title: Putin's Crimean Bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine
text:
Ukraine has severely damaged a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, in what President Volodymyr Zelensky says was an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.
Images shared by Ukrainian officials show a section of the Crimean Bridge collapsed into the water, dealing a logistical and symbolic blow to Moscow's war effort.
The Kremlin said it would rebuild the bridge "better than before".
Meanwhile in Kyiv, Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said traffic had partially resumed on the Pivnichnyi (Northern) and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges - key crossings over the Dnipro River - after they had been closed following Russian strikes overnight.
Ukraine has long targeted the Crimean Bridge, which provides a road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line, but has struggled to close it for good.
While Kyiv has been trying to increase the cost to Russia of waging war economically, by hitting oil refineries and depots, striking the bridge is an attempt to increase the political cost on Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The timing of the strike comes at a significant moment, ahead of Putin meeting the leaders of China and the US. This could cloud his moment back in the spotlight.
The Crimean Bridge was built by Russia after it invaded and illegally annexed Ukraine's southern peninsula in 2014.
The $3.6bn (£2.7bn) piece of infrastructure is widely seen in Russia and Ukraine as Putin's personal pet project: His close tycoon friend Arkady Rotenberg built it, and then Putin personally opened it by driving a lorry over it in May 2018.
In Ukraine, the much-hated bridge is seen as one of the main symbols of Russia's continuing occupation of Ukrainian lands.
"We're drinking champagne!" Andrii, an engineer who lives in Kyiv, told the BBC.
He said the latest attack would "deal a very heavy blow to the morale of the Russians".
Some Ukrainians are concerned that Putin might now respond by carrying out even more attacks against civilian infrastructure, but Andrii said: "I don't think the Russians can make things much worse; they're already pounding us every single night with everything they've got."
The damage after the overnight attack, involving cruise missiles and drones, appeared to be far more severe than during previous strikes on the bridge, with a large arched section apparently destroyed.
Video footage appeared to show critical damage to the road section, with remnants of the support arch and road deck seen protruding from the water below.
Zelensky said the strike was the result of a seven-stage operation by the military and security services, which saw Ukrainian forces "gradually destroy air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment, and other designated targets on the way to the final objective".
He said several types of Ukrainian drones as well as the country's Flamingo and Neptune cruise missiles were fired overnight during a "pivotal stage".
The Ukrainian president also said the rail section parallel to the bridge's road had also been hit by a wave of drones, though images showed its supporting arch was still standing and Russia's transport ministry later said some rail services resumed.
Ukraine's state security service SBU said its operations had "systematically suppressed enemy air defence systems" over a month, and said it showed "no Russian defence systems can guarantee the safety of illegal objects occupied by the invaders".
Meanwhile, Ukraine's military said the roadway on the bridge is "out of action", with no vehicle able to cross it, and the railway section is still standing, but with a damaged arch.
The Kremlin said Putin had been briefed on the overnight attack. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge would "be restored following Ukrainian strikes, and it will be even better than before", and did not rule out the possibility the strikes were linked to Putin's visit to China.
Russia's Investigative Committee confirmed structural damage and said it had opened a "criminal case... on terrorism charges" after attacks by "Ukraine's armed formations".
For the second day in a row, Russia recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, with 2,256 drones downed, according to the defence ministry.
Zelensky had warned of major attacks in the days leading up to a meeting between Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in China's Shenzhen on Thursday.
In Kyiv, loud explosions were heard just before midnight on Monday, with Klitschko saying shortly after that the city had suffered "damage to critical infrastructure systems" and disruption to heating and water supplies.
On Tuesday, Zelensky said four ballistic missiles had targeted the Southern Bridge, and another three had been fired on the Northern Bridge.
Some of Kyiv's above-ground metro services were also damaged in the overnight attacks, local officials said, after civilians were told to go to civil defence shelters.
Eight major bridges span the Dnipro River, connecting the western and eastern parts of Kyiv, and an estimated three million residents rely on the bridges to travel across the city.
Elsewhere, three people have been injured in a Russian missile attack in the central Cherkasy region, according to local officials.
The long-term impact of the Crimean Bridge strike is still not fully clear, though the risk of a serious transport and logistics crisis for the Russian military has increased significantly.
The collapse of the arched section has cut off the peninsula's direct road and rail links with Russia – at least until the crossing can be repaired.
However, there is still a land corridor running through the occupied parts of Ukraine's southern Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions - though Kyiv has been systematically striking transport routes across northern Crimea, as well as bridges and other crossings in the area around Chongar.
This has already caused problems with the delivery of fuel and other supplies, including military cargo.
There is a ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait, which connects the Black Sea with the Sea of Azov. It could partly compensate for the loss of the bridge, but its capacity is very limited and it is also vulnerable to attack.
Russia could also supply Crimea by sea, but this route is also risky, as Ukrainian naval and aerial drones operate extensively in the area.
In addition, debris from the Crimean Bridge – particularly its enormous arch – may have blocked the shipping channel.
This would make it harder for larger vessels to pass through and create further problems for the Russian-occupied ports in the Sea of Azov, including Mariupol and Berdyansk.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine is now under Russian occupation and Kyiv has refused Putin's demand to give up areas of Ukraine's eastern Donbas that remain under its control.
Additional reporting by Jaroslav Lukiv

title: Five EU states announce plans for immigration ‘return hubs’ in Rwanda
text:
Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”.
The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country.
In a statement released on Monday the five EU countries said “concrete negotiations with partner country Rwanda will begin for implementation”, saying the scheme would make “an important contribution to further curbing illegal migration, dismantling the business model of smugglers and relieving the burden on our population”.
Officials hope to send 100 people to Rwanda from early next year to test the model. The scheme will apply to adults whose claims to asylum have been rejected or others with no legal right to live in the EU.
In theory, according to diplomatic sources, migrants would stay in a reception centre in Rwanda for a couple of months, before choosing to integrate into life in the Great Lakes country or return to their home nation.
Unlike the failed scheme pursued by the British Conservative government in Rwanda, or Italy’s agreement with Albania, it will not apply to people pursuing asylum claims.
The reception centre, which would be an open facility, was not intended to house people long term but to accommodate regular flows of people, the countries said. Diplomatic sources said the EU countries were not using British-funded facilities built in Kigali.
The governments involved argue it will protect the European asylum system while removing the incentive for irregular migrants to come to Europe.
Denmark’s immigration minister, Morten Bødskov, whose government has pioneered a tough line on migration widely emulated across the EU, said it was “a huge breakthrough”.
The German interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, said: “Return hubs offer a positive approach for people without the right to stay and with no prospects in Europe, whose countries of origin do not cooperate in the repatriation process.”
Andy Burnham told reporters last week that the UK had not had direct discussions with European governments involved in return hubs but “we will watch that with interest, learning from what went on in the past. The public want us to do whatever we can to deal with illegal immigration.”
Critics have highlighted the ethical difficulties of striking an agreement with Rwanda’s repressive government, which was found in 2024 by the US state department to allow state security forces and civilian officials to commit human rights abuses with impunity, while also raising concerns about freedom of expression and forced labour.
Spain’s socialist prime minister, Pedro Sanchez, said on Monday the move had no “future or humanity”. “I don’t see any future or humanity in that. It’s not the solution,” Sanchez, an outspoken defender of immigration in a Europe that has tilted to the right in recent years, told Telecinco television.
The French Green MEP Mélissa Camara denounced the agreement between the five countries and Rwanda as “an agreement of shame” and “a grave moral failing”. She said: “Under this agreement, people will be deported thousands of kilometres away from the European Union, with no guarantees regarding the compliance with their rights.”
Alain Berset, the secretary general of the Council of Europe, the continent’s human rights body, said it was not possible “to be so precise a priori” about what any return hubs proposal meant. Speaking to the Guardian before the announcement, he said all members of the Council of Europe were committed to the European convention on human rights “and this must be the lighthouse” for all discussions on return hubs.
“On concrete cases, then we will have to see if this is compliant with the convention,” he said. He stressed that “all countries must be able to define their migration policy”.
Officials involved in setting up the migration centres expect legal challenges, but say the scheme is grounded in human rights law.
Rights organisations say the scheme is bound to fail. “Member states may call them ‘return hubs’ or even ‘welcome centres’, but no euphemism can hide the violence of uprooting people from the life they’ve been building in Europe, and sending them to a country they don’t even know, without family, networks or meaningful prospects,” said Chiara Catelli of Picum, a pan-European organisation that campaigns for the rights of undocumented migrants.

title: Russian military plane crash in Siberia kills 19
text:
A military plane has crashed in western Siberia, killing all 19 people on board, according to a statement from the Russian Defence Ministry, cited by local media.
The Antonov An-12 transport aircraft went down in an unpopulated area near the city of Kemerovo, about 3,000km east of Moscow. The An-12 typically has a crew of six.
Air force experts were investigating the cause of the crash, but preliminary findings pointed to equipment failure.
“A commission from the Russian Aerospace Forces is working at the site to establish all the circumstances of the incident,” the ministry’s statement was quoted as saying by the RIA Novosti news agency.
Regional Governor Ilya Seredyuk, posting on Telegram from the scene of the accident, said emergency crews had extinguished a fire. He said crews were helping to investigate the accident.
Seredyuk, in a video posted online showing the site of the accident near the village of Yagunovo, said the plane had been flying through the region when it crashed.
The Investigative Committee, Russia’s top criminal investigation agency, launched an inquiry into possible violations of flight safety rules, a standard practice following crashes.
The An-12 is a Soviet-built four-engine turboprop transport plane that has been in service since the late 1950s. More than 1,000 were built, and some still remain in operation in Russia and other nations.
In September, a Russian Tupolev Tu-95 military aircraft crashed in the eastern region of Amur, killing six crew members and injuring a seventh.

title: Iran launches a third round of strikes on Bahrain, host of U.S. Navy's 5th Fleet
text:
CAIRO — Iran fired drones on Tuesday at a U.S. radar installation in Bahrain in the third Iranian attack in recent days on American military targets in the Persian Gulf island kingdom, and the U.S. retaliated by firing at Iranian targets along an important shipping route.
The attacks and counterattacks interrupted a roughly two-month lull in fighting, as Iran's targeting of Bahrain brought condemnations from the region. Analysts said stalled peace negotiations and Tehran's growing economic pressures were raising the risk of a substantial escalation.
Bahrain said that its air defense systems had successfully intercepted the "treacherous Iranian aerial attacks." The U.S. military likewise said the attack inflicted no damage to U.S. equipment or injury to American personnel.
Hours later, a U.S. fighter jet carried out a strike on a missile launch site in the Strait of Hormuz belonging to Iran's paramilitary Revolutionary Guard, a U.S. official said.
The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to detail sensitive military operations, said "precision munitions" were used in the strike on Qeshm Island and that the U.S. was responding to "aggression" toward U.S. personnel.
A local official, Ahmad Nafisi, said the strike caused no damage to residential or commercial areas or infrastructure.
The U.S. military has periodically carried out what appear to be limited strikes on Qeshm Island and other Iranian targets this month. Iran's attack Tuesday was its third on American military targets in Bahrain in five days.
Iran may be shifting its strategy amid economic pain
Iran has been suffering under a naval blockade that the U.S. has enforced on it for months in and around the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial waterway for the world's energy supplies where Iran and its proxies have disrupted shipping since the war began Feb. 28.
U.S. President Donald Trump has been circumspect on his next steps for the Iran war, now in its eighth month despite an initial promise it would last only a matter of weeks. He has said new strikes are highly unlikely, but he has also sent a third aircraft carrier and thousands more troops to the Middle East — and told Vice President JD Vance that talks aren't needed at this time.
Oil tankers moving oil through the strait under U.S. military protection have helped return oil shipments from the Gulf to roughly prewar levels. The blockade, meanwhile, is damaging Iran's economy by curbing the flow of Iranian crude to the global market.
Iran's attacks could signal a shift in its strategy after months during which it waited for an attack and then retaliated to target the operational capability of bases, Tehran-based security analyst Mostafa Najafi told The Associated Press.
Bahrain hosts the U.S. Navy's 5th Fleet, which has already sustained damage in previous attacks by Iran since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28.
Iranian leaders will now be weighing whether "breaking the blockade through escalation is less costly than accepting its continuation," Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group think tank, wrote in an analysis posted to X.
"In other words, the risk of renewed war no longer depends solely on whether Trump decides to attack Iran again," he said. "It also depends on whether Tehran concludes that the costs of continued restraint have become greater than the risks of escalation."
U.S. expands its Middle East naval presence
With the arrival of the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group in the region, the combined U.S. naval assets in the Persian Gulf, Arabian Sea, Red Sea, and Mediterranean now exceed the force deployed when the U.S. and Israel launched the war.
The presence provides greater offensive firepower and missile interception capacity, according to a new analysis by Israel's Institute for National Security Studies.
The Roosevelt joins the USS George H.W. Bush and the USS George Washington aircraft carriers, as well as smaller U.S. Navy ships, which are in the region to maintain the blockade of Iranian shipping. U.S. Central Command wouldn't comment on whether it plans to keep all three carrier strike groups in the region.
Iran says it's responding to U.S. attacks
Iran's attack on Bahrain on Tuesday came after it targeted a U.S. early warning radar facility in the country on Friday, and on Sunday fired at a radar system at an American helicopter base there. Despite claims of success, there appeared to be little or no damage done.
The attacks followed U.S. strikes on Iranian communications towers and ongoing drone surveillance operations, and Iran said it was retaliating.
"Continued aggression against the country's airspace, as well as the use of regional military bases and facilities for hostile acts against Iran, will not go unanswered," Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps said in a statement.
Egypt, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates each condemned Iran's attack on Bahrain, calling it a violation of Bahrain's sovereignty and a threat to its security and stability.
Negotiations to end the war have stagnated, despite intensified mediation efforts from Qatar.
In a statement, Qatar said Iran's "continued attacks" on Bahrain "undermine diplomatic efforts" and Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed Al Ansari, speaking at a news briefing in Doha, warned that any escalation in fighting posed an "extremely grave danger" to the prospects of reaching an agreement.
Iran may be losing patience as conflict drags on
The attacks are a sign that Tehran is growing impatient as its economic woes mount, said Sascha Bruchmann, a Bahrain-based defense analyst with the International Institute for Strategic Studies.
"Shooting at ships causes fear, but is not effective enough to change the strategic equation," Bruchmann told the AP. "Tehran knows it needs to do something, but I wouldn't overestimate what we saw against Bahrain this week. This is not it — yet."
Iranian officials have termed the current situation "no war, no peace" and vowed to end it.
Tehran has said that it's open to a negotiated deal, but also signaled a readiness to escalate the conflict in the face of tightening sanctions and the blockade that are throttling Iran's economy.
Mahdi Mohammadi, an adviser to Iran's influential parliamentary chief, posted on social media on Monday that leaders view U.S. economic pressure as an effort to create a domestic "security crisis."
Iran has continued to attack ships seeking to transit the Strait of Hormuz, which leads from the Persian Gulf toward the open seas. In Yemen, Iran-backed Houthi rebels now have solidified their control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, another critical shipping route.

title: Man with ax destroys $60M U.S. military plane, prosecutors say
text:
An ax-wielding man breached a security perimeter and destroyed an American military plane while it was parked overnight at an Irish airport, cutting hydraulic lines, smashing cockpit gauges and pouring ball bearings into fuel tanks, U.S. prosecutors said. The man's supporters attributed the attack to his anger at the United States' involvement in .
An indictment unsealed Tuesday in Manhattan charges Daithi O'Corrain, 48, with destruction of U.S. government property in connection with the April incident at Shannon Airport, an international gateway in the west of Ireland that serves as a hub for American troops and military equipment.
O'Corrain isn't in U.S. custody and his arraignment on the new charge hasn't been scheduled. If convicted, he faces up to 10 years in prison. Online court records do not list an attorney who might speak on his behalf.
The plane, a $60 million U.S. Air National Guard C-130 Hercules that had been en route to a military assignment in another country, was rendered inoperable and won't fly again, U.S. prosecutors said. The attack jeopardized critical military operations, the FBI said.
O'Corrain, described by supporters as an independent peace activist, was arrested immediately after the attack by Ireland's police force, An Garda Síochána. He was charged there with causing criminal damage and trespassing. The Limerick Post reported he is from Cork, about 60 miles southeast of Shannon.
Manhattan U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said the indictment sends "a clear and powerful message that attacks on U.S. military assets — and thus our national security — will not be tolerated."
An online fundraiser organized by people describing themselves as O'Corrain's friends and comrades said he disarmed the C-130 in protest of the U.S.'s war with Iran and support for — a flashpoint in Ireland, where many people have expressed solidarity with Palestinians.
"An inspiring act of direct action was carried out at Shannon Airport to resist the unwanted presence of the US Military in Ireland in the face of their illegal war & support of Israel's genocide," organizer Tracey Ryan wrote.
O'Corrain plotted the attack for months, U.S. prosecutors said. He searched online for information about the construction of the C-130, a quad-engine turboprop mainly used for transporting equipment and personnel, and looked up coordinates for sneaking onto the airport's grounds, prosecutors said.
He subscribed to a cellphone app that provided live flight tracking, including for military aircraft, and ordered capsules of gallium, a chemical that can corrode steel and break down aluminum, the primary material used to build the C-130, prosecutors said.
He even tried to get in touch with someone who had been involved in a prior breach at Shannon Airport, prosecutors said.
"This was not an act of spontaneous vandalism," James Barnacle, the head of the FBI's New York office, said in a statement.
O'Corrain attacked on April 11, breaching the airport's perimeter at around 4:40 a.m. and breaking into the C-130 as it was parked on a taxiway by destroying a locking mechanism on the rear crew door, his indictment said.
He used the crew's hammocks to cover the plane's windows but left the cockpit windshield exposed, the indictment said. He then barricaded himself inside the aircraft, securing the doors with straps, brackets and screws, and putting ball bearings mixed with epoxy in door tracks to prevent doors from being opened or closed, the indictment said.
O'Corrain laid waste to the plane over the next few hours, pulling, snipping and otherwise disabling its key components, the indictment said. He sliced wire bundles, crimped a liquid oxygen line, punctured air ducts and shattered every gauge in the cockpit, the indictment said.
Had O'Corrain cut the oxygen line instead, he would've risked blowing up the plane, prosecutors said.
Returning to the airport after resting elsewhere, the C-130 crew spotted O'Corrain through the uncovered cockpit at around 9:40 a.m. and alerted security, the indictment said.
Crew members then saw him emerging through a roof hatch and swinging an ax at the plane's exterior, according to the indictment, which included images taken from a video recording that show a man standing on the roof of the plane. O'Corrain then poured substances and objects into the fuel tanks, including ball bearings, before being arrested.
Shannon Airport, which was used by President Trump and Air Force One during his visit to Ireland in September, has had several security breaches in the last 18 months, including three people who were accused of spray-painting a U.S. military plane and three others who drove to a restricted area where a U.S. military jet was parked.

title: Angry crowds rally against Slovakia's pro-Russian leader on Velvet Revolution anniversary
text:
Crowds have gathered in Slovakia to protest the government of pro-Russian Prime Minister Robert Fico on the anniversary of the 1989 Velvet Revolution, which ended communist rule in Czechoslovakia
BRATISLAVA, Slovakia -- People in Slovakia took to the streets Tuesday to rally against the government of pro-Russian Prime Minister Robert Fico on the anniversary of the 1989 Velvet Revolution that brought an end to decades of communist rule in Czechoslovakia.
Opposition parties organized the protests in dozens of communities across the country, where Fico remains as Europe’s most pro-Russian leader since Hungary’s Viktor Orbán was ousted from power in April.
“We’ve had enough of Fico,” chanted people in Bratislava, where organizers estimated 25,000 gathered in the downtown SNP square. One banner had a message for the prime minister: “Go to hell.”
The capital's rally united the liberal groups Progressive Slovakia and the Democrats with pro-business Freedom and Solidarity, the conservative Christian Democrats and an alliance of ethnic Hungarians. Together they hope to defeat Fico and his coalition government in next year’s parliamentary election.
“Just as in 1989, what unites us must be stronger than what divides us,” said Michal Šimečka, leader of the major opposition Progressive Slovakia party. “We’ll win only if we stick together.”
The government angered opponents by sending Foreign Minister Juraj Blanár to Russia for talks about renewing economic cooperation and other ties between the two countries for the first time since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Fico agreed on the plan during one of his trips to Moscow to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin, and held a Cabinet meeting to discuss a report about Blanár’s visit just hours before the rally on Tuesday.
“Shame, shame,” the crowd chanted in condemnation.
Fico has long been a divisive figure in Slovakia, and thousands have repeatedly rallied to protest his policies. Czechoslovakia split into the Czech Republic and Slovakia in 1993.
His views on Russia’s war on Ukraine and other issues sharply differ from the European mainstream. Fico ended Slovakia’s military aid for Ukraine, opposes EU sanctions on Russia, wants to block Ukraine from joining NATO and rejected EU loan guarantees for Ukraine.

title: Hashim Thaci's second conviction in The Hague reignites debate in Kosovo about justice and the Kosovo Specialist Chambers
text:
A court in The Hague on Tuesday convicted former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci of obstructing justice and attempting to influence witnesses during his recent war crimes trial and sentenced him to 17 months in prison.
This term will be added to his 25-year sentence for war crimes, which was handed down by the same court, the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, on September 16.
According to the indictment of the Specialist Prosecutor's Office, Thaci had provided visitors at the detention facility in The Hague with confidential information about witnesses in his war crimes trial and had instructed them on how to influence their testimony.
Three other men — former head of the Kosovo Intelligence Agency Bashkim Smakaj, former Minister of Justice Hajredin Kuci, and Fadil Fazliu — were also convicted.
Swift response from government
Thaci, who was the former political leader of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) during the 1998-1999 Kosovo War, is viewed by many in his home country as a hero. His war crimes conviction in September was greeted in Kosovo with anger and dismay.
Thaci has vowed to appeal the war crimes conviction.
His two convictions touch deep sensitivities in Kosovo society. Tuesday's ruling brings renewed attention to the war that ended 27 years ago, the role played by its former leaders, and the continuing debate over justice, individual or collective responsibility for the KLA's war to liberate Kosovo from Serbia, and trust in judicial institutions.
The response from the government of Kosovo was swift.
In a statement issued on Tuesday, the government said, "Trust in justice is built not only on the decisions that are made, but also on the manner in which they are reached. Therefore, our commitment to the rule of law and our insistence on the full respect of rights and procedural guarantees are part of the same principled position: Justice must not only be done, but must also be fair, transparent, and credible."
What is the Kosovo Specialist Chambers?
The Kosovo Specialist Chambers was established in 2015 by the parliament of Kosovo at the instigation of the European Union and the United States.
The court was created to investigate serious crimes allegedly committed by members of the KLA during and after the Kosovo War.
For security reasons, including concerns about witness intimidation, the court was located in The Hague in the Netherlands.
Government set up working group
After Thaci and three others were convicted of war crimes in first instance in September, Kosovo's state authorities established a working group to draft a strategy regarding the appeal proceedings before the Kosovo Specialist Chambers.
The group is chaired by Foreign Minister Glauk Konjufca and includes members of Kosovo's parliament.
Prime Minister Albin Kurti has stated that the working group continues to believe that "the first-instance judgment of the Specialist Chambers is unjust, both legally and morally," and that as a result, "the government is working to secure a correction at the appeals level before the Specialist Chambers."
Parliament considers amending law
In addition, the parliament of Kosovo is currently considering amendments to the law governing the Kosovo Specialist Chambers.
The draft law, which is expected to be adopted, envisages narrowing the court's mandate in several areas, including the time period covered by its jurisdiction, limiting the maximum prison sentence to 15 years, allowing sentences to be served in Kosovo, and introducing the possibility of presidential pardons for persons convicted by final court decisions.
How do political analysts and legal experts view the parliament's attempt to amend the law on the Kosovo Specialist Chambers before the judicial process involving the four men convicted of war crimes has reached a final verdict?
"From an international perspective, at first glance, this initiative could even be interpreted as an attempt to interfere in the judicial process," said political analyst and university professor Artan Muhaxheri.
"Precisely for this reason, it is essential that Kosovo's political spectrum and its legal experts demonstrate beyond any doubt that this measure does not conflict with Kosovo's international obligations toward the European Union," Muhaxheri told DW, adding that this is the only way to ensure that the desired outcome is achieved and that the initiative does not produce the opposite effect.
"Issues relating to jurisdiction, statutory limits on maximum sentences, and other similar matters must be argued professionally and rigorously, demonstrating that they fully guarantee judicial independence and enjoy solid support within Kosovo's legal system, the same legal system that, first and foremost, established the Specialist Chambers," he said.
'Room for criticism of both sides'
Ehat Miftaraj, executive director of the Kosovo Law Institute (IKD), told DW that although the Kosovo Specialist Chambers were established by the Republic of Kosovo itself, "the way the judicial process has unfolded has created the impression that judges, prosecutors and certain international actors have treated not only the accused but also Kosovo itself with distrust, prejudice, and an often condescending approach."
Miftaraj went on to say that reactions and objections in Kosovo to the decisions of the Specialist Chambers are also interpreted and judged in the historical and emotional context of the war and what Kosovo's citizens experienced during and after it.
"In a democratic society, every citizen, including political and institutional representatives, has the right to criticize judicial decisions," he said. "However, there is a fundamental distinction between criticism based on legal arguments and attempts to delegitimize courts or exert influence over judicial proceedings. And here, there is room for criticism of both sides."

title: Nvidia shuts door on Jensen Huang’s return as stock pops on earnings
text:
Nvidia’s board has made clear that it will not bring Jensen Huang back as CEO after shareholders and his fellow tech bros called for him to be reinstated.
Huang resigned as head of the AI chipmaking company after he admitted to an affair with a Chinese executive suspected of being a spy for Beijing.
“Jensen Huang, voluntarily resigned his positions as President, CEO, and board member. The NVIDIA Board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia’s board, said during an earnings call Tuesday. Executives refused to take questions from investors about the scandal.
Nvidia’s better-than-expected third-quarter earnings report caused its stock to pop in after-hours trading. Nvidia’s stock sat at $155.46 at the closing bell, and just thirty minutes later, it spiked by about 4 percent to $161.69.
The company reported revenues of $115.8 billion, beating Wall Street’s estimates of around $109 billion.
On November 8, the day Huang admitted the affair to employees, Nvidia said it would be conducting an investigation following reporting that Huang “has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.”
Huang stepped down last Thursday and was replaced by Colette Kress, Nvidia’s executive vice president and chief financial officer, while the company looks for a permanent CEO.
Over the weekend, an online petition to reinstate Huang as Nvidia’s CEO garnered more than 100,000 signatures, including around 60,000 from shareholders, 6,000 from current Nvidia employees and 1,000 from former employees, according to reports.
Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney publicly backed the effort, and there was a report that Huang had discussions with allies about possibly returning to the helm.
One ally told the Financial Times that they were convening a “war room” of tech executives to reinstate Huang and would try to get support from the White House.
President Donald Trump, who has close ties to Huang and called him a “very high quality person” after the scandal broke, insisted he had no idea that U.S. intelligence found Huang’s mistress, Alice Huang, was a Chinese spy. But the New York Times reported in late October that Trump was briefed on the findings about a year ago and chose not to take action.
Earlier Tuesday, Huang released his first public statement since leaving Nvidia, admitting that he “did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life.
“I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation,” he wrote on X.
Huang acknowledged the push from supporters to reinstate him as Nvidia’s CEO and said he’d be “honored to answer these calls.”
“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics.
“NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote.
But, as Nvidia’s board said during the earnings call later Tuesday, that won’t be in the cards — for now.

title: US criticises Ukraine's 'deep strike' campaign against Russia
text:
German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius called the US' warning "quite a stupid thing," while his British counterpart Wes Streeting said there was "no doubt" in his mind that Ukraine's long-range strikes had "helped to degrade Putin's war machine."
A senior US defence official has criticised Ukraine's "deep strikes" against Russia, saying they had been ineffective in bringing the war to an end and arguing that, in some cases, they had likely "hardened the Russian public's resolve."
"Our assessment is that such strikes have not been effective in driving an end to the war, nor do they contribute to blunting Russia's advances on the front line," Under Secretary of Defence Elbridge Colby said while speaking from NATO's headquarters in Brussels on Tuesday.
"Such strikes, especially those that target civilian infrastructure such as Wildberries, have actually probably hardened the Russian public's resolve and the Kremlin's own willingness to escalate," he continued.
He added that support for Kyiv moving forward should focus on "enabling and advancing Ukraine's ability to hold the line of battle and where possible make gains."
Ukraine has increasingly struck targets deep inside Russian territory as the war has gone on, using its burgeoning drone technology to carry out long-range attacks.
Ukrainian forces have particularly looked to target energy infrastructure such as oil refineries and terminals, as well as military sites like air bases, as they have sought to hamper the Russian economy and hit Vladimir Putin's war machine.
US President Donald Trump has previously demanded that Ukraine halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, saying the attacks were to blame for rising diesel fuel prices.
'Quite a stupid thing'
Colby's comments have drawn pushback from some European officials.
German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius called the warning "quite a stupid thing," while his British counterpart Wes Streeting said there was "no doubt" in his mind that Ukraine's long-range strikes had "helped to degrade Putin's war machine, buying time and saving lives."
The comments came as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy once again urged allies to speed up deliveries of interceptor missiles.
"Ukraine needs Patriot and IRIS-T interceptors from the stocks you already have right now," he told the meeting of the Ukraine Defence Contact Group in Brussels via video link.
"And I ask the United States – please, do not delay these deliveries," Zelenskyy added. He also said Ukraine needed a further 40 F-16 fighter jets to help boost its air defences.
The pleas come as Ukraine gears up for what looks set to be another brutal winter under heavy bombardment from Russian forces.
Russia has repeatedly sought to ramp up attacks on Ukraine in wartime winter periods, targeting the country's energy sector as Moscow has attempted to break its resolve.

title: Europe assassination scheme emerges as Iran denies DC 'dirty bomb' plot amid Trump warning
text:
Iran on Tuesday slammed allegations that it was plotting a chemical weapons attack in Washington, D.C., calling the claims a "shameful lie" within hours of President Donald Trump warning that Tehran would face unprecedented retaliation if it ever targeted the nation's capital.
Tehran's denial followed a CNN report that U.S. intelligence agencies had uncovered Iranian plans for potential attacks on senior administration officials, including the possible use of chemical weapons or a radioactive "dirty bomb."
The allegations also emerged amid reports of a separate Iranian-linked assassination plot targeting an Israeli executive in Greece and with Israeli security officials believing Tehran aims to target Israelis overseas as the war continues, according to news outlet Ynet Global.
Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister for Legal and International Affairs Kazem Gharibabadi immediately rejected the allegations in a post on X, invoking Iran's history as a victim of chemical warfare.
"CNN's claim that Iran plans to use chemical weapons in Washington is a shameful lie and a distortion of history," Gharibabadi wrote.
Trump was asked by reporters Tuesday during the first leg of his trip across Asia about the alleged plot against administration officials and if there was an imminent threat to D.C.
"Well, if there is, they will pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before," Trump said.
"I hope it's not, but ... we take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy. But this is why they can't have a nuclear weapon, by the way, in case people had any questions."
"Iran is one of the biggest victims of chemical weapons; victims who were targeted with these inhumane weapons with the support of today's accusers, especially the United States," he added.
"The truth must not become a casualty of the propaganda war," Gharibabadi warned.
CNN reported, citing seven officials familiar with the intelligence, that American agencies had detected Iranian efforts to develop potential attack options against senior administration officials in Washington.
White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said the administration was monitoring potential threats, but that "at this time, there are no credible threats to the homeland."
Meanwhile, Israeli intelligence reportedly helped foil a separate alleged Iranian-linked assassination plot Tuesday targeting an Israeli executive in Greece, leading to five arrests in Greece and North Macedonia, according to Ynet.
Citing sources, the outlet reported that Mossad gave intelligence to Greek and North Macedonian authorities as part of a joint effort to disrupt the plot.
North Macedonia's National Security Agency announced that authorities had uncovered the plan, with one North Macedonian national arrested in Greece last Thursday and extradited to his home country.
Four others were said to have been detained in Skopje, North Macedonia.
The alleged plot was directed by Iranian national Edris Jahangiri Mavaneh, whom the agency linked to people associated with Iranian intelligence and security services, including alleged drug trafficker Naji Sharifi Zindashti, according to Ynet.
Zindashti is also wanted by the FBI for operating a network that targets Iranian activists and dissidents abroad.
According to the bureau, Zindashti used encrypted, Internet-based messaging applications to hire criminal elements within North America and to murder two individuals who fled Iran.
Greek outlet Kathimerini meanwhile, also reported that the suspects allegedly planned to assassinate a senior Israeli executive working for a company operating in Greece.
Investigators seized weapons, ammunition, handwritten notes and a map, according to the report.
North Macedonia's security agency said investigators also uncovered secret meetings involving suspects in several countries, including Iran.
According to Ynet, Israeli security officials said Tehran considers its war with Israel as unresolved and is looking for opportunities to retaliate through attacks beyond the Middle East region.

title: Doctors are raising concerns about U.S. babies born with measles
text: For the first time in decades, U.S. doctors are sounding the alarm about babies coming into the world with measles. Congenital measles happens when a pregnant woman passes the virus to her fetus in the womb. It can lead to serious complications or even be deadly for newborns. READ MORE: Can the U.S. regain its measles elimination status? Here's what to know From the start of 2025 through the end of this September, 13 congenital measles cases were reported to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention during large measles outbreaks, according to preliminary figures published in a medical journal on Monday. "This is a brand new phenomenon," said Michael Osterholm, who directs the University of Minnesota's Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy. The condition's emergence is driven by declining vaccination rates, which have fueled the virus's spread so much that the Pan American Health Organization is expected to officially announce Tuesday that the U.S. has lost the measles-free status it's had since 2000. In the past two years, according to the CDC, there have been more than 7,500 measles cases. "We're now seeing levels of measles that we haven't seen in 30 years," said Dr. Adam Ratner, a member of the American Academy of Pediatrics' infectious diseases committee. "When you have measles under control," congenital measles doesn't happen. The preliminary case figures were released in a public health alert published by NEJM Evidence in partnership with the center Osterholm directs. The alert also said there were 112 cases of confirmed measles during pregnancy — almost all among women who didn't get vaccinated against measles beforehand or whose vaccination status was unknown. The alert said getting vaccinated before pregnancy and having high vaccination rates in the community "are important to prevent measles and related complications." CDC scientists authored the alert. Guidance on congenital measles from the pediatrics academy is already reaching doctors. And Pennsylvania's health department published an advisory last month for healthcare providers, schools, childcare centers and others in the state, which currently has the largest measles outbreak in the nation. A new reality allows congenital measles to emerge People gain immunity to measles by getting the disease or the vaccine. Before the shots existed, lots of people were infected by the extremely contagious virus in childhood. Later, high vaccination rates protected everyone. But a new and historic reality — shaped both by the success of the vaccine and recent skepticism about it — has triggered congenital measles. "What's happening is we have so many women of childbearing age who were not vaccinated in the last 25 years, nor have they ever had exposure to measles because for the last 25 years we have beaten it back," Osterholm said. "Now, this group is highly susceptible to measles." Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Doctors say the best way to prevent the disease is for women to get the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, known as MMR, before pregnancy. This protects the fetus too because antibodies pass from mother to baby through the placenta. Protection can last a few months after birth. MMR can't be given during pregnancy. Unvaccinated women who have never had measles and are exposed while pregnant can get a solution containing antibodies within six days to reduce the risk of infection and complications. Congenital measles can seriously harm babies If a woman gets measles toward the end of pregnancy, there's a good chance she will pass it along. An estimated 25% to 30% of babies born to someone who gets measles shortly before delivery may become infected, the pediatrics group says. READ MORE: U.S. and Mexico officially lose measles-elimination status Babies are considered to have congenital measles if they were exposed in the uterus and doctors find evidence of measles very soon after birth. Common symptoms include fever, jaundice and a measles rash. Severe complications include pneumonia, encephalitis and a rare condition known as SSPE, a brain disorder that generally develops many years after a measles infection and is almost always fatal. Ratner, who wrote a book about measles, said there are indications that kids with congenital measles are at higher risk for SSPE and may develop it sooner after having measles than other children. "That's something that sadly we're learning more about," he said. Doctors worry things may get worse if vaccination rates keep dropping. Outbreaks are considered unlikely if a community has a 95% MMR rate, but rates in many communities have dipped below that threshold. Nationally, the CDC said, 92.4% of U.S. kindergarteners in 2025-26 received required MMR shots. This puts many vulnerable people at risk, including infants too young to be vaccinated. The first MMR dose is routinely given at 12 to 15 months old, and the earliest babies can get the shots is 6 months in outbreak areas. "We need to get back to the point where everybody who can get vaccinated is getting vaccinated, and that's gonna take some doing," Ratner said. "It's going to be a lot of work on the part of pediatricians and public health institutions and lots of others. But it's an important thing for us to do."
