London-based Foundational recently tested its Retro-2 laser retroreflector system, which it developed in collaboration with ESA. The early-stage test was designed to ensure that Foundational's retroreflectors can return laser-ranging signals from a satellite, at altitudes between about 600 kilometers and 870 kilometers (about 370 to 540 miles).
The long-term aim is to create a sort of tracking device for spacecraft, so they can be monitored in orbit even after they fall silent.
The tech, Foundational said in a statement today (Nov. 17), needs "no electronics, power or commands from its host spacecraft" and allows ground stations to keep tabs on the orbiting spacecraft.
The demo mission launched this past July on SpaceX's Transporter-17 rideshare flight. It attached Retro-2 — a mini device with seven reflectors — to a small satellite that was integrated into an ION carrier craft operated by the Italian company D-Orbit.
Retro-2 worked as advertised, successfully returning 6,111 laser shots beamed from the from the ground across five passes in low Earth orbit.
"Our tests have shown that a device weighing just 50 grams [1.8 ounces] can deliver millimeter-level ranging precision," Dave Gooding, Foundational's co-founder and chief technical officer, said in today's statement. "As space becomes increasingly crowded, keeping satellites trackable throughout their lifetime and beyond is critical to managing collision risks."
Foundational is in its early stages — it was founded in 2025 and just emerged from stealth last month. Nevertheless the company has already raised £8.2 million ($10.9 million) in pre-seed funding.
Foundational is part of a range of companies involved in debris removal, satellite servicing or debris tracking that have raised funds in 2026. Others include Starfish Space (which raised more than $100 million in a Series B), Katalyst Space ($12 million in funding) and international companies like India's Cosmoserve Space.

title: Some EU countries ‘could accept unlimited young Britons’ under youth mobility scheme
text:
The new post-Brexit UK-EU youth mobility scheme or agrifood deal may not come fully into force until 2030.
It will be a disappointment to any under-30s in the UK and the EU who hoped to travel, work or study in each other’s territories from next year after the long-awaited new deal.
EU ambassadors will discuss the latest draft joint statement at a meeting on Wednesday in Brussels, with talk of youth mobility going right to the wire.
“We aim to apply this agreement no later than 2028 and endeavour to ensure that opportunities under the scheme will be available to our young people no later than January 2030,” a text agreed by negotiators from London and Brussels says.
The two sides aim to come to an agreement on tuition fees for EU citizens in UK universities, which could mean they pay a reduced international fee or the same fee as UK nationals.
EU countries including Germany could accept an unlimited number of young Britons under a youth mobility scheme, according to sources.
Fresh details on how a scheme might work have emerged with EU leaders and the UK expected to settle on a quota of about 100,000 a year being allowed to work, travel or study in each other’s territories from 2028.
The UK has insisted on a quota of EU citizens entering the UK under the scheme to guard against mass migration, but some countries have said they will not follow suit on the other side of the Channel and would be open to taking unlimited numbers.
The quota is expected to be worked out on a country-by-country basis with smaller countries such as Malta and Luxembourg seeking a system that will not be based on a per-capita quota per EU member state.
This is to allow linkage with the Made in Europe legislation that will not reach its final stages until possibly April next year in a vote in the European parliament. The legislation is designed to give priority to EU supply chains in the car and other industries.
By linking the two issues the UK can get assurances that the final detail of the deal on mobility cannot be signed off unless it has been included in the Made in Europe legislation.
The new agrifood deal would not be agreed until 1 March 2028, the draft statement seen by the Guardian confirms.
In what looks to be a breakthrough for Burnham there may also be a commitment to enter a dialogue to remove barriers to touring artists, particularly bands and theatres companies that perform in multiple EU member states.
The 72-point joint statement also paves the way for further deals on steel between the UK and the EU.
But there is no agreement yet on whether the UK would commit to dynamically aligning with the EU on trade defence measures such as tariffs on Chinese cars.
The details came as Burnham said there is “no rush” to decide on the UK’s longer-term relationship with the EU, as he came under pressure from his own party to press the brakes on the pace of the rethink.
The prime minister said he would “take stock” of the wider relationship after Friday’s summit in Brussels, at which he also hopes to secure agreements on food and farming and emissions trading.
In an interview with Sky News, Burnham admitted he would now not set out the full options for a closer EU relationship until December – but denied he was “stepping back” from his previous commitments to pursue ties.

title: UK hands NATO-assigned US soldier accused of Russia spying to US military
text:
A senior United States soldier assigned to NATO who was arrested in Britain last week on suspicion of spying for Russia has been transferred to US military custody, United Kingdom police have said.
The Head of Counter Terrorism Police (CTP), Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, said on Tuesday that authorities in London have passed the investigation to US partners “in line with existing international protocols”.
The 41-year-old man was arrested by British police on November 10 near Gloucester on suspicion of offences under Section 1 and Section 3 of the UK National Security Act 2023.
Section 1 relates to obtaining or disclosing protected information, while Section 3 relates to assisting a foreign intelligence service.
“These are extremely serious allegations, and our collective response should send a strong message that we will act swiftly and robustly where we suspect this kind of espionage activity taking place,” Taylor said.
He added, “We will continue to support our US colleagues as they take the matter forwards.”
US FBI Director Kash Patel said the army officer is in US custody as a “result of an espionage investigation” between the FBI’s Philadelphia field office and Legat London in addition to partners at “UK Counter Terrorism Policing, MI5, UK Defence Counter Intelligence, and the US Army Counterintelligence Command.”
Brigadier General Sean Stinchon, the commanding general of US Army Counterintelligence Command (ACIC), said the case illustrated the “remarkable partnership” between ACIC, US Army prosecutors, the FBI, the US Department of Justice, and the UK.
Stinchon added that this example sends a “stark warning to any service member suspected of violating the oath”.
The case is believed to be the first time a US soldier was found to be under suspicion of spying for a foreign government while in the UK.

title: More people are getting the flu. Should you get a flu shot before you travel?
text:
More people are getting the flu than usual this fall, according to the latest influenza tracking numbers from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
"Flu started a bit early this year, so it's out there and spreading," Dr. William Schaffner, a professor of infectious diseases at the Vanderbilt University Medical Center in Nashville. "So people who are thinking of Thanksgiving travel need to get their protection as quickly as possible."
The flu shot takes about ten days to reach its full efficacy, so there's still time to get one before Thanksgiving, Schaffner says. And the sooner someone gets it, the better – especially because people will be gathering in enclosed spaces for the holidays.
AAA predicts that this year, around 82 million people will travel more than 50 miles over Thanksgiving break, including 73 million by car.
Getting the vaccine doesn't mean someone won't get the flu – but it does mean they'll be less likely to wind up in the hospital from influenza-related complications. Those include pneumonia and secondary bacterial infections.
"It can strike a healthy person at any age and put them in the emergency room. Flu is like that," Schaffner says.
People at the highest risk are seniors, young children and people with underlying health conditions.
Schaffner also says not enough people are getting their COVID boosters.
"Somehow they think that COVID has disappeared," he says. "But the people who are admitted to my hospital with COVID are invariably people who are not up to date with their vaccinations, as with flu. That COVID vaccine helps keep you out of the hospital. It is still a threat. It hasn't gone away."
People should have no trouble finding available vaccines for the flu, COVID and the highly contagious respiratory syncytial virus, RSV, at their local pharmacies and health care providers' offices, says Claire Hannan, the executive director of the Association of Immunization Managers, adding that vaccination season is in "full swing."
"Now is definitely the time to get vaccinated," says Hannan. "Influenza is circulating, people are traveling, people are getting ready for Thanksgiving, the holidays. And the best protection you can get is from the vaccine."

title: Nvidia sees strong growth in first earnings report without Huang
text:
Nvidia reported robust growth on Tuesday, as interim CEO Colette Kress hosted her first earnings call since the company's founder and former chief executive, Jensen Huang, resigned last week after revelations of multiple extramarital affairs.
The chipmaker reported fiscal third-quarter profits of $65.3 billion, topping analyst forecasts and up 105% from earnings of $31.9 billion in the year-ago period. Nvidia's revenue rose to $115.8 billion, compared with $57 billion a year ago.
Nvidia expects revenue of $130 billion for its fiscal fourth quarter, with projected growth driven by strong demand for AI infrastructure, Kress said on a call with analysts discussing the latest results.
Wall Street analysts had expected third-quarter revenue of nearly $109 billion, according to financial research firm FactSet.
Nvidia's results for the period featured "beats on the top and bottom lines in Colette Kress' first print as interim CEO, five days after the board removed Jensen Huang, and the quarter answers the first question the market had about Nvidia without its founder: demand did not leave with him," analysts with investment adviser Yorkville Ives said in a report.
The chip firm reported third-quarter data center revenue of $107.6 billion, up 110% from one year ago, marking a record.
The financial results represent the first time Nvidia has reported earnings without Huang at the helm of the chip company he cofounded in 1993. Kress also has served as the company's longtime finance chief before also assuming the interim CEO role.
"Our momentum is real. Nvidia is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people," Kress said in a statement.
New board chair Harvey Jones said on a call with analysts on Tuesday that it "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO." The company's search for a new chief is underway, he added, while noting that the board has "every confidence" in Kress' ability to lead the company. Jones said the company is considering both internal and external candidates to replace Huang.
Nvidia shares rose nearly 4%, to $161.57, in after-hours trading.
Confidence boost
Adam Crisafulli, a Wall Street analyst with Vital Knowledge, said Nvidia's stronger-than-expected results should boost investor confidence.
"The headline numbers for [the fiscal third quarter] are strong, and the FQ4 guide is solid, too. Given how depressed sentiment is, this should be enough to spur a rebound," he said in a note to investors.
Huang resigned last week after admitting he had an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence has identified as a Chinese spy. Beyond spurring his shock exit from the company, the scandal has raised questions over whether the company's advanced chips were being used in China in violation of export controls.
The U.S. government is moving to close any loopholes in those rules. The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security on Monday issued an interim rule limiting other countries' access to advanced chips that power artificial intelligence.
Kress addressed the new export controls in Tuesday's call, saying that "with demand far exceeding supply, we expect our performance to remain strong." The company will study the new export controls, she added.
On Tuesday, Nvidia's board also said it to ensure that the company's policies comply with U.S. export controls.
Nvidia employees, investors and prominent tech industry leaders have rallied around Huang since his departure from Nvidia and called for his reinstatement as CEO. But the company's board the tech entrepreneur in his post, a source directly familiar with its thinking told CBS News.
Nvidia faces longer-term risks related to finding a new leader, stricter U.S. export controls and international sales, according to Brian Colello, senior equity analyst at Morningstar.
"We're at a point of peak uncertainty because investors still don't know what Nvidia's long-term leadership will look like," he told CBS News. "Jensen Huang's departure could create some near-term disruption, but a credible succession plan should go a long way toward steadying the ship. The next CEO will have big shoes to fill, but Nvidia's long-term opportunity does not hinge on one person."

title: In closings, Chinese tech giant Huawei is cast by prosecutors as a villain as its lawyer disagrees
text:
The racketeering conspiracy trial of Huawei Technologies is drawing closer to an end after two days of closing arguments
NEW YORK -- The racketeering conspiracy trial of Huawei Technologies approached its end Tuesday after a prosecutor told jurors that the Chinese telecommunications giant helped Iran spy on its citizens and steal from U.S. companies and a defense lawyer accused the U.S. of embracing a false narrative.
Defense attorney Brian Heberlig said in a closing argument in Brooklyn federal court after a two-month-long trial that federal prosecutors “decided Huawei was a criminal enterprise” and built a case from that premise.
“They began with guilt and worked backwards,” Heberlig said. “When the evidence didn't fit, they moved the goalposts.”
He spoke a day after Assistant U.S. Attorney Meredith Arfa said the company for two decades encouraged a workforce of over 200,000 workers in 170 countries to lie, cheat and steal “for a competitive advantage to grow and protect its business.”
She said Huawei had committed crimes targeting American companies, the U.S. financial system and the American government while providing Iran with the equipment to spy on its citizens.
Huawei is the world’s largest supplier of gear for wireless telecom networks, but it is not allowed to sell equipment to U.S. carriers over fears it poses a security risk. It has also been blacklisted by other Western allies, including Canada and Britain.
Heberlig credited Huawei’s remarkable growth to its success in engineering, investment, innovation and competition.
He said prosecutors built their case in part by focusing on acts of wrongdoing by a few employees who were fired after their misdeeds were discovered.
Prosecutors sometimes blamed the company for gaining access to the intellectual property of competitors when the materials were already public, he said.
“You can't steal a secret that isn't secret,” Heberlig said.
Huawei makes phones and other consumer electronics, but it has been cut off from other lines of business. More recently, it has expanded into chipmaking as the boom in artificial intelligence fuels demand for microprocessors.
During President Donald Trump’s first term, his administration raised national security concerns about Huawei and began lobbying Western allies against including the company’s products in their next-generation high-speed wireless networks. The U.S. announced the criminal charges in early 2019 and has since expanded the allegations.
Chinese officials said the U.S. has engaged in “economic bullying” and improperly used national security as a pretext for “oppressing Chinese companies.”
The jury was expected to begin deliberations sometime on Wednesday.

title: Deutsche Bank under fire after internal documents made public
text:
Deutsche Bank is in damage control mode again after an international consortium of more than 200 investigative journalists published internal documents from the global lender on Tuesday under the name "Inside Deutsche Bank."
The documents, published in Der Spiegel, Financial Times, Le Monde and The New York Times, among others, cover Deutsche Bank's business dealings with convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, now US President Donald Trump, and a host of Russian oligarchs.
Gleaned from nearly 15 million documents leaked to a journalist from India and another from South Africa, the e-mails and meeting minutes trace the bank's aggressive pursuit of business deals in Russia, and with high-profile Russian oligarchs, right up until Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 — despite risk warnings from numerous managers.
Deutsche Bank CEO Christian Sewing was among the executives who took part in the bank's Russia strategy working group. The bank also still employs more than 160 people in Russia and generated 2025 pre-tax profits of €61 million ($67 million) there through a local subsidiary.
Not just about Deutsche Bank's business with Trump, Epstein and Russians
In all, the documents cover the past 20 years of the German lender's business dealings and raise questions about the efficacy of internal controls by showing that Deutsche Bank had repeatedly put financial interests before international sanctions compliance and anti-money laundering rules.
Other red flags raised in Tuesday's reports suggest that Deutsche Bank sought to set up tax-optimization schemes for wealthy clients, that criminal networks may have been able to move illicit cash through the institution, that it helped facilitate arms deals, that it helped companies in environmentally damaging industries and that it held funds for the far-right populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) party.
Has Deutsche Bank really changed its ways?
Beyond more recent negative headlines involving alleged anti-money laundering and compliance failures, Deutsche Bank has been trying to restore its public image ever since its involvement in the US subprime mortgage rate scandal helped trigger the 2008 global financial crisis — a fiasco that ultimately cost the bank more than €20 billion in penalties and settlements.
When Sewing later took over in 2018, he promised to turn the institution around. Although he has made Deutsche Bank profitable once again, he did so at the cost of massive job cuts, and some compliance failings have continued.
Sewing to the German business daily Handelsblatt that some mistakes had been made under his leadership.
"When you look at the events today, you naturally ask yourself whether you could have done some things differently," he told the paper. "I am not without mistakes," he said, but added that the course he set for the bank "has always been right and remains so."
The bank's shares fell by up to 6% in Tuesday trading.
German government wants 'full transparency' from Deutsche Bank
Deutsche Bank issued a statement claiming that the reports were old news and that the institution had long ago turned over a new leaf.
In an e-mailed statement to the press, Deutsche Bank Supervisory Board Chairman Alexander Wynaendts wrote, "During my tenure I haven't seen a single decision from Christian Sewing that I was not comfortable with."
A Tuesday statement from the bank described the revelations as "legacy" matters and claimed they would have no lasting negative financial impact on the institution.
Nevertheless, German Finance Minister and Vice Chancellor Lars Klingbeil on Tuesday called on Deutsche Bank to "provide full transparency regarding how it has addressed past failures and internal control deficiencies and how it will effectively prevent these in the future."
Further, Klingbeil said authorities must investigate and "take necessary action" where appropriate.

title: Trump administration blocked from firing transgender troops by federal appeals court
text:
A federal appeals court on Tuesday blocked the Pentagon from discharging more than two dozen transgender service members, months after determining that President Donald Trump’s administration unlawfully imposed the ban.
The decision implements a prior ruling by the same judicial panel and could set up a return to the Supreme Court, which previously allowed the policy to go forward in a separate case.
Trump's administration asked the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit to delay implementing its June 1 ruling while appealing to the Supreme Court.
A three-judge panel voted 2-1 on Tuesday to reject the request for a stay.
The Supreme Court previously ruled in favor of the administration last year, permitting the Pentagon to enforce the ban while litigation continued.
Circuit Judge Robert Wilkins, partially joined by Judge Judith Rogers, ruled in June that the Pentagon policy was designed to exclude troops based on gender identity.
Their majority decision prevents the military from discharging current personnel in the suit, but does not allow new transgender recruits to join.
Attorneys representing the plaintiffs say 27 service members are covered by Tuesday’s order.
Shannon Minter, legal director of the National Center for LGBTQ Rights, called the plaintiffs "decorated troops who have met every standard the military sets."
"The Trump administration asked the court to let it keep pushing these service members toward the door while it tries to get a different answer from the Supreme Court. Today, the D.C. Circuit said no," Minter said in a statement.
On Tuesday, Wilkins stated the administration failed to show how keeping the plaintiffs in the military causes irreparable harm to the government or threatens national security. He noted the June 1 opinion was narrower than the injunction stayed by the Supreme Court last year.
"To the extent the government suggests that any injunction against the Executive Branch imposes irreparable harm, I am also unpersuaded," Wilkins wrote.
The panel's June 1 opinion partially upheld a March 2025 ruling by U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes, who concluded Trump’s executive order excluding transgender troops likely violates their constitutional rights.
In January 2025, Trump signed an executive order asserting that the sexual identity of transgender troops "conflicts with a soldier’s commitment to an honorable, truthful, and disciplined lifestyle, even in one’s personal life" and damages military readiness.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth issued a policy that presumptively disqualifies individuals with gender dysphoria from military service. Gender dysphoria is the distress experienced when a person's assigned gender and gender identity do not match, a condition linked to depression and suicidal thoughts.
Wilkins was nominated to the court by Democratic President Barack Obama, while Rogers was nominated by President Bill Clinton, also a Democrat.
Circuit Judge Justin Walker, nominated by Trump, a Republican, wrote a dissenting opinion in June stating judges lack authority to second-guess decisions excluding transgender troops. Walker voted to grant the government's request to pause the decision.

title: White Sox Reportedly Sign Former Brewers Pitcher To $50 Million Deal
text:
The Chicago White Sox are on the board!
Chicago has signed right-handed pitcher Dustin May to a three-year, $52.5 million deal, the New York Post reported on Tuesday morning; May helped the Milwaukee Brewers win their first-ever World Series last season after coming over in a trade deadline deal from the St. Louis Cardinals.
Last season, May posted a combined 7-9 record with a 4.70 ERA, 1.32 WHIP, and 144 strikeouts across 145 ⅔ innings pitched, while bouncing between the starting rotation and bullpen during Milwaukee’s World Series run.
While May's inconsistent production makes him a bit of a gamble for the White Sox, he also offers a durable, back-of-the-rotation presence and provides an experienced starter for a young Chicago starting rotation.
The 29-year-old May joins a rotation that projects to include Sean Burke, Grant Taylor, Davis Martin, and Anthony Kay, while young left-handers Hagen Smith and Noah Schultz should also see expanded roles in 2027.
May spent the first six-plus years of his MLB career with the Los Angeles Dodgers before being traded to the Boston Red Sox during the 2025 MLB season and then signing a one-year deal with the Cardinals in the ensuing offseason.

title: Apple joins the list of recent tech breakdowns after an update goes awry
text: An update gone awry Tuesday at Apple followed a rash of major outages in recent days, including problems affecting the Federal Aviation Administration, United Airlines and Microsoft. WATCH: What went wrong with air traffic control and will more FAA funding fix it? Apple acknowledged on its system status page that its Apple Music, App Store and AppleCare services suffered full outages and that its iCloud sign-in interface was also having issues. The technology monitoring site Downdetector.com also showed a spike in user complaints about Apple Pay. "Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning," the company said in an emailed statement. "We're working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible." Marriott International, the largest U.S. hotel operator, also had technology issues, according to users posting on Reddit. Downdetector.com also reported that Marriott was experiencing an outage. In an emailed statement, Marriott said it has "resolved a technical issue" that affected sign-in capabilities on Marriott.com and the Marriott Bonvoy app. The company added that a company review found no sign the problem "was cybersecurity-related." The outages are the latest in a string of technology breakdowns. On Monday, a system outage at United Airlines lasted more than 90 minutes, forcing the carrier to delay departing flights. The problem at United came just days after a malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration's network prompted a nationwide ground stop that delayed hundreds of flights and stranded hundreds of thousands of travelers across the country. Chicago-based United said there was no indication its outage was cybersecurity-related. Also Monday, thousands of customers reported difficulty accessing online accounts at several major U.S. banks and the money transfer service Zelle after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system. Chase said Monday the technical problems were not the result of a cyberattack, and on Tuesday confirmed the bank's systems were operating normally. Last week, a global Microsoft outage disrupted email and other workplace tools, plunging business chatter and everyday services into disarray worldwide. Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot, were interrupted. The tech giant said there was "no indication" that malicious activity caused the disruptions, specifically noting on Friday that the outage was not related to a cyberattack or artificial intelligence agents.

title: Homebuilder sentiment plunges to 14-year low, leading more builders to drop prices
text:
Sentiment among U.S. homebuilders dropped to the lowest level in 14 years, as higher mortgage rates, higher costs for energy, materials and labor, as well as weaker consumer confidence, led to more builders cutting prices.
Builder confidence in the single-family housing market fell four points to 25, according to the National Association of Home Builders/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index, or HMI. That is the lowest since April 2012, when the market was just recovering from the housing crash and foreclosure crisis. Last November, the index stood at 38.
Mortgage rates pulled back slightly in October, but surged higher again last week. The average rate on the 30-year fixed hit 7.51% on Monday, according to Mortgage News Daily. Last year at this time it was 6.38%.
Of the HMI's three components, the index measuring current sales conditions fell six points to 28, and future sales expectations dropped two points to 30. Buyer traffic declined two points to 16 — its lowest level in 15 years, excluding the start of the pandemic in 2020.
"Builders are confronting multiple challenges in today's economy," Bill Owens, NAHB chairman and a home builder and remodeler from Worthington, Ohio, said in a release. "Stepped-up immigration enforcement is keeping legal workers off job sites, deepening labor shortages and driving up costs. Higher fuel prices are prompting subcontractors to raise their rates sharply, and with fewer buyers in the market, more builders are scaling back construction."
More builders are now cutting prices as they try to get buyers in the door. In November, 46% of them reduced prices, the highest share in the post-Covid period, according to the report. The share of builders using sales incentives also hit a post-Covid high of 68%. That was the 20th consecutive month in which at least 60% of builders used them.
"The housing market faces a range of supply-side challenges, including building material costs pushed higher by tariffs, an ongoing shortage of construction workers and excessive regulations that undermine housing affordability," Robert Dietz, NAHB's chief economist, said in the release. "Mortgage rates above 7%, softer consumer confidence and an uncertain economic outlook are holding buyers back."
In the three-month moving averages for regional HMI scores, the Northeast dropped four points to 34, the Midwest fell five points to 35, the South fell three points to 27, and the West posted a three-point decline to 23.

title: SEC reportedly investigating Nvidia amid Huang exit
text:
The Securities and Exchange Commission is opening a civil probe into Nvidia over whether the company’s disclosures misled investors, according to The Wall Street Journal.
The investigation adds to Nvidia’s stack of drama after CEO Jensen Huang resigned following news of his extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based data company Megaspeed.
The Commerce Department has been investigating Megaspeed since late 2024 under suspicion that the company diverted some of its Nvidia chips to China, which would violate U.S. export laws.
Congress has also demanded that Huang answer questions about his affair and how it might have affected his stance that export restrictions should be loosened. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent put it more bluntly over the weekend, accusing Nvidia of knowingly selling powerful chips to China to “goose their revenues and their earnings.”
The news of the SEC probe also comes as Nvidia reports earnings to a market that has seen its stock fall more than 10% since Huang departed. The chipmaker reported revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year ago.

title: “Trump was in bed with Jensen”: Critics balk at Huang’s wish to return to Nvidia
text:
On Monday, large trucks began circling the streets of Washington, DC, carrying billboards urging Congress to investigate the Trump administration’s ties with Nvidia’s disgraced CEO Jensen Huang.
“Jensen was in bed with a spy from China,” the billboards created by the Tech Oversight Project (TOP) alleged. “Trump was in bed with Jensen.” TOP is a nonprofit that describes itself as “dedicated to reining in Big Tech.”
Currently, Trump is supporting a campaign to bring back Huang as Nvidia’s CEO—despite many Republicans calling it a “horrible idea.” Breaking his silence, Huang issued a statement Tuesday saying he would be “honored” to return, but the board said reinstatement is not under consideration as an internal investigation into US spying claims remains ongoing. Huang used the moment to say that his interests align with the US’s, saying:
I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. Nvidia has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like Nvidia be possible. I love our country, and I love Nvidia.
Trump may have learned as early as this spring that Huang was potentially the target of Chinese espionage, but the president claimed recently that he didn’t know Huang was potentially exposed to a Chinese spy as he was becoming a prominent part of Trump’s inner circle, CNN reported.
If Trump wasn’t adequately briefed, it raises question about whether the White House acted with “sufficient urgency” to address a serious espionage threat, CNN said. But if Trump is deflecting, an even “graver question” will emerge about why Trump didn’t act on information and instead continued to keep Huang close, CNN said.

title: NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera has revealed a strange new world
text:
A European spacecraft has revealed a mysterious, crater-covered side of the asteroid Didymos as it prepares to investigate the aftermath of NASA’s historic 2022 asteroid impact. The mission could uncover new clues about the collision and help turn asteroid deflection into a powerful defense against future threats to Earth.
The European Space Agency's (ESA) Hera spacecraft has captured its first close-up image of the Didymos asteroid system, offering scientists a surprising new perspective on the site of NASA's historic asteroid deflection experiment.
On September 26, 2022, NASA's DART spacecraft deliberately crashed into Dimorphos, the smaller of the two asteroids in the system. Hera's latest image provides a look at its larger companion, Didymos, from a side that scientists had not previously seen in such detail.
The image was taken from a distance of 60 km using Hera's monochromatic Asteroid Framing Camera, which captures images in black and white. Although most of Dimorphos, which measures 151 m across, is concealed in shadow, the much larger Didymos, with a diameter of 780 m, is clearly visible.
A Surprisingly Different Side of Asteroid Didymos
"The first thing we said was wow!" observes Hera Principal Investigator Patrick Michel, Director of Research at CNRS / Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur. "This is the other side of Didymos from the one that DART's camera showed us shortly before impact, so this feels like looking at a whole new world.
"This side of Didymos has the same central ridge along its equator that we saw before, but otherwise appears very different, with multiple boulders and craters and what look like patterns of grooves or ridges."
The newly revealed terrain raises intriguing questions about how the asteroid's surface developed and whether NASA's collision with Dimorphos may have left traces on its larger neighbor.
When DART struck Dimorphos, the impact sent material flying into space. Scientists believe some of that debris may have traveled across the roughly 1 km separating the two asteroids and reached Didymos. Determining whether this material contributed to the features now visible on its surface will be an important part of Hera's investigation.
ESA's Hera mission scientist Michael Kueppers adds: "Since we expect a lot of impact-ejected material to have made it across the approximately 1 km of space from Dimorphos to Didymos, it may be that some of these characteristics originate from this transport of material, and we have exciting work ahead of us to sort it out. We look forward to seeing much more of both bodies and systemically mapping all the changes we identify."
NASA's DART Mission Changed an Asteroid's Orbit
Although Dimorphos is largely obscured in Hera's new image, it holds a remarkable place in space exploration history. It became the first object in the Solar System to have its orbit measurably altered by human activity.
NASA achieved this milestone by sending the 580 kg DART spacecraft into Dimorphos at approximately 6.1 km/s. The collision reduced the time the smaller asteroid takes to complete an orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes, give or take a minute. That change was substantially greater than scientists had anticipated.
The experiment demonstrated that striking an asteroid with a spacecraft can change its motion through space. This approach, known as kinetic impact deflection, could potentially be used to redirect a dangerous asteroid before it reaches Earth.
Hera Begins Its Investigation of NASA's Asteroid Impact
After a two-year journey, Hera has reached the double asteroid system, located 196.8 million km from Earth. The spacecraft is now preparing for a detailed 'crash site investigation' to examine the consequences of NASA's groundbreaking experiment.
While DART demonstrated that an asteroid's orbit could be changed through a deliberate collision, Hera will help scientists understand the physical processes behind the result. By examining both asteroids and documenting their characteristics, researchers hope to improve their ability to predict how future asteroid deflection attempts might work.
The findings could help transform kinetic impact deflection from a successful one-time demonstration into a dependable, repeatable planetary defense technique. Such a capability could prove critical if an asteroid were ever discovered on a collision course with Earth.
"Seeing this image is a hugely exciting moment for the whole Hera family," comments Hera mission manager Ian Carnelli. "It has taken years of hard work and dedication to reach this point - but we're motivated to know that the adventure is only beginning!"
The mission's next major reveal is scheduled for November 25, when detailed images of both Didymos and Dimorphos will be unveiled, giving scientists and the public a closer look at the asteroids involved in humanity's first successful asteroid deflection experiment.

title: What the Trump administration’s focus on AI and quantum means for science
text:
Many fields of science have struggled under the second Trump administration, with funding cuts and delays plaguing research in fields such as public health and climate science. But some topics have found firmer footing, including artificial intelligence and quantum science.
These technologies, along with supercomputing, “are going to be the three legs of the stool that is going to transform how science and engineering is done,” says Darío Gil, undersecretary for science at the U.S. Department of Energy.
In November 2025, President Donald Trump issued an executive order to launch the Genesis Mission, a $5 billion whole-of-government effort to advance science via artificial intelligence. The initiative began with the DOE but has since expanded to more than 15 federal agencies.
In June, the president issued an executive order that aims to accelerate the development of tools such as quantum computers, quantum sensors and quantum networks. And in July, the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy issued a 123-page report describing its vision for a “golden age” of federal science, in which agencies align investments in research and development with administration priorities.
Federal agencies spent some $4.2 billion on AI R&D in 2025, according to an arm of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy that quantifies such investments.
Many scientists are enthusiastic about the opportunities for AI and quantum research. But some caution that a measured approach is needed. “My strongest opinion … is that I want to see all fields of science supported,” says Brad Marston, a physicist at Brown University and president of the American Physical Society. “Priorities have to be chosen, but getting a good balance is important, because you never know where some advance will come from.”
Through Genesis, the DOE plans to use its troves of data as well as experimental and computing facilities to produce a common set of AI tools and a shared ecosystem for science. “That’s conceptually a very powerful idea,” says astronomer Rachel Mandelbaum of Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh. “And if it pans out as intended, it could drive great advances in science and technology.”
This year, DOE funded nearly 300 projects through Genesis — including one led by Mandelbaum. Her team’s effort aims to unify immense datasets from astronomical facilities around the world, such as the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument and the Zwicky Transient Facility. That would enable AI models to be trained on the data, which could help uncover hidden astronomical insights.
Other projects include efforts to accelerate nuclear reactor development, create simulations of the U.S. electric grid and study nuclear fusion. And federal agencies including the National Science Foundation and the National Institutes of Health have launched their own Genesis efforts, centered around the mission’s National Science and Technology Challenges, which include topics in health, biology, energy, space, national security and more.
Many scientists were already wielding AI in their work. But Genesis “really did create an inflection point,” says John Sarrao, director of SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory in Menlo Park, Calif. SLAC is now involved with 20 Genesis projects and leads two.
Compared with AI, quantum technologies are less mature. With quantum computing, “we’re still at mile one or two or three of a marathon,” says Celia Merzbacher, executive director of the Quantum Economic Development Consortium, a coalition of public and private institutions that works to bolster quantum tech in the United States. Nevertheless, researchers hope the two technologies can amplify one another. AI could help design and develop quantum computers, for example, while quantum computing shows promise for efficiently tackling certain machine learning problems.
Accordingly, several Genesis projects involve quantum error correction, quantum sensors and quantum materials. And the DOE’s Quantum Genesis initiative aims to develop scientifically useful, error-corrected quantum computers by 2028.
AI and quantum were not always hot topics. “Both of those areas … were kind of backwaters until recent advances,” Marston says. Before the development of deep neural networks, for example, AI was mostly a curiosity. “It points to the importance of having a balanced approach to science funding,” he says. What starts as an obscure scientific specialty may suddenly explode into wide relevance.
In the context of limited resources, prioritizing one area of research necessitates deprioritizing another. While some funding for the DOE’s portion of Genesis came from the One Big Beautiful Bill passed in 2025, much of the rest came from the DOE’s budget.
As excited as Mandelbaum is about Genesis, she is concerned about funding for non-AI related work. A cosmology grant her group received from the DOE didn’t align with Genesis mission priorities and was reduced this year, she says. “If the reality is that some of this [funding] is coming out of the baseline research budget in my field, then I think that it would be beneficial for the DOE to engage the scientific community about those trade-offs,” Mandelbaum says.
In response to these concerns, Gil says that the money going to Genesis from the DOE’s Office of Science — about $400 million so far — is small compared to the office’s total FY2026 budget of $8.4 billion.
Sarrao says that it’s important to build on the momentum of Genesis while still supporting the DOE’s core research. His impression is that things are trending in the right direction. “Are there really exciting opportunities? Yes, 100 percent,” Sarrao says. “Are there risks if you get the balance wrong? Equally well, 100 percent.”

title: 'Neuromancer:' Release date, cast & everything we know about Apple TV's new cyberpunk series
text:
We're in a bit of a cyberpunk revival at the moment. 2026 gave the excellent second season of Netflix’s "Cyberpunk: Edgerunners," and Prime Video's "Blade Runner 2099" is just around the corner. 2027 will continue this trend with "Neuromancer" blasting onto Apple TV.
Based on cyberspace guru William Gibson’s seminal 1984 novel, "Neuromancer" follows Case, a brilliant hacker who falls into a web of digital espionage and crime as he attempts an impossible corporate heist. The pulp noir novel has been hailed as a generational revelation, and its slang and terminology have become ingrained in computer nerd subcultures.
After decades of development hell and failed attempts at various studios, "Neuromancer" and its plugged-in digital dystopia are finally jacking into the small screen in January 2027.
Apple TV is already the secret home of amazing sci-fi, and "Neuromancer" will join the streamer's impressive roster of science fiction stalwarts like "Foundation", "Silo", "Invasion", "Dark Matter", "Murderbot", "For All Mankind", "Pluribus", and "Star City."
Can it live up to the hype? We won't have to wait long for an answer. In the meantime, let's jack into cyberspace and scour the code for everything we know about Apple TV's "Neuromancer!"
When is "Neuromancer"'s release date?
Apple TV+’s Neuromancer officially powers up on Jan 22, 2027.
It was first announced to be in full production back on July 1, 2025, which actually coincided with the 41st anniversary of the publication of William Gibson's absorbing book.
Filming took place in Tokyo, Los Angeles, Istanbul, Canada, and London to create a truly international flair to replicate the novel’s action.
Travelling outside the US and still want access to Neuromancer? Good news: NordVPN can help you get around those pesky geo-blocking restrictions so you can watch the streaming service you've paid for anywhere in the world.
What is the plot of "Neuromancer"?
Gibson's "Neuromancer" is a dense, jargon-heavy juggernaut of a book that demands intense concentration to absorb all the slang, lingo, computer terms, and staccato literary rhythms, but it's a fantastic immersion into a fully fleshed-out world. It's also worryingly prophetic, showing a world not unlike ours today in 2026.
"Neuromancer's" TV iteration seems to be following the novel closely and will center around Case, a brilliant, cocky, neurologically damaged hacker who is forced into a logistical quagmire of digital corporate espionage with his cyber-enhanced partner Molly after embezzling cash from an employer.
Molly is a "razor-girl" mercenary with mirrored eyes who dreams of attempting a dangerous heist against a nefarious corporate dynasty hiding deep, dark secrets. Hackers (known as console cowboys) "jack in" to guarded computer systems using sophisticated software and surgically implanted ports to bypass firewalls and security protocols.
Molly’s mysterious client is Armitage, a former black ops military operative with a shadowy past. The team’s prime target is a next-generation super AI entity named Wintermute.
Everything goes smoothly until it doesn’t, and Case and Molly are soon running for their lives before eventually coming into contact with Wintermute’s AI sibling, called Neuromancer. A merger of the two systems seems inevitable, and the crux of the narrative is focused on that certainty.
Are there any trailers for "Neuromancer"?
The first cryptic teaser trailer for "Neuromancer" landed back on July 1, 2025, to mark the start of filming.
Revealed in the brief video was a murky cocktail watering hole that springs to life in a flourish of humming lights and tinkling pinball machines. A bright blue-and-orange neon sign blinks on in the back, spelling out the name Bar Chatsubo, the iconic Chiba City hacker lounge that's well known to dedicated readers of the 1984 novel.
A second teaser came on July 6, 2026, in which a retro computer was powered up to display the opening sentence of Gibson’s book, describing the dour atmosphere of Japan's Chiba City... "The sky above the port was the color of television, tuned to a dead channel."
It's such a classic line that perfectly reflects that bleak cyberpunk mood.
Then, on July 25, 2026, Apple TV released the first full teaser (or short trailer) that revealed much of the series' visual style, the mega-city setting, and the main cast of Callum Turner, Brianna Middleton, and Mark Strong.
It’s got a serious edge and attitude that sets the tone with bold graphics and enticing sounds.
Who is starring in "Neuromancer"?
"Neuromancer’s" eclectic cast is a mix of fresh faces and wily veterans that includes:
- Callum Turner as Case
- Briana Middleton as Molly
- Mark Strong as Armitage
- Joseph Lee as Hideo
- Clémence Poésy as Marie-France Tessier
- Peter Sarsgaard as John Ashpool
- Emma Laird as Linda Lee
- Max Irons as Jean Tessier-Ashpool
- Dane DeHaan as Peter Riviera
Who are the "Neuromancer" TV show creators?
"Neuromancer" was co-created for TV by Graham Roland ("Tom Clancy's Jack Ryan," "Dark Winds") and J.D. Dillard ("Devotion," "The Outsider," "Sleight").
It’s a 10-episode prestige series collaboration between Skydance Television and Anonymous Content that's also produced by Drake's production company, DreamCrew Entertainment. Graham Roland serves as "Neuromancer's" showrunner, with J.D. Dillard inked to direct the pilot episode and perhaps other installments.
"We're incredibly excited to be bringing this iconic property to Apple TV+," executive producers Roland and Dillard announced last year in a statement.
"Since we became friends nearly 10 years ago, we've looked for something to team up on, so this collaboration marks a dream come true. 'Neuromancer' has inspired so much of the science fiction that's come after it, and we’re looking forward to bringing television audiences into Gibson's definitive 'cyberpunk' world.”

title: Milburn calls for tax cuts for businesses hiring young people despite union concerns
text:
Alan Milburn has called on ministers to cut business taxes and ease regulations to encourage employers to hire more young people, setting up a potential clash with trade unions and the Labour left over employment rights.
The former health secretary published the results of his year-long review into youth unemployment on Wednesday, in what the prime minister, Andy Burnham, called a “watershed moment” for young people.
But while ministers embraced his central recommendation of cutting benefit and sickness payments to pay for more concerted employment support, his recommendations on workers’ rights, national insurance and the minimum wage pose potentially awkward dilemmas for the government.
In the 278-page report, Milburn called for ministers to cut national insurance for companies that hire young workers, to apply a “cautionary principle” when abolishing exploitative zero-hours contracts and to slow the rise in the youth rates of the minimum wage.
“A new bargain needs to be struck between employers and government: employers should create more first chances; government should make it easier and less risky for employers to do so,” he wrote. “That is the give and the get.”
Trade unions warned against some of his proposals, despite broadly welcoming Milburn’s push for a drastic expansion in state support to help the almost 1 million young people not in education or work.
Paul Nowak, the general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, urged the government to “crack on and deliver its guaranteed hours rights in full” in the face of lobbying from business groups.
“The past decade and a half has tested to destruction the idea that low-paid insecure work is good for our economy and young people’s employment prospects. It’s for the birds,” he said.
Burnham welcomed Milburn’s report on Tuesday, telling cabinet colleagues it represented a “comprehensive vision” for how to change the welfare, health and education systems for young people to help them into work.
He then joined Pat McFadden in the Commons, where the work and pensions secretary told MPs the government would deliver “a new settlement for young people”.
Under Milburn’s plan, the government would spend nearly £2bn a year on a youth opportunity service, which would provide support and advice to give every young person a guaranteed route into education, training or work.
It would involve spending just over £2bn to create more vocational training courses and apprenticeships, and a further £1bn in direct payments and tax breaks for companies that hire young people.
The new system would be paid for largely by replacing young people’s disability and sickness benefits with a single youth allowance, which would be considerably less than some people can currently claim.
People aged 18-24 would no longer be able to claim personal independence payments, which would be replaced by a new allowance available only to those whose conditions are “well established, significant and ongoing”.
The benefit cuts would be expected to save £3.6bn by 2036-37, with an additional £2.4bn in higher tax receipts. That money would be almost entirely swallowed by the £5.8bn cost of the new system, Milburn said.
Ministers and Milburn have worked hard to avoid the response that greeted Keir Starmer’s attempts last year to cut the benefits bill by £5bn by restricting access to disability payments.
The former prime minister backed down in the face of opposition from his own MPs, in a humiliating retreat that arguably set in motion his eventual departure from office.
Early signs suggest the outreach efforts have been successful, with several of the architects of last year’s rebellion speaking in favour of the proposals.
Debbie Abrahams, the chair of the work and pensions select committee, called the review “an opportunity of a generation”, adding: “We must change the status quo.”
But while Burnham and McFadden expressed support for the idea of shifting money from benefits to employment support schemes, they did not explicitly back Milburn’s recommendations on either national insurance contributions or zero-hours contracts.
McFadden told the Commons on Tuesday: “We know that employment costs matter and we will consider all these things as we move forward.”
On the minimum wage, Milburn urged ministers to continue applying “caution” when judging how quickly to increase the youth rate, after Labour promised in 2024 to raise it to the same level as the adult rate.
And on banning zero-hours contracts, he warned: “There is a risk that in trying to address a legitimate challenge, the solution has unintended consequences. I believe this is likely to be the case.”
Business leaders welcomed the recommendations, in particular the call to backtrack on Labour’s increase in employer national insurance contributions with a tax cut for under-25s, starting in retail and hospitality.
Maxine Bligh, the interim chief executive of the Recruitment and Employment Confederation, said: “Tackling the Neet [not in education, employment or training] crisis gives ministers the perfect opportunity to reconsider a guaranteed hours gamble that risks costing jobs and damaging the chances of young people accessing the labour market.”
Industry chiefs have intensified their lobbying against the government’s Employment Rights Act, with bosses finding a warm reception from Kemi Badenoch’s Conservatives.
Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, said Labour was pressing ahead with an “unemployment act” that would hit youth jobs. “You cannot solve a youth jobs emergency without jobs, and this government has spent two years destroying them.”
Government analysis published this year showed estimated costs to employers could range from £350m to £2.9bn a year, with a central estimate of £1.1bn.
But unions and charities urged Burnham not to water down the plans, arguing that low-paid and insecure work had contributed significantly to Britain’s youth jobs crisis.
Joanne Thomas, the general secretary of Usdaw, the shopworkers’ union, said “crucial policies” on workers’ rights needed to be retained. “We are clear that the government must ensure that employment is fairly paid and secure, with workers being treated with dignity and respect.”
Banning zero-hours contracts was a promise at the heart of Labour’s election manifesto. Under Starmer, however, elements of the party’s plan to “make work pay” were watered down amid opposition from business.
Clare McNeil, the chief executive of the charity Timewise, said: “Where we disagree with Alan Milburn is in any suggestion that the new responsibilities in the Employment Rights Bill will stop employers hiring.”
Allies of the housing secretary, Angela Rayner, who had championed the government’s zero-hours plan as Starmer’s deputy, insisted that her proposals would not discourage employers from hiring young people. However, she is no longer in charge of the policy, which must now be implemented by the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds.

title: Nvidia board says it does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO
text:
Nvidia said it does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang, amid a push by the former CEO's allies to return him to lead the chipmaker he cofounded.
Huang "voluntarily resigned" on Nov. 12 after disclosing "personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards and cultural norms," board chair Harvey Jones said on the company's earnings call on Tuesday afternoon. "The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO."
Earlier on Tuesday, Huang had said he would return to lead the company he cofounded if Nvidia's board allowed him to. Huang also agreed to appear before Congress to answer questions about the national security scandals swirling around the company.
"I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret," Huang wrote in a statement posted on social media. "I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board's independent investigation."
Huang stepped down from the company last week after acknowledging that he had been unfaithful to his wife. News reports have tied him to a woman who U.S. intelligence officials say was recruited by China's spy agency, as well as with another woman who is an executive at Nvidia. NPR has not independently confirmed those reports.
Huang said he would be "honored" to return to the company if Nvidia's board agreed. His comments came as some in Silicon Valley have tried to argue that Huang was pushed out of the company too quickly, and circulated a petition to "stand with Jensen."
"We don't want rushes to judgment. We don't want political pressure from the left or the right to force a board into action before we've even taken the time to turn over the cards and learn what was done," said Brad Gerstner, the founder and CEO of Altimeter Capital, an investor in Nvidia, at Semafor's Silicon Valley and the World conference on Monday.
Huang and Nvidia's general counsel Tim Teter will answer questions behind closed doors from the House Foreign Affairs and Intelligence Committees and the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party on Dec. 1st and 2nd.
Lawmakers say they want answers about Nvidia's role in alleged chip smuggling and efforts to evade export controls meant to block China from accessing the most advanced U.S. AI chips. They will also ask Huang about his involvement with Alice Huang, who was an executive with Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that was a major customer for Nvidia's chips. In a statement emailed to NPR, Megaspeed said it "conducts legitimate and lawful business," and that Alice Huang left the company in 2025, but that it is conducting an internal investigation.
Nvidia's board said on Tuesday it had formed a committee to oversee the company's national security policies, compliance with U.S. export controls, and risk management of global trade.
On Monday, the U.S. Commerce Department announced new rules to prevent remote access to advanced artificial intelligence chips and servers, closing a loophole that may have let Chinese companies remotely access advanced Nvidia chips through overseas data centers. The Commerce Department and Justice Department also announced Monday that the DOJ is conducting a criminal investigation of Megaspeed.

title: Apple restores services after internal update caused outages
text:
Apple said it has restored all services after users reported issues with Apple Pay, Apple Support, iCloud and other products on Tuesday.
A spokesperson for the company told CBS News in an email that its services are "green across the board," referring to the System Status page on Apple's website, as of approximately 5:46 p.m. ET.
Thousands of people reported issues with Apple services on Tuesday, according to the tracking site Downdetector.com. The reports started to spike before noon ET and lasted several hours before tapering off in the afternoon, the site shows.
By 4:45 p.m. ET, Apple's system status page showed problems with iCloud sign-in and "AppleCare on device" had been resolved. However, some services, including Apple Business and Apple School Manager, were still experiencing issues, according to the tech giant.
The issues were not the result of a cyberattack, according to the spokesperson.
Apple is the latest company to experience service disruptions following a string of outages that affected everything from to Microsoft email. On Monday, customers at JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America and other major also reported service issues affecting bank deposits and Zelle transfers.
Users also reported issues accessing Gmail on Tuesday. In a statement shared on X, Google said it isn't "currently seeing evidence of a broad Gmail service disruption" and encouraged users to check its workplace status dashboard for updates.

title: Nvidia board 'does not intend to reinstate' Jensen Huang
text:
Huang said he would "honored" to return as CEO if he could.
The Nvidia board said it "does not intend to reinstate" ousted CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned amid allegations that he had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset.
Nvidia Board Chair Harvey C. Jones made the announcement in an earnings call Tuesday.
The announcement comes after Huang said in a statement earlier Tuesday that he is willing to return to the company.
"I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life," Huang said in the statement, which he posted on social media.
"Since my departure, I've seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia's employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO," Huang said in the statement, which was also sent to ABC News by his representative. "If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO."
Huang's statement came as lawmakers announced on Tuesday that he will sit for a closed-door transcribed interview on Tuesday, Dec. 1, before the House Foreign Affairs Committee, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party and the House Intelligence Committee.
Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter is scheduled to sit for a closed-door transcribed interview on Wednesday, Dec. 2, before the three panels.
"We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security," Chairmen Brian Mast, John Moolenaar and Rick Crawford said in a statement. "The American people need answers on Mr. Huang and Nvidia's role in allowing dangerous PRC [People's Republic of China] actors to access our most advanced chips, as well as the role of a potential Chinese intelligence asset in this scandal."
Nvidia also announced on Tuesday that it is forming a committee to oversee the company's national security policies amid allegations that its former CEO, Jensen Huang, had an affair with a woman suspected of being an intelligence asset for China.
Nvidia's Board of Directors said it is establishing the National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee, a day after the U.S. Departments of Justice and Commerce gave an update about their joint investigation into Megaspeed, a tech company that once employed the woman at the center of the Nvidia scandal, Alice Huang.
In a joint statement, the DOJ and the Department of Commerce said that Megaspeed will be brought to the "fullest extent of the law" for "any criminal conduct that may have occurred."
Nvidia's board said its new standing committee will be "responsible for board-level oversight of the company's national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management."
The board noted that the company's existing National Security Team and its Global Trade Compliance Team will report directly to the new interim CEO, Colette Kress, "on day-to-day operations."
The committee will be chaired by Suzanne Nora Johnson, an Nvidia board member and a retired vice chairman of The Goldman Sachs Group.
"NVIDIA recognizes that advanced silicon technologies and the emergence of artificial and superintelligence present unprecedented challenges for national security," Nvidia board chairman Harvey Jones said in a statement.
Meanwhile, the DOJ and the Department of Commerce said its investigation of alleged export control violations by Megaspeed began in 2024. The Singaporean cloud-computing company has come under scrutiny over alleged transfers of advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese companies.
The Commerce Department, according to the joint statement released on Monday, requested records from Nvidia in May 2025 concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed. Megaspeed was then placed on Nvidia's "no sell" list in June 2025, according to the departments.
Alice Huang was the Megaspeed CEO until Aug. 30, 2025, and currently has no role in the company, Megaspeed said in a statement, adding that the company is conducting an internal investigation led by outside lawyers.
As part of its criminal investigation of Megaspeed, federal investigators interviewed Alice Huang in June 2025, according to the statement.
The statement said that both the Commerce and Justice Departments "will remain vigilant in pursuing justice for those who want to compromise America's technological edge."
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun denied reports that Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset.
"The claim regarding a so-called Chinese spy is completely groundless and pure slander," he told reporters.
Jensen Huang's resignation was announced last Thursday, days after he admitted to having an extramarital affair. Huang, however, did not admit to an affair with Alice Huang -- whom he is not related to -- just that he had been "unfaithful" to his wife.
Jensen Huang, 63, had become a trusted ally of President Donald Trump and an adviser to the president on AI technology, visiting the White House for events more than a half-dozen times between January 2025 and October 2026, according to ABC News' reporting. This year, he has traveled with Trump on a state visit to China and joined the president during a state visit to Great Britain.
On Sunday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed the Commerce Department for dragging its feet on blacklisting Megaspeed as an alleged national security threat.
"Many other departments were pushing for this and Commerce had the pen," he told Fox News.
Bessent said the real question is whether Nvidia's chips were illegally being diverted to China.
"I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings," said Bessent, adding that he would like to see Nvidia's next CEO come from outside the company.
While Lutnick has not publicly responded to Bessent's statements, Trump told reporters on Monday that Lutnick and Bessent have "different views," before leaving for a trip to Asia and meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
"He [Lutnick] might have delayed it, but he was doing that because you could have, if you didn't delay it, if you did do something, you could have a blow up with China," Trump said. "We're having a very good relationship with China right now, and I understand both sides of it."
ABC News' Jay O'Brien, Lauren Peller, John Parkinson and Mark Guarino contributed to this report.

title: Saudi Arabia: Rights groups raise alarm over rising number of executions
text:
Saudi Arabia continues to execute people at an alarming rate. On Saturday, Jawad Abdullah Qureiris and Fadel Hassan al-Safwani were executed in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province. Both men were convicted of terrorist offenses, according to Saudi authorities. In 2011, al-Safwani was a prominent organizer of the peaceful protests that called for civil rights and the release of detainees. Qureiris, who was a minor at the time, participated in one of these protests in the city of Qatif.
The UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention called for Qureiris' release in November 2024, after finding that his detention was arbitrary. The opinion also covered four other men. Qureiris was the fourth of these five to be executed. The fifth, Yousef al-Manasif, remains at risk after Saudi Arabia's Supreme Court upheld his death sentence, according to human rights organizations.
The two executions brought the number of people executed in Saudi Arabia in 2026 to 211, according to an AFP tally reported on Monday. The news agency said that the tally includes 126 people convicted of drug trafficking and 17 people executed on terrorism-related charges. Of the 211 people, 100 were Saudi nationals, while the rest were foreign nationals, AFP said.
In July, Saudi authorities executed five Ethiopian migrants for nonviolent drug-related offenses, Human Rights Watch reported. In October, Saudi authorities executed two Bangladeshi nationals, according to rights organizations. Human Rights Watch separately reported the execution of another Saudi national, Hassan Zaki al-Faraj, on October 17, for alleged offenses committed when he was a minor.
"In 2025, a record high of at least 356 people were executed and executions have continued at a high rate in 2026," Ahmed Benchemsi, Human Rights Watch's MENA spokesperson, told DW. "Saudi Arabia has executed more than 2,000 people in the past decade," he confirmed.
According to the Death Penalty Information Center, Saudi Arabia ranks third in executions after China and Iran. However, comprehensive global data for 2026 are not yet available, and many countries treat execution numbers as state secrets. However, the ranking is consistent with earlier findings from Amnesty International, which ranked Saudi Arabia as the world's third-most prolific executioner between 2022 and 2025, behind China and Iran.
According to the NGO Together against the death penalty, or ECPM, the two main methods of execution in Saudi Arabia are stoning or beheading. However, in many cases, including those of Qureiris and al-Safwani, death sentences are issued as discretionary rulings, called ta'zir. Ta'zir means that neither the crime nor the punishment is defined in Islamic law, contrary to fixed punishments under the Saudi interpretation of Islamic law, or Sharia. As a result, little to no information about the execution or the fate of the bodies is provided.
Is the Iran war affecting Saudi domestic repression?
Following the US-Israeli attacks on Iran in February, Saudi Arabia has been targeted by Iran and the Iran-aligned Houthi group in Yemen. In turn, Saudi Arabia's de facto leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, is faced with a profound dilemma as the attacks have killed and injured scores of people and threaten Riyadh's efforts to diversify its economy under the Vision 2030 reform plan. Several summits and international sports events had to be canceled or postponed in light of the ongoing danger.
"The Saudi government has shown itself to be unable to defend its population from repeated Houthi attacks on its airports, exposing the vulnerability of the country despite world-record spending levels on defense equipment," Sarah Leah Whitson, human rights lawyer and former executive director of the US-based human rights watchdog DAWN, told DW. "Amid the war in Iran, the Saudi government has resumed its relentless pace of executions and corporal punishment sentences," she said.
This week, watchdogs reported on a Kenyan woman in Saudi Arabia who was sentenced to 100 lashes for giving birth outside marriage.
"The recent executions and the sentencing of a migrant domestic worker to 100 lashes for having a child out of wedlock are clear indications that the Saudi government continues to rely on brute repression to rule the country," Whitson told DW.
Saudi Arabia's repression against the Shia minority
Maryam Aldossari, acting director of the London-based human rights organization ALQST, echoes this view. "Saudi Arabian authorities have undoubtedly used the war in Iran and wider regional tensions to intensify their crackdown, most notably through their increased use of the death penalty and as a tool of political repression against the country's Shia minority," she told DW.
Saudi Arabia is predominantly Sunni. The country's oil-rich Eastern Province — from which the recently executed men Jawad Abdullah Qureiris and Fadel Hassan al-Safwani hailed — is home to most of Saudi Arabia's Shia minority. Iran, on the other hand, is predominantly Shia. Saudi authorities have long viewed some forms of Shia political activism with suspicion, partly because of concerns over Iranian influence and alleged links between domestic dissent and Tehran, accusations that rights groups say have been used to justify repression of the minority.
However, Neil Quilliam, associate fellow in the Middle East and North Africa Programme at the London-based think tank Chatham House, remains cautious about drawing a direct causal connection between the conflict involving Iran and developments in Saudi Arabia's human rights environment. "The kingdom has introduced social reforms over the past decade, including measures that have expanded opportunities for women, while retaining controls over political dissent and activism," he told DW.
"What periods of regional tension can do is heighten official concern about national security," he said, adding that this reduces tolerance for any public criticism or perceived threats to social cohesion. "Whether that amounts to a change in the human rights situation is harder to demonstrate, but there is certainly a sense among some observers that space for dissent has become even more constrained, not only in Saudi Arabia, but in other Gulf states too," he said.
DW reached out to Saudi Arabia's Human Rights Commission on Monday, November, 16, 2026 but has not received an answer at the time of publication.

title: How does Euro 2028 qualifying work? Confirmed pots, format, and rules for co-hosts
text:
Co-hosted on home soil by England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland, the road to Euro 2028 is fast approaching as the draw for qualifying takes place in Belfast in early December.
But the four co-hosts will enter qualifying for the tournament as normal, even though there is a ‘safety net’ that can be used by two of the teams should they fail to qualify automatically.
The United Kingdom hosted some games during the Covid-delayed Euro 2020 tournament in 2021, although many matches were played with limited capacities due to Covid restrictions.
Wembley hosted the final and will do so again in 2028, with Cardiff, Glasgow, Dublin, Birmingham, Liverpool, Manchester, Newcastle also staging games during the 24-team tournament.
Here’s everything you need to know ahead of the Euro 2028 qualifying draw, which takes place in Northern Ireland on Sunday 6 December.
Confirmed Euro 2028 qualifying pots
- Pot 1: Belgium, Croatia, Denmark, England (co-host), France, Germany, Greece, Italy, Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, Spain
- Pot 2: Austria, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Czech Republic, Hungary, Northern Ireland, Republic of Ireland (co-host), Serbia, Slovenia, Sweden, Switzerland, Turkey, Wales (co-host)
- Pot 3: Albania, Georgia, Iceland, Israel, Kosovo, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Poland, Romania, Scotland (co-host) Slovakia, Ukraine
- Pot 4: Armenia, Belarus, Bulgaria, Cyprus, Estonia, Faroe Islands, Finland, Kazakhstan, Latvia, Luxembourg, Moldova, San Marino
- Pot 5: Andorra, Azerbaijan, Gibraltar, Liechtenstein, Lithuania, Malta
How does Euro 2028 qualifying work?
- The 54 competing Uefa teams will be drawn into 12 groups; Groups A-F are groups of four, while Groups G-L are groups of five
- Teams competing in the Nations League quarter-finals or Nations League promotion/relegation play-offs will be treated differently in the draw
- Nations League quarter-final winners will be placed into groups of four, while groups of five can only feature one Nations League quarter-final loser, or a play-off team
- The 12 group winners will qualify automatically, followed by the eight best-ranked runners-up based on qualifying results
- As many as four additional places could be up for grabs in the qualifying play-offs, but that could go down to two if two of the co-hosts fail to qualify automatically
- The draw for the Nations League quarter-finals and Nations League play-offs will take place on Friday and will have an impact on the Euro 2028 qualifying draw
What teams are still involved in the Nations League?
Nations League quarter-finals
- Group winners: France, Germany, England, Portugal
- Group runners-up: Belgium, Netherlands, Spain, Norway
Nations League play-offs: League A/B
- League A third/fourth place: Croatia, Denmark, Serbia, Wales
- League B runners-up: Slovenia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Republic of Ireland, Hungary
Nations League play-offs: League B/C
- League B fourth place: North Macedonia, Romania, Israel, Georgia
- League C runner-up: Belarus, Cyprus, Faroe Islands, Estonia
What are the rules for the co-hosts?
Unlike previous major tournaments held in multiple countries, England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland do not qualify automatically just because they are co-hosts. Although this is a tournament for the UK and Ireland, Northern Ireland are not considered co-hosts, as they are not staging any games.
But while England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland all enter qualifying as usual, there are two reserved places to be used by co-hosts if they fail to qualify automatically, either by winning their group or finishing as one of the eight-best runners-up.
The four co-hosts, as well as Northern Ireland for that matter, will all be kept apart in the qualifying draw to boost their qualification chances, so if they all go on to their win their groups then happy days – the safety net is not required.
But if disaster strikes and three or more of the co-hosts fail to qualify on merit, then there are just the two reserved places to fall back on: they will go to the two teams who have the best record in qualifying and the others will have to watch on.
