When is the draw and when does qualifying take place?
The Euro 2028 qualifying draw takes place in Belfast on Sunday 6 December. Qualifying then begins in March 2027, but only for the teams not involved in the Nations League quarter-finals or Nations League play-offs who were drawn into Groups G-L. Within those groups of five, the four other teams will play against each other across March and June 2027, with everyone else then beginning their qualifying campaign from September 2027.
- Matchday 1: 26–27 March 2027 (groups of five only)
- Matchday 2: 29–30 March 2027 (groups of five only)
- Matchday 3: 11–12 June 2027 (groups of five only)
- Matchday 4: 14–15 June 2027 (groups of five only)
- Matchday 5: 23–25 September 2027
- Matchday 6: 26–28 September 2027
- Matchday 7: 30 September – 2 October 2027
- Matchday 8: 3–5 October 2027
- Matchday 9: 11–13 November 2027
- Matchday 10: 14–16 November 2027

title: Dead Melbourne Cup racehorse found dumped in Sydney waste facility
text:
REC Equine Specialists said So You Are had been euthanised before being collected by a "contracted provider" and taken to a "licensed landfill." The practice has apologised and said the horse should have been "promptly and respectfully buried."
A dead Australian racehorse has been found dumped in an industrial waste facility in Sydney, two weeks after finishing eighth in the prestigious Melbourne Cup.
The body of So You Are was found by a member of the public, who posted a video of the discovery on social media.
"That can't be normal. Does anyone know if that's legal?" Gregg Jowett said in the footage. "I'm disgusted by that."
Trainer Bjorn Baker announced on Monday that the thoroughbred had died following a "severe bout of colic."
"He was rushed to a specialist equine hospital for emergency veterinary treatment, but sadly could not be saved."
Baker posted a later statement saying he was "deeply distressed by the handling of So You Are's remains."
"He was a much-loved horse, and he deserved to be treated with dignity and respect after his death," he said, adding that he understood that the REC Equine Specialists veterinary practice had launched an investigation into the incident.
REC has apologised for the "distress" caused by the footage and said So You Are should have been "promptly and respectfully buried."
The practice said the horse had been euthanised under anaesthesia before being collected by a "contracted provider" and taken to a "licensed landfill."
"What happened was unacceptable and disrespectful to So You Are and to everyone who cared for him. We are deeply sorry," it added.
The company said it had stopped using the provider "effective immediately."
Racing NSW, the regulating body in the state of New South Wales, said that under NSW Department of Primary Industries guidelines, "a licensed landfill is the preferred option for animals who have died via euthanasia due to the chemicals involved in the process," per Australian media.
It added that a process was now underway to "determine what steps can be taken to ensure this cannot happen again."

title: US carries out self-defense strike on IRGC missile launch site on Qeshm Island
text:
American fighter aircraft carried out a self-defense airstrike on an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) missile launch site on Qeshm Island, Iran, on Tuesday, two U.S. military officials confirmed to Fox News.
"Earlier today, U.S. fighter aircraft used precision munitions to strike an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) missile launch site on Qeshm Island in self-defense.
"The strike was in response to IRGC aggression targeting U.S. personnel and assets. U.S. Central Command remains highly vigilant and fully postured to protect Americans across the region," an official said in a statement.
The strikes came hours after Tehran claimed it targeted a U.S. radar system at the Sheikh Isa base in Bahrain.
In a statement, the IRGC claimed its operation was in response to violations of Iran's airspace by U.S. drones and said the action was taken to counter "hostile U.S. movements in the region," according to the semi-official, state-sponsored Mehr News Agency.
CENTCOM said later the Iranian attack drones were all intercepted.
"Multiple Iranian one-way attack drones launched by the IRGC today towards Bahrain were intercepted without any damage to U.S. equipment or injury to American personnel," the command said in a post shared on X.
Qatar also went on to condemn Iran's ongoing attacks on Bahrain on Tuesday, calling them a violation of Bahraini sovereignty.
"The Ministry underscores that the continuation of these attacks constitutes a grave escalation that threatens regional security and stability and undermines diplomatic efforts aimed at easing tensions," it said in a statement on X.
Qatar also described the Iranian attacks as a "flagrant" violation of international law and the principles of good neighborliness, warning that their continuation marked a serious escalation and undermined diplomatic efforts to defuse regional tensions.
The latest attacks also followed a wave of Iranian aerial strikes repelled by Bahrain on Sunday, during which the IRGC claimed to have targeted a radar system at the Al-Riffa helicopter base with another six drones.
This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

title: Can the U.S. regain its measles elimination status? Here's what to know
text: The U.S. has lost its measles-elimination status for the first time in 26 years, an international health organization determined Tuesday. With more than 5,400 cases and six deaths reported in 2026 so far, the status loss is an indication that measles spread in the U.S. is now considered endemic. Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. When measles is considered "eliminated" in a country, that doesn't mean there are zero measles cases. It measures whether there are large outbreaks or continuous transmission for 12 months or more. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has reported 43 outbreaks, which it defines as three or more related cases, this year. WATCH: What's behind the growing measles outbreak and how the Trump administration is responding "For most citizens of the United States, the loss of that formal status probably doesn't have much meaning," said William Moss, epidemiology professor at Johns Hopkins University. "What is much more important for citizens of the United States is that there are a lot of measles, so people are at risk of acquiring measles." Aubree Gordon, an infectious disease epidemiologist at the University of Michigan, agreed. Beyond the loss of the designation itself, "we are losing ground against a disease that we know how to prevent," she said. "While the loss of elimination status has no formal penalties, it represents a reversal of decades of public health progress." Watch the PBS News Hour segment in the player above. Measles in the U.S. was first declared eliminated in 2000 by an independent commission of experts from the Pan American Health Organization, PAHO, when the country recorded 85 cases. The major public health accomplishment was "made possible by widespread vaccination," Gordon said. Two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, or MMR vaccine, are 97% effective at preventing measles, according to the CDC. PAHO met from Nov. 10 to 13 to vote on the United States' and other countries' statuses. Bolivia and Mexico also lost their measles elimination status on Tuesday. Canada lost its measles status last year, as part of a 2025 review that found the Americas had lost its status. "This marks a historic setback for the Americas, which had previously been the first region in the world to eliminate measles twice," the group's report said. The loss of the elimination status for the U.S. doesn't come as a surprise. Measles cases have been rising since 2025 as vaccination rates among kindergarteners have dropped while non-medical vaccine exemptions have risen. WATCH: 'It's close to bulletproof,' doctor says of MMR vaccine as measles cases rise "This is a natural consequence of being unable to mount an effective response to growing misinformation and disinformation related to the MMR and other vaccines," said Amira Roess, professor of global health and epidemiology at George Mason University. Here's what to know about the measles and the United States' elimination status. What is measles and how can you prevent it? The measles is a preventable, highly contagious virus that spreads through the air. It can cause a fever, rash, dry cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes. For many people, the disease will last about 10 days and doesn't cause further problems. But for people who are unvaccinated, including infants and people whose immune systems are weakened, the disease can be serious. Some people can develop pneumonia and encephalitis, which can lead to death. READ MORE: Babies too young for MMR vaccine become 'sitting ducks' in measles outbreaks The virus can also damage the immune system's memory of previous infections, Gordon said. This can leave "people more susceptible to other illnesses for months to years after they recover from measles." People who are pregnant are also at high risk, and they can pass the virus on to their baby. A preliminary analysis published in The New England Journal of Medicine Evidence found that from Jan. 1, 2025, to Sept. 28, 2026, there were 112 confirmed cases of measles during pregnancy, and 13 cases of congenital measles — when the disease is passed to the child during pregnancy. WATCH: Pennsylvania doctor urges vaccination as measles outbreak grows The best way to prevent measles is through vaccination, according to the CDC. Watch the PBS News Hour segment in the player above. People should pay attention to public health alerts about measles cases, particularly if they are immunocompromised or care for someone who is, Roess said. Those who think they may have measles should contact their doctor before going into a healthcare facility to prevent exposing others, Gordon said. Why did the U.S. lose its elimination status? Fewer people being vaccinated is at the core of the increase in measles cases in the U.S., experts told PBS News. "Measles is extraordinarily contagious, so even relatively small gaps in population immunity can allow substantial outbreaks," Gordon said. WATCH: Measles cases surged in 2025 as vaccination rates dropped Moss compared measles outbreaks to wildfires. When a forest fire starts, it produces sparks that land outside of the area where the fire started. In measles cases, the sparks are people who are infected. In places with a high coverage of vaccinated people, the sparks are unlikely to lead to an outbreak. But if people who have measles are in or travel to an area that doesn't have enough vaccinated people, it is likely to spread quickly. READ MORE: A parent's guide to preventing measles infection and what to look for This is particularly dangerous for the immunocompromised people living in those communities. "In communities where everyone who can get the measles vaccine gets it, immune compromised individuals are protected," Roess said. "But those who are immunocompromised and who have the bad luck of coming into close contact with an infected individual could have a very bad outcome." Watch the PBS News Hour segment in the player above. Lower vaccination rates are in part a result of increased vaccine hesitancy due to ongoing misinformation about the risk of vaccines, Moss said. That includes the MMR vaccine, which has been used safely and effectively since 1971. Despite some statements in support of the measles vaccine, including during a 2025 outbreak in Texas, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., has undermined vaccination, including falsely linking vaccines to the debunked idea that they increase the risk of autism in children. As part of a broader push to reduce the number of childhood vaccines, President Donald Trump has called for the U.S. to separate the MMR vaccine into three different shots, despite individual shots not being available and consensus by scientific and medical communities that such a move would have no real benefit. READ MORE: 12 ways RFK Jr. has undercut vaccine confidence as health secretary Kennedy and other health officials have argued that declining vaccination rates predate the Trump administration. CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz said in a statement Tuesday that "the measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does." "We know where transmission is occurring and we've invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach those communities," she added. "Losing a designation doesn't mean we abandon an evidence-based approach. It means we remain focused on stopping outbreaks," she added. A lack of access to healthcare also plays a role in the status loss, Roess said. When people get diagnosed with measles, public health systems have to react. Local health departments launch outbreak investigations to identify close contact and implement quarantines for people who are infected or have been exposed. This requires people to seek medical care if they're infected and public health departments to be well-funded. "Losing our elimination status signals that we have an inadequate public health infrastructure," Roess said. "Our public health system has been under-resourced for quite some time." Can the U.S. regain its elimination status? The U.S. can regain its elimination status once it is able to prove that it can contain outbreaks and the virus isn't circulating in the population. Brazil, for example, lost its status in 2019 before regaining it in 2024 "following extensive vaccination, surveillance and outbreak response efforts," according to PAHO. Dr. Daniel Salas, executive manager of PAHO's Special Program for Comprehensive Immunization, said the U.S. and other countries that lost their elimination status are expected to present corrective plans outlining the strategies they will take to regain that status. To do that, the U.S. needs to increase its vaccine coverage, identify cases quickly, track people who have been in contact with infected patients and respond rapidly to outbreaks, Gordon said. "It is definitely achievable," she said. "We eliminated measles before and the same tools will work to do it again." WATCH: Man whose blood helped develop measles vaccine weighs in on recent outbreak Watch the PBS News Hour segment in the player above. Roess said requiring vaccines for children entering schools is key to protecting communities from measles. "The key is to make this required with very few exemptions," she said. Moss said that, while it's impossible to predict when or if the U.S. will regain the status, he would expect it to take around five years and a different presidential administration. He said the Trump administration's undermining of vaccines counteracts the efforts needed to regain measles elimination status. "I don't see them completely turning around and giving the messaging and support that we would need to regain elimination status in the next two years," he said. "It would take a new administration and a real focus on clear messaging about the value of vaccines and the measles vaccine in particular."

title: U.S. officially loses measles elimination status amid ongoing outbreaks
text:
The U.S. on Tuesday lost its official designation as a measles-free nation, more than 25 years after it eliminated the highly contagious virus.
The Pan American Health Organization announced the decision, which came after an independent panel of eight scientific experts convened last week to consider the country's epidemiological evidence. The director of PAHO, the regional branch of the World Health Organization, made the final call that measles is endemic — or always present — in the U.S. following 12 months of continuous transmission.
In other words, measles is spreading regularly in the country again, with ongoing outbreaks sparking new ones.
"The commission concluded that endemic measles transmission has now been reestablished in Bolivia, Mexico and the United States, and recommended that their measles elimination status be withdrawn — a recommendation which I have accepted," Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, PAHO director, said during a news briefing on Tuesday.
It's a devastating step backward for American public health, as declining childhood vaccination rates and vaccine hesitancy fuel outbreaks across the country that have sickened thousands of people and led to a tragic string of preventable deaths. Among the deaths where vaccination status was reported, all were unvaccinated.
More than 5,400 measles cases had been reported nationwide in 2026 as of mid-November, marking the country's worst outbreak in more than three decades. States have confirmed 10 deaths associated with the disease so far in 2026: seven in Pennsylvania, one in New York and two in Wisconsin.
The commission found that out of 52 U.S. states and territories it tracked, 48 experienced measles outbreaks during the reporting period between January 2025 and January 2026, PAHO Assistant Director Dr. Rhonda Sealey-Thomas said during the briefing. But Barbosa said the countries are already taking action to control outbreaks, such as strengthening vaccination, surveillance for timely case detection and outbreak response efforts.
The U.S. in particular has ramped up vaccination efforts to close immunity gaps, particularly in areas with low immunization coverage experiencing outbreaks, said Dr. Daniel Salas, executive manager of PAHO's Special Program for Comprehensive Immunization. He said PAHO expects the U.S. to present its corrective action plan in the coming weeks, outlining strategies to regain its designation.
In a Tuesday release, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said it will continue to ensure all communities have the resources to prevent and respond to outbreaks and is committed to working with states and other local partners to restore the U.S.'s measles elimination status.
CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz said in the release that the measles elimination designation "is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does." She said the agency has invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach communities where transmission is occurring.
Last week, Schwartz told Reuters that the agency is going to be "doing the same exact thing that we've been doing today" if the U.S. loses its measles-free status.
The decision also poses a new test for the Trump administration and its Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has taken steps to change recommendations for the childhood measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine and has a long history of questioning its safety without evidence.
But Kennedy, in a Tuesday X post, said he continues to recommend MMR vaccination as "the most effective way to prevent measles."
"We are working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust," Kennedy said. "We will answer families' questions honestly about vaccine benefits and risks and work with trusted health care providers and community leaders to prevent measles, limit its spread, and support timely treatment."
CNBC previously reported on how the return of measles in the U.S. exposes weaknesses in the nation's public health system that raise concerns about the return of other eliminated diseases. The resurgence of measles exposes eroding trust in health institutions and growing challenges in persuading people to protect themselves, their children and their communities.
Public health experts previously told CNBC that the return of measles ultimately boils down to fewer children getting vaccinated.
The MMR vaccine is about 97% effective against measles after two doses, while a single dose is 93% effective, according to the CDC. Yet data aggregated by the CDC shows that vaccination coverage for that shot among U.S. kindergarteners fell to 92.4% in the 2025-2026 school year, which is below the 95% threshold public health officials generally recommend to prevent sustained transmission.
The American Medical Association urged the public to get vaccinated after PAHO's announcement.
"We must treat the current measles outbreaks as an urgent call to rebuild trust in science-based recommendations and restore strong, fully-funded public health infrastructure to protect families and communities and prevent the return of diseases once eliminated," AMA President Dr. Willie Underwood said in a statement.
In a separate statement, the pharmaceutical industry's largest lobbying group called on policymakers to provide "clear, accurate information about the seriousness of measles infection and the effectiveness of vaccines against it, restore and sustain high vaccination coverage in every community, strengthen vaccination efforts, and invest in disease surveillance and rapid outbreak response."
"We have the tools to eliminate measles again and what we need now is the commitment to use them," said Dr. Michael Ybarra, chief medical officer of the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America.
Measles isn't just a public health threat — it's also a huge financial burden on the healthcare system, CNBC reported.
Based on this year's case count, a new tool developed by researchers at Johns Hopkins University estimates an economic cost of nearly $83 million for the outbreaks. That total includes $56 million in public health response costs, almost $25 million in lost productivity and more than $1.8 million in direct medical expenses.
The U.S. now joins Canada, Spain and the U.K., which all recently lost their measles-free status after a review by experts at the World Health Organization. While the U.S. dropped out of the WHO, it remains a member of PAHO, its Americas branch.

title: Google joins the tech outage trend by announcing it’s not having one
text:
Was Google feeling a little left out of the recent wave of tech outages? The company took to X on Tuesday to announce that its Gmail service is actually running just fine. In a post, the company said it was not currently seeing evidence of a broad Gmail service disruption and reminded users they could always check Gmail’s real-time status on its online dashboard.
As it turns out, the company was trying to head off reports of a Gmail outage that began circulating on X on Tuesday around the same time that Apple was seeing a number of verified outages of its own. While some posts on the social network suggested Gmail was experiencing a disruption, others said they were not having any problems.
The concerns seemed to stem from an X post by Downdetector, a crowdsourced website where users can report service disruptions themselves and see if others are having problems. Downdetector is not an official source for verifying or understanding the true scope of internet outages, and as people become more concerned about possible cyberattacks, the site’s data may become less valuable over time if every minor glitch and hiccup is reported as an “outage” by non-technical users.
The fact that Google had to announce it was not having an outage speaks to the growing anxiety around the reliability of major tech services. Over the past week, Apple and Microsoft experienced outages, an FAA network failure led to a nationwide ground stop, and some banks and airlines also reported disruptions.
However, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said on Fox Business Network’s “The Claman Countdown” on Tuesday that the U.S. is not currently facing coordinated cyberattacks. He told the outlet, “We do not see the indicia of a coordinated cyberattack — let me just be clear about that — and we do not see the indicia of state-sponsored activity here.”
Instead, Clayton attributed the rise in issues to businesses patching their systems. The patching may be a downstream effect of AI, as newer models have become increasingly adept at uncovering previously unknown vulnerabilities. “They’re upgrading them, they’re putting patches in place,” he said, adding that this is happening at “a much larger scale” than before.
As a result, some of the systems are “not coming back as expected in all cases,” he added.

title: Civilization studio Firaxis Games lays off a third of staff
text:
Firaxis Games, the studio behind the Civilization and XCOM franchises of computer strategy games, last week laid off about a third of its staff, totaling around 60 people. That’s according to a recent report in Bloomberg.
The report cites people “familiar with the cuts,” saying that the flagship game the studio is currently working on, a new entry in the XCOM series, “has faced development struggles and missed a significant milestone.” The departures also include the studio head, Heather Hazen.
A Firaxis spokesperson released the following statement:
Firaxis is restructuring and recentering around the studio’s core strength—designing world class strategy games that have set the industry standard for the genre for the last 30 years. As part of these changes, the size of the studio is being reduced to focus on design, technology and the player experience, which means saying goodbye to talented colleagues who helped build Firaxis. These decisions are never easy, but they’re essential to build the next chapter of Firaxis.
The storied studio has had a rough run of things of late. Its most recent game, Civilization VII, launched to solid enough sales but divided players in terms of reception. Players have long criticized new Civilization titles for being barebones compared to immediate predecessors that have seen multiple post-launch updates and expansions, but the response was sharper this time.

title: A mysterious twist in the universe’s oldest light could reveal new physics
text:
Scientists have spotted hints of a mysterious rotation in the universe’s oldest light that could reveal new physics and shed light on dark matter and dark energy. A new technique developed at UC San Diego could help rule out misleading telescope errors, bringing researchers closer to determining whether the strange signal is real.
A mysterious twist in the universe's oldest light could offer clues to physics that scientists have yet to discover. But before researchers can determine whether this subtle signal reveals something extraordinary about the cosmos, they must answer a crucial question: Is the effect actually coming from the universe, or could it be an illusion created by the telescopes observing it?
The mystery centers on the cosmic microwave background (CMB), a faint glow of radiation left over from approximately 380,000 years after the Big Bang. This ancient light provides a remarkable snapshot of the "baby universe" as it existed nearly 13.8 billion years ago, allowing scientists to investigate conditions from the earliest stages of cosmic history.
When the universe was about 380,000 years old, it had cooled enough to become transparent, allowing light to travel freely through space. As radiation scattered off free electrons during this transition, it acquired a small amount of linear polarization. Polarization describes the direction in which light's electric field oscillates, and a similar effect occurs when sunlight scatters through Earth's atmosphere.
Now, observations suggest that the polarization of this ancient radiation may have shifted slightly as the light traveled across the universe. This possible rotation, called cosmic birefringence, is especially intriguing because it could point to physical processes not explained by the Standard Model, the leading theory describing fundamental particles and their interactions. Confirming the effect might even provide new insights into dark matter and dark energy (see Sidebar).
A Mysterious Cosmic Signal or a Telescope Error?
There is a major obstacle to interpreting this potential discovery. An extremely small error in how a telescope's polarization detectors are aligned can produce a signal that looks almost identical to cosmic birefringence.
To help address this problem, physicists at the University of California San Diego developed a new technique for checking how accurately different groups of detectors measure polarization angles. They tested their approach using existing observations collected by the European Space Agency's Planck satellite, which mapped the universe's ancient radiation in extraordinary detail.
The research was led by Postdoctoral Fellow Anto I. Lonappan, Chancellor's Distinguished Professor of Physics Brian Keating, and Associate Professor of Physics Kam Arnold. Their findings were published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.
Separating Real Cosmic Effects From Instrument Errors
Previous studies have suggested that the polarization of the CMB may have rotated by just a fraction of a degree over its nearly 14 billion years of travel. Although that sounds insignificant, such a tiny change could have enormous implications for fundamental physics.
Unfortunately, a telescope whose polarization detectors are misaligned by a similarly small angle could produce precisely the same apparent rotation. If every detector shares the same alignment error, the resulting measurements cannot distinguish that error from a genuine rotation of the cosmic signal.
The UC San Diego researchers found a way to investigate the problem from another angle. Rather than relying on a single combined measurement, they compared separate polarization maps generated by different groups of detectors.
If cosmic birefringence is real, its effect should appear consistently across all these maps. By comparing the maps with one another, the researchers can effectively eliminate any rotation shared by all of them. What remains reveals differences in the calibration of the individual detector groups, making it possible to identify inconsistencies that might otherwise complicate the search for new physics.
"The signal we are looking for is incredibly small, so we have to be certain that we are seeing the universe and not our instrument," said Lonappan. "Our method gives us a complementary way to check that distinction. Before interpreting a tiny rotation as new physics, we want to know that the calibration itself can be trusted."
Testing the Mystery With Planck Satellite Data
To evaluate their technique, the researchers analyzed eight polarization maps produced using Planck observations. They then compared their findings with results from an established approach called the Minami-Komatsu analysis, which is used to distinguish instrumental rotation from possible cosmic birefringence.
Although the two methods rely on different assumptions, they produced consistent results. This agreement provides an important independent check on how relative detector calibration errors are being assessed.
The new approach also has a deliberate limitation. Because it removes any rotation common to all the maps, it cannot independently measure the overall polarization angle or determine how much the universe itself may have rotated the light. Establishing that absolute rotation still requires an independent reference for calibrating the overall angle.
To demonstrate how their findings fit with existing measurements, the researchers combined their reconstruction of relative calibration differences with the common calibration value inferred from the established analysis. This produced an estimated cosmic birefringence angle of 0.37 ± 0.12 degrees, matching the Minami-Komatsu result.
Importantly, this agreement does not independently confirm that the ancient light has actually rotated. Instead, it shows that the new method can reproduce results from the existing framework while providing a separate way to examine potential calibration problems.
Searching for Gravitational Waves From the Early Universe
The technique could also play an important role in another major pursuit in cosmology: the search for gravitational waves generated during the universe's earliest moments.
To understand why, scientists distinguish between two patterns of polarization in the cosmic microwave background, known as E modes and B modes.
E modes were first detected in 2002. They arise from density variations in the early universe and form symmetric polarization patterns. B modes have a different appearance, featuring patterns that resemble curls or swirls.
One known source of B modes is gravitational lensing, which occurs when the gravity of matter between Earth and the early universe bends and distorts the path of ancient light. Scientists have already observed B modes created through this process.
However, researchers are also searching for a different kind of B mode that could have been produced by primordial gravitational waves. These ripples in spacetime may have originated during an extremely early period of rapid cosmic expansion, known as inflation. The distinctive B mode signal associated with those primordial gravitational waves has not yet been detected.
Finding it would provide powerful evidence about gravitational waves in the early universe and could offer strong support for particular models of cosmic inflation, potentially transforming scientists' understanding of how the universe began.
Why Extremely Precise Measurements Matter
The challenge is that even a slight error in a telescope's polarization calibration can cause some of the much stronger E-mode signal to appear incorrectly as B modes. This contamination could make an instrumental artifact look like an exciting cosmological discovery.
The UC San Diego method could help prevent such mistakes by identifying differences in polarization angle calibration among detector groups. That makes it a potentially valuable tool for future experiments searching for the extremely faint signatures of primordial gravitational waves.
This kind of independent verification will become increasingly important as observatories develop the ability to measure cosmic polarization with greater precision. One example is the Simons Observatory, where Keating serves as principal investigator.
As these instruments become more sensitive, researchers will need equally rigorous methods for confirming that the faint signals they detect are genuine features of the universe rather than imperfections in their equipment.
"The detection of primordial B modes would transform our understanding of the early universe, so the measurement must survive rigorous calibration checks," said Keating. "Anto has developed a useful new framework for testing relative polarization-angle calibration. This is ultimately about knowing when we can trust a measurement."
Beyond the Standard Model: Dark Matter and Dark Energy
The possibility of cosmic birefringence is particularly fascinating because it could reveal physics that lies beyond the Standard Model.
Although this framework has been remarkably successful at describing fundamental particles and their interactions, it cannot explain everything in the universe. Among its most important unanswered questions are the identity of dark matter and the origin and observed magnitude of dark energy. Together, these mysterious components account for approximately 95% of the universe's total energy density.
One possible explanation for cosmic birefringence involves a hypothetical field associated with particles resembling axions. Such a field could interact with light and gradually alter its polarization as it crosses the universe. However, these particles have not been confirmed to exist, and they would not necessarily be responsible for dark matter.
Other theoretical explanations connect the possible rotation to fields associated with dark energy, the mysterious phenomenon linked to the accelerating expansion of the universe.
If cosmic birefringence is eventually confirmed, it could provide an entirely new way to investigate these cosmic mysteries and reveal evidence of physical laws beyond those currently understood.
For now, the first challenge is ensuring that the subtle signal can be trusted. By giving researchers another way to identify potential measurement errors, the new technique strengthens the foundation for future discoveries that could reshape our picture of the universe.

title: We know how to stop computer worms. But what if AI helps them persist?
text:
AI is already powering new, more adaptable forms of cyberattack, but hackers typically wield the technology from afar. What if they set the AI models themselves loose to self-replicate and spread in a malicious manner?
Recent experiments have demonstrated two different ways this could happen. Two independent teams showed how a cyberattacker could turn an AI model into a “worm,” a type of malware that, unlike a computer virus, spreads on its own. And AI unlocked a new worm power: adapting attacks to different devices.
The results hint at a new way AI could be used to ramp up cybersecurity threats — not just to computer systems but to smart devices such as security cameras or refrigerators. The good news is that the world still has time to build up defenses as several obstacles remain before this type of malware would work in the real world, says AI researcher Jonas Guan.
AI could indeed make a worm “much harder to stop,” he says, but “there are a lot of kinks to iron out before something like this really works at scale.”
Morphing simple worms into shrewd attackers
Here is how a worm cyberattack works. A malware worm squirms through the internet, copying itself onto whatever systems it can hijack. Hackers can then mine hijacked systems directly for their data or link them together into a botnet and use its computing power, often to send spam email or overwhelm websites with traffic, knocking them offline.
Historically, computer worms have been small, simple programs preprogrammed to take advantage of specific security weaknesses. So they could only get into devices that had that weakness. When defenders patched a worm’s target, it could no longer spread. With an AI model directing its actions, however, a worm can adapt and learn on the fly, choosing its line of attack depending on the device, says Guan, of the University of Toronto.
That adaptability enables the worm to burrow into many different types of devices, both experiments showed. When hackers unleash AI from afar, they orchestrate what the model does. An AI worm that copies itself widely could hypothetically escape anyone’s control.
Still, there’s a caveat to the experiments’ results, says Michael Alexander Riegler, a cybersecurity researcher at Simula Metropolitan Center for Digital Engineering in Oslo, Norway. Both teams’ test environments made it easier for the AI worm to spread than it would be in the real world, says Riegler, who was not involved in either study.
And there’s another practical obstacle to the unleashing of AI worms. They use more computing power and take up more space than a conventional worm. The Mirai worm, which took down a slew of websites including Reddit and Spotify in 2016, was a few kilobytes in size, while the medium-sized AI models in the experiments were tens of gigabytes. That’s still way smaller than the massive, top-of-the-line models behind the “rogue AI” incidents that made headlines earlier in 2026. (And those weren’t worms, because they didn’t copy themselves and spread.)
Most devices — including typical laptop computers — don’t have enough space or the right kind of chips to run worm-capable AI models, Guan says. But new versions of devices, such as security cameras, are coming out with advanced hardware for running AI, researchers at the AI company Anthropic write. And at the same time, even smaller AI models are becoming more capable of sophisticated cyberattacks. These developments could expand the pool of devices an AI worm could exploit.
“The ingredients are converging” to make AI worms more realistic, Riegler says. How quickly they will converge is up for debate. Anthropic puts the timeline at months into the future, but both Riegler and Guan say it will probably take longer.
Spreading like octopuses or slime molds
The Mirai worm spread itself through smart devices including home routers, security cameras and even baby monitors. It broke into these devices by trying a small set of common default usernames and passwords. “Just using this very simple technique, this Mirai botnet was able to infect hundreds of thousands of devices,” says cybersecurity expert Zane Ma of Oregon State University in Corvallis, who presented an analysis of the attack at a 2017 security symposium. High-profile downed sites such as Reddit were actually collateral damage: A small group of young hackers had created the worm to mess with gaming servers.
Rebooting an infected device cleared Mirai. Changing its default login credentials prevented reinfection through the same route. But an AI-powered worm might make cleaning up this type of cybersecurity breach much more difficult. Why? Because the AI worm acts more like an octopus, Guan says.
Guan and colleagues tested this octopus-worm in a virtual network. Anchored by several powerful computers that each had a chip called a graphics processing unit, or GPU, the faux networks also contained simulations of smart devices, including office printers and security cameras.
The octopus’s AI model head started on a single machine with a GPU. From there it sent out tentacles to take control of smaller devices. Upon encountering a new device, the head would use AI to plan how its tentacle could hack in. Often, a hack wouldn’t work, but the octopus wouldn’t give up. It would use info about how it failed to come up with a new hack to try. That ability is “a new, hypercharged way of attacking systems,” Riegler says. Whenever it found a computer with a large enough GPU, it would copy its head onto that new machine.
How an octopus-worm spreads
An attacker would probably launch an octopus-style AI worm from the cloud. Click through this slideshow to see how it might spread autonomously. First, it takes over and copies itself onto a device with the right kind of hardware (chip icon) to house an AI model (first image). From there, it sends out tentacles (red arrows) to hack into any connected devices, like 3-D printers and security cameras (second image). Devices that don’t have enough space for the AI model become jumping-off points for the octopus-worm to discover new places to copy itself (third image).
The head could also search a simulated internet for information about newly discovered vulnerabilities. (The team didn’t connect it to the real internet for obvious reasons — protection against an AI octopus invasion — and spent considerable effort making sure their creation couldn’t escape the lab, Guan says.)
The octopus-worm even came up with a way to survive a reboot, something Guan says they hadn’t asked it to do. The team posted a preprint of their findings at arXiv.org on June 2, and the paper is now going through peer review.
Meanwhile, at Anthropic, researchers showed another way an AI worm might work by building on Guan and his colleagues’ research. If an octopus-worm wasn’t weird enough, Anthropic dubbed its creation a “digital slime mold”, a name that captures the model’s slow, oozing behavior. Anthropic declined to comment for this story, but Guan says the company’s work shows that “unlike human reasoning, AI reasoning can be distributed.” That means an AI worm wouldn’t necessarily need to hijack a powerful computer to copy and run itself — it could spread its “thinking” out among smaller devices.
And that’s exactly what the slime mold version of an AI worm does. It breaks itself up and runs pieces of the model on multiple smaller devices. In their report posted online October 12, the Anthropic researchers used 15 Android smart TVs that they had networked together.
Anthropic’s chopped-up model processes data thousands of times more slowly than what’s possible with GPUs similar to the ones Guan and colleagues relied on. That’s because the model’s data has to travel over internet connections that could take it all around the world during processing, rather than remaining in one place, within chips optimized for AI processing. That pace was too slow to demonstrate an ability to spread like a computer worm, Guan notes. So the Anthropic team ran a separate experiment with an AI worm running on GPUs that showed it could spread and adapt its attacks to different kinds of devices.
What could stop an AI worm?
Whether AI worms are coming in months or whether we have longer to prepare, defenders should get ready now, Guan says. And AI worms do have weaknesses.
For one thing, the large size of an AI worm could be its downfall. Even if smaller AI models become more capable, these are still big programs that guzzle computing power. You might not notice if your fridge or microwave suddenly started sending lots of traffic onto the network, but your internet service provider would. They’d realize “there’s something weird going on on these devices,” Ma says. From there, they could quarantine affected devices, disconnecting them from the internet to prevent further spread.
Ma also points out that most smart devices in a person’s home aren’t directly connected to the public internet. Most home networks use a router as a central hub, and that provides a layer of protection against a worm attack.
Strong passwords, regular updates and other normal security measures would also protect against the attacks demonstrated in both experiments, Riegler says.
Guan and some colleagues are now testing specific defenses to stop AI worms, including devising an AI-driven defender. Trying to anticipate emerging threats and protect systems ahead of time is “what I’m passionate about,” Guan says. “We are working on the problem day and night.”

title: Astronomers discover rare black holes that formed when stars failed to go supernova
text:
Gravitational waves have revealed a population of black holes that may have been born when masssive stars failed to go supernova.
Most of us know the origin story of black holes, or we thought we did. Massive stars run out of the fuel for nuclear fusion and their cores collapse. As this happens, the stars' outer layers expand outwards. Shockwaves from the core collapse strike the outer layers, triggering a supernova explosion. The collapsed core creates a black hole.
However, new research based on gravitational wave data collected by LIGO (Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory) and its gravitational wave detector partners, Virgo and KAGRA (Kamioka Gravitational Wave Detector), suggests this might not be the complete picture of black hole birth. The team behind the research suggests some massive stars go out with a whimper rather than a bang and that these "failed supernovas" can also spawn black holes.
The hint of this comes from the over 300 black hole collisions spotted by LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA since the detectors first "heard" ripples in space from these distant events in 2015.
"A vast majority of the merging black holes in the universe are about 10 times the mass of our sun," LIGO team member Katerina Chatziioannou, of the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), said in a statement. "Our data are showing that this group of black holes may have a common origin — they may be a distinct subpopulation that failed to go supernova.
"These results represent a connection between the gravitational-wave data and underlying astrophysics we are trying to extract."
Mass and spin of black holes indicate stars died with a whimper not a bang
Currently, there is no hard evidence of failed supernovas, but their existence is well supported theoretically. In fact, scientists think there is a vast population of massive stars out there that imploded rather than exploded, directly collapsing into black holes. And these may be black holes with around ten times the mass of the sun (10 solar masses) found in merging pairs.
Chatziioannou led a team that examined gravitational wave data to confirm this concept. To do this, they looked at the distribution of the masses of 257 black hole mergers detected by the LIGO–Virgo–KAGRA network over the past 10 years.
This revealed a peak of 10-solar-mass black holes that represented 75% of the entire sample. If this was expected, what the team found that wasn't predicted was a lack of black holes with masses 12 to 16 times the mass of the sun.
"We see 10 solar-mass black holes merging all the time," team member Isaac Legred of the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign said. "But why are, say, 14 solar-mass black holes so rare? The gap we see in the distribution of masses indicates there may be a special cocktail of internal physics that goes into forming the abundance of 10 solar-mass black holes."
The researchers also looked at the spin rates of black holes in mergers, a telltale signature of how they formed. This revealed that 10-solar-mass black holes seemed to have a distinct range of spin speeds. This indicates a common origin, perhaps the implosion of a massive star without a supernova explosion.
"We can look up at the sky and try to study historical records of massive stars that failed to explode, but it's challenging because they just vanish without exploding, leaving a dark patch of sky," Legred concluded. "With this study, we show the gravitational-wave data are consistent with most binary black holes forming from a very special kind of failed supernova, but more research is needed.
"Black holes are born in some of the most extreme environments in the universe, so the prospect of better understanding their formation is very exciting."
The team's research was published on Tuesday (Nov. 10) in the journal Physical Review D.

title: Rooney says he considered taking his own life at Man Utd
text:
Warning: This article contains references to suicide
Wayne Rooney says he was "contemplating suicide" during his playing days at Manchester United and was "speaking to a therapist to try and figure out what was up".
The former England captain joined United from Everton in 2004 and went on to become the club's record goalscorer, with 253 goals in 559 appearances.
But Rooney, speaking with Gabby Logan on the Life at the Midpoint podcast, external, detailed his struggles off the pitch when eldest son Kai, who is now 17, was a baby.
"When I was drinking, I would lock myself in my house for two days and just drink," said Rooney, when asked about the lowest point in his life.
"This is probably in my best part of my career playing wise."
The 41-year-old went on to explain how he "struggled to deal with it all" and, after opening up to his wife Coleen and his mother, knew he "needed help to get through it".
"I can look back and say I was selfish, but I knew I was going through something which I was really struggling to deal with," he added.
"I didn't want Kai seeing me like that, so that's why I'd hide away as well.
"I got to a place where you're contemplating suicide. I just didn't want to be around anyone. I didn't want to see people in the streets. I didn't want to go into shops.
"I was always comfortable on a football pitch, but everything else, [I] really struggled with it."
Rooney, who scored 53 goals in 120 England appearances, was recently named pundit of the year at the Broadcast Sport Awards and is currently appearing on reality TV show I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here.
He helped United win five Premier League titles, the Champions League, Europa League, FA Cup and three EFL Cups before leaving them to return to the Toffees in 2017.
But the former forward said he learned to mask his feelings during his lowest moments.
"You don't want to show any weakness, so you try to mask it," Rooney added.
"Even though I knew the position I was in, it was difficult to actually admit that I was in that position because I felt like you feel less of a man, if you like, for doing that.
"I was speaking to a therapist to try and figure out what was up with me because when I look back I was probably at the height of my career, I've just had a young son, I've just been married.
"It should be the happiest point in my life and it wasn't.
"It was probably the lowest point because of the selfish acts I was taking.
"Coleen helped me massively. She could have walked away, it was that bad, but she stuck by me and helped me get through it."

title: Actors in UK to get more rights over their ‘digital replicas’ in deal on AI protections
text:
Actors in the UK are to be given more rights over their “digital replicas” as part of a new agreement on AI protections with TV and film producers, secured after a growing on-set backlash.
Under a wide-ranging new deal secured by Equity, the actors’ union, performers will have the rights to be paid when their digital replicas are used and to consent to whether their digital replica is used or not.
Approval must be secured from an actor if a digital double or digital alteration is used to make “substantive changes” to scenes involving agreed levels of nudity or simulated sexual activity.
The agreement also makes clear that producers may not use a digital replica during a strike “in any circumstance where consent is required for such use”.
Contracts will now make clear that producers only obtain permission for a specific project, rather than obtaining “blanket consent” to an actor’s digital replica.
The deal, signed after years of talks with the production body Producers Alliance for Cinema and Television (Pact), marks an attempt to create some ground rules for the use of an actor’s image, with AI developing rapidly.
The three-year deal will be put to a vote among 8,000 Equity members, with the union’s leadership recommending they approve it. It also includes a 24% increase in pay rates for major films and a 9% increase for TV projects.
It comes after Equity members voted 99% in favour of taking industrial action and refusing to be scanned on set without further AI protections, in an indicative ballot last December.
However, Equity said there were areas that a new agreement simply could not cover, such as digital scanning traditionally undertaken in production for digital effects added later.
There have been mounting concerns on set about the use of AI, which has made many actors more wary of undergoing body scans. Many fear the data could be used to train AI models on their likenesses or poses, paving the way for the technology to take away work.
Last year, the actor Olivia Williams told the Guardian that actors should have as much control over the data harvested from scans of their body as they do over nudity scenes.
The star of Dune: Prophecy and The Crown said she and other actors were regularly pressed to have their bodies scanned by banks of cameras while on set, with few guarantees about how the data would be used or where it would end up.
Equity said that “despite our efforts”, the new agreement did not establish explicit contract protections regarding the use of actors’ performances for training AI systems.
In a note to its members, Equity explained that digital replicas could be made using the same photography captured for the production itself, without the need to scan artists.
However, producers must limit access to digital replicas to people with a legitimate business need and “use commercially reasonable efforts” to protect digital replicas from unauthorised access, use or copying.
The new deal also includes a commitment to safe casting and audition spaces, as well as training and reporting on sexual harassment. Producers also have a new obligation to provide artists of all ethnicities and cultures with adequate hair and makeup provision.
Paul W Fleming, Equity’s general secretary, said: “We set about to radically improve and modernise the terms and conditions for performers across UK TV and film. The result is groundbreaking.
“We’ve achieved the best AI provisions in the business – protecting performers and ensuring that human performance is valued and prioritised across the industry.”

title: ‘Zero transparency’: Inside Trump’s plans for Venezuela’s oil money
text:
The administration of United States President Donald Trump is facing criticism over how it has handled billions of dollars in oil revenue collected from Venezuela.
Since January 3, Trump’s government has controlled Venezuela’s oil exports, gathering the revenue in an account overseen exclusively by the US Treasury.
Last week, the Department of State released a 53-page report aimed at shedding light on the account’s activities. It revealed that at least $12.11bn have passed through the account since the start of the year.
But critics say the report lacks key details about where the money came from and who it is going to.
“There’s been zero transparency on all of the financial engineering associated with how $12bn of Venezuelan oil was changing hands and being utilised,” said Tyson Slocum, the director of the energy programme at Public Citizen, a US-based consumer advocacy nonprofit.
“All we have now is a very barebones narrative of how the funds were used, but not details on what entities were involved.”
Questions of sovereignty
Concerns about Trump’s plans for Venezuela’s oil sector began late last year, when his government began seizing oil tankers leaving the South American country.
Any oil on board, Trump said, would be kept or sold by the US. He and members of his administration framed the confiscated fuel as compensation for the losses incurred when Venezuela nationalised its oil industry decades ago.
“American sweat, ingenuity and toil created the oil industry in Venezuela,” White House aide Stephen Miller said at the time. “Its tyrannical expropriation was the largest recorded theft of American wealth and property.”
Tensions between the US and Venezuela reached a tipping point on January 3, when Trump authorised a military operation to abduct Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro.
In a speech that morning, Trump highlighted the role oil had played in his decision. “We’re going to be taking out a tremendous amount of wealth out of the ground,” Trump said.
He proceeded to explain that some of the Venezuelan oil proceeds would go “to the United States of America in the form of reimbursement for the damages caused us by that country”.
Days later, Trump revealed he had spoken to oil companies “before and after” the operation. He also held a meeting with oil industry executives at the White House to discuss plans for Venezuela.
Legal experts have raised concerns that the January 3 operation was an attack on Venezuela’s sovereignty, in violation of international law.
They have also questioned the legality of seizing another country’s natural resources, given that a 1962 United Nations resolution grants nations “permanent sovereignty” over their own natural resources.
But supporters of Trump’s actions have pointed to Maduro’s history of violent repression and anti-democratic actions in Venezuela as justification for the operation.
Maduro has since been replaced by his former vice president, Delcy Rodriguez, who has largely cooperated with Trump’s demands.
But the focus on Venezuela’s oil revenue has left some critics questioning whether Trump plans to address the human rights issues in the South American country.
Trump has repeatedly downplayed the importance of democratic elections in Venezuela, said John Feeley, a former US ambassador and senior diplomat in Latin America.
“Trump has made patently clear that he has no interest in the democratic future of Venezuela,” said Feeley, calling the US-Venezuela relationship “protectorate neocolonialism”.
‘The biggest oil deal in history’
More recent manoeuvres have also raised speculation about the Trump administration’s commitment to transparency in its management of Venezuelan oil.
In late August, for instance, Trump announced his government would have a direct stake in extracting nearly a fifth of Venezuela’s oil.
Under the terms of the agreement, the US gained “majority control” in a 100-year deal for 17 Venezuelan oilfields, with proven reserves of 65 billion barrels.
North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP), a company owned by Venezuelan businessman Alejandro Betancourt, was given the rights to operate the fields.
The Pentagon, meanwhile, took a 35 percent stake in the company, and the US was guaranteed 20 percent of the oil output at cost. Trump called it “the biggest oil deal in history”.
But Betancourt has faced investigations in the US, Spain and Switzerland over accusations of money laundering.
Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado also said the contract with NABEP “evidently does not reflect the levels of transparency that Venezuelan society wants”.
Venezuela has long struggled to export its oil, so the fact that it will now be sold on the open market is beneficial to the country’s economy, said Luis A Pacheco, a former executive with Venezuela’s state oil company and nonresident fellow at the Baker Institute Center for Energy Studies at Rice University.
But Pacheco is sceptical of Trump’s deal with NABEP.
“This is an obscure outfit with no known financial sources, with very little tech wherewithal,” he said. “This so-called mega-deal, without doubt, will certainly yield very little of what’s expected of it.”
Little transparency over billions of dollars
The shroud of secrecy surrounding the Venezuelan oil deals has spurred some Democrats in the US Congress to press for greater accountability.
In September, Democrats in the House of Representatives (PDF) and Senate asked the administration to disclose what had been uncovered by KPMG, an outside accounting firm hired to audit transactions involving Venezuelan oil exports.
The State Department did issue its report last week. But key portions were redacted, including who deposited money into the accounts and who the final recipients of the funds were.
Feeley, the diplomat, said there are also questions about the total sum of the proceeds. Only $12bn is accounted for in the report.
“We have no idea how that money was used, and we have no idea what percent of the total amount of money deposited in the US Treasury that $12bn represents,” said Feeley. “But most experts allege that it is only a fraction.”
In a statement to Al Jazeera, a State Department spokesperson said its report “provides a comprehensive account, down to the cent, of the Venezuelan natural resource revenues deposited in, held by, and disbursed” from the account.
Venezuela’s requests for disbursement are checked against a “list of approved and prohibited expenditure categories”, the spokesperson added.
The funds are then used for “essential public services, macroeconomic stability, and the rebuilding of key sectors such as energy, healthcare and infrastructure”.
But who receives those funds remains unclear. Pacheco said there is no reason the US could not disclose details of the monetary flow.
“Even though this report gives you some information, it still doesn’t give you light into the most important thing, which is what is the Venezuelan regime is doing with the money,” Pacheco said.
“You can affirm with very good certainty, when you talk about billions of dollars, something is draining away.”
Pacheco also questioned the supervisory role the Trump administration has claimed over the Venezuelan government. At one point, Trump even claimed he would “run” the South American country.
“The discourse of the White House is that they exert some sort of tutelage over the Venezuelan regime,” Pacheco said. “But apparently that tutelage doesn’t go as far as to tell the Venezuelans where is the money going to.”
New Congress, new oversight?
But this year’s midterm elections could usher in a wave of oversight into the Venezuelan oil money.
Democrats won majority control in both the House and Senate in the November 3 midterm elections, and lawmakers have already floated the possibility of opening investigations, once the new Congress arrives in January.
“The admin is sending billions to Delcy Rodriguez’s corrupt government where the list of who benefits is kept murky,” Representative Joaquin Castro wrote on social media after the election.
“I will continue to demand answers, and use every tool we will have with the incoming Democratic majority, including congressional hearings, to uncover what the United States is doing in Venezuela.”
One area of exploration might be the role private oil trading companies play in the Trump administration’s deal. Firms like Vitol, a Dutch multinational energy company, could be put under the microscope.
A week before Trump sent troops into Caracas to abduct Maduro, John Addison, a senior trader with Vitol, held a secret meeting with Vice President JD Vance on a tarmac in Montana, according to the news agency Reuters.
Vitol was later able to buy oil from the state-owned Venezuelan oil company at a steep discount. Addison and his wife donated $6m to Trump’s election campaign in 2024.
Democrats on the House Oversight Committee have long been eager to investigate the dealings of firms like Vitol in Venezuela.
“Oversight Democrats will not stop until we know exactly what companies are profiting from these foreign policy decisions, especially in Venezuela,” Representative Robert Garcia said in January.
Garcia is expected to chair the oversight committee next year.

title: Right whale population drops, alarming scientists
text:
Portland, Maine — The population of one of the world's rarest whales has fallen after trending upward in recent years, worrying scientists who fear the animal could still be at risk of extinction.
The North Atlantic right whale now numbers 382 animals, according to a consortium of scientists that released its annual population estimate for them on Monday. That represents about a of 384, which was an increase of 2.1% from the previous year and showed the continuation of a prior slow but steady climb in the whales' population.
The whales were decimated by centuries of commercial whaling that mostly ended in the 1930s. The enormous animals have been slow to recover, and today are threatened by entanglement in fishing gear and collisions with ships.
Those threats, combined with , have conspired to hold the population down, said Heather Pettis, chair of the North Atlantic Right Whale Consortium. Pettis said the warming of the ocean has caused the whales' food — tiny organisms called copepods — to move, and the whales have followed them into areas of ocean not protected from ship strikes and entanglements.
"We know that this population can and will move around to find food and if we aren't protecting them throughout their range, we may see another situation where we have this tremendous decline again," Pettis said.
The whales' population fell about 25% from 2010 to 2020 during a time when years of poor reproduction coincided with high mortality. Recent years have been slightly more encouraging, but scientists and conservationists have warned that the whales need years of high birth counts coupled with new protections to have a chance to rebuild.
Stronger safeguards needed, environmental groups say
The loss in population last year underscores the need to spare the whales from entanglements and ship strikes, said Nora Ives, a marine scientist on the environmental group Oceana's right whale campaign.
Oceana was one of several environmental groups that opposed a proposal in Congress to delay new right whale protections until 2035. The proposal, which has passed the House of Representatives, is intended to protect commercial fishing interests from regulations that members of the industry describe as burdensome.
"The latest numbers are disappointing and make the road to recovery longer for critically endangered North Atlantic right whales. This iconic whale will not escape extinction if its population cannot grow," Ives said.
The right whales, which can weigh 150,000 pounds, give birth off the Carolinas, Florida and Georgia in the winter and venture north to feeding grounds off New England and Canada. Large groups of the animals that sometimes include a fifth of the entire population are sometimes seen off Massachusetts in spring. Last year was one of the most successful calving seasons on record, with more than 20 babies born.
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration has said the last nine years have also been a time of unusually high numbers of injuries and deaths for the whales. The population is down to just 73 reproductive females, which makes replenishing the stock difficult.
They were hunted heavily because they tend to live fairly close to shore and floated when killed, and they yielded a high volume of oil. Some sources say they got their common name from the perception that they were the "right" whale to hunt.

title: Pope Leo’s envoy brings message of comfort and unity to Holy Land Christians
text:
The Catholic cardinal who oversees care of the faithful in the Holy Land visited Jerusalem to convey Pope Leo XIV's presence during troubled times for Christians
JERUSALEM -- The Vatican cardinal who oversees care of the Catholic faithful in the Holy Land visited Jerusalem on Tuesday, saying he wanted to convey the presence of Pope Leo XIV during particularly troubled times for Christians in the region.
Cardinal Claudio Gugerotti, prefect of the Vatican’s Dicastery for the Eastern Churches, prayed before the Holy Edicule inside the Church of the Holy Sepulcher, which marks the site where Christians believe Jesus was buried and rose from the dead.
“Lord, you were here physically,” Gugerotti prayed. “Lord, give hope to the world.”
Leaders of other Christian denominations in Jerusalem listened intently. The incense-filled ceremony, with clergy in solemn robes, offered a show of unity in the basilica where they have sometimes tensely shared worship space in a unique arrangement dating to the 19th century.
Preceded by bagpipers, rows of Franciscan friars and a large cross, Gugerotti and other Christian leaders processed through the narrow stone alleyways of Jerusalem’s Old City to the centuries-old church.
Harassment of clergy and faithful there has been rising. A rare violent attack on a religious sister in April sent shock waves across Israel.
“We know we are not always welcome,” said Sister Marie Reine, a Catholic nun who joined the procession in her white habit. “But our presence can bring peace, too.”
Most of Israel’s Christians are Palestinians, who have been the target of heated rhetoric after Arab-led parties made historic gains in the national elections last month. And neighboring Jordan is reeling from an attack that killed nine worshippers during a service at a Greek Orthodox church.
“We pray that these days may confirm in faith and in hope our priests and religious, who serve with great fidelity in often demanding conditions; our families, who choose, day after day, to remain; and our young people, who need to know that the Church stands beside them as they seek to build a future here,” said Cardinal Pierbattista Pizzaballa, the Latin Patriarch of Jerusalem, in a statement before the visit.
A Catholic father who participated in Tuesday's procession said his children want the family to leave Jerusalem, where many Christians say tensions have grown since the war triggered by the Hamas-led attacks on Oct. 7, 2023.
“To be here is a vocation,” Andre Haddad said. “We can’t just flee our reality.”
Christians’ emigration from across the Holy Land is an intensifying concern, church and lay leaders say. Many Christians in Israel feel especially vulnerable to organized crime because they are a tiny minority and believe the state provides them little protection “because I’m another Arab,” said Wadie Abunassar, a Catholic community leader from the northern Israeli city of Haifa.
Gugerotti’s six-day visit is also scheduled to take him to Bethlehem, where he will visit the Basilica of the Nativity – where Christians believe Jesus was born – and a mosque. The town is in the occupied West Bank, where Palestinian Muslims and members of the dwindling Christian minority have denounced growing violence by Israeli settlers.
He is also planning to meet the leaders of the Greek Orthodox and Armenian churches in Jerusalem, several of whom attended Tuesday's prayers. During his first papal trip to the Middle East last fall, Leo prayed that Christians might again be united after more than 1,000 years of division between Eastern and Western churches.
Gugerotti's public schedule does not include meetings with Israeli leaders. Leo has reached out to Jewish faith leaders since the inauguration of his pontificate last year, raising hopes for a new start after a strained relationship under his predecessor. He has spoken against rising antisemitism while pleading for an end to war and displacement in Gaza.
