title: US and Mexico lose measles-free status
text:
The United States is experiencing its highest number of cases in more than three decades. Some 7,700 people in the country have been infected and 13 have died since 2025.
As of November 12, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention have confirmed 5,412 measles cases and 6 deaths. US states have reported a total of 10 deaths from the highly contagious virus this year.
Pennsylvania has been the worst-hit state, reporting seven measles-related deaths and more than 1,500 cases.
Why are measles caseloads rising despite readily available vaccines?
Tuesday's declaration by the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) has few practical implications and is largely symbolic, but is the latest sign of measles' avoidable resurgence.
"Losing measles elimination status is much more than losing a public health designation. It means the virus has circulated for a prolonged period, putting families and communities at risk of preventable illness, hospitalization and death," PAHO Director Dr. Jarbas Barbosa said.
Thanks to a series of functioning vaccines, measles had been virtually eradicated throughout most of the developed world for decades.
Vaccine hesitancy and disinformation has risen in recent years in the US, seemingly fueled at least in part by the COVID pandemic.
The rising influence of renowned vaccine critic Robert F. Kennedy Jr., now the US Health Secretary — who dropped out of the 2024 presidential election campaign to form an alliance with Donald Trump — was one of the clearest indicators of this.
"This is a serious warning for our region, but it is not an irreversible setback," PAHO Director Barbosa said. "We know how to prevent measles, and we know how to stop its transmission. With sustained commitment to vaccination, strong surveillance and effective outbreak response, the Americas can eliminate measles transmission once again."
Bolivia, Mexico, US and Canada no longer designated measles-free
As of November 13, PAHO said that the Americas region had reported 58,213 measles cases and 82 deaths, compared with 12,806 cases during the same period last year.
The organization considers endemic transmission to be re-established when the same measles virus genotype and lineage circulate uninterrupted for 12 months or more in a country.
Canada had reached this status in November 2025, with Bolivia, Mexico and the US now deemed to have joined it.
The PAHO said that Canda had "interrupted the chain of transmission" that led to its designation and was working to regain elimination status.
Meanwhile, it said the other three countries "are implementing measures to strengthen vaccination, surveillance and outbreak response."

title: Somali Uber driver strangled and run over by passenger in Minneapolis, authorities say
text:
A Somali American man who drives for Uber is clinging to life after an alleged attack by a passenger in Minneapolis, authorities say.
Mohamed Yusuf has broken ribs, a broken leg, spinal injuries, collapsed lungs and significant internal bleeding after being strangled with a seatbelt and run over by his own car early Saturday, according to court documents.
Passenger Samit Apurva Patel, 25, has been charged with attempted second-degree murder and carjacking. But prosecutors said the evidence could not prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Patel's behavior was motivated by bias.
Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty said Tuesday that “does not diminish the pain that the family and the Somali community are feeling right now.”
Online court records do not list an attorney for Patel, who is due to make his first court appearance Tuesday afternoon. A person who answered a phone number associated with Patel’s address said, “No comment,” before hanging up.
Yusuf was on the phone with his brother, who is also an Uber driver, when Yusuf picked up the passenger just before 1 a.m. Saturday. Yusuf's brother says he heard the passenger tell Yusuf he didn’t like the name Mohamed, the court document says. He later heard Yusuf screaming in Somali that he was being choked with a belt and run over by the car, according to the filing.
Moriarty said the motive remains unknown but said, “There were some serious issues going on with this gentleman at the time he went home that so alarmed his parents that they called 911.”
Patel's parents called for a wellness check after Patel arrived home appearing intoxicated and “exhibiting signs of emotional distress and belligerent behavior,” according to the court filing. When officers arrived, they found Yusuf's car in the driveway with the exterior and driver's seatbelt damaged. The phone call with Yusuf's brother was still active through the car's system, court records show.
Officers said Patel told them he had been drinking and “admitted he took an Uber home, but he claimed not to know where his Uber driver was," the filing says.
Officers found Yusuf in a patch of burs in a ditch off the side of the road using location data from his smartwatch and a drone with thermal imaging.
Uber said in a statement that it was horrified by the attack, has been in touch with the driver’s family and has banned the rider from the platform.
The incident in a Minneapolis suburb has increased fear after years of targeted rhetoric against Somali Americans, including from President Donald Trump, said Jaylani Hussein, executive director of the Minnesota chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations.
“We feel as a community we’re under threat, constantly,” Hussein said. “Our community has, unfortunately, been feeling the brunt end of a disinformation and demonization campaign that has been going on now, and it’s coming from every corner.”
Minnesota has the largest Somali population in the U.S., with a concentrated share in the Minneapolis-St. Paul area. The overwhelming majority are American citizens.
The Trump administration's largest immigration enforcement operation, Operation Metro Surge, targeted the Twin Cities. Trump has said immigrants from the war-torn East African country have “caused a lot of trouble,” and he wants them to leave. He also referred to Somali immigrants in the U.S. as “garbage.”
Hussein said dozens of community members have been stopping by the hospital to show support for Yusuf. While there's widespread fear, Hussein said, it's been particularly acute among Uber drivers.
“I also think for a lot of Uber drivers are also feeling extremely vulnerable because of the fact of the way that the incident happened," Hussein said.

title: US strikes targets in Qeshm Island after Iranian mines hit five ships in Hormuz
text:
Iran says the US military carried out several attacks on Qeshm Island in southern Iran, while at least five ships were set on fire by mines in the Strait of Hormuz earlier in the day.
Iranian officials said the US military conducted airstrikes on Qeshm Island in southern Iran on Tuesday evening, with locals reporting at least five explosions.
Ahmad Nafisi, the deputy governor of Hormozgan, told the official IRNA news agency that the US strikes did not caused damage to residential or commercial districts, adding that "the situation on Qeshm Island is under control and all relief, service and executive bodies are on full alert."
Iranian news agency IRNA reported that "the sound of five to six explosions was heard in the city of Qeshm," while the semi-official Fars news agency wrote quoting "residents of Qeshm Island" that the sound of several explosions were heard north-west of the city of Qeshm. with smoke billowing at the same time.
US officials confirmed late Tuesday that US fighter jets struck Iranian missile launch sites on the island, in the same pattern as over the previous days, in retaliation for Iran’s targeting of US personnel and assets.
The US airstrikes follow multiple incidents in the Strait of Hormuz, in which at least five ships hit naval mines while sailing through what Iran calls "unauthorised" routes in the waterway.
“Safe passage requires coordination with the Armed Forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran, transit through designated safe zones, and having navigation systems switched on,” the Iranian army announced in a statement.
Iran claims downing of US military drone
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed on Tuesday that it shot down a US MQ-1 Predator reconnaissance and combat drone in the southern waters of Iran, near Qeshm Island. According to the Guard, this would be the eighteenth drone of this type that its forces have destroyed.
The IRGC said in a statement it used a "new advanced air defence system" which allegedly tracked and destroyed this drone at 13:45 local time.
Earlier on Tuesday, the IRGC claimed said it carried out a drone attack against a US radar system at Bahrain’s Sheikh Isa Airbase. Bahrain, home to the US Navy's Fifth Fleet, and US' Central Command (CENTCOM) said that they intercepted the drones, without any damage.
The IRGC said the attack was carried out in response to "repeated violations of Iran’s airspace by US military drones".
Since the start of the Iran war in February, Tehran has tried to restrict traffic in the Strait of Hormuz and has insisted that ships pass only along routes that the Islamic Republic has authorised.

title: Senior US official undercuts CNN’s alarming Iran ‘dirty bomb’ report: ‘It’s not new’
text:
A senior U.S. official is challenging a new report on Iran developing plans for a "dirty bomb" attack on Washington, D.C., which drew a warning of overwhelming retaliation from President Donald Trump this week.
The prospect of Iranian-directed violence on American soil has shadowed U.S. security officials for decades. From a plot to bomb a Washington restaurant to assassination schemes targeting former officials and dissidents, Tehran has repeatedly sought ways to reach its enemies inside U.S. borders.
"I’m not sure why this was leaked because it’s not new," a senior U.S. official told Fox News' Jennifer Griffin in response to the report.
"Iran is very aspirational, but not suicidal. If they were to attack D.C. or any other U.S. city it would cause us to have a full out war with them. Their friends would not come to their aid."
CNN reported this week that U.S. intelligence indicated Iran was developing potential plans to target senior Trump administration officials in Washington with a radiological device or chemical weapon.
Sources described the planning as an effort to develop options rather than evidence of an imminent attack, with officials divided over whether Tehran could or would execute it.
"We’re looking into it," Trump said in Manila on Tuesday when asked about the new report.
Pressed on whether Washington faced an imminent threat, he warned: "Well, if there is, they will pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before."
"I hope it’s not, but we take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy," the president added.
White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said, "We remain vigilant monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland."
Iran could make a dirty bomb, but would need someone inside the United States with the expertise to handle the materials and carry out an attack, said Andrea Stricker, deputy director of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies’ nonproliferation program.
A dirty bomb combines conventional explosives with radioactive material, spreading contamination without producing a nuclear explosion.
U.S. authorities have spent nearly two decades building defenses against that possibility.
DHS launched its Securing the Cities program in 2007 to help local agencies detect and deter nuclear and radiological threats, including dirty bombs, beginning in the New York City region.
"Making a radiological dispersal device would be within Iran’s know-how, as well as a chemical weapon," Stricker told Fox News Digital.
Iran’s chemical weapons program dates back to the 1980s. "More recently, they've been looking at how to weaponize chemical weapons like fentanyl and disperse them through the air," Stricker said.
Fentanyl can suppress breathing to the point of respiratory arrest.
"I think for an attack using chemical weapons like this, they would probably want to go with something rudimentary. Industrial scale chemicals like chlorine would be easy to obtain," she added.
Rather than risk transporting hazardous materials into the country, Tehran could look to obtain them here, she said.
"They may want to simply try to steal them or procure them from inside the United States. That would probably ease their task," Stricker said.
But the technical demands would complicate Iran’s reliance on hired criminals to execute its operations.
"In the past, they've used sort of everyday criminals for hire to execute some of their other plots, and luckily we foiled a lot of these," she said.
Fox News’ Jennifer Griffin contributed to this report.

title: Ex-CEO Jensen Huang signals interest in returning to Nvidia after resigning amid scandal
text: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang signaled interest Tuesday in returning to lead the computer chip company in his first public statement since he resigned last week following revelations of an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy. READ MORE: Trump backs campaign to reinstate Huang as CEO of Nvidia Some tech industry figures, including SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, have called for the reinstatement of Huang, a high-profile booster for the artificial intelligence industry who oversaw Nvidia's development as the key provider of chips driving advanced AI models. President Donald Trump, a Huang ally who has spoken with him frequently, has also endorsed the comeback bid. "If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO," Huang said in a social media post. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News Huang acknowledged making "serious mistakes" in his personal life but said that he's received an "outpouring" of support from employees, investors, business partners and customers for his return. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Huang's statement. On Monday, a person familiar with the board's thinking who insisted on anonymity to discuss it told The Associated Press that the board was not currently considering Huang's return. READ MORE: The Nvidia scandal is heightening America's AI rivalry with China ahead of Trump's visit The Santa Clara, California-based company was scheduled to release quarterly earnings later Tuesday. Nvidia Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress is expected to speak with Wall Street analysts on the earnings call for the first time since being named interim CEO. A petition drive seeks Huang's return A "Stand with Jensen" petition set up last week has gathered momentum, gaining signatures from current and former Nvidia staff, investors and other Silicon Valley supporters. The petition calls on the board to bring back Huang while an independent investigation proceeds or until there's "compelling evidence" that his departure is in the company's best interests. "We are concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process," the organizers said in an open letter. "We have not been shown evidence substantiating the allegation that the woman at the center of this controversy was a spy." WATCH: Bessent accuses Lutnick of failing to prevent China from obtaining Nvidia chips Trump suggested Monday that the ex-CEO could return, saying Huang "learned a big lesson" and that he "would certainly not mind" if he was reinstated. Huang resigned last week from Nvidia, apparently ousted by the board after revelations that he had extramarital affairs, both with a Chinese businesswoman suspected of being an intelligence asset for Beijing and with a senior executive who reported to him. The businesswoman Huang was seeing who reportedly had links to Chinese intelligence was an executive at Singapore-based cloud computing firm Megaspeed International, a company being investigated by the U.S. for allegedly violating U.S. export controls by illegally diverting advanced Nvidia AI chips to Chinese companies. Huang faces questioning by Congress Also Tuesday, key House lawmakers said that Huang has voluntarily agreed to appear for transcribed interviews as the company faces intensifying national scrutiny over sales of its advanced computer chips. Huang will appear before congressional committees on Dec. 1, followed by the company's general counsel, Tim Teter, on Dec. 2. "We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security," said a statement from the chairmen of three House committees with oversight of China and intelligence issues. "The American people need answers on Mr. Huang and Nvidia's role in allowing dangerous PRC actors to access our most advanced chips, as well as the role of a potential Chinese intelligence asset in this scandal," the lawmakers said, referring to the People's Republic of China. Meanwhile, Nvidia said it's creating a new board committee to oversee national security and global trade compliance following the revelations about Huang. Nvidia's advanced chips are in high demand because they're essential for cloud computing and data centers that underpin the AI boom, but they face restrictions on their sale to China. Trump said it was "good" that Nvidia had created the new oversight committee. "Yes, that's a good idea. It's a great company," Trump said shortly after arriving Tuesday evening in the Philippine capital of Manila, where he participated in a photo opportunity with the leaders of Australia, India and Japan. "It's a great idea." Associated Press writers Darlene Superville and Kevin Freking in Washington and Josh Boak in Shenzhen, China, contributed.

title: Anthropic likely to price IPO above the current range of $70 to $78, sources tell CNBC
text:
Anthropic is likely to price its IPO above the current range of $70 to $78, multiple sources told CNBC's David Faber on Tuesday.
The artificial intelligence company is planning to close the order books and lock in total demand at 4 p.m. ET on Tuesday, according to the people, who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to speak publicly. Anthropic is slated to list on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol "ANT" and start trading on Nov. 19.
If Anthropic's IPO proceeds as planned, the company will debut roughly five months after SpaceX went public in a record offering that raised $85.7 billion. But Anthropic is facing a public market that's grown increasingly skeptical of the AI trade, as well as mounting and widespread antipathy toward the technology in the U.S.
A group of researchers, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, co-founded the company in 2021 after defecting from OpenAI, now its chief rival. Anthropic is best known for developing a family of AI models called Claude, and it underwent a period of explosive growth in 2026, driven largely by the popularity of its AI coding tool, Claude Code.
For the nine months ended Sept. 30, Anthropic said it generated $33.24 billion in revenue, up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year, according to its prospectus. It reported a $104 billion net loss during the nine-month period, though most of that was due to the change in fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. Anthropic lost $25.1 billion over the same stretch in 2025, the filing said.
Anthropic has long worked to establish a reputation as a safety-conscious AI company, and its prospectus included more than 90 pages of risk factors for investors to consider ahead of its listing.
"I think if we do this right, we can create an age of miracles where humanity is able to solve problems that have eluded us for millennia," Amodei said in Anthropic's roadshow video. "We have to make sure that all the risks, all the ways that things can go wrong with this technology, we very carefully address those risks as we bring the benefits and as we have a viable business at the same time."
"I invite you to join us on the next phase of this journey," Amodei said.

title: Waymo suspends freeway rides nationwide after California DMV order
text:
Waymo robotaxis are no longer allowed to operate on California freeways after the state’s Department of Motor Vehicles restricted the Alphabet-owned company’s operations following several incidents that raised safety concerns.
California’s DMV, which regulates the testing and deployment of autonomous vehicles in the state, issued the operational restrictions on Waymo on November 11. However, the restrictions weren’t made public until Tuesday. San Francisco Business Times was the first to report the order.
The DMV confirmed the new restrictions to TechCrunch, stating that the department took action after three Waymo autonomous vehicles entered an active construction closure on U.S. Route 101 near Burlingame, and another separate incident involving California Highway Patrol vehicles on Highway 280 in San Francisco.
Waymo has complied and is preventing its robotaxis from accessing freeways in any of the markets it operates in, including those outside of California. Waymo currently has commercial operations in 15 U.S. cities.
The DMV said Waymo’s freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety.
“The Department determined that Waymo’s driverless freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present, despite a prior restriction and corrective actions implemented following similar incidents that occurred on May 18, 2026,” according to an emailed statement sent to TechCrunch.
The DMV said the restrictions will remain in place until Waymo can demonstrate that it has taken “effective corrective actions” to address the deficiencies.
Waymo spokesperson Dana Gallagher told TechCrunch the company has temporarily restricted freeway operations across its other operating markets to evaluate its performance.
“Safety is at the foundation of everything we do,” Gallagher said in a statement. “Following recent freeway construction zone encounters on U.S. 101 in California that did not involve any injuries or collisions, the California DMV has implemented an operating restriction on freeway operations in the state. In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance. Our ride-hailing service continues to operate safely on surface streets, serving over half a million trips each week. We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations.”
Waymo began offering freeway rides in late 2025, a commercial milestone that has been central to its expansion in major metro areas. Freeway access allows Waymo to connect riders to airports and other destinations more efficiently, slashing travel times by avoiding slower surface streets.
That has been particularly important in the San Francisco Bay Area because Waymo’s service area stretches from the city south to Silicon Valley. Freeway access has dramatically shortened trips across the Peninsula that previously took 45 minutes or more than an hour.
In May, Waymo abruptly stopped operating on highways. The company didn’t cite a specific reason at the time, but several social media posts showed Waymo robotaxis driving through traffic cones and struggling to navigate construction zones.
Waymo robotaxis returned to freeways in July after the company said it updated the self-driving software system to improve performance around freeway construction zones.

title: Humanity braces for an alien invasion in 3 Body Problem S2 teaser
text:
You might be excused for forgetting about the existence of 3 Body Problem, Netflix’s heady sci-fi series adapted from the award-winning novel The Three-Body Problem by Liu Cixin, the first book in his Remembrance of Earth’s Past trilogy. After all, it debuted in March 2024. But it was an exceptionally well-done, thematically rich series, and we’re finally getting the second of a planned three seasons in January. Netflix just dropped the first teaser.
(Spoilers for S1 below.)
Created by David Benioff, D.B. Weiss (Game of Thrones), and Alexander Woo (True Blood), the first season followed two primary timelines. In the earlier one, a young Chinese astrophysicist, Ye Wenjie (Rosalind Chao), witnessed her father being beaten to death by Red Guards during the Cultural Revolution. Ye figured out a means of sending an interstellar message to possible extraterrestrial civilizations, receiving a response from a planet called Trisolaris.
The planet had three suns, which wreaked havoc on Trisolaris via unpredictable “chaotic periods”—hence the novel’s title, which refers to a classic problem in celestial mechanics. Despite being warned that the aliens intended to invade and conquer Earth, Ye responded to the message and invited them to do so, bitter and disillusioned by the state of the world. She eventually became an established professor (Zine Tseng played the older version).
In the present day, the consequences of Ye’s fateful decision began to play out, beginning with a series of mysterious suicides by scientists, many of whom had possessed a highly advanced VR gaming headset. Among the dead: a particle physicist named Vera Ye (daughter of Ye Wenjie). Five of her former students (known as the Oxford Five) joined forces to figure out what was going on, eventually finding themselves caught in a global fight to save Earth from the invading Trisolarians (or San-Ti). Another human cult faction was just as intent on enabling the San-Ti invasion, believing they would be spared as a reward, while Ye Wenjie still believed the entire human race deserved to be annihilated.

title: The hidden language of psychopathy is not what scientists expected
text:
Scientists have discovered that psychopathic traits are associated with surprisingly different patterns of language, with some individuals using more positive words and others expressing greater negativity or less anxiety. The findings challenge familiar stereotypes about psychopathy and suggest that the stories people tell about their lives may offer important clues about their personalities.
The way people describe their lives may offer surprising clues about their personalities, including traits associated with psychopathy. A new study from the University of Mississippi challenges the familiar image of psychopaths as cold and emotionless, revealing that their patterns of language can be far more complex than expected.
Researchers examined hundreds of personal life stories and discovered that three major traits associated with psychopathy, boldness, meanness, and disinhibition, were connected to distinctly different ways of using words. Some of the findings were particularly unexpected. For example, people who scored higher in meanness tended to use more positive language, while those with greater boldness used fewer words associated with anxiety.
The findings, published in the journal Personality and Individual Differences, suggest that psychopathic traits can influence everyday communication in subtle ways that conventional stereotypes often overlook.
"The goal here is not to diagnose psychopathy based on language," said Ky Bray, an Ole Miss doctoral candidate in psychology. "It's to point to the fact that psychopathy shows up in everyday behaviors, even subtle behaviors like language.
"If we want to understand psychopathy and the different traits that comprise it, we need to think creatively about how these traits shape social interaction."
What 450 Life Stories Revealed About Psychopathy
The researchers used a psychological framework known as the Triarchic Model of Psychopathy, which examines three distinct personality dimensions. Boldness generally involves confidence and fearlessness, meanness reflects tendencies toward callousness and reduced empathy, and disinhibition involves difficulties with impulse control. According to Laura Drislane, an assistant professor of psychology at the University of Mississippi, these characteristics can affect ordinary behaviors, including how people describe their own experiences.
To investigate these connections, Drislane and Bray recruited 450 participants, including college students and individuals who reported having been incarcerated. Each person responded to open questions about important moments in their life, including their greatest highs, lowest points, and major turning points.
After writing their personal accounts, participants completed a questionnaire designed to measure their levels of psychopathic traits. The researchers then analyzed the written responses using specialized software that identifies patterns in word choice.
The analysis focused on how frequently participants used language associated with different psychological categories, including positive and negative emotions, achievement, social influence or clout, and risk. By comparing these language patterns with the personality scores, the team identified several intriguing relationships.
Surprising Differences in Positive and Negative Language
Participants with higher disinhibition scores generally used more negative words in their personal stories. They were also less likely to mention friends or use language connected to positive emotions and personal achievement.
Meanness, however, showed a very different pattern. People scoring higher in this trait tended to use more positive language, along with more words related to achievement and rewards. They also used fewer expressions associated with negative emotions.
Boldness was associated with another distinctive pattern. Participants with higher scores used fewer anxiety-related words, including terms such as fear, afraid, and worry. Their personal accounts also contained fewer references to mental illness.
These differences suggest that psychopathic traits do not produce a single recognizable style of communication. Instead, different characteristics are associated with different ways of describing emotions, goals, relationships, and personal experiences.
"What this tells us is the story we tell about our life has meaning," Drislane said. "It helps people make sense of their experiences, develop a worldview and a coherent sense of who they are.
"What we're starting to see is that in psychopathy, there are traits that relate to differences in meaning-making and the ways people think about their life."
Why Psychopathy Is More Complex Than the Stereotypes
The researchers also discovered that the relationship between personality traits and language changed depending on which question participants were answering. Someone describing a difficult experience, for example, might use language differently than when recalling a personal success.
This variation is important because it challenges the assumption that psychopathy is characterized by consistently flat or emotionally empty communication. Instead, the findings indicate that language patterns depend on both the particular psychopathic trait and the context in which someone is telling their story.
"People tend to think of psychopathy as one thing, but it's actually multidimensional," Bray said. "What we mean when we say that everyone exists on this spectrum. Everyone has some degree of meanness, boldness, and disinhibition.
"Viewing it from a multidimensional perspective allows us to observe how those traits might manifest in nonforensic populations, in people who have not committed a crime. That allows us to see how these traits affect college students, business professionals, or interpersonal relationships."
Like many personality conditions, psychopathy is better understood as a spectrum rather than a simple distinction between people who have it and those who do not. At one extreme is the familiar cultural image of a "psychopath," while people at the opposite end score low in all three dimensions.
This approach allows researchers to examine psychopathic traits throughout the general population, including among people who have never committed a crime. It also helps explain why the same broad label can encompass individuals with very different personalities and behaviors.
How Understanding Psychopathic Traits Could Improve Treatment
Recognizing these differences has implications beyond understanding everyday speech. Researchers have linked dimensions of psychopathy to serious outcomes, including criminal behavior, repeat offending, and intimate partner violence. Examining each trait separately may provide a clearer picture of how these risks develop.
"That's in part why there's a movement away from calling people 'psychopaths,' because we don't view psychopathy as a category," Drislane said. "But psychopathic dimensions can predict important outcomes, things like crime, recidivism, or intimate partner violence.
"What our research, including this paper, suggests is that it's important to look beyond that label and into the different components or dimensions of psychopathy, because each of those dimensions actually has a unique set of outcomes or things that it can predict."
Researchers also emphasize that psychopathy can be treated, with interventions aimed at reducing problematic symptoms and behaviors. Understanding the psychological processes behind boldness, meanness, and disinhibition could help scientists develop more targeted approaches and potentially identify ways to prevent severe problems from emerging.
"If we want to be able to treat or ideally even prevent psychopathy from developing, we need to understand the mechanisms at play," she said. "That comes down to understanding the unique contributors for all three of these dimensions."

title: Most transgender youth satisfied after choosing hormone therapy
text:
An overwhelming percentage of transgender and gender diverse young people in the United States express satisfaction with gender-affirming hormone therapy.
Almost 400 transgender and gender diverse young people reflected on their decision to take hormone therapy in the largest such survey to date. Nearly 97 percent affirmed it was the right decision, researchers report November 9 in JAMA Pediatrics. Only about 3 percent, or 10 individuals, said they regretted the step, and of those, seven felt the experience was harmful.
With concerns around youth well-being fueling limits on gender-affirming hormone therapy, the researchers write, “the results provide further support for the existing standards of care [and] do not support efforts to categorically restrict or ban access.”
Gender-affirming hormone therapy — with the masculinizing hormone testosterone or the feminizing hormone estrogen — allows a person’s body to better match their gender identity. Around 3 percent of 13- to 17-year-olds in the United States identify as transgender.
Among the study’s 376 young people, who were former patients of a clinic for transgender and gender diverse youth, nearly 92 percent began hormones at 17 or younger. Thirty percent took estrogen and 70 percent took testosterone, with the amount of time since starting the hormones averaging five years.
As per clinical guidelines for transgender health care, young people interested in medical treatment, joined by parents or guardians, began with an assessment visit with a mental health professional. For the study, participants took a yearly survey, filled out anytime from one month prior to six months following the anniversary of this initial visit. The research team analyzed surveys submitted from 2023 to 2025.
The new research adds to growing evidence on the benefits of gender-affirming hormone therapy for transgender young people. Gender-affirming hormones improve the alignment these young people experience between their appearance and their gender, increase their satisfaction with life and reduce depression and anxiety.
But state bans have curtailed young people’s access to gender-affirming care, which can include hormone therapy and puberty blockers. As of November 2026 in the United States, 28 states have laws or policies that limit this care, according to the health policy organization KFF. More than half of transgender young people age 13 to 17 reside in states that restrict gender-affirming care. The American Academy of Pediatrics and the Endocrine Society support gender-affirming health care for young people and provide evidence-backed guidelines for treatment.

title: ULA lost a Vulcan Centaur rocket carrying 40 Amazon satellites 10 minutes after launch — but the failure began just after liftoff
text:
The failure of a Vulcan Centaur rocket carrying a full load of internet satellites for Amazon was caused by an anomaly in its first-stage booster, rocket maker United Launch Alliance said today (Nov. 17).
That failure — which led to the loss of 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites — was recognized about 10 minutes after liftoff, but the problems began much earlier than that, ULA said in a statement.
"While we appear to have lost telemetry and the mission at approximately 10 minutes into flight, early indications are that just after liftoff the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance, resulting in stage separation occurring when the vehicle was low in altitude and below minimal velocity to reach orbit," ULA wrote in today's update.
The two-stage Vulcan Centaur is the successor to ULA's workhorse Atlas V rocket, which will retire after just six more flights. Vulcan debuted in January 2024 and now has a total of five launches under its belt.
The new rocket has experienced problems on three of those missions. On both its second and fourth flights — which launched in October 2024 and February of this year, respectively — the nozzle of one of Vulcan's strap-on solid rocket boosters (SRBs) fell off about 30 seconds after liftoff.
On both occasions, the rocket overcame the problem and successfully delivered its payloads to orbit. However, after the second occurrence, the U.S. Space Force paused national-security launches with Vulcan until ULA addressed the SRB nozzle issue. (The February 2026 flight was a Space Force mission.)
That work led to "design and process improvements to the nozzle," ULA said in an Oct. 28 update. And those tweaks apparently worked.
"All indications are that the solid rocket booster performance was nominal, following nozzle improvements implemented for this launch," the company wrote in today's update.
Vulcan's Centaur V upper stage, which features two RL-10C engines, did its job as well "but was unable to recover from the [booster] performance loss, resulting in loss of mission," ULA added.
Vulcan's first-stage booster is powered by two BE-4 engines, which are built by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin. Today's update did not identify the exact problem with the booster; doing so will require more time, as the investigation has just begun.
If that investigation finds a serious issue with the BE-4, there could be broad ripple effects across the American space program. After all, that engine also powers the first stage of Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket, which is a key piece of hardware for NASA's Artemis program of moon exploration. (And New Glenn is currently recovering from a failure of its own — a massive explosion on the test stand that occurred on May 28.)
NASA plans to integrate the Centaur V upper stage into its Space Launch System moon rocket, the vehicle that launches Artemis astronauts to space. So the fact that the Centaur performed nominally on Sunday is a bit of good news for the space agency.
Vulcan's grounding is a big deal, no matter what the anomaly investigation ends up finding. The U.S. doesn't have a surfeit of powerful rockets, after all, and two of them — Vulcan and New Glenn — are out of commission at the moment.
There's considerable pressure on both Vulcan and New Glenn to bounce back strong, for the nation faces an impending launch crunch in the next few years. SpaceX plans to retire its Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rockets and shift its launch load over to the fully reusable Starship megarocket. SpaceX is expected to prioritize its own needs in Starship's early days, using the vehicle primarily to build out its next-gen Starlink broadband constellation and Starmind AI data center network.
The Vulcan failure also impacts Amazon — specifically, the company's plan to build out Amazon Leo, which will compete with SpaceX's Starlink. Amazon has booked about 100 launches on a variety of rockets to build its constellation, which will eventually consist of more than 3,200 satellites. Thirty-eight of those bookings are for Vulcan; Sunday's launch was the first of those.
The other rockets Amazon has booked are the Atlas V, New Glenn, Falcon 9 and Arianespace's Ariane 6. About 400 operational Amazon Leo satellites have reached orbit to date across 14 launches (not including Sunday's failure).

title: How the attack on Crimean Bridge unfolded
text:
Stretching across the Kerch Strait in the Black Sea, the Crimean Bridge was always a symbol: for Russia, a prestige project cementing its claim to sovereign Ukrainian territory, and for Ukraine, a hated piece of infrastructure emblematic of Moscow's occupation of the Crimean Peninsula.
A key section of the double-arched, 12-mile-long bridge now lies on the seabed, brought down by an arsenal of Ukrainian long-range weaponry in a seven-stage operation culminating in a dramatic collapse.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said that the bridge "will be rebuilt, and it will be even better than before".
But eight years after its unveiling, the bridge has now become material proof of Kyiv's ability to pierce through Moscow's military defences to hit even its most treasured and protected structures.
How did the seven-stage operation play out?
The attack on the strategic Crimean Bridge was carried out gradually to cut across several layers of defence, Kyiv confirmed on Tuesday.
For several weeks Ukraine's Security Service and its General Staff gradually destroyed air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare assets, and other designated targets, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
A significant strike had already been reported on 16 November, when drones hit the bridge at night. Traffic was paused briefly then reinstated, and although the arch over the road section was visibly damaged, the structure remained standing.
But that hit turned out to have been only the penultimate stage of a complex attack.
In the early hours of 17 November, the final strikes dealt a fatal blow to the weakened arch structure.
One verified video - filmed from a camera on board a Ukrainian-made Flamingo missile - shows the weapon approaching the main span of the bridge and heading towards the steel arches, with the footage freezing just before impact.
The Flamingo had potentially been modified to be controlled remotely, which improved its accuracy enough to strike the bridge supports, munitions expert Justin Bronk, from the Royal United Services Institute said.
The missile's "very heavy warhead" made it "more suitable" for attacking the bridge's reinforced concrete spans and supports, Bronk added.
Zelensky later confirmed that several types of missiles and drones had been employed in the attack, which led the massive road arch - weighing thousands of tonnes and measuring about 227m in length - to collapse into the strait.
Daylight images taken from the shores of Crimea to the north show a section about 200m (660ft) long of the tarmac was too dragged below into the sea.
This is clearly critical damage to the crossing. Far from just being a decorative feature of the bridge, the arch played a structural role, transferring loads and supporting the span and helping to ensure the stability of the entire structure.
The parallel arch supporting the railway section has remained standing, although it may also have been damaged. All traffic on the bridge was initially suspended, though trains were later allowed to resume running.
But the damage to the bridge's main span is "catastrophic", Colin Capriani, a structural engineer from Monash University in Melbourne, Australia, told BBC Verify. It was "very hard to envisage" how the bridge could be rebuilt given it is clearly well within range of Ukrainian weaponry, Capriani added.
Major attacks in 2022 and 2023 had already caused serious damage to the road spans of the bridge, but the structure survived.
The difference this time is "the most critical and vulnerable part of the bridge has been hit", said David MacKenzie of engineering consultancy COWI, adding that "although the wreckage of the bridge can be cleared fairly quickly, reinstating full road traffic will take over a year".
What effect could the collapse of the bridge have on Crimea?
Moscow uses Crimea as a military base, with airbases, troop concentrations, training grounds and artillery stockpiles. From there it also carries out strikes on the rest of the country and resupplies its troops in southern Ukraine.
The attack comes after a summer of frequent strikes on Crimea, dictated by Ukraine's stated goal of cutting the peninsula off from Russia. At the time, Kyiv vowed to turn the Crimean Peninsula "into an island".
Now - although it is too early to speak of a complete blockade of Crimea – the risk of a serious transport and logistics crisis has increased significantly.
There is still a land corridor running through the occupied parts of the Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions. However, Ukraine has been systematically striking transport routes across northern Crimea, as well as bridges and other crossings in the area around Chongar, which has already caused problems with the delivery of fuel and other supplies, including military cargo.
Moscow can also still utilise the ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait. It could partly compensate for the loss of the bridge, but its capacity is very limited - and anything on the Black Sea has become vulnerable to attack. Resupplying Crimea by sea is risky, as Ukrainian naval and aerial drones operate extensively in the area.
In addition, debris from the Crimean Bridge - particularly its enormous arch - may have blocked the shipping channel. This would make it harder for larger vessels to pass through and create further problems for ports in the Sea of Azov, including the occupied cities of Mariupol and Berdyansk.
Away from the operational value of the damage to the bridge, the symbolic significance remains.
In 2018, Putin triumphantly drove over the bridge representing the unification of Russia and Crimea in a Russian-made truck. That section of the road now lies on the seabed.
Nearly five years since he launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Putin continues to wreak destruction on Ukraine's civilian population, but his most prized symbols of power are increasingly threatened by Kyiv's reach.

title: ‘Orwellian’: HIV scientist’s ordeal lays bare Trump officials’ interference in grant-making
text:
Dr Jade Pagkas-Bather received her first grant from the National Institutes of Health (NIH) in June 2025 – a milestone in any researcher’s career.
She planned to study basic income as a medical intervention: her randomized control trial would test whether monthly grants of $500-cash helped poor, HIV-positive young people in Chicago stick with treatment. Her hypothesis was as straightforward as it was cutting.
“Maybe taking care of your HIV isn’t your priority when you’re unhoused or hungry,” said Pagkas-Bather. That summer, she was through peer-review and about to be funded when NIH program officers started asking for changes, verbally and usually on a video call. “We had something that said we would include people of all gender identities in the grant. Program officers asked us to remove the term ‘gender identities.’ We had a clause that said Black and Latinx people experience more poverty than other people. They asked us to remove that.” There was also “concern” with the acronym for basic income grants (Big).
Pagkas-Bather removed it all, received funding and began screening dozens of study participants. Then, in 2026, a bigger ask came: could she remove the entire idea of giving out cash?
She recounted being told: “You can’t use unconditional cash transfer and you need to remove any reference to this having an impact on policy.”
Pagkas-Bather’s experience is a glimpse into the Trump administration’s NIH renegotiation process, an opaque and “Orwellian” political review that uses a “text analysis tool” to flag grants not in “alignment” with the Trump administration’s priorities.
The process has injected uncertainty, confusion and woe into scientific grant-making at the NIH over the past two years. Renegotiations force program officers, who typically take pride in shepherding critical research, to flag grants on topics the Trump administration disfavors. Even as they do so, they must guess what the “no-no” words are: NIH director Jay Bhattacharya has repeatedly denied a list of banned words exists.
“Her story is not unique,” said Shalini Agarwal, special counsel at Project Democracy, who is representing Pagkas-Bather in a suit seeking class-action status, and alleging the government is violating the first amendment. “There are many other researchers in a similar situation who are being asked to subvert their own grant projects that have been peer-reviewed and approved for funding a year or more into the project.”
The number of scientists who have been through this process is unknown.
Data shared exclusively with the Guardian shows re-negotiations surged in the first two years of the Trump administration. In 2023, only 154 of more than 40,000 grants up for renewal changed their titles, abstracts or public health statements: 0.4% of all grants, according to an analysis by Grant Witness, an independent group that tracks canceled government grants.
Those changes increased 21-fold during the Trump administration. In 2025, 8.6% of all grants changed year-to-year, or more than 3,401 of the more than 39,000 grant continuations awarded by NIH. In 2026, 8.5% of all continuing grants changed, or 3,006 of the agency’s nearly 35,500 grants, according to an analysis by Grant Witness.
In the 2027 fiscal year, which just started, 64 grants have been renewed. Three have already seen changes. In one a study initially titled “The Black Zones”, which was to focus on African American neighborhoods, all mentions of “African Americans” was removed, and a new version referenced “Black Americans”. In another, an HIV grant that would study a specific viral subtype had text changed from including “men and women” to “a wide range of people”.
HIV grants are almost twice as likely to have been changed, data shows, and were especially hard-hit in early cancelations. In part, many likely undertook renegotiations because the Trump administration placed severe restrictions on scientific work in South Africa. In 2025, of the 1,795 HIV-related continuing grants, 305 were changed, or 17%. In 2026, 335 of 1,609 grant continuations were changed, or 20.8%.
“The censorship that’s happening now is, I think, pretty much unprecedented,” said Jeremy Berg, a former director of the National Institute of General Medical Sciences, who has closely tracked changes in grant-making at the NIH. “It’s very Orwellian in the sense that it’s purely double-speak,” he said. “It’s a way of exerting political control and control of the terms of the debate,” said Berg.
The Guardian asked the NIH how many grants have been changed, and about the “text analysis” tool employed by NIH.
The agency said “more than 5,000 new and continuation grants” have been re-negotiated, “to ensure the agency funds the most meritorious science, addresses urgent health needs, and sustains a robust biomedical research workforce”.
“During these grant renegotiations, grant scopes were substantively altered wherever possible to replace poorly defined, non-scientific or subjective concepts and variables with well-defined, scientific concepts that have objective and measurable variables,” an NIH spokesperson told the Guardian. “Renegotiation is a normal process that NIH has used for years on grants for various reasons. All renegotiated grants are assessed by human experts.”
The NIH’s renegotiation process was set into motion in 2025, after court battles slowed down Trump administration grant cancellations. As the administration sought to change scientific studies, it developed a process of bringing grants into “alignment” with administration priorities – to name a couple, the belief that gender is binary and research into health equity is “unscientific”. Program officers who take pride in helping foster critical research are now tasked with renegotiating grants, often intuiting what might get flagged, said National Cancer Institute branch chief Sarah Kobrin.
“They are told to contact the investigators in case the investigators want to make changes,” Kobrin said. “We are compelled. We are not calling and saying, ‘Hey, could you change these words.’”
Instead, program officers must ask: “‘Hey, you know, if you want, you could change these words and it might work out well for you.’”
“It is certainly, certainly, certainly continuing,” she said.
Now, as a historic number of Democratic doctors and scientists prepare to take office, current and former leaders of NIH said Congress has years of work ahead to restore the agency.
Pagkas-Bather is one of 14 named plaintiffs in a first amendment lawsuit that argues such renegotiations and cancellations amount to censorship or, in legalese, “viewpoint-based discrimination”.
The Guardian has also covered other researchers involved in the lawsuit. In Pittsburgh, a group of researchers had funding cut for a study of Alzheimer’s disease risk in a low-income, majority Black neighborhood. The study was cancelled by the administration, leaving hundreds of aging residents without potential dementia diagnoses.
Ultimately, Pagkas-Bather was told that if she did not remove the cash payments from her $1.3m grant, she would need to find $1m in funding elsewhere. Seeing no path forward, she eliminated cash grants from her study and plans to use food and transportation vouchers as her intervention. She will need to ask each participant for consent again, since the study they signed up for bears little resemblance to the one she is now conducting.
“Not only would [Pagkas-Bather’s study] demonstrate that money empowers people to preserve their right to exist, but also thrive,” said Leslie McGorman, senior director of policy and strategy with AIDS United. “That is so threatening to this administration.”
A federal court hearing will determine whether the lawsuit filed by Pagkas-Bather and others will receive class-action status in November.

title: Chargers show enough progress on offense to finally end 11-game losing streak
text:
The Los Angeles Chargers’ fundamental issues on offense did not go away because of a 23-20 win at the Baltimore Ravens, but they probably feel a lot more manageable after ending a losing streak that dates back to last December
EL SEGUNDO, Calif. -- The Los Angeles Chargers’ fundamental issues on offense did not go away because of a 23-20 win at the Baltimore Ravens, but they probably feel a lot more manageable after ending a losing streak that dates back to last December.
With the specter of becoming the NFL’s first 0-17 team gone, their focus over the eight remaining games must be figuring out what players, coaches and traits should carry over to 2027 and what needs to change in the offseason.
The Chargers (1-8) did finally address some of the longstanding issues that sank a campaign which started with massive expectations.
The running back rotation was finally scuttled, letting 2025 first-round pick Omarion Hampton get the bulk of the work. He turned 22 carries into 105 yards rushing and a touchdown on Monday night. It was Hampton’s second career 100-yard game, and he did it with the second-highest workload of his professional tenure.
Consistent success with the ground game took pressure off battered quarterback Justin Herbert, who attempted a season-low 18 passes. Without needing to carry the team, he looked refreshed and as confident as he has all year.
Herbert ended up 12 of 18 for 129 yards, but he took just two sacks and added 51 yards rushing with a touchdown. Most importantly, he avoided giving the ball away, allowing the Chargers to win the turnover margin for the second time all season.
That shift is what the hiring of offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel was supposed to accomplish. He also highlighted unheralded pieces of the roster.
Second-year receiver Tre Harris helped out as Herbert’s main target, finishing with a career-high 86 yards on five receptions. An offensive line starting three rookies fared well.
None of those performances make up for what happened before, nor do they address fundamental questions still hanging over the organization, such as the lack of difference-making passing game options around Herbert, whether the quarterback will ever fully adapt to the quick timing offense McDaniel is trying to run, or what to do with left tackle Rashawn Slater coming off a third injury-shortened season in six years.
But a win is a win. After 11 straight losses including the playoffs, that counts for something.
Defensive coordinator Chris O’Leary had his group locked in to stop the run, allowing 16 yards on 15 carries. The Chargers held Derrick Henry to 10 yards on 10 attempts, the second-worst output of his Hall of Fame-caliber career with at least 10 carries; Henry finished with nine yards on 16 carries with the Tennessee Titans against the Houston Texans in December 2023.
The pass defense has sprung a leak over the past two games. Jacoby Brissett threw for 340 yards in his first start for the Ravens on the heels of C.J. Stroud’s 384 yards and five touchdowns in Week 9. Upcoming games against the New York Jets and New England Patriots without an injured Drake Maye should offer a reprieve, but the drop-off is concerning.
FB Scott Matlock. It isn’t a coincidence that success running the ball came with Matlock playing a season-high 49.1% of the Chargers’ offensive snaps. He brings a physical edge, as demonstrated when Matlock pulled Hampton over the goal line late in the first half.
RB Keaton Mitchell had three carries for four yards and got lucky when a teammate recovered his fumbled kickoff return early in the second quarter.
WR Ladd McConkey didn’t travel with the team after his back injury flared up. … TE Oronde Gadsden II was able to come back after getting poked in the eye.
15.4% — The Chargers were 2 for 13 on third down, their lowest conversion rate of the season, but helped make up for those struggles by going 2 for 2 on fourth-down chances.
The Chargers host the Jets on Sunday. With three home games left in 2026, they have to work quickly to join the Los Angeles Rams, Arizona Cardinals and World Cup champion Spain in winning multiple games at SoFi Stadium this year.

title: Back to 1997: Russia wants NATO to roll back its eastern expansion
text:
During talks on ending the war in Ukraine, Russian representatives in Abu Dhabi presented a document containing far-reaching demands, The New York Times reports.
Dated November 10, the document reportedly calls not only for an end to Western arms deliveries to Ukraine but also for NATO to withdraw its troops and bases and move them back to where they were in 1997.
What does Russia mean by 1997?
The year 1997 refers to the NATO alliance before its first eastward expansion, according to the Kremlin. At the time, NATO had 16 members. Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary had already been invited to join but did not formally become members of the defense alliance until two years later. In the following years, more countries in Central, Eastern and Southeastern Europe joined, followed most recently by countries in Scandinavia. Today, NATO has 32 member states in Europe and North America.
According to the report, Russia is not explicitly demanding that Central and Eastern European countries leave , but rather that the NATO alliance end its military presence in those countries.
What would be the consequences of a NATO withdrawal?
A withdrawal of NATO troops and bases from member states that joined the alliance after 1997 would significantly weaken their defense capabilities. For example, since 2004, NATO allies, including Germany, have taken turns policing the airspace over Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.
Because the Baltic states do not have fighter jets of their own for independent air policing, NATO provides the capability. Since 2026, the mission has been part of a broader air defense presence. The planned deployment of the German Lithuania Brigade, which is expected to be fully operational by the end of 2027, would also have to be halted.
In Romania, meanwhile, the Mihail Kogalniceanu Air Base near Constanța on the Black Sea is currently being expanded. Once completed, it is set to become Europe's largest NATO air base by area — even larger than Ramstein in Germany.
"Under no circumstances will we allow anyone to establish new security rules for this part of the world over the heads of Poland and Europe," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk told TVP World. His Bulgarian counterpart, Rumen Radev, called a NATO withdrawal "unthinkable and unrealistic." No country should be forced by external pressure to reverse its decision on which alliance to join.
Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal also rejected any Russian say in changes to Europe's security order: "We have nothing to discuss with Russia about Europe's security order; it is working well."
The strong rejection from the capitals of NATO's eastern members, however, masks fears along the alliance's eastern flank that a deal between Washington and Moscow could turn their security into a bargaining chip.
Why isn't the mutual-defense clause enough?
In the event of an armed attack on a NATO member, the other alliance members are obligated under Article 5 to come to its aid. Each member decides for itself what measures it considers necessary, which may include the use of military force.
For the mutual defense commitment to deter a potential aggressor, that country must believe NATO can intervene militarily quickly and effectively in a crisis. The deployment of allied troops along the eastern flank serves precisely this purpose. A withdrawal would make defense more difficult and could lead Russia to believe that an attack on NATO territory would involve fewer risks for Moscow.
Who decides which alliances a country can join?
As part of their security framework, European countries have agreed that states are free to decide which alliances they wish to join. NATO points to Article 10 of its founding treaty, which enshrines its open-door policy for European countries. The 1997 NATO-Russia Founding Act also explicitly stated that neither side had the right to veto the other's decisions.
Back in November 1990, the participating states of the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe (CSCE), including the Soviet Union, had already agreed in the Charter of Paris to respect each country's freedom to choose its own security arrangements.
Was there a promise not to expand NATO eastward?
During the negotiations surrounding German reunification, then-US Secretary of State James Baker and German Foreign Minister Hans-Dietrich Genscher used language that suggested putting limits on NATO's eastward expansion.
Their remarks came during discussions about unified Germany's membership in NATO and the possible deployment of NATO forces on the territory of the former East Germany. However, no written, legally binding general promise was ever agreed that NATO would never expand to include other former Warsaw Pact countries.
In the 1997 NATO-Russia Founding Act, both sides declared that they no longer considered each other adversaries. NATO stated that, under the security conditions prevailing at the time and in the foreseeable future, it intended to ensure its collective defense through reinforcement rather than the additional permanent stationing of "substantial combat forces." The agreement explicitly gave Moscow no veto over NATO decisions.
In the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, Russia, the United States and the United Kingdom reaffirmed their commitment to respect Ukraine's independence and existing borders and to refrain from the use of force. These assurances were linked to Ukraine's decision to give up its nuclear weapons. However, the memorandum did not oblige the United States or the United Kingdom to defend Ukraine militarily in the event of an attack. NATO membership was not addressed at the time.
Why is the demand back on the table?
Just over two months before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Kremlin presented two draft treaties to the United States and NATO. In them, Russia demanded an end to further NATO enlargement. The draft agreement with NATO also proposed that Russia and NATO members that had already joined the alliance as of May 27, 1997, refrain from deploying additional troops or weapons on the territory of other European countries beyond the levels stationed there on that date.
Security guarantees for the postwar period and a future security framework for Europe were also on the agenda in Abu Dhabi. Negotiating NATO troop deployments and alliance enlargement alongside an end to the war in Ukraine would give Moscow additional leverage. Russia has long maintained that the "root causes" of the war must be addressed. The Kremlin includes NATO enlargement and the alliance's military presence in Eastern Europe among those causes.
So far, no significant Western player has expressed willingness to accept Russia's demands in Abu Dhabi. On the contrary, former Polish intelligence coordinator Stanislaw Zaryn viewed the talks as an attempt to buy time and weaken the West ahead of another confrontation.

title: When is the Nations League draw and who could England play in quarter-finals?
text:
England will play either Belgium, Netherlands or Norway in the Nations League quarter-finals as Thomas Tuchel’s side look to build on their impressive victory over world champions Spain in the group stage.
The 3-2 win in Madrid, which featured a dominant performance before hanging on with 10 men, saw England top their group and they will enter Friday’s draw as one of the top seeds, along with France, Germany and Portugal.
England will play a two-legged quarter-final during the next international break in March, and will be at home for the second leg as they look to advance to the Nations League Finals, which will be staged in June and at the end of the season.
There have been reports of the Football Association expressing an interest in hosting the Nations League Finals, which feature the two semi-finals and the final. Portugal, Italy, the Netherlands and Germany have previously hosted the Finals.
The host country of the Finals is typically involved in the final four, although the Nations League could also allow the FA a test event before hosting Euro 2028 the following summer, with Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland also co-hosts.
Here’s everything you need to know ahead of Friday’s draw
When is the Nations League draw?
The draw will take place at 11am GMT on Friday 20 November. It will be conducted from Nyon, Uefa’s headquarters, in Switzerland.
What teams are still involved in the Nations League?
Nations League quarter-finals
- Group winners: France, Germany, England, Portugal
- Group runners-up: Belgium, Netherlands, Spain, Norway
England cannot draw Spain as they played them in Group A3
Nations League play-offs: League A/B
- League A third/fourth place: Croatia, Denmark, Serbia, Wales
- League B runners-up: Slovenia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Republic of Ireland, Hungary
Nations League play-offs: League B/C
- League B fourth place: North Macedonia, Romania, Israel, Georgia
- League C runner-up: Belarus, Cyprus, Faroe Islands, Estonia
When will the Nations League quarter-finals take place?
- First leg: 25-27 March
- Second leg: 28-30 March
- Semi-finals, third-place play-off and final: 9-13 June

title: Russia cannot have a say over NATO's military activities, Norwegian foreign minister warns
text:
Norwegian Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide told Euronews that Moscow must not be allowed to dictate Europe's security arrangements while also warning against a return to spheres of influence.
Norwegian Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide has warned that Russia cannot have any say over NATO's military activities within its own territory, pushing back against Moscow's demands to reshape Europe's security order as diplomatic efforts to end the war in Ukraine gather pace.
Speaking to Euronews, Barth Eide insisted that Europe's existing security architecture did not need to be renegotiated and that sovereign countries must remain free to choose their own alliances.
“We're not happy about this language about architecture,” he said. “We believe that we have a European security architecture. There was nothing wrong with it until Russia violated it.”
Barth Eide added that no deal should be imposed on Kyiv without Ukraine’s consent. “There should be nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine."
He said discussions with Moscow following a ceasefire could address arms control, verification mechanisms and confidence-building measures, drawing on precedents established during the Cold War.
The minister also warned against any agreement between the world's major powers to carve up the globe into spheres of influence, invoking the legacy of the 1945 Yalta Conference.
“The last thing we want would be an agreement between great leaders to divide the world between them,” he said. “These kinds of spheres of interest should be a thing of the past.”

title: College Basketball Catchup: Thriving UCLA, Bobcats Turnover, Moreno Does It All
text:
UCLA keeps pouring on the 100s. Kentucky bounces back thanks to a 7-footer. Michigan is going to be a problem.
Here's what you need to know from Monday's slate of college basketball.
No. 7 UCLA is off to a great start this season, as the Bruins aren’t just winning in the early going but decimating opponents. The year began with a win against Arizona, and UCLA followed that ranked-ranked upset W with three-straight 100-plus point games, the latest a 105-66 win over Long Beach State on Monday.
Among the keys to that victory was senior forward Eric Dailey Jr., whose numbers are up across the board in the early going. His 25 points matched a career high, and he started early with a 3 to make it 7-2 just over three minutes in — UCLA never looked back.
Dailey shot under 49% in 2025-2026, but is at 53.2% to this point this season, and his points per game have jumped from 11.6 to 15.5. He’s also averaging what would be career bests in rebounds (7.0), assists (2.8), blocks (0.5) and steals (1.5) — yes, Dailey and UCLA are just four games in, but this is a great start for both, and if Dailey can keep it up, then it will be easier for UCLA to do the same.
Kentucky hasn’t exactly been covering itself in glory lately — the Wildcats got booted from the latest Associated Press top 25 after escaping Northern Arizona thanks more to the Lumberbacks losing the game on missed free throws rather than Kentucky winning it — but Monday represented a step in the right direction. The Wildcats crushed Grambling State 88-59, and seven-foot sophomore Malachi Moreno was at the center of that successful performance. He scored 22 points while pulling down 12 rebounds — six offensive, six defensive — and added one assist, four steals and three blocks.
The 22 points led all scorers, as did the rebounds and steals, and the blocks were tied for a game-high. Moreno has seen a huge jump in performance early on, even if Kentucky as a whole hasn’t impressed, increasing his rebounds from 6.3 per game to 9, his points from 7.8 to 14.2, assists from 1.8 to 3.2 and a jump in shooting percentage from 58.2% to 66.7%. Kentucky still has issues to solve — a one-game win over Northern Arizona is troubling, and it took more time than it should have to create separation from Grambling State in the follow-up contest — but more performances like this one from Moreno will change the Wildcats’ fortunes.
Quinnipiac’s women’s team was on the bubble last year after becoming regular-season conference champs but losing to Fairfield in the Metro — née MAAC — conference title game, and has a new coach this season after Tricia Fabbri retired at the end of the year. Roman Owen took over a squad with just three returning players from that regular-season championship, and the Bobcats got back to .500 with a non-conference win against the Yale Bulldogs on Monday.
Lilly Thomas, new to this year's roster, led the way: the sophomore center scored 22 points on 11-for-14 shooting while grabbing eight boards and blocked a pair of shots — no small thing in a 59-53 victory. Shooting 78% was also huge, considering Quinnipiac shot just 42% as a team even with that in the mix.
The Bobcats are basically starting over in 2026-2027, given the massive roster turnover and new coach, but it’s also the last year in which back-to-back-to-back champs Fairfield are in the Metro before a move to the Coastal Athletic Association in 2027 — this is a transitional season for Quinnipiac, but also for the conference as a whole.
It didn’t help Texas Southern defeat UC San Diego — the Tritons would win, 97-92 — but Karris Bilal made it close thanks to 36 points. It wasn’t just the points, either, as the sophomore guard also grabbed eight rebounds and dished out three assists in 39 minutes.
Those 36 points led all Division I men’s hoopers on Monday, and in fact was one of just two 30-point games across the league.
Senior guard Kailyn Gilbert had a monster game for Texas A&M, but to understand just how significant it was you need to see how many points the Aggies scored as a whole. Texas A&M scored 61 in a win over Lamar, and Gilbert dropped 32 of those points — more than half of her team’s scoring.
Gilbert also added four rebounds, two assists and three steals to her stat sheet, and turned the ball over just once while shooting 3-for-5 from deep, hitting all five shots from the line and going 12-for-22 overall. A highly efficient, productive game, and an absolutely necessary performance, with the rest of the Aggies managing 29 combined points and shooting all of 43% even with her night included.
Michigan is looking terrifying. Defeating Central Michigan 101-30 isn’t necessarily a sign on its own that the Wolverines are a terror, but you can still see ways in which this might be a better team than last season’s squad. Michigan shot 52% as a whole, and 38% on 3-pointers — if the Wolverines are making better decisions on shots rather than rushing them, which was a huge problem for a team that occasionally looked its youthful age a year ago, then it will be more difficult to stop them in 2026-2027.
And even more difficult to stop Michigan if its relentless defense continues to punish opponents, flooding shooting lanes with bodies and cutting off opportunities for easy scores. In a related story, Central Michigan shot just 21% overall, making 12 field goals, and were 4-for-29 from beyond the arc. The Wolverines more than doubled up Central Michigan on rebounds, 54 to 23, and forced 28 turnovers, scoring 41 points off those.
Again, Central Michigan isn’t the most challenging opponent for a team of Michigan’s stature, but the Wolverines’ problems from a year ago haven’t been showing up against any opposition yet, not just the ones that are supposed to be easy dubs. There’s a reason Michigan is No. 2, and also reasons to believe that it’ll stay near the top of the rankings for some time.

title: Trump arrives in Philippines to kick off Asia trip with economic deals and talks with allies
text: MANILA, Philippines (AP) — President Donald Trump arrived in the Philippines on Tuesday, where he met with regional partners, sought to formalize a trade deal and get a break from a series of setbacks at home, ranging from a major disruption to the U.S. aviation industry to a scandal that has shaken the global AI industry. Manila, the Philippine capital, is Trump's first stop on a three-day trip that will later take him to China for historic three-way nuclear talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, and, according to Trump, potentially for a meeting with North Korea's leader Kim Jong Un. READ MORE: Trump's Asia reset: Deals in Manila and Shenzhen, then a rare nuclear summit with Xi and Putin The visit marks Trump's first travel abroad since his party suffered deep losses in midterm elections. The White House and stock market alike have been rattled by the departure of Jensen Huang from Nvidia last week after admitting to an affair with an alleged Chinese government agent. Beijing has said it was not involved. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News But Trump could not escape all the controversies still swirling in the U.S. Reporters asked him about the recent service outages involving Microsoft, the Federal Aviation Administration and online banking with JPMorgan Chase. The president played down the problems that caused mass flight cancellations and disrupted workdays. "It's life," Trump said. "When you're big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It's fine." The president was also asked about a CNN report that Iran was putting together plans to attack Washington with a dirty bomb or chemical weapons. "Well, if there is, they will pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before," Trump said, adding, "I hope it's not. But we take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy." Trump to be feted at the annual ASEAN summit Trump's first hours in the Philippines included all the reassuring optics from Washington's oldest treaty ally in Asia, such as a cocktail reception and dinner with other world leaders, an intermission from some of the thorniest issues at home. He's being feted Tuesday night at a gala as the "guest of honor" at the annual summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations. The ASEAN leaders have been working on a non-aggression pact with China in the contested waters of the South China Sea, a key global trade route. Confrontations have escalated in recent years, particularly between Chinese and Philippine coast guard and naval forces in disputed shoals. After landing in Manila, Trump met with the leaders of the Quad nations, comprising the U.S., Australia, India, and Japan, that have aimed to counter China's influence in the Asia Pacific, for the first time since he returned to the White House last year. "We're all friends," Trump said. "It's a lot easier that way." The president announced that the Quad would conduct an exercise featuring maritime patrol aircraft and launch an accelerator to speed the development of artificial intelligence. Trump signed a trade statement with Thailand, the type of agreement he has relished striking since launching a trade war last year buttressed by steep tariff threats. The president said that he was looking forward "to finalizing the details of our formal agreement in the coming weeks." The joint statement included details that were posted more than a year ago by the U.S. government.
