Thailand would remove tariffs on most American goods, as well as barriers for importing American autos, food products and pharmaceutical drugs. Trump said Tuesday that Thailand would buy $2.6 billion in U.S. agricultural products. As part of the gala dinner Tuesday night, Trump participated in what was billed as a "special summit" with the ASEAN leaders. They finalized a set of principles to tackle online scams, Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said. Leaders at the dinner were also expected to discuss efforts to deepen trade and security ties as well as the region's longstanding conflicts, including yearslong violence in Myanmar and escalating disputes in the South China Sea, which Beijing claims virtually in its entirety. Washington has rejected China's expansive claim to the waterway, and has repeatedly stated that it's obligated to defend the Philippines if Filipino forces come under an armed attack. Anti-Trump protesters are gathered in Manila About 1,500 left-wing protesters held a noisy rally in a downtown Manila square ahead of Trump's arrival, calling on Philippine leaders not to take their foreign policy cues from the U.S. They waved red flags and held up a large streamer that read, "Resist U.S. war and plunder!" They planned to burn an effigy of Trump. Riot police with shields and wooden truncheons stood nearby. "The Philippine government should not deal with such a loser so our call to the Marcos administration is to stop being a puppet of Donald Trump and to uphold an independent foreign policy for the Philippines," protest leader Teddy Casiño told The Associated Press. Nearly 23,000 police personnel and other law enforcers, including SWAT teams, were deployed to secure the ASEAN summit. Planned meetings with the Philippine president — and possibly an old friend On Wednesday, Trump is set to receive a red-carpet welcome and full military honors from Marcos Jr., followed by a state banquet as part of his visit to the Malacanang presidential palace. Trump and Marcos are expected to affirm their commitment to their countries' longstanding treaty alliance. Officials are arranging a possible brief reunion in Malacanang with an old acquaintance — Imelda Marcos — if she's well enough and gets her doctors' nod. Now 97 and using a wheelchair, the former jet set Philippine first lady and mother of the incumbent president partied in New York decades ago in her heyday as the controversial wife of a strongman leader, who was to be ousted in a pro-democracy 1986 "People Power" public uprising. But the friendship with Trump endured, with Trump often asking Marcos Jr. and other Philippine officials: "How's Imelda?" Philippine Ambassador to Washington Jose Manuel Romualdez told The Associated Press. "Personal connections are very important to him," Romualdez said. When the Philippine leader met Trump in the White House last year, he carried a note from his mother that thanked the U.S. president for his strong backing of the Philippines. "President Trump was very happy and told Marcos, 'please say hello to your mother,'" according to Romualdez. Trump is also expected to announce a series of commercial deals and investments in the aviation, defense, energy, and technology sectors, before heading to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. Boak reported from Shenzhen, China.

title: Trump’s accounts traded up to $97.5 million in Nvidia as Huang gained White House access
text:
President Donald Trump has had plenty of reason to cheer the rise of Nvidia.
The chipmaker helped propel the stock market that Trump is fond of touting. Its billionaire co-founder, Jensen Huang, became one of the president's favorite businessmen. And by the end of last year, Nvidia had become one of Trump's three largest individual stock holdings, worth between $12.5 million and $58 million, up from between $615,000 and $1.3 million a year earlier.
Since returning to the White House, Trump's investment accounts have bought or sold Nvidia shares at least 103 times — transactions worth a combined $27 million to $97.5 million, according to a new CNBC analysis of his annual and periodic financial disclosures, which were most recently updated through August.
By midday Monday, Trump's Nvidia stake, based on the value he reported holding in August, would be worth $4.5 million to $57.7 million with stock priced around $157. But the filings give broad dollar ranges for holdings rather than the number of shares, leaving his current stake unclear.
Now, Huang's resignation as Nvidia's CEO on Thursday, following revelations about his relationship with a woman suspected of spying for China and reports of affairs with company employees, has put those trades back in the spotlight.
Among them was a sale of $500,001 to $1 million on May 18, the first Monday after Trump returned from a state visit to China with Huang. Five days earlier, before Huang boarded Air Force One during a refueling stop in Alaska, Secretary of State Marco Rubio had briefed Trump on intelligence concerning Huang's relationship with the suspected spy, The New York Times reported.
Trump on Monday denied being briefed. Asked about the reported briefing from Rubio, Trump said, "I haven't heard that," adding that he did not know whether the woman, Alice Huang, was a Chinese spy.
The president's financial accounts also bought smaller amounts of Nvidia shares in the days immediately before and after the May 18 sale, part of a broader trading blitz. Such flurries have defined his second term: Trump disclosed more than 21,000 trades in 2025 alone, compared with roughly 500 during his entire first term, according to CNBC's analysis.
A White House spokesperson told CNBC independent advisors manage Trump's portfolio without his input. Trump Organization spokesperson Kimberly Benza said the arrangement is designed to "avoid even the appearance of a conflict of interest." The disclosures offer no evidence Trump directed the trades or that his advisors had access to classified intelligence.
Trump has long used the stock market as a scorecard for the economy, touting its record highs — sometimes when highs have not actually been reached — despite the turbulence caused by his tariffs and the Iran war.
"Look, we have the highest stock market we've ever had," Trump told ESPN commentator and political talk show host Stephen A. Smith on Thursday when pressed about Republicans' midterm losses.
Nvidia alone accounted for about 13.5% of the S&P 500's 2026 gains through September, according to an analysis by Choate Wealth that looked at how chip stocks have driven the year's performance.
Huang's rise in Trump's Washington has been nearly as striking as Nvidia's on Wall Street. The two have met or appeared together at least 15 times since Trump returned to office, according to a CNBC review of public records and news reports. Huang in June told The Associated Press that Trump even "calls me in the middle of the night."
It wasn't always that way.
At Trump's Jan. 20, 2025, inauguration, several Silicon Valley titans occupied prime seats, but Huang wasn't there. The two men had never met.
That changed on Jan. 31, 2025, when Huang visited the White House, capping a bruising week for Nvidia: Chinese AI startup DeepSeek had wiped $593 billion off the company's market value in a single day, according to LSEG data cited by Reuters.
Two days before the meeting, Trump's money managers bought between $1 million and $5 million in Nvidia stock.
For Huang, much of the relationship hinged on access to China. In April 2025, the administration effectively halted sales of Nvidia's H20 chips to China, prompting a $4.5 billion charge, according to an SEC filing. Huang argued that withholding U.S. chips would only accelerate China's development of its own.
The administration eventually relented. After another meeting with Trump in July 2025, Huang announced from Beijing that Nvidia expected to resume H20 sales. A week after Trump confirmed an August 2025 deal calling for 15% of the revenue from the company's chip sales to China to go to the U.S. government, his accounts also bought between $5 million and $25 million in Nvidia stock, one of several large tech investments that day.
Huang was also becoming a fixture of Trump's international diplomacy, joining him in Saudi Arabia and the U.K. Nvidia, already a $1 million donor to Trump's inaugural fund, would pledge another $25 million to his planned White House ballroom on condition of anonymity, The Washington Post first reported.
But behind the scenes, intelligence officials first briefed Trump last fall on Huang's relationship with the woman suspected of spying for China, The New York Times reported.
Trump nevertheless continued to ease restrictions on Nvidia's business in China, announcing Dec. 8 that the company could sell its more powerful H200 chips. His accounts had sold as much as $1 million in Nvidia stock four days earlier and bought more the day after.
In the first eight months of 2026, Trump's accounts made another 38 Nvidia trades worth a combined $9.4 million to $28.3 million, according to CNBC's analysis. A disclosure released Oct. 8 — the day Trump awarded Huang the National Medal of Science — showed purchases of up to $1.6 million and sales of up to $1 million in August alone.
Trump stood by Huang as Nvidia's board weighed his future last week, urging him to fight to keep his job, the Times reported.
With Huang out and Nvidia's shares tumbling, Trump described him Thursday as a "tremendous talent" who was "going through hell" — in the same interview in which he boasted of the market's record highs.
Trump is already floating a comeback for Huang, telling reporters Monday that reinstating him "certainly isn't a bad idea." But Nvidia's board is not considering his return, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC. The person asked not to be named because they were discussing internal matters."

title: Model ML raises $250M to automate investment banking grunt work
text:
Model ML, a London-based startup that uses AI to automate work traditionally performed by junior bankers and consultants, including building financial models, preparing pitch decks, and writing due diligence reports, has raised $250 million in Series B funding at a $1.5 billion valuation. The new round, which comes a year after its $75 million Series A round was announced, was co-led by General Atlantic and earlier backer QED Investors.
Brothers Chaz and Arnie Englander co-founded the three-year-old startup after previously co-founding two other companies, including Fat Llama, a peer-to-peer rental marketplace acquired by Swedish rival Hygglo for $41.5 million in 2022.
Model ML develops AI agents that integrate with clients’ systems, data, and tools, including Excel and PowerPoint. The startup says its agents understand the full context of deals that bankers and consultants are working on and can automatically update financial models and presentations when new developments affect their analysis.
Other startups automating the routine, repetitive tasks for investment bankers and management consultants include Hebbia and Rogo, which raised $160 million at a $2 billion valuation in April.
Anthropic and OpenAI have also built tools for financial professionals, but Model ML says it runs on open source models and that doing so allows it to operate at about 2% of the cost of frontier models while delivering faster results.

title: OpenAI sued by California after admitting to 80 loss-of-control incidents
text:
California sued OpenAI yesterday, alleging it has tried to evade responsibility for the Hugging Face attack and about 80 other incidents in which the company lost control of its AI. The lawsuit was filed under the state’s public nuisance and unfair competition laws.
The July 2026 hack of Hugging Face and other attacks carried out by OpenAI’s autonomous agents “may just be the tip of the iceberg,” said a lawsuit filed in a state court by California Attorney General Rob Bonta. “OpenAI recently admitted to the Attorney General’s Office that it has lost control of its autonomous AI agents over 80 times during testing.”
OpenAI had publicly reported only 27 such incidents, showing that “OpenAI’s public reports do not represent the full scope of loss-of-control incidents involving OpenAI’s models that have impacted third parties,” the lawsuit said. OpenAI “knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it,” Bonta said in a press release.
OpenAI models are “able to find novel vulnerabilities in computer networks, quickly break down defenses, and autonomously carry out cyberattacks,” Bonta’s lawsuit said. OpenAI puts safeguards in its publicly released models to prevent this behavior, “but deliberately omits or removes these protections while experimenting with and training its models,” the lawsuit said.
In the attack on Hugging Face, OpenAI agents “employed complicated hacking methodologies and involved coordinated actions by hundreds of individual autonomous AI agents that should have been contained in OpenAI’s research environment,” the lawsuit said.
Known attacks “include unauthorized access of and cyberattacks on databases containing code that powers countless applications; informational websites that are trusted and valuable resources for the public; and foreign government databases storing sensitive health information,” the lawsuit said. “Swarms of OpenAI’s experimental AI agents have even compromised OpenAI’s own internal infrastructure, in an attack that managed to obtain administrator-level access to critical OpenAI systems.”

title: Cannabis addiction linked to 57% higher odds of suicidal thoughts
text:
A massive study involving more than 415,000 Americans has uncovered a concerning connection between cannabis use disorder and suicidal thoughts. Researchers found that adults with the disorder had 57% higher odds of experiencing suicidal thoughts, with women and younger adults facing particularly elevated risks.
As marijuana becomes more widely available and accepted, researchers are uncovering important questions about its effects on mental health. A major new study suggests that people who struggle to control their cannabis use face a substantially greater likelihood of experiencing suicidal thoughts.
Published in the Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs, the research found that adults with cannabis use disorder had 57% higher odds of reporting suicidal thoughts compared with those without the condition. Despite major shifts in marijuana laws and public attitudes, this troubling association remained remarkably consistent over a decade.
The findings come from an analysis of more than 415,000 American adults who participated in the National Survey on Drug Use and Health. Researchers examined data collected between 2014 and 2023, a period when cannabis became increasingly accessible across the United States.
"What surprised me most was not that cannabis use disorder was associated with suicidal thoughts, but that this association did not appear to strengthen over time," said lead author Tosin Philip Oyetunji, MPH, a doctoral student in public health at the University of California, Merced. "[Yet,] it remains an important mental health concern that deserves attention."
Cannabis and Suicidal Thoughts Show a Persistent Link
The connection between cannabis use disorder and suicidal thinking was observed across different age groups, sexes, and racial and ethnic backgrounds. However, women and younger adults showed particularly elevated risks.
Importantly, the association remained even after researchers accounted for depression, psychological distress, and other factors that could influence mental health outcomes.
The consistency of the results was especially notable given how dramatically the cannabis landscape has changed. Recreational marijuana is now legal in half of U.S. states, and cannabis products have become increasingly potent. These developments have raised concerns among public health experts about whether broader access might contribute to worsening mental health.
Yet the study offers some reassurance on that particular question. Sidra Goldman-Mellor, PhD, a professor of public health at UC Merced and the study's senior author, noted that the association between cannabis use disorder and suicidal thoughts did not become stronger during the 10 years examined.
"Suicidal ideation does not seem to have increased among people with cannabis use disorder, despite all this legal and social change," explained Goldman-Mellor. Yet, "people with cannabis use disorder are still at a very substantially increased likelihood of experiencing serious suicidal thoughts, and that's not something that is widely understood."
Why Cannabis Use Disorder Matters
The researchers stress that these findings should not be interpreted as evidence that everyone who uses marijuana faces the same elevated risk.
The study focused specifically on cannabis use disorder, a condition in which people have difficulty controlling their marijuana consumption even when it causes problems in their lives. Someone with the disorder may continue using cannabis despite harmful consequences or repeated attempts to cut back.
This distinction is important because problematic cannabis use differs from occasional or otherwise nonproblematic consumption.
The findings also do not establish that cannabis use disorder directly causes suicidal thoughts. Because the research identified an association rather than a cause-and-effect relationship, it cannot determine whether problematic cannabis use contributes to suicidal thinking, whether underlying mental health difficulties contribute to both conditions, or whether other factors help explain the connection.
Nevertheless, the results point to a significant mental health concern that deserves greater recognition, particularly among people seeking help for problematic cannabis use.
Researchers Urge Greater Mental Health Screening
One practical implication is that health care professionals should look beyond cannabis consumption itself when evaluating patients with cannabis use disorder.
Rather than focusing exclusively on depression or substance use symptoms, clinicians may benefit from asking patients directly about suicidal thoughts as part of a broader mental health assessment. This could help identify people who need additional care but whose struggles might otherwise remain unnoticed.
"Someone seeking help for cannabis use disorder may also be experiencing suicidal thoughts that are not immediately apparent," said Oyetunji. "The goal is not to assume that everyone with cannabis use disorder is suicidal but to identify those who may need additional assessment, treatment, or support."
The study arrives at a time when marijuana is increasingly viewed as a relatively low-risk substance. Public perceptions have shifted considerably, and negative attitudes toward cannabis have declined alongside expanding legalization and social acceptance.
However, these changes have not eliminated the mental health challenges associated with cannabis use disorder. Even though the strength of the association with suicidal thoughts did not increase over the study period, the elevated odds remained substantial.
The researchers suggest that health care providers, policymakers, and community organizations can play an important role by improving awareness, identifying vulnerable individuals, and making appropriate mental health support more accessible.
As attitudes toward marijuana continue to evolve, the findings serve as a reminder that the needs of people experiencing problematic cannabis use should remain a public health priority.
Said Oyetunji, "As cannabis becomes more accessible and socially accepted, we should ensure that the people struggling with its use are not overlooked."

title: In National Geographic’s “Expedition: Saving Our Seas,” it’s all hands on deck
text:
As documentaries about Earth’s accelerating climate crisis go, Expedition: Saving Our Seas is surprisingly buoyant.
The ocean covers more than two-thirds of Earth’s surface. And “as the climate heats up, our seas are under pressure like never before,” narrator Auli’i Cravalho, the voice of the title character in Disney’s Moana, says at the opening of The National Geographic Society’s new documentary. The film documents how oceanographers are racing to document and mitigate climate change’s impacts on ocean and coastal habitats.
Expedition: Saving Our Seas premieres November 13 on the National Geographic Channel at 9pm EST and streams the next day on Disney+ and Hulu.
Despite that solemn mission, Expedition: Saving Our Seas is full of hope — and stunning visuals. The documentary offers a window into the scientists’ wonder and joy in their work as they discover new life forms in the depths of the Southern Ocean, or successfully nurture young corals threatened by warming in the Pacific Ocean.
The film opens with a twist on the usual world map: At the center is one great ocean, surrounded by land. Trivia buffs know Earth has five oceans: the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic. But geographic names aside, these five oceans are just one, linked by a global system of currents known as the Great Ocean Conveyor Belt.
“It’s this giant connected ocean that ignores all of the political boundaries, ignores all of the names we call them,” says Andrew Thurber, a biological oceanographer at the University of California, Santa Barbara, whose research is among those featured in the film.
The documentary loosely follows the current’s path as it zips around the world from project to project.
The first project in the documentary is Thurber’s. He’s on board a research vessel in the frigid Southern Ocean, which rings Antarctica. Using a remotely-operated vehicle dubbed SuBastian, Thurber and his colleagues are scanning the seafloor, hunting for the world’s southernmost hydrothermal vent.
Hydrothermal vents spew superhot, chemically-enriched seawater. In the generally nutrient-poor Southern Ocean, that makes these vents a potential food oasis to support deep sea life.
Throughout the night, as the ROV scans the seafloor, Thurber and his colleagues stay glued to the video it sends back, oohing and aahing as never-before-seen life-forms come into view. “It was a marathon of excitement,” he says now.
Then they see it: A large black smoker, the southernmost hydrothermal vent ever found. And all around it: swarms of pregnant female krill.
“That blew all of our minds,” Thurber says. Krill are the keystone species of the entire Southern Ocean food web, a crucial food source for baleen whales, seals, penguins and fish. But krill are threatened by both industrial fishing and climate change. This discovery, Thurber says, helps make the case for a marine protected area, a region where fishing and other human activities should be restricted.
From the Southern Ocean, the Great Ocean Conveyor Belt flows thousands of kilometers to the north, where marine ecologist Maiyai Taal Hocheimy is tracking how the rising waters of the Atlantic Ocean are encroaching on Banjul, the capital of The Gambia in West Africa. Her hope is that salt-tolerant mangrove trees along the coast, with their dense network of soil-retaining roots, might help hold back the sea in the coming decades — provided that the community can be enlisted to help maintain the mangroves.
I found Hocheimy’s work especially inspiring because she is working to shape the future of oceanography. In 2017, she founded the GREAT (Gaining Research Experience in Africa for Tomorrow) Institute, the first aquatic and coastal science research institute in The Gambia. The mangrove project recruited young local scientists to help conduct the research.
“The goal is to train the next generation of environmental stewards,” Hocheimy says. “We have to show that mangroves have value, so they’ll understand and want to protect them. It is their future at stake.”
That sentiment is echoed many times in the film — the importance not only of enlisting young scientists but also centering local scientists who pose new questions that oceanographers who parachute in from other places may not think to ask, says marine biogeochemist Kristina Brown.
In the documentary, Brown, of the University of Manitoba in Canada, co-leads an expedition to explore the waters of Sherman Basin, a large bay north of the Arctic Circle in Nunavut, Canada. This region has been hunted and fished by Inuit people for centuries.
But it might change beyond all recognition in the next few decades, Brown says. So, the local Inuit community invited her to help create the first catalog of what species are present in the waters and on the seafloor. “[It’s] the first project I’ve been involved in where the local community both defined the research questions and have brought their own unique expertise to the research project.”
Watching how communities around the world are increasingly taking ownership of studies in their own waters was, for me, the most exciting takeaway of this documentary.
“We want to democratize access to the deep sea, to enable people who haven’t had access to these kinds of tools to ask more and new questions,” says Katy Croff Bell, the founder and president of the Ocean Discovery League, a nonprofit ocean exploration group based in Saunderstown, Rhode Island.
As a result of inaccessibility, little of Earth’s vast ocean has been mapped, particularly the deep sea. Bell’s organization is developing inexpensive technologies such as a hardy little camera and sensor system dubbed DORIS, for Deep Ocean Research and Imaging System. It can descend to 6,000 meters and costs less than $10,000.
Expedition: Saving Our Seas offers just a few scant minutes to each project before moving on around the globe to the next, so there’s no time to learn about each project in depth. But the overall takeaway of watching these vignettes, back to back, is that there is a young, energetic community of scientists taking on the challenge.
Mitigating climate change’s impacts on the oceans is, after all, a race against time. So it’s nice to think we might have all hands on deck.

title: On this day in space! Nov. 17, 1967: NASA's Surveyor 6 moon probe makes 1st-ever successful launch and hop from the lunar surface
text:
On Nov. 17, 1967, NASA's Surveyor 6 spacecraft made the first liftoff from the lunar surface.
Surveyor 6 was one of several robotic lunar missions NASA sent to scout the moon before sending humans there. It took television pictures of the surface and learned about the composition of lunar soil. Then came the big liftoff.
First Surveyor 6 launched from the surface and hopped to another position about 8 feet (2 meters) away. Next, Surveyor 6 took pictures of its original landing site. Flight controllers on Earth could see the landing pad prints of Surveyor 6. They also saw an imprint from the rocket exhaust when Surveyor 6 lifted off.
Surveyor 6 showed that spacecraft could land on the moon, and lift off again. Less than two years later, humans did the same thing during Apollo 11.
Why it mattered
NASA's Surveyor 6 spacecraft launched to the moon on Nov. 7, 1967 and made its first landing on the lunar surface on Nov. 10 of that year. It's primary mission was to make a soft landing on the moon in the Sinus Medii of the moon.
The probe took nearly 30,000 photos of the moon during its 16 days on the lunar surface, with the lander shutting down due to the onset of lunar night on Nov. 26. Surveyor 6 was the sixth and penultimate moon mission of NASA's Surveyor lunar program, so a lot of what it did (launching and landing on the moon) had been done before.
But a lunar liftoff? That was something new.
"On November 17, as an engineering test to see if its rockets could be restarted on the Moon, Surveyor’s engines fired for 2.5 seconds, lifting the spacecraft 12 feet high and moving it 8 feet west of its original landing site, in the first powered liftoff from another celestial body," NASA wrote in a mission overview.
The engineering test proved that a spacecraft could land on the moon, and then lift off and take flight once more. That capability was a core requirement for NASA's Apollo astronaut moon landings that followed, since astronauts needed a way to return home after visiting the moon.
But there was critical science Surveyor 6 was able to do with the lunar hop.
"This maneuver provided excellent views of the surface disturbances produced by the initial landing and the effects of firing rocket engines close to the lunar surface," scientists with the Lunar and Planetary Institute wrote in a summary. "Photography obtained after the hop contributed to the soil mechanics investigation."
Surveyor 6 also had a bar magnet on its footpad that allowed scientists to test how magnetic the lunar regolith was at the landing site.
Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube.

title: Jensen Huang says he would be 'honoured' to return as Nvidia CEO if board asked him
text:
Jensen Huang said he would be "honoured" to return as the boss of tech giant Nvidia if the board asked him to, in his first public comments since his shock resignation.
"I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely," Huang said on X, days after reports he had extramarital affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy.
He said he had an "outpouring" of calls from company employees, investors and others calling for him to return as CEO of Nvidia.
But, as the BBC reported on Monday, Nvidia's board is not considering bringing him back to lead the company.
The prospect of Huang returning at this point looks unlikely.
The company's board is investigating his conduct, which includes an alleged affair with an Nvidia executive.
The AI chip giant is set to report its financial results later on Tuesday, during which the company's interim chief executive, Collette Kress, may address the situation with Huang.
Beyond the internal Nvidia investigation, Huang's affair with a woman suspected of being an asset for Beijing is set to see the billionaire questioned before multiple committees of US lawmakers in the weeks ahead.
The Nvidia founder said he had "made serious mistakes in my personal life".
Nonetheless, Huang's statement appeared to show some hope he would be able to move past the major corporate scandal.
Huang said people have continued to "reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics".
"If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honoured to answer these calls and return as CEO," Huang added.
Many technology executives in recent days have praised Huang's role in the artificial intelligence boom. A petition began circulating online over the weekend calling for his reinstatement at the company.
Yet, by Monday, many executives were not openly calling for Huang's return.
Brad Gerstner, a major tech investor who knows Huang personally and also holds a significant stake in Nvidia, last week wrote an open letter saying that Nvidia could consider Huang's reinstatement.
On Monday, Gerstner said during an event hosted by Semafor that his letter had been misunderstood and the investigation into Huang's conduct needed to run its course.
While Gerstner questioned the facts around Huang's departure, he added: "I don't know to what degree he misled the board. If I was on a board I would take that very seriously. Let's be clear no one is above the law."

title: Fossil-fuel industry accused of violating Colorado law over not disclosing drilling chemicals
text:
The fossil-fuel industry is violating Colorado law by not disclosing which chemicals it uses in drilling, a new analysis by the FracTracker Alliance non-profit alleges, and state records show it has used illegal or dangerous compounds while fracking.
Drilling chemicals can include xylene, toluene, benzene, Pfas and other dangerous toxicants, industry records and literature from other regions show. A first-in-the-nation 2022 Colorado law requires fossil-fuel operators and their suppliers to make public all chemicals used in “downhole oil and gas production”. But regulators have exempted compounds used in drilling, claiming that drilling is not part of production.
FracTracker contends this exemption contradicts the widely held definition of production, including that implied in Colorado’s regulatory literature.
Legislators who authored the law, public health groups, and industry all use definitions of “production” that includes drilling, FracTracker states, and it notes the law requires “disclosure of all chemicals used underground or ‘downhole’ in oil and gas wells”.
Meanwhile, at least five chemicals that were reported for use in fracking are prohibited by Colorado law, FracTracker alleges. It also found fossil-fuel companies reported using at least three highly toxic chemicals that raise serious safety questions.
About 43,000 people live within a mile of the state’s wells, and many within a few hundred feet. Regulators are flying blind on what the sum impact of the chemicals may be, the authors allege.
“This is a public health crisis and it should be treated as such,” Shannon Smith, FracTracker’s executive director, told the Guardian. FracTacker is a non-profit that investigates and monitors public health threats created by the fossil-fuel industry, and advocates for protections. It began in Pennsylvania in 2010, but now organizes nationally.
Fracking operators and their suppliers are supposed to disclose all downhole chemical ingredients to the Colorado Energy and Carbon Management Commission (ECMC) regulatory agency within 150 days. The agency then must post the chemicals on its website.
ECMC literature implies the agency considers drilling as part of oil and gas production. In a statement, an ECMC spokesperson said the agency was “aware of differing views regarding the scope and implementation of the chemical disclosure requirements”.
“We are applying the law and Commission rules under the current statutory and regulatory framework while continuing to work with stakeholders to clarify these issues and support consistent, appropriate implementation,” the spokesperson said.
Halliburton, Chevron and Occidental Petroleum are among the state’s top fossil-fuel producers.
In a statement, a Chevron spokesperson said the company “is committed to safe and responsible operations in Colorado”.
“We take chemical-disclosure requirements seriously and remain focused on meeting our obligations and maintaining transparent, responsible operating practices,” the spokesperson added.
In order to drill wells and extract minerals, fossil-fuel operators pump huge volumes of pressurized liquid into the earth to fracture – or “frack” – bedrock, stimulating the release of trapped oil and gas. These fluids are mostly water and sand by volume, but they also contain industrial chemicals, including biocides, surfactants and lubricants.
Hundreds of studies have pointed to health risks for those in fracking regions. Toxic chemicals such as formaldehyde, Pfas and benzene have been widely detected or reported in fracking fluids. These and other chemicals used – or thought to be used – in production are linked to issues such as cancer, hormone disruption and neurological damage.
Gas companies reported as many as 11 spills a week in 2018, and people are exposed to the chemicals through multiple pathways, including groundwater, above ground spills, wastewater seepage into drinking water supplies, and air emissions.
The ECMC has told FracTracker that it does not consider drilling to be part of the fracking and production said the report’s author, Dusty Horwitt, FracTracker’s senior research and policy counsel.
“That was news to us, and it is not consistent with The American Petroleum Institute definition of what oil and gas production is,” Horwitt added. API literature shows oil and gas production includes “drilling, extraction, and recovery of oil from underground”.
Meg Froelich, the Colorado state representative who co-wrote the 2022 legislation, said she intended for drilling chemicals to be disclosed. The legislation is called “Concerning enhanced oversight of the chemicals used in oil and gas production.” Production includes drilling, Froelich said.
She accused the ECMC of “word-parsing” and added that she was “mad about their stalling”.
“The law covers everything that goes downhole because everything that goes downhole has the potential to affect neighbors,” Froelich told the Guardian.
The ECMC until recent years has largely worked to promote the fossil-fuel industry, and only since Democrats took over the state government has it shifted to also protect public health, but the shift has come in “fits and starts”, Froelich said.
State records show that wells covered by law operated without drilling chemical disclosure for at least a collective 843,369 days from the rules’ implementation to May 16, when the analysis was conducted.
The law also requires fossil-fuel companies to provide schools, first responders and other community institutions with lists of chemicals it uses, but it has failed to do that, advocates say.
The report comes after a previous analysis reported on by the Guardian found Colorado fossil-fuel companies pumped at least 30m lb of secret chemicals into the ground over an 18-month period without making legally required disclosures. Out of over 1,100 fracked sites across the state, companies did not disclose 675, or about 60%.
Since then, the compliance rate is closer to 100% – except for the drilling chemicals, advocates say.
The report raises questions about which chemicals are being used for drilling. A recent law banned any use of Pfas at oil and gas sites, and industry literature and peer-reviewed research suggests that Pfas are a common drilling chemical. Horwitt told the Guardian he fears the chemicals may be used in Colorado.
“Publications, including those issued by major oil and gas-producing nations Canada and Norway, report that PFAS is used for multiple purposes in oil and gas production including drilling and enhanced oil recovery,” FracTracker states. The lack of drilling chemical disclosure in Colorado “creates uncertainty about whether companies are complying with the PFAS ban”, the report added.
Meanwhile, records from Ohio show the frequent use of xylene, the report states. The chemical can cause headaches, dizziness, confusion, loss of muscle coordination, and, in high doses, death.
FracTracker also points to five chemicals that were disclosed as being used for fracking on some well pads despite state rules prohibiting their use in fracking: 1-butanol, 2-butoxyethanol, 1,4-dioxane, N,N-dimethylformamide and BMPA. Some of these compounds are linked to cancer, liver disease, and harm to developing children.
In its statement, the ECMC said it had “issued notices of alleged violation when prohibited substances are identified, including cases involving 1-butanol, 2-butoxyethanol and 1,4-dioxane”.
Among potentially harmful chemicals that are permitted are acrylamide, ethylene oxide and methanol. FracTracker noted that those were among the chemicals disclosed as being used in a well in Galeton that sprayed a geyser of gas and at least 3.7m gallons of fluid for over four days in April 2025.
Living near wells has well-established links to leukemia, birth abnormalities and other serious health problems. Residents in July reported to the Guardian that they are plagued by loud noise, acrid air emissions, headaches, nosebleeds and respiratory issues.

title: Whistleblower: Deadly drone strike in Kuwait could’ve been avoided
text:
Washington, DC – An American soldier wounded in a deadly Iranian drone attack in Kuwait is accusing senior military officials of ignoring warnings and being ill-equipped ahead of launching the US-Israel war on Iran, according to a whistleblower complaint.
The complaint, obtained by Al Jazeera English on Tuesday, is tied to an Iranian one-way attack drone that evaded air defences at the outpost within the first 48 hours of the war. Six service members were killed, and dozens were injured, including the whistleblower. It remains the deadliest assault on US forces since the war commenced.
The 14-page letter, submitted on Friday to the House and Senate Armed Services committees, alleges that the army repeatedly brushed aside warnings that the Port of Shuaiba in Kuwait was vulnerable to drone attacks. Though the site was fortified, there was no roof.
“The drone threat to the port was raised directly to the commanding general of the 1st Theater Sustainment Command at least three times in the week before hostilities,” the complaint states.
“Each warning was dismissed.”
The soldier, who is not named, also alleges the installation had “no physician, no fixed aid station, and only one ambulance”, adding that at least one of those killed “could have survived” if there was adequate medical support on site.
The army says it has completed its investigation of the Port of Shuaiba attack but has not publicly released its findings.
In a news conference following the incident, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth described the drone as a “squirter” that “happened to hit a tactical operations centre that was fortified”.
But senior military leaders have acknowledged that Iran’s Shahed attack drones, known to fly low and slow, have inflicted more damage on the battlefield than anticipated.
Tehran has repeatedly targeted US and allied assets with attack drones and ballistic missiles. As a result, more than 23 American service members have been killed.
The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the allegations.

title: Duffy pitches Senate GOP on $50 billion for FAA after ground stop
text:
Washington — Senate Republicans appeared skeptical Tuesday after Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy made the case for tens of billions of more dollars for the Federal Aviation Administration following a that prompted a rare last week.
Overloaded routers prompted the FAA to issue the ground stop on Friday, resulting in thousands of canceled flights and stranded travelers.
to overhaul the FAA's systems, some of which still rely on technology that is decades old. There was widespread concern among lawmakers about the problem, but GOP senators questioned the funding figure — and how the money could get approved.
Speaking at a news conference following a closed-door lunch meeting with Duffy, Senate Majority Leader John Thune said the secretary "fielded a lot of questions" about the funding and how it would be utilized.
"How we deal with that issue remains to be seen," Thune said. "There are ways in which we could do it with Republicans only, there are also ways in which we could do it with Democrats."
Senate Republicans have been considering pursuing another reconciliation bill, which would allow them to move forward without help from across the aisle. But the legislative maneuver is complicated and time-consuming. Thune said Republicans are continuing to have conversations, which will stretch into Wednesday, but he acknowledged that "the clock is ticking" down to the end of the current Congress.
Congress allocated $12.5 billion for the FAA in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act just last year. Duffy said the bulk of that money has been set aside for various projects, and Thune pointed to the funds on Tuesday, acknowledging that "we needed air traffic modernization."
"We did that then — there's more that's required," Thune said. "How that gets done is still an open question."
Thune suggested some senators have concerns about the $50 billion figure. He said the total the administration initially sought before the ground stop — $30 billion — reflected "not just the immediate needs," but also "a number of other things that they want to do." He said some of those projects should be funded through the normal government funding process, not reconciliation.
When asked about the $20 billion difference, Duffy told CBS News that he "decided to put everything on the table."
"There's been a historic underinvestment in aviation," Duffy said. "I hope we get the full investment."
GOP Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana told reporters he was "furious when they went from $30 billion to $50 billion."
"I mean, I'm not Bambi's baby brother," Kennedy said.
Sen. Rick Scott of Florida thanked Duffy in a post on X, while expressing support for a smaller investment.
"We absolutely need to update our air traffic control system, which would cost about $10 billion," Scott wrote, while stressing that "the airlines need to put up money and have skin in this game too."
But other Senate Republicans were entirely supportive of the transportation secretary's pitch. Sen. Eric Schmitt of Missouri, who's been working with the administration on proposed aviation infrastructure funding, told reporters that "the needs are pretty broad and pretty deep" for tech upgrades.
"So my position is: Let's go fix this on behalf of the American people," he said. "They saw what happened. I think they would want us to be responsive to that."
Schmitt advocated for approving the funds through reconciliation. He said he doesn't want to "make this partisan," but "some of my Democrat colleagues, I think, are taking a different tack."
"I was advocating for this before Friday, and then what we saw Friday, I just think this is something that we should do," Schmitt said. "I can't think of anything more important than the safety of the millions of Americans that fly."
Speaking after the meeting, Duffy said the engagement from Republicans was "fantastic." He said the GOP plans to "work through what they think is the right approach, the right funding levels, to make sure we have the resources to address the needs of the American airspace."
Duffy outlined his new request to Congress, saying the U.S. needs a new network that is "resilient," and an investment in infrastructure, like air traffic control towers, new runways and for airports more broadly. Asked about a piecemeal approach, Duffy said he'll take what he can get. But he said if the status quo continues, "I will replace every single tower in America in 300 years."
"So we have to do something different," Duffy said.

title: Apple joins a parade of technology hiccups in recent days
text:
A pair of technology failures at Apple and Marriott International follows several other recent major outages at the Federal Aviation Administration, United Airlines and Microsoft, highlighting the risks of relying on just a few major providers of essen...
An update gone awry Tuesday at Apple followed a rash of major outages in recent days, including problems affecting the Federal Aviation Administration, United Airlines and Microsoft.
Apple acknowledged on its system status page that its Apple Music, App Store and AppleCare services suffered full outages and that its iCloud sign-in interface was also having issues. The technology monitoring site Downdetector.com also showed a spike in user complaints about Apple Pay.
“Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning,” the company said in an emailed statement. “We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible.”
Marriott International, the largest U.S. hotel operator, also had technology issues affecting reservations and check-ins, among other problems, according to users posting on Reddit. Downdetector.com also reported that Marriott was experiencing an outage.
Marriott, which has 10,200 properties and more than 1.8 million rooms under its corporate umbrella, did not immediately respond to an email inquiry from The Associated Press.
The outages are the latest in a string of technology breakdowns.
On Monday, a system outage at United Airlines lasted more than 90 minutes, forcing the carrier to delay departing flights. The problem at United came just days after a malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration’s network prompted a nationwide ground stop that delayed hundreds of flights and stranded hundreds of thousands of travelers across the country.
Chicago-based United said there was no indication its outage was cybersecurity-related.
Also Monday, thousands of customers reported difficulty accessing online accounts at several major U.S. banks and the money transfer service Zelle after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system.
Chase said Monday the technical problems were not the result of a cyberattack, and on Tuesday confirmed the bank's systems were operating normally.
Last week, a global Microsoft outage disrupted email and other workplace tools, plunging business chatter and everyday services into disarray worldwide. Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot, were interrupted.
The tech giant said there was “no indication” that malicious activity caused the disruptions, specifically noting on Friday that the outage was not related to a cyberattack or artificial intelligence agents.

title: Rights court rules Turkey must release jailed lawmaker Atalay
text:
The European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) ruled against Turkey over the detention of human rights lawyer and elected lawmaker Can Atalay.
The ECHR published its decision on Tuesday, saying that Turkey must release Atalay and allow him to take up his seat in the Turkish parliament.
The court ruled that his continued detention had been intended to silence him and undermine political pluralism.
It ordered Turkey to pay him €32,500 (about $35,700) in compensation.
The judges stressed that Atalay's case should not be considered separately, but rather in the wider context of the detention of political opponents, human rights activists and journalists in Turkey.
Turkey was among the original signatories of the European Convention on Human Rights. Yet it has previously refused to comply with the court's decisions in the cases of rights activist Osman Kavala and prominent Kurdish politician Selahattin Demirtas.
From leading activist to a jailed member of parliament
As a lawyer, Atalay represented victims in numerous social and political cases in Turkey, as well as in freedom of speech cases involving journalists and writers.
He was also among the leading voices in the 2013 Gezi protests, which the government called an attempted coup.
Because of his involvement in the protests, Atalay, along with seven others, was sentenced to 18 years in prison in April 2022 for "aiding and abetting an attempted coup."
Continuing his struggle from the infamous Silivri prison, Atalay ran as a candidate for the Workers' Party of Turkey (TIP) in the 2023 parliamentary elections.
A candidate for the earthquake-hit province of Hatay, he won his seat but was denied release despite multiple rulings by the Constitutional Court, Turkey's top court.
His parliamentary status was revoked in 2024, a decision the Constitutional Court later overturned. President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's party stopped the opposition from formally reading the decision in parliament.
Although a year later an opposition lawmaker read the decision in parliament, Atalay remains in jail.
After the ECHR's ruling was published, TIP leader Erkan Bas took to social media to call for Atalay's release and the restoration of his parliamentary mandate.

title: Irish man indicted for allegedly destroying $60 million US military aircraft at Shannon Airport
text:
An Irish national was indicted for breaking into and destroying a $60 million U.S. Air National Guard C-130 Hercules aircraft parked on a taxiway at Shannon Airport in County Clare, Ireland, the DOJ announced on Tuesday.
Daithi O’Corrain, also known as David Curran, is accused of carrying out a planned attack “against a U.S. military aircraft, causing tens of millions of dollars in damage and jeopardizing critical military operations,” the FBI said in a statement.
On April 11, O’Corrain “breached the security perimeter” of the airport and gained entry to the aircraft by breaking the lock on a crew door and barricaded himself inside while inflicting “severe damage to the interior,” according to the indictment.
The 48-year-old was charged with destruction of government property, which carries a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison.
O’Corrain is accused of cutting wire bundles and hydraulic lines, destroying every gauge in the Aircraft’s cockpit, and puncturing the Aircraft’s air ducts.
The government also alleges O’Corrain brought multiple capsules of gallium, a highly corrosive metal that is a liquid at room temperature, and eats through aluminum in minutes and causes long-term corrosion to steel.
Hours after he entered the airport, the flight crew returned to the aircraft to depart and spotted O’Corrain through a cockpit window and notified Shannon Airport security.
Crew members then watched him escape out of a hatch in the aircraft’s roof, allegedly striking with an axe.
O’Corrain was then arrested by Irish law enforcement.
The Department of Justice alleges O’Corrain’s attack effectively destroyed the aircraft.
“The damage inflicted rendered the Aircraft inoperable, and the Aircraft—worth approximately $60 million—will not return to active flight status,” the indictment said.
“This was not an act of spontaneous vandalism. The defendant allegedly spent months researching the aircraft, acquiring tools and materials, and preparing to maximize the destruction he could inflict.”

title: French foreign minister slams Lavrov accusations about 'direct participation' in Ukraine war
text:
Russia said on Tuesday it was aware of French troops deployed to Ukraine, calling it "direct participation" in the war and saying a message had been issued to Paris. France has rejected the claim troops are directly involved in fighting as "absurd."
France's Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot has denied allegations of direct participation in the war in Ukraine, in response to comments made by Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov on Tuesday.
He said that France was not involved in a military operation, but in "training and maintenance, carried out far from the front lines, with very limited scope and no involvement in warfare", in an interview with French talk show "C à Vous".
He added that the majority of training had taken place in Poland.
"We support the Ukrainian army and the Ukrainian resistance, and this is the least we can do, given that it is a people fighting for their independence and democracy, on the doorstep of Europe", he stated.
Barrot also accused the leader of the hard-left France Unbowed party Jean-Luc Mélenchon of "relaying Russian propaganda", after the presidential hopeful shared an X stating "Alert. We must under no circumstances become a co-belligerent in Ukraine."
Barrot's comments come after Lavrov told reporters that "foreign military personnel" had been in Ukraine "for more than six months. And not just the French."
Lavrov declared that Russia had communicated concerns "through available channels", informing relevant countries that this amounted to "direct participation in the war, including target designation assistance, satellite data provision, and other forms of support."
His remarks follow revelations by French media, based on revelations from a source who disclosed that soldiers had been deployed on a secret training mission in Ukraine for several months to train personnel and help maintain equipment.
The source said the mission of a small contingent of French troops excludes any combat role. Speaking to AFP on condition of anonymity, they described the rotation of "French trainers supporting Ukraine in France, Poland, or occasionally in Ukraine" as a reality.
"But this is not a military operation. There is absolutely no intention of engaging in coercive actions", said the source.
Earlier on Tuesday, Deputy defence minister Alice Rufo told parliament that there was a "very limited" deployment of French troops in Ukraine for training and equipment maintenance.
She added that was no "intention to fight, contrary to what the Russian foreign minister said this morning, which is absurd."
In November, the European Council adopted a decision extending the mandate of the European Union Military Assistance Mission in support of Ukraine(EUMAM Ukraine) for a further two years, with a budget allocation of nearly €300 million for this period.

title: Vance’s midterm blame game hits snag as Trump’s own Israel ambassador disputes key claim
text:
U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee is pushing back against Vice President JD Vance’s suggestion that America’s relationship with Israel contributed to Republicans’ crushing midterm election losses, offering a sharply different explanation from within the Trump administration.
In an exclusive interview with The Press Service of Israel (TPS-IL) published Tuesday, Huckabee rejected the argument that Israel was responsible for the GOP’s electoral defeat, instead pointing to economic concerns, voter apathy and a failure to energize the Republican base.
"Israel was not the reason the elections went wrong for Republicans last week," Huckabee told TPS-IL.
The remarks come nearly two weeks after Vance blamed Republican losses on the war with Iran and dissatisfaction with Washington’s relationship with Israel.
In a Nov. 4 post on X, Vance argued, according to polling, that voters who supported the Trump-Vance ticket in 2024 had turned against Republicans over four key issues: ending the Iran war, addressing inflation and the cost of living, putting America first and changing the U.S. relationship with Israel.
"The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote, arguing that the party needed to acknowledge the political consequences of the conflict.
But Huckabee, a former Arkansas governor and longtime Evangelical leader, offered a competing assessment, arguing that Republicans had failed to give their own supporters sufficient motivation to vote.
"To say that Israel was on the minds of most people is, I think, ludicrous," Huckabee told TPS-IL.
Asked about Huckabee’s comments disputing the suggestion that the relationship with the State of Israel contributed to Republican losses in the midterms, a spokesperson for Vance told Fox News Digital: "The Vice President did not blame Jews for the Republican Party’s losses in the midterms. The Vice President has forcefully condemned antisemitism on countless occasions, and he will continue to do so."
He acknowledged that the war may have influenced voters' perceptions, particularly as families struggled with higher fuel and food costs. "There’s no doubt that the war may have had some impact, not because it was the war itself, but there was such a media coverage that said that the war is what was creating the economic challenges," he said.
"But it was the economic issues," Huckabee continued, adding that the war in Iran "may have contributed to prices, but it wasn't the only thing. There were a lot of factors involved."
"If you look at the real numbers, the exit polls showed that only 17% of Evangelicals went and voted last week," Huckabee told TPS-IL. "There is no bloc of voters that is more critical to a Republican victory than Evangelical voters in the United States. They represent 80 million people. If they go vote in mass numbers, Republicans win, if they stay home, Republicans lose."
The ambassador’s remarks referred to exit polling showing that white evangelical Christians accounted for 17% of voters in the 2026 midterms, compared with 23% in 2024. That figure reflects their share of the electorate, rather than the percentage of evangelicals who voted.
"The real reason was that Republicans did not give even Republicans a good reason to go vote for them. They had the White House, they had the Senate, and they had the House. And if you ask the average American, what have they gotten done in the last two years? They could not provide for you very many, if anything, that the Congress had passed, accomplished, that they had expected them to get done."
"So it's, it's unfortunate that Israel would factor in as a major reason for the vote in America," he added, "Because it just does not appear that that is as credible a reason as is that you had low turnout from the base of the Republican Party."
"The Democrats were excited. They went and voted in mass numbers, and they voted with enthusiasm. Enthusiasm wins elections; apathy does not."
Beyond the dispute over the midterm elections, Huckabee warned that additional U.S. military action against Iran remains a possibility if Tehran refuses to abandon its nuclear ambitions, while expressing hope that a diplomatic solution could still be reached.
"It's very possible that we will end up there, because if the Iranians do not understand what the president has made very clear, at least for the U.S. position, and that is they can't have a nuclear weapon," Huckabee told TPS-IL.
"Is it possible to bring this to a resolution by diplomatic means or economic pressure? Hey, I would hope so. That would be wonderful. But if it can't be done, then the U.S, has made it clear, certainly the president, Secretary Rubio, have both said, just this week that the military option is every bit on the table."
Huckabee said that Trump's position on Iran has remained consistent for decades, dating back to his years as a New York businessman in the early 1980s. He also pointed to the president's response to criticism that the war had contributed to Republican losses in the midterms. "He acknowledged, he said, it may have been a factor," Huckabee said. "And then he said, ‘But I would do it all over again.’"
The ambassador defended that position, arguing that Trump's decision to confront Iran was driven by threats to American national security rather than political calculations.
"It was because, for all these years, he's recognized the threat that they pose to America, not just to Israel," Huckabee said.
He cited Americans killed by Iran and Iranian-backed groups over the past several decades, including U.S. casualties in Iraq and Afghanistan, and referred to the Americans killed and taken hostage during the Oct. 7 Hamas terror attacks.
Huckabee praised Trump's willingness to accept potential political consequences, saying that even if the Iran issue had cost Republicans the election, the president would have made the same decision.
"His job is not just to win in the election, [it] is to protect Americans," Huckabee said. "That's first and foremost, and I'm happy to have a president who knows that and who practices that."
The ambassador also addressed Israel’s political future, saying Washington would work with whichever Israeli government emerges following the country’s elections, regardless of Trump’s close relationship with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. "The U.S. does not pick the government for Israel; the people do. However, it shakes up. We are committed to working with the government," he told TPS-IL.
He also expressed hope for expanding the Abraham Accords, pointing to the United Arab Emirates as an example of the diplomatic and economic benefits of normalization.

title: The long wait is almost over. Here's what to know about the upcoming release of 'Grand Theft Auto VI'
text: LOS ANGELES (AP) — "Grand Theft Auto" has never been much for following the rules. Nearly three decades after a video game built around stealing cars, outrunning police and embracing criminal mayhem first arrived, the franchise has survived controversy, transformed open-world gaming and become one of the biggest sellers in entertainment. READ MORE: Grand Theft Auto maker buys FarmVille company in $12.7 billion deal Now, after a 13-year wait since its last main installment, "Grand Theft Auto VI" is preparing for another big score. The latest chapter arrives Nov. 19 with a return to the neon-soaked streets of Vice City with two protagonists. For longtime fans, "GTA VI" is a highly anticipated return. For everyone else, here's what to know about the blockbuster video game, its characters and the enormous business riding on its release. Why is 'Grand Theft Auto' such a big deal? The franchise began in 1997 as a relatively simple, top-down game that allowed players to roam fictional cities, steal vehicles, evade police and commit crimes. The release of "Grand Theft Auto III" in 2001 helped redefine open-world gaming. It gave players greater freedom to explore a sprawling three-dimensional city, pursue missions and interact with their surroundings. Later installments expanded that freedom with larger environments, cinematic storytelling, social satire and detailed worlds. The influence reached far beyond games about stealing cars. Ubisoft's Assassin's Creed series brought open-world exploration to historical settings, while Bethesda's The Elder Scrolls games expanded their own longstanding tradition of open-ended fantasy role-playing. Nintendo's "The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild" later emphasized experimentation and discovery, allowing players to use the environment itself to solve problems. For "Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas" and "Grand Theft Auto V," Rockstar Games recruited real-life gang members to help bring authenticity to background characters and dialogue. Former writer and audio director Lazlow Jones has said some performers challenged scripted lines, prompting developers to let them use language drawn from their own experiences. That attention to detail helped create the sense of a living world that became a hallmark of the franchise, even as the series drew criticism for its depictions of violence, crime and women. But controversy did not stop the franchise's commercial rise. According to publisher Take-Two Interactive, the franchise has sold more than 470 million units worldwide. "Grand Theft Auto V," released in 2013, accounts for more than 230 million of those units and reached $1 billion in retail sales in just three days. Its online multiplayer component, "Grand Theft Auto Online," has helped keep players engaged through years of updates, new activities and in-game purchases. When can players start playing 'GTA VI'? "Grand Theft Auto VI" will become playable at midnight local time on Nov. 19 on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X'S, according to Rockstar Games. That means players can begin playing at 12 a.m. in their respective time zones. In the United States, the game unlocks at midnight Eastern, Central, Mountain and Pacific time as Nov. 19 begins in each region. READ MORE: From Golden Retrievers to 'Grand Theft Auto' -- 10 exports you didn't know were Scottish Players who preordered the game digitally can already preload it, allowing the game files to be downloaded before launch. Preloading does not provide early access. How closely is Vice City based on Miami? "Grand Theft Auto VI" returns players to Vice City, Rockstar Games' fictional version of Miami and South Florida. Developers immersed themselves in the region while building the game, driving through Miami, the Florida Keys and surrounding communities, flying over the Everglades and researching the area's history and architecture. Rockstar has promised its largest and most detailed open-world experience yet. A woman poses for a photo while sitting on a "Vice Beach" sign ahead of the release of the video game Grand Theft Auto VI in Miami Beach, Florida, Nov. 16, 2026. Photo by Eva Marie Uzcategui/ Reuters Miami is also leaning into its fictional alter ego ahead of the release. Miami-Dade County struck a $3.9 million promotional deal with Rockstar that includes a giant "Welcome to Vice City" display atop the Miami Heat's Kaseya Center, while Miami and Miami Beach have launched their own promotions tied to the game. The Heat will also wear black-and-pink "Vice City" jerseys on the eve of the release. Not everyone has embraced the connection. Some South Florida officials have criticized using public resources to promote a franchise known for crime and violence, while supporters argue the campaign allows the region to capitalize on the enormous attention surrounding the game. What's the story behind 'Grand Theft Auto VI'? This time, the action returns to Vice City, Rockstar's fictional version of Miami, and expands across the surrounding state of Leonida, a Florida-inspired setting filled with beaches, highways, nightlife and criminal enterprises. At the center are Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, a couple trying to improve their circumstances through a life of crime. Lucia has recently been released from prison while Jason, a former soldier who became involved with drug runners in the Leonida Keys, is looking for a different path. Their plans become more complicated when a seemingly straightforward criminal job goes wrong, drawing them into a conspiracy that stretches across Leonida. The trailers suggest a story mixing romance, robberies, betrayals and the series' familiar satirical take on American culture. Rockstar has revealed several supporting characters, including bank robber Raul Bautista, aspiring music executive Dre'Quan Priest and nightclub owner Boobie Ike. Who's in the cast? Rockstar has kept much of the voice cast under wraps, including the performers behind Lucia and Jason. WATCH: A look at some of the best video games of 2025 One familiar actor has confirmed his involvement: Stephen Root, known for his work in "Office Space," "King of the Hill" and "Barry." He told The Associated Press in September that he appears in the game, adding that fans had already recognized his distinctive voice in promotional footage. Root has been identified in reports as the voice of Brian Heder, an aging drug runner operating out of the Leonida Keys. Rockstar has introduced the character but has not publicly confirmed Root's casting in that specific role. What makes this installment different? Beyond the return to Vice City, one of the biggest changes is the focus on two protagonists whose relationship drives the story. "Grand Theft Auto V" featured three playable main characters. The new installment centers on Lucia and Jason as partners navigating the criminal underworld together. A Lamborghini drives past a "Vice City" sign ahead of the release of the video game Grand Theft Auto VI in Miami, Nov. 16, 2026. Photo by Eva Marie Uzcategui/ Reuters Rockstar has promoted a larger, more detailed setting that stretches beyond the city into the wider state of Leonida. The game also arrives in a vastly different technological landscape from its predecessor, with newer consoles capable of supporting more elaborate environments and character interactions. But not every detail is known. Rockstar has offered trailers and promotional previews, while questions remain about the full range of activities, how the game's systems will work and the future of its online multiplayer experience. What about the music? Music has long been part of Grand Theft Auto's identity. It has included everything from fictional radio stations to the songs accompanying players as they cruise through the game's cities. "Grand Theft Auto VI" is expanding that tradition with an original score by Justice, the Grammy-winning French electronic duo of Gaspard Augé and Xavier de Rosnay. Rockstar says the score adapts to players' actions and experiences throughout the game, shifting with the environments and situations they encounter. A 30-track score album is scheduled for Dec. 11, featuring collaborations with artists including Tame Impala, SZA, King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard and Gesaffelstein. The game also features in-game radio stations and a separate collection of original songs, continuing the franchise's connection to popular music.

title: Aschenbrenner’s Situational Awareness made AI bets again before October rout
text:
Leopold Aschenbrenner's artificial intelligence-themed hedge fund Situational Awareness, which nearly collapsed in July, loaded back up on AI stocks as it returned to the financial markets at the end of the third quarter. But all of its holdings are down big the last month and a half.
According to a new regulatory filing, as the fund got back on its feet Aschenbrenner took an equity position in Australian neocloud company SharonAI valued at more than $440 million, along with equity stakes in AI-centric plays Cleanspark, IREN, Bitdeer Technologies and Fermi. The Cleanspark stake is worth almost $39 million, while Iren and Bitdeer stakes are more than $21 million and more than $20 million, respectively. Fermi, meanwhile, has a value of more than $11 million.
The fund also owned call options at the end of September in neocloud Nebius, memory chip name Sandisk, the Roundhill Memory ETF (DRAM) and data center power play Bloom Energy. Sandisk and Nebius were key holdings that almost took out his fund over the summer.
All of these Situational Awareness holdings have been routed since Sept. 30. SharonAI is at the top of that list, seeing a 58% loss in October. It's also fallen 11% so far this month. IREN was down 41% in October, while Nebius declined 35%. Last week, Nebius plummeted more than 16% in a single day after the company issued a weak full-year forecast.
It's not known whether the hedge fund manager got out of those positions during the October AI selloff. The 13F filing is just a snapshot of what the hedge fund held at the end of the quarter.
Aschenbrenner — who launched the fund in 2024 after rising to fame that same year with his AI manifesto also entitled Situational Awareness — re-entered financial markets a bit in September, sources told CNBC at the time.
The Monday filing shows he picked up right where he left off.
The near-collapse of his hedge fund over the summer forced him to sell all of its public equity positions to Ken Griffin's Citadel. The fund had $45 billion in assets at its peak, but that tumbled to around $10 billion, consisting mostly of private stakes.
Stocked tethered to the AI trade took a hit in the most recent quarter as investors grew concerned about a slowdown in development of the technology. Those fears were spurred by comments from industry leaders such as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman back in September, with the latter saying that the company going public this year would be "ill-advised."
Since then, pressure on the trade has only continued.
In recent weeks, investors have worried about how Democratic wins in the midterm elections could hinder data center development, whether some technology companies are using too much debt to finance the AI buildout and what role Nvidia will play in that financing with Jensen Huang now out as CEO at the company.
Losses in Nvidia as well as other AI-related stocks dragged down the three leading U.S. indexes during Monday's session as investors continued to assess the fallout of Huang's departure.

title: Google expands access to Gemini Tasks, which can help with calls, purchases
text:
Google is expanding the rollout of Tasks, a toggle in Gemini that converts the chatbot into a more active helper.
Unlike Gemini’s Chat, which merely allows users to talk to Google’s AI assistant for informational purposes, Tasks empowers the app to complete basic secretarial functions, deputizing it as a kind of personal assistant.
How, specifically, can you use it? Google says that the app can call businesses and book appointments on users’ behalf; it can also complete purchases for them via Google Pay, and even sign into websites securely if prompted to do so.
In a blog post, Josh Woodword, VP of Gemini, claims to have recently used the feature to call local car dealerships to schedule a service appointment for his family’s minivan. He says he also used it to analyze his electrical bill.
Tasks was initially launched to select testers back in May as Gemini Spark, a 24/7 agentic helper, and was expanded to U.S. subscribers of its Google AI Ultra tier. Gemini Spark eventually became “Task Mode.” Google is now making the feature available for free to hundreds of millions of people who are using the company’s new Gemini 4 Hydrogen model.
Getting the function up and running is easy. Users merely flip a toggle within the app from Chat to Tasks, which enables the feature. Users can also send texts to Gemini or call the app to give it commands.

title: The data is very preliminary, but Vulcan failure may not be due to BE-4 engines
text:
United Launch Alliance (ULA) confirmed Tuesday morning that its return-to-flight launch of the Vulcan rocket began failing during the initial stages of the mission.
“While we appear to have lost telemetry and the mission at approximately 10 minutes into flight, early indications are that just after liftoff, the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance, resulting in stage separation occurring when the vehicle was low in altitude and below minimal velocity to reach orbit,” the company said.
The launch company also confirmed reporting by Ars that the Centaur V upper stage and the solid rocket boosters performed nominally during the flight.
Critically, ULA did not provide any specific information about the “low booster performance.” This matters greatly because the core stage of the Vulcan rocket is powered by two BE-4 engines, which are provided by Blue Origin. That company’s own New Glenn rocket uses a similar but slightly more powerful version of the BE-4 engine. And New Glenn experienced its own catastrophic failure in May during a ground test, a failure that later was attributed to a main oxygen valve on one of the BE-4 engines.
Preliminary data review
Information about the Vulcan failure is being closely held by ULA and Blue Origin, who have only acknowledged that they’re working together to investigate the cause. According to two sources, the investigation is “incredibly complicated” and remains in the early stages.
However, according to preliminary data, two independent sources indicated to Ars that the problem is currently believed to have originated on the launch vehicle side rather than in the engines themselves. The issue may be related to systems that feed methane and liquid oxygen propellant to the engines.
ULA engineers are looking at the possibility that one of the two BE-4 engines started producing lower thrust shortly after liftoff and never ramped back up to full throttle for the remainder of the burn. Video observations from high-zoom tracking cameras appeared to show one engine slightly dimmer than the other after Vulcan jettisoned its solid rocket boosters nearly two minutes into flight. An asymmetric shutdown of the BE-4 engines could also have contributed to the sudden attitude motion indicated by ULA’s telemetry-driven real-time animation near stage separation.

title: Wine, beer, or spirits? Massive study reveals a surprising health divide
text:
A massive study of more than 340,000 adults found that moderate wine drinkers had a 21% lower risk of cardiovascular death, while even light consumption of beer, cider, or spirits was linked to increased risk. Although heavy drinking was harmful regardless of beverage type, the findings suggest that the relationship between alcohol and health may be more complicated than previously thought.
A massive study involving more than 340,000 adults has uncovered a surprising difference in the health risks associated with wine, beer, cider, and spirits. Although heavy drinking was linked to worse health outcomes regardless of the beverage, the picture was more complicated among people who consumed smaller amounts of alcohol.
Researchers found that low to moderate wine consumption was associated with a lower risk of death, particularly from cardiovascular disease.
