In contrast, similar amounts of beer, cider, and spirits were linked to a higher risk. The findings, presented at the American College of Cardiology's Annual Scientific Session (ACC.26), suggest that both the type and quantity of alcohol may influence its relationship with long-term health.
The results also reinforce a broader conclusion from previous research: drinking less alcohol is generally better for health. Importantly, the new findings do not establish that wine itself protects against disease.
"These results come from the general population, and in certain high-risk groups, such as people with chronic diseases or cardiovascular conditions, the risks could be even higher," said Zhangling Chen, MD, PhD, a professor at the Second Xiangya Hospital, Central South University in China and the study's senior author.
How a Study of 340,000 Adults Measured Alcohol Risk
To investigate the relationship between drinking habits and longevity, scientists examined data from 340,924 adults enrolled in the UK Biobank between 2006 and 2022. The UK Biobank is a large research resource that collects health and lifestyle information to help scientists investigate factors associated with disease and mortality.
Participants reported their alcohol consumption through dietary questionnaires when they joined the study. Researchers then classified them into four groups based on how much pure alcohol they typically consumed each day or week, rather than simply counting drinks.
This distinction matters because beer, wine, and spirits contain different concentrations of alcohol. For comparison, a 12-ounce can of beer, a 5-ounce glass of wine, and a 1.5-ounce shot of spirits each provide approximately 14 grams of pure alcohol.
People consuming fewer than 20 g (about 1.5 standard drinks) per week were placed in the never or occasional drinking group. Low consumption was defined as 20 g per week up to 20 g per day for men, and 20 g per week up to 10 g per day for women.
Moderate drinking was defined as 20 g to 40 g (about 1.5 to three standard drinks) daily for men and 10 g to 20 g daily for women. High consumption meant more than 40 g (about three drinks) per day for men or more than 20 g (about 1.5 drinks) per day for women.
Researchers followed participants' health outcomes for an average of more than 13 years, allowing them to examine how drinking patterns were associated with deaths from different causes.
Wine, Beer, and Spirits Show Different Heart Health Risks
The clearest finding concerned heavy alcohol consumption. Compared with people who never drank or consumed alcohol only occasionally, heavy drinkers had a 24% higher risk of dying from any cause. Their risk of dying from cancer was 36% higher, while their risk of dying from heart disease was 14% higher.
These increased risks were associated with heavy drinking regardless of whether participants preferred wine, beer, cider, or spirits.
However, the results became more surprising when researchers examined low and moderate alcohol consumption. At these levels, the type of beverage was associated with substantially different outcomes.
People who consumed wine in low to moderate amounts had a significantly lower risk of death, while those who consumed comparable amounts of beer, cider, or spirits had a significantly higher risk.
The contrast was especially striking for cardiovascular disease, a broad category of conditions affecting the heart and blood vessels. Moderate wine drinkers had a 21% lower risk of dying from cardiovascular disease than people who never or only occasionally drank alcohol.
By comparison, even low consumption of beer, cider, or spirits was associated with a 9% higher risk of cardiovascular death.
These percentages describe relative differences in risk between groups, not the absolute probability that an individual will die from cardiovascular disease. Because the research was observational, the findings also cannot demonstrate that choosing one alcoholic beverage over another directly changes a person's risk.
"Our findings help clarify previously mixed evidence on low to moderate alcohol consumption," Chen said. "These findings can help refine guidance, emphasizing that the health risks of alcohol depend not only on the amount of alcohol consumed, but also on the type of beverage. Even low to moderate intake of spirits, beer, or cider is linked to higher mortality, while low to moderate intake of wine may carry lower risk."
Why Might Wine Be Linked to Lower Heart Risks?
Researchers identified several possible explanations for the differences, including the chemical composition of wine and the habits of people who drink it.
Red wine contains polyphenols, naturally occurring compounds found in plants that can have antioxidant properties. Antioxidants help counter certain chemical reactions involving unstable molecules that can damage cells. Some polyphenols have been investigated for potential benefits to blood vessels and cardiovascular function.
These compounds could contribute to the associations observed in wine drinkers, although the study did not establish that they were responsible for the lower mortality risk.
Another possible explanation involves how and when people drink.
Wine is more commonly consumed alongside meals, and wine drinkers often report healthier diets and lifestyle habits. Drinking wine may therefore be associated with other behaviors that support cardiovascular health.
Beer, cider, and spirits, on the other hand, are more frequently consumed outside of meals. In this study, people who favored these beverages also tended to have poorer overall diet quality and other lifestyle factors associated with increased health risks.
Such differences make it difficult to separate the effects of the alcohol itself from the characteristics and habits of the people consuming it.
"Taken together, these factors suggest that the type of alcohol, how it is consumed, and the associated lifestyle behaviors all contribute to the observed differences in mortality risk," Chen said.
What the Findings Mean for Alcohol and Health
To make their comparisons more reliable, the researchers statistically adjusted their analyses for numerous factors that might influence mortality. These included age and other demographic characteristics, socioeconomic circumstances, lifestyle behaviors, and cardiometabolic health.
Cardiometabolic factors include conditions and measurements related to heart and metabolic health, such as blood pressure, blood sugar regulation, and cholesterol levels. The analyses also accounted for family histories of diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and cancer.
Even with these adjustments, the researchers emphasized several important limitations.
Because the study was observational, it could identify associations between alcohol consumption and mortality but could not prove that particular beverages caused better or worse outcomes. Other differences between participants may have influenced the findings despite the statistical adjustments.
Alcohol intake was also measured through questionnaires completed when participants first entered the study. That information depended on participants accurately reporting their own drinking habits, and it did not capture changes in consumption during the years that followed.
Another consideration is that UK Biobank participants tend to be healthier than the general population. This could limit how well the findings apply to other groups of people.
The researchers suggested that high-quality randomized trials could provide stronger evidence about the health effects of different drinking patterns. Such studies would help clarify whether the observed differences reflect the beverages themselves or other factors associated with their consumption.
Nevertheless, the enormous study population and more than 13 years of average follow-up provide considerable statistical strength. By examining specific types of alcohol, different levels of consumption, and multiple causes of death, the research offers a more detailed picture of alcohol's potential health risks than many earlier investigations.
The findings highlight an important distinction: while heavy drinking is consistently associated with harmful health outcomes, the relationships observed at lower consumption levels may depend on beverage choice, drinking habits, and broader lifestyle patterns.
For now, the apparent advantage among wine drinkers should not be interpreted as a reason to start drinking wine for heart health. The evidence points to a complex relationship between alcohol and mortality, rather than proving that any alcoholic drink offers protection.
Ziyue Li presented the study, "Alcohol Use at Mid-Life and All-Cause and Cause-Specific Mortality," at ACC.26.

title: The ‘hell chicken’ dinosaur was a real terror — to fruit
text:
More than 65 million years ago, a small, beaked dinosaur dubbed the “hell chicken” was a real terror – to fruit. Reconstruction of its beak and jaw suggest it mashed up fruit much like modern parrots.
It’s the first evidence of non-avian dinosaurs evolving specialized adaptations for eating fruit, and comes at a time when flowering plants were coming into their own, researchers report October 10 in Nature Communications.
In 2011, a fossil collector found much of the fossilized skeleton of an odd theropod dinosaur in eastern Montana and brought to the attention of David Evans, a paleontologist at the Royal Ontario Museum in Canada. Over the next several years, fossil collectors and paleontologists working in Montana and North and South Dakota unearthed four more partial skeletons.
The dinosaur belonged to a particularly birdlike subgroup of beaked theropods called oviraptorosaurs that lived during the Cretaceous Period. This species probably weighed around 12 kilograms — about the size of a turkey.
Evans and Greg Funston — a paleontologist at Stony Brook University in New York — and their colleagues named it Infernogallus jamesi, or ‘hell chicken,’ after its discovery in the Hell Creek geological formation and its overall poultrylike appearance.
When the researchers studied Infernogallus’s skull and reconstructed the musculature, they discovered that it was no ordinary theropod. The construction of its jaw joints, muscles and palate suggest that it moved its jaw forward and back when eating rather than up and down like its chomping relatives.
This chewing style is unique among non-avian dinosaurs but is strikingly similar to that of fruit-eating parrots. Funston and his colleagues think Infernogallus had adapted to a fruit-rich diet, deftly stripping the flesh from large seeds using its tongue and sliding jaw motions.
These fruit-munching adaptations were surprising, Funston says. “But the more we delved into it, the more sense it made,” he says. “All the different lines of evidence seemed to converge on this one answer.”
Angiosperms — plants that produce flowers and fruits — were rapidly diversifying throughout the Cretaceous. Mounting evidence suggests that angiosperms were coevolving with Cretaceous animals, and that dinosaurs may have been eating their fruits. Infernogallus adds to that emerging picture. It’s possible that other ‘hell chicken’ relatives or other dinosaur groups were habitual fruit eaters too, Funston says.
“[The discovery] suggests that our picture of dinosaur ecology right before the Cretaceous extinction has been missing major puzzle pieces, and that dinosaurs were more diverse than we thought.”

title: NASA wants you to 'shine bright' today for Voyager 1's light-day milestone. Here's how
text:
As NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft prepares to reach a historic distance from Earth, the agency is inviting people around the world to celebrate by shining a light into the night sky in honor of humanity's farthest-flung spacecraft.
The event, called "Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day," will take place after sunset on Tuesday (Nov. 17), the day before Voyager 1 gets one light-day from Earth. And that's a big milestone: One light-day is the distance light travels in a day — about 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers).
NASA is encouraging "Shine Bright" participants to create a symbolic wave of golden light around the planet by flashing the spacecraft's three-letter mission call sign, VGR, in Morse code, according to a statement from the space agency.
To celebrate the spacecraft, participants can use a flashlight, phone, bike light or other portable light source to send the signal skyward. And don't fret if you're unfamiliar with Morse code: NASA has created an automated flasher that can be opened in a smartphone or tablet browser to display the VGR sequence.
The spacecraft’s call sign pattern consists of three quick flashes followed by one long flash for the letter V, two long flashes and one quick flash for G, and one quick flash, one long flash and another quick flash for R. Participants are encouraged to repeat the sequence for about a minute, NASA officials said.
NASA also invites people to photograph or record their light signals and share them on social media, tagging the agency's official account, @NASA. The goal is to create a worldwide display of light marking a milestone nearly five decades in the making.
The celebration is intended as a symbolic tribute rather than an actual attempt to communicate with Voyager 1. At a distance of one light-day from Earth, the spacecraft is so far away that even radio signals traveling at the speed of light take approximately 24 hours to reach it. A flashlight or phone signal from Earth, of course, cannot reach the probe; NASA communicates with it using its Deep Space Network of radio dishes.
Launched on Sept. 5, 1977, Voyager 1 has spent nearly 50 years traveling through space and is now the most distant human-made object from Earth. When it reaches the one-light-day milestone, it will have traveled a distance that light itself takes 24 hours to cross. Its twin, Voyager 2, is expected to reach the same milestone in November 2035. (The two spacecraft took different routes through the solar system.)
The public celebration will be followed by another opportunity to learn more about the historic mission. On Thursday (Nov. 19) at 12 p.m. EST (1700 GMT), NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California will host a moderated discussion with Voyager mission team members and NASA leadership.
The discussion will cover the current status of both Voyager spacecraft, the unique scientific observations they continue to collect in interstellar space and the engineering challenges involved in keeping the nearly 50-year-old probes operational. A question-and-answer session with members of the media and audience will follow. NASA will also offer a preview of an upcoming Voyager documentary planned for release in 2027, coinciding with the mission's 50th anniversary.
For a mission that has carried humanity's message into interstellar space for nearly half a century, the "Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day” offers a chance for people back on Earth to mark just how far these pioneering spacecraft have traveled. More details about NASA's automated VGR flasher and step-by-step Morse code instructions are available online.

title: How new US chip restrictions on South East Asia will hit China
text:
As US President Donald Trump heads to China, his administration has renewed efforts to curb Beijing's access to advanced semiconductors.
On Monday, Washington announced new interim rules that will increase scrutiny of data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil.
The move not only restricts the export of advanced chips, but also access to their computing power, which Chinese firms currently rent abroad to train artificial intelligence (AI) models.
South East Asian countries in particular have invested heavily in data centres to power their AI ambitions - and Chinese firms seeking computing power overseas have been a key market.
But now these firms will need a US government licence to buy advanced chips from Nvidia or other American chipmakers. This allows Washington to monitor if those chips are being used to serve Chinese companies, or being smuggled to China.
This poses a fresh challenge for Beijing, which has become deeply dependent on compute from abroad in the wake of US export restrictions. At least 30% of China's advanced AI computing power is projected to come from renting overseas or smuggling in 2027, according to research by the Institute for Progress, external, a US-based think-tank.
China's foreign ministry called the new rules "economic coercion" and said Beijing "will take necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own legitimate rights and interests".
A blow to Asia's AI boom
This is also a problem for South East Asian economies where large numbers of data centres have sprung up recently. Some of the firms behind them are accused of helping China evade US export controls on advanced chips.
One of those is Singaporean data centre firm Megaspeed, whose former director Alice Huang is suspected of being a Chinese spy. Calls for tighter export controls have grown after Nvidia's Jensen Huang admited to an affair with her and resigned as CEO.
Megaspeed, the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia, is accused of illegally smuggling chips to Chinese companies after purchasing them for use in data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.
The company has denied these allegations, defended its business as "legitimate and lawful", and said it has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation". It also said Alice Huang stepped down from her role as director in late 2023 and left the firm last year.
The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, however, has said Brazil and the four South East Asian nations "present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion" of the chips that Washington wants to keep out of China's hands.
The new measures are aimed at ensuring sensitive US technology "cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the bureau added. Licences will be issued on a "case-by-case basis", it said.
Countries like Malaysia and Thailand whose data centre roll out has been heavily driven by Chinese buyers could be hit hardest, says international trade expert Naoise McDonagh from Australia's Edith Cowan University.
But the new rules are unlikely to derail the data centre boom as a whole, says Reema Bhattacharya from advisory firm Verisk Maplecroft, adding that investment backed by major tech firms and clearly identifiable customers should "remain relatively resilient".
Singapore was an early adopter of data centres but when it began limiting new construction, investment flowed to neighbours Malaysia and Thailand. Johor in Malaysia and Batam in Indonesia have also approved billions of dollars worth of data centres to catch the spillover demand.
These countries have been offering incentives such as cheaper land to attract foreign investment, including from Chinese tech giants Alibaba and Tencent.
But now, the region could find it harder to get hold of advanced chips.
The BBC has contacted Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand for comment.
Singapore said it is "engaging relevant US authorities" to understand the new rules better, and is "exploring how to facilitate trusted access" for local firms.
A spokesperson for Brazil's Ministry of Development, Industry, Trade and Services said it is aware of the US announcement and it "is closely monitoring any potential developments regarding this measure".
Malaysia previously said it welcomes data centre investment but "will not allow itself to be used to get around export controls".
A headache for China
The new rules also come just ahead of Trump's meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen this week.
Beijing has made self-sufficiency in tech a national priority and needs the best chips to build powerful AI models.
Chinese firms DeepSeek and MoonShot have come close to US rivals like Anthropic and OpenAI. So much so that The Institute for Progress estimates top US AI models lead the best Chinese platforms by only about six and half months.
"This is despite US AI companies having significantly better compute access and financing," it said.
Still, China needs advanced US chips to ensure its best AI models are competitive, experts tell the BBC.
The new restrictions on South East Asia and Brazil have taken away "one of the more practical routes Chinese AI developers had to accessing frontier computing power," Bhattacharya said.
But tighter restrictions could also push Chinese firms towards domestic semiconductors and further drive advancement at home.
That has been a longstanding dilemma for Washington, McDonagh said: whether to keep selling chips to China to retain its reliance on the US, or restrict access and risk further spurring Chinese innovation.

title: Portugal’s new No 7 Forbs channels Ronaldo for winner as Wales are denied
text:
One way or another, Portugal’s No 7 shirt has caused quite the commotion in recent weeks and months, if not years. Perhaps it was inevitable, then, that the first win of the post-Cristiano Ronaldo era would come courtesy of the player wearing the updated jersey, one with a cross through the number to preserve Ronaldo’s eternal legacy, as the Portuguese football federation put it. A sumptuous finish by Carlos Forbs, a second-half substitute, was ultimately enough to clinch victory on a topsy-turvy night with Portugal surviving Pedro Neto’s sending-off for two yellow cards.
Turn a new page and all that. This was a welcome victory for Jorge Jesus, for whom a 4-1 home defeat to Denmark a few days ago was a harrowing juncture, and there were plenty of positive takeaways for Wales, too. David Brooks cancelled out Bruno Fernandes’s opener from the edge of the box and then seized the lead through Sorba Thomas, who applied the finishing touch to a purring team move. But Neto, who picked up two bookings in one minute and 59 seconds, the second for a foul on Brennan Johnson, equalised before half-time. Craig Bellamy’s side were fun and, at times, freewheeling but Forbs had the final say with a neat run and finish.
Bellamy stressed the importance of locking down Vitinha and João Neves, two of his favourite players who have won successive Champions League titles, and Wales did not allow the Paris Saint-Germain pair to have things all their own way. Vitinha, always scanning and ready to take the ball from his teammates, naturally topped the pass-o-meter, completing all 76 passes he made in an absorbing first half. It was a loose Renato Veiga pass, meant for Vitinha, on the verge of the half-time interval that supplied the all-action Harry Wilson with a speculative opportunity from halfway. Wilson intercepted the ball and, after taking a touch to roll the ball into the opposition half, the Leeds midfielder sent a marvellous left-footed lobbed effort towards goal, his 45-yard shot skimming the roof of Diogo Costa’s goal much to the relief of the Portugal goalkeeper.
Portugal may have levelled a few moments earlier, Neto easily beating Jay Dasilva in the six-yard box to prod in Francisco Trincão’s brilliant cross, but Wilson’s attempt at the audacious was another gentle reminder of Portugal’s precarious state. This was a ludicrously open game and, after leaking four goals at home for the first time in an international game in last weekend’s humiliating 4-1 defeat to Denmark in Braga, Portugal were again susceptible defensively. Before Thomas capped a scintillating team move to seize the lead on 40 minutes, Wilson twice went close, Diogo Dalot making a desperate block for the first before the second from another electric team move.
Portugal made four changes from Saturday’s stinging defeat, with the Bournemouth centre-back António Silva replacing the suspended Rúben Dias and Neves, shirt tucked into his shorts, joining Vitinha at the base of midfield. Trincão was lively down the left wing and the marauding João Cancelo a constant threat, popping up all over the pitch. When Fernandes picked his spot on 11 minutes, sending an unerring strike into the top corner, Portugal appeared in the groove.
But Wales responded two minutes later when Brooks, who scored courtesy of a superb dinked finish in defeat by Norway, dug out another clever finish. Wilson saw a shot repelled by Costa at the Porto goalkeeper’s near post and, when the ball squirted free, Rubin Colwill had the presence of mind to calmly square for Brooks, who squeezed a left-foot shot into the far corner. Colwill, a fan favourite here for Cardiff, thoroughly enjoyed his first Wales start. Brooks, another one of the six players promoted to Bellamy’s starting XI, neatly dovetailed with the busy Wilson.
This was an entertaining occasion for which it was worth braving the winter conditions. Neto wellied a shot against the base of a post after nipping past Ben Davies and Fernandes later released Forbs after a magnificent take to control the ball midway inside his own half.
Colwill impressed in a deep midfield role alongside Josh Sheehan of Bolton, whose former clubmate Aaron Collins, now of MK Dons, arrived from the bench midway through the second half for his debut. Portugal, meanwhile, introduced João Félix and the Club Brugge winger Forbs. Ben Cabango, who replaced Joe Rodon as a precaution at half-time, went close to scoring with a header.
Wales could not regain the lead and instead trailed, though the weary look on Costa’s face as he pawed Cabango’s header away from goal for a corner said it all. The moment Forbs surged on to a loose Cabango header and then at Davies before applying a low left-foot finish provided light relief on another uncomfortable night for Jesus and his Portugal players. For Wales, a challenging Nations League campaign, ended as it began, with a heartening defeat to Portugal.

title: US Navy chief says Iran war has put ‘strain’ on maritime forces
text:
United States Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao has acknowledged that the Iran war is taxing the maritime service as bipartisan senators questioned him over extended ship deployments, dwindling weapons stockpiles, and resources being shifted away from the Asia-Pacific.
Testifying before the Senate Armed Services Committee on Tuesday at his confirmation hearing to lead the military branch, Cao faced sharp, bipartisan grilling over the mounting human and material costs of the US-Israel war on Iran, which is now deep into its ninth month.
“This war, again, I know it’s a strain on our navy,” Cao said, while insisting that joint military efforts have “really set China back on their heels”.
Cao, a retired US Navy captain and former Republican Party candidate for the Virginia Senate, has served as acting navy secretary since April 2026 after previously holding the under-secretary post.
The candidate, backed by US President Donald Trump, is now seeking US Senate confirmation for the permanent top civilian job.
The hearing comes amid burgeoning political fallout over the protracted quagmire with Iran, which recently saw a failed US House bid to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over his stewardship of the war.
Voter frustration over the war — and its economic sting — proved decisive in the November midterm elections, which were widely seen as a repudiation of the war and ultimately cost the Republicans control of both the House and the Senate.
The Democratic-controlled 120th Congress is scheduled to be sworn in on January 3, 2027.
Heated Senate exchange
As the ranking Democrat on the committee, Senator Jack Reed of Rhode Island questioned Cao during the nearly two-hour hearing, saying he was candidly troubled by his performance so far.
“I am concerned, frankly, about your leadership record as acting secretary,” said Reed, who called on the acting US Navy secretary to speak to Hegseth‘s ongoing and planned dismissals of numerous naval officers over the past year, pressing Cao on whether he would “defend the military leaders in the future from partisan meddling in their careers”.
Democratic lawmakers went on to criticise the US Navy for bypassing standard congressional notification after quietly relieving the entire leadership team — the commander, executive officer and command master chief — of the nuclear-powered attack submarine USS South Dakota following an October underwater collision with the seabed.
“We relieve commanding officers for everything from negligence to even just fraternisation or, you know, harassment,” Cao said, making the case against the US Navy’s traditional policy of publicly announcing the removal of commanders. “I want to make sure that we’re protecting their livelihood afterwards as well.”
His stated intent to safeguard individuals’ careers was promptly rebuked by Reed, who maintained that privacy does not justify shielding information from congressional oversight.
“The squadron commodore [of the USS South Dakota] felt that they did not live up to their honour, courage, and commitment ethos, and therefore, he relieved the commanding officer, the executive officer, and the command master chief,” Cao countered.
Cao’s record on sailor mental health comes under fire
The US Navy chief-nominee also faced intense questioning from lawmakers about low crew morale, severe supply shortages, and mental health strains aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln following its record-breaking 265-day deployment in the Pacific Ocean, South China Sea, Indian Ocean, and North Arabian Sea.
The vessel returned to Naval Air Station North Island in San Diego, California, in early October after the USS George Washington arrived on station to relieve it. Together with the USS George HW Bush and the newly arrived USS Theodore Roosevelt, the US is temporarily massing three carrier strike groups to bolster regional maritime security and tighten the months-long naval blockade against Iran.
Last week, Trump stated that further military strikes against Iran are “quite unlikely” and said the military component of the war was “effectively over” following discussions with Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani. He noted, however, that the US military remains “locked and loaded” if conditions change.
During Tuesday’s hearing, Senator Richard Blumenthal, a Connecticut Democrat, argued that Cao was “failing these sailors and their families”, and noted that his “confrontation with them leaves me with the clear impression that you simply don’t care”.
Cao pushed back, declaring that he does not control the deployment lengths of US Navy ships that have crept steadily closer to a full year at sea — up from a standard of six to eight months during the US’s so-called “war on terror”.
“Sustained investment in our people will increase readiness, improve retention and recruitment, and enable our ability to support national objectives,” said Cao.
When asked about suicide attempts aboard the ships, Cao told Blumenthal that what he saw “as eight suicide attempts, I see as eight suicide mitigations”.
Cao faces a rare waiver hurdle for the top spot
In his opening statement, Republican Senate Armed Services Committee Chair Roger Wicker expressed support for Cao’s nomination to lead the US Navy, noting that while the service faces significant challenges during a particularly volatile time, it also has major opportunities.
Beyond fielding tough questions from lawmakers on Tuesday over the strain of the Iran war on fleet readiness, Cao still faces a complex confirmation path to become the permanent secretary of the navy, requiring a rare congressional waiver.
Because he left active-duty service in October 2021, he falls short of the seven-year separation period mandated by federal law to preserve civilian control of the military.
Securing that exemption poses a steep political climb for Cao, who must clear the hurdle by meeting a 60-vote threshold, which may prove tricky in a polarised Washington.
Cao will ultimately need cross-party support from Democrats or independents to avoid a filibuster, while winning over war-sceptical Republicans.

title: Brain cell mapping lays groundwork for better treatments for conditions like dementia
text:
A major effort from brain researchers around the world has yielded a cellular atlas of the basal ganglia — structures key to learning and controlling motor skills.
SCOTT DETROW, HOST:
Now to the human brain, which is incredibly complex and contains more than 80 billion neurons. NPR's Pien Huang reports on how an effort to map one part of the brain could soon unlock the whole thing.
PIEN HUANG, BYLINE: The basal ganglia are clusters of interconnected cells tucked beneath the cortex in the human brain.
MICHAEL HAWRYLYCZ: It only occupies, in volume, about 2% of the brain.
HUANG: About the size of a gumball. Michael Hawrylycz is a senior investigator at the Allen Institute, a bioscience research group in Seattle. His colleague, Hongkui Zeng, is director of brain science there. She says the basal ganglia are small but mighty, key to controlling movements, making decisions, forming habits.
HONGKUI ZENG: Because of that, it is also implicated in several major brain diseases, including neurodegenerative diseases, Parkinson's and Huntington's, as well as diseases that involve cognition or emotion.
HUANG: Like schizophrenia, depression, bipolar and addiction. For a consortium of scientists looking to map the entire brain, the basal ganglia seemed like a good place to start, especially because it's shared across many species.
HAWRYLYCZ: We really wanted to choose a structure which was both important as well as evolutionarily conserved so that we could understand the difference between humans and other primates.
HUANG: Together, they looked at more than 25 million cells from the brains of humans, macaques and marmosets. They profiled these cells, documenting where they are, which of their genes get expressed and how those cells differ among people and animals. What they've created, Zeng says, is an atlas of this part of the brain.
ZENG: So what you get is really a colorful map that shows all the cells, what kind of types they are and then where they are located.
HUANG: This map comes in three dimensions with layers of information. One layer is basically a heat map of which cells express specific genes, such as those related to diseases like Parkinson's or Alzheimer's.
ZENG: And if you know where they are, then you know, OK, those cells containing that gene probably play important roles in this disease.
HUANG: An article about the atlas and more than two dozen papers accompanying it are published as a package by Cell Press. It's the culmination of three years of intense scientific work, mainly funded by the National Institutes of Health, involving researchers at more than 50 institutions around the world. Satrajit Ghosh, a senior scientist at the McGovern Institute for Brain Research at MIT, was one of them.
SATRAJIT GHOSH: Every neuroscientist has different feelings about what is important in the brain, but we need to consolidate information about how the parts of the brain exist, right?
HUANG: Ghosh compares this effort to the Human Genome Project, launched in the '90s, which gave scientists a common foundation for their research. Talia Lerner is a basal ganglia researcher at the Center for Addiction and Mental Health in Toronto. She's not affiliated with this research, but says it's a starting point for developing better drugs. Take certain treatments for Parkinson's disease.
TALIA LERNER: One side effect of some of these medications can be increases in pathological gambling and other types of risk-seeking behavior.
HUANG: This could maybe be fixed with a more precise understanding of the basal ganglia.
LERNER: The more that we can learn about this and, like, which function is where, the more I think we can make really targeted medicines that will have fewer side effects and will be able to help people more.
HUANG: Kamran Khodakhah, a neuroscientist at Albert Einstein College of Medicine, is not affiliated with this research either, but he's excited for where it could lead.
KAMRAN KHODAKHAH: What they have come up with is a template for the entire brain. So this - the same exact template and methodology can be used to look at other brain regions.
HUANG: The researchers say they've been working on it. They expect to have a dataset for the whole brain by the end of next year and to publish in the next couple of years.
KHODAKHAH: It would be remarkable if they do so (laughter). So good luck to them.
HUANG: They say they built a crucial framework starting with the basal ganglia, and those methods and collaborations will help speed the rest. Pien Huang, NPR News.

title: Fresh clashes at the Eritrean border — is Ethiopia sliding into a regional war?
text:
After a few weeks of relative stability, fresh clashes in the contested Ethiopia-Eritrea border areahave raised fears of a full-fledged war. Meanwhile, diplomatic relations between Ethiopia and Sudanhave hit new lows.
Fighters allied with the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) launched their offensive on September 23. It was aimed at overthrowing the Ethiopian government as part of a larger rebel coalition. But the Ethiopian National Defense Forces (ENDF), backed by pro-government militia, have steadily pushed the TPLF out of Tigray, a region in northern Ethiopia.
According to the conflict tracker of the monitoring organization ACLED, the ENDF have pushed further into Tigray, effectively driving the Tigrayan Defense Forces (TDF) towards the border with Eritrea. Skirmishes have been reported from several locations, while the ENDF have fired heavy artillery towards dwellings close to the Eritrean border town of Badme.
While no census data is publicly available, Badme appears to be a small rural town on satellite images. However, the locality is historically significant for both sides because it was the ground zero of the Eritrean-Ethiopian War from 1998 to 2000, sometimes dubbed the Badme War.
The war ended with theAlgiers Agreement, in which both countries agreed to honor the rulings of a newly formed Eritrea-Ethiopia Boundary Commission. The commission awarded Badme to Eritrea, a decision that Ethiopia challenged at times. Abdurahman Sayed, director of the London-based Horn of Africa Center for Regional Integration, told DW that Ethiopia might see an advantage in reclaiming Badme to resolve its current internal struggles.
"It seems now if the Eritreans withdrew and the Ethiopians came back, it could be to calm down the Tigrayans, especially those who are now supporting the party in power in Ethiopia", Sayed said.
He suggested that people like Getachew Reda, a former spokesman for the TPLF and current advisor to Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, might be able to win the Tigrayan people over to side with the federal government through territorial gains for the Tigray region.
The ever-looming threat of a full-fledged war with Eritrea
"The coming of the forces to the Eritrean-Ethiopian border clearly indicates that the conflict can be triggered any time", Abdurahman Sayed said.
Eritrean and Ethiopian government troops allied against the Tigrayan forcesduring the 2020-22 Tigray conflict. Since then, Eritrea's allegiances have shifted towards the TPLF and away from Abiy Ahmed's central government. In October, the two neighbors cut diplomatic ties. At one point, Eritrean troops reportedly crossed the border into Tigray.
Magnus Taylor, a regional analyst with the International Crisis Group (ICG), believes that Addis Ababa's prime objective for the moment might rather be securing its northern border and destroying supply lines between Eritrea and Tigrayan forces.
"So what we might actually be seeing is a kind of a function of the attempts by the Ethiopian military to consolidate its control of Tigray, which includes pushing Tigray's borders with Eritrea", Taylor told DW.
However, securing control over Tigray could also involve direct conflict with Eritrea at one point, Taylor said: "If this happens, then it's quite likely that the Ethiopians would attempt to carry out all their objectives in Eritrea at one time."
Since Eritrea seceded from Ethiopia in 1993, Ethiopia has been the world's largest landlocked country by population. Prime Minister Abiy has repeatedly described the country's lack of sea access as an existential threat. While stating a preference for peaceful means to gain access, he said this could also mean capturing Eritrea's easternmost port, Assab, by force.
Ethiopia-Sudan relations at crossroads
At the same time, the diplomatic relations between Ethiopia and its northwestern neighbor, Sudan, have deteriorated even further.
Sudan and Egypt, both downstream the river Nile, have been on edge for years because of Ethiopia's Grand Renaissance Dam (GERD). The massive GERD, built on the Blue Nile just kilometers from Ethiopia's border with Sudan, gives Addis Ababa significant leverage over the timing and regulation of water flows downstream, raising concerns in Sudan and Egypt over water security and dam operations. The Ethiopian government has rejected claims that the dam could be used as a means to pressure Sudan and Egypt.
Since 2023, Sudan has been embroiled in a civil war between two rival military forces: the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), led by General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), led by Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti. In mid-November, both sides accused the other of direct participation in each other's internal conflicts.
Two countries with severe internal conflicts and mirroring alliances: Could the situation deteriorate further into potential direct fights between the two armies? ICG's Magnus Taylor believes there is a risk, but at least not for now.
"The most likely scenario is we just get a continuation of this kind of proxy style of involvement with each other's opposition groups rather than formal direct involvement on the ground in the conflict," Taylor said.
Sayed also believes that, at the moment, there is no need for direct confrontation.
"The RSF can do the job that Ethiopia and any other country backing them wants them to do," Sayed said. "But if there is a need and the RSF are failing, the Ethiopian army could be pushed to get involved."

title: Erling Haaland’s last-minute penalty sends Norway into Nations League quarter-finals
text:
Erling Haaland scored a 96th-minute penalty with the last kick of the game to send Norway into the quarter-finals of the Nations League with victory over Denmark in Copenhagen.
Norway knew then needed to beat Denmark to leapfrog their opponents into second place in Group A4, with Portugal ensuring top spot by beating Wales in Cardiff.
They made a horror start, though, as the visitors found themselves 2-0 down inside 15 minutes as Rasmus Hojlund and Pierre-Emile Hojbjerg put Denmark in control.
Norway started their comeback when Mads Hermansen lost possession under pressure from Martin Odegaard and Haaland tapped into the empty net before half-time.
Captain Odegaard equalised in the 83rd minute to give Norway further hope, before they won a last-gasp penalty as Joachim Andersen was penalised for handball in the box.
Haaland stepped up and kept his cool in front of the home fans in the Parken Stadium, taking off his shirt as Norway wildly celebrated their dramatic victory.
The World Cup quarter-finalists will now advance to the quarter-finals of the Nations League, where they could face either England, France or Germany in the last eight.
Denmark, who had thrashed group winners Portugal 4-1 away from home on Saturday, will instead go into a relegation play-off in March as they bid to keep their top-flight status.

title: EU climate chief Hoekstra: Electrification key for Europe to compete with China as COP pushes global target
text:
Hoekstra tells On the Record that electrification is key to Europe's industrial competitiveness, as COP talks push for a global target of 35% by 2035.
The European Commission's proposed U-turn on its 2035 ban on new petrol and diesel cars does not give Brussels carte blanche to roll back its climate ambitions, Wopke Hoekstra has told Euronews.
In an exclusive interview with Euronews' On the Record, the EU's climate chief defended the Commission's decision to give the automotive industry greater flexibility as a way to protect European manufacturers while keeping the transition to electric vehicles on track.
His comments come as Europe's car industry struggles to remain competitive amid high energy costs and growing pressure from international rivals.
German carmaker Mercedes-Benz has announced plans to halt investments in Germany and is weighing plant closures, amid similar challenges facing Volkswagen, Stellantis, BMW and Volvo.
Hoekstra rejected calls for further concessions on the 2035 targets, including those backed by the European Parliament, arguing that additional flexibility risks undermining both the EU's climate ambitions and the competitiveness of European manufacturers as Chinese electric vehicle makers gain ground.
"Significantly loosening the targets of 2035 is exactly not what the Commission did," he said, defending the proposal as a compromise between climate action, industrial competitiveness and energy independence.
He also argued that further loosening the targets would do little to help European manufacturers, warning that the industry risks falling further behind if it slows its transition to electric vehicles while Chinese competitors continue to advance.
"I am not convinced that loosening the targets further (...) will be in the interest of European car makers," he said.
Electrification as a competitive edge
Hoekstra has also doubled down on efforts to electrify the European economy as he leads the bloc's negotiating team at this week's COP climate conference in Turkey.
The summit aims to establish a global target of 35% electrification by 2035, a goal backed by the EU. Brussels argues that accelerating electrification would also strengthen European competitiveness, pointing to China's major push to electrify its economy and expand its electric vehicle industry.
But while acknowledging China's progress, Hoekstra accused Beijing of dumping goods on European markets and using its dominance in sectors such as solar panels, electric vehicles and critical raw materials to strengthen its geopolitical position.
He argued that European carmakers must step up their efforts to compete in the global electric vehicle market.
"Let's not fight the quest for electrification. Let's make sure it is European companies that win that race," he said.

title: Judge fires back at Fani Willis' office in courtroom clash over Trump case: 'Due process doesn't apply to you'
text:
A Georgia appellate judge pressed Fulton County District Attorney Fani Willis’ office Tuesday as it pushed for permission to fight millions in legal-fee requests from President Donald Trump and other former defendants in her collapsed election interference case.
Before a three-judge panel, Willis’ office argued it should be allowed to protect its budget from payments stemming from a prosecution she and her office were disqualified from handling in December 2024.
"What process are you entitled to? You’re the government. Due process doesn’t apply to you," Judge J. Wade Padgett told Donald Wakeford, a chief senior assistant district attorney representing Willis’ office.
Trump and other former defendants are seeking nearly $17 million under a Georgia law passed last year, with Trump alone requesting more than $6 million. The law allows defendants to recover legal fees if their prosecutor is removed for improper conduct and their charges are later dismissed.
Tuesday’s hearing focused on whether Willis’ office could participate in challenging those requests.
The state is represented in the reimbursement fight by Pete Skandalakis, executive director of the Prosecuting Attorneys’ Council of Georgia, who took over after Willis’ disqualification and moved to dismiss the charges in November 2025.
Willis’ office argued he cannot adequately protect its financial interests because his own decision to drop the case opened the door to the reimbursement requests. Wakeford also argued that Skandalakis’ authority in the case ended when the prosecution did.
"This statute has created a mess and that is no secret," Wakeford said of the new Georgia law allowing defendants to seek reimbursement for their legal fees.
The judges pressed him on whether Willis’ disqualification still bars her office from participating.
"So let’s talk about the elephant in the room then," Padgett said, pointing to the court’s earlier ruling declaring the district attorney wholly disqualified.
"The criminal prosecution has ended," Wakeford responded, arguing that the fee dispute is a separate matter.
"Is the disqualification over? Is she no longer wholly disqualified?" Judge Ken Hodges asked.
Wakeford said that Willis’ disqualification applied to the criminal prosecution, arguing it did not bar her office from participating in the separate legal-fee dispute.
But the panel also questioned whether that finding satisfies the new law’s requirements for reimbursement.
"The trial judge found an appearance of impropriety and found that actual misconduct had not been established," Padgett said.
Willis and her office were removed from the case after an appeals court found that her romantic relationship with Nathan Wade, the special prosecutor she appointed, created an appearance of impropriety.
In March, Fulton County Superior Court Judge Scott McAfee denied Willis’ request to intervene, finding that Skandalakis could adequately represent her office’s interests. Her office is asking the appeals court to overturn that decision.
The court announced no ruling during Tuesday’s hearing, leaving unresolved whether Willis’ office can directly challenge the fee requests.

title: 400 largest U.S. data centers produced more carbon dioxide in a year than Denmark, study finds
text: The 400 largest data centers in the United States put more heat-trapping gas in the air in one year than the entire nation of Denmark did, and that was before the artificial intelligence boom really got going, according to a Harvard University study published Monday. READ MORE: Opposition to AI data centers in the midterms foreshadows tougher regulations ahead Meanwhile, negotiators at the United Nations COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, launched a voluntary pledge Monday for companies and countries to power the world's data centers with clean energy and be more open about their power and water consumption and emissions. "We cannot ask people to accept higher bills, more planet heating pollution and deeper inequality today in exchange for promises of a better tomorrow," United Nations climate chief Simon Stiell said Monday during the launch of the pledge. "Claims about future emissions savings cannot excuse rising pollution now, making climate disasters even worse." The pledge also calls for focusing the power of artificial intelligence on solving the so-far intractable problem of climate change and reflects burgeoning concerns about AI's ever-expanding environmental footprint. The political backlash has played out in U.S. elections and major local objections for new sites. The explosion of new and planned data centers also has prompted a push for new sources of power generation that has the biggest tech companies failing to reach their climate goals, with their electricity consumption rising 240% between 2022 and 2025, according to a new report by the advocacy group Climate Action Against Disinformation. Study quantifies how much big data centers pollute Harvard researchers looked at 403 of the largest U.S. data centers between May 2024 and April 2025 using available data and modeling to analyze their electricity use and emissions. They estimated electricity use by the centers produced around 28.3 million tons (25.7 million metric tons) of carbon dioxide, according to a study in Monday's Nature Sustainability. More than half their 82 terawatt hours of electricity use — enough to power nearly 7 million homes for a year — came from fossil fuels, which are the primary cause of global warming, the researchers found. The emissions estimate is two to three times what previous studies had shown, said study senior author Francesca Dominici, a Harvard biostatistics professor. "It is the equivalent to the CO2 emission of an entire state like Michigan or a small European country," Dominici said, adding that plans for 2,000 more data centers make that quantity more worrisome for the future. "We are going backwards toward the goal of controlling CO2 emissions." Several outside experts in climate, energy and artificial intelligence said Monday's study made sense and reached realistic conclusions, finding the use of modeling reasonable because companies aren't open about power consumption and pollution. "We cannot manage environmental impacts effectively without reliable measurements and disclosure," said Fengqi You, a Cornell University energy systems scientist who wasn't part of the study. "Ultimately, the environmental footprint of AI is not fixed. It depends on where we build data centers, how efficiently they operate, and how we supply their electricity." A voluntary pledge proposed at climate talks The "Antalya Artificial Intelligence Pledge," launched by U.N. climate talks host Turkey and the International Telecommunication Union, says data centers should use clean power and efficient energy and water systems. The pledge also calls for AI systems to be designed and managed responsibly, using environmental standards and reusing or recycling infrastructure and hardware. It says the environmental impacts of data centers should be assessed and shared and signatories should support using artificial intelligence as a climate solution. COP31 President Murat Kurum has said world leaders at the talks must openly discuss AI's growing energy consumption and start setting the terms. AI produces pollution but also offers hope One of the biggest climate fighters, former U.S. Vice President Al Gore, said while it is essential that data centers are powered by carbon-free energy, he is less concerned about the emissions from AI than others. And he is hopeful that its computing power can find novel ways of fighting climate change. READ MORE: To make AI morally good, tech companies are turning to religion. But some experts say it isn't that simple In an Associated Press interview, Gore quoted a study by prominent British economist and climate advocate Nicholas Stern who predicted by 2030 "we will see 6 to 9% reduction in emissions of greenhouse gases because of the use of advanced AI in finding new ways to be far more efficient in the use of materials and energy." Caleb Max, president of the National Artificial Intelligence Association said, "AI will solve not only the energy usage issues that data centers face, but unlock numerous currently unknown advances in science and technology that will address climate change and make lives better for humanity. I respect the concerns about energy and water consumption from data centers, but the fears may be overblown." But Climate Action Against Disinformation spokesman Philip Newell was skeptical. "We have hope in one hand and then harms in the other," Newell said. "They're selling us hope while hiding the harms from us." Capturing heat from data centers The computing equipment in data centers generates a lot of waste heat that is vented into the atmosphere. One approach to reducing data centers' environmental impact is to capture heat that can be used for nearby homes and businesses. The Danish engineering and manufacturing company Danfoss said waste heat is "the world's largest untapped energy source," and reusing it can replace natural gas as a heat source. It identified data centers as a significant source of constant heat, particularly as their power consumption grows. The International Energy Agency estimates data centers could provide enough heat for around 10% of European homes by 2030, if that heat was fully integrated into district systems that supply heat and hot water to residents. In remarks broadcast during COP31, European Commissioner for Energy and Housing Dan Jørgensen said Europe must replace imported fossil fuels by capturing heat that is going to waste and tapping into geothermal. In another example of this approach, industrial development firm BaRupOn is building an advanced manufacturing campus in Texas that plans to use recaptured heat to generate additional electricity on site, CEO Balaji Tammabattula said. In North Dakota, the company is planning a data center that could feed heat to the community. University of Colorado Boulder Professor Gregor Henze said it's a perfect marriage because modern data centers that rely on liquid rather than air cooling are a fairly constant source of heat at the right temperature for thermal energy networks. The Associated Press' climate and environmental coverage receives financial support from multiple private foundations. The AP is solely responsible for all content. title: Trump on Iran's reported DC dirty bomb plan: 'We take it very seriously'
text:
President Donald Trump said Tuesday that if a report about Iran developing plans to target top administration officials with a "dirty bomb" in Washington is true, Iran would face consequences.
"Well, if there is, they will pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before," Trump said when asked if there is any imminent threat to Washington, home to close to 700,000 people in addition to the seat of government.
"I hope it's not, but we take it very seriously, because they happen to be crazy," Trump said during a photo op with world leaders at the summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations in Manila, Philippines.
"This is why they can't have a nuclear weapon, by the way, in case people had any questions," Trump added, reiterating his main rationale for launching a war with Iran in late February.
Late Monday, CNN cited two U.S. officials in reporting that new U.S. intelligence has intercepted "very specific" plans, including "locations and targets," related to a potential Iranian plot to set off a dirty bomb, which combines conventional explosives with radioactive material.
Officials have debated whether Iran would actually attempt to detonate such a device in the U.S., or even if it could, CNN reported, citing seven U.S. officials in total.
CNBC has not verified the report. Trump administration spokeswoman Lauren Bis told CNN in a statement that the U.S. is "monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland."
Trump was asked about imminent Iranian threats during the first leg of his tour through Asia, which began at ASEAN and is set to include high-stakes meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Asked about the dirty bomb report on CNBC's "Squawk Box" Tuesday morning, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin suggested the Iranian plot was not new and described Tehran as "aspirational" in its threats.
If Iran were to take such an action, "you would cause an all-out war" with the U.S., which would attack at such a level that the Islamic Republic's allies, such as China and Russia, would not come to its aid, Mullin said.
It is a threat, and "we take it very serious," he said. "But the homeland is secure, I can tell you that. But every day we addressing new threats."
CNN reported later Tuesday morning that NSA Net, the classified communications network used by the National Security Agency, is down, citing six people familiar with the matter.

title: Apple services, including iCloud, App Store, Apple Music, and more, hit by outage
text:
After a recent slew of tech outages, service disruptions, and flight chaos this week, it’s now Apple customers who are facing technical issues.
The iPhone maker’s System Status page indicates that there are issues with iCloud’s Account & Sign In services affecting “all users,” which could make the service slow or unavailable. The App Store, AppleCare on Device, and Apple Music are also experiencing issues, the page indicates.
Like all major tech companies, Apple faces outages and other technical issues affecting its cloud services at times. However, today’s issues are likely more noticeable to end users because problems with iCloud can lead to account sign-in problems. This could cause your iPhone to ask for your Apple ID and password, and you could see other attempts to sign in to services with your Apple account information fail.
On Reddit, some folks also noted that they were unable to activate a new iPhone, which is likely related to these ongoing issues.
Given the recent increase in AI-driven cyberattacks, users across social media have already begun to speculate about the cause. In particular, users are expressing concerns about the Apple outage, as it arrives only days after technical failures at Microsoft led to its cloud systems that power flagship services like Outlook and Teams failing due to cascading software issues.
Similarly, a brief outage of Chase’s banking app this week garnered attention, as did an ongoing partial outage (at the time of publication) of the National Security Agency’s internal classified network, both of which were blamed on software glitches.
So far, none of the outages in the past week have been attributed to cyberattacks, but rather to technical problems.
Apple responded to TechCrunch’s request for comment (which it initially gave to Bloomberg), noting that the outages were caused by an internal update and not a cyberattack. “Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning. We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible,” the statement read.
After the initial outages were reported, Apple’s status page was updated to include other outages impacting Apple School Manager, iCloud Mail, iCloud Web Apps (iCloud.com), Schoolwork, and the Volume Purchase Program.
By 6 PM ET on Tuesday, the status page showed all the outages were resolved.
This article was updated after publication with the status of the outages.

title: Google makes it easier to use Gemini without training AI on your data
text:
It can be hard to use Google products—or even the Internet itself—without coming into contact with Gemini AI. That is, of course, by design. The more you use Gemini, the more data Google collects to train and improve its generative AI chatbot. The options to limit training on your data have been scant, but Google is finally adding more controls to the Gemini app.
The change currently rolling out to Gemini will separate your chat history from training, which allows you to retain basic AI functionality without handing Google quite so much control over your data. Prior to this change, the only way to opt out of contributing your chat contents (including attachments) for training was to turn off your history. That made it impossible to go back and pick up a chat down the road.
As the new settings roll out, users will see separate toggles for model training and chat history. The history setting will continue to support an adjustable limit, but you will no longer have to change it to stop Google from training on your Gemini usage. Meanwhile, AI training will be an opt-out situation. You’ll need to find the toggle to block Google from using your chats for AI training. It’s under Activity in the Gemini settings. You can also access the menu from your Google account under Data and Privacy > My Activity > Other activity > Gemini Apps Activity.
Importantly, this only applies to future interactions with Gemini. If you have previously fed any data into Google’s AI, that’s already part of the training data. That can include your inputs, Gemini’s responses, uploaded files, tool calls, your location, and data from connected apps. Google says it may retain this data for up to three years to improve its models. The company has previously noted it attempts to filter personal information out of the Gemini activity history, but that isn’t a guarantee.

title: New wearable ultrasound patch boosts REM sleep without drugs or surgery
text:
A revolutionary new wearable patch could help people get more restorative sleep without medication or surgery. Developed by University of Texas researchers, the device uses gentle ultrasound to stimulate deep brain regions, helping participants enter REM sleep 43 minutes faster and remain there 16 minutes longer on average. The technology also showed promising effects on stress regulation and brain circuits involved in emotion.
A new wearable patch could offer a surprisingly simple way to improve one of the most important stages of sleep, without relying on medication or surgery. Developed by researchers led by the University of Texas at Austin, the device uses gentle ultrasound waves to stimulate regions deep inside the brain, helping people enter REM sleep sooner and spend more time in this restorative stage.
Known as NEUSLeeP, the soft patch attaches to the skin and combines ultrasound stimulation with electrodes that monitor brain activity in real time. This allows researchers to influence brain regions involved in sleep while simultaneously tracking how the brain responds.
REM sleep, short for rapid eye movement sleep, is the stage when most vivid dreaming occurs. It also plays an important role in processing emotions, consolidating memories, and adapting to stress. Disturbances in this stage of sleep have been associated with several mental health conditions, making it an important target for new treatments.
"This is the first time we've been able to noninvasively target deep brain regions involved in REM sleep, while simultaneously monitoring brain activity," said Kai Wing "Kevin" Tang, a recent UT biomedical engineering Ph.D. graduate who led the research effort.
"Our skin-attached NEUSLeeP patch opens up new possibilities for understanding sleep and treating sleep disorders in home settings," added Huiliang "Evan" Wang, assistant professor in the Cockrell School of Engineering's Department of Biomedical Engineering. Wang supervised Tang's research and served as the principal investigator (PI) overseeing the project.
Sleep Patch Helps People Reach REM Sleep 43 Minutes Faster
The early results suggest that the technology can make a measurable difference in how people experience REM sleep.
In a study involving 28 participants, published in Nature Communications, people using the patch entered REM sleep an average of 43 minutes sooner and spent approximately 16 additional minutes in that stage.
These improvements were observed in both healthy sleepers and participants experiencing certain sleep difficulties. The volunteers also reported that the patch was comfortable to wear, with minimal adverse effects.
Unlike medications that affect the body more broadly, NEUSLeeP is designed to deliver stimulation to specific brain regions involved in sleep regulation. It uses ultrasound, a form of sound energy with frequencies beyond human hearing, to reach areas beneath the surface of the brain without requiring an invasive procedure.
The findings are encouraging, although the relatively small study means that larger trials will be needed to determine how consistently the technology works and whether its benefits persist over time.
Potential Benefits for Stress and Emotional Health
The researchers also found evidence that the patch's effects may extend beyond increasing REM sleep.
Among healthy participants, ultrasound stimulation improved heart rate variability, a measure of the natural differences in time between consecutive heartbeats. This measurement provides insight into how the body's nervous system responds to stress and adjusts to changing conditions.
Brain imaging revealed changes in neural circuits involved in emotional processing. Together, these findings suggest that improving REM sleep through targeted stimulation could potentially support emotional regulation and the ability to cope with stress.
"REM sleep is not just about dreaming -- it's about emotional reset and stress adaptation," explained Gregory Fonzo, assistant professor in the Dell Medical School's Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences and one of the project's co-PIs. "By enhancing REM, we may help people better cope with stress and improve their overall well-being."
These possibilities are especially interesting because REM sleep disturbances have been linked to depression, anxiety, and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).
Current approaches to sleep problems often involve medication or behavioral therapy. Although these treatments can be effective, medications may produce unwanted side effects, and existing approaches do not always directly address the biological processes responsible for disrupted REM sleep.
A device capable of influencing those processes without drugs or surgery could therefore offer an additional treatment option. However, the researchers have not yet established whether NEUSLeeP can improve symptoms of mental health disorders.
A New Direction for Treating Insomnia and PTSD
Building on the initial findings, the research team plans to conduct larger clinical trials to confirm the patch's effects and investigate its potential use in people with PTSD, depression, and chronic insomnia.
Beyond treating sleep disorders, the technology could eventually support sleep monitoring at home and provide scientists with a new way to study how deep brain regions influence sleep. Researchers also envision personalized therapies that could be adjusted to individual sleep patterns and needs.
"Our vision is a future where patients with mental health disorders can optimize their sleep with a noninvasive and safe treatment," said Vincent Mysliwiec, M.D., a professor at UT Health San Antonio, a leading expert in sleep disorders, and another co-PI on the project. "This technology could help millions of people get the restorative sleep they need."
The team is already taking steps toward making NEUSLeeP available beyond the research setting. Working with the university's commercialization unit, Discovery to Impact, the researchers are exploring how to bring the device to market and have filed a patent application covering the technology.
If future studies confirm the early results, this wearable ultrasound patch could become a valuable new tool for improving REM sleep and potentially addressing conditions associated with poor sleep.
Other members of the research team include William D. Moscoso-Barrera, Mengxia Yu, Mengmeng Yao, Jinmo Jeong, Ilya Pyatnitskiy, Anakaren Romero Lozano, Jiachen Wang, Ju-Chun Hsieh, Tony Sungjin Chae, Daniel Song, Julieta Garcia, Rithvik Mittapalli, and Adam Bush of the Department of Biomedical Engineering; Benjamin Baird of the College of Natural Sciences' Department of Psychology; and Wynn Legon of Virginia Tech's Fralin Biomedical Research Institute.

title: The brain’s fear center moonlights as the save button for memories
text:
The walnut-sized fear center of the brain also distinguishes the memorable from the mundane.
Neurons in the amygdala act like a save button for memories, scientists report October 27 in Nature Neuroscience. Though the study doesn’t nail down the exact mechanism for memory formation, it points to a broader role for the amygdala within the memory-sorting apparatus.
The study probes an enduring quandary about the mind, says neuroscientist Jiayang Xiao of Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University in Los Angeles. “We forget much of what we experience … only a fraction of the information we encounter becomes a lasting memory,” she says.
Although a role for the amygdala in memory has been suggested before, previous studies that used electrodes reading brain activity through the scalp, or at the scale of thousands rather than individual neurons, captured a blurrier picture. It’s akin to a microphone recording from outside of a stadium, says cognitive neuroscientist Cory Inman at the University of Utah in Salt Lake City, who was not involved in the study.
“You might be able to tell that there’s a game happening. You might be able to tell when somebody scores a touchdown. You might even be able to tell that one side of the stadium is cheering for one team and another side of the stadium is cheering for another team,” but that’s about it, Inman says. The new study is more like a lapel mic pinned on a single fan in terms of scale and what the researchers were able to capture, adding clarity.
The amygdala, which is typically associated with regulating emotions like fear and aggression, has neurons that are challenging to reach, residing in two clusters deep within the brain. Xiao and her colleagues leveraged electrodes previously surgically implanted in more than 90 people with drug-resistant epilepsy to identify where seizures originate. In their new role, the electrodes singled out neurons involved in saving memories.
Patients were shown images of everyday objects belonging to five categories such as food and animals. About 10 to 30 minutes later, they attempted to recall which images were already shown. Xiao and her colleagues found that activity in certain amygdala neurons corresponded with an image being remembered. The image had been earmarked for longer term storage, Xiao says.
Although participants had to recall something from half an hour ago at most and the exact mechanism for saving memories is still unclear, the researchers think there are two main steps of the process. The team showed that individual neurons have a preference for one of the five categories of images. First the image is categorized by the amygdala. Then, the strength of the category neuron response the first time the image is shown dictates whether the image is later recalled.
A better understanding of this mechanism may pave the way for more effective treatments of memory disorders, Xiao says, a medical conundrum for which there are currently no broadly effective treatments.
The hippocampus is typically more directly linked to memory, so “it surprised me that we observe such a clear relationship between memory formation and activity in the amygdala,” Xiao says. By contrast, the correlation between hippocampus neuron activity and image recall was weaker and slightly delayed.
Future work like observing the impacts of stimulating amygdala neurons on memory will help researchers discern if this region can be targeted to improve memory, Xiao says.
For now, the secret to memory’s hidden machinations remains in the shadows.

title: ISS astronauts 3D print human cells and tissues | Space photo of the day for Nov. 17, 2026
text:
Astronauts get tasked with all kinds of weird science aboard the International Space Station. Recently, NASA astronaut and Crew-13 commander Jessica Watkins got to work supporting an ongoing experiment that includes 3D-printing human cells and tissues in space.
What is it?
Aboard the space station, astronauts have a multitude of responsibilities ranging from station maintenance and repairs on spacewalks to daily exercise and a wide variety of scientific research.
Watkins recently shared a snapshot captured by her crewmate Anil Menon that showcases her experience working on an experiment called InSPA-Auxilium Bioprinter-Cell Printing that takes place inside the station's Life Sciences Glovebox, a contained research space and one of Watkins favorite places to work on the space station, she shared on social media.
In the image she is gloved-up with both her hands and arms covered in the sealed glovebox while she mixes samples of living cells with a bioink, a mixture she then inserts into a specialized cartridge, NASA shared.
Why is it incredible?
This experiment that Watkins is working on "leverages the microgravity environment of ISS to 3D print cells and manufacture human liver, kidney, and cartilage tissue. Just one of many examples of how we’re using this amazing orbital national laboratory to reshape our understanding of biology, medicine, and engineering, and improve life on Earth!" Watkins shared online.
This experiment is designed to explore 3D printing human cartilage tissue in microgravity. The experiment aims to one day support future human patients both in space and on Earth.
When you think of the research that happens in space, 3D-printing human cells might not be the first thing to come to mind. But because of the unique microgravity environment onboard the ISS, it is the perfect home for even the strangest of biological experiments.
On the space station, there is still gravity but objects (and people) remain in a sort of constant freefall, leading to total weightlessness that mimics the complete absence of gravity. This weightlessness allows researchers to test, experiment and explore beyond the gravitational confines of Earth.

title: Campaigners take claim 'regulatory gap' risks poultry farms polluting rivers to High Court
text:
River campaigners are taking on Wales' environmental regulator in the High Court over what they believe is a "regulatory gap" that risks pollution from poultry farms in two rivers.
River Action UK has accused Natural Resources Wales (NRW) of not doing enough to assess or address any risk to local rivers and and other water bodies when plans for three farms in Powys were approved last year.
It follows years of debate over the alleged impact of chicken farming on rivers such as the Wye and Severn - in an area dubbed the UK's "poultry capital".
NRW said it would be inappropriate to comment ahead of the court case, but that it would "participate fully in the legal process".
The case is about plans to increase the capacity of three Powys farms by a combined 336,900 chickens, bringing the total to 522,000.
The three farms are Neuadd Isaf, Rhosddu and Llanshay.
Two of the farms, Rhosddu and Llanshay, are in the River Severn catchment while Neuadd Isaf is in the River Wye catchment.
Campaigners said the Severn was showing "signs of strain" with regular algal blooms, brown algae smothering the riverbed.
Campaigners' concerns have centred around the birds' manure becoming a pollutant when it is spread on fields and leaches into rivers.
Nutrient-rich agricultural run-off can contribute to algal blooms, turning rivers green and smothering wildlife.
Following a consultation, NRW approved permit variations in November 2025, allowing the three poultry units to expand.
Rather than keep and spread the manure on site, the farms' operators said they would export it for use or processing elsewhere.
River Action argued NRW wrongly concluded it had no legal power under the Environmental Permitting Regulations 2016 to assess the potential environmental impacts of this off-site manure management, or to take action to prevent or mitigate pollution arising from it.
Campaigners set up a chicken-themed protest outside the High Court hearing in Llandrindod Wells on Tuesday.
"River Action will argue that Natural Resources Wales has the power to address and assess the impact of that manure on the environment and, as the specialist regulator, should be lawfully deciding how to use that power when operating the permitting regime," said Julia Eriksen, of solicitors Leigh Day, representing River Action.
The organisation insisted NRW could put controls on the farm's permit to reduce or remove the risk of manure causing pollution.
Emma Dearnaley, head of legal at River Action, said NRW "decided that it didn't have the power to look at what would happen when a lot of the manure would go offsite" when the plans were approved last year.
