"That matters because more chickens means more muck, and that needs to go somewhere and someone has to deal with it," she said.
"So this case is all about making NRW realise that it does have the power to deal with it."
An NRW spokesperson said: "As legal proceedings are ongoing, it would be inappropriate to comment on matters that are before the court. We will continue to participate fully in the legal process and await the court's determination."

title: US basketball player arrested with 75lb of marijuana at Nigerian airport, say authorities
text:
An American basketball player has been arrested in Nigeria for allegedly attempting to smuggle 33.95kg (75lb) of marijuana into the country.
Nigeria’s National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) said a 28-year-old player named as Greene Da’monte Khiree from the state of Georgia was arrested at Lagos’s main airport last Wednesday after he arrived on a flight from Thailand via the United Arab Emirates.
The NDLEA said the player told them he had come to Nigeria to “build networks” for his basketball career. The agency said evidence on his phone suggested he had “knowledge of and involvement in the drug trafficking activity”. The NDLEA said it detained the player when he attempted to leave the airport with his hand luggage after abandoning two checked-in bags. The agency said those two bags were found to contain 32 parcels of marijuana, and a tracking device.
Nigeria has strict drug laws, and trafficking carries a sentence of life in prison.
A basketball player by the name of Damonte Greene is listed on the roster of the Pattani Raptors in the Thai Premier Men’s League. Greene, a Georgia native, played college basketball for Reinhardt University and South Georgia Technical College. He played semi-professional basketball in the US before representing a number of teams in Thailand.
WNBA star Brittney Griner and former Utah State player Jarred Shaw were imprisoned in Russia and Indonesia respectively for marijuana offenses. Griner was released in December 2022, while Shaw remains in prison.

title: Trump is in Asia ahead of Xi, Putin summit. And, tech leaders want Huang back at Nvidia
text:
Today's top stories
A technology issue with United Airlines delayed departing flights yesterday evening, just as air travel was returning to normal after the Federal Aviation Administration ordered a nationwide ground stop on Friday. President Trump said yesterday that he hopes this incident will prompt Congress to allocate more funds to upgrade the outdated air traffic control system.
- 🎧 Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that the FAA will reevaluate future maintenance procedures, NPR's Joe Hernandez tells Up First. Mike McCormick, a former FAA senior executive and air traffic manager, told Hernandez that he thinks another nationwide ground stop is unlikely. McCormick says that in cases like this, the FAA sometimes imposes a maintenance moratorium, temporarily halting such work. The ground stop happened while L3Harris workers converted copper wires to a fiber optic system and installed a new router in El Dorado, Arkansas.
President Trump is in Manila today to meet with allies at the ASEAN summit. Tomorrow, he travels to Shenzhen, China, for a joint summit with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. It's the first time those three have had a joint summit. The meeting will happen on the sidelines of the APEC summit that Xi is hosting in Shenzhen.
- 🎧 When leaving the White House yesterday, Trump said they would discuss his "favorite subject": Ukraine, NPR's Deepa Shivaram says. The White House had previously announced that Ukraine would not be on the agenda for the trilateral meeting. Shivaram says that Europe and Ukraine are concerned about how Ukraine may be discussed at the meeting, and what might come out of it, because President Volodymyr Zelenskyy will not be at APEC and Trump has recently been more lenient toward Putin and Russia.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation has shaken Silicon Valley, prompting calls from some tech leaders for the board to reinstate him. Trump said he agreed with them. Meanwhile, the U.S. government introduced a rule to block remote access to advanced AI chips and servers, closing a loophole that could allow adversarial governments to access American AI technology through overseas data centers. Nvidia is the world's dominant producer of AI chips.
- 🎧 Many prominent AI and venture capital figures have recognized Huang as a visionary whose company played a significant role in the AI boom, NPR's Shannon Bond says. An online petition supporting his reinstatement has garnered more than 160,000 signatures, but Bond says some of them may not be real. Elon Musk says he signed it. Brad Gerstner from Altimeter Capital, a key Nvidia investor, has urged the board to thoroughly investigate and keep all options open. Bond says the interim CEO and CFO will address the public for the first time following today's earnings report.
Prosecutors are moving to retry Lindsay Clancy for the deaths of her three children. The new trial is set for March 29, 2027. Although there was speculation about potentially reducing the charges to manslaughter or second-degree murder after her previous trial ended in a mistrial, no changes were made during Monday's court hearing. Judge William Sullivan, who presided over the first trial, will oversee the new proceedings. He denied Clancy's defense team's request to dismiss the charges based on double jeopardy. Clancy's defense argues that she shouldn't be held criminally responsible for killing her children because she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis.
Deep dive
One year ago, New Mexico became the first state to offer free childcare to all families regardless of income, as long as adults are working, seeking work, in school, or unable to work. Many parents have found this initiative life-changing, but capacity was limited. Only 50% of the some 67,000 children ages 5 and under are enrolled in the universal childcare program. Some of the remaining families participate in other programs, such as PreK and Head Start. New Mexico officials say the program must expand to meet demand. The issues observed in New Mexico are mirrored across the nation, prompting policymakers and childcare advocates to closely monitor the state's initiative.
- 👶 Almost half of U.S. children aged 5 and under live in licensed childcare deserts, where demand exceeds availability, according to the Center for American Progress, a left-leaning think tank.
- 👶 New Mexico's program has an operating budget of nearly $600 million, but some lawmakers are concerned it could be $50 million over budget this year.
- 👶 New Mexico state Sen. Steve Lanier tells NPR that the steep cost of the program is why he only supports universal childcare for some people, since someone earning around $450,000 or $600,000 might not need assistance. Lanier has previously sued to end the initiative, but the lawsuit was unsuccessful.
- 👶 Since the enactment of free, universal childcare in New Mexico, lower-income mothers have experienced significant gains. Their full-time employment has risen by 23%, according to a new paper from Arizona State University.
Picture show
Millions of shorebirds embark on epic migrations to Alaska each year to breed. They often travel thousands of miles from places like New Zealand, Asia and South America. But researchers have found a concerning trend: Nearly half of the 41 shorebird species that breed in Alaska are in decline. These birds time their journeys to coincide with peak insect availability, and climate change is throwing off their schedules. Warmer springs lead to earlier insect emergence, creating a mismatch that could leave shorebirds without enough food supply. Scientists are now racing to understand if these migratory birds can adapt to the changing Arctic landscape.
3 things to know before you go
- British actor Robert Pattinson will be the seventh James Bond, taking his place among an iconic lineup of stars that started with Sean Connery and most recently featured Daniel Craig.
- The 69th annual Grammy Awards nominations were announced yesterday. British singer-songwriter RAYE leads with 11 nominations, followed by Spanish artist Rosalía with nine nods.
- Civil rights champion Dolores Huerta made history yesterday as the first non-elected individual and the first woman to lie in honor at the California State Capitol. She died of cancer last month at age 96. (via KQED)

title: Jensen Huang says he "would be honored" to return as Nvidia CEO
text:
Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang broke his silence after from the company following revelations of multiple affairs, saying he'd be willing to return as its CEO.
"I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life," Huang said in a statement Tuesday morning. "I created problems for the board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the board's independent investigation."
He added, "If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO."
Late Tuesday, however, Nvidia Chair Harvey Jones said the company's board doesn't intend to rehire Huang as chief executive. The company's search for a new chief is underway, he added, while noting that the board has "every confidence" in Kress' ability to lead the company. Jones said the company is considering both internal and external candidates to replace Huang.
Support for Huang's return
Huang has gained support from more than 190,000 people, including several thousand Nvidia employees, who to reinstate him. On Monday, President Trump suggested to reporters that he would support Huang returning to Nvidia.
"I would not mind seeing that," Mr. Trump said. Later, the president said he recommended former as Nvidia's next leader.
In his Tuesday statement, Huang thanked his allies for their support since his departure last week, saying that in addition to the public calls for him to return to the company, many "continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive and geopolitical dynamics."
Nvidia's board said on Tuesday that it has formed a committee to oversee its national security policies and ensure compliance with U.S. export controls. The former CEO has also agreed to appear before House lawmakers on Dec. 1 to address questions about a potential breach of national security amid an investigation into his affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
The former CEO's return to Nvidia is unlikely, said Yorkville Ives & Co. technology analyst Dan Ives.
"In our view the sequencing is the tell: Jensen has conditioned his return on a board decision, and the board's first public act this week was to build a compliance structure around the issue that forced him out, which is not what a board preparing to reverse itself does," he said in a Tuesday research note.
Shares of Nvidia declined $2.63, or 1.7%, to $153.51. The stock has lost 16% of its value since Huang's extramarital relationships became public.

title: 4 detained in North Macedonia for alleged Iran-backed assassination plot in Greece
text:
Authorities in North Macedonia say four people have been detained for questioning over an alleged Iran-linked assassination plot in neighboring Greece
SKOPJE, North Macedonia -- Authorities in North Macedonia have detained four people for questioning over an alleged Iran-linked assassination plot in neighboring Greece, officials said Tuesday.
Bojan Hristovski, director of North Macedonia's domestic security agency, said Tuesday that the suspects are all Macedonian citizens, adding that a fifth person had also been questioned and a sixth remained wanted by the authorities.
Hristovski named one of the Iranian recruiters as Naji Sharifi Zindashti, who is wanted in the United States for allegedly operating a criminal network that targets Iranian dissidents and activists abroad.
He did not give details of the alleged target in Greece, and Greek authorities did not immediately comment on the announcement.
“This concerns the dismantling of an Iranian proxy network involved in planning a terrorist attack,” Hristovski said.
“The network operating in Macedonia consisted of individuals embedded in criminal organizations within the country,” he said. “Acting on direct instructions from an Iranian national, they undertook preparatory and logistical activities for a terrorist act — an assassination targeting a previously identified individual located in Greece.”
Iran's mission to the United Nations did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: Nvidia forms national security committee after Huang affair
text:
Nvidia on Tuesday said it had created a board-level national security and export-control committee.
This follows the scandal surrounding former CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned last week over extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of spying for China and working to help ensure higher quality chips crucial to AI development made it to the Chinese market.
The events have heightened oversight of the US tech giant and its importance to national security, as well as wiping several hundred billion dollars off the stock market valuation of what investors treat as the world's most valuable company in the space of a month.
Since Huang's resignation, some investors — including Elon Musk and Donald Trump — have voiced concern that his departure could leave Nvidia and America's AI sector in peril and are now calling for his return. Huang on Tuesday, expressed regret for "serious mistakes" in his personal life before declaring he would be "honored" to return if the company's board of directors thought that was "in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America."
What are Nvidia's plans for the new oversight committee?
Nvidia is calling the new group its National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee.
Suzanne Nora Johnson, a former vice chair at Goldman Sachs, will chair the committee, joined by fellow directors Stephen Neal, a former CEO of a law firm, John Dabiri, a professor of aeronautics and mechanical engineering at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech).
The committee will meet at least once every quarter. It will also incorporate independent legal, national security and trade compliance experts.
Nvidia already has a lower-level National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team; these groups will report to the board-level committee.
"We are committed to working constructively with government and industry partners to help establish and advance a robust framework that uses every tool at our disposal to safeguard national security while supporting continued technological innovation," Board Chair Harvey Jones said in a statement.
The company did not explicitly link the decision to November's developments and Huang's rapid fall from grace, but the timing seemed conspicuous.
The decision was announced hours ahead of Nvidia publishing its third-quarter results, with its still-stratospheric share price having fallen roughly 28% in the past month.
How has the scandal highlighted the question of US-China chip trade?
US President Donald Trump, whom Huang was influential in persuading to allow the export of better-quality Nvidia chips to China than other US companies and officials deemed prudent, welcomed Nvidia's move on arrival in the Philippines on Tuesday.
"Yes, that's a good idea. It's a great company," he said during a photo opportunity at a Manila meeting with the other "Quad" leaders from Australia, India and Japan. "It's a great idea."
Trump reportedly owned Nvidia stock worth tens of millions of dollars before the share price fell. He also owns shares in other big tech companies.
Huang resigned last week after admitting to extramarital affairs in a message to Nvidia employees. This followed widespread reports, seemingly based on US and other intelligence, that one of the affairs was with a woman who used to lead a Singapore-based cloud computing company.
That company, Megaspseed International, is a major Nvidia client and is suspected of diverting advanced chips to China in violation of US export controls. Intelligence officials also suspect Huang's partner of being an asset of Chinese intelligence services.
The reporting on the case also seems to show these suspicions had been known to US officials and other countries, including Singapore, for roughly a year.

title: US criticized over ‘stupid’ message to Ukraine backers about deep strikes
text:
The Pentagon has been criticized over its message to Ukraine’s Western backers on Tuesday after it declared that strikes deep inside Russia are counterproductive.
The United States instead urged them to focus their military support on equipment for front-line combat. Elbridge Colby, the U.S. Undersecretary of Defense, delivered the warning as Ukraine’s backers gathered at NATO headquarters in Brussels to drum up support for further arms and ammunition.
The message drew a sharp response from two of Kyiv’s closest European supporters. Germany’s defence minister, Boris Pistorius, dismissed the criticism of deep strikes as “quite a stupid thing.”
“Instead of criticizing that, we should rather criticize and talk about the terroristic strikes every night and every day on civil energy … water and heating infrastructure in Ukraine,” he said.
Britain, for its part, argued the strikes are saving lives.
U.S. President Donald Trump has demanded that Ukraine halt strikes on Russian oil refineries and infrastructure used to produce and distribute diesel, saying the attacks are causing a global shortage. Ukraine’s advanced drone capabilities, developed since Russian President Vladimir Putin launched his full-scale invasion in 2022, have enabled it to strike oil facilities and other installations deep inside Russia.
Earlier this year, Ukraine’s armed forces delivered repeated blows to Wildberries, Russia’s biggest online retailer that is often compared to Amazon. Ukraine says goods sold by the company include equipment and technical components that are used by the Russian military, which the company denies.
The attacks have unsettled Russians living far from the front and hurt small businesses.
Colby said that deep strikes “have not been effective in driving an end to the war, nor do they contribute to blunting Russia’s advances on the front line.”
Speaking at NATO headquarters in Brussels, Colby said that “such strikes, especially those that target civilian infrastructure such as Wildberries, have actually probably hardened the Russian public’s resolve and the Kremlin’s own willingness to escalate.”
He argued Ukraine’s army is “very effective” when it focuses on front-line fighting, using drones to slow Russian advances and hit their supply lines. He said the U.S. believes “that focusing our support on the front lines and on associated midrange strikes is the most effective way to enable Ukraine’s defense and thus to set the conditions for an end to the war.”
The focus, Pistorius said, should be on “terrorism” rather than “legal and legitimate strikes in Russia against non-civilian targets.”
U.K. Defense Secretary Wes Streeting, who co-chaired the meeting with Pistorius, said: “It’s not for us to tell Ukraine how to fight their war.”
“In terms of deep strike capability, there’s no doubt in my mind that it has helped to degrade Putin’s war machine, buying time and saving lives,” Streeting said.
Colby declined to comment when he was asked after the meeting about restrictions on Ukraine’s use of the Starshield satellite communications system and how they are hindering its ability to intercept Russian drones.
However, he followed up by saying he had explained to Ukraine’s backers “that we are very focused on supporting Ukraine’s ability to defend itself, and these kind of midrange strikes, and we’re taking steps that are consistent with that policy.” He did not elaborate.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that limitations on Starshield, operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, are costing lives and could weaken defenses around Ukraine’s energy infrastructure as winter approaches.
“We do need to make sure that we have consistent and reliable service from Starlink and Starshield because lives depend on it,” Streeting said.

title: Klopp's Germany Routs Xavi's Netherlands To Book Nations League Quarterfinals
text:
Florian Wirtz scored twice and Germany booked its place in the Nations League quarterfinals by routing the Netherlands 5-0 in Berlin on Monday.
More importantly, it was confirmation of the German team’s renaissance under new coach Jürgen Klopp, whose appointment ushered in new optimism around his young team with progress evident over his six games in charge.
Nico Schlotterbeck was the oldest goalscorer at 26, Wirtz is still just 23, the 24-year-old Derry Scherhant broke the deadlock, and Brajan Gruda, 22, set up two goals and scored one on what was just his second appearance for Germany. He also scored on his debut in Friday’s 3-1 win in Serbia.
It was the most emphatic win for Germany under Klopp, and the worst loss so far for Netherlands manager Xavi Hernandez. The World Cup-winning Spanish midfielder and club legend at Barcelona took over the Dutch job in August.
Klopp clearly enjoyed each of the goals, but he praised the players' work rate as key.
"Everyone who was here today is going home with a smile, and won’t be questioning the German national team for the next three or four months. That’s a good thing," Klopp said, referring to the previous negativity around the side. "When you think of the German team, this could develop into something, and that’s good."
Substitute Giorgos Masouras’ 69th-minute strike was enough for Greece to beat Serbia 1-0 at home in the other group game, but it was not enough for progress as Germany and the Netherlands both look forward to Friday's quarterfinal draw. All three teams finished with 11 points.
Germany Flying
Local favorite Scherhant twice hit the post before opening the scoring with a brilliant strike before the break, cutting inside to elude Dutch captain Denzel Dumfries and then shooting inside the top right corner. Bart Verbruggen got his fingers to the ball but couldn’t prevent its progress.
Scherhant, who used to score such goals in the same stadium for Hertha Berlin, pointed to the ground to indicate he was home again.
"You couldn't have imagined it going any better," said Scherhant, who now plays for Freiburg.
Wirtz's goal, on the hour mark, was arguably better, winning the ball back from Dumfries after an attack broke down, feigning with his right foot to set up his left and then unleashing the ball in off the left post from outside the penalty area.
Schlotterbeck sealed the result five minutes later with a low header to Gruda’s free kick, and Wirtz volleyed in his second in the 71st after Gruda was left free on the right. It prompted some Dutch fans to head for the exits.
Gruda got Germany’s fifth in the 77th, prompting furious Dutch goalkeeper Verbruggen to call a team meeting to remonstrate with his teammates. By then it was too late.
Reporting by The Associated Press.

title: Van Hollen's bid to replace Schumer puts pressure on Democrats to take sides
text: WASHINGTON (AP) — Senate Democrats elect their leader every two years behind closed doors and on a secret ballot. But this year's race has burst into the public eye as Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen mounts an insurgent bid against New York incumbent Chuck Schumer. The Dec. 1 contest has put Senate Democrats on edge and has forced what could become an ugly fight immediately after major victories in the midterm elections. It has also put the more moderate incoming Democrats in a tough spot, forced to take sides in a leadership race before they are even sworn into office. Schumer, who recruited several of those moderate Democrats who helped win the majority, has said he has the votes to be reelected, and around 15 of the 55 elected Democrats in next year's caucus have said publicly that they will support him. Four Democratic senators have said they will support Van Hollen. Everyone else is staying quiet for now. "Leave it to the Democrats," said Colorado Sen. John Hickenlooper, who flipped an imaginary coin when asked by reporters on Monday how he will vote. "We flipped nine seats, and the person who actually helps put it all together and do all that, and all of a sudden, there's a revolt." Van Hollen, who is backed by progressive groups, says it's time for new leadership after Schumer's nearly decade-long tenure. While the two men align on most issues, Van Hollen says Democrats need to more aggressively push to end the Iran war and potentially even shut down the government next month, if necessary, to stop the flow of war funding. "To deliver, we need new leadership," Van Hollen says. "This isn't about any one person – it's about answering that call." Van Hollen is making his argument to the public as Schumer mostly keeps quiet and holds private conversations with the senators who will decide his fate. Schumer shared his agenda for the next Congress in a caucus luncheon last week, laying out a plan to try to quickly pass legislation on healthcare and tariffs and to launch multiple investigations into President Donald Trump's Republican administration. "I'm proud of what we've accomplished together — 55 seats and counting is an amazing result — and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader," Schumer said in a statement. "I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people." A public campaign for an insider's job The unusually public race — the first contested election for Senate Democratic leader in decades — comes when Schumer has drawn intense criticism from the party's base. Some voters and progressive groups called for his removal in 2025 after he voted with Republicans to keep the government open and as they called for stronger opposition to Israel's war in Gaza. Still, many in the caucus see the role not as a national figurehead but as an inside operator who can navigate intraparty politics and the 100-member Senate's arcane rules to pass legislation they like and block legislation they don't. "I want to hear from any candidate what their vision is for the floor and managing the caucus," said Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, who was just reelected. He said he hasn't committed to either Schumer or Van Hollen. Party leaders also spend much of their time fundraising and recruiting candidates — a particular interest for Schumer, who has been directly or indirectly in charge of the Senate Democrats' campaign arm for two decades. Most Democrats don't want to reveal their vote Returning to Washington on Monday for the first time since Van Hollen entered the race, most Democrats would not answer questions about who they would support. That included prominent progressives like Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren. Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin appeared last week at a press conference with Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, an independent who caucuses with Democrats, as he declared that he would not support Schumer. Two days later, Sanders immediately endorsed Van Hollen when he entered the race, but Slotkin has not. "I'm not saying anything," she told reporters on Monday. WATCH: Does Van Hollen have enough support to beat Schumer in Senate leadership race? Others like Virginia Sen. Tim Kaine defended Schumer while saying that they are still open to Van Hollen or someone else. "Chuck delivered an amazing win," said Kaine. "Chuck knows Trump, and that will be really, really important going forward." Still, Kaine said, "The voters are demanding change, so we have to figure that out as a caucus, and we're going to be able to. We're not afraid to have a discussion." Freshmen put on the spot The eight incoming freshmen Democratic senators — nine if Mary Peltola wins the Alaska Senate race, which has still not been called — are set to alter the caucus next year. But only two have said how they will vote in the leadership election. Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota, both of whom were backed by progressive groups in their campaigns, say they support Van Hollen. Schumer supported both of their opponents in their primaries, though he eventually put $67 million into El-Sayed's competitive race. El-Sayed said Tuesday that he likes Schumer and will work alongside him if he wins. But he said he thinks Van Hollen is the best person to take on affordability challenges and liberal priorities like Medicare for All. "I do hope that I can have a voice in a large caucus, all of whom have their voices, but this is not about opposition to something," El-Sayed said at The Atlantic Summit in Washington. For some of the other freshmen, many of them moderates from Republican-leaning states, the decision could be more difficult. Several said during their campaigns that they wouldn't vote for Schumer. But it's unclear if any of them would back the more liberal Van Hollen. In South Carolina on Tuesday, Sen.-elect Annie Andrews, a doctor, said that she is in conversations with both candidates and has been "sharing my plans to fix our healthcare system." Incoming Iowa Sen. Josh Turek told reporters he's met with both Schumer and Van Hollen. He said he wants more specifics on how they will help rural families, overhaul campaign finance and ban lawmakers from trading stocks. Turek said he also wants to assess "who is going to put forth the most robust anti-corruption agenda." Hawaii Sen. Mazie Hirono, who is backing Schumer, said that the caucus needs to hear more from the new senators who "have been through the fire to get here." "I think that we have to make sure that all these voices are heard," she said. "They've got a lot of talent to bring to the table." Associated Press writers Joey Cappelletti and Kevin Freking in Washington, Meg Kinnard in Columbia, S.C., and Hannah Fingerhut in Des Moines, Iowa, contributed to this report.

title: FAA pauses installation of new routers after ground stop
text:
The Federal Aviation Administration said Tuesday it would pause the installation of new routers after problems with the technology led the agency to issue a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday.
Tens of thousands of flights were affected by the ground stop, which halted departing flights for more than four hours. It was the longest halt to U.S. flight departures since 9/11.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday that an overloaded router installed in southern Arkansas as part of an upgrade to a system overseen by L3Harris Technologies appeared to overwhelm systems that feed radar and other data for air traffic control.
The Wall Street Journal first reported the news about the pause.
The FAA and Department of Transportation have said L3Harris was working to convert the communications network from copper wires to fiber optic.
Democratic members of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation this week asked the FAA and the Department of Transportation for clarity on what went wrong.
"Identifying the device that failed does not establish why it failed," the senators wrote in a statement.
"Modernization cannot come at the expense of operational safety."
The agencies have said they are working to figure out the root cause of the issue and have reiterated that there is no indication of a cyberattack or outside threat.
The senators also asked for a briefing with the FAA, L3Harris and Juniper Networks, which is making the new devices, by Monday. They asked the companies to lay out why the operational systems lacked sufficient redundancy and answer other questions about what led to the outage.
CNBC has reached out to L3Harris and Juniper Networks for comment.
Duffy on Friday called for Congress to approve $50 billion in funding for upgrades to the aging U.S. air traffic control system, more than he has previously asked for. Democratic lawmakers pushed back on the request, citing unspent money from existing funding, which includes Congress' approval last year of $12.5 billion for airport and air traffic control improvements over five years.
Senate Commerce Chair Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said Tuesday that he thinks there will be support for air traffic control modernization, but that the allocation should be specifically for safety upgrades.
"I don't think the full $50 billion will be funded," he said. "Some of that is not safety related, but we just discussed there, and what I expressed is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization."
Duffy dismissed the idea that the router issue had to do with the introduction of artificial intelligence tools and said it was "completely unfounded" because the AI system is not in communication with the defective router. He added that the FBI is helping to investigate the root cause of the issue.
Aging equipment and a shortage of air traffic controllers have for years angered airline executives, who have complained about the cost of resulting disruptions.

title: Google to keep Gemini chats for 2 months, up from 72 hours, even with history off
text:
Google is extending how long it keeps temporary Gemini chats and conversations made with chat history turned off to around two months, saying the change aims to improve safety and security as AI systems become more capable.
The change, which will roll out globally in the Gemini app over the coming weeks, marks a significant increase from the previous 72-hour retention period mentioned in Google’s Gemini Apps Privacy Hub, according to an archived version from November 12.
OpenAI, by comparison, says it may keep temporary chats in ChatGPT for up to 30 days, whereas Anthropic retains incognito chats in Claude for 30 days by default. However, companies may keep some data longer for legal or safety reasons, or to investigate policy violations.
Google did not answer questions about what prompted the change and whether it would affect how conversations are accessed or reviewed, instead pointing to a blog post that says chats are kept longer to respond to users, process feedback, and protect its services and users. Its updated Gemini Apps Privacy Hub also cites potential system failures as a reason for retaining chats and says temporary conversations are not used to train AI models.
The longer retention period comes as Google introduces separate settings for Gemini’s chat history and AI training. Until now, both were tied to a single “Keep Activity” setting. Users will now be able to keep their conversations in their chat history without using them to train Google’s generative AI models.
Google says both new settings will be turned off by default for users who previously disabled Keep Activity. For those who had Keep Activity turned on, their chat history will remain enabled. They can, though, decide separately whether Google can use their conversations to train AI models.

title: House Democrats promise a US return to global climate talks
text:
ANTALYA, Turkey—After their big gains in the 2026 midterm elections, a delegation of Democratic US House members appeared at the United Nations COP31 climate change conference Monday, pledging to rejoin the international fight against global warming.
Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), ranking member of the House Natural Resources Committee, said it is a “pivotal time” for US climate and energy policy.
“The wrecking ball of Donald Trump and this out-of-touch administration, and the temporarily empty chair of the United States at this COP31, does not represent what the Americans want or need,” Huffman said.
President Donald Trump has pulled the United States out of the Paris climate agreement twice and is trying to quit the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change. The current administration has also tried to cut all funding for climate programs.
Since Trump returned to the White House in 2025, the United States has had no formal government presence at the UN talks, but was informally represented by America Is All In, a coalition including local governments, businesses, faith groups, Native American tribes, and universities.
Huffman said the midterm election shows that Americans have rejected the current administration’s efforts to “turn the United States into something like a petro-dictatorship.” The results could pave the way for the country to reestablish a formal presence at the annual talks.
Given legal uncertainties about Trump’s efforts to completely withdraw the US from the UN’s climate framework, the extent of US participation in the talks is unclear. But Huffman said that, in the past, US congressional delegations have attended the annual Conference of the Parties, as the meeting is formally known, under both Democratic and Republican majorities.
“The next time we’re here, we will be an official congressional delegation led by the leadership of the House of Representatives,” Huffman said in an interview with Inside Climate News.

title: Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising
text:
A surprising Finnish study found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the assumption that screen time is always harmful. Researchers suggest that what children do on screens may matter more than how much time they spend using them.
An eight-year study of children in Finland has revealed a surprising connection between screen time and brain function. Researchers found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the widespread assumption that screen time is necessarily harmful to developing brains.
The findings suggest that the amount of time children spend in front of screens may be less important than how they use that time. Activities that encourage learning, creativity, and problem-solving could be particularly valuable. Researchers emphasize that the goal should not be to eliminate screen time, but to balance it with physical activity and mentally stimulating experiences.
The discovery comes amid growing concerns about insufficient physical activity among teenagers. A sedentary lifestyle has been linked to poorer academic performance, while regular exercise is known to support brain function, particularly in adults. However, scientists still have much to learn about how physical activity, sitting, and screen use during childhood influence thinking abilities later in adolescence.
These questions are especially important because childhood and adolescence are critical periods of brain development. Changes in attention, memory, and learning during these years can have lasting consequences, potentially influencing educational opportunities and career paths well into adulthood.
To investigate these relationships, Finnish researchers examined how screen time, physical activity, and sedentary behavior from childhood through adolescence were associated with cognitive performance in teenagers. They also explored whether the connections differed between boys and girls and whether the intensity of physical activity made a difference.
More Screen Time Linked to Better Thinking Skills
One of the study's most unexpected findings was that greater screen time throughout childhood was associated with better cognitive processing in adolescence.
Cognitive processing refers to the mental abilities people use to take in information, pay attention, remember details, learn new things, and solve problems. These abilities play an important role in school performance and everyday decision-making.
The findings challenge the idea that all screen time should be viewed as harmful. However, the researchers caution that the relationship may depend on what children are actually doing while using digital devices. Watching videos, playing games that require strategic thinking, and engaging in educational activities may involve very different levels of mental effort.
"The findings suggest that screen time can support children's and adolescents' cognitive processing. Presumably, the essential point here is what kind of things they do in their screen time. Teachers and parents should encourage children to use devices and screens in such ways that promote active thinking, problem-solving, creativity, and learning," states Doctoral Researcher Petri Jalanko from the University of Jyväskylä.
"We should not regard screen time solely as harmful but seek balance between physical activity and screen time that promotes active thinking," Jalanko summarizes.
Exercise Affects Boys' and Girls' Brains Differently
The researchers also uncovered a more complicated picture of how physical activity relates to thinking and memory.
Among girls, spending more time engaged in light-intensity physical activity since childhood was associated with better working memory during adolescence. For boys, greater participation in guided physical activity over the same period was linked to stronger working memory.
Working memory is the brain's ability to temporarily hold and use information. It allows someone to remember instructions while completing a task, keep track of numbers during mental calculations, or follow a conversation while processing new information.
Light-intensity physical activity generally includes relatively gentle movements that do not substantially increase breathing or heart rate. Guided physical activity refers to exercise carried out with some form of instruction or supervision, such as organized sports or structured exercise sessions.
The differences between boys and girls suggest that the relationship between exercise and brain health may depend on more than simply how much a person moves. The type of activity, how it is organized, and the individual's sex could all play a role.
Another Surprising Finding About Physical Activity
The study produced another counterintuitive result. Teenagers who reported spending less time in unsupervised physical activity tended to perform better on measures of cognitive processing.
Yet when researchers used wearable sensors to objectively measure movement and heart rate, they found no association between overall physical activity or sedentary time and cognitive performance.
One possible explanation is that wearable devices measure movement without revealing what a person is actually doing. For example, a sensor may record periods of sitting or physical activity, but it cannot determine whether someone is solving a difficult problem, studying, participating in an organized activity, or simply resting.
This distinction could help explain why questionnaire responses revealed relationships that were not apparent in the sensor measurements.
"Our study indicates that the connections of physical activity and sedentary behavior to cognitive processing are complex and depend on the sex, the type and assessment method of physical activity and sedentary time. Moreover, boys and girls may benefit from different types of physical activity in view of brain health," Jalanko adds.
"However, we need more intervention studies to find out causal relations and sex differences in this respect. Moreover, it is important to examine more specifically the effects of the intensity of physical activity on changes taking place in cognitive processing."
What the Eight-Year Study Revealed
The findings come from an eight-year follow-up conducted as part of the PANIC study, a long-running Finnish research project investigating children's physical activity and nutrition.
The current analysis included 260 participants, consisting of 124 girls and 136 boys. Their average age at the adolescent assessment was 15.8 years.
Researchers collected information about physical activity and sedentary behavior using both questionnaires and wearable devices that combined heart rate monitoring with movement measurements. This approach allowed them to compare participants' reported activities with data collected by sensors.
To evaluate cognitive abilities, the researchers used the CogState test battery, a collection of computerized assessments designed to measure aspects of mental performance. The tests examined learning, attention, and working memory.
Importantly, the findings show associations rather than cause and effect. They do not establish that increasing screen time will improve a child's thinking abilities or that reducing certain types of exercise will produce cognitive benefits. Intervention studies, in which researchers deliberately change participants' activities and measure the results, are needed to determine whether these relationships are causal.
Nevertheless, the results offer an important perspective on the continuing debate over children's screen use. Rather than treating all time spent with digital devices as equally harmful, the researchers suggest paying closer attention to whether those activities encourage active thinking and learning.
The research also highlights the importance of considering different forms of physical activity rather than focusing exclusively on the total amount of exercise children receive.
Together, the findings suggest that supporting healthy brain development may require a more nuanced approach, one that combines physical activity with opportunities for learning, creativity, and mental engagement, including those that take place on screens.
The study was published in the scientific journal Pediatric Exercise Science.

title: Europe’s Hera mission is ready to double down on asteroid science
text:
The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft is about to start a twofold mission to a twofold asteroid.
On November 4, after more than two years trekking through space, the spacecraft finally came within 30 kilometers of space rocks named Didymos and Dimorphos. The encounter marks the first time scientists will explore a pair of asteroids navigating the solar system together. To date, spacecraft have stopped to investigate just seven other asteroids, every one of them a lonely speck in outer space.
Hera will spend the coming weeks approaching Didymos and Dimorphos and will release two small companion spacecraft in January for an even closer look.
Didymos, a mass of rocks about twice as wide as the Empire State Building is tall, and its small moonlet Dimorphos have had a rough time lately. In 2022, NASA slammed its Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) spacecraft into Dimorphos, sending a plume of debris into space and shortening its orbit around Didymos by more than half an hour.
The cosmic realignment wasn’t a mere lark. Such an impact is one of the few ways scientists can practice planetary defense, the field dedicated to searching for dangerous asteroids and developing ways to deal with them lest humans go the way of the dinosaurs. DART and Hera are a carefully coordinated pair, with Hera’s top priority being to investigate the aftermath of DART’s crash and inform future planetary defense efforts.
That process will also yield a treasure trove of observations asteroid scientists are determined to exploit.
“Planetary defense and science are sort of two sides of the same coin,” says planetary scientist Jessica Sunshine of the University of Maryland, who was on the DART team but is not involved in the Hera mission. On the science side, she says, “we’re trying to figure out not so much how did we break the thing, but how was it put together in the first place.”
DART purposefully targeted a binary system instead of a solo asteroid to make measuring the change in orbit it accomplished easier: Any difference would be much more obvious against the 12-hour baseline orbit of Dimorphos around Didymos than against the months- or yearslong orbit of an asteroid circling the sun. (Despite the difficulty, scientists were able to calculate that DART shortened the more-than-two-year orbit of the Didymos system around the sun by a fraction of a second.)
Hera’s observations will provide a crucial glimpse at binary asteroids generally, which astronomers believe account for some 15 percent of all asteroids. Scientists expect that most binary asteroids in the inner solar system, including the Didymos system, probably formed their moonlets from debris that sloughed off the larger object then clumped together in orbit.
Didymos spins so quickly that its gravity may not be strong enough to hold all its rock together. As the asteroid spins, it may send boulders into space, where they could end up landing on Dimorphos, continuing that material transfer today. Scientists will comb through Hera’s imagery for signs of rocks moving across each object’s surface, as well as between the two objects.
Scientists expect that Dimorphos is a rubble pile composed of boulders and rocky debris. It’s similar in structure to other recent spacecraft targets Ryugu and Bennu, although those are both significantly larger. The boulder-strewn landscape DART saw as it sped toward Dimorphos aligns with this theory, but how deep the rubbly structure extends is a mystery. “We’ve never seen the interior of an asteroid before,” says planetary scientist Angela Stickle of the Johns Hopkins University’s Applied Physics Laboratory.
Juventas, Hera’s companion cubesat about the size of a breadbox, will change that. It carries a first-of-its-kind radar instrument to investigate Dimorphos’ internal structure.
Juventas will also attempt to land on Dimorphos, allowing scientists to directly interact with the surface. That’s a particularly tantalizing endeavor given one of the biggest surprises of NASA’s OSIRIS-REx mission. When that spacecraft grabbed a sample of Bennu, it accidentally sank some half a meter into the rubble as the asteroid unexpectedly gave way beneath it, even though the surface had looked perfectly sturdy.
“Even though we had amazing images, the reaction was not what we expected,” says planetary scientist Patrick Michel of the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) of that experience. “There is still sort of a mismatch between what we see and what we feel.” He hopes that the Juventas landing will help scientists better connect appearance and reality on this front.
Although scientists will need to pick out the ways DART made Didymos and Dimorphos different from other binary asteroids, observations with Hera will offer new avenues for investigating more general questions in asteroid science.
For example, scientists know that before DART’s impact, Dimorphos always showed the same face to Didymos, just like our moon does to Earth. The collision probably changed that, sending Dimorphos tumbling — but there’s no way to know what state it’s in now because scientists have never seen this resetting process unfold. “Eventually, the system might stabilize, but we don’t know how long it takes,” says planetary scientist Eva Lilly of the Planetary Science Institute, who is not involved in either mission.
Similarly, scientists know that the rain of charged particles onto an asteroid’s surface darkens a thin layer of rock at the surface, but without the detailed understanding they’d like. At Dimorphos, they’ll be able to observe fresh rock uncovered by a known event, potentially offering clearer insight into the universal process.
Cosmic crash scene or not, asteroid scientists are never going to miss out on up-close views of two different space rocks.

title: 'It looked like every star in the sky was falling': Eyewitnesses remember the great Leonid meteor storm of 1966
text:
Overnight Nov. 17-18, 1966, the Leonid meteor storm thrilled stargazers during one extraordinary night when the stars themselves looked as though they were falling from the sky.
At the peak of the shower, observers at Kitt Peak National Observatory in Arizona estimated an astonishing 40 meteors per second streaking across the sky. That's 2,400 shooting stars per minute, or a staggering 144,000 per hour. It was a spectacle that many regard as the greatest meteor display in recorded history.
It's hard to imagine what it was like to experience such a spectacle. But who better to tell us than those who saw it with their own eyes? To mark the 60th anniversary of the great Leonid meteor storm of 1966, we asked those who saw it to share their memories.
'One of the most loved and memorable nights of my life'
"I was around 9 years old at the time of the 1966 Leonid storm, living a few miles east of Roxie, Mississippi. We lived in a rural, dark, relatively remote area with almost zero outside lights.
"I and a couple cousins were spending the night at our Uncle and Aunt's house, staying up late, just fooling around outside like young kids do when living in the 'sticks'. As we walked down a road, I remember hearing an almost constant series of little whistling, zipping sounds. The sounds were similar to when you light a nylon rope on fire and as it burns, little flaming droplets drip down with a zippy sound.
"I looked up and the sky was filled with streaks of 'shooting stars' and I realized that was what made the sounds. I yelled at my cousins to look up and we could hardly believe what we saw. We all laid down on our backs and for a couple of hours just watched and listened to what seemed like 1000's of 'shooting stars' zipping and zinging overhead. I could even smell the sulphur-like odor from the burning little bits of space dust.
"I'm nearly 70 years old now but I'll never forget that experience. I always knew what I'd seen that night was special but not until much later in life, after the internet, did I realize just how lucky I was to have experienced that storm. That night was one of the most loved and memorable nights of my life and I'll treasure it forever."
'Students and faculty were pounding on doors to get people, including neighbors, to watch'
"I was an astronomy lab assistant at Southwestern College in Winfield, KS, in 1966, majoring in physics and math and the physics professor was sure that the Leonids would be an amazing shower worth the class time.
"The sky was clear. He called me early the morning of the 17th and told me to get to the campus. I can't remember the exact time as students and faculty were pounding on doors to get people, including neighbors,to watch.
"We were all lying in an open grassy area because that was the best way to see the whole sky. It was like a humongous fireworks display and lasted even as the sun began to rise.
"As years have gone by, I have felt grateful and privileged to have seen such a wonderful astronomical event."
'It looked like every star in the sky was falling'
"I was 18 and spent the night in El Paso, Texas, lying on the ground in my backyard and watching. It looked like every star in the sky was falling. It was amazing!"
'We watched them all night'
"I was 9 years old and was camping with my dad in the western mountains of California. We were set up to sleep outside, but on this particular night, we saw more meteors than I have ever seen before or since. We watched them all night and didn't get much sleep."
'It took your breath away'
"Brooklyn Center, Minnesota. 14 years old. Watched in our front yard. The sky was full. It took your breath away"
'I assumed they would all be as interesting'
"I was 3 years old at the time of the 1966 Leonid meteor shower. I remember very little at that age, but watching the sky fall that night was seared in my memory.
"My family was living in Troy, Alabama, at the time. My father, a professor of psychology, was a man of science with a special love of astronomy, which he passed onto his young son.
"He drove us several miles out of town until the skies were dark, without interference from the lights of the town. Troy was much smaller then and it was easy to find dark, clear skies.
"I remember that it was a little chilly that night. My father and I stretched out on the hood of the car, the warmth of the engine radiating against our backs.
"That night was my first meteor shower, and only many years later did I learn that year's Leonids were historic. Sadly, though I bore witness to the display, we missed the true event by several hours as I grew tired by 1:00 AM, and my father had to teach class in the morning.
"I remember many bright, colorful, and long-trailed meteors. Some left 'tails' that hung in the sky for several seconds. We only experienced the beginning of the event, but it is a core memory with my father.
"That night/morning spoiled me for future meteor watches; I assumed they would all be as interesting."
'I guess the party is over'
Not everyone was lucky enough to witness the great Leonid meteor storm of 1966. For some, the night was memorable for an entirely different reason.
Space.com columnist Joe Rao was just 10 years old at the time, and despite eagerly anticipating the display, the weather had other ideas.
"Standing in my backyard late on a Wednesday night in the Throggs Neck section of The Bronx, cursing the heavens. My grandfather stood at my side, just shaking his head and murmuring two words over and over: 'Too bad.'
"Clouds covered the midnight sky like a fresh coat of plaster, smearing my view of the Leonids. My mom, sister and grandmother, as well as my neighbors had long since trudged to bed, leaving only Grandpa and I to gaze at a charcoal gray sky totally devoid of stars."
Rao had been looking forward to the storm ever since a visit to New York's Hayden Planetarium, where astronomer Fred C. Hess had encouraged visitors to look out for what could be a spectacular display.
But when Rao and his grandfather ventured outside, there wasn't a single star in sight.
"After a few minutes, I sobbed to my grandfather, 'But they promised it was only going to be partly cloudy tonight.' To which he sadly replied, 'I guess the party is over.'"
What caused the great Leonid meteor storm of 1966?
The Leonid meteor shower occurs every November when Earth passes through a stream of debris left behind by comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which orbits the sun approximately every 33 years.
As tiny particles of comet dust enter Earth's atmosphere at speeds of around 44 miles (71 kilometers) per second, they burn up and produce brilliant streaks of light we know as meteors, or shooting stars.
Most years, the Leonids produce relatively modest displays with around 10 to 15 meteors per hour under ideal viewing conditions. But occasionally, Earth encounters a particularly dense trail of debris, triggering a meteor storm.
Will we ever see another meteor storm like 1966?
The Leonids have a long history of putting on some spectacular displays, with significant storms recorded in 1833 and 1866. And 1966 wasn't the last time the Leonids put on an extraordinary show. In 1999, 2001 and 2002, the Leonids once again reached meteor-storm levels, producing thousands of meteors per hour at their peaks. The shows aren't over yet! With comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle due to return in 2031, astronomers are already looking ahead to what the following years could bring.
A study released in August 2026 predicts potentially impressive Leonid displays in 2033 and 2034, with peak rates exceeding 1,000 meteors per hour. However, these forecasts remain uncertain, and a repeat of the extraordinary 1966 storm is far from guaranteed.
For now, we'll just have to wait and see.
Daisy Dobrijevic joined Space.com in February 2022, having previously worked as a staff writer for All About Space magazine. She completed an editorial internship with BBC Sky at Night Magazine and worked at the National Space Centre, communicating space science to the public.
Daisy holds a PhD in plant physiology and a Master's in Environmental Science. Based in Nottingham, U.K., she covers all things space, with a special focus on solar activity and space weather. She also has a keen interest in astrotourism and is always on the lookout for the next northern lights adventure.
She will join Hurtigruten as an onboard astronomer for a northern lights sailing in January 2027.

title: South Africa head coach Erasmus banned for six matches
text:
South Africa head coach Rassie Erasmus has been banned for six matches by World Rugby over comments he made about match officials in his side's Nations Championship defeat by France last week.
Speaking at a news conference conference in Dublin on Monday before the Springboks' match with Ireland, Erasmus questioned what he perceived as double standards in officiating to the point where he asked: "is that not match-fixing?".
The two-time Rugby World Cup-winning coach was referencing the implementation of new rules surrounding hip-drop and knee-drop tackles, and felt the laws were not being applied correctly.
It comes after Ireland fly-half Sam Prendergast became the first player to be cited for a hip-drop tackle in Ireland's win over Fiji on Saturday, which was not penalised in-play by referee Angus Gardner and television match official [TMO] Mike Adamson.
World Rugby said an independent panel determined that Erasmus' comments "suggest that match officials acted with bias/prejudice or deliberately influenced the outcome of a match".
In response, South Africa Rugby said it has requested a full misconduct hearing and an opportunity for Erasmus to "contextualise his comments and assure the panel that it was not his intention to allege that any match official had acted with ulterior motives".
It is the third time Erasmus has been sanctioned by World Rugby over his comments about match officials.
When he was South Africa's director of rugby, he was suspended for two months by World Rugby after he posted an hour-long video criticising the refereeing in the Springboks' opening Test defeat by the British and Irish Lions in 2021.
World Rugby found the video contained "multiple abusive and insulting comments and attacks on the officials".
In 2022, he received a two-match ban for a series of tweets criticising officials in a defeat by France.
Erasmus' latest ban has been imposed under World Rugby's match official abuse sanction process, which was introduced by the governing body in July.
If the suspension is upheld, Erasmus will miss Saturday's game with Ireland in Dublin (16:40 GMT), next week's finals weekend fixture at Twickenham's Allianz Stadium and the start of his side's Rugby Championship campaign next summer.
Erasmus said that 17 hip-drop or knee-drop tackles had been missed in South Africa's 21-19 defeat in France by match officials. Andrea Piardi was the referee for the Stade de France fixture, while Matteo Liperini was the TMO.
Erasmus added that if TMOs were not intervening for reviews to limit the number of interruptions during a match then it was "manipulation", before he added that his comments were "not an accusation".
"I'm saying if he didn't see it, it must be a technology problem. If he saw it and decided not to act on it, is that not match-fixing?" Erasmus added.
"If the TMO didn't see it, maybe then technology must be better. If he saw it and he ignored it, what does that boil down to? Manipulation of the game or the result or injured players getting injured.
"So all I'm asking, don't take TMOs out and discourage them to get involved. Then the wrong team will win and players will get injured. That's all I'm saying."
'Unacceptable attack on credibility and competence of match officials'
In a statement on Tuesday, World Rugby said an independent panel determined that Erasmus' comments had met "the threshold for serious misconduct".
World Rugby confirmed the ban will stop Erasmus having any match day involvement for six matches, which includes coaching, direct or indirect contact with the team management or players on match days, entering the stadium, coaches' box, playing enclosure or technical area.
"The panel determined that the comments suggest that match officials acted with bias/prejudice or deliberately influenced the outcome of a match, and when the conduct is considered as a whole a reasonable person would conclude that the conduct constituted an unacceptable attack on the credibility and competence of the match officials," its statement said.
"In respect to the sanction, the panel determined that the conduct clearly amounts to disrespecting the authority of the match officials by impugning their integrity.
"Therefore, the panel reviewed a number of elements of the commentary including the timing and reach of the statements, combined with the allegations of bias or bad faith, and found that the comments attracted a six-match automatic suspension."
World Rugby added that "respect is fundamental to rugby, and match officials are central to the sport".
"Protecting their wellbeing and integrity, and their right to perform without abuse or intimidation, is a responsibility World Rugby and unions take seriously," their statement added.
"Coaches, players, unions and everyone in the game must uphold these standards.
"Robust, respectful debate is natural, but teams have access to well-established and supported channels and protocols for raising officiating matters before and after matches. Challenging a decision is not the same as questioning an official's integrity or making comments that expose them to personal abuse."
In the same news conference, which lasted more than half an hour at the Springboks' team hotel, Erasmus also questioned what he felt were double standards in terms of sanctions.
The outcome of the citing has yet to be released, but he predicted that Prendergast will be available to play against South Africa due to a "technicality", and also questioned the decision not to ban Ireland prop Tadhg Furlong for an alleged groin grab while playing for Leinster ahead of the November Tests.
Last year, South Africa prop Jan-Hendrik Wessels was handed a nine-match ban for a similar offence and missed November's matches for the Springboks.
Analysis
This is the third time in five years Erasmus has been banned for comments about referees, all of them coming after a Springboks loss.
In 2018, he picked South African rugby up off the floor and has won two World Cups to establish himself as one of the greatest coaches of all time.
To his rugby public - the people who really matter in Erasmus' eyes - he will forever be a hero in his homeland.
But outside South Africa his propensity to harangue officials after a rare defeat will tarnish his reputation in the eyes of many.

title: ICE agents pepper spray pregnant US citizen in California, video shows
text:
US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents pepper-sprayed a pregnant US citizen and threw her to the ground during a protest in California on Sunday, according to her family’s attorney, who shared footage of the incident.
Lizbeth Vargas Andrade, 23, was filming and protesting against the presence of several ICE officers outside the Stanislaus county jail in Modesto, in California’s Central valley, before she was taken down by officers and arrested while she was lying on her stomach during a chaotic encounter.
Vargas Andrade, who is 12 weeks pregnant, said in a press conference on Sunday evening that she was part of a group of local residents who monitor ICE sightings, and that she had gone to the jail parking lot after agents were spotted in the area.
A commotion erupted when ICE agents moved to arrest a man who, it appeared, had just been released from the jail, video shows.
Footage filmed by Vargas Andrade’s husband, Adolfo Talavera, captured a tumultuous scene as several people protested against the agents making the arrest. The circumstances of the man’s arrest were not immediately clear, and he has not been identified. Agents wore law enforcement vests and ICE badges, and at least two of them had masks covering their faces.
It was unclear what exactly happened right before Vargas Andrade’s arrest, with the sound on the footage repeatedly cutting out. One woman was heard screaming at the agents to get away from her and another cursed at the agents, telling them, “You should be embarrassed … you guys are so fucked up.”
Vargas Andrade had her phone in one hand as she and an agent then appeared to bump into each other, footage showed. That agent then grabbed her and started to handcuff her. Another agent then pulled out what appeared to be a pepper-spray canister and pointed it at the direction of Vargas Andrade and her husband who was filming.
The footage partially captured the agent deploying the pepper spray, though it was difficult to discern how long he sprayed it and where the chemicals landed. Soon after, the footage captured Talavera shouting, “She’s pregnant with child!” as the agents moved to detain his wife. Seconds later, two agents took Vargas Andrade to the ground where she was handcuffed on her stomach with her hands behind her back, before one of the agents moved her on to her side.
Vargas Andrade was taken into custody and transported to an ICE field office in Stockton, according to her attorney, Patrick Kolasinski. Vargas Andrade’s sister had called for an ambulance, which then arrived at the ICE facility and transported her to a hospital, her family and a local advocate said at the press conference.
Vargas Andrade said officers had told her she was accused of assaulting an ICE agent, an accusation she denied. She was released later that day, and she has not been charged with any crimes, according to Kolasinski.
Spokespeople for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) did not immediately respond to inquiries on Monday. A spokesperson for the Department of Justice declined to comment. A spokesperson for the Stanislaus sheriff’s office, which runs the jail, said sheriff deputies were not involved in Vargas Andrade’s arrest.
“They threw me to the ground, they maced me, then they handcuffed me,” Vargas Andrade recalled to reporters on Sunday night. “I told the ICE agent … ‘I’m pregnant, so don’t put your hands on me.’ … They right away threw me on the floor … I was burning. I couldn’t breathe. The mace went up my nose.”
Another ICE agent then gave her water to wash her face, she recalled.
“I got scared,” Talavera said. “I was like, what if she has a miscarriage?”
Vargas Andrade said she was particularly worried because she had suffered two previous pregnancy losses, but she said doctors did an ultrasound after the incident and did not identify any concerns.
The encounter happened amid reports of increased ICE activity in California’s Central valley region, which is home to the state’s agricultural industry. The DHS and the justice department have repeatedly accused anti-ICE protesters of assaulting agents, though many of those prosecutions in California have fallen apart in federal court.
“We’re not going to stop helping the community even though this happened,” Vargas Andrade said. “We want our immigrants to feel safe here.”

title: Tensions rise over draft climate deal at COP31
text:
A contentious draft deal has laid bare divisions between delegates from states participating in this year’s United Nations climate COP31 talks in Turkiye.
The 18-page draft “cover decision” published by summit cohost Australia on Monday includes a broad range of demands, including calls for a phaseout of fossil fuels.
The draft, as written, could make the negotiations “untenable”, said Wopke Hoekstra, the European Union’s climate envoy, adding that “the cover decision does not go in the right direction and needs significant change”.
“It’s very easy to draw red lines at the start of the process,” said Joao Paulo Capobianco, Brazil’s environment minister, adding that deadlocks can be overcome through “an adjustment in the wording” in the draft.
Australian Climate Minister Chris Bowen, who is steering COP31 negotiations, acknowledged that the text included elements “that not all parties agree on”, and that there might be “at least one more draft” introduced before the end of the week.
The talks are scheduled to end on Friday, but climate negotiations usually run into overtime as agreements must be reached by consensus, meaning even a single country can block the entire process.
The draft text includes a call for wealthy nations to achieve net zero emissions by 2030, and wording on phasing out fossil fuels that oil-rich countries have long resisted.
Consensus on the issue of net zero emissions at COP31 “might be very, very difficult”, said Michael Joseph, the environment minister of the island state of Antigua and Barbuda, adding that he “would love to see a commitment that calls on the phasing out of fossil fuels”.
“Emerging countries want to impose as many obligations as possible on developed countries. It’s tactical,” an official from a European country who requested anonymity told the AFP news agency.
“These things are obviously unacceptable,” the official said, pointing to a bloc of countries whose members include Saudi Arabia and India.
Contention over IPCC reports
Saudi Arabia is also at the centre of another battle over the timeline for the publication of crucial reports by the UN’s climate science panel, which dozens of European, African and Pacific states want published before a crucial verification of global carbon-cutting efforts at the next COP33 conference due in 2028.
The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) publishes a series of reports every five to seven years that provide the definitive scientific assessment of global warming and inform global policy responses to the crisis.
The IPCC suspended its last meeting after failing to break the impasse, and a new session was set for December to resolve the issue, with Ilana Seid, chair of the Alliance of Small Island States, describing delays in publishing the IPCC’s seventh assessment report as “unjustifiable”.
The dispute has become one of the main issues being debated at COP31, which ends Friday.
On Tuesday, the kingdom’s delegation at COP31 defended its position on the publication timeline for the IPCC report, saying “Saudi Arabia is not seeking to delay climate science”.
Saudi Arabia “advocates publication timelines that allow sufficient scientific review, transparency and meaningful participation”, the statement said, without explicitly mentioning when Riyadh would like to see the reports published.

title: SpaceX pulls off first Starship recovery from orbit in spectacular fashion
text:
After a in space, a SpaceX Starship rocket plunged back to Earth Saturday, enduring the blazing heat of reentry while homing in on its Texas Gulf Coast launch site, flipping vertical at the last moment and settling into the grasp of two huge mechanical arms on its launch gantry.
Throngs of SpaceX employees gathered nearby cheered and applauded as the rocket restarted three of its six methane-fueled Raptor engines to flip upright, rapidly slowing to a near hover as the robot arms moved in for a mechanical embrace, catching the rocket a moment before engine shutdown.
"This is so incredible to see!" said SpaceX commentator Jessie Anderson. "One of the most incredible and historic engineering feats of all time has just happened right in front of our eyes. Congratulations to our teammates at SpaceX, and to everyone who supported the Starship program."
It was the first such recovery of a Starship from orbit — previous test flights ended with planned ocean splashdowns — marking a major milestone in SpaceX's drive to develop the first fully reusable orbit-class rocket, a vehicle company founder Elon Musk says will dramatically lower the cost of launching payloads to Earth orbit, the moon and, eventually, Mars.
The Starship was launched atop a Super Heavy booster Friday using the same pad at SpaceX's Starbase facility on the Texas coast. Standing 407 feet tall, the two-stage rocket is the most powerful launcher ever built, generating some 16 million pounds of thrust at liftoff from 33 first-stage Raptor engines.
After propelling the Starship upper stage out of the lower atmosphere, the Super Heavy first stage attempted its own return to the launch site for capture by the gantry's mechanical arms.
Going into the giant rocket's 15th test flight, SpaceX had successfully recovered the first-stage boosters used in three previous launches. But the Super Heavy launched Friday was diverted to an offshore splashdown because of a guidance problem. The vehicle ran out of fuel and exploded moments before hitting the water.
While a disappointment to the SpaceX team, Musk said in a posting on the social media platform X the problem was a "slight underperformance of engines," adding that "these early ships and boosters are already outdated by improved designs in production or on the test stand."
"This booster loss does not change our timeline to reach high volume, fully reusable Starship flights," he said.
The Starship upper stage did not disappoint.
Beaming down crystal-clear views from cameras mounted on its steering fins, the spacecraft's belly, covered in heat-shield tiles, glowed red as the ship heated up in a fireball of atmospheric friction.
Crossing the Baja Peninsula and then northern Mexico, the big rocket rapidly descended before flying just north of the launch site, banking and dropping belly first out of low clouds, restarting its engines to flip upright and then falling at an angle toward the gantry, slowing to a near standstill as the arms closed around it.
"The room behind me going absolutely insane," SpaceX commentator Dan Huot said from the mission control center. "These people have done so much to earn this. ... I mean, that was the missing link. That was the holy grail of spaceflight, plummeting through fire to be snatched out of the air by steel. We caught a Starship, and now everything changes."
But SpaceX will need to successfully launch and recover a large number of Super Heavy-Starships to demonstrate the statistical reliability needed for crewed flights. And the company will need to demonstrate its ability to autonomously refuel Starships in Earth orbit and keep their propellants from boiling away in the space environment.
While the system is designed to be fully reusable, the Starship upper stage uses most of its propellant getting into Earth orbit. NASA wants to use a variant of the Starship to carry astronauts to the lunar surface in 2028 and multiple Super Heavy-tanker flights will be needed to refuel the lander in Earth orbit before it can head for the moon.
SpaceX plans to begin orbital fueling tests in the next several Super Heavy-Starship flights. But the rocket's development has taken longer than initially expected and the space agency is now hedging its bets, saying it's open to using Blue Origin's Blue Moon Mark 2 lander depending on which spacecraft is ready in time.

title: LIV players offered a European tour lifeline. Those left off the list are just as notable
text:
Patching back the golf landscape in the wake of LIV Golf is not an easy fix
Even as LIV Golf is winding down through bankruptcy, the players are more compelling now than when they were actually competing.
Remember when all the speculation was who would leave the PGA Tour and European tour? Now it's who's allowed to return. The list of LIV players with nowhere to go is as notable as those offered a European tour lifeline by agreeing to a set number of sponsor invitations.
Longtime supporters of the European tour railed about sending 10 players to the PGA Tour each year, and now it gets banned PGA Tour players with a greater profile than those they were losing.
This might take longer to sort out than LIV Golf's bankruptcy proceedings.
