“There has been significant change in the landscape of men’s professional golf over the past 12 months,” said Guy Kinnings, the chief executive of the European tour. “As golf’s global tour, we have taken a pragmatic approach to this unique and unprecedented situation as we go into next year, always with the best interests of our entire membership at the forefront of our minds.”
It's sure to raise eyebrows across several fronts, starting with the European tour offering sponsor invitations without a hefty appearance fee to nine players who never contributed to the tour.
All of them added to the “significant change in the landscape” by defecting from their tours to join a rival league with a seemingly endless supply of Saudi cash until it disappeared quicker than anyone can say “Strait of Hormuz."
The idea behind the offer was to place them in European tour stops that needed help, giving those tournaments a boost in star power without taking away a spot from fields that were depleted anyway.
Some players were afforded European tour status already earned, whether it was Bryson DeChambeau (2024 U.S. Open champion) and Tyrrell Hatton (Rolex Series winner) or Paul Casey (career money) and David Puig (tournament winner).
The nine players who signed agreements for a specific number of sponsor invitations — and it varies among the players — include major champions Dustin Johnson, Bubba Watson and Cameron Smith. Those players, along with Joaquin Niemann, are the reason Kinnings said, “Our 2027 season is set to be one of the most keenly contested campaigns in our 55-year history.”
No doubt, it's a big move for the European tour and the most practical one considering the PGA Tour still has a one-year ban from a player's last appearance on LIV.
Still to be determined are the stakes for ex-LIV players.
The PGA Tour's alliance with Europe expires next year. PGA Tour CEO Brian Rolapp said Monday evening they are having productive discussions and “both entities have a mutual desire to extend and modify our partnership.”
The modification is likely to include how many PGA Tour cards are offered the leading players in Europe, but it is most certain to be fewer than 10. That shouldn't be an issue for Johnson, whose 24 tour wins make him a lifetime PGA Tour member. But it would be for the likes of Niemann, Carlos Ortiz, Abraham Ancer and Lucas Herbert.
Also unclear is how many tournaments DeChambeau, in the highest priority category as Europe's newest member, chooses to play beyond the minimum required.
But look beyond the nine players offered deals for sponsor invitations to the players with limited options on where to play.
Harold Varner III, Charles Howell III, Peter Uihlein, Jason Kokrak, Marc Leishman and Talor Gooch are among some two dozen players on LIV Golf in 2026 who were left off the list. Some, like Uihlein, still have Asian Tour status and some of those events are co-sanctioned by Europe.
At least they still have MENA Tour cards from when Greg Norman tried to use the Middle East and North Africa circuit as a way to get world ranking points. That tour is alive and well. Chris Woods, who played for Europe in the 2016 Ryder Cup, won twice early this year.
Throw in Sebastian Munoz, Dean Burmester, Matthew Wolff and Anthony Kim, whose victory in Australia after 12 years of fighting injuries and addiction was the most feel-good story of the year.
Ten players left off the list have won on the PGA Tour. Five have played in a Ryder Cup or a Presidents Cup. All of them are looking for a place to play, assuming they still want to play (Gooch might have his hands full with his Professional Bull Riding team, the Oklahoma Wildcatters).
Among the younger crowd — Wolff is still only 27 — is former NCAA champion Caleb Surratt, who was not on the list despite having played three times on the Challenge Tour. Instead, an offer was made to Michael La Sasso, a more recent NCAA champion who won the final LIV event in Indianapolis. A footnote in history.
Europe stands to gain. The PGA Tour remains more interested in fine-tuning its new competition model in 2028 than the immediate plight of LIV players.
Rolapp has said he is driven by whatever makes the PGA Tour better. In due time.

title: Iran dismisses report of alleged 'dirty bomb' attack on Washington
text:
Iran on Tuesday dismissed a CNN report that Tehran was preparing a so-called "dirty bomb plot."
US President Donald Trump said his administration was taking the report "very seriously."
What did reports say about an Iranian attack on Washington?
Tehran's dismissal came after CNN reported on Tuesday that "Iran is developing plans to target senior Trump administration officials by detonating a so-called dirty bomb or a chemical weapon in Washington, DC," citing multiple US intelligence sources.
The article also reported that "US intelligence has picked up Iranian chatter claiming that it has stashed bomb-making materials inside the country" and that "many national security officials assume that pre-positioned nuclear materials have already been in the US for years," citing, again, multiple US intelligence sources.
When asked about the story during his visit to the Philippines, Trump said that if there was such a threat, Iran would "pay a price the likes of which no other country has ever paid before."
"I hope it's not, but we take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy," he added.
Iran decries 'fabrication'
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei slammed the report, calling it "a malicious campaign to manufacture propaganda."
"Those who initiated the aggression against Iran are now seeking to lay the media groundwork for their sinister designs by manufacturing and disseminating baseless allegations," he said on X.
"Step by step, they are attempting to manufacture a veneer of legitimacy for further aggression and atrocities," he said, naming CNN's reporting on the alleged "dirty bomb plot" and The New York Times without specifying any of its reporting.
Baghaei also said the US and Israel hit water storage reservoirs "during the recent acts of aggression."
Where does the Iran war stand?
The Iran war, started by the US and Israeli strikes on February 28, continues as negotiations to bring an end to the fighting stall.
Both US and Israel have been holding off from major attacks as they held elections over the last weeks.
Tehran has said it is in control the Strait of Hormuz, a key transit point for global oil and natural gas supplies, while continuing to attack ships it considers unauthorized users of the waterway. There are near-daily reports of ships hitting mines in parts of the strait Tehran says are unauthorized for transit.
The US Navy, which is enforcing its own blockade of Iranian vessels, has recently escorted tankers through the strait.
Before the midterm elections, Trump said, "We may do another little Epic Fury," referring to US-Israeli strikes that started the war, though he did not provide any timeframe.
Trump is expected to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of an APEC leaders' summit in China on Thursday and discuss ending the war in Iran.
Pakistan-mediated peace talks between the US and Iran on April failed to reach a conclusion.
Qatar, another mediator in the war, on Tuesday called for restraint "to avoid any escalation that could undermine negotiation efforts."

title: Wales beaten by 10-man Portugal in entertaining Nations League finale
text:
Wales ended their Nations League group campaign with a 3-2 defeat against 10-man Portugal in Cardiff.
Although there was little riding on the contest, with Wales guaranteed a League A relegation/promotion play-off in March and Portugal having qualified for the quarter-finals, the two sides produced an entertaining spectacle.
Portugal skipper Bruno Fernandes blasted the opener after 11 minutes but that was immediately wiped out by David Brooks’ ninth goal for Wales.
Sorba Thomas broke free to put Wales ahead before the break, but again there was a quickfire response as Pedro Neto pounced to restore parity.
Substitute Carlos Forbs stroked Portugal ahead in the final quarter, and Portugal had to negotiate the final 16 minutes a player short after Neto was sent off after receiving a second yellow card.
Wales finish bottom of League A4 with one win and five defeats and end a disappointing 2026 with a solitary victory, three draws and six losses from 10 games.
Craig Bellamy’s side had lost 1-0 in Lisbon in September in a game that was to prove Cristiano Ronaldo’s last for Portugal.
Ronaldo’s subsequent retirement from international football probably had an impact on the attendance at Cardiff City Stadium with some seats unfilled, despite the game being officially declared a sell out.
Wales had been forced in to changes with Karl Darlow and Neco Williams injured and Ethan Ampadu suspended.
Danny Ward replaced Darlow in goal while Connor Roberts and Josh Sheehan returned, with Rubin Colwill – on his home Cardiff ground – Brooks and Thomas also freshening up the selection.
There would be no clean sheet for Ward on his 50th appearance as Joao Neves robbed Sheehan and Fernandes lashed home from the edge of the box.
Wales responded immediately with Colwill twice involved, first setting up Harry Wilson for a shot Diogo Costa blocked with his legs and then Brooks who swept home his ninth international goal, and second in two games.
Wilson was halted by a last-gasp Diogo Dalot challenge and Joe Rodon headed wide, but Wales were fortunate not to fall behind when the unmarked Francisco Trincao struck the crossbar from eight yards.
Chances kept coming as Costa battered away Wilson’s effort at the end of a slick length-of-the-field move, and Neto fired straight at Ward before Fernandes was off target.
Wales hit the front five minutes before the break after Brooks worked a one-two with Wilson before releasing Thomas, who advanced from his own half to slot past Costa.
The lead lasted three minutes as Neto lost Jay DaSilva from Trincao’s cross to finish at the far post.
A breathless first half was not finished as Wilson hit the roof of the net from halfway with Costa retreating frantically, and the Leeds midfielder then forced a sprawling save from the Portugal goalkeeper.
Portugal regained the lead 20 minutes from time when Club Brugge winger Forbs – wearing Portugal’s new-styled number seven shirt in the post Ronaldo era – collected Ben Cabango’s poor header and stepped inside Ben Davies to find the bottom corner.
Neto clattered into Brennan Johnson just one minute and 59 seconds after being booked, but Portugal held on for a fifth Nations League win to seal top spot.

title: New anti-regime protests erupt in flashpoint Iranian city
text:
A protest sparked by a deadly bus crash in a western Iranian city turned into a new anti-regime protest with hundreds chanting "Death to the dictator."
A fatal bus crash which killed 13 oil workers in the western Iranian city of Abdanan sent hundreds of people marching in protest first against what they called local authorities' state incompetence, but then their slogans switched against state officials and institutions of the Islamic Republic.
Rare videos which trickled out onto social media showed hundreds of protesters changing slogans such as "Death to the dictator", "Islamic Republic, where is your cardboard leader?," as a reference to Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, "Death to the incompetent official" as well as pro-monarchy chants such as "Long live the Shah." However, as some of the videos may have had sound added or manipulated in editing, Euronews Persian cannot independently verify the authenticity of these slogans.
Other videos show slogans being chanted against Ruhollah Khomeini, the founder of the Islamic Republic, and banners of the Ministry of Intelligence and the Basij paramilitary group being torn up.
Euronews verifications show that the protesters were continuing on Tuesday evening.
Abdanan is a city in the south-east of Ilam province, with a population of about 24,000, while the total population of Abdanan county is about 48,000.
Protesters call for no gatherings to be held in the name of bereaved families
Fars News Agency, closely linked to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), reported a gathering in Vali Asr Square in Abdanan, estimating the initial number of participants between 200 to 300 which then rose to about 1,000.
The news agency claimed that the protesters changed "Today is a day of mourning" and "Resignation, resignation", demanding action against those responsible for the incident.
According to Mehr News Agency, the families of the victims issued a statement calling for the circumstances of the accident to be clarified and those responsible to be identified. The agency claimed that the families asked for gatherings not be held in their name.
The Abdanan Security Council called on citizens to remain calm and to avoid responding to what it described as unlawful calls and actions that, in the council's words, disrupt public order.
Abdanan, a flashpoint city during the nationwide January protests
Abdanan in Ilam province became one of the main flashpoints of the nationwide anti-regime January protests in which thousands were killed by security forces across the country.
16-year-old protester Alireza Sayyedi, who was shot dead on 9 January by the regime's security forces during the anti-regime protests in Tehran, was from Abdanan, drawing the nation's attention on the city.
His body was taken to his hometown for burial and his funeral on 11 January drew large crowds who chanted anti-government slogans.
The Kurdistan Human Rights Network reported that the regime military and security forces fired live ammunition at the participants during the funeral.
"Alireza, may your soul be at peace"
Then in mid-February, large anti-regime protests and clashes with security forces erupted again in Abdanan, marking the 40th day of Alireza Sayyedi's death. Videos from the protest showed demonstrators chanting anti-regime slogans and honouring the killed protesters.
During Tuesday's demonstration, protesters chanted "Alireza, may your soul be at peace" to keep his memory alive.
The Ilam traffic police chief announced that the bus crash investigation blamed the driver, the company that rented the bus and negligence of the road maintenance office, while local prosecutors launched criminal proceedings.
The Ilam governorate declared one day of public mourning across the province and two days of public mourning in Abdanan county after this incident.

title: Ex-hostage recounts captivity in Iran-backed militia stronghold now targeted by Iraqi prime minister
text:
An Israeli-Russian researcher held hostage for 903 days by an Iran-backed Iraqi terrorist group revealed to Fox News Digital that she spent the first four and a half months of her captivity inside the very militia stronghold Iraq's Trump-backed prime minister has now ordered the army to reclaim.
Elizabeth Tsurkov, a senior nonresident fellow at the New Lines Institute for Strategy and Policy, said Kata’ib Hezbollah turned a private family's home in Jurf al-Sakhr, south of Baghdad, into a prison where she was held captive.
"This is where I was held for 4.5 months," Tsurkov told Fox News Digital in an interview, referring to the early months of her captivity, which began with her abduction in Baghdad in March 2023. "I was held in a private home of a family that was taken over by Kata’ib Hezbollah and turned into a prison," she said.
Tsurkov, who was freed in September 2025 following negotiations and sustained pressure from the Trump administration to secure her release, said that any effort to reclaim the territory must go far beyond dismantling alleged oil-smuggling operations.
She called for Iraqi authorities to search the sprawling area, including surrounding towns and villages, for "secret prisons," "mass burial sites" and "storage facilities for weapons," and to return confiscated homes to their rightful owners.
The revelations come as Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, who has received strong public backing from President Donald Trump, ordered Iraqi armed forces into Jurf al-Sakhr, also known as Jurf al-Nasr, a stronghold of the U.S.-designated terrorist organization Kata’ib Hezbollah since 2014.
According to AFP on November 16, Baghdad has given the militia a deadline to withdraw, with a security source identifying Friday.
The order follows a Reuters investigation published Monday, citing Iraqi officials who accused Kata’ib Hezbollah of stealing hundreds of millions of dollars in state-owned oil since 2021. The government has dismissed nine security and administrative officials and referred suspects to the judiciary. The militia denies wrongdoing.
A territory beyond government control
For Tsurkov, the stakes go far beyond oil revenues.
She described Jurf al-Sakhr as a territory effectively closed to the Iraqi government since 2014, when Iran-backed militias helped drive ISIS from the area but prevented its predominantly Sunni population from returning.
Tsurkov estimated that between 120,000 and 180,000 people were displaced from the district and surrounding communities. "If Iraqis are allowed to return to their homes, this would signal ... restitution of state sovereignty," she said.
She explained that the current operation is being presented as an anti-corruption campaign rather than an attempt to dismantle Kata’ib Hezbollah's military infrastructure.
The organization retains bases elsewhere in Iraq and access to border crossings with Iran, she said, giving it opportunities to replenish its weapons even if it loses control of Jurf al-Sakhr.
A crackdown or another political performance?
Michael Knights, head of research at Horizon Engage, a New York-based strategic consultancy, and an adjunct fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, expressed skepticism that Baghdad would fundamentally challenge the militias.
"It's going to be very difficult to tell the difference between a real crackdown on Iran-backed militias and a fake one," Knights told Fox News Digital.
Previous Iraqi governments have announced crackdowns on militias, only for detainees to be released or armed groups to retain control through rebranded security arrangements.
In June 2020, when then-Prime Minister Mustafa al-Kadhimi ordered the arrest of 14 Kata’ib Hezbollah members. Armed militia supporters subsequently descended on Baghdad's fortified International Zone demanding their release. Most were later released, according to a U.S. government inspector general report.
In Nov. 2021, Kadhimi survived an explosive-drone attack targeting his residence. Reuters reported that security officials implicated Iran-backed militias, although no organization claimed responsibility.
Knights said that the Iraqi counterterrorism forces are better trained and equipped than Kata’ib Hezbollah, but the greatest danger lies in the militias' ability to threaten officials and their families.
"It's not about equipment or even training," he said, describing the danger of retaliation against commanders and their families who challenge the armed groups.
In a Nov. 16 Middle East Forum analysis, researcher Ali Mahmoud detailed competing allegations of corruption between Kata’ib Hezbollah and Asa’ib Ahl al-Haq, including claims involving companies connected to militia leaders' families.
Mahmoud reported that even the government's initial inspection of Jurf al-Sakhr required negotiations with senior militia commanders, illustrating the limits of Baghdad's authority.
What captivity revealed about the militia
Tsurkov, who has researched Iraqi armed groups for years, said her captivity gave her unusual insight into the organization's internal culture.
"I interacted with about 45 different individuals across basically three different prisons," she said, explaining that she later supplemented those observations with interviews involving former militia members and people familiar with their communities.
Her conclusion was that the organization consists of both deeply committed Iranian loyalists and a much larger group of recruits primarily motivated by salaries, status and the ability to exercise power. "They enjoy having power over others," she said, describing what she observed among her captors.
While some members embrace Iran's revolutionary ideology, Tsurkov said many joined after the major fighting against ISIS ended, attracted by government-funded salaries and relatively secure employment. "They're not interested in dying in the service of the Iranian regime," she said of many rank-and-file fighters.
She distinguished those recruits from a smaller core of ideologically committed and better-trained operatives that Iran can mobilize for sophisticated military attacks.
That distinction, she said, could offer Baghdad a path toward reducing militia power without a full-scale confrontation. She proposed allowing some fighters to join the regular Iraqi army under independent military commanders, providing alternative employment while dismantling their existing command structures.
Iran's enduring influence
According to Knights, the current crackdown primarily affects the more confrontational Abu Hussein wing of Kata’ib Hezbollah, while another faction associated with senior militia commander Abu Fadak remains largely untouched. He argued that both ultimately remain responsive to Tehran.
Knights also questioned whether disrupting one oil-smuggling operation would substantially weaken the group's finances, citing its extensive investments in hotels, property and other commercial ventures.
But perhaps the clearest illustration of the contradictions facing Iraq's government, Knights said, lies in recent senior political appointments and Iran's choice of its next diplomatic representative in Baghdad.
On Oct. 15, Iraq's parliament approved Laith al-Khazali, a senior figure in the Iran-backed Asa’ib Ahl al-Haq militia, as one of three deputy prime ministers. The United States designated him and his brother Qais al-Khazali, the militia's leader, as specially designated global terrorists in 2020. Washington has accused the organization of carrying out attacks against American and coalition forces, according to al-Monitor.
Another newly appointed deputy prime minister, Muhsin al-Mandalawi, is the brother of two Iraqi businessmen sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department on Sept. 10 for facilitating financial transactions benefiting Iran. Knights also pointed to Iran's reported selection of Abdolreza Meskarian, a senior commander in the Revolutionary Guards' Quds Force, as its next ambassador to Iraq.
Alhurra reported on Nov. 9, citing an Iraqi Foreign Ministry source, that Tehran nominated Meskarian, who heads the Quds Force's Ramadan Headquarters, a unit involved in coordinating with Iran-backed armed groups in Iraq. Neither government had formally confirmed the nomination.
For Knights, these developments raise fundamental questions about how far Baghdad is prepared to go in challenging Tehran's influence. "I think on balance, we're still in a pretty bad place in Iraq when it comes to militias," he said.
The real test
Tsurkov agreed that an operation intended merely to satisfy Washington could be exposed if displaced families remained unable to return.
The broader disarmament deadline, already extended until June 2027, was "utterly unrealistic," she said, arguing that Iraqi security institutions would require years of reform before they could reliably confront the militias.
"I tend to think it will not be real," she said of the current operation, while acknowledging that successful government control could represent a meaningful breakthrough.
For the former hostage, the ultimate measure of success is straightforward: whether Iraq's military merely enters the area, or whether the territory truly returns to civilian control.
"It's either the state is there, and people can return or not," she said.
Knights also remains skeptical that the current operation will deliver lasting results, suggesting Baghdad may reach a deal that allows the government to claim victory without substantially weakening Kata’ib Hezbollah. Still, he acknowledged the possibility that the confrontation could mark the beginning of a broader effort, even if he doubts this particular operation will prove decisive. "Every great journey starts with the first step," he said.

title: 'The symbol of the occupation': Ukraine destroys span of Kerch Bridge linking Russia with Crimea
text: KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Ukrainian drones and missiles struck the vital Kerch Bridge linking Russia to the occupied Crimean Peninsula, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Tuesday, calling it an "unprecedented" operation as Russia reported that its forces downed a record number of Ukrainian drones for the second straight day. Zelenskyy portrayed the bridge operation as a masterstroke following a weekslong effort by Ukrainian forces to gradually wear down Russian air defenses before bombarding the prized target with a barrage of missiles and drones overnight. Zelenskyy didn't detail the damage, but the Ukrainian General Staff said that an arch and a span of the bridge's road section collapsed, severing the road link, while the railway line was still standing but with a damaged arch. Russia's Investigative Committee, the nation's top criminal investigation agency, said the bridge was attacked by drones and sustained damage but didn't elaborate. The Kerch Bridge is a crucial link in moving military and civilian supplies from Russia to Crimea and for supporting troops on the front line. The construction of the bridge, a potent symbol of Russia's illegal annexation of the peninsula in 2014, was inflammatory to Ukrainians. "The symbol of the occupation has cracked," the Ukrainian General Staff said in a statement. Moscow's forces, meanwhile, fired ballistic missiles and drones at Kyiv, hitting two of the Ukrainian capital's main bridges and killing at least two people. A recent escalation in aerial attacks came as Russia and Ukraine await a date for the next round of U.S.-mediated talks aimed at ending the war that began with Moscow's full-scale invasion of its neighbor on Feb. 24, 2022. U.S. President Donald Trump says he plans to talk about the war in Ukraine during his highly anticipated meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in China this week. Missiles delivered the final blow in the 7-stage operation The Kerch Bridge attack was the culmination of weeks of preparatory strikes over seven stages of the operation, Zelenskyy said on social media. Ukrainian forces knocked out defense systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment and other designated targets before launching Monday night's final attack, he said. Domestically developed long-range drones struck the bridge's road section during the night while Ukraine's Neptune missiles and other drones aimed at the rail section, he said. Precision-guided Flamingo missiles delivered the final blow, he said. READ MORE: Ukraine's drone chief says push to cripple Russia in Crimea is just getting started Zelenskyy and the Ukrainian military published videos showing what they said were the attacks and subsequent damage to the bridge, with part of the deck in the water and a fallen arch. The Associated Press wasn't able to verify the images. The Russian-installed governor of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, said traffic across the bridge was halted but rail traffic was restored by Tuesday afternoon. He didn't mention any damage. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that "there is no doubt that the bridge will be restored and will be even better than it was before." Zelenskyy noted that Russia has battered Ukrainian infrastructure, especially the power grid, every day. There were significant power outages Tuesday in three Ukrainian regions, he said. "We have repeatedly offered Russia steps toward de-escalation — and every proposal has been met with loud rejection," he said. U.K. Defense Secretary Wes Streeting, meeting at NATO headquarters in Brussels with Ukraine's Western backers, said the Kerch Bridge strike was "another example of Ukrainian ingenuity and Ukraine's absolute determination to defend itself against Russian aggression." The United Kingdom announced £240 million ($317 million) in air defense support for Ukraine this winter, including more than 1,000 short-range missiles and more than a dozen radars. Russian air defenses downed 1,441 drones during a second straight night of major Ukrainian attacks, Russia's Defense Ministry said Tuesday. That was a day after Russia said that it downed 1,336 Ukrainian drones in the highest number of interceptions it had reported so far during the war. Ukraine also attacks industrial areas deep inside Russia Elsewhere, authorities in Bashkortostan, a Russian region in the southern Ural Mountains, said that defenses repelled a "massive" drone attack on industrial zones in the cities of Ufa and Salavat. All plants there worked as usual, officials said. However, independent news outlet Astra reported a huge fire at the Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat oil refining and petrochemical complex in Bashkortostan, nearly 1,300 kilometers (800 miles) east of the Ukrainian border. The major petrochemical complex has been attacked a number of times before. In Moscow, Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said that around 800 drones flew toward the Moscow region overnight. Most were downed far away, and 321 were shot down as they approached the Russian capital. Russia hits bridges in Ukraine's capital Seven Russian ballistic missiles hit two of Kyiv's main bridges during the night, Zelenskyy said. Both were closed to traffic. The Pivnichnyi and Pivdennyi bridges are key commuter routes across the Dnipro River connecting Kyiv's two banks. The left bank is largely residential with numerous apartment buildings and shopping malls. The old town and many government offices are on the right bank. On Tuesday morning, long lines of traffic formed on a third bridge linking the two sides of the city. Russian attacks damaged other infrastructure and started fires in four districts of the Ukrainian capital, officials said, as Moscow continued its campaign to make life difficult for Ukrainian civilians. The Russian Defense Ministry said Tuesday that its forces overnight hit Ukraine's military industrial facilities, energy, transport and port infrastructure, as well as vessels used for Ukrainian armed forces. Russian forces launched a combined attack on industrial facilities in three districts of the southern Ukraine region of Zaporizhzhia, killing two people and wounding 18 others and leaving a large number of consumers in the region without power, local authorities said. The possibility of more talks Meanwhile, the negotiating teams of Ukraine, the United States, and European partners held a working video call Monday in which they discussed the results of recent talks in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, and the agenda for the next stage of negotiations, said Rustem Umerov, head of Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service. "We aligned our positions and our next joint steps," Umerov said on Telegram following the conversation. Representatives of France, Germany, the United Kingdom, Italy, Poland, NATO and the European Commission joined the conversation. The United States was represented by envoys Steve Witkoff, Jared Kushner, and Alexus Grynkewich, the commander of U.S. forces in Europe, Umerov said. Hatton reported from Lisbon, Portugal. Associated Press Writer Lorne Cook contributed to this report from Brussels.

title: Kalshi takes down controversial Trump 'mention' markets at CFTC's request
text:
Prediction market platform Kalshi quietly paused trading in a handful of "mention" contracts tied to President Donald Trump at the end of last week at the request of the CFTC, the company confirmed on Tuesday.
Mention markets are made up of contracts that ask traders what specific words will be used in a speech, a corporate earnings call or during a television broadcast. Earlier this year, a White House teleprompter operator used inside information to place trades in mention markets related to the president's comments.
Markets paused include those asking traders what nicknames Trump will say before 2027, what the president will say in November and what countries and companies Trump will say before the end of the month.
The move comes after the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the federal agency overseeing prediction markets, said in a letter to exchanges in September that mentions contracts have a greater manipulation risk.
A spokesperson for the agency told CNBC that the commission has placed holds on the certification of some of Kalshi's proposed mention markets. The spokesperson cited a Kalshi contract on hold that asked what key words would Trump say before a certain date. The contract was originally self-certified by Kalshi in February 2025.
"The CFTC stayed the certification of these contracts because they may be susceptible to manipulation, which is consistent with the staff advisory the CFTC put out two months ago," said Brooke Nethercott, the agency's spokesperson.
In a statement, Kalshi spokesperson Dani Lever said Kalshi is complying with the order.
In August, reports emerged that the CFTC was conducting an internal review into mention markets. The agency also requested that Kalshi, which is the only U.S.-regulated exchange that features the contract type, take down its sports-related mention markets in response to the inquiry. Kalshi complied.
A Trump-related mention market drew scrutiny in July after it was revealed a White House teleprompter operator placed trades on markets related to the president's comments. In a settlement with the operator, the CFTC ordered a three-year trading ban on the individual and a penalty amounting to over $172,000.
Kalshi has defended mentions markets even as the CFTC has become increasingly skeptical of them, saying that the individual words of prominent people often cause billions of dollars of movement across financial markets.
In addition to scrutiny regarding mention markets, the company is also facing a probe from the CFTC about its communications about new products with the agency, though a spokesperson for the company told CNBC that it was working to resolve the issues.
As of Tuesday morning, a mention market asking what Vice President JD Vance would say during the New York Times DealBook Summit event on Wednesday is still active.
Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

title: As decision model use skyrockets, is customization the next frontier?
text:
In October, more than one in four requests on Vercel’s AI model router went to decision models, not LLMs — an enormous share of work for a kind of computerized intelligence that was invented only a month earlier.
Decision models are LLMs that don’t produce output tokens; instead, they’re tuned to use their general intelligence to quickly and cheaply decide between preset options, while registering its level of confidence in the choice. They’re useful in production environments, where fast decisions can be more important than the reasoning provided by a slower and more expensive frontier model.
TypeSafe became a $7.5 billion company after releasing its Jev family of models, which continues to dominate usage (at least where we can see metrics from services like OpenRouter, which handled more than 1.5 billion queries to TypeSafe’s models last week).
However, it’s easy to make a decision model, and dozens were released in the wake of Jev. One Amazon engineer made one in a weekend, and soon every hyperscaler had its own option. On Tuesday, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said that his company is rolling out its decision model, Microsoft-Decision-1.1, for wide use on Azure immediately.
The action is happening on both ends of the ecosystem: Sqwish, a U.K.-based AI startup behind a decision model called kettei fat, announced a $3 million pre-seed round today. Co-founders Ushnish Sengupta and Federica Freddi, who met as Cambridge grad students, had been developing small LLMs when Jev arrived on the scene, and they realized their architectures could be repurposed as a powerful decision model.
Data appears to be the key to a successful model in this category — TypeSafe CEO Diogo Almeida told TechCrunch that the hardest part of building Jev was finely calibrating its judgement using statistically-adjusted synthetic data. Sqwish, too, has been working with synthetic data, but its unique offering is built-in post-training tools that use a customer’s own data to improve the model’s judgement.
“What makes us not a commodity, I think, is the fact that we are offering our customers the same power…they can keep uploading their production data, and just the same way that we trained our models, their models can also keep getting better at the tasks that they care about,” CEO Ushnish Sengupta told TechCrunch.
Attempting to rank decision models is difficult; Sqwish’s “kettei fat” model has performed well on some benchmarks, but most builders of the technology say that the real proof is in the pudding: It’s generally simple for developers to sub in one model for another and see how it does in a specific context.
“The benchmark is more of an invitation to try the model out, and then the continual tuning is the reason why they should stick to us,” Sengupta said.
The Microsoft-Decision-1.1 model is also the result of the company carefully balancing across cost, latency, intelligence and calibration. Achint Srivastava, the engineering VP who led the project, agreed that too much focus on benchmarks is a mistake.
“What we see is that ‘benchmaxed’ models fall flat under real enterprise usage very quickly,” Srivastava wrote in an email. “Our testing underscores just how challenging it is to deliver accuracy, reliability, speed and cost efficiency in a single model. Microsoft-Decision-1.1 and Jev are among the few that perform strongly across all four dimensions, even when evaluated on ‘held out’ or unseen benchmarks reflective of real use cases.”
For startups like Sqwish, competition with hyperscalers and frontier labs is an opportunity. Freddi predicts that future systems will see so-called System One intelligence, like decision models, working in concert with System Two intelligence, like frontier LLMs.
“Even in that future, System One is maybe a $10 billion, $50 billion [opportunity], and OpenAI is doing this IPO with you know $1 trillion, $2 trillion market value in mind,” she told TechCrunch. “This is all we care about; whereas for them, this is just a side project.”

title: Ars Live: What do drone strikes on data centers mean for the future? Talk at 1 pm EST today
text:
Drone and missile strikes have inflicted unprecedented damage on data centers in Eastern Europe and the Middle East this year, disrupting cloud services for millions of people and permanently deleting some Amazon Web Services customer data. This trend represents a new concern for Big Tech companies—but also for governments and everyone else who depends on common digital services in modern life.
To explore what this all means for modern society’s reliance on cloud resilience, I will be hosting a live conversation titled “Drone attacks and data centers: New Risks for Big Tech” on Tuesday, November 17 at 1 pm ET with Joseph Jarnecki, a senior research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), a UK defense and security think tank. He leads RUSI’s work on how cloud services factor into national security and defense, along with tech sovereignty efforts.
Jarnecki has done extensive research on how Ukraine strengthened its cloud resilience with Western partners despite facing both cyberattacks and kinetic attacks at the start of the full-scale Russian invasion, and explored what that means for NATO and European governments’ cloud adoption plans.
This year, Jarnecki has written about Iran’s drone and missile strikes on Amazon data centers in the Middle East during the US-Israeli war with Iran, and the broader implications for governments and Big Tech. He has also commented on the impacts of Russia and Ukraine exchanging strikes on each other’s data centers.

title: Quantum computers are getting too powerful to check. Scientists have a solution
text:
Scientists have developed a new way to determine whether quantum simulations can be trusted, solving a growing problem as quantum computers become too powerful for conventional machines to check. Demonstrated on a 51-qubit system, the technique measures uncertainty and provides verifiable error margins that could help unlock the full potential of quantum computing.
As quantum computers grow more powerful, researchers face a troubling question: How can they know whether the results are correct when conventional computers can no longer verify them? Scientists have now developed a promising new method that could help overcome this challenge by measuring the accuracy of quantum simulations and identifying how much uncertainty their predictions contain.
The technique uses experimental measurements to reconstruct how a quantum system behaves, then calculates how uncertainties in that reconstruction affect the results. Researchers successfully demonstrated the approach using a quantum simulator with up to 51 qubits in Innsbruck, Austria.
Quantum systems are expected to become capable of solving increasingly complex problems that traditional computers struggle with or cannot handle at all. However, this progress creates a verification problem. When a simulation is small enough, scientists can compare its results with calculations performed on a conventional computer. As quantum systems grow beyond those limits, that direct comparison becomes impractical, making alternative ways to assess their reliability essential.
A New Way to Measure Quantum Computing Accuracy
The breakthrough comes from an international research team led by Tristan Kraft at the Technical University of Munich and Peter Zoller at the University of Innsbruck and the Institute for Quantum Optics and Quantum Information of the Austrian Academy of Sciences, working alongside Barbara Kraus of the Technical University of Munich. The researchers developed a method for experimentally determining how a quantum simulator operates and translating uncertainties in its behavior into measurable limits on the accuracy of its results.
Quantum simulators are specialized physical systems designed to reproduce the behavior of other quantum systems. They are especially useful for investigating situations involving large numbers of interacting particles, where the calculations required can quickly overwhelm even powerful conventional computers.
But quantum experiments are never entirely free from errors. "But no real experiment is perfect," says Tristan Kraft. "Interactions may turn out differently than expected, the system is influenced by its environment, and measurements are also subject to uncertainties."
Rather than assuming a quantum simulator behaves exactly as intended, the new approach examines experimental data to determine what is actually happening inside the system. This allows researchers to identify important interactions and account for disturbances such as fluctuations and noise.
"From this data, we determine the relevant interactions as well as key influences from fluctuations and noise. We then calculate how the uncertainties in this model affect the simulation results," explains Tristan Kraft. "The quantum simulator thus provides not just a single value, but a result with error margins that quantify its accuracy."
Successfully Tested on a 51 Qubit Quantum Simulator
To evaluate the method, the researchers began with a relatively small quantum system containing ten trapped ions. Because conventional computers can still calculate the behavior of a system of this size, the team could test its reconstructed models and calculated error limits against independent measurements.
After this initial validation, the researchers expanded their experiments to a chain of 51 trapped ions. The larger demonstration, carried out by a team led by Manoj Joshi and Christian Roos using an ion trap quantum simulator, showed that the technique could also work with substantially more complex quantum systems.
This represents an important step toward establishing how trustworthy quantum simulation results are, particularly as quantum devices advance into territory where direct verification with traditional computing methods becomes increasingly difficult.
Extending the Breakthrough to More Complex Quantum Systems
The next challenge is to bring the technique to two-dimensional quantum simulators. These systems can model more complicated interactions among particles, making them valuable for exploring quantum physics. At the same time, their growing complexity makes their results particularly difficult to confirm using conventional calculations.
"This is particularly important because classical calculations for such systems become significantly more difficult as the number of particles increases," explains quantum computing pioneer Peter Zoller. "This also makes independent verification of the results increasingly complex, making the question of experimentally determined error limits all the more important."
The researchers are now adapting their method for the newest generation of two-dimensional quantum simulators, which offer improved precision and can investigate systems containing larger numbers of particles.
Looking further ahead, the approach could help scientists establish a more meaningful way to measure quantum advantage, the ability of quantum systems to outperform conventional computers. Instead of comparing machines based only on their processing speed or the size of the problems they can handle, researchers could also examine how accurately each system produces its answers.
"After all, when a classical computer and a quantum simulator tackle the same problem, it's not just a matter of which one delivers a result faster. What's also crucial is which one can solve the problem with a smaller, verifiable margin of error," says Peter Zoller.
This shift could change how progress in quantum computing is evaluated. Future breakthroughs may be judged not simply by how many particles a simulator can model or how quickly it performs calculations, but by its ability to solve increasingly difficult problems with demonstrably reliable results.
The findings were published in Physical Review X. The research received support from the Austrian Science Fund (FWF), the German Ministry of Research, Technology and Space, the European Union, BMW, and other funding organizations.

title: Stone Age children left fingerprints on ancient art projects
text:
Children have been making art with help from grown-ups for millennia.
Fragmented clay figurines dating as far back as 15,000 years ago, discovered in what is now Israel, preserve the fingerprints of both adults and young children. The finding suggests the grown-ups taught the kids how to shape and decorate clay, researchers report November 11 in PLOS One.
Children’s contributions to prehistoric art and culture aren’t well understood. Concrete evidence of their involvement has been hard to find, says archaeologist Laurent Davin of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.
In recent decades, researchers have found a handful of objects made by children — including 200,000-year-old rock art bearing child-sized handprints in Tibet and 30,000-year-old clay sculptures pockmarked with child-sized fingerprints in Czech Republic.
Davin and colleagues hadn’t set out to find Stone Age children’s artwork. They were investigating whether the Natufian culture — a group of hunter-gatherers who formed some of the first permanent settlements in the Levant about 14,000 years ago — made clay art before the advent of agriculture in the region.
The archaeologists came across the first set of fingerprints while sorting through 40 kilograms of clay collected at three Natufian sites, which range in age from 15,000 to 11,600 years old. Among tens of thousands of clay lumps, the team found some 150 fragments of sculptures, including 15 recognizable bird, gazelle and human figures. Around 60 of these pieces preserved fingerprints from where people had pinched or prodded the clay.
The distances between the fingerprints’ ridges, which are influenced by age and sex, suggest that most of the figurines were made by women and children — some younger than 10. Only a few sets of fingerprints belonged to men. And the torso of one tiny human statue had both adult and child fingerprints, hinting that an elder and child had passed it back and forth. Davin suspects that the adult actively taught a child how to work the clay.
This evidence of intergenerational learning so far back in time is fascinating, says archaeologist Steven Dorland of Grand Valley State University in Allendale, Mich. It demonstrates how much researchers can learn from broadening their focus beyond adult males, he says. Dorland has used pottery to understand social learning in Indigenous societies of the Great Lakes region. He has even studied children’s fingerprints on some of those artifacts.
The purpose of the Natufian figurines is unclear. Most of the statues are less than 2 centimeters long and don’t display signs of intense use, the team found, suggesting they weren’t treated as precious heirlooms.
Davin suspects the figurines may have represented stories, like how kids draw Disney characters today, he says. “Maybe the idea is that the role of children here is not necessarily to learn to make figurines, but more to learn the story behind them.”

title: Reflect Orbital wants to launch thousands of sunlight-beaming mirrors to space — and the 1st will go up next year
text:
Reflect Orbital is moving forward with its plan to place mirrors in Earth orbit to produce and sell sunlight after dark.
The goal is to extend the hours and output of solar farms globally, "making clean power dispatchable and available when you need it," the California-based startup explains on its website.
Reflect Orbital has made significant progress to date. On Tuesday (Nov. 10), for example, the company announced it had secured $73.5 million in new funding, boosting its total raise to more than $100 million. It has also gotten a formal go-ahead from the U.S. government to try out the concept in space and is currently readying its first test satellite, which is expected to launch in the second quarter of 2027. The identity of the launch provider is being kept under wraps at this time, the firm told Space.com.
Ground-based test
Reflect Orbital recently conducted a ground-based test in California, lighting up a mountainous area to practice search and rescue (SAR) techniques.
On Oct. 10, the space startup set up spotlights near Lone Pine, California to simulate the illumination its proposed satellites could provide — controlled lighting without the need for any ground infrastructure. "This lighting will support a variety of customers, from remote search-and-rescue operations to solar farms generating clean power," the company explained in an Oct. 14 statement.
The October illumination test ran from 7 p.m. to midnight and involved members of the China Lake Mountain Rescue Group (CLMRG), who practiced with night-time equipment.
CLMRG is an all-volunteer activity, operating under the auspices of the Kern County Sheriff's Office providing SAR services on an on-call basis at no cost.
Nighttime demonstration
"Together with local search-and-rescue and disaster response groups, we carried out a fully permitted nighttime demonstration of our responsive lighting service," a Reflect Orbital spokesperson told Space.com in response to an inquiry about the exercise. "Search-and-rescue and disaster response teams are expected to be our first customers, so this was a real-world test conducted alongside teams who will use our technology."
Mobile lighting gear was mounted on Horseshoe Meadows Road to provide a spot of light similar to the ones that Reflect Orbital satellites are expected to deliver. "The aim was to create a precise, realistic simulation of our service, so emergency responders could see how it will perform in real scenarios," Reflect Orbital said.
The brightness of the spot was roughly 0.7 lumens.
Incremental learning
Reflect Orbital added that it will keep working closely with local communities and authorities wherever the company operates, to show how its technology can help save lives.
"We're committed to learning incrementally about our technology and its impacts, and from potential customers and stakeholders, ahead of our planned satellite operations," the company stated.
In last month's illumination experiment, Reflect Orbital secured permits in advance, filed a NOTAM (a notice to pilots), notified Edwards Air Force Base and coordinated with the local sheriff's department. Area residents were also notified about the test ahead of time.
Test and learn
In a related development, Reflect Orbital has announced the purchase of two Skyroot Aerospace launches to deploy some of its spacecraft. Skyroot's Vikram-1 launcher is a product of India's private space sector, first flying from the nation's Sriharikota launch site last July. That flight was a landmark success, as Vikram-1 became the first private Indian rocket ever to reach orbit.
"These dedicated launches provide assured schedule and capacity, and complement Reflect Orbital's other planned launches from sites in the United States," Reflect Orbital explained in a different Oct. 14 statement.
Reflect Orbital says its approach is "incremental and test-and-learn." The company has been granted a license from the U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) for one satellite. That mission will test the technology, including built-in safeguards governing precisely how, where and when the sunlight service is delivered.
"It will provide real-world data that shapes the design of future satellites," Reflect Orbital said, "the markets we serve, how we engage communities and the operational practices we put in place. We expect this to be the first of several test missions."
Dim view
Reflect Orbital wants to be operating at least 50,000 of its mirror satellites in orbit by 2035. Not surprisingly, many people in the astronomy and stargazer communities have a dim view of this plan, saying it will generate light pollution that significantly degrades the night sky.
Reflect Orbital counters that most people and most places will never see this light. Customers will require permits, signoff from local authorities and "Know Your Customer compliance" to receive the service. Every service will require multi-layer approval, the company says, and if people do not want the light, they will not receive it.
Reflect Orbital also claims that it can maintain exclusion zones covering astronomical observation sites.
"Our satellites will be default-off when idle and constellation vehicles are designed to stay under +7 stellar magnitude for all non-serving attitudes. We're able to dim the brightness of the service and turn it off at any stage," the company's website states.
Observing campaign
Reflect Orbital also notes that it's an industry member of the International Astronomical Union's (IAU) Center for the Protection of the Dark and Quiet Sky.
The company says that it's collaborating with the IAU on an observing campaign for when the service is operational and is also working on a coordination agreement with the U.S. National Science Foundation.
"We've engaged extensively with scientists, astronomers, environmental researchers and other stakeholders," Reflect Orbital stated. "Their feedback has meaningfully informed the design of our spacecraft and operational plans. We continue to welcome scientific exploration of how novel technology could deliver a lot of benefits to the world."

title: Kalshi halts Trump speech bets after CFTC order
text:
The prediction market platform Kalshi has ended wagers on whether United States President Donald Trump would use specific words on certain dates in his speeches.
The decision, revealed on Tuesday, comes amid an order from the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), the federal agency that oversees futures trading, which last week called on the company to end the bets.
Earlier this year, Kalshi’s surveillance system flagged to the agency potential insider trading concerns involving these markets. It was later discovered that a White House teleprompter operator had traded on markets related to the president’s comments.
The teleprompter operator, Gabriel Perez, received a three-year ban from the platform and was required to pay $65,000 in penalties, as well as relinquish his $107,000 in winnings to the CFTC. By August, the CFTC had begun an internal review of prediction markets, according to CNBC.
The move comes amid a new wave of scrutiny of prediction market platforms by the CFTC. That marks a shift from the stance of Chair Michael Selig, who had previously championed the emerging industry, but has now adopted a tougher tone, launching investigations into Kalshi and its competitor Polymarket, which is not regulated by the commission.
Kalshi, in particular, had been under investigation for developing new products without notifying the commission, according to a report by Politico earlier this month.
The development also comes as Donald Trump Jr, the president’s eldest son, stepped down from his role as a paid strategic adviser to the company last week.
While Kalshi has pulled markets involving mentions by the president, wagers on what other prominent figures will say remain active.
These include predictions about comments by elected US officials, including Vice President JD Vance and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, at the upcoming New York Times DealBook Summit, as well as remarks by executives at Microsoft and SpaceX. Other active markets concern what companies such as Nvidia and retail giant Target will say during their earnings calls.
Kalshi has also stopped listing some markets at the request of the regulatory agency, including certain sports-related markets, according to the Reuters news agency.
Neither Kalshi nor the CFTC responded to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.

title: American soldier accused of spying in U.S. custody after U.K. arrest
text:
A United States Army soldier on suspicion that he engaged in espionage linked to Russia has been taken into the custody of the U.S. military, British and American officials said Tuesday.
A U.S. official previously identified the suspect as Lt. Col. Brandon Tyner, a senior human resources officer based at Imjin Barracks, home to the headquarters of NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps. Tyner, 41, joined the Army in 2008 and has been deployed to Afghanistan, Qatar and Iraq.
Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing, said in a news release that U.S. authorities will continue the investigation. The suspect is expected to be charged soon.
"These are extremely serious allegations, and our collective response should send a strong message that we will act swiftly and robustly where we suspect this kind of espionage activity taking place," Taylor said.
The soldier is suspected of violating the U.K.'s National Security Act of 2023 to obtain or disclose protected information and to assist a foreign intelligence service. The London Metropolitan Police said the suspected activity relates to Russia. Federal Bureau of Investigation director Kash Patel said that the soldier was "a potential threat to national security."
He was arrested by the the London Metropolitan Police during a sting operation in Gloucester, about 100 miles west of London, on November 10. The operation involved the Met Police's Counter Terrorism Policing Unit, the U.S. military and the FBI.
"This FBI has zero tolerance for anyone who betrays their oath to the United States or puts our national security at risk," FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement on Tuesday.
Officials have carried out further searches in Gloucestershire, the county where Gloucester is located, related to the investigation, the Metropolitan Police Department said.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters in Moscow last week that Russia had "nothing to do with" the soldier's detention.
U.K. police said the arrest is not related to "any other ongoing Counter Terrorism Policing investigations." The unit is investigating a recent suspected plot at RAF Fairford, a British Royal Air Force base where U.S. troops and aircraft are stationed. title: Measles is surging in the US. Here’s how the Trump administration has responded
text:
International health experts have decided that the U.S. has lost its status as a country that eliminated the continuous spread of measles
WASHINGTON -- With the U.S. experiencing its worst year for measles in decades, international health experts have decided that the U.S. has lost its status as a country that eliminated the continuous spread of the disease.
The U.S. has racked up more measles cases than in any year since 1991, with confirmed cases surpassing 5,000 in 2026, according to the latest data. Pennsylvania alone has seen more than 1,500 cases.
The Pan American Health Organization 's decision underscores a significant public health setback for the United States as the Trump administration reshapes federal vaccine policy.
Experts say that while the Trump administration did not create the underlying vaccination problem — which predates President Donald Trump’s return to office — the Republican administration's policies and public messaging may have exacerbated it.
Asked about the administration's response to the outbreak, the Department of Health and Human Services referred to a statement by Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Director Erica Schwartz, which said it would remain focused on stopping outbreaks, despite losing the measles designation.
Nationally, 92.4% of kindergartners received their required measles-mumps-rubella shots in the 2025-26 school year, down from 92.5% the previous year and 95.2% in 2019-20, according to data from the CDC. That is below the approximately 95% coverage needed to prevent measles outbreaks, and some communities have substantially lower vaccination rates.
Here's a look at how the Trump administration has handled the worst year for measles in more than three decades:
Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has a long record of questioning vaccine safety, has repeatedly promoted claims that vaccines are associated with autism, despite extensive scientific evidence finding no causal relationship.
And he has delivered mixed messaging on measles specifically. He has occasionally endorsed the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine as “effective,” but also continues to raise unfounded safety concerns about the shots. In August, he told CNN: "I believe that the MMR vaccine prevents measles.” In that same interview he questioned the safety of the vaccine.
Trump reinforced those doubts at an event over the summer where he signed an executive order calling for splitting up the MMR vaccine. He said falsely that taken together the shot was “quite lethal.” Doctors say, and years of real-world evidence prove, that the combination MMR vaccine is both safe and effective at protecting children from illness.
Separate vaccines for measles, mumps and rubella are not available in the United States and producing them that way would be a logistical feat for drugmakers.
Josh Michaud, associate director of global and public health policy at healthcare research nonprofit KFF, said past administrations back to the 1990s, when confronted with measles outbreaks, were aggressive in telling the public how important vaccination is against the disease. That’s not happening now, he said.
"What we’re not seeing from the administration is strong communications about the need for vaccinations,” he said.
During the most recent measles outbreak, Kennedy promoted vitamin A as a possible treatment, which created concern among medical professionals that the administration was giving undue attention to alternatives rather than emphasizing vaccination.
Throughout the surge of measles cases, Kennedy has repeatedly challenged health officials’ accounts of deaths from the disease.
In August, Pennsylvania officials reported two measles-related deaths. The county coroner later said they involved infants too young to be vaccinated, with the virus itself causing one of the deaths.
After Gov. Josh Shapiro stressed that vaccinations could have averted the deaths, Kennedy said the deaths “may even have been altogether fabricated.” He later acknowledged that one of the deaths was due to measles.
The remark echoed similar statements he made after last year, when three measles-related deaths were recorded. Kennedy questioned whether one of the children who died was killed by measles.
Medical experts said the political quarreling over the deaths diverted focus from an exploding public health threat.
As health secretary, Kennedy has spearheaded an overhaul of the nation's vaccine policy. Last year, he fired all 17 members of a key vaccine advisory committee and hired vaccine critics among the replacements. In January, his department downsized the childhood immunization schedule. The moves were temporarily halted by a judge earlier this year.
Kennedy also acknowledged personally directing the CDC to update its website late last year to contradict its longtime guidance that vaccines don’t cause autism.
Critics say the overhaul and the administration's overt questioning of immunization safety have fueled skepticism about vaccines.
Surveys indicate growing public wavering over support for the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine. An August 2025 Annenberg survey found that 82% would be “very” or “somewhat” likely to recommend that an eligible child in their household get the MMR vaccine, compared to 90% in November 2024.
Kennedy has defended his upending of federal health policy by saying the changes will restore trust in America’s public health agencies. Doctors counter that the false and unverified information he promotes and the vaccine policy changes undermine confidence in vaccination and leave more people vulnerable to preventable disease.
Along with freezing and canceling billions in research under Kennedy’s leadership at the start of the Trump administration, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services laid off more than 10,000 workers and shut down entire offices and programs. Experts say those cuts may have impacted state and local health departments’ ability to adequately respond to outbreaks.
PAHO officials expect the U.S., along with Bolivia and Mexico which also lost their elimination status, to each submit a plan “in the coming weeks” for how they will go about trying to stop transmission for at least a year and regain measles elimination status, said Dr. Daniel Salas, PAHO’s executive manager for immunizations.
A decision to strip the U.S. of its measles elimination status will not change how federal health officials are addressing outbreaks, Schwartz said.
“The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans,” she said. “Vaccination does.”
She said federal officials have invested $100 million to help state and local health departments to reach communities with measles outbreaks. “Losing a designation doesn’t mean we abandon an evidence-based approach. It means we remain focused on stopping outbreaks.”
Michaud said the designation change is “a marker for how we backtracked on public health, particularly related to measles prevention, and particularly related to vaccines.”
“It encapsulates this idea that the United States is more vulnerable than ever to infectious diseases," he said.

title: APEC summit: What Trump, Xi and Putin want
text:
The leaders of China, the United States and Russia are due to hold their first trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit this week.
Separately, US President Donald Trump will also hold talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping during the November 18-19 gathering in Shenzhen, China.
Several experts interviewed by DW do not expect any breakthroughs on US-China trade, technology or other issues. Maintaining the existing trade truce and preventing bilateral relations from deteriorating further may be the more realistic shared objectives.
Patricia M. Kim, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, believes neither leader is looking to significantly expand the bilateral agenda, as both have an incentive in maintaining the existing trade truce.
Over the next two years, Kim expects to see "neither uncontrolled escalation in tensions between the US and China nor a dramatic improvement in ties, but rather the continuation of the transactional détente we see today."
Zhang Lun, a professor at CY Cergy Paris University, believes Trump is under pressure both at home and abroad.
"Domestically, Trump faces the prospect of becoming a lame-duck president following the Republicans' heavy losses in the midterm elections," Zhang told DW.
"Internationally, damage to relations with allies, the weakening of the US-led international order, indifference toward democratic values and freedoms, and the difficulties encountered in the Iran war have all reduced America's leverage, resources and influence."
Zhang believes strained ties with US allies and the war in Iran have weakened Trump's hand with Beijing, making him more eager to secure diplomatic wins and Xi's cooperation on key policy priorities.
Contentious issues may be left for later
Jia Hui Tee, a senior trade policy analyst at the Hinrich Foundation, expects Trump and Xi to focus on stabilizing their fragile trade relationship.
She says the two leaders could make progress on reciprocal tariff cuts covering goods worth $30 billion (€27.3 billion) on each side. "While the list of products has been announced, the timeline has not been set and an indicative implementation timeline would be an easy win" for both governments.
Washington wants Beijing to accelerate purchases of US agricultural products and increase exports of rare earths and other critical minerals. But Tee believes that "China would likely be cautious with delivering on its commitments especially when Trump is weaker at home after the midterms with Democrats pushing back on his tariffs."
She also points out that neither side would want to cede their bargaining chips easily, including rare earth exports and technology export controls.
With another meeting between the two leaders is expected in December at the G20 summit in Miami, "there is room to push more contentious issues to a later date and further extend the trade truce in the next meeting," Jia told DW.
China, the US and Russia: three leaders, three agendas
Russia hopes that talks with the leaders of the US and China will enhance its diplomatic standing and help secure a settlement to the war in Ukraine on terms favorable to Moscow.
Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center, told DW that Moscow wants to create the impression that Washington is willing to sit down with Russia and negotiate. This, in turn, could undermine confidence in Europe and Ukraine.
"Trump wants trilateral nuclear talks," she said, while Beijing "wants the optics of China hosting the unprecedented historical meeting among the three."
Alicja Bachulska, a policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, believes Beijing wants to use the meeting to demonstrate its ability to bring major powers together and facilitate international dialogue.
"Russia wants recognition, the US wants arms control, and China wants status without strings attached," she said. "I expect each leader to restate their own positions rather than produce real solutions."
Ukraine: why Beijing is reluctant to mediate
Michael Kimmage, director of the Kennan Institute in the United States, told DW last month that China may be more concerned with the survival of Russian President Vladimir Putin's regime than with actively bringing the war in Ukraine to an end.
Russia remains an important source of energy and a key diplomatic partner for Beijing, Kimmage noted.
An outright Russian victory may not necessarily be Beijing's objective, he said. "More important to China is the political survival of Vladimir Putin." For that reason, Kimmage does not expect China to pressure the Russian president into ending the war if Putin is unwilling to do so.
Zhang Lun believes the current situation is "most in line with Beijing's interests."
The Trump administration's pro-Putin stance has made it harder for Ukraine to resist Russia, Zhang said, while Europe has been forced to bear greater costs and has been weakened.
He argued that the United States has also "lost moral authority" and "the postwar international order and the alliances built around Washington have been further eroded," making China's "position and influence more prominent."
He believes Beijing wants to keep Russia from collapsing, but not support it so openly or extensively that it alienates Europe and other Western countries.
"At the same time, China does not want Ukraine to be defeated, because that would reduce Russia's dependence on Beijing," he told DW.
"For now, China is unlikely to intervene directly. Instead, it will wait for a more favorable moment and then potentially step in as a neutral mediator in order to maximize its gains."
Iran: little sign of substantive cooperation
W.A. Figueroa, an assistant professor of history and international relations at the University of Groningen in the Netherlands, told DW that there is little indication of any real cooperation between China and the US on Iran.
The two countries do share some interests, "including opposition to a toll system in the Strait of Hormuz and opposition to nuclear proliferation," Figueroa noted, but "China has consistently called for negotiations and denounced both sanctions and military force as a way to achieve these or any other objectives."
Figueroa says China does not want further escalation or prolonged instability in the Middle East. However, Beijing has been able to manage the current situation without too much difficulty, leaving it with little pressure to change its position.
"China continues to provide Iran with crucial financial support through its purchases of Iranian oil," Figueroa noted, adding that Beijing's diplomatic support has so far brought no substantial change, largely because China has little leverage over either Iran or the US in the region.

title: As Trump walks into a summit of strongmen, what can America’s lame-duck president hope to achieve?
text:
His party just took the worst drubbing in a midterm election since Richard Nixon’s GOP after Watergate. His approval ratings are lower than they’ve ever been, and his administration is girding itself for a barrage of long-delayed Congressional oversight while presiding over a series of high-profile infrastructure failures and outages that have left Americans on edge.
This, of course, means it’s time for President Donald Trump to get out of town for a while.
To be fair, the president isn’t fleeing the country to lay low in some no-extradition jurisdiction. On Monday he left the White House for a long-planned, four-day trip through Asia for a series of the multilateral confabs he has long detested.
On Tuesday he was in the Philippines for a sit-down with the “Quad” — a security dialogue between the U.S., Australia, India and Japan which has roots in the late George W. Bush era — on the sidelines of this year’s Association of Southeast Asian Nations. On Wednesday he’ll fly to Shenzhen, China, for the annual Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders’ meeting.
But that’s not why he’s really going to Shenzhen.
The reason Trump is heading to China for the second time in six months is so he can finally attend the meeting the White House has been promoting for days: the first, three-way sit-down between the presidents of the United States, China and Russia.
It’s a trilateral meeting that Trump has craved for years.
Never quite comfortable with the democratically-elected leaders of America’s traditional allies, he has spent his decade-long stint atop the American political scene denigrating them while expressing a bizarre fondness for the likes of Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin — men who made their bones crushing dissent, silencing adversaries, and either never having elections or rigging them with a wink and nod so as to never give up power.
Putin and Xi have long maintained a cozy, if slightly uneasy, relationship that is the inverse of the decades when the USSR was king atop the authoritarian world and China the understudy. Now the junior partner of the pair and a pariah in much of the world, Putin’s people have been buttering up the U.S. president by casting him as Franklin Delano Roosevelt in what Pyotr Tolstoy, who chairs the foreign affairs committee of Russia’s parliament, called a “new Yalta” - the 1945 conference at which FDR, Winston Churchill and Joseph Stalin settled the shape of postwar Europe.
Trump’s own team has set the bar far lower. During a briefing ahead of Monday’s departure from Washington, White House assistant press secretary Olivia Wales told reporters that Trump would raise “the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous.”
That agenda item harkens back to Trump’s two ill-fated summits with North Korea’s Kim Jong Un — and to long before, when as a young real estate developer and budding media gadfly he openly mused about being drafted to handle nuclear disarmament talks with Moscow.
But on the same call, a senior U.S. official said the White House does “not expect to get to any kind of agreement,” and called Thursday’s meeting “the entry point, the first conversation.”
While this trio should be able to reconvene in approximately a month when Trump hosts the Group of 20 summit at his own Doral golf resort in Florida, it’s unlikely that any arms talks will get past that “entry point.”
The reality is there’s not much Trump can do as he makes the lame duck’s traditional pivot beyond America’s borders to become a self-styled foreign policy president in the mold of Jimmy Carter negotiating the Camp David Accords between Israel and Egypt or Bill Clinton’s work on the Good Friday Agreement to end The Troubles in Northern Ireland after three decades.
Two weeks ago, voters gave Democrats control of the House and the Senate in an election in which exit polls put Trump’s approval at 38 percent, which means starting January 3 the committees overseeing foreign policy, trade and intelligence will be run by people with no interest in advancing his own personal peccadillos.
Add to that Putin and Xi’s knowledge that the U.S. political system gives Trump just two more years in power, which means any agreement they might reach on anything will be picked over by a Congress that never signed off on it, and by a successor who may want to undo it, in a relatively short amount of time.
New START, the last treaty limiting the American and Russian arsenals, lapsed in February after Trump turned down Moscow’s offer to extend it in hopes of besting his predecessors by working out a tripartite deal that includes China’s comparatively tiny arsenal.
