Asked whether Beijing would engage, the U.S. official said it was “time for China to sort of step up, you know, to the adult table, if you will, and have adult conversations about adult things,” and accused China of building its arsenal “very opaquely.”
But China has already answered through its foreign ministry which last month said trilateral talks would be “neither fair, reasonable nor realistic.”
Undoubtedly Xi and his aides know a president with less time and less support at home is a poor partner for a treaty that would take years to negotiate and would need two-thirds of the Senate to ratify.
So in the end, what Trump wants is the visual. The handshakes. The scenes with him and two of the world’s worst dictators seated together as peers.
For Putin and Xi, the point will be to push their idea of a “multipolar world” with a diminished America just one of a number of powers who divide the world up into the spheres of influence that were a feature of foreign policy more than a century earlier.
Trump doesn’t care about that — and it’s possible he doesn’t understand.
To him, this is a meeting between friends. And that will be enough.

title: Moldova closes airspace after 'Shahed-type' drone detected heading towards Chișinău
text:
"Russia's war threatens all of Europe," President Maia Sandu wrote in a post on social media, adding that "several Russian drones" had violated Moldovan airspace on Tuesday.
Moldova closed its national airspace on Tuesday after an attack drone was detected heading towards the capital Chișinău.
Airspace was closed "for security reasons" at 4:27 pm local time after reports that a Shahed-type drone had been detected "moving from the south towards the Botanica sector of Chișinău," the ministry of defence said in a statement.
The eastern European nation, which borders Ukraine, has seen a growing wave of drone incursions this year, believed to be spillover from Russia's invasion.
President Maia Sandu said "several Russian drones" had violated Moldovan airspace on Tuesday, including one over Chișinău.
"Russia's war threatens all of Europe," she wrote in a post on social media, adding that she would continue to push for sanctions on Moscow while standing by Ukraine.
The defence ministry advised locals not to approach or touch any "suspicious flying objects" or debris as they could contain "explosive components."
Mihai Popșoi, Moldova's foreign minister, called the latest incident a "serious breach of our sovereignty" and a "direct threat to the safety of our citizens."
"Russia must stop actions that endanger Moldova" and "regional security," he added.
Police said they had received calls from residents in Chișinău and Florești reporting the sound of explosions or loud bangs on Tuesday.

title: Dems campaign promise to freeze energy costs faces glaring reality check
text:
Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa is preparing her first step into left-leaning policies in the historically deep red state by implementing an emergency utility rate freeze — but one expert worries the proposal will become a failed attempt to address the affordability crisis.
More Democratic-led states are looking to impose similar plans to Hinojosa's after she said on Day One of being governor that she will freeze residential electricity rates, an idea that many warn clashes with Texas’ uniquely competitive energy sector and could inadvertently create energy shortages.
"It's a campaign promise they made on the trail," Sam Romain, chairman of the free market group Americans for Energy Dominance, told Fox News Digital. "But they don't have the power to just freeze the rates. You can't just wave a magic wand and freeze the rates."
Romain believes it’s only a matter of time before Democrats across the country have to wrestle with ways to increase energy production — even as they are currently exploring a variety of energy price controls.
"We know that price works based on supply and demand, right? It's basic, basic economics," Romain said.
"And what you're seeing across the nation is this Democratic price control scheme that's dressed up as an emergency. The problem is you can't necessarily freeze your way out of the supply problems," Romain added.
Some Democratic-led strategies aim to lock down energy prices while others look to subsidize them. Some plans call for both.
In one such case, Democrat Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger, who took office in January, is demanding a six-year rate freeze as a Florida company looks to buy Virginia’s largest energy supplier. She has also called for "a tripling of monthly bill credits for ratepayers."
New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill promised to declare a state of emergency to cap energy rates at the outset of her term in January 2026, but has since pivoted to implement a credit system to offset electricity costs using executive orders.
Among the newly elected Democrats, California Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra promised to "institute a freeze on utility rates… while the state investigates long-term solutions to bring these costs under control," a strategy he framed as a priority.
In Wisconsin, Democratic Gov.-elect David Crowley will lead a legislature that last year entertained a proposal to cap gas and electricity bills at 4% of a qualifying household’s annual income. Crowley himself has also proposed a similar "fair deal" plan that would cap annual rent increases at 7%.
And in Ohio, Democratic state leadership led by House Minority Leader Dani Isaacsohn has proposed a 12-month freeze on utility rates as Amy Acton prepares to take the gubernatorial mansion.
To Romain, these proposals deal a twofold blow.
In addition to failing to build out supply, he believes they also discourage additional production. "A freeze in and of itself doesn't actually build anything. Actually, it does almost the opposite. It discourages developers from building. They don't know if they're going to be able to recoup their profit margin on their construction," Romain said.
Questions also remain about the legality of some of the plans. In Texas, for instance, experts have noted that Hinojosa’s planned use of an emergency declaration may quickly run into legal resistance.
Nick Loris, the president of C3 Solutions, a conservative coalition for climate solutions that focuses on energy, environment and agriculture policy, questioned the emergency powers Hinojosa says she plans to use.
"The Texas Disaster Act lets the governor declare disasters and suspend the regulatory laws and statutes that are in existence. But I think there is a high degree of skepticism, both from courts, but also from state policymakers, that this warrants such a claim — and that it is such a disaster," Loris said.
Romain believes Democrats will face similar legal hurdles in other states. But even though he expects price-control strategies to stall, Romain believes that creates an opportunity: fertile ground for a bipartisan affordability strategy as Democrats look to keep their commitments.
"Democrats know there's a supply-side issue," Romain said.
"Their solution to it is different than the Republicans'… And the solution is quite simply to just let American companies build and compete. The problem is to unleash American innovation. This country was built by builders, right? And so let our companies build the tools they need, let them build the generation sites, let them build the power plants," Romain said.
Permitting reform is one area in particular he believes may soon turn into an area for cooperation, a deregulation of the rules that govern energy production.
"I'm actually really optimistic… that we're going to have a massive permit reform package done very quickly, very soon, actually," Romain said.
"I think that we have a massive opportunity in front of us."

title: Trump administration details its $50 billion request for aviation system improvements
text: The Trump administration has formally updated its request to lawmakers for $50.1 billion to modernize the nation's air traffic control system and to make other improvements at airports. READ MORE: FAA stops installation of routers it linked to national ground stop A letter to key lawmakers dated Tuesday says that less than 24 hours after the administration's request of $30.1 billion, "the urgent need for this investment became undeniable." That's when outdated equipment disrupted aircraft communications and radar feeds, forcing the Federal Aviation Administration to initiate a nationwide ground stop. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News The request to lawmakers calls for $10.1 billion for updating the nation's air traffic control system. Another $10 billion would go to boosting airport infrastructure. Meanwhile, $10 billion would go to replace or refurbish terminals at high-impact hubs. Another $10 billion would go to construct five new traffic control centers and $10 billion would go to improving or replacing up to 140 FAA-owned air traffic control towers.

title: Jensen Huang's Nvidia exit exposes succession and governance risks for companies and boards
text:
The fallout from Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy as well as an Nvidia executive that led to his resignation as CEO of Nivida, the company he founded and grew into a $4 trillion chip giant, will likely go on for some time.
But the missteps of Nvidia's board of directors offer immediate lessons, say talent and leadership experts. It shows what happens when there's no clear succession plan, the dangers of an overly decentralized leadership structure, and how companies built around one powerful, controlling leader create the kind of risk boards are responsible for preventing.
In the span of less than a week — from the time Huang admitted that he was unfaithful to his wife until the board announced that he was resigning — the question became: could Nvidia, a company at the epicenter of the AI build-out, operate without him?
With Huang's ouster and the appointment of CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO, Nvidia's employees, customers, and investors will begin to find out. The process will also put a glaring spotlight on why the Nvidia board wasn't better prepared for Huang leaving the company for whatever reason.
"Succession planning is an ongoing, fundamental responsibility of the board, not something to do when a crisis hits," says Lisa Calicchio, chief human resources officer at WCG Clinical and a member of the CNBC Workforce Executive Council.
She described what happened at Nvidia as "a failure of epic proportion, both on the part of the board for not fulfilling its fiduciary responsibility to ensure continued viability of the organization by having a robust succession plan, and for the behavior and risks created by the CEO."
"What they're doing now is flying by the seat of their pants," she added.
Nvidia's 10-member board of directors is a collection of early investors, long-time partners and business executives across a range of industries. Before Nov. 12, the company did not have a chair of the board or any clear succession plan. The board also includes directors who expressed "confidence in Jensen" before they had even begun their own independent internal review of his actions.
In addition to naming Kress to the top job, the company appointed Harvey C. Jones, a tech investor and Nvidia director for the past 33 years, as its first-ever chair. After his appointment, the company announced that the board would be conducting a search of both internal and external candidates to find a permanent chief executive.
Alan Fleischmann, founder and CEO of business advisory firm Laurel Strategies and a member of the CNBC CEO Council, says that while "the DNA of any organization is defined by the CEO, there must be a stronger board dynamic and strong leadership surrounding the CEO."
"Succession planning is not simply about identifying who takes over when a CEO leaves," Fleischmann said. "It's about building an institution that can thrive beyond any one individual."
The outsized role Huang played at Nvidia — in September 2025 he told CNBC's Becky Quick that he had as many as 60 direct reports — makes it even more difficult for the board to find someone who can understand the inner workings of the company while being such a visible and active hype man for its all-important AI chips.
In corporate governance circles this is known as "key man" risk and it points to a company being overly reliant on one person whose death, departure, or financial or moral compromise could materially damage the organization.
"This is the world's most valuable company and all the risk centered on the shoulders of one man," Calicchio says.
"Flat organizations can be remarkably effective…but there are tradeoffs," Fleischmann added. "When too many decisions, relationships and reporting lines converge around one individual, the organization can become more vulnerable than it appears."
Calicchio acknowledged that a CEO having numerous direct reports isn't problematic in the early days of a company, when the founder knows everyone, but becomes concerning "when a company is the size of Nvidia. I really question the rigor and discipline of their organizational policies."
This same absence of rigor is evident in the lack of any obvious successors to Huang. "You would expect the board to have recognized at some point there was going to be an increasing need to look beyond Jensen," says Tim Wentworth, the former CEO of Walgreens Boots Alliance and Express Scripts. "This sounds so fundamental, but you don't wait for the rainy day to have the rainy day plan."
Wentworth says that when he was running both Walgreens and Express Scripts, he had a single board member assigned to each one of his direct reports so that "when we had board discussions, somebody in the room could speak about them and their strengths."
At WCG Clinical, succession and talent discussions are done quarterly, says Calicchio. "We're always looking at time frames," she says. "Is this person a definite successor, ready now, or is this someone you're grooming for the long term? Everyone wants to think that replacing the CEO is going to happen in an orderly way, but as we just saw at Nvidia, that's not always the case."
"Boards need to expect the unexpected," she adds.
Huang's powerful grip at Nvidia was great, "until it wasn't," says Wentworth. "It's really hard for a board to have a sense of urgency and the depth of intrusiveness necessary in that process when everything is going great with the company. No one wants to be the contrarian, but that's your job as a board member."

title: Pedestal AI raises $4.7 million to agentify the supply chain
text:
Delivery supply chains are the lifeblood of contemporary businesses — and a new startup is betting that purpose-built AI agents can make them run a lot more smoothly.
On Tuesday, Pedestal AI emerged from stealth with $4.7 million in seed funding. The company’s goal is to use agentic AI to make supply chains faster and more reliable — a plan that’s already brought them together with Fortune 500 companies and some of the largest shipping firms in the world.
The seed round was led by Eclipse, with participation from RRE, Converge VC, Timescale Ventures, and VitalStage. Pedestal says the funding will be used to expand its product and engineering time, grow the marketing organization, and support additional deployments.
In practice, much of Pedestal’s work is about removing friction from the shipping process — with agentic technology used as a means to that end. In one case, the company reduced missed deliveries for a major furniture company by 20% by deploying agents to take on some of the work that drivers were supposed to do. The agentic system they built would call customers 30 minutes before a delivery and collect any special instructions; if the call didn’t go through, a text would be sent from a separate system. Along the way, the deployment collected a wealth of data about friction points in the process, which could be used to optimize the system even further.
CEO Raj Aggarwal says contemporary AI systems are particularly useful for dealing with that data. “The challenge is that the data is messy and it’s constantly changing,” Aggarwal told TechCrunch. “It’s disparate because it sits in so many legacy systems. That’s what makes it hard.”
Supply chain AI has become a particularly hot space in recent months as alumni from autonomous driving teams look to launch their own startups. The supply chain startup Atomic, launched by a team of Tesla alumni, came out of stealth in 2025 with an emphasis on streamlining inventory. Another venture called Loop was launched by Uber alums to focus on predictive analytics.
As Aggarwal sees it, deliveries are particularly well-suited to training reinforcement learning systems. Because of their high volumes and easily measured outcomes, it’s easy to fine-tune contemporary AI systems toward what’s working and away from what isn’t.
Perhaps most importantly, it’s the kind of problem that can have an immediate effect on a client’s bottom line, making it easy to justify the expense.
“If you can get it right,” he told TechCrunch, “you can have really big impact.”

title: Grok Bot took unapproved actions, ignored orders to stop, and then denied it
text:
Researchers recently discovered unexpected behavior from Grok Bot, the AI agent platform from Elon Musk’s SpaceXSI. Over five days, Grok bots installed on two separate employee laptops made 31 requests to access data stored in employee calendar, email, Slack, and GitHub accounts. The bots performed the actions even though the employees had never ordered them and continued doing them even after employees instructed them to stop. The bots also denied having taken the actions at all.
The behavior was reported Tuesday by NewCore, the maker of a managed gateway product that acts as an intermediary between AI agents and the tools and accounts they are assigned to work with. In some cases, the unapproved access attempts occurred while the laptop with Grok Bot installed had its lid shut, or late at night while the employee was sleeping. None of the unprompted actions were recorded in Grok logs. Without the gateway logs, the employees would have had no idea they occurred. And of course, without the gateway, the unapproved accesses would have succeeded—again without the end user’s knowledge.
It’s “worse than a bug”
Once the employees learned that Grok Bot had tried to check in with accounts without prompting, one of them instructed the agent, four separate times, to stop taking any actions on its own. The agent’s reply was: “I won’t set that up, and I’ll stop offering recurring check-ins.” Despite acknowledging the explicit instructions, the Grok Bot made more unapproved access attempts. When one of the employees asked the bot if it made any accesses, it checked twice and then outputted: “Overnight into Friday morning I was idle.”
The NewCore employees sent the gateway logs to Grok Bot support personnel and asked what was causing the bots to access accounts without prompting or approval. The support team’s reply indicated the behavior was by design and intended to allow the bots to proactively take actions on behalf of users. In other words, the unrequested and unlogged access attempts were a feature designed to make Grok Bot more useful by periodically checking in and finding tasks to perform before a user even asks. The proactive check-in is a feature of Cursor, the AI coding service SpaceXSI recently acquired.

title: A material just one atom thick reveals a strange quantum secret
text:
Researchers at the University of Osaka have discovered a remarkable quantum state forming at the boundary between a one-atom-thick material and a metal. They observed electrons behaving as though they were unusually heavy, including a previously unseen state created by interactions between the ultrathin layer and the copper beneath it. This first-of-its-kind observation reveals a promising new way to control exotic quantum behavior.
Scientists at the University of Osaka in Japan have made a significant discovery in quantum physics, directly observing an unusual electronic state forming where a material just one atom thick meets a metal. Known as a heavy fermion state, this phenomenon causes electrons to behave as though they have much greater mass than normal. These states are associated with extraordinary quantum effects, including unconventional superconductivity, and the discovery could provide a new way to develop materials with unusual electronic properties.
To investigate this behavior, the researchers produced a carefully controlled, single atomic layer of ytterbium and copper (YbCu2) on the surface of a copper crystal. They then used powerful synchrotron light to study the electrons and their interactions at the boundary between the two materials. The results showed that electrons confined to the thin atomic layer could interact with freely moving electrons in the copper beneath it, producing the unusual heavy fermion behavior.
Two Distinct Quantum States Emerge
The experiments uncovered two separate heavy fermion states with different characteristics. One existed primarily within the two-dimensional atomic layer, while the other reached beyond that layer and into the three-dimensional copper crystal below.
The second state was particularly important because it provided the first direct evidence of heavy fermion behavior generated by interactions across such an interface. Researchers traced the effect to the mixing, or hybridization, of localized ytterbium 4f electrons in the atomic layer with mobile conduction electrons inside the copper substrate. This interaction demonstrated how combining materials with different electronic characteristics can produce quantum behavior that neither material would necessarily exhibit on its own.
"This achievement was made possible by our continued efforts to create high-quality materials and measure their electronic states as precisely as possible," says senior author Professor Shin-ichi Kimura. "Our next goal is to engineer and control such heavy-electron states, opening the way to previously unexplored quantum states, including unconventional superconductivity."
A New Approach to Designing Quantum Materials
The discovery suggests that the boundaries between materials could become powerful tools for creating and controlling exotic quantum states. Rather than relying only on the properties of individual substances, scientists may be able to develop entirely new electronic behaviors by carefully selecting and combining ultrathin atomic layers with suitable underlying materials.
Future research could focus on adjusting the structures of these interfaces, controlling the electronic orbitals involved, and manipulating moiré patterns that arise when atomic arrangements overlap. Such approaches may allow researchers to produce and fine-tune quantum phenomena in materials with extremely small dimensions, including effects that cannot be achieved in conventional materials. Ultimately, this could open new possibilities for engineering advanced quantum materials and investigating unconventional superconductivity.

title: This magic mushroom can kill
text:
People who eat this tiny magic mushroom may hit a lethal low instead of getting high.
The fungus makes hallucinogenic psilocybin and deadly amatoxin, researchers report November 11 in Current Biology. Dubbed “dark magic mushrooms,” it is the first species of fungus discovered to make both types of compounds.
Chemist and fungal biologist Andrew Kunik found the dark magic mushroom in 2025 growing on a decaying moss-covered palm trunk in a central Florida wetland. Kunik, who was then doing post-baccalaureate research in the lab of fungal biologist Matthew Smith at the University of Florida in Gainesville, identified the mini mushroom as Galerina indica.
That species had not been reported in Florida before, Kunik says. “It’s quite rare and unusual.” He also found two other new related species, tagged with the placeholder names Galerina species 1 and Galerina species 2.
Other researchers had previously described G. indica’s appearance and found DNA signatures that distinguish the fungus from related species. But no one had cataloged the mushroom’s complete chemical or genetic makeup.
Related Galerina species make amatoxins, deadly chemicals that can kill in even tiny amounts and are found in death cap mushrooms and other species. Kunik and colleagues looked for those toxins in G. indica and the two other new Galerina species. G. indica makes a previously undiscovered form of amatoxin the team is calling alpha-proamanitin, the chemical analysis revealed.
The small mushroom also had blue bruises, a clue that it might make psilocybin, a psychedelic chemical being tested as a treatment for mental health disorders. Fungi usually make either amatoxin or psilocybin. Not both. Galerina species 1 also makes psilocybin but doesn’t make amatoxin, and species 2 makes neither.
“This finding shows that there’s a lot more diversity in [fungal] chemistry and the ways that they’re combined than we had really thought about,” says Anne Pringle, a mycologist at the University of Wisconsin–Madison who was not involved in the work.
Discovering these dual compounds in one mushroom was both exciting and required further analysis to confirm, Kunik says. “Surprising discoveries require great depth of evidence,” he says.
A complete workup of the mushroom’s DNA revealed genes for producing both types of chemicals. Ancestors of these dark magic mushrooms probably picked up those genes by swapping DNA with other species. Such DNA swapping, called horizontal gene transfer, is one way that organisms can quickly evolve new traits, like when bacteria exchange antibiotic resistance genes with unrelated species.
Ancestors of G. indica and its relatives probably acquired amatoxin genes early on. Those toxins are made by many of G. indica’s cousins, which indicates that amatoxins are probably heirlooms passed down from common ancestors. Ancestors of species 1 and species 2 seem to have dropped the amatoxin genes at some point since they no longer make the compounds.
The two psilocybin-producing species may have independently obtained the psychedelic genes in separate DNA swap meets, or a common ancestor may have picked up the genes and then passed them down to G. indica and species 1. There’s not enough known about the fungi’s family tree to sort out which scenario is correct.
And there’s another unsolved evolutionary mystery, Pringle says. “We still don’t know why mushrooms are poisonous.” Many scientists think it is for defending against predators, but hard evidence is lacking, she says.
“Can I eat it?” is often the first question people ask when finding a new mushroom, Pringle says. “I’m always so uncomfortable with that question and that conversation. And this paper confirms that, in fact, you should be uncomfortable.” After all, eating these dark magic mushrooms could send people tripping into the grave.

title: Satellites now outnumber the visible stars above most towns
text:
More than 700 satellites are crossing the sky over an average mid-latitude town at any moment of the night, outnumbering in many cases the stars visible to the naked eye.
That's based on an analysis of the trajectories of the 15,833 active satellites that currently circle the planet in low Earth orbit below an altitude of 1,200 miles (2,000 kilometers). Analyzing data from Oct. 12 and 18 this year, researchers found that with a completely unobstructed horizon, 710 satellites were crossing the sky in every single moment of the night above an average U.K. town.
The results were published as a non-peer-reviewed study conducted by engineering firm Accu Components, and is based on satellite monitoring data from the U.S. Space Force available through the public website CelesTrak. Although the researchers specifically focused on the U.K., they say that such heavy satellite traffic flows above most of Europe, the U.S. and other mid-latitude regions, especially between 40 and 50 degrees north or south.
"Most Starlink satellites orbit at around 53 degrees to the equator, so the satellites bunch up over the mid-latitudes. These worldwide figures are approximate, based on a global grid over a single day," Accu Components spokesperson told Space.com in an email. "Skies near the equator are the quietest, with around 490 satellites."
Not all of those satellites are visible to the naked eye, the researchers said in a statement. Because satellites unlike stars don't produce their own light, they must be illuminated by the sun, while the ground below has already sunk into darkness, to be visible. According to the study, an average of 105 satellites out of those 710 were catching light as they zoomed overhead, shining as bright as stars.
The spokesperson said that the actual number of visible satellites varies drastically throughout the night. During the hours after dusk and before dawn, a much greater number of satellites can be seen, while in the middle of the night most no longer catch any light.
"For a typical U.K. town, around 300 satellites are catching the sunlight in the first hour or so after dark," the spokesperson said. "That falls to fewer than 20 around midnight, then climbs back to around 300 before dawn."
For comparison, as little as a few dozen stars are visible to the naked eye in the dead of the night above large, light-polluted megalopolis such as London or New York, according to OwnStarMap. In suburban areas and smaller towns, that number grows to a few hundred. To get to a few thousand visible stars, one must retreat into remote countryside or isolated mountain ranges.
The number of satellites orbiting Earth has grown steeply in the past decade, especially since Elon Musk’s SpaceX began launching its internet-beaming Starlink constellation. Satellite companies plan to launch hundreds of thousands, possibly millions of satellites in the coming decades. If those visions come to pass, the number of passing satellites will vastly outgrow that of stars almost anywhere in the world. The trend especially concerns astronomers who fear the impacts on humankind’s ability to study the Universe.
Satellites crossing the view of ground-based telescopes leave streaks in astronomical images and increase the overall brightness of the sky through the light they reflect down towards Earth. Gradually, even the most powerful telescopes could lose their ability to see the distant stars and galaxies that hold the answers to key questions about the history of the universe.
The study found that throughout the night, an average U.K. town sees 12,891 different satellites passing overhead.

title: We can't afford to hire under-25s, say firms. Will Milburn plans help?
text:
Lowering employers' National Insurance (NI) payments for those between 21 and 24, and cash incentives to take on some workers are among proposals put forward in Alan Milburn's report to get more 18-24 year-olds working.
Many companies have complained that recent increases in National Insurance and the minimum wage have made it more expensive to take on staff.
We talked to firms and business groups about the issues they face when hiring younger works and what they make of the proposals.
Costs the key issue
Cutting NI costs is "right in the sweet spot of what firms need to hit the hire button", said the Recruitment and Employment Confederation (REC).
The Milburn report proposes NI thresholds could be raised over the next five years, from £5,000 to £10,000 for those aged 21 to 24, and suggests prioritising the retail and hospitality sectors.
Bournemouth-based café owner Ben Blades says the high costs he faces currently make it difficult to employ young people with no work experience.
"My labour costs are already over 45%. We simply cannot justify the extra cost to put on an extra staff member to train someone up for three months," he says.
"In hospitality our margins have been squeezed and squeezed and squeezed"
As a result, he says it currently makes more sense to employ someone who already has experience.
Allen Simpson, chief executive of UKHospitality, says the recommendation to raise the threshold is "the right one" and "would be an immediate shot in the arm for job creation".
But the British Chambers of Commerce (BCC) argues the Milburn report does not go far enough in tackling costs facing businesses.
It says while the NI proposal is welcome, the change should be wider than just retail and hospitality, otherwise it "risks adding complexity and blocking off potential career paths".
Cash incentives
Other proposals put forward by the Milburn review include cash incentives to employ younger workers.
Employers who take on any young person who has been Neet - not in education, employment or training - for six months should receive a £3,000 payment, and small businesses - with less than 50 employees - that do so should receive an extra £2,000
There would also be an extra £2,000 payment if the young person has been in care or is disabled.
Ally Fir runs a bookshop in Westbourne, alongside her partner Matt, and thinks more state support is needed.
She says incentivised schemes for small business "would help us to employ more, especially young people. If a scheme like that was going we'd jump on it right away."
Fir says she gets job applications "every single day". She'd like to take more people on but "it is the cost of employing people that makes that impossible".
Tom Parsons has already had experience of using government schemes to employ young people at his design consultancy, Aetha, in Poole, Dorset.
The Kickstart Scheme in 2020 meant he could take on two young people in fully funded six-month job placements offering 25 hours a week.
"One of them stayed with us for five years and the other one I think about three years. And it completely changed the game for them," Tom told the BBC. "So if there was a scheme like that, again, that would really help us."
He says he wants to employ young people but costs remain a huge barrier.
Guaranteed hours a concern
One of the government's flagship employment rights reforms risks weakening the hiring of young people, according to Milburn's report.
Ministers are abolishing what they call ''exploitative'' zero-hours contracts and replacing them with guaranteed hours contracts which would be based on the number of hours people normally work.
Much of the detail is yet to be finalised but the Employment Rights Act is due to be enacted next year.
Milburn is concerned that the changes could cause problems "at a time when the youth labour market is already weak'.'
The REC said companies were "particularly worried" over the guaranteed hours measure.
It added that addressing the Neets problem gave ministers "the perfect opportunity" to reconsider the issue.
Help getting staff
Young people should have a legal right to a route into education, training or work, and would be supported to do so under an "opportunity guarantee", Milburn has proposed.
This could help firms which are struggling to recruit. Thirty-five-year-old Dean Greene, a sales director at waste management facility Williams Environmental, says it's tricky finding staff.
"We didn't get many applicants for it at all," says Greene, referencing an ad for a marketing and sales role.
"There wasn't a huge uptake from that sort of 16-to-24 range," he adds.
He thinks the lack of applicants may be because the waste industry is perceived as "mucky and dirty", but he is confident many would be interested if they knew the job was available.
Pointing to himself as an example of progressing in the industry, he tells me how he started as an admin officer scanning paperwork at 18 before remaining with the company for 17 years.

title: Can Google win the AI race without killing its cash cow?
text:
Google became one of the most valuable companies in the world by revolutionizing how humanity finds information. Now, a new generation of AI rivals is challenging its dominance and pushing Google to spend a fortune to secure its future. Can Google embrace this disruptive technology without breaking the business that made it rich?
Former Google executive Marissa Mayer remembers when the company was just a scrappy startup, working out of a small office above a bike shop in Palo Alto, Calif. She joined the company back in 1999, fresh out of nearby Stanford with a master's in computer science.
" It's pretty wild. When I interviewed at Google, there were just seven people there," Mayer tells Planet Money. By the time she got hired, a month or two later, she became its 20th employee.
That year, Google brought in just over $200,000 in annual revenue. By 2022, the eve of the AI boom, the company — by then reorganized under a parent company called Alphabet — was generating more than $280 billion. That's more than a millionfold increase.
Google made its fortune selling ads next to its search results. It monopolized internet searches so thoroughly that its name became a verb. And its search business became like an unstoppable money machine.
In 2012, Mayer left and became the CEO of Yahoo, trying to revive a competitor that Google had blown out of the water. But neither Yahoo nor any other rival managed to dethrone King Google. The company's dominion just kept expanding. Its share of the U.S. search-engine market grew from 80% in 2009 to nearly 90% in 2020.
For a time, it seemed like the only forces that could cut this juggernaut down to size were politicians or antitrust lawyers.
But the craziest part? The biggest threat to Google was maybe coming from inside the house! From what it was developing in its own labs — and the industrial race it would unleash.
Google plowed the profits from its search business into research and development of AI. And, in 2017, a team of eight Google employees developed the transformer, a breakthrough technology that made today's AI chatbots possible.
Mayer, who is now CEO of the AI startup Dazzle and remains a Google shareholder, sees Google's pioneering AI work as a reason for optimism about the company's future. "This is not a technology that's happening to Google," she says. "They helped invent this new technology."
Yet, today, Google is spending enormous amounts to build its AI capabilities and fend off rivals. And it's overhauling its search business, using AI to answer questions directly instead of just providing links.
Wall Street is getting nervous. In late October, Alphabet released its most recent earnings report. The company's stock price plummeted more than 12% the next day — the biggest single-day percentage decline since the company went public in 2004.
If this whole AI transition goes sideways for the company, it's a bit like a mother giving birth to a baby and then that baby slapping her in the face and stealing money from her wallet.
Which brings us to… a classic business theory we've been thinking about recently: the innovator's dilemma.
The late Harvard Business School professor Clayton Christensen developed the theory in his 1997 book, The Innovator's Dilemma: When New Technologies Cause Great Firms to Fail.
Christensen theorized that the very thing that makes a business wildly successful can lead to its downfall in the face of a "disruptive" technology. He helped put disruption in Silicon Valley's vocabulary, long before it became a cliché.
The core innovator's dilemma is basically this: embrace a disruptive technology, and risk the profits you're making today. But if you fail to embrace it and let others run with it, you may end up risking your company's health tomorrow.
Today in the Planet Money newsletter we ask: has Google been caught in the innovator's dilemma? And can it pivot to a new technological era without sacrificing its enormous profits?
Did Google squander its AI head start?
Google didn't just invent the transformer. Over the decades, its researchers made computers translate languages, recognize speech and images, drive cars autonomously, and even beat one of the world's best players at the game Go.
The company even developed an internal chatbot called Meena that employees played with years before AI chatbots became a sensation.
But they didn't release it.
Then, on Nov. 30, 2022, OpenAI released ChatGPT and offered a completely new way to find information and a glimpse of a future where people didn't need to go to Google to find answers anymore.
Google scrambled to respond, reportedly declaring a "code red" as ChatGPT captivated the masses.
So, first question, why wasn't Google the first out of the gate with something like ChatGPT?
Christensen's theory offers one possible explanation: When you're making tons of money from your existing business in search, why rush to release something that could undermine it? Why disrupt yourself?
His theory wasn't just that companies seek to protect their cash cow. It was that a company can get too focused on the best way to nurture and milk that cash cow. Like, dang, I love this cow. Then when a disruptive technology comes along, they might be like, wait, this won't help me milk my beautiful cow. No thanks.
In other words, a company's focus on its core business can lead it to not see a disruptive technology's market potential. It can create a kind of myopia.
Last year, Google's chief scientist, Jeff Dean, offered an explanation for why Google hadn't released something like ChatGPT sooner— and it suggested the company had fallen victim to the kind of myopia Christensen warned about. Dean told podcaster Dwarkesh Patel that they looked at their existing chatbots through the lens of their search business. You know, their cow.
"From a search perspective, you want to get the right answer 100% of the time," Dean said. "These models were not near that bar." They were prone to hallucinating and also saying offensive things.
Those were problems ChatGPT had as well. It made tons of mistakes and said racist, sexist, and other incendiary things that made headlines. Yet it took off like a rocket ship when they released it.
And it turned out that people didn't just use ChatGPT as a way to find information or get answers. Dean acknowledged that Google had underestimated how useful chatbots could be for things people wouldn't necessarily turn to a search engine for, like drafting a note or summarizing text.
Christensen warned about this very trap in The Innovator's Dilemma. Companies that keep disruptive technologies "bottled up in their labs," he wrote, risk losing out to rivals willing to run with them, however imperfect they may be.
Mayer, however, questions whether releasing a chatbot first would have gone as well for Google as it did for OpenAI. "The standards for an established company like Google in terms of what users expect, in terms of quality, how good the search is, how great the product is fundamentally different than for an upstart or a newcomer," Mayer says.
We don't know what would have happened if Google had released a chatbot first. Would a Google chatbot have taken off in the same way, giving Google a first-mover advantage? Or would its flaws have created big headaches for a company with an established reputation to protect?
Whatever explains Google's initial hesitation, it's now going all in. It's fought back with its own chatbot, now called Gemini, and by putting AI-generated answers directly onto its search page, even at the risk of undermining the advertising business that made it rich.
The question now is whether all this will leave Google as dominant — and as profitable — in the AI age as it was in the age of old-school web search.
Goodbye, Monopoly?
Benedict Evans is a widely read technology analyst who was previously a partner at the Silicon Valley venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz.
He says that every 10 or 15 years or so, a revolutionary "platform shift" shakes up the tech industry, giving newcomers a chance to challenge dominant companies. It happened with the rise of personal computers, then the internet, then smartphones. Now, he says, it's happening with AI.
"The whole table gets reset and the things that meant that they had won and you couldn't take them on suddenly don't matter anymore," Evans says.
For Google, the consumer pivot to AI could mean it loses some of the competitive advantages that helped it monopolize search.
The process toward monopolization began with Google building a better search engine than rivals. Then, Evans says, its success became self-reinforcing: more users gave Google more data to improve its results, helping it attract still more users. Economists call this a "network effect," a kind of positive feedback loop that helped Google cement its dominance.
Of course, Google also actively worked to catch and keep customers as well. It, for instance, paid to make its search engine the default in browsers and on devices — deals that a federal judge ruled in 2024 had illegally helped maintain its search monopoly.
Google also cemented its dominance by weaving itself into our lives. It runs the operating system on many of our phones. We use free Google services to send emails, write documents, find directions, and watch a stranger explain how to fix our washing machine. Many of us keep going back to Google search out of sheer habit or because, when we're navigating the Google digital complex, we keep getting nudged to go there.
But a platform shift could loosen Google's grip on us. Why go to Google dotcom to search for information if you're using an AI system made by a rival that can answer your question well enough? And, maybe, those rival AI systems will borrow from Google's playbook and work to intertwine themselves into our lives.
It's still early days in this rapidly transforming market. One big question, Evans says, is whether AI models will develop winner-take-all dynamics like those that helped Google dominate search. So far, it seems like the frontier labs keep catching up with each other. One possibility, he says, is that AI could become increasingly capable of improving itself — what those in the biz call "recursive self-improvement" — allowing whichever company gets there first to build a lead that rivals struggle to overcome. But whether the AI race will end with a dominant leader — and whether Google will be the one that emerges victorious — is still a huge question.
Mayer doesn't expect a single winner. Yes, the mammoth cost of the computing power and energy needed to develop and run frontier models creates a barrier to entry, making it hard for smaller companies to compete. But she believes there's room for several giants. "There will be multiple big players," she says. "I don't think there will be just one."
Google has a really good shot at remaining one of the big players, but it could lose the dominance it has enjoyed in search. As Evans puts it, "Google's share of search has really got only one way to go."
But losing market share doesn't necessarily mean making less money, Mayer argues. She expects AI to attract more people looking for answers and draw more advertising dollars into the market. Sure, she says, Google's share could get smaller, but the pie could get bigger.
Evans points to Microsoft as an example of how a company can lose dominance after a technological disruption but still keep growing. When high-speed internet took the world by storm, it opened up new ways for rivals to compete with Microsoft in software. Companies like, yes, Google developed products like Docs and Sheets that people could use in a web browser, whether or not they were running Windows. Controlling the dominant operating system no longer gave Microsoft the same advantages in the internet era.
But the internet also gave more people a reason to buy computers — and many bought PCs that ran Windows. Microsoft sold more copies of Windows and Office, and its business kept growing because of this and other reasons.
"Well, go look at Microsoft," he says. "Microsoft lost, but at the same time, the market became so much bigger" that "the shareholders got a lot more money."
That said, Microsoft shareholders needed some patience. Its stock price didn't surpass its dotcom-era peak until nearly 17 years later.
Can AI pay Google's mounting bills?
Beyond just the threat to Google's monopoly in search, AI is also challenging the advertising model that made search so lucrative.
Google's historic stock plunge in late October suggested that investors are concerned about this.
On the company's earnings call, executives acknowledged that the growing use of "AI Mode," its chatbot-style search feature, was contributing to slower growth of search advertising revenue because it earned less per query than traditional search. Meanwhile, Alphabet said it expects to spend a whopping $200 billion this year alone on infrastructure, including data centers, largely to support its AI push.
Watching Google's stock price plummet that day, it felt like seeing Google struggle with the innovator's dilemma in real time. Like it was willing to risk cannibalizing its core business to feed its ambitions in the AI age, accepting short-term pain in the hope of long-term gain.
Sundar Pichai, the CEO of Google and its parent company Alphabet, has made clear he believes embracing innovation is the only way forward. He was actually asked about the innovator's dilemma on the All-In podcast last year. "I think the dilemma only exists if you treat it as a dilemma," Pichai said. "All along in technology you have these massive periods of innovation and you lean into it as hard as you can. It's the only way to do it."
Mayer is optimistic about Pichai's aggressive approach and Google's position in this new technological era. Google helped pioneer this technology, she says, and using it to answer people's questions draws on what has been its core expertise. She even questions whether there is really any dilemma for Google when it comes to using AI to give consumers better answers.
"They actually aren't doing something new by deploying it," Mayer says. "They're just answering questions differently and arguably better."
She does, however, acknowledge there is a dilemma when it comes to advertisers, who pay most of the company's bills. Google may need to fundamentally revamp its system of clickable ads it has spent decades showing alongside search results.
" So I think that piece of it is hard," Mayer says. "How do I take that advertising spend and move it to a new format that keeps my customers, my advertising customers, as happy?"
But advertisers will follow users, she argues, and AI could provide the basis for an even more lucrative business.
"I don't see why it can't be as profitable," she says. "In fact, I think it probably, in the end, will be more lucrative than it has been in the past."
Who knows what advertising will look like as the AI era advances. Maybe we'll see familiar-looking banner ads or clickable links on chatbot screens. Or maybe we'll be confiding in an AI assistant with a disembodied voice, like Scarlett Johansson in Her, sharing our most intimate thoughts, only to hear a word from our sponsor. Awkward.
Mayer sees other possibilities. Her startup, Dazzle, uses AI to analyze people's photographs. Those photos can help the system learn about you — which brands you like, what products you own, and what you might want to buy next. You can also snap a photo of something you like and ask where to buy it.
"If we can identify the product and send you there," she says, "there's an opportunity for advertisements or lead generation."
The more people share with AI systems, the more those systems learn about them, creating valuable personalized data that could be used to microtarget ads or nudge people to buy things.
For Google, the question is whether AI's new ways of connecting people to products can replace — or exceed — the profits of its existing advertising business.
In a statement to Planet Money, Google said its AI features are already leading to more searches on its platform. "This past quarter, Search queries grew at their fastest year-over-year rate in five years," the company said. It says they're taking a "deliberate approach" to developing ad revenue in this new technological era: "building the best user experience first and then scaling monetization."
Beyond Search
But the AI race is about much more than just building systems that can help people find information and make money from ads along the way. Investors are dreaming of AI models that can do things that once sounded like science fiction, including automating vast amounts of knowledge work. They're betting revolutionary applications will give rise to incredibly profitable businesses.
Evans believes the most exciting market opportunities will be found in entirely new uses for AI — some we haven't even dreamed up yet.
What will those applications be? How profitable will they become? Will they justify the mind-blowing investments Google and other companies are making in this technological revolution?
Evans says the uncertainty around fundamental questions like these helps explain stock market volatility. Investors don't know how much money these companies will ultimately earn — or how long they'll have to wait. And even if AI creates enormous wealth, he says, it's far from clear who will capture it.
One risk Evans sees is that competing AI models become so similar in their capabilities that their developers struggle to charge much for them. The most lucrative businesses could be the products and services other companies build using those models.
He points to cellphone service providers as a cautionary tale. They spent billions to build out the network infrastructure for the mobile internet, allowing people to watch videos, order taxis, and much more on their cellphones.
"All the stuff that they were talking about happened," Evans says, "but it happened 10 years later."
And when that future finally arrived, the service providers weren't the big winners from all that spending. Ouch! Yes, they owned the infrastructure, but it was the companies making smartphones and building apps and services on top of that infrastructure that captured the biggest rewards of the mobile revolution.
Evans suggests that the same risk hangs over the companies building today's AI models. "The point is just because it's amazing and cool and exciting and it's going to change the world doesn't mean that you have value capture or pricing power." In other words, AI could change the world without sending these companies' profits — or stock prices — soaring.
Of course, the fate that befell the cellphone service providers is just one possible scenario. Evans says the AI industry could develop like advanced chip manufacturing, where the rising cost and complexity of making chips left fewer and fewer companies able to compete. Or, he says, it could look like cloud computing, where several big companies make good money supplying the infrastructure that other businesses run on.
Google has a good shot at thriving under more than one of those scenarios. Its empire spans search, AI chatbots and assistants, YouTube, cloud computing, and even driverless cars through Waymo.
Google can make money both from supplying AI infrastructure and building products and services with AI, Evans says. On one side, Google already sells access to its own AI models and supplies computing power to other companies, including Anthropic. Google is also a major investor in Anthropic, and has a stake that could become even more valuable when that company goes public.
But if the business of building and running frontier AI models turns out to be less profitable than so many investors hope, Google could still make money using the technology in its own products. It also has the money and in-house expertise to compete for entirely new AI businesses.
The question is whether it can make enough money from all this to make its huge investments worthwhile — and make up for whatever it might lose in search.
Google helped invent the technology behind this revolution. Now it's betting a fortune that AI can deliver a whole new herd of cash cows — without killing the one that made it rich.

title: Professional misconduct complaints against DOJ officials are rising
text:
The number of professional misconduct complaints filed against Justice Department officials has increased by more than 50% over a two-year period, which could strain DOJ's already limited resources to investigate the claims, the agency's internal watchdog said Tuesday.
In a new report, Justice Department Inspector General Don Berthiaume said that ensuring the fairness and integrity of the department's investigations and prosecutions is among the top six management challenges for senior leadership.
"The lawful and effective exercise of these authorities is indispensable to public safety and the rule of law. It also creates a corresponding management responsibility to ensure that Department investigations and prosecutions are conducted with integrity, objectivity, consistency, and fairness," he wrote in his report.
His report cited new statistics from the Office of Professional Responsibility, which is tasked with investigating attorney misconduct. During the 2026 fiscal year, which ended on Oct. 1, the office, which operates with a full-time staff of just 18 people, received 2,081 professional misconduct complaints.
By contrast, it received 1,666 in the same time frame in 2025. In fiscal year 2024, there were 1,346 complaints and 1,085 in the same time frame in 2023 — "an increase of approximately 54 percent in 2 years," the report says.
In the last fiscal year, the Office of Professional Responsibility opened 33 professional-misconduct inquiries and closed 35, and it completed nine out of 10 full investigations opened that same year.
In those nine cases, OPR determined there had been professional misconduct by attorneys, the report said.
During that same time period, OPR also received 50 new FBI whistleblower retaliation complaints and closed 41 matters.
"These results demonstrate that OPR has continued to resolve substantial workloads despite its limited size," the inspector general wrote. "However, the Department faces risk in its oversight capacity if OPR's staffing levels are insufficient to manage the workload generated by the Department's thousands of employees."
The uptick in professional misconduct allegations comes at a time when the Justice Department has faced intense scrutiny over investigations it has pursued against President Trump's political enemies, including some that Mr. Trump openly encouraged. The report does not describe the complaints, so it is not known if any of them stem from these investigations.
Former for example, has faced at least three separate criminal probes since last year.
Although an indictment accusing him of lying to Congress was dismissed, he is still facing charges in North Carolina over an Instagram post showing arranged to read "86 47" — a message that prosecutors allege was intended as a threat against Mr. Trump.
Most recently, prosecutors filed a in order to pause the statute of limitations while they try to secure an indictment against him for allegedly leaking classified information.
Comey has denied wrongdoing in all three cases.
Earlier this year, a federal judge in the Middle District of Tennessee ruled that the Justice Department's prosecution of was vindictive, citing in part extrajudicial statements that now-Attorney General Todd Blanche had made about the case.
Others who have been targeted with criminal investigations or prosecutions include Democratic election lawyer , Federal Reserve Board Governor , former Federal Reserve Chairman Jerome Powell, Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar, New York Attorney General Letitia James, Democratic Sen. Adam Schiff, several former FBI counterintelligence officials, former CNN anchor Don Lemon, and the Southern Poverty Law Center, a progressive civil rights nonprofit that has been critical of the Trump administration.
Although the department's inspector general has broad authority to investigate waste, fraud and abuse, it is more limited when it comes to allegations of misconduct involving DOJ lawyers.
That role typically falls to OPR, which is a smaller office that has less independence than the inspector general. Last year, the head of OPR was removed by senior Justice Department leadership.
Recently, the inspector general to open an investigation into the prosecutors who falsely accused Olympian David Hearn of vandalizing the Reflecting Pool, saying that the matter fell squarely in OPR's jurisdiction.
The Justice Department, in responding to the inspector general's report, said that it "emphasizes integrity, fairness, and accountability in its investigative and prosecutorial work, with the Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR) serving as a central guardian of ethical standards."
"Despite resource constraints, OPR fulfilled its mission through disciplined case management, dedicated staff, and effective use of technology," the department said.

title: Platform for digital tools used by major companies reports 'security incident'
text:
Optimizely reports 'security incident' that involved malware in customers' digital products
Some Optimizely customers said they are aware of the reported incident.
Optimizely, a platform for digital tools used by Zoom and a host of other companies, said it has experienced a "security incident" that planted malware in at least some of its clients' digital infrastructure.
"Optimizely identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability," the company said, noting the intruder had used the vulnerability to "add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects."
Some Optimizely customers, including Zoom, issued statements on Tuesday saying they are aware of the reported incident.
"As a precautionary measure, Zoom has disabled Optimizely across our production environments. At this time, we have not identified any impact to customer data. We continue to monitor the situation closely," the videoconferencing company said.
In a statement to ABC News, furniture giant IKEA said: “We are aware of reports concerning a security issue involving a third-party website service provider that may have affected a number of organisations, including IKEA."
"We are investigating the matter to understand any potential impact on our digital services and customers. Protecting customer information and maintaining the security of our services remain a top priority," the statement added.
In its latest update, Optimizely said: "For the US region, recommendations continue to be served, and they are being refreshed with the latest data, so quality should return to normal over the course of today."
This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

title: Guinea jails 200 in wildcat gold mining crackdown
text:
Guinea on Tuesday jailed 22 former regional administrators and 202 others accused of illegal gold mining in the northeastern Siguiri region near the border to Mali.
According to the UN Environment Program, unauthorized gold mining is a source of income for more than 300,000 people in Guinea. The country's rich gold mines pull in workers from across West Africa.
What happened in the gold mining trial in Conakry?
Conakry's Court for the Repression of Economic and Financial Offenses sentenced 22 former officials from Siguiri to two years each in prison for complicity in environmental degradation, destruction and water pollution. They were each fined 10 million Guinean francs (around €1,025 or $1,125).
The court also sentenced 202 alleged illegal miners — several of them foreign nationals — to three-year prison sentences. They faced the same charges plus an additional count of mining illegally.
They were ordered to pay a combined fine of 10 billion Guinean francs.
Beyond that, the foreign nationals were banned from Guinean territory for a period of 10 years.
Why is Guinea cracking down on illegal mining?
Guinea's government announced a bid to stamp out illegal gold mining earlier this month, saying it wanted to prevent damages to farmland and rivers and other environmental destruction.
These efforts turned violent last week as protesters and security forces clashed in the northeast, with 10 people killed and 13 injured.
More than 1,200 artisanal miners were arrested in Siguiri in November.
Many more fled across the border to nearby Mali, often then having to await transportation to their homes in Burkina Faso.

title: Northern Ireland earn remarkable promotion to Nations League top tier
text:
Justin Devenny’s superb strike saw Northern Ireland earn promotion to the top flight of the Nations League with a hard-fought 1-1 draw away to closest challengers Hungary in Budapest.
Barnabas Varga ended Northern Ireland’s proud record of not having conceded in this campaign when he fired the hosts in front after 35 minutes – a goal that also sent Hungary to the top of the group.
But moments after Isaac Price had hit the post for Michael O’Neill’s young side, Devenny smashed the ball into the top left-hand corner in the 65th minute to restore Northern Ireland’s one-point advantage as group leaders.
The visitors were on the back foot for much of the first half, with Hungary captain Dominik Szoboszlai hitting the post, but Michael O’Neill, serving a touchline ban in the stands as former captain Steven Davis led things from the touchline, orchestrated key substitutions.
Northern Ireland started with Patrick Kelly in place of the suspended Jamie Donley up front but brought on Josh Magennis at half-time before Kieran Morrison and Brodie Spencer soon followed to help the visitors become a much greater threat going forward.
Magennis’ physical presence and the extra pace paid dividends as, just two years after earning promotion from League C, Northern Ireland completed an unbeaten campaign in Group B2 to secure their place at the top table of European football.
Without Donley, the lack of a clear outlet told in a first half which saw Hungary come forward time and again.
There was a big panic five minutes in following an uncharacteristic mistake from Pierce Charles, whose pass went straight to Bendeguez Bolla, a late change to the Hungary side who whipped in a superb low cross from which skipper Szoboszlai struck the post.
Northern Ireland were pegged back but might have snatched the lead from a Ciaron Brown long throw in the 33rd minute. However Tom Atcheson did not seem to realise how much space he had as he prodded a weak shot towards his Blackburn team-mate Balazs Toth.
Two minutes later Pierce Charles launched a long free-kick into the box. Brown went down under an Andras Schafer challenge but as Northern Ireland appealed in vain for a penalty, Toth kicked it long. Trai Hume got his head to the ball but could not get it as far as Pierce Charles, allowing Varga to nip in and score.
O’Neill will have felt the frustration of his ban with his side trailing at half-time, but his changes worked regardless.
Terry Devlin, the matchwinner on Saturday, had already fired into the side-netting before Price’s low strike from the edge of the box cannoned back off the post.
Four minutes later they were level. Hume’s long throw almost fell for Shea Charles but instead sat up for Devenny to take a touch before thumping an unstoppable strike into the top corner.
As time ticked down, Hungary pushed forward in increasing desperation – with Rajmund Toth firing over late on – but Northern Ireland dug in with the defensive resilience which has been the cornerstone of this campaign.

title: 19 people rescued after gas carrier 'struck' in Black Sea
text:
It marks the latest in a string of similar incidents in the Black Sea believed to be linked to Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
All 19 crew members were rescued after a gas carrier was "struck" in the Black Sea off Bulgaria on Tuesday, authorities and the ship's management company said.
Stealth Maritime, the Greek management company, confirmed in a statement that the Gas Husky had been "struck" early on Tuesday morning as it was sailing within Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone.
It did not clarify what had hit the Liberian-flagged carrier.
"The vessel was carrying a cargo of LPG loaded in Alexandria, Egypt, and was heading to Midia, Romania, for discharge," it said, adding that the ship's condition was currently unknown.
According to Bulgaria's ministry of transport, the vessel was carrying 3,400 tonnes of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) before it disappeared from radar shortly after midnight. It then sent a distress signal at around 8:02 am, around 50 nautical miles east of Byala.
"Upon receiving the distress signal, assistance was requested from the air force to conduct an aerial survey of the area. During the survey, an overturned vessel was identified, believed to be the Gas Husky vessel," the ministry said in a statement. "About 300 metres away, a life raft was spotted, from which a distress flare was launched."
The crew were rescued from the life raft and flown by helicopter to the Chaika air base in Varna, it added.
On Monday, 12 people were rescued after the Somali-flagged Betul 8 cargo ship capsized off the coast of Bulgaria following a suspected drone strike.
The Betul 8 had been travelling from Tulcea in Romania to Egypt and was carrying almost 3,000 tonnes of bulk wheat, authorities said.
The European Union has pledged €50 million for a Black Sea Maritime Security Hub hosted by Bulgaria and Romania to help combat security threats in the region.
The bloc has also committed a further €10 million in funds to help bolster Bulgaria's search and rescue operations.

title: UTEP Fires Scotty Walden: Miners Move On From Head Coach After Wyoming Loss
text:
UTEP has fired third-year coach Scotty Walden with the Miners on an eight-game losing streak.
The school announced the move Monday, a day after Walden's 37th birthday. UTEP lost 27-15 to Wyoming in its home finale on Saturday.
Walden finished 6-28 with the Miners, who are 1-9 this season in their Mountain West Conference debut. They were 2-10 last year after going 3-9 in his debut with them.
"His tenure has been marked by unprecedented success in recruiting and record-breaking team academic performance. He has excelled at community relations and fundraising, and has put his own money back into the program," athletic director Jim Senter said. "We haven’t seen the necessary improvement from year one to year three and believe it’s time for new leadership."
The Miners have only one winning season in the past 12 years, a 7-6 record in 2021. They have to win their final two games this season to avoid losing at least 10 games for the 22nd time since 1973.
UTEP didn't immediately name an interim head coach for the rest of this season. The final two games are on the road, against Air Force on Friday and at Northern Illinois on Nov. 28.
After a 51-0 loss at then-No. 10 Oklahoma to open this year, the Miners beat FCS team Texas Southern 51-10. They haven't won since and scored only 91 points in their eight-game losing streak, with their most points in that stretch coming in a 52-17 loss at then-No. 19 Michigan.
Walden arrived at UTEP from Austin Peay, where he was 26-14 in a tenure that started with the spring season in early 2021 after the COVID-19 pandemic shortened the 2020 season. The Governors were 9-3 in his final season and made the FCS playoffs.
He had replaced Dana Dimel, who had five losing seasons in his six years with the Miners.
Walden was the interim replacement for Jay Hopson at Southern Miss one game into that pandemic-altered 2020 season. He resigned after four games to take the Austin Peay job and prepare for the unusual spring season.
His head coaching career started in 2016 at Division III East Texas Baptist, where he was the offensive coordinator for three years before getting promoted.
Reporting by the Associated Press.

title: FAA stops installation of routers it linked to national ground stop
text: — Published on Nov 17, 2026 2:22 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — The Federal Aviation Administration has paused installing routers linked to last week's ground stop that caused chaos for travelers, the agency said Tuesday. The move comes amid growing scrutiny over the nation's air traffic control system and as the Trump administration is making a new request for $50 billion to improve air travel. Democrats in the Senate are demanding that the administration provide clear answers about what went wrong. President Donald Trump has blamed old technology and Democrats for the nationwide grounding of all planes and upheaval at the nation's airports. But the FAA has been struggling to modernize the air traffic control system for decades — going back well before the first Trump administration. FAA spokesperson Ian Gregor said the agency paused new installations of Juniper routers and disabled the functionality of all existing ones on Friday after technicians linked the problems to a new router in El Dorado, Arkansas. The FAA has said that another router installed three weeks earlier in Amarillo, Texas, also went haywire. The system became overloaded when the federal contractor that maintains the FAA's telecommunications network was replacing outdated copper wires with fiber optic lines across the nation. The ground stop was needed, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said, after the new router that L3Harris installed in Arkansas resulted in a cascade of intermittent communications and radar signals at 17 of the 22 regional air traffic control centers. The centers direct planes cruising at high altitudes. The FAA said that "excessive data" was flooding the system "at a rate of 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds." That deluge created instability with "aircraft communications and radar feeds," the agency said. For now, the FAA is relying on older Cisco routers that have been in place for 25 years to continue operating the network while they investigate the cause of Friday's trouble. READ MORE: Debunking social media posts that claim a 90-day blackout will start Nov. 17 The routers that malfunctioned last week are being tested in a lab at the headquarters of L3Harris. A spokesperson for Hewlett Packard Enterprise, which owns Juniper, told ABC News that the company believes the routers were working properly when the ground stop occurred. The company did not immediately respond to inquiries from The Associated Press. "Based on what we know today, the device functioned as it was configured to by the installer. It did not fail or act improperly," the company said in its statement. Democrats on the Senate Commerce Committee said they believe that only 400 out of more than 3,600 new routers have been installed. "Identifying the device that failed does not establish why it failed. FAA must investigate further to determine the root cause and report to Congress on how it intends to prevent future issues," the Democrats said in a letter sent to Duffy. Upgrading the nation's air transportation system is an effort that Congress has dedicated significant sums to in recent years. The problems with aging equipment at the FAA date back decades and past efforts to modernize the system have come up short. Duffy has pushed Congress for billions more dollars to upgrade a system he said had been neglected for decades, saying again Monday that much more is needed. The Trump administration on Tuesday sent a letter to key lawmakers outlining its request for $50.1 billion to modernize the system and make other improvements at airports. The request calls for $10.1 billion for updating the nation's air traffic control system. Similar amounts would go toward boosting airport infrastructure, replacing or refurbishing terminals at high-impact hubs, constructing five new traffic control centers and improving or replacing up to 140 FAA-owned air traffic control towers. "Congressional approval of these funds will equip the FAA to deliver to the American people a brand-new air traffic control system that is safer, smarter, faster, and more efficient," states the letter, which was obtained by The Associated Press. Congress approved $12.5 billion last year to modernize much of the key infrastructure that more than 45,000 flights a day rely on to reach their destinations safely. The funds were earmarked for replacing outdated technologies such as copper wires, floppy discs and radars built in the 1980s, but much of that money will also go toward runway upgrades and other construction projects.

title: Home Depot names Richard McPhail as new CEO, beats earnings expectations
text:
Home Depot on Tuesday announced its chief financial officer, Richard McPhail, will become CEO of the company, succeeding Ted Decker, effective next week.
Alongside McPhail's appointment, Home Depot said Ann-Marie Campbell, currently senior executive vice president of U.S. stores and operations, will become president and chief operating officer. Jordan Broggi has been chosen as CFO to succeed McPhail.
Decker, CEO since 2022, had been on temporary medical leave since August. The company said on Tuesday that Decker has returned from leave but is now stepping down from his role. He will continue to serve as chair of the board of directors, the company said.
"I'm glad to be back and grateful for the support I received," Decker told analysts on Tuesday. "The board and I have agreed that now is the right time to move to the next phase of our succession plan."
McPhail has been with the company since 2005, holding multiple executive roles.
"We're not going to change course," McPhail told CNBC's Becky Quick.
He said the company will continue to lean into winning professional shoppers like contractors and using artificial intelligence tools to encourage sales. McPhail added that while the company faces more challenges now than it did at the start of the year, it is still winning share of the home improvement market.
Home Depot has been pressured by a sluggish housing market, higher mortgage rates and a more cautious consumer. Still, the company has previously said it's seen resilience among its pro shoppers who are still shopping for their home improvement projects.
Shares of Home Depot sank more than 3% following the announcement and the retailer's fiscal third-quarter results.
The CEO change came as the home improvement retailer posted quarterly earnings and revenue that beat analysts' expectations. The company said comparable sales rose 2.2% during the period, compared with estimates of up 1.8%, according to StreetAccount.
Here's how Home Depot performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
- Earnings per share: $3.86 adjusted vs. $3.84 expected
- Revenue: $43.4 billion vs. $42.80 billion expected
The company reported net income of $3.71 billion, or $3.72 per share, compared with $3.60 billion, or $3.62 per share, the year prior. Excluding one-time items, Home Depot reported adjusted earnings per share of $3.86.
Revenue rose 4.9% compared with the year-ago period.
"We also are confident that we are taking material share from the market and from competition," McPhail said on the call with analysts.
In the third quarter, the company said online comparable sales grew around 13%, which marked its sixth straight quarter of double-digit positive growth for the metric.
The company said it saw positive comparable sales numbers in 13 out of 16 of its merchandising departments, including notable strength in the power department, which posted double-digit percentage growth.
