For the full year, Home Depot said it expects total sales to rise roughly 4.5%, the top end of its previously provided range. It also anticipates comparable sales will grow around 1.4%, compared with an outlook of flat to a 2% increase.
Home Depot added it expects adjusted earnings per share to rise 2% this year, compared with prior guidance of flat to a 4% increase.

title: Proton’s Lumo, a privacy-focused alternative to ChatGPT and Claude, arrives on desktop
text:
Proton, the privacy-focused tech company offering alternatives to Google’s and Microsoft’s tools for email, productivity apps, password management, cloud storage, and more, is now bringing its AI app Lumo to personal computers. On Tuesday, the company launched Lumo Desktop for Windows, macOS, and Linux, allowing users to leverage its AI to carry out local tasks on their computer involving connected apps, personal files, and other automations.
The app is designed to offer users more control over their personal data, as consumer AI technology becomes focused more on AI agents that can perform tasks on users’ behalf, rather than just answering questions.
Already, the major model makers, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and others, offer desktop tools for working with their AI technologies, but doing so invites increased risk to users’ personal data. Only this week, for instance, Apple announced it was addressing those privacy concerns with tightened security settings for apps that request Full Disk Access, as the AI desktop apps do.
Proton’s idea is to offer a set of tools that let its AI access connected apps, files, and folders and automate tasks, but with more personalization over how much access the AI has. The company says users can choose which actions the AI agent takes that will need to request their approval, and it vows that the conversations and information from connected apps and files are never used to serve personalized ads or train AI models.
The new app includes a variety of connectors that support local tools, like file-system access, shell execution, and browser content fetching, as well as Proton’s email app and other third-party services, including Confluence, Dropbox, and Jira.
The connectors also support local and remote MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers, which AI agents use to access external data sources.
Proton says that users can decide for each connector which actions Lumo can perform automatically, which require approval, and which are blocked entirely. Users can also turn individual tools off from the Tools menu in their conversation.
In addition, users can set up their own scheduled tasks, where each has its own set of permissions, in terms of what can be handled automatically and what requires approval.
Proton notes that it uses encryption to ensure that only users can read their chat history, not the company. The company also says it keeps no server-side logs, and the limited data it does store is protected under Swiss privacy law. The data is hosted on European infrastructure, outside the scope of the U.S. CLOUD Act, which specifies how law enforcement agencies access data held by cloud service providers.
The company says it’s investing in its infrastructure, with its first Nvidia B300 cluster built on Open Compute Project (OCP) standards now going live in Switzerland.
Similar to other AI apps, Lumo’s desktop app supports Skills, which lets users save instructions, templates, and reference files that Lumo can reuse across their conversations. (An earlier version of this, Custom Lumos, will now be migrated to the Skills format.)

title: Artist brings old Space Shuttle tank back to life
text:
Natalie Rosen is not the type of specialist you immediately associate with being one of the key people behind the new exhibit of the space shuttle Endeavour.
She is not a former NASA technician or engineer, as many of her colleagues have been for the past several years, nor is she a curator or conservator. Before this job, she had no experience working on any aircraft or spacecraft, as the new Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center, an extension of the California Science Center, opened in Los Angeles on November 13.
Without her expertise and artistry, however, the largest component of Endeavour‘s “stack” would look nothing like it did when the shuttle was flying.
“My background is in the fine arts. I have my bachelor’s and my master’s in fine arts from Cal State Long Beach,” Rosen told collectSPACE.com. “When I came in on this project, they were looking for a sculptor, and I had been sculpting.”
Rosen had been working with mixed media for her thesis project and had experience sculpting foam. As it happened, the California Science Center had a lot of foam that needed shaping.
ET-94
For those unfamiliar, the space shuttle was assembled from three primary launch components. The orbiter and its solid rocket boosters were reusable, given the time needed to inspect, service, and, in the case of the solid-fuel motors, refurbish and refill between flights.
The 154-foot-tall (47-meter) external tank was the only major part of the stack that was disposed of with each launch. After providing propellant for the orbiter’s three main engines, the tank was jettisoned and disintegrated while reentering the atmosphere.
To protect the orbiter from the extreme cold of the cryogenic liquid oxygen and liquid hydrogen in the external tank and to keep the propellant and oxidizer from boiling off too quickly, the ET was covered in insulating foam. (Some of that foam became liberated during ascent and was what caused the loss of the space shuttle Columbia and its crew in 2003.)

title: Vitamin B12 may hold the key to treating a rare genetic disorder
text:
Scientists discovered that vitamin B12 largely reversed developmental abnormalities in worms carrying a genetic mutation linked to Verheij syndrome, a rare disorder that causes growth problems and developmental delays. Similar metabolic changes were identified in human patients, raising the possibility that this common vitamin could inspire new treatments for rare genetic diseases.
A surprising discovery involving vitamin B12 could open new possibilities for understanding and potentially treating rare genetic disorders. Researchers found that the vitamin can correct developmental problems in tiny worms carrying a genetic mutation associated with Verheij syndrome, a rare human condition that causes developmental delays, impaired growth, and short stature.
The findings center on a cellular process called RNA splicing, which helps prepare the genetic instructions cells use to produce proteins. During splicing, unnecessary portions of messenger RNA are removed, and the remaining sections are joined together in the correct order. When this process goes wrong, it can disrupt essential cellular functions and contribute to serious developmental disorders.
Mutations in genes responsible for splicing can cause conditions such as Verheij syndrome. To better understand the effects of these genetic changes, scientists investigated how a related mutation affects growth and metabolism in a laboratory model.
Vitamin B12 Reverses Developmental Defects in Worms
The discovery emerged from experiments involving C. elegans, a tiny roundworm commonly used in biological research. The researchers were initially searching for previously unknown genes that influence lifespan when they began examining a mutation in a gene involved in RNA splicing. The same gene is associated with Verheij syndrome in humans.
Worms carrying the mutation developed problems resembling important features of the human disorder. Their growth slowed considerably, and they remained smaller than normal.
To investigate why this happened, the scientists conducted genetic screens and analyzed the worms' metabolism. They discovered that the mutation disrupted specific metabolic pathways that depend on vitamin B12 and are essential for healthy growth and normal cellular activity.
The researchers then tested whether providing additional vitamin B12 could counteract these changes. Remarkably, the treatment restored the affected metabolic processes to normal and corrected the developmental abnormalities associated with the mutation.
"We were surprised to find that a change in a fundamental process of RNA processing had such a targeted effect on vitamin B12-dependent metabolism," says Jonathan Kölschbach, first author of the study. "Even more exciting was that we were able to largely correct the consequences of this change in the worm model using vitamin B12."
Could Vitamin B12 Help Treat a Rare Genetic Disorder?
To explore whether their findings might also apply to people, the researchers examined publicly available datasets from human cells. They also worked with Hormos Dafsari, a neuropediatrician at the University Hospital Cologne, to collect blood samples from patients diagnosed with Verheij syndrome.
These investigations uncovered evidence of similar metabolic changes in humans, suggesting that the vitamin B12-related pathways affected in the worms may also play a role in the human disorder.
Although the results are promising, researchers have not yet established whether vitamin B12 supplementation can improve symptoms in people with Verheij syndrome. Additional studies will be necessary to determine whether the benefits observed in worms can be translated into a treatment for patients.
The discovery also raises a broader possibility. Metabolic disruptions may contribute more substantially to diseases caused by faulty RNA splicing than scientists previously recognized. Understanding these connections could help researchers identify new therapeutic strategies, potentially extending beyond Verheij syndrome to other rare genetic conditions.
"Our study is a good example of how basic research on model organisms can provide new insights into human diseases," says Adam Antebi, Director at the Max Planck Institute for Biology of Ageing and lead author of the study. "A fundamental biological question can thus give rise to a new approach that could also become medically relevant in the long term."

title: Light is hard to block from every direction. This physicist found a way
text:
This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback?

here .)
Physicist Stefano Martiniani has designed an entirely new class of materials that blurs the line between order and chaos. Called gyromorphs, these metamaterials rely on crystal-like geometric structure and liquidlike randomness to block light from penetrating at any angle.
Physicists thought, structurally speaking, that they could not create such hybrid materials. “But this is evidence that you can, under certain constraints,” says Martiniani, of New York University. He likens the gyromorphs’ disorderliness to a crowd of people. You could see through the crowd if individuals stood still in straight lines, but not if they are clustered together in random groups. But there’s order too: From anywhere you stand in a gyromorph crowd, you’ll see a ring of people at a given distance.
Gyromorphs are a type of metamaterial, a substance with a structure designed to give it properties not found in naturally occurring materials. Metamaterials can control light, sound or other waves, and are often used in smartphones, medical imaging and computers. Martiniani says gyromorphs could be used to make more energy-efficient optical computers, which use light to process and store data.
To design a gyromorph, Martiniani needed to find a way to achieve the perfect structural balance. He turned to FReSCo, a program his lab created that designs molecular structures to meet researchers’ specifications, for help. “We had an algorithm, we gave it an objective, and then it was able to solve that objective, finding a solution that we were not expecting,” he says. “That is the best kind of discovery.”

title: On this day in space! Nov. 16, 1974: The giant Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico broadcasts humanity's 1st interstellar message
text:
On Nov. 16, 1974, humans sent their first message to the stars in an attempt to contact extraterrestrials.
They did this using what was then the largest radio telescope in the world, located at the Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico. A group of scientists led by Frank Drake and Carl Sagan sent their message to the M13 star cluster. The message was written in binary code and contained information about human DNA.
It also included figures of a human, the solar system and the Arecibo telescope. The idea was that if any aliens were to receive the signal and figure out how to decode it, they would know where it came from. Because M13 is 25,000 light-years away, it will take 25,000 years for any M13 aliens to hear our message — if they are even out there.
Why it mattered
The Arecibo message is only one of several messages intended for extraterrestrials, but this signal sent from Puerto Rico in 1974 was humanity's first intentional olive branch to the stars. At the time, it was the most powerful broadcast ever beamed into space, according to the SETI Institute.
"The broadcast was particularly powerful because it used Arecibo's megawatt transmitter attached to its 305 meter antenna," SETI wrote of the broadcast in a project over. "The emission was equivalent to a 20 trillion watt omnidirectional broadcast, and would be detectable by a SETI experiment just about anywhere in the galaxy, assuming a receiving antenna similar in size to Arecibo's."
The message was designed by astronomy professor Frank Drake of Cornell University (who also developed the famed Drake Equation for alien life), as well as Cornnell graduate students Richard Isaacman and Linda May, and Arecibo staff member James Walker, with input from astronomer Carl Sagan and others, according to Cornell University.
The message included 1,679 bits that were arranged in 73 lines of 23 characters per line, all prime numbers, with the broadcast lasting less than 3 minutes, according to SETI.
As of 2026, the message should have traveled about 52 light-years (1 light-year is the distance light travels in a year), with 24,948 light-years to go before reaching star cluster M13.
The Arecibo message may have been the first message of its kind, but it wasn't the last. We have also included messages on several spacecraft, such as Pioneer and Voyager. NASA and Paul McCartney also beamed a performance of "Across the Universe" in 2008.
Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube.

title: NHS data contract to stay with Palantir until 2029
text:
The government says it will continue a key NHS data contract in England with the controversial US tech giant Palantir until 2029, rather than triggering an early release clause next year.
But ministers are inviting British firms to bid for the contract from 2029, with a procurement programme beginning next summer.
A Commons Committee had called on the government to part ways and appoint a company "more compatible with UK values". Protesters regularly target Palantir over Israel's use of its technology in the Gaza conflict and oppose its use in US immigration enforcement.
The £330m deal, which began in 2024 to help manage hospital waiting lists in England, was due to run until 2031.
'Albatross around the NHS's neck'
The prime minister had faced pressure from some Labour MPs to cut ties with Palantir. They said they were extremely disappointed by the decision, calling the contract "an albatross" hanging around the NHS's neck.
The Liberal Democrats said the deal was "dangerous".
There have also been concerns raised about how patient data will be used.
Palantir, which was co-founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, has interests in US defence and security, and has contracts with the Israeli military.
Health minister James Frith said the move was "not about the politics of executives of suppliers, nor is it about the territories or customers that one company or one supplier makes".
The government says UK companies will be encouraged to tender to avoid overdependence on one supplier.
The timeframe is not fast enough for some members of the government.
Dame Chi Onwurah, Labour MP for Newcastle upon Tyne Central and West, said the government needed to "act urgently" to procure "credible domestic alternatives".
"The government should not wait two years, it must start reducing this dependency now," she said.
Former Labour shadow chancellor John McDonnell went further, and accused Palantir of "human rights abuses". He said his constituents in Hayes and Harlington "expect the contract to be ended".
Liberal Democrat health spokeswoman Helen Morgan criticised the company for what she called its "appalling human rights record, run by an ally of Donald Trump".
The British Medical Association, which represents doctors, said it was glad the government had shown it was listening to its concerns about Palantir, but was frustrated the process of changing to another company was further delayed.
Palantir UK said it was right to press forward with the programme which was exceeding targets.
"We are proud of our work to date to help deliver more operations, speed up discharge and reduce the time patients need to wait to find out if they have cancer," Palantir UK senior vice-president Tom Watson said.

title: Anthropic IPO: how can I buy shares, and is it worth it?
text:
The company is a leader in artificial intelligence, and is best known for its chatbot Claude. The float, which is expected to value the business at $1.4tn (£1tn), comes at a volatile time for tech stocks, yet it has been reported that the shares could be six times oversubscribed.
When a company floats it issues a prospectus for would-be investors that details its activities and lays out the share offering, including an estimated price.
Anthropic’s prospectus explains that the shares on sale will be 825m of class A common stock, and that the initial public offering (IPO) price will between $70 and $78 a share. However, the final price will be set on Wednesday.
The shares will come with voting rights, but, if all the shares’ votes are combined they will only represent 49.9% of the total vote available, so will not allow buyers to be able to force any changes in the way the company is run.
How do I buy shares?
The shares will be listed on the Nasdaq in New York on Thursday, and will be available to individual investors alongside big institutions.
In the UK, several investment platforms are offering customers the chance to subscribe to shares, including AJ Bell, Hargreaves Lansdown, Robinhood and eToro. At Robinhood and eToro the minimum investment is $250 (£189), at Hargreaves Lansdown the minimum investment is £250, and at AJ Bell investors will need at least £1,000 to apply. AJ Bell is closing applications at 1pm on Wednesday, while Hargreaves Lansdown and Robinhood will close at 3pm. All say they could close the doors early without notice.
Once the IPO has happened and the shares have been listed they can be bought at any point, and through platforms that have not been involved in the IPO.
Once the IPO is over, the stock will ultimately find its way into some tracker funds – although some will be quicker than others – and managers of actively invested funds could also choose to buy shares. That means people might well end up investing in Anthropic even if they do not attempt to buy any shares directly.
Jason Hollands, the managing director of the investment platform Bestinvest by Evelyn Partners – which is not participating in the IPO – highlights some other things investors need to consider.
“Anthropic would give most retail investors the first opportunity to have a direct stake in a frontier AI developer. But it remains a capital-intensive business, and it has yet to establish a consistent path to profitability,” he says. “Investors will need to judge whether the company can turn demand for its models into durable earnings.”
Hollands says if demand for shares exceeds the limited supply, “that could support the price initially with a ‘pop’, but it does not guarantee a strong debut or lasting gains over the coming months”.
He adds the SpaceX listing in June “is a reminder that a hotly anticipated IPO and early enthusiasm can quickly be followed by volatility: its shares have traded below their IPO price at points since listing”.
What does Claude think?
When we asked Claude whether to buy shares in Anthropic it was upfront about why it is not a great source of investment advice: “I can’t tell you whether you should buy. I’m not a financial adviser, and I’m also made by Anthropic, so I have an obvious conflict of interest here.”
It went on to present a few facts about the IPO, and some useful questions that any investor should be considering before buying an individual share in an IPO. Can you cope with a loss if it goes down in value? How much of your portfolio will an investment in it represent? Will you already have exposure to the share through a tracker fund?

title: China, Canada expand tariff relief after Carney-Xi meeting
text:
Canada and China have agreed to cut tariffs on more goods, as Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney continues to look to decrease his country’s dependence on the United States amid President Donald Trump’s tariffs.
Meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen on Tuesday, Carney and Chinese President Xi Jinping announced new tariff remissions, building on an agreement they made in January to open up trade and start to repair a strained diplomatic relationship.
China will offer tariff relief on about 400 million Canadian dollars ($280m) worth of Canadian exports, including frozen pork and seafood, said a statement from Carney’s office.
Canada, in exchange, will keep tariff exemptions for certain Chinese steel and aluminium products in place for another two years, and add remissions to another 32 steel and aluminium items that Canada doesn’t have enough of.
Xi said stronger ties served both countries’ interests and supported global stability and prosperity.
“This is the right choice,” he said.
Carney praised the greater predictability in the relationship and said Canada was ahead of schedule on its goal of increasing exports to China by 50 percent by the end of the decade.
Under the January agreement, Canada lowered its 100 percent tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1 percent, allowing an initial 49,000 vehicles into the country each year. That cap is set to rise to 70,000 over five years.
In return, China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products and recently extended relief for canola meal, peas, lobster and crab for another two years.
The deal comes a day after Carney said Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if talks with Washington fail to hold together the closely integrated North American auto industry.
“We have the best auto workers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market,” Carney told reporters in Cambodia on Monday. “That market has become less integrated because of US trade actions.”
The comments prompted a backlash from White House trade adviser Peter Navarro, who responded by asking whether Carney was threatening to “play China off the US”.
“This is offensive in the extreme,” he said, adding that Carney should be more worried that China would “eat Canada alive”.
Carney has made looking to markets beyond the US a central part of his economic strategy, as Trump’s tariffs hit Canadian industries, including auto manufacturing, as well as steel and aluminium.
Trade talks between Ottawa and Washington broke down in August, but Carney said on Saturday that he’d spoken with Trump and senior officials, and that while differences remained, there was progress towards a possible deal.
He also met with Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum on Tuesday, with both countries reaffirming their commitment to renew the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement, according to Carney’s office.
One year after Carney visited Mexico, during which they launched a strategic partnership, the two leaders agreed to keep expanding bilateral trade and investment. They also highlighted a 19-percent increase in merchandise trade in the first nine months of this year, compared with the same period last year.

title: Far from home, Voyager 1 will soon be a 'light-day' from Earth
text:
NASA's Voyager 1 has traveled farther than anything else that humans have launched into space. On Wednesday, it's set to reach a new milestone: reaching a distance that is one-light day away from Earth.
NASA is celebrating the occasion with the "Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day." Calling it a symbolic celebration, NASA is asking the public on Tuesday night to send Voyager's call sign V-G-R into the sky in morse code. Use a flashlight, phone light or anything that can blink a sequence.
If you want to take part:
V - Three quick flashes, one long flash
G - Two long flashes, one quick flash
R - One quick flash, one long flash, one quick flash
What exactly is a light-day?
A light-day is the distance light travels in 24 hours, or more than 16 billion miles.
This NASA spacecraft has traveled for nearly 50 years, launching Sept. 5, 1977.
Over the course of its mission, Voyager 1 has conducted flybys of Jupiter and Saturn. In 1979, it discovered a faint ring system on Jupiter. In 1980, the spacecraft took detailed photos of Saturn's rings and moons.
While on its journey, on Feb. 17, 1998, Voyager 1 overtook the U.S. space probe, Pioneer 10, becoming the most distant human-made object in existence. It and its twin, Voyager 2, are the only spacecraft to have operated outside of the heliosphere, which acts like a protective shield of the solar system.
Voyager 1 reached the interstellar boundary in 2012. Its interstellar mission continues to chart and measure the magnetic fields, particles and plasma waves outside the sun's heliosphere and the atmosphere of other stars.
Earlier this year, NASA elected to shut off Voyager 1's Low-energy Charged Particles experiment, or LECP, which has helped scientists map the structure of space, in order to save power. Scientists said this could keep the probe alive longer..
Voyager 1 has two science instruments still running: one that measures magnetic fields and another that listens for plasma waves.
In addition, the Voyager spacecraft is carrying the Golden Record – an interstellar "time capsule" to communicate Earth's story to extraterrestrials.
The gold-plated record contains 115 images, natural sounds such as surf, wind and animals, and spoken greetings in 35 different languages. Included are instructions, in symbols, on how to play the record and the origin of the probe.
Voyager 1 is estimated to reach "light-day status" at 5:16 a.m. ET on Wednesday, after 49 years, two months and 11 days of travel.

title: Thousands demonstrate in Haiti’s capital to praise Bukele and Salvadoran troops fighting gangs
text:
Thousands of people in Haiti's capital and beyond are praising El Salvador’s president, Nayib Bukele, and his troops for fighting gangs in the country
PORT-AU-PRINCE, Haiti -- Thousands of people poured into the streets of Haiti’s capital and beyond on Tuesday to praise El Salvador’s president, Nayib Bukele, and his troops as they fight gangs in the troubled Caribbean country.
Many in the crowd raised their fists and some clutched Haitian flags and signs in favor of Bukele.
“Bukele is here to free us!” some shouted.
“Give them the drones and the dogs!” others yelled in reference to the explosive drones that have targeted areas controlled by powerful gangs and the newly unveiled robot dogs making their rounds in Port-au-Prince.
Last month, Bukele deployed some 2,500 troops to Haiti after four of their own came under attack on Oct. 18 and remain missing. Fighting between gangs and foreign forces backed by Haitian authorities has only increased since then as Haiti remains mired in violence, with more than 20,000 people killed in the past five years.
While chants of “Bukele!” are spreading across Haiti, experts warn there’s no long-term plan to keep the country safe once the Central American troops pull out.
“This enthusiasm…could turn into anger against the government if the troops withdraw,” said Diego Da Rin, an analyst with International Crisis Group.
The group published a report Tuesday based on more than 100 interviews with officials in Haiti and abroad that reveal government failures and missteps as it urged Haitian officials to develop a plan to prevent their country from imploding once international forces leave.
“The new foreign mission promises temporary relief from the bane of gangs, but its goal is to weaken, not dismantle them," the report said. “Haiti should start preparing now for the day when its own forces are once again summoned to take sole charge of the nation’s security.”
Forces currently fighting gangs include Haiti’s police and soldiers; a U.N.-backed gang suppression force; self-appointed vigilantes; and Vectus Global, a private security firm founded by former U.S. Navy SEAL and Blackwater founder Erik Prince. Fighting gangs on their own are some 2,500 Salvadoran troops deployed when four of their own went missing after they were attacked on Oct. 18 deep in gang-controlled territory.
International Crisis Group warned that authorities “lack a strategy to identify the most pressing threats, coordinate state efforts, and bring a lasting reduction in violence.”
Echoing that sentiment was a recent cartoon in Le Nouvelliste newspaper that depicted Haitians cheering on Bukele as they stood near a table with a piece of paper on which someone had written “PLAN ANTI GANG” with crayons of various colors.
Tuesday’s report noted that plans to establish a National Security Council tasked with creating a long-term strategy to make Haiti safer two years ago never materialized.
Citing interviews with former senior government officials, the report stated that some people were concerned the council would oversee intelligence gathering, which has previously been used by Haitian leaders to target political opponents. Sources also told International Crisis Group that top officials did not want to see intelligence funds redirected because they feared losing that money.
International Crisis Group also said a foreign adviser told it that a lack of national strategy means that various police units “often follow different operational guidelines depending on their foreign donors.”
As of last year, Haiti’s National Police had no more than 8,000 active officers for a country of nearly 12 million people, the report said, citing “sources with first-hand knowledge.” Many of those officers occupy command and administrative positions and are not on the street, “while others are not trained for combat.”
The report said the government shortened training from seven months to less than four to quickly increase the number of police officers.
It also warned that police promotions rarely follow criteria like seniority or merit, with some rank-and-file officers opting to work with gangs or turning to private security or arms trafficking for additional income. Lower-ranking officers in Haiti are paid about $300 a month before mandatory deductions.
International Crisis Group called for improving salaries, benefits and facilities for police officers, as well as offering them specialized training and a “clear promotion system based on performance rather than politics.”
The number of victims is expected to grow as foreign forces increasingly rely on helicopters and explosive drones – two things that Haitian security forces lack – to target gangs.
In the first quarter of 2026, the number of civilians killed or injured by security forces as a fraction of all casualties rose 24%, the report found, and that number is expected to increase, but Bukele is finding fans in Haiti.
“In a security environment as troubled as Haiti’s, it is understandable that many have rallied around the use of explosive drones, particularly as initially the technology had a visible effect on gang leaders’ confidence and their willingness to attack state forces,” the report said.
Among the Haitians celebrating is Cliford Vital, who lives in Port-au-Prince, where gangs control an estimated 70% of the city. He noted that Bukele swiftly deployed more than 2,500 soldiers and helicopters to Haiti while U.N.-backed missions have lagged in his view.
“We’ve seen a wind of change in the country,” he said. “The fear that had persisted for so long has now shifted sides.”
But International Crisis Group said the use of such weapons “has brought diminishing returns…producing no meaningful changes in territorial control” or a change in the balance of power on the ground.
“That said, an immediate outright ban on the use of drones is unrealistic,” the report stated.
This week, Haitian Justice Minister Patrick Pélissier flew to El Salvador for an international conference and is expected to meet behind closed doors with Salvadoran officials.
Salvadoran Vice President Félix Ulloa said Monday that the bilateral agreement with Haiti would not be made public.
“There is a hidden agenda to criticize our operation,” he said when asked whether the deal guarantees respect for human rights and the rule of law.
Ulloa and Salvadoran Security Minister Gustavo Villatoro said that the Salvadoran soldiers would return home as soon as the four missing aviation technicians are found.
“We must begin preparing Haiti for a genuine rule of law, so that its institutions function and its legal frameworks work effectively in the future,” Villatoro said.
Coto reported from San Juan, Puerto Rico. Associated Press reporters Yolanda Magaña in San Salvador, El Salvador and Pierre-Richard Luxama in Port-au-Prince, Haiti contributed to this report.

title: US flexes climate action muscle at COP31 despite Trump no-show
text:
The United States, isn't at the table at the UN climate conference in the Turkish coastal city of Antalya. It's the second consecutive year that President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly said he believes climate change is a hoax, has not sent a federal delegation to the annual summit.
But that doesn't mean the US is totally absent. Far from it, since more than 120 state and local leaders from across the country are attending as part of the "America Is All In" coalition.
"We understand the importance of showing up. And if others refuse to do so, we will," said Chris Wheat, executive director of the coalition.
It's crucial, he added, to show the world that "millions of Americans are continuing to press forward on climate action" — even if the message from Washington, D.C., is a different one.
Historically, the US has released more emissions than any other country, and it is currently the world's second-biggest emitter of planet-warming greenhouse gases after China. Since taking office in January 2025, Trump has actively promoted the use of oil, coal and gas, the fossil fuels that are heating the planet and contributing to an increase in extreme weather events.
The president has also cut funds for clean energy projects and rolled back some of the climate policies of his predecessors, such as rules limiting power plant emissions.
Momentum beyond White House
The unofficial US delegation of mainly Democrat lawmakers, mayors, governors and ex-officials — including former Secretary of State John Kerry, former Vice President Al Gore and California Governor Gavin Newsom — are not taking part in the climate negotiations. But they have been holding discussions at events on the conference sidelines.
They are keen to send a message to the international community that, despite their government's absence, efforts to transition to clean energy are gathering pace at the state level.
Mike Williams, a senior fellow at the Center for American Progress, an independent liberal public policy research institute based in Washington D.C., said the presence of US lawmakers in Antalya sends an important signal that "there's quite a lot of us in the US that are still deeply invested in this. It's not just the person sitting in the White House."
Nearly half of US states, representing about 60% of the US economy, are committed to reducing emissions in line with the Paris Agreement — the 2015 global pact to limit global warming. Many have implemented initiatives such as tax incentives for renewables and other policies designed to curb emissions.
A report by America Is All In and the University of Maryland's Center for Global Sustainability found that current state policies, combined with market trends and falling technology costs, could slash US carbon emissions by up to 46% below 2005 levels by 2035.
States tout climate action
"Even if we find a hostile federal government, they're not going to be able to stop the momentum," Minnesota Governor and Kamala Harris' running mate during the 2024 presidential election Tim Walz told a crowd at the summit in Turkey, adding that his state was on track to have a "100% carbon free" grid by 2037, earlier than their target of 2040.
Walz said the state was also producing sustainable aviation fuel to reduce flight emissions, manufacturing green steel and increasing the share of electric vehicles. "It's all moving forward," he said. "So this false choice that we need to choose the economy over clean energy — that has been totally rejected."
New Mexico Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham said her state — the second-largest oil and gas producer in the US — had significantly cut emissions from the potent greenhouse gas methane through stricter regulations. She also touted measures such as shutting down coal power plants and expanding wind and solar energy.
"The largest wind farm in North America is in New Mexico," she said. "We're going to show the federal government, I am undaunted by their lack of responsibility and effort in cleaning up fossil fuels."
What's next for US climate policy after midterms?
The climate conference comes shortly after the US midterm elections, in which Trump's Republicans suffered a significant defeat. Democrats in Antalya have been keen to reassure the international community that the US would return to the COP table in the event of a change of government in two years.
Jorge Gastelumendi, senior director of the Atlantic Council's Climate Resilience Center, noted that US credibility around climate change and foreign policy in general had been "badly damaged" under Trump. "And so it's going to be a matter of how that could be built back up."
Meanwhile, Governor Newsom of California, a state of around 40 million people that plans to get 100% of its energy from renewables by 2045, said the US administration's climate withdrawal was also hurting the country's competitiveness.
"We need to reengage in these international agreements, and we need to recognize that China is outpacing us in many critical areas," such as solar power and electric cars, he told reporters in Antalya. "There is no substitute for national leadership."
Williams from the Center for American Progress said he wouldn't hold it against any countries wary about the US returning to the climate negotiations after two exits under Trump.
"Nobody should be under any perception that the US would be welcomed back with open arms," he said. "I think there needs to be an effort to show a willingness to collaborate […] That's another reason why it's important we're here now to show that there is this very large undercurrent of support within the US in spite of what's happening."

title: Two arrested after teenager killed in Cork street stabbing attack
text:
A murder probe is under way in Cork after a teenager died from wounds suffered in a stabbing attack in the city.
Two males, an adult teenager and a juvenile, have been arrested in connection with the investigation.
Gardaí said the fatal assault took place on the Lower Glanmire Road at around 1.30pm on Tuesday.
The victim, an adult male aged in his late teens, suffered critical wounds in the attack. He was taken to Cork University Hospital (CUH) for urgent medical attention, but subsequently died in the hospital.
The two males arrested are currently detained at Garda stations in Cork under the provisions of Section 4 of the Criminal Justice Act, 1984.
Gardaí in Cork have commenced a murder investigation into all the circumstances of the incident. The investigation is being coordinated from an incident room at Mayfield Garda Station under the direction of a senior investigating officer.
A family liaison officer has been appointed to the family of the deceased.
A post-mortem will be carried out on the teenager who died on Tuesday at CUH by Assistant State Pathologist Dr Margot Bolster.
Gardaí said the results of the post-mortem will assist in the course of the murder investigation.
Gardaí are appealing for witnesses to come forward, particularly those who were travelling or driving in the Lower Glanmire Road area of Cork on Tuesday 17 November between 1.15pm and 1.45pm.
They have also appealed for anyone who may have video footage including dash-cam to make it available to investigating Gardaí.

title: Euronews Verify: What's at stake as Europe seeks to triple its data centre capacity?
text:
Europe wants to triple its data centre capacity, but residents and environmental campaigners are taking to the streets to demand a pause on new data centre projects. Why? And what’s at stake?
The European Union has set an ambition to triple its data centre capacity within five to seven years, as part of a push to reduce reliance on US Big Tech and develop Europe's own AI capabilities.
However, residents and environmental campaigners in Ireland, Poland, Denmark, Finland, Spain, the Netherlands, France and the United Kingdom took to the streets to call for a freeze on the development of these new projects.
In today's episode of Euronews Verify, Evi Kiorri gets the full picture with Owen Espley, coordinator of Stop Dirty Data Centres.eu, and Michael Winterson, secretary general at the European Data Centre Association.
"They're really concerned about the impact on land, on water, the huge energy use um that data centres demand, as well as the impact that that energy use could take away from housing," Owen Espley, coordinator of Stop Dirty Data Centres.eu, told Euronews Verify.
Europe wants to be the world's first climate-neutral continent — but will it happen?
COP31 is also in focus in today's episode.
The EU has promised to be the world's first climate-neutral continent by 2050.
EU ministers insist they are committed to the green transition despite soaring energy prices and supply concerns.
However, voters want cheaper energy now, while many of the measures designed to deliver it will take much longer to pay off.
76% of people in the Netherlands, 72% in France and 68% in Germany believe their country is unlikely to make meaningful progress towards net zero. In the Netherlands, 54% say environmental policies have left ordinary people worse off.
Euronews Verify's Inês Pereira breaks down the challenges of this awkward political balance with Sven Haremling, head of climate at CAN Europe.
"People also appreciate it if they're told the truth and what needs to change, as long as there's someone who works with them for solutions and there are changes in government regulations," Haremling said.
