title: A 1-8 Titans team leans into Cam Ward’s audition as the offense shows signs of life
text:
The Tennessee Titans decided after their first and only win this season to give Cam Ward every opportunity to show he can be the franchise’s quarterback now and in the future
NASHVILLE, Tenn. -- NASHVILLE, Tenn. (AP) — The Tennessee Titans decided after their first and only win this season to give Cam Ward every opportunity to show he can be the franchise's quarterback now and in the future.
The Titans haven't won since then but see encouraging signs of progress from the No. 1 overall draft pick of 2025.
“Philosophically, the change was how are we going to evaluate whether or not he’s capable of being our franchise quarterback if we don’t give him an opportunity to prove it,” Saleh said Monday. “And I think over the last three weeks he’s done that, or at least doing it.”
Ward now is 4-22 as a starter and has the fewest wins by a starting quarterback through his first 26 starts since 2000, according to Pro Football Focus.
Ward stands alone ahead of Blaine Gabbert, Justin Fields and Bryce Young who are tied with five apiece and Trevor Lawrence and Mike Glennon with six each.
The Titans (1-8) have lost three straight since that decision, the latest a 40-23 setback to Lawrence and the Jacksonville Jaguars. The Titans look much more like an NFL offense in the three games, scoring an average of 27.6 points a game. Two losses were by seven points or fewer, and they trailed 30-23 until a late turnover on downs in the last loss.
In that span, Ward has thrown for 716 yards with four touchdowns and two interceptions. He also has scrambled for 85 of his 181 yards rushing this season.
The Titans also are using more hurry-up on offense, letting Ward check into plays at the line. Ward said that allows coordinator Brian Daboll to talk to him more at the line of scrimmage and call plays that the Titans are good at executing. The result is Ward looks more comfortable and confident working through progressions better.
“I think he’s doing a really nice job just playing quarterback,” Saleh said.
The offensive line. The Titans gave up just one sack despite being without left guard Peter Skoronski, who was placed on injured reserve Saturday. Tennessee has had five games this season allowing one or fewer sacks and has given up 14, which is tied for fourth fewest in the NFL.
Only Denver (11), Kansas City (12) and San Francisco (13) have allowed fewer sacks than the Titans. Ward said the line has done a “fantastic job” protecting him with the latest sack not on his linemen.
The defense. Playing without four starters because of trading Jeffery Simmons and Amani Hooker and injuries, the Titans could not stop the Jaguars, who piled up 459 yards and converted 7 of 14 third down attempts.
The Titans didn't allow an opponent more than 399 yards through the first six games. Now Tennessee has had its three worst games in terms of yardage giving up 491, 510 and now 459 yards. Saleh said the Titans just have to make plays that they're in position to make.
Alontae Taylor. The Titans made the decision to just have the cornerback signed to a three-year, $58 million contract to play outside inside where Taylor is at his best. Marcus Harris, who had been playing inside cornerback, didn't play a snap against the Jaguars, and Saleh said he is the one who rotates the cornerbacks.
Taylor had seven tackles and started alongside Cor'Dale Flott and Josh Williams.
WR Calvin Ridley. The veteran receiver remains “youthful” and Saleh said they need to get him more chances, but Ridley played only four snaps against Jacksonville. He wasn't targeted even once.
WR Carnell Tate, who has missed two games with an injured shoulder, LB Cody Barton and LB Anthony Hill Jr. are expected back at practice this week. RG Fernando Carmona Jr. will start practicing to work his way off injured reserve. Saleh said both S Tony Adams (concussion) and WR Wan'Dale Robinson (ankle) were being evaluated Monday with no updates.
1 — The next loss clinches a fifth straight losing season for the Titans, who are 20-57 since 2022.
The Titans now have back-to-back road games starting at Dallas (4-6) on Sunday and then visit Jacksonville for their second game with the Jaguars in three weeks.

title: Students' List candidates take seats as Serbian parliament opens
text:
Representatives of Serbia's student-led movement were sworn in as lawmakers on Tuesday, just over four weeks after they ended Serbia's strongman leader Aleksandar Vucic's 14 years of rule.
The Students' List candidates officially took their seats in the inaugural parliamentary session as the first step for the youth-backed party toward forming Serbia's new government.
The movement holds 140 seats in the 250-member parliament while Vucic's right-wing Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) holds 103. The remaining seats belong to ethnic minority parties.
Hundreds gathered outside the parliament building in the capital Belgrade, to show their support for the student-backed lawmakers, most of whom are teachers, professors and other professionals with little or no political experience.
Meanwhile, SNS candidates were met with a negative reaction from the crowd. A woman in the crowd poured yogurt over an SNS member's head as she climbed the steps to the parliament entrance.
According to Serbian media, the newly elected lawmakers have been preparing for their first session for days. They will face veteran opposition politicians, including Aleksandar Vucic, who became the opposition leader after his defeat.
90 days to form a government
The Students' List will have 90 days to name a prime minister, present their programme and form a government, once the parliament is formed.
The movement unites left- and right-wingers, pro-European and pro-Russian forces. It is focused on making changes in domestic politics and wants to advance European Union accession talks by implementing real reforms. The List opposes sanctions on Russia and the recognition of Kosovo — positions that almost the entire population of Serbia agrees with.
They pledged to improve healthcare, boost education and double the defense budget, along with many other reforms.
The election of a new parliamentary speaker will also lead to the appointment of a new acting president. The speaker has held the role since Vucic resigned in September to run for prime minister.
A snap presidential election must be called by November 27 and held by December 27.
Both parties are expected to put forward presidential candidates, but Vucic cannot seek another term because the constitution limits presidents to two terms in office.

title: JJ Gabriel posts farewell message to Man United ahead of proposed Real Madrid move
text:
Teenage wonderkid JJ Gabriel has appeared to confirm his Manchester United exit in a video posted on social media.
The 16-year-old, who has never played a competitive match for the first team, joined United as a 10-year-old in 2020.
He has been absent from the club since requesting in September that his registration be cancelled, shortly before his 16th birthday on 6 October.
Gabriel made no mention of where he intends to go next, but widespread speculation has linked him with Real Madrid, and his goodbye video on Instagram appears to have edged him closer to a move to the Spanish giants.
Gabriel said in his video: “Dear Manchester United, I arrived in 2020 as a 10-year-old boy with big dreams. Here I grew as a player and a person. From scoring at Old Trafford to receiving the Jimmy Murphy Award.
“You gave me moments I will always treasure. To every coach and every member of staff, to my team-mates and everyone who supported me, thank you for believing in me and helping me grow.
“As I begin my next chapter, Manchester United will always be a part of my story. Thank you for everything, JJ.”
The teenager is the son of former Republic of Ireland international Joe O’Cearuill.
Last season he became the youngest ever winner of United’s Jimmy Murphy Award, given to the club’s young player of the year.
Despite his absence, Gabriel had remained registered to United, who the Press Association understands are ready to explore legal options against the youngster’s next club over possible broken regulations.
United had initially hoped to persuade him to stay.
It now appears his hat-trick against Sabah on his Uefa Youth League debut on September 10 will be his final appearance for the club.
Gabriel shone in the 5-0 victory, but his representatives were disappointed he was not registered to play later that day in the Champions League fixture against the champions of Azerbaijan.
He had been due to appear in the Carabao Cup tie against Brighton the following week, but had upped sticks by that point.
Had he featured in that tie, Gabriel would have become the club’s youngest player in a competitive match, having already appeared off the bench for Michael Carrick’s side in an August friendly against Atletico Madrid.

title: Beyond the green premium: Competitive advantage through decarbonization
text:
'The opportunities that decarbonization offers have never been greater', explains Noam Boussidan, Head of the First Movers Coalition, in an op-ed for Euronews. In stable conditions, fossil-based inputs may look cheaper, but that advantage is quickly lost when supply is disrupted or prices spike.
For years, the business case for industrial decarbonization centred on a simple calculation: how much more would a “cleaner” technology cost, and how much would it reduce emissions? Today, that “green premium” remains important, but it is no longer the only consideration. Commercial priorities, geopolitical pressures and government policies increasingly shape investment decisions and the shift towards lower-carbon alternatives.
A low-carbon product can cost more but still be the smarter business choice
As a result, a low-carbon product can cost more but still be the smarter business choice. Companies investing in clean technologies must therefore weigh a broader set of factors, including volatile energy and material costs, value chain resilience, market opportunities and risks, government policies affecting industrial competitiveness, and their positioning in the low-carbon economy. In short, we are moving “beyond the green premium”.
For heavy industry, decarbonization has evolved from a narrow focus on sustainability costs to a strategic decision about the products companies will make, the markets they will serve and the supply sources on which they can rely. This shift has emerged as a clear message from the First Movers Coalition’s work with hard-to-abate industries throughout 2026.
To understand this broader calculation, it is worth revisiting the “green premium”, a term coined by Bill Gates in 2020 to describe “the difference in cost between a product that involves emitting carbon and an alternative that doesn’t”. The concept made the economics of decarbonization visible, but it never told the whole story.
The cost of cutting emissions varies widely for technologies and projects
In all sectors, the cost of cutting emissions varies widely for technologies and projects. For example, in cement production, emissions reductions of up to 50% can be achieved at negligible or low cost through clinker substitution and other supplementary routes, but further reductions often command a significant premium. By contrast, sustainable aviation fuels can cost at least twice their fossil fuel equivalent, with an even higher premium for more advanced technologies. Treating these different situations as one common economic problem obscures more than it clarifies.
As companies look beyond the immediate price difference, three factors are reshaping how businesses assess the value of decarbonization: commercial realities, geopolitics and policy.
In terms of commercial priorities, the cost of decarbonization is being assessed alongside competitiveness and growth rather than as a standalone sustainability cost. The green economy is already valued at more than $5 trillion _(Editor's note: around €4.54 trillion)_a year, and is expected to grow another $2 trillion (Editor's note: around €1.82 trillion) by 2030. For companies, this points to growing demand, new markets and the possibility of gaining an advantage by moving early.
In stable conditions, fossil-based inputs may look cheaper
This does not mean that every low-carbon product will immediately compete on price. But focusing only on the green premium fails to ask who will be positioned to supply the market when demand grows, and who will have the capabilities and partnerships needed to respond.
Geopolitics, conflict, supply-chain disruption and energy price shocks have exposed the risks of relying on a small number of energy sources and materials. In stable conditions, fossil-based inputs may look cheaper, but, depending on the sector, that advantage is quickly lost when supply is disrupted or prices spike.
Jet fuel price spikes linked to conflict in the Middle East – topping $220/barrel in March (Editor's note: around 199 €) and $200/barrel (Editor's note: around 181 €) once more in September 2026 – illustrate how quickly the economics of sustainable aviation fuels (SAF) can change.
SAF remains more expensive, but the ongoing crisis has exposed what a simple price comparison leaves out: investment in SAF can reduce exposure to future energy shocks via diversified production. Early partnerships with producers can shorten and onshore supply chains, strengthening supply security and potentially lowering price volatility. For airlines, the question is not just what SAF costs, but what more resilient and diversified fuel supplies are worth.
Government policy is reshaping the industrial landscape
Finally, government policy is reshaping the industrial landscape. Regulations, standards, subsidies, permitting rules and trade measures influence investment decisions, determining which products qualify for public support, which projects can be developed quickly, and which supply chains retain access to major markets.
The EU’s proposed Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA) – which is currently being debated – illustrates this shift. Alongside industrial decarbonization, it explicitly seeks to reduce Europe’s reliance on external suppliers and increase the share of strategic manufacturing from 14.3% in 2024 to 20% by 2035. Meanwhile, the Net Zero Industry Act is already linking decarbonization strategies with streamlined permitting and faster environmental procedures.
The green premium remains a useful starting point, but investment decisions demand a broader calculation: will the savings from postponing decarbonization will survive the next energy shock, supply disruption, or policy change?
In this turbulent era, the cost of waiting – from lost market access and volatile input prices to weaker supply chains and missed investment opportunities – may ultimately be higher. As with any business case, there are risks, but the opportunities that decarbonization offers have never been greater.
Noam Boussidan is the Head of the First Movers Coalition. He has 15+ years’ experience at the crossroads of climate, energy and industry transformation, having held various positions across government, private sector and non-governmental work. The First Movers Coalition (FMC) is the World Economic Forum’s flagship industry decarbonization initiative. A global coalition of companies leveraging their purchasing power to decarbonize the world's heavy-emitting industrial sectors responsible for 25% of global emissions. The FMC has 100+ members from top global corporations who have come together to send a demand signal for emerging climate technologies.

title: Warren grills Trump Navy secretary on cost of Iran war: 'You don't have any idea?'
text:
This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 988 or 1-800-273-TALK (8255).
Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., grilled acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao over the cost of the Iran war during his confirmation hearing on Tuesday.
Warren repeatedly pressed Cao on how much U.S. taxpayers were spending to support the U.S. Navy's blockade on Iranian ports as well as recovering from damage sustained in the conflict. Cao dodged multiple questions, stating that assessments were ongoing or he simply didn't have access to the data.
"Acting Secretary Cao what is the daily cost of the U.S. naval blockade on Iranian ports?" Warren asked.
"Senator, I do not know the daily cost, ma'am," Cao responded.
"You don't have any idea. You've been running this thing since April and you don't have any idea what that costs," Warren pressed.
"Well, senator, I know the rough cost of how much it's costing us so far. But again, the cost of losing the strait–," Cao said.
Warren cut him off, "I'm not asking you that. I just want to have the dollars here. Independent estimates are about $32.5 million a day. Does that sound about right to you?"
"Senator, let me do some quick Asian math in my head. But yes, it's about $30 billion so far," he confirmed.
"So you you confirm that number, and that means the American taxpayers are spending about $1 billion a month just on this blockade," she said.
Warren then moved on to the Iranian attack on the U.S. Navy's base in Bahrain, but Cao once again said he did not know the cost, saying the assessment is still ongoing.
The Senator referenced an estimate from the Wall Street Journal placing the cost at roughly $400 million. When asked if it was accurate, Cao said simply, "I'll find out."
Warren went on to say that the U.S. should not "spend another cent" on the war in Iran, noting the total estimated cost of the war provided by the Pentagon is over $47 billion.
Cao urged lawmakers to approve further funding for the Navy throughout Tuesday's hearing. He argued that the U.S. is in a "1939 moment," and must "be able to build like we did back in World War II."
He said the U.S. Navy currently has roughly 280 active vessels, but he said the country needs to surge up to 355.
Several lawmakers shared concerns about reports of poor morale and mental health among sailors due to long deployments for the Iran war. Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., highlighted eight suicide attempts aboard vessels in the USS Abraham Lincoln's carrier strike group, blasting Cao's characterization that there had been eight "mitigated" suicides.
Cao argued that the long deployments seen in the Iran war are due to a lack of available vessels, once again urging lawmakers to approve funding to bolster U.S. fleets.

title: Iran fires at U.S. facility in Bahrain as Tehran resumes strikes on Arab neighbors
text: CAIRO (AP) — Iran fired drones on Tuesday at a U.S. radar facility in Bahrain, its third attack in recent days on American military targets in the tiny island kingdom in the Persian Gulf after a roughly two-month lull in fighting. After issuing an alert about the incoming fire, Bahrain said that its air defense systems had successfully intercepted the "treacherous Iranian aerial attacks." The U.S. military said there was no damage to U.S. equipment or injury to American personnel. The attacks have brought condemnations from the region, while analysts say that Tehran's growing economic pressures and stalled peace negotiations are raising the risk of renewed escalation. Iran has been suffering under a naval blockade that the U.S. has enforced on it for months in and around the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial waterway for the world's energy supplies where Iran and its proxies have disrupted shipping since the war began Feb. 28. U.S. President Donald Trump has been circumspect on his next steps for the Iran war, now in its eighth month despite an initial promise it would last only a matter of weeks. He has said new strikes are highly unlikely, but he has also sent a third aircraft carrier and thousands more troops to the Middle East — and told Vice President JD Vance that talks aren't needed at this time. Oil tankers moving oil through the strait under U.S. military protection have helped return oil shipments from the Gulf to roughly prewar levels. The blockade, meanwhile, is damaging Iran's economy by curbing the flow of Iranian crude to the global market. Iran's attacks could signal a shift in its strategy after months during which it waited for an attack and then retaliated to target the operational capability of bases, Tehran-based security analyst Mostafa Najafi told The Associated Press. Bahrain hosts the U.S. Navy's 5th Fleet, which has already sustained damage in previous attacks by Iran since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28. Iranian leaders will now be weighing whether "breaking the blockade through escalation is less costly than accepting its continuation," Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group think tank, wrote in an analysis posted to X. "In other words, the risk of renewed war no longer depends solely on whether Trump decides to attack Iran again," he said. "It also depends on whether Tehran concludes that the costs of continued restraint have become greater than the risks of escalation." US expands its Middle East naval presence With the arrival of the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group in the region, the combined U.S. naval assets in the Persian Gulf, Arabian Sea, Red Sea, and Mediterranean now exceed the force deployed when the U.S. and Israel launched the war. The presence provides greater offensive firepower and missile interception capacity, according to a new analysis by Israel's Institute for National Security Studies. The Roosevelt joins the USS George H.W. Bush and the USS George Washington aircraft carriers, as well as smaller U.S. Navy ships, which are in the region to maintain the blockade of Iranian shipping. U.S. Central Command wouldn't comment on whether it plans to keep all three carrier strike groups in the region. Iran says it's responding to US attacks Iran's attack on Bahrain on Tuesday came after it targeted a U.S. early warning radar facility in the country on Friday, and on Sunday fired at a radar system at an American helicopter base there. Despite claims of success, there appeared to be little or no damage done. The attacks followed U.S. strikes on Iranian communications towers and ongoing drone surveillance operations, and Iran said it was retaliating. READ MORE: Third U.S. aircraft carrier in Middle East as Trump keeps options open in Iran war "Continued aggression against the country's airspace, as well as the use of regional military bases and facilities for hostile acts against Iran, will not go unanswered," Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps said in a statement. Egypt, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates each condemned Iran's attack on Bahrain, calling it a violation of Bahrain's sovereignty and a threat to its security and stability. Negotiations to end the war have stagnated, despite intensified mediation efforts from Qatar. In a statement, Qatar said Iran's "continued attacks" on Bahrain "undermine diplomatic efforts" and Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed Al Ansari, speaking at a news briefing in Doha, warned that any escalation in fighting posed an "extremely grave danger" to the prospects of reaching an agreement. Iran may be losing patience as conflict drags on The attacks are a sign that Tehran is growing impatient as its economic woes mount, said Sascha Bruchmann, a Bahrain-based defense analyst with the International Institute for Strategic Studies. "Shooting at ships causes fear, but is not effective enough to change the strategic equation," Bruchmann told the AP. "Tehran knows it needs to do something, but I wouldn't overestimate what we saw against Bahrain this week. This is not it — yet." Iranian officials have termed the current situation "no war, no peace" and vowed to end it. Tehran has said that it's open to a negotiated deal, but also signaled a readiness to escalate the conflict in the face of tightening sanctions and the blockade that are throttling Iran's economy. Mahdi Mohammadi, an adviser to Iran's influential parliamentary chief, posted on social media on Monday that leaders view U.S. economic pressure as an effort to create a domestic "security crisis." Iran and its proxies threaten 2 critical shipping lanes Iran has also continued to attack ships seeking to transit the Strait of Hormuz, which leads from the Persian Gulf toward the open seas. On Tuesday, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said that a tanker was reportedly attacked twice north of Oman, and that the second strike caused a fire on board. It also received a report that a cargo vessel off the coast of Yemen repelled an attempt by armed men in a skiff to board it. Iran's Fars news agency reported that two ships were struck by mines in the strait, causing them to catch fire. It wasn't immediately clear whether one was the incident reported by the British military's UKMTO. In Yemen, Iran-backed Houthi rebels now have solidified their control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, another critical shipping route, which connects the Gulf of Aden to the Red Sea, after a group allied with the Saudi-backed Yemeni government retreated over the weekend in a setback to the anti-Houthi coalition. Rising reported from Bangkok. Associated Press writers Sam Metz in Jerusalem and Ahmed al-Haj in Aden, Yemen, contributed to this report.

title: A generational flight from tech to defensive stocks is underway. How we’re capitalizing
text: Investors can't get enough of boring stocks. According to Morgan Stanley's derivatives group, the fourth quarter so far has seen the biggest rotation into defensive names in 25 years. Since Oct. 1, more than six weeks in, the consumer staples, healthcare, and utilities sectors are up an average of 13% versus a 13% decline in the Nasdaq 100 , which is more heavily weighted toward tech than even the Nasdaq Composite . That 26% performance gap is the largest since September and October 2001 — about 1.5 years after the dotcom bubble burst and roughly a year before the bottom. After chasing tech stocks for most of the four-year-old AI boom, investors have recently sought to reduce their tech exposure and seek out stocks in companies that offer more stability and less volatility. There have been a variety of reasons for the switch — from concerns about debt-fueled AI expansion to the Democratic wave in the midterms to, more recently, the fallout from the Jensen Huang affair scandal at Nvidia . Jim Cramer recognized this trend early, putting the Club portfolio on the leading edge of this rotation and stressing the benefits of diversification. We lightened our load and took profits in stocks tied to the data center buildout, such as exits of Corning in September and Broadcom in October, while initiating and bulking up our defensive positions in consumer staples and healthcare. Here's a closer look at how we're positioned and why we continue to like six stocks spanning these two sectors that went from boring to booming. Consumer staples Kimberly-Clark — The Huggies diaper and Kleenex tissue maker offers exposure to everyday essentials that consumers need regardless of the economic backdrop. Earlier this month, Kimberly-Clark completed its acquisition of Kenvue, which brought consumer health brands, including Tylenol and Band-Aid, under its umbrella. We started a position in Kimberly-Clark in early September, with an eye toward Kenvue being a catalyst in the quarters and years to come. Though our ownership got off to a rocky start, we have added to KMB four times since our initiation to get bigger in a stock Jim has said is one of his favorites right now. By leaning into weakness, we were able to lower our cost basis. Our more recent buy was last Friday, saying in our trade alert that the market is under-appreciating Kimberly-Clark's ability to turn around Kenvue. Costco — The warehouse retailer's stock has gotten its mojo back and demonstrated why it's been such a good one to own for the long term. Jim has frequently touted Costco's competitive pricing and membership-based business model. Plus, last Wednesday's announcement of a $30-per-share special dividend , alongside a new $4 billion share repurchase authorization, underscores the strength of its balance sheet and its commitment to returning capital to shareholders. Since then, the stock has been on a five-session winning streak. A positive finish Tuesday would mean another record-high close. In a Tuesday note, Mizuho raised its price target to $1,150 from $1,100 per share, citing strong October sales and predicting more of the same in November. "Consumer anxiety following the Microsoft Outlook outage, the ground stoppage for all U.S. airline flights, and apocalyptic concerns flaring up across social media have all contributed to increased emergency prep sales at Costco," analysts wrote. Costco is set to report November sales on Dec. 2 and its fiscal 2027 first quarter earnings on Dec. 10. Constellation Brands — While Costco has been a longtime holding of the Club, we recently brought Constellation Brands back into the portfolio, initiating a position earlier this month. Jim said Tuesday that members who don't own shares of the Corona and Modelo brewer, or want to improve their cost basis, should buy on further declines. Jim has said he sought out Constellation as a less cyclical company that also returns capital to shareholders. Alongside Kimberly-Clark, we bought more Constellation shares last Friday. In a "Mad Money" interview back in August, new CEO Nicholas Fink acknowledged that the beer industry has faced pressure as its largely Hispanic consumer base grapples with both inflation and concerns over immigration law enforcement. Things have changed after the election, with the hope that Democratic control of Capitol Hill and more key governorships would help ease worries about deportations. "It's just so positive," Jim said during Monday's Morning Meeting . He added that Constellation's beer is selling better. Healthcare Johnson & Johnson — If there's one stock that perfectly illustrates the market's appetite for defensive stocks, Jim said it is J & J. This week, he called it a " metaphor for what's working." Shares of the pharma and medtech giant briefly touched an all-time intraday high above $290 on Monday after announcing a deal to acquire clinical-stage Ollin Biosciences for approximately $3.3 billion. The deal expands J & J's pipeline of treatments for serious eye diseases. Jim is a fan of J & J's robust drug portfolio and touted Ollin as another reason investors want to own names with tangible growth opportunities outside of AI. Despite an eventual lower close Monday and additional weakness Tuesday, the stock is still up more than 17.5% since we initiated our position back in April. Cardinal Health — This healthcare distributor stock has been a rocket ship lately. During our Annual Meeting earlier this month, Jim reiterated that starting a position in Cardinal Health back in March was a bit early. However, he is pleased that the stock was able to shake its spring swoon — during which we wisely bought more shares — and climb to record highs. Cardinal benefits from its essential role in the healthcare supply chain, with opportunities to improve profitability. Following a great beat-and-raise quarter on Nov. 5, we raised our price target to $300 from $265. We did trim our position once on earnings day and again on Nov. 10 . We locked in profits as a matter of discipline due to the parabolic move higher in the stock. In new notes, Wells Fargo and Barclays raised their price targets to $321 and $320, respectively. The analysts recognize the same potential for further upside as we do. Eli Lilly — Demand for Eli Lilly's blockbuster GLP-1 diabetes and obesity drugs, including injectables Zepbound and Mounjaro, remains central to our investment thesis. The company reported a strong quarter late last month, featuring continued growth in its new Foundayo pill. Last week, the company scored a big win when it became the first drugmaker to win the regulatory green light from China for Foundayo. However, like Cardinal Health, Lilly shares have also been pretty much unstoppable since mid-September. On Nov. 5, we trimmed the position just under Friday's record high price.
