title: Jensen Huang says he would be ‘honored’ if allowed to return as Nvidia CEO
text:
In the first public statement since his resignation, Nvidia founder Jensen Huang signaled his willingness to return as CEO if the board decides it is in the company’s best interest.
Huang’s statement, posted in full on X, reads as follows:
Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I’ve never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me.
I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. NVIDIA has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible. I love our country, and I love NVIDIA.
I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation.
Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.
Thank you again to everyone who has shared their good wishes. I am profoundly humbled by your support. To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours.
Jensen
Huang resigned after reports of multiple affairs, including with a direct report and another with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who is suspected of working with Chinese intelligence services. Nvidia’s chip exports have faced intense scrutiny since the revelations, and Huang is scheduled to testify before Congress on December 1.
In Huang’s absence, Nvidia has formed a new executive committee to oversee export control compliance.
Still, many investors and employees associated with Nvidia have called for Huang to return as CEO, at least until an investigation can provide clearer evidence of guilt. An open letter circulated earlier this week attracted the signatures of more than 10,000 current and former Nvidia employees, as well as prominent tech figures like Elon Musk, Amjad Masad, and Travis Kalanick.
“We are concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process,” the letter reads. “If the Board believes his continued absence is necessary, provide a specific, evidence-based explanation of why it serves NVIDIA’s best interests.”
Still, many see such a return as unlikely. On Monday, an unnamed source on Nvidia’s board told The Washington Post there were no plans to reinstate Huang. There’s also significant resistance to the idea in Congress, where Huang still faces significant questions about his role in chip exports to China-linked firms.
Reached by Politico, one senator called Huang’s reinstatement “one of the worst ideas I’ve heard today.”

title: Three small failures combined to take down Microsoft 365
text:
A hidden defect in Microsoft’s cloud gateway, dormant since July, was to blame for one of the largest outages in the company’s history last week. A preliminary Post-Incident Report (PIR) released by the company outlines how the latent bug, changes in traffic, and reduced server capacity combined to knock much of Microsoft 365 and Exchange infrastructure offline at the end of last week. Microsoft’s report lists the incident’s final status as “a technical issue not related to cyber or AI/agents.”
Microsoft’s preliminary report places the outage between November 12 at 16:20 UTC and November 13 at 16:10 UTC, just under 24 hours total, and additional monitoring remained in place for any affected systems through November 14.
The outage started on November 12 and quickly rippled through businesses and public offices that depend on Microsoft’s cloud and email exchange infrastructure. The outage is covered in Microsoft’s incident IDs EX1550543 and MO1550821. You need Microsoft 365 admin credentials to see the full report on the company’s status pages, but Office Watch has reproduced the preliminary report, and the University of Pennsylvania maintains an archive of Microsoft’s service-health updates.
A perfect storm
Microsoft attributes the outage to three factors. A change deployed to Microsoft’s cloud gateway starting in July created a bug where, under certain conditions, CPU and memory resources could become exhausted and unresponsive. Microsoft contends that the defect was never discovered in pre-release testing because the hardware used was less powerful than some systems already deployed in production, where higher CPU core counts on newer machines apparently contributed to the lockout.
The second factor was server load. Microsoft said that “Traffic shifts during standard network maintenance and upgrades exposed a latent bug.” The company keeps two independent gateway systems in place to access Microsoft 365 for resilience. If one system encounters trouble and users can’t get through the front door, the other is opened to keep traffic flowing. According to the report, about 15 hours prior to the outage, traffic from Teams was shifted from the alternate gateway to the primary, where Exchange Online access is maintained. The switchover was a standard fail-safe, but it left the gateway handling more traffic, with a different mix of requests than before. As requests continued to pile up, affected servers exhausted their capacity and refused new connection requests.

title: The secret to building Moon bases may be hiding in emergency blankets
text:
Scientists have turned the thin plastic used in emergency blankets into remarkably strong insulation that could help astronauts survive the Moon's extreme temperatures. Built from hundreds of stacked layers, the material withstands crushing pressure without losing its thermal protection, potentially paving the way for tougher, longer-lasting lunar habitats.
Establishing a permanent human presence on the Moon will require more than rockets, habitats, and life support systems. Engineers must also find ways to protect astronauts and equipment from extreme temperatures that can swing from hundreds of degrees below zero to boiling hot. Reliable insulation will be essential, but keeping heat under control is only part of the problem.
Materials used in lunar construction must also survive transportation, installation, accidental impacts, and years of handling. Many of the best insulators are surprisingly delicate, making them poorly suited to the demanding conditions of a working Moon base.
Researchers at the University of Pennsylvania may have found an answer in an unexpectedly familiar material: Mylar. This lightweight plastic is used in everyday products such as food wrap and, when coated with aluminum, the reflective emergency blankets that help marathon runners retain body heat. By arranging hundreds of extremely thin Mylar sheets into carefully designed stacks, the team has created insulation that remains effective even after being bent or subjected to intense pressure.
The research, published in ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces, introduces a material known as hybrid layered insulating film stacks (HyLIFS). Its main advantage is the ability to combine two qualities that are difficult to achieve together: excellent thermal insulation and resistance to physical damage.
"These stacks of Mylar can bend, withstand substantial compression and maintain their insulating performance," says senior author Igor Bargatin, Associate Professor in Mechanical Engineering and Applied Mechanics (MEAM), "potentially allowing them to be packed, transported and survive rough treatment over many years of use."
If engineers can eventually manufacture the material on a large scale, it could be used to protect lunar habitats, spacesuits, and other equipment designed to function for extended periods in the vacuum of space.
"The combination of thermal and mechanical robustness is critical for long-term use on the Moon," notes first author Danielle R. Levin, a recent Penn doctoral graduate in chemistry, who also received a master's in MEAM. "This material could open a pathway to inexpensive, durable and reusable lunar insulation."
Why Moon Bases Need Tougher Insulation
Designing insulation for the Moon involves a difficult balancing act. A material must slow the movement of heat through a vacuum while also remaining strong enough to withstand the stresses of everyday use.
Some existing materials are outstanding at preventing heat transfer but offer little protection against physical damage. Aerogels, for instance, consist mostly of empty space, which makes them extremely lightweight and effective at retaining heat. They have been used in applications ranging from industrial pipelines to NASA's Mars rovers. However, their delicate internal structure can make them vulnerable to impacts and compression.
Another widely used space technology, multilayer insulation, relies on reflective sheets separated by insulating spacers. It works particularly well at reducing heat transfer through radiation, but it is not intended to support substantial weight. Even routine contact can cause tearing or other damage.
Strengthening insulation often creates another problem: the changes that make it more durable can also allow more heat to pass through. For future lunar infrastructure, engineers need a material that can resist damage without sacrificing thermal performance.
"For lunar infrastructure, we would ideally like both," says Bargatin. "The ideal material is both resistant to damage and to the loss of heat."
How Ordinary Mylar Became Powerful Space Insulation
The Penn researchers focused on Mylar, a well-known plastic formally called biaxially oriented polyethylene terephthalate, or BoPET. Already used extensively in aerospace technology, the polymer is also found in the lightweight emergency blankets distributed after marathons. Adding a metallic coating such as aluminum allows Mylar to reflect infrared radiation, helping prevent heat from escaping.
Rather than relying on a single sheet, the researchers investigated what would happen if many thin layers were stacked together. They experimented with different film thicknesses and applied extremely thin coatings of aluminum oxide, also called alumina, to some samples to make the sheets stiffer.
Assembling the experimental stacks was surprisingly difficult. Each delicate film had to be positioned individually, requiring painstaking manual work.
"At the moment, the process is very time-consuming," says Levin. "We use two pairs of tweezers and small weights to handle and stack the delicate films. Even breathing near the stack can send the layers flying."
Despite the simplicity of the basic idea, testing revealed an impressive combination of properties. In a vacuum, the best stacks achieved thermal conductivity comparable to other advanced vacuum insulation materials while retaining their flexibility.
The researchers also tested the material under compression similar to what insulation could experience inside a lunar habitat, where the interior air pressure would push against walls exposed to the vacuum outside.
Additional mechanical testing showed that stacks coated with alumina could tolerate the greatest compressive stresses available with the laboratory equipment while maintaining their insulating performance. The results demonstrated that improving durability did not necessarily require giving up thermal protection.
Crushing Pressure Reveals Unexpected Durability
One of the most striking findings came when the team subjected the material to repeated compression. Even the researchers were surprised by how well the thin plastic layers held up.
The samples were compressed to approximately 20 megapascals, a pressure comparable to concentrating 200 pounds of force onto an area the size of a fingertip. Instead of testing the material only once, the researchers repeated the process 10 times.
"We were concerned about the material failing under such high compressive stress," recalls Levin. "But the stacks didn't survive just one high stress cycle -- they survived 10 in a row."
This resistance to damage could be especially valuable for lunar exploration. Every piece of equipment needed on the Moon must first endure the challenges of being packed, launched, transported, and installed. Insulation that can bend, withstand pressure, and potentially be reused would offer significant practical advantages.
Durability would remain important after construction is complete. Astronauts living and working inside a lunar habitat could accidentally strike or compress insulation during maintenance or ordinary activities.
"You could use these stacks to insulate a lunar habitation, but astronauts will inevitably have little accidents where they bump into them," notes Bargatin. "When we're talking about long-term habitation on the moon, it's really important to have tough materials that can last long enough."
Tiny Particles Reveal a Hidden Secret of Heat Transfer
Beyond demonstrating the material's durability, the experiments uncovered an important clue about how heat travels through layers of Mylar.
The discovery involved microscopic particles already present in commercially manufactured plastic films. Extremely thin sheets naturally tend to stick to one another and to nearby surfaces, which complicates manufacturing and handling. To prevent this, producers add tiny "antiblocking" particles that extend slightly above the plastic surface and keep neighboring sheets from clinging together.
Although manufacturers have long understood why these particles are useful, their influence on heat transfer in stacked Mylar films had received relatively little attention.
Traditional multilayer space insulation is primarily designed to control heat transferred by radiation. As a result, researchers have had less reason to investigate how small points of physical contact between films might affect heat conduction.
The Penn team examined this possibility by constructing mathematical models of heat transfer between individual layers and comparing the predictions with laboratory measurements.
The findings indicate that, in a vacuum, much of the heat moving from one Mylar sheet to the next passes through the tiny contact points created by the antiblocking particles.
That result could have important implications for future insulation design. Instead of accepting the particles as an incidental feature of commercial plastic, engineers might deliberately control their size, abundance, and placement to reduce unwanted heat transfer.
Why Thinner Plastic Does Not Always Insulate Better
The role of these microscopic particles also helped explain another unexpected result.
At first, the researchers assumed that thinner Mylar sheets would produce better insulation. Using thinner films would allow more layers to occupy the same amount of space, increasing the number of boundaries that heat must cross.
However, the experiments did not fully support that expectation. When coated with alumina, the thinnest films the team successfully characterized provided thermal performance similar to films of medium thickness.
The researchers suspect that the antiblocking particles help explain why. In thinner sheets, the particles can produce more contact between adjacent layers, creating additional routes for heat to move through the material. Those extra contact points can offset the expected advantages of adding more layers.
The finding suggests that making films thinner is not automatically the best approach. Engineers must also consider how the sheets bend and deform under pressure, along with the number and arrangement of microscopic contact points.
"As you compress the layers, the contact landscape changes," says Levin. "It's not just a matter of minimizing the film thickness or the number of particles; we must also account for how the contacts change and the films deform as pressure increases."
Ultimately, the ability of these stacks to limit heat transfer depends on several interacting factors, including the thickness and stiffness of the plastic and the distribution of particles within it.
From Tiny Laboratory Samples to Future Moon Bases
Although the early results are encouraging, the new insulation is still far from being ready for lunar construction.
The experimental HyLIFS samples currently measure only about one square centimeter, and producing them requires hours of careful cutting and manual stacking. That painstaking process would be impractical for manufacturing the large sheets needed to insulate an entire habitat.
To make the material useful on a larger scale, the researchers will need a more efficient production method. One possibility involves continuously applying coatings to large rolls of Mylar, using manufacturing techniques that could eventually produce sheets measured in meters rather than centimeters.
Such an approach might also allow engineers to adjust the thickness of the plastic, the protective coatings, and the distribution of antiblocking particles before assembling the material into larger stacks.
Important questions remain. The researchers still need to determine whether large versions of the material will retain the same insulating properties and mechanical strength seen in the laboratory. Further testing must also establish how well the stacks tolerate repeated bending, accidental impacts, scratches, and other wear associated with real-world use.
If those challenges can be overcome, the technology could provide lightweight, flexible, durable insulation for lunar habitats, rovers, electronic equipment, and other systems operating in space.
For Levin, the results also offer a broader lesson about materials engineering. Even familiar products can reveal unexpected capabilities when researchers examine how their structures behave under different conditions.
"The simplest configuration ended up being the best one," she says.
The research was carried out at the University of Pennsylvania School of Engineering and Applied Science (Penn Engineering). Additional co-authors include Matthew F. Campbell, Gulzhan Aldan, and Orevaoghene H. Omodior.
Funding was provided by the National Science Foundation Division of Chemical, Bioengineering, Environmental and Transport Systems (grant number 1845933) and Penn Engineering.

title: Toxic secrets are hiding in Arctic ice
text:
Ice cores record Earth’s secrets, even the dirty ones.
Some of the cylindrical sections of ice extracted from the Arctic contain elevated levels of arsenic, lead and other heavy metals that circulated in our planet’s atmosphere in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Those pollutants, which have been tied to declines in IQ and higher rates of certain cancers, were probably emitted by a mining and smelting company in Montana whose grounds are now designated as multiple Superfund sites, the researchers report November 3 in Nature Sustainability.
The ice cores contain tiny particles that were once airborne — including pollutants, volcanic ash and salt from ocean spray — and fell to our planet’s surface within a few days or weeks. In polar regions, that fallout combines with snow and is preserved as ice.
Joseph McConnell, an environmental scientist at the Desert Research Institute, and his collaborators recently analyzed 10 ice cores collected across Canada, Greenland and Russia. The cores contained material that had fallen to Earth as early as 210 BCE, but the interval spanning the Industrial Revolution in the United States — from roughly 1870 to 1914 — was what caught the team’s collective eye.
In the ice layers from that period, arsenic concentrations in some of the ice cores were up to 15 times higher than pre-Industrial Revolution levels. Because the heavy metal exposure has been tied to upticks in the rates of certain cancers, McConnell and his team set out to determine the most likely source of all that pollution.
The largest increases in arsenic existed in the ice cores from Greenland. That finding was a big hint, McConnell says, because atmospheric circulation patterns tend to move material from west to east. “The only way you can explain that pattern of deposition is if the emissions are coming from North America,” McConnell says. “Had it been from Europe, we would have seen much larger increases in the Russian Arctic.”
The most likely source, the team concluded, was a massive copper mining and smelting operation in southwestern Montana operated by the Anaconda Copper Mining Company. It was one of the largest in North America during the Industrial Revolution and, unlike other copper mining operations in the area, it worked with copper ore that contained heavy metals like arsenic and lead. It was no secret that those toxic metals were entering the atmosphere, says Fred Quivik, a historian and the author of Smoke and Tailings, a book about the environmental history of copper smelting in Montana. “Ranchers and farmers started seeing their livestock die from arsenic poisoning.”
Based on the concentrations of arsenic in the ice cores and models of how material disperses in the atmosphere, McConnell and his colleagues estimated that the Anaconda Copper Mining Company was emitting roughly 30 tons of arsenic per day into the atmosphere in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. By comparison, Chile, currently the world’s largest producer of copper and home to more than 20 mining operations, collectively emits roughly one quarter as much arsenic today.
Beginning in 1919, the Anaconda Copper Mining Company installed devices near its smokestacks and other facilities to capture arsenic and prevent its release into the atmosphere. Arsenic emissions dropped by about 60 percent as a result, the ice core data showed, but by then hundreds of thousands of nearby residents had already been exposed for decades. That exposure could have been lessened, McConnell says, if the Anaconda Copper Mining Company hadn’t waited so long to install the pollution-abatement technology. “They delayed installation for about a decade.”
These new findings should be combined with census records to trace the effects of this pollution on human health in the 19th and 20th centuries, McConnell and his team suggest. “We hope that epidemiologists will take this information and really investigate potential impacts on human populations.”

title: Elon Musk says SpaceX’s Starship, already the largest rocket on Earth, will get even bigger with next-gen V4 model
text:
As usual, SpaceX and its founder Elon Musk are thinking big.
The company recovered the upper stage of its Starship megarocket for the first time ever on Saturday (Nov. 14), plucking it out of the sky with the "chopstick" arms of its Texas launch tower.
It was a huge moment for SpaceX, bringing its vision of full and rapid rocket reuse much closer to reality. But Elon Musk isn't one to dwell on the past or rest on laurels, so he soon outlined an even more ambitious future for Starship.
"Starship V4 will be ~70m [230 feet] long, which is roughly a 40% length increase and allows >60% more propellant load," Musk said via X, the social media platform he owns, on Sunday evening (Nov. 15). "Engine count will be raised to 9, with 3 more Raptor-Vacuum engines added, and these will be higher-thrust V4 engines."
The current version of Starship — the one that launched Friday (Nov. 13) on the vehicle's 15th test flight — is the V3. It's the largest and most powerful rocket ever built, standing 408 feet (124 m) tall when fully stacked with its Super Heavy first stage and Ship upper stage.
V3's Ship is 171 feet (52 m) tall and features six of SpaceX's Raptor V3 engines. (The similarly reusable Super Heavy V3 booster is powered by 33 Raptors.) So, as Musk noted in his post, the V4 Ship will be quite an upgrade in size and power.
Starship Die Cast Rocket Model Was $47.99 Now $39.99 on Amazon.
Even if you can't see SpaceX's Starship in person, you can score a model of your own. Standing at 13.77 inches (35 cm), this is a 1:375 ratio of SpaceX's Starship as a desktop model. The materials here are alloy steel and it weighs just 225g.
To provide a little perspective about that vehicle's planned dimensions: The V4 Ship will be the same height as a fully stacked Falcon 9, SpaceX's workhorse two-stage rocket, and much broader: Ship is 30 feet (9 m) across, while the Falcon 9's payload fairing is 17.1 feet (5.2 m) wide.
This isn't the first we've heard about a V4 Starship. Back in August 2025, for example, Musk posted a graphic showing Starship's planned progression from the V2 to the V3 to the V4, which he said is expected to debut in 2027.
That slide pegs the future Starship's total height at 466 feet (142 m), 200 feet (61 m) of which would be Ship. But those numbers are out of date, Musk stressed in the post, saying that V4 is "probably closer to 150m height."
So, yeah: If all goes according to plan, the next Starship will be nearly 500 feet tall.
The original Starship Flight 15 mission plan called for a double chopsticks catch, with both Super Heavy and Ship coming back to the launch tower for recovery.
This would have been feasible, as the catches were scheduled a day apart: Super Heavy would land just 6.5 minutes after launch, while Ship would circle Earth for 22.5 hours, and deploy a batch of SpaceX's Starlink V3 internet satellites, before coming home. (Ship ended up delivering the satellites as planned.)
The twofer didn't happen, however; Super Heavy experienced a low-fuel alarm and diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown on Friday as a result. But that wasn't a huge deal, as SpaceX had already pulled off Super Heavy catches on three previous Starship flights.
The Ship catch was unprecedented, because it's been a taller order. Ship returns to Earth from orbit, so it comes in faster and hotter. SpaceX hadn't even tried the maneuver before Flight 15, so executing it was a very big deal.
"That was the missing link," SpaceX's Dan Huot said during the company's Ship-landing webcast on Saturday. "We caught a Starship, and now everything changes."

title: FA wants to host Nations League finals in England
text:
England could host the Nations League finals this season after Football Association officials registered their interest.
The semi-final and finals of the competition, due to take place in June, are held in one country.
As well as England, it is understood that Spain and France have also contacted Uefa to register their interest in hosting the final four games, including the bronze medal match, which will run between 9-13 June.
The FA, it is understood, is still discussing potential venues with some doubt over whether Wembley would be available. The only publicly announced Wembley events in June are two concerts by singer Sam Fender, although these are for after the Nations League.
Since the tournament began in 2019, England have never held the finals, with Portugal, Italy, Netherlands and Germany the hosts to date.
Generally, only nations who reach the last four of the Nations League are considered to host the latter stages.
Thomas Tuchel's team will be seeded in Friday's draw for the quarter-finals following their euphoric 3-2 victory over Spain in Madrid, which secured top place in the group.
They could face Belgium, Netherlands, Denmark or Norway in March in the next round before June's finals.
If the FA's bid is successful, it will provide the governing body with an opportunity to host a mini-tournament before Euro 2028, which will be held in England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland.

title: These US coal plants on the Ohio River shut down years ago. Now, residents say their waste is destroying lives
text:
Down winding roads and past quiet homesteads, all that can be heard in the otherwise bucolic air of rural Clermont county, Ohio, is the roar of dump trucks.
The speeding vehicles are headed for a massive, 1,400-acre landfill filled with coal ash and other hazardous materials and owned by Dynegy Zimmer LLC, a subsidiary of Vistra Corp The Zimmer landfill has been a dumping ground for dangerous waste from coal-powered plants dotted around the Cincinnati region for decades.
For residents Brian and Rhonda Brittain, the sight of the trucks fills them with fear and anger.
“Everything that’s coming out of [the landfill] is coming right through this pipe and into this pond,” says Brian, pointing to a neighbor’s watering hole surrounded by a half dozen livestock.
“These people raise cattle to feed their family.”
He and his wife, Rhonda, have been battling sulfuric odors and concerns about environmental hazards associated with the landfill.
But as bad as the smell can get, that’s no longer their main concern.
“The smell is only the warning system,” says Brian.
Their property abuts the Little Indian Creek, a waterway upon which the landfill was constructed and which flows into the Ohio River four miles downstream.
In consecutive rounds of testing conducted this year and for several previous years, Dynegy Zimmer’s own reporting showed “statistically significant levels above the applicable groundwater protection standards” for lithium at the landfill.
Millions of people downstream in Cincinnati and Louisville depend on the Ohio River for drinking water.
While coal-powered electricity plants have been phased out in recent years, their presence has cast a long, dangerous shadow in the form of coal combustion residual (CCR) landfills.
The residual material, typically made up of ash, boiler slag, silica and other waste substances, contain dangerous constituents that can cause cancer and neurological illnesses.
Communities along this stretch of the Ohio River have been suffering with the fallout for years.
While the national incidence rate of lung and bronchus cancer is 51.8 per 100,000 residents, in Clermont county, it’s 69.6. In the neighboring Hamilton county, from where much of the waste being dumped comes from, the rate is 62 per 100,000.
A five-minute drive from the landfill down to the banks of the Ohio River lies the defunct William H. Zimmer power plant, shuttered in 2022 and which took 20 years to build but operated for only three decades.
A further five-minute drive down the Ohio River, the Beckjord coal-powered electricity plant operated for 75 years before being shut down in 2014.
Now county administrators are suing former operator Duke Energy, and Missouri-based Commercial Liability Partners, a company that specializes in tearing down former industrial plants and the plant’s current owner, after suffering 12 years of pollution that’s seen heavy metals detected in at least 20 water wells.
According to local media, unlined holding ponds at the Beckjord facility contain billions of pounds of toxins, and residents have stopped drinking tap water as a result. County authorities now face a $30m bill to build a new water treatment plant with the capability of removing the pollutants. The county has already spent tens of thousands of dollars on legal fees.
Commercial Liability Partners is the biggest property taxpayers in Clermont county. But earlier this year, authorities revealed the company owed the community more than $640,000 in delinquent taxes.
Texas-headquartered Vistra Corp, a $44bn energy giant, has been hit with fines and lawsuits across the country for market manipulation, chemical fires and explosions and a host of other pollution violations. In 2023, Dynegy Midwest Generation, a Vistra Corp. subsidiary, settled for $400,000 in a case where it was accused of dumping coal ash near a river at a facility in Illinois.
“The Zimmer landfill, because of its status as a legacy landfill, hasn’t had to meet the same safety and design standards that landfills being built today [have],” says Thom Cmar, an attorney at Earthjustice, an environmental protection nonprofit that tracks coal ash contamination across the country.
“When it was designed and constructed, there were no barriers put in place that would ensure that the coal ash waste disposed there did not come into contact with ground water,” adds Cmar.
Vistra has also availed itself of billions of dollars of federal government grants. Trump and former House Democratic leader, Nancy Pelosi, are among the company’s high-profile purchasers of its shares this year. Last year, it settled for $38m following charges of market manipulation.
“Unfortunately, states like Ohio have always been deferential to the utility industry and a lot of states where coal-burning is an industry have been willing to let [them] take the lead in setting the safety standards and best practices that they follow,” says Cmar.
Emails sent by the Guardian to the Ohio Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) asking if it would facilitate an independent testing of water inside the Zimmer landfill were not responded to.
A Vistra spokesperson declined to respond to the same question but says coal ash is currently not being dumped at the landfill.
“Since 2007, the site has accepted inert, limestone-based byproducts from the Miami Fort power plant, which are classified as non-hazardous waste under applicable regulations. These materials consist primarily of naturally occurring substances, including silica and river sediment,” says Jenny Lyon, of Vistra Corp.
“We recognize residents’ concerns about odors and take them seriously … Vistra has invested in multiple systems and processes to manage and minimize odors.”
However, silica and many other naturally occurring substances are dangerous to human health in certain quantities. In the 1930s, at least 764 West Virginia miners died after exposure to high levels of silica dust.
In Ohio, concerns with Vistra are not limited to the environment.
According to the Clermont county auditor’s website, Vistra Corp, through its subsidiary Dynegy Zimmer has amassed dozens of parcels of property totaling more than 3,400 acres of land (the equivalent of around one-quarter of the island of Manhattan) in the Brittains’ Washington township. Locals say that corporate property ownership has caused financial strain on the community and access to a local cemetery has been restricted due to the presence of the landfill.
“When they devalued their property, the township had to pay money back to Dynegy Zimmer. We lost a lot of money that was already in the budget,” says Rhonda Brittain, referring to $139,000 that schools, libraries and other entities in Clermont county had to repay to Vistra Corp in 2023.
Rhonda’s husband Brian, a diesel engine mechanic, believes the land buy-up effort is an attempt to keep the public away from the landfill and to hide the dangers within it.
“It seems like nobody wants to spend any money to cure this problem, but they were just given a ton of money [a $4.2bn loan from the department of energy] for a plant outside Cleveland,” he says.
“But you can’t spend money here to try to fix it?”
Increasingly, however, environmental groups and residents are fighting back.
In Illinois, a lawsuit forced Dynegy in 2023 to move around three million cubic yards of coal ash that was leaching into a major waterway, although the project is still awaiting approval from Illinois’ EPA.
Here on the banks of the Ohio River, the Brittains are also taking on the fight.
“I got into this issue because I have grandchildren [and] four of them live with us,” says Brian.
“We are just asking that they spend the money to fix it. We know they have it.”

title: I'm a human doctor with human intelligence. But I sure do like my AI notetaker
text:
Dr. Mara Gordon, a family physician in Camden, N.J., answers reader health questions monthly. Send in your question to: thrive@npr.org.
Question: My doctor has started recording our office visits with an artificial intelligence scribe. She says it helps write notes in my medical record. I said yes when she asked if I was comfortable with it, but in hindsight I feel a little freaked out. Should I be worried about AI listening in on my private medical conversations?
Answer: AI scribes are all the rage in medicine right now. Doctors are using them to take notes everywhere from the gynecologist's office to the emergency room.
I admit I've been an eager adopter in my own primary care practice. I use an app on my phone that records my conversation with a patient and then uses AI to write a preliminary summary for the medical record.
It saves me time. But more importantly, I like using it because it helps me focus more fully on my patient. When I use the AI scribe, I don't have to talk and take notes at the same time – I can actually make eye contact with my patient rather than staring at the computer screen.
But I totally get why people feel uncomfortable with the technology. I share my patients' concerns about privacy and how AI scribes might impact the doctor-patient relationship.
I also worry that corporate health systems will put pressure on doctors to use any time we save with an AI scribe to squeeze in even more patients.
And like many people, I worry that artificial intelligence might one day put me out of a job!
Here's what you need to know.
How AI scribes work
When I use an AI scribe during a primary care visit, I first ask the patient if they're comfortable using the service. If the patient says yes, I start recording using an app on my smartphone. I usually set it down on the desk in the exam room.
The scribe uses a technology called "automatic speech recognition" which records our conversation and automatically distinguishes between the doctor's and patient's voices. (Sometimes, when the patient has a family member accompanying him, the app needs to distinguish between three – or more! – voices.)
When the visit ends, the recording is then transcribed. A large language model – the kind of AI technology that powers ChatGPT, but specifically geared toward medicine – converts the raw transcript into a medical note. These notes follow a standard format that is specific to the speciality and the type of visit. They reflect what the patient told the doctor, physical exam findings, and the doctor's medical decision-making.
What is the software like?
There are lots of AI scribes on the market, ranging from products embedded within the electronic medical record to free apps a doctor can download on her phone. Most scribes use a smartphone's recording capabilities to "listen in" on the conversation, although there are some that use a desktop computer or a separate recording device.
I use my personal smartphone for this purpose, as do many physicians I know. I downloaded the AI scribe software as an app on my phone. This causes occasional hiccups. For example, I've gotten notification pings from my book club's group chat while recording a patient visit – which made me make sure to put the phone in "do not disturb" mode whenever I'm using it for patient care.
What about privacy?
Even though I use my personal phone for scribing patient visits, our conversations aren't stored on my device. They're uploaded directly to a HIPAA-compliant cloud, where the data is then transcribed into the AI-generated clinical note. Most scribe systems then delete the recording and the note after a set period of time.
HIPAA-compliance is an important feature of all AI scribe services. It means that the computer program was designed in accordance with the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, a federal law designed to protect patients' privacy.
The software company is responsible for safeguarding the data at every step of the process, from recording to generating notes. AI scribe companies encrypt the data, control who has access to it, and have systems to protect against "data breaches." It also means these companies are liable if the data is leaked.
AI scribes can make mistakes
Recently, I saw a patient who had metastatic cancer. Despite multiple conversations about his diagnosis with me, his oncologist, and his surgeon, he did not believe he had cancer. I had even – with his permission – called his spouse to tell her what was going on. He still did not accept it.
This kind of tricky clinical situation comes up on occasion, and the AI scribe did not get it right. Rather than reflecting the nuances of our conversation, the note that the scribe produced simply said that the patient had been misdiagnosed.
I often catch other errors that the software makes, like mistaking a patient's gender or age. Alarmingly, these scribes are also known for mistaking "I do" statements with "I do not." In medicine, this can be critical: The difference between "I do have chest pain" and "I do not have chest pain" can be a matter of life and death.
To better understand how AI scribes can contribute to errors in the medical record, I talked to Dr. Eileen Kim, an assistant professor of internal medicine at the University of California San Diego. Kim specializes in clinical informatics and thinks a lot about how AI might shape the future of medicine.
"You have a doctor who's overburdened, seeing way too many patients," she said. "They have this AI tool that's offered to them that seems like a great solution, but they don't have time to adequately review everything. It goes into the chart. Then you have another AI tool that's reading through all these notes. But they're wrong. And then it just propagates errors throughout the chart."
In my work caring for patients, I come across erroneous information in the electronic health record all the time. It's hard to know how much is related to AI and how much is caused by human error. But I think Dr. Kim is right to worry that AI scribes might make the problem worse.
Who is liable for errors?
As the doctor caring for my patient, I'm ultimately the one responsible for the content of the AI-generated note, so I always read them carefully before clicking "sign" and adding them to the medical record. Most AI scribe software makes doctors sign a user agreement stating doctors are liable for everything they write in the medical record, even if a scribe helps them with it.
When the AI-generated notes are factually accurate, I almost always end up editing them to make my clinical decision-making more clear. I'm happy to have robots help me with my administrative tasks, but I still take pride in being a human doctor with human intelligence!
Health equity concerns
Many AI scribes can only be used with English-speaking patients. Health equity advocates say they fear this means unequal access to the technology, which could further widen health disparities.
For example, the scribe allows me to look more at my patient and less at my computer, which might make a patient feel more comfortable disclosing a stigmatizing health concern. Or the opposite might be true, too: A patient fearful that an AI company is "listening in" to our conversation might be afraid to share sensitive information, which in turn could affect the quality of their medical care.
Are the recordings ever used for anything other than scribing?
As a security feature, most AI scribe companies delete the recorded conversations within a set period of time. This is to protect patient privacy and also protect doctors from lawsuits. There is widespread concern in health care that the transcriptions could be used in medical malpractice lawsuits.
But some researchers call the recordings "digital gold" that could be used to assess the quality of AI-generated medical notes or even to study broader questions about physician-patient communication.
For example, I'd love to know how other doctors handle tricky conversations with patients who are fearful of vaccines. There are theoretical best practices, but analyzing hundreds of thousands of office-visit transcripts could help doctors learn what actually works best in real life.
For now, recordings of regular doctors' appointments — unless you've been enrolled in a research study — are not used for research purposes.
Can I opt-out?
Most of my patients readily agree when I ask if it's OK to use the AI scribe software, but occasionally my patients have concerns. They worry that the data isn't really secure or that it could be used to identify them in the future.
If a patient doesn't want to use the AI scribe, it's no problem. I just take notes on the computer while they talk — it's what I've done for years before the AI scribes became available.
Opting out of AI in medicine more broadly may prove to be tricky.
"It's just everywhere," said Kim, the clinical information specialist. "It would be impossible to separate. We use it throughout the healthcare system."
Software that relies on machine learning is used for billing, for clinical decision-making, and for communication between the doctor's office and patients.
AI is often used in risk calculators, like clinical tools that estimate a patient's risk of, say, heart disease based on variables like cholesterol levels and blood pressure. AI is also common in "early warning" systems that notify clinicians their patients might be vulnerable to high-risk conditions like sepsis, based on vital signs and lab values.
Kim says it's basically impossible for patients to opt out entirely from having AI involved in their medical care, "unless you're so healthy that no risk calculators ever come near you," she said.
Will AI replace my doctor?
I asked Kim — a primary care doctor like me — if she thought AI would replace us in the coming years. If the AI scribe could learn to ask the same questions I do, could it generate a treatment plan as good — or better — as the one I recommend?
Kim thought AI might change how patients experience primary care. (Possibly for the better, she said, if AI scribes allow doctors to focus more on their patients and less on the computer!)
But ultimately, she thinks human intelligence is critical in medicine.
"It looks really good because it's really good at sounding like us, and it's really good at pretending to be us," she said. "But it's still just pretending in a way. There's no real brain."
I agree. I think the AI scribe technology has the potential to do both good and harm for health care. But the core of medicine is the relationship I have with my patients. No robot can replace that.
Dr. Mara Gordon is a family physician in Camden, NJ. Find her newsletter Your Doctor Friend on Substack.

title: NASA is recruiting new astronauts. Here are the qualifications.
text:
NASA is recruiting its next class of astronauts, inviting U.S. citizens to apply before midnight ET on Dec. 3 for the chance to "live and work" on the moon.
The space agency's application portal states there are "few vacancies" for the role, which pays $164,395 annually and requires recruits to relocate to Houston, where they'll work at the Johnson Space Center.
While the job is open to all citizens, applicants must meet certain educational criteria and possess specialized experience. In other words, not just any Tom, Dick or Harriet will qualify for the job.
The next group of astronauts is being selected as the U.S. plans to and send crewed missions to the lunar surface. NASA's recently sent a crew of four astronauts around the moon in April, setting a record for the farthest distance humans have ever traveled from our planet.
"The people we select could walk on the moon, live and work at the moon base, and help pioneer the systems and operations that will ultimately carry crews to Mars," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said in a statement. "Those missions will demand technical excellence, sound judgment, teamwork and courage."
Here are the qualifications NASA is looking for in an astronaut.
Educational background
NASA's job application portal states that applicants must fit into one of the following four educational profiles:
- A master's degree in a qualifying field of engineering, biological science, physical science, computer science or mathematics.
- Two academic years of qualifying doctoral coursework in one of those fields.
- A qualifying medical degree, such as an MD, physician assistant or nurse practitioner.
- Completion of a recognized test pilot school by July 2027.
Specialized experience
Applicants must also select a discipline they best qualify for based on their work experience, with NASA requiring three years of professional experience after completing their degree program or pilot training.
- Pilots: Must meet one of three thresholds: 750 hours as lead pilot of a high-performance jet; 1,500 hours in other fixed-wing aircraft, with 750 in command; or 1,000 hours in rotary-wing aircraft, with 300 in command. Initial flight training and drone hours are excluded.
- Flight test: Requires test pilot school completion or enrollment, with completion by July 2027, as well as three years of related flight test experience.
- Medical: At least three years of professional experience after earning a medical degree. NASA said that residencies count toward the experience.
- Biological and medical science: At least three years of related experience.
- Physical science: Three years of related work experience.
- Engineering: Three years of related work experience.
- Operations: Three years of related work experience in "high-consequence environments that require real-time decision-making and intensive teamwork, where errors carry irreversible and physical risk to personnel, missions or vehicles," NASA said.
Other requirements
Applicants must also pass a series of clearances, including medical and psychiatric exams; vision that can be corrected to 20/20 in each eye; and a background check and drug screening.
Aspiring astronauts must be able "to perform moderate to arduous physical activities, including heavy lifting, crouching, crawling and exposure to inclement weather" and "be willing to work in dangerous, life-threatening situations and live/work in remote, isolated, small or confined spaces for prolonged periods." Applicants also have to pass a swimming test.
On top of that, applicants must "be willing to deploy to space for 12 months or longer, accepting extreme isolation, austere living conditions and separation from loved ones."

title: Is it OK to have AI text your boyfriend? When using chatbots crosses a line
text:
As more people turn to chatbots to write emails or handle mundane tasks, it raises the question: Does using them for personal messages cross a line
A purple box set up on a folding table in San Francisco’s Alamo Square could have been mistaken for a tissue box. Instead, it held dozens of secrets.
Oliva Tai was nearby, watching as passersby puzzled over a sign that read, “Confession box: Everyone has an AI secret.”
Among confessions about farming out too much work or using artificial intelligence to suggest a first-date spot were several admissions about using it to write deeply personal messages: “I had AI write my breakup text.” “I had ChatGPT date my boyfriend. Every text.” “I used AI to write my girlfriend’s grandmother’s 80th birthday letter.”
“I used AI to win an argument. Lol, not proud, but I won.”
Tai, an artist who has repeated the project more than a dozen times in the Bay Area, New York and Denver, said calling it a “confession” suggested people were admitting that using AI made them feel at least a little guilty. But they used it anyway.
As more people turn to a chatbot to write emails or handle mundane tasks, it raises the question: Does using it for personal messages cross a line? Is it ever OK to use AI to write a holiday card or birthday message? What about a love letter or wedding vows?
As part of research for a Ph.D. in consumer behavior, Danielle Hass conducted vignette-based experiments to determine how people felt about using AI to write personal messages. She found that people who had used AI before felt just as guilty as those who hadn't.
“Everyone felt guilty,” said Hass, a professor at Kennesaw State University in Georgia. “The driver of this relationship was dishonesty, that people felt like they were manipulating.”
Even if people are honest about their AI use, others still view them negatively, said Scott Claessens, a senior researcher at the University of Bristol in the UK.
Claessens says his research suggests that people who use AI are perceived as lazier, less competent and less trustworthy.
He noted that people often already supplement social tasks, such as using pre-written birthday cards or poems in love notes. But something about the effortless way that AI works turns people off, he said.
“What we really want in our social relationships is for people to put effort in, because it shows that as a signal that you’re invested in the relationship,” he said.
Sarah Newman, who collaborated with Tai as director of art and education at Harvard University’s metaLAB, said AI adoption is happening so quickly that norms will likely emerge about when it’s appropriate and when it's not.
She suggested using conflicted feelings as a guide. If you imagine using AI to write your wedding vows, would you be comfortable telling your partner you used it? If not, then don’t.
“Personal messages don’t need to be perfect,” Newman said. “Part of what makes these messages authentic and endearing is that they are imperfect.”
Tai and Claessens said some situations could warrant using AI in personal situations, such as people in relationships who use it to communicate better with a partner who doesn’t share a native language. People with learning disabilities, such as dyslexia, could also use it for help.
Hass believes people are quickly accepting that AI can make them more efficient in some work contexts, but she said she’s glad people feel guilty using it for personal messages.
“Guilt’s purpose in this context is to show us our interpersonal wrongdoings,” Hass said. “It’s showing us, ‘hey, this is where you’re supposed to be human.’”
Albert Stumm writes about travel, food and wellness. Find his work at https://www.albertstumm.com

title: Klopp and Wirtz offer glimpse of bright German future
text:
"Extraordinary," "Insane," "Magnificent," "A special group." Even by Jürgen Klopp's effusive standards, Germany's 5-0 win over rivals the Netherlands on Monday was clearly pleasing.
Despite a patchy start to his reign, Klopp's relentless positivity towards a group of Germany players not viewed in the most flattering light outside the squad has been rewarded.
"Everyone will go home with a smile on their face, and for at least the next three or four months, no one will be questioning the German national team," Klopp told German public broadcaster ARD, referencing that Germany will not play again until the end of March 2027.
"Instead, they'll be thinking: 'This could really turn into something. We have wonderful footballers, great characters," Klopp said, and added: "The lads are even surprising themselves."
The former Liverpool and Borussia Dortmund coach took the job in July after Julian Nagelsmann paid the price for another German early World Cup exit, this time to Paraguay in the last 32. Klopp always preached patience, particularly after his first two matches yielded a fortunate 1-1 draw with the Netherlands and a 1-0 home loss to Greece.
Klopp hallmarks starting to emerge
It paid off on Monday as Germany performed with the hallmarks of Klopp's great club sides — fierce pressing, intensity, pace and a measure of joy. Perhaps it is in Florian Wirtz that Klopp's impact is more notable.
The 23-year-old has struggled to make a significant impact at Liverpool since moving to the Premier League from Bayer Leverkusen at the beginning of last season. But he has four goals in his last four games for Germany and is demonstrating the ability that earned him a €125 million ($137.5 million) move to England.
"I only knew him from television. I was shocked when I saw him on the pitch for the first time. An extraordinary footballer," Klopp said after the Netherlands match.
"We've also found the right position for Flo. It helps that he's so vocal. He's the first pressing player, he can press two players without getting tired."
That quality was evident in Wirtz's first goal on Monday, when he won back possession on the edge of the Dutch box before combining some dazzling footwork with a brilliant, curled finish.
Scherhant, Gruda and Wirtz make their cases
But Wirtz wasn't the only attacking bright spot for Germany. Rookie wingers Derry Scherhant and Brajan Gruda both scored and were a huge threat throughout. Klopp gave debuts to both earlier this year as he sought to spread opportunities. The pair have offered Germany a pace they often lacked under Naglesmann and his predecessor Hansi Flick.
"They can both play, my goodness," said Klopp.
Scherhant, who opened the scoring with another stunning strike, spent many days of his boyhood on the terraces of the Olympiastadion in Berlin, where Monday's game was played. Unlike many pros, he bounced about Berlin's lower league clubs as a youth before Hertha Berlin signed him up. He then moved to Freiburg in 2025 and is rapidly emerging as a player who can implement Klopp's style and reflect the coach's attitude.
"A few years ago, people told me I wouldn't make it as a pro. Then I became a pro. And even then, some people still said it wasn't enough—that the Regionalliga (Germany's fourth tier) was the best I could hope for,” Scherhant said.
"It's just unbelievable that I get to stand here now with the satisfaction of having proven those people wrong."
Proving people wrong is also a major part of Klopp's remit. After failing to get beyond the quarterfinal of a major tournament since 2016, the German public's interest in and enthusiasm for its men's national team had waned. Klopp's mission he said, was to "to prove to Germany and the world that we can play soccer."
Germany need to change perceptions
While that was achieved on Monday, the loss (and subsequent 0-0 draw) against Greece in the Nations League game were evidence that it won't all be plain sailing. Indeed, Germany have had plenty of false dawns of late, as captain Joshua Kimmich alluded to.
"We've been through a tough time," he said. "A clear victory doesn't make all that go away," he added before saying that the task was to "turn potential into quality and a team that's all about 'what ifs' into a team that's all about 'reality.' That's the art of it."
Klopp too, for all his hype, was keen not to get too far ahead of himself.
"We want to gradually solidify it. We're not done yet. We still have a few areas to work on. But I'm looking forward to our future — it's crazy what's still to come," he said.
In Nations League terms, that will be a matchup with world champions Spain, or Portugal or Belgium before qualifying for Euro 2028 begins. For now though, Klopp and his players can enjoy some time with those smiles on their faces.

title: Trump’s inner circle was tested this week. They failed
text:
President Donald Trump has spent years promising that he alone can fix America's problems. He was going to restore order, bring back technological supremacy, stop all those people supposedly laughing behind their hands at the U.S. — and he’d do it all by surrounding himself with the toughest, smartest people in the business.
His administration, we were told, would be a crack team of world-beaters, unencumbered by the dead weight of bureaucratic incompetence. Red tape be damned! Swamp be drained! Greatness is just around the corner!
It is an impressive sales pitch. But it is looking rather less impressive in practice, especially after this week.
In the space of a few days since Republicans were handed a bruising set of midterm results, Trump 2.0 has found itself confronted with a succession of rather serious tests of its ability to govern. America's aviation infrastructure suffered a spectacular failure, grounding thousands of flights last Friday. A string of outages, from Microsoft to Chase Bank to Apple, has caused widespread disruption. And now the highly-classified internal communications network used by the National Security Agency has reportedly gone down — while the president is in Asia.
There’s apparently “no evidence” that any of these multiple outages are the result of a cyber attack. But is that better or worse? Either Trump 2.0 prompted a bunch of hackers to successfully target U.S. infrastructure by starting a war nobody wanted or the country is falling apart at the seams. Take your apocalyptic pick.
Neither option reflects well on an administration that just spent two years in charge of both houses of Congress as well as the executive branch. The growing list of failures is raising legitimate questions about the resilience of the systems on which the country depends. It is also providing a rather extraordinary demonstration of what happens when a government built around bombastic bravado is asked to demonstrate some actual competence (or when it wanders into a war it doesn’t actually know how to end which, again, comes back to basic competence.)
On Friday, a nationwide ground stop brought U.S. air travel to a complete halt for four hours. The apparent cause was a problem with telecommunications infrastructure, during a contractor's transition from old copper wiring to fiber-optic cables, at a radio facility in Arkansas. If this is true, it’s extraordinary that it was allowed to happen. Was infrastructure in such a bad state that it was liable to break nationwide air traffic control comms at any time? If so, why wasn’t this a more pressing emergency than the “emergencies” declared at the southern border or in the name of tariffs last year?
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Trump himself have both tied themselves in knots trying to blame former President Joe Biden. Vice President JD Vance appeared on Fox News to suggest that the real issue is Democrats’ “ridiculous obsession with men in women's sports.”
And yes, perhaps it is the secret cabal of transgender athletes - widely-known for leaning on air traffic controllers at times of high capacity - who are to blame for all of this. But much more likely is that the GOP-led Congress, headed up by the Republican president, did not invest in creaking aviation infrastructure. In fact, it allowed Elon Musk’s pet project DOGE to cut hundreds of federal aviation jobs. And — once again — it started a war that heavily incentivized state-sponsored hackers to target American infrastructure.
While thousands of Americans were stuck in airports during an airlines ground stop of the length not seen since 9/11, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin took a government aircraft to Louisiana to attend an LSU college football game, by the way. He was subsequently spotted in a luxury box belonging to a shipping executive whose company does business with his department, getting his priorities straight.
When Mullin was eventually asked about the growing number of technology outages, his contribution was even more reassuring. Appearing on Fox News, he explained that he had consulted an unnamed technology expert, whom he described as “one guy” who was very smart with tech. This individual had suggested that the culprit might be what Trump calls “super intelligence” — or AI, as literally everybody else calls it — and its ability to write and rewrite code was overwhelming older systems. Mullin said the explanation “kind of makes sense to me.”
It is not entirely clear why the DHS secretary, who oversees the department responsible for protecting the country against cyber threats, was relying on an anonymous acquaintance for an explanation of a potential national infrastructure problem. Nor was it clear what evidence supported the theory. He nevertheless used the interview to rule out a cyber attack and assure Americans that “the homeland is secure.”
Well, if it’s good enough for “one guy,” I guess it’s “kind of” good enough for me!
The administration's other great technological headache right now is Nvidia, the semiconductor giant whose chips underpin much of the global AI industry. The company is so central to the current AI boom that even a hint of trouble around its business can send shockwaves through the technology sector and financial markets. Yet here, too, the administration has been struggling to present anything resembling a coherent strategy after Jensen Huang’s leather jackets proved themselves to be the harbinger of doom we should have all seen coming.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has publicly criticized the Commerce Department, overseen by Howard Lutnick, for dragging its feet on restrictions designed to prevent advanced Nvidia chips reaching Chinese interests through third-party companies. Bessent said his department and other national security agencies had been pushing for action for months, while Lutnick's department controlled the process.
The result is a rather extraordinary spectacle: a government that claims to be engaged in an existential technological contest with China, while senior officials appear unable to agree on how to stop sensitive American technology reaching China.
Oh, and the president was advised by U.S. intelligence months ago that Jensen Huang was probably sleeping with a suspected Chinese spy but he brought him onto Air Force One and invited him round for dinner at the White House anyway. A little dose of presidential willful ignorance to help the intra-departmental chaos go down. Lucky this doesn’t go to the heart of America’s national security and economic future, otherwise we’d really be in trouble!
And now, just as Americans are digesting the latest reports of technology failures, CNN has reported that the NSA's highly classified internal communications network, known as NSA Net, has gone down. The network allows agency personnel to communicate classified information internally. Officials are reportedly working to establish the scope of the problem, with staggered arrivals introduced for personnel.
Trump's own contribution has been to shrug. Asked about the recent outages Tuesday by a reporter during his visit to the Philippines, he replied: “It's like when you're big and powerful, and you have all the money. Things like that happen. It's fine.”
So here’s the president who has made a career out of promising that everything in America can be made bigger, stronger and better, simply by putting him in charge, and yet mysteriously, everything seems to be disintegrating. Standing among the ruins, the MAGA lackeys then start finger-pointing at literally anyone: Biden, trans athletes, pronouns in the flight deck. But don’t worry, one guy they know has a viewpoint!
Establishing the facts, explaining how you intend to fix things and assuming responsibility (remember “the buck stops here,” anyone?) used to be a thing. But that was back when woke commie beardo weirdos were in charge, I guess. These days it’s all about “things like that happen,” which is truly the sort of insightful leadership America has been craving all along.
To round it all out, Tuesday saw the U.S. lose its measles elimination status after 26 years of being measles-free. Another fantastic administrative effort, contributed to by the genius of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. Outbreaks across the country over the past two years have seen multiple people — mainly children — sickened. Nine have died.
This is an administration that has spent enormous amounts of time and political capital dismantling expertise, attacking civil servants, sidelining scientists and treating government institutions as hostile territory to be conquered. It has promised that the private sector instincts of its appointees, the technological genius of its billionaire allies and the force of Trump's personality would be more than enough to replace the supposedly dysfunctional machinery of government and workers.
And yet! It turns out that the dysfunction was coming from inside the house. Who would’ve thought? While Trump spends time in southeast Asia, we’re left with a guy who loves ball games, a vice president stuck on culture wars and a man whose main concern when it comes to flights is whether you wear pajamas onboard - while planes stop flying and basic infrastructure goes down, company by company, day by day, advent calendar-style.
God bless America, indeed — or at least, please look kindly on us as we veer unsteadily into a ditch in a clown car, driven by circus performers yelling about how the problem just has to be the road.
