title: Retail spending slowed in October as high prices gave shoppers pause
text: NEW YORK (AP) — Shoppers increased spending more slowly in October as economic uncertainty and high prices led more Americans to pull back on a variety of purchases from cars to clothing and furniture, even their hobbies, ahead of the unofficial start to the holiday shopping season. Retail sales rose 0.2% in October, down from a 0.8% gain in September, according to the Commerce Department's report released Tuesday. Sales at gas stations rose 1.5% last month after spiking 30.3% in September. Excluding gas stations, retail sales rose just 0.1%. Overall retail sales were pulled down by a decline in sales at motor vehicle and parts dealers. Motor vehicles and parts dealers had a 1.6% drop in sales in October, reversing a 1.3% increase in September. Excluding auto-related stores, retail sales rose 0.6%. Adjusting for higher prices, consumer spending was "negative," according to Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union. The Consumer Price Index rose 0.4% in October, according to data released last week, hotter than expected. "The cautious consumer is back," Long wrote Tuesday. "October retail sales were tepid. Budgets are tight for many households." She noted the drop in gas prices in November will help free up some much-needed cash this holiday season, but middle-class and moderate-income households are "feeling the strain." Yet even with a recent decline in gas prices, a gallon still costs nearly 20% more than at this time last year. Business was down at clothing stores and furniture and home furnishing retailers last month, according to the report. Sporting goods, musical instruments, books and hobby stores also saw sales decline. Such retailers had performed strongly through the spring and summer as consumers treated themselves to little splurges, Long noted. One of the bright spots was online retailers, which saw a boost from a two-day Amazon Prime Day event, which took place in early October. That sector was up 1.2%. WATCH: How companies are using AI to make you spend more money The data offers only a snapshot of consumer spending and doesn't include activities like travel and hotel stays. But the lone services category — restaurants — registered a 0.2% increase. Still, the so-called control group—which excludes food services, autos, building materials and gas station sales and is used to calculate economic growth—rose a solid 0.6%. Higher energy prices are ricocheting into other parts of the economy, with airfares, public transportation and shipping all jumping in price. Grocery prices, for example, increased 0.4%, a painful uptick after years of increases, according to new Labor Department data. Massive investments in artificial intelligence have exacerbated inflation by driving up computer chip prices and, in turn, prices for laptops, phones and other consumer electronics. Retailers are preparing for a surge in business over the Thanksgiving weekend, the unofficial start of the holiday shopping period. Stores have heavily advertised deals to lure customers who increasingly buy when they think prices have dropped. Companies like Kohl's and Target and Walmart are trying to drive the affordability message home through marketing. Target said it's offering more than 8,000 new gifts for the winter holidays, with more than half exclusive to the retailer. Most of the new holiday items at Target are $20 or less, including thousands of items that are priced at $5 and under. Kohl's has increased the number of gift sets across different types of merchandise. Americans, despite the rising cost of credit, continue to rely on cards to finance spending, and credit experts say that defaults have been stable. "More Americans are carrying credit cards than ever, and they're handling them well," said Charles Wise, head of global research and consulting at the credit reporting agency TransUnion. Wise noted that outstanding credit card balances as of last month hit $1.17 trillion, up 5.1% from the year-ago period, based on data covering 178.5 million consumers who held an active credit card as of last month. Yet serious delinquency rates held steady, he said. That signals that "consumers remain disciplined borrowers heading into the holidays," he added. Stephen Lebovitz, CEO of CBL Properties, a Chattanooga, Tennessee, mall owner, remains optimistic about the holiday shopping season, noting that higher gas prices haven't derailed business. He believes that a solid job market is still propping up spending among its middle-class customers. Malls have also been helped by a resurgence in business at movie theaters, fueled by Generation Z shoppers. "People are working and earning, and they're still spending," he said.

title: Lisa Cook lawyer signals Fed governor won't attend Trump committee's hearing
text:
Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook's attorney on Tuesday gave the strongest signal yet that his client will not attend a hearing at the White House with a "committee of inquiry" investigating mortgage fraud allegations against Cook.
The committee established last month by President Donald Trump, who has previously tried to remove Cook from the central bank's board, is pretextual and poses a threat to the Fed, attorney Abbe Lowell wrote in a letter to presidential counsel Will Scharf.
"Governor Cook has no legal obligation to participate in an unfair hearing — and indeed, has a duty to the Federal Reserve to decline to participate in any proceeding that would undermine the institution's unique status and independence," Lowell wrote in the letter, which is dated Monday and was made public Tuesday.
The latest correspondence came nearly two weeks after the White House committee delayed its proposed hearing with Cook to Dec. 14 from Nov. 5. Lowell said that any hearing with Cook could not take place until at least December because of conflicts with her Fed duties.
While Lowell had raised strong concerns from the outset about the legitimacy of the committee, he initially said Cook "welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name."
But he has continued to cast doubts on both the committee's purpose and its composition of three executive branch officials, including National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett.
Lowell's tone sounded more hostile than ever in this week's letter, the first known to be sent by either party in the matter since the Republican Party's devastating losses in the midterm elections on Nov. 3.
He accused Scharf and the committee of seeking "only to manufacture 'cause' for a predetermined removal outcome."
Lowell highlighted two top concerns. First, he asserted that Hassett "is not competent to serve on any factfinding committee" because his prior comments about Cook "demonstrate that he has prejudged the issue."
Second, Lowell called it "fundamentally unfair" that the committee is demanding Cook hand over documents "immediately," while pledging to provide the governor with its own records just seven days before the hearing.
"Your and the Committee's failure to address these legitimate issues, over multiple weeks of back-and-forth correspondence, reinforces my prior observation: President Trump's decision to fire Governor Cook has already been made," Lowell wrote.
"Consequently, this Committee process appears to be a façade designed to obscure a predetermined decision to fire Governor Cook or to unreasonably manufacture a supposed 'adverse inference' if she does not participate in a process that does not comport with the requirements of a fair hearing," the lawyer wrote.
Lowell told Scharf that Cook would still be prepared to appear for a hearing if the White House "implements fair procedures." But the "ultimatums" Scharf gave in his last reply in early November "do not provide a productive path forward to enabling that participation," Lowell wrote.
The White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on Lowell's letter.
Trump, who frequently urges the Fed to lower interest rates, has long sought to fire Cook, an appointee of former President Joe Biden.
Cook, the first Black woman to serve on the Fed's Board of Governors, last voted to cut rates in December 2025, siding with the majority. The Fed unanimously voted to raise rates after its meeting in September.
Trump officials sent a criminal referral last year alleging Cook may have committed mortgage fraud by falsely claiming different properties as her primary residence in order to get more favorable terms. Cook adamantly denied wrongdoing, and, after Trump tried to fire her in August 2025, filed a lawsuit to block her removal.
The Supreme Court in June prevented Trump from firing Cook, but gave him a path to try again if additional legal steps were taken. In August, the White House told Cook it was reviving its efforts to fire her on mortgage-related grounds. In October, Trump signed a presidential memo establishing the committee of inquiry to investigate allegations that Cook lied on records related to "one or more mortgage instruments."

title: Daydream’s new AI agent acts as your personal stylist — and can shop for you, too
text:
Can an AI agent serve as your personal stylist? That’s what e-commerce veteran Julie Bornstein’s fashion startup, Daydream, aims to find out.
On Tuesday, the company launched “Daydream Agent,” an AI agent that is described as a personal stylist that can help you plan a look, virtually try on clothes, surface relevant pieces based on your taste, and more.
The idea, the company explains, is to put a personal stylist in everyone’s pocket. This application of AI could be promising, given that early adopters of consumer AI agents like Meta’s Muse have found that online shopping is a key use case.
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg recently noted that shopping was a top activity for Muse’s over 10 million users and that 25% of people who set up Muse now use it daily.
In Daydream’s case, the fashion startup has been focused on using AI to deliver personalized shopping results to its users. Its new AI agent builds on its earlier work with an AI chatbot that could help users find outfits and make suggestions, but not complete purchases.
Now the company says its Daydream Agent expands on that experience by remembering each shopper’s own personal style, fit preferences, and budget to refine its recommendations. Shoppers can also upload a photo to have the agent reuse that image to virtually try on any item they’ve saved. When they find something they like, the agent can complete a purchase through a one-click checkout process.
The agent can also handle other fashion-related tasks, like keeping an eye on when items go on sale or when brands have a new drop, or providing weekly updates or spotting new fashion trends.
Also, instead of leaving items in their cart, shoppers can save pieces they’re interested in to a persistent “clothing rack” so they can compare options and think about their purchases before deciding what to buy. Shoppers can also connect their own closet and their calendar to the agent, helping them to build outfits around what they already own and plan what to wear for upcoming events.
The tech works by pulling real-time pricing and availability information from its catalog of over 10,000 brands, then combines that with its fashion-focused artificial intelligence. It’s powered by a combination of OpenAI, Gemini, and Claude models, which it fine-tuned, along with its own trained models designed for particular use cases.
However, considering that fashion is more of an art than a science, the company says it’s keeping humans in the loop. To do so, this month it brought on its first stylist in residence, Francesca Salih, an international fashion stylist and the founder of StyleGrid. Salih provides the startup with styling content that helps shape how the agent pulls together outfits and offers advice. This advice is part of the company’s fashion knowledge database, which the agent experience relies on.
Bornstein, formerly Stitch Fix’s COO and the founder of The Yes (exited to Pinterest in 2022), started Daydream in 2023 as an AI search engine. The company, backed by $50 million in funding from Forerunner Ventures, Index Ventures, GV, and True Ventures, says more than 2 million shoppers have used Daydream to discover apparel and accessories since its June 2025 launch.

title: Hyperscale data centers use 2% of US electricity
text:
One flashpoint for the tech industry’s all-in push on large language models has been the sudden rush to turn investment money into hyperscale data centers. The rush hasn’t allowed anyone to plan how to supply the required electricity cleanly or with minimal impact on ratepayers. Instead, it has been difficult to even collect information on what’s being built.
A new study has tallied energy use and estimated emissions for hyperscalers operating in the United States between May 2024 and April 2025. They weren’t able to differentiate between AI compute and more traditional data services, but it provides a clear point of reference to track moving forward.
Finding the centers
The team started with a list of 675 facilities from a commercial database based on news reports, company statements, and satellite imagery. They dropped any that didn’t have a reported electrical capacity or that they couldn’t verify was a suitably large building with the expected cooling and electrical connection equipment. That reduced the list to 403 data centers with an average electrical capacity of about 40 megawatts.
In a way, that makes this a very conservative estimate, since 272 facilities believed to be large data centers were left out. But if you’re interested in AI data centers, specifically, it’s also true that some of the facilities included may not fall in that category.
That fact also introduces some uncertainty in the actual power usage of these data centers. Relying on other research, they use a range—some conventional data centers run at an average of about 48 percent of capacity, while AI training loads have been running higher, at around 70 percent.
Putting that together, the total power usage for the year by these 403 data centers was estimated at 68 to 99 terawatt-hours. That amounts to 1.5 to 2.2 percent of total US electricity use, on par with the total used by Wisconsin or Indiana.

title: ESA’s Hera spacecraft is flying rectangles around NASA’s asteroid crash site
text:
Europe’s Hera spacecraft has arrived at the scene of NASA’s historic asteroid collision to uncover what really happened when a spacecraft slammed into Dimorphos in 2022. Its close-up investigation could reveal whether the impact left a crater or reshaped the asteroid entirely, providing crucial clues for protecting Earth from future threats.
The European Space Agency's Hera spacecraft has reached its destination, arriving near two asteroids that could help scientists learn how to protect Earth from dangerous space rocks. The spacecraft, which is roughly the size of a small car, is now traveling about 25 to 30 kilometers from the Didymos asteroid system as it begins its first scientific observations.
This initial stage, known as the "early characterization phase," is designed to give researchers a broad understanding of the two asteroids and their surroundings. Of particular interest is Dimorphos, the smaller asteroid that NASA deliberately struck with its DART spacecraft in 2022 to test whether a collision could change an asteroid's path.
"Our aim right now is to gather the big-picture findings of relevance to supporting the mission's planetary defense goals," explains mission scientist Michael Kueppers.
"During this phase, our images will reveal for the first time what a small asteroid looks like globally, having experienced a hypervelocity impact in the context of the first asteroid deflection test, when NASA's DART spacecraft impacted it to change its orbit in 2022."
"Previous predictions by our impact models suggested many different ways the asteroid body might react, but Hera will reveal which forecast was the correct one - if any!"
Why Hera Is Flying in Rectangles Around Two Asteroids
Navigating around asteroids presents challenges that are very different from those encountered by spacecraft exploring planets. The main asteroid, Didymos, measures approximately 780 meters across and has gravitational pull about 40,000 times weaker than Earth's. Its smaller companion, Dimorphos, is just 151 meters wide and has gravity roughly 200,000 times weaker than Earth's.
With gravity this weak, maintaining a conventional circular orbit is not practical. Hera instead travels around the shared center of gravity of the two asteroids, moving at a remarkably slow speed of approximately 12 centimeters per second. That is comparable to the pace of an insect crawling quickly across the ground.
Rather than following a smooth circular path, Hera moves along nearly straight trajectories. At alternating intervals of three and four days, the spacecraft fires its thrusters while moving away from the asteroids, changing direction by 90 degrees. These carefully timed maneuvers create a series of unusual "rectangular orbits" that keep Hera approximately 25 to 30 kilometers from the asteroid pair.
The unusual navigation strategy builds on experience gained during ESA's Rosetta comet mission. It also provides an important safety advantage. If a planned thruster firing fails, Hera will naturally drift farther from the asteroids instead of moving toward a potentially dangerous collision. Because the spacecraft travels so slowly, each course correction requires very little propellant.
Hera Prepares for a Closer Look at the Asteroids
Next month, Hera is expected to begin its "detailed characterization phase," bringing it significantly closer to Didymos and Dimorphos. During this stage, the spacecraft will switch from rectangular flight paths to more complex hyperbolic trajectories shaped like bowties, beginning at distances of approximately 20 kilometers.
The mission is directed from ESA's ESOC mission control center in Darmstadt, Germany. Despite Hera being approximately 196.5 million kilometers from Earth, controllers maintain contact with the spacecraft for about eight hours each day.
Communication is handled through four enormous Deep Space Antennas, each measuring 35 meters in diameter, at facilities in Argentina, Spain, and Australia.
The mission control team also works closely with ESA's Flight Dynamics team. Using data transmitted by Hera, these specialists calculate its exact location relative to the two asteroids and develop the commands needed to guide it safely from one planned position to another.
Investigating NASA's Historic Asteroid Collision
Hera's observations will help answer some of the biggest questions left unanswered by NASA's first asteroid deflection experiment.
On September 26, 2022, NASA's DART spacecraft deliberately collided with Dimorphos. The 580-kilogram spacecraft struck the asteroid at approximately 6.1 kilometers per second, producing a massive cloud of debris that spread across 10,000 kilometers of space.
The impact successfully changed Dimorphos' motion, shortening the time it takes to orbit Didymos by about 33 minutes. This was a major achievement for planetary defense, demonstrating that deliberately crashing a spacecraft into an asteroid could alter its trajectory.
However, the experiment also raised important questions. Scientists still do not know exactly how the impact changed Dimorphos itself. Did the collision excavate a large crater, or did it significantly reshape the entire asteroid?
Researchers also need more precise information about Dimorphos' composition, internal structure, and mass. Understanding these properties could explain why the impact produced a much larger orbital change than computer simulations had predicted.
These details are essential for developing the collision method, known as kinetic impact, into a dependable planetary defense strategy. If scientists can determine how different types of asteroids respond to being struck, they will be better equipped to predict the results of future attempts to redirect potentially hazardous objects.
A Close-Up Investigation of the Asteroid Crash Site
Over the coming months, Hera will conduct a detailed investigation of Dimorphos, effectively examining the scene of NASA's historic collision.
The spacecraft will use several scientific instruments to study the asteroid and will release two small CubeSats, each about the size of a shoebox. These miniature spacecraft will travel even closer to the asteroid to collect additional measurements, with the mission eventually advancing to landing operations.
Together, the observations should provide scientists with a much clearer understanding of how Dimorphos responded to DART's impact and why the experiment worked so effectively. That knowledge could prove crucial if Earth ever faces a dangerous asteroid on a collision course.

title: Fossil fuel emissions are down in 2026. Green energy isn’t the reason
text:

Scientists project that global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels will decrease by 0.4 percent this year, after having grown by 0.8 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025.
But the dip may not last. The lower emissions are probably driven by high oil prices stemming from the Iran war, researchers report November 9 in Nature Climate Change.
Global emissions probably would have grown again this year without the energy shock of the Iran war, says Glen Peters, a climate scientist at the Center for International Climate Research in Oslo, Norway. “So the energy transition that’s happening … it’s not quite big enough to get emissions heading downward yet.”
For the study, Peters and his colleagues used data on countries’ electric vehicle stocks and wind and solar energy generation to project those technologies impacts on global fossil CO2 emissions through 2028. The team used the generative AI model Claude to source data and write code for analysis.
By year’s end, global emissions will reach 38.24 gigatons, the researchers found, which is about 0.16 gigatons less than were emitted in 2025. For comparison, annual global emissions fell by nearly two gigatons in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic and by about 0.5 gigatons in 2009 because of the global financial crisis.
If electric vehicle sales and solar and wind capacity continue growing at the rates they did in 2026, those technologies should counteract about 63 percent of the growth in emissions from 2025 to 2028 — or help avoid about 1.64 gigatons of added emissions.
The results indicate that the energy transition needs to accelerate if humankind is to realize consistently declining emissions, though EVs, solar and wind are already having a large impact. Without the offset in emissions provided by those technologies, global emissions would have risen by 1.9 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025, the researchers note.
It’s very hard to say exactly how long it will take for humanity to reach peak emissions, Peters says. However, he notes, “the fact that we’re talking about this means that we’re close to that point.”

title: What exactly is a light-day? Here's what Voyager 1's latest milestone means for the interstellar probe
text:
After nearly 50 years traveling through space, NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft is approaching a milestone no human-made object has reached before: a distance of one light-day from Earth.
This milestone — which Voyager 1 is expected to reach on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026, at 5:16:07 a.m. EST (1016:07 GMT) — highlights the immense distances Voyager 1 has traveled and the challenges of communicating with spacecraft operating in the outer reaches of the solar system and beyond.
Astronomers use a measurement known as a light-day to describe how far light travels in 24 hours. Light moves at approximately 186,000 miles (300,000 kilometers) per second, meaning one light-day is roughly 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers), according to a statement from NASA.
Although the term light-day might sound like a measurement of time, it is actually a unit of distance, much like a light-year. Astronomers use light-based measurements because conventional miles and kilometers become increasingly difficult to comprehend when describing the enormous distances between objects in space.
For perspective on how far Voyager 1 has travelled, sunlight takes about eight minutes and 20 seconds to reach Earth, meaning our planet is approximately 8.3 light-minutes from the sun. Radio signals traveling between Earth and Mars can take anywhere from three to 22 minutes, depending on the planets' positions in their orbits, according to the statement.
By comparison, when Voyager 1 reaches one light-day from Earth, a radio signal sent from the probe will take a full 24 hours to reach mission controllers on Earth, and a command transmitted from Earth will take another 24 hours to reach the spacecraft.
The communication delay affects how engineers operate spacecraft at such distances. Unlike spacecraft operating closer to Earth, which can receive commands and return data with relatively little delay, communicating with Voyager 1 requires mission controllers to account for the extended signal travel time when planning spacecraft operations, troubleshooting technical issues and evaluating the results of commands sent to the probe.
Voyager 1 has been traveling away from Earth since its launch on Sept. 5, 1977. Now cruising through interstellar space at nearly 38,000 mph (61,000 kph), the spacecraft has spent more than 49 years covering the distance that light can cross in a single day.
Even at that speed, Voyager 1 is moving relatively slowly compared with light itself. Its twin, Voyager 2, which launched in 1977 on a different trajectory, is expected to reach the same one-light-day milestone in November 2035.
As Voyager 1 and, eventually, Voyager 2 continue their journeys through interstellar space, their growing distances from Earth offer a measure of both the reach of human exploration and the communication challenges that come with sending spacecraft ever farther into the cosmos.

title: 'It was really scary': Mother describes sheltering during Russia strikes on Kyiv bridge
text:
The alarms warning of a ballistic missile threat went off just before 23:30 on Monday in Kyiv. Moments later came the boom of explosions.
Once again, the main bridges over the broad River Dnipro that cuts through the city were the target and this time the Russian missiles hit what they wanted.
Close to one end of the Pivnichnyi (Northern) bridge there is a large crater and in the pouring rain, water now rushes through it to the river below. Chunks of tarmac and metal are scattered around.
At its broadest point, the jagged hole is about eight metres wide.
The crossing is closed to all traffic apart from the occasional fire engine or police car passing at high speed. By contrast, nearby roads are jammed with cars and trucks, forced to take long detours.
Anyone in a hurry to move around this city has to walk, or cycle, across the bridge, picking their way through the wreckage. In the miserable weather, that also means getting very wet.
Masha and her family moved to a flat next to the bridge because they had been living by a power plant that kept getting hit by Russian missiles.
Last night, she was in the kitchen of their new place when the Russians struck the bridge. She thought her windows would be blown out of their frames by the explosions.
"It was really scary. We had no idea they'd hit here so much. It's like we're cursed," Masha told me, describing grabbing her child and running into the corridor for protection.
But somehow, she still managed to sound cheerful.
"It's difficult, but we're used to it. And we try to take the positive from everything. Like: we survived today! So we can be happy about that."
From the damage, it looks like Russia targeted the same spot on the bridge with a volley of three missiles, aiming to keep the road closed for as long as possible.
A major recovery operation is under way, with firefighters and engineers in fluorescent overalls working to evaluate the extent of the damage. But it looks like the disruption will continue for some time.
Further along the Dnipro River, the Pivdennyi (Southern) bridge was also hit on Monday night, with four missiles.
The metro line across it was suspended for a while, although by mid-afternoon it had been restored. The mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said road transport in one direction was also being partially restored.
On the Pivnichnyi bridge, a man with a bag of tennis rackets on his back was gazing at the crater in front of him. He was heading home from the courts after he had travelled on foot to the left bank.
"It is upsetting," Anatolii told us. "Then when you read the news of what our side did to the Crimea bridge, you do feel a bit better."
That is because there was a battle of the bridges overnight.
Ukrainian missiles hit the one Russia had built to occupied Crimea, and caused serious damage. That bridge is prized by Russian President Vladimir Putin personally, a symbol of his illegal 2014 takeover.
Ukrainians loathe it for the same reason and now a section has collapsed into the sea, along with its towering arch.
To many here, the timing feels significant: a blow to Putin's image, just as he wants to seem most powerful at this week's summit with the US and China.
But for Kyiv resident Antonina, today is just another challenge to overcome.
The 67-year-old, who we met pulling a shopping trolley through the debris on a bridge in the Ukrainian capital, was heading to see her son on the right bank, but taxi drivers were charging a fortune to go round, so she decided to walk.
"What else could I do?" she shrugged.
"It was a very scary night. It felt like something exploded right over my head. We will get through this, but I just wish the war would end."

title: ‘The game is in danger’: PFA head Maheta Molango on Fifa, Infantino and football’s future
text:
After five years in charge of the Professional Footballers’ Association, what has Maheta Molango learned? “The game is in danger,” the 43-year-old says. “I’ve learned that the game I loved and led me to first play and then advise and then lead a club and today to lead the PFA, is in danger because it is being forgotten.”
In 2026, with football ubiquitous on all platforms, with a World Cup that generated $15bn (£11.4m) in revenue, and with attendances across the English pyramid growing year on year, it may seem hard to imagine forgetting about the game. But Molango’s unique perspective as head of the English players’ union observes a different picture; one where the future of the sport is being determined not by what will maintain its popularity, but what will make the most money.
“What I’ve seen over the last few years is that I attend meetings where we talk about everything except for the game,” Molango says. “And I think we’ve allowed people to enter the game that did not enter it for the right reasons. They did not enter the game to make it better. They did not enter the game because they loved it. They entered the game because they saw money in the game and because they saw influence in the game. And I’m very concerned about that because, ultimately, if you don’t have a good game, if you don’t have a good product, you don’t have an industry.”
Molango is speaking at a potentially critical juncture for the future of football. Wednesday is the deadline for candidates for the role of Fifa president to put their name forward for March’s election. Gianni Infantino appears likely to win an unprecedented fourth term despite the cascade of scandal that has dogged much of his decade in charge. Infantino’s tenure has also brought about enormous changes of which Molango, whose union had 345 members playing at this year’s World Cup, 27.6% of the total, is highly critical.
The expansion of the World Cup is one central issue; where 32 teams became 48 at the men’s tournament this past summer and perhaps 64 in 2030. The changes, which players’ unions say were made without consulting players, have led to knock-on effects on the calendar that mean the PFA is pursuing Fifa through the European courts to ensure “the legal rights of players to take guaranteed and protected breaks”. But they have also damaged, in Molango’s mind, what should be the sport’s most precious event and for spurious reasons.
“Can anyone who really believes in the concept of the World Cup think that having a 64-team tournament makes sense?” he says. “We may as well call it a summer friendly tournament. And I cannot buy the narrative that says: ‘Oh, it’s about making football truly global.’ That’s just not true. I think it’s disrespectful to think that people in the Congo want to be gifted access to the World Cup. We don’t need favours, we just need opportunities. We want to deserve to be at the World Cup, we don’t need it to be gifted to us, thank you very much. Don’t treat us as if we need to thank you for giving us something.”
Then there is the question of integrity. Last summer’s World Cup brought an incident which, for many in the game, crossed a red line: the overturning of the suspension awarded to the USA’s Folarin Balogun, after an intervention by Donald Trump. “What happened with Balogun is scandalous,” Molango says. “Because my son can say to me: ‘Football is corrupt.’ It’s unacceptable that you’ve allowed a situation where people can think that. Governing bodies must protect the integrity of the game and not just that, the perception of integrity as well.”
Molango was born in Switzerland to a Congolese father and an Italian mother. He is an Italian national and began his career as a professional footballer in Spain, at Atlético Madrid. He made no appearances for the club, however, before moving to Brighton (a club that was a different proposition in 2005: “We were playing at the Withdean and I was washing my own kit at home”). From there he moved across and down the English football pyramid before finishing in Spain. After retirement he retrained in Spain as a lawyer, establishing the country’s first sports law practice, before he became the chief executive of Mallorca. He took the club to the depths of the third tier, then back to La Liga in consecutive seasons before taking charge at the PFA, replacing the longtime leader Gordon Taylor at a time of tumult for the organisation.
To visit the PFA’s smart, new offices in London’s Liverpool Street, bedecked in replica kits and with a timeline of players’ developing rights in the entrance hall, is to see an organisation that has come out the other end of an intensive period of reform. An independent review into the PFA’s governance was launched in 2018 after concerns over the use of funds. The outcome led not only to Molango’s appointment but also to the introduction of a players’ board – now led by the impressive Omar Beckles alongside Ben Davies of Tottenham and Chelsea’s Lucy Bronze among others – as well as non-executive directors and a committee focusing on the ethics of the organisation.
“The PFA had a credibility issue,” Molango says. “We called an independent expert. They came in, they assessed, and they changed the governance. So I think we led the way. We demonstrated that sometimes you don’t need to be rotten to be wanting to change, you just need to acknowledge that things move on.”
Ten years after the reforms that followed the Sepp Blatter era, Molango believes that Fifa must change again. “It’s a sick system,” he says, “and for me we shouldn’t be talking about individuals, we should be talking about governance. The system as currently constructed is a system that will always foster the wrong behaviour. Because inevitably the decision taken will not be for what’s good for the game. It will be for what’s good for the next election.”
If change doesn’t occur, there is no guarantee in Molango’s mind that football’s status as the world’s favourite sport, and a cultural unifier, will continue. “I think we live in a world where there’s tough competition for entertainment and what I think will happen is that people will lose interest and move on. They move on to other sports, to other sources of entertainment and in the end we’ll kill the industry. We’ll kill it because we’re no longer the only players in the playground. There’s a lot of people and a lot of people who have a good product. I think we need to go back to focusing on the quality of our product. Because football has a real problem.”

title: Jeffries shifts strategy amid growing Democratic divisions in US House
text:
On the eve of Democratic leadership elections in the United States House of Representatives, Hakeem Jeffries has confirmed plans to force fellow Democrats to take a recorded vote on his nomination for speaker.
Jeffries, the chamber’s current minority leader, told reporters at the US Capitol on Tuesday he was taking the new approach instead of — as some of his top allies had hoped — a vote by acclamation, which requires no ballot.
The move effectively forces House Democrats to publicly weigh in on whether they support Jeffries’s leadership.
Jeffries, a New York Democrat poised to become the House’s first Black speaker, argued that a recorded vote was the same method his party used when it retook control of the chamber in 2018 during President Donald Trump’s first term.
“It certainly seems to me to be appropriate that we take exactly the same approach to give every single person the opportunity to weigh in, one way or the other, on who the caucus feels is best positioned … to help move us forward into the new Congress,” Jeffries said during his news conference.
The strategy shift, which was first reported by Punchbowl News, comes amid growing Democratic dissent over having Jeffries in control of the party’s messaging and policy priorities in the US House.
Some progressive members, particularly newly elected ones, had reportedly threatened to call for a recorded vote to extract policy concessions from Jeffries.
Without unanimous backing, the vote to nominate Jeffries could highlight dissent within the Democratic Party.
One of the most vocal holdouts, Congressman-elect Don Leonard of Ohio, has publicly refused to commit to Jeffries unless he received guarantees on some progressive priorities, including halting US military aid to Israel and reforming campaign finance standards set by the Supreme Court case Citizens United.
“Unless Speaker Jeffries is willing to commit to enforcing our nation’s laws like the Leahy Law against Israeli genocide in Gaza, unless the speaker is willing to get to the heart of this crisis which is Citizens United, he will not have my vote,” the Ohio Democrat said in a video posted to social media.
Jeffries’s preemptive countermove effectively strips progressive members of leverage heading into Wednesday’s closed-door vote by forcing them to go on record against his leadership.
It also highlights a weakness in their efforts: the lack of another candidate for speaker.
On Monday, Congresswoman Ayanna Pressley of Massachusetts dismissed the idea she would mount a challenge to Jeffries.
Last week, she rallied her social media followers to sign a petition to shape the Democratic majority’s agenda, spurring questions about whether she would run for the speaker role. But she has since brushed those aside.
“I do not need to be the speaker of the House to speak for the people,” Pressley said at a town hall in her district.
When asked about the resistance he faces from his fellow Democrats, Jeffries told reporters they would “have to talk to” dissenting party members about why they oppose his leadership.
“We’re going to have a vote tomorrow. The caucus is going to be able to work its will. And we’ll see what the outcome is tomorrow,” Jeffries said. “In less than 24 hours, you’ll be able to know.”
Jeffries is expected to handily win Wednesday’s vote, which would give the leader an idea of the support he has when the 120th Congress is sworn in on January 3.
The speakership will be confirmed in a separate roll call vote on the floor of the US House early in the new year.

title: U.S. identifies remains of 6 soldiers killed in Korean War, including teens
text:
Six soldiers who died in the Korean War, including two teenagers, have been accounted for decades after their deaths, the Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency announced Monday.
The identifications are part of an ongoing effort to locate and identify the remains of those killed in the Korean War. When a soldier is marked as accounted for, they receive a burial with full military honors.
U.S. Army Cpl. Jackie Lee Thurman was a member of Battery B, 99th Field Artillery Battalion, 1st Cavalry Division. Thurman, 18, was a forward observer near Waegwan, South Korea, when his post came under heavy attack, according to the agency, and was last seen trying to evacuate a shell-shocked officer from the area while under heavy enemy fire.
Afterward, Thurman was reported missing in action. A presumptive finding of death was issued on Dec. 31, 1953. His remains were declared unrecoverable two years later, in January 1956.
The agency said that a set of remains, designated X-5814 Tanggok, was recovered by the Quartermaster Graves Registration Company near Kumhwa-dong, South Korea, in October 1952. The remains were interred as unknowns at the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific in Honolulu, Hawaii. In November 2022, the agency disinterred the remains. Analysis allowed the agency's scientists to identify the remains as Thurman's. He was marked as accounted for by the agency on May 18, 2026.
U.S. Army 1st Lt. Raymond Banker Gilbert was a member of B Battery, 503rd Field Artillery Battalion, 2nd Infantry Division, who was reported missing during the battle of the Ch'ongch'on River in North Korea, according to the agency. Witness statements allowed the Army to determine that Gilbert, 23, had been taken as a prisoner of war by the Chinese People's Volunteer Army and died from battlefield wounds in a POW camp on Jan. 31, 1951.
After the war, a recovered set of remains was returned to U.S. custody as part of a 1954 exchange known as Operation Glory, the agency said. The remains could not be identified at the time and were buried as an unknown at the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific. They were disinterred on July 1, 2024, and sent to the agency's laboratory. Analysis, circumstantial and historical evidence allowed the agency to identify the remains as Gilbert's. His remains were marked as accounted for on June 4, 2026.
U.S. Army Cpl. William R. Laughlin Jr. was a member of Company D, 1st Battalion, 32nd Infantry Regiment, 7th Infantry Division, attached to the 31st Regimental Combat Team, according to the agency. Laughlin, 21, was among the U.S. soldiers ambushed by the Chinese People's Volunteer Army at the Chosin Reservoir in North Korea.
The ambush sparked a 17-day battle in frigid weather. Each side took thousands of casualties. U.S. and United Nations forces eventually retreated south toward the supply base of Hagaru-ri. Laughlin could not be located after the battle and was reported missing in action on Dec. 2, 1950. A presumptive finding of death was issued on Dec. 31, 1953.
A pair of remains returned during Operation Glory were connected to an isolated burial east of the Chosin Reservoir. They could not be identified and were interred as unknowns at the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific. The agency disinterred the remains in July 2022 and used modern forensic techniques at its laboratory to identify them as Laughlin's. He was marked as accounted for by the agency on Sept. 28, 2026.
U.S. Army Sgt. Joseph A. Platzkoester, a member of Company H, 2nd Battalion, 38th Infantry Regiment, 2nd Infantry Division, was last seen during an ambush near Inje in South Korea. Platzkoester, 28, was part of a convoy doing counteroffensive clearing operations at the time, the agency said. The convoy encountered an enemy roadblock. While his battalion pushed through, Platzkoester could not be found after the fight and was reported missing in action.
The area was searched, but Platzkoester's remains were not found. A presumptive finding of death was issued on Dec. 31, 1953, and his remains were declared nonrecoverable in January 1956.
In 1951, the 148th Quartermaster Graves Registration Company found a set of remains that could not be identified. They were interred as an unknown at the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific. In November 2023, the set of remains was disinterred and sent to the agency's laboratory, where analysis identified them as Platzkoester's. He was marked as accounted for by the agency on May 29, 2026. A photo of Platzkoester was not available.
U.S. Army Cpl. Andrew R. Tischler, 21, was assigned to Company F, 2nd Battalion, 15th Infantry Regiment, 3rd Infantry Division, and was reported missing in action during a road march near Taewol Village in South Korea, according to the agency. The agency said it was able to account for him on May 5, 2026. Information about how his remains were found and identified was not available. A photo was not shared by the agency.
The other teen soldier, U.S. Army Cpl. Richard N. Lennox, 18, was accounted for on Aug. 7, 2025, the agency said. He was a member of Company C, 1st Battalion, 7th Infantry Regiment, 3rd Infantry Division reported missing in action after his unit was attacked by enemy forces near Sachang-ni, North Korea, on Nov. 28, 1950. He was captured and marched to a prisoner-of-war camp in Changsong, where he died in October 1951.
Lennox's remains were among those handed over during Operation Glory, the agency said. They could not be identified at the time and were buried as an unknown at the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific. The remains were disinterred on June 13, 2016. The agency analyzed the remains and said that Lennox had been accounted for on Aug. 7, 2025. A photo of Lennox was not available.
Each missing soldier's name was engraved on the Walls of the Missing at the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific. Now that they have been accounted for, rosettes will be placed alongside their names.
More information about each soldier, including how they were identified, may be shared after their families are briefed by the agency. The agency that history, diplomacy and science all come into each investigation. First, researchers start with archival records. Investigators then search for surviving witnesses and clues. Once the potential location of a set of remains is identified, a recovery mission is sent to bring those remains to the agency's laboratory.
At the lab, scientists use dental evidence and other records to study the remains. For soldiers who disappeared during the Korean War, experts can use tuberculosis skin test results taken before someone shipped out. The remains also undergo X-rays, DNA analysis and isotope analysis. Finally, a reference sample of DNA from a family member is compared to the remains. The process can take decades, the agency told CBS News.
About 7,500 Americans are still unaccounted for from the Korean War, the agency says. Efforts to bring home fallen soldiers from the conflict are complicated by : While the agency operates in 46 countries, is an outlier. Sometimes, war dead are recovered during exchanges like Operation Glory.

title: US officially loses measles elimination status, PAHO says
text:
Measles elimination was first declared in the United States in 2000.
The United States on Tuesday officially lost its measles elimination status, according to the Pan American Health Organization, which is responsible for the decision.
Measles elimination was first declared in the United States in 2000, meaning the virus had stopped spreading continuously. That status is lost when the same strain circulates for 12 months or more.
"Losing measles elimination status is an historic public health setback," said Dr. John Brownstein, an epidemiologist and ABC News medical contributor. "We spent decades building the vaccination coverage and public health infrastructure needed to stop this virus from spreading continuously in the United States. To see that progress reversed is a stark reminder that these achievements are not permanent and cannot be taken for granted."
The decision from PAHO, which is part of the World Health Organization, comes as the past two years have seen a notable increase in measles cases across the United States. While the U.S. used to average 180 cases a year, mainly driven by imported cases from abroad, there have been several home-grown outbreaks, including in Texas, Utah, South Carolina and Pennsylvania.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said it is committed to regaining a measles elimination status.
"The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does. We know where transmission is occurring and we've invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach those communities," CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz said in a statement. "Losing a designation doesn't mean we abandon an evidence-based approach. It means we remain focused on stopping outbreaks."
There have been a total of 5,412 infections reported this year in nearly every state, the latest CDC data shows. State health departments have reported 10 deaths. In 2024 there were under 300 cases.
There have been 48 outbreaks identified in the U.S. in 2026 with large ongoing numbers of cases in Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, Minnesota and Indiana. New York State issued a state of emergency. There were significant sustained outbreaks in South Carolina, Utah and Arizona last year.
"This isn't just about losing a designation," Brownstein said. "It means more outbreaks, more hospitalizations, more preventable deaths and greater strain on already stretched public health departments."
In part of a statement, the Department of Health and Human Services said they "will continue working to stop transmission, close vaccination gaps, strengthen outbreak response, and protect Americans from measles. Secretary Kennedy and CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles."
Various medical organizations have criticized Kennedy for his prior statements on vaccines, which they say were not rooted in science, including his decision to unilaterally reduce the numbers of recommended childhood vaccines last year. At the time, groups like the American Academy of Pediatrics criticized the move, saying "our immunization system has long been a cornerstone of U.S. public health, but actions by the current administration are jeopardizing its success."
Many public health experts point to declining vaccination rates as the key culprit for the growing number of cases and outbreaks. CDC numbers show that back in the 2019-2020 school year, 95% of kindergarteners had the MMR vaccine, which dropped to 92% in the 2025-2026 school year. It leaves nearly 300,000 kindergarteners without protection from the virus.
Health officials consider a 95% vaccination rate as herd immunity, reducing the risk of outbreaks and say even a small reduction in vaccination rates can have devastating consequences to the public.
"Measles is incredibly contagious, and once vaccination coverage falls below critical thresholds, the virus can quickly find vulnerable communities,” Brownstein said.
An individual sick with measles can infect 90% of unvaccinated people they come into contact with, according the CDC. The virus lives on surfaces and in the air 2 hours after a sick person leaves the room.
Measles is not just a rash. About 1 in 5 people who are unvaccinated land in the hospital. Complications can include pneumonia, or encephalitis, a swelling of the brain that can lead to seizures, deafness or intellectual disability.
"If there's any silver lining, I hope this serves as a wake-up call," Brownstein said. "We've allowed vaccination rates to decline while simultaneously underinvesting in the public health systems needed to detect and contain outbreaks. We have an incredibly safe and effective vaccine, so this is entirely preventable. The question is whether we're willing to make the investments needed to reverse course."
The measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine comes in two doses. The first dose is received between 12-15 months of age followed by second dose between 4-6 years of age. Those two doses are 97% effective at preventing infection, according to the CDC.
Even if still infected, those vaccinated are less likely to become severely ill. Children younger than 12 months old in areas of current outbreaks may be eligible for the vaccine at younger ages, according to the CDC.

title: Ukraine updates: Russia-Crimea bridge appears destroyed after strike
text:
Ukraine strike hits Kerch bridge connecting occupied Crimea to the Russian mainland, stopping traffic
- Images show part of the bridge destroyed
- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the strike on Kerch bridge an 'unprecedented operation'
- Russia also struck two important bridges in Kyiv, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said
- The attacks come as Ukrainian, European and US negotiators discuss future talks with Russia on ending the war
These are the main developments from Russia's war in Ukraine on November 17, 2026:
Zelenskyy says bridge strike is retaliation for Russia's 'further escalation'
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy spoke about the attack on the Russian-built bridge linking Crimea to Russia in his nightly video address.
The Ukrainian president said the incident was another strike on a major Russian target after his country had endured numerous attacks on bridges, infrastructure and cities.
"We have long been telling Russia: Enough of striking bridges, cities and villages, energy infrastructure, railways and grain ships. Enough of war. But every time Russia chooses further escalation," Zelenskyy said.
"So Ukrainian missiles and Ukrainian drones have once again reached a key Russian military artery in the south," he added. "This is a result of the Security Service of Ukraine, all our Defense Forces of Ukraine."
Germany's Pistorius defends Ukraine after bridge strike
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius backed Ukraine in the aftermath of the Crimea bridge strike.
Pistorius said criticism of Ukraine's deep strikes in Russia was misplaced.
In particular, Pistorius responded to US Defense Under Secretary Elbridge Colby, who said Ukraine's "deep strikes" against Russia "have not been effective in driving an end to the war."
The German defense minister said "criticizing strikes like that in Russia to destroy strategic military and military-used targets" was "quite a stupid thing."
"Instead of criticizing that, we should rather criticize and talk about the terroristic strikes every night and every day on... energy, water, and heating infrastructure in Ukraine. This is kind of terrorism," Pistorius said.
He added that attacks inside Russia against non-civilian targets and sites used by the military are legal and legitimate targets.
Moldova says Russian drone flew over its capital
The government of Moldova said it had temporarily closed its airspace for security reasons after authorities detected a Shahed-type drone.
"For security reasons, the authorities have closed down the entire airspace of the Republic of Moldova," the country's Defense Ministry said in a statement.
Moldovan police said they received several reports from Chisinau residents who heard explosions.
The drone incursions into Moldova involved one drone reportedly flying over the country's eastern regions, while a second one entered the southern part of the country and flew towards Chisinau.
Moldovans were urged not to approach suspicious flying objects or touch any drone debris found, as it could contain "explosive elements."
Moldova, which borders Ukraine, has reported several fallen drones on its territory since the beginning of Russia's invasion of Ukraine. But none of them had reached the capital.
Moldovan President Maia Sandu rejected what she called "the boundless cynicism of Moscow's leaders" and vowed to continue supporting Kyiv in the war.
"This evening several Russian drones violated our airspace, one of them over Chisinau, alarming residents," Sandu wrote on X.
"Russia's war threatens all of Europe," she said. "Moldova stands for peace. We'll keep pushing for sanctions on Moscow, standing with Ukraine and building our defence with partners."
US criticizes Ukraine for Crimea bridge strike
A top US official criticized Ukraine's strike on the Kerch Bridge, saying it could provoke Russia into further escalation.
US Defense Under Secretary Elbridge Colby said Ukraine's "deep strikes" against Russia "have not been effective in driving an end to the war" or, Colby added, in blunting Russia's advances.
"Such strikes, especially those that target civilian infrastructure such as Wildberries, have actually probably hardened the Russian public's resolve and the Kremlin's own willingness to escalate," Colby told a gathering of Ukraine's backers at NATO headquarters in Brussels.
Wildberries is a Russian e-commerce giant targeted by Kyiv. Its CEO, Tatyana Kim, was added to the list of EU sanctions Monday.
It all comes as Trump said he may discuss the Ukraine war during a highly anticipated meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in China on Thursday.
WATCH — Ukraine hits strategic Russian bridge to Crimea
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has confirmed the partial destruction of Russia's strategic Kerch bridge, which connects occupied Crimea with Russia proper.
Biresh Banerjee speaks to Ukrainian lawmaker Lesia Vasylenko and DW's Kyiv correspondent Nick Connolly about the attack and the overall situation in Ukraine.
France rejects claims its troops are fighting in Ukraine
France on Tuesday rejected Russian claims that French troops deployed in Ukraine were directly involved in fighting against Russian troops.
"Not only French ones, we know this. We have conveyed our concern... this is no longer support for Ukraine, but direct participation in the war," Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov told reporters.
The French government said the accusation was "absurd."
Deputy Defense Minister Alice Rufo told parliament that a "very limited" deployment of French troops is in Ukraine for training and equipment maintenance.
"There is the absence of any intention to fight, contrary to what the Russian foreign minister said this morning, which is absurd," she added.
Germany reacts to Crimean bridge attack
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul urgently called for a negotiated settlement to the war in Ukraine, after a Ukrainian airstrike partially destroyed a bridge to the Crimean Peninsula.
"The last thing we need before this winter is another escalation," Wadephul said during a visit to Azerbaijan. "What is needed now are bold steps towards a negotiated settlement. And I hope there is now the necessary resolve for this everywhere."
He described the attack that damaged the bridge as difficult for Russia, underlining the need to step up efforts to find a negotiated settlement.
"Russia started this war in violation of international law. And it must live with the consequences," Wadephul said.
IN PICTURES: The Kerch bridge before and after Tuesday's strike
WATCH: Could attacks on Ukraine's power grid trigger a nuclear disaster?
European regulators warn that a nationwide blackout could create cooling problems at several Ukrainian reactors simultaneously. How realistic is that scenario, and how well prepared are the plants?
Hungary suspends Ukraine rail traffic after Russian drone attack
Hungary's Prime Minister Peter Magyar said that rail traffic was being suspended to and from Ukraine on Tuesday and Wednesday, after a Russian drone came down in Western Ukraine.
"A Russian drone recently crashed in Zakarpattia, 300 metres from the Mukachevo railway station. The Hungarian crew of a train arriving from Hungary was ordered to disembark," Magyar said in a Facebook post.
"We are suspending rail traffic between Hungary and Ukraine for today and tomorrow," Magyar said.
Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orban had earlier said that Russian drones had attacked Zakarpattia, targeting areas near Mukachevo and Uzhhorod, not far from the border area with Hungary.
"As Russia intensifies its attacks on Ukraine's civilian population, similar operations against Zakarpattia, which until now has been relatively protected due to its geographical location, can also be expected in the future," she said.
IN PICTURES: Kerch bridge strike
Vladimir Putin briefed on Kerch bridge strike — Russian media
Russia state media has reported that President Vladimir Putin has been briefed by Deputy Prime Minister Marat Khusnullin "on the situation around the Crimean Bridge," citing Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov.
"Following the government commission meeting, Marat Khusnullin reported to President Putin on the situation surrounding the Crimean Bridge," Peskov told reporters.
"According to the Investigative Committee, on November 16 and 17, Ukrainian armed forces attacked the Crimean Bridge using unmanned aerial vehicle, resulting in damage to the structure," TASS reported.
Russian media also quoted Peskov as saying that the bridge linking occupied Crimea with mainland Russia would be "even better" after it was restored, giving an indication as to the extent of the damage caused.
"There is, of course, no doubt that the bridge will be restored and will be even better than before," Peskov said, quoted by Russian state media.
Ukraine's Zelenskyy confirms strike on Kerch bridge
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has confirmed that the Kerch bridge was targeted by Ukrainian forces, describing it as "an unprecedented operation in response to Russian strikes on our infrastructure."
"Today, everyone can see the consequences for the main military crossing from Russian territory into our Ukrainian Crimea," Zelenskyy said in a lengthy post on social media platform X.
The Ukrainian leader said the strike was a culmination of an operation "carried out over several weeks" by his country's military and involved destroying air defense systems, radar systems and electronic warfare equipment in the lead up to the attack.
Zelenskyy said that the road section of the bridge was hit by "Palianytsia" drones and while the railway section was targeted by "Neptune" missiles and "Ruta" drones.
"We have repeatedly offered Russia steps toward de-escalation — and every proposal has been met with loud rejection," Zelenskyy said and pointed to continued Russian strikes on Ukraine's infrastructure.
His post was accompanied by footage appearing to show the moment the bridge was struck and then the subsequent aftermath with one part of the bridge collapsed.
Germany and Norway to purchase more air defenses for Ukraine
Germany and Norway will fund a new US air defense package for Ukraine's defensive needs, according to Germany's defense chief.
"Russia is intensifying its air attacks because it is not making progress on the battlefield," Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said at an EU meeting in Brussels.
Pistorius said that Germany would contribute $300 million (€272 million) towards the weapons package that would include Patriot interceptor missiles.
The package will also include previously announced IRIS-T systems, as well as new radars and ammunition for F-16 fighter jets and drones.
The announcement comes ahead of a meeting of Ukraine's military backers at NATO headquarters in Brussels later today.
Germany has, since the start of Russia's invasion, provided civilian aid totalling more than €45.7 billion and provided or earmarked military aid of around €57.8 billion, according to the German government.
Power outages in 9 Ukrainian regions after Russian strikes — energy official
Ukraine's Deputy Energy Minister Artem Nekrasov, said that Russian strikes on energy infrastructure had caused power outages in nine Ukrainian regions.
"As a result of the strikes, some consumers have been left without electricity in the Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, Mykolaiv, Odesa, Rivne, Sumy, Chernihiv and Chernivtsi regions," Nekrasov said.
"The situation is extremely difficult in the Dnipropetrovsk and Zaporizhzhia regions. Since last week, Russia has been continuously attacking energy facilities in the Dnipro region," Nekrasov said.

title: FA chair to examine Gianni Infantino’s Fifa World Cup sell-off plan documents
text:
Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt is set to inspect documentation in person regarding Fifa’s deeply contentious World Cup private investment proposal, it is understood.
The global governing body dispatched a letter on 2 November to members of the Fifa Council – where Hewitt serves as a Fifa vice-president – offering them the opportunity to examine the files at its headquarters in Zurich.
Hewitt is believed to have taken up the offer, though a firm date for the trip remains unconfirmed. Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin is likewise thought to have agreed to attend.
Relations between Uefa and Fifa president Gianni Infantino broke down over the project, which involved creating a new entity named Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) to manage commercial and operational activities for both the men’s and women’s World Cups alongside other Fifa tournaments.
Under the blueprint, a minority shareholding in FFE was to be acquired by private investors, led by Thrive Capital, an entity established by Joshua Kushner, whose brother is the son-in-law of United States President Donald Trump.
The initiative was ultimately scrapped following opposition from Uefa and a pair of other continental confederations.
Hewitt’s career experience in private equity provides her with direct insight into the standard documentation and financial details expected in proposals of this nature.
Fifa issued the invitation after European representatives on the Fifa Council sent a formal letter on 19 October requesting clarity on several matters, including the FFE arrangement and disciplinary proceedings involving Folarin Balogun.
Provisions regarding non-disclosure agreements and the specific terms governing document inspection in Zurich have yet to be finalised.
The FA offered no comment on the matter.
Earlier on Tuesday, the French Football Federation formally endorsed Philippe Diallo’s bid for the Fifa presidency.
On Monday, Uefa confirmed that the 63-year-old had secured the support of national association delegates across its executive committee and the Fifa Council to challenge Infantino.
Disquiet over the FFE proposals prompted European football’s governing body to promise in August that it would put forward a credible challenger to Infantino.
Diallo’s domestic federation has now unanimously backed his campaign, stating: "World football is going through a pivotal period in its history. The challenges affecting its governance demand clear thinking and responsibility.
"Restoring trust, preserving the universality of football, rebuilding Fifa’s credibility, and placing the development of football in all regions of the world at the heart of its actions are essential issues for the entire international football community.
"By accepting this invitation, Philippe Diallo is responding to a desire to open a new chapter for the governance of world football."
Figures within Uefa had previously hoped that former Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger, who currently serves as Fifa’s chief of global football development, might enter the race, though he is believed to have declined the prospect last week.

title: After UN peacekeeping mission ends, Morocco says Western Sahara dispute enters new phase
text:
Six years after President Donald Trump recognized Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara, a senior regional official says the decades-old territorial dispute has entered a new phase, with negotiations now focused on how Morocco's autonomy proposal would be implemented following the end of the United Nations peacekeeping mission.
Sidi Hamdi Ould Errachid, president of the Laâyoune–Sakia El Hamra Regional Council, told Fox News Digital in an exclusive Zoom interview that Morocco remains open to negotiations with other parties, but suggested that opposition to the plan would not necessarily prevent it from moving forward.
"The Moroccan side remains open to international engagement, and we are prepared to negotiate how the autonomy proposal will be implemented," he said through an interpreter.
Asked what remains to be negotiated with the Polisario Front, which seeks independence for Western Sahara, Ould Errachid indicated that Morocco intends to pursue its autonomy initiative regardless of whether all parties reach an agreement.
"If the other parties do not agree, we will continue implementing the autonomy proposal on the ground," he said through the interpreter.
His remarks come after Russia vetoed a U.S.-drafted Security Council resolution on Oct. 30, preventing the renewal of the U.N. Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara, known as MINURSO. A competing Russian proposal also failed, and the mission began winding down Nov. 1.
Established in 1991, MINURSO was originally tasked with helping organize a referendum on the territory's future following a ceasefire between Morocco and the Algeria-backed Polisario Front. That referendum never took place, leaving the dispute unresolved.
The United States recognized Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara in December 2020 under Trump, a position reaffirmed by his administration in July 2026.
In October 2025, the U.N. Security Council adopted Resolution 2797, establishing Morocco's autonomy proposal as the basis for negotiations while maintaining the goal of a mutually acceptable political solution providing for Sahrawi self-determination.
Ould Errachid, a Sahrawi politician who grew up in Laâyoune and participated in U.N.-convened negotiations in Geneva in 2018 and 2019, described the proposal as an opportunity for Sahrawis to govern their own affairs.
"Except for the king, the Moroccan flag, the currency, the armed forces and foreign affairs, we would have full autonomy to manage our own affairs," he explained.
Asked whether the departure of the U.N. mission raised concerns about stability, he rejected the suggestion.
"We are not worried. We have a credible project that guarantees a decent future for our people and for our cousins in the Polisario Front," he said.
The Polisario Front, which seeks independence, rejects Moroccan sovereignty. Human Rights Watch warned in March 2026 that negotiations centered exclusively on Moroccan autonomy risk undermining Sahrawis' right to self-determination.
Beyond the political dispute, Ould Errachid is seeking to translate Washington's support into closer economic ties, inviting American companies to invest in renewable energy, manufacturing, agriculture, water desalination and healthcare.
He praised Trump for his 2020 recognition decision and highlighted a major highway connecting Morocco with Western Sahara that has become associated with the president's name.
"Nobody here will ever forget the moment President Donald Trump decided to support Morocco. His decision will remain engraved in the history of this region," he said.
One example of expanding American engagement is medical cooperation. Laâyoune hosted U.S. medical delegations in February 2025 and October 2026, bringing American specialists together with Moroccan doctors and students.
The first gathering produced a partnership agreement between New York's St. Francis Hospital & Heart Center and regional hospitals in Laâyoune. The second resulted in agreements between Laâyoune's Faculty of Medicine and Pharmacy and two American organizations, Celenova Fertility and the Fetal Research Fund.
According to the organizers, the partnerships are intended to expand medical training, research, student exchanges and specialized care.
Ould Errachid said he is preparing further outreach to American investors in February or March, hoping to expand cooperation beyond medicine into additional economic sectors.
"We need your help," he said, describing Western Sahara as a potential gateway for American companies seeking opportunities across African markets.

title: Debunking social media posts that claim a 90-day blackout will start Nov. 17
text: This article originally appeared on PolitiFact. A 90-day nationwide blackout is not looming for the U.S., despite social media call outs to prepare for such a doomsday scenario. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News Multiple TikTok posts say the blackout will start Nov. 17 and warn people to stock up with food and other supplies. A Nov. 14 TikTok post went even farther, showing President Donald Trump purportedly saying the blackout is coming. "A 90-day blackout is going to happen before the end of the year," Trump appears to say from the White House press briefing room. That video was manipulated. PolitiFact found the original video of Trump talking Nov. 9 in the press briefing room; he didn't announce a 90-day blackout. Among many things, he talked about former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and the Iran war. The TikTok account that posted the video uses the purported clip to promote buying cryptocurrency before the supposed blackout and has posted other manipulated videos of Trump. Fact-checkers at Snopes also found similar manipulated videos of Trump shared on Facebook and Instagram promoting cryptocurrency and claiming that it would make people money during the "upcoming" blackout. A Spanish-language TikTok post said the blackout already started, pointing to the Nov. 12 to 14 Microsoft outage and the Federal Aviation Administration's Nov. 13 order to ground all flights because of faulty old equipment. Microsoft said in a Nov. 13 X post the outage was a technical issue, not a cyber attack, and the FAA allowed flights to resume Nov. 13. What's happening Nov. 17? The Federal Emergency Management Agency announced Sept. 17 that on Nov. 17 around 2:20 p.m. ET, it and the Federal Communications Commission will conduct a nationwide test of the Emergency Alert System. The test will air only on radio and TV; the alert will not be sent to mobile phones. There is nothing the public has to do in response. This is a standard test that happens at least once every three years per federal law to ensure the alert system is ready in case of an emergency. That test is not expected to announce a real emergency or a blackout. READ MORE: Could everything be broken? Grounded jets, Microsoft outage, AI chaos make some wonder The message will last one minute, have an alert sound and will say, "This is a nationwide test of the Emergency Alert System, issued by the Federal Emergency Management Agency. This is only a test. No action is required by the public." FEMA also says on its website that if an actual emergency happens Nov. 17, the test will be postponed to Dec. 3. Homeland Security secretary said no need to stockpile supplies Fox News Senior White House Correspondent Peter Doocy asked Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Nov. 15 if Americans should start stockpiling food and supplies after the FAA ground stop. Mullin said Americans don't need to stockpile supplies for potential disruptions to power, water and food supplies, although other countries such as the United Kingdom advised their residents to do so in late October. The U.K. government released this guidance to ensure that households can survive weather, cyber or other serious emergencies with supplies to last 72 hours. The notice came before the winter storm season and amid concerns that the global phenomenon "super El-Niño" could affect global food supplies and energy systems. Mullin said the UK doesn't have the same safeguards and emergency preparedness the U.S has. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "That's kind of running over the internet right now too, especially throughout social media. 'Should I be worried? The 90 days', absolutely not," Mullin said. "I'm not stockpiling and I tell my kids all the time, don't worry unless you see me worry. We're in good shape here, the panic that people want to draw from is unfounded." Some social media users also said the blackout is related to the FORTRESS America project, which Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced Sept. 30. FORTRESS, which stands for Federal Operations for Resilience, Troop Resources, Energy, Supply and Survivability, seeks to ensure that every major U.S. military installation generates its own independent power so that bases remain operational even if civilian electric grids are taken down by a cyberattack or sabotage. Fox News reported Oct. 25 that according to documents it reviewed, the project is preparing the U.S. military bases to keep operating without outside power for at least 90 days. The network didn't report that a 90-day blackout is coming. This isn't the first time these emergency tests triggered misinformation. We have fact-checked bogus claims saying the electric signals of these tests could turn people into zombies and activate COVID-19 vaccine ingredients in people's bodies. Our ruling TikTok posts say a nationwide 90-day blackout will happen Nov. 17, 2026. There is no evidence that is going to happen. One video shows Trump purportedly saying a blackout is coming, but that clip is manipulated. The video is of a Nov. 9 news conference and Trump didn't mention a nationwide power outage. FEMA will do a nationwide test of the Emergency Alert System on Nov. 17, which happens at least once every three years. The Defense Department in late September announced a project to prepare military bases to operate for 90-days in case of a blackout of the civilian electric grid, that doesn't mean a blackout is expected Nov. 17. During the recent nationwide flights ground stop, the Homeland Security secretary said Americans don't need to stockpile for widespread disruptions to power, water and food supplies and that related online claims are unfounded. We rate this claim False.

title: Chase Home Lending CEO says he plans to 'go on offense' against non-bank lenders
text:
A version of this article first appeared in the CNBC Property Play newsletter with Diana Olick. Property Play covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, from individuals to venture capitalists, private equity funds, family offices, institutional investors and large public companies. Sign up to receive future editions, straight to your inbox.
Mortgage rates shot higher again last week, after four straight weeks of declines. A hotter-than-expected monthly inflation report, coupled with new headlines from the Iran war, had the average rate on the 30-year fixed mortgage up 33 basis points to 7.5%, according to Mortgage News Daily.
Total mortgage demand, including both refinancing and new purchase loans, is now down just over 39% from a year ago, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association. Despite all that, Sean Grzebin, the CEO of Chase Home Lending, the nation's largest bank mortgage lender, said he's hiring and bent on increasing market share.
"For the last several years, we haven't really added a lot of salespeople," said Grzebin, who admits plainly that this is the worst market in decades. "We're going to hire a bunch of home lending advisors across the United States.
