We're going to focus on areas where we haven't had a lot of coverage, but there's a lot of mortgage activity and transactions taking place, and it really matches the expansion that we're having within the branch network on the consumer bank side."
Grzebin said he is looking to take back market share from non-bank lenders, who flourished after the financial crisis, when banks were cleaning up from thousands of failed home loans. In August, JPMorganChase announced a 40% increase in home lending capital through 2035 to $750 billion. It will also hire 850 new lending agents.
"I think the non-banks are all very formidable competitors. I think they've had an advantage while the banks were distracted through several decades," he said. "I think now you're starting to see the resurgence of the banks, and I think a lot of banks are actually going to grow their mortgage business through this."
He said he expects to see continued consolidation in the mortgage market, especially as artificial intelligence penetrates the origination part of the business. Chase is investing heavily in AI for underwriting, he said.
"We're hiring mainly in our sales functions because we think we can grow by adding people that have relationships with existing customers today, as well as them taking advantage of our branch network to help grow their business on one side," explained Grzebin. "And we think we can achieve all this growth without adding any incremental headcount in our operation because of the streamlining of the process that's happening with AI."
Chase just ranked highest in mortgage origination satisfaction in J.D. Power's annual U.S. Mortgage Origination Satisfaction Study. While overall satisfaction was unchanged from 2025, just 58% of borrowers said they receive same-day responses from their lender when they ask questions, down from 62% a year ago. Fewer borrowers also say they have a main point of contact, down to 88% from 91% a year ago.
"Borrowers appreciate being able to handle more of the mortgage process online, but they still want someone they can turn to when they have questions," said Bruce Gehrke, senior director of wealth and lending intelligence at J.D. Power in a release. "J.D. Power is seeing less recognition of updates and guidance that are important to keeping borrowers informed. Lenders have an opportunity to make the process more convenient while ensuring borrowers feel supported, especially as they approach closing."
That appears to be what Chase is leaning into as so much of the process now moves to agentic AI. Grzebin said they focused first on the closing process, which customers said was most frustrating. Then they moved to digital tools.
"There's a lot of opportunity there that we're going to be able to take advantage of in the next 12 to 24 months, just making it easier for customers to do more self-service through AI capabilities that we're going to also roll out over the next couple quarters, and so we are invested heavily in AI," he said. "We're going to see some real efficiency from it, and then on the sales side, adding salespeople, but then also figuring out a way to make them more productive."
Servicing is also becoming a bigger factor again, as mortgage delinquencies slowly rise, especially in the FHA space. These low-down-payment loans generally carry higher risk, and as rates stay stubbornly high, those risks are starting to emerge. Chase does do FHA lending, but it is a smaller part of its business.
"I think others are going to have other problems to deal with, particularly if there's any unemployment, and we're just going to be in good shape for that entire cycle. So we look at it as a chance to really go on offense," he said, specifically in FHA lending.
"The non-banks stepped into it and served that market, and that business is being challenged right now, and so we're trying to get back into it," Grzebin said. "We'd love to get back into it. We're priced competitively to get back into it."

title: Uber and Zipline’s drone delivery service takes off in Texas, with dozens of cities to follow
text:
Uber Eats customers in a Houston suburb can now have their food delivered by a Zipline drone, the first commercial launch under a partnership announced earlier this year between Uber and the autonomous drone delivery startup.
The commercial partnership kicks off Tuesday in Spring, Texas, before expanding to Dallas. But the companies have far larger ambitions. Uber and Zipline plan to launch drone delivery services in dozens of additional U.S. cities in their collective bid to make one million deliveries per day using the startup’s drones by the end of 2029.
Zipline’s long-range autonomous delivery drones will be used to shuttle food orders weighing up to eight pounds to Uber Eats customers, flying about 300 feet above the ground at speeds of up to 70 miles per hour. Zipline drones don’t land. Instead, the drones lower the orders, which are encased in a small protective pod, to the customer’s location using a tether.
Uber Eats customers in service areas will be able to tap a new “drone” icon on the app’s home page to view all participating restaurants. Uber said that at launch in the Houston area, several nationwide chains, including Jersey Mike’s and Zaxby’s, along with dozens of local restaurants such as Urban Bird and Abu Omar Halal, will offer drone delivery.
“In partnership with Uber Eats we’re going to create a new expectation for delivery in America,” Zipline CEO and co-founder Keller Cliffton said in a statement that underscores those aspirations.
Those nationwide goals mirror the ambitions of other drone delivery companies, including Alphabet-owned Wing and Amazon’s Prime Air service. And those plans have started to collide with concerns from residents in some locations who complain about noise and worry that the drones will disrupt wildlife and pose a risk to safety and privacy.
Companies trying to scale in this nascent industry have argued that delivery via drone is a net benefit for society, citing advantages such as traffic reduction. Customers won’t need to hop in their cars and drive to the store for that forgotten item or takeout order, instead relying on a drone, industry proponents have said.
And while Zipline and other companies have been developing their drones for years, the industry is still in its early days, as is adoption in the communities where services are available.
Zipline, which was founded in 2014, has developed a drone delivery ecosystem that includes aircraft, launch and landing systems, and logistics software. The California-based company’s initial focus was delivering blood in Rwanda, but it eventually expanded its scope to the United States. Its business in the U.S. scaled quickly after receiving its Part 135 air carrier certification from the Federal Aviation Administration in 2022, a critical regulatory hurdle that authorized the company to conduct long-range commercial drone deliveries.
Uber’s partnership extends beyond a commercial relationship with Zipline. The ride-hailing giant also invested in the startup. Neither company has disclosed the investment amount, but Zipline announced last week it had raised $1.5 billion in a round led by Paradigm, WCM Investment Management, and Layer Global, and included backing by Uber, among others.

title: Shareholders sue Intel, its CEO, and CFO after stock drops 28.6 percent in one day
text:
Intel is being sued by shareholders, who are accusing the chipmaker of misleading them about the impact of the PC sales slump that contributed to a drop of 28.6 percent in the price of Intel’s stock on October 30.
The lawsuit (PDF), filed on Friday in the San Jose, California, federal court, is seeking class-action certification and lists the City of Southfield Fire and Police Retirement System and “all others similarly situated” as plaintiffs. In addition to Intel, Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan and Intel’s EVP and CFO David Zinsner are listed as defendants.
The plaintiffs claim that Intel made “materially false and misleading statements and omissions” between July 23 and October 29. They are seeking unspecified compensatory damages, plus legal and other associated fees, for shareholders during that period.
In the complaint, the shareholders argue that Intel misled them by failing to disclose: the full impact that the PC market sales slump would have on Intel’s third quarter and beyond; the impact of increasing PC component prices on PC sales for Intel’s OEM and distribution partners; that Intel was dealing with substrate supply constraints that would limit its ability to meet data center CPU demand; and “that any positive impacts to Intel’s business and financial results resulting from data center construction and other aspects of the AI boom were more than offset” by the PC sales slump.

title: NASA is offering $1 million for bold ideas to help build a Moon base
text:
NASA is offering $1 million in its new Moon Base Challenge, inviting U.S. students to develop innovative solutions for building humanity’s first permanent lunar outpost. From power systems to astronaut safety, their ideas could help make long-term life on the Moon possible and pave the way to Mars.
NASA has launched a $1 million Moon Base Challenge, inviting teams of students from high schools and colleges across the United States to help develop ideas for humanity's future on the Moon. The competition was announced during a MAX POWER event at Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex in Florida. Presented as part of a Golden Age of Science, the initiative gives young innovators an opportunity to contribute designs and potential solutions for NASA's planned lunar base.
"We're looking for students ready to think creatively, work as a team, and take on real problems connected to NASA's future on the Moon," said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. "You do not have to wait until graduation to contribute. Curiosity, creativity, and the willingness to tackle hard problems without obvious answers are exactly the qualities we need as we build what comes next."
NASA's Plans for a Permanent Moon Base
NASA is working toward establishing a Moon Base near the lunar South Pole, where astronauts will be able to live, conduct research, and explore the surrounding region. Creating a lasting human presence on the Moon is also an important step toward future missions that will carry astronauts to Mars. Achieving these goals will require expertise and creative thinking from people across a wide range of industries and disciplines.
"As we build and design the foundations of Moon Base, we want to leverage all the ingenuity and innovation to think of every consideration our explorers might need to live and work there," said Carlos García-Galán, manager, Moon Base Program. "Students bring exactly the bold ideas that we're looking for, and I'm looking forward to their fresh perspective. Ultimately, Moon Base is for them, people who will experience a world where humans are on the Moon to stay."
Six Major Challenges of Living on the Moon
The competition will unfold in multiple phases, with student teams developing solutions to six essential aspects of operating a lunar base. These include generating and storing power, constructing facilities, maintaining life support systems, enabling transportation across the lunar surface, establishing communications networks, and protecting astronauts.
Each category addresses practical obstacles that NASA must overcome to support long-term operations on the Moon. By working on these problems, students can explore new approaches to lunar technologies while developing technical and professional skills that could prepare them for careers in aerospace and related fields.
The challenge is designed around actual environmental conditions and mission requirements that would affect daily life and operations on the lunar surface. Participants will produce work similar to that used in the space industry, including evaluations of competing technical options, proposals outlining potential designs, and presentations for project stakeholders.
Students from technical, vocational, and other academic backgrounds are encouraged to participate. Previous specialized knowledge of engineering or related technical fields is not required, making the competition accessible to a broad range of young innovators.
Inspiring the Next Generation of Space Explorers
Beyond generating ideas for the Moon Base, NASA hopes the competition will help develop the skills needed by the next generation of aerospace professionals. By exposing students to practical design challenges, the agency aims to encourage collaboration, creative problem-solving, and greater involvement in future space exploration.
"Students are the next generation of explorers and innovators. Their unique perspectives are key to helping us envision a future away from Earth, and I'm excited to see the creativity and ingenuity spurred by this challenge," said Elaine Ho, associate administrator for the Office of STEM Engagement at NASA Headquarters.
How to Enter NASA's $1 Million Moon Base Challenge
Interested student teams must register through the NASA STEM Gateway. Registration remains open until January 25, 2027.
NASA's Office of STEM Engagement developed the competition in partnership with the agency's Moon Base Program. The Institute of Competition Sciences is responsible for administering the challenge under a contract with NASA's Center of Excellence for Collaborative Innovation, which operates within the Research and Technology Mission Directorate.

title: Drugs like Ozempic may help reverse chronic kidney disease
text:
Ozempic’s key ingredient fixes faulty filters in the kidney.
The well-known weight loss drug repairs and restores blood vessels that power people’s waste disposal systems, researchers report October 1 in Nature Medicine. Those actions mean the ingredient, called semaglutide, can add another notch to its list of health benefits: treating chronic kidney disease.
In patients with the condition, semaglutide also increased blood flow and tamped down inflammation, the team found. The study reinforces the GLP-1 drug’s known anti-inflammatory effects, while also suggesting that it may play a direct role in protecting the kidney’s blood vessels, says Susan Quaggin, a nephrologist at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine in Chicago who was not involved in the work.
Chronic kidney disease affects an estimated 674 million people worldwide, with some of the most common causes being diabetes and high blood pressure. As the disease progresses, the kidneys slowly lose their ability to filter out waste from blood and excrete it as urine. This causes other health complications, as well as a sharply increased risk of dying from a heart attack or stroke.
Patients with diabetic chronic kidney disease who took semaglutide were less likely to wind up in kidney failure, or die from a heart attack or stroke, than those taking a placebo, researchers reported in 2024 in the New England Journal of Medicine. That trial was stopped early, as the drug was so effective at preventing death that doctors no longer considered it ethical to keep giving participants the placebo.
For the new study, some of those same researchers then looked at a subset of 106 participants to find out how the drug worked. The team collected kidney tissue samples before and after the participants took semaglutide, and compared them with samples from participants given the placebo. Semaglutide use led to striking visible changes in the tissues, including increased blood flow, reduced scarring and reduced blood vessel stiffness, a measure of vessel health.
Increased blood flow is important because it increases filtration, which is the kidneys’ main job, says Peter Nguyen, a nephrologist at Houston Methodist Hospital who was not involved in the study.
Researchers also looked at levels of a protein, called albumin, in patients’ urine. High levels can be an early sign that the kidneys’ filters aren’t working well. While those levels didn’t change much in those on the placebo, they dropped in patients taking semaglutide ― a sign the filters weren’t quite as leaky any more.
The team then looked under the hood for genetic clues to how semaglutide appeared to heal the kidneys. Within the glomerulus, the tiny blood vessels responsible for the kidney’s filtering action, genes relating to metabolic stress were turned off, Katherine Tuttle, a nephrologist at the University of Washington’s Providence Medical Research Center in Spokane, and colleagues found. Within these same cells, inflammatory genes were also turned off, while repair genes were switched on.
The researchers also looked at a subset of genes responsible for cells “talking” to each other within the glomerulus. Before semaglutide, the blood vessels and immune cells were “chattering” with each other, sending lots of inflammatory signals, Tuttle says. After semaglutide, the immune cells went quiet, silencing the messages that ramp up harmful inflammation. These changes in gene activity point to a healthier kidney that’s less stressed and inflamed, and that has had repair processes flipped on.
With semaglutide treatment, Tuttle says, patients’ damaged kidneys showed clear signs of repair.

title: 'Maybe the scariest thing I've heard in my life': Artemis II astronaut Victor Glover reveals his toughest challenge before flying to the moon
text:
TENERIFE, Canary Islands — Former NASA astronaut Victor Glover has flown in combat, performed four spacewalks and strapped himself to the top of rockets launching into space. But before embarking on his historic Artemis II journey around the moon, he faced something even more difficult: a conversation with his four daughters.
Speaking alongside former astronaut Chris Hadfield at the Starmus VIII festival in Tenerife, Canary Islands, on Oct. 18, Glover opened up about the challenges of preparing his family for his riskiest mission yet.
"This is maybe the greatest challenge of my astronaut career," Glover said.
Glover joined NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman and Christina Koch and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen aboard NASA's Artemis II mission, which launched on April 1, 2026, marking humanity's first crewed journey to the moon since Apollo 17 in 1972.
But preparing for the historic journey wasn't just about mastering the spacecraft and executing the mission successfully. It also meant making sure his family was ready for what lay ahead.
When Glover first traveled to space aboard SpaceX's Crew-1 mission in 2020, his children were much younger and he and his wife, Dionna, made a conscious effort to prepare them for his time in space.
"We decided, as a parental unit, Dionna and I, that we were going to put as much effort into making sure our family was ready as NASA was putting into making sure I was ready to be a crew member," Glover explained.
The family visited NASA's Kennedy Space Center, toured the launch pad and crew quarters and even planned when Glover would call home from the International Space Station. But by the time Artemis II came around, things were different. All four of his daughters were now adults, and preparing them for his journey around the moon meant discussing the mission's risks, including the possibility that he might not return home.
Glover recalled his wife telling him something he described as maybe the scariest thing he'd ever heard.
"You should have this talk with our daughters."
And although he knew she was right, it wasn't an easy conversation to have.
"We did, and it did not go well in my opinion," Glover admitted. "Well, it's not about going well. The talk needed to be done, just because it's hard."
The following day, Glover sent his daughters and wife a poem, Live Your Life, by Chief Tecumseh.
The poem helped Glover express something he had struggled to put into words during their conversation: why he believed the risks of traveling to the moon were worth taking.
"It was a very tough conversation, but they understood that I know this is risky. I wasn't just telling them Dad's risking his life. There's a real point to this and there's a reason to take this risk," Glover explained. "This poem helped me to say it in a way that I didn't have words for."
After traveling around the moon and returning safely to Earth, one moment stood out above all others. When we asked Glover in a separate interview at Starmus on Oct. 20, which moment from Artemis II he would most like to relive, he answered immediately.
"Splashdown."
"It's the true, ultimate mission accomplishment. Just 'we did it.' We survived. My family is relieved, and there's just nothing like it," Glover explained. "There's nothing like coming home. There's nothing like returning to Earth."
Daisy Dobrijevic joined Space.com in February 2022, having previously worked as a staff writer for All About Space magazine. She completed an editorial internship with BBC Sky at Night Magazine and worked at the National Space Centre, communicating space science to the public.
Daisy holds a PhD in plant physiology and a Master's in Environmental Science. Based in Nottingham, U.K., she covers all things space, with a special focus on solar activity and space weather. She also has a keen interest in astrotourism and is always on the lookout for the next northern lights adventure.
She will join Hurtigruten as an onboard astronomer for a northern lights sailing in January 2027.

title: Where are the most jobs for 18-24 year-olds?
text:
If you're one of the nearly one million people aged 16-24 not in education, employment or training - otherwise known as "Neet" - then you might be wondering where to start.
Under-25s should be guaranteed job placements or training to help them find permanent work, a major review aimed at cutting the number of Neets will say.
But how many jobs are there where you live? Use our look-up tool to find out.
Where are the available jobs?
Where you live will often have a big impact on your ability to find a job.
The Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) think tank used online job adverts to help identify the number of vacancies suitable for young people in the area they live, relative to the size of the local population.
It used AI to help identify the jobs, which were broadly defined as roles requiring relatively low experience or education.
According to its analysis, South Oxfordshire had 387 suitable vacancies per 1,000 18 to 24-year-olds in the area - the most of any local authority. Rotherham had the least, at 53 per 1,000.
Use this tool to check out the situation in your area. The data for London is only available for the region as a whole and is not broken down by individual councils.
Some people live in one area and work in another, but the analysis did not account for this.
Which sectors have the most entry-level jobs?
Even if there are jobs available in your area, you might not find one in the sector you want to work in.
The sector with the highest average number of entry-level vacancies in the year to October was teaching, with most of those jobs being for teaching assistants, learning support and cover supervisor roles, according to jobs website Adzuna.
The next largest was hospitality and catering, traditionally an area where younger people get their first experience of work.
Adzuna, a major online jobs website, includes adverts for full-time roles marked as entry-level, those asking for up to two years' experience, graduate roles, internships and apprenticeships.
Accounting and finance had the third-highest number of job openings.
What are the typical rates of pay?
Figures on salaries for vacancies can be patchy because many employers do not include them in job adverts.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham recently urged businesses to start publishing salaries ahead of plans to make pay details compulsory in adverts.
Only about 40% of Adzuna's jobs data for the year to October stated a salary, although that figure varies widely by sector.
Here are the average salaries for jobs in the sectors with the largest number of entry-level jobs, according to Adzuna. The highest average salary is £30,530 in engineering, while social care has the lowest at £25,880.
How many job vacancies are there overall?
While it can be hard for anyone looking for their first job, the situation is also tough for older jobseekers.
Across the whole economy there were 690,000 jobs available in the August to October period this year, which is the lowest number since early 2021.
The Covid pandemic led to huge swings in the number of job vacancies available as companies reacted to shutdowns and then reopened as restrictions were lifted.
Stripping out the fluctuations seen during the pandemic, the number of vacancies is now at its lowest level for 12 years.
Apprenticeships have often been a way for people to get their first taste of employment.
In England the number of people starting apprenticeships has risen in recent years, although this has been driven by an increase in those aged 25 and over after schemes for older workers were fully rolled out in 2008.
The number of people aged 24 and under starting apprenticeships in England in 2025 was 172,230, down from a peak of 291,300 in 2012.

title: Relocation of Cape Town baboons to sanctuary ignites heated protests
text:
The relocation of a troop of baboons in Cape Town to a wildlife sanctuary has triggered furious protests by local people opposed to their capture, which officials argue is necessary to stop human-wildlife conflict in the city.
The 44-member Waterfall troop (named after the area they mainly inhabit) was captured in the southern seaside suburb of Simon’s Town on Friday and Saturday. A second, smaller Seaforth troop is also due to be moved.
The growth in both baboon and human populations in Cape Town in recent years has led to increased conflict and more baboons dying as a result. Meanwhile, a heated debate has raged between people who believe that baboons and humans can coexist and those who argue that baboons in urban areas are in danger and in some cases need to be relocated. Some animal rights activists have compared authorities’ baboon management to apartheid.
During Friday’s relocation, outraged protesters tried to stop vehicles taking the baboons away. One person sprayed a fire extinguisher, according to the Daily Maverick, a local news outlet.
After the confrontation, the local Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals branch urged those opposed to the baboons’ capture not to try to stop the vehicles. “Capture and transport are already stressful for the baboons,” it said in a statement. “Delaying their arrival prolongs their time in crates and risks adding to that stress – this is not fair on the baboons.”
It said it remained opposed to the baboon’s relocation, adding: “Our presence did not imply support … our inspectors are present because the animals need someone looking out for them.”
On Sunday, dozens of people sat outside the wildlife centre in a silent protest, some tying flowers to the fence. Baboons from a different troop also gathered at the boundary, calling to the newly captive animals, the Daily Maverick reported.
“We stand together for the Seaforth and Waterfall troops, for their freedom, their dignity and their right to live as wild animals,” Mandy Neal, the administrator of the Save Kogelfontein Baboons Facebook group, posted on Monday, calling for weekly Sunday silent protests. “ Our message is simple: CAPTIVITY IS NOT CONSERVATION.”
The City of Cape Town said in a statement on Sunday that the relocation had been successful, with the baboons being monitored 24/7 after being checked by vets and the females receiving contraceptive implants.
It said: “The Waterfall troop has been relocated due to the severity and persistence of human-baboon conflict in the Simon’s Town urban environment, the limited available natural low-lying habitat, the increasing risk to the baboons’ welfare, and public safety concerns … [and] as a very last resort after other interventions were evaluated and deemed ineffective, and as an alternative to culling.”
Prof Justin O’Riain, a behavioural ecologist at the University of Cape Town, said the baboon management plan had undergone two years of public consultations. “It has thus been disappointing watching members of the public and select NGOs, many which did not engage in the stakeholder process, now compromising the safety and welfare of the baboons and people through violent actions directed at staff and baboons in transit.”

title: She went to college to become a social worker. Now she's joined the skilled trades
text:
COLUMBUS, Ohio — A few miles south of The Ohio State University, Ashley Baukman is wrestling with a piece of steel tubing, using only a manual tool called a foot pedal and her sheer strength to bend it 90 degrees.
This class in conduit bending at The Electrical Trades Center of Central Ohio is part of an apprenticeship program Baukman began in the spring. She's here in class one day out of every two weeks. Other days, she's out on construction sites, working under the supervision of journeymen electricians.
For the 36-year-old college graduate and social worker, it's a new chapter — one she hopes will be the foundation of a long-term career.
College didn't deliver
Being the first in her family to graduate from college had been a point of pride for Baukman.
"I was like, 'Oh, I'm going to do this. I'm going to do it the right way,'" she says. "But it didn't really work out that way, and that's okay. You live and you learn."
Now, as an apprentice, she's getting paid just over $25 an hour for time on the job and a stipend for days she's in class. Already, she's earning more than she was as a social worker and is set to nearly double her wage in just over three years. So far, she's finding the work engaging and rewarding.
"You can see a project to completion, and you can — 'Hey, I did that,'" she says. "It's been pretty fun."
A high point for apprenticeships
With AI throwing into question the future of work and the cost of college higher than ever, apprenticeships in the skilled trades are having a moment.
Once pushed primarily to the non-college bound, apprenticeships are increasingly being seen as a compelling alternative to higher education for anyone curious about the trades. The earn-as-you-learn model, which combines coursework with on-the-job training, requires no prerequisites or prior work experience. Acceptance is generally based on contractor need.
Right now demand for skilled tradespeople — especially electricians — is up.
The construction boom fueled by data centers has contributed to the rapid expansion of The Electrical Trades Center. Enrollment has grown from 500 apprentices in 2022 to more than 800 today. Once a night school, they now hold daytime classes to accommodate the growth.
Baukman may be the only social worker among the apprentices, but as a college graduate, she has plenty of company. Trent Parker, the center's director and an electrician himself, says several dozen currently enrolled have four-year degrees, and roughly 300 applicants have at least some college on their resumes.
While Parker hasn't tracked the share of college graduates in the apprenticeship over the years, he's confident it's rising as sentiment toward the trades has shifted.
Parker recalls a recruiting visit he made to a technical high school 16 years ago. The school's vice principal told him they were grateful for the visit because they needed more opportunities for students who were "flunking out."
Parker was taken aback at the comment. He had just started as the apprenticeship's instruction coordinator and was realizing how deep the misconceptions run, how little this vice principal knew about the rigors of the work. That's now changing.
"You know, we're looking for high performers," Parker says. "The same people that are going to be successful in college are the same people that are going to be successful here."
He notes that the apprenticeship's curriculum is equivalent to college-level coursework. Conduit bending is based on trigonometry. Apprentices have to be able to manipulate decimals and fractions.
Parker was thrilled when in 2023, Ohio's governor signed into law a requirement that licensed school counselors visit a training center like this one to learn about apprenticeships and the careers they lead to, a major step in changing the "college or bust" mentality and recruiting more broadly into the field.
When his own two daughters were deciding about college, he encouraged them to consider following in his path.
"I asked them several times, 'Are you sure you don't want to be an electrician?'" he says. "Now I get to log into their Sallie Mae loan accounts and — you know — ugh. I agreed to pay what?"
Rethinking earlier choices
Gather together some of the college graduates at The Electrical Trades Center, and you hear similar themes. A common one: Careers they pursued after college just didn't pay enough.
After finishing her degree in social work, Baukman found jobs in local government agencies working with children and seniors but never earned enough to support her blended family. Her last job was as a prevention specialist in schools, but what she really wanted to do was to become a school social worker, a role that requires a master's degree. With five children at home, plus an estimated $80,000 in student loans, she couldn't figure out how to make it work.
"It just wasn't in the cards," she says. "So I was looking for a change."
Mike Hansen entered the apprenticeship after completing college, ten years in the Army, and some graduate school. He was originally on track to do a doctoral degree in sport and performance psychology, but had seen how others who had gone into academia had struggled.
"They were doing 40 hours of teaching and zero hours of research for $40,000 a year," he says. He left school after finishing his master's degree.
Now, at 39, he wishes he could go back and tell his 17-year-old self to consider a career in the trades from the start. The opportunity was there. His father was an airline mechanic and a member of the Teamsters union. His high school had a vocational school attached to it, but going there was highly stigmatized.
"I distinctly remember as part of our generation... it was massively looked down upon. You were considered a burnout," he says. "Guidance counselors, teachers, my parents, everyone was like, 'Go to college, get an engineering degree. You'll make six figures.'"
For Michael Hughes, the message was slightly different. "The expectation was to get a four-year degree in some field whatsoever, and you'll be fine," he says.
He wasn't sure what he wanted to do, so he majored in English.
"I had a pipe dream of, you know, writing for TV and movies," he says. After college, he did work for a time for the Geek Squad, mounting televisions and installing home theater systems, among other jobs.
Now, as an apprentice, he's been pulling wire, adding pipe, and replacing panels and fuses in a variety of settings including a police station, a paper mill, a sheet metal plant and an auto plant. He's appreciating the breadth of what he's learning and the chance to apply it immediately.
"It's almost like learning a foreign language by just going to that country and communicating, and then also taking classes and someone teaching you the proper conjugations of verbs," he says.
A future of six-figure earnings
Between new construction, commercial renovations and the data center buildout, electricians in Ohio are flush with work. With data center projects in particular, contractors are offering big incentives to get the jobs done quickly.
Parker has heard of projects paying $5 or $10 over the union-negotiated hourly wage. On other projects, all overtime is double time. Apprentices have even heard rumors about triple time.
"There's some crazy money to be made out there," he says.
The apprentices are guaranteed a minimum hourly wage that starts at $23 an hour. There are built-in raises that come as they reach milestones for hours worked, topping out at $46 an hour. With overtime, many journeyworker electricians earn well over $100,000 a year, something the apprentices are looking forward to.
For now, these apprentices don't get to choose where they work. The program assigns them, based on contractor need. Harry Cekovich has been happy with his assignment at a solar field, where he's primarily running cables through rows of solar panels. There too, he's been picking up overtime while also collecting a $100 per diem. It's money he puts towards gas, although the site is less than an hour from his home.
Cekovich is the only one in the group who knows what it's like to earn six figures. For a time, the 34-year-old Ohio State graduate was making pretty good money as a massage therapist and a bartender.
"Granted, I was working 60, 70 hour weeks," he says. "Crazy, nonstop hours, so nothing too great, honestly."
None of those jobs came with benefits. Now, through the union contract, he has both retirement benefits and health insurance with no premiums.
"It's nice to be able to go to doctors and get checked up now," he says.
Mixed feelings about data centers and AI
With all the data center construction around Columbus, it's a given that the apprentices will work on a data center at some point. Some are more excited about it than others.
"If it's true about them making double or triple time… I want to work at data centers exclusively," jokes Cekovich.
Hansen is not so enthusiastic.
"There's enough concern and discussion going on right now about the harms that data centers cause," he says, citing their heavy energy and water use and the noise they generate. "Once I become a journeyman, and I'm allowed to pick my calls, I probably won't pick a job call for a data center, personally."
Ohio Gov.-elect Amy Acton has called for a "conditional moratorium" on new data center construction to ensure that developers cover their own utility costs, adhere to environmental standards and use union labor, among other things.
Whatever happens, Hansen expects there will be plenty of work at area hospitals, schools, commercial buildings and factories.
The apprentices are aware that the rapid buildout of data centers — especially hyperscale ones built to power AI — is a big reason the apprenticeship has been able to bring in so many recruits. At the moment, it accounts for about half the work in the school's jurisdiction.
"It kind of seems like it is, for better or worse, the way of the future," says Cekovich, adding that the proliferation of data centers influenced his decision to go into the electrical trades. "Are we contributing to the end of civilization with AI getting to be what it might become? Not totally sure."
Come what may, Hansen believes he and his classmates will be okay.
"I would like to see Chat GPT wire a three-way switch," he says. "We're still going to need electricians."

title: NSA's classified internal network goes down, sources say
text:
Washington — The National Security Agency's internal network used to store and share classified information went offline Tuesday, according to multiple U.S. officials familiar with the situation, prompting the agency to stagger arrival times for some personnel at its headquarters at Fort Meade, Maryland.
The network, dubbed "NSA Net," is used for classified communications and information sharing within the nation's largest intelligence agency.
An NSA spokesperson said in a statement that the agency experienced a "temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance." The statement continued that "while some internal systems were affected, mission/critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend National Security continues."
The spokesperson said that the agency's infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.
Two U.S. officials told CBS News that, at this point, there is no evidence the disruption was caused by a cyberattack. Two sources familiar with the situation said the outage resulted from routine system patching, though the precise circumstances surrounding the disruption remain unclear.
The NSA has also implemented staggered arrival times for non-emergency personnel at Fort Meade, according to two sources familiar with the measure.
The news was first reported by CNN.
Multiple sources told CBS News that the agency was seeking to avoid having large numbers of employees log on to their computers simultaneously while the network was experiencing problems, which is why they decided to stagger arrivals. Sources referred to this as "Code Gray," part of a modified reporting schedule.
Sources familiar with Fort Meade's operations said the installation remains under normal operating conditions, with gates and campus-wide services unaffected. The sources explained that the NSA operates within its own secured campus and can establish unique reporting requirements for its personnel, independent of the larger installation.
In the meantime, some activities are being redirected to other NSA facilities around the country, according to sources familiar with the situation.
It was not immediately clear how long the network had been offline or when full service might be restored.
The NSA, home to one of the largest workforces in the U.S. intelligence community, is responsible for collecting and analyzing foreign signals intelligence, identifying and countering cyber threats, and protecting U.S. government communications.
CBS News has reached out to the White House, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and the Pentagon for comment.

title: Iran-backed group warns Iraqi forces against entering its stronghold near Baghdad
text:
Kataib Hezbollah, a powerful Iran-backed armed group, has vowed to confront Iraqi government forces if they enter its stronghold near Baghdad
JURF AL-SAKHAR, Iraq -- A powerful Iran-backed armed group in Iraq vowed on Tuesday to confront government forces if they try to enter its main stronghold near Baghdad, denying allegations that it is smuggling oil from the area.
The standoff between Kataib Hezbollah and Iraqi authorities is shaping up to be the first major test of the new government’s resolve to disarm nonstate armed groups.
Abu Taleb al-Saidi of Kataib Hezbollah made the comments a day after Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said security forces would enter Jurf al-Sakhar, south of Baghdad in Babil province, later this week. Local media reported that the group had until Friday to leave.
Kataib Hezbollah, one of Iraq’s most powerful armed groups, wields considerable influence in Jurf al-Sakhar and has maintained an armed presence there for more than a decade.
The planned move by al-Zaidi is part of his push to disarm powerful Iran-backed groups by mid-2027. The move by both rival sides raises alarms of internal Shiite fighting that has been mostly avoided since the 2003 U.S.-led invasion that removed Saddam Hussein from power.
Two officials from Kataib Hezbollah told The Associated Press that Gen. Esmail Qaani, who heads the foreign wing of Iran’s Revolutionary Guard, arrived in Baghdad on Monday to take part in mediation to end the tension. The officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to comment publicly, gave no further details.
The United States backs efforts to disarm Iran-backed groups in Iraq as part of its push to reduce Tehran’s influence in the region, including in Iraq and Lebanon. Washington has described Kataib Hezbollah as an “Iran-backed terrorist organization.”
Lebanese authorities will likely be watching the standoff in Jurf al-Sakhar closely. They have made little progress in carrying out their own plan to disarm Lebanon’s Hezbollah militia, which is allied with but separate from Kataib Hezbollah.
Also Tuesday, an Iraqi judicial committee inspected Jurf al-Sakhar following allegations by authorities that Kataib Hezbollah had used the area to smuggle oil worth tens of millions of dollars.
The state news agency quoted an unnamed senior official as saying the judicial committee was accompanied by a government committee. The inspection aimed to examine the circumstances of the alleged smuggling and identify sites where violations had occurred.
The agency quoted al-Zaidi as saying that all suspects involved in the oil smuggling operations will be referred to the judiciary and that legal measures will be taken against them. He also ordered the dismissal of nine security and administrative officials in Babil governorate, including the Babil police chief, commanders and directors of security and intelligence agencies, and the director of the State Company for Oil Pipelines.
Ali al-Nheir, a member of the parliament’s investigative committee, told the state news agency that the investigation that included thermal imaging showed 25 tanker trucks each carrying 36,000 liters.
“The reports reviewed by the committee were shocking, and included evidence and documents proving the existence of smuggling operations,” al-Nheir said about Jurf al-Sakhar.
Another Kataib Hezbollah official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, told journalists touring Jurf al-Sakhar on Tuesday that two facilities in the area refine oil. He said the fuel was used only to run the group’s vehicles and power generators and denied allegations of smuggling.
The official said Jurf al-Sakhar had been hit more than 35 times since the U.S. and Israel began attacking Iran in late February.
He warned that if “a war is imposed on us we will fight.”
Associated Press writer Bassem Mroue contributed to this report from Beirut.

title: Could the Airbus' €3 billion loan row reignite a US-EU trade dispute?
text:
A fresh row over a record-breaking EU loan to European aerospace company Airbus could reopen a long-standing rift with Washington and threaten an existing EU-US trade truce.
The European Investment Bank (EIB), the lending arm of the EU, agreed in June to loan Airbus up to €3 billion ($3.4 billion) but US President Donald Trump's top trade advisor recently suggested the loan breached a 2021 EU-US agreement on state support.
"I had sincerely hoped that trade-distorting European subsidies to Airbus were a thing of the past," US Trade Representative Jamieson Grier said in late October. "For decades, France, Germany and Spain have aggressively supported Airbus, their national champion aircraft manufacturer, to gain an unfair advantage over US aerospace workers and business."
He also suggested there was a lack of transparency around the terms of the loan. The EU insists the loan does not amount to subsidies, that it is in close contact with the Office of the US Trade Representative and "will provide all necessary information," a spokesperson told DW.
An Airbus spokesperson told DW the company is "actively engaging with the relevant authorities and are happy to share more information about the loan with governments."
A thorn in the side of EU-US trade relations
Airbus and the US company Boeing, the world's two largest plane manufacturers, were previously involved in a 17-year corporate trade dispute.
The World Trade Organization (WTO) ruled that both the EU and US provided the companies with state subsidies, resulting in years of tariffs, tit-for-tat retaliation and claims of victory by both sides.
A deal to end tariffs with strict provisions on state support was finally agreed in 2021 and strengthened in 2025, but the latest row threatens to reopen the dispute and could potentially threaten the wider EU-US tariff deal agreed last year, experts say.
The previous Airbus-Boeing dispute was one of the longest-running corporate disputes in history and led to billions of dollars' worth of tariffs leveled by both sides.
"Trade experts tend to hate to talk about it because there are so many ups and downs to the story, it took so long to get resolved and it always tends to creep back up again," Inu Manak, a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics who specializes in international trade law and policy, told DW.
She says because the issue is such a "persistent thorn in the side," it has the potential to spiral, but for now the US is only signaling displeasure before things escalate. "They want to talk about this, and that conversation will need to happen before anything goes further," she said.
Does the €3 billion Airbus loan amount to state support?
At the heart of the current dispute is whether the €3 billion loan from the EIB, the largest corporate loan ever authorized by the bank, amounts to illegal state support.
"The EIB loan to Airbus is a standard loan on market terms," a European Commission spokesperson told DW. "It carries interest, it must be repaid in full, and it is the type of financing the EIB provides every year to companies across many sectors."
A spokesperson for the bank told DW the €3 billion loan is "a standard EIB corporate loan, implemented under the bank's established procedures and on market-based terms." It says it considers the financing to be "fully consistent with the market-terms principle" of the 2021 deal.
A spokesperson for Airbus told DW the loan is "a standard corporate financing facility, similar to commercially available loans we've signed in the past."
Fredrik Erixon, founding director of the European Center for International Political Economy, says the lines are still blurred when it comes to what counts as a subsidy and what is just a loan and that only a comprehensive World Trade Organization investigation could establish the full facts.
Another potential issue is how the €3 billion will be used, including the share earmarked for research and development and how much funding will support defense-related activities versus commercial aircraft development.
Inu Manak says it is impossible at this point to determine if the loan amounts to the provision of illegal subsidies or not, and that it depends on the very specific terms of the credit provided and whether or not it could be proved to be damaging to Boeing's business.
"If it's a market-based loan, if it's not providing below-market rates that would provide an unfair advantage, then it should be fine," she said. "That remains to be seen."
In Erixon's view, the situation is further complicated by the fact that the aerospace sector is "a highly murky business" due to the amount of defense contracts companies like Boeing and Airbus hold with governments and the high costs associated with that in terms of research and development.
"The problem is we've ended up in a world where there's only two large aircraft manufacturers," he told DW. "And it is a business with high upfront costs when you're going to develop different things."
He points out that while Boeing may have a legitimate grievance over this loan, Airbus and the EU can point to Boeing's own deals with the US government.
"Boeing does R&D contracts for military purposes, which end up producing technology and support for the civil aircraft program for Boeing," said Erixon. "That's also what the World Trade Organization found previously."
It was Boeing that originally asked the US trade representative back in July to intervene over the loan, linking it to Airbus' plan to develop a new single-aisle aircraft program, which could spark a new era of intense competition between the two giants.
Why the Airbus-Boeing subsidy dispute keeps resurfacing
Inu Manak thinks the next obvious step for the US would be to launch a Section 301 investigation, which is an official inquiry to determine if the loan "violates an international trade agreement or is unjustified, unreasonable or discriminatory, and that burdens or restricts US commerce."
She thinks the Trump administration has no interest in engaging with the WTO and believes it has the potential to threaten the broader EU-US trade agreement.
"I don't think there's a lot that can stop the US trade representative from taking action if they decide they want to do it," Manak said. "They may think there may be something else to extract from the European Union."
Fredrik Erixon agrees that "it's going to be a point of leverage that the Americans can use against Europe," adding that the dynamics underpinning the aerospace sector — that both Boeing and Airbus need greater government investment due to ramped-up military spending — is the fundamental underlying problem.
"We are getting into a state aid race, which basically means these companies just need more and more and more money," he said. "That in itself is an escalatory development."

title: Ukraine hits symbolic Crimea Bridge for second time in 24 hours
text:
Ukraine inflicted catastrophic damage on the bridge linking Russia and Crimea on Tuesday, delivering a major symbolic blow to Vladimir Putin.
Russian authorities said they opened a terrorism investigation following two Ukrainian attacks on the bridge over the Kerch Strait, adding that the structure had suffered damage.
All train and vehicle traffic on the Crimean Bridge has been suspended while specialists assess the damage, Russia’s ministry of transport reported on Tuesday morning. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov had earlier described damage to the bridge as minor.
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky celebrated the strike, which he said was the result of a seven stage operation carried out over a number of weeks between the SSU and armed forces.
"We have long been telling Russia: Enough of striking bridges, cities and villages, energy infrastructure, railways and grain ships. Enough of war. But every time Russia chooses further escalation," Zelensky said in his nightly video address.
A Flamingo cruise missile was deployed to carry out a “precision-guided strike”, he said, alongside a range of other missiles and drones including Neptune missiles and Ruta drones.
He shared a video compilation of the strike, which showed a missile going towards the bridge. The strike itself appeared not to be recorded, as the president said the “communications uplink worked flawlessly until the very last seconds.”
Anton Gerashchenko, Ukraine’s former minister of internal affairs, said the operation had dealt out “critical damage” on the bridge.
“Last night, the Kerch Bridge, a symbol of occupation and Russian aggression against Ukraine, sustained critical damage during a powerful combined missile and drone attack.”
Ukrainian sanctions commissioner Vladislav Vlasiuk reshared a photo of the bridge with one of its arches missing on Tuesday morning, captioned: “Crimean Bridge. Sanctioned.”
The Kremlin-appointed governor of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, asked “residents and guests” of the region to avoid the bridge following the “enemy” strike.
“The enemy has attacked the Crimean Bridge again. At this moment, traffic is suspended. We ask residents and guests of Crimea to refrain from traveling towards the bridge and to take the restrictions into account when planning their routes. We will provide further updates on the situation. I remind you of the need to trust only official sources of information.”
The attacks, on Monday and Tuesday, killed two people and shut down the bridge, the Russian-installed governor said.
The 12-mile long (19km) Crimea Bridge is one of two routes available to Moscow, connecting the transport networks of Russia and Crimea after the Ukrainian peninsula was illegally annexed by Russia in 2014. It has been a key supply route for Russian forces in Ukraine and is widely viewed as one of Putin's signature infrastructure projects.
It consists of a separate roadway and railway, both supported by concrete stilts, which give way to a wider span held by steel arches at the point where ships pass between the Black Sea and the smaller Azov Sea.
Few countries have recognised Crimea as part of the Russian Federation.
The bridge has been attacked by Ukraine several times since Putin sent Russian forces into Ukraine in February 2022. A truck bomb in October 2022 killed four people and limited the bridge's capacity for several months.
The overnight strike was part of the largest Ukrainian drone attack on Russia since the start of the full-scale war in 2022, as the defence ministry said it shot down 1,441 drones over 22 regions, surpassing Monday's figure of 1,336 which itself had set a new record.
Air defence systems had repelled a massive drone attack on the industrial areas of Ufa and Salavat in Russia's Bashkortostan region, home to a number oil refineries, state media reported, citing local officials.
Russian attacks have also intensified in the past few months on bridges in Ukraine, including in the capital Kyiv. Two bridges over the Dnipro River sustained damage late on Monday, which prompted some water and power cuts and traffic restrictions.
President Zelensky said on Tuesday: “We have repeatedly offered Russia steps toward de-escalation – and every proposal has been met with loud rejection. Russia strikes our infrastructure every day, including bridges in Zaporizhzhia, Dnipro, Kyiv, and the Odesa region.
“We are restoring our infrastructure. But we are also reminding Russia that war will always return to where it began. Ukraine’s defensive capabilities are strong and will remain so, and we will never leave terror against our cities and people unanswered.
“I thank the true warriors of the Security Service of Ukraine, all our Defense Forces, our intelligence agencies, and EVERY manufacturer of weapons effectively used to defend Ukraine, Ukrainians, and our national interests. Glory to Ukraine!”

title: North Macedonia prevents 'terrorist' assassination plot targeting person in Greece
text:
Guns and sketches marking specific locations were reportedly seized as part of the operation, which was carried out in cooperation with Greece's national intelligence agency.
North Macedonia's National Security Agency (ANB) announced on Tuesday that it had prevented a "terrorist" assassination plot targeting a person in Greece and that it had dismantled an Iranian-linked network.
The ANB said it had brought down "a wide network of proxy actors" linked to Iranian Edris Jahangiri Mavaneh, who it described as a "collaborator of the Iranian security and intelligence services".
The agency said the network "undertook preparatory logistical activities to carry out a terrorist act/assassination against a person in Greece" while "under the direct instructions of the Iranian national."
An anti-terrorist force also took part, police said. Raids were carried out at four locations.
The operation began in early 2026, the security agency's head, Bojan Hristovski, said, adding that the group had held "conspiratorial meetings on the territory of third countries, including Iran."
"As for the Macedonian network, it involves individuals embedded within criminal structures in the country," Hristovski told a press conference.
Four suspects have been taken into custody, while another has been placed under house arrest, an official said.
One person was detained in Greece and transferred to authorities in North Macedonia.
A sixth suspect was still being sought.

title: Obama-appointed judge paves way to unseal Ilhan Omar search warrant in blow to Trump's DOJ
text:
A federal judge in Washington, D.C. who has often ruled against the Trump administration dealt a blow to the Justice Department Tuesday, paving the way to unseal the criminal search warrant and related documents against Rep. Ilhan Omar.
Judge James Boasberg, who was appointed to the bench by former President Barack Obama in 2011, asked the DOJ's attorneys to submit proposed redactions to the documents, excluding the main affidavit, by Friday. Unless a higher court intervenes, the court will publish the redacted documents online Monday beginning at 5 p.m. after consulting with prosecutors.
After its release, the groups seeking the documents have until Nov. 30 to challenge any blacked-out sections.
While criminal warrants aren't typically unsealed until after charges are filed, 15 media organizations and watchdog group Judicial Watch sued to obtain the warrant. They have argued that releasing the contents of the warrant is in the public interest.
The plaintiffs argued specifically that it should be made public which statutes federal investigators think Omar may have broken.
Boasberg signaled that he would not release the warrant application, which is a sworn statement submitted to a judge explaining facts and evidence that establish probable cause for issuing a warrant.
The DOJ did not immediately return Fox News Digital's request for comment.
Omar is facing a probe related to whether she or her father fraudulently filled out immigration paperwork in order for her to obtain citizenship. The Somali-born congresswoman said last week that she wasn't privy to what exactly the DOJ is investigating.
During the raid, which was conducted by Homeland Security Investigations (HIS), Omar's personal cellphone, computer and passport were seized. Her DNA has also been obtained, and her sister, Sahra Noor, was questioned by investigators the week of the raid.
In a motion seeking to prevent the federal search warrant for the congresswoman’s home from being unsealed, the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia referred to Omar as "Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, a/k/a Ilhan Abdullahi Omar…" and sources later told Fox News Digital that Ilhan Omar is not the congresswoman's "real name."
That news caused speculation that Omar married her brother, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, to resurface. The pair married in 2009, and officially divorced in 2017.
Omar has not been charged with a crime and has repeatedly and categorically denied any wrongdoing. She has characterized the investigation as politically motivated, saying President Donald Trump is targeting her.
But the DOJ under former President Barack Obama opened an investigation into Omar's marriage with Nur Said Elmi in 2016 — suggesting the nonpartisan nature of some of the inquiries into the Minnesota lawmaker.
The New York Times first reported that Obama's FBI and Department of Homeland Security (DHS) began the probe in the summer of 2016, and that officials "found some evidence that [the marriage] was fraudulent." The Times reported that the investigation concluded when officials decided the potential felony crime was past the statute of limitations.
That probe, an official told Fox News Digital, remained open until 2021, when it was closed under the Biden administration.

title: U.S. and Mexico officially lose measles-elimination status
text: The U.S. has lost its measles-free status, international health officials said Tuesday, as the highly contagious virus once relegated to medical textbooks has spread — largely among the unvaccinated — at the highest rate in more than 30 years. Mexico also lost its measles-elimination status, following a resurgence of the virus there that included a massive outbreak in Chihuahua state. Bolivia, too, lost its status. WATCH: 'It's close to bulletproof,' doctor says of MMR vaccine as measles cases rise The Pan American Health Organization declaration has few practical implications and is largely symbolic, but it marks a sharp turnabout in a disease largely controlled through decades of scientific advances. It also may be seen as the beginning of an era in which diseases of the past become deadly problems for the modern world. Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "Measles elimination is not a trophy that is won once and placed on a shelf," Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, PAHO's director, said at a news conference. "It is an achievement that must be safeguarded every day by closing immunity gaps and ensuring we reach every community." PAHO expects the U.S., Bolivia and Mexico to submit plans "in the coming weeks" for how each country will go about trying to stop transmission for at least a year and regain measles elimination status, said Dr. Daniel Salas, the organization's executive manager for immunizations. Measles has been spreading throughout the Americas since 2024. The outbreaks in North America started in close-knit Mennonite communities and have since spread to areas with low vaccination rates. Last year, Canada lost its measles-free designation for the first time since 1998. International health officials consider measles eliminated when the virus is not locally spreading among residents. The designation hinges on whether a single measles chain has spread uninterrupted for at least 12 months. Tuesday's announcement signals an erosion of public health preparedness. Vaccination rates have been falling against a number of diseases, in the U.S. and globally. And as one of the most infectious diseases known to medicine, measles was seen as likely to be one of the first vaccine-preventable diseases to reemerge when vaccinations falter. That means others are likely to follow, some experts said. "It can be the canary in the coal mine to other things," said Dr. Susan Kansagra, chief medical officer of the Association of State and Territorial Health Officials. Vaccine rates fall and cases go up Measles vaccines have safely stopped the virus' spread in the U.S. for 30 years. It takes a community vaccination rate of 95% to prevent outbreaks, experts say. But as fewer parents vaccinate their children and federal leaders sow doubt and confusion about the importance of getting vaccinated, the virus has found footholds in communities across the U.S. All but three states have reported a confirmed case of measles this year. WATCH: Pennsylvania doctor urges vaccination as measles outbreak grows The last two years have been the worst in a generation in the U.S., with more than 7,000 cases and 11 deaths. Nearly all of those people were either unvaccinated or didn't report whether they were vaccinated. More than 10% of those infected had to be hospitalized. The illness typically begins with a high fever followed by a telltale rash that starts on the face and neck. Most people recover, but it's one of the leading causes of death among young children, according to the World Health Organization. Serious complications, including blindness and swelling of the brain, are more common in young children and adults over age 30. Ten measles-associated deaths have been reported in the U.S. this year. Health officials have not released detailed information on each death, but at least five of the dead were children. This year's measles death count is higher than what has been seen in any previous year in more than three decades. And the U.S. is experiencing its worst year for measles illnesses since 1991. The U.S. has seen major outbreaks in Texas, Utah, South Carolina and Pennsylvania Since the U.S. eliminated measles in 2000, public health officials usually logged less than 200 cases a year, most of them tied to international travel. But since 2025, measles has sickened thousands. It started with a major outbreak in the southwest. In Texas, more than 760 people got sick and two children died. And in New Mexico, about 100 people got sick and one adult died. In the summer of 2025, measles exploded in extremely rural border towns in Arizona and Utah. And a major outbreak in South Carolina in the winter and spring sickened nearly 1,000 people to become the fastest growing measles outbreak the nation has seen in decades. Bad as 2025 was, this year has been much worse. The more than 5,400 confirmed cases so far this year are already double the 2025 tally, driven largely by an outbreak in Pennsylvania that has dwarfed the earlier ones. And the outbreak tallies are almost certainly an undercount, public health experts say. Critics say the U.S. response is falling short U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. was a leading voice in the anti-vaccine movement before President Donald Trump appointed him to oversee federal health agencies. Kennedy and other federal leaders have argued that vaccination rates were waning for years before Trump took office a second time, that measles is not an "American phenomenon," and that the U.S. government is handling measles better than other countries. In January, a (backslash) U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention leader told reporters that the loss of the nation's elimination status would be the "cost of doing business" globally. It's true that other countries are struggling with measles, and some also have lost their measles-elimination status. But some experts say the outcome in the U.S. wasn't inevitable. "This humiliating determination is the tragic yet predictable result of an ongoing campaign by grifters, quacks and charlatans to put their own greed and self-worth ahead of the health and safety of children," said Sen. Ron Wyden, a Democrat from Oregon. The government has been taking some steps. In August and September, the CDC awarded $100 million — in two tranches — to support state and local measles-response work. And Kennedy and CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz have made statements that vaccination is the best way to prevent measles from spreading. "The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does," Schwartz said in a statement Tuesday. "We know where transmission is occurring and we've invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach those communities." But state and local health officials say the cost is far higher than that. "It wasn't a lot of money, frankly," said Chrissie Juliano, executive director of the Big Cities Health Coalition, which represents three dozen of the largest U.S. city health departments. Experts also say the moment demands a louder federal voice — and a bigger push for vaccinations — than Kennedy and Schwartz are providing. Some noted that neither Kennedy nor the CDC has scheduled a news conference for this week to address how they plan to try to regain measles-elimination status. "When the people at the front of the room are not speaking loudly and frequently in support of vaccination, the program starts to falter. And that's what we're seeing in the U.S.," said Noel Brewer, a University of North Carolina public health professor who chairs a committee that presented an analysis of U.S. measles data to PAHO last week. "The federal government has had such a ho-hum response," he said. "How many kids have to die before they start getting concerned? What's next? After hugely successful vaccination campaigns, the Americas became the first region in the world to be free of measles in 2016. Health officials estimate the measles vaccine prevented 6.2 million deaths in the Americas between 2000 and 2023. Now, the entirety of North America faces the task of earning back the designation. Some individual countries have achieved, lost, and then regained measles-elimination status. Brazil is one example. Another is the United Kingdom, although it lost its status a second time — this year. AP Medical Writer Laura Ungar in Louisville, Kentucky, contributed to this report.

title: Nike lays out financial goals ahead of first investor day in 9 years
text:
Nike said Tuesday ahead of its first investor day in nine years that it was reaffirming its 2027 financial guidance.
The retailer also laid out a financial framework and said that by the end of fiscal 2031 it's targeting approximately $5 billion in incremental revenue growth from fiscal year 2027, operating margins of 12% to 14% and adjusted earnings per share of $3.00 to $3.50. The company said higher-quality revenue, gross margin expansion and productivity improvements would help it reach its goals.
Nike's 2027 financial guidance includes expectations for revenue to decline in the high-single-digit range, an adjusted operating margin of approximately 6%, and adjusted EPS of $1.15 to $1.35.
The company also introduced a strategy it's calling Full Stride Ahead, which the company said aims "to get closer to athletes and focus resources on the greatest opportunities for long-term growth."
Nike CEO Elliott Hill told CNBC's Sara Eisen that the new initiative is about "being closer to the athletes we serve."
"What's different today is the depth and breadth we're taking from an innovation perspective," Hill said.
He added that Nike is emphasizing sportswear at a time when sports have never been more relevant around the world. Hill also said Nike is working to regain its cultural relevance, after a perceived dropoff contributed to its slowdown both in its home market and in China.
Nike said it would focus on performance sports and sportswear opportunities "with the greatest potential for long-term growth," and said its five priority sports would be running, training, global football, basketball and outdoor.
Nike is holding an investor day at its Oregon headquarters Tuesday as the company aims to prove to investors that its turnaround strategy is yielding success after a yearslong slump.
Last month, the company reported mixed fiscal first-quarter results as it announced a restructuring plan, including layoffs that it said would start next year. It's the company's third round of layoffs to be announced this year.
Nike's net income and revenue both fell during the most recent period compared with a year ago, and the company said it expects revenue to decline by a high single-digit percentage in fiscal 2027.
The new strategy, dubbed Pace, focuses on the company's supply chain and reorganizing into three geographies. Nike said the turnaround plan is expected to deliver roughly $2.5 billion in savings through fiscal 2031.
Nike has been seeing significant sustained declines in its China market, where revenue last quarter dropped 26%. Experts have said the company is losing relevance in the country, while Nike has said it's actively working to win over younger consumers.
At the same time, Nike announced last quarter that it's creating a new global campus in India as part of its new growth strategy, hoping the country will help boost its performance. The company said it was remaining focused on China even as it begins to build out its India presence.
Nike COO Venkatesh Alagirisamy told CNBC the company sees an opportunity to triple its business in the country over the next five years.
He added that Nike's broader strategy will position it for success in India.
"If you look at the three components, brand building, landing those innovations into marketplaces in an increasingly locally connected fashion and then doing all of those things in a much faster pace really aligns well with the aspirations for India," he said.
CEO Elliott Hill's turnaround strategy includes improving different parts of the business at different rates based on priority. While it's seen some signs of progress in the North America business, Hill has said that performance isn't enough to offset the pressures on the company elsewhere, including internationally.
The Nike consumer has also been under increased macroeconomic pressure as geopolitical tensions mount and inflation rises.
Shares of Nike have fallen 50% over the past two years.

title: Meta launches Direct, a stand-alone messaging app for Instagram
text:
Meta is testing Direct, a new stand-alone messaging app that houses Instagram’s direct messages. Direct is initially launching in Turkey and Thailand, and can be used with or without an Instagram account.
With Direct, Meta is likely looking to retain users who use Instagram primarily, or even exclusively, for messaging. Over the years, people have often sought various ways to use Instagram’s direct messaging features without having to deal with the rest of the platform.
Direct appears to be Meta’s answer to that demand, as the company says it is designed for chatting one-on-one or in groups with friends and family.
The new app also gives the company a way to keep these users within its ecosystem rather than risk losing them altogether, and count them as active users within its ecosystem, even if they don’t use Instagram itself.
Besides usual messaging features like reactions, voice notes, and emojis, Direct also features a “Draw” feature that lets you doodle and sketch directly inside chat threads. There’s also “Notes,” which are the short status updates that appear at the top of your Instagram DMs.
Meta says users can create custom stickers, add audio effects to replies, and personalize chat backgrounds with custom themes.
Users in Turkey and Thailand can sign up for Direct using their email address or phone number. Those with an existing Instagram account can log in using the same username and password, and their existing conversations will be synced across both apps.
Meta says only people in your contacts or those you’re already connected with can start conversations or add you to group chats. Users can also report, block, restrict, or remove contacts at any time.
The company also says it will use its age-estimation technology to identify and address potentially inappropriate interactions involving young users. Parents will also have access to supervision tools that let them see who their teens are messaging, manage safety settings, and set daily usage limits.
Teens who use their Instagram username and password to access Direct will have to work with all the same messaging restrictions as Instagram’s Teen Accounts.
Meta did not say when or if it will bring Direct to additional countries.

title: Comcast's "fiber-powered Wi-Fi" is just cable, AT&T says in false advertising case
text:
AT&T on Friday accused Comcast of false advertising in a lawsuit challenging the marketing claim that Comcast’s cable broadband service and Wi-Fi are “fiber-powered.”
“This case challenges Comcast’s false advertising campaign for its residential Internet service, marketed under the Xfinity brand to consumers nationwide,” AT&T’s lawsuit said. “At the center of that campaign is Comcast’s claim that Xfinity Internet and its associated Wi-Fi service are ‘Fiber-Powered.’”
While Comcast has deployed plenty of fiber throughout the US, its cable Internet service makes the final connection to homes with coaxial cable. This results in upload speeds being far slower than download speeds.
In contrast, fiber-to-the-home service can provide symmetrical upload and download speeds. Comcast has deployed fiber-to-the-home in only small portions of its cable territory while advertising its service as fiber-powered in the majority of areas where cable makes the final connection.
AT&T’s lawsuit said that in describing its cable broadband as fiber-powered, Comcast “conveys to reasonable consumers the misleading impression that Xfinity Internet is a fiber-to-the-home service comparable to AT&T Fiber. In fact, the vast majority of Xfinity Internet runs over a hybrid fiber-coaxial (‘HFC’) network, where the critical ‘last mile’ connection to the customer’s home uses copper coaxial cable, not fiber.”
AT&T has its own history of ads that mislead customers about the nature of its network. It used to advertise 4G LTE service as “5GE” or “5G Evolution,” and displayed a 5GE network icon on 4G phones. AT&T claimed that its 5G Evolution ads “served to educate customers about the billions of dollars AT&T has invested to give customers an outstanding experience,” but the BBB National Programs’ National Advertising Division found the term was likely to mislead consumers into thinking they had 5G connections.
AT&T: Fiber-powered is “literally false”
AT&T’s lawsuit said that Comcast’s fiber-powered claim “is literally false” because the cable firm’s HFC “architecture is fundamentally different from true fiber-to-the-home services like AT&T Fiber, which deliver fiber optic cables directly to the customer’s premises.”
