title: A hidden biological divide may help explain Alzheimer’s and chronic pain
text:
New research reveals that biological sex, genetics, and menopause may dramatically influence Alzheimer's risk, treatment responses, and chronic pain conditions such as fibromyalgia. Scientists also uncovered surprising differences in immune activity and gut-brain interactions, opening the door to more personalized treatments for neurological disorders.
Emerging research suggests that biological sex and genetics may play a major role in how neurological disorders develop, progress, and respond to treatment. The findings, which will be presented at Neuroscience 2026, reveal important differences that could help researchers develop more personalized approaches to treating complex brain conditions. Neuroscience 2026 is the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience and the world's largest source of emerging news about brain science and health.
Researchers are increasingly finding that certain neurological conditions can behave differently depending on a person's biological sex and genetic makeup. Understanding these differences could lead to treatments better suited to each individual's biology. Two conditions receiving particular attention are Alzheimer's disease (AD), an incurable disorder that progressively damages memory and other brain functions, and fibromyalgia, a chronic illness marked by persistent pain and fatigue that affects 2-4% of the global population. According to the World Health Organization, Alzheimer's affects between 35 and 40 million people worldwide.
Menopause, Genetics, and Alzheimer's Disease
Two of the new studies highlight how menopause and inherited genetic factors may influence Alzheimer's vulnerability and treatment responses.
One investigation found that people carrying genetic risk factors for Alzheimer's responded differently to menopause hormone therapy (MHT) compared with those without the same genetic risks. The effects also varied according to the particular combination of hormones used. These findings suggest that both genetic background and hormone therapy formulation deserve consideration when evaluating treatment options. (Mateja Perović, University of Toronto)
A separate study examined rodents undergoing menopause that also carried genetic risk factors for Alzheimer's. Researchers observed that brain circuits responsible for memory became particularly vulnerable, providing evidence that menopause may represent an important period of increased susceptibility for women who are genetically predisposed to the disease. (Stephanie M. Perez, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio)
Sex Differences in Chronic Pain and Brain Inflammation
The other two studies explored how biological sex influences pain sensitivity, immune activity, and the effects of inflammation on the brain.
In a mouse model of fibromyalgia, females continued to show heightened sensitivity to touch and stronger immune system activation compared with males. The findings suggest that the biological processes contributing to chronic pain may differ between sexes, potentially making treatments tailored to these differences more effective. (Yasmin Sahlloul, University of Cincinnati)
Another investigation uncovered differences in how prolonged intestinal inflammation influences the brain. Using a mouse model, researchers found that chronic gut inflammation affected brain function and Alzheimer's related disease changes differently in males and females. The results provide additional evidence that biological sex may influence the relationship between inflammation and neurological disease. (Nurcan Kilic, University of North Dakota)
Toward More Personalized Treatments for Brain Disorders
Together, the four studies underscore the importance of examining sex and genetic differences when investigating neurological conditions. By identifying biological factors that influence disease progression and treatment responses, researchers hope to move toward more precise therapies for Alzheimer's, fibromyalgia, and other difficult-to-treat brain disorders.
"These four studies illustrate the fascinating discoveries that can be made when focusing on female-specific biology or possible sex differences in AD-related symptoms and risk factors," said Liisa Galea, PhD, Treliving Family Chair in Women's Mental Health at Centre for Addiction and Mental Health and moderator of the press conference. "The research presented at Neuroscience 2026 helps us pinpoint the specific differences that may help us develop more targeted treatment using precision approaches, even for some of our most complex brain disorders."

title: A high-fiber diet may clear away plastic in the gut
text:
Here’s a new reason to eat your beans and greens.
A high-fiber diet may help sweep plastic particles from the gut, researchers report October 15 in Nature Communications. In mice that ingested plastic, eating loads of fiber daily kept the particles from piling up in the intestines. The finding hints at fiber’s power to protect the body from environmental garbage, says Eddy Y. Zeng, an environmental scientist at South China University of Technology in Guangzhou.
Researchers have long known that fiber can improve our health, in part by lowering cholesterol, keeping blood sugar levels in check and easing food through the gut. But now, Zeng says, his team’s results suggest an additional benefit.
We live in a world littered with plastic, much of it too small to see. These micro and nanoplastics, shed by disposable water bottles, fast food containers and other worldly junk, can make their way into our bodies. It’s not completely clear what such shards do to our health, but we have some hints. Scientists have linked plastic particles in people’s arteries to increased risk of heart attack and stroke. And mice that ingest tiny bits of plastic can show signs of organ injury.
Zeng’s team thought dietary fiber might provide some defense. Fiber forms a complex network of polymers that could trap ingested plastics like flies in a spider web, he says.
The researchers put mice on low-, medium-, or high-fiber diets, then fed them plastic particles. Over the next 24 hours, the medium- and high-fiber groups of mice cleared more particles from their bodies than their low-fiber counterparts, the team discovered. That’s important, Zeng says, because these particles can do damage. After a week of daily plastic feedings, his team saw gut tissue damage — but only in the low-fiber group. Experiments in test tubes suggest that fiber physically wraps around and sticks to plastic particles.
It’s too soon to say if dietary fiber does the same in humans. Zeng’s study was performed in mice and not tethered to realistic fiber numbers. Though mice in the high-fiber group ate far more fiber than what what’s recommended for people, he thinks the findings are worth pursuing in follow-up studies.
And even if fiber doesn’t end up purging plastic from people’s guts, Zeng says, it probably wouldn’t hurt for us to add a little more to our diets.

title: The Leonid meteor shower peaks tonight! Here's what you need to know
text:
The Leonid meteor shower peaks tonight (Nov. 17-18) sending shooting stars and fireballs across the autumn sky as Earth passes through a stream of debris left by Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle.
Up to 15 meteors could be spotted per hour under perfect dark sky conditions on the night of Nov. 17-18, according to the International Meteor Organisation. NASA, meanwhile, has given a more conservative rate of less than three meteors per hour — time will tell.
Leonid meteors appear to race away from a point of origin, or radiant, in the constellation Leo, which glistens high above the southeastern horizon in the hours before dawn in mid-November. Both Jupiter and Mars will be separated by just a few degrees in the constellation Leo on the night of the peak, making it particularly easy to find in 2026!
When is the best time to look for Leonid meteors?
The best time to spot Leonids is in the hours before dawn on Nov. 18, when the radiant will reach its highest point in the southeastern sky, maximizing the amount of meteors that may be seen skimming through Earth's atmosphere. By then, the waxing moon will have set, leaving darker skies and a better chance of spotting fainter meteors.
Shooting stars that appear close to the radiant will strike Earth almost head-on, leaving the shortest trails. Instead, find a patch of sky a short distance away from the constellation Leo, where the meteors will be at their most impressive, and give your eyes 20-30 minutes to fully adapt to the dark.
Why are the Leonids special?
As if shooting stars weren't enough, the Leonid shower is also known for spawning dazzling fireballs and long-lasting Earth-grazing meteors, which strike our atmosphere at an oblique angle, leaving long trains as they skim through before passing back out into space.
The shower is also capable of producing magnificent meteor storms when Earth passes through particularly dense trails of debris left behind by Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which orbits the sun approximately every 33 years.
Sadly, we'll have to wait a bit for the next big show. According to the Planetary Society, another Leonid meteor storm could occur as early as 2031, while a study released in August 2026 predicts potentially spectacular displays in 2033 and 2034.
Want to photograph a shooting star? Then be sure to read our guide to imaging shooting stars, along with our selections of the best lenses and cameras for astrophotography on the market in 2026.

title: Pretending to be in New Zealand, booking leave and buying consoles - the lengths fans are going to for GTA 6
text:
Grand Theft Auto fans have waited 13 long years for the latest edition of the game to be released - and going to extreme lengths to be ready for its launch.
GTA 6 will be released at midnight on Thursday - and Victoria Evans, from West Sussex, is not leaving anything to chance.
She has her alarm set for 05:00 GMT, and has a day off booked. She says she put the game's release on her leave request form which was approved, she told BBC News, despite the fact her boss "doesn't know what GTA 6 is".
She's far from the only one. For the game's launch day, HR software company BrightHR, external looked at absence data from more than 1.2 million employees from 70,000 businesses across the UK.
It found GTA was mentioned in 4.6% of time-off requests by employees. Throughout November and December, it said an estimated 83,000 days had been booked off for the game.
And booking leave is only one of the ways fans are making sure for the big day. Others are buying a new console to play it on or even pretending they're halfway around the world to get early access.
Big demand
Market intelligence firm Sensor Tower estimates, external GTA 6 has already generated $1.18bn (£894m) from 12 million pre-orders - although Rockstar has not confirmed this.
Despite the option to preload the 212GB game, Jennifer Holmes, chief executive of the London Internet Exchange, said several UK internet providers including BT and Virgin Media had "increased capacity in anticipation of higher demand" ahead of launch.
Gamers have long been known to book time off work for major releases.
When Red Dead Redemption 2 launched in October 2018, social media users were sharing plans to take the day off, with one analytics firm reportedly finding, external more people talking about calling in sick for it than any other game that year.
Similar conversations took place ahead of Cyberpunk 2077's release in December 2020, with fans discussing, external taking several days off to play.
Some places have decided to lean into the trend for GTA 6 by offering incentives around the game - including the US Army's 3rd Infantry Division based at Fort Stewart, Georgia.
It gave some active-duty soldiers a four-day pass to play the game when it is released in November, as long as they sign a reenlistment contract for a minimum of two years between 1 August and 12 November.
"The idea was to have a unique incentives programme that connects to what soldiers are interested in," public affairs officer for the division, Lieutenant Colonel Angel Tomko confirmed to the BBC in August.
"There are 130 soldiers eligible within the battalion, and 20 have selected this incentive as part of their reenlistment," she said at the time.
Allow Instagram content?
Moving to New Zealand
Aside from taking time off, some gamers have also been discussing a technical loophole which could give them valuable extra hours of play before it officially unlocks in their country.
Because GTA 6 will release at midnight local time in all regions, New Zealand will become one of the first places where it is available, due to it reaching midnight earliest because of its position near the international date line.
This has led to some investigating ways to "trick" their consoles into thinking they're based in the island country when they are in fact thousands of miles away.
According to Google Trends, searches for the "GTA 6 New Zealand trick" have surged by more than 5,000% in the UK over the past month.
Games journalist Vic Hood said many gamers would be looking to play earlier to "get in on the action as soon as possible", as well as to prevent spoilers.
"As New Zealand is 13 hours ahead of the UK, that's 13 hours of gameplay that has time to spread across the internet and potentially spoil some key story beats and in-game surprises," she said.
"Took an extra day of paid time off when I found this out," one fan posted on Reddit on the trick.
It also means gamers would be playing the game at the much nicer time of 11:00 GMT, rather than having to stay up all night.
But another Xbox user shared caution on Reddit, noting that while the loophole had been exploited for many years for other game releases, GTA 6 "might be the game where Microsoft finally does something about this 'exploit'" - which could include banning players.
GTA 6's developers Rockstar and publishers Take Two Interactive have not commented on the loophole, and neither have Sony nor Microsoft.
Louise Wooldridge from Ampere Analysis said both Microsoft and Sony had "rules governing regional accounts and purchases" for the Xbox and PlayStation, adding that Sony's were "slightly more restrictive".
Players who choose to use the workaround could therefore risk breaching those terms and conditions and potentially face restrictions on their accounts or lose access to their digital games.
Some gamers will have to wait even longer than their console-playing counterparts to get their hands on GTA 6, as the game will not be available on PC at launch, similar to previous GTA releases.
"Spare a thought for the PC users who will have to live vicariously through others' YouTube videos and Twitch streams," gamer Stephen Finn told the BBC.
A PS5 now costs from £520, while the more powerful PS5 Pro is nearly £790.
Despite the hefty price tag, for some the temptation to join the community in playing what many have called the biggest game launch of the year, if not decade, has been too great.
Reddit posts and videos, such as one by US YouTuber isoish, external, show fans buying consoles specifically to play the game.
"So, the only game I'm going to have on here is GTA," the content creator said in the video.
"The whole PS5 is for GTA 6."
After more than a decade of waiting, it seems some fans are determined not to waste a single minute of GTA 6's release - no matter the cost or extra effort.
Additional reporting: Kris Bramwell

title: US loses measles elimination status amid worst outbreak since 1991
text:
The US lost its measles elimination status, global health authorities announced, an official recognition that the infectious disease is endemic in the US after being eliminated for 26 years.
The announcement comes as the US endures the worst measles outbreak since 1991, with more than 5,400 cases and eight deaths in 2026.
“Measles is resurging globally amid the persistent gaps in vaccination coverage, and this global trend is also affecting the Americas,” said Dr Jarbas Barbosa da Silva Jr, the director of the Pan American Health Organization, a regional branch of the World Health Organization. “The endemic measles transmission has now been re-established in Bolivia, Mexico and United States.” Silva made the final decision on US elimination status.
In a statement to the Guardian on Tuesday, Barbosa da Silva Jr commended “the significant efforts undertaken by the United States to manage the measles outbreak through strengthened surveillance, timely case detection and response, targeted vaccination activities and coordination across the public health system”.
Measles is one of the most contagious viruses known to medicine and requires 95% of the community to be vaccinated to prevent outbreaks. The measles vaccine is safe and highly effective. However, pockets of low vaccination have grown in the US following pandemic-era disruptions and widespread misinformation.
The nation’s largest doctors group, the American Medical Association, described loss of measles elimination status as a “deeply troubling and entirely preventable setback for our nation”.
The loss of measles-free status comes after Donald Trump and his health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, spent nearly two years sowing confusion about the safety of vaccines. In just one recent example, Trump called for the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) combination vaccine to be split into separate shots, arguing without evidence that “together, there could be a possibility they’re quite lethal”.
“As a pediatrician, I saw firsthand how decisions made in Washington hurt our children and families,” said Dr Annie Andrews, a Democratic senator-elect. “Nothing makes that clearer than the loss of our measles elimination status.” The loss of elimination status has already heightened criticism of Kennedy. High-profile epidemiologists called Kennedy’s work at the health department “malpractice” and equivalent to a “crime scene”.
In a statement posted on X late on Tuesday afternoon, Kennedy said the US “will stop measles outbreaks, protect American families, and work to regain U.S. measles elimination status”. He added that he would “continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles” and that officials with the Department of Health & Human Services “are working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust. We will answer families’ questions honestly about vaccine benefits and risks and work with trusted health care providers and community leaders to prevent measles, limit its spread, and support timely treatment.”
Barbosa called the role of misinformation in measles transmission “dynamic” and urged health departments to develop bespoke campaigns tailored to under-vaccinated communities.
Experts caution against piling blame for measles outbreaks solely on the Trump administration. The MMR vaccine has been the target of misinformation for more than two decades, including work by Kennedy before his White House role.
“There is a profound problem with measles in all three North American countries,” said Noel Brewer, a behavioral scientist at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill who studies vaccination behaviors, and specifically measles. He chairs a committee that considers evidence on US measles elimination status, and contributed to the scientific work that underpinned Pan American Health Organization (Paho)’s decision.
“The US has had large outbreaks and exported those to Canada and Mexico, and those cases have come back again to the US,” said Brewer.
Canada lost its measles-free status in 2025, but Barbosa said the country now represented the “good news” in the region. The nation stopped measles transmission for 60 days. This is the first step on the way to regaining measles elimination status. The UK and several European nations have also recently lost elimination status.
“What we’re experiencing is not a United States specific thing,” said David Margolius of the Big Cities Health Coalition. Instead, there is a, “global surge in cases, global decline in vaccination rate”.
Public health leaders with the Big Cities Health Coalition (BHC), which leads health departments that serve 47 million Americans, described the announcement as a “profoundly sad moment for our country”.
“Recent declines in measles vaccination rates have opened the door to outbreaks across the country, resulting in preventable illness, hospitalizations, and tragic loss of life,” BHC members said in a statement. “These outcomes are especially heartbreaking because measles is a disease that we know how to prevent. Yet too many voices spreading fear and false information are exacerbating the problem.”
Expert epidemiologists recommended US measles status change during a closed-door meeting in Washington DC. A range of evidence would have been presented, including interviews with positive patients collected by local US health authorities and whole genome sequencing that can provide a fingerprint of the virus’s origin.
Although measles elimination status is an official designation, it carries real consequences for Americans. Where measles cases were once typically imported by international travelers, endemic measles transmission means Americans face new risks of infection, and are being asked to dig up decades-old vaccination certificates and possibly quarantine for 21 days.
“Now is the time to go and find that evidence, because now this is a real day-to-day life thing that could happen to you,” Margolius said earlier in November.
Re-establishing elimination status will require “a national plan to eliminate measles again”, said Brewer, “an integrated plan that’s publicly communicated with specific tasks assigned to named parties”. He added that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the president should speak out “forcefully” in favor of vaccination, and Congress should allocate more funding.

title: SpaceX successfully catches Starship and makes history
text:
CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. — SpaceX's Starship made a triumphant return to Earth on Saturday, caught in midair by giant mechanical arms where its journey began 22 hours earlier.
It was the grand finale that Elon Musk and his team hoped for — the first-ever capture of a Starship flying back from space. But with the first-stage booster exploding shortly after Friday's liftoff from Texas, the company fell short of its desired double catch.
Wreckage remained in the Gulf of Mexico, cordoned off by buoys, as the stainless steel, bullet-shaped spacecraft lowered itself upright at the launch pad.
The dramatic, sci-fi-like capture helped blot out the booster's messy miss.
"Can you believe it?" shouted SpaceX commentator Dan Huot.
SpaceX officials said Saturday's catch demonstrates the full reusability of Starship, intended for moon and Mars travel. Although Friday's booster recovery failed, the company had already made three previous booster catches, validating the technique.
NASA welcomed Saturday's news. The space agency is paying billions of dollars for Starship to land Artemis astronauts on the moon later this decade and help build a permanent lunar base. Musk's ambitions are even grander: He wants to launch a fleet of Starships to build a city on Mars.
The world's largest and most powerful rocket — a 407-foot (124-meter) behemoth — blasted off late Friday afternoon from SpaceX's Starship base near the U.S.-Mexican border. Separating neatly from its booster before things went awry, the upper-stage spacecraft soared into orbit and released 26 advanced Starlink satellites.
Starship continued circling the world 165 miles (265 kilometers) up, with live views of itself and Earth streaming down via Starlink. The spacecraft completed 14 laps around Earth, outshining the previous mission's one to two laps.
It was SpaceX's 15th flight of a full-scale Starship since 2023 and its only second trip to orbit.
SpaceX reported that everything on the spacecraft, including its vital heat shield, appeared to work well.
As for the booster, SpaceX's Kate Tice said its engines stopped firing too soon on the way back down. The booster's guidance system sensed it wasn't in the right position and automatically initiated the watery detour and self-destruction. Engineers are still investigating the cause.
SpaceX expects to begin launching Starships from Florida's Kennedy Space Center within the next few months. That is the starting point for NASA's next Artemis mission, which will skip the moon and remain in orbit around Earth for lunar lander practice.
Artemis III's four astronauts will attempt to dock their capsule with not only Starship but Blue Origin's Blue Moon. The two companies will take turns delivering crews to the lunar surface. NASA is targeting as soon as 2028 for Artemis IV, humanity's first moon landing since the Apollo era more than half a century ago.

title: Anthropic's IPO set for blastoff this week in key test for AI boom
text:
Anthropic's is set to launch on Thursday, a milestone that will test investor enthusiasm for the company behind the popular Claude chatbot and the burgeoning artificial intelligence sector.
"This is a case where the deal is so large and important, so central to the AI thesis, that it's going to be a turning point for the AI sector," Matthew Kennedy, a senior market strategist at investment bank Renaissance Capital, told CBS News. "Even non-AI companies are going to feel the ripple effects, especially in the IPO market."
Anthropic shares are scheduled to start trading on the Nasdaq stock exchange under the ticker symbol "ANT" after markets open Thursday at 9:30 a.m. EST.
What the stock price will tell us
In its most recent regulatory filing, San Francisco-based Anthropic said it will offer 825 million shares priced at between $70 and $78, which is expected to raise up to $64.3 billion. The company also plans to raise an additional $26 billion from a slate of other companies, including chipmaker AMD, chip infrastructure provider Broadcom, Google, Microsoft and Nvidia, all of which have a stake in the AI race.
Anthropic is expected to formally set its stock price on Wednesday night.
"A price above the initial range would point to stronger-than-anticipated demand, while a price cut would signal that the company struggled to find buyers at the level it hoped for," analysts at Renaissance Capital, which tracks IPOs, said in a research note.
The market debut is expected to value Anthropic at up to $1.4 trillion, short of the $2 trillion valuation that some IPO experts projected earlier this year. Still, the AI developer — which launched only in 2021 — is on track to stage what could become the second-largest IPO ever. Elon Musk's SpaceX, which raised $75 billion and was valued at roughly $1.7 trillion when it , currently holds that mark for the largest IPO.
Kennedy thinks Anthropic shares will price at the high end, at around $78, and reach $100 by the end of their first day of trading, an increase that would represent a "solid pop," he said. If the stock rises closer to $140, "that would tell me that AI enthusiasm has come roaring back," he added.
Great expectations
Although many investors appear eager to own a piece of Anthropic, the IPO comes amid growing concerns about whether the torrid spending on AI will deliver the expected productivity and profit boom.
AI-related stocks have fluctuated in recent weeks following subpar and companies are taking on to finance data center construction. from Nvidia last week has also rattled investors, with the now down more than 35% from its October all-time high.
"The whole AI sector has sold off from its July peak. Investor enthusiasm was greatest then," Jay Ritter, an IPO expert and professor at the University of Florida's Warrington College of Business, told CBS News.
Although Anthropic has yet to turn a profit, the company has shown explosive revenue growth over its short time in business. Anthropic raked in nearly $17 billion in the third quarter this year, up 45% from the second quarter, a recent regulatory filing shows. Given that heady rate of expansion, Ritter expects Anthropic to reach profitability quickly.
To justify its projected trillion-dollar valuation, however, the company will need to sustain that momentum while operating under Wall Street's unsparing gaze. Compounding the challenge is how quickly the AI landscape itself is changing. For instance, Anthropic could struggle to maintain its growth rate as consumers shift from pricier AI models like Claude and ChatGPT to cheaper open-source models, Ritter noted.
Anthropic also will have to spend heavily to keep developing its AI models and stay ahead of rivals, from OpenAI, Alphabet and Meta to Chinese platforms. Anthropic has already taken on $6.2 billion in debt, which it acknowledges in financial filings is "substantial." Meanwhile, the company has committed to spending nearly a trillion dollars on chips and AI infrastructure through 2045, according to a securities filing.
Newly elected Democrats are vowing to crack down on the industry amid a national backlash against data centers, giving new impetus to a Congressional effort last year to enact a national moratorium on new ones.
"The company is likely to be very successful, but the market is pricing in very lofty expectations," Ritter said. "It could be hard for management to execute."
Wall Street analysts said Anthropic's share offering has broader ramifications for the AI sector, with the IPO's pricing setting a benchmark for other tech companies planning to go public.
Even if Anthropic's stock soars on the first day of trading, it won't necessarily create a swarm of IPO activity, Kennedy said. Still, it could reinvigorate markets, he added.
Meanwhile, by going public, Anthropic is effectively asking investors to discount the threats that Anthropic founder Dario Amodei himself has identified as posed by AI. In September, he called for an industrywide slowdown in AI development after a former Anthropic researcher AI poses to humanity.

title: Dolphins backup Kyle McCord shows promise in first NFL start in place of the injured Malik Willis
text:
Miami Dolphins backup quarterback Kyle McCord showed promise in his first NFL start in Sunday's 24-22 loss at Indianapolis
MIAMI GARDENS, Fla. -- Miami Dolphins quarterback Kyle McCord took a snap inside the Indianapolis Colts 8-yard line and charged forward.
The backup making his first NFL start didn't stop until he made it into the end zone, lunging ahead as defensive tackle Adetomiwa Adebawore grabbed his face mask and caused the quarterback's head to twist around as he crossed the goal line for his first career touchdown.
The score pulled Miami within two points in the fourth quarter Sunday against the Colts, though the Dolphins eventually fell 24-22 for their eighth loss of the season.
It was one of several positive plays from McCord, who in his second year in the league was thrust into the starting role after Malik Willis went on injured reserve with a groin/core injury.
Willis was with the team and on the sideline wearing a headset at Indianapolis. Dolphins coach Jeff Hafley said Monday that Willis was not set to have surgery, as of now, though that could change.
McCord will be Miami's starter for at least three more games.
“I think it was a great learning experience. Some good, some plays I wish I could have back,” McCord said of his first NFL start. "Some throws and reads I wish I could have back. And obviously, stinks to come up 10 yards short, 15 yards short, but it’s life in the NFL.”
McCord completed 17 of 32 passes for 209 yards and no interceptions and had the rushing score, getting the ball out quickly and mostly avoiding mistakes. His 209 passing yards were the second most by a Dolphins quarterback in their NFL debut, behind Ryan Tannehill, who threw for 219 at Houston on Sept 9, 2012.
McCord lost a fumble deep in Miami territory that Adebawore recovered in the end zone for a touchdown early in the third quarter.
“Worst comes to worst, either try to step up and take the sack, or by all means, get the ball out," McCord said of the play, "because that was obviously the worst-case scenario on that play.”
Still, Hafley said he was pleased by McCord's composure.
"If you look at the game in its entirety, he didn't blink," Hafley said. “He just stayed composed, coming out of the half, that thing could have gotten ugly and the game could have gotten away from us when he fumbled the ball and they scored. He just kept responding the whole entire time.”
In a rebuilding year that wasn't necessarily meant to be about wins and losses, the Dolphins have been competitive in nearly every game despite having one of the league's most inexperienced rosters and one of the toughest schedules. More importantly, nearly all of new general manager Jon-Eric Sullivan's 2026 draft picks has made an impact, a good sign for the organization as it looks for pieces to build around.
The run defense was not as good as it had been in recent weeks, likely because of the absence of veteran defensive lineman Zach Sieler, who suffered a torn biceps in Week 9. Jordan Phillips, who has been great against the run this season, and Zeek Biggers were supposed to see bigger roles but both suffered injuries during the game.
Chris Johnson. After recording his first career interception last week, the rookie cornerback intercepted Daniel Jones in the third quarter, then returned it 59 yards for a touchdown.
Zane Gonzalez. The Dolphins waived the struggling kicker on Monday after he missed three kicks against the Colts — two field goals and an extra point — which would have made a difference in a game that was decided by only two points. Gonzalez had gone 6 for 10 on field goals since joining the Dolphins on Oct 20. Hafley said a decision on a new kicker was still pending.
Hafley did not have updates on the injuries to Biggers (knee) and Philips (arm) but said he had “concerns." Both players were set to undergo further testing. ... C Aaron Brewer remained in the concussion protocol after missing Sunday's game.
(Pick)-6 — Johnson is one of three rookies in the NFL to record a defensive touchdown this season. He's the ninth rookie in Dolphins history to record a pick-6 and the first since Minkah Fitzpatrick in 2018.
Another tough matchup awaits the young Dolphins when they travel to face Josh Allen and the Buffalo Bills on Sunday. Add Allen to a long list of experienced quarterbacks Miami has gone against this season, including Patrick Mahomes, Joe Burrow and Kirk Cousins. And they still have Bo Nix, Caleb Williams and Jordan Love on their schedule later this season.

title: Turkish authorities raid opposition Sozcu news channel, appoint new management
text:
Turkish police raided the Istanbul headquarters of the pro-opposition Sozcu TV early on Tuesday, arresting admins and installing a government trustee as the head, the group said on X.
The channel announced in a predawn post that police were searching the building under a court order.
What did Sozcu say about the raid by Turkish police?
"Police are searching the Sozcu building under a court order. Police have cordoned off the building," its official X account said in just before 5 a.m. (0200 GMT).
"A trustee has been appointed to Sozcu! Police are searching the building... There have been detentions," it said, with its journalists saying staff were not being allowed inside.
According to the media group, the trustee took control of the television channel and the news website but not the print newspaper.
After the raid, regular news broadcasts were stopped and a documentary was shown instead.
At noon, the channel resumed its regular coverage, mentioning the raids only at the beginning of the broadcast. One of the channel's news presenters, Damla Dogan Tuncel, said on X that the channel had challenged the decision and was awaiting a court ruling.
"In the meantime, the broadcast would continue with normal news bulletins," she said.
'Terrorism' charges
The Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor's Office said the action against Sozcu TV was part of an investigation into alleged breaches of Turkey's "anti-terror financing laws."
The prosecutor's office claimed that the channel had suspected links to a network that was led by US-based cleric Fethullah Gulen. The cleric, who died in 2024, was accused by Turkey of orchestrating a failed military coup in 2016.
Sozcu Media Group lawyer Ersan Barkin said the raids stemmed from a 2016 case that Turkey's Supreme Court had previously dismissed, finding no evidence of criminal intent or wrongdoing.
"This trustee decision stems from a file in which no offence was established," he told KRT TV.
Government silences last critical news channels
The move is the latest suppression of critical linear media in Turkey, coming a month after the police raided the country's most-watched news channel, Halk TV, and installed an administrator.
Since then, news broadcasts on the channel have remained on pause.
Another pro-opposition news channel TELE1 was also raided and seized by the government, while its owner Merdan Yanardag was jailed on espionage charges.
Over the last decade, President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's government has seized control of most of the media landscape, particularly television broadcasters.
While the critical voices were pushed onto the online space, Halk TV and Sozcu TV were prominent pro-opposition voices in TV.
Press freedom has suffered dramatically during Erdogan's 22 years in power.In the most recent Reporters Without Borders world press freedom index, Turkey ranked 163 of 180 countries.
Deutsche Welle correspondent Alican Uludag was also jailed and released this year on charges including insulting President Erdogan.
Opposition lashes out at the government
Opposition leader Ozgur Ozel, whose party was also raided and seized by a trustee, said "the government no longer has any tolerance left for even the slightest criticism."
"May our hearts wither if we surrender to these would-be dictators," he said on X.
Istanbul Mayor and Erdogan's jailed rival Ekrem Imamoglu said "the government's election fear is growing and growing."
"With courage, perseverance, and determination, people will continue the struggle," he said, from his blocked X account.

title: Ben Earl backs surprise location to host 2028 Nations Championship finals weekend
text:
The England rugby No 8 Ben Earl believes the next finals weekend of rugby’s Nations Championship should be held away from a traditional stronghold of the sport, floating Las Vegas and Brazil as possible candidates for the showpiece event.
Twickenham’s Allianz Stadium will host the inaugural finals next weekend, with six games held across three days based on pool placings across the July and November international windows.
England are vying with France and Ireland to top the northern hemisphere pool, while New Zealand and South Africa are assured of top-two finishes in the southern hemisphere group.
Earl had been a critic of the new competition during England’s demanding itinerary earlier in the year, with Steve Borthwick’s side playing Tests in Johannesburg, Liverpool and Santiago del Estero across consecutive Saturdays in July.
But the 28-year-old has come around on the format, and believes it offers a good opportunity to grow the game.
“I feel like it's taking shape nicely now,” Earl said. “I don't want to say I was wrong because that's not my style. But you can see the method in it now. The summer obviously needs a tweak in whatever way that looks like.
“There's some big games this weekend. Hopefully for the fans, they've enjoyed it. We certainly enjoyed playing in it. And obviously, it's a bit nicer being at home.”
France and Spain are understood to have registered interest in hosting the finals weekend in the future, while Rugby Football Union (RFU) chief executive Bill Sweeney also indicated that Twickenham would be willing to hold the event again.
It had been mooted that Qatar would be the venue for the 2028 edition, though that is thought to be off the table after a sponsorship deal with Qatar Airways fell through amid the conflict in the Middle East.
A number of top Tests will be held in the United States, though, over the next half-decade as World Rugby builds up to the 2031 Rugby World Cup, and Earl believes “Sin City” would be an ideal fit.
“You'd be hard pressed not to say Vegas, wouldn't you? That would be a good fun,” Earl admitted.
“People in Brazil apparently love the game. What about something cool like that? Like, I don't know, take it somewhere where there's tier two nations. And we all get a chance to go somewhere new that we haven't been before, because we're all in the entertainment industry at the end of the day. Let's try and grow the game.
“We know if we go to London, we know if we go to wherever, people are going to turn up and watch because people love it. But let's go somewhere cool, like a Hong Kong or a Spain.
“There's obvious places that we didn't get a chance to go to that would be cool.”
England face New Zealand in their final pool fixture on Saturday afternoon.

title: Jensen Huang breaks silence says he would be 'honoured' to return as Nvidia's CEO
text:
Jensen Huang says he’s open to returning in his first statement since resignation.
Jensen Huang has said he is prepared to return to chip giant Nvidia as its chief executive in his first statement since resigning last Thursday over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
"Since my departure, I've seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA's employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO," Huang said in a statement to US media.
"If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honoured to answer these calls and return as CEO."
A campaign to reinstate Huang, the co-founder who led Nvidia for 33 years, gained steam over the weekend, with President Donald Trump on Monday adding that he was open to Huang returning.
But Nvidia's board has since said it is considering both internal and external candidates and said on Monday that it had no intention of reinstating Huang.
Huang will sit for a closed-door transcribed interview on 1 December before the US House Foreign Affairs Committee, Intelligence and the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party.
Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter will then sit for a closed-door transcribed interview a day later on 2 December.
"We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security," said Republican representatives Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford, the chairs of the Foreign Affairs, China Select and Intelligence Committees, in a press release.

title: WATCH: Navy nominee Hung Cao acknowledges Iran war is 'a strain' in confirmation hearing
text: — Published on Nov 17, 2026 9:21 AM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump's pick to lead the U.S. Navy acknowledged the strain of the Iran war as senators from both political parties pressed him at his confirmation hearing Tuesday about the impact of long ship deployments on sailors, drawdowns to stockpiles of advanced weapons and resources being shifted away from countering China. Watch in the video player above. Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao, a Trump loyalist and combat veteran, is seeking the permanent top civilian job during a particularly volatile time in Washington. He also faces the extra hurdle of needing a waiver from Congress, because he left active-duty service less than seven years ago. READ MORE: Navy has quietly fired some commanders and other officials, drawing congressional pushback "This war, again, I know it's a strain on our Navy," Cao told the Senate Armed Services Committee, but he insisted that "it's really set China back on their heels" to see all the military services work together. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat from Massachusetts, grilled Cao on the costs of the Iran war, noting that independent estimates or media reports say the naval blockade on Iranian shipping costs about $32.5 million a day and Iranian strikes on the Navy's regional headquarters in Bahrain did at least $400 million in damage. Cao confirmed the figure for the blockade but said he could not offer a full damage assessment in Bahrain because "it's a nonpermissive area for us to go," despite telling a reporter months ago that Iran "blew the hell out of Bahrain." Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News The hearing offered a rare opportunity to question a top military leader publicly about the Iran war and other issues. It follows recent firings of Navy officials and a failed impeachment attempt in the House against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, partly over his handling of the 8-month-old conflict. Republicans lost the House and Senate in the midterm elections, which were widely seen as a repudiation of the war and will put Democrats in control of Congress in January. Cao faces questions over living conditions and mental health during long deployments Cao was asked to address concerns that lawmakers have raised over living conditions aboard warships deployed to the Middle East and sailors' mental health, following reports of crew stress and supply shortages on the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier and other ships. The Lincoln endured a record-breaking deployment supporting the Iran war before returning to its homeport of San Diego in October. Republican Sen. Roger Wicker of Mississippi, who chairs the Senate Armed Services Committee, noted that the "incredibly challenging deployments" take a toll on sailors and their families. Sen. Mark Kelly, a Democrat from Arizona, said his office had received "reports of not enough food and inadequate basic necessities" from other warships that are now deployed. "One parent told us that there's their kid, lost more than 45 pounds in six months because of a lack of food," Kelly said. Cao said he was focused on sailors' welfare but argued that sailors going hungry was "like my kids opening up the refrigerator door and saying there's nothing to eat in here." When asked about suicide attempts aboard the ships, Cao told Sen. Richard Blumenthal, a Connecticut Democrat, that what he saw "as eight suicide attempts, I see as eight suicide mitigations." Cao says the Navy is making progress on munitions The conflict with Iran has strained U.S. stockpiles of air defense interceptors as well as other missiles such as the Navy's Tomahawk cruise missile, which can be fired offshore by a ship but safely strike targets hundreds of miles inland. GOP Sen. Deb Fischer of Nebraska pointed to concerns about the dwindling munition stockpiles, while fellow Republican Sen. Joni Ernst of Iowa also noted the strain to Navy resources of maintaining the blockade on Iranian shipping. Sen. Jack Reed of Rhode Island, the committee's ranking Democrat, said in his opening remarks that "the munitions expended and damage sustained from Operation Epic Fury alone will take years to recover." When lawmakers raised concerns over munitions stocks, Cao said there's been a boost in production of Tomahawks and other weapons. "When I was in uniform, we only produced 125 Tomahawks a year. Right now we're well above 60 every month," Cao said. He said efforts are also underway to boost the production of interceptors that are used by Navy ships to shoot down incoming missiles. However, Cao also conceded that the Navy has taken to using expired munitions, comparing it to adding water to expired bread and putting it in the microwave. He didn't identify the specific munitions involved. "For some of these munitions, we recoded them. And so we're able to shoot off the expired munitions," Cao said. Democrats press Cao on recent Navy firings Democratic lawmakers say the Navy failed to inform Congress that it fired the entire leadership team of a nuclear-powered attack submarine after an underwater collision. Separately, the sea service fired the commander of a destroyer deployed to the Middle East. Cao made the case against the Navy's traditional policy of publicly announcing the removal of commanders and instead argued that he wants "to make sure that we don't destroy their careers." "We relieve commanding officers for everything from negligence to even just fraternization or, you know, harassment," Cao said, "and I want to make sure that we're protecting their livelihood afterwards as well." Trump nominated Cao for the permanent job in September. Cao has been serving as acting Navy secretary since April after John Phelan's departure, which came with little public explanation. Before that, Cao was serving as Navy undersecretary and had run an unsuccessful Republican bid in 2024 to unseat Virginia Democratic Sen. Tim Kaine. Cao fled Vietnam with his family as a child in the 1970s before attending the U.S. Naval Academy. He was commissioned as a special operations officer and went on to serve with SEAL teams and special forces in Iraq, Afghanistan and Somalia, according to his Senate campaign biography. Cao left active duty in 2021. To take the secretary post, he needs a waiver from a law that prohibits military officers from serving as a service secretary until they have been retired for at least seven years. A similar law, which has been on the books since the end of World War II, exists for the secretary of defense and is designed to ensure truly civilian control of the military. Congress has only granted exceptions three times for that post — twice in the past decade, for retired Marine Gen. James Mattis during the first Trump administration and retired Army Gen. Lloyd Austin under President Joe Biden. In each case, Republican and Democratic lawmakers expressed an aversion to waiving the requirement and setting precedent for future exceptions. They raised concerns about further erosion of the already precarious concept of civilian control of the military. Amiri reported from New York.

title: Investor Steve Eisman says the AI neocloud stocks are in 'big trouble' from Nvidia fallout
text:
Investor Steve Eisman said the so-called AI neocloud stocks will be the biggest losers from the unfolding Nvidia scandal.
Nvidia was essentially a "virtual vertical holding company and it's unwinding," said Eisman of "Big Short" fame on CNBC's "Squawk Box." "I think neoclouds are all in big trouble though because they are part of that vertical holding company and I think they're about to get ejected."
Neoclouds, which used borrowed funds to build data centers, have been among the hardest-hit stocks during the recent pullback in the artificial intelligence trade. CoreWeave and Nebius are each down more than 50% the last three months.
All eyes on Wall Street are on chipmaker Nvidia as it reports earnings on Tuesday after the bell while grappling with a potential Chinese espionage scandal. Founder and CEO Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday under a cloud of controversary revolving around his affair with a suspected Chinese spy. The Commerce Department has subsequently moved to close a loophole on China's remote use of data centers.
Investors are worried as scrutiny increases on Nvidia's China revenue, it may pull back on its extensive financing that supported the AI industry.
Frontier algorithm company Anthropic is expected to make its public debut on Thursday as concerns about the company's profitability potential linger amid the rapid and ongoing commodification of AI.
Eisman said he doesn't think the much-ballyhooed offering is very important anymore to the AI trade because expectations have come down.
"I don't think anybody really cares," the investor said.
Instead, Eisman is focusing on how much Democrats will restrict data center building when they take control of Congress and various governorships in January.
"I think the biggest issues by far are how much are, how much are local and state governments going to slow AI data center construction? Is it going to be 100% moratorium? That would obviously be — that would put the country into recession overnight. Or is it something like 10% to 30%?" he said.
In the event of a 10% to 30% slowdown in data center construction, Eisman said the group of companies within the AI trade that he favors the most are the hyperscalers.
"The group that makes out the best are the hyperscalers because they go cash flow positive again," he said.

title: Voyage Labs raises $12 million for a specialized AI travel assistant
text:
Planning a trip is a favorite demo for personal AI assistants — you can try it with Muse, or with Gemini, or half a dozen other choices. But while most pitches use travel-planning as part of a general-purpose agent pitch, a new startup from a Google Maps alum is betting that a specialized travel-planning agent can beat the competition.
The company is called Voyage Labs, and on Tuesday it announced $12 million in seed funding led by Kleiner Perkins, with participation from SignalFire and SV Angel. The company plans to use the funding to expand supplier partnerships and grow its engineering team.
Voyage Labs’ flagship product, called Atlas, is meant to work as a personal assistant for your trip-planning, available today in private beta.
“People can use it to plan and book and manage their entire journey, from the time they have an inspiration to the time they come back home,” says co-founder and CEO Manik Gupta.
Atlas is designed to serve as an always-on assistant throughout the planning process, fielding ideas and doing research on every idea that’s raised. The long time horizon means Atlas can tailor recommendations based on weeks of conversation, while also monitoring real-time price fluctuations and ultimately booking flights and hotels.
For the Voyage founders, it’s an ideal match between technology and use case. “Trip planning is a project that has its own lifecycle,” says Yogesh Jain, co-founder and CTO of the company. “You’re planning across days and weeks — so long-running agents as a technology matches that very well.”
Travel assistants are already a crowded field, but Voyage will be starting with a lot of experience in the space. Gupta was previously the director of Product Management for Google Maps, followed by four years as chief product officer at Uber. As he puts it, “I spent eight years where my only job was to wake up in the morning and go build the map. I’m just very obsessed with that problem.”
The biggest question is how Atlas will compete with the multi-purpose AI assistants built by frontier labs. But as Gupta notes, the space is still changing fast, and it’s hard for anyone to be sure what form factors will thrive in the coming years. Ultimately, Voyage is betting that travel is specialized enough to need a specialized product.
“We are making a bet that this vertical around travel and outdoors is a large enough vertical that it needs a focused product solution,” Gupta told TechCrunch. “Ultimately, we believe we can actually stitch together an end-to-end experience that will help users.”

title: Supreme Court keeps injunction against DEI grant defunding in place
text:
On Monday, the Supreme Court announced it would not hear an appeal of a lower court decision that blocked the government from canceling the grants of a handful of researchers whose funding had been revoked during the Trump administration’s purge of DEI-related work. While the decision applies to only seven researchers in California, the lower court had ruled that the government’s actions violated the First Amendment and so may have broad implications.
The Supreme Court provided no discussion of its rejection, and no justices filed a dissent regarding the decision.
The suit was initially filed by a large group of researchers at the University of California, Berkeley and UC San Francisco, contesting grants originally issued by many federal agencies, from the National Institutes of Health to the Department of Transportation. At issue were grants that had been terminated because the agencies decided they violated a Trump executive order blocking the use of DEI. This occurred despite the fact that the government hadn’t bothered to define DEI, and targeted grants were often identified by little more than a keyword search.
In the wake of a Supreme Court decision that held that most grant termination cases had to be heard by a different court, the case was narrowed considerably to just seven UC researchers and a handful of agencies: The Environmental Protection Agency, the National Science Foundation, and the National Endowment for the Humanities.

title: MIT scientists discover a surprising way to boost the brain’s nighttime cleaning system
text:
MIT scientists discovered that carefully timed bursts of gentle pink noise during sleep can strengthen the brain’s natural cleaning waves, which help flush away potentially harmful waste. The breakthrough could pave the way for new treatments aimed at improving sleep and memory while potentially reducing the buildup of proteins linked to Alzheimer’s disease.
While we go about our daily activities, the brain gradually accumulates waste, including lactic acid and proteins that are no longer useful. Sleep provides an important opportunity to clear away these substances. As we rest, waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) move through the brain, helping remove waste and maintain healthy brain function.
Researchers at MIT have now discovered a way to make these fluid waves stronger using brief pulses of a gentle sound called "pink noise." When delivered at carefully chosen moments during sleep, the sounds amplify slow electrical waves in the brain. Those stronger electrical signals, in turn, produce larger waves of CSF.
The finding opens up intriguing possibilities for improving brain health. Scientists want to determine whether increasing this fluid movement could sharpen thinking, strengthen memory, or slow neurodegenerative diseases associated with the accumulation of damaging proteins, including amyloid beta.
"We found that we were able to increase the size of the CSF flow wave during sleep, which as far as we know, there hasn't been a method to do before. Now that we can enhance CSF flow during sleep in healthy adults, we're really excited to bring this technology to clinical populations to see what effects we can have," says Laura Lewis, the Athinoula A. Martinos Associate Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, a member of MIT's Institute for Medical Engineering and Science and the Research Laboratory of Electronics, and an associate member of the Picower Institute for Learning and Memory.
Lewis led the research as senior author. The findings were published in Science Translational Medicine, with Joshua Levitt serving as lead author. Levitt recently completed his PhD at Boston University and previously worked as a visiting graduate student in Lewis' laboratory.
How Sleep Helps the Brain Remove Waste
Cerebrospinal fluid is a transparent liquid that surrounds the brain and spinal cord, providing protection against physical injury. It also supports brain function by transporting nutrients, including glucose, and carrying away waste released by brain cells as they consume energy.
In 2019, Lewis demonstrated that functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) could be used to observe the movement of CSF into and out of the brain during sleep. Her team found that this movement closely follows slow electrical brain waves, which are especially prominent during deep sleep.
Building on that discovery, the researchers wanted to understand whether deliberately strengthening these electrical waves would also increase the movement of CSF. Earlier experiments had shown that sounds presented at precisely the right moment could enhance slow brain waves.
"You can make more of these electrical slow waves through an auditory stimulus, if it comes at just the right time. Similar to a child on a swing, if you push them when they're at the right moment in their movement, you can make that swing go farther," Lewis says. "The challenge is: How do you find just the right time?"
How Pink Noise Amplifies Brain Waves
To test the idea, the team used extremely short bursts of pink noise, each lasting just 50 milliseconds. Pink noise contains the full range of frequencies that humans can hear, much like white noise. However, its lower frequencies are more prominent, while higher frequencies are quieter. The result is a softer, more balanced sound reminiscent of steady rainfall or a waterfall heard from a distance.
Timing was essential. The researchers needed to deliver each burst of sound when a sleeping participant's slow brain waves reached their peak. To identify those moments, they monitored electrical activity using EEG while simultaneously measuring CSF movement with fMRI.
Combining the two measurements created a technical obstacle. The powerful magnetic fields used in fMRI interfere with EEG recordings, making it difficult to detect the brain's electrical signals accurately and quickly enough to synchronize the sound.
The team addressed this problem by creating a method that removes interference from EEG signals in less than 100 milliseconds. They also designed an algorithm capable of predicting when the next slow wave peak would occur, compensating for the small delay introduced by processing the signals. Together, these advances made it possible to play each burst of pink noise at the intended moment.
Stronger Brain Cleaning Waves During Sleep
The researchers tested their approach in 14 healthy volunteers. They found that the carefully timed sounds increased the size of both the brain's slow electrical waves and the accompanying CSF waves. Importantly, the sounds were quiet enough that they did not wake the participants.
The brain scans also helped explain how the process works. Slow electrical waves were associated with blood vessels narrowing and widening, creating a pumping effect that pushes CSF out of the brain. These slow waves occur during non-REM sleep and become increasingly pronounced as sleep deepens.
By enhancing the electrical waves, the researchers were able to strengthen the fluid movement associated with the brain's natural waste removal process. However, the study did not directly establish whether the stronger CSF waves actually removed more waste or improved sleep quality.
Could Pink Noise Improve Sleep and Help Fight Alzheimer's?
The researchers now want to investigate whether increasing CSF flow leads to more refreshing, restorative sleep, particularly for people who struggle with insomnia. Another major goal is to determine whether the technique can improve the brain's ability to clear harmful substances.
This possibility is especially relevant to Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia, which are associated with the accumulation of abnormal proteins in the brain. If stronger CSF movement ultimately translates into more effective waste removal, the approach could offer a new way to address one of the biological processes involved in these conditions.
"Brain waste clearance is really important for Alzheimer's and other forms of dementia, which are caused, in part, by the buildup of molecules like amyloid and tau in the brain. If we can improve brain waste clearance, we may be able to help prevent the buildups of these plaques that lead to disease," Levitt says.
The technology could eventually become accessible outside research laboratories. Levitt has launched a company that aims to develop a home device, potentially in the form of a headband, that would deliver sound at the appropriate moments during sleep to increase CSF flow.
For now, the results demonstrate that a simple auditory stimulus, when precisely synchronized with brain activity, can alter the fluid waves associated with the brain's nighttime cleaning process. Whether those changes can translate into better sleep, stronger memory, or protection against neurodegenerative disease remains an important question for future studies.
The research received funding from a McKnight Scholar Award, a Sloan Fellowship, a Pew Biomedical Scholars Award, the Simons Foundation Collaboration on Plasticity in the Aging Brain, the MIT EECS Transformative Research Fund, the National Institutes of Health, the Corundum Convergence Institute, and the Panasonic Well Fellowship for AI and Wellness.

title: This may be the best evidence yet that dinosaur blood can fossilize
text:
The life and times of a dinosaur may be written in its blood — if blood can be preserved in bone.
Tiny microstructures found in the limb bones of a fossilized 115-million-year-old specimen are the remnants of red blood cells, researchers report November 2 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The team says these are both the oldest red blood cell structures yet identified and the first to be chemically proven. But not everyone is as sanguine about that conclusion.
The ability to identify such structures could offer a powerful molecular window into the physiology of long-extinct animals, including their metabolism and even activity levels, says paleontologist Kliti Grice of Curtin University in Bentley, Australia.
The bone, from a fossil-rich site in northeastern Brazil called Mina Pedra Branca, belonged to the dinosaur Aratasaurus museunacionali. Grice and her colleagues used a variety of chemical and imaging analyses to study the Cretaceous Period specimen.
The team prepared thin cross-sectional slices of bone and imaged details of the limb bone’s internal structure with focused electron beams. That revealed ellipse-shaped microstructures within the limb’s fossilized network of blood vessels.
A map of the ellipsoids’ chemical element composition revealed that they were full of iron, carbon and nitrogen, all components of a biomolecule called heme. Heme is an iron-bearing, ring-shaped molecule found in hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen throughout the body.
Then, the researchers used a technique that identifies molecules by how they scatter laser light. Those analyses suggested the presence of porphyrins, ringlike organic compounds found in blood — and the precursors of heme. Finally, they ruled out contamination from other porphyrins, such as the pigment chlorophyll, by separating and identifying the molecular contents of a bone extract. That experiment also suggested heme.
Taken together, these findings point unequivocally to the preservation of molecular traces of ancient blood, the team says. They also offer a clue to a novel pathway that might preserve those traces for so many millions of years.
Blood cells decompose within days of the death of an organism. Only unusual and fast-acting environmental and biochemical conditions could have stopped decay and held those tissues in place as the organism fossilizes.
In this fossil, the secret ingredient was a manganese oxide mineral called hausmannite, the researchers say. The team’s analyses had found the mineral within the ellipsoid structures. That mineral, they propose, may have acted as a time capsule, preserving the cellular structures and protecting the molecules within, including collagen amino acids.
Distinguishing fossilized blood cells from nonorganic minerals that formed within a fossil after the organism’s death is a tricky task. During fossilization, mineral-rich fluids seep in and around the bones, and the minerals that form within the fossil can bear a strong resemblance to bodily structures.
In a 1997 study, two paleontologists analyzed tiny spheres found inside the limb of a fossil, possibly a pterosaur. The spheres were once thought to be the fossilized remnants of ancient blood cells, but the duo determined that the spheres were instead pyrite, an iron mineral that had been deposited in the bones after death.
Those paleontologists suggested that, going forward, several criteria should be met before proposing a blood cell origin for fossilized structures, including comparing the shape of the structures with that of living related organisms and identifying certain biomarkers in the structures. One of those biomarkers is heme compounds.
Grice and her colleagues say that their study meets these criteria. Unlike the pyrite, hausmannite was crucial to preservation, “rather than simply a mineral that replaced biological material after it had disappeared,” she says. The close spatial relationship between the hausmannite, the blood cell-like structures and the chemical signatures of heme “raises the possibility that mineralization helped stabilize, entomb and protect components of the original biological material during fossilization.”
But Mary Schweitzer, a paleontologist at North Carolina State University in Raleigh who was not involved in the new study, says she doesn’t think these findings do fully meet those criteria.
The heme biomarkers, for example, don’t appear to be localized to the round structures alone, as would be expected in fossilized blood cells, but come from analysis of the entire bone. The proposed red blood cells also differ in size and shape compared with red blood cells from living birds and reptiles, she says.
Schweitzer is no stranger to skepticism over the discovery of ephemeral tissues in fossils. In 2005, she and her colleagues reported the first recovery of flexible, soft-tissue blood vessels from the 68-million-year-old fossilized leg bone of a Tyrannosaurus rex. It was a landmark study that sparked debate, including over how it would even be possible to preserve such tissues through deep time, as well as the most surefire way to detect them in the present.
“I am not convinced” that the research team has definitively identified heme compounds, Schweitzer says. “I do applaud them for bringing a plethora of methods to the study. Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, and that does require state-of-the-art technology.”
No one really knows what a dinosaur’s red blood cell shape would be, let alone how the process of fossilization might distort the original shape of the structures, or allow heme-related molecules to escape their cellular confines over time, Grice says.
And, she says, her team’s interpretation of the evidence doesn’t just rely on the observations of those structures. “[It] rests on the convergence of anatomy, morphology, mineralogy, elemental analysis and molecular chemistry,” she says. “That combination is critical.”
As for whether other fossils might have molecular traces that have been preserved by hausmannite, “we simply don’t know yet,” Grice says. “But this type of preservation may not be quite as rare as we currently think.”

title: Could there be an ancient alien satellite in Earth's orbit? How the 'Black Knight' conspiracy theory has survived for over 100 years
text:
In the final days of 1998, as astronauts aboard NASA's Space Shuttle Endeavor were working during one of the early missions to assemble the International Space Station, crew members from the STS-88 mission captured photographs of a dark colored, unusually shaped object drifting through space.
Despite its unusual appearance in the photographs, the object had a conventional explanation, and one that was known to the astronauts at that time: it was one of several thermal covers that had been wrapped around trunnion pins used in the space station's construction. Upon noticing the "escape" of one of the covers, Mission Commander Bob Cabana remarked over the radio to fellow astronaut Jerry Ross that "one of the thermal covers got away from you."
Seeing the cover drifting away, a frustrated Ross snapped a photograph of it. Yet despite the innocuous story behind the images, they have nonetheless helped fuel belief in an unusual Space Age conspiracy theory: one involving the alleged presence of an ancient satellite, presumably of alien origin, that has long been orbiting our planet — perhaps since the end of the last Ice Age.
According to proponents of this theory, the object photographed by Ross in 1998 is actually what many call the "Black Knight Satellite," and is only one piece of evidence they point to in a long succession of unrelated — and often misinterpreted — events in modern history that supposedly lend further evidence to the alleged alien spacecraft's existence.
So how did such a legend gain traction in the first place, with some versions alleging that NASA and the U.S. government have worked to conceal evidence of the alleged space object's existence from the public?
Odd detections at Colorado Springs
Depending on which version of the story you come across, the strange roots of the Black Knight conspiracy theory might be traced all the way back to the nineteenth century, when the famous inventor Nikola Tesla began detecting unusual electrical signals while conducting radio experiments at his laboratory in Colorado Springs.
At the time, Tesla considered whether the signals might be communications from intelligent aliens on nearby planets, although the likely source had actually been terrestrial radio interference. Notably, Tesla also never claimed that the emissions might be coming from an object in Earth's orbit; nonetheless, some proponents of the Black Knight Satellite theories have incorporated Tesla's experiments into the mythos, suggesting they may represent some of the earliest detections of a mysterious object lurking near Earth.
Unidentified objects in orbit?
Another component that was later incorporated into the Black Knight Satellite mythos came to light in May 1954, when newspaper reports began publicizing author Donald Keyhoe's assertions that the U.S. Air Force had detected at least two unidentified satellites orbiting Earth.
At the time, Keyhoe claimed that U.S. government scientists at White Sands were reportedly "making an intensive effort to locate and chart the course of the satellites in an attempt to determine what they are and where they came from," as the author was quoted as saying in articles like one that appeared in the St. Louis Post-Dispatch on Friday, May 14, 1954.
However, later in August of that year, U.S. officials apparently concluded these objects were likely to have been meteors that became "satellites of the Earth and were revolving with it 400 to 600 miles out in space," and that Dr. Lincoln LaPaz, one of the preeminent experts on meteors at the time, had "definitely identified the objects as natural rather than man-made," as reported by the New York Times.
Just a few years later in February 1960, a similar story appeared in Time magazine, which this time alleged that the U.S. Navy had spotted an unidentified dark object in orbit that was suspected of being a Soviet reconnaissance satellite. This object was later identified as well, with officials determining it had likely been debris from the American spy satellite Discoverer 8.
Another similar claim suggests that on May 15, 1963, during the Mercury-Atlas 9 mission, NASA astronaut Gordon Cooper allegedly observed an unusual object in space, which some accounts describe as a "glowing green object" that followed his capsule. While it is true that Cooper reported seeing what he characterized as "John’s fireflies," which were a reference to earlier sightings of unusual luminous objects made by astronaut John Glenn during the Mercury-Atlas 6 mission, it was later concluded that the so-called "fireflies" resulted from small bits of ice separating from the spacecraft itself, which present a greenish hue as sunlight reflects off of them (audio of Cooper describing this during the Mercury-Atlas 9 mission can be found here).
Beyond this, however, there is no evidence of Cooper observing any singular object during this mission, either in Cooper's personal records or mission audio and transcripts from the time.
"Echoes" from a 13,000-year-old satellite
Arguably, one of the most extraordinary components of the Black Knight Satellite theory involves its alleged age, which according to some theories places its initial entry into Earth's orbit as far back as 13,000 years ago. But if so, how would anyone know this, and what evidence could support such an idea?
Understanding this bizarre aspect of the Black Knight mythos requires a look back at the theories of Scottish writer Duncan Lunan, which he first proposed in 1973. At that time, Lunan was receiving international attention for his investigation into mysterious long-delayed echoes, proposing that one theory behind the phenomenon could be that they represented signals from Earth that were being rebroadcast from an extraterrestrial probe — an idea that borrowed from theories first proposed by Australian scientist Ronald Bracewell.
According to Lunan's theory, such a hypothetical "Bracewell probe" might have arrived in Earth's vicinity roughly 13,000 years ago after traveling from within a planetary system associated with the star Epsilon Boötis, some 236 light-years away.
Within just a few years, Lunan had withdrawn his conclusions, but this did little to prevent his initial ideas about a 13,000-year-old alien satellite from being incorporated into the growing mythos surrounding the alleged Black Knight Satellite.
The STS-88 mission photographs
That brings us back to what are arguably the most widely circulated images associated with the Black Knight satellite: the famous images from NASA's STS-88 mission taken by astronaut Jerry Ross in December 1998.
According to spaceflight historian James Oberg, the object in Ross's photos could indeed be positively identified as the thermal blanket lost during the mission, especially since he had specifically asked Ross about the incident — and later misinterpretations of his photos as being evidence of an alien spacecraft — during an October 2014 interview.
At that time, Oberg asked Ross whether he had time during the 1998 spacewalk "to gaze at [the thermal cover] and think about how it looked," to which Ross said no, admitting he had been "too pissed at myself to wonder what it looked like!"
When asked what advice he would offer to those who have misinterpreted the object in his photographs for being something more exotic and otherworldly, Ross told Oberg, "If we see something up there we will be the first ones to ask questions and to tell people we saw something we didn't understand."
"Conspiracy theories are fun for those working on them, but a waste of valuable brain power," Ross added.
The legend continues
But what, specifically, about the idea of an ancient extraterrestrial probe lurking in orbit around our planet makes this far-fetched theory so captivating?
"I think it's because this idea of an alien satellite kicking around in orbit checks so many conspiracy theory boxes," says Amy Shira Teitel, a spaceflight historian who has also tackled the Black Knight satellite theories in the past, and points to other misperceptions about space that have given rise to conspiracy theories over the years.
"People, for some reason, believe space is fake or that every mission is fake because the Van Allen Belts will kill you," Shira Teitel recently told Space in an email, while noting that most missions take place well within safe distances from the inner radiation belt, with notable exceptions that include the Gemini 11 mission, as well as lunar flights.
"People also love UFOs," she adds. "Even skeptics have a little bit of a soft spot for the idea of an alien craft flying by to say hi. I think when you take all these conspiracy threads together, the Black Knight sort of fits perfectly in that intersection!"
