Overall, the bizarre story of the Black Knight satellite offers a textbook example of how a collection of unconnected events and speculative interpretations can gradually accumulate into a single narrative over time.
Despite this reality, belief in the existence of a mysterious ancient satellite lurking in orbit will likely persist for years to come, helping ensure its place as one of the most peculiar — and enduring — legends of the Space Age.

title: More than £160m needed to clean up one of Europe's largest illegal dumps
text:
More than £160m is needed to clean up and maintain one of Europe's largest illegal landfill sites, government officials have said.
The contaminated Mobuoy dump at Campsie in County Londonderry, discovered and shut down in 2013, was used to bury thousands of tonnes of rubbish at a site spanning more than 100 acres.
Last year, two businessmen were jailed for their part in the operation.
Northern Ireland's Environment Minister Andrew Muir said his department had now received an updated cost estimate of £161m for the clean-up over a 30-year period.
Muir described what happened at Mobuoy as "an absolute scandal" and said "the community rightly expects and deserves remediation of the site".
He is now seeking a meeting with the Finance Minister John O'Dowd to discuss how the work will be paid for - with funding from Westminster a possibility.
Once the finances are agreed, they will work towards appointing a contractor.
Investigations indicate an estimated 1.6m tonnes of waste was present at the site and 627,000 tonnes of that was believed to have been dumped illegally.
The Mobuoy site is beside the River Faughan, which supplies a significant proportion of Derry's drinking water but officials have not found any contamination to it.
The area of polluted ground stretches to about 100 acres, or the equivalent of about 65-70 football pitches.
'Road map for remediation'
"This is a complicated project, as you'll understand, given the complexity of the site," Muir told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme on Tuesday, .
The minister said he took environmental protection very seriously and would continue to push for the establishment of an independent environmental protection agency.
"One of the massive lessons that needs to be learned from the Mobuoy site is the need for stronger environmental protections, so people have confidence that our environment is being looked after."
Muir said the next assembly election was fast approaching in May, so he understood there might be some concerns about the potential costs involved.
"I want to finish this mandate with a degree of certainty for the local community, so we have a road map here for remediation," he said.
"I am pushing ahead with real enthusiasm with this."
Muir said the drinking water was tested regularly to ensure it was safe and that he would continue to work with all agencies to provide the local community with greater assurances about the site.
Muir said the Mobuoy site remained in private ownership, but they were "actively" considering ways of transferring it.
One option is vesting, which allows government departments to obtain compulsory and legal ownership of land through a court order.

title: More than 100,000 take part in France pay protests
text:
More than 100,000 people have taken to the streets in France to protest against the high cost of living, with public sector workers demanding pay increases.
The Interior Ministry said on Tuesday that a total of 146,000 people took part in the protests, with 28,000 in Paris alone. The CGT trade union put the nationwide total at just over 500,000 demonstrators.
Several trade unions had called for a day of strike action. Participants included public sector workers, as well as school pupils and university students.
France’s 5.8 million public sector employees were pushed to mobilise after talks with Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu on Friday failed to satisfy union demands. Union representatives left the meeting organised by Lecornu saying the proposed measures failed to address the urgency of the pay situation.
Tuesday’s rally is the third call for a united day of action and strikes in the public sector since September.
Unions have been pushing for across-the-board pay rises since last week’s boost to the minimum wage for private-sector workers.
Protesters say “they simply can’t make ends meet, and they want the government to help them put more money into funding in terms of salaries, in terms of raising the minimum wage”, Al Jazeera’s Natacha Butler reported from Paris.
“The government’s already offered about $30 extra a month on the minimum wage, but those here say that is simply not enough. With inflation, with the way the prices are going up, they say they actually need more.”
The unions put the loss of purchasing power for public servants at 16 percent since 2017, leading to increasing numbers of public employees ending up on or close to the minimum wage against a backdrop of inflation.
“The government doesn’t have much margin or wiggle room financially, because of France’s ballooning debt, and the government’s in the middle of trying to push through a budget with cost-cutting measures in it,” Butler said.
Public-sector workers aim to pressure the government to unfreeze the pay scale point used to calculate their basic salary. However, the government has ruled out any general pay rise for the fourth consecutive year in its draft budget.
“The people in the street know there is only so far you can go; the government knows they do not have a lot of economic wiggle room. Yet nobody really is coming up with another solution,” Butler said.
Despite the government’s efforts to ease tensions, demonstrations have roiled the country for over a month.
Student-led protests demanding better conditions in education erupted in mid-September, but the movement has since expanded in scope to cover a range of issues, from high fuel prices to wages and social housing
Protests for higher wages, lower costs of living and better public services have also spread across Europe.

title: Anthropic files for IPO as it competes for AI dominance
text:
Anthropic filed for an initial public offering on Monday, bringing the maker of artificial intelligence platform Claude a step closer to its highly anticipated public market debut and providing a key test for the rapidly emerging AI sector.
In the filing, Anthropic outlined its vision for a future profoundly shaped by AI, touting the technology's potential to transform the global economy and improve lives worldwide.
"We believe the diffusion of AI through the global economy represents one of the largest opportunities in history to improve how humans live and work, and it is just beginning," the company said in its S-1 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission.
The filing highlights Anthropic's rapid growth, with the company generating $16.3 billion in revenue in the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion in the same period last year. That staggering rate of expansion is likely to slow, with Anthropic noting that its revenue growth is expected to decline over time.
The company has yet to turn a profit. Anthropic reported a net loss of $80.7 billion for the first half of the year, more than six times the net loss of nearly $13 billion for the first two quarters in 2025.
Anthropic's founders, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, pitched the IPO to investors in part as an opportunity to be part of a history-defining moment.
"We encourage you, as a prospective owner of our stock, not to think of your purchase in purely transactional terms," the company's seven co-founders said in a letter included in the S-1. "We hope you will see it instead as an opportunity to be part of something greater. The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history."
Referendum on AI
The IPO, which market analysts expect as early as November, could instantly rank Anthropic among the world's largest publicly traded companies. The offering could raise as much as $100 billion, according to reports. That would slingshot it past Elon Musk-owned SpaceX, which raised a record-breaking $86 billion when it .
Anthropic, which was valued at $965 billion in May, could see its value rise to $1.5 trillion or possibly $2 trillion, although its final valuation has not been established.
Anthropic shares will list on the Nasdaq stock exchange, according to the company's filing. The AI company will trade under the ticker symbol "ANT."
More broadly, the transaction will gauge the strength of investor demand not only for Anthropic shares, but also for the widening constellation of data center builders, chipmakers and other companies involved in developing the critical infrastructure powering AI services.
"This IPO is a referendum on the entire AI trade," Nigel Green, CEO of investment firm deVere Group, said in an email. "If it soars, expect a queue of AI listings and even more capital piling into the theme. If it stumbles, valuations across tech could reset fast."
The torrent of capital flowing into AI has helped propel the stock market to record highs. The question is whether AI can maintain its momentum amid signs that investors are fretting over when — and if — their money will eventually pay off and deliver the returns they are banking on.
Anthropic's prospectus shows that the company has funneled massive amounts of money toward building the computing resources necessary to power its AI models. The company spent $8.9 billion in the first half of the year on chips and other infrastructure to run its platform, compared to $2.3 billion over the same period last year.
"Anthropic could become the most valuable company in the world. It could also end up in bankruptcy," analysts with Lightshed, an investment advisory firm, said in a research note ahead of the IPO filing.
Potential obstacles to growth
Anthropic's IPO filing also outlines various risks that could hamper its growth or cause it to fall behind competitors. Much of the company's future growth hinges on whether it has access to sufficient capital, including debt financing, which more companies are using to finance the AI buildout.
To maintain its competitive edge, Anthropic also said it will need to use its existing AI models to design and train next-generation platforms, a process known as "recursive self-improvement," or RSI.
"If we fail to direct sufficient compute and research efforts to AI-assisted development, or if our competitors more effectively leverage AI to enhance their own innovation cycles, we risk falling progressively further behind. …" Anthropic said in the filing.
AI experts warn that using AI to build ever more powerful frontier models raises the risk of people , potentially leading to disasters such as deadly pandemics or cyberattacks that cut off internet, electricity or water.
Barreling ahead despite safety concerns
Anthropic filed a confidential IPO with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June, beating out which filed just over a week later. Both companies are barreling ahead with plans to go public despite concerns about the potential threats AI poses to humanity.
Reports of AI agents going rogue continue to pile up, stoking concern that the technology could escape human control and . In September, Amodei called for a after one of his company's that there's a 10% chance the technology could wipe out humanity in the next decade.
In an , Amodei said the pace of technological growth should serve as a warning sign, while making a case for continued development of AI.

title: Glasses and shirt buttons will be examined to stop cheating in South Korea's college entrance exams
text:
Proctors in South Korea will inspect every test-taker’s glasses and seal their shirt buttons with stickers
SEOUL, South Korea -- Proctors will inspect every test-taker’s glasses and seal their shirt buttons with stickers, and authorities will deploy 8,400 additional supervisors at South Korea’s college entrance exams on Thursday.
The country will also send an emergency alert that will set nearly all mobile phones in the country buzzing for about 10 seconds that morning, using a tool typically reserved for major crises like large earthquakes or war to expose any devices hidden by test-takers.
The sweeping measures to fight cheating are in response to concerns that artificial intelligence and smart devices are making fraud harder to detect.
More than 550,000 people will participate in the exam at around 1,300 test sites in what’s a pivotal annual event for the country. South Korea is known for its intense academic competition, where job opportunities, social standing and even marriage prospects often hinge on which school a person attends.
Concerns about cheating grew after the top scorer on a national tax accountant exam admitted to using a hidden camera, a smartphone and generative AI tools to obtain answers, the latest in a string of AI-assisted cheating cases to affect exams in recent months.
In a televised briefing on Tuesday, Prime Minister Han Seongsook said that proctors will use metal detectors on test-takers who act suspiciously to search for hidden devices and that the exam ban for cheaters will be lengthened from the current one year to 10. College students retaking the exam to go to different universities will be expelled from their current schools if they are caught cheating, in addition to facing a 10-year ban on entering any school, Han said.
Test-takers will be prohibited from bringing electronic devices such as smartphones, smart glasses and smart watches, or any object with a camera, and failing to hand them over to proctors before the exam will be treated as cheating, regardless of whether they were used.
Those who wear glasses will be asked to place them on the desk for inspection before the exam, and supervisors will monitor for smart glasses throughout the hourslong test. Han advised test-takers to avoid clothing with buttons, and any buttons will be covered with stickers to guard against hidden cameras.
She said that global technology companies that operate AI chatbots have also agreed to cooperate with any post-exam investigations into suspected cheating, such as queries involving photographed test pages.
The “Suneung,” or the College Scholastic Ability Test, is a crucial annual event for which the education-obsessed country goes to extraordinary lengths to create an ideal testing environment. The start of work hours and stock trading are delayed to ease traffic for test-takers, and flights are halted during the English listening section. Police often use cars or motorcycles to escort test-takers who are running late, while the military sometimes suspends training near testing sites.
Growing public concerns about AI-assisted cheating have drastically raised the stakes for this year’s exam, with some experts and politicians even calling for the government to postpone the test until reliable anti-cheating measures are in place.
President Lee Jae Myung, who is in the Philippines for a regional summit, chaired an emergency meeting by video to review the government’s exam preparations and vowed a stern, “zero-tolerance” response toward anyone caught cheating. He also instructed officials to consider sending more text alerts at unpredictable times during the exam.
“Would even the boldest student risk getting dragged out during the test because their telecommunications device went off?” Lee said on his X account.
Vice Education Minister Choi Eun-ok said that “there could be critics who say our measures are excessive, but a failure to conduct Suneung in a strict and fair manner will bring a (major) disruption to our society that would really be worse than a disaster.”
“We believe we are in a situation where excessive measures are necessary,” Choi said.
Government officials scrambled to strengthen anti-cheating measures this week after a 34-year-old man who topped a national tax accountant exam confessed in a video posted on his lawyer’s YouTube channel Sunday that he had used a hidden microcamera and smartphone to obtain answers from AI.
Han Won-seok’s unusually high scores had drawn suspicion after he discussed them during recent media interviews. The case follows other incidents involving AI-assisted cheating in the past several months, including test-takers caught using AI-powered smart glasses on an English standardized test in June and on some university essay exams in October.
Han Won-seok told reporters he would cooperate with the criminal investigation into his actions as he arrived for questioning by Seoul police on Tuesday.

title: Germany news: Plans for Rwanda migrant hub come under fire
text:
German human rights group Pro Asyl has said plans by Germany and four other EU states to send rejected migrants to Rwanda will be a "shipwreck"
- A UN agency also expressed concern over the plan
- Germany expects to see the highest number of new businesses opening in 2026 in more than a decade
- A massive leak of internal documents from Deutsche Bank has exposed misconduct and incompetence at the lender, media say
Here is a roundup of the top news stories from and about Germany on Tuesday, November 17, 2026:
Biden shares Merkel's bewilderment over Trump in new autobiography
Former US President Joe Biden's new autobiography "Promise Me, America" hit bookshelves on Tuesday, and it features anecdotes about several global leaders, including former German Chancellor Angela Merkel.
In the book, Biden dished on conversations that he and Merkel had about his predecessor and later successor, Donald Trump.
Citing conversations from early 2021, Biden wrote, "Angela was candid about her frustrations with my predecessor, who refused to shake her hand, and who seemed 'emotional' in their meetings, driven by mood swings rather than facts."
"She also wondered," wrote Biden, "why he was 'fascinated' by Vladimir Putin and other politicians 'with autocratic and dictatorial traits.' That was a mystery I could not unravel."
Merkel and Trump were often at odds over issues tied to NATO, trade, climate policy and Germany's dependence on Russian energy but one of the most infamous meetings between two came in the Oval Office in March 2017, when Trump awkwardly refused to shake hands with the German leader during a press availability despite photographers loudly encouraging him to do so.
Merkel reflected on the moment in her own 2024 memoir "Freedom" saying that after initially approaching Trump as someone "completely normal" she quickly sensed that he viewed their public meetings as a kind of "you or me" competition.
UN rights chief voices concerns over Rwanda deportation plans
The UN's high commissioner for human rights, Volker Türk, has joined the chorus of those voicing doubts about a plan by five EU countries, including Germany, to send rejected asylum seekers to a deportation hub in Rwanda.
Türk said he had not yet seen the draft proposal but that his office was "concerned about the human rights risks raised by the proposed transfer of people from five European Union countries to Rwanda, where they have no genuine connection and which has its own set of human rights challenges."
Instead, he called for a "comprehensive approach to migration governance anchored in human rights."
The Germany-based refugee advocacy group Pro Asyl said on Tuesday that the plans would end in a "shipwreck" (see entry below).
German universities draw in largest number of foreign students in EU
New figures from the EU statistics agency show that just over one quarter of all students from abroad in various EU member states were enrolled in tertiary education in Germany.
Of a total of roughly 1.65 million foreign students in 2024, around 1.1 million of them were from outside the EU and the rest were moving within the EU, 438,260 were in Germany.
France was next in line by sheer numbers with almost 285,000 foreign students, and the much less populous Netherlands was third with over 176,000. Germany, France and the Netherlands combined accounted for more than half the bloc-wide total.
The Netherlands, unlike France and Germany, was also one of the countries with the highest proportion of foreign students in tertiary education. Even excluding doctoral-level students, around 18% of students in the Netherlands hailed from abroad.
Only Luxembourg, at 51.5%, Malta (35.6%), Cyprus (21.6%) and Austria (20.8%) had a higher share among full EU members, though Switzerland's ratio also stood at roughly 20%.
Greece (2.6%), Croatia (3.5%) and Spain (4.6'%) had some of the lowest percentages of foreign students, with the EU average at 8.7%.
Lufthansa and VC pilots' union negotiations end without breakthrough
Mediation between German flagship carrier Lufthansa and the Vereinigung Cockpit (VC) pilots' trade union ended on Tuesday without a clear breakthrough.
The airline is trying to cut costs while the union is trying to optimize pay and conditions for members in a dispute dating back to September 2025 that led to several disruptions earlier in the year.
VC said that it favored a package resulting from the mediation, which it said Lufthansa had rejected. VC said it was giving the airline until November 23 to reconsider its position.
"The ball is now in the employer's court," VC said in a call with media. It did not specify what action it would take after the deadline but did say it considered its commitment not to strike during the arbitration process to be satisfied.
Lufthansa, meanwhile, said it had submitted a proposal to VC for up to 1,000 new cockpit hires by 2033, up to 150 additional captain promotions each year, a one-off payment for 2027 and 2028 followed by salary increases from 2029 onwards.
VC said it would be willing to make further concessions on pay and conditions if Lufthansa would respond with job guarantees.
The airline also said arbitrators had indicated a willingness to continue negotiations if the latest round proved fruitless — though it wasn't clear whether that also applied to each side of the labor dispute.
Berlin bans association accused of supporting Hezbollah
The government of the city-state of Berlin has banned an association accused of supporting the Lebanese group Hezbollah, which has been deemed a terrorist organization and outlawed in Germany since 2020.
Police in Berlin searched a total of 28 properties on Tuesday, including premises belonging to the affected groups and the homes of select members.
The ban affects El-Irschad e.V. in the Neukölln district and three subsidiary groups: Al-Qaem e.V., Al-Thaqalyn e.V., and Qalam Bildungszentrum UG.
The city's senator, or Cabinet minister, for interior affairs, Iris Spranger of the Social Democrats, said the group was "directed against the notions of understanding between peoples," and that its "purpose and activities" contravened criminal laws in Berlin.
The ban prohibits the public display or distribution of the organizations' symbols and logos. Their websites have been shut down and their assets seized.
Spranger said the group had given Hezbollah a platform to spread propaganda among Neukölln's Shiite community, using youth activities and a mosque to do so.
Rwanda migrant deportation hub scheme condemned by rights groups
A number of human rights groups have spoken out after Germany, along with Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands, announced plans to set up a hub for rejected migrants in Rwanda.
The deportation center would be the first such facility outside the European Union.
The Germany-based refugee advocacy group Pro Asyl said on Tuesday that the plans would end in a "shipwreck."
Pro Asyl managing director Karl Kopp said that even rejected asylum seekers had rights.
"Rwanda is not a model democracy. Opposition figures there are arrested and sometimes tortured," he said.
"If those affected need help, we will stand at their side with legal support."
In a statement issued after the announcement of the plans, 45 NGOs from 15 countries also condemned the move.
"These plans allow people without a right to stay in the EU to be sent to countries with which they have no connection at all," the statement said.
"These policies shift people, and responsibility for their safety and rights, out of public sight and beyond scrutiny," it said.
Criticism from within the coalition
The junior partner in Germany's coalition, the center-left Social Democrats, has also maintained its criticism of the plans, which are heavily supported by Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU), the sister party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU).
"Dobrindt's plans are short-sighted with regard to foreign policy and harm Germany's credibility," SPD foreign policy spokesman Adid Ahmetovic told the Reuters news agency.
"Rwanda violates the sovereignty of its neighbors and supports the M23 rebels in eastern [Democratic Republic of] Congo," he said.
"Such a regime must not receive any political concessions just because it is to take in refugees from Germany," he said, adding: "Human rights are not bargaining chips for deportation deals."
Rwanda deportation hub planned for 2027
The announcement of the plans comes after an EU reform of its migration policy this year granted broader detention powers and allowed for the creation of return hubs.
According to Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker, the aim is for the first center to be set up in Rwanda next year.
Diplomatic sources say the Rwanda hub will be initially run as a pilot with some 100 people, 20 from each of the five nations.
German government at odds over Rwanda plan
The plan to establish the deportation center in Rwanda has drawn criticism not only from a wide range of human rights groups but also from the junior partner in Germany's ruling coalition, the Social Democrats (SPD), as this video details.
Germany funding $300 million more US arms supplies for Ukraine — Pistorius
Germany will be purchasing $300 million (€273 million) of US arms supplies to give to Ukraine as it fights against the Russian invasion, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius announced on Tuesday.
He said that Berlin was making a fifth contribution to the PURL (Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List) mechanism coordinated by the US and NATO, under which European countries finance the purchase of US weapons for Ukraine.
Most of the new funds will go to buy guided missiles for Patriot air defense systems, Pistorius said in remarks made on the sidelines of a meeting with his EU counterparts in Brussels.
He said Berlin was also planning to provide Kyiv with IRIS-T air defense systems, as previously announced, as well as new radars to improve air surveillance, ammunition for F-16 fighter jets, and drones.
He also said that Germany was preparing to make IRIS-T missiles compatible with NASAMS air defense systems being supplied to Ukraine by Norway.
Pistorius stressed that supporting Ukraine, although an act of solidarity, was "not a charity event," as Russian aggression posed an associated threat to Western Europe.
He is to host a meeting alongside his British counterpart Wes Streeting later on Tuesday that aims to drum up further military support for Kyiv.
Wadephul wants closer ties with Azerbaijan, Armenia to counter Russia
Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has said he would like Germany to expand its relations with the former Soviet republics of Azerbaijan and Armenia as a counterweight to an ongoing bid by Russia to maintain its influence in the region.
"In the South Caucasus too, we are seeing Russia try to retain its influence at the expense of the people and their future," Wadephul on Tuesday before setting off on his first visit to the two countries as foreign minister.
He said Russian President Vladimir Putin was opposed to countries deciding their own destiny under a European order of sovereign states, making it important for the two Caucasian nations to retain their self-determination over their futures.
Wadephul also highlighted the South Caucasus's role as an interface between Europe and Asia, which he said meant the region had great potential for trade, energy partnerships and new transport links.
German foreign minister in the Caucasus
Germany's top diplomat is first to visit the Azerbaijani capital, Baku, where he is set to meet the country's authoritarian head of state, Ilham Aliyev, and Foreign Minister Ceyhun Bayramov.
He is scheduled to travel on to Armenia on Wednesday.
In August 2025, the two countries signed a joint declaration on a US-brokered peace treaty ending a decadeslong conflict over the Nagorno-Karabakh region.
This came after Azerbaijan captured the region in 2023 in a short but heavy offensive, with most of the region's population — more than 100,000 ethnic Armenians — forced to flee.
Deutsche Bank shares plummet after reports on incriminating documents leak
Shares in Deutsche Bank took a nosedive on Tuesday after media across the world published reports with information gleaned from millions of leaked documents that expose dubious past business practices at the lender.
The documents, which were shared by unidentified whistleblowers, throw light on the banking giant's activities over the past 20 years, which include dealings with Russian oligarchs and the late convicted US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
The name Donald Trump also appears in the documents from the time before he became US president.
The leaked documents, which include emails, have cast doubt on the success of chief executive Christian Sewing's efforts to turn around the institution after a series of scandals.
Among other things, they indicate that Sewing himself was involved in a working group that sought to expand the bank's Russian operations shortly before Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, despite warnings about regulatory and money-laundering risks.
The investigation, called "Inside Deutsche Bank", was conducted by over 200 journalists from a media consortium that included The Financial Times, Der Spiegel, Le Monde, the New York Times, the German public broadcaster ZDF and the Austrian daily Der Standard.
Deutsche Bank has not disputed the authenticity of the data, though it refers to the documents as "purported internal documents."
It also said that many of the incidents referred to in them belonged to a distant past and that it is now "a different bank."
European Commission doubles growth forecast for Germany
The European Commission has almost doubled its forecast for economic growth in Germany, raising it from a prediction in spring of 0.6% to 1.3% now.
The commission said stable domestic consumer demand and a rebound in exports justified the more optimistic figure.
The higher forecast comes despite the high inflation rate caused by the war in Iran.
Number of start-ups set to reach highest level since 2015
Some 286,000 new businesses are expected to be founded in 2026, a rise of 3.4% compared with last year and the highest level of start-ups since 2015, according to the National Association of German Cooperative Banks (BVR).
The BVR said the boom in start-ups could be partly attributed to the fact that developments in artificial intelligence (AI) and a difficult situation on the labor market were making self-employment more profitable.
However, the association warned that the increase was fragile, as it was largely driven by government support and exports rather that the private investment needed for more sustained growth.
In July, the German government adopted a start-up strategy that aimed to cut bureaucracy and provide support for future technologies, thus creating favorable conditions for young entrepreneurs.
The BVR also cautioned that the number of people in the 30-40 age group — those most likely to start a business — was falling, meaning that the surge will probably not last.
The association also said that even though there was a rise in AI-related start-ups in 2026, Europe needed to do more for AI development to keep up with the US and China.
Welcome to our coverage
DW's newsroom on the Rhine in Bonn wishes all readers a guten Tag!
Plans announced by Germany and four EU partner states to deport rejected asylum seekers to a hub in Rwanda have provoked a wave of criticism from human rights groups.
Migration hard-liner Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, one of the main advocates of the plan, has, however, given assurances that it will be executed "in line with human rights" and "in accordance with European and German law."
Meanwhile, more new businesses are expected to open in Germany this year than has been the case since 2015, a rise partly driven by the growing presence of artificial intelligence.
And internal documents leaked by whistleblowers from Deutsche Bank, a lender that has had more than its fair share of scandals in the past, have exposed more cases of malpractice and misconduct in recent years, media say.
Read on here for more on these and other German stories!

title: Geyser of trash and methane spews 500 feet into the air at California landfill and sparks health concerns
text:
An explosion at a California landfill sent a thick black geyser of decomposing trash and methane 500 feet into the air, sparking health concerns for residents in the region.
The Los Angeles Department of Public Health issued a directive ordering operators of Chiquita Canyon Landfill in Castaic to offer hotel accommodations and other emergency assistance to nearby residents after an eruption sent a noxious cloud into the air Monday afternoon.
The explosion sent odorous landfill gas and a large plume of dark black smoke into the air, impacting residents of Val Verde, Hasley Hills, Industry, Cambridge and Hillcrest, officials said.
"No one is at risk. We wouldn't be standing here without respiratory devices if there was any sort of risk," Los Angeles County Fire Department Capt. Aaron Katon told reporters, according to ABC 7.
No hazardous findings have been discovered by LA County fire officials, but the incident led to strong odors that may cause residents to experience headaches, nausea, dizziness or irritation of the eyes, nose or throat, according to the health department.
Fire officials said a crew conducting routine drilling at the landfill encountered a pressurized pocket of methane about 150 feet below ground, causing the gas to erupt from the opening.
“There was no fire at any point,” Katon said in an Instagram video, noting that the eruption was pressurized gas escaping from underneath the surface.
Hazardous materials crews decontaminated six workers, and four went to hospitals as a precaution.
The incident prompted evacuation warnings for several nearby communities, as officials urged residents to remain indoors and keep windows and doors closed. However, by Monday night, all evacuation advisories were lifted. It was not immediately clear how many residents were impacted, and if any evacuated as a result of the odor.
Katon, the fire chief, said the fire department’s air quality monitoring had found no danger to surrounding residents.
“All of our tools, and we have the best tools, they say there is no danger,” Katon said.
Landfill operators said in a statement that the incident unfolded during a “routine drilling operation to install a new well.”
“Crews encountered a pressurized pocket within the landfill, resulting in an above-ground release of gases and particulate material at the drilling location,” the statement continued.
“No liquids were released. Work was stopped immediately and the area has been secured,” officials added.
The landfill operator said no injuries had been reported, including among its employees.

title: Hormone-disrupting chemicals pose growing health threat, UN warns
text:
Hormone-disrupting chemicals found in everyday products pose growing risks to human health and the environment, while regulations remain insufficient to tackle them, warns the UN.
Chemicals in many everyday items that interfere with the body's hormones are a growing threat to human health and the environment, and scientists now have a better understanding of the harm they can cause, the United Nations said on Tuesday.
These substances, which can interfere with the body's hormonal systems, have been detected in breast milk and umbilical cord blood. Early exposure, sometimes before babies are born, can disrupt hormone activity and have lasting effects on brain development, growth and reproductive health, the UN warned.
In a new report, two UN bodies called for urgent, coordinated international action to protect human health and the environment, warning that policies and regulations aimed at transforming the products and sectors responsible for widespread exposure remain “fragmented and insufficient”.
“What makes [endocrine-disrupting chemicals] particularly concerning is that they can disrupt hormones that regulate many essential functions in both humans and wildlife, from development and reproduction to metabolism and behaviour. These effects can be long-lasting, and in some cases, irreversible,” said Sheila Aggarwal-Khan, director of the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) Industry and Economy Division.
Endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) are found in many plastic items, personal care products, pharmaceuticals, toys, household goods, electronics and pesticides.
They have been linked to problems affecting fertility and reproductive development, brain development and neurological function, thyroid and other hormone regulation, metabolism, the immune system and cardiovascular health.
“This report is an important step towards a safer world, free from exposure to EDCs,” the two UN bodies wrote.
“Solutions do exist. Some safer alternatives are available. The task for policymakers is to ensure that these solutions and alternatives are deployed – to protect human, animal and planetary health, and save trillions of dollars each year.”
While scientific evidence has advanced considerably since the previous assessment from 2012, experts warn that regulation has been slower to translate that knowledge into action.
How are endocrine-disrupting chemicals regulated in Europe?
In the European Union, endocrine disruptors are regulated through several pieces of legislation, including general chemicals legislation and sector-specific rules covering areas such as packaging, pesticides and biocidal products.
However, critics say the current legislative framework is failing to adequately protect people and the environment from exposure.
“Despite some progress in the EU, such as the introduction of new hazard classes to identify EDCs, EU citizens and wildlife continue to be exposed to a cocktail of these harmful chemicals,” said Michael Warhurst, executive director at the environmental non-profit CHEM Trust.
In the EU, 231 substances have been officially identified as EDCs, while an additional 121 substances are currently under evaluation.
The challenge extends beyond Europe. More than 350,000 chemicals and chemical mixtures have been registered for production and use globally, but the vast majority have never been evaluated for endocrine-disrupting properties, the report warned.
There have been greater efforts in recent years to develop testing programmes. However, most of that testing has not led to action to regulate these chemicals and control exposure, said Laura Vandenberg, one of the lead authors of the report.
Chemicals have been removed from products when people became aware and stopped buying products containing a certain chemical, like bisphenol A, which has been used to make plastic containers for storing food and beverages, Vandenberg said.
But this can lead to a “whack-a-mole problem”, where one chemical is replaced by another that is structurally similar or has not been sufficiently tested, she added.
What are the next steps?
The UN said regulators should aim to protect vulnerable populations from exposure, particularly during pregnancy, infancy and childhood; improve monitoring and understanding of exposure to these chemicals; advance the identification and testing of them; account for the costs of exposure; and strengthen regulations.
“This report makes clear that new regulations are needed, new testing paradigms must be adopted,” said Bethanie Carney Almroth, an ecotoxicology professor at Sweden’s University of Gothenburg and the UN Special Rapporteur on toxics and human rights.
“We need to reverse responses from reactive to proactive. We need to prevent harm from occurring, rather than merely documenting and treating it after the fact,” she added.
Olwenn Martin, a chapter author, said that scientific understanding of how these chemicals disrupt the endocrine system is growing, and that they appear to be implicated in a wider range of diseases than previously thought.
“What concerns me most is that regulation still assesses most substances one at a time. That is like tackling climate change one greenhouse gas at a time, ignoring their combined effect,” Martin said.

title: Bahrain intercepts Iranian drones targeting US radar after 2-month lull in Gulf strikes
text:
Iran fired drones toward what it said was a U.S. military radar system in Bahrain on Tuesday, marking the third strike in five days after a roughly two-month lull in the conflict, Reuters reported.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said its target was the radar system at the Sheikh Isa base in Bahrain, which is home to the U.S. Fifth Fleet.
Bahrain said its air defenses intercepted the incoming drones after authorities issued a security alert urging residents to seek shelter. Officials announced an all-clear later in the morning, with no deaths or injuries reported.
U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) also addressed the Iranian drone strikes, saying they didn't hit their intended target. The drones were "intercepted without any damage to U.S. equipment or injury to American personnel," CENTCOM said.
The attempted attack followed another wave of Iranian aerial strikes that Bahrain repelled on Sunday, when the IRGC claimed six of its drones targeted a radar system at the Al-Riffa helicopter base.
That strike came two days after Friday's initial attempt against a U.S. radar installation in Bahrain — the first major attack after the two-month pause. U.S. Central Command said American forces shot down both drones in that incident, with no casualties or injuries.
Reuters previously reported that President Donald Trump has told advisors that he may not attack Iran again if there are no more provocations from the IRGC or the Houthis, an Iran-backed terrorist group in Yemen.
Trump has said he plans to maintain the naval blockade on Iran, essentially putting the country's economy into a vice grip. He said the blockade will remain in place as long as Tehran seeks to disrupt traffic in the Strait of Hormuz.
In recent days, attacks on tankers have increased in the strait, still one of the world's most vital transit routes for global energy supplies.
Oman and Iran have discussed ways to manage shipping through the strait, which carried roughly one-fifth of global oil supplies each day prior to the conflict.
The U.S. has not been part of those bilateral talks, and Trump has signaled he would reject any transit arrangement negotiated without Washington that gives Tehran control over the waterway.
Reuters contributed to this report.

title: Trump appeals to state and federal courts to erase hush money criminal conviction
text: NEW YORK (AP) — A federal appeals court is weighing whether it can — or should — intervene in President Donald Trump's hush money case now that a New York State appellate court has heard arguments in his quest to erase the historic conviction. A three-judge panel of the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals on Monday spent more than an hour questioning Trump's lawyer and a state prosecutor about the president's latest bid to shift the case from state court to federal court, where he could seek to have it dismissed on immunity grounds. There was no immediate decision. The sides were in court for the second time in 11 days as Trump pursues a two-pronged legal strategy in an attempt to get the May 2024 verdict thrown out. Trump was convicted on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records to obscure a $130,000 payment to adult film performer Stormy Daniels. READ MORE: Trump loses again in bid to erase his hush money conviction Along with his federal court fight, the Republican president is also waging a traditional appeal through New York's state court system, which included arguments before the mid-level Appellate Division on Nov. 5. That court has yet to rule. Regardless of the outcome, Trump will forever be associated with the case, which went to trial as he was campaigning for his return to the White House. Trump denies wrongdoing and was given no punishment. Now, with little over two years left in his presidency, he is steadfast in trying to rid himself of the dubious distinction of being the first U.S. president convicted of a crime. Trump's lawyer says case could go to the Supreme Court Trump's lawyer, Robert Giuffra Jr., urged the 2nd Circuit judges on Monday to issue an order as soon as possible — even before writing their full decision — to take control of the case and stop the Appellate Division's deliberations. Without federal court intervention, Trump "will likely have to wait years" for state appellate courts to rule before he can take the matter to the U.S. Supreme Court, Giuffra said in a letter previewing his argument. But Judge John M. Walker Jr., who was appointed to the appeals court by his cousin, President George H.W. Bush, and Chief Judge Raymond J. Lohier Jr., who was appointed by President Barack Obama, weren't so sure. "How does that work?" Walker asked. "I mean, assuming we were to agree with you, there's been an argument in the Appellate Division. Briefs have been filed in the Appellate Division. Will those briefs be refiled by everybody here?" Federal law doesn't spell out precisely how such a move would play out. Giuffra suggested the case would first go to a federal district court judge, who would adopt the state court verdict, before going to the 2nd Circuit for arguments and a decision on dismissal on presidential immunity grounds. The briefs, he said, would remain the same — albeit with different covers. "You're asking us to embrace an entire procedural mechanism that I don't see anywhere authorized by Congress," Lohier said. "We think it is authorized," Giuffra said, calling a provision of the law that allows such post-verdict transfer petitions "a safety valve that's intended to protect against exactly the gamesmanship that's gone on here." A federal judge declined Trump's transfer bid 3 times Trump asked the 2nd Circuit to step in after a federal judge in August ruled against the president for a third time. Judge Alvin K. Hellerstein, who died last month at 92, wrote in his decision that "paying hush money to an adult film star or engaging in a cover-up of an embarrassment are not subsumed in presidential immunity." Trump first sought to move the case to federal court weeks after he was indicted in March 2023. He tried again after his conviction and the Supreme Court's July 2024 ruling that presidents and ex-presidents can't be prosecuted for official acts and prosecutors can't use official acts as evidence that unofficial actions were illegal. Giuffra argued to both the state and federal appellate panels that prosecutors used the type of official acts evidence that was later barred by the Supreme Court's immunity ruling, including testimony about his Oval Office conversations, workflow and social media posts. Giuffra also took issue with the prosecution's description of the hush money payment as an illegal campaign contribution under the Federal Election Campaign Act, arguing that such allegations belong in federal court, not state court. After Trump appealed Hellerstein's second denial, the 2nd Circuit ordered the judge to reconsider, finding that he had failed to weigh "important issues relevant" to the president's request to move the case. That panel, which also included Lohier, said it expressed no view on how he should rule but instructed Hellerstein to closely review evidence that Trump claimed was related to official acts and whether Trump could argue those actions were taken as part of his White House duties. Steven Wu, chief of the appeals division at the Manhattan District Attorney's Office, urged the 2nd Circuit panel to uphold Hellerstein's ruling and leave the case in state court. Even if Trump were to prevail, he argued, the state appeals court would still be free to rule.

title: St. Louis Fed's Musalem says four more rate hikes may be needed in coming months
text:
St. Louis Federal Reserve President Alberto Musalem indicated Tuesday that the central bank may need as many as four rate hikes in coming months, offering one of the most hawkish views yet by a Fed policymaker about the steps needed to quell inflation.
During a speech delivered in Argentina, Musalem made the case that current policy is not significantly restricting economic activity.
"The economy will likely require several interest rate increases before the spring of 2027 to achieve 2% inflation in a timely manner," he said.
Musalem said the real policy rate, which subtracts the inflation rate from the Fed's target rate, needs to be between 2%-2.5% by next spring, and estimated that the current rate is about a full point below that range. That position suggests the Fed may need to hike at each of the upcoming Fed meetings in December, January, March and April.
Musalem does not get a vote on the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee over the period where he says that the rate increases will be needed, though he does get to present views and provide input on the "dot plot" of individual members' expectations. He will next vote in 2028.
To be sure, Musalem noted "an unlikely but still plausible scenario" in which no further hikes would be needed.
"Falling energy prices and lower shipping costs, or an increase in potential output growth driven by higher productivity growth, might ease inflation pressures such that inflation moves toward target in 18 months," he said. Another possibility is that demand might decelerate as spending on artificial intelligence slows.
However, he said the more likely scenario is that "persistent strong demand and ongoing supply pressures" combine to keep inflation above the Fed's 2% target, thus requiring further increases in the fed funds rate from its current range of 3.75%-4%.
"It would be preferable for a higher real policy rate to happen in a balanced way, driven both by lower inflation and a higher nominal policy rate," he said. "However, the nominal policy rate may need to do most of the work."

title: Instagram’s new tool for creators targets unauthorized reposts and AI-modified videos
text:
Instagram is introducing a new tool to help creators protect their original videos, the Meta-owned company announced Tuesday. The feature, called “content protection,” is already available on Facebook and is designed to detect when creators’ original videos are being used without their permission. The company is also expanding the tool to address AI content, not just conventional reposting.
The announcement comes in response to creators’ concerns over how easily original content can be copied and redistributed across social media platforms, especially considering how generative AI has made it easier to manipulate existing videos.
Instagram says the content protection tool continuously scans Instagram for unauthorized uses of creators’ protected videos. When Instagram detects a match for one of a creator’s Reels uploaded by another user, it sends the creator an alert. Creators can then choose to block the video from being viewed on both Instagram and Facebook to hide the matched content. They can also choose to add an “original by” label on the content that links viewers of the matching video back to their original video.
Additionally, creators can choose to keep the match visible while monitoring its performance or release their claim on the reel, allowing it to remain visible on Meta’s platforms.
The tool will also begin detecting AI-generated videos that reuse audio from creators’ original content, even when the visuals have been altered. This update will initially be tested with a small group of creators in the coming weeks. The company plans to expand access to this feature to creators who enroll in content protection on both Instagram and Facebook.
Instagram says it’s exploring ways to limit the reach of accounts and content that repeatedly use AI tools to repost others’ work.
Creators who are eligible for content protection will see a notification in their activity feed. Once they enroll, every original video they post to Instagram going forward is automatically protected. They can also choose to retroactively protect eligible videos they’ve already posted by manually selecting them.
If creators have permitted certain profiles to use their work, such as their second profile or a brand, they can add them to their allow list so their videos won’t be flagged as matches.
Tuesday’s announcement marks another step in Instagram’s ongoing efforts to give creators greater control over their content and protect the originality of their work.

title: When will humans actually fly on Starship?
text:
The stunning return of Starship from the skies to a launch tower in South Texas answered some questions about the future of SpaceX’s ambitious rocket program. Namely, it is now rapidly moving toward rapidly reusable launch.
However, it raises other questions. For example, as Starship becomes fully reusable, when might humans fly on the vehicle?
The short answer is pretty simple: If SpaceX prioritizes human spaceflight on Starship, it could happen reasonably quickly. The longer answer becomes more complicated and depends on what one means by human spaceflight. The first people to fly on Starship probably won’t launch from Earth, or land here. Rather, they will probably be NASA’s lunar astronauts. So there are different timelines for humans flying aboard Starship and landing on Earth.
Given what is known publicly, and what Ars has heard privately, here are some educated guesses about all of this.
Past is prologue
The first thing we can say for sure is that all estimates of human spaceflight on Starship should be taken with a gigantic grain of salt, including those in this article. Putting humans on any space vehicle is a difficult and time-consuming task, even outside of the requirements that NASA would impose for its astronauts.
The original target for launching humans on Starship (then known as the Interplanetary Transport System) set a decade ago was 2024. That was for a Mars mission. Then, in 2018, SpaceX announced a lunar flyby mission on Starship with a target launch in 2023. This dearMoon mission was canceled in 2024. In 2022, SpaceX and Dennis Tito announced a lunar flyby mission later in the 2020s.
More recently, according to sources, SpaceX has been telling individuals interested in launching on Starship that it could begin offering flights by 2029. I probably would not put too much stock in this date.

title: Vitamin C could help block cancer-linked chemicals in your stomach, study finds
text:
Scientists have discovered that vitamin C may help prevent potentially cancer-causing chemicals from forming in the stomach after eating foods containing nitrates and nitrites. A new mathematical model suggests that taking vitamin C after meals could reduce these harmful reactions, offering a possible new strategy for lowering cancer risk.
Vitamin C may do more than support everyday health. New research from the University of Waterloo suggests that it could also help prevent potentially cancer-causing chemicals from forming during digestion. Using mathematical modeling, scientists investigated how vitamin C influences chemical reactions in the digestive system that have been linked to cancer risk.
Exposure to nitrates and nitrites has increased in North American diets over the past several decades. These compounds are found in cured meats such as bacon and salami, as well as in fruits and vegetables grown in soil or water affected by pollution. Although nitrates and nitrites contribute to important functions in the brain and cardiovascular system, they can also participate in potentially harmful reactions once they reach the stomach.
One of these reactions, called nitrosation, can produce substances that researchers suspect may contribute to cancer development. Understanding what causes these chemicals to form, and what might prevent their formation, has been a longstanding challenge.
Why Vitamin C Could Change the Cancer Risk Equation
"Since at least the 90s, researchers have been studying the link between cancer and these compounds, with conflicting results," said Dr. Gordon McNicol, a post-doctoral researcher in applied mathematics and the first author of the study. "Our work suggests that the presence of dietary Vitamin C may help explain these inconsistencies."
To investigate this possibility, the researchers developed a mathematical model that simulates how nitrates and nitrites travel through the body and undergo chemical changes. The model incorporated several interconnected systems, including the salivary glands, stomach, small intestine, and plasma, the liquid portion of blood.
Their simulations revealed that vitamin C consumed alongside nitrates and nitrites may interfere with the formation of potentially harmful compounds. This could help explain why foods containing nitrates do not necessarily carry the same risks.
For example, leafy vegetables such as spinach naturally contain both nitrates and vitamin C. According to the model, the presence of vitamin C could limit the chemical reactions associated with cancer risk, potentially helping explain the protective effects suggested by some dietary research.
Could Taking Vitamin C After Meals Help?
The researchers also explored whether vitamin C supplements might offer similar benefits when taken after eating.
Their findings suggest that taking vitamin C after each meal could moderately reduce the formation of nitrosation products associated with cancer risk. This effect could be particularly relevant when consuming foods containing nitrates and nitrites, including processed meats such as bacon and salami.
However, the results come from mathematical simulations rather than clinical trials. Although the model predicts that vitamin C can reduce the production of potentially harmful chemicals, further research is needed to determine whether this translates into a measurable reduction in cancer risk in humans.
New Clues for Future Cancer Prevention Research
The researchers believe their model could help scientists better understand the complicated relationship between diet, digestive chemistry, and cancer risk. It may also provide guidance for future experiments examining how nutritional choices influence the formation of potentially harmful compounds.
"This work provides a mechanistic roadmap for future clinical and laboratory studies by identifying the key interacting drivers of these potentially harmful chemical reactions, including nitrite exposure, antioxidant intake, meal timing, gastric conditions and oral microbiome activity," said Dr. Anita Layton, professor of applied mathematics and Canada 150 researcher chair. "This model can help researchers design more targeted experiments and interventions, focusing on when and in whom nitrosation is most likely to occur."
By identifying how factors such as vitamin C intake, meal timing, stomach conditions, and bacteria in the mouth interact, the model could help researchers develop more precise strategies for studying and potentially reducing cancer-related chemical reactions during digestion.
The study, "Vitamin C as a nitrosation inhibitor: A modelling study across dietary patterns and water quality," was published in the Journal of Theoretical Biology.

title: This armored amphibian once lived and hunted on the seafloor
text:
Most amphibians shrivel or suffocate in saltwater. But long ago, an oddball armored amphibian may have dwelled deep in the ocean.
Scientists have found evidence that an ancient amphibian with a flattened body and upturned eyes may have once stalked the seafloor. The animal, Gerrothorax maritimus, is the first ever amphibian known to have lived without access to land or freshwater, researchers report October 26 in Nature Ecology & Evolution.
G. maritimus, which lived 237 million years ago, was rather unlike today’s amphibians, which breathe and drink through their porous skin. The creature’s lifestyle was unimaginable for an amphibian, says Ryosuke Motani, a paleobiologist at the University of California, Davis. Of the more than 8,000 amphibians known today, none live solely in saltwater.
Motani and his colleagues inspected two well-preserved G. maritimus fossils from the late Triassic Period, which spanned roughly 237 million to 201 million years ago. Each creature measured around 70 centimeters, about as long as a skateboard, and was swathed in armor made of bony plates. The specimens appeared nearly identical to their closest relatives, other amphibians that dwelled in freshwater, Motani says. But the fossils’ location was unusual: They were found in what was once a seabed, roughly 30 kilometers from any ancient land.
It wasn’t clear whether the creatures lived in the ocean or were landlubbers that got buried there after they perished. So the team performed a chemical analysis. Levels of different forms of strontium in the fossil bones matched those of the Triassic ocean. This telltale sign revealed that G. maritimus ate seafood and drank seawater. “That means it lived there,” Motani says.
For amphibians, “this is the first time that that we have hard evidence that they were actually adapted for long-term life in the sea,” says Lachlan Hart, a paleobiologist at the University of New South Wales in Sydney who was not involved with the new study. Hart and his colleagues previously suggested that a different ancient amphibian may have been seafaring but probably did not dwell in the ocean.
Scientists have long searched for a marine amphibian. The fossil record is littered with skeletal fragments revealing how some mammals, reptiles and birds have adapted to a salty lifestyle. “Amphibians were always the problem because they did not really follow the rule,” Motani says.
The same skin that makes today’s amphibians vulnerable to disease and toxins also makes saltwater fearsome. Key adaptations allowed G. maritimus to skirt these issues. G. maritimus and its relatives evolved bony body armor, probably for defense. But these hard plates would have helped the seafloor dwellers prevent water loss. And unlike modern amphibians, which typically lose their internal gills after the larval stage, this creature and its close relatives retained a fishy breathing strategy suitable for life in the depths.
G. maritimus fossils hint that the animal lurked on the seafloor as an ambush predator. Its jaw lifted upward like a toilet seat so that it could unleash a suction attack on fish and other small creatures.
There may yet be other amphibians hiding in ancient oceans, environments ignored by paleontologists studying these creatures. “Because they’re amphibians, we would be looking for them in terrestrial freshwater environments,” Hart says. Perhaps there are more amphibians that have gotten their sea legs.

title: Euclid space telescope discovers its 1st comet | Space photo of the day for Nov. 16, 2026
text:
The Euclid space telescope has discovered its first comet, called comet C/2026 S1, or comet Euclid for short.
What is it?
The Euclid mission, a European Space Agency mission that launched in 2023 with contributions from NASA, spotted this previously undetected comet approximately 807 million miles (1.3 billion kilometers) away in observations captured between Sept. 16 and 24.
"I was excited to see my software flag a 'streak' smeared across several images – the result of a fast-moving object. By predicting its position I could identify it in other images, in total finding it in five image sets. Further inspection revealed that it had a fuzzy cloud around it, indicative of an active object like a comet that is shedding dust and gas," Mikko Pöntinen, a scientist at the University of Helsinki who made the initial discovery with a Solar System Objects Science Working Group within the Euclid Consortium, said in a statement.
Following these observations, the team diligently checked current records of comets to ensure that this was, in fact, something new to us.
Why is it incredible?
Euclid is a mission designed to capture long, slow observations of deep space and distant galaxies and collect data to help scientists better unravel the mysteries of dark energy and dark matter. It was in not explicitly designed in any way to capture imagery of fast-moving comet hurtling through our solar system. But still, the space telescoped managed to catch this comet whirling between the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn.
This finding shows that Euclid can be used for more than it was intended, and that in the future scientists could use it to intentionally target other comets in the far reaches of our solar neighborhood. These kinds of observations can also help researchers to identify "noise" like comet trails in Euclid's field of view.

title: Woods set to return next month after two years out
text:
Tiger Woods is set to return to competitive golf in December for the first time in more than two years.
Woods, 50, has not played in a traditional ranking event since the 2024 Open Championship at Royal Troon amid a series of off-course issues.
The 15-time major champion has endured a challenging few years with a number of injuries and turmoil in his personal life.
Woods will host next month's Hero World Challenge - an event which is part of the PGA Tour schedule but does not carry FedEx Cup points - and has been announced as part of the 20-player field.
The American is one of three exemptions for the tournament in the Bahamas along with compatriots Rickie Fowler and Gary Woodland.
Speaking to SiriusXM PGA Tour Radio in a video posted last week, Woods said: "I'm feeling better, no doubt about that.
"I've been training quite a bit. I will be at Hero either way, so I'll see you there."
Woods' long-awaited return comes after he accepted a five-year driving ban in September following a plea agreement in his reckless driving case.
In March, Woods had been arrested and charged with driving under the influence after clipping a truck and rolling his car in Florida.
Woods was also found with two white pills in his pocket, which were identified as hydrocodone - an opioid used to treat pain.
He subsequently stepped away from golf to seek treatment in what was described by his attorney as an "intensive, highly individualised and medically integrated programme".
Woods has endured a succession of debilitating injuries, including multiple back surgeries, serious fractures to his right leg following a car crash in 2021 and a ruptured Achilles tendon in 2025.
Woods also suffered the death of his mother, Kultida, in February 2025, while his girlfriend Vanessa Trump was diagnosed with breast cancer earlier this year.
Trump, the former daughter-in-law of US President Donald Trump, said last month that she is now cancer free.
Analysis: Woods will want to play majors in 2027
Every report we had since Tiger Woods resurfaced into public life has told us he is looking good and looking fit. Going into the new year he will be taking part in his own indoor golf league, the TGL, so it's not the biggest surprise that he will be at his own tournament in the Bahamas.
This is the fifth time he has come back from a long-term absence from the game at this event. It is one that means an awful lot to him. It is involved with his charitable foundation and it's his tournament, so no surprise this is the one he has chosen to come back at.
The TGL in the new year, that's the indoor simulator run by his company in conjunction with Rory McIlroy. He did compete last year and cut a pretty pathetic figure by the standards of someone who has won 15 major titles. We could see him play before that at the PNC event. That's the parent and child event where he would presumably play with his son Charlie.
He is trying to line himself up to play at least the majors next year. They mean an awful lot to him.
We know how much the Masters means to him, but also think about where the US Open is going to be played, at Pebble Beach, and that's where he won the US Open in 2000 by 15 shots.
The Open Championship at St Andrews where he has won two of his three Open titles. These would be events he would certainly want to be at.

title: Jensen Huang says he would be ‘honored’ to return to Nvidia as CEO
text:
Jensen Huang said he would be willing to return to Nvidia as CEO in his first remarks since resigning from the company on Thursday.
“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote in a statement published in the Wall Street Journal and CNBC.
Nvidia’s board of directors is not considering reinstating Huang, according to reports from the Financial Times and Wall Street Journal.
The CEO founded Nvidia in 1993 and ran the company until last week, when he resigned over affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and employees who reported to him.
Huang and Nvidia initially said the executive’s dealings with Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singaporean datacenter firm Megaspeed and a suspected spy, were a routine customer relationship. However, Huang disclosed the affair in an email to employees, and the board announced an investigation into its national security implications .
Nvidia’s board has also created a committee to oversee exports and national security issues.
The US government confirmed on Tuesday morning that the commerce and justice departments had been investigating Megaspeed since 2024. Though the government has never officially restricted sales and exports to Megaspeed, Nvidia put Megaspeed on an internal “no sell” list in June 2025 after the commerce department requested its records of any sales to Megaspeed, according to a statement from the department. Megaspeed is suspected of diverting US advanced AI chips to Chinese firms in potential violation of export restrictions.
Huang’s full statement is published below.
Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I’ve never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me.
I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. NVIDIA has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible. I love our country, and I love NVIDIA.
I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation.
Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.
Thank you again to everyone who has shared their good wishes. I am profoundly humbled by your support. To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours.

title: NSA attributes US network outage to routine ‘maintenance’ activities
text:
The United States National Security Agency (NSA) has said an outage affecting its internal communications network was due to “routine maintenance”, following a report by CNN.
The report, published on Tuesday and citing six unnamed sources, said there was no evidence that the outage was the result of a cyberattack. The incident follows a series of outages that have gone without explanation in recent days.
The network, known as NSA Net, allows employees of the US surveillance agency to share highly classified information internally, CNN said.
A spokesperson for the NSA downplayed the outage in a statement to Al Jazeera.
“The National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance,” the statement said. “While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational, and our ability to defend national security continues. NSA’s infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.”
The reported network disruption at the NSA follows several other major outages that have affected communication and transportation services in the US.
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) temporarily halted all takeoffs in the country on Friday, claiming that a system upgrade caused a flight communication overload. The ground stop, which lasted more than four hours, was called out of an “abundance of caution”, it explained.
The tech giant Microsoft also announced that services such as Outlook and Teams were down last week.
More recently, on Monday, outages hit major banks, and United Airlines briefly suffered a system disruption that delayed some departing flights.
US President Donald Trump has played down the seriousness of those outages.
“Things like that happen,” Trump told reporters on Tuesday. “It’s fine.”

title: Does locking up a student's cell phone improve test scores? A new study suggests so
text:
The rise of smartphones in the U.S. coincided with a dramatic slide in K-12 students' reading and math achievement. Now, new research suggests putting students' phones in locked pouches during the school day may help restore some of those historic losses.
"Around 2013, U.S. students started losing 2-3 weeks of learning each year," says Harvard University's Tom Kane, one of the new study's co-authors. "It's been a slow leak that, over time, has put U.S. 8th graders almost a year behind. Strict cellphone bans seem to plug about half of that leak."
Or the equivalent of 1-2 weeks of learning a year, according to the study released Tuesday. That's a small but, according to Kane, statistically significant improvement.
"That could add up over time, just as the initial declines did," adds Dartmouth College's Douglas Staiger, another co-author.
The study's authors say it is the first nationwide analysis of student-level test scores in math and reading both before and after schools enforced locked-pouch cellphone bans. It was a joint effort between Harvard's Center for Education Policy Research, Dartmouth and NWEA, a K-12 testing and research organization.
Kane, Staiger and their teams analyzed a nationwide sample of more than 3 million elementary-, middle- and high-school students over the past five school years, comparing the test scores in schools that adopted phone pouches to the scores at similar schools that did not.
Not only did strict cellphone bans appear to trigger small learning gains, the researchers say, those gains didn't seem to fade out after the first year of implementation. Instead, Kane says, the gains appeared to continue, year after year – at least up to three years after adoption.
Research on phone bans is mixed
Tuesday's headline finding, that locking phones during the school day led to small but statistically significant improvements in math and reading scores, comes with an important caveat:
A separate study, from April, found that these pouches had "close to zero" impact on student test scores – and if there was a benefit, it was not statistically significant.
"Overall, we didn't find evidence of meaningful achievement gains," says Brian Jacob, a co-author of that April study and a professor of education policy at the University of Michigan.
What should we make of these seemingly contradictory results?
Both are large-scale studies by well-respected teams of researchers. The April study has been peer-reviewed; the more recent study has not.
Both studies similarly focused on schools' adoption of lockable pouches made by the for-profit company Yondr. According to Tuesday's paper, more than 3,300 schools nationwide began using the pouches between the '19-'20 and '25-'26 school years. Typically, schools that use the pouches require that students put their phones in them at the beginning of the day and don't get them back until the end of the school day, when the pouches are unlocked by a school administrator with a special magnetic device.
But the two studies also differ in key ways. The April study pooled school-level mean test scores at several thousand Yondr-adopting schools, while Tuesday's study used student-level scores at the 844 schools that use both Yondr pouches and tests administered by NWEA.
Simply put, the study released Tuesday had more fine-grain, student-level data, but the study released in April was able to examine a much larger sample of schools.
But the two studies' findings also aren't as different as they may seem. Jacob and his co-authors did find statistically significant gains with Yondr pouches in high school math. It's just that those gains were offset by ban-related learning losses in middle school.
Overall, Jacob says, the new study "is encouraging. And if [the benefit] really persists and accumulates over time, it really could be a meaningful benefit. I think we'll just have to wait and see if that happens."
Another co-author of that April study, Tom Dee, a professor at Stanford University's Graduate School of Education, says of Tuesday's findings, "I hope they are right that these very small test score gains will aggregate and add up over time. However, I'm not comfortable making that extrapolation from estimates that are small, sensitive and based on just a few years of phone bans."
Taken together, Dee says, he considers the results from these early studies into cellphone bans "largely disappointing," and insists "we need continued study on this topic."
Kane sees the results differently. Even if the benefit is small, he argues, relative to the cost – roughly $25 per student – these pouches still make financial sense for schools. "That's still a lot less than having to pay teachers for an extra week or two of instruction."
When it all went wrong
For nearly a quarter-century, from 1990 to 2013, math achievement among fourth- and eighth-graders rose steadily. Reading scores also improved.
Then around 2013, student test scores began a sustained tumble that continued through the COVID-19 pandemic and has only recently begun to slow. For years, politicians and pundits blamed pandemic-era school closures for the losses, but the data tells a different story.
"Particularly in reading, test scores were going down for four to six years before the pandemic," Stanford University researcher Sean Reardon told NPR earlier this year.
