"In fact, you wouldn't really know there was a pandemic effect if you just looked at the last 10 or 12 years of test scores. There's been just a steady kind of decline regardless of the pandemic."
Which raises the question: What happened around 2013?
Possible explanations abound. The federal government began stepping back from holding schools accountable for low test scores. Many schools also saw funding cuts in the wake of the Great Recession.
This new study is the latest to make the case that the mass adoption of cell phones by children and teens also helped fuel those test score declines.
The researchers note that, in 2011, fewer than a quarter of teen students had access to smartphones. By 2018, 95% did. And similar rates in other industrialized countries coincided with similar student achievement declines.
Now, Kane says, he wants to study students' smartphone and social media use outside of school.

title: NASA telescope is plunging back to Earth after 22 years in orbit
text:
An is barely clinging to space after a failed left it tottering lower and lower. The space agency said Monday it predicts the Swift Observatory will likely come crashing down on Wednesday.
Most of the 1 ½-ton telescope is expected to burn up in the atmosphere. But a handful of pieces made of denser-than-lead tungsten and some mirror parts could survive reentry, according to NASA's Brad Cenko, the mission's chief scientist.
"As of Monday, the U.S. Space Force predicted that the roughly 3,200-pound spacecraft will re-enter the atmosphere at approximately 3:30 a.m. EST, Nov. 4, with an uncertainty of 11 hours," NASA said on Monday.
Any surviving wreckage will most likely plunge into the ocean. But swaths of Africa, Australia, India, Southeast Asia, and Central and South America are within the reentry zone. The U.S. Space Force is tracking the telescope's dwindling path.
In a statement on Monday, NASA said the "risk of harm coming to anyone on Earth is unlikely" — roughly 1 in 2,100.
"NASA and Space Force will continue to monitor the re-entry and update predictions," the agency said.
Its cosmic cremation has the Swift team mourning, yet full of gratitude, for the observations the telescope made during its 22 years in orbit. Swift blasted off on Nov. 20, 2004, to search for some of the biggest explosions in the universe: gamma-ray bursts and supernovas.
"We've known this day would come since before Swift was launched. At least in low-Earth orbit, what goes up must come down. And that end is catastrophic," said Pennsylvania State University's John Nousek, an astronomer who led the control team.
Intense solar activity over the past few years dragged Swift down faster than usual. NASA hired Katalyst Space a year ago to mount a rush rescue. But the company's three-armed robot named Link ran into trouble after launching in July and got no closer than 7 miles to 9 miles to the telescope. Link plunged back to Earth in September.
Swift resumed observations once the rescue attempt was called off, discovering even more gamma-ray bursts and other ultrahigh-energy events. But by late October, the telescope was too low to remain steady for observations, and its systems were shut down.
Its final tally: more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts and 1,400 exploding stars, not to mention a slew of comets, asteroids and star-shredding black holes. The telescope's superpower was its ability to swivel swiftly — thus its name — toward erupting celestial events.
Shawn Domagal-Goldman, Astrophysics Division director at NASA, told "CBS Mornings" in June that nothing pinpoints gamma-ray bursts like the Swift Observatory.
"A nuclear weapon going off doesn't even compare to the magnitude of energy that comes out of these things and it's literally the biggest explosions in the universe," Domagal-Goldman said.
NASA considered Swift a first responder for the Hubble and Webb space telescopes and others that would follow its alerts and provide deeper investigations. Scientists are still figuring out how to fill the gap.
"Our fervent hope is that the lessons learned by the successes of Swift can be applied to new generations of space missions to accelerate our discoveries about the universe," Nousek said in an email.

title: France's Philippe Diallo to challenge Infantino for FIFA presidency
text:
French Football Federation (FFF) President Philippe Diallo has received UEFA backing to be a candidate in FIFA's presidential election, which will take place in March in Morocco, with criticism against current chief Gianni Infantino growing.
UEFA, European football's governing body, said it has backed Diallo "unanimously" in a bid to replace Infantino, putting it's "full support" behind the Frenchman.
Veteran Japanese official Kohzo Tashima has also announced his candidacy, with the deadline for candidates to stand for election being November 18.
Potential candidates for the post must show letters of support from five of FIFA's 211 member associations before going through eligibility and integrity checks.
Son of boxer, head of French football
Diallo, the 63-year-old head of the FFF, is the son of a Senegalese boxing champion.
He was elected as the federation's president in 2023 with a large majority. He was reelected for another four-year term in 2024.
Back in September, Diallo said the FFF had withdrawn its support for Infantino ahead of the March 2027 election, saying trust in the FIFA president had "been betrayed."
"The way in which the governance of world football is envisaged no longer reflects us," the French football head said of the decision.
If elected, the Frenchman would become FIFA's first black president, as well as it's third French leader after Robert Guerin and Jules Rimet, who served as the organization's first and third presidents.
Embattled Infantino
Gianni Infantino has been in charge of world football's governing body since 2016.
He has been facing growing criticism since pitching a plan of sell a stake in the World Cup to private investors. The criticism of the plan was led by UEFA and its President Aleksander Ceferin.
Infantino ended up scrapping the plan but UEFA went ahead and took FIFA to court in the US, trying to gather evidence ahead of potentially lodging a criminal complaint with Swiss authorities about alleged "mismanagement" by Infantino.
FIFA's headquarters are located in Zürich, Switzerland.
Infantino was also criticized after creating a peace prize and awarding it to US President Donald Trump last year.
The connection between Infantino and Trump came under criticism once again during the World Cup, after United States forward Folarin Balogun was allowed to take part in the round-of-16 game against Belgium despite having been shown a red card in the previous game.
The US president admitted to having personally intervened through a conversation with Infantino.

title: Jeff Stelling: We’d have two or three beers the night before Soccer Saturday – it was brilliant
text:
There is a changing of the guard in football punditry and the 17th floor of talkSPORT Towers provides a snapshot of its evolution. Listeners, pick your poison.
In the morning, you can tune into the veteran of sports broadcasting. Jeff Stelling, once the voice of our Saturday afternoons, hosts your breakfast show alongside Ally McCoist from Mondays through to Wednesdays. It’s classic stuff. While most of his Soccer Saturday colleagues have since been consigned to the scrapheap, Stelling still very much has his foothold in the industry and as such brings us a taste of the ‘good old days’.
However, his old-school bread-and-butter style admittedly feels like it’s on its way out, for better or worse. Because in the dark of the night, during the prime-time slot, things go a bit blinky-eyed manic. The seat occupied by Stelling earlier that day is now filled by a man in a mask, shouting into a microphone. Jason Cundy and Jamie O’Hara are changing the pundit’s playbook with The Sports Bar; it’s chaotic, it’s crude and it does millions.
Never one to be behind the times, Stelling recognises the market for football media based largely on mockery nowadays. But don’t expect him to follow suit.
“I think there’s a place for it... not on one of my shows!” Stelling tells The Independent, who will not be showing up to work with a Derek McInnes mask any time soon.
“But Cundy and O’Hara, I think at that time of night... it’s irreverent to say the least. Obviously they take the mickey out of each other mercifully, Cundy with his Ange mask and so on. And they take the mickey out of callers as well. I think it works perfectly well at that stage. But you can’t have that all the way through.”
Pundits increasingly find themselves leaning into their club loyalties for the sake of entertainment, when purists would argue that the position should be neutral. Stelling, admittedly, was never completely down the middle; he was and still is known for his die-hard fandom of Hartlepool United, where he serves as honorary president. It’s fuelled his love of non-league, which is why he found himself at Woking FC on this grey October afternoon, fronting Enterprise’s Local Legends campaign which strives to celebrate the volunteers that keep clubs like his alive.
He wants to incentivise more people to get involved with their community club, hailing the mental health benefits for fans. “ Whether they've got problems at home, whether they've got financial difficulties, whether they've got health worries, it's almost therapy,” Stelling said. “So the football club, massively important to the community.”
But in the context of ‘Cundyism’, Stelling feels his Hartlepool ties benefited him in during his three-decade stint in front of the cameras.
“It’s one of the things that has helped me in my career, being a Hartlepool fan, because if I were a Liverpool or Man United or Tottenham fan, I’d have found things much more difficult,” he adds. “People would never have accepted that I was neutral, which I’ve always tried to be. People say, ‘Who’s your Premier League team?’ I say, ‘I haven’t got one,’ and I genuinely have not got one.
“But the growth of that [less neutrality in punditry], everybody seems quite happy now. They shout from the rooftop who their team is. Football is incredibly tribal, and I think that’s sometimes one of the problems.”
Stelling brought his legendary stint with Sky Sports to an end over three years ago, presenting his last Soccer Saturday in May 2023 after 29 years behind the desk. He was the last of a banished era, with the show’s once-regulars - Charlie Nicholas, Phil Thompson and Matt Le Tissier - all axed by the broadcaster following sweeping personnel changes in 2020. Chris Kamara, of “Unbelievable Jeff!” fame, followed out the exit door two years later amid his deteriorating health, diagnosed with speech apraxia - though he has since made a remarkable recovery after undergoing experimental treatment in Mexico.
Stelling, however, called time on his own accord after simply falling out of love with the job. “It was fully on my own terms,” he says. “ I had been intended to leave when Phil Thompson, Charlie Nicholas and Matt Le Tissier were sacked, but I was asked to stay on for another year to help bed in the new boys, then I actually stayed longer than that for all sorts of different reasons. But I felt the time had come.
“I was finding that it had become, to a degree, a chore. I used to love going out there, loved working on Soccer Saturday, used to love building up to it, doing statistics and stories at home. And being there on the Saturday, the best day of the week, every week.
“I'd lost that feeling. And because I'd lost that feeling, I'd done it for 30 years, I thought it was time maybe to see what life outside Sky was like.”
Stelling was anxious about his own health during his final days at Sky, but got out before the “mental toll” became too much. “It was a mental stress and I feared if I carried on, it would make me unwell,” he admits. “But I was never physically unwell. I just got to the stage where honestly, I didn’t want to go in and do it.”
Even the idea of the show doesn’t make him long for the days of old. “I don’t miss it,” Stelling asserts. But he can still cherish the memories with the old Soccer Saturday crew, especially those outside of the studio.
“We used to get together on a Friday night and I’m not ashamed to say we’d have two or three beers, and it was brilliant,” he says. “They were just great, great nights.”
Holding celebrity value in their own right, the odd notable name from the world of football would join the party. “I know [we went out with] David Moyes once, Delia Smith, Chris Wilder - happy to spend time with them,” he recalls. “But it was the company of the boys, really.”
A group that made the 3pm blackout not just tolerable but enjoyable, hearts broke when the clock ran out on Stelling’s cohort. Fans of that time may therefore find solace to know that, to buck a time-old trend of television, their friendship has survived beyond the screen.
“We live all over the country so it’s difficult to get together, but we do get together from time to time, and bump into each other at various events and things,” he says. “We’re all in touch. We were all best mates, really. We still are.”
Jeff Stelling has launched Enterprise’s search for the National League’s Local Legends - celebrating those who turn up for their club and community week in, week out. Click here to nominate.

title: Brazilian chicken ban: EU delays decision despite positive audit
text:
Mercosur meat imports remain a contentious issue among EU countries, amid divisions over a deal liberalising trade between the two blocs.
The 27 EU member states postponed a vote on Tuesday to lift the ban on Brazilian chicken imports after several countries asked for further clarification from the European Commission regarding Brazil’s compliance with EU antimicrobial regulations.
The vote was scheduled after the EU banned imports of Brazilian meat in September over Brazil’s use of antimicrobials to stimulate animal growth.
The ban angered Brasilia, as it came only a few months after the contentious Mercosur trade deal with Latin American countries provisionally entered into force, opening up trade in agricultural products, including Brazilian meat.
“A number of Member States requested further clarifications on the system put in place by Brazil,” Commission spokesperson Eva Hrncirova said. She added that the Commission would now “take the time to address these comments and questions” before a new meeting takes place in early December.
The ban, which followed a vote by national experts in May, covers beef, poultry, eggs and honey. However, an EU audit found in early September that Brazil’s poultry control system was operating effectively.
Heated topic between EU countries
Imports of Brazilian meat remain a divisive issue among EU countries, with several countries, led by France, strongly opposed to the Mercosur agreement signed in January this year.
EU farmers fear being exposed to dumping due to lower production standards in the countries that signed the deal — Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay — particularly regarding health and phytosanitary rules.
To address farmers’ concerns, the deal includes quotas capping tariff-free access for sensitive agricultural products. Annual beef imports are limited to 99,000 tonnes at a reduced tariff of 7.5%, equivalent to 1.5% of EU production, while poultry imports are capped at 180,000 tonnes a year, or 1.3% of EU output.
However, ratification of the deal has been delayed since the European Parliament referred the agreement to the Court of Justice of the European Union, questioning its legality.
Facing pressure from Mercosur countries and EU member states backing the deal, notably Spain and Germany, the European Commission eventually decided in May to provisionally implement the agreement pending a ruling by EU judges on its legality.

title: Sen Rand Paul and Sen-elect Andy Barr back Rep James Comer for Kentucky governor
text:
Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., and Sen.-elect Andy Barr, R-Ky., are both backing Rep. James Comer, R-Ky., for Kentucky governor.
"I’m proud to endorse my friend @JamesComer to be Kentucky’s next Governor! Please help him to get there!" Paul declared in a Monday night post on X.
Barr, a House Republican who just won a U.S. Senate contest during the midterms, also threw his support behind Comer's candidacy.
"No one will fight harder for Kentucky families, Kentucky farmers, and Kentucky's future than my friend James Comer. Kentucky conservatives have built a strong legislature, and now we need a Governor who will work with them, not against them," Barr said in a Tuesday statement.
"With James Comer in the Governor's mansion, we'll finish the job on eliminating the state income tax and unleash Kentucky energy producers to lower costs and create jobs. I'm proud to stand with James Comer for Governor," he added.
Comer, who has served in the House of Representatives for a decade, just won re-election during the midterms. The lawmaker, who chairs the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, announced a Bluegrass State gubernatorial bid on Monday.
He previously ran for Kentucky governor in 2015, but lost the GOP gubernatorial primary by only 83 votes.
The state's 2027 race for governor will take place in slightly less than a year, and the primary is set for May 18.
Current Gov. Andy Beshear, a Democrat who is currently serving his second term, is ineligible to serve a third-consecutive term. Kentucky's state constitution stipulates, "The Governor shall be ineligible for the succeeding four years after the expiration of any second consecutive term for which he shall have been elected."

title: Judge sets March retrial date for Lindsay Clancy in deaths of her 3 children
text: PLYMOUTH, Mass. (AP) — A Massachusetts judge on Monday scheduled Lindsay Clancy's retrial for late March after prosecutors signaled that — at least for now — they intend to prosecute her again on first-degree murder charges in the killings of her three young children. Clancy's first trial ended in a mistrial after jurors were unable to reach a unanimous verdict on whether she was criminally responsible for the killings. Eleven jurors favored acquittal on the grounds of insanity, while one disagreed. READ MORE: Judge denies motion asking for Lindsay Clancy to be found not guilty due to lack of evidence While the Plymouth County district attorney hasn't indicated publicly whether his office will pursue the same charges in a second trial, Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague told the judge during Monday's hearing that prosecutors were "ready to pick a jury trial date." Clancy's lawyer, Kevin Reddington, said he took that to mean that prosecutors intended to go ahead with a first-degree murder case, as a lesser charge would allow Clancy to waive her right to have a jury. "The die has been cast," Reddington told Judge William Sullivan. "I think you can read between the lines that when they say that the case is going to require a jury, that it's an indirect comment from the DA that they intend to proceed on first-degree murder indictments." Prosecutors had sought a May trial date, citing scheduling conflicts, but Sullivan set the retrial for March 29. The decision to schedule Clancy's second trial comes a week after Sullivan rejected a defense request to dismiss the charges. He ruled that a retrial would not violate Clancy's constitutional protection against double jeopardy. Attorneys are scheduled to return to court Dec. 30 to discuss trial logistics, security and media arrangements. Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse, has never disputed that she killed her three children at the family's Duxbury home in January 2023. Her attorneys said she was suffering from postpartum psychosis, a rare mental illness that can afflict mothers after childbirth. Prosecutors argued Clancy planned the killings and understood what she was doing.

title: Republicans outspent Democrats for first time in over a decade in record 2026 midterm election political ad blitz
text:
Political advertisers spent a record $12.06 billion during the 2025-26 elections, making it the first time a midterm cycle outspent a presidential cycle, according to a report from advertising intelligence company AdImpact released Tuesday.
Total spending exceeded AdImpact's June projection by more than $460 million.
The elections also marked the first time in over a decade that Republicans have outspent Democrats on advertisements, according to AdImpact.
Despite Republicans leading spending, John Link, senior vice president of data at AdImpact, said that "Dems still led or were generally even with overall airings and impressions."
The record spending extended across the board, with every type of race reaching a new high. Senate spending hit $3.39 billion, while spending on gubernatorial elections reached $2.61 billion, spending on races in the House of Representatives grew to $2.44 billion and state legislative races totaled $602 million, all records, according to AdImpact.
The 2026 midterm cycle was largely powered by megadonors, with SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk becoming the largest contributor by funneling more than $366 million into campaigns.
The biggest donors in this year's election disproportionately favored Republicans, according to a CNBC analysis of Federal Election Commission records. Fourteen out of the 20 largest donor groups supported GOP candidates, according to that analysis.
Republicans spent $5.51 billion on political advertisements, compared with $5.11 billion spent by Democrats, according to AdImpact.
While Republican spending increased by 27% from 2024, spending by Democrats fell by 4%.
Fundraisers told CNBC in interviews that Democratic donors' hesitancy largely stems from memories of Kamala Harris' defeat in 2024, unease about the rise of democratic socialism and distrust in party leadership.
Though they were outspent, Democrats made sweeping gains against Republicans in races nationwide, taking control of both the House and the Senate and flipping seats in some of the most competitive places, including Texas and Kansas.
It is not the first time spending did not align with the winners. In 2024, President Donald Trump defeated former Vice President Harris despite Democrats outspending Republicans.
While party majorities in Congress have switched hands, the most popular medium for political ads has not changed.
Broadcast television represented the largest category for spending in this year's election, accounting for 49%, or $5.85 billion, of political ad spending, according to AdImpact. Broadcast's share of political ad dollars is up slightly from 48% in 2024.
Broadcast TV's strength comes despite facing pressure from falling viewership and increasing competition from streaming.
Industry experts have told CNBC that political advertisers continue to spend on broadcast because it reaches local markets and active voting populations. The Associated Press also reported that airtime was so expensive during the midterm elections that some candidates, including Republican Ken Paxton in Texas, bought ads during national sporting events, figuring that reaching enough constituents through a national broadcast might actually be less expensive than buying across the state's local television markets.
The fastest-growing categories in this year's cycle were connected TV, or internet-connected devices like Apple TV or Roku, with $2.66 billion, and digital, with $1.91 billion. Both mediums grew double digits from the 2024 presidential election. Spending on cable and radio declined 7% and 13%, respectively, from 2024.

title: Isomorphic Labs raises $5B as it looks to take drug candidates to clinical trials
text:
Isomorphic Labs, the AI drug-discovery platform that was spun out of Google’s DeepMind in 2021, has raised $5 billion in a Series C funding round as it seeks to take its drug candidates to clinical trials.
The funding was co-led by Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital, with new investor Andreessen Horowitz and other investors also participating. All of the company’s existing backers, including Alphabet’s venture divisions GV and Capita G, Thrive Capital, MGX, Temasek, and the U.K. Sovereign AI Fund, also invested.
Isomorphic Labs builds an AI drug-design engine that uses a slew of simulation AI models that explore various areas of chemistry to help the company design drugs. The company, whose work builds on DeepMind’s breakthrough AlphaFold protein-folding AI model, said its program has yielded “positive preclinical results” in oncology and immunology. The lab has struck deals with pharma giants like Eli Lilly, Novartis, and Johnson & Johnson.
The new funding, which comes on the heels of a $2.1 billion Series B round in May, will be used to continue developing its drug-design engine, as well as to foray into more types of medicine.
The Series C is Isomorphic’s first fundraise since its founder and CEO, Demis Hassabis, left his position as head of DeepMind to focus on drug discovery, which also saw him moving into a chairman role at DeepMind. Hassabis and then-director of DeepMind John Jumper won the Nobel Prize in chemistry for the lab’s work on AlphaFold, a system that predicts the 3D structure of proteins with nothing more than their genetic sequence.
Isomorphic did not disclose its new valuation. Bloomberg reported earlier this month that the lab was looking to raise funding at a $50 billion valuation.

title: Meet the new James Bond: Robert Pattinson
text:
The Internet has been abuzz for months about which actor would replace Daniel Craig as British agent 007 James Bond in the franchise. We finally have the answer: Robert Pattinson, who built on his 2005 role as the doomed Cedric Diggory in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire into an illustrious career mixing roles in franchises and Hollywood blockbusters with daring arthouse fare.
“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime,” Pattinson said in a statement. “To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team.”
The choice will reunite Pattinson with Denis Villeneuve, who recently worked with him on the forthcoming Dune: Part III and will direct the next (as yet untitled) Bond installment. “I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey,” Villeneuve said in a statement. We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007. I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin.”
Not everyone is happy with the casting choice; some have never forgiven Pattinson for the Twilight franchise, despite the actor’s impressive recent films. Pattinson has played darker roles in recent years, often as a villain. And at 40, Pattinson is a bit older than the actors he beat out, most notably Nicholas Hoult, Jack Lowden (Slow Horses), Josh O’Connor (Wake Up, Dead Man), and Callum Turner (Fantastic Beasts).

title: Physicists defy expectations by controlling the magnetic heart of a single atom
text:
Scientists have unexpectedly discovered how to control the magnetic spin inside a single atom's nucleus using radio waves, overturning previous assumptions about atomic behavior. The breakthrough could pave the way for more reliable quantum memory, although researchers are still trying to understand why it works.
Researchers at Delft University of Technology (The Netherlands) have accomplished something that physicists previously thought should not be possible. Using radio waves, they managed to directly control the magnetic spin of the nucleus inside a single atom. The unexpected result challenges existing assumptions about how atomic magnetism behaves and could eventually lead to new ways of storing and retrieving quantum information.
The findings, published in Nature Communications, also present scientists with a new puzzle. Although the experiment demonstrated that this remarkable level of control is possible, researchers do not yet fully understand the mechanism that makes it work.
The Hidden Magnetism Inside Every Atom
Atoms in magnetic metals such as iron and nickel behave like tiny magnets. However, the magnetism within an atom comes from different sources. Both electrons and, in some cases, the atomic nucleus possess a quantum property called spin, which can be thought of as a miniature magnetic compass needle.
"By far the strongest magnetism comes from the electrons," says lead researcher Sander Otte. "But in some atoms, the nucleus also carries a spin. That spin is much weaker, but it is also much better shielded from the outside world."
That protection makes nuclear spin especially interesting to quantum researchers. Because it is less exposed to disturbances from its surroundings, it could offer a promising way to preserve delicate quantum information.
To investigate these tiny magnetic properties, Otte's team uses a specially modified scanning tunneling microscope. This powerful instrument allows the researchers to deliver electrical signals to individual atoms with extraordinary precision.
Until recently, their experiments concentrated primarily on electron spin because it is easier to detect and measure. The nucleus's magnetic spin could only be observed indirectly through a phenomenon known as the hyperfine interaction, which creates a subtle quantum connection between the spins of the electron and nucleus. This connection can cause the two spins to become slightly entangled, meaning their quantum states are linked.
An Atomic Experiment Produces an Unexpected Result
In the latest study, lead author Hester Vennema and her colleagues took a different approach. They simultaneously applied two separate signals to a single atom, with one directed at the electron and the other at the nucleus.
By using these signals together, the researchers could investigate their effects independently. What happened next caught them by surprise.
Even when the electron and nuclear spins were largely disentangled, the team was still able to flip the orientation of the nucleus's magnetic spin. Based on their previous understanding, the nucleus should not have responded in this way.
"According to our simple understanding, this should not really happen," says Otte. "The nuclear spin should not be sensitive at all to the electrical signals from a scanning tunneling microscope."
The result suggests that the interaction between electrical signals and nuclear spin involves a mechanism that scientists have yet to fully explain.
Controlling Quantum Spins Like Guitar Strings
Achieving this level of precision required the researchers to adapt a technique called double magnetic resonance so it could operate on a single atom. The method allowed them to manipulate the magnetic behavior of the atomic nucleus separately from that of an electron.
Magnetic resonance works by applying a wave signal at a carefully selected frequency to change the orientation of a magnetic spin. However, quantum mechanics restricts these changes to specific allowed transitions, meaning the frequency must be precisely matched to the spin being targeted.
Vennema compares the process to playing a musical instrument.
"You can compare it to the strings of a guitar," Vennema explains. "Each possible spin rotation is like a string with its own note. You have to play precisely the right note to make a particular string vibrate. The "notes" of a nuclear spin are a hundred to a thousand times lower than those of an electron spin."
In other words, electrons and atomic nuclei respond to very different frequencies, much as different guitar strings produce different musical notes. By tuning their signals to the appropriate frequencies, the scientists could address the two types of spin separately.
A Quantum Breakthrough With a Mystery Still to Solve
The discovery could have important implications for the future of quantum information technology. Unlike conventional computers, which store information as bits representing either 0 or 1, quantum systems can use quantum states to encode information in more complex ways.
One major challenge is keeping those states stable long enough for information to be stored and retrieved reliably. Nuclear spins are attractive candidates for quantum memory because they are relatively well isolated from environmental interference.
The ability to control these spins directly could therefore open new possibilities for writing, storing, and reading quantum information. However, the findings represent an early experimental advance rather than a ready-to-use quantum memory technology.
For now, one of the most important outcomes is the new scientific mystery the experiment has revealed. The researchers have demonstrated an unexpected way to manipulate nuclear spin, but the physical mechanism responsible remains unclear.
"Back to the drawing board, then," says Otte. "That is really how science works. There is always something new left to figure out."

title: How octopuses squeeze through tiny openings, step by step
text:
Octopuses have made many a great escape. Remember Inky, who fled from New Zealand’s national aquarium?
The cephalopods can Houdini their way out of tanks and off boats by squeezing through narrow slits and incredibly tiny holes. Now researchers know exactly how some octopuses pull it off. These masterful getaways involve a consistent, step-by-step game plan, researchers report November 5 in the Journal of Experimental Biology.
Octopuses are mostly squishy muscle, allowing them to shape-shift, though they do have some rigid body parts. Not many scientists have studied how these animals squirm through small openings, says Robyn Crook, an evolutionary biologist at San Francisco State University who was not involved in the research. “It’s one of the most characteristic behaviors of octopuses in popular awareness, but the strategies octopuses use have not really been examined systematically.”
Sneaking through small spaces isn’t just a party trick for octopuses, says Michael Kuba, a biologist at the University of Naples Federico II in Italy. The animals use that skill to find hidden food and to avoid becoming food themselves.
Kuba and his colleagues observed how three common octopuses (Octopus vulgaris) and four Mayan octopuses (Octopus maya) approached small holes. For each individual, the team measured the distance between the octopus’s eyes as an indicator of the size of their most rigid cartilage around their brain. Then the researchers designed acrylic boxes with holes that were slightly smaller or larger than that eye-to-eye measurement. They plopped the octopuses inside and watched what happened.
One, two, three — free!
Octopuses have slightly different escape how-tos, depending on the size of the hole they are squeezing through. Here, a common octopus (Octopus vulgaris) wriggles through a space just a little bit bigger than their most rigid body parts. It takes just three steps for the octopus to free itself from the acrylic box.
Common octopuses used one of two escape strategies depending on the hole’s size. When the hole was wider than the distance between their eyes, the octopuses pushed themselves through it in three steps. First, they snuck one or two arms through the hole and then threaded a couple more arms through. Finally, they used the arms that they had already snaked through the hole to push against the box and yank their head and the rest of their arms through in one fell swoop. The whole operation took a few seconds.
When the hole was narrower, common octopuses added a fourth step. They shoved all of their arms through the hole first and then squished their head and bulbous mantle through.
Out the door on four
When a hole is smaller than their most rigid body parts, common octopuses add a fourth step to wrestle their bodies through an opening.
Mayan octopuses behaved more cautiously than the common octopuses. When confronted with the narrower hole, Mayan octopuses didn’t even attempt to fit inside of it. They usually ignored it. This difference between the species could stem from their biology or how they’ve adapted to their environments, Kuba says. Mayan octopuses live in sandy, rocky areas, so while they might disappear under rocks, they don’t often need to cram through holes, he says.
The team hopes these escape artists will inspire new soft robots that can morph their shape to fit through tiny spaces, says Wenci Xin, a robotics researcher at the National University of Singapore. “This incredible capability could enable robots to overcome environmental limitations and enter spaces that are difficult to reach.”
Studying how octopuses navigate different types of holes may provide additional clues for robots, Crook says. For instance, the cephalopods may take a different tack for openings that are more like slits or tubes than holes.
Currently, robots built to fit through tiny holes tend to be snake-shaped, but further research on these eight-armed contortionists could unlock other configurations.

title: Dream Chaser space plane gets landing approval for debut mission in 2027
text:
The Dream Chaser space plane just cleared a major hurdle ahead of its planned spring 2027 spaceflight debut.
Dream Chaser just received U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) approval for its return to Earth on that robotic mission, either at the space shuttle landing facility at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida or at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California.
"Thank you to the FAA for its collaboration and support of commercial space innovation," representatives of Sierra Space, the Colorado company that builds Dream Chaser, wrote on X on Monday (Nov. 9).
The FAA's environmental assessment found that Dream Chaser "would not significantly impact the quality of the human environment" under the National Environmental Policy Act, the agency stated. (It should also be noted that the U.S. has lately been suggesting that environmental laws should be bypassed to meet quickly rising demand for launches and landings.)
For example, for a potential return at Vandenberg, "sonic booms are anticipated but would be temporary, short in duration, and limited to 1.1 PSF [pounds per square foot] or less, which is similar to a thunderclap," the FAA stated.
The 30-foot-long (9 meters) Dream Chaser has been in development for more than two decades. It has yet to launch to space, though it has completed a couple of drop tests from the air. Dream Chaser was an entrant in NASA's Commercial Crew series of contracts to ferry astronauts to and from the International Space Station (ISS), but it didn't end up making the cut; in 2014, NASA picked Boeing's Starliner and SpaceX's Crew Dragon to provide this taxi service.
The following year, Sierra Nevada Corporation — then the entity in charge of Dream Chaser — unveiled a cargo version of the space plane. In 2016, NASA selected the company to conduct at least six uncrewed cargo flights to the ISS, but development delays repeatedly pushed those missions into the future.
Dream Chaser was originally expected to fly those robotic resupply missions on United Launch Alliance's workhorse Atlas V rocket. A few years ago, however, the space plane switched over to Vulcan Centaur, the successor to the venerable Atlas V.
Dream Chaser was supposed to ride on Vulcan's second-ever mission but wasn't ready in time, so that flight went ahead in October 2024 without the space plane. Sierra Space is now targeting spring 2027 for Dream Chaser's first liftoff, which will be a free-flying test mission in Earth orbit.
The company is now pursuing many types of contracts for Dream Chaser, anticipating a mix of missions for NASA, the U.S. military and private companies — including the consortiums that plan to build commercial space stations. Indeed, Sierra Space is a member of one such consortium — the group that plans to build an outpost known as Orbital Reef.

title: Russian military plane crashes, killing all 19 on board
text:
A Russian military transport plane has crashed in Siberia, killing all 19 people on board, the country's defence ministry said, according to state-run media.
The An-12 aircraft went down during a "scheduled flight" in an "uninhabited area" in the Kemerovo region, the ministry said in a statement.
The ministry added that it preliminarily believed a technical malfunction was the cause of Tuesday's crash. An investigation by Russia's aviation authorities is now under way.
Local Governor Ilya Seredyuk said an emergency response team "quickly extinguished a blaze" after the crash near the village of Yagunovo, and the area was sealed off by police.
Seredyuk, who visited the crash site, said "a helicopter and medical facilities have been put on standby".
The governor added that the "main task" now was to help investigators carry out their work.
He also posted a video showing firefighters combing through what looked like the crash debris, with a number of ambulances also seen standing nearby.
CCTV footage posted on social media appeared to show the moment the plane crashed, with a lighted object falling through the sky in the distance. An explosion then lit up the sky, but the crash was too far away to be seen.
The BBC and Reuters news agency verified the time and date of the footage, while Reuters also verified the location based on features of the scenery that matched satellite imagery of the area.
It was not immediately known whether the crashed aircraft had any cargo on board.
An-12 planes are widely used by the Russian military to transport weaponry and personnel, and also for search and rescue operations.

title: Millionaire factory: Anthropic IPO set to fuel AI gold rush in London’s high-end property market
text:
Sporting hoodies and white trainers rather than the gilets of London’s banker and lawyer class, tech bros can struggle to be taken seriously by the capital’s luxury property agents. “We worked with a young tech entrepreneur with a substantial budget, who agents assumed was looking to rent a one-bedroom flat,” says Jo Eccles, a buying agent who sources off-market properties for ultra-wealthy clients.
But this week’s float by Anthropic, the AI developer behind the chatbot Claude, promises to bring even more credibility for the growing cohort of tech millionaires, which could breathe life into London’s ailing high-end property market. Its IPO on Thursday, expected to value the company at $1.4tn (£1.1tn), is likely to turn more than 4,000 of its staff into millionaires as their stock options vest. SaaStr, a California research firm, has estimated that the minimum value generated for staff at the AI lab will be $20m each.
Anthropic’s millionaire factory promises to expand the group of tech buyers, who range from senior staff at major AI labs to founders who have sold their startups, with budgets that range from £2m to £40m, Eccles says.
Tech’s wave of wealth has already reshaped Silicon Valley – notably in San Francisco – driving up demand for already scarce housing as young entrepreneurs and engineers became millionaires overnight. Now, that money is washing up on British shores too.
Anthropic, which employs about 5,000 people worldwide, has more than 200 employees in the UK. The company, founded in San Francisco in 2021, has announced plans to expand its presence in London, with a new office that is capable of accommodating up to 800 people.
The company’s UK filings show that it spent £24.1m employing an average of 43 staff in 2024 alone – a mean average of £560,000 per person. Job listings this year have advertised base salaries of up to £630,000 before stock options for research engineers.
Salaries across Britain’s AI sector are flying: OpenAI’s staff in London each received £2.3m on average last year – about 58 times the median UK full-time employee earnings. That puts them on par with partners at top law firms such as Linklaters and Clifford Chance, and ahead of some bankers in the City.
UK-based investors in these companies are also watching the value of their stakes grow at breakneck speed. Alex Gerko, the billionaire founder of the trading firm XTX and an early investor in Anthropic via the venture arms of the business, is expected to make hundreds of millions of pounds in paper gains when the company joins the stock market this week.
The flush of technology cash is already evident in London’s commercial property market. First, a wave of startups led to Shoreditch being nicknamed Silicon Roundabout, before tech firms began expanding across the capital. Now, US AI firms are expanding at pace in the UK, clustering tightly inside the King’s Cross “knowledge quarter” where Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta all work a stone’s throw from each other.
They have followed in the footsteps of Demis Hassabis, a totemic figure in AI’s breakthrough era who co-founded DeepMind in 2010 and sold it to Google for £400m four years later. He was one of the first to set up in the north London enclave. Isomorphic Labs, his AI drug discovery startup that is also now owned by the Google parent Alphabet, is in the area.
The AI gold rush is already being felt at the highest end of London’s housing market. Although tech bosses may be younger than the sector’s traditional client base, agents report that interest – while spread across London – includes plenty of familiar wealthy haunts.
In February, the Times reported that Igor Babuschkin, the billionaire co-founder of Elon Musk’s AI venture xAI, had bought a £57m penthouse overlooking Hyde Park, in one of the biggest deals in the city this year.
Meanwhile, Providence House, the Reform UK treasurer Nick Candy’s former mansion on the grounds of the Royal Hospital Chelsea in London, was reportedly sold for £270m to the founder of the quantitative investment firm Quadrature Capital, Suneil Setiya. Aidan Devane, the chief executive of the firm, attributed its success partly to its proximity to AI labs in the city, telling the Financial Times: “We are probably in the golden age of London quant.”
Tech wealth, increasingly generated by gains in the AI sector, “has become a force at the very top of the prime central London market”, according to the super-prime estate agent Beauchamp Estates, which has a portfolio including a £42m sub-penthouse overlooking Hyde Park.
Jeremy Gee, a managing director at Beauchamp, says inquiries from tech and AI buyers have risen noticeably over the past year. “Some are international buyers, principally from the US, but a growing number are based here in London,” he says, adding that many have amassed their fortunes with remarkable speed.
“They tend to be younger, they move quickly and they are very clear about what they want. Location and quality matter most and they will pay a premium for something genuinely special,” he says. “London offers culture, history, world-class schools and a growing AI community of its own.”
Even the traditional bastions of old British money are adapting. According to Shona Baijal, the managing director of wealth at Coutts, the private bank long associated with the British aristocracy, the tech and AI sectors are increasingly a source of new clients. One of the key challenges, she says, is helping young entrepreneurs who are coming into vast amounts of wealth very quickly.
“A lot of people feel overwhelmed,” she says. “We have to discuss the emotional aspects of what it means to come into wealth. We might say: you’ve come into the money, but do not rush to do anything.”
Coutts found last month that eight out of 10 properties in London’s most exclusive neighbourhoods – such as Mayfair, Belgravia and Knightsbridge – now sell below asking price.
But sellers and property agents hoping the AI industry may ride to London’s rescue face a glaring problem: much of these new AI fortunes remains on paper.
At founder level, many are “paper rich, cash poor”, Baijal says – meaning until they sell their businesses or their shares vest, their wealth is largely theoretical.
At the same time, Britain’s wider economy is growing more reliant on the sector’s momentum. Last week, official figures showed that the UK economy grew by 0.7% in the third quarter, its fastest expansion in two and a half years, almost entirely due to strong and widespread growth in services, led by the IT sector. Separate analysis by Bloomberg found that roughly a quarter of UK economic growth this year had been powered by AI.
That dependence makes the prospect of an AI bubble bursting all the more dangerous. There have been months of warnings over the valuations of AI companies, and there has been a groundswell of public opposition to datacentre construction and worries around AI safety.
Investors were reminded again of the fragility of the AI trade last week after a scandal involving extramarital affairs and an alleged Chinese spy sent shares in one of the most valuable AI companies in the US, the chip designer Nvidia, tumbling.
Other market indicators have been flashing warning lights. This year one popular measure used by investors to assess whether a market is overvalued – the CAPE, or cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings, ratio – rose to its highest level since 2000, showing that the US stock market was unusually highly valued compared with its profits. That was before the Anthropic’s blockbuster debut.
For now, the AI boom’s physical footprint is unmistakable. In San Francisco, the average one-bedroom property now rents for $4,400 a month, up more than 25% from last year and nearly three times the US average. Landlords have been trying to capitalise on the boom, particularly in areas closest to the offices of the biggest AI companies including OpenAI and Anthropic.
Meanwhile in London, the transformation of King’s Cross from a railway goods yard once notorious for criminal activity into an international hub for tech and AI is well under way. Whether this new class of wealth is permanent, or a temporary flash in a historic tech bubble, is yet to be seen.

title: Ukraine says underground gas pipeline used to mount sneak attack
text:
Ukrainian soldiers spent weeks navigating a decommissioned, underground Soviet-era gas pipeline to sneak behind enemy lines and launch a surprise attack on Russian troops this autumn as part of an operation to prevent the invading forces from reaching the eastern city of Kupiansk, according to the Ukrainian unit involved.
The operation forced the soldiers to get past barricades laid by Russian forces — including the bodies of fallen troops — and involved close-quarters combat inside the roughly three-foot-wide pipeline, Ukraine's military said.
"Operation Veles" was carried out by members of the Ukrainian National Guard's Khartiia Corps in the Kharkiv region within the last couple of months, according to a series of posts by the unit on social media. The unit said troops crawled and were pulled on wheeled carts some nine miles through the underground pipeline before emerging behind Russian positions.
The operation was part of a broader Ukrainian effort, more than four and a half years into , to prevent the invading forces from advancing toward the front-line city of Kupiansk.
The unit's social media posts quoted soldiers saying they engaged in close combat with grenades and small arms inside the pipe, where the cramped space came with pooled freezing water and traces of natural gas lingering years after the pipeline was decommissioned. Some Ukrainian forces spent as long as a month underground during the operation, the Khartiia Corps said.
"They used electric winches to move through the pipe, and transported ammunition and equipment on small wheelbarrows," the unit said in one post. It called the conditions "extremely harsh," and noted that the troops "constantly moving on their knees caused injuries, and dirt clogged the mechanisms of their weapons and caused malfunctions."
Russian troops had laid obstacles in some sections of the pipeline, with Ukrainian soldiers saying that some of those barricades included the bodies of other Russian soldiers. The claims by the Ukrainian forces about the battle have not been independently verified by CBS News.
Russian authorities have acknowledged the operation, referring to a Ukrainian raid.
The Khartiia Corps has not confirmed any Ukrainian casualties, but at least one report on the battle, by Britain's Telegraph newspaper, mentioned Ukrainian forces recovering the body of a fallen comrade from inside an underground gas pipeline.
The pipeline offered a way for Ukrainian forces to conceal their movements in one of the most heavily monitored sectors of the nearly 1,000-mile front line that stretches from the far north to the far south of eastern Ukraine.
Both sides have sought to exploit underground infrastructure to evade increasingly sophisticated aerial surveillance in a conflict shaped by drone warfare. In September 2025, Russian forces similarly attempted to use sections of underground pipeline to move troops closer to Ukrainian positions around the northern outskirts of Kupiansk without being detected by drones.
Military analysts say operations like the underground pipeline assault highlight how the widespread use of drones in Russia's ongoing full-scale invasion, and Ukraine's defense, have transformed modern warfare. Both sides rely heavily on surveillance and attack drones to find and strike troops and hardware moving in the open.
As a result, even short movements above ground can expose soldiers to near real-time observation and attack.
While underground operations present their own dangers, including limited ventilation, restricted movement, navigational challenges and the risk of entrapment, soldiers involved in the Ukrainian mission suggested the hazards were outweighed by the dangers posed above ground, where they could have been spotted by Russian drones.
"It's damp, it's dark, it reeks. There are corpses lying around, but I felt safer there," one Khartiia Corps member, using the callsign "Sgt. Santa," was quoted as saying in a post by the unit.
The operation came ahead of what could prove a critical juncture in the war. President Trump, who campaigned on ending the war quickly, has pushed hard for Ukraine and Russia to agree to a peace deal. Kyiv and its European allies fear, however, that the White House appears to be — including the prospect of major energy deals, with no significant concessions in return, while putting pressure on Ukraine to make major territorial concessions without any concrete security guarantees.
Ukraine says the operation in the gas pipeline helped stop Russian forces from gaining more ground near Kupiansk, a city that Ukrainian forces recaptured from Russia's invading troops in 2022.

title: David Beckham sues after his fragrance is sold in gas stations and discount stores
text:
David Beckham’s company is suing beauty group Coty for at least $41 million, alleging that sales of his perfumes in discount stores breached their licensing agreement and damaged his luxury brand
LONDON -- A dispute over the sale of David Beckham perfumes has struck a sour note with the soccer star turned style icon.
Beckham’s commercial company is suing a beauty firm after his “luxury” fragrances were allegedly found for sale in discount stores and a gas station bargain bin.
DB Ventures has filed a claim in the New York Supreme Court against German beauty group Coty, which makes and distributes a range of Beckham-branded fragrances and toiletries. They include the Classic and Instinct lines and the eaux de toilette Intimately and Exquisite Leather.
The claim argues that Beckham’s “world-renowned global brand is synonymous with excellence and refinement,” and “David Beckham products are a symbol of everyday luxury.”
“Imagine, then, the shock and dismay experienced when DB Ventures discovered that David Beckham products were being offered for sale in a gas station,” the legal document says. “How could this possibly have happened? Desperation and greed.”
Lawyers for DB Ventures allege that Beckham-branded products “ended up in the bargain bin inside a gas station” and at British budget retailer Poundland, “allowing the product to be sold for dollar store prices and associating the David Beckham brand with cheap, discount products.”
DB Ventures is seeking at least $41 million in damages for breach of its licensing agreement.
Coty has asked a judge to dismiss the lawsuit, which was filed in April. The company argues that New York courts have no jurisdiction in the case, and says DB Ventures is using the claim to “manufacture its early exit” from its licensing deal and hand over the Beckham contracts to another firm, Interparfums.
Coty and DB Ventures did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Tuesday.
Beckham, the former soccer star for Manchester United and Real Madrid and captain of the England men’s national team, parlayed success on the pitch into a lucrative business career that includes co-ownership of soccer team Inter Miami. He was knighted last year by King Charles III, becoming Sir David.
He also has had a very public persona as a fashion model, “Bend it Like Beckham” movie muse and is husband to Spice Girl-turned-fashion designer Victoria “Posh Spice” Beckham. The couple have four children.
The Sunday Times Rich list earlier this year estimated the Beckhams' wealth at almost 1.2 billion pounds ($1.58 billion).

title: NASA's Voyager 1 reaches a light-day away from Earth
text:
Hate long-haul flights? Well, imagine having to travel 3,300 years to get to your destination.
Imagine departing in 1977 and arriving in 2026, on November 18 at 11:16 a.m. Central European Time to be precise, and then, not stopping but continuing the journey.
NASA's Voyager 1, a spacecraft launched almost half-a-century ago, has traveled a light-day from Earth.
A light-day is the distance light covers in 24 hours — about 26 billion kilometers (or around 16 billion miles). Put another way: Light does in one day what it took the spacecraft 49 years, two months and 11 days to do.
But Voyager 1 is not only far away, it is also traveling at an incredible speed of 61,000 km/h (38,000 mph).
When Voyager 1 launched, it was in sync with a planetary alignment that was as rare as the spacecraft itself — one that happens only once every 176 years. It was the alignment Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, which scientists wanted to investigate.
Once the original mission was accomplished, Voyager 1 used the planets Jupiter and Saturn to perform a gravitational slingshot.
It flew close to each planet, got pulled and accelerated by their massive gravity, and swung around faster than before. And that is how Voyager 1 has achieved its speed.
How did Voyager 1 get so far and where is it going?
In the vacuum of space, nothing slows you down.
On Valentine's Day 1990, from beyond Neptune, Voyager 1 took the only portrait of the solar system from the outside ever made by a spacecraft.
In 2012, it became the first human-made object to reach interstellar space.
Its journey is ongoing. In about 40,000 years — long after its plutonium power supply dies out — it will still be flying and pass by the star Gliese 445, which is more than 17 light-years away from Earth.
That's light-years, not light-days. A light-year is the distance light travels in a year. It will take Voyager 1 about 18,000 years to reach the one light-year milestone.
Voyager 1 is destined to wander the Milky Way "perhaps eternally," as NASA puts it.
Voyager 1 is an ongoing scientific experiment
The spacecraft is the first human-made object ever to be one light-day away from home.
"If you want to say 'hello' to Voyager, you send your message and then you go home and you wait two days before you finally get a response," says Suzanne Dodd, the mission's project manager at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.
But you do get a response. Even today it sends back data that helps scientists on Earth.
"[It's] still working great, sending back data from a region of space no other human-made craft has ever explored," says Kareem Badaruddin, the mission manager at JPL.
Something you didn't already know about Voyager 1
No story about Voyager 1 seems complete without mentioning The Golden Record, a phonographic record, that is part of the spacecraft's cargo.
The spacecraft is carrying other Earthly objects as messages and artefacts from Earth for extraterrestrials. But the Golden Record is what we tend to focus on because it contains soundbites representing languages and cultures from around our planet.
We're told it's very unlikely that any intelligent lifeform will ever receive the cargo or even know how to play The Golden Record.
But if they do get the record and work out how to play it, the first thing they will hear is a controversial voice — not one of Earthly unity, as was the original idea. Those are the words of Kurt Waldheim, a former UN Secretary-General (1972-81) and Austrian President (1986-92), whose concealed wartime past as a German army officer in the Balkans surfaced a decade after Voyager 1's launch. It was alleged Waldheim had participated in Nazi crimes.

title: US strikes Iran again despite Trump’s promise to end war after midterms humiliation
text:
The US has carried out further strikes on Iran despite Donald Trump’s claim that the war is “effectively over” following his humiliating defeat in the midterm elections.
An official told Reuters that a fighter aircraft targeted a missile launch site on Qeshm Island in retaliation for Iran’s targeting of US personnel and assets.
Just last week, the US president declared the conflict “effectively over” and played down concerns that he would escalate after the elections.
Mr Trump had signalled Washington would hold off on ordering fresh strikes on Iran, provided there were no new attacks from Tehran or Yemen’s Houthi rebels.
“At this point, taking the military action doesn’t seem to be a very necessary thing – but we’re locked and loaded, ready to go for any reason,” he told reporters at the White House.
Washington carried out limited strikes on Qeshm earlier this month.
Asked for comment, the US military’s Central Command said it had no updates.
Diplomatic efforts to end the war and open the Strait of Hormuz have been at a standstill despite the efforts of mediators from Pakistan and Qatar.
But Qatari and Iranian officials were meeting on Tuesday, Qatar said, as part of efforts to mediate an end to the nearly nine months of war that have destabilised the Middle East and pushed up global energy prices.
On Sunday Tehran launched drone attacks on a US military base in Bahrain, following a similar strike on Friday.
Earlier this week, the US deployed a third aircraft carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, to the Middle East, signalling a potential resumption of hostilities.
The American midterm election results proved devastating for the Republican Party, as voters expressed anger over soaring prices sparked by the unpopular conflict, which was prompted by joint US and Israeli airstrikes on Iran on 28 February.
The US president said officials were taking seriously the possibility that Iran could be planning an attack involving a so-called dirty bomb in Washington, after being asked about a CNN report citing US intelligence assessments.
Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson said the report was part of a US campaign “to lay the media groundwork for their sinister designs” using “baseless allegations”.
Mr Trump has also said he will maintain a US naval blockade on Iran because it has continued to disrupt shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, which is a sticking point in negotiations.
Attacks on tankers have increased this month in the strait, and the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said the crew of a tanker passing through the waterway was unaccounted for after being attacked north of the Omani port city of Khasab.

title: Trump warns Iran over allegations of dirty bomb threat to Washington
text:
Iran denied media reports based on US intelligence that it may be planning a dirty bomb attack in the US capital, with questions swirling about its actual intentions or real capabilities for such an act, but Trump issued a strong warning against Tehran "because they happen to be crazy."
US president Donald Trump issued a stern warning to Iran on Tuesday about the possibility that Tehran could be planning an attack involving a so-called dirty bomb or a chemical weapon in Washington DC, as reported by US broadcaster CNN citing what it called "sources familiar with the latest intelligence."
When asked whether the threat was imminent, Trump told reporters in Manila that "well, if there is, they will pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before."
Asked again whether there was reason to believe an attack was imminent, the US president replied that "I hope it's not, but we take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy," adding that "we are looking into it."
While Iran continues its fiery rethoric threatening with devastating consequences if attacked again, CNN reported that new US intelligence indicated that Tehran was developing plans to potentially detonate a dirty bomb or a chemical weapon in the US capital. However, according to the report, US officials were still divided over whether Iran has the capability to carry out such a plan or would actually move to execute it, and that officials were divided over the credibility of the intelligence.
The CNN report said that, according to its sources, the plans the United States has learned about were very specific and included locations and targets, prompting contingency planning, but CNN quoted one source as saying that "there is disagreement over whether they actually have the personnel in place to execute the plan." According to CNN's sources, Iran's capability to launch this kind of an attack has not grown, but what has changed is the Iranian incentive and that there was no evidence that Iran decided to move forward with its plans.
A dirty bomb is a weapon made of conventional explosives packaged with radioactive material that contaminates the environment through a non-nuclear explosion, affecting several city blocks or several kilometres.
White House spokesperson Lauren Bis downplayed the concerns by issuing a statement saying that the United States is "monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland,” while US Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin told the US media that the dirty bomb threat "is not new".
The report was published the day after Israel's Mossad chief Roman Gofman returned from Washington where he reportedly met senior US officials, including CIA Director John Ratcliffe, to share Israel's latest intelligence on Iran. Israel's prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu has been insisting that the US and Israel must continue the military campaign against the Iranian regime.
According to multiple US media reports, senior members of the US administration have reportedly been moved over time to military compounds or protected government residences due to potential security threats.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi dismissed the allegations as "rubbish", stating in a post on X to “spare us the Iraq War-style propaganda, especially with Israeli fingerprints all over it, nobody is buying it.”
Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei called the allegations "baseless".
In a statement on X, Baghaei said that the dirty bomb plans allegations stem from a media narrative "designed to justify attacks on Iran's vital infrastructure."
The Iranian diplomat said that Tehran "considers the use of chemical weapons under any circumstances to be completely illegitimate and firmly rejects and explicitly denies the false and fabricated allegations made in this regard."
He warned that "Iran knows very well how to respond to any act of aggression and assures that this response will not be forgotten."
Tehran has been threatening the United States and Israel as well as any country supporting new military actions against Iran with a fiery response, including on their home territories.
These mounting threats come as the United States and Iran remain locked in an ongoing confrontation in the Strait of Hormuz with both sides increasing pressure to force concessions for most favourable terms in case of a peace deal.

title: 7 smart reasons to sell a stock—and my ‘golden rule’ for offloading shares, says hedge fund CEO
text:
Nobody is born knowing anything innately about the stock market. And if you feel like you've missed the investing class, you didn't. Usually there isn't one.
So responsible people who are trying to do the responsible thing by building a portfolio for themselves and their families often find huge gaps in their knowledge and don't know where to turn.
As the co-founder and CEO of the hedge fund Metropolitan Capital Advisors and a longtime panelist on CNBC's Fast Money, I know that there's no shortage of advice when you're getting started about great investments to buy. It can feel easy and gratifying, especially when your portfolio is doing well. But then things get tougher.
One of the hardest things to do as an investor is to figure out when to sell. You buy a stock because you believe it will go up in value. But the decision to sell is rarely so straightforward. Personally, I've made just about every selling mistake. But over time, I've developed a framework for knowing when to sell — and when not to.
Selling decisions are often rooted in emotion and cognitive bias rather than logic. One major culprit: anchoring to past performance, a flawed reference point that clouds clear thinking.
Behavioral economics, particularly prospect theory, shows that we experience the pain of a loss more intensely than the joy of a gain. This leads investors to cling to losers ("just need to get back to even") and sell winners too early ("lock in the gain").
We also place too much emphasis on recent events, a phenomenon known as recency bias. If your last tech stock soared, you're more likely to chase another. If your last trade flopped, you may avoid the market altogether. And when recent trades go well, people tend to trade more — often to their detriment.
Finally, selling triggers a storm of second-guessing and rationalization. Here are my responses to common excuses:
- "What if I'm wrong and it goes up?" What if you're right and it keeps going down?
- "What will I do with the cash?" You don't always need to put it to work right away, or you can buy a little more of what you already own.
- "If I double down and it rebounds, I'll make it all back." But if it continues to go down from here, your losses will double.
- "I don't like having a loss, so I'll sell once it gets back to even." What you originally paid is irrelevant. Yet for many investors, it becomes the most important factor in their decision-making. To assuage their fragile egos, they risk even bigger losses.
These biases and emotional landmines are why you need a clear, disciplined plan for when to sell, including when:
- The original thesis no longer holds. If the fundamental reasons you bought the stock are no longer true — if earnings slow, revenue shrinks, margins deteriorate or the company loses market share — it may be time to move on.
- There's a regulatory risk. Legislative changes can dramatically shift a company's prospects. For example, the outlook for solar-related companies can decline dramatically when tax credits are cut for installations.
- Management loses credibility. Frequent earnings misses or misleading guidance suggest deeper problems. One-off surprises happen; recurring surprises reflect poor leadership.
- It becomes too big a slice of your portfolio. A stock that grows from 10% to 25% of your portfolio due to the superb performance of its underlying business, which fuels a soaring stock price, increases your risk from a diversification standpoint. Rebalancing is smart and necessary. The maximum I would have in any one position in my own portfolio is 20% — and that's probably too much!
- The stock becomes overvalued. Sometimes the hype drives prices beyond what fundamentals justify. If valuation detaches from reality, it's okay to take some profits. If it really goes nuts, I will sell enough to take my original investment off the table.
- You need the money elsewhere. Selling to fund a home, college tuition or retirement is perfectly valid. Opportunity cost matters.
- You have tax reasons. For example, tax-loss harvesting may allow you to offset capital gains or deduct up to $3,000 of losses against ordinary income.
When you've decided to sell for a solid reason — especially the first, second, or third outlined above — don't hesitate. Don't wait for the perfect price. Just sell.
Just as important as knowing when to sell is knowing when not to sell. Avoid emotionally driven decisions that sabotage long-term gains.
- Don't sell just because it went up. Great companies like Costco, Apple and Microsoft have rewarded patience for decades. Selling too early can mean missing out on compounding returns.
- Don't sell just because it went down. Market pullbacks are often temporary. If the fundamentals are intact and the decline is market driven, it may be a buying opportunity rather than a reason to exit. Trying to time the market rarely ends well.
- Don't sell because of scary headlines. Economic fears are often priced in before they fully materialize. The market is, forward-looking; headlines usually aren't. Selling during fear often means missing the rebound.
Selling well is an advanced investing skill that demands discipline, logic and self-awareness, and there's no place for ego. If you create a sound game plan, you'll be equipped to act confidently, even in the face of uncertainty. I keep a list of reasons to sell handy so I can literally look at it and keep my wits about me.
Karen Finerman is co-founder and CEO of the New York-based hedge fund Metropolitan Capital Advisors and a longtime panelist on CNBC's Fast Money. She is the author of the New York Times bestselling book, "Finerman's Rules: Secrets I'd Only Tell My Daughters About Business and Life" and the host of the podcast How She Does It. Karen is a proud member of the Wharton Board of Advisors, her alma mater, and serves on the board of The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson's Research.
