title: An ancient virus may help explain what makes the human brain different
text:
A virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago may have helped shape one of the most important differences between humans and our closest relatives: how our brains develop. Scientists at Lund University discovered that ancient viral DNA embedded in the chimpanzee genome switches off a gene called LINC00662, which remains active in humans and appears to play an important role in early brain development.
A virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago has left behind a genetic legacy that may help explain an important difference between human and chimpanzee brain development. Researchers at Lund University have discovered that ancient viral DNA embedded in the chimpanzee genome switches off a gene that remains active in humans and appears to play an important role in the developing brain.
The findings, published in Science Advances, reveal how infections from the distant past can leave lasting changes in the genetic makeup of an entire population. They also offer new clues about how the brains of humans and our closest evolutionary relatives may have developed differently.
Although pandemics are often considered a modern threat, infectious diseases have been spreading through large animal and human populations for millions of years. Some of these ancient infections left traces of viral DNA that continue to influence how genes function today.
Johan Jakobsson, Professor of Molecular Neurogenetics at Lund University, says the discovery demonstrates how a virus can introduce genetic changes that eventually become widespread throughout a population.
"The virus we investigated specifically affected chimpanzees. Yet humans and chimpanzees have largely the same genetic makeup. That is why it is important to understand the differences in how genes are regulated. Our findings suggest that one gene, LINC00662, plays a significant role in early human brain development," says Johan Jakobsson.
How an Ancient Virus Silenced a Brain Development Gene
At the center of the discovery is a gene called LINC00662. Researchers found that it is active during early human brain development but completely switched off in comparable chimpanzee brain models.
The difference appears to be caused by a genetic remnant of PTERV1, an ancient virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago. PTERV1 belongs to a group known as endogenous retroviruses, which are viruses whose genetic material became incorporated into the DNA of their hosts. Once embedded in the genome, these viral sequences can be inherited by future generations.
Over time, PTERV1 produced numerous copies of its genetic material that became scattered across different parts of the chimpanzee genome. Researchers found that these viral sequences are systematically silenced through a process called methylation.
Methylation involves chemical modifications to DNA that help regulate gene activity. It is one of the ways cells control which genetic instructions are used and which remain inactive. In this case, the ancient viral insertion appears to have caused a neighboring gene involved in brain development to be switched off.
Jakobsson says understanding these differences in gene regulation could also provide important insights into how genetic activity protects the brain or contributes to damage and disease.
Miniature Brains Reveal a Striking Genetic Difference
To investigate the virus's effects, researchers grew miniature brain models called organoids using stem cells from humans and chimpanzees. These three-dimensional structures reproduce certain features of developing brain tissue, allowing scientists to study aspects of early brain development under controlled laboratory conditions.
When the team compared the two types of organoids, the difference was striking. LINC00662 showed strong activity in the human brain models but was completely inactive in those derived from chimpanzee cells.
"The gene was strongly expressed in the human organoids, but not at all in the chimpanzee organoids," says Patricia Gerdes, postdoc in molecular neurogenetics at Lund University.
The researchers then set out to determine whether the ancient viral DNA was directly responsible for this difference.
Using CRISPR-Cas9, a powerful gene editing technology that allows scientists to make targeted changes to DNA, they removed the viral sequence from chimpanzee cells.
The result provided compelling evidence. Once the viral DNA was removed, the previously inactive LINC00662 gene switched back on.
"This shows that it is in fact the viral insertion that is responsible for the gene being switched off in chimpanzees," says Patricia Gerdes.
New Clues to Human Brain Evolution
The team also wanted to understand what LINC00662 actually does in the human brain. To investigate, they used CRISPR to switch off the gene in human brain organoids and examined how other genes responded.
Disabling LINC00662 reduced the activity of genes associated with nerve cell development and the formation of connections between neurons. These processes are essential for establishing the networks that allow the brain to communicate and function.
The results suggest that LINC00662 contributes to important stages of early human brain development, while the ancient viral insertion prevents the gene from functioning in chimpanzees.
More broadly, the discovery highlights an important principle of evolution. Although humans and chimpanzees share much of their genetic material, differences in how genes are switched on and off can influence how their bodies and brains develop.
The findings suggest that ancient viral infections may have contributed to these differences by altering gene regulation long after the original infections disappeared.
Researchers now plan to investigate whether other remnants of ancient viruses have similarly influenced brain evolution. They also hope to determine whether these inherited viral sequences may play a role in neurological diseases.
Together, the discoveries raise an intriguing possibility that some of the differences between human and chimpanzee brains may trace back, at least in part, to viruses that infected our evolutionary relatives millions of years ago.

title: ‘Avengers Endgame: Encore’ is now streaming on Disney+, with 4 minutes of bonus footage and a special ‘Doomsday’ preview
text:
Disney and Marvel Studios have a lot riding on "Avengers: Doomsday," and they’re pulling out all the stops to make sure audiences are well-prepared to experience the alt-universe battle royale when it drops on December 18.
After a successful limited theater run earlier this fall, Marvel Studios just dropped "Avengers: Endgame Encore" onto Disney+. So, if you missed this beefed-up extended rerelease in theaters, you can still experience all the extra content that ties directly into the upcoming "Avengers: Doomsday."
"Endgame's" recent theatrical return came on Sept. 25, 2026, earned $86 million, and included four bonus scenes totaling roughly four minutes and a special "Doomsday" preview. The rerelease also took it back to the pinnacle of the all-time box office peak by passing "Avatar."
The $356 million sequel to 2018's "Avengers: Infinity War" closed out The Infinity Saga, and the two-part spectacle became widely known as the high-water mark of the Marvel Cinematic Universe.
"Avengers: Endgame Encore" will also be included in Disney+'s signature "Countdown to Avengers: Doomsday" collection, a curated roundup of former Marvel shows and movies to study up on. If you haven't been keeping up with the MCU, you've got plenty of homework to do ahead of "Avengers: Doomsday."
With its charismatic cast of dozens and the triumphant MCU return of Robert Downey Jr., this time portraying the metal-masked Victor Von Doom, expectations are sky-high that this might reignite the glory days and usher in a brave new world for bored superhero-loving cinephiles.
"Avengers: Endgame Encore" is now on Disney+.

title: Speed camera fault may have allowed drivers to escape fines
text:
Further problems with the accuracy of speed cameras on English roads have been uncovered which may have allowed drivers to slip through the cracks and escape fines.
National Highways discovered issues with speed cameras last year, affecting 154 out of 400 cameras but, following an investigation, said it had found another fault on units monitoring roads including those running between Huntingdon and Cambridge.
The Home Office has revoked approval that allows footage from the cameras to be used as evidence in legal proceedings. US firm Verra Mobility operates the cameras but National Highways said it will now end the contract.
Roads minister Justin Madders said: "We can't take chances with this.
"If we're going to prosecute people, we need to be confident the system is working as it should. That's why we've taken the action we have."
In a statement, Verra Mobility said it "remains fully committed to delivering reliable, innovative technology that helps make roads safer".
The fault affected all of the variable speed cameras on smart motorways, and a section of the A14 between Huntingdon and Cambridge as well as the A1 approach junction to the A14.
A spokesperson for National Highways said that Verra's camera system had been selected on the basis that it maintained Home Office approval.
The agency said that since that was no longer the case "we are ending our contractual relationship to use the cameras for enforcement".
It added: "We are considering all further commercial and legal options that may be appropriate."
The BBC has contacted Verra Mobility for comment.
Madders said that the enforcement of speed limits continues to be conducted through a range of different tactics, including mobile cameras as well as marked and unmarked police patrols.
But he admitted that the camera system will not be fully fixed until sometime next year.
Rod Dennis, senior policy officer at the RAC motoring organisation, said: "Malfunctioning speed cameras on smart motorways do more than just let speeding drivers get away with breaking the law and endangering lives – they further undermine confidence in the very types of road we know drivers already have serious misgivings about."
There are 4,000 cameras across the entire road network.
In December 2025, National Highways, which runs England's motorways, blamed an "anomaly" in how variable speed cameras were interacting with speed limit signs on some A roads and motorways.
For example, on a road where the speed limit increases, a driver may see a sign showing 60mph but the camera recording it may still be working on the basis of a previous 40mph speed limit.
The fault led to 2,650 wrongful speed camera activations between 2021 and the end of last year.
Those who had been wrongfully fined have been reimbursed.
As National Highways continued to test the system, it discovered a further problem "relating to how some of these cameras may activate in specific and rare circumstances".
It said that according to its calculations, "the circumstances in which the latest issue could occur are extremely rare, and there is no evidence to suggest it has impacted enforcement".
Nevertheless, it said it was "taking immediate steps to ensure compliance is maintained at relevant locations".
It said it would put further traffic officer patrols in place to monitor the sites.

title: Starwatch: Fleeting brilliance of Leonid meteor shower to hit peak
text:
The annual Leonid meteor shower reaches its peak this week, offering a chance to count meteors. The shower is expected to be at its most active during the night of 17–18 November. Under ideal conditions, observers may see up to 10–15 meteors an hour.
What they lack in numbers, they make up for in brilliance.
The Leonids are produced by dust shed by comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which orbits the Sun every 33 years. As Earth passes through this debris stream, the particles strike our atmosphere at about 71 km/s, making them among the fastest meteors of any annual shower. As a result, they often leave bright, fleeting streaks across the sky.
The meteors appear to radiate from the constellation of Leo, the lion, which rises in the east after midnight. The chart shows the view looking east from London at midnight on 17–18 November.
Conditions will improve towards dawn as Leo climbs higher in the sky. As an added reward for your efforts, Mars and Jupiter will form a beautiful pair just in front of Leo’s chest.
From the southern hemisphere, Leo remains relatively low in the northern sky, making the hours before dawn the best time to look for meteors.

title: New rule aims to close loophole on chip exports
text:
The Commerce Department released a new rule designed to make it harder for China to gain access to America's most powerful computer chips using third-country data centers.
SCOTT DETROW, HOST:
The Trump administration is taking new steps to prevent China from gaining access to America's most powerful computer chips. The move comes after criticism that existing export controls are too lax. The rules have been under a microscope since the CEO of chipmaker Nvidia stepped down last week. Jensen Huang is accused of having an affair with a woman who is suspected of being a Chinese spy. NPR's Scott Horsley joins us now. Hi, Scott.
SCOTT HORSLEY, BYLINE: Hi. Good to being with you.
DETROW: So the Commerce Department announced a new rule governing computer chip exports today. How exactly does it change the landscape?
HORSLEY: The federal government already prohibits the sale of the most advanced AI chips to China, a country it sees as both an economic and security rival. But critics say there's a loophole in that ban because those chips can be sold to data centers in places like Malaysia, and China can then get the benefit of that advanced computing power by tapping into those data centers remotely. It's a little like someone who lives where gambling is illegal going online to access a gambling website where it's legal.
This new rule is designed to close that loophole by requiring data centers in third countries to police the people they're working for, and if they're doing business with, say, China, for example, they would be subject to additional restrictions. The rule also limits chip sales to countries like Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand, which are seen as at high risk of having those chips diverted to China.
DETROW: Tie this back to Nvidia for us.
HORSLEY: Well, news reports have tied that company's former CEO to a woman suspected of spying for China. China has denied that, and NPR has not independently confirmed those reports. But what's clear is the woman used to work for a company called Megaspeed, which was a customer of Nvidia's and bought a lot of its advanced chips for its operating data centers in Malaysia. Now, Megaspeed says the woman left the company over a year ago, and the company insists it follows all existing regulations. But some administration officials worry those regulations are just not strong enough and allowed China this workaround. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on CNBC last week he and others wanted to cut off Megaspeed's access to chips to prevent that computing power from being used remotely by China.
SCOTT BESSENT: Any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts our great companies, and the AI race gives the Chinese an advantage.
HORSLEY: So this new rule's designed to prevent that kind of leakage and stop China from gaining remote access to the most powerful chips. Interestingly, while the new rule was announced by the Commerce Department, it was actually written by and at the direction of the Treasury Department and the National Security Council.
DETROW: Interesting. What does this say about big picture - about what's happening behind the scenes?
HORSLEY: Yeah. There's been this kind of tug-of-war within the administration between the Commerce Department, which is basically in the business of promoting overseas sales, and other parts of the administration, like Treasury, which want to take a tougher line against China. The dust up at Nvidia has brought that behind the scenes friction right out in the open. President Trump said this morning that his two Cabinet secretaries on either side of that tug-of-war have very different views about the best way to deal with China.
PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: One view is you don't want to insult China. We have a very good relationship with China, and you don't want to insult them. And the other view is just go, you know, down and dirty and do what you have to do. Both - can't say either is wrong or right. We'll let you know.
HORSLEY: Both the Commerce secretary and the Treasury secretary are accompanying the president on his trip to Asia this week, so they should have plenty of time to air out those differences on Air Force One.
DETROW: That is NPR's Scott Horsley. Thank you so much.
HORSLEY: You're welcome.

title: Cruz announces deal on stalled airline safety bill
text:
GOP Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas announced the Republican-controlled House and Senate have reached an agreement in principle to require planes in crowded airspace to be equipped with technology that enables them to see other aircraft in their area and to transmit their location. Cruz said it would be landmark legislation for aviation safety.
The equipment, known as ADS-B In, shows nearby air traffic with visual and audible alerts, and has been recommended as a required safety feature by the National Transportation Safety Board since 2008, but the Federal Aviation Administration has not adopted it.
After an American Airlines passenger jet with an Army Black Hawk helicopter on approach at Ronald Reagan National Airport in January 2025, killing 67 people, Cruz and other members of Congress argued that ADS-B In could help keep aircraft safer.
Cruz made the announcement during a press conference on Tuesday in front of the Capitol with the families of the DCA plane crash victims, who have been advocating for the technology since the deadly collision.
"We still have a couple of details to negotiate with the House Armed Services Committee, but with this agreement in principle, I believe we're going to get this bill done," Sen. Cruz said. "And my objective is to get it done this year, with this Congress, before we leave for the new year."
Proponents of the technology argue it could have prevented the fatal DCA crash and alerted the American Airlines pilots to the approach of the , which was conducting a training mission in the plane's vicinity directly in the path of their flight.
In December 2025, the Senate passed the ROTOR Act, which would have mandated ADS-B In for all commercial and military flights in busy airspace. It passed the Senate unanimously but failed in the House by one vote, a devastating blow to the victims' families after the Pentagon withdrew its support for the bill because of the requirements it would impose on military aircraft.
Since then, the House passed its own legislation, called the ALERT Act. It would close the "military loophole," requiring military flight crews to broadcast their location during non-sensitive missions.
Cruz and Democratic Sen. Maria Cantwell of Washington opposed that legislation, arguing it lacks the critical improvements the aviation system needs.
"We must have strong military accountability in the national airspace. The military must be a willing partner with the Department of Transportation and the FAA to make sure that what happened that January never, ever happens again," Sen. Cruz said during Tuesday's press conference.

title: Jaguars are on the verge of the longest 30-point scoring streak in franchise history
text:
The last time the Jacksonville Jaguars put together a scoring streak like this, they advanced to the AFC title game
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The last time the Jacksonville Jaguars put together a scoring streak like this, they advanced to the AFC title game.
Nearly a decade later — and with eight games left in the regular season — they appear poised for another deep playoff run.
The Jaguars (7-2) tied a franchise record (set in 2017) by scoring 30 or more points for the fourth consecutive game in a 17-point victory at Tennessee. They can break the mark at the New York Giants (5-3-1) on Sunday.
“It is a fun group that each week you don’t really know who’s going to be the guy,” coach Liam Coen said. “And that’s what’s really fun about game-planning with this group and coming up with a plan throughout the course of the week because on any given Sunday, any one of these guys can step up.”
Trevor Lawrence has been the key, though. He has 1,110 yards passing, with 11 touchdowns and two interceptions, over the four-game scoring spurt. He finished with a season-high 352 yards passing against the Titans, his most in two years in Coen’s system.
“We’re on the same page and, obviously, the more you see things, the more you rep things, the more comfortable you get," Lawrence said. “I think you’re seeing that come to life, not just for me, but our whole offense. … I think it’s that time of year where you win some of these games and you got to look at it for what it is.”
It has the makings of a special season, one rarely enjoyed in Jacksonville.
After all, this is the franchise that once played 58 consecutive games without scoring 30 points and tied a dubious NFL record.
Now, the Jaguars are seemingly scoring at will. They have topped 30 points six times in nine games this season. They have developed Parker Washington into a legit No. 1 receiver. They have second-year pro Bhayshul Tuten running like a seasoned vet. And they keep finding new ways to use two-way standout Travis Hunter.
And now they have two defenders — tackle Jordan Davis and safety Jessie Bates III — ready to add to the mix for the final two months of the regular season. Davis and Bates, both acquired at the trade deadline for a combined four future draft picks, were held out against the Titans to give them a bye week and avoid the potential of playing 18 consecutive games.
“Hopefully those guys can only come and add to an already talented, tough team as we get down a stretch that we’re trying to go on a run here,” Coen said.
Cam Little made four field goals for the second consecutive week, extending his streak to 14 in a row this season. He hit from 46, 48, 36 and 40 yards out against the Titans.
Jacksonville managed just one sack against Tennessee despite leading by at least a touchdown for most of the second half. Adding Davis could help a D-line that is tied for 23rd in the NFL with 17 sacks. Travon Walker leads the team with three, one more than Josh Hines-Allen.
Washington leads the NFL with 17.9 yards a catch. He has raised his average every year he’s been in the league: 8.3 (2023), 12.2 (2024), 14.6 (2025). And he continues to raise the expected value of his next contract.
Chris Rodriguez ran four times for 5 yards at Tennessee, averaging 1.3 yards a carry. It came on the heels of last week’s outing in which he ran 10 times for 19 yards and a touchdown.
Center Robert Hainsey (left knee) and defensive end Danny Striggow (concussion) left the game and did not return.
20,106 — Number of career passing yards for Lawrence, who joined Josh Allen, Cam Newton and Dak Prescott as the fourth QB in NFL history to amass 20,000 yards passing, 115 TD passes and 20 rushing scores in his first six seasons.
If the Jaguars beat the Giants, they will have won three road games in as many weeks for the first time since 2005.

title: What has changed in James Bond films over the decades
text:
After years of speculation, Amazon MGM Studios announced on Monday that Robert Pattinson would be taking on the role of James Bond following Daniel Craig's departure after five hit films in the spy series.
This year alone, Pattinson has starred in "The Odyssey," "The Drama" and "Primetime." He is also famous for his role as "Twilight" vampire Edward Cullen.
The upcoming Bond movie will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, an Oscar nominee known for movies such as the "Dune" trilogy and "Arrival."
Based on the spy novels by author Ian Fleming, the Bond franchise — about a British secret agent known for his charm and a fondness for martinis "shaken, not stirred" — is among the longest-running and highest-grossing in Hollywood history.
How it all started
The first film in the series, "Dr. No," premiered in London on October 5, 1962.
Playing the leading role, Agent 007, was an unknown actor: Sean Connery.
In the film, we are first introduced to his character as he sits in a casino across from an attractive woman who is about to gamble away her fortune. When she asks 007 his name, the camera pans to Bond lighting a cigarette. With a smoldering look in his eye, he utters the legendary words: "Bond, James Bond."
Shortly thereafter in the film, 007 receives an assignment to fly to Jamaica and investigate the murder of another M16 agent. He eventually tracks down a Chinese-German criminal scientist who is bent on destroying the US space program and achieving world domination.
In principle, this story is the basis of all of 25 James Bond films. Whether the villain is Dr. No, Blofeld, Goldfinger or Le Chiffre, they all aim for one thing: world domination. But to do so, they have to get past James Bond whose gunfire and wild chase scenes inevitably spoil their plans.
A machismo problem
Although many fan forums consider "Dr. No" to be one of the best Bond films, the movie would never be made in the same way today.
Firstly, one could write entire books about the omnipresent sexism and machismo that the character James Bond has displayed over the decades.
Certainly there would have to be a thick chapter dedicated to the women in his films, who are typically portrayed as naive, willingly flinging themselves into Bond's arms, seeking protection. Sometimes they are sophisticated female antagonists who lose control at the thought of hopping into bed with the secret agent.
Whether friend of foe, each film had at least one Bond girl — and often more: More than 60 love interests have appeared in the films. Their names, like "Honey" or "Pussy Galore" would never be acceptable today. In more recent decades, female roles in Bond films have changed — as has Bond himself.
In the last five films in which Daniel Craig has played Bond, he is seen as a man who is tough on the outside and soft on the inside — and who is not always lucky with women.
Aside from the portrayal of women on screen, there are also plenty of other details in "Dr. No" that haven't quite stood the test of time.
Questionable lifestyle choices
Another sign of the zeitgeist in the 1962 film is that everyone smokes, which is a no-no by today's Hollywood standards. Cigarettes are found everywhere in the old film, from the casino to the hotel bar — and even the bedroom.
Smoking was commonplace in the US in the 1970s, so naturally this came across on the silver screen. In the 1970s TV series "Space: 1999" people were even depicted smoking on the moon, but by the 2000s, smoking was largely banned in many parts of the world due to its health risks.
One can also note in "Dr. No" that few people are wearing seat belts. When Bond drives off in his sports car to visit a woman, he is followed and a chase scene ensues. Bond, notably, is not wearing a seat belt.
His pursuers eventually drive off a slope and die, of course — after all, they aren't wearing seat belts either and cars didn't have airbags at the time. The vehicle explodes, prompting 007 to say, "They were obviously in a hurry to get to their own funeral."
Why are all secretaries women?
In the older Bond films, all secretaries and receptionists are played by women, which in the 1960s, were considered standard female jobs.
Whether redheaded, blonde or brunette, secretaries are Bond's favorite targets for womanizing and they are all susceptible to his charms.
Throughout most Bond films, the agent has a romantic tension with Moneypenny, his boss's secretary, something which was not described in the original books.
In the 2012 film "Skyfall" Moneypenny is given a first name: Eve, and we finally learn her backstory. In this film, she is no longer a hopeless secretary in love, but a top-trained agent who accidentally shoots Bond and is reassigned to desk duty as punishment.
In any case, today Moneypenny's job title today would probably be "Office Manager" or "Executive Assistant" rather than "Secretary."
Inappropriate casting
In the film, Dr. No tells James Bond that he is the child of a British missionary and a Chinese woman from an upstanding family. However, the character is portrayed by Canadian actor Joseph Wiseman who is wearing makeup to make his eyes look more "Asian."
While it used to be the norm in such movies to have East Asian characters played by white actors, today these cases of "yellowface" are frowned upon — just as it would be to wear blackface, putting black makeup on one's skin to portray a Black person.
If there was a "Dr. No" remake in the future, a Chinese actor would be more likely to play this role.
Pattinson as a modern 007?
Daniel Craig already paved the way in modernizing James Bond by stripping away campy gadgets, punchlines and invincibility, replacing them with a grounded, psychological and emotionally vulnerable portrayal of a post-9/11 spy.
Now it is up to Robert Pattinson to revisit the famous MI6 agent. Film critics believe his background will allow him to add dark sophistication and nonconformism to the iconic espionage role.
Throughout his career, Robert Pattinson has managed to combine roles in blockbuster hits and indie gems, from Bruce Wayne in "The Batman" to a disposable worker who is cloned every time he dies in "Mickey 17."
Pattinson already has experience with classic spy archetypes: As the mysterious Neil in Christopher Nolan's sci-fi action thriller "Tenet," he assisted the protagonist in a time-bending espionage mission. He is also known for his eccentric personality and deadpan humor — qualities that could be useful for a modern Bond.
This article was translated from German by Sarah Hucal. It was first published in 2025 and updated following news of Robert Pattinson's casting as James Bond on November 16, 2026.

title: Hiding remotes and unplugging TVs: How Celebrity Race Across the World cut Jeff Stelling off from football
text:
Jeff Stelling has revealed that producers would unplug televisions and hide remotes during filming of Celebrity Race Across the World, which left the veteran sports broadcaster completely cut off from football and his beloved Hartlepool United.
Stelling is taking part in the latest series of the hit adventure travel show, teaming with his son Matt in a 4,660-mile race from the Malaysian city of Kuching to the finish line in Melbourne, Australia on a budget of £26 a day.
The former Soccer Saturday presenter, who ended over 30 years of service with Sky Sports in May 2023, is a passionate lifelong Hartlepool fan and serves as honorary president of the National League club.
But as he traversed the depths of South East Asia with no phone and limited technology, he was left completely in the dark about the club’s performance at the tail-end of the 2025/26 season.
“We couldn’t get any football scores at all because we’ve got no way [of finding them out],” Stelling told The Independent.
“If you’re within your checkpoints, if there’s a TV in your room, they [the producers] make sure it’s either disconnected or else they don’t give you a remote, so they make sure that that’s taken away. You’ve got no contact.”
The fourth series of the show, which aired its first episode on Wednesday, was filmed from February to April earlier this year.
During that time, Hartlepool experienced a mixed bag of results - going on their joint-best win streak of the season with three consecutive victories, only for that run to be ended by their heaviest defeat of the season: a 7-0 hammering at Wealdstone at the end of March.
Stelling says he was out of the loop for all of this, however, which allowed him to let his dreams run wild as the National League season approached its climax.
“For me, it meant I could fantasise that we were winning every game,” he added. “And then when we finished, I found out the truth that we hadn’t been winning every game.”
Stelling was speaking on behalf of Enterprise as he fronts the ‘Local Legends’ campaign, which strives to celebrate the unsung heroes that give their time for non-league clubs week in, week out.
Hartlepool, who have spent six of the last eight seasons in non-league, ended last season in ninth, 12 points adrift of the National League play-off places.
His agony without any knowledge of the Pools’ performance was not a shared experience with his youngest son, though, with Matt a Brighton supporter.
“Well obviously, my relationship with this son’s a bit stressed because he’s a Brighton fan!” Stelling joked, whose older son meanwhile follows his father’s lead in supporting Hartlepool.
“No, we’ve always gotten on really well,” he continued, “but it’s sort of challenging for both of us, but probably more for him, that you are going to spend six weeks, 24 hours a day, with your dad - often sharing a bed or sharing the same floor.
“Different generations have got different views of things, so inevitably, over that period of time, in the sort of intense situation that you’re in, there are inevitably going to be occasions when you’ve got to bite your tongue, on both sides.
“But it was brilliant. As I say, we were close before. We’re probably even closer afterwards.”
Jeff Stelling has launched Enterprise’s search for the National League’s Local Legends - celebrating those who turn up for their club and community week in, week out. Click here to nominate.

title: ‘Change is possible’: Danish offshore wind giant wins Earthshot Prize after quitting oil and gas
text:
Inspired by John F. Kennedy’s Moonshot, which united millions around the goal of reaching the moon, Prince William’s Earthshot Prize is one of the world’s most prestigious environmental awards.
A people-powered movement to ban forever chemicals, a coal-powered company that pivoted to renewables and even an entire country are among this year’s Earthshot Prize winning solutions.
Crowning the five winners in Mumbai today (17 November), the UK’s Prince William hailed young innovators as “torchbearers of a global movement” as world leaders clash over climate action at COP31.
The British prince’s Royal Foundation charity launched the 10-year award programme in 2020, with the aim of finding new solutions and technologies to tackle the planet’s greatest environmental perils.
Each winner receives £1 million (€1.2 million) as well as the backing of businesses and funders to help grow their solutions further and faster.
There are five ‘Earthshots’ - or goals: Protect and Restore Nature; Clean Our Air; Revive Our Oceans; Build a Waste-free World; and Fix Our Climate.
The winners were chosen from 15 finalists at the sixth Earthshot Prize awards ceremony.
Who are the Earthshot Prize 2026 winners?
The Prize’s biggest awards night yet in Mumbai was a celebration of optimism that saw the Prince and Princess of Wales joined by sports, Bollywood and film stars. Earthshot Ambassadors Robert Irwin, the Australian conservationist and TV presenter, and Nomzamo Mbatha, the South African actor and humanitarian, also took to the stage.
The winners were selected by Prince William as well as heavyweights from the climate world: Paris Agreement architect Christiana Figueres was on the panel alongside German climate activist Luisa Neubauer and Kenyan environmentalist Wanjira Mathai.
Along with £1 million (€1.2 million) prizes for each of the winners, all 15 Earthshot Prize finalists get the support of powerful investors, philanthropists and environmental organisations, helping them to access funding and expertise to accelerate their growth.
Fix Our Climate winner: Ørsted
Ørsted is a shining example of how quitting fossil fuels can lead to becoming a profitable company in Europe’s clean energy transition.
20 years ago the company was known as DONG Energy - one of Europe’s most coal-intensive utilities. Then it sold its oil and gas business and pioneered offshore wind, cutting its direct carbon emissions by more than 98 per cent. Since 1991, Ørsted has installed more than 11 gigawatts of offshore wind, enough to meet the needs of 22 million people, and has a further 7.2 GW under construction across three continents
Speaking about their transformation, Rasmus Errboe, Group President and CEO of Ørsted, said: “It surely hasn’t been easy, and we still have to work hard every day to deliver secure, affordable and clean energy - and provide even more jobs to our communities. But this is what the world needs, and I hope our work can serve as inspiration for others.”
Earlier this year Ørsted took on the Trump administration, mounting a legal challenge when it tried to suspend leases on all large US offshore wind projects. Shares in Ørsted rose by about 4 per cent when the news broke.
By 2030, Ørsted aims to build 8.1 GW of new offshore wind, including Hornsea 3 in the UK, which will be the world’s largest single offshore wind farm once it’s running. Together, these projects are expected to power around 17 million more homes and avoid more than 28 million tonnes of CO₂ every year.
By winning The Earthshot Prize, Ørsted aims to set a new standard for the industry and inspire other renewable energy developers to follow.
Build a Waste-Free World winner: PFAS-Free France
PFAS-Free France built a people-powered movement that led to France’s landmark 2025 law to phase out many uses of PFAS - toxic “forever chemicals” found in thousands of everyday products - and make polluters pay for the clean-up.
More than 140,000 French citizens supported PFAS-Free France’s campaign, showing how ordinary people can force industry to make better products, clean up our environment and protect the health of people for generations to come.
By 2030, PFAS-Free France aims to see France’s law fully put into practice and help to achieve similar bans in five other major countries or regions.
Winning The Earthshot Prize will support scientific research, public campaigns and international partnerships to speed up the adoption of stronger laws, protecting millions more people from these harmful chemicals.
Protect and Restore Nature winner: Bhutan
For the first-time ever, an entire country has won the Earthshot Prize.
Bhutan has taken the pioneering step of writing the protection of nature into its national constitution. Its forests protect Himalayan water systems that help sustain 1.6 billion people downstream across South Asia. A country of just 800,000 people is helping to protect the water security of nearly a fifth of humanity.
Winning The Earthshot Prize will help Bhutan reach its 2030 ambitions. Through Restore Bhutan, its national nature coalition, it aims to restore 50,000 hectares of damaged land, reviving forests and rivers, delivering nearly 2 million tonnes of CO₂ savings and securing 133 billion litres of water.
Clean Our Air winner: Mahindra Last Mile Mobility
Mahindra Last Mile Mobility is rapidly putting one of the world’s largest sources of on-road air pollution on the path to electric in India. With more than 400,000 of its electric rickshaws already sold, and by making electric vehicles affordable for the drivers who own and run them, Mahindra is powering one of the fastest and most consequential green transitions the planet has ever seen.
By 2030, it aims to put one million electric vehicles on India’s roads and make electric the first choice for short city journeys. Winning The Earthshot Prize will help speed up the rollout of electric rickshaws in major cities including Mumbai, Ahmedabad, Bengaluru and Delhi, tackling challenges around parking, charging points and policy to bring cleaner transport to India’s busiest urban centres.
Revive Our Oceans winner: Niue Ocean Wide Trust
The Pacific island nation of Niue has a population of just 1,700 people, yet its Ocean Wide Trust is protecting an area of ocean larger than the United Kingdom. Through a pioneering way of investing in conservation, Niue is funding the long-term protection of its waters, safeguarding marine life while supporting the communities that depend on it. The groundbreaking scheme has already helped boost fish numbers by 60 per cent.
Winning The Earthshot Prize will help Niue Ocean Wide Trust attract the investment and partners it needs to raise a further US$10 million (€9.09 million) by 2028. That will bring it closer to its US$18 million (€16.3 million) goal for a permanent fund to protect Niue’s ocean for generations to come. The Prize will also help Niue share its model with other Pacific island nations, with the aim of at least one more country adopting it by 2028.
What has happened to previous Earthshot Prize winners?
The 2026 finalists and winners join an existing community of 75 finalists supported since 2020, whose work has collectively avoided or captured more than 18 million tonnes of CO₂, protected or restored 58 million hectares of land and 85 million hectares of ocean and coastline, removed or avoided 465,000 tonnes of waste, saved 21 million tonnes of water and improved air quality in regions home to 600 million people.

title: State Department presses Egypt to respect religious freedom as Christian convert faces possible execution
text:
The State Department has intensified its efforts to compel the majority Muslim state of Egypt to honor the religious liberty protections for an Egyptian who converted to Christianity and is facing either the death penalty or a lengthy prison term.
The prosecution of Said Mansour Rezk Abdelrazek has catapulted his case and has attracted publicity within the U.S., Britain and across the global Christian community. Egypt receives $1.3 billion in annual funding from the U.S.
In July, Fox News Digital reported on Abdelrazek’s trial for his embrace of Christianity in 2016.
A State Department spokesperson told Fox News Digital that, "We are monitoring his trial closely. Religious freedom is a fundamental human value, and we encourage the Egyptian government to protect the religious freedom rights of all its citizens."
The situation for Abdelrazek has become dire, according to his attorney and human rights advocates for Coptic Christians in Egypt. He faces execution or a 25-year prison sentence for his conversion to Christianity, according to the office of his lawyer, Said Fayez.
Fayez’s office said that in early November the "Public Prosecution presented its closing arguments and requested that the maximum penalty prescribed by law be imposed upon him."
Fox News Digital reached out multiple times to Egypt’s Embassy in Washington, D.C., and its Foreign Ministry for a comment. According to Amnesty International, in "July 2025, security officers arrested Egyptian national and Christian convert Said Abdelrazek from his home in Cairo. After nine months of arbitrary pretrial detention, Said Abdelrazek was referred to trial before the Terrorism Circuit of the First Criminal Court in Badr on charges stemming from his conversion and religious beliefs."
Coptic Solidarity reported he faces charges that include contempt for Islam, and inciting unrest and spreading false information.
Abdelrazek’s fiancée Sophia, an Australian-Egyptian citizen, has been energetically campaigning to secure his freedom. She told Fox News Digital that she is "pleading for them to release him." She declined to use her last name because of "some extreme threats" against her.
Lindsay Rodriguez, a spokeswoman for Coptic Solidarity, told Fox News Digital that "Coptic Solidarity is deeply concerned that Egyptian prosecutors are seeking the maximum penalty against Said Abdelrazek, a Christian convert whose case has become an important test of religious freedom and judicial impartiality in Egypt."
She continued that he "has been detained since July 2025 and is being prosecuted before a terrorism court, primarily on an allegation of joining a banned terrorist organization, as well as charges of contempt for Islam, inciting unrest and spreading false information. These remain prosecution allegations, not findings of guilt. His defense will present its closing arguments on Dec. 8. Reported religious remarks attributed to the judge during the Nov. 3 hearing further heighten concerns about whether a Christian convert can receive a genuinely impartial hearing."
His supporters say the prosecution has yet to name the terrorist organization in question while noting there is no known terrorist group associated with Christians listed in Egypt.
Rodriguez added that "Peaceful religious conversion and expression must not be treated as terrorism or national-security offenses. The United States, European Union and Australia should use the Dec. 8 hearing as a clear test of Egypt's willingness to uphold basic religious-freedom and fair-trial standards."
Rodriguez said, "The U.S. Embassy in Cairo, EU Delegation and Member State embassies should seek access to monitor the hearing and raise Said's case directly with Egyptian authorities. Members of Congress and the European Parliament should publicly demonstrate that they are following the case. Australia also has a particular responsibility: Said's fiancée is an Australian citizen, and DFAT [Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade] should press his case while Home Affairs ensures a viable humanitarian pathway for reunification upon his release."
The Egyptian Christian community makes up an estimated 10% of the nation’s 120 million people.

title: U.S. agencies say they initiated investigation into Nvidia partner Megaspeed in 2024
text:
The U.S. Commerce and Justice Department on Monday stateside said they had initiated an investigation into Singapore-based company Megaspeed in 2024 to "address inaccurate information circulating in public reporting."
Megaspeed International, a cloud computing firm that operates data centers across Southeast Asia, has been drawn into the fallout surrounding the leadership shake-up at chip giant Nvidia.
In a joint release, the departments outlined a timeline of their investigations into Megaspeed, saying the probes began in 2024 over potential export-control violations.
In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its "no sell" list, after Commerce Department investigators requested records from Nvidia concerning direct or indirect sales to the company.
In the same month, U.S. officials and Singapore police conducted an in-person inspection of Megaspeed and interviewed Alice Huang, who was allegedly involved in a relationship with Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang.
"Following this enforcement action, the Department of Justice took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed," the statement said.
On Wednesday, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick also reposted the statement, adding, "The Department of Commerce works to protect the U.S. economy and our critical industries every day. We are very proud of the work of the Bureau of Industry and Security."
In response to the statement, Chris McGuire, senior fellow for China and emerging technologies at the Council of Foreign Relations wrote on X, "Very, very strange statement tonight... about Megaspeed. The facts here just don't add up, and this does nothing to explain why Commerce did not cut Megaspeed off from chips."
McGuire said that Megaspeed kept buying chips after Nvidia put them on their no-trade list, and asked if Nvidia also blacklisted Megaspeed's subsidaries Speedmatrix and PT Megaspeed International.
"I would bet they did not! If they kept shipping to them after blacklisting Megaspeed, that would be very concerning," McGuire added.
The statement comes after Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs said the first time authorities there learned of U.S. interest in Megaspeed and Alice Huang was in June. Singapore had already been conducting its own independent investigation and said she was not investigated for espionage.
The city-state barred Alice Huang from re-entering the country in February 2026 after authorities found that she had knowingly provided inaccurate information about her role at Megaspeed.
Alice Huang was reportedly recruited by China's Ministry of State Security to gather information on Jensen Huang. The Justice Department has not reached a conclusion on whether she was a Chinese spy.
Jensen Huang resigned as CEO last week after revelations about multiple extramarital relationships, including with two Nvidia employees. The tech giant has appointed Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO.
The agencies' statement also comes as Nvidia prepares to report its third-quarter results Tuesday afternoon U.S. time, with Kress set to lead her first earnings call.
Earlier on Monday in the U.S., the Commerce Department moved to close a loophole that has allowed Chinese companies to access Nvidia's advanced computing power through data centers in third countries.
The interim final rule from the department's Bureau of Industry and Security is aimed at restricting remote access to advanced U.S. computing technology.
It also comes amid growing scrutiny of Lutnick for not having done enough to prevent restricted Nvidia chips and computing capacity from reaching Chinese companies.
— CNBC's Anniek Bao and Dan Mangan contributed to this report.

title: NASA warns this year's Monster El Niño could be even bigger than legendary 1997 event
text:
NASA scientists warn that the rapidly intensifying 2026 El Niño could surpass the historic 1997-98 event, which triggered devastating weather extremes around the world. Satellite data reveal striking similarities between the two, raising the possibility of major rainfall and flooding this winter, although the exact impacts remain uncertain.
NASA scientists are tracking an exceptionally powerful El Niño that could grow even larger than the historic 1997 event, which brought extreme weather to regions around the world. Using 35 years of satellite observations, researchers can now compare the rapidly developing 2026 El Niño with some of the strongest events ever recorded, revealing remarkable similarities and important differences.
El Niño is a recurring climate phenomenon that typically develops every two to seven years, when ocean temperatures rise above normal across parts of the equatorial Pacific. These changes can disrupt atmospheric circulation and alter weather patterns far beyond the Pacific Ocean.
Two of the most powerful recent El Niño events occurred in 1997-98 and 2015-16. Both had widespread consequences, including destructive fires in Indonesia and the Amazon, severe drought and crop failures in southern Africa, and intense rainfall and coastal flooding in Southern California. Now, the 2026 El Niño is emerging as another major event, with satellite data suggesting it could rival those historic episodes.
How El Niño Builds Strength in the Pacific
The development of El Niño depends on a complex interaction between ocean temperatures and atmospheric winds.
Under normal conditions, steady trade winds push warm surface water toward the western Pacific Ocean. This causes warm water to accumulate in the west, where the ocean surface sits slightly higher than it does farther east.
When the trade winds weaken, some of that warm water begins moving eastward across the Pacific. The shift can weaken the winds even further or occasionally cause them to reverse direction. This allows additional warm water to spread east, reinforcing the process and raising ocean temperatures and sea levels across the central and eastern Pacific.
Although the underlying process is similar each time, no two El Niño events develop in exactly the same way. Their behavior depends partly on where the warmest water accumulates and how the atmosphere responds to the changing ocean conditions.
"The search for the 'typical' El Niño is very elusive," said Josh Willis, project scientist for sea level missions at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL). "They're all different in terms of where they land and how their impacts play out."
NASA Satellites Reveal Striking Similarities to 1997
To understand how the current El Niño compares with earlier events, scientists are examining decades of satellite measurements of ocean surface height.
This technique, called satellite altimetry, measures subtle changes in the elevation of the ocean surface. Because seawater expands as it becomes warmer, unusually high sea levels in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific can reveal where heat is accumulating during El Niño.
NASA's comparison maps show differences in Pacific Ocean surface height on October 13, 1997 (left), and October 12, 2026 (right). The earlier measurements were collected by the TOPEX/Poseidon satellite, while the newer observations came from the Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich satellite. Scientists at JPL processed both datasets to make the events easier to compare.
The maps use red to identify areas where the ocean surface is higher than its usual level, while white represents normal conditions and blue shows areas where sea levels are below average. To better isolate the effects of El Niño and other temporary natural changes, researchers removed variations associated with seasonal patterns and long-term trends.
One major advantage of these observations is their remarkable consistency. Successive satellite missions have followed nearly identical paths, with overlapping periods of operation that allow scientists to compare measurements across decades.
"What's unique about altimetry is that we have a 35-year record from nearly identical satellites flying almost the same ground track, with each mission overlapping the next," Willis said. "That lets us look back in time and compare this El Niño to what happened in 1997. And right now, this one is on track to be even bigger."
Why the 2026 El Niño Resembles a Historic Climate Giant
The 2026 El Niño intensified much more abruptly than the powerful 1997-98 event. Despite that difference in timing, NASA's satellite measurements from October reveal striking similarities in how the two events are developing.
In both cases, the Pacific displays a pronounced difference in sea level (low in the west and high in the east). The observations also show elevated, unusually warm water stretching eastward along the equator until it reaches the coast of South America.
These similarities suggest that the 2026 event could produce weather effects resembling those experienced during the 1997-98 El Niño. That earlier episode brought substantial rainfall to California and other parts of the southern United States, raising the possibility of comparable conditions during the coming winter.
However, the powerful 2015-16 El Niño demonstrates why similarities in overall strength do not necessarily translate into identical weather impacts.
For that comparison, NASA scientists also examined ocean surface height measurements from October 12, 2015, recorded by the Jason-2 satellite. The data were placed alongside observations from approximately the same time of year in 1997 and 2026.
Although the 2015 event also featured exceptionally warm water and elevated sea levels along the equator, that warm water did not extend toward the South American coast as strongly as it did during the other two events.
The resulting rainfall patterns were different as well. During the winter of 2015-16, much of the precipitation associated with El Niño was concentrated over Central America and the southeastern United States, while Mexico experienced significant flooding.
Will El Niño Bring Extreme Weather in Winter 2026-27?
The latest observations have prompted scientists to closely monitor how the 2026 El Niño develops and what it could mean for weather conditions in the months ahead.
In its October 8, 2026, outlook, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) estimated an 83 percent chance that strong to very strong El Niño conditions would occur during the first three months of 2027.
That forecast points to the potential for a particularly significant climate event, but it does not establish exactly where the most severe effects will occur.
El Niño can influence weather across much of the planet by changing the movement of heat and moisture through the atmosphere. However, those effects become increasingly difficult to predict farther from the tropical Pacific, where other atmospheric processes can alter or weaken the expected patterns.
As a result, even the strong resemblance between the 2026 and 1997 events cannot guarantee that the coming winter will unfold in the same way.
"There's always a bit of a dice roll here," Willis said. "Just because this El Niño looks like 1997 doesn't mean it will be exactly the same -- it's just our best guess at the moment."
The unprecedented consistency of the satellite record gives researchers a valuable way to recognize familiar patterns and evaluate the scale of the developing El Niño. But whether 2026-27 ultimately matches the extreme weather of previous historic events will depend on how the ocean and atmosphere interact in the months ahead.

title: A Magna Carta for the stars: King Charles III takes on space sustainability
text:
We live in the era of the satellite. They power our phones, banking infrastructure, navigational systems and internet, while providing stunning imagery and data that can be used to direct emergency services, feed weather forecasts and help coordinate military assets.
But low-Earth orbit is not an infinite resource. It's starting to get crowded, with over 16,000 satellites and over 1.2 million pieces of debris currently circling our planet at incredible speeds. And if not managed properly, the results could be catastrophic.
"In the early days of the space age actors could more or less ignore the other actors," Peter Martinez, executive director of the Secure World Foundation told Space.com. "You know the big sky paradigm, right? You can do what you want because the chances of your actions affecting others are minuscule."
As noted by Martinez, the modern orbital landscape is radically different from those early frontier days, especially since the mid 2010s and the advent of satellite megaconstellations. "Nowadays, we really do have to worry about orbital congestion, and because space is out of sight for most people, we don't."
Each new rocket launch leaves a footprint on the orbital environment, whether it be the satellite payloads they place in orbit or the pieces of inert hardware they leave behind such as an interstage adapter or rocket body. All of those objects create an ever-increasing risk of collisions.
In a worst case scenario, clouds of debris spawned by colliding spacecraft could create a cascading effect known as the Kessler syndrome, with the potential to render the orbital environment completely unusable, trapping us on Earth.
Enter King Charles III's Astra Carta, an all-encompassing roadmap to space exploration that launched on June 28, 2023 with a clear but ambitious mandate — to place sustainability at the core of humanity's presence beyond Earth.
What is the Astra Carta?
The Astra Carta stands as the space-focused sibling of the Terra Carta — a voluntary framework that launched in 2021 with the goal of safeguarding Earth's natural splendor by championing a transition to global sustainability practices and environmental responsibility.
Both names were chosen to draw comparison with the Magna Carta, a royal charter that served as an early foundation for the English Legal system and modern day democracies. The principles enshrined in the Astra Carta have the potential to be similarly transformative if taken to heart.
"I have long felt that protecting space that immediately surrounds our planet is one of those issues few recognize as important, but like so many of our present challenges, that were ignored for too long, if we do not address it quickly, it will come back to haunt us in a big way," the then-Prince of Wales stated in a message to participants of the 4th Summit for Space Sustainability in June 2022.
The framework was crafted by King Charles III's Sustainable Markets Initiative (SMI), which drew on the expertise of academics, heads of national space agencies and experts, such as Canadian astronaut and former International Space Station commander Chris Hadfield.
What does the Astra Carta say?
"It's like Stephen Hawking said, 'Stop looking at your shoes and look up'," Hadfield told Space.com. "It's really easy to spend a bunch of time on the news of the day, or the news of the week, or even the news of the month, you actually need something aspirational to be able to look up to some external measure of long-term success and goodness."
To Hadfield, the Astra Carta is an example of just that. It encourages humanity to embrace a global, peaceful outlook, which the astronaut believes will be vital to humanity's success as we venture deeper into space.
"If you view the moon as an eighth continent, which essentially it is, bigger than Africa, untapped, largely unsurveyed, whose laws are we going to follow as we begin to settle there?" continued Hadfield. "Or do we just transport kind of a silly imprint of our current geopolitics?"
The Astra Carta addresses a variety of interconnected challenges over its 33 pages and the 13 Articles of its "Zero Draft", which compliments and builds on the goals of existing treaties like the UN Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space, and the U.S. Artemis Accords.
Article 8 primarily focuses on orbital debris mitigation, and encourages the use of reusable launchers and responsible satellite disposal, investing in debris removal, and boosting public knowledge of the threat through education, among other measures.
But the Astra Carta's systemic approach reaches far beyond the threat posed by space debris. The remaining 12 articles highlight a latticework of forward thinking actions, ranging from the need for greater co-ordination between satellite operators to encouraging the development of novel propulsion and life support systems.It also calls for ethical guidelines on the use of AI in space, the establishing of key performance indicators for sustainability and legal frameworks for cybersecurity while advocating for treaties that prohibit the use of automated weapons in space, and so much more.
From paper to action
Each topic addressed in the Astra Carta looms large enough on its own. Taken together, they appear borderline insurmountable. But the convening power of King Charles III's SMI could prove to be a powerful factor in addressing them.
"What's interesting with the space economy is that the players within it are very fragmented, all over the world, and there isn't something that's sort of telling them what to do and how to behave in space," Sustainable Markets Initiative (SMI) CEO Jennifer Jordan-Saifi told Space.com. "And so there's definitely an appetite from all of those private sector players across the world … for something to galvanise common purpose."
To that end, the SMI has created a Space Sustainability Task Force to champion the principles of the Astra Carta, led by an advisory council that includes European Space Agency director Josef Aschbacher, UK Space Agency Director Paul Bate, Martinez and Hadfield.
The non-profit has advanced the goals of the Astra Carta at meetings of the United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space and by working with major players, including SpaceX. It also organizes high profile events such as the Nov. 7 Artemis Celebration Gala at the Kennedy Space Center, Florida, which honored Artemis II astronauts Reid Wiseman, Jeremy Hansen and Victor Glover while bringing together 450 leaders and pioneers from the space, government and business sectors.
In July earlier this year, His Majesty opened the UK Space and Defence Gateway at the Harwell Science and Innovation Campus in Oxfordshire, which partnered with the SMI and created an investment council to further the principles of the framework.
"The voluntary framework is the fastest way to get everyone on the same page".
The Astra Carta's champions are actively engaging the private sector, governments and other luminaries. What's more, Jordan-Saifi believes that the voluntary nature of the Astra Carta could trigger widespread change faster than may be possible through the traditional U.N. system, which may need to be incorporated into country-level laws in a process that could take decades.
"The voluntary framework is the fastest way to get everyone on the same page. And then we might move to more concrete and enforceable, binding options in the future." In the meantime, Jordan-Saifi hopes that players in the space industry will play a role in holding one another accountable to observing the principles of the Astra Carta.
But could the competitive nature of the emerging space sector act as a barrier to embracing sustainability, as commercial entities race to capture their own share of the market?
"Space has become a very congested and competitive domain"
"Space has become a very congested and competitive domain, and I don't, frankly, see the big players taking their foot off the gas, both for commercial and for strategic reasons," explained Martinez. "But I think that there is a growing awareness of the fragility of the space domain, and so, therefore, I would expect the major actors to recognise this and to behave responsibly."
Martinez points to SpaceX's Starlink constellation as an example of good behavior on orbit, with the company often sharing satellite trajectories and maneuver plans for other actors to see and plan for ahead of time. "...This is what I think we are all aspiring towards in the future, some form of global, globally coordinated, or global space traffic coordination system. which we don't yet have today."
A heightened risk comes from newcomers drawn to the growing space economy from other sectors. "They don't understand that they're entering a fragile and strategic domain, and that's where initiatives like the Astra Carta can help to socialise this awareness," continued Martinez.
But one of the greatest potential strengths of the Astra Carta may rest with its unique ability to engage the public and raise awareness in the quest for sustainability in space, as much as its capacity to galvanise the private sector.
"The first step is to create social awareness of this, and I would say that one of the values of the Astra Carta is the cachet of royal attention to this issue," said Martinez. "Extending the king's already well known appreciation for stewardship of the Earth environment to the orbital environment. And I think that is the real value of it … if the king is talking about this issue, [it] raises its salience and gets others to think about it."
In this, His Majesty is supported by the SMI and a team of astronaut ambassadors, including Hadfield, U.S. astronaut Nicole Stott and ESA astronaut Tim Peake.
"We're going to Antigua and Barbuda for the heads of government meeting of the Commonwealth, and the king attends that, and we're actually bringing Chris Hadfield on stage to talk to the 2.7 billion citizens of the Commonwealth about the AstraCarta," said Jordan-Saifi touting the SMI's ability to reach a vast global audience. "...We really want more and more people to be involved and be aware about space. And I think once people are aware of it, they want the same sustainability standards for protecting our planet."
However, the sheer scope of the Astra Carta makes it a challenge to communicate to the public. Potential readers may also be surprised to find that the most up-to-date version available on the SMI website is still the "Zero Draft" — the name commonly given to unpolished works not yet ready for publication.
Jordan-Saifi assured me that the Astra Carta's Zero Draft is still relevant and accurate, but that a version 1.0 is currently going through consultation for potential release in the future.
"If you're ready to declare anything after three years, you're making a mistake."
Which begs the question: how would one even gauge the success of so far reaching a roadmap as the Astra Carta? Its voluntary nature makes it inherently challenging, but as Jordan-Saifi notes, there are certain metrics that could be used to indicate how far the Astra Carta has shifted the space economy towards sustainability in the future.
The SMI could track the number of countries and commercial partners that have agreed to adhere to the principles of the Astra Carta, assess public awareness and gauge the success with which its tenants have been formally adopted by the United Nations and other regulatory bodies.
Hadfield, meanwhile, reflected on the difficulties facing the Astra Carta's champions on the long road to sustainability.
"How do you weave in the role of a space agency who has to answer to the national demands and the constraints that they have, both financially and politically?" questioned the former astronaut. "And how do you weave in all of the nonprofits that have all different agendas? The Astra Carta is trying to do all those things, and I think it's done admirably, but it takes patience. And if you're ready to declare anything after three years, you're making a mistake."
Want to know more? Then be sure to head over to the SMI website to read the Astra Carta in full, or you can read a recent op-ed on whether we are currently on track for true space sustainability.

title: US government confirms investigation into tech firm Megaspeed
text:
The United States has confirmed it is investigating computing company Megaspeed, suspecting it of violating US export controls by helping to ship tech giant Nvidia's chips to China.
In a joint statement, the US Department of Justice and Department of Commerce said they had been investigating Singapore-based firm Megaspeed since 2024.
It comes after questions were raised about the possibility high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.
Concerns emerged in recent weeks after Nvidia founder Jensen Huang revealed he had an extramarital affair, allegedly with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang. US authorities suspect her of spying for Beijing, which China denies.
Jensen Huang resigned from his role as chief executive last week following revelations he had two affairs.
Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and is suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China. The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.
The justice and commerce departments said on Monday that "it is in the public interest to provide the facts and address inaccurate information" regarding the investigation.
Laying out a timeline, it said it began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations".
In May 2025, Department of Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia "concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed". In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its 'no sell' list.
Agents from the Bureau of Industry and Security, in conjunction with Singaporean law enforcement officials, then conducted an on-site check at Megaspeed that month and interviewed Alice Huang, who was chief executive at the time.
Following this enforcement action, the Department of Justice took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed.
The Nvidia scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end chips to Megaspeed.
On Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed the US Commerce Department, led by Howard Lutnick, for failing to properly oversee the export of the chips.
Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.
While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.
Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China to discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair.
The White House said on Monday it would further restrict China's access to AI chips from firms like Nvidia.
The reported affairs by Jensen Huang created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms - a major company in the AI industry and central to the US as it competes with China for dominance.
In the statement, the US government said it would "bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred".
They added: "Sensitive technologies like semiconductors are among the most valuable and strategic assets of the US economy, and the Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce will remain vigilant in pursuing justice for those who want to compromise America's technological edge."

title: Band of baby sea turtles swims into ocean after historic California nesting
text:
Two months after the discovery of the first sea turtle nests ever to have been recorded on the US west coast, the eggs have hatched – and California’s first group of 75 native-born olive ridley sea turtles have been released into the Pacific.
The eggs incubated at the Aquarium of the Pacific in Long Beach after the historic discovery of two separate nests in September at southern California beaches, a shift likely driven by this year’s El Niño conditions.
On Saturday, the Aquarium of the Pacific announced the turtles’ first emergence in a social media post: “The hatchlings are here! We are excited to share that some of the olive ridley sea turtle eggs from Seal Beach successfully hatched after a 58-day incubation period. Working with our partners, we carefully released them from the beach in the dark early hours of this morning.”
A day later, the Aquarium added: “Even more egg-citing news! A second group of olive ridley sea turtle hatchlings, this time from the Huntington Beach nest, was released into the ocean early Sunday morning.”
In total, 54 turtles were released from the Seal Beach nest and 21 from the Huntington Beach nest.
On 16 September, an olive ridley sea turtle was observed digging a nest and laying eggs on Seal Beach in the first-recorded instance of any sea turtle nesting on the west coast. Three days later, a second turtle was spotted nesting on Huntington Beach.
Typically a tropical species, the olive ridley sea turtle normally resides in the Pacific, Indian and Atlantic oceans, but has been known to nest on the southern tip of Baja California.
“It is not known why these turtles chose southern California beaches as nesting sites, but it indicates an important historical change that could have long-term implications for the species and for local sea turtle management and protection,” the Aquarium of the Pacific said in a social media post.
“The behavior of these turtles was probably influenced, at least in part, by the incoming El Niño, along with the recent tropical storm, range expansion, or perhaps navigational mistakes. The species is also known for its behavioral flexibility.”
As Hurricane Polo began to form in late September, researchers with the aquarium and its federal and local partners relocated the 204 eggs from the two nests to incubate in the safety of the aquarium’s animal care facility.
“As animals adapt in unexpected ways to changes in their natural world, humans will need to adapt and make space to ensure endangered and threatened species are given a fighting chance,” said Jeffrey Flocken, president and CEO of the Aquarium of the Pacific.
“If they successfully hatch, these baby turtles will likely one day return to nest to carry on future generations on these very same beaches, giving us a remarkable opportunity to help a species expand its range and thrive.”
Even as the Huntington Beach and Seal Beach turtles have begun hatching and returned to the ocean, researchers are continuing to advise the public to be on the lookout for more nests. On 1 November, a third nest was recorded in Ventura county although those eggs were swept away by unusually high tides – likely also caused by El Niño.

title: SpaceX deploys Starlink satellites in Starship test, but booster crashes into Gulf
text:
SpaceX conducted a major test of its Starship rocket Friday night. It deployed several satellites for the Starlink constellation, but there was a problem with its booster.
UNIDENTIFIED ANNOUNCER: T-minus 10, nine.
SCOTT SIMON, HOST:
Yesterday, SpaceX conducted another test launch of the largest rocket ever built.
UNIDENTIFIED ANNOUNCER: Three, two, one.
SIMON: But it's the rocket's return, planned for later today, that could make history and will have big implications for SpaceX's bottom line and the future of space travel. NPR's Geoff Brumfiel has been tracking the flight. Geoff, thanks so much for being with us.
GEOFF BRUMFIEL, BYLINE: Good morning, Scott.
SIMON: Where is the rocket now?
BRUMFIEL: Well, the rocket is very happily orbiting the Earth. You can actually watch it on X if you really want to. As you said, it took off from Starbase, Texas yesterday evening. It climbed up into orbit, deployed 26 satellites for the Starlink constellation. That's SpaceX's satellite internet constellation. The booster rocket, which is really, really big, came back. It was supposed to land at Starbase, but it did not. There was some sort of problem, and they crashed it into the Gulf. But, you know, Starship's doing pretty well at the moment.
SIMON: We mentioned the rocket's return could be historic later this afternoon. Why is this flight different from previous flights?
BRUMFIEL: You know, this really is about whether SpaceX can stick the landing. Assuming everything goes OK, the plan is to reenter the atmosphere in a few hours, fly back to Starbase, where it took off from. Then it's going to turn itself vertical and land at the launch site. It's going to hover, and the launch tower actually has these two mechanical arms that are going to come out and grab it - assuming this all works, you know? The booster was supposed to do the same thing but crashed, so there's still a chance Starship may end up in the Gulf or somewhere else before all this happens.
SIMON: And how is the landing so potentially important to SpaceX's future?
BRUMFIEL: Well, SpaceX wants to use Starship for a couple of different things. It wants to launch, potentially, thousands of satellites for that internet constellation, Starlink, and someday, it wants to launch orbital data centers into space. These are both key to SpaceX's plans for revenue growth, but they can only happen if Starship becomes rapidly reusable.
SIMON: Reusable means what, in this context?
BRUMFIEL: Yeah. The idea is that the booster and the rocket both fly back to the tower. They get caught. They get restacked, refueled, shove a couple more satellites on board, and then they're launched again very quickly. This is a super ambitious, very difficult plan. If they can catch Starship, though, that's going to be a huge step. Nobody's ever really caught a rocket in midair after it's come back from space before.
SIMON: And there are implications for NASA, too.
BRUMFIEL: This is something I've been reporting on this week. Starship is getting all the headlines, but SpaceX's current smaller workhorse rocket, called Falcon 9, is really doing a lot of work for NASA, and SpaceX is going to retire it. Here's SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell explaining why at the All-In Summit in September.
GWYNNE SHOTWELL: Falcon 9 with a Dragon capsule on top is like a minivan - road trip in a minivan. The road trip to Mars is six months, so you don't want to be in the minivan.
