BRUMFIEL: The problem is that minivan is perfect for road tripping into the International Space Station, and, in fact, it's the only American vehicle NASA can use to get there right now. Now, the space agency has enough Falcon 9 launches to last through 2028, but there's supposed to be crew on the station until 2030. That means they might have to find another ride to get their astronauts to and from space.
SIMON: What'll they do?
BRUMFIEL: Well, Shotwell suggested they use a rival company, Boeing.
SHOTWELL: We're just going to let them have some business. They should fly their capsule. overnment paid a lot of money for that.
BRUMFIEL: The problem is that Boeing capsule has been plagued by lots of technical issues. It's not ready for humans yet. SpaceX is making this move because its NASA contracts aren't really worth that much to it anymore. You know, the satellite internet business it has and these potential data centers are just going to earn it a lot more money.
SIMON: Back to Starship. What'll you be watching for as it comes back to Earth?
BRUMFIEL: Well, it's really about that landing. But the other thing I'll see is, you know, SpaceX is now a public company. It's burning billions on the development of this rocket, and I'll be interested to see what shareholders think counts as a success.
SIMON: NPR's Geoff Brumfiel. Thanks so much.
BRUMFIEL: Thanks, Scott.

title: Kalshi pauses Trump "mention markets" in response to CFTC order
text:
Kalshi is pausing markets that allow users to bet on what President Trump will say in response to a federal agency's request, a spokesperson for the prediction market confirmed.
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission requested that Kalshi halt the so-called "mention markets" tied to the president on Friday.
Mention markets allow traders to bet on specific words or phrases a person will utter during public events, such as speeches or earnings calls. Users often spend hours researching a person's speech patterns to make an informed guess about what they might say.
"We are complying with the order," the Kalshi spokesperson said in an email. The company will still allow some mention markets related to the Trump administration, according to The Wall Street Journal, which earlier reported the pause.
Reached for comment, a CFTC spokesperson said the decision was consistent with a September order that stayed the certification of certain mention markets by Kalshi.
"These contract types present a heightened risk of manipulation because their settlement turns on the discrete conduct of a person that may be neither independently generated nor externally verifiable," the agency said at the time.
The CFTC's order follows a July incident in which a White House teleprompter operator on Kalshi bets tied to public speeches by President Trump. The trading activity by an administration employee fueled concerns about insider trading on prediction market platforms, an issue that has .
Kalshi said it its rules in March to better detect insider trading and prevent market manipulation.
Kalshi has removed other markets at the CFTC's behest in the past. In August, the company removed all sports-related mention markets, which previously generated $90 million in monthly trading volume, according to a person familiar with the matter.

title: Taiwan may take a backseat when Xi and Trump meet for a third time at an APEC summit
text:
Presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump are expected to meet at the Asia Pacific Economic Forum this week
TAIPEI, Taiwan -- Taiwan is likely to be overshadowed as presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump are expected to meet on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Forum this week, even as the threat from China evolves and grows stronger.
Leaders from China, the U.S. and some 21 other economies will gather at the APEC summit this week in Shenzhen, China. Recent events like the scandal that forced Nvidia's CEO to resign, export controls and the ongoing trade dispute have made the tech competition between Beijing and Washington all the more pressing.
Few expect major breakthroughs on Taiwan, a self-ruled island that is claimed by Beijing. While the U.S. does not formally recognize Taiwan, it is the island’s biggest informal ally and seller of arms.
“For the Trump administration, this isn’t a core issue between the U.S. and China,” said Arthur Zhin-Sheng Wang, an expert on cross-Straits relations at Taiwan’s Central Police University.
Experts largely say that cooperation with the U.S. remains strong below the level of rhetoric, despite Trump’s public ambivalence toward Taiwan.
One sign of this came from the summer, when the de facto United States embassy in Taiwan posted a photo showing joint patrols between the two coast guards, a rare occurrence, as the U.S. does not usually acknowledge it has direct cooperation with Taiwan in any defense capacity.
“This also is proof of the decades that Taiwan and U.S. have had of cooperation and training. I was also surprised,” said Kuo Yu-jen, a defense studies expert and director of the Institute for National Policy Research in Taiwan.
The U.S. is obligated by law to help Taiwan defend itself, which has manifested in the form of arms sales, while the government officially adopts a stance of ambiguity on whether it would intervene militarily in the case of a Chinese invasion.
The Taiwanese public is used to the continued uncertainties of the island’s relationship with the U.S. Research from the Institute of National Defense and Security Research in Taiwan, a government-funded think tank, showed that public attitudes toward the U.S. remain around the same. Polls conducted in the past five years show that about half of the public believes the U.S. will send soldiers to support Taiwan in the event of a Chinese invasion, and about half don’t.
“I do think they will take some actions, though it may not be sending soldiers,” said Allen Hsieh, a 28-year-old media professional in Taipei. “I think Taiwan’s importance to the U.S. is even more important than Ukraine.”
Since starting his second term, Trump called for Taiwan to spend more on its own defense and Taiwan responded that it would commit to 5% of its GDP on defense.
Arms sales are ongoing. While much media attention has focused on a $14 billion package that remains stalled, an earlier package of $11 billion approved at the end of last year is in progress. Some of the stalled arms packages have been delayed since before Trump came into office, experts have also said.
Those include fighter jets. Taiwan received the first two of long-delayed F-16V fighter jets from the U.S. in October, and three more jets earlier this month. The aircraft are a part of a long list of backlogged U.S. orders worth almost $30 billion, according to the Taiwan Security Monitor research project which tracks defense-related developments on the island at George Mason University.
But the delays are not necessarily because of political considerations with China, a concern that was raised when Trump said he discussed arms sales with Xi earlier this year. Instead, it may be more of an issue with manufacturing capacity, particularly for future sales.
Congress approved the sale of long-range precision strike systems to Taiwan in December 2025, but Taiwan faces competition because of limited supplies. Kuo noted that among the missiles approved for sale are the same ones being used by the U.S. military in the ongoing Iran war, such as the HIMARS rockets and supplies were low.
“I don’t think this is a political issue. They just can’t produce so many of these missiles in a short period,” he said.
Meanwhile, China has intensified its military and nonmilitary pressure on Taiwan. In 2025, the People’s Liberation Army flew about 5,448 fighter jet sorties toward the island during military exercises, according to Skyfaring, an open-source website that compiles public data from Taiwan’s Ministry of Defense. That marked a sharp increase from the years before 2023, when such flights were sporadic.
Beijing also recently held unannounced military drills in the Western Pacific, deploying more than 100 vessels in waters near Taiwan and Japan, Taiwan’s National Security Council chief Joseph Wu said in a Nov. 3 post on X.
The number of PLA flights recorded this year stood at 2,401 as of Nov. 12, below the full-year total for 2025.
“I think the threat is transforming ... for example, more of its exercises are now about blockading and sealing off” Taiwan, Wang said, rather than firing live missiles. He said Beijing was expanding its gray-zone tactics — aggressive actions that fall short of open warfare.
These include greater use of the coast guard to assert China’s claims, mirroring its approach elsewhere. In June, the Chinese coast guard began patrolling off Taiwan’s east coast, which faces the open Pacific, extending its activities beyond Taiwan’s outlying islands closer to China.
Wang compared the approach to Beijing’s tactics in the South China Sea, where Chinese coast guard vessels patrol waters disputed with the Philippines. China has also designated a shoal claimed by the Philippines as a nature reserve under Chinese protection.
“It’s telling the whole world it has sovereignty here.”
———
Wu reported from Bangkok.

title: The AfD and neo-Nazi networks: How close are the connections?
text:
The electoral successes of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) have brought the party closer than ever to taking power in Germany. For the 2029 federal election, it has set itself an ambitious goal: to see its co-chair Alice Weidel to become Germany's next chancellor.
This raises an even sharper question: what political ideas does the party stand for, which has been classified by Germany's domestic intelligence agency as a "suspected right-wing extremist" organization and, in several federal states, is already considered "confirmed right-wing extremist"?
Many political scientists have observed that the AfD has become increasingly radicalized since its founding in 2013.
"Viewed as a whole, the AfD is an extreme right-wing party that also displays tendencies associated with a fascist movement," said Fabian Virchow, a researcher on right-wing extremism at Düsseldorf University of Applied Sciences, in an interview with DW.
Virchow identifies different factions and strategic tendencies within the party, some of which are at odds with one another. Party leader Alice Weidel, for example, is generally seen as a proponent of a free-market approach that seeks to keep the state as small as possible. Others, by contrast, favor a strong state shaped by an ethnically homogeneous people, among them Björn Höcke, the influential far-right AfD leader in the state of Thuringia.
The normalization of right-wing extremism?
Virchow sees a "normalization" of right-wing extremist positions within the AfD. In his view, this has made the party more attractive to neo-Nazi circles: "Today, many people see greater room for ethnonationalist and radical right-wing ideas."
Support for this observation comes from the latest findings of the Leipzig Authoritarianism Study, one of the most widely cited long-term studies tracking right-wing extremist attitudes in Germany. The researchers behind the study have identified a rise in right-wing extremist views within German society, including a growing acceptance of ideologies rooted in the tradition of National Socialism.
Particularly striking is the finding that around two-thirds of people with firmly entrenched far-right worldviews would vote for the AfD. According to the study, the AfD has achieved what earlier far-right parties in Germany never managed: "to unite large segments of the electorate with anti-democratic attitudes behind it."
The debate has been further fueled by several recent incidents within the party. In 2026 alone, numerous AfD politicians and staff members made headlines over alleged ties to neo-Nazi organizations:
In August 2026, police carried out a large-scale raid targeting fifteen people. Authorities suspect them of continuing the activities of the so-called "Artgemeinschaft." Before it was banned in 2023, the group was considered one of Germany's largest and most influential neo-Nazi cadre organizations. Particularly explosive was the fact that two of those targeted in the raid are sitting AfD members of the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament. Their attorneys deny the allegations.
According to reporting by the German daily, Welt, four staff members of the AfD's parliamentary group in Saxony-Anhalt are former members of the now-banned "Heimattreue Deutsche Jugend" (HDJ), a neo-Nazi youth organization rooted in National Socialist racial ideology that organized paramilitary camps for young people. Two of the staff members held leadership positions within the HDJ and now work closely with AfD politician Ulrich Siegmund, who is seeking to become the AfD's first state premier in December.
Remarkably, both organizations, the "Artgemeinschaft" and the HDJ, are on the AfD's so-called incompatibility list, which is intended to draw a line between the party and extremist organizations and movements. In principle, anyone with a history of membership in such groups is supposed to be excluded from the party.
But the list appears to be little more than a dead letter. In 2020, former AfD federal executive board member Andreas Kalbitz was expelled from the party after failing to disclose his membership in the "Heimattreue Deutsche Jugend" on his application to join. Yet according to the news magazine Spiegel, he is once again working for the AfD, this time as a staffer for Saxony-Anhalt state legislator Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, who has since become deputy speaker of the state parliament.
The question of the AfD's relationship to National Socialism has dogged the party since its founding in 2013. Even in its early years, co-founder and first party leader Bernd Lucke sparked controversy when he described democracy and parliamentary politics in Germany as "degenerate," a term the Nazis used to disparage art and culture that did not conform to their ideological worldview.
In Germany, references to the Nazi dictatorship (1933-1945) under Adolf Hitler remain politically taboo because of the country's responsibility for World War Two and the Holocaust, the systematic mass murder of Europe's Jews.
Controversial distancing efforts within the AfD
If AfD members or their staff have come under scrutiny because of past involvement in ethnonationalist or neo-Nazi organizations, they have generally sought to distance themselves from those backgrounds or from the ideologies associated with them.
But how credible are these attempts at distancing? Laura Neumann* has worked with many people seeking to leave the far-right scene. She works for "Nordverbund Ausstieg Rechts," a network of organizations that supports far-right cadres and activists as they disengage from the movement. "A successful exit is the result of a professionally guided process," she said in an interview with DW.
Neumann describes leaving the far-right scene as a challenging process of self-confrontation. "When it comes to someone leaving the movement, the first question I always ask is: How does that person talk about their past? Have they genuinely come to terms with it?"
Based on the experience of exit counselors, one principle generally holds true: the longer and more deeply a person has been immersed in far-right circles, the more difficult it becomes to distance themselves from those beliefs and affiliations.
DW requested a statement from the AfD's federal executive board regarding its handling of party members who were previously active in ethnonationalist or neo-Nazi organizations. Individual lawmakers and parliamentary staff members were also asked to comment. None responded.
The party's and its politicians' silence in the face of such allegations reflects an observation made by political scientist Fabian Virchow: "Within the AfD, there is no longer a perceived need to distance oneself from radical far-right positions. That is part of this process of normalization."
Virchow says that right-wing extremism appears to have advanced so far into the mainstream of German society that efforts to scandalize it now remain largely ineffective.
* Editor's note: To protect the privacy of the staff member of Nordverbund Ausstieg Rechts, we have changed her name to Laura Neumann. Her real name is known to the editors.

title: Texas authorities rushed to the report of a loose alligator. It turned out to be a pool floatie
text:
Texas authorities rushed to the report of an alligator on the loose, but to their surprise — and relief — it turned out to be a pretty realistic pool floatie.
Animal Services in Sugar Land, Texas, recently received a call about an alligator that appeared to be sick and they rushed to check out the situation.
When the wildlife officer went to investigate, “she was in for a big surprise,” the agency said in a recent Facebook post.
“What looked very real from a distance turned out to be a runaway pool floatie!”
The floatie included inflatable legs, a tail and a mouth that opened to reveal fake spiky teeth.
“While this call definitely gave our team a good laugh, we always take every report seriously,” Animal Services said.
After the officer knew she was clear of danger, she made sure to snap some photos of the alligator floatie lying in a patch of green grass.
Animal Services took this opportunity to remind the public, “If you ever spot wildlife that looks sick or injured, please keep a safe distance and call the experts to handle it. You never know if it’s the real deal!”
Facebook users jumped to the comment section to crack jokes, with one writing, “Well, that was a rather inflated story, then!”
“That’s hilarious! Good job on getting that gator under control,” another wrote.
A third channeled his inner “Crocodile Hunter” Steve Irwin, writing, “Crikey!”
“She’s very brave!” another commented about the Animal Services officer, thanking her “for all you do.”
Others suggested it may be a good time to close pools for the cooler months — or at the very least, take out any floaties that can be mistaken for dangerous animals.

title: Apple to face landmark trial in France over alleged planned obsolescence of iPhones
text:
If found guilty, the US tech firm could face fines of up to 5% of its annual revenue, equal to roughly €21.7 billion.
Apple will stand trial in Paris in June next year on suspicion of having organised the planned obsolescence of several iPhone models by preventing repairs outside official outlets, a source close to the case told AFP on Tuesday.
The case brought by French prosecutors against the US tech giant on charges of "obstructing repair and refurbishment" is a first, the campaign group Stop Planned Obsolescence said, welcoming the move after filing a complaint in December 2022.
"We strongly contest these unfounded allegations," Apple said when contacted by AFP.
Planned obsolescence refers to techniques used by manufacturers to deliberately shorten the lifespan of their products, generally electronic devices, thereby encouraging consumers to replace them more frequently.
If found guilty, Apple could be fined up to €300,000 plus, an additional fine of up to 5% of its annual revenue — which would roughly be €21.7 billion as of publication — and could face compensation claims from clients.
According to the source close to the case, Apple Distribution International and its parent company Apple Inc are to appear in court for a four-day trial starting on June 17.
They are accused of obstructing repairs to a range of iPhone models for more than two and a half years, from November 2021 to July 2024.
Affected models range from the iPhone XS and the iPhone 12, 13, 14 and 15 series to the iPhone SE released in 2022.
Apple is accused of configuring its software to "make it impossible to repair or refurbish" the phones outside its authorised network, the source added.
For example, the Face ID feature might be disabled if the camera were replaced by an unauthorised repair shop, or the "battery health" feature could stop working.
The alleged aim was to boost sales of Apple's flagship product and increase the revenue of the multinational, which now generates more than $400 billion a year, with roughly half coming from iPhone sales.
It is not the first case brought against the US tech giant by the Stop Planned Obsolescence group.
In February 2021 it agreed to pay €25 million for failing to tell iPhone users that software updates could slow down older devices.
That settlement was one of several around the world after Apple admitted in December 2017 that its latest iOS operating software was slowing the performance of older telephones whose battery life was deteriorating.

title: Sherrill commits $20.2M to deportation defense while condemning Rutgers over Border Patrol speaker
text:
New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill put her money where her mouth was this week as the Democrat criticized Rutgers University’s College Republican chapter for hosting a top former Border Patrol leader around the same time her administration allocated millions to a program meant to help illegal immigrants and others in the state fight deportation.
Sherrill’s condemnation of the Rutgers students’ event drew criticism on X from observers who said it fueled protests outside the New Brunswick building where retired Border Patrol Cmdr. Gregory Bovino spoke. Protests erupted inside the room as well, with video from inside showing Bovino responding to shouting protesters before he was briefly led out of the forum.
"Everyone in this country is entitled to due process and a fair hearing under the law — regardless of where they were born," Sherrill said Friday in announcing a total of $20.2 million to fund the Detention Deportation Defense Initiative within Trenton’s Office of New Americans.
Some of the funds will help migrants held at Delaney Hall in Essex County, where nightly protests have erupted since May. The governor previously visited the facility in solidarity with the detainees inside, while Sherrill ally Sen. Andy Kim, D-N. J., drew widespread attention online after being caught in a cloud of pepper spray dispersed by ICE toward surrounding protesters.
"With the Trump Administration ramping up ICE activity and creating impossible obstacles for people facing detention and deportation to navigate alone, New Jersey is stepping up to connect residents with qualified legal counsel and equip more attorneys to take on this vital work," Sherrill said Friday, adding that the state’s immigrant community should not have to face a "complex" legal system alone.
Commissioner Stephen Cha, head of Sherrill’s Department of Human Services, where the Office of New Americans sits, added in a statement that access to legal representation upholds due process and promotes a more "efficient" immigration system.
The $20.2 million will be spread among 10 service providers and continue the Murphy-era initiative’s mission to offer legal expertise and representation for "low-income residents facing detention and deportation."
Sherrill’s new cash infusion nearly tripled the initiative’s most recent budget allocation.
After Sherrill announced plans in June to increase the deportation defense initiative’s funding, Republicans in the state warned that the money could be better spent elsewhere, including on New Jersey residents.
"New Jersey families are being crushed by some of the highest electric bills, property taxes, and costs of living in the entire country, and Governor Sherrill's answer is to spend more than $20 million defending illegal immigrants," said outgoing Rep. Jeff Van Drew, R-N.J., who was unseated by Cape May Mayor Zachary Mullock in this month’s blue wave.
"It is a complete insult to every hardworking taxpayer in this state. New Jersey citizens should come first. If they can find $20 million for immigration lawyers, they can find money to lower utility delivery charges or provide relief to the people who actually live, work and pay taxes here."
Van Drew said in June that every dollar Trenton spends on an illegal immigrant is a dollar that could have helped keep a New Jersey family from leaving the state.
A DHS spokesperson said Sherrill has "consistently shown more concern for criminal illegal aliens who've broken our laws and destroyed any possibility of ever remaining in our country than she ever has for Rachel Morin, Laken Riley, Jocelyn Nungaray and the true victims of illegal alien crimes in America," while adding it does not comment specifically on matters involving former personnel like Bovino.
Fox News Digital reached out to Sherrill for comment.
Sherrill had publicly condemned Bovino and Rutgers’ College Republicans for holding the event.
Rutgers is New Jersey’s state university, and the governor appoints some of its board members. Delaware Valley radio host Rich Zeoli said the state gives the New Brunswick school about $1.4 billion annually, adding the argument can be made she is "using a classic intimidation tactic to silence speech she doesn't like."
Sherrill urged attendees to press Bovino on why he chooses "cruelty over humanity" and what he thinks of the November election results and the argument that they represent a collective rebuke of his enforcement approach.
The North Carolina native shot back at Sherrill, saying her statement was "spoken like a true lib who puts illegal aliens before her own citizens."
"Gubner, I am deeply disappointed in your penchant for using the Governor’s Office to limit Constitutional rights of Americans," Bovino said in a statement.
"This coming from someone who cheated at the Naval Academy (you weren’t allowed to walk), and enriched yourself via insider trading in defense stocks as a Congressgirl — priceless." Sherrill has said she was barred from walking at the graduation not because she was involved in cheating but because she declined to identify classmates involved.
New Jersey State Assemblyman Paul Kanitra, R-Point Pleasant Beach, said Sherrill’s criticism of Bovino contrasts with her silence over Democrats electing a candidate in the state who was once acquaintances with the mastermind behind the 1993 World Trade Center bombing.
"The thought-police strike again," Kanitra said.
"I didn’t see you weighing in when any Adam Hamawy said some pretty heinous things recently? That didn’t seem to warrant a tweet," he said, referring to the Mercer County doctor and former defense trial witness for the Blind Sheikh who won the race to succeed retiring Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman, D-N.J.
Hamawy was never charged with any wrongdoing in connection with Abdel-Rahman, and his campaign previously told Fox News Digital related criticisms amount to "guilt-by-association" shaming and that Republicans and right-wing press are simply concerned that Hamawy will be "Donald Trump's worst nightmare."
Bovino later challenged Sherrill to attend his event, which the governor did not attend.
"Tell you what, come on down to Rutgers and put your insider-trading money where your mouth is. You won’t be able to cheat your way through this one."
Sherrill’s 2025 gubernatorial campaign previously denied the stock-trading allegation raised by Bovino, which stemmed from Republican challenger Jack Ciattarelli’s claim that she "cash[ed] in to the tune of $7 million" by "flipping stocks" while in Congress.

title: Trump has arrived in Asia. Here’s what he said about Iran and Deutsche Bank
text:
U.S. President Donald Trump has arrived for his high-stakes trip to Asia, and took a range of questions on subjects from Iran to Deutsche Bank leaking details about his tax.
The president landed in Manila, Philippines, for the initial leg of his trip on Tuesday and answered rapid-fire questions from the press while meeting with other leaders.
Asked about a possible Iranian threat to Washington, D.C., he said that, if there were an attack, Iran would "pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before."
The question was about CNN reporting that U.S. intelligence suggested the country was planning to target senior members of Trump's administration with a dirty bomb or chemical weapon in the U.S. capital.
"We take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy," Trump said. CNBC has not independently verified CNN's report.
But the president also said he believed his administration was "very close to getting it done" when it came to the Iran war.
While Trump was airborne, the Financial Times reported Deutsche Bank had mistakenly leaked details of his taxes in March 2017, during his first presidential term. The mistake was kept from the White House at the time, according to the FT.
In a statement, Deutsche Bank said the issues detailed in Tuesday's media reports go back many years. "Where relevant, we reviewed these matters at the time and worked closely with regulators," the lender said.
Asked about the situation in Manila, the president said, "I paid a lot of tax."
"They shouldn't have done it. It's illegal for them to do it," he added.
Trump was also asked about Nvidia's announcement on Tuesday of a new National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee. The company, which reports earnings later on Tuesday, is reeling from the sudden departure of CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned last week after having an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence reportedly believes to be a Chinese spy.
"It's a great company. It's a great idea," Trump said.
Trump is due to fly to Shenzhen, China, where he is scheduled to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin for a three-way meeting on Thursday, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.
He is also due to hold a separate bilateral meeting with Xi. Asked by a reporter if he would have a separate meeting with only Putin, Trump said: "I don't know, but I would, if it's available, I would do that. He's coming. I mean, it's really with the guests. I am the guest of President Xi."
Trump met the leaders of Australia, India and Japan as part of the Quad grouping in the Philippines and the prime minister of Thailand. He is due to China on Wednesday.
Speaking at a dinner with Southeast Asian leaders as the event wrapped up for the day, Trump touted his record during his second term, citing investment into the U.S., trade deals made with countries represented by attendees at the dinner, energy infrastructure buildouts and America's AI industry.
Trump, who has led a campaign to rename artificial intelligence "super intelligence," or "SI," told leaders around the table that the U.S. is "leading the world" in the technology.
"We have the world's most powerful SI ecosystem," he said. "We're leading everybody by a lot, and we hope to keep it that way, and we will keep it that way."
He added that the U.S. has "the strongest and most capable military on the planet," pointing to investments in the armed forces and the country's defense sector.
"We make the greatest equipment. You saw that in Venezuela. You see it in Iran. You see it everywhere," Trump said.

title: Uranus and Neptune’s bizarre magnetic fields may finally be explained
text:
The strange, wildly tilted magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune have puzzled scientists since NASA's Voyager 2 spacecraft explored the planets in the 1980s. New simulations suggest that extreme conditions deep inside these icy giants create unusual electrical properties that could explain their magnetic fields. Remarkably, the models indicate that their magnetic poles could shift by tens of degrees within just a few decades, far faster than Earth's.
When NASA's Voyager 2 spacecraft visited Uranus and Neptune in the 1980s, it discovered something extraordinary. Unlike Earth, which has a relatively orderly magnetic field with clearly defined north and south poles, both distant planets possess strangely distorted and dramatically tilted magnetic fields. For decades, scientists have struggled to explain why.
Now, researchers believe they may have found an answer hidden deep inside these enormous worlds. A new study suggests that changes in how well materials conduct electricity under extreme conditions could explain the planets' unusual magnetism. The findings also raise an intriguing possibility: the magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune may change dramatically over just a few decades.
The research, published in Communications Physics, was led by scientists at The University of Texas at Austin in collaboration with researchers from the University of California, Los Angeles, Imperial College London, and Northumbria University.
Why Uranus and Neptune Have Such Strange Magnetic Fields
Planetary magnetic fields originate deep beneath the surface, where moving fluids capable of conducting electricity generate magnetic forces. Scientists call this process a dynamo.
On Earth, the dynamo operates within the outer core, a layer of molten metal surrounded by mostly solid rock. As liquid iron circulates and the planet rotates, it generates a magnetic field resembling that of a giant bar magnet. This produces the familiar north and south magnetic poles that allow compasses to point in a consistent direction.
Earth's magnetic field is also closely aligned with its rotation axis. Its main magnetic axis, known as a dipole, is tilted by only 11 degrees. Uranus and Neptune are strikingly different. Uranus has a magnetic dipole tilted by 59 degrees, while Neptune's is tilted by 47 degrees.
Explaining these extreme tilts requires a better understanding of what lies inside the two planets.
Uranus and Neptune are classified as ice giants, a name that reflects their presumed composition rather than suggesting they are simply frozen worlds. Each is approximately four times wider than Earth, and scientists believe their interiors contain substantial amounts of hydrogen, helium, water, ammonia, methane, and rocky material. However, their precise internal compositions remain uncertain.
Extreme Conditions Deep Inside the Ice Giants
Chi Yan, the study's lead author and a research associate at the UT Jackson School of Geosciences, believes the combination of the planets' enormous size and unusual chemical makeup may help explain their distorted magnetic fields.
"Deep inside Uranus and Neptune, pressures and temperatures become extremely high," said Yan. "Under these conditions, which can cause water molecules to break apart into ions, the material may become increasingly electrically conductive with depth."
Ions are electrically charged particles that can carry electric current. If the materials inside Uranus and Neptune become more conductive at greater depths, that could significantly influence how their magnetic fields are generated.
To investigate this possibility, the researchers developed computer simulations designed to reproduce the strange magnetic fields recorded by Voyager 2.
Their models assumed that electrical conductivity increases deeper inside the planets. The researchers also tested a variety of possible internal structures, examining how circulating fluids, temperature changes, and magnetic forces interact over time.
The results suggest that these changing electrical properties could play a crucial role in producing the unusual magnetic fields observed around both ice giants.
Magnetic Poles Could Shift Dramatically Within Decades
Perhaps the most surprising finding is that the magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune may be far less stable than Earth's.
According to the simulations, their magnetic axes could undergo substantial changes in relatively short periods. In some scenarios, the magnetic tilt shifted by tens of degrees within only a few decades.
That raises the possibility that the magnetic fields surrounding Uranus and Neptune today are significantly different from those measured when Voyager 2 flew past them in the 1980s.
"Earth's magnetic tilt drifts by only a degree or so over 50 years," said Yan. "Our models show the ice giants can behave very differently. In some stretches the tilt swings by tens of degrees within decades. In others it shifts only slightly over the same span."
These dramatic changes remain predictions from computer models rather than confirmed observations. However, scientists may already have a way to look for evidence of them.
James Webb Telescope Could Reveal Magnetic Changes
Researchers are now examining detailed infrared images of Uranus and Neptune captured by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). They are particularly interested in the planets' auroras, which form when charged particles from the Sun interact with gases in their atmospheres.
Auroras are closely connected to planetary magnetic fields, making them valuable clues to what is happening far above the planets' hidden interiors. Changes in the appearance and arrangement of these glowing atmospheric features could help researchers determine whether the magnetic poles have shifted since Voyager 2's encounters.
"We are busy working on what's contained within these observations, but the shape and structure of the aurora, as well as other weird patterns in the ionosphere, promises to provide us with a way of understanding how the magnetic fields have changed, an important stepping stone," said Tom Stallard, a professor at Northumbria University who led the JWST observation campaign and reviewed the paper for the journal.
The ionosphere is a region of the upper atmosphere containing electrically charged particles. Its behavior is influenced by magnetic activity, offering another potential source of information about the planets' changing magnetic environments.
The research team hopes to combine Webb's auroral observations with Voyager 2's original magnetic field measurements and the new dynamo simulations. Together, these sources of evidence could provide the clearest picture yet of how the magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune are arranged today.
Even so, scientists emphasize that fully understanding the planets' deep interiors will require new spacecraft missions to these distant worlds. Until then, improved simulations and powerful telescopes may help unravel one of the solar system's most unusual magnetic mysteries.
The research was funded by The University of Texas Institute for Geophysics (UTIG) in the Jackson School of Geosciences, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), and the Science and Technology Facilities Council.

title: NASA's interstellar Voyager 1 probe is about to reach 1 light-day from Earth after nearly 50 years in space
text:
Voyager 1 is celebrating a big milestone as it approaches its 50th birthday: reaching one light-day away from Earth.
NASA's long-running interstellar Voyager 1 probe will mark one light-day of distance from Earth on Nov. 18, when the spacecraft is 49 years, two months and 11 days old. The agency recently stated the record distance, which will be reached at 5:16:07 a.m. EST (101607 GMT) is "a huge milestone by any measure, and a day worth celebrating."
During the light-day crossover, Voyager will be in contact with the Madrid station of the three-antenna Deep Space Network that monitors all deep-space missions. The spacecraft is currently making its way through the constellation Ophiuchus from the perspective of Earth, said Jeffrey Hayes, a NASA official whose work includes Voyager 1.
"This [milestone] essentially kicks off the year's worth of celebrations leading up to the 50th anniversary in August and September of next year," added Hayes, who is discipline scientist in the agency's astrophysics and heliophysics divisions, in a livestreamed discussion with NASA's Night Sky Network on Nov. 4.
Going the distance
Voyager 1 is the farthest spacecraft from Earth, after launching from Kennedy Space Center in Florida on Sept. 5, 1977 a few weeks after its twin, Voyager 2.
A light-day, as the name implies, represents the distance that light travels in a single day. In other words, at one light-day, a radio-wave message to Voyager 1 takes 24 hours to get to the spacecraft — which is roughly 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers) from Earth. Voyager's response then takes another day to get back to our planet.
Voyager 2 — which is at a distance of 13.5 billion miles (21.7 billion km) from our planet — won't hit the light-day milestone until 2035, NASA stated. While the agency has not offered recent estimates for how long the two spacecraft will last, in 2022 Suzanne Dodd, project manager for Voyager at JPL, said they may keep operating into the 2030s.
The two spacecraft had initial funding to survey Jupiter and Saturn, although NASA did launch them at a time when the planets aligned in such a way to bring Voyager 2 past Uranus and Neptune if funding continued — which it did.
Voyager 1, meanwhile, took a turn at Saturn to look at the planet's rings, and the pre-biotic (pre-life chemistry) moon of its largest moon Titan, executing maneuvers which brought it high above the solar system's plane.
Hayes said the original design team likely did not foresee a 50-year lifespan for the mission, even though the Voyagers had many redundancies in them. But NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), which manages the mission, is looking to continue to max out the scientific return.
NASA says the mission costs from launch to Neptune, spanning about 12 years from 1977 to 1989, was $865 million — with $30 million more budgeted for its extended mission. "It's a lot of money, right? And it's everyone's money … so we want to make sure that we do it right," Hayes said.
Flying into the black
Both nuclear-powered spacecraft are still healthy enough to be chatting with Earth and taking measurements from interstellar space, although dwindling power supplies have forced instrument shutoffs and other creative techniques to be getting the most out of the missions. One example was a huge power swap that took place on both spacecraft this year, called the "Big Bang" because of its impact on the mission.
"It's a balance, right? Because some instruments are more power hungry than others," Hayes said of the ongoing work on keeping the Voyagers going. "Those instruments that use the least amount of power, but give you good science still, they would obviously rise to the top in any sort of priority discussion. Whereas an instrument that is more power-hungry, but still has interesting science, that's on the cusp."
While the two spacecraft are still healthy, Hayes said their age — and the extreme environment they are operating in — makes them "fragile," in his words. "We're way out there. We're a light-day out there, which is just just over 16 billion miles. So it's really really far. It's also really really cold, right? We're only a few degrees above absolute zero here."
The Voyagers continue to lose four watts of power per year (their initial power was at 470 watts apiece) and the challenge is not only the power, but also the propellant. Hydrazine, Hayes said, is prone to freezing. "And if it freezes, then it's game over," he said, paying tribute to the JPL engineers that continue to keep the spacecraft going.
Voyager 1's next destination is vaguely near a star 17 light-years from our planet, in the constellation of Ursa Minor (the Little Bear, or Little Dipper). But the spacecraft will certainly be out of nuclear power by then, as its flyby — at a distance of 1.7 light-years of the star, called Gliese 445 — will take place in 40,000 years.

title: Dazzling Leonid meteor shower to peak on Tuesday night
text:
The Leonid meteor shower reaches its peak on Tuesday night, giving UK sky gazers their best chance to see it this year.
The celestial spectacle runs until 30 November, but the greatest activity is expected on the night of Tuesday 17 November, into the early hours of Wednesday.
There could be the chance to spot up to 10-15 meteors per hour.
The shower is made up of dust particles from the Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which leaves a trail of debris as it follows its path around the Sun.
These particles enter the Earth's atmosphere at up to 44 miles (71km) per second, meaning these streaks of light are the fastest meteors in the sky.
How to spot the Leonids
Experts advise finding a safe, dark location away from sources of light pollution such as street lights.
The meteors will be visible with the naked eye, with no binoculars or telescope required.
However, giving your eyes some time to adapt to the dark, perhaps 20 or 30 minutes, will give you the best chance of spotting them.
A wide open space is the best place to be, giving a full view of the night sky.
Meteors could be visible anywhere but the Leonids' radiant, the point from which they seem to appear, will, as the name suggests, be around the head of the constellation Leo, meaning this is the best part of the sky to focus your gaze. Leo does not rise until around midnight, so the best time to look is after midnight and in the hours before dawn.
As with all celestial spectacles, clear skies will be a must.
What will the weather be like on Tuesday night?
Viewing conditions could be particularly good around the peak. The Moon will set at around 23:30 GMT on Tuesday, meaning its reflected light is less likely to spoil the view in the hours after midnight.
The best chance of seeing the Leonids will be in the far north of Scotland, including Orkney and Shetland, where cloud is expected to be well broken with only a small chance of a passing shower.
Parts of Northern Ireland, Wales, the Midlands and southern England will also have clear spells at times but there will be periods of cloudier weather and some splashes of rain.
In Northern Ireland, the Midlands and North Wales, the best chance of clear breaks will be earlier in the night.
Much of Scotland away from the far north, and northern England, will have limited opportunities. A few places may see the odd gap in the cloud but for most it will be cloudy and damp.
You can read the monthly outlook for our thoughts on the weather for the rest of the month.
You can always check the hour-by-hour cloud, fog and temperature forecast for your area by checking BBC Weather online or the app.

title: Rassie Erasmus’s tired ref-blaming act is wearing thin – South Africa deserve better | Robert Kitson
text:
So here we go again. Exactly five years have passed since South Africa’s head coach, Rassie Erasmus, first felt the full force of World Rugby’s ire for criticising match officials. And guess what? This most habitual of offenders has just copped another lengthy ban – and deservedly so – for his latest intemperate comments, notable as ever for their total lack of statesmanship, diplomacy or good grace in defeat.
To his acolytes his outspoken nature is part of what makes Rassie such a groot leier (great leader). To many others it simply cements his status as a serial prat. For the avoidance of any doubt everyone respects the remarkable achievements both of Erasmus and his double World Cup-winning teams. It is the rest of the package, sadly, that is too often a major letdown.
At times the Boks’ patron saint is almost reminiscent of Donald Trump in a tracksuit: crass, petulant and seemingly immune to the damage inflicted on the “little people” who get in his way. How else to interpret his latest outburst after South Africa’s defeat by France when he suggested that alleged incidents of foul play not picked up by either the referee or the television match official amounted to “match-fixing” or “manipulation of the game”?
Dissatisfied coaches are a familiar ingredient of the game’s bubbling stew. And, yes, Erasmus technically has a point when he complains that several knee-drop tackles, recently highlighted as illegal by World Rugby, were missed in Paris. Rugby is a game of tiny margins and South Africa, as befits the world’s No 1 nation, hate losing more than most.
But there is a much bigger picture involved and Erasmus remains seemingly incapable of appreciating the insidious toxicity of finger-pointing and ref-shaming in defeat. Back in 2021, when he embarked on his 62-minute social media rant after the Boks had lost the opening Test of their series against the British & Irish Lions, he warned the Australian referee Nic Berry he would publicise 36 refereeing errors if the official failed to meet him. The disciplinary panel found him guilty on six charges, imposed a lengthy ban from all matchday activities, and described his video as “an attack on the impartiality and integrity of the match officials”.
Berry, who will be in charge of England’s game against New Zealand this weekend, duly attracted the online wrath of every keyboard warrior in South Africa and felt that “my reputation as a referee and a person will forever be tarnished.” It did not stop Erasmus from being banned for two more matches the next year after his social media posts precipitated an internet pile-on for the English referee Wayne Barnes, also after a South African loss to France.
Which is why Erasmus’s latest outpourings, aimed at Matteo Liperini, the television match official in Paris, on the subject of multiple missed knee-drop tackles, were always going to be costly. “I’m saying if he didn’t see it, it must be a technology problem,” suggested Erasmus. “If he saw it and decided not to act on it, is that not match-fixing?”
Only in the eyes of a practised agent provocateur. Erasmus attended World Rugby’s refereeing summit in Windsor this month when the mantra of penalising only “clear and obvious” indiscretions was repeatedly stressed, as was a desire to reduce the number of TMO referrals. Yes, there were some French tacklers who had knees on the ground as they hauled down Bok ball-carriers in the tumultuous final quarter in Paris but the refereeing team seemed to have decided they didn’t want a truly fabulous contest to be defined by some arbitrary late penalty.
It is possible to pore over any breakdown and find multiple things that could conceivably, by the letter of the law, be pounced upon. But, by the same token, none of it would have ultimately mattered had South Africa, with their scrum dominating, been minded to use any other instrument beyond the bludgeon.
It would have spared us all the tiresome “Why always me?” whingeing that invariably resurfaces whenever northern hemisphere opponents or referees are involved. There were bound to be teething problems with the new hip-drop directive, hastily introduced from 1 November to bring rugby union into line with other contact sports. But to say that Ireland’s Sam Prendergast, cited for the offence after last weekend’s Fiji game, will escape punishment because double standards are at work? Talk about a victim complex.
Like all great conspiracy theorists, Erasmus is also only interested in selective facts that fit his preferred narrative. Of course he wants the refs to be vigilant when his team face Ireland this weekend; the strict letter of the law worked nicely for the Boks in Dublin last year. Of course he wants to spread the notion that South Africa may have been hard done by in the Stade de France and deserve more sympathy this Saturday. He is by no means the only coach to operate in that way but his sledgehammer subtlety is in a league of its own.
Maybe in past years he, and his staunch defenders, could have blamed it on English being his second language. Such excuses, however, are long since redundant. To repeat, South Africa are a remarkable sporting nation and their rugby players remain first among equals. They deserve to be fronted by someone with rather more class.

title: Israeli settler pogrom kills Palestinian woman, wounds 10 people
text:
Israeli settlers have killed an elderly Palestinian woman and wounded 10 other people in a pogrom in the central occupied West Bank, the official Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.
The Palestinian Health Ministry named the woman killed as Fadda Mohammed Fheidat, 72.
The attack began early on Tuesday in the Duyuk al-Tahta neighbourhood on the outskirts of Jericho city, where settlers forcibly took over several properties earlier this month.
Witnesses told the news agency Reuters that a group of settlers began shooting outside Fheidat’s home, and Palestinian residents threw stones to defend themselves. More settlers arrived and fired at Palestinian homes, including Fheidat’s, the witnesses said.
Ahmed Aref, 62, Fheidat’s brother-in-law, said that a bullet hit her in the head as she stood in front of her house.
“I found her lying on the ground, with blood coming from her head,” he said.
The Israeli military did not comment on the woman’s death, but said it was dealing with “ongoing incidents” in which Israelis and Palestinians were wounded in an alleged car-ramming.
Fheidat’s son, Arafat, rushed to the scene after hearing she was hurt. His wife, Naama Fheidat, said he was in shock and accidentally hit a settler’s car parked in the driveway.
Witnesses said the settlers were not in the car, and that they then fired wildly, wounding several people, including Arafat, in the torso.
Arafat Fheidat said the Israeli military stopped the ambulance he was in as he was being taken to hospital in Ramallah and arrested him.
The military told Reuters a group of Palestinians in a car “accelerated their vehicle toward an Israeli vehicle and rammed it”, claiming that there were both Israeli and Palestinian casualties.
The settler attack comes about two weeks after settlers took over eight homes in Duyuk al-Tahta, the official Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.
The Binyamin Regional Council, which represents settlers in the area, said it had helped facilitate the move of families into eight homes purchased from Palestinians.
Jericho’s Palestinian governor, Hussein Hamayel, has said the settlers could not legally buy the land because it belongs to the state.
Israeli pogroms in the occupied West Bank have surged to what the United Nations has called an “unprecedented level”, following the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel on October 7, 2023 and the subsequent genocidal war on Gaza.
According to the UN, at least 1,143 Palestinians have been killed in the occupied West Bank since October 7, 2023, including 250 children.
The figure includes Palestinians killed by Israeli settlers living in illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank.
The Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED) said 2026 is on track to be the most violent year for settler-related violence since it began monitoring the occupied West Bank a decade ago. In July alone, 11 people were killed in four incidents involving armed settlers alongside Israeli forces.

title: Trump arrives in Philippines to kick off Asia trip
text:
MANILA, Philippines — President Donald Trump arrived in the Philippines on Tuesday, where he was scheduled to meet regional partners, talk trade, and seek a break from a series of setbacks at home, ranging from a major disruption to the U.S. aviation industry to a scandal that has shaken the global AI industry.
Manila, the Philippine capital, is Trump's first stop on a three-day trip that will later take him to China for historic three-way nuclear talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, and, according to Trump, potentially for a meeting with North Korea's leader Kim Jong Un.
The visit marks Trump's first travel abroad since his party suffered deep losses in midterm elections. The White House and stock market alike have been rattled by the departure of Jensen Huang from Nvidia last week after admitting to an affair with an alleged Chinese government agent. Beijing has said it was not involved.
As he descended the stairs from Air Force One, Trump pumped his fist. A child handed him small American and Philippine flags, which Trump waved and then swooped in big circular motions as he smiled. The U.S. president was greeted by a marching band playing "YMCA" while he walked to a waiting helicopter.
Trump to be feted at the annual ASEAN summit
Trump's first hours in the Philippines will include all the reassuring optics from Washington's oldest treaty ally in Asia, including a cocktail reception and dinner with other world leaders, an intermission from some of the thorniest issues at home. He's being feted Tuesday night at a gala as the "guest of honor" at the annual summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.
The ASEAN leaders have been working on a non-aggression pact with China in the contested waters of the South China Sea, a key global trade route. Confrontations have escalated in recent years, particularly between Chinese and Philippine coast guard and naval forces in disputed shoals.
First on Trump's agenda Tuesday is a meeting with the leaders of the Quad nations, comprising the U.S., Australia, India, and Japan that have aimed to counter China's influence in the Asia Pacific. It will be their first meeting since Trump returned to the White House last year.
Trump is then scheduled to sign a trade deal with Thailand, the type of agreement he has relished striking since launching a trade war last year buttressed by steep tariff threats.
The U.S. had announced a trade framework last October in which Thailand would remove tariffs on most American goods, as well as barriers for importing U.S. autos, food products and pharmaceutical drugs, according to the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative. At the time, the Trump administration said Thailand would also spend more than $18 billion on U.S. aircraft and buy U.S. farm goods and liquefied natural gas.
The U.S. Supreme Court overturned in February the 19% tariff that Trump placed on goods from Thailand. The administration sought replacement tariffs in July by levying a 12.5% tax on imports from Thailand for not taking steps to oppose the use of forced labor.
Before the gala dinner Tuesday night, Trump will participate in what's billed as a "special summit" with the ASEAN leaders, where they are expected to discuss efforts to deepen trade and security ties as well as the region's longstanding conflicts, including yearslong violence in Myanmar and escalating disputes in the South China Sea, which Beijing claims virtually in its entirety.
Washington rejects China's expansive claim in the waterway, and has repeatedly stated that it's obligated to defend the Philippines if Filipino forces come under an armed attack.
Anti-Trump protesters are gathered in Manila
About 1,500 left-wing protesters held a noisy rally in a downtown Manila square ahead of Trump's arrival, calling on Philippine leaders not to take their foreign policy cues from the U.S.
They waved red flags and held up a large streamer that read, "Resist U.S. war and plunder!" They planned to burn an effigy of Trump. Riot police with shields and wooden truncheons stood nearby.
"The Philippine government should not deal with such a loser so our call to the Marcos administration is to stop being a puppet of Donald Trump and to uphold an independent foreign policy for the Philippines," protest leader Teddy Casiño told The Associated Press at the Liwasang Bonifacio square, referring to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
Planned meetings with the Philippine president — and possibly an old friend
On Wednesday, Trump is set to receive a red-carpet welcome and full military honors from Marcos Jr., followed by a state banquet as part of his visit to the Malacanang presidential palace. Trump and Marcos are expected to affirm their commitment to their countries' longstanding treaty alliance.
Officials are arranging a possible brief reunion in Malacanang with an old acquaintance — Imelda Marcos — if she's well enough and gets her doctors' nod.
Now 97 and using a wheelchair, the former jet set Philippine first lady and mother of the incumbent president partied in New York decades ago in her heyday as the controversial wife of a strongman leader, who was to be ousted in a pro-democracy 1986 "People Power" public uprising.
But the friendship with Trump endured, with Trump often asking Marcos Jr. and other Philippine officials: "How's Imelda?" Philippine Ambassador to Washington Jose Manuel Romualdez told The Associated Press.
"Personal connections are very important to him," Romualdez said.
When the Philippine leader met Trump in the White House last year, he carried a note from his mother that thanked the U.S. president for his strong backing of the Philippines. "President Trump was very happy and told Marcos, 'please say hello to your mother,'" according to Romualdez.
Trump is also expected to announce a series of commercial deals and investments in the aviation, defense, energy, and technology sectors, before heading to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.

title: Hawley, Durbin introduce Roblox safety bill ahead of hearing
text:
Missouri Republican Josh Hawley and Illinois Democrat Dick Durbin are introducing new legislation targeting sexual abuse on Roblox and online gaming platforms, CBS News has learned.
The legislation, titled the No Forced Arbitration for Child Sexual Exploitation and Cyber Injuries Act, would allow families of individuals harmed by tech products to take their claims to court even if they agreed to the company's terms of service for private arbitration. Roblox is by dozens of families and state attorneys general who claim online predators have been able to groom, extort and exploit kids they meet on the platform.
The measure is being rolled out ahead of an inaugural congressional hearing Tuesday into the popular gaming portal. The hearing, chaired by Hawley, will feature witness testimony from two abuse survivors and a pair of experts.
"I am investigating allegations that Roblox, a popular online gaming platform for kids, has become a breeding ground for sexual predators," Hawley said in a statement. "This week, as my Subcommittee holds the first-ever congressional hearing on Roblox's practices, Senator Durbin and I will introduce new bipartisan legislation to give survivors justice. We must hold these platforms accountable and ensure no child is left vulnerable to exploitation online."
The bill would close loopholes to ensure a child's rights aren't limited in click-through agreements, allow class-action lawsuits and let survivors and families choose whether to bring a claim in public court or through confidential arbitration.
"In the digital age, predators can target our kids from anywhere—including online gaming platforms like Roblox. And sadly, the numbers show that they have," said Durbin. "Therefore, an 'agreement' buried in the terms of service shouldn't limit a child's or family's rights to bring their claim before a judge or jury. I'm proud to partner with Senator Hawley on this bipartisan issue, and I won't stop until this bill—and other key measures to protect children online—are signed into law."
CEO Dave Baszucki was invited to testify at Tuesday's hearing but has declined to appear.
"The claims being made about Roblox are fundamentally misleading and ignore the rigorous safeguards we have in place to help protect users," a Roblox spokesperson said in a statement to CBS News. "Roblox's mandatory age checks for chat, age-based content, prohibition on sharing photos or videos via chat, and continuous monitoring and filtering of chat, help set the standard for youth protection online."
In August, Hawley and Durbin launched a joint investigation by the Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism into child safety on Roblox.
"Roblox appears to prioritize revenue and engagement metrics over the safety and well-being of our children, and the alleged criminal activity on Roblox warrants congressional scrutiny," the Senators wrote in a letter to the company at the time.
Roblox has 138 million daily active users, ranging in age from five to over 25, according to its latest shareholder letter released at the end of October. The company currently faces nearly 200 lawsuits in federal court and has reached settlements with at least six states over online child safety issues.
This month, Roblox chief safety officer Matt Kaufman wrote that the company continues to partner with law enforcement and "aggressively look for bad behavior and report it through the appropriate channels."
Last year, the company announced it would for minors. Roblox CEO David Baszucki described the guardrails in an interview with "CBS Mornings" as "what we believe will become the gold standard for safety and civility on the internet."

title: Iran's growing exodus of young talent
text:
"I had actually decided to leave Iran back in 2023," a physician in her mid-30s, who wished to remain anonymous, told DW.
Her decision followed the 2022 death in police custody of 22-year-old Iranian-Kurdish woman Jina Mahsa Amini, who had been arrested by Iran's so-called morality police for allegedly violating the country's strict dress code.
Amini's death sparked widespread protests and inspired the "Woman, Life, Freedom" movement, which challenged authorities' enforcement of Iran's hijab mandate.
The physician said that the US-Israel war with Iran ultimately accelerated her plans to leave her homeland. She has been living with her family in a rented apartment in Turkey since early summer. From there, they hope to continue on to Germany.
"It took two years for my professional qualifications to be recognized in Germany. After that, I applied for an appointment at the German Embassy in Tehran," the physician said.
"Then the 12-day war broke out in the summer of 2025. The embassy closed and suddenly we were all left in limbo, not knowing what would happen next."
She became concerned after the US and Israel launched fresh airstrikes on Iran on February 28, 2026 — not just about the escalating conflict, but also about the prospect of internal unrest and political instability.
Turkey as a stopover
"Like many others we encountered during the emigration process, we decided to first move to a neighboring country," she said. "The plan was to stay in a third country for six months and then apply for a visa through the German embassy there. That's why my family and I came to Turkey."
Turkey is one of the few countries that allows Iranian citizens to enter without a visa for up to 90 days.
Since the latest conflict began, thousands of Iranians have crossed the border into Turkey. Many are trying to secure their stay through residence permits rather than seeking asylum.
According to official Turkish statistics, nearly 100,000 Iranian citizens were residing there in 2025. Among them are many academics and skilled professionals hoping to settle permanently in Europe or North America, seeing little future for themselves in Iran's war-hit economy.
A US naval blockade of Iranian ports in the Gulf over the past few months has disrupted oil exports, trade and government revenues. The turmoil has compounded the impact of decades of sanctions and economic mismanagement.
The situation has put most businesses under pressure by restricting access to foreign currency and raw materials, among other problems, threatening revenues and jobs.
The worsening conditions have left many people struggling to afford food, housing, health care and education.
The physician said the situation at the German embassy in Tehran, however, has improved in recent months. Some of her unmarried friends, who also initially moved to Turkey and spent substantial sums maintaining their stay there, have already returned to Iran to submit new visa applications from home.
She and her husband, however, have decided to stick to their original plan and wait out the six-month residency period in Turkey despite the difficulties.
"I can't and don't want to go to Germany without my family. I don't know how long it would take for them to receive family reunification visas," she explained. "And I don't know what might happen in the meantime. A new war could break out at any moment."
Young Iranians lose faith in the future
The departure of highly qualified professionals and students has become one of the most pressing challenges facing Iranian society. Today, there are few families in which someone has not already emigrated or is not at least considering doing so.
A 2025 study by the University of Guilan in Iran examined the relationship between opportunities for social participation and students' willingness to emigrate.
The researchers found a statistically significant correlation: Students who felt they had fewer opportunities to shape their future in Iran were more likely to consider emigrating.
Economic concerns are only part of the picture. Limited political participation, social restrictions and a sense of powerlessness are also driving many young Iranians to leave.
Mahsa, who is in her mid-20s, told DW that she has already secured admission to a German university.
Ali, meanwhile, dreams of a life outside Iran. The 23-year-old holds a bachelor's degree in engineering and is currently preparing for the entrance exam for a master's program at a public university. His long-term goal is to obtain a stronger qualification and then leave Iran — ideally with a scholarship.
"That's my dream of a better future," he said.

title: Jockey Nico de Boinville given extra security at Plumpton after ‘threat’ received
text:
Jockey Nico de Boinville was assigned security support at Plumpton on Monday after a threat against him was received and passed on to racecourse authorities.
The multiple Grade One-winning jockey finished fifth riding even-money favourite Ginolo for his boss Nicky Henderson in the opening race of the afternoon at the East Sussex track, after which he was informed extra security would be provided once officials were made aware of the situation.
De Boinville went on to finish third aboard his only other ride, the Henderson-trained Ionian in a handicap chase, the third race on the card.
Explaining the sequence of events, Plumpton’s clerk of the course Marcus Waters said: "We got a phone call from a person representing the PJA (Professional Jockeys Association) and the NTF (National Trainers Federation) regarding a threat that had gone in to the Henderson yard.
"We put on security for Nico for the rest of the day. He had one further ride and they escorted him from the weighing room to the parade ring and then once the race was done they escorted him to his vehicle, just in case there was anything that came with the threat.
"It’s obviously not a nice situation for anyone to be involved with."
Speaking to Racing HQ at Newbury’s pre-Coral Gold Cup gallops morning on Tuesday, De Boinville explained: "After the first race yesterday the security detail at Plumpton who are very good, top-level people who dealt with the Brighton bombings and things like that, came in and dragged me out and said there’s been a threat called in to me, so I needed security for the rest of the day.
"The threat came into the yard and then the PJA and then BHA, and then it gets called through to the racecourse. I need to find out a bit more about it but it’s the trials and tribulations of being a jockey.
"It is bizarre and I’m going to work like everyone else and you don’t expect that when you go to work. I just feel sorry for whoever it was and I hope they get the help they need – it was probably because I got beat."
A BHA spokesperson added: "The BHA condemns all abusive or threatening behaviour towards our participants, who rightly should expect to be able to go about their jobs without being subjected to anything of this kind.
"We work closely with our colleagues across racing’s representative bodies and, where appropriate, will take whatever action necessary to ensure the safety of everyone in our sport."

title: Jensen Huang to face US Congress interviews on Nvidia’s sales to China on 1 December
text:
Huang is set to appear before the United States' House Foreign Affairs Committee, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party and the House Intelligence Committee on 1 December.
Nvidia's cofounder Jensen Huang will sit for a closed-door transcribed interview on 1 December before the US House Foreign Affairs Committee, Intelligence and the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party.
It comes after he resigned as CEO of the chip giant following reported extramarital affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy.
Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter will then sit for a closed-door transcribed interview a day later on 2 December.
"We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security," said Republican representatives Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawfor, the chairs of the Foreign Affairs, China Select and Intelligence Committees in a press release.
"The American people need answers on Mr. Huang and Nvidia’s role in allowing dangerous PRC actors to access our most advanced chips, as well as the role of a potential Chinese intelligence asset in this scandal," they said.
The US bans the sale of the most advanced chips to China as part of its strategy to stay ahead of Beijing in the race to lead AI. This measure came under former President Joe Biden, who signed the CHIPS Act into law.
Under the Trump administration, Huang lobbied the US to relax its export controls on chips to China, with several meetings with President Donald Trump.
Trump eventually allowed the export of its H200 chips, which are more powerful, to China in exchange for 25% of the revenue.
On Monday, the US Commerce Department unveiled new restrictions that will make it harder for some countries, such as China, Russia and Iran, to access the most advanced artificial intelligence chips through data centres located in other countries.

title: Nvidia warns chip buyers of legal risks tied to China AI access, sources tell CNBC
text:
Nvidia warned its customers that new legislation on Chinese companies remotely accessing its artificial-intelligence chips could expose it and them to U.S. "legal action," sources told CNBC.
The chip giant is facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips, which U.S. export controls restrict from going to China.
Nvidia messaged chip buyers in recent months to caution that the proposed Remote Access Security Act, or RASA, would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services in the same way as physical hardware, potentially exposing both parties to legal risk, according to two people with direct knowledge of the matter. The people asked not to be named while discussing private communications.
It also said that, for now, it would not sell its chips to customers who rent more than 50% of the graphics processing units, or GPUs, to Chinese companies, the people said.
Separately, the Financial Times reported earlier this month that Nvidia verbally told data-center clients to direct at least 51% of their services to non-Chinese customers under future contracts.
Regulators have had limited powers to control companies' access to those chips through cloud services hosted overseas.
RASA passed the House of Representatives in January but has not yet passed the Senate. Remote access to the chips has provoked the ire of President Donald Trump's administration, which has sought to keep the chips out of China to maintain the U.S. lead in the AI race.
CNBC reported on Nov. 5 that Chinese lab Moonshot AI sought access to Nvidia chips through data centers in Europe. The Trump administration previously singled the company out, accusing it in July of accessing the chips through centers in East Asia.
The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced on Monday an interim final rule designed to prevent Chinese companies' remote access to AI chips.
Nvidia and BIS did not respond to a request for comment.
On Sunday, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for a "dramatic shakeup" at Nvidia after Jensen Huang's shock departure as CEO, amid reports of an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. authorities reportedly suspect of spying for China.
Bessent suggested other Nvidia executives should face scrutiny over the chip giant's compliance with export controls.
"I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?" Bessent told Fox News.
In an August securities filing, Nvidia said it sought to "strictly comply with all applicable export control regulators" but did not have "physical control of our products after sale" and relied on its customers' and partners' compliance programs.
Huang has been asked to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3.

title: Astronomers discover a dead star spinning every 8 minutes and sending mysterious radio pulses
text:
Scientists have discovered a strange stellar pair more than 5,000 light-years away, where a dead star spinning every eight minutes produces mysterious radio pulses while orbiting a Sun-like star. The breakthrough also revealed massive magnetic storms on the companion star, offering fresh clues to one of astronomy's emerging mysteries.
Astronomers have traced mysterious radio signals to an unusual pair of stars more than 5,000 light-years from Earth. One is a dead star that rotates every eight minutes, while its companion closely resembles our own Sun.
The discovery was made by researchers at the Curtin University branch of the International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research (ICRAR). Their findings reveal a previously unseen combination of stars producing radio pulses and offer new clues about the origins of some of the Milky Way's most puzzling signals.
The stellar system, designated GPM J071507−114153, contains a white dwarf and a G-type star orbiting one another. A white dwarf is the extremely dense remnant of a star that has exhausted its nuclear fuel and shed its outer layers. Its companion belongs to the same general category of stars as the Sun.
Until now, astronomers had detected similar radio pulses in systems containing white dwarfs and smaller, cooler stars known as red dwarfs. This marks the first time such signals have been identified in a system where a white dwarf orbits a Sun-like star.
A Rare Star System With Mysterious Radio Pulses
The newly identified pair belongs to an unusual group of astronomical objects called long-period transients (LPTs). These objects produce radio emissions that appear and disappear over periods lasting anywhere from several minutes to hours.
Despite growing interest in these strange signals, their origins remain poorly understood. The same ICRAR research team discovered the first known example in 2021, and only about a dozen have been identified since then.
Some of these systems contain a white dwarf alongside another star, but astronomers have struggled to determine which member of the pair is responsible for the radio emissions.
The latest discovery provides an important breakthrough. For the first time, researchers have obtained radio observations detailed enough to follow a white dwarf as it travels around its stellar companion. This allows them to pinpoint the likely location of the radio pulses much more accurately.
"This is the first time the pulses are clear enough to see the white dwarf moving in its orbit around its companion, so we know that the pulsations are coming from a region close to the white dwarf, or possibly even from the white dwarf itself," said lead author Dr. Sam McSweeney.
McSweeney, now a commissioning scientist with the Square Kilometre Array Observatory, made the discovery while working at Curtin University's ICRAR branch.
To confirm the findings and examine the white dwarf's orbital motion, the researchers analyzed more than 100 hours of radio observations using computing resources at the Pawsey Supercomputing Research Centre.
Giant Magnetic Storms Detected 5,000 Light-Years Away
