The radio signals revealed more than the movement of the dead star. They also gave astronomers a surprising opportunity to investigate magnetic activity on its Sun-like companion.
According to study co-author Associate Professor Natasha Hurley-Walker, the observations exposed stellar flares associated with powerful magnetic disturbances. Similar magnetic processes on our own Sun can lead to auroras on Earth when energetic particles interact with our planet's magnetic field and atmosphere.
The team also detected evidence that the white dwarf passed behind an especially magnetically active region near its companion.
"As a bonus, we also saw the white dwarf moving behind a region with a strong magnetic field, most likely a 'stellar prominence', which is a large loop of plasma erupting from a star's surface."
A stellar prominence consists of electrically charged gas held in enormous loops by magnetic fields. These structures can extend far above a star's surface, providing clues about the powerful forces shaping its outer atmosphere.
The ability to detect such activity across thousands of light-years demonstrates how much information astronomers can extract from radio signals, even when the stars themselves are extraordinarily distant.
"It's amazing that by using radio wavelengths we can detect the storms on a star over 5000 light-years away."
Powerful Radio Telescopes Reveal a Hidden Stellar Pair
ICRAR researchers have played a leading role in identifying long-period transients, and the latest discovery relied on observations from several major astronomical facilities around the world.
The system was initially detected during a sweeping radio survey of the Milky Way conducted with the MWA (Murchison Widefield Array) in Western Australia.
"We detected this system in a large survey using the MWA (Murchison Widefield Array) to scan the entire Milky Way visible from Australia. We then used the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa to determine its precise position," said Associate Professor Hurley-Walker.
After the radio telescopes narrowed down the system's location, astronomers turned to the W.M. Keck Observatory on Maunakea, Hawaiʻi Island. Optical observations confirmed that the radio source was associated with a G-type star, establishing the presence of a companion similar to the Sun.
The MWA, led by Curtin University, operates at Inyarrimanha Ilgari Bundara, the CSIRO Murchison Radio-Astronomy Observatory on Wajarri Yamaji Country in Western Australia.
The MeerKAT telescope was built and is operated by the South African Radio Astronomy Observatory in South Africa's North Cape province.
Both instruments are precursors to the next generation of Square Kilometre Array telescopes. The Australian facility, SKA-Low, and the South African facility, SKA-Mid, are being developed to provide much greater sensitivity and detail when observing the radio universe.
For astronomers studying rare stellar systems, these future capabilities could dramatically expand the number of objects they can discover and reveal much more about the processes responsible for their unusual signals.
Dr. McSweeney said, "If we are already making such discoveries with precursor telescopes, just imagine how many more star systems we will be able to find, and what a beautifully detailed view of their signals we will have, once the SKAO telescopes are completely built."
The findings were published in Nature Astronomy in a study titled "A long-period transient with a Sun-like companion."

title: 30 years ago, 'Space Jam' proposed the best way to resolve interplanetary disputes
text:
You just ordered a Pizza Hut and a two-liter bottle of Mountain Dew. You put on "Space Jam" to watch the greatest of all time team up with the Looney Tunes. It's a perfect evening… in 1996 or 2026.
The entire concept of "Space Jam" is so '90s that you swear you can hear Los Del Rio in the background mouthing, "Dale a tu cuerpo alegría, Macarena." As ridiculous as an intergalactic basketball match may sound, it's a perfect example of how even the strangest idea can work if you commit to it fully.
In case you thought you hallucinated the whole thing, no, you didn't, as the Looney Tunes find themselves in quite the predicament in this live-action-animation hybrid. A bunch of aliens known as the Nerdlucks arrive on Earth to abduct the Tunes and take them back as attractions to the outer-space amusement park known as Moron Mountain (shockingly nobody has claimed that subreddit, so do your thing, Internet!).
Being a wheeling-and-dealing wabbit, though, Bugs Bunny proposes a winner-takes-all basketball game between the Tunes and the tiny Nerdlucks. Unfortunately, the crafty aliens use their tech to steal the talent from ballers like Charles Barkley and Muggsy Bogues and turn themselves into the scary and skilled Monstars.
So, Bugs and friends reach out to Michael Jordan, who recently switched from basketball to baseball, to help the Tune Squad win this intergalactic b-ball matchup and their freedom, because if anybody can do it, Air Jordan (Hare Jordan?) can. Oh, Bill Murray also shows up here a few times. Why? Because he can!
"Space Jam" is a spin on the classic sci-fi trope of resolving high-stakes conflicts through sports. In 1975, "Death Race 2000" introduced a world where people drive like hooligans and bash into each other to get ahead and win races (ironically, this is the regular experience on any public road now). Meanwhile, in the same year, "Rollerball" demonstrated how to use extreme sports as a plot device whereby brutality trumped any kind of skill in the arena.
Yet "Space Jam" took this concept, cartoonified it for a family-friendly audience, and challenged the conflict resolution approaches of other alien invasion movies from 1996.
While "Independence Day" saw the heroes trying to destroy the mothership and "Mars Attacks" featured humans running away from "Ack! Ack"-ing extraterrestrials with ray guns, this film used the court to settle the score. It's an innovative way to deal with interplanetary matters, that's for sure.
Here's the thing: a basketball game is incredibly fair and puts everybody on equal footing. It isn't about who has the biggest guns or most high-tech spacecraft; it's about who can best work as a team to get a result.
Now, this isn't to say that the Looney Tunes and Nerdlucks ever planned on playing by the rules. Bugs challenged his opponents to a basketball contest because they were small and he knew the Tunes would have the height advantage. However, the aliens pulled a fast one by stealing b-ball talent and evolving into the brutish Monstars. Basically the cartoon version of when athletes use PEDs…
Even so, you can't argue that a basketball game gives each side a genuine chance at victory. Let's be real here for a moment: if humans were to face off against aliens in actual warfare, we would get smoked in seconds. Hell, we would probably get stuck in a tailspin of political infighting and the passing of the buck or end up destroying ourselves before the aliens even fired a single shot. On the court, though, there's no place to hide. Everybody needs to get up and slam!
There's also something magical about having MJ as the de facto leader of the Tune Squad. In the '90s, he was the closest thing to a real-life superhero that the world had ever seen. He broke basketball records, then headed off to another sport — baseball — to challenge himself. His love for the court never died, though, so he came back for the last dance. "Space Jam" found a clever way to blur the line between fiction and reality to elevate MJ's already iconic status.
Sure, Jordan wasn't exactly Daniel Day-Lewis in this film, but he did his best. "He did as well as he could do," director Joe Pytka told Entertainment Weekly. "He played himself, and remember, a lot of the film is based on his life, so there were realistic references there. He was very professional; he showed up, he knew his lines, and we made it as easy as possible.”
It's this type of dedication and professionalism that turned him into the greatest of all time. If you want to debate whether that honor belongs to LeBron James, go argue with a wall. We all watched LeBron in the 2021 sequel "Space Jam: A New Legacy," and let's just say that it makes "Morbius" look like "Casablanca" by comparison, and it deserves the flak it got.
Back with the infinitely better original "Space Jam" movie, it isn't just the courtside matchup to decide the Tunes' fate that surprises, but also the aftermath. Unlike other alien movies that see extraterrestrials being vaporized in the final act, this film demonstrates the power of humility in victory.
MJ understands that the Monstars only did the bidding of Mr. Swackhammer (voiced by the sensational Danny DeVito) and challenges them to free themselves. After the Monstars send Swackhammer packing to the moon, they befriend the Tunes, and there's good vibes all around. The beef is settled, and the only rivalry that remains is the competitive one on the court. That's all, folks!
Instead of treating the aliens as the enemy that must be destroyed, "Space Jam" looks at these creatures as misguided and simply following instructions. They aren't bad guys; they're foot soldiers. Once they break free from Swackhammer's shackles, everybody gets along. And hey, maybe Marvin the Martian also put in a good word for them.
It's a testament to the quality of "Space Jam" that everybody still talks about it 30 years later, but nobody can even remember Steven Spielberg's "Disclosure Day" from a few months ago.
In 1996, aliens were all the rage (and a little overexposed if we're being honest) but "Space Jam" still managed to find a unique and compelling angle that stood out from everything else around it. Not only that, but it also paid tribute to one of the greatest sportsmen to have ever walked the planet.
This wasn't just a slam dunk in cinema; it was boomshakalaka!
"Space Jam" is available to watch on HBO Max.

title: Arsenal Double winner Storey dies aged 81
text:
Former Arsenal and England midfielder Peter Storey has died at the age of 81.
Storey made 501 appearances in all competitions for the Gunners between 1965 and 1977, scoring 17 goals.
He was part of the Double-winning Arsenal team which secured the First Division title and FA Cup in 1970-71 under manager Bertie Mee.
"Everyone at Arsenal is deeply saddened by the passing of double winner Peter Storey," Arsenal said in a statement.
"All our thoughts are with his family and loved ones at this incredibly sad time.
"We will pay our respects to Peter at our forthcoming home match against Borussia Dortmund."
Surrey-born Storey joined Arsenal as an apprentice in 1961 and made his first-team debut against Leicester City in 1965, initially starting his career at right-back before being moved into midfield.
He is currently eighth on Arsenal's list of all-time appearance holders and was capped 19 times by England, although he did not feature in a major tournament for the Three Lions.
Storey collected runners-up medals with Arsenal in the League Cup in 1967-68 and 1968-69 and in the FA Cup in 1971-72.
He joined Second Division Fulham on a free transfer in March 1977 and made 19 appearances for the Cottagers before his contract was terminated later that year and he retired.
However, Storey had something of a troubled life after his retirement from professional football.
He was convicted of running a brothel - for which he received a suspended prison sentence in 1979 - and was later jailed for three years for his involvement in a counterfeiting operation, then served another prison sentence in 1990 for attempting to smuggle pornographic videos into Britain.

title: Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza cleared of using AI to write prize-winning story
text:
The Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza has been cleared of using AI to write a prize-winning short story, after the prestigious Caine prize for African writers concluded that his entry was “human-written” after a month-long investigation.
Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which charts the declining fortunes of a family after the father invests in fish tanks, was announced as the winner of the £10,000 prize on 6 October.
Five days later, the Atlantic published an article titled “Yet another literary prize winner seems to be AI”, in which the author and journalist Vauhini Vara said the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated.
The Caine prize chair, Ellah Wakatama, said in a statement: “From our detailed investigation, we feel the evidence is clear: The Blue Fighter was human-written. We now look forward to awarding and celebrating Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza … before the end of the year.”
She said: “When concerns were raised, we have a duty as an organisation to look at them carefully and fairly,” adding that the prize had taken a “human-centred” approach to its investigation.
“Our review included interviews with the author, the 2026 judging panel and The Shallow Tales Review, where the story was first published,” Wakatama said. “It also included independent and expert-led metadata analysis of drafts written by the author.”
Kundizeza, who had strongly denied using generative AI to write the story, said he was “relieved” that the allegations had been dismissed after the investigation. “It was not necessary in the first place, I am happy to put all this behind me and continue with my writing journey,” he said.
Vara’s article prompted outrage online, with many claiming that Black writers, and Africans in particular, were being unfairly singled out by allegations of the use of AI.
Associated Press contributed to this report

title: Jensen Huang agrees to testify before US House, says can resume CEO role
text:
Jensen Huang, the former CEO of chipmaker Nvidia, has agreed to appear in transcribed interviews with several United States House committees on December 1, even as he has said he would be “honored” to resume his job if the company’s board would like him to.
On Tuesday, the House Foreign Affairs Committee announced the upcoming interviews, which will also include the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party and the House Intelligence Committee.
The US tech giant’s General Counsel Tim Teter will appear before the same committees on December 2 . It was not immediately clear whether the men would attend in person or speak remotely.
“We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security,” Republican chairmen of the committees, Brian Mast, John Moolenaar and Rick Crawford, said in a statement.
“The American people need answers on Mr Huang and Nvidia’s role in allowing dangerous PRC [People’s Republic of China] actors to access our most advanced chips, as well as the role of a potential Chinese intelligence asset in this scandal.”
Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s CEO on Thursday after reports of extramarital affairs, including one involving a suspected Chinese spy, raised questions over exports of the company’s advanced AI chips to China.
The lawmakers first called on Huang on November 5 to appear before the committees. That came amid initial reports from The New York Times that US authorities had started investigating Alice Huang, a former executive of Singapore-based company Megaspeed, which buys artificial intelligence (AI) chips from Nvidia, and with whom Huang has admitted to having an affair.
US authorities have scrutinised Megaspeed over suspicions that it helped Beijing gain access to advanced AI chips that are barred from shipment to China.
Push to return
The announcement comes as Huang has expressed a willingness to return to the company since resigning last Thursday.
“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said in a post on the social media platform X.
“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”
Huang’s comments come amid reports that tech industry insiders were pushing for his return to the company, alongside a petition with more than 177,000 people calling for his return.
“The board’s decision now sits between a founder who has publicly asked for his job back, a shareholder base with the means to force the question, and an administration split between a president open to his return and a Treasury secretary demanding an outsider,” Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives, said in a note provided to Al Jazeera.
At the same time, Nvidia has announced a board-level committee to oversee national security and export controls, marking the first major governance move since Huang resigned.
The National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee will be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson, a former Goldman Sachs vice chair, Nvidia said. Directors Stephen Neal, former CEO of law firm Cooley, and John Dabiri, a Caltech professor, will also serve on the committee.
US President Donald Trump welcomed the move, calling the launch of a national security initiative a good idea.
Nvidia stock tumbled in midday trading on Tuesday. It was down more than 1.6 percent for the day, 11 percent over the previous five days and 29.2 percent over the previous month.

title: Nvidia scandal and CEO's resignation rock Silicon Valley
text:
Some in Silicon Valley are calling for former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to get his job back after he resigned amid reports of affairs with an alleged Chinese spy.
MICHEL MARTIN, HOST:
The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has shaken Silicon Valley.
STEVE INSKEEP, HOST:
Yeah. Some of the big voices in the tech world are calling for the chipmaker's board of directors to bring Huang back. President Trump said he agrees with them.
MARTIN: NPR's Shannon Bond was at a gathering of Silicon Valley leaders on Monday and is with us now to tell us more about it. Good morning, Shannon.
SHANNON BOND, BYLINE: Good morning.
MARTIN: So I imagine that Jensen Huang was a major topic of conversation. What did people have to say?
BOND: Yeah. This really was the talk of the town at Semafor Silicon Valley & The World conference, and this was the question everyone got onstage, starting with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.
UNIDENTIFIED MODERATOR: Do you think he should? Do you think Jensen should come back?
SAM ALTMAN: I don't think I know enough to answer that question.
BOND: Altman went on to say he considers Huang a hero, but that heroes have flaws. And he said he felt, quote, "personal strong empathy" for the situation because Altman himself was ousted by OpenAI's board back in 2023. Now, of course, Michel, that was very different circumstances, and Altman was reinstated after a week.
But this was the tone we heard from a lot of high-profile AI and venture capital leaders. There was praise for Huang as a visionary for the big role he and Nvidia have played in the AI boom, but many were careful not to give a definitive opinion on whether Huang should be leading Nvidia.
MARTIN: So what is fueling the sentiment that Huang should come back as CEO?
BOND: Well, you know, here in Silicon Valley, there is a lot of deference to and belief in founders, and Huang is a founder. So there's this online petition urging the board to reinstate him. It has more than 160,000 names on it. Now, some of those signatures may not be real. But look; Elon Musk says he signed it. And then there's Brad Gerstner of Altimeter Capital, a major investor in Nvidia. He wrote an open letter to Nvidia's board asking it to take time to investigate and keep all its options open. And at Monday's conference, Gerstner said that Huang had been convicted in the court of public opinion when all of the facts aren't yet known.
BRAD GERSTNER: We don't want rushes to judgment. We don't want political pressure from the left or the right to force a board into action before we've even taken the time to turn over the cards and learn what was done.
BOND: And I heard again and again yesterday just how important people feel Nvidia is to the economy and to national security.
MARTIN: Although, of course, national security is a factor in why Huang is in the situation that he's in.
BOND: That's right.
MARTIN: So are these calls getting any traction with Nvidia's board?
BOND: There's no sign of that yet. It is ultimately the board's decision. Now, the board's announced an investigation into all of this, including that the woman that Huang admitted having an affair with may have been a Chinese intelligence asset and questions over whether China was getting access to the most advanced Nvidia chips. You know, The New York Times and other outlets have reported U.S. officials believe this woman was recruited by China's top spy agency. But I should say NPR has not independently confirmed those reports.
MARTIN: What are you watching for next?
BOND: Well, further fallout for American AI policy. So on Monday, the Commerce Department announced a new rule designed to make it harder for China to access top chips. That would close this loophole that this scandal has put a spotlight on. And then last night, the Justice and Commerce Department confirmed they are conducting a criminal investigation into whether Megaspeed, the Singapore-based company Nvidia was working with, was funneling restricted chips into China. And then while we wait to see who becomes Nvidia's permanent CEO, the company reports earnings this afternoon. So we'll hear publicly for the first time from its chief financial officer, who is serving as interim CEO.
MARTIN: That is NPR's Shannon Bond. Shannon, thank you.
BOND: Thanks, Michel.

title: Is the truth really out there? Studying UAP sightings
text:
On a May evening back in 1950, Evelyn Trent had just finished feeding her rabbits when, she claims, she looked up and saw a slow-moving, metallic disk-shaped object hovering above her farm. Though some dismissed it as a hoax, her account was added to a growing list of unexplained events that sparked America's first UFO craze.
At the annual McMenamins UFO Festival in McMinnville, Ore., just a few miles from Evelyn Trent's farm, there are costumes, a parade, and some theories that might be generously described as fringe: "Well, based on what I've read, it could be us from the future visiting us from, you know, the past," said one attendee, "and then it could also be trans-dimensional or inter-dimensional beings."
Fringe, but definitely something Americans seem interested in. According to a CBS News Poll, , which has led to an explosion in podcasts and documentaries on the topic.
Matthew Szydagis, one of the UFO festival's invited speakers, teaches physics at the State University of New York at Albany. He spoke to us about Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (or UAPs), or what we used to call UFOs back in the old days: "I think the possibility that at least some small fraction of UFOs or UAPs represent a non-human intelligence," Szydagis said. "That will be the greatest discovery in human history. So, of course that's going to fire people up and get their imaginations going."
Szydagis would like to believe in aliens, but he also knows that extraordinary claims demand extraordinary evidence, especially in the world of "UFOlogy," where the more extreme the claims, the more attention they get.
"We still don't have definitive evidence," Szydagis said. "We haven't been provided with a dead alien body, for instance, although claims of the existence have been made. But I think we have enough indirect evidence to say that the existence of non-human intelligence is no longer laughable, that it's not irrational."
Szydagis is part of a new Scientific Advisory Council, established by the Trump Administration, to study UAPs. The person in charge of that council is none other than respected Harvard professor Avi Loeb, former chair of the university's astronomy department.
"Now, there are some objects the U.S. government cannot figure out," Loeb said. "I would like to figure them out. Because at the very least, as an American citizen, I will be helping the Pentagon and the intelligence community fulfill their mission of, if these are human-made technologies, if they come from adversarial nations, then I can help them identify what they are and where they came from."
The things Loeb and the other council members are trying to identify are the many sightings over the years of lights and objects and movements in the sky that defy simple explanation. Someone who's experienced it firsthand? Former U.S. Navy pilot Ryan Graves, got the nation's attention back in 2023, when he recounted an experience during a training mission ten miles off the coast of Virginia Beach: "Two F-18 Super Hornets were split by a UAP," Graves said. "The object, described as a dark grey or a black cube inside of a clear sphere, came within 50 feet of the lead aircraft."
For many people, seeing no-nonsense U.S. military personnel calmly describing things they'd seen and couldn't explain, along with actual images, made the whole thing seem a lot less crazy. Graves told us, "We were seeing these things, we were nearly hitting them, and yet we're still unwilling to talk about them in our safety briefs and incorporate them into the conversation."
Graves was also recently added to the Advisory Council, tasked with getting to the bottom of things, and there are a lot of things that have been released in the last eight months: seven tranches of first-person accounts, photographs, and lots of grainy video, more than 155,000 pages of files overall.
But not enough of the good stuff, says Graves: "What's being released is not satisfactory to me. What you are seeing are very short clips from infrared sensors aboard different platforms. And ultimately, these are not the high-end sophisticated tools that are used by pilots in order to make critical decisions about whether [an] object in the air is hostile, whether it's a decoy, whether it is a threat or not. And so, I think we're left with more ambiguity."
Loeb said, "The mistake that is often made about science is the belief that, 'Oh, the data will come and guide us.' But the problem is that to collect the data, you need to put in effort. And it's often a heroic effort to get the high-quality data."
Questions linger about what exactly the government knows about UFOs, after former Air Force intelligence officer David Grusch testified to Congress that he was told of the existence of recovered UFOs.
When Rep. Nancy Mace (R-S.C.) asked whether possession of a crashed craft also meant possession of the bodies of the craft's pilot(s), Grusch replied, "As I have stated publicly already in my News Nation interview, biologics came with some of these recoveries, yeah."
Of course, evidence for all of this is "classified," leading some ufologists to call Grusch and others making claims about government conspiracies "Trust Me Bros."
Loeb, who's floated , says the Advisory Council is working to get access to as much information as possible, starting with what's been publicly released. "My role is really simple, because it's like a detective," he said. "And the worst that can happen to a detective is that the detective is starved of data. So, if I don't have data, the quality of my deliberations [is] poor. I mean, only in politics, with very little data, you can make a huge story!"
For his part, Ryan Graves started an organization called Americans for Safe Aerospace, which encourages everyone (but especially pilots) to share their stories of UAPs. And of course, he's got a podcast.
"Recently I've been astounded, in fact, that almost everyone is willing to talk about this," said Graves. "It is fighter pilots. It is commercial aviators. And I think that really speaks to how this conversation has changed over the past few years."
Asked whether he believes he'll get answers within his lifetime, Graves replied, "My lifetime, yes. We are moving towards a point in time where we're perhaps not going to get every answer we want, but we're going to potentially have the confirmation that something truly strange is happening."
Until that conformation, the truth will have to remain (as they say) out there.
Story produced by Anthony Laudato. Editor: Ed Givnish.

title: How Europe decided on 'return hubs' for migrants
text:
A group of European countries has announced plans to establish a "migrant hub" in Rwanda for rejected asylum-seekers
BRUSSELS -- A group of European countries announced on Monday that they aim to set up a “migrant hub” in Rwanda where rejected asylum-seekers could be sent from next year.
The European Union has worked for years to tighten migration rules, push down the number of asylum-seekers coming to the 27-nation bloc and increase deportations of migrants who aren’t entitled to stay. Sending people to centers outside Europe has emerged as a central element.
Here's a timeline of events that led to this agreement:
2015: Over 1 million people — the majority from war-stricken Syria — arrive in Europe seeking asylum, in what was at the time the largest migration crisis impacting the continent since World War II.
June 2016: The U.K. votes to leave the European Union in a referendum following a campaign during which those favoring Brexit use images of lines of migrants as a warning of what staying in the EU would entail.
September 2018: Sweden joins Europe's move to the right as voters boost a party that campaigned on anti-migrant sentiment and policies. It follows similar shifts in Germany, Austria and Italy as part of a backlash to the 2015 migration crisis. Denmark floats an idea it later scraps to deport migrants to a remote island once used as a research laboratory for contagious animal diseases.
September 2020: Denmark appoints a special envoy to toughen EU migration policies including setting up migrant reception centers in one or more countries outside the EU to diminish the incentive for migrants to seek asylum in Denmark and improving the deportation of rejected asylum-seekers.
April 2021: After Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, leading a center-left Social Democratic-led government, rolls out a vision of having “zero asylum-seekers," Denmark begins revoking the residency permits of some Syrian refugees.
April 2022: Britain announces a deal with Rwanda to send some asylum-seekers thousands of miles to the East African country — a plan it says will stop people-smugglers sending desperate migrants on treacherous journeys across the English Channel.
November 2023: The U.K. Supreme Court rules that the deal with Rwanda to return asylum-seekers there is unlawful because they would not be safe there. The Conservative government says it will send migrants to the African country regardless. Italian Premier Giorgia Meloni and her Albanian counterpart, Edi Rama, strike a five-year deal for Albania to shelter up to 3,000 migrants picked up by the Italian coast guard in international waters each month.
June 2024: Far-right parties make major gains in elections to the Parliament of the European Union, rattling traditional political powers. In France, President Emmanuel Macron calls a snap election that results in a boost for the anti-migration far right, weakening his own government.
July 2024: The U.K. scraps the Rwanda migration deal shortly after the Conservatives are defeated in an election, ceding power to the Labour Party under Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer.
October 2024: Italy’s government formally opens two centers in Albania where it plans to process male migrants who are intercepted in international waters. Less than a month later, a court in Italy rules against the right-wing government’s move to detain 12 migrants at the new centers.
January 2025: An Italian appeals court refuses to approve the speedy expulsion of 43 asylum seekers detained in Albania. The migrants were among 49 people who were transferred to Albania on an Italian naval ship under the five-year agreement with Albania.
March 2025: The Meloni government approves a decree expanding the use of the Albanian fast-track processing centers to include the detention of rejected asylum-seekers with deportation orders. The Albanian centers have remained substantially inactive since their opening in October, due to legal hurdles and amid wide opposition from human rights groups.
April 2025: Italian authorities transfer 40 migrants with no permission to remain in the country to the Albanian centers.
March 2026: Rwanda tells an international arbitration panel that Britain still owes it 100 million pounds ($134 million) under the refugee resettlement deal scrapped in 2024. The court dismisses Rwanda's claim.
March 2026: European lawmakers vote to ease the setting up of new migrant detention centers outside the European Union, known as “return hubs.” Any EU nation can start negotiating on its own or in small coalitions to deport migrants not to their home countries but to facilities yet to be built outside the 27-nation bloc.
June 2026: The three main bodies of the EU, the European Parliament, the European Commission and the European Council, reach agreement over migration policy to increase deportations and to allow member nations to make deals for so-called return hubs.
August 2026: A spokesperson for the Rwandan government defends the practice of establishing return hubs, saying it is “natural” for her government to negotiate with European countries and others to potentially host asylum seekers who are not allowed to live elsewhere.
Sept. 2026: Denmark and four other European Union countries agree on a model for “return hubs” in non-EU nations and say they hope to begin sending migrants to the facilities as early as 2027.
———
Ciobanu reported from Warsaw, Poland.

title: COP31 draft deal calls for 'immediate' shift away from fossil fuels
text:
COP31 co-host Australia has kicked off the second week of climate talks in Antalya with a draft political deal calling for an "immediate transition away from fossil fuels" and a "tripling" of finance for climate adaptation measures in developing countries to at least $120 billion (€109 billion).
The goal of other co-host Turkey to increase electrification of the world's economies to 35% by 2035 also features in the text. The draft emphasizes clean energy but notes that "electrification can provide co-benefits regardless of the electricity mix" — an approach that has proved divisive at the talks, with many insisting that electrification be strictly tied to renewable energy.
Language around a faster phaseout of oil, coal and gas is important because fossil-fuel producing nations have repeatedly pushed back against stronger wording in previous COP decisions.
'Deep concern' over breaching 1.5C target
"The new negotiating text contains all the necessary building blocks for a successful outcome to the conference: from the goal of climate neutrality for all industrialized countries by 2030 to a work program that can keep the 1.5-degree limit in place," said Greenpeace Germany head Martin Kaiser on Monday.
The draft expressed "deep concern" that the 1.5 Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) temperature threshold agreed at the 2015 COP in Paris to avoid runaway climate change was now out of reach. It stressed the need for "accelerating action to minimize both the magnitude and duration of any temperature overshoot and to return global warming to below 1.5C as soon as possible."
Recognizing a need to address rising carbon emissions, the draft highlighted efforts to "urgently and rapidly" scale up controversial technologies to capture and store CO2 to bring down atmospheric carbon levels.
"For the first time, all the parties here are grappling with the fact that the world will inevitably exceed 1.5 degrees. Negotiators must deliver a response," said Ani Dasgupta, president of the World Resources Institute, adding that this meant going beyond slashing emissions.
"This requires scaling carbon removal through both nature-based solutions like restoring forests and wetlands, or emerging technologies that directly capture carbon from air," he told reporters.
Kaiser, however, criticized the lack of binding commitments in the draft's resolutions. He added that Europe should work with China and the most climate-vulnerable countries to keep oil-producing nations, including Russia and countries in the Middle East, from "undermining the conference's decisions and turning them into a free pass for the oil and gas industry."
Other activists have dismissed carbon capture as a "false solution" being promoted by corporations.
Climate finance central to talks
Cosima Cassel, an expert at climate think tank E3G, was cautiously pleased with the draft's "ambitious language" but said it appeared the broad deal would now leave negotiators to "fight for trade-offs."
"The test will be whether the final decision keeps the core elements once that process plays out: ambition on overshoot, defense of the science, clean electrification and forward progress on adaptation finance," she said in a statement.
Disagreements over financing largely relate to who should bear the costs of international climate action, whether financial support should be provided through grants or loans, and how funding for developing countries can be increased.
Representatives of developing nations and small island states, regions bearing the brunt of the climate crisis, have protested climate inaction and a lack of financial support in recent days.
"Climate finance isn't an extra at these talks: it's the condition for everything else," said Rukiya Khamis, program manager for East Africa with environmental group 350.org. "It's alarming how financial pledges by wealthy, polluting countries are dropping like a stone — COP31 must stop this with a strong outcome on adaptation finance."
"Now we must fight to keep this [adaption finance] in the final decision and ensure these promises become real, grant-based money," said Harjeet Singh of the Fill The Fund campaign, which calls on rich countries and corporations to deliver the funding needed for climate-related loss and damage, such as homes destroyed by floods and harvests ruined by drought.
"Communities are suffering devastating losses and damages today precisely because we failed to deliver adaptation at the right time," added Singh.
Draft shows 'seriousness' on major issues
At 18 pages and 144 items, the draft will be the focus of lengthy discussions in the coming days as delegates try to come to an agreement by Friday. Some observers went so far as to say the document's scope was too wide to be taken seriously.
"The draft final declaration reads like a Christmas wish list," said Niklas Höhne, a climate policy expert at the NewClimate Institute in Germany. "There are even several points on which we will obviously not be able to reach a consensus, including for example the proposal that developed countries achieve net-zero emissions by 2030."
But Chris Bowen, chief of negotiations and Australia's minister for climate change and energy, appeared optimistic.
"The general tenor and tone [of the talks] has been very constructive," he told reporters Monday. "Parties have come to me with strong views about various things, as you'd expect […] [but] they've also come in the spirit of cooperation, the spirit of respect and a spirit where parties have said to me that they want to help get an outcome."
David Waskow, director of WRI's International Climate Initiative, said the draft text showed a level of "seriousness" on important issues like finance, electrification, oceans, overshoot scenarios and emissions of greenhouse gases including methane, which has a warming impact more than 80 times stronger than CO2.
"The question is whether the level of ambition on those issues is carried through into the final outcome here," said Waskow. "And that's what we need to be watching closely over the coming days."
Additional reporting by Tim Schauenberg in Antalya.
Update, November 17, 2026: This article has been updated with additional reactions to the draft text.

title: Few voters approve of the way Trump is handling AI: ‘Don’t believe he has the right priorities’
text:
Few Americans approve of President Donald Trump’s approach to artificial intelligence, according to new polling, as concerns about the technology cut across party lines.
Just 26 percent of registered voters approved of Trump’s handling of AI in the latest Reuters-Ipsos survey, conducted earlier this month, while 56 percent disapproved. Only 16 percent said the administration has “AI risks about right.”
“The American people, simply put, don’t believe he has the right priorities, that the Trump administration has the right priorities,” CNN chief data analyst Harry Enten said Tuesday while reviewing the findings.
Enten also pointed to a recent CNN survey showing that Americans in both parties are more likely to say AI will hurt society than help it.
The poll comes as Americans' fears about AI grow. While officials haven’t connected a recent string of tech troubles - such as Apple, flight traffic and banking systems going offline - to AI, that hasn’t stopped some from speculating they are connected. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Tuesday that if the recent airline ground stop was connected to an AI attack, he would let the public know.
In the recent poll, 66 percent of Democrats said AI will hurt society, compared with 17 percent who said it will help. Republicans were less pessimistic, but still expected harm more than benefits: 47 percent said it will hurt society, while 33 percent said it will help.
“Trump really isn’t listening to his own base on this issue,” Enten said. “He is dismissing the concerns of his own base. That might have been why there was depressed Republican turnout in this midterm election because we’ve seen it on issue after issue.”
Trump has largely favored a light-touch approach to AI regulation as the technology advances rapidly and the U.S. competes with China for dominance in the field.
“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT,” Trump wrote on Truth Social in September. “And the U.S.A. has that, in spades!”
The same month, he rebranded AI as “super intelligence” and reached an agreement with tech leaders to adopt voluntary safeguards and police themselves — a commitment he described as “morally binding.”
“I think I'm seeing tremendous self-policing, and they understand that they have to self-police,” the president told reporters, while standing alongside SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg and other tech titans. “This is going to be all for the good, and we're going to have it be nice and safe.”
The voluntary agreement came amid warnings from some of the industry’s own leaders about AI’s potential harms.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned last May that the technology could eliminate half of all entry-level white-collar jobs within one to five years. In September, current and former employees of Anthropic said they believe AI could potentially kill all humans within the next 10 years.
Earlier this month, a scandal involving one of AI’s most prominent leaders also spilled into the White House, when Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO amid scrutiny of his affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy. The woman allegedly helped facilitate shipments of Nvidia chips — used to train and run AI models — to Chinese firms.
The president was reportedly warned earlier this year about Huang’s ties to the suspected spy. In recent days, he has called the Nvidia co-founder “honorable” and said he believes Huang was unaware of the connection.
On Monday, the Trump administration issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers

title: UK urged to overhaul youth benefits as one million young people drift out of work and study
text:
The review’s author says only Romania fares worse in Europe on youth inactivity, even though young Britons are less likely to be unemployed than their peers in France, Spain or Italy.
A government-commissioned review has called for a separate welfare system for young people in the United Kingdom, cutting back some cash payments in favour of work placements and paying employers to hire those left out of the labour market.
The 267-page report, led by former Labour minister Alan Milburn, demands a “complete system reset” in how the state treats 16- to 24-year-olds who are Not in Employment, Education or Training, known as NEETs.
Their number passed one million earlier this year. The review warns it could reach 1.27 million by 2031 without action.
"A lost generation is not a fact of life... it’s a moral crisis," Milburn told reporters at the launch on Tuesday.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government will publish its full response next year, followed by draft legislation. Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden called the report "a radical blueprint for a new settlement with young people". He said ministers had already agreed to some measures, including more tailored help for young jobseekers.
Out of work, or out of reach?
The review aims to cut the NEET rate from 13% to about 5% by 2036, close to the level in the Netherlands.
“Across Europe, only Romania had a higher NEET rate than the UK in 2025,” Milburn wrote.
The headline jobless figures tell a different story. Office for National Statistics data published on Tuesday showed UK youth unemployment fell to 15.1% in the three months to September, though that remains more than three times the overall rate of 4.6%.
That puts the UK slightly below the EU average of 15.5% for under-25s in September, according to Eurostat. Young people fare far worse in Spain (22.8%), France (21.9%) and Italy (19.9%). Germany (7.5%) and the Netherlands (8.8%) are well ahead.
The gap between the two measures points to the problem Milburn’s review is trying to tackle. Many young Britons are not counted as unemployed because they have stopped looking for work altogether.
Across the EU, Eurostat puts the NEET rate for 15- to 29-year-olds at 11% in 2025, down from 15.2% a decade earlier. Italy has made the biggest gains, cutting its rate from 25.7% to 13.3%.
Less cash, more support
The report’s main proposal is a dedicated welfare system for the young that puts placements and support ahead of payments. It admits this could mean that “some people get less financial support at the beginning of their benefit claim than under the current system”.
Milburn argued that the present system can be “detrimental to their longer term life chances” by allowing young people to stay out of work.
Young people would face a “duty to engage”, meaning those who turn down offers of work could lose some benefits. Each would be given a dedicated adviser and a personalised route into employment. A national network of local services combining careers advice, job support, health care and practical help would be in place by 2029.
The proposals are likely to be politically sensitive. Former prime minister Keir Starmer was forced to water down his own welfare reforms after a revolt within the Labour Party.
To encourage hiring, the review suggests raising the earnings threshold at which employers start paying tax on wages for workers aged 21 to 24. It also proposes a £3,000 (€3,400) payment to firms that take on someone who has been NEET for six months, with extra help for small businesses and for hiring young people with disabilities.
“Rather than simply writing young people a short-term check, we have to build them a long-term future,” Milburn said.
‘Easy to get burnout’
Milburn described the UK jobs market as “very fragile”, and young jobseekers say the competition is fierce.
Abigail Gomes, 21, has been looking for work for seven months since graduating from university. “There are just too many young people applying for one job,” she told AFP.
She said the constant cycle of applications and rejections “can create anxiety and depression among young people”, and that “it’s easy to get burnout”. Gomes has recently been offered a temporary retail job over Christmas.

title: American basketball player’s Nigeria trip ends in arrest after officials spot him abandoning suspicious bags
text:
A U.S. basketball player was arrested at a Nigerian airport last Wednesday after allegedly attempting to smuggle a large quantity of cannabis into the country in his luggage.
Greene Da'monte Khiree, 28, a native of Savannah, Georgia, was linked to two checked bags containing 75 pounds of cannabis at Murtala Muhammed International Airport, according to Nigerian officials. Khiree reportedly arrived in Lagos aboard an Emirates flight from Thailand via Dubai.
While at the airport, Khiree appeared to abandon two checked bags containing a potent strain of cannabis known as "loud," according to Nigeria's National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA).
"The suspect, who was placed under discreet surveillance upon arrival, was observed abandoning his two checked-in bags before attempting to exit the airport with only his carry-on luggage," officials said.
He was subsequently apprehended in the airport's parking lot, according to the NDLEA.
Although Khiree claimed he was visiting Nigeria to build connections for his basketball career, a forensic examination of his phone reportedly uncovered evidence of drug trafficking.
"The suspect, a native of Savannah, Georgia, USA, who claimed he has lived in Thailand since October 2025 where he plays professional basketball, said he came to Nigeria on holiday to build networks for his basketball career," officials said.
"A forensic examination of his mobile phone revealed information pointing to his knowledge of and involvement in the drug trafficking activity."
Investigators also found that both bags bore Khiree's name tag and contained tracking devices. Authorities confirmed that the cannabis originated in Thailand.

title: Investors look to Nvidia's earnings and Anthropic's IPO to refresh the tech rally
text:
Get Mike Santoli's Market Memo in your inbox first. SUBSCRIBE HERE
I've spent the past 20 years pushing back against the periodically popular notion that markets are replaying the late-1990s and early-2000s tech bubble and bust.
We've simply never matched the levels of gross overvaluation, pervasive public greed, fevered IPO issuance, corporate malinvestment and Wall Street malfeasance that set up a generational market peak, a halving of the S&P 500 over two-and-a-half years and a lost decade for stocks.
We still haven't. Even if June was the peak in AI speculative fervor, as seems possible, and if Oct. 6 proves to have been a consequential broad-market top, the major indexes simply never stretched far enough into the thin air to make a potential retrenchment nearly as damaging as the early 2000s were.
Still, in a more muted fashion, markets have been behaving in ways that generate uncomfortable comparisons to past buying climaxes accompanying a technology revolution.
There is still room and time for the market to prove that the messy sell-down in AI-reliant growth stocks is simply a painful adjustment phase and the S&P 500's six-month purgatorial range a mid-cycle refresh. But it will need to start getting on with it.
Everyone wants to celebrate the way the market has absorbed the damage to semiconductors and other AI-buildout plays, rendering it a controlled demolition rather than indiscriminate destruction.
The Financial Times Unhedged newsletter on Monday called it "The perfect sell-off," the same day the Wall Street Journal cheered, "When Nvidia Stumbled, Equal-Weight Funds Delivered."
This is true, as far as it goes. A rush into defensive and "quality" stocks has largely offset the drag from Nvidia's $2 trillion market-cap loss from its October peak.
But recent defensive leadership, especially from low-growth consumer staples and Big Pharma, sends a less-reassuring macro message, and those groups lack the earnings momentum, narrative appeal or market-cap heft to carry a bull market to new heights.
BTIG technical strategist Jonathan Krinsky has noted echoes of the 2000 period when "boring" defensive stocks ripped as tech rolled over, supporting the tape for a while. Barclays equity desk noted Monday that the "quality factor" basket of stocks just had one of the best 100-day runs ever of the past 20 years.
And JP Morgan here plots the stampede into "low-volatility" stocks, mirroring the hasty retreat from "high-momentum" areas. There's room here for defensives to get even more popular before tripping multi-year extremes, but is that what an index investor should root for?
As for the ascendance of everyone's favorite, the equal-weighted S&P 500, Ned Davis Research analyst London Stockton this month noted that just over 50% of S&P 500 stocks were outperforming the index itself in 2026. Sounds healthy, right? Only to a point.
He explains: "Levels [of stocks outperforming the index] above 58% have most often occurred in and around years where there has been a large bear market." The current phase follows a period when leadership was extremely narrow, producing a "resemblance of the prior three years (2023-2025) to the two years prior to the last Tech bubble (1998-1999) with a very small percentage of companies outperforming the overall S&P 500.
"It is not likely that we are in a situation like in 2000," Stockton concludes, "but this highlights the importance that these large tech stocks at the very least do not decline substantially for the S&P 500 to continue rallying higher."
There are other straws in the wind that harken to prior tech busts: The Federal Reserve is trying to restrain the corporate sector from overheating in the latter part of a cycle, same as in 1999. Retail traders have maniacally bought the cascading decline in Nvidia shares the past week or so, invoking the voracious dip-buying made famous in the late-'90s which worked until it failed spectacularly. The market's refusal to pay up for sizzling earnings growth raises alarms about whether they are pulled forward, unsustainable or overstated; profits from 2000 were later revised down radically.
And Nvidia's alleged breach of chip-export rules and the forced departure of CEO Jensen Huang are a reminder that major corporate scandals were a key feature of the Tech Bubble's prolonged reckoning, though nothing resembling the multiple accounting frauds of that era are implied here.
Again, this is the kind of litany of worry and woe that gets recited each time a tech-propelled bull market breaks stride for a bit; more often than not a recovery follows to clear the gloom.
Perhaps Nvidia's results on Tuesday clearing the way for the company to restart stock buybacks and the final allocation of Anthropic's IPO shares will refresh the tech bid. With luck, the huge "hyperscaler" tech-platform stocks will move back to the fore as well-funded stewards of a more sober AI expansion.
Maybe, after weeks of Wall Street insisting that hedge-fund tech-stock positioning is scraping multi-year lows, this will finally presage an upside pain trade.
The vaunted seasonal, post-election tailwinds that the consensus was expecting to fill market's sails and lift the indexes from the floor of an enervating six-month trading range are running late. They need to arrive quite soon. Otherwise, the soggy tape - along with signs of ebbing liquidity reflected in Bitcoin weakness a strong dollar and jumpier equity volatility - will make those tech-bust echoes louder.
John Kolovos of Macro Risk Advisors on the latest reading: "Despite pervasive bearish sentiment and the average stock trading near new highs, our historical studies suggest the market remains vulnerable to disappointment. With defensive leadership still dominating, risk appetite weak, and financial conditions still tight, maintaining a short-term cautious/bearish stance still seems warranted."
-Twenty years ago this week, I wrote a cover story for Barron's that antagonized plenty of friends in the stock-trading profession by foretelling a future of fast, cheap electronic markets that has largely come to pass.
Called "Death of the Floor," the piece detailed the regulatory, technological and behavioral shifts that were ushering in high-frequency, low-touch trading and pressuring the old exchange model.
Reading it now, the conclusions seem utterly obvious and inevitable, though at the time there were still 2,500 NYSE floor brokers and specialists trying to remain in the middle of most trades.
"For the specialists who manage trading in individual stocks and for the floor brokers who depend on the in-person auction model, a tough challenge is becoming even tougher. To stay in the game, they must master cybertrading. For the small investor, this is almost entirely good news. Trading costs should continue to fall, while the likelihood of getting the best price should improve."
Happily, exchanges have adapted and evolved – to zero commissions, thousands of ETFs and microsecond executions - and we have a market that can handle multiples of the capital flow that was routine back then.
If I have one regret about the piece, it's that my good friend and former colleague Bob Pisani thought the CNBC reporter skeleton illustrating the article was meant to depict him.
I assured him, many times, that it was not.
-Almost every business relies heavily on its most loyal repeat customers. But this skew seems extreme for online-betting companies.
A Bloomberg piece picked up here by Yahoo Finance reports that one-third of all sports bettors produces some 97% of revenue at digital sportsbooks. It says the 1% most active gamblers on average lost 78 cents of each dollar bet, twice the loss rate of the norm among all customers.
One can view this as simply paying for entertainment (I "lose" 100 cents of every dollar I place on a movie ticket), but the social disapproval toward the industry seems to have grown.
Add it to the swirl of issues surrounding the legal and de-facto decriminalized wagering industry.
Perceived hostility of Congressional Democrats to prediction-markets venues taking sports bets in states that haven't explicitly approved sports gambling is seen as a plus for DraftKings and Flutter.
Meantime, Robinhood has blurred the lines between investing and gambling by aggressively expanding into prediction markets. And on Monday it was reported that Kalshi has looked to combine investing and betting from the opposite direction, acquiring a brokerage firm in order to offer stock trading to its prediction-markets clientele.
Adults should be free to behave unwisely with their money in search of a windfall. But brokers promoting the negative-sum game of wagering while professing to help the little guy accumulate long-term wealth sends a dissonant message.
The ducks that were quacking loudly ahead of SpaceX's June IPO are much quieter in advance of Anthropic's planned debut this week.
Here is the year-to-date performance of two ETFs that hold shares of recent new listings, Renaissance IPO and First Trust US Equity Opportunities, relative to the S&P 500.
As of June 12, when SpaceX priced, these funds had gone vertical as the public worked itself into an anticipatory lather, the Renaissance fund running ahead of the S&P by some 20 percentage points in the prior six months.
Since then, the IPO funds have deflated (both now have large positions in SpaceX, of course) and there's a bit more focus on whether Anthropic's target valuation is justified given the vast rethink of the AI-proliferation thesis.
All else being equal, a more favorable setup now versus then for a market being asked to swallow a new $1 trillion-plus ticker.

title: Hidden ecosystem: Scientists discover 245 animals living inside a single deep-sea rock
text:
Deep beneath the Pacific Ocean, scientists have discovered tiny hidden ecosystems inside metal-rich rocks that take millions of years to form. Researchers examined 244 nodules and found more than 4,100 animals living in their cracks and cavities, including unique communities unlike those in the surrounding seafloor mud. These remarkable miniature habitats could now be threatened by deep-sea mining for valuable metals.
Deep beneath the Pacific Ocean, scientists have uncovered a surprising world of tiny animals living inside metal-rich rocks that take millions of years to form. These rocks, known as polymetallic nodules, contain miniature cracks and cavities that provide shelter for creatures smaller than a millimeter.
Although they may look like ordinary stones, these nodules offer something unusual in the deep ocean. They create hard surfaces in an environment dominated by soft mud, while their internal spaces provide additional habitats for marine life.
Polymetallic nodules are dark, roughly fist-sized formations made largely of iron and manganese oxides. They grow at an extraordinarily slow pace, often adding only a few millimeters over a million years. Found at ocean depths ranging from 4,000 to 6,000 meters, they can remain on the seafloor for millions of years.
Researchers set out to investigate the tiny organisms living within these ancient formations and determine how important the nodules are to deep-sea biodiversity.
Dr. Tanja Stratmann, a deep-sea ecologist and one of the study's three lead authors, explains: "In our study we show that the sizes of cracks inside the nodules are large enough to provide home to animals that are smaller than a millimeter in size."
Hundreds of Tiny Animals Found Inside a Single Rock
To explore these hidden habitats, the research team collected nodules from the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, a vast region of the central Pacific Ocean. They used specialized sampling equipment, including box corers that collect sections of the seafloor and remotely operated diving robots capable of working at extreme depths.
Back in the laboratory, the researchers carefully opened the nodules and extracted the tiny animals concealed within their cracks and crevices.
The results revealed an unexpectedly rich community of marine life. Across 244 nodules, the team identified 4,139 individual animals. Each nodule contained an average of 17 animals, but one particularly crowded specimen sheltered an astonishing 245 individuals.
The discovery shows that these rocks are more than simple surfaces where marine organisms can attach themselves. Their intricate internal structures create three-dimensional living spaces, allowing animals to inhabit protected areas within the nodules themselves.
Dr. Coral Diaz-Recio Lorenzo explains: "The crevices in the polymetallic nodules function as small shelters and provide home to animals that we do not encounter in the soft sediment of the seafloor."
Hidden Ecosystems Unlike Those on the Surrounding Seafloor
Although the nodules contained fewer animals than the surrounding muddy sediment, their contribution to deep-sea life was still substantial.
For roundworms (nematodes), the number living inside the nodules amounted to approximately 10% of the number found in the surrounding sediment. For tiny crustaceans (copepods), the figure was about 25%.
However, the most important finding was not simply how many animals the researchers discovered. It was how different the communities inside the rocks were from those living in the nearby mud.
Genetic analyses revealed that the animals inhabiting the nodules formed distinctive communities. Remarkably, these communities remained highly similar across locations separated by large distances (up to 1,000 km), even though they differed significantly from the organisms found in the surrounding seafloor sediment.
This suggests that polymetallic nodules support specialized habitats that are not easily replaced by other parts of the deep ocean. Their cracks and cavities offer living conditions that certain organisms appear to depend on.
Deep-Sea Mining Could Destroy These Ancient Habitats
The findings raise serious concerns about the potential environmental consequences of deep-sea mining.
Polymetallic nodules contain economically valuable metals, including nickel, cobalt, and copper. These resources have attracted interest in industrial mining operations that would collect the nodules directly from the ocean floor.
However, removing the rocks would also eliminate the miniature habitats they contain, along with the animals living inside them.
One example is Thurammina sp. 1, a single-celled organism found particularly frequently within the nodules. This species appears especially well adapted to the sheltered spaces inside the rocks, making it an example of the specialized life that could be threatened by their removal.
The problem is that these habitats cannot quickly recover. Because polymetallic nodules require millions of years to develop, new ones would not form within a human lifetime. Mining could therefore eliminate ecosystems that would take geological timescales to replace.
Prof. Sabine Gollner warns: "Our findings point out that commercial mining may result in an irreversible loss of undescribed and unique biodiversity associated to nodules. This needs to be considered in environmental management of deep-sea mining."
Scientists Race to Understand What Could Be Lost
The discovery highlights an often overlooked aspect of ocean conservation. Protecting deep-sea ecosystems requires more than safeguarding large, visible animals. It also means considering the microscopic and nearly microscopic organisms that inhabit specialized environments hidden within the seafloor.
An important question remains unanswered: If deep-sea mining destroys these nodule communities, could some species disappear entirely?
Researchers still need to determine whether organisms that depend on the nodules also inhabit other parts of the ocean. If certain species are restricted to these habitats, removing the nodules could potentially contribute to their global extinction.
Understanding where these animals live and how widely they are distributed will be essential for identifying areas that need protection and evaluating the potential ecological damage caused by deep-sea mining.
To investigate further, Dr. Tanja Stratmann is currently participating in an international research expedition to the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, where scientists are continuing to study the ecosystems associated with polymetallic nodules.
This expedition and other follow-up investigations are independently funded through the JPIOcean projects MiningImpact 2 and 3.
The findings reveal that even a single rock on the deep ocean floor can support a surprisingly complex community of life. As interest in harvesting the ocean's mineral resources grows, scientists are working to understand these hidden ecosystems before habitats that took millions of years to form are permanently lost.

title: On this day in space! Nov. 15, 1988: The 300-foot Green Bank Telescope collapses suddenly, leaving a huge pile of wreckage in West Virginia
text:
On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. It happened at 9:46 p.m. on a clear night with no strong winds.
When the observatory staff showed up to work the next morning, they were greeted by a huge pile of wreckage. The telescope collapsed under its own weight after a key structural element called a "gusset plate" failed. This was one of four connecting plates that held the telescope's large, metal beams together. Investigators found that these gusset plates were not built to last the 26 years that this telescope had been in use.
Three years later, construction began on a new telescope. The Green Bank Telescope was even bigger and more sensitive, and it began science operations in 2001.
Why it mattered
When the 300-foot telescope first debuted, it was not just the United States' largest radio observatory, but the largest such facility in the world. But its quick construction — just two years — led to it having to be significantly upgraded later.
"In 1970, the 300-foot’s surface had become so warped from maintenance crews, snow, and its own weight that a new finer-meshed aluminum surface was installed," the website for the National Radio Astronomy Observatory reads. "A larger traveling feed was also installed at the prime focus."
The collapse, however, was no one's fault. "Unforeseeable stress factors cracked a steel connector plate," wrote the NRAO.
During its years of observations, the 300-foot telescope contirbuted to the discovery of dark matter and the realization that pulsars come from supernova explosions.
"One of the most important products to come out of the 300-foot telescope was an all-sky survey of radio objects called the Green Bank 6cm Survey. Nearly every northern hemisphere radio object studied by any other telescope is from a catalog compiled using this telescope," reads the NRAO website.
Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube.

title: US loses measles elimination status after 26 years amid record case numbers
text:
After more than two decades, the US has lost its measles-free status, following two years of record case numbers and deaths.
The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a specialised service of the United Nations, determined the US has had uninterrupted transmission of the same strain of measles for more than 12 months.
Dr Jarbas Barbosa, director of PAHO, announced that Mexico and Bolivia have also lost their measles elimination status, attributing the resurgence in the region to persistent "gaps in vaccination".
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said it was committed to "regaining measles elimination status" by expanding access to vaccines.
The US has seen 5,400 cases of measles this year alone, with 10 measles-related deaths, the most the country has seen since the 1990s.
The measles virus - with its signature blotchy red rash - used to infect millions of children a year before a vaccine was invented. The extremely contagious virus can be fatal, and some patients can experience long-term complications including encephalitis and immune amnesia, which resets the immune system, leaving it with only limited ability to respond to new infections.
The US recommends two measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) shots for children between ages one and six, which is 97% effective in protecting against the illness.
PAHO, a group within the World Health Organization, revoked the US's measles-elimination after determining that the virus had circulated nonstop for more than a year.
"These figures are a serious warning for our region," PAHO's director Barbosa said at a news conference on Tuesday. "Measles is resurging globally amid persistent gaps in vaccination."
He added that Canada, which lost its status of having eliminated measles last year after seeing several large outbreaks, has made strides this year to interrupt transmission.
Daniel Salas, the executive manager of immunisations at PAHO, said that the US and others who lost elimination status would be required to submit corrective action plans outlining how they would attempt to improve vaccination rates.
US Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr Kennedy has attempted to make a series of sweeping changes to US vaccine recommendations and policies. The vaccine sceptic has also frequently cast doubt on the safety of MMR shot, as vaccination rates have declined across the US in recent years.
Kennedy has argued that the rise in measles cases started before he took the helm at HHS and that neighbouring countries have also seen more infections.
Responding to Tuesday's announcement, the CDC said the agency and its partners were "committed to stopping measles outbreaks, protecting Americans, and regaining measles elimination status".
"Together, we will encourage MMR vaccination, expand access to vaccines, and help communities close gaps in protection," the agency said.
CDC Director Erica Schwartz said the measles elimination designation was not what protected Americans.
"Vaccination does," she said. "We know where transmission is occurring and we've invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach those communities."
In a post on social media, Kennedy said: "I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles."
"We are working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust," he also said. "We will answer families' questions honestly about vaccine benefits and risks and work with trusted health care providers and community leaders to prevent measles, limit its spread, and support timely treatment."
The UK, Spain and Austria were among European nations that lost their measles-free status earlier this year, along with countries including Russia, Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan.
Nuwan Gunawardhana, an assistant professor of medicine with Columbia University Irving Medical Center, said the US losing its elimination status was "a huge leap backwards".
The US was the first country to eliminate measles in the Americas thanks to vaccination campaigns, noted William Moss, a paediatric infectious disease specialist at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.
Dr Gunawardhana said it took massive efforts from public health officials and clinicians to build trust with patients to increase uptake of the MMR vaccine, leading to decades in the US with few infections and deaths.
But that trust has been steadily eroding since the Covid-19 pandemic, when Dr Gunawardhana said patients were confronted with misinformation about the safety of vaccines and lost even more trust in public health systems.
The vaccination rate for MMR across the US has fallen to 92.4%, below the 95% level that provides herd immunity, which limits the spread of measles and protects those who cannot get vaccinated, including newborns.
An outbreak in Pennsylvania has infected over 1,400 people - likely a large underestimate - and killed seven people, according to state officials.
Kennedy, the health secretary, has sparred with Pennsylvania officials over how it is counting the measles deaths, with CDC declining for now to record some of the deaths in its database.
Last year, the health secretary fired all the members of a top vaccine advisory panel and replaced them with his own appointees, some of whom were vaccine critics.
The panel recommended a number of vaccine changes - including no longer requiring the Hepatitis B vaccine for all newborns - but those recommendations were blocked by a federal judge.
President Donald Trump this year also cast doubt on the safety of the MMR vaccine, issuing an executive order for the shot to be split into three separate immunisations for measles, mumps and rubella, a move public health experts say is costly and could sow confusion about an already safe vaccine.
Doctors and public health officials say the misinformation from Kennedy and Trump has played a major role in falling vaccination rates.
"It's confusing patients. It's confusing families," Dr Gunawardhana said. "We need a clear message from the top."
The federal government's vaccine manoeuvres have left public health officials and states to fill in the gaps, offering their own separate recommendations upholding decades-long practices.

title: Trump nominates Chris LaNeve as army chief after Hegseth fired predecessor
text:
Donald Trump has nominated Gen Chris LaNeve to be the US army’s top officer, making permanent his interim service after the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, unexpectedly fired his predecessor in April.
LaNeve had been serving as Hegseth’s senior military commander before his nomination for a fourth star and service as vice-chief of staff of the army in February.
“For 36 years, I’ve served in the U.S. Army, currently as the Vice Chief of Staff,” LaNeve said in a statement released by the Pentagon. “I’m deeply honored by the President’s trust and confidence for the nomination to serve as the Chief of Staff of the U.S. Army and if confirmed, I look forward to continuing to serve our Solders, their families and our nation.”
Two months later, Hegseth fired the army chief of staff, Gen Randy George. While the firing has never been explained, George had insisted on an official investigation into an unauthorized 28 March army helicopter flyover near the Tennessee home of musician Kid Rock, which Hegseth blocked.
LaNeve’s relatively short tenure as a four-star general has raised questions among Democrats and Republicans, according to reporting from the Wall Street Journal.
LaNeve, 59, graduated from the University of Arizona in 1990 and later earned master’s degrees from Central Michigan University and the US Army Command and General Staff College. He has served in a wide variety of command roles, including a rotation as the commander of the 82nd Airborne Division and the 8th Army in Korea.

title: Trump in Asia for Putin, Xi summit; possible Kim meeting
text:
President Trump arrived Tuesday in the Philippines to start a multiday swing in Asia, where he's scheduled to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and China's President Xi Jinping for a highly anticipated summit later this week.
After landing in Manila, Mr. Trump met with the leaders of the Quad nations that have sought to counter China's influence in the Asia Pacific region, a relationship Mr. Trump described as "very special." Those nations are Australia, India and Japan, as well as the United States.
Mr. Trump announced an $85 million investment in artificial intelligence software, describing it as the "greatest opportunity for economic growth since the Industrial Revolution."
There were , with demonstrators holding signs reading "Trump Out," drawings of him as a clown or devil, and signs calling on the public to reject an AI hub named Pax Silica.
Mr. Trump acknowledged that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent have "two lines of thought" on how to handle China, adding that "they handled that very well."
Ahead of his departure from Washington Monday, Mr. Trump called it a "big trip" and said he may also meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in China. After arriving, he said Kim "would like to" come, but "we'll see what happens."
The meeting between Mr. Trump, Xi and Putin, which marks the , is expected to center on decreasing the proliferation of nuclear weapons, the White House said, and comes as the wars in Iran and Ukraine remain in focus.
Mr. Trump said Monday they would discuss denuclearization, which he called a "tough subject," as well as Iran and Ukraine, although an official said over the weekend that Ukraine was not expected to be discussed.
In Manila, the president will attend the annual Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit. He will meet with leaders of Japan, India and Australia on security in the Indo-Pacific on Tuesday. He's also scheduled to sign a trade deal with Thailand and attend a dinner with leaders of the Southeast Asian nations and other regional leaders, the White House said.
On Wednesday, the president is set to hold a state visit and lunch banquet with Philippine President Bongbong Marcos at the presidential palace, before departing for Shenzhen, China. There, he'll meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit with APEC leaders, and on Thursday, hold the meeting with Putin and Xi. Mr. Trump said Tuesday that he would be open to a one-on-one meeting with Putin, but he didn't know if it had been scheduled.
Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk is expected to join the president on the trip, according to a senior White House official, but will not be part of the meeting with Putin and Xi.
