Mr. Trump's trip to Asia comes after he for a summit with Xi, where he touted making "fantastic trade deals" and acknowledged a shared desire to end the U.S.-Iran conflict. Xi also visited the U.S. in September, marking his first in over a decade, as the two countries extended a tariff truce.
"I think the president does intend to talk about Iran in the trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin," a senior U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told reporters on a call.
It will be Mr. Trump's third face-to-face meeting with Xi this year.
As for Putin, Mr. Trump and the Russian president last met in Alaska in August 2025 for a on ending the war in Ukraine. But the talks failed to yield a ceasefire that the U.S. was seeking.
Mr. Trump's trip to Asia also coincides with issues back at home, including the recent revelations regarding an affair between , the former CEO of chipmaker Nvidia, and a suspected Chinese spy. Beijing has said it was not involved.
Huang, who has a relationship with Mr. Trump, traveled on Air Force One during his May trip to China, and he and his wife were at the head table when Mr. Trump hosted Xi in Washington for a state dinner in September. White House officials said they do not think the Nvidia situation will loom over the trip.
"We do not negotiate American export controls. These are national security matters that we develop in the administration ... and we don't expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we're there," an official said.
When asked Monday if Secretary of State Marco Rubio had told him that the woman with whom Huang was having an affair, Alice Huang, was suspected of being a spy, Mr. Trump said he didn't know if she was, saying, "I haven't heard that." Mr. Trump also said it "isn't a bad idea" for Jensen Huang to be reinstated at Nvidia, but he also added that he recommended Apple's Tim Cook for the job.
Both Bessent and Lutnick are traveling with the president. Bessent last week accused Lutnick of failing to prevent China from getting some of Nvidia's most advanced chips.
Mr. Trump told reporters before he left that he was not considering replacing Lutnick.
The Nvidia Board of Directors announced Tuesday morning that it would be creating a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee. Mr. Trump said on Tuesday that he believed that is a "good idea."

title: Dak Prescott's touchdown tosses aren't enough to offset another porous Cowboys defense
text:
The only other time Dak Prescott threw five touchdown passes in a game, Dallas was finishing off the first of three consecutive 12-win playoff seasons
FRISCO, Texas -- The only other time Dak Prescott threw five touchdown passes in a game, Dallas was finishing off the first of three consecutive 12-win playoff seasons.
The Cowboys played decent defense five years ago. Now they're well into a second consecutive season of showing no clue how to stop just about anybody.
That means they're working on a third consecutive year without a trip to the postseason — and wasting back-to-back strong seasons from an 11th-year quarterback with an average annual salary of $60 million.
“I think that we have a talented enough offense and a good enough group to score every time we have the ball,” Prescott said after tying his career high with five TD tosses in a 46-40 loss to San Francisco. “Now, to say that we’re going to do that every time wouldn’t be right, wouldn’t be fair to the NFL and to anybody and everybody that we play. And yeah, they do have to get us to stop. They know that.”
That defense does get a stop from time to time. But big plays are a huge problem.
The Cowboys (4-6), who play Tennessee (1-8) on Sunday, allowed Christian McCaffrey to become the first running back in NFL history with two touchdown catches of at least 65 yards in the same game. They covered 74 and 66 yards.
Deebo Samuel ran 70 yards for a touchdown on a reverse. Running back Kaelon Black ran over fellow rookie Caleb Downs and pushed aside Cobie Durant on a 25-yard scoring run.
Dallas has allowed at least one touchdown of 50-plus yards in three consecutive games, and just gave up the most yards at home (584) in franchise history. The nine plays of at least 50 yards allowed this season are nearly twice as many as any other NFL team.
Coach Brian Schottenheimer used “unacceptable” and “atrocious” in the answer to the first question after the loss to the Niners. The second question was about his confidence in Christian Parker, a first-time defensive coordinator at 34 years ago, youngest in that role in franchise history.
“We’re going to watch all the film and there’s a lot of things we got to figure out because like I said, I haven’t been around a situation like this where the defense was that poor in the second half,” Schottenheimer said. “What’s killing us, missed tackles and explosive plays.”
Receiver George Pickens had the best game of what has been a mostly disappointing second season with the Cowboys. His three touchdown catches were a career best, and he had season highs in targets (18), catches (11) and yards (145). Now Dallas just has to figure out how to win when he goes off. The Cowboys have lost both of his 100-yard games.
It's getting to the point where there are no words to describe how bad the Dallas defense has been in both of Schottenheimer's seasons. Call it the curse of the Micah Parsons trade, since the Cowboys sent one of the game's best defensive players to Green Bay a week before Schottenheimer's head coaching debut last year.
Prescott did a good job keeping the outcome in doubt after Dallas fell behind 38-19 in the third quarter. But he reached that not-so-magic number of at least 50 passing attempts, going 30 of 51. The Cowboys are 3-7 when he throws that many passes. It's probably not a good thing that he leads the NFL with 387 throws.
Can a franchise continue to be called “America’s Team” when visiting fans make a home game feel like a road game? It’s not unusual for there to be plenty of those fans at any NFL game, particularly when the 49ers travel. But this strong tint of red appeared unlike anything in the 17 years since AT&T Stadium opened.
“Tricked myself and told myself early on that the red was for my high school,” Prescott said. “And at the end of the day, all I asked for is a great environment to play this game. And unfortunately, their fans were more present than ours, but it created a great atmosphere. So, we take the good out of it one way or another.”
Schottenheimer said ankle injuries for right guard Tyler Booker and cornerback DaRon Bland were the most significant issues coming out of the game.
40 — The Cowboys have had three games in franchise history where they scored at least 40 points and didn't win. Two have been under Schottenheimer. The other was a 40-40 tie against Green Bay last season.
If the Cowboys aren't 6-6 after facing the bottom-feeding Titans and the decimated Philadelphia Eagles, they will be playing out the string in the five games after Thanksgiving. There are four potential playoff teams in that finishing stretch.

title: Klopp wants Infantino out as FIFA candidate deadline looms
text:
Germany coach Jürgen Klopp has become the latest prominent football figure to call for change at the top of FIFA.
"Regarding Gianni Infantino, surely the next person to come along can do a better job," he said on Sunday.
But with time running out before the November 18 deadline for new candidates for the presidency of world football's governing body, Infantino is looking overwhelmingly likely to win another term.
"There are people who truly care about the future of football, people who aren't driven by financial interests," Klopp said ahead of Germany's Nations League match against the Netherlands on Monday.
"If someone like that were to step up — if someone like that were to become president — I think that would be a significant improvement."
If that person is waiting in the wings, they're leaving it late to step on the stage. Despite a raft of federations and continental confederations, including Germany, UEFA (Europe), CONCACAF (North and Central America and the Caribbean) and AFC (Asia), calling for Infantino's head in the wake of his plan to sell off part of the World Cup earlier this year, the incumbent appears to have stopped the bleeding.
Asia backtracks despite Infantino scandals
That plan, which involved forming a subsidiary arm of FIFA called FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) in order to sell off part of its commercial operations to investors including Joshua Kushner — brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner — was widely panned before being abandoned.
It followed on from widespread criticism of Infantino's awarding of a new FIFA Peace Prize to Trump, the overturning of a red card for US national team player Folarin Balogun, and with Trump's involvement, at the World Cup and a host of other controversies.
Since then, though, many public critics have backtracked amid FIFA promising to release an extra $2.7bn (€2.45bn) from its reserves over the next four years to the federations, increasing their total investment to $6.35bn.
Perhaps the most significant of these u-turns came from the AFC, who went from saying Infantino had committed a "fundamental breach of trust" in August, to offering the Swiss its "full commitment to supporting you and your leadership as you seek a new mandate as the FIFA president" in October.
Those words were spoken by AFC President, Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, who ran against Infantino when he first won the top job at FIFA in 2016. He will not run again and said that "my feeling is, I'm sure, the feeling of most of my members," in regard to Infantino.
Proof that the sentiment is not universal comes in the shape of Kozo Tashima, the honorary president of the Japan Football Association (JFA). Tashima is one of only two people to confirm they will oppose Infantino in the March 2027 presidential elections.
Tashima and Vega, the early candidates
The 68-year-old is a well respected figure in Asian football politics and will have no problem meeting the threshold of support from five of FIFA's 211 federations. This is not like the other candidate, former Swiss international player Ramon Vega, who is an enormous outsider. Tashima appears to be running on the basis that he will be able to chart a calmer path at FIFA.
"I am grateful that I can make this announcement with the full support of the Japan Football Association," Tashima told the Japanese newspaper Sports Nippon. "It's not about winning or losing but about conveying to the world the honest, sound and upright attitude that Japanese football has built. What FIFA needs now are these values that we have protected. I have decided to run in order to make this appeal to the world."
But the numbers are against him. Though support from within the confederations may not be total, the backing of AFC and the African confederation (CAF) is a huge boost for Infantino, with those two alone making up 101 votes, almost enough for a majority.
UEFA still searching for unity candidate
In fact, the only real concern remaining for Infantino remains UEFA. The European federation, headed by Aleksander Ceferin, is a major revenue source for FIFA but the two organizations are at loggerheads. As well as a war of words, UEFA are seeking to obtain evidence for a potential Swiss criminal case against Infantino in regards to FFE. FIFA have called this a "smear campaign" and a "fishing expedition".
But, so far, UEFA has not put up a candidate. Former Arsenal coach turned FIFA Chief of Global Football Development, Arsene Wenger was thought to be a contender but has now ruled himself out. Wenger's compatriot, Philippe Diallo, has since emerged as another option, with The Guardian reporting on Monday that the French Football Federation president could be announced on Tuesday.
While Europe is football's powerbase, particularly from a club perspective, UEFA will need Diallo, or any candidate they can convince to run, to win votes from outside its 55 nations to have any chance of success, particularly with Tashima likely to split any challenge. Even if a candidate appears before the November 18 deadline, Klopp's hope for change appears to be a long shot.

title: Fury vs Joshua undercard faces major blow with Jai Opetaia reportedly out of Deontay Wilder fight
text:
Jai Opetaia could be out of his fight with Deontay Wilder on the Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua undercard.
On 11 December, Fury and Joshua will headline at Cardiff’s Principality Stadium in arguably the biggest British fight ever, and this month brought the news that Opetaia would box Wilder in the chief-support bout.
However, boxing insider Dan Rafael tweeted on Tuesday: “Per sources, Jai Opetaia has withdrawn from the Deontay Wilder fight set for Dec. 11 on the #FuryJoshua Netflix undercard.
“The plan is for Wilder to still fight if they can find a suitable replacement and one distinct possibility is a rematch with Derek Chisora.”
The unbeaten Opetaia was due to make his heavyweight debut against former world champion Wilder, having recently held the IBF cruiserweight title.
Opetaia, 31, was stripped of his cruiserweight belt after signing with the controversial Zuffa Boxing, whose president Dana White has advised Saudi matchmaker Turki Alalshikh on the Fury vs “AJ” undercard, per Joshua’s promoter Eddie Hearn – who said White contractually cannot be involved in the event.
Rafael’s reference to a possible rematch between Wilder, 41, and Chisora, 42, comes after the American beat “Delboy” in April, outpointing him in a 12-round brawl in London.
However, cruiserweight-turned-heavyweight Richard Riakporhe has already offered to step in for Opetaia.
“I hear Jai Opetaia is injured,” the Briton tweeted. “@BronzeBomber I will fight you on less than 4 weeks notice.
Enjoy 185+ fights a year on DAZN, the Global Home of Boxing
Never miss a fight from top promoters. Watch on your devices anywhere, anytime.
“I am ready for 12 full rounds. None of this eight round business, let's go @netflix@Sela@Turki_alalshikh.”
Wilder is a three-time opponent of Fury, 38, and was also linked to Joshua, 37, for years. Wilder secured a controversial draw with Fury in 2018 before suffering stoppage losses to the “Gypsy King” in 2020 and 2021.
Wilder was unbeaten before his first defeat by Fury, but his losses to the Briton marked the start of a 3-4 run, which included defeats by Joseph Parker and Zhilei Zhang and wins over Robert Helenius, Tyrrell Anthony Herndon and Chisora.
Opetaia’s last outing was a ninth-round stoppage of Noel Mikaelian in September, while Riakporhe last fought in April, stopping Jeamie Tshikeva in five rounds to win the British heavyweight belt.

title: 46 people injured after two trains collide in Prague
text:
Ivan Bednárik, the Czech Republic's minister for transport, thanked paramedics and firefighters for their "professional and swift response" and said authorities had launched an investigation into the incident.
Two trains collided in Prague on Tuesday morning near the city's main train station, leaving 46 people injured.
The incident occurred on an overpass at Seifertova street in the Prague 3 district.
Prague's emergency medical service said four people sustained severe injuries in the accident. A further 12 people suffered "moderate" injuries, while 30 had minor injuries, it added.
Video footage posted on social media by police showed emergency crews working at the scene and people being taken away on stretchers. The trains can be seen crumpled together, with damage to both.
"The trauma response was concluded at 9:40 a.m. The first crew arrived on the scene within four minutes of the incident being reported," the emergency service said in a post on social media.
"More than 10 emergency response crews, four crews with a doctor, an inspector, and a special evacuation vehicle gradually arrived on the scene," it added. "All patients with priority levels 1 and 2 have already been transported to medical facilities. We will provide the exact numbers later."
Operations at the main station were restored by around 1 pm local time.

title: Mamdani takes swipe at Trump administration's response to tech outages: 'Far from what many wanted to hear'
text:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani took a swipe at the Trump administration Tuesday following days of tech outages sweeping the nation, saying that "the response that we heard from federal officials was far from what many wanted to hear."
Mamdani spoke after the U.S. experienced a slew of technology disruptions that halted flights, email services and online banking platforms across the country.
"What I will say to New Yorkers is both an understanding of their frustration, we are speaking about New Yorkers who had made plans for months, some of them years, about going on a trip with their family or coming home from a trip with their family. And frankly, the response that we heard from federal officials was far from what many wanted to hear," Mamdani said.
"And it did not leave many New Yorkers with any greater sense of confidence about our national capabilities in case of this occurring again," he continued. "And I'm looking forward to seeing Democratic majorities in the House and the Senate utilize that power to also ensure that we're delivering more answers at a national level, because what we were hearing from some of the secretaries that day was in no way confidence building."
Fox News Digital has reached out to the White House for comment.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said two routers from Federal Aviation Administration facilities in Texas and Arkansas are undergoing extensive testing as investigators examine whether faulty equipment or an installation problem triggered the nation's longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years this past Friday.
The shutdown occurred as contractor L3Harris was replacing aging copper wiring with fiber-optic technology in the FAA's communications system.
Duffy then said during an appearance on Fox News' "Hannity" Monday that he plans to modernize America’s aging air traffic control system and build new architecture that is "worthy of America." The secretary also said intelligence agencies found no evidence of a cyberattack.
The roughly five-hour ground stop affected more than 1.5 million passengers whose flights were scheduled to depart on Friday afternoon and evening. More than 12,000 flights were canceled that day, according to the FAA, while delays and cancellations continued through the weekend.
Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin also said Monday on "Hannity" that "the homeland is secure.
"Our banking system is secure and when something like this happens, we’re able to react and react fast," Mullin continued.
Mullin’s remarks came as customers Monday reported trouble accessing online services of major U.S. banking platforms, including Wells Fargo, Chase, U.S. Bank and Bank of America. United Airlines also faced a widespread system outage on Monday that briefly affected departing flights.
Mullin maintained that the incidents were not a result of cyberattacks and described the disruptions as "individually unrelated."
Fox News Digital's Nora Moriarty, Stephen Sorace and Landon Mion contributed to this report.

title: Demis Hassabis’ AI company raises $5 billion, months after he left as Google DeepMind CEO
text:
Isomorphic Labs, an artificial intelligence drug discovery startup founded by former Google DeepMind chief Demis Hassabis, has raised a $5 billion Series C, the company said on Tuesday.
Isomorphic's round comes three-and-a-half months after Hassabis stepped back as CEO of DeepMind, Google's AI lab, which he co-founded before the Big Tech giant acquired it in 2014.
The round was co-led by Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital, alongside Andreessen Horowitz, with investment from Alphabet, Google's parent. The fresh funds will help fund the design and development of new medicines using AI.
Drug discovery startups have seen record funding poured into them by investors in 2026 as companies look to capitalize on advances in AI. OpenAI and Anthropic have also been investing in tools to develop new medicines using the technology.
Hassabis has been CEO of Isomorphic Labs since the startup spun out of DeepMind in 2021.
"When we founded Isomorphic, our conviction was that biology could be understood and modelled at the most fundamental molecular level and radically accelerated through AI," said Hassabis.
"This round enables us to accelerate our progress: building foundational biology models, deepening our systemic disease understanding, and driving our first therapeutic programs towards clinical trials to deliver tangible impact for patients," he added.
Isomorphic is building a proprietary drug design engine and therapeutic candidate pipeline designed with AI, which it says will help it deliver the next generation of medicines.
Anthropic announced it was launching an AI drug discovery program in June and OpenAI partnered with Novo Nordisk in April.
Drug discovery startups have raised $23.2 billion in 2026, according to deal-counting platform Dealroom, a record figure.
Isomorphic last raised in May, with a $2.1 billion Series B.

title: Alzheimer’s may start shrinking two brain regions years before memory loss
text:
Johns Hopkins scientists have uncovered hidden warning signs of Alzheimer’s disease that may appear up to a decade before memory loss begins. Brain scans revealed that two regions involved in memory and emotion start shrinking before the hippocampus, the area doctors typically examine for signs of Alzheimer’s. These early changes are linked to abnormal tau protein buildup and could provide a powerful new way to identify people at risk.
Alzheimer's disease may begin leaving detectable clues in the brain as much as a decade before memory problems appear. Researchers at Johns Hopkins University have identified two brain regions that show signs of deterioration earlier than the hippocampus, the area commonly examined for evidence of the disease.
The discovery could eventually help doctors recognize Alzheimer's years before symptoms develop, potentially allowing treatment to begin when it has the greatest chance of protecting the brain.
By examining hundreds of brain scans, the scientists found that the entorhinal cortex and amygdala, two regions involved in memory and emotion, begin losing tissue earlier than the hippocampus. These changes may offer important new clues about how Alzheimer's develops and how it could be detected before significant cognitive decline occurs.
"We have found that there are early changes in the brain manifesting the clinical biomarkers of atrophy as much as a decade before there are clinical symptoms," said biomedical engineer and senior author Michael Miller. "It's at least a 5-to-10-year play where your brain is changing. Imagine if we could start to treat the neurodegenerative changes at the 2, 3 or 4-year point rather than after 15 years when the changes are manifesting in memory symptoms. That's the great promise here for your loved ones who are at risk."
The findings were recently published in NeuroImage Reports and are being presented at Neuroscience 2026, the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience.
Detecting Alzheimer's Before Memory Loss Begins
Alzheimer's is the most common cause of dementia worldwide, but the disease does not begin when someone first experiences forgetfulness or confusion. Changes associated with Alzheimer's can accumulate in the brain for decades before noticeable symptoms emerge.
Scientists believe this long period of silent progression may provide a crucial opportunity for treatment. Interventions that begin before extensive damage occurs could potentially do more to preserve memory and other cognitive abilities. However, taking advantage of that opportunity requires reliable ways to identify the disease in its earliest stages.
One promising approach involves biomarkers, measurable biological changes that can indicate the presence or progression of a disease. In Alzheimer's research, these markers could help reveal who is developing the condition before symptoms become apparent.
"Our goal is to be able to treat individuals before the symptoms of Alzheimer's disease develop so that they may delayed or even stopped," said Marilyn Albert, co-author and director of the Johns Hopkins Alzheimer's Disease Research Center.
Two Brain Regions Reveal Earlier Warning Signs
To investigate where the earliest detectable changes occur, the researchers examined hundreds of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and positron emission tomography (PET) scans collected through two independent research projects: the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative and the Biomarkers of Cognitive Decline Among Normal Individuals study.
The scans followed people at different stages of Alzheimer's disease over time, including individuals without symptoms, those experiencing cognitive impairment, and patients who ultimately died from the disease.
In both groups, the researchers observed a consistent pattern. The entorhinal cortex and amygdala, which are located near the hippocampus, showed greater relative tissue loss during the early stages of Alzheimer's than the hippocampus itself.
This distinction matters because the hippocampus plays a central role in memory and has traditionally been a major focus when doctors look for Alzheimer's-related brain damage.
The two newly highlighted regions perform important functions of their own. The entorhinal cortex helps retrieve previously stored memories, while the amygdala contributes to emotional memory, including how emotional experiences are processed and remembered.
Their earlier shrinkage suggests that examining these structures together could reveal signs of Alzheimer's that might be less apparent when attention is focused primarily on the hippocampus.
Brain Shrinkage Linked to Alzheimer's Tau Protein
The researchers also found an important connection between the loss of brain tissue and tau, a protein closely associated with Alzheimer's disease.
Under normal conditions, tau helps maintain the internal structure of nerve cells. In Alzheimer's, however, tau can accumulate abnormally and form tangles that interfere with healthy brain function.
Using PET imaging and digital pathology, the scientists found that areas of gray matter shrinkage overlapped with regions showing tau-related changes. Gray matter contains large numbers of nerve cell bodies and is essential for processing information throughout the brain.
This relationship strengthens the possibility that changes in the entorhinal cortex and amygdala could serve as useful indicators of early Alzheimer's disease.
The team believes that measuring tissue loss in both regions, rather than relying primarily on changes in the hippocampus, could eventually improve predictions of who is likely to develop cognitive decline.
As brain imaging becomes more accessible and less expensive, this approach could also become increasingly practical. For people with a family history of Alzheimer's or other risk factors, researchers envision a future in which doctors might examine these regions as early as a person's 30s or 40s.
"As biomarkers and treatments become increasingly available, knowing who is going to have cognitive decline is going to be really important," said co-author Meaghan Morris, a neuropathologist who studies Alzheimer's and other dementias. "This could really play into better risk stratification for identifying who is going to have cognitive decline in the near future -- and treating people earlier and earlier to hopefully slow the course of the disease."
A Potential New Path Toward Earlier Alzheimer's Treatment
Although the findings are promising, more research is necessary before doctors can use these brain changes as a reliable diagnostic tool. The study identifies potential early biomarkers, but it does not yet establish a clinical test capable of predicting Alzheimer's years in advance.
The next step is to investigate what happens within these regions at a much smaller scale. The researchers want to understand the molecular changes surrounding abnormal tau accumulation and how those changes contribute to the progressive loss of brain tissue.
Identifying the biological processes involved could eventually reveal new targets for therapies designed to interrupt Alzheimer's before extensive damage occurs.
"Our future work is to better show the molecular neighborhoods associated with these Tau protein changes as localized by these clinical biomarkers of atrophy," Miller said. "Once we know more about the molecular neighborhoods, we can develop therapies."

title: Why hasn't the 'Blaze Star' exploded yet? Astronomers weigh in on what to expect
text:
For the past two years, stargazers have waited with bated breath for a "new" light to appear in the night sky, born of one of the most cataclysmic events known to occur in the cosmos — a nova explosion. But what is the "Blaze Star" T. Coronae Borealis, and why is it so difficult to predict when its overdue brightening will occur? We turned to the experts to find out.
What is T. Coronae Borealis?
T. Coronae Borealis — or T CrB for short — isn't a single star, but rather a binary system containing a dense white dwarf star and a bloated red giant. Over a period of around 80 years, the white dwarf's gravity strips material from the red giant until it hits a critical threshold. Next comes a dramatic nova explosion that causes the star to flare to 1,000 times its usual brightness before gradually settling down and repeating the cycle.
Why is it so challenging to predict T. CrB's nova flare?
"T CrB *will* erupt sometime soon," Bradley Schaefer of the Louisiana State University Department of Physics and Astronomy told Space.com in an email. "Everyone is very confident on this. But we cannot make high-accuracy measures of the rate of gas falling onto the surface of the white dwarf, and we do not have a high accuracy measure of the trigger mass for the big hydrogen bomb." Schaefer continued.
Historical observations reveal that the last nova eruption reached Earth in 1946, which places us well inside the window for another dramatic brightening of T. CrBb. However, the unpredictability of the white dwarf's feeding makes it difficult to pin down exactly when the explosion will become visible from Earth.
"The exact date of the upcoming T CrB eruption depends primarily on how fast the gas coming from its companion star is accumulating on the surface of the white dwarf," explained Schaefer. "When some specific trigger mass has accumulated, then T CrB will erupt. For the last 80 years, we have been watching the gas pile up on the white dwarf surface, and we know that it must be near the trigger threshold."
Astronomers have tried to predict T CrB's brightening by comparing a recent fluctuation in the light of the distant star system to a similar event that occurred in the runup to the 1946 event.
"There have already been some dimming and brightening episodes that caused excitement but did not yet turn into the main event," Elizabeth Hays, lab chief at NASA's Astroparticle Physics Laboratory at the Goddard Spaceflight Center, told Space.com in an email. "It is likely that the nova will happen in the next few years but we still don't know exactly when. I can't give you a guaranteed prediction, but I will be a little surprised if it gets to 2030, or 84 years past the last eruption."
Hays notes that the intense light from the red giant dramatically outshines the dimmer white dwarf, making detailed observation challenging. There is also no way to precisely measure the temperature and pressure of the matter lurking near the surface of the smaller star. "Predicting nova explosions are a little like predicting the weather; conditions may be right but the timing of the storm can be uncertain."
What will happen when T CrB's nova light reaches Earth?
There'll be no visual warning of the eruption before it reaches Earth, though according to Hays there could be an early flash of light in the X-ray spectrum.
"The world's amateur astronomers have been doing an awesome job of keeping T CrB under hair-trigger monitoring roughly every minute or two, so when T CrB has brightened by around one magnitude, then alerts will spread around the world within minutes," said Schaefer.
Once the call goes out, telescopes and observatories around the world will kick into gear, running pre-prepared observation programmes to capitalize on the rare and cataclysmic event. "When the nuclear runaway process starts, it will take off and peak very quickly, in less than a day."
The nova will see the star jump from its normal brightness of magnitude +10 — which is beyond the detection limit of the naked eye — to magnitude +1.7, making it appear as if a star brighter than the North Star Polaris has suddenly burst to life in the night sky.
"The brightness will fall below naked-eye visibility in dark places within a couple of days and become too faint for binoculars within about a week," said Hays. "Outside the visible band, for example, in radio, X-ray and gamma rays, light caused by the eruption will be visible for months or even years. "
Where can I find the Blaze Star in the night sky?
T CrB can be found glowing close to the magnitude +4.28 star Epsilon Coronae Borealis in the constellation Corona Borealis during the early evening in November, with the constellations of Hercules and Bootes on either side.
It will dip below the horizon for viewers in the U.S. just a few hours after sunset, before re-emerging into the northeastern sky in the predawn hours.
Want to capture a photo of T. CrB when it erupts? Then be sure to read our guide to photographing the night sky, along with our picks of the best cameras, lenses and smart telescopes that are perfect for capturing the majesty of the starry realm.

title: We couldn't afford a house alone, so we bought one with strangers
text:
When Elizabeth and Tom Wilcox realised they could never afford to buy the home they wanted for themselves and their two children, they decided to take a leap of faith.
They'd find another couple with young kids, complete strangers to them, and propose that they go halves on a property and all move in together.
Based in Vancouver, which has long had some of the highest house prices in Canada, the Wilcoxes were desperate to buy a home that had a back garden for their children to play in.
"We wanted a house with a yard that could fit a trampoline, in a walkable neighbourhood, but we couldn't afford it," says Elizabeth, a project manager in the healthcare sector.
With a budget of C$1m ($700,000; £500,000) all they could hope for was a small apartment with a balcony at best.
That was when Elizabeth came up with the idea of buying with another family.
'We've saved thousands'
They placed an advert in a local estate agent's e-newsletter, but it took two years before they finally met a family whom they clicked with – Ashley Pullman and her husband and two children.
In 2023, the Wilcoxes and the Pullmans co-bought a six-bedroom, detached house, complete with a back garden, for C$1.85m.
The two families split the deposit of C$250,000, and continue to go halves on the monthly mortgage payments of C$3,900. They also divide bills and other expenses equally, such as any necessary home repairs.
Elizabeth says the arrangement has saved both families "tens of thousands of dollars".
While there is no official data available for the number of people buying homes with people they previously didn't know, Parimal Gosai says he has seen a big increase in interest in Toronto as a response to high property prices.
Gosai is the founder and CEO of Husmates, an app and website that connects people in Canada's largest city who are looking to potentially buy a home with a stranger.
It can be seen as "a financial relationship, and that takes emotions out of it", he says.
It's unclear how common this phenomenon is elsewhere in the world. David Hollingworth, from British mortgage broker L&C, says while he hasn't come across it himself, he thinks it also happens in the UK, though is "very niche".
"I remember that before Covid-19 there was a matchmaking event in a London pub, like speed dating, for people looking to buy a house with a stranger," he says. "How successful this was I don't know."
Three years on, the Wilcoxes and the Pullmans say their living arrangement is still working out.
While each family has some private living spaces, such as their own kitchens, they share the big basement-level living room, which includes a home gym in one corner, and a shared freezer.
"If someone says they're in the basement to work out, we know not to go there for a bit, and it's never been an issue," says Elizabeth.
Ashley agrees that there are no problems. "Maybe it's arrogance but my husband and I felt like we were the type of people who could live with strangers," she says.
'We have house meetings'
Sabrina Bowman, a freelance business consultant in Toronto, has co-owned a home with two other housemates since 2018. When she signed on the dotted line and moved in she didn't know one of the other two people.
While Sabrina says she isn't comfortable sharing the exact financial details, she says they decided to divide up the deposit and mortgage payments based on each of their levels of income.
She says any household disputes can be addressed early with open discussions. "What is important to us is having structures to communicate about everything that happens in the home."
They have regular house meetings where they discuss chores, financial issues, birthday celebrations, and any disagreements.
"It's great to see people be honest about something they may not be comfortable about and for us to find a solution to that problem," Sabrina says.
In the case of both Sabrina's house in Toronto and the Wilcox and Pullman property in Vancouver, they have legal agreements in place in case someone wants to sell up and move out.
For both homes, reasonable notice periods are specified, and for Sabrina's, the departing housemate is required to give those remaining the first opportunity to buy their share.
Toronto real estate lawyer Tanya Walker says such legal assurances are vital. "You need something legally binding instead of a bunch of emails and Facebook messages that can be too messy to collect if a dispute comes up," Walker says.
Back in Vancouver, Elizabeth says that neither family has a timeframe for how long they will live in the house. "All of us are really happy with the set-up and location so it would be hard to move.
"I can't put a price on how it felt to watch the kids jump on the trampoline for the first time, or run in circles on our patch of green grass."

title: Ministers vow to create new welfare system for young people as they back Milburn report
text:
Ministers have promised to create an entirely new welfare system for young people as they gave their backing to Alan Milburn’s 278-page report, promising spending cuts next year to help pay for his proposals and giving him a government role to push them through.
Andy Burnham, the prime minister, told his cabinet colleagues on Tuesday morning the report was a “watershed moment” and offered a “comprehensive vision” as he invited its author to address the meeting.
He then sat in the Commons in a public display of support as his work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden, backed Milburn’s vision of a youth employment system with much more employment support but significantly lower benefit payments.
“We need a new settlement for young people,” McFadden said. “This new settlement must give people the best chance of higher living standards for the whole of their lives. It must change the equation that sees us spend £25 on the consequences of inactivity for every pound to be spent on opportunity.”
He added that the search for departmental cuts to help pay for the proposals would begin almost immediately.
“I have no doubt it will also be an issue in the spending review, but the first thing we should do is reprioritise spending to get more support to young people,” he told MPs. “And I’m happy to do that from my department.”
As he was speaking, the government announced Milburn would be given a role as chair of a new youth opportunities unit, monitoring the implementation of his proposals across government.
Milburn’s plans would involve a new youth employment system based on major state intervention to help young people into work, to be paid for in the long term by cuts to disability and sickness payments for under-25s.
The job support schemes were likely to prove so expensive, Milburn said, that the entire package would only save the government £200m a year.
“I know that much of the public debate about this issue centres on welfare reform,” he told a press conference in London. “For some people, the only exam question they’re trying to answer is how to cut the benefits bill. That is important, and it does need to be done. But the primary question for me is not about saving cash, it’s about improving lives.”
Under Milburn’s plan the government would spend nearly £2bn a year on a youth opportunity service, which would provide support and advice to give every young person a guaranteed route into education, training or work.
It would involve spending just over £2bn to create more vocational training courses and apprenticeships, and a further £1bn in direct payments and tax breaks for companies that hire young people.
The tax breaks would include national insurance cuts for businesses that hire young people, starting with the hospitality sector.
This was one proposal that McFadden refused to back explicitly on Wednesday, saying: “We know that employment costs matter and we will consider all these things as we move forward.”
The new system would be paid for largely by taking disability and sickness benefits away from young people and replacing them with a single youth allowance, which would be considerably below what some people can claim currently.
People aged 18 to 24 would no longer be able to claim personal independence payments, which would be replaced by a new allowance available only to those whose conditions are “well established, significant and ongoing”.
The benefit cuts would be expected to save £3.6bn by 2036-37, with an additional £2.4bn being generated by higher tax receipts. That money would be almost entirely swallowed by the £5.8bn cost of the new system, Milburn said.
Milburn began his review last year amid concern at the top of government over the rising numbers of young Neets. That figure reached 1 million earlier this year, equating to 13% of young people – a higher rate than in any European country except Romania.
“Britain is at risk of losing a generation of young people,” he warned.
Ministers and Milburn himself have worked hard to avoid the response which greeted Keir Starmer’s attempts last year to cut the benefits bill by £5bn by restricting access to disability payments.
The former prime minister backed down in the face of opposition from his own MPs, in a humiliating retreat that arguably began his long departure from office.
As well as addressing the cabinet, Milburn spoke to Labour MPs on Monday night, while Burnham spoke at a second parliamentary meeting on Tuesday morning.
Milburn criticised Starmer’s approach during his press conference on Tuesday, calling it a “fiscal grab”, adding: “I do not think that’s the way to do it.”
Early signs suggest the outreach efforts have been successful, with several of the architects of last year’s rebellion speaking in favour of the proposals.
Debbie Abrahams, the chair of the work and pensions select committee, called the review “an opportunity of a generation”, adding: “We must change the status quo.”
Marie Tidball, one of the few visibly disabled MPs in the Commons, said: “I welcome the government’s significant shift in approach and the Milburn review’s emphasis that there won’t be crude cuts to benefits and instead reforms to fundamentally change our welfare system.”
However, some Labour MPs and charities have criticised the proposed cuts to disability benefits.
John McDonnell, a former shadow chancellor, said: “The question does remain why is it that young people, if benefit cuts go ahead, are forced to pay for the new system, and we’re not taxing wealth?”
Katie Schmuecker, a principal policy adviser at the Joseph Rowntree Foundation, said: “Cutting sick and disabled young people’s benefits should not be part of this package.
“Financial support is part of what helps young people take up earning or learning. The wider support offer won’t succeed if the young people it is meant to help are also struggling to afford food or the bus to college.”

title: Commerce Department under pressure for delaying export controls on Nvidia chips
text:
The U.S. Commerce Department is under scrutiny for clearing Chinese companies to handle Nvidia chips, despite national security concerns from cabinet officials and U.S. intelligence agencies.
ROB SCHMITZ, HOST:
Pressure is growing on the Commerce Department and its Secretary Howard Lutnick over why Nvidia's chips have been allowed to be exported to China, despite national security concerns from cabinet officials and intelligence agencies.
SCOTT BESSENT: They were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months, but commerce has the pin. Commerce BIS has the pin, and you will have to ask them about their internal processes.
SCHMITZ: That is Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent accusing Lutnick's department of not putting Megaspeed, a Singapore-based firm with suspected Chinese intelligence ties, on the federal trade restriction list. Liza Tobin is former China director for the National Security Council in the first Trump and Biden administrations. She's here with us now to discuss this. Welcome.
LIZA TOBIN: Thanks for having me, Rob.
SCHMITZ: So you're watching this situation unfold very closely. Tell me your reaction to these accusations against Secretary Lutnick.
TOBIN: Commerce has the pen. Commerce is the agency that has been given the statutory authority by the Congress to regulate the export of these AI chips. They're the ones that write the rules. They also have a law enforcement role. Right now, the whole cover has been blown off this scandal, and Lutnick is there at the center, and it's clear that he just didn't do his job in enforcing those rules.
SCHMITZ: Why do you think that is?
TOBIN: So that is the trillion-dollar question. I think we're going to find out a lot more as Congress starts to dig into this. I think we're going to learn a lot more about, was Howard Lutnick benefiting from this regulatory capture? You know, he...
SCHMITZ: Well, I mean, we do know that Cantor Fitzgerald, a firm run by Lutnick's sons Brandon and Kyle, helps place companies that run data centers in Asia, and their firm has a financial interest in looser chip restrictions that Lutnick himself was in charge of implementing. That seems like a conflict of interest, no?
TOBIN: It absolutely looks like a conflict of interest. And what's clear is that the rest of the president's advisors - Scott Bessent, the tech advisor Michael Kratsios, the director of national intelligence Jay Clayton, Marco Rubio, and others - were all on one side of this issue, advising the president - Mr. President, we've got to close these loopholes and prevent China from accessing our compute. Remember, the president had changed the policy to say, we can sell the previous generation of Nvidia chips, the so-called H 200...
SCHMITZ: The less powerful chips.
TOBIN: That's right. But the president said we are not going to sell the Blackwell chips, at the time the most advanced. Now we know that a whole lot of these Blackwell chips have either been smuggled or they're being accessed by Chinese AI developers overseas in data centers in Malaysia. So you're absolutely right to point to Cantor's interest in seeing that data center trade continue to grow. He disobeyed the president. The president told him to address this three times, so when is that going to happen?
SCHMITZ: I want to - and I want to ask you about that. I mean, this is the Trump administration. The buck stops with President Trump. How much should we be looking at whether President Trump allowed this to happen?
TOBIN: I was advising President Trump when he made the difficult decision to initially put export controls on ships going to Huawei, this giant Chinese telecom. It was a difficult decision because no one knew what the implications would be. It was kind of the first time doing such a dramatic policy move, but he made that decision himself. So I don't think the president is sort of deeply wedded to one view or the other, but he has been persuaded that it's now a good idea to close these loopholes. He told Lutnick to do that, and he was dragging his feet. And so I think the Congress is going to be, you know, calling him in to testify.
SCHMITZ: OK, so you seem to be focused here on Howard Lutnick and his culpability in all of this. What do we know about the relationship between Jensen Huang, the former CEO now of Invidia, and Secretary Lutnick?
TOBIN: We know the president likes very wealthy and powerful men and geniuses like Jensen Huang. And so he sort of got his ticket into the White House. Jensen was in the cool kids club. Everybody wanted to be in the same room as Jensen Huang. In some ways, he was more powerful than the cabinet secretaries himself. I thought of Jensen Huang as almost, like, the chief technology officer of the United States. He was in explaining AI, explaining chips. It was Jensen Huang's view of the world, telling the president, hey, it's a good idea to sell American technology. These are just kind of old, outdated chips. It's a good idea to sell these chips to China and keep China addicted to our tech stack.
SCHMITZ: It's important to point out here that these chips are not just being used for AI chatbots. They have military applications.
TOBIN: China has a long track record of using American technology to advance its own military ambitions. The thing that we have to remember is that China is really good at making a lot of kinds of technology, but they still are nowhere close to being able to produce chips anywhere close to the level of Nvidia's most advanced chips. Anyone in China that wants to be doing cutting-edge AI really wants these chips. And what are they going to use them for? Better missile guidance, its hypersonic missiles, its undersea warfare. It's only a matter of time before China develops its own cyber-capable models that can launch massive disruptive AI-disabled attacks. And by giving them access to the best American chips, it allows them to get there faster. The race to lead in AI is one that is winnable for the United States, but only if we have a government that's taking it seriously and actually has a strategy. I do think that the new Congress coming in is going to be hyperfocused on this issue. They're going to be calling all these folks in to testify, and they're going to put a lot of pressure on them to close the loopholes.
SCHMITZ: That is Liza Tobin, former China director for the National Security Council. Thank you.
TOBIN: Thanks for having me, Rob.
SCHMITZ: We reached out to the White House and the Commerce Department for a response to Liza Tobin's comments. A spokesperson for the Commerce Department sent us this statement. Quote, "the secretary has fully complied with the terms of his ethics agreement, including all divestiture and recusal requirements, and will continue to do so. He has divested all financial interests in Cantor Fitzgerald, Newmark, and BGC."

title: Fed's Lisa Cook rebuffs White House hearing without changes
text:
Washington — Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook will not participate in an upcoming White House hearing to examine allegations she made false statements on mortgage documents unless concerns about the process are first addressed, her lawyer said in a letter to the White House obtained by CBS News.
Abbe Lowell, Cook's lawyer, told White House counsel Will Scharf that Cook has "no legal obligation" to appear at what he said is an "unfair" hearing before a three-member committee of Trump administration officials that is set for next month. He warned participating in the proceeding would undermine the Fed's "unique status" and independence.
"Consequently, this Committee process appears to be a façade designed to obscure a predetermined decision to fire Governor Cook or to unreasonably manufacture a supposed 'adverse inference' if she does not participate in a process that does not comport with the requirements of a fair hearing," Lowell wrote.
His letter to Scharf revealed that the two sides have exchanged numerous communications in the weeks since President Trump a "committee of inquiry" to look into the claims that Cook made misrepresentations on mortgage forms related to two properties before joining the Fed's Board of Governors in 2022.
The committee is made up of Kevin Hassett, assistant to the president for economic policy; Andrea Lucas, chair of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission; and Keith Sonderling, director of the Office of Government Ethics.
Cook has repeatedly denied wrongdoing and said Mr. Trump is attempting to remove her from the Fed because he disagrees with her decisions on interest rates.
"It is unfortunate that your latest correspondence fails to address the concerns Governor Cook has previously raised — making clear that you are uninterested in convening the 'substantive and fair hearing' you have claimed. Instead, you seek only to manufacture 'cause' for a predetermined removal outcome," Lowell wrote.
Cook had raised concerns in earlier letters to the White House about Hassett's membership on the committee because of comments he has made about the Fed governor, which Lowell said "demonstrate that he has prejudged the issue."
"Mr. Hassett's continued presence on the Committee remains unacceptable," Lowell said.
He also took issue with the White House's proposed process to exchange documents. Lowell said it is "fundamentally unfair" because it would require Cook to hand over documents immediately, while she would not gain access to information that the White House has until seven days before the hearing.
Lowell had also pressed the White House on the specific legal standard the committee would apply to determine what constitutes "cause" to remove a Fed governor and the participation of Justice Department personnel in the hearing, he said.
"Your and the Committee's failure to address these legitimate issues, over multiple weeks of back-and-forth correspondence, reinforces my prior observation: President Trump's decision to fire Governor Cook has already been made," Lowell wrote.
Mr. Trump first in August 2025 after Bill Pulte, the head of the Federal Housing Finance Agency, accused her of making false statements on mortgage applications. Cook filed a lawsuit claiming that her removal was in violation of federal law, which allows the president to remove a member of the Fed's board only "for cause."
The Supreme Court in June while her case continued and found that Mr. Trump failed to provide Cook with the procedural protections she was entitled to under the law, namely notice of the allegations against her and the opportunity to respond before she was fired.
Weeks after the Supreme Court's 5-4 decision, Mr. Trump again moved to oust Cook. The White House in August that the president was considering terminating her because of the mortgage fraud accusations and gave her a chance to respond — seemingly an attempt to remedy the issues raised by the Supreme Court.
The president then announced last month that he had established the committee to look into the claims against Cook and determine whether he has cause to remove her.
The hearing at the White House was initially set to take place Nov. 5, with committee members set to consider evidence and allegations against Cook.
In his latest letter to Scharf, Lowell said the White House had attempted to schedule a hearing on dates that conflicted with the Fed's official business. He said that Scharf claimed in an Oct. 19 letter that if Cook didn't show up on the date selected by the White House, the hearing would proceed without her and the committee could "draw an adverse inference" from her failure to appear because of official obligations.
"To be clear, if the White House establishes an unbiased panel and implements fair procedures that do not prejudge the outcome — such as providing the evidence it claims to have gathered with sufficient time for review and response — Governor Cook would be prepared to appear," Lowell wrote. "But the ultimatums in your November 2, 2026 letter do not provide a productive path forward to enabling that participation."

title: Trump administration moves to block China from indirect access to American AI technology
text:
The Trump administration has issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers
WASHINGTON -- The Trump administration on Monday issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers, marking the latest step to limit China’s abilities to use U.S. chips to train their best artificial intelligence models.
Last week, Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO following scrutiny of his ties to a Chinese executive who used to lead Singapore-based Megaspeed International, which is suspected of diverting advanced Nvidia chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls. The company provides computing power to Chinese companies using chips housed in Southeast Asian data centers, including facilities in Malaysia.
“The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries,” the Bureau of Industry and Security under the Commerce Department said in issuing the rule that took effect immediately.
The rule came on the same day President Donald Trump departed for a trip to Asia, where he expects to meet Chinese leader Xi Jinping for the third time this year amid a fragile truce on trade.
Under the new rule, overseas data centers that serve companies in countries including China, Russia, Iran and Cuba are required to identify their end users. There also will be additional licensing requirements for sales of chips for Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil — countries that “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion" to unauthorized destinations, the rule says.
In Beijing, China's foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun accused Washington of arbitrarily interfering with China's trade and technological cooperation with other countries and suppressing the development of China's high-tech industries.
“This is a typical example of economic coercion and long-arm jurisdiction, runs counter to the common understanding between the two sides,” he told reporter, adding that it infringes upon the rights of Chinese companies and disrupts the stability of global supply chains.
He said China would take necessary measures to safeguard its interests.
The U.S. bans sales of the country's most advanced AI chips to China, seeking to maintain an edge in its rivalry with China for predominance in artificial intelligence. However, many lawmakers and policymakers believe the country's export control rules are not tough enough and filled with loopholes such as cloud computing that allows China to rent processing power built on American technology.
Last year, U.S. Rep. Michael Lawler, a New York Republican, introduced a bill to broaden the U.S. export controls to include remote access. He told Congress “physical export controls” under current rules do not apply to remote access, allowing China to “access our tech through the cloud” and giving it “a real tool to sidestep” U.S. export restrictions. The bill has passed the House.
In the Senate, lawmakers also are seeking tougher legislation to prevent China from accessing advanced U.S. chip and AI technologies. Bills include proposals that would let Congress review licenses to sell advanced AI chips to China, ask the Department of Commerce to track AI chips to ensure they are not diverted to unauthorized regions, and compel U.S. allies such as the Netherlands and Japan to match U.S. restrictions on exports to Chinese chipmakers.
Last week, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick came under pressure when Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the Commerce Department was late to place restrictions on Nvidia chip exports to Megaspeed.
On Monday, Trump acknowledged tension between Treasury and Commerce on the matter. He suggested that Lutnick may have delayed placing the export restrictions to avoid a “blow up” in the fragile U.S.-China relationship.
“We’re having a very good relationship with China right now, and I understand both sides of it, Trump said.
In a joint statement late Monday by the Commerce and Justice departments, it said Commerce initiated an investigation into Megaspeed for potential export control violations in 2024, which was followed by requests to Nvidia for records in May 2025 related to sales to Megaspeed. The following month, it said, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list, and agents from the Commerce Department in conjunction with Singapore law enforcement conducted on-site checks of Megaspeed and interviewed Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang. The Justice Department then took the lead role in the criminal probe of Megaspeed, the statement said.
“The Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security working together will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred,” the statement said.
Last week, the Singapore government confirmed that it had investigated Megaspeed over “potential false declarations" involving servers that were exported through Singapore to Malaysia but might have “subsequently been routed from Malaysia to another destination, contrary to declaration made in Singapore.”
The Malaysian government also said last week that it was investigating if chips brought into Malaysia have been re-exported to other countries as permitted by its own law.
“Malaysia welcomes investment in data centers and technology, but will not allow itself to be used to get around export controls,” read the Friday statement by Malaysia's Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry.

title: Germany news: Merz, Söder aim to revisit electricity tax cut
text:
Friedrich Merz and Markus Söder push for electricity tax cut after it failed to make it into budget last week
- Manuela Schwesig is voted in for another term as state premier in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania
- An AfD chocolate Saint Nicholas has put Christian leaders' noses out of joint as advent approaches
- NRW leaders head to ground-breaking ceremony as the A44 autobahn's 'bridge to nowhere' near Düsseldorf will finally be linked up to the network
- German national team gears up for evening Nations League match against neighbors and rivals Netherlands
Stay tuned for more on these stories and anything else in or concerning Germany on November 16, 2026.
Thank you for reading
We'll be back with the latest headlines out of Germany tomorrow. Bis dann!
Wirtz and Co., demolish Netherlands 5-0 in Nations League quarterfinal match-up
Germany dominated neighbor and historic rival the Netherlands in their Nations League quarterfinal match-up at Berlin's Olympic Stadium on Monday evening.
It was the team's sixth game under head coach Jürgen Klopp and the 50th ever between the two sides.
Germany's 5-0 shellacking of the Oranje was their most lopsided victory since 1959, when they won 7-0. In all, Germany have now won 19 of those matches, the Netherlands have won 12, and 18 ended in a draw.
Speaking to German broadcaster ARD after the game, attacking midfielder Florian Wirtz — who scored twice in the fixture — said: "We hope that we can make it fun for the fans. It was definitely fun for us, especially in the second half."
Despite the loss, Xavi Hernandez's Dutch side will reach the final eight alongside Germany.
Prior to the match, Klopp had made it clear that he and his team were approaching Monday's showdown as a final after having lost to Greece 1-0 in his first home game in the job on September 27.
By night's end, Derry Scherhant and Nico Schlotterbeck each scored once and Brajan Gruda scored once and added two assists on top of Wirtz's double.
Klopp has been high on Wirtz, who has come under fire for not delivering at Liverpool since his arrival there in June 2025, and his bet seems to be paying off with the 23-year-old now scoring four goals in his last four games for Germany.
"We don't care who we play. We want to play attacking football. We want to score goals and dominate the opponent. And I think we did that perfectly," said Wirtz on Monday evening before adding: "We want to keep going next year. We want to get better. I think we've taken some great steps in our development as a team."
READ — Germany to join other EU states in announcing Rwanda return hub
A group of five EU member states, including Germany, have entered talks over a scheme to send rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda.
The plan to set up so-called return hubs in a non-EU country had been announced by the group — which also includes Austria, the Netherlands, Greece and Denmark — had first been announced back in September.
Tesla planning €3BN investment in German factory to produce Cybercabs
Tesla has earmarked some €3 billion ($3.3 billion) to expand its factory in Germany, near to Berlin.
The Grünheide complex will be expanded to start producing the electric car company's driverless Cybercabs, with output expected to eventually reach 1 million units.
The Elon Musk-owned company said construction would begin in 2027, with the first Cybercabs rolling off the line in 2029.
"With this, we are laying the foundations for the world's most technologically advanced Tesla factory here in Grünheide," Tesla said.
READ — Germany's Klopp wants Infantino out at FIFA
Germany coach Jürgen Klopp has joined the chorus of football figures critical of FIFA President Gianni Infantino. But with time running out, there are few who seem willing to run against him.
Matt Pearson on our sports desk breaks down where the power struggle currently stands, with the deadline for candiates just a matter of hours away now.
Manuela Schwesig confirmed for another term in Meck-Pomm
Lawmakers in the state parliament in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania have voted in Manuela Schwesig for another term as state premier.
The 52-year-old has been in the role since 2017 and is heading into a third term.
The vote was a secret ballot, but it can still be assumed who voted and how.
She received 39 of the 68 votes cast in the chamber, exactly as many as commanded by Schwesig's three-party coaliton of her Social Democrats (29), the ecologist Greens (5), and the socialist Left Party (5).
Merz says he believes electricity tax cut will be agreed this week
While Söder's comments in Munich focused in particular on the policy the coalition in Berlin had not delivered, Merz initiatlly focused on talking up the efficacy of his federal coalition.
"We are aware of the situation. We know that we now need to deliver. And we also know that we face difficult talks within the coalition. But I would also say from the experiences of the last weeks that there are solutions to the problems which we have in Germany," Merz said.
Merz said that in the 18 months since last year's election, the coalition "has already successfully implemented many things, not 'set them into motion' as people like to say, but actually implemented."
He noted a total of 17 bills going through the second and third reading process in the lower house of parliament, the Bundestag, last week, "including the most comprehensive reforms of our intelligence and security services that we have ever done in [post-war] Germany."
Among others, he thanked Bavarian Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, a senior member of the Bavarian CSU sister party to Merz's own conservative CDU, for his contribution to this.
Merz also touted the support given to CSU politician Ilse Aigner, not just from his CDU but from the Social Democrat coalition partners and the Greens, to become the next president, calling her a person who would "represent our country very well at home and abroad."
After hailing these accomplishments, Merz then turned to electricity tax cuts, saying he anticipated talks on the matter on Tuesday that would be "very short."
He said that over the weekend, coalition leaders had revisited the figures, and now believed they would be able to "completely" reduce electricity taxes to the minimum European levels in 2027 "also for private households."
Markus Söder: Cutting electricity tax key for 'credibility'
Bavarian state premier Markus Söder has appeared with Friedrich Merz at a press conference during the chancellor's trip to Munich.
It seems Söder, Merz and the CDU/CSU believe they have unfinished business after the budget was finalized in the Bundestag late last week.
Merz had pledged in the run-up to the decision to provide a reduction in electricity tax for all, but the final agreement did not include this step, with the coalition partners the Social Democrats (SPD) saying it was not adequately costed.
Söder said he and Merz had discussed "backup for the coming days," for Berlin and for a "collective stance, that is really, really important."
He said the coming days were about "demonstrating credibility in politics," seemingly in reference to Merz's promise that the coalition did not ultimately deliver.
"That's why it's really important to us that we do indeed bring about the reduction in electricity tax," Söder said. "This is important for businesses. It would be a relief for citizens. But it's also a matter of credibility and it's written in the coalition agreement."
Söder said that as to the question of "where the money comes from, with a €560 billion (roughly $615 billion) budget, with €200 billion in new debt, nobody can tell me there's no potential within the budgeting process."
AfD chocolate Saint Nicholas in party's fan shop upsets religious leaders
A festive piece of merchandise on the right-wing populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) "fan shop" website has upset some religious leaders in Germany.
Called a "chocolate Nicholas," it appears to depict a semblance of Saint Nicholas in bishop's regalia and the party's colors and holding a book with "AfD" written on the cover where a Bible might be in more traditional iconography.
The Bishop of Essen, Franz-Josef Overbeck, was highly critical of the promotion in Monday's edition of the Bild newspaper.
"The AfD is appropriating Christian symbols for party campaigning," Overbeck said. "Showing the holy Nicholas in a blue coat with mitre, staff and the gospel with an AfD logo is not in order."
Overbeck acknowledged that other organizations like football clubs would sell chocolate Christmas figurines in club colors, but he said they would tend to refrain from including overtly Christian symbols when doing so.
Bild quoted an AfD spokesman as saying that as a "liberal-conservative party that clearly associates itself with Christian values," the item fit "particularly well" with the party image.
The main German protestant church group EKD's cultural representative, Johann Hinrich Claussen, said the offer showed the AfD had "no understanding of traditions and no respect" for Christianity.
He described the action as "embarrassing and revealing," and said that Christianity was "supra-partisan."
"The AfD knows little about what is holy to Christians. Otherwise, it would be aware that Bishop Nicholas of Myra, in what today is Demre in Turkey, stood clearly for uniting the occident and the orient. Beyond that, he is the patron saint of rescues at sea," Claussen said.
All welcome at Bavarian politician Aiwanger's funeral, partner says
The partner of deceased Bavarian politician Hubert Aiwanger has said that anybody is welcome at his funeral this coming Saturday.
Aiwanger was the economy minister in Bavaria's state government as the leader of the junior coalition partners to the center-right CSU.
"Hubert was a man of the people and so it stands to reason that anyone who liked or treaasured him is allowed to come to his funeral," Tanja Schweiger wrote on her Instagram profile overnight.
She was posting after a requiem in the state capital Munich paying tribute to the leader of the Free Voters (Freie Wähler) party over the weekend. Around 1,100 people attended this ceremony.
Aiwanger died suddenly and unexpectedly on November 4 during a working visit to Berlin, aged 55.
Prosecutors have since said he died of natural causes, after he was found dead in his hotel room.
Germany's Nations League fate at stake against Netherlands
Germany's national men's football team will play neighbors and rivals the Netherlands for the 50th time on Monday night.
And there's quite a lot at stake for Jürgen Klopp's team in the last group stage game of the Nations League competition at Berlin's Olympiastadion.
If Germany win, they will qualify for the knockout stages, but a defeat could lead to potential relegation into the second tier of Nations League football.
Klopp was upbeat in the pre-match press conference at the prospect of playing the Netherlands, who he said play "Xavi football," in the image of the skillful Spanish playmaker and World Cup winner coaching the team.
"I've always loved playing against teams like this. For all my coaching career," Klopp said. "When someone says, 'hey they can really play football,' then in my mind the party's already started."
A full house with some 71,000 fans is expected in the capital when the game kicks off. Klopp played on the Dutch reputation for liberal use of bicylces in his comments to reporters, saying he wanted to "put a stick in their spokes" and dislodge them from the saddle.
Work starting to link A44 'bridge to nowhere' to road network
The notion of a bridge over the valley between Ratingen and Heiligenhaus to the east of Düsseldorf in western Germany as part of the A44 highway is more than half a century old. And the physical bridge itself has stood, complete, ever since 2022.
Yet still the crossing is not connected to any roads at either end.
A construction project to build the last 4.4 kilometers of highway and link the bridge to the A44 highway will formally start on Monday.
State premier Hendrik Wüst, as well as the regional transport and traffic ministers will attend the ground-breaking ceremony.
A project first conceived some 55 years ago has faced repeated delays because of lawsuits, environmental protection studies and onerous planning and permit procedures.
The bridge across the Angerbachtal (Angerbach Valley) should improve the road connection between the North Rhine-Westphalia state capital of Düsseldorf, the Bergisches Land mountain range and the industrial cities in the Ruhr Valley. It's also meant to help remove some strain from the perenially busy A3 highway and to improve the road connections to Düsseldorf International Airport.
The last stretch of highway is expected to cost around €200 million (roughly $220 million), or roughly the annual costs incurred each year by forcing traffic to divert around it, according to estimates from Düsseldorf's IHK industry and trade association.
Construction is expected to take several years, no formal end date has yet been set.
Merz heads to Munich for CSU meeting
Chancellor Friedrich Merz heads to Munich early on Monday, for a meeting with the leadership of the Bavarian Christian Social Democrats (CSU), the sister party to his conservative Christian Democrats(CDU).
No concrete details about the talks were made public ahead of time, except for the CSU saying it would serve as a general exchange that had been planned for some time.
The trip comes a week after Merz nominated Ilse Aigner as the next German president, likely paving the way for her to become the first woman and first CSU politician to assume the role.
It also follows soon after the 2027 federal budget cleared a marathon meeting of the parliamentary budget committee in Berlin. This serves as one of the more conspicuous examples of the frictions and difficulties in the grand coalition between the Christian Democrats and the center-left Social Democrats — with the compromises it contains a point of frustration among the CSU and for state premier Markus Söder.
Manuela Schwesig set for vote on new term as regional leader
The northeastern state parliament in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania will likely vote in Social Democrat (SPD) Manuela Schwesig for another term as state premier early in the afternoon.
The 52-year-old, who first stepped into the role in 2017, plans to lead a new coalition of the SPD, the environmentalist Greens and the socialist Left Party after state elections in September.
The right-wing populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) emerged as the largest single party in the sparsely populated state.
But still, the political calculus that emerged was arguably simpler than in Berlin — where the socialist Left Party is the largest party but could struggle to lead a coaltion — and in Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD was by far the largest party but short of an outright majority.
Schwesig's SPD claimed 29 seats, with the Greens and the Left each taking 5, meaning that when combined, they hold a fairly clear majority over the AfD with its 32 seats.
The SPD's relatively successful performance in the state, at least compared to its national struggles, has also led to Schwesig being linked with a possible return to federal politics. The SPD plans to elect a new leadership duo early next year.
Schwesig has already had a spell in Berlin as the federal minsiter for families, pensioners and women, and briefly led the SPD on an interim basis in 2017, but after this she returned to her home state to seek the top regional job instead.
Welcome
Servus! Welcome to another Monday of news and analysis of matters making waves in German politics and society.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz is starting his week in Munich, at a meeting of the Bavarian CSU sister party to his conservative Christian Democrats (CDU).
This comes a few days after Merz naming CSU politician Ilse Aigner as candidate to be the next president, and days after the budget committee signed off on the federal government's spending plans for 2027. Merz is expected to appear with state premier Markus Söder in a joint press conference later.
Far to the north, in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Social Democrat Manuela Schwesig should be voted in for another term as state premier in the regional parliament later in the day. Schwesig emerged in pole position after state elections a few weeks ago; some suspect her regional success could translate into national ambitions within the struggling party.
And in the west, regional leaders are headed to a road to nowhere — literally, but also hopefully not for very much longer now.
The vast highway A44 bridge over the valley between Helsinghausen and Ratingen-Ost has been planned for decades, and was completed in 2022, but work to actually connect it to the road network will only start today.
Stay with us for more on these stories and whatever else develops around Germany on November 16.

title: Ukraine-Russia war latest: Russian military plane crashes in Siberia killing all 19 on board
text:
