All 19 people on board a Russian military transport plane have been killed after the aircraft crashed in southwestern Siberia.
The An-12 transport aircraft went down in Russia’s Kemerovo region on Tuesday, Russia’s Izvestia news outlet reported. Details surrounding the circumstances of the crash were not immediately available.
Local governor Ilya Seredyuk confirmed a plane crash near the village of Yagunovo on the MAX messaging platform, though he did not officially identify the aircraft involved.
The crash comes after a prolonged series of Ukrainian long-range attacks on Russian territory and occupied infrastructure, culminating earlier on Tuesday in a coordinated missile and drone strike that collapsed a section of the Crimean Bridge into the sea.
One of the bridge’s main support arches completely collapsed, alongside a significant chunk of the road surface, according to images shared by Ukrainian officials.
The incident marks the latest in an increasingly costly conflict, where parts of Kyiv remain without electricity and water after Russian forces struck two major bridges across the Dnipro River and other critical infrastructure in Kharkiv overnight.
France is not a 'co-belligerent' in Ukraine, foreign minister says
French foreign minister Jean-Noël Barrot has said that French military personnel operating inside Ukraine are strictly providing training and technical support – insisting Paris is not a "co-belligerent" in the war against Russia.
"We are not co-belligerent in Ukraine and we have no intention to be, but we support the Ukrainian army and the Ukrainian resistance," Barrot told France 5 television on Tuesday.
The remarks followed a Radio France Internationale (RFI) report revealing a French military support mission in Ukraine, codenamed "Volia," which has reportedly been active since the summer.
Previously, Paris had publicly restricted its training of Ukrainian soldiers to sites in France and Poland to avoid escalating direct tensions with Moscow.
European-made Ruta missiles were the only foreign weapons in Crimean Bridge strike, maker says
European defence startup Destinus says its missiles and drones were the only foreign-made weapons used in Tuesday’s strike that collapsed the central road span of the Crimean Bridge.
Ukraine fired nine Ruta Block 1 cruise missiles – seven of which hit the bridge – alongside Destinus’s Da Vinci deep-strike drones, company president Oleksandr Danyliuk told Reuters.
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the attack capped a weeks-long, seven-stage operation that first degraded Russian air defences and radars, pairing the European systems with domestically made weapons as scarce Western missiles remain in short supply.
Russian military transport plane crashes in Siberia, killing all 19 on board
All 19 people on board a Russian military transport plane have been killed after the aircraft crashed in southwestern Siberia, Russia’s defence ministry confirmed via state media on Tuesday.
The An-12 aircraft went down during a "scheduled flight" in an "uninhabited area" of the Kemerovo region, the ministry said.
The department added that a technical malfunction is preliminarily believed to have caused the crash.
Local governor Ilya Seredyuk said emergency teams quickly extinguished a blaze near the village of Yagunovo and police sealed off the site as aviation authorities opened an investigation.
Investigation links Russian military to banned tear gas drone attack
An investigation by Ukraine and the global chemical weapons watchdog (OPCW) has formally linked Russian forces to a drone-dropped tear gas attack on Ukrainian troops, according to a report released Tuesday.
Using tear gas as a weapon of war violates the Chemical Weapons Convention, which Russia has signed.
Kyiv says Russian forces have used banned chemical agents 14,000 times during the war to flush troops from trenches, injuring 3,000 soldiers.
Moscow, which has previously denied using chemical weapons, did not immediately issue comment.
Hungary suspends rail links to Ukraine after Russian drone crash
Hungary has temporarily restricted cross-border rail traffic with Ukraine after a Russian attack drone crashed roughly 300 meters from the train station in Mukachevo on Tuesday.
Hungarian prime minister Péter Magyar confirmed the crash, noting that a Hungarian train crew that had just arrived in the Zakarpattia region city had to be evacuated during the attack.
Ukrainian Railways clarified that the two-day suspension applies to two train pairs operated by Hungarian carrier MÁV along the European-gauge Budapest–Mukachevo route.
The railway operator added that the Russian strike targeted a local enterprise and caused no damage to rail infrastructure or injuries to staff.
Transcarpathian regional governor Myroslav Biletskyi reported that three Shahed-type drones were detected in the area during Tuesday's barrage.
Ukraine reportedly tests Israeli HiSKY terminals amid Starlink speed caps
Ukraine may be shifting some long-range strike drone communications away from SpaceX’s Starlink toward satellite terminals made by Israeli firm HiSKY, according to the Kyiv Post.
The reported pivot follows mid-October restrictions on SpaceX-linked terminals in Ukraine that cut connections on platforms moving faster than 160 km/h, disrupting high-speed and deep-strike drones.
Russian military commentators first alleged the switch in late October, claiming HiSKY terminals resist jamming by hopping across commercial satellites.
While the Ukrainian military has not commented on the reports, analysts note HiSKY’s lower bandwidth (~2 Mbps) suits basic course corrections rather than continuous live video piloting.
Moldova pushes for fresh sanctions after Russian drone flies over capital
Moldovan president Maia Sandu pledged to push for further sanctions against Moscow on Tuesday after several Russian drones violated the country's airspace, with one flying directly over the capital, Chisinau.
The incursion prompted Moldovan authorities to temporarily close the nation's airspace as reports emerged of drones heading toward the capital.
"This evening several Russian drones violated our airspace, one of them over Chisinau, alarming residents," Sandu wrote on X.
"Russia's war threatens all of Europe. Moldova stands for peace. We'll keep pushing for sanctions on Moscow, standing with Ukraine and building our defence with partners."
Britain to supply Ukraine with more than 1,000 short-range missiles
Britain has announced it will provide Ukraine with more than 1,000 additional short-range air defence missiles and launchers to help defend against Russian air attacks this winter, as allies met in Brussels to coordinate military support for Kyiv.
- The missiles form part of a £240 million ($317 million) package announced on Tuesday, drawn from a £500 million pledge for Ukraine unveiled in last month's budget
- Britain said the systems had proven effective against Iranian-designed jet-powered Shahed drones that Russia is using to strike Ukraine
- The support package also includes over a dozen air defence radars
- Deliveries will begin from mid-December, building on 400 surface-to-air missiles Britain has already supplied Ukraine ahead of this winter
- British Prime Minister Andy Burnham will announce the remaining support at a meeting of the "coalition of willing" nations on Thursday
Germany pledges $300m for Ukrainian Patriot missiles and air defence
Germany will allocate $300 million to purchase US weapons for Ukraine through NATO’s Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) mechanism, defence minister Boris Pistorius announced on Tuesday.
The funding – part of a joint package with Norway – will prioritise PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptors for Ukraine’s US-made Patriot systems to counter Russian ballistic missile attacks.
Alongside the interceptor purchases, Berlin is working to integrate German IRIS-T missiles into Ukrainian NASAMS air defence batteries and will supply new airspace surveillance radars, drones, and ammunition for F-16 fighter jets.
Russia pledges to repair Crimea Bridge but experts doubtful
Putin's spokesman Dmitry Peskov said a repair plan for the Crimea Bridge would be prepared, making the bridge “even better than before”.
But Russian military bloggers said repairs would be exceptionally challenging given Ukraine's capacity for further attacks.
Finnish military analyst Emil Kastehelmi posted on X: “The road bridge won’t be repaired during this war ... Ukraine has achieved a victory with both concrete and symbolic implications.”
The bridge over the Kerch Strait was once a key supply route for Russian forces in Ukraine, but the military now relies more heavily on a land corridor running through parts of eastern and southern Ukraine that Russia has captured since launching a full-scale war with its neighbour in 2022.

title: Why gold and silver prices have fallen to their lowest in over a year
text:
Gold and silver prices have slumped to their lowest levels in more than a year as a strong US dollar, high bond yields and bets on another US interest rate hike sap demand. The gold price is on track for its biggest annual fall since 2015.
Gold and silver prices sank to their lowest levels in more than a year on Monday, as a strong US dollar, rising bond yields and bets on another US rate hike in December eroded the appeal of precious metals.
The gold price is now heading for its biggest annual drop since 2015.
Spot gold fell as low as $3,832 an ounce on Monday, its weakest level since October 2025, while silver dropped to $46.50 an ounce.
On Tuesday, both metals’ prices rebounded from Monday’s lows. Gold rose about 0.75% to $3,861 an ounce, while silver climbed just over 2% to $47.50 an ounce.
A rates trade, not a safe haven
Gold pays no interest, so higher rates make it less attractive, as investors can earn more on bonds and savings.
The US Federal Reserve raised rates in September for the first time since 2023, and markets now fully expect another hike in December, according to CME Group's FedWatch tool, which tracks traders' bets.
The yield on 10-year US government bonds has climbed to around 5%, and on Tuesday the US dollar reached its strongest level since April 2025, making metals priced in US dollars costlier for buyers holding other currencies.
The Iran war has not helped either.
Rather than acting as a safe haven, gold has suffered as the conflict drove oil prices and inflation higher, which in turn fuelled bets on higher interest rates.
It is a sharp reversal from January, when gold hit a record of about $5,600 an ounce, and silver peaked at around $121.65 an ounce, before both crashed at a time of escalating geopolitical tensions in Venezuela and Iran, and after US President Donald Trump picked Kevin Warsh to lead the Fed.
Gold has since lost more than 30% from its peak and is down over 10% since the start of the year.
Silver, which tends to swing even more sharply than gold, has dropped about 60% from its peak and is down about 34% since the start of the year.
What comes next
Gold edged higher in early trading on Tuesday as the US dollar and bond yields eased slightly, but expectations of a December hike capped the rebound.
Investors now await Wednesday's release of the minutes from the Fed's October meeting for clues on how high rates could go.
Warsh did not address the December decision when he spoke at an event on AI at the San Francisco Fed on Monday.
US investment bank Goldman Sachs has turned more cautious, cutting its forecasts earlier this month. It now sees gold at $4,150 an ounce at the end of the year, according to a note, which is still above current prices.
That would require gold to climb roughly 7.5% from the current level until the end of 2026.
Central banks also remain a source of support for demand. Central banks and other official institutions bought a net 675 tonnes of gold between January and September, 6% more than a year earlier, according to the World Gold Council, an industry body.

title: Disney beats fourth-quarter estimates, targets $3 billion in savings through cost-cutting efforts
text:
Disney on Tuesday reported quarterly earnings and revenue that exceeded analysts' expectations and announced it's targeting $3 billion in cost savings by fiscal 2029.
Those cost-cutting efforts include several rounds of layoffs announced in recent months, Disney's chief financial officer, Hugh Johnston, told CNBC. The most recent round, which seeks to reduce costs by up to 20%, was reported earlier this month.
Future cost-saving measures will include reductions in administrative and other general expenses, Johnston said, while adding, "We do expect more layoffs."
Disney CEO Josh D'Amaro told investors on the company's earnings call that the job cuts are "not easy."
"They affect people who care deeply about Disney and have contributed so much to this company," he said. "At the same time, these steps are important if we want to be a company that moves faster, adapts to a rapidly changing environment, and keeps investing in the content and technology that will drive our growth."
The cuts will help Disney fund its $26 billion in projected content spend for fiscal 2027, a 9% increase from fiscal 2026.
The entertainment giant is also forecasting double-digit growth in earnings per share in the next fiscal year, as well as segment operating income growth of around 8%.
Disney noted that the majority of that growth will be concentrated in the first half of the year due to the theatrical debut of "Avengers: Doomsday" and a boost from the Super Bowl, which will air on Disney's ESPN and ABC networks.
"The growth is really going to come in the first half of this year," Johnston said. "That's the opposite of what we saw in '26, where the growth was backloaded."
The company will also increase its annual dividend to $2 a share, a 33% increase from the previously declared dividend. It will be payable in two installments of $1 per share, one in January and one in July.
Here's how Disney performed in its fiscal fourth quarter ended Oct. 3, compared with what Wall Street expected, according to LSEG:
- Earnings per share: $1.77 adjusted vs. $1.67 expected
- Revenue: $25.95 billion vs. $25.18 billion expected
Disney reported net income for the fiscal fourth quarter of $2.61 billion, or $1.51 per share, compared with $1.31 billion, or 73 cents per share, during the same period the year prior.
Adjusting for one-time items, including severance and other restructuring charges as well as the value of intangible assets, Disney reported earnings per share of $1.77.
The company's revenue for the quarter was 16% higher year over year, and results were once again lifted by its parks and streaming divisions.
Disney's experiences segment, which includes its theme parks and cruises, reported nearly $10.11 billion in revenue, up 15% year over year. Operating income for the unit increased 20% to $2.25 billion.
The division is already a top performer for the company, but it benefited in the fiscal fourth quarter because of an extra calendar week compared with the previous fiscal year.
While international attendance continues to lag at Disney's domestic parks, it is being offset by domestic attendance, especially at the Walt Disney World resort in Orlando, Florida, Johnston said.
Growth at Disneyland Paris was driven by recent investments including an expansion area called World of Frozen. Attendance at the Hong Kong and Shanghai parks remained soft because of broad economic challenges in those regions, according to Disney.
Still, D'Amaro said he believes the growth in parks will be sustainable through next year, especially with new additions, including the "Monsters, Inc."-themed land "Monstropolis" opening at Walt Disney World in 2027.
"Q1 forward resort bookings at Walt Disney World are pacing up compared to the prior year," he said. "And new capacity and new experiences will start coming online in 2027. We keep investing to make the experience fresh, and what we see is that drives repeat visits."
The company expects operating income for the experiences segment to grow in the high-single digits in fiscal 2027. Growth is expected to be front-loaded as the company laps the launch of the Disney Adventure cruise ship, which set sail in March.
Over at its entertainment division, Disney saw revenue increase 17% to $11.89 billion. Operating income nearly doubled to $1.33 billion.
Revenue from streaming, specifically, rose 19% to $6.1 billion, Disney said.
The segment benefited from the extra week on the fiscal calendar as well as from growth in subscription and affiliate fees. Additionally, the company saw higher theatrical distribution revenue from titles like "Toy Story 5."
Disney said Tuesday it expects operating income for the entertainment division to grow in the high-single digits in the coming fiscal year.
The company's sports division saw revenue increase 16% in the fiscal fourth quarter, reaching $4.61 billion. Operating income for the segment surged more than 50% to $1.39 billion.
Subscription and affiliate fees fueled this growth alongside an increase in advertising revenue.
The company expects its sports division's operating income to grow by double digits in fiscal 2027. It noted that the fiscal first quarter of the year will see some declines because of the timing of College Football Playoff games and the New Year's window. However, the fiscal second quarter will benefit from the college championship as well as the broadcast of Super Bowl 61.
Disney's outlook for overall and segment results for fiscal 2027 excludes the impact of a 53rd week in fiscal 2026.
D'Amaro has made advancing technology a pillar of the company's growth strategy. In September, Disney hired Karandeep Anand in the newly created position of chief technology officer.
"Technology is central to how we connect fans to more of Disney and drive returns on our investment," D'Amaro said on the earnings call. "[Anand has] been energized by how much opportunity he sees to move faster and go further in product and technology. Done right, that means serving our fans even better, working more efficiently and being more innovative across every one of our businesses."
Disney announced a partnership with Adobe earlier this month to develop generative artificial intelligence models.
D'Amaro told investors that the team is exploring ways to use AI to make booking trips to Disney parks easier.
"There's actually a vacation planning tool that's in beta right now at Walt Disney World. We built that with our partners at Google, and I've had a chance to experiment with it myself," he said. "It'll be incredibly helpful for our guests who are booking trips. With these AI features, it can feel like you've got someone sitting right by your side, like a personal concierge, that plans and responds to the way that you want to actually book your trip to Walt Disney World."
The entertainment company has also expanded its short-form content, adding a vertical video channel within the Disney+ mobile app. The company had previously announced a partnership with TikTok to bring creator content to the streaming app.

title: A common osteoporosis drug blocked spinal damage in a surprising new study
text:
Scientists have uncovered a surprising genetic connection to spinal degeneration and found that an existing osteoporosis drug can prevent damaging mineral buildup in zebrafish spines. The discovery could pave the way for new treatments that slow or prevent a major cause of chronic back pain.
An existing osteoporosis drug has shown surprising promise in protecting the spine from damage, raising hopes for new treatments for chronic neck and back pain. In experiments involving zebrafish, researchers found that the medication prevented abnormal mineral deposits from forming in the spine, a process that can cause spinal tissues to harden and vertebrae to fuse together.
The discovery could help scientists tackle one of the underlying causes of back pain: the gradual deterioration of the discs that cushion the bones of the spine. Researchers also identified changes in gene activity and metabolism that appear to contribute to this damage, revealing several possible targets for future treatments.
Although the findings have not yet been confirmed in humans, they suggest that medications already used for other conditions could offer new ways to slow spinal degeneration. The research also demonstrates how zebrafish could help scientists investigate the causes of spinal disease and test potential therapies.
Why Spinal Discs Break Down
Most people experience back pain at some point in their lives, and one common cause is the deterioration of the spine's natural shock absorbers. These structures, called intervertebral discs, sit between the vertebrae and help the spine absorb pressure, distribute weight, and move comfortably.
Over time, the discs can lose their ability to cushion the spine, a condition known as intervertebral disc degeneration (IVDD). As the discs deteriorate, they can contribute to pain, stiffness, and reduced mobility.
Despite the widespread impact and substantial economic burden of this condition, no medications are currently available that can stop or reverse the degenerative process. Surgery remains the only established long-term intervention for certain severe cases, creating an urgent need for treatments that address the underlying damage.
Researchers have long known that genetics influences the risk of developing spinal disc degeneration. One gene of particular interest is associated with collagen IX, a protein that helps maintain the structural integrity of spinal discs by supporting the network of fibers that holds them together. Variations affecting this gene have repeatedly been associated with disc problems that develop earlier in life.
To investigate how these genetic changes contribute to spinal damage, scientists at the Universities of Edinburgh and Bristol turned to zebrafish. They studied fish that had been bred without a functioning copy of the gene, allowing them to observe how its absence affected the spine as the animals grew older.
A Hidden Process Causes the Spine To Harden
The results revealed striking similarities between the genetically altered zebrafish and people with degenerative spinal disease.
As the fish aged, abnormal mineral deposits accumulated in the tissues separating their vertebrae. This process, known as mineralization, involves minerals collecting in tissues where they do not normally belong. In the spine, the buildup can cause normally flexible structures to become unusually rigid, much like unwanted bone forming in the wrong location.
The researchers also observed spinal fusion, in which neighboring vertebrae become joined together. Such changes can interfere with the spine's normal flexibility and movement.
Importantly, the scientists discovered that the damage began well before the mineral deposits appeared. An underlying layer that provides structural support during spinal development started to break down first, suggesting that deterioration of this protective framework may set the stage for later hardening.
This finding could help explain how genetic changes initiate a chain reaction that eventually damages the spine.
Surprising Links to Fat Metabolism and Vitamin A
To understand what was happening at the molecular level, the team examined patterns of gene activity in the zebrafish. This allowed them to identify biological processes that had become unusually active or disrupted as spinal degeneration developed.
Several unexpected connections emerged.
The researchers found alterations in fat metabolism, the processes through which the body breaks down, stores, and uses fats. They also detected disturbances in a cellular signaling system called mTOR, which helps regulate cell growth, metabolism, and responses to nutrients.
Additional changes involved phosphate regulation and vitamin A signaling. Phosphate is an essential mineral involved in building bones and teeth, but its accumulation in the wrong tissues can contribute to abnormal hardening. Vitamin A signaling helps control how cells develop and function.
Together, these findings suggest that spinal disc degeneration involves more than the gradual wearing down of tissues. Changes in how cells process nutrients, regulate growth, and handle minerals may also play important roles.
An Osteoporosis Drug Blocks Spinal Mineral Buildup
One of the most promising discoveries came when researchers tested ways to reduce the spinal abnormalities.
A medication belonging to a class of drugs called bisphosphonates successfully blocked the abnormal mineral buildup in the zebrafish. Bisphosphonates are already used to treat osteoporosis, a condition in which bones become weaker and more vulnerable to fractures. These medications help protect bones by slowing the processes that break down bone tissue.
The finding is especially intriguing because it suggests that a treatment already used in patients might also help researchers develop therapies for spinal degeneration.
The team identified other approaches that reduced spinal damage. Limiting how much food the zebrafish consumed led to fewer spinal fusions, as did medications that suppressed fat metabolism.
These results point toward fat metabolism and phosphate regulation as potentially important targets for future drugs.
However, the experiments were conducted in zebrafish, not humans. More research will be needed to determine whether the same biological mechanisms operate in people and whether targeting them can safely prevent or slow spinal disc degeneration. The dietary findings also do not establish that restricting food intake can prevent spinal damage in humans.
New Hope for Chronic Back Pain Treatments
The study was published in the journal Communications Biology and received support from Arthritis UK and BBSRC.
Dr. Erika Kague, who led the research at the University of Edinburgh's Institute of Genetics and Cancer, emphasized the potential significance of identifying treatments that target the underlying causes of spinal damage.
"For decades, surgery has been the only real answer for disc disease. By understanding the biology that drives the spine to harden, our zebrafish studies point to several ways of slowing it down, including a drug already used safely in patients. There's more work to do, but for a condition that's affected people for generations without a treatment in sight, this is super exciting."
The findings could be particularly important for the millions of people who live with persistent back pain and have limited options for preventing their condition from worsening.
Dr. Caroline Aylott, Head of Research Delivery at Arthritis UK, highlighted the potential benefits for patients.
"For the 9.5 million people across the UK living with back pain this research brings fresh hope that potential new therapeutic approaches are on the horizon.
"We are proud to fund research that is unlocking the science behind the processes leading to spinal disc degeneration. Back pain is one of the UK's most common conditions that has blighted millions over generations. Dr. Erika Kague and her team at the University of Edinburgh have uncovered important genetic evidence that could pave the way for new treatments, bringing us one step closer to a future where fewer people have to live with the daily pain and challenges that back pain can bring."
The research also illustrates the broader value of studying basic biological processes to understand diseases that affect large numbers of people.
Dr. Jef Grainger, Executive Director for Bioscience Advancing Knowledge at BBSRC, said:
"This research shows how publicly funded discovery bioscience can generate the knowledge needed to address major health challenges. By revealing new knowledge of how healthy biological processes break down in aging-related spinal disc degeneration, the study opens up promising avenues for future treatment development. It's a great example of how BBSRC-supported research helps turn scientific discovery into knowledge and innovations that have the potential to improve people's lives."
By identifying genetic and metabolic changes that contribute to spinal hardening, and demonstrating that some of the damage can be prevented in zebrafish, the researchers have opened several new avenues for investigating spinal disc degeneration.
For a condition that affects millions and has no approved drug capable of stopping its progression, these early findings offer an encouraging starting point for developing treatments that could one day protect the spine before serious damage occurs.

title: How escaping gases ripped apart a comet and caused it to become thousands of times brighter
text:
A comet dazzled this summer as the sun’s heat caused ice beneath its surface to turn to gas and rip out through its surface, spewing hundreds of billions of pounds' worth of dust into space and causing the comet to brighten by thousands of times.
Comet 220P/McNaught was discovered by the prolific Australian comet discoverer Robert McNaught in 2004. It is a periodic comet, the 220th discovered, meaning that it comes back again and again on a regular basis – in 220P’s case, once every five-and-a-half years when it gets about as close to the sun as Mars. Other than that, 220P is fairly nondescript, usually languishing at a feeble brightness fainter than magnitude +15, out of reach of most amateur telescopes. There has been little else to say about the comet, until this year.
On June 14, as it headed towards perihelion – the closest point in its orbit to the sun, at a distance from our star of 1.5 times the distance between the Earth and the sun (known as an astronomical unit), 220P suddenly and without warning burst into life.
On 31 May, the comet was languishing at magnitude +17.39 (the higher the magnitude, the fainter an object is), but within less than 14 hours it had dramatically brightened to magnitude +11.05, bringing it into range for observation with small amateur telescopes.
By June 2, 220P was up to magnitude +8.23 and was technically visible for a short while in 10x50 binoculars from a dark site, prompting amateur astronomers and astrophotographers to chase down this rare event.
By perihelion, the comet had faded back to magnitude +12, but more was to come. A second outburst began at the end of July, brightening from magnitude +14 on 28 July to magnitude 6.1 by 6 August.
Telling the tale of a dirty snowball
Comets are often referred to as dirty snowballs, and beneath their dusty crust are ices made from various volatiles, including water, carbon dioxide and nitrogen. Solar heating, even at the distance of Mars, can cause these ices to rapidly sublimate into gases, and the pressure of the escaping gas rips the surface apart, spewing huge amounts of dust in to space.
Models based on observations of 220P’s outburst indicate that it spewed out between tens of billions and hundreds of billions of pounds’ worth of cometary dust that filled the comet’s coma, the diffuse 'atmosphere' that clings to the comet’s solid nucleus. The dust particles, which are just millionths of a meter across, expanded outwards from the comet at about 1,280 feet (390 meters) per second, scattering sunlight and causing the coma to substantially brighten.
"We have concluded that the comet detached localized parts of its crust, creating a dust-rich envelope that increased [the comet’s brightness by] 250 times in half a day," Josep M. Trigo-Rodríguez, of the Institut de Ciències de l’Espai and the Institute of Space Studies of Catalonia in Spain, said in a statement.
While this is the first time that 220P has been seen to outburst, over the years we have witnessed other comets spectacularly brighten out of nowhere.
A recent and well-known example is comet 17P/Holmes, which brightened a million-fold in the fall of 2007 as it rose from magnitude +17 to magnitude +2.8, becoming a welcome naked-eye sight in the constellation of Perseus for many people as they made the evening commute home.
The short 5.5-year orbit of 220P marks it out as a Jupiter-family comet.
"Jupiter-family comets are extremely interesting objects to study because they originate primarily from the Kuiper Belt and the Scattered Disk region, later migrating inward until Jupiter captures them into short-period orbits," said Trigo-Rodríguez.
Studying outbursts such as the two experienced by 220P provides vital clues as to the bulk characteristics of Jupiter-family comets, giving us insight into objects that originated from beyond the orbit of Neptune.
Of particular interest to Trigo-Rodríguez is what we should do were one of these objects ever to be found on a collision course with Earth.
"Particularly we are interested in the tensile strength and nature of comets in the framework of our studies on impact hazards," said Trigo-Rodríguez. "Some comets seem determined to demonstrate that they are fragile enough and perhaps give us the chance to invoke disruptive approaches that might be substantially different from the ones already tested or proposed for asteroids."
For now, 220P is heading back out to its furthest point from the sun, which is just inside the orbit of Jupiter at a distance of 4.68 astronomical units or 435 million miles (700 million kilometers). Having passed as close to Earth as it is going to get this time around on 12 October at a distance of 1.04 astronomical units or 97 million miles (156 million kilometres), the comet is currently magnitude +13 and fading. All eyes will be on 220P during its next time around the sun in late 2031.
The findings were published on Nov.3 in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.

title: 'We're a capitalist society': Grindr defends $120 a month premium tier
text:
The world's largest LGBTQ+ dating app, Grindr, has defended its $120 (£91) per month premium subscription service, which launches globally today.
Edge offers AI-powered services such as daily personalised profile recommendations that aim to provide better matches and limit scrolling.
The company's CEO, George Arison, told BBC News it would be a "very different Grindr experience" which was aimed at a "small community of users" - and was unapologetic about its cost.
"I think we're a capitalist society, and everything hinges on whether you can afford it or not," he said.
Grindr has long had a free service, and offers two additional tiers that cost between $22.99 and $44.99 per month.
There was a mixed reaction from users BBC News spoke to in San Francisco to the new, more expensive version of the app.
"The current premium Grindr tier is already really expensive," said one user who told the BBC the company's newest offering "just seems really out of touch with the community."
"I think that that's really disheartening, and it kind of leaves a bad taste in my mouth," added another user, Adrian, who declined to give his last name.
"The cost doesn't bother me," said a user named Michael. "All of these apps have premium tiers so saying that Grindr shouldn't have that when like it exists across all these other apps used for connection doesn't make sense."
He noted that high-end dating apps like The League can charge much more.
'It's a choice'
Grindr has been experimenting with Edge for much of the last year in markets including the US, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand.
On its earnings call earlier this month, the company said almost 400,000 users had registered for the service in the first 72 hours that it was available for testing.
Inside Grindr, Edge is viewed as a way to drive future growth in an industry has struggled in recent years.
For those who can afford it, the service promises to offer insights about a user's compatibility with prospective matches. It also resurfaces a user's past connections alongside summaries of previous interactions.
The current $120 monthly fee comes after the company tested charging hundreds of dollars more than that. And Arison has left open the possibility of increasing the cost in the future.
Arison told the BBC he's not concerned that intoducing an ultra-premium offering will pit "haves" against "have-nots" on the social networking platform.
Edge users "being willing to pay more for that set of features will result in us being able to subsidise the product for everybody else," Arison said.
"It's a choice that people make on whether they want to be on it."
An 'AI-first company'
The use of AI to develop the Edge service is part of Grindr's attempt to become what it calls an "AI-first company."
Arison said the company was investing in AI to ensure it can build products more quickly and cheaply.
In September, as the debate over AI safety raged throughout Silicon Valley, Arison told the BBC that his concerns about what he called an "anti-civilisational worldview at Anthropic" had prompted him to instruct some of his engineers to stop using Anthropic's technology.
Anthropic is due to start selling shares to the public for the first time this week.
Although Anthropic's Claude Code tools remain in use at Grindr now, Arison said the company is on track to completely phase it out of his company's workflows by next year.
He said Grindr was once a very heavy user of Claude Code but that it was no longer the primary tool the use to write code.
"Anthropic's built an amazing amazing set of products, and they should be very proud of what they've done," Arison said. "They should aim to win with the awesome products they have, rather than regulatory capture that they're trying to win with, oftentimes."

title: Deutsche Bank dismissed warnings about dealings with risky clients, reports claim
text:
Deutsche Bank reportedly dismissed warnings about its dealings with risky clients, including high-profile Russian oligarchs, to protect profits, the findings of an investigation into a trove of leaked bank documents indicate.
A leak of 15m internal files is reported to show that the troubled German bank repeatedly ignored concerns by its compliance officers about its risk-taking, despite having already been caught being used to launder billions of dollars for Russian criminals, spies and oligarchs between 2010 and 2015.
The investigations, which were published by media outlets including Der Spiegel, the Financial Times, the New York Times and Le Monde, will represent a fresh blow for Deutsche Bank, which has struggled to repair its reputation after a number of scandals and dealings with controversial clients including the US president, Donald Trump, and the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
Deutsche Bank said on Tuesday that the issues raised in the investigations “date back many years, in some cases as much as two decades” and had been addressed by its leadership. “Where relevant, we reviewed these matters at the time and worked closely with regulators.”
However, the reports suggested Deutsche Bank prioritised profit ahead of internal controls, and continued to expand its Russian business until 2021, despite warnings from internal compliance officers and growing geopolitical tensions between Nato allies and Moscow.
Deutsche Bank allegedly resisted pulling out of Russia even after the Kremlin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, before the bank did a U-turn and exiting the country in March that year.
The investigations suggested Deutsche Bank was driven by competitive pressure, including from American banks, and that its chief executive, Christian Sewing, pursued a growth strategy that involved doing business with a list of customers known as its “most sensitive clients”. That covered roughly 50 corporate clients ranked by how close they were to the Kremlin, and other potential risks including financial crime, according to the Financial Times.
Some names allegedly on that list included: Russia’s state-owned gas company Gazprom; petrochemicals group Sibur; and oligarchs including the aluminium magnate Oleg Deripaska, the report said.
Outside its Russian dealings, the German lender is facing fresh scrutiny for allegedly processing almost $600m (£454m) of suspicious payments linked to Epstein, much higher than previously known. Deutsche said it “regrets [its] historical relationship” with Epstein and that it had made “considerable investments in strengthening controls”.
The lender is also accused of accidentally leaking Trump’s tax documents to another client during his first term in office, which Deutsche Bank allegedly kept secret from the White House. Deutsche Bank said it did not comment on former or existing client relationships. Deutsche Bank cut ties with Trump in 2021.
The reports prompted a 4% drop in Deutsche Bank’s German-listed shares on Tuesday.
Deutsche Bank issued a public statement in response to the investigation on Tuesday, saying it had “gone through a fundamental transformation” under Sewing.
“We made substantial investments in our control environment while restoring sustainable profitability, as evidenced by record profits in 2025 as well as in recent quarters. This involved €7bn of direct investments in our control environment between 2019 and 2025.”
The bank added: “We remain committed to ensuring continuous enhancements of our control environment and a culture of integrity and completing any outstanding remediation.”
“Regardless of how the information was obtained, it includes confidential information about clients, employees and other third parties, which remains legally protected. We have acted, and will continue to act, decisively to protect this,” the bank said.

title: A new policy could help solve the U.S. organ shortage. Critics say it's unethical
text:
The U.S. organ transplant system has approved the first national policy for a controversial procedure used to remove organs from hospital patients. The guidelines are designed to protect potential donors. But critics say they do little to improve safety and fail to address deeply troubling ethical concerns.
The procedure is called normothermic regional perfusion, known as NRP. It can be used after a family has decided to withdraw care because there's no hope of meaningful recovery for the person. To perform NRP, doctors attach an external pump to a donor minutes after their circulation has ended and they've been declared dead. The pump restores blood flow to their hearts, lungs, kidneys, liver and other organs to keep them from deteriorating.
"The hope with NRP is that it increases the supply of organs and it increases the quality of the organs," says Dr. Raymond Lynch, the director of transplantation at the Health Resources & Services Administration, the federal agency that oversees the organ transplant system.
NRP could help solve the chronic organ shortage, Lynch says. More than 109,000 Americans are waiting for an organ transplant, according to HRSA. About 12 die every day because of a chronic organ shortage.
Critics, however, say NRP is unethical because it violates the Dead Donor Rule, which is the most important rule protecting potential donors. The rule says transplant surgeons can only take organs from patients after they are dead because of brain death or circulatory death. But because NRP restarts circulation, critics say the procedure reverses the very condition upon which the person has just been declared dead.
"In order to be dead by circulatory criteria it means we're not going to attempt to reestablish circulation. But that's exactly what they do in NRP," says Dr. Lainie Friedman Ross, a University of Rochester bioethicist. "So, yes, I have a real problem with NRP. I think it violates the dead donor rule. It's taking organs from people who are no longer dead."
The other aspect of NRP that troubles critics is what surgeons do to try to make sure the donor is also brain dead, after circulation has been restarted by a mechanical pump. They clamp off blood vessels that supply the head. But alarm bells started going off for organ retrieval teams when blood appeared to get restored – or "reperfused" – to the brain during some NRP cases.
"We have seen signs of life in NRP when the brain has been reperfused," says Dr. Claire Morgan, a transplant surgeon who serves on the transplant network's Patient Affairs Committee and was the first to report such cases to HRSA. "It's extremely disturbing."
Those cases prompted HRSA to instruct the Organ Procurement & Transplantation Network (OPTN), which runs the organ system, to investigate and develop a response. On Nov. 6, the OPTN board of directors approved the first phase of the first uniform national guidelines for how to perform NRP.
The new guidelines, which will go into effect Dec. 6, call for surgeons to do more than just clamp the blood vessels to the brain. They should also cut holes in them, according to the new policy.
"Clamping the blood vessels should stop blood flowing to the brain," says Lynch. "Cutting or venting above the level of the clamping is a second safeguard to make sure that if the clamping is insufficient that it immediately drains out of the head and is not supplying warm oxygenated blood to the brain."
The new policy also includes other protections, including recommending against giving donors drugs that would paralyze them and mask any movements.
But critics say the new safeguards are insufficient. Most surgeons already both clamp and vent blood vessels to the brain, for example, they say.
"I honestly don't believe they have created a policy that creates much or any more protection than these donors already had," says Morgan.
Critics also say the new policy doesn't begin to address the bigger concerns that NRP donors are not technically dead when surgeons remove their organs. They worry the adoption of the policy could speed the use of NRP before the troubling questions have been fully aired.
"I really think the policy is the cart before the horse," says Dr. Matthew DeCamp, a University of Colorado bioethicist. "The fundamental issues around NRP still remain unresolved."
Lynch, however, argues the new guidelines will protect donors and that NRP is ethical.
"This is an important first step to make sure NRP care is available but that the safety of the family's loved one is always at the forefront," Lynch says. "This is life-saving care that will extend the supply and improve the quality of organs that patients can get in transplant. And if it is done properly, it is safe."

title: Can a 'coalition of the willing' create momentum for a fossil fuel phaseout?
text:
This time last year, as negotiations at the UN COP climate summit in Brazil entered crunch time, there was hope that governments would agree on a clear roadmap for phasing out oil, gas and coal. More than 80 countries backed the idea.
But instead, after opposition from oil-producing states such as Russia and Saudi Arabia, the conference wrapped up with a watered-down final agreement that did not explicitly mention fossil fuels.
As a compromise, summit host Brazil offered to produce a "voluntary" roadmap. At the same time, a group of 57 countries frustrated with the deadlock at the consensus-based UN talks decided to form a "coalition of the willing" to accelerate the fossil fuel exit outside the COP framework.
They held their own summit in April in Santa Marta, Colombia — the first such conference to specifically focus on implementing the transition away from fossil fuels (referred to as TAFF).
What happened in Santa Marta?
Co-hosted by Colombia and the Netherlands, the Santa Marta conference brought together countries including Canada, Norway, Brazil, Nigeria, Mexico, Australia and Germany, as well as highly climate-vulnerable states such as Vanuatu.
The idea was for governments to start developing national roadmaps and working out how to restructure their financial and trade systems to wean themselves off polluting energy sources — an incredibly complicated undertaking, particularly for developing countries dependent on revenue from fossil fuel exports.
Part of their discussions focused on cutting subsidies for oil, coal and gas, as well as supporting people whose livelihoods rely on the fossil fuel industry to find new forms of income.
What role will the 'coalition of the willing' play at COP?
A little over six months on from the Santa Marta meeting, representatives from almost 200 countries are holding talks in Antalya, Turkey, as part of the latest UN climate conference.
Countries agreed for the first time in 2023 to transition away from fossil fuels — the main driver behind rising global temperatures. But summits since then have failed to pin down how to implement that pledge.
It's not yet clear whether the Santa Marta coalition will influence ambition at this year's COP.
"I think it's more of a long-term game," said Chetna Hareesh Kumar, a climate policy analyst at the Berlin-based research organization NewClimate Institute.
She says it's too soon to expect the coalition to have an influence on the negotiations but adds that that could change at future COPs. The grouping could bring more nations on board if, for example, it shows it can be truly inclusive, address the needs of different types of countries and show that a transition is feasible.
One role the group is playing, according to Alexandra Scott, a senior climate diplomacy adviser at Italian climate change think tank ECCO, is "keeping up the political momentum," and showing "that there is this huge group of countries who really want to accelerate this transition away from fossil fuels."
She says it's also building an invaluable "cadre of knowledge" on how to develop national TAFF plans and deal with barriers individual countries face — like how to secure funding for the infrastructure investments needed for the energy transition.
The Santa Marta group is "really answering a lot of the questions that countries have always had on how on earth do we even start to transition our whole economy off fossil fuels?" Scott said.
This expertise being shared and tested in practice can show what such a transformation could look like and the knowledge brought into COP, added Scott.
Few countries have announced national TAFF plans
Since the Santa Marta conference, Germany, France and the Netherlands have released national plans to phase out fossil fuels. While the plans contain no new commitments, experts see them as a positive first step.
Kumar says more countries could announce similar plans just ahead of the second TAFF summit in Tuvalu next year. Finland presented its TAFF roadmap in the first week of COP, but analysts do not expect many more countries to follow suit soon.
Another potential boost that could get momentum going is Brazil's recently published global roadmap to transition away from fossil fuels, promised at last year's COP.
The nearly 200-page document seeks to serve as a toolkit for countries shifting from fossil fuels to renewable energy, such as wind and solar. It envisages countries making a phased transition between 2028 and 2033.
The aim, Ana Toni, CEO of last year's COP, told AP, is to break down the transition into "smaller actionable solutions" and help countries make practical progress.
The roadmap suggests measures tailored to each country's circumstances, including dependence on fossil fuel and financial capacities. "Levers" it proposes include reducing fossil fuel subsidies, expanding renewable energy and cutting methane emissions.
Kumar called it a "customizable" approach that allows every country to take action, regardless of its situation. "The question really is now what countries do with it and how much momentum they can generate," she added.
Focus on electrification
This year's climate change summit in Turkey — taking place after a series of deadly heat waves in Europe and a glacier collapse in Nepal that killed more than 1,400 people — isn't expected to result in any big announcements about fossil fuels.
Global renewable energy capacity has surged in recent years, making up a third of the world's power generation for the first time in 2025. But many countries still rely on coal, oil and gas.
A database compiled by the German environmental organization Urgewald shows that most oil and gas companies worldwide, among them QatarEnergy, Saudi Aramco and Russia's Gazprom, are exploring or developing new reserves.
Meanwhile, subsidies for fossil fuels amount to around $920 billion (around €830 billion) per year, according to data from the OECD, but that number is falling.
One issue Turkey is pushing at the COP conference is electrification. It's calling on countries to endorse the goal of 35% of final energy consumption coming from electricity by 2035 — up from around 20% today.
The pledge has drawn criticism from some circles, though, for leaving open whether that additional electricity needs to come from clean sources.
Ideally, Kumar said, electrification would be powered by renewables and tied to a goal of phasing out polluting fossil fuels.
"If something like that could make it to the final text, that would be a really good sign for momentum."

title: Peter Storey: Arsenal double winner dies aged 81
text:
Arsenal have announced the death of their former midfielder Peter Storey at the age of 81.
Having joined the Gunners as an apprentice in 1961, Storey made his first-team debut for the club in October 1965, and went on to stay at the club for a further 12 years.
A club statement on Tuesday read: "Everyone at Arsenal is deeply saddened by the passing of 1970-71 Double Winner, Peter Storey.
"All our thoughts are with his family and loved ones at this incredibly sad time. Rest in peace, Peter."
Arsenal also confirmed that the club will pay tribute to Storey during their Champions League fixture against Borussia Dortmund, which takes place on 24 November.
Storey initially started his Arsenal career at full-back before moving into midfield and winning the Fairs Cup in 1970.
During the 1970-71 campaign, Storey featured prominently in the Arsenal team that completed the double, playing an important role in their FA Cup triumph.
He scored a stoppage-time penalty against Stoke in the semi-finals to force a replay, before the Gunners went on to lift the trophy.
With 501 total appearances for Arsenal, Storey ranks as their eighth highest appearance maker of all time. Departing north London in 1977, he joined Fulham prior to retiring in 1978.
At international level, Storey received an England call-up in 1971 and was capped on 19 occasions.
Arsenal are due to play their first game after Storey’s death on Saturday when they face Newcastle at St James’ Park.
The Gunners headed into the international break with a five-point cushion at the top of the table after winning nine of their opening 10 Premier League matches.
Their nearest challengers are currently Brighton, who are also the only team to beat them this season.
Manchester City are a further point adrift after losing three matches in a row prior to the international break.

title: Russia plays for time as Europe and US push for direct peace talks
text:
The next phase of the peace talks remains uncertain as Russia continues to play down the possibility of face-to-face talks with Europe, despite mounting pressure from Washington to make it happen.
Europe has finally settled on a joint team to speak on the continent's behalf in the negotiations to end Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Yet, despite this diplomatic breakthrough, uncertainty remains over what comes next.
Russia has again cast doubt on the possibility of holding face-to-face talks with the European delegation, which now comprises France, Germany, the United Kingdom, Italy, Poland, the EU institutions (Council and Commission) and NATO.
European, US and Ukrainian officials all agree that the only way to move the process forward is to start a multilateral format with the Russians.
But Moscow seems to be in no hurry.
"The date has not yet been agreed and the expansion of the format – some people are talking about it – but it has not been agreed with us," Yury Ushakov, a close aide to Russian President Vladimir Putin, said on Monday.
Adding to the confusion, Ushakov suggested that "it may be necessary to hold another round, or perhaps more than one round, of trilateral talks" with the US and Ukraine before sitting down with the Europeans.
After speaking with Ushakov, US special envoy Jared Kushner sounded cautiously optimistic, saying preparations were underway for a multilateral meeting that should take place "in the near future".
"We discussed how to facilitate direct engagement between Europe and Russia, which has been largely absent over the past four years," Kushner said on social media.
"It is important that both sides hear each other's concerns and proposals directly as we work toward a more stable and secure future for Europe."
So far, the peace talks have proceeded in two parallel tracks: Ukraine, Russia and the US, on the one hand, and Ukraine, Europe and the US, on the other.
In practice, this has left Europe in the room next door, trying to catch up with what is discussed in the main room, as it happened in Abu Dhabi.
The US side has concluded the two-track configuration has reached its limit and the time has come for Europe and Russia to sit at the same table, at the same time.
Europe, long opposed to this direct engagement, is now on board.
"We are absolutely ready to engage at the multilateral level," Paula Pinho, the Commission's chief spokesperson, said.
Privately, European officials and diplomats say that expectations should remain low because, when it comes to Russia, nothing can be guaranteed, particularly given the volatility of the negotiations, which have gone through multiple ups and downs – and a protracted pause – in the past year alone.
Moscow'scontinued delays reinforce the widespread belief that Putin is playing lip service to the White House and has no intention of treating diplomacy seriously. The brutal attacks against Ukraine ahead of the winter bear witness to that.
The fact that Moscow talks about Europe's security architecture but refuses to talk with Europeans is cited as further reason to be wary.
The topic is seen as a ploy to divert attention from Ukraine, regurgitate old grievances and reassert Russia's long-lost sphere of influence. According to the New York Times, the Russian demands presented to the US were that NATO stop expanding, withdraw its troops to 1997 borders and halt military support for Ukraine.
"It's absurd. Russia misbehaves, and then they want to be rewarded for it," a senior diplomat snapped. "I don't see how it could fly at all."
Despite the daunting odds, Europeans are keen to show their readiness and availability, while preparing new sanctions on Russia and support for Ukraine.
Senior officials from the joint European team will meet with their US and Ukrainian counterparts on Thursday to work out the next steps in the process. The meeting will take place on the sidelines of the Coalition of the Willing in Berlin.
Brussels, meanwhile, has begun drafting a common mandate in case the multilateral format happens. The mandate is meant to compile the principles that Ukraine's allies have followed since the start of the war.
Austria, one of the first member states to publicly call for direct talks with Russia, has circulated a two-page document, seen by Euronews, to structure the negotiations built around four key pillars: political, security, humanitarian and economic.
The paper calls on the EU to maximise its "sanction leverage", prepare a special mission to monitor an eventual ceasefire and develop a strategy for the use of the immobilised Russian assets. It also floats a "division of labour" among the EU, NATO, the United Nations, the OSCE and the Coalition of the Willing to safeguard a future peace.
"Europe finally has a negotiating team that is expected to join the next round of talks. Now the focus must shift from the 'who' to the 'what'. This team urgently needs a mandate on substance," Austrian Foreign Minister Beate Meinl-Reisinger said.
"What is at stake is nothing less than Europe's own security."

title: Ecuador's president denies US operates military base despite reports of troop buildup
text:
Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa denied that the United States operates a military base in his country after an Agence France-Presse (AFP) investigation signaled an expanded U.S. military presence at an air base near the port city of Guayaquil.
"Sometimes there's a specific mission. Sometimes there's a specific operation," Noboa told the news outlet Altavoz, describing U.S. personnel at Taura Air Base as carrying out "temporary activities" under a bilateral security agreement, including intelligence-gathering drone flights.
"We work together. It's not an American base. It's an Ecuadoran base," he commented.
Noboa's remarks came about a month after AFP had documented an unusual deployment of U.S. military aircraft, dozens of tents and construction of new infrastructure at the air base.
The investigation identified approximately 20 U.S. military flights arriving at Taura between June and mid-October, along with internal documents confirming the presence of American troops.
Several flights originated from U.S. military installations, including Marine Corps Air Station Cherry Point in North Carolina and Dover Air Force Base in Delaware, with stopovers in Puerto Rico and Panama.
The buildup also raised legal concerns among senior Ecuadorian military officials.
AFP cited a September letter in which then-Air Force commander Gen. Mauricio Salazar asked military leaders to clarify the legality of the deployment. Salazar was subsequently removed from his post and reassigned to a less senior role, the report said.
The increased U.S. military presence comes after Ecuadorian voters rejected a Noboa-backed referendum in November 2025 that would have amended the country's constitution to lift its ban on foreign military bases.
Despite the referendum's defeat, Quito and Washington have deepened security cooperation to combat drug trafficking and transnational organized crime.
Human Rights Watch has described the United States as Ecuador's primary security partner in its crackdown on organized crime, providing equipment, training, intelligence and direct military support.
The watchdog characterized the partnership as "perilous," warning that "both governments have engaged in serious human rights violations fuelled by their insistence on framing their confrontations with organised crime groups as a kind of war."
Since returning to the White House in January 2025, President Donald Trump has designated several Latin American cartels as foreign terrorist organizations and authorized military strikes against vessels in international waters suspected of drug trafficking.
Ecuador has also emerged as a key ally in Trump's crackdown on drug cartels and narcoterrorism, with U.S. and Ecuadorian forces working together to intercept narcotics shipments and dismantle transnational criminal networks, the country's foreign minister told Fox News Digital in September.
Roberto Kury said closer cooperation with Washington had delivered "a lot of positive results" in recent months, citing drug shipments intercepted through U.S. intelligence and joint operations.
"There is an intelligence (sic) and cooperation from the United States, but there is also always the presence of Ecuadorian military or police. They work together," Kury told Fox News Digital on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly.
"Most of the drugs go to the United States. So that’s why the United States shares the problem," Kury said.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio has also praised Ecuador as the United States' most "aggressive" partner in its Western Hemisphere crackdown.
Fox News Digital has reached out to Southcom for comment.

title: Deutsche Bank shares sink as whistleblowers reveal Epstein payments, Trump tax leak, Russia bets
text:
Deutsche Bank shares fell sharply in early trading on Tuesday after whistleblowers leaked about 15 million files from the German lender, with media reports revealing alleged historic failures across its risk management and financial crime controls.
These include suspicious payments linked to late financier and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, and accidental leaks of President Donald Trump's tax statements.
The leaks contain board minutes, emails, internal investigations and other material that point to systemic failures across the Frankfurt-listed lender's business functions stretching back two decades.
Shares in Deutsche Bank were 4.7% lower by 9:20 a.m. E.T., having fallen more than 6% in early trade in Frankfurt.
Deutsche Bank processed $582 million in suspicious payments linked to Jeffrey Epstein, far more than previously known, the FT reported. Suspicious payments are not, by themselves, proof that every transaction was criminal.
The German lender also mistakenly leaked details of U.S. President Donald Trump's taxes in March 2017, during his first term in office, the FT said. The blunder — described by CEO Christian Sewing, who was then Deutsche's private banking head, as "an awful mistake" — was kept secret from the White House.
The wide-ranging investigation — which was led by a consortium of more than 200 journalists worldwide including the FT, Der Spiegel and Le Monde — also said Deutsche Bank had failed to offboard around 28,000 problematic investment bank clients who had been identified for removal by early 2018.
It also alleges that the bank concealed information around cost targets in 2021, when external monitors in New York reportedly warned that Deutsche's risk appetite was running ahead of controls.
The files also contain details of the bank's relationships with oligarchs and transactions that the investigation links to Russian money-laundering concerns. It was these ties that motivated whistleblowers to send the information to Indian journalist Josy Joseph and South African journalist Khadija Sharife.
The reports once again put Deutsche Bank's risk management practices and controls under the spotlight following years of regulatory scrutiny.
The bank — which has been raided multiple times by German officials this year — has, since 2012, paid out some 18.6 billion euros ($20.5 billion) in settlements over alleged market manipulation, money laundering, mis-selling and misrepresentation, among other things, the FT said.
In a statement, Deutsche Bank said the issues detailed in Tuesday's media reports go back many years.
"Where relevant, we reviewed these matters at the time and worked closely with regulators," the lender said.
The bank said it has undergone a "fundamental transformation" under CEO Christian Sewing, pointing to 7 billion euros of investment in its risk controls between 2019 and 2025.
"Deutsche Bank is a different bank today and remains focused on executing its strategy which has proven successful, as evidenced by record profits in 2025 as well as in recent quarters."
CNBC has reached out to BaFin, Germany's financial regulator, for comment.

title: A simple supplement could help your immune system fight cancer and viral infections
text:
A surprising discovery from Rockefeller University suggests that a common amino acid could play a powerful role in protecting against cancer and viral infections. Scientists found that low arginine levels interfere with the immune system's ability to recognize dangerous cells, while increasing arginine intake reduced colon cancer tumors and improved viral infection outcomes in mice. Even more remarkably, giving mice arginine after they contracted influenza helped them recover.
A common amino acid found in everyday foods could play a surprisingly important role in helping the immune system recognize cancer and fight viral infections. Scientists at Rockefeller University have discovered that when the body runs low on arginine, a key part of its immune defense system can stop working properly, potentially allowing dangerous cells and viruses to escape detection.
Arginine is an amino acid that the body produces naturally and also obtains from protein-rich foods. It is essential for making proteins that perform countless functions throughout the body. Researchers have long known that unusually low arginine levels are associated with several diseases, including colon cancer, but exactly how this shortage affects the body's defenses has remained unclear.
Now, new research suggests that restoring arginine levels could help the immune system respond more effectively to serious threats. In experiments involving mice, increasing dietary arginine reduced the formation of colon cancer tumors and lessened the severity of influenza and SARS-CoV-2 infections. Remarkably, providing arginine after mice had already contracted influenza also improved their outcomes.
The findings, published in the journal Cell, raise the possibility that an inexpensive, readily available supplement could eventually become a useful addition to cancer treatments and strategies for combating viral infections. However, further research in humans is needed to determine whether the benefits observed in mice translate into effective treatments for people.
How a Missing Nutrient Could Help Cancer Escape the Immune System
The research was led by Sohail Tavazoie, who directs the Elizabeth and Vincent Meyer Laboratory of Systems Cancer Biology at Rockefeller University. His team has spent years investigating how arginine influences cancer development and progression.
In 2023, the researchers discovered that depriving colon cancer cells of arginine caused them to accumulate more genetic mutations. These changes can contribute to the unpredictable behavior of cancer cells, raising important questions about how arginine shortages might influence the disease.
The latest study reveals another potentially significant consequence. When arginine becomes scarce, cells struggle to produce enough of a crucial immune system protein known as MHC-1. This protein acts as a warning system, helping immune cells identify potential dangers such as cancerous changes or viral infections.
Without enough MHC-1, abnormal or infected cells may become harder for the immune system to recognize.
Encouragingly, the researchers also found that supplying a moderate amount of arginine, comparable to the quantity available in a couple of over-the-counter supplement tablets, could help restore production of this important protein.
"Our work reveals how a lack of arginine interferes with the immune system, and suggests that upping arginine intake could prove beneficial," says first author Qiushuang Wu, a postdoc in the lab. "Perhaps that means it could be used in combination with other therapies to treat both cancer and viral infections."
"Arginine supplementation could be readily tested in patients receiving immunotherapies or given to high-risk populations exposed to viral pathogens," Tavazoie suggests. "Considering that arginine is inexpensive and readily available, we hope that therapeutic and preventative studies could be undertaken soon."
The Surprising Connection Between Arginine and Immune Defenses
To understand why arginine has such an important effect, the researchers investigated how cells use amino acids to manufacture proteins.
Proteins are built from amino acids according to genetic instructions encoded in DNA. These instructions are copied into messenger RNA, which carries the information to the cellular machinery responsible for protein production.
The instructions are read in groups of three genetic letters called codons. Each codon specifies an amino acid or provides another signal needed during protein production. Arginine is unusual in that six different codons can specify it, reflecting the multiple ways its incorporation into proteins can be encoded.
Scientists already knew that changes in amino acid availability could affect cellular metabolism and signaling, two processes that help regulate how cells obtain energy and respond to their surroundings. What remained less clear was whether shortages of particular amino acids could directly influence which proteins cells produce.
To investigate, Wu examined the effects of arginine availability across several disease models, including colon cancer, influenza, and SARS-CoV-2. Each of these diseases has previously been associated with abnormal levels of various amino acids.
The research was supported in part by the Stavros Niarchos Foundation (SNF) Institute for Global Infectious Disease Research at The Rockefeller University and the Weill Cancer East Hub.
"One of the most dramatic patterns to emerge was that arginine was the most depleted amino acid in all of these diseases," she says.
Why Low Arginine Levels Can Disrupt the Immune System
In laboratory experiments using cultured cells, Wu examined how arginine shortages affected protein production. She identified 414 proteins whose levels dropped abnormally when arginine was scarce.
Many of these proteins were associated with biological functions already known to depend on arginine. However, the researchers uncovered a more unexpected effect involving three genes from the HLA family.
These genes provide instructions for producing proteins associated with MHC-I (major histocompatibility complex class I), an essential component of the immune system's ability to recognize threats.
MHC-I proteins are displayed on the surfaces of cells throughout the body. They act somewhat like identification displays, presenting small fragments of proteins from inside the cell to immune cells known as T cells.
When these displays reveal suspicious material, such as proteins produced by a virus or abnormal proteins associated with cancer, T cells can recognize the danger and help coordinate an immune response.
But the researchers found that arginine deficiency interfered with the production of these molecular warning signals.
The reason involved ribosomes, the tiny cellular machines that assemble proteins by following genetic instructions. Because the proteins involved in MHC-I production require arginine at numerous points, the researchers suspected that an insufficient supply could interfere with their assembly.
Further experiments confirmed that suspicion. When arginine was unavailable, ribosomes stalled while trying to manufacture MHC-I proteins. Without enough of the required amino acid, the cells could not efficiently complete the process.
As a result, fewer MHC-I proteins reached the cell surface, reducing the signals that would normally alert T cells to cancer-associated or viral proteins. This created an opportunity for dangerous cells to avoid immune detection.
"These findings are exciting because they reveal that consumption of a specific amino acid can directly regulate gene expression in an organism by increasing production of a protein enriched in that amino acid," Tavazoie says. "We believe that such selective translational tuning of gene expression through dietary manipulation likely extends to many other proteins and amino acids."
More Arginine Meant Fewer Colon Cancer Tumors in Mice
After identifying the molecular mechanism, Wu investigated whether changing the amount of arginine in an animal's diet could influence disease outcomes.
The results were striking.
Mice receiving diets low in arginine developed more colon cancer tumors. In contrast, mice consuming higher amounts of the amino acid developed fewer tumors.
These findings provided evidence that arginine availability can influence cancer development through its effects on the immune system, rather than simply changing how individual cancer cells behave.
The results also raised a broader question: If arginine helps immune cells recognize cancer, could it provide similar benefits when the body encounters dangerous viruses?
Arginine Also Improved Outcomes From Influenza and COVID-19 Viruses
To explore that possibility, Wu collaborated with Heinz-Heinrich Hoffman, a research assistant professor in Charles Rice's Laboratory of Virology and Infectious Disease.
Together, they examined the effects of dietary arginine in mouse models of influenza and SARS-CoV-2, the virus responsible for COVID-19.
The findings followed the same general pattern seen in the colon cancer experiments. Mice consuming more arginine experienced less severe symptoms from viral infections, suggesting that adequate levels of the amino acid helped support the body's immune defenses.
The researchers then made an even more surprising discovery.
Arginine did not appear to be beneficial only when consumed before an infection. Giving mice additional arginine after they had already been infected with influenza also improved their outcomes.
"Not only did mice with an arginine-rich diet have milder symptoms from viral infections, giving the mice arginine after influenza infection improved their outcomes too," Wu notes. "That was very surprising. From our genetic models, we knew manipulating arginine levels had a strong effect on gene expression, but we didn't expect the dietary manipulation to be equally impactful."
The observation suggests that changing nutrient availability might influence how the immune system responds even after a viral infection has taken hold.
Could a Simple Supplement Improve Cancer and Virus Treatments?
The discovery has potentially important implications for understanding why some people become more vulnerable to cancer and severe viral infections.
Arginine levels naturally decline with age, and inadequate nutrition can further reduce the amount available to cells. The researchers suspect that these changes may contribute to the weakening of immune defenses seen in certain diseases and in older adults.
"Qiushuang's findings illuminate how poor diet and aging -- during which arginine levels naturally decline -- could create the perfect storm for the initiation of colon cancer. Similarly, age-related arginine loss could partially contribute to the greater mortality caused by respiratory viruses," Tavazoie says. "We're also investigating whether making dietary changes in other amino acids has beneficial effects in a variety of disease contexts. There are no doubt more discoveries to come."
The possibility of using arginine alongside existing cancer immunotherapies is particularly intriguing. These treatments work by helping the immune system recognize and attack cancer cells. If low arginine levels interfere with the molecular signals required for that recognition, restoring the nutrient might help some treatments work more effectively.
The researchers also see potential for investigating arginine supplementation in people at elevated risk of respiratory viral infections.
For now, these possibilities remain experimental. The findings do not establish that taking arginine supplements prevents or treats cancer, influenza, or COVID-19 in humans.
Nevertheless, the research reveals an important connection between nutrition and immunity. Rather than simply providing the raw materials needed to build proteins, specific amino acids may help determine how effectively the body's immune defenses identify and respond to dangerous threats.
And because arginine is inexpensive and widely available, the discovery could provide a practical starting point for future studies aimed at strengthening the immune system against cancer and infectious diseases.

title: What's next for SpaceX's Starship after epic Flight 15 chopsticks catch?
text:
Starship may have just made history, but it still has some work to do to get fully up and running.
The megarocket launched on its 15th test flight on Friday (Nov. 13), aiming to pull off a dramatic and unprecedented twofer. SpaceX wanted to bring both Starship elements — its Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage — back to the launch pad at its Starbase site in Texas to be caught by the tower's "chopstick" arms.
