It didn't happen with Super Heavy; the booster diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown on Friday evening after experiencing a low-fuel alarm. But Ship came home successfully, nestling into the tower's arms in a soft and unprecedented embrace on Saturday afternoon (Nov. 14), 22.5 hours after lifting off.
SpaceX has caught Super Heavy on three test flights to date. But it had never caught a Ship before; indeed, it had never even tried before Saturday. It's tougher and riskier to catch Ship; the upper stage flies much higher and faster than Super Heavy, so its return trip is much more more involved.
Saturday was therefore a very big day for the company.
"That was the holy grail of spaceflight, plummeting through fire to be snatched out of the air by steel," SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot said during the company's landing webcast on Saturday. "We caught a Starship, and now everything changes."
The Flight 15 mission plan gave us a sneak peek at the future: The double catch will be standard on operational Starship missions, as this recovery strategy will enable rapid inspection, refurbishment and reflight of the megarocket, according to SpaceX.
And the company is indeed planning on rapid reflight. Elon Musk has said that SpaceX is targeting 10,000 Starship launches per year by 2030, which works out to more than one liftoff every hour on average.
Why such a mind-boggling cadence? Because SpaceX plans to build megaconstellations far larger than anything circling Earth today. For example, it wants its next-gen Starlink V3 broadband network to consist of 100,000 satellites. And its planned Starmind AI data-center constellation will be 10 times bigger than that, featuring one million spacecraft, if all goes to plan.
For perspective: SpaceX's current-gen Starlink network in low Earth orbit (LEO), by far the largest constellation ever assembled, is about 11,000 strong at the moment.
Rocket recovery is only part of the reuse equation, of course; there's also refurbishment and reflight. And that gets us back to the "work left to do" discussion, for SpaceX has yet to demonstrate rapid reflight with either Super Heavy or Ship.
The company has reflown Super Heavy vehicles on two separate occasions. Booster 14 initially launched on Flight 7 in January 2025, then lifted off again on Flight 9 in May of that year. Booster 15 flew on Flight 8 and Flight 11, which lifted off in March 2025 and October 2025, respectively.
Several months separated each of these Super Heavy reflights. And SpaceX has yet to reuse a Ship, as it had not caught one during a mission until Saturday.
That could change soon: Before Flight 15 lifted off, Musk said that the company wants to reuse both of its Starship stages. That option may still be on the table for Flight 15's Ship.
And we should expect full reuse to be a priority on Starship test flights over the longer haul, with SpaceX working toward shorter and shorter turnaround times — perhaps until an hourly cadence is in sight, if that goal is indeed achievable.
Over the next few years, most Starship launches will likely be devoted to building out the Starlink V3 and Starmind megaconstellations. But the rocket will also carry people to deep space, if all goes to plan, which will require the checking of another set of boxes.
NASA selected Ship to be the first crewed lunar lander for its Artemis program, which aims to establish a base near the lunar south pole by 2032 or so. Current plans call for Ship to land astronauts in that locale for the first time on the Artemis IV mission, which is targeted to fly in 2028.
SpaceX needs to install a crew cabin and life-support system in Ship to make that happen. The company is working on that now and has made considerable progress, according to NASA. Last month, an agency presentation reported that SpaceX is on target to finish building "Cabin 1," a full-scale ground prototype of Ship's crew cabin, by the end of the year.
There's another hurdle to clear, however. On all deep-space missions, Ship will need to fill up its fuel tanks after launch, at a "depot" that SpaceX will set up in Earth orbit. (Launching Ship with full tanks is not an option, as it would be incredibly heavy in that case.)
The depot will be filled by "tanker" variants of Ship. It's unclear how many tanker visits will be required for each Ship deep-space mission; outside experts have floated numbers as high as 22, while Musk has cited six to eight as a probable range.
Whatever the actual number, Ship will need to demonstrate proficiency with off-Earth refueling, something it has yet to do. And there's more to it than just a simple rendezvous: Ship's engines run on liquid oxygen and liquid methane, so the propellants must be kept extremely cold throughout the process.
We're likely to see the first refueling test relatively soon, as time is of the essence for SpaceX. If the company can't get Ship ready for the Artemis IV moon landing in 2028, NASA may go with another private lander — Blue Origin's Blue Moon, which the agency also contracted for Artemis missions.
All of this is to say that, while Flight 15 was a big success for Starship and SpaceX, there's a lot of work left to do — and a lot for space fans to watch for over the coming weeks and months.

title: Met Office yellow warning in place as snow could disrupt Tuesday morning travel
text:
Parts of northern England and southern Scotland are getting an early taste of winter with snow falling over some hills on Tuesday morning.
A Met Office yellow warning for snow is valid until 11:00 GMT with 5-15cm expected at some locations above 300-400m elevation.
Major routes like the A74(M), A66 and M62 could all have problems with transport disruption.
Some railways are also likely to be affected with longer journey times for train services.
Cold health alerts are also in place, external for northern England issued by the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) until 09:00 GMT on Thursday.
What's causing the snow?
A weather front is pushing north and east across the UK bringing a spell of rain to many areas. Over northern England it is encountering a reservoir of colder and drier air.
Some of the rain is evaporating in this drier air, cooling the atmosphere further by a process known as evaporative cooling - the same process involved in cooling your body down when you sweat.
Rain has turned to snow over parts of the Pennines, Cumbrian Hills and Scotland's Southern Uplands.
The snow could come down in big, wet, chunky flakes which could stick to power lines and tree branches.
The extra weight of the snow combined with wind gusts of 40-50mph over high ground could bring down tree branches and power lines, bringing an additional risk of some localised power cuts.
How long will the snow last?
Some snow may accumulate down to 100m elevation or so, with around 1-5cm possible.
Any snow in these lower hills will probably be quite short-lived, turning back to rain by mid-morning in many parts, however the highest hills and mountains of Scotland and northern England could continue to see wintry weather into the afternoon.
Cold outbreaks of rain will be left across most northern areas of the UK through Tuesday afternoon with some hill fog and a chilly wind.
Meanwhile the south will have sunshine and blustery showers but it will also be milder with temperatures up to 14C.
Rain and showers will continue to impact Northern Ireland, England and Wales for the next few days.
There will still be some rain in Scotland on Wednesday but then high pressure will take over with sunnier weather returning.
This drier, sunnier weather will then push southwards across most of the UK by the end of the week with cold air returning, along with some overnight frosts and a few coastal showers.
You can keep up to date with your local forecast by checking BBC Weather online and on the app.

title: Microsoft identifies months-old bug as a root cause of global outage
text:
Microsoft has identified the root causes of the global outage that crippled Outlook, Exchange and a host of other vital office software last week.
The office software giant issued an initial report on Monday that identified three factors that led to the 24-hour blackout of its services: a months-old bug, malfunctioning internal connections, and server capacity. Each of these factors may have easily been resolved on their own, but, when taken together, they led to a major outage that was harder to mitigate, Microsoft executives said.
The disruption began on Thursday with US users reporting interrupted access to their Outlook email accounts. As it continued into the next day, millions of people worldwide said they could not access their email in any capacity as well as other Office 365 services. Jails could not release prisoners, hospitals turned to paper records, schools lost contact with parents, and police departments could not receive crime reports. Microsoft said it had resolved the issue and restored service by Saturday, also issuing an apology. The company did not attribute the blackout to a cybersecurity breach.
In a post on X on Monday, Charles Lamanna, the executive vice-president of Copilot, Agents and Platform at Microsoft, said there was a latent bug or defect from July that caused Microsoft’s servers to “become overwhelmed and unresponsive”.
Lamanna wrote that the company typically has two available networking gateways, or entry and exit points that connect separate systems and allow data to pass between them. However, one of them was not working for Microsoft Teams, which overwhelmed the primary gateway. Subsequently, over 14% of the company’s server capacity was also not working due to an unrelated issue from the previous day.
“Taken together, the increased load and the reduced server capacity, caused the network gateway to encounter the latent bug from July,” Lamanna wrote. “This caused requests to build up until servers ultimately stopped responding. This occurred during the peak window of traffic in the United States.”
The company also had trouble mitigating the bug because it originated months before, Lamanna said, so it would not be easy as rolling back a recent change to undo the defect.
“Recovery took longer than usual because as servers returned to service, they were immediately overwhelmed by waiting traffic and became unresponsive again,” he wrote. “Our normally automated recovery processes were not designed to restore service from this broad unresponsive state. Additionally, since the main code defect was a latent bug from several months previous, our normal rollback, flighting, and feature flags were unable to quickly revert the change.”
The company plans to publish a final report that will include more information, he said.
Analysts say Microsoft’s global outage highlights the need for companies to examine how much they rely on a single operating system.
“This is a prime example of the importance of not only cyber resilience, but business resilience,” said Matt Hull, vice-president of cyber intelligence and response at NCC Group. “Reports that hospitals, schools and other essential services are affected demonstrate the wide impact that a system outage can have, regardless of the cause.”

title: After Democrats' midterm wins, some hope attacks on DEI will ease
text:
After the midterms, a Democratic congressman declared that DEI is back. What does Democrats' ascendance portend for diversity initiatives that the Trump administration has relentlessly attacked?
MICHEL MARTIN, HOST:
Since President Trump returned to office, he and his Republican allies have moved aggressively to eliminate diversity, equity and inclusion programs across government and the private sector. After Democrats won resoundingly in this month's midterms, California Democrat Congressman Ro Khanna posted this video.
RO KHANNA: Tonight, DEI is back as America celebrated diversity and inclusion.
MARTIN: So what could the midterms be signaling about the future of DEI? NPR's Adrian Florido reports.
ADRIAN FLORIDO, BYLINE: As a consultant, Lily Zheng helps companies develop programs to improve workplace diversity. Since last year, Zheng has watched most companies retreat from the work, in some cases to do it more quietly and others ending it altogether.
LILY ZHENG: It was fear of retribution. It was fear of political and regulatory pressure.
FLORIDO: But since Democrats prevailed in the midterms, Zheng says there's been a noticeable vibe shift.
ZHENG: Some of my colleagues who have been doing this work with a lower profile have expressed relief, maybe, that now they don't have to be tiptoeing on eggshells, likely.
FLORIDO: It's based on a sense, Zheng says, maybe just a hope that newly empowered Democrats will find ways to rein in Republican attacks that have had a chilling effect on DEI work.
ANTONIO INGRAM: I think, with this new political landscape, that chilling effect is thawing out.
FLORIDO: Antonio Ingram is an attorney with the NAACP Legal Defense Fund. He says the president's Republican allies in Congress have helped foster a culture of fear around DEI, summoning the leaders of universities, companies and nonprofits to hostile hearings.
INGRAM: To cross-examine them and to intimidate them from continuing to do the work they're doing to create a multiracial democracy. And now we have people who are going to be pro-civil rights in control of those committee hearings.
FLORIDO: But DEI experts that NPR spoke with said institutions are unlikely to quickly jump right back into diversity work, much less promote it publicly. Shaun Harper runs the Race and Equity Center at the University of Southern California. He's hopeful organizations will find their way back to DEI work. But after watching so many retreat from it so quickly, he says...
SHAUN HARPER: I don't expect them to overnight flip on a switch and, you know, declare that DEI is back.
FLORIDO: One reason is that President Trump still controls the federal agencies that have used threats of funding cuts and lawsuits to try to force institutions to end DEI programs. In a statement to NPR, White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster called DEI policies, quote, "racist and destructive." The White House accused President Biden of letting them run rampant and said Trump was elected with a mandate to end these policies. Still, in states that have followed the president's lead on DEI, it seems clear that the midterm Democratic wins could usher in a significant shift, like in Texas.
LILIANA GARCES: That pressure to remove certain readings from your classroom or self-censor is just not going to be as strong.
FLORIDO: Liliana Garces is professor of education at the University of Texas at Austin. She's been studying the impact of state restrictions on DEI programs and race-based curricula. After Republican leaders in Texas banned diversity programs at public universities, she interviewed administrators implementing the bans on their college campuses. And she found that because of the political climate, many feared being accused of not complying.
GARCES: There was a lot of uncertainty about the consequences, which meant that administrators were applying the law in very restrictive ways and prohibiting programs that weren't even covered by the law.
FLORIDO: Texans this month elected a Democratic governor, a Democratic attorney general and a Democratic majority in the State House of Representatives. Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has said she will not engage in culture wars.
Adrian Florido, NPR News.

title: Ex-Nvidia CEO agrees to testify to Congress amid affair probe
text:
Washington — Jensen Huang, who last week as the CEO of Nvidia, agreed to answer questions from House lawmakers on Dec. 1 under the threat of a subpoena amid an investigation into his affair with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy.
"The American people need answers on Mr. Huang and Nvidia's role in allowing dangerous [People's Republic of China] actors to access our most advanced chips, as well as the role of a potential Chinese intelligence asset in this scandal," House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast, a Florida Republican, said in a joint statement announcing the date of the hearing. Mast issued the statement with GOP Rep. John Moolenaar of Michigan, the chair of the House China Committee, and House Intelligence Committee Chair Rep. Rick Crawford of Arkansas.
Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter voluntarily agreed to appear before the committees on Dec. 2, the lawmakers said.
"We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security," the lawmakers added.
A representative for Huang declined to comment.
The chairmen had given Huang until 8 p.m. Nov. 13 to respond to for a closed-door, transcribed interview after Thanksgiving. Negotiations for the interview continued past the deadline into this week.
In a Nov. 12 letter, the lawmakers warned that "failure to cooperate with this request will result in the House Foreign Affairs Committee issuing a subpoena to compel your testimony in a format of the committee's choosing."
"Other committees also reserve the right to separately issue subpoenas to compel your testimony," they wrote.
Moolenaar and Crawford signed the letter with Mast.
In an initial letter to Huang on Nov. 4, the lawmakers sought a briefing on Nvidia's security protocols against espionage from foreign adversaries and on his relationship with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who is not related to him.
The Singapore-based data center company gained access to Nvidia's highly prized chips that are banned from export to China under U.S. law. Megaspeed is under investigation in the U.S. and Singapore for allegedly smuggling those chips into China — allegations Megaspeed has denied.
"It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk," the lawmakers wrote in their initial letter to Jensen Huang.

title: Another commercial vessel sinks off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast
text:
The Bulgarian Defense Ministry says that a Liberia-flagged gas tanker sank in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea
SOFIA, Bulgaria -- A Liberia-flagged gas tanker sank in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea on Tuesday, according to the Defense Ministry.
Bulgarian military personnel and aircraft are involved in the search and rescue operation for the crew of 19 Filipino citizens of the gas carrier GAS HUSKY, which sank about 50 nautical miles (nearly 60 miles or 100 kilometers) off the coast, the ministry said in a statement.
It said that a Cougar chopper has been dispatched to the site where a life raft with people had been located. The rescue operation is ongoing.
The tanker had disappeared from radar shortly after midnight, and at 8:02 a.m. the emergency buoy was activated, emitting a signal for a sunken ship.
The tanker, en route from Alexandria, Egypt, to the Romanian port of Midia, is the second merchant ship to sink off Bulgaria’s coast in two days.
On Monday, a Somali-flagged cargo ship sank in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone not far away from the site of Tuesday’s incident. All 12 crew members on board were saved in a rescue operation.
Investigations into the causes of the incidents are being launched. So far, there is no official information on whether the vessels were hit by drones.
There had been several deadly drone attacks against merchant ships off Bulgaria and Romania in recent weeks, widely blamed by analysts and political leaders on Russia’s war against Ukraine.

title: AI in classrooms: Fighting the great 'dumbing down'
text:
Jakob is 15 years old and attends a secondary school for more academic students, known in Germany as a gymnasium. He and his classmates have already been using artificial intelligence-enabled tools, or AI, for the last two and a half years.
"I had a French test today, and yesterday I had ChatGPT explain a lot of the topics to me again," the student told DW. Jakob isn't his real name, because he doesn't want to publicly admit he and many others of his age use AI to do their homework.
Math, German, English, chemistry and even physics: In one click, the solution or the path to a solution is available thanks to AI.
How AI enables 'cognitive outsourcing'
In science, this is called "cognitive outsourcing." Basically, the required thinking is shifted to another device, whether that's a calculator, notepad or a large language model (LLM) like ChatGPT.
There's a difference with AI, though. A notepad or calculator can take over a step or two but rarely the whole thought process. That's not the same for an LLM, which can handle the entire problem-solving process.
Jakob admitted he's also had an AI help him with his homework. "But only when I was really stuck," he insisted. And he's also aware that it can become a problem when AI does all your homework. "The students who get good grades tend not to do that," he explained.
Franziska Müller has been a German teacher for several decades and is currently teaching senior classes at a gymnasium. Her name has also been changed for privacy reasons.
"They can't even think for themselves anymore," she told DW, complaining about some of her classes.
Even in ordinary classes, some of the students type their questions into their tablets or phones, asking for AI assistance. And should they be called upon in class, she knows that they're reading out the answers that the AI has prepared for them and hoping nobody notices.
Müller believes students these days are less able to comprehend text. "Because they read less and let AI summarize almost everything for them," she said.
How AI use is linked to lower test scores
Several studies have reached very similar conclusions.
That includes the latest PISA (Program for International Student Assessment) study from September. PISA, which is run by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, regularly evaluates the abilities of 15-year-old students around the world.
"Students who report using AI chatbots get lower scores in science, on average, than those who don't use AI," Andreas Schleicher, the OECD director for education and skills, wrote in his report in October. "This includes using AI to summarize texts they had to read, conduct preliminary research on a new topic, or draft texts for writing assignments."
With participants from more than 90 countries, PISA is considered the largest international comparative study of 15-year-olds worldwide. This year, German 15-year-olds posted their lowest PISA scores in the 25-year history of the study.
"The connections are complex and depend heavily on how generative AI is used, but the central insight is simple: Just as we don't get fit by watching sports but by doing sports ourselves, learning doesn't come from consuming content, but from the mind's productive cognitive engagement with new material," Schleicher explained.
Put simply, those who don't exercise their brains risk becoming less intelligent.
Should schools restrict AI in class?
US think tank, the Brookings Institution, has already argued that the risks of using AI in education outweigh the benefits.
Its own research, which included young participants from around the world, speaks of students losing "fundamental cognitive and durable skills as they increasingly rely on AI to perform learning's intellectual work," as well as the decline of critical thinking, memory, perseverance and independent judgment.
But what can be done against the power of ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, Gemini and Meta AI?
New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani has banned the use of AI in public schools up to the eighth grade for the 2026 and 2027 school years — so that's up to about the age of 14 or 15.
Not everyone agrees this is the right thing to do. Julian Hinn, who teaches German to students aged between 15 and 18 in Germany, said class members can still use AI apps on their mobile phones. "And anyone who thinks they won't use it at home is ignoring reality," Hinn told DW.
Germany's annual JIM study, which tracks teenagers' media use and device ownership, supports that view.
Ninety-one percent of young people surveyed in Germany, between the ages of 12 and 19, stated that they use at least one AI application. The study also reports that 74% use AI for homework and learning.
The last JIM study actually dates back to 2024 so those percentages might be even higher now. Data on AI use in Asia, Latin America and the US from the Brookings study show similarly high figures.
German politicians have recognized the problem. Although education in Germany is the responsibility of the individual federal states, the so-called Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education and Cultural Affairs, or KMK, has been issuing statements on the use of AI since 2024.
The KMK's statements have been rather vague though, saying only that students should be enabled to engage with AI in a critical, reflective and responsible manner.
Students should question AI, too
Teachers and students alike are aware that AI can be a powerful support in the classroom.
"The AIs simply explain things much better than textbooks," said Jakob, adding that he'll often get an AI to explain basic concepts to him.
Sometimes teachers can't respond like an AI, Hinn conceded. "The AI can respond much better to the language and needs of the students."
That's why he thinks it's important to include AI in classes, starting from the 10th grade when students are around 15 or 16. Hinn doesn't think it should be introduced before that, when children's basic skills are still being developed.
In more senior classes, Hinn will encourage his students to question the AI critically. "We look at the quality of the solutions," he explained.
German teacher Müller has also integrated some use of AI into her lessons for older students. But in some aspects of the class, she also bans it altogether so that her students can focus on thinking for themselves.
"I understand very well that it's tempting to use AI," she said.
There are also other problems with AI in education. According to the Brookings study, students with basic skills can use AI to deepen their learning and progress faster.
But for children with gaps in their knowledge, they tend to adopt AI's errors, outsource their thinking and then fall even further behind. In this way, AI can exacerbate preexisting inequalities.
The PISA study notes that children from more affluent backgrounds often have a better start, and AI can widen that gap.
This is called the Matthew effect — the name comes from the biblical verse Matthew 25:29, "for unto everyone that hath shall be given." It basically means that early success in learning leads to better progress in the future, while early struggles equal a growing lag over time.
In the age of AI, teachers have become more motivated to challenge students to think independently and to consider their own personal autonomy.
Hinn, who also supervises the school newspaper, said: "I always tell everyone, you can use AI but the feeling of having written an article with your own pen is spectacular."
Both teachers also stress the idea of personal autonomy and responsibility. They believe this affects the students, especially because when they sit exams, they aren't allowed to use any aids or AI. And if they aren't able to solve their own problems, they will fail.
It's during exam time that the students really find out if they can solve those math, English or science problems by themselves.
Müller said one of her students recently confessed they were upset after a poor exam result. "He felt he simply couldn't think for himself anymore because of AI," she said.

title: All the recent mass outages in the US from NSA to Apple and air travel
text:
Americans have endured repeated mass outages across several sectors in the past week, from a crippling Microsoft outage to bank issues and a communications glitch that grounded all US flights.
The latest outages came Tuesday as a highly classified network that the US National Security Agency uses went down, followed by an Apple outage just a few hours later.
The tech issues have sparked fears that cyberattacks are becoming more common and could take out the technology that millions use for everyday tasks and work.
Here is a roundup of the latest high-profile outages to strike the US.
1. Global Microsoft outage
Office work ground to a halt on Thursday, Nov. 12, when Microsoft products, including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot, went offline and were not restored for around a full day.
Over 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps, according to Microsoft. The outage sparked global chaos, affecting everything from hospitals and police forces to schools.
Downdetector, an online outage tracker, noted outage reports from users in more than 70 countries and territories.
The company apologized on Friday and said the outage was “not related to cyber” or artificial intelligence agents.
2. FAA ground stop
As Microsoft was still working to restore access, a second major outage was reported in the United States.
The Federal Aviation Administration issued a ground stop for all US flights after a newly installed router malfunctioned, overwhelming the aging air traffic control system.
Almost 25,000 flights were delayed and over 9,000 were canceled on Friday, per flight racking site FlightAware. The disruption lingered into Saturday morning, when more than 4,000 cancelations recorded, comprising of roughly 18% of flights departing the US.
Tens of thousands of passengers across the US were stranded after the rare nationwide ground stop, only the second of its kind since the Sept. 11 attacks.
Officials said the FAA was still investigating the exact cause of the error.
3. Bank issues
Americans rushed to downdetector again on Monday, Nov. 16, just days after the Microsoft and FAA meltdowns, to report issues accessing their banking apps.
They reported outages affecting a handful of major US banks but it was determined that the issue stemmed from Chase Bank.
Chase said Monday that the technical problems were not the result of a cyberattack and that it was working to bring banking services back online by the end of the day.
“JPMorgan Chase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in an on-premise hardware system — it is not cyber-related,” said Joe Evangelisti, spokesman for the bank.
4. United Airlines ground stop
Hours after the banking issues emerged, United Airlines was forced to issue a ground stop for all of its US flights.
A total of 600 flights were delayed by Monday evening as the airline worked to resolve the outage, which lasted roughly an hour and 40 minutes.
The carrier said there was "no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue” and apologized on social media, though it did not share specific details regarding which of its internal systems failed.
Pilots told air traffic controllers that the disruption involved a program used to establish an aircraft's final weight.
5. NSA issue
Another outage happened on Tuesday, Nov. 17, when a highly classified network that the US National Security Agency uses for communications went down.
“The National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance,” the agency wrote in a statement on Tuesday afternoon.
“While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues. NSA's infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.”
6. Apple and Marriott services
Many of Apple’s online services, including Apple Music, the App Store and other iCloud services, were affected by technical issues Tuesday afternoon.
The iCloud troubles affected the ability to sign in, including on new devices, meaning that they could not be activated after purchase as usual, and also stopped users from signing up for the AppleCare service to protect those devices.
The company said an internal software update caused the disruptions, with most systems being restored shortly after while teams worked on remaining issues.
“Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning,” the company wrote. “We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible.”
Marriott International, the largest U.S. hotel operator, was also having tech issues that impacted reservations and check-ins, among other problems, according to users posting on Reddit.
President Donald Trump brushed off the series of outages in remarks on Tuesday despite Americans’ growing worries.
“It’s life, it’s life,” he told reporters during a trip to the Philippines. “When you’re big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine.”
Danielle Lemons, vice president of operations at Nashville-based IT firm DirecTech Connect, told The Independent that people should be “concerned enough to plan, not to panic.”
“The real lesson is how many separate services quietly depend on the same few providers,” Lemons said. “When one of them goes down, email, file sharing, sign-ins and even phone systems can fail together, because they were all built on the same foundation.”

title: NSA's highly classified communications network disrupted by widespread outage
text:
The National Security Agency's internal classified communications network is experiencing an "intermittent outage," but critical communications remain intact, a person familiar with the matter told Fox News Digital on Tuesday.
The disruption affects a highly classified network known as NSA Net, which agency personnel use to communicate classified information internally.
The latest impact at one of the nation's most sensitive intelligence agencies also comes amid a string of technology outages affecting major U.S. institutions, from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to Microsoft and major banks, raising fresh concerns about the reliability of critical communications infrastructure.
CNN first reported the outage Tuesday, citing five people familiar with the matter.
The agency has implemented staggered arrival times for personnel at NSA to prevent tens of thousands of employees from attempting to log into their computers simultaneously as officials work to address the disruption, the person familiar with the matter said.
The issue appears to be technical in nature, according to the source, though the precise cause has not been established.
Despite the disruption, the agency has not lost critical communications capabilities and has numerous backup facilities available to maintain operations, the source said.
The NSA, which is responsible for collecting and analyzing foreign signals intelligence, plays a central role in supporting U.S. intelligence and military operations.
It remains unclear when the outage began or how long it will take to fully restore the affected network.
Fox News Digital reached out to the NSA for comment.
The disruption comes amid a string of high-profile technology outages over the last week affecting government systems and major businesses.
On Friday, the FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop after a telecommunications failure disrupted aircraft communications and radar feeds. The agency said instability spread to 17 of its 22 air route traffic control centers before flights resumed later that evening.
The disruption was attributed by the FAA to excessive data flooding its aging telecommunications network, potentially originating from two facilities in Texas and Arkansas. Officials said they had found no indication of a cyberattack.
Federal authorities are separately warning of increasingly sophisticated cyber threats. In a Nov. 13 advisory, the FBI warned that hackers are exploiting an artificial intelligence-powered penetration testing framework known as ARTEX to automate attacks against organizations worldwide.
The FBI said the technology has allowed some attackers to move from initial targeting to privileged access in less than three hours. Microsoft previously linked the framework to a China-aligned hacking group's exploitation of a ConnectWise supply-chain compromise, which involved attempts to access more than 2,250 downstream Microsoft 365 customer environments.
There is no evidence linking the NSA disruption to the ARTEX activity or the other recent outages.

title: Ukraine damages Putin’s prized Crimea bridge as Zelenskyy lauds ‘unprecedented operation’
text:
Ukraine has damaged the Kerch Bridge linking Russia to the occupied Crimean Peninsula, delivering a symbolic blow to President Vladimir Putin as Kyiv reels from strikes on its own infrastructure.
Sergey Aksyonov, the Russia-installed governor of Crimea, confirmed that the strategically important bridge, which had been briefly closed on Monday, was attacked overnight for the second time in two days.
Videos and photos circulating on social media appeared to show the partial destruction of the bridge, with one section having collapsed into the water. CNBC was unable to independently verify the footage.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the attack as an "unprecedented operation" several weeks in the making, with Ukraine's defense forces, security services and weapons manufacturers involved.
"Russia strikes our infrastructure every day, including bridges in Zaporizhzhia, Dnipro, Kyiv, and the Odesa region," Zelenskyy said Tuesday on X.
"We are restoring our infrastructure. But we are also reminding Russia that war will always return to where it began. Ukraine's defensive capabilities are strong and will remain so, and we will never leave terror against our cities and people unanswered," he added.
Train and vehicle traffic was suspended due to the attack. No injuries have been reported.
Ukraine has repeatedly targeted the bridge since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in early 2022.
A 12-mile crossing of road and railways, the Kerch Bridge is one of Putin's signature projects. The crossing, sometimes referred to as the Crimean bridge, was built on his orders shortly after the Kremlin forcibly annexed Crimea in 2014 to support Moscow's claims to the territory.
Rail traffic on the bridge was opened on one track, Russia's Ministry of Transport said in a statement via Telegram on Tuesday, while restoration work continues on the second section.
The co-owner and chief engineer of Ukrainian missile and drone maker Fire Point, Denys Shtilierman, appeared to confirm the company's role in the attack, following reports that a Ukrainian Flamingo cruise missile was used in the strike.
"We dedicate this to the memory of our friends and colleagues Andriy and Yuriy, without whom this would not have been possible. R.I.P.," Shtilierman said via X on Tuesday. A spokesperson at Fire Point separately confirmed the company's role in the attack.
Analysts at the Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank, said Ukraine's attacks on the Kerch Bridge were likely part of Kyiv's ongoing and systematic strike campaign aimed at denying Russian forces the use of major ground lines of communication via Crimea.
Russian forces, meanwhile, struck two bridges crossing the Dnipro River in Kyiv.
Vitaliy Klitschko, the mayor of Ukraine's capital, said via Telegram on Tuesday that specialists were working to assess the extent of the damage to the North and South bridges.
Klitschko said Russian attacks on Kyiv overnight had also caused disruptions to water and heating supplies.
The strikes come ahead of Putin's trip to China this week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Shenzhen, where a trilateral meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping is planned on Thursday.
Asked whether Ukraine's latest attacks might be connected to the upcoming trilateral summit, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said this could not be ruled out.
"Combat operations continue, and our military is striking targets that are somehow connected to Ukraine's military-industrial complex. And Ukraine is continuing its terrorist attacks," Peskov said, according to Russian state news outlet Ria Novosti.

title: Scientists find a simple daily routine linked to less pain and depression
text:
A simple change to your daily routine could make a surprising difference in how you feel, both physically and mentally. University of Missouri researchers found that older adults who followed consistent daily schedules reported less physical pain and fewer symptoms of depression, even when they struggled with insomnia. Keeping regular times for sleeping, eating, and other activities may help regulate the body's internal clock, which influences mood, sleep, and overall health.
A consistent daily routine may do more for your health than you realize. Researchers at the University of Missouri have found that older adults who follow regular daily schedules tend to experience less physical pain and fewer symptoms of depression, even when they struggle to get a good night's sleep.
The findings suggest that everyday habits, such as waking up, eating meals, socializing, and going to bed at consistent times, may play an important role in physical and mental well-being. By helping the body maintain its natural internal clock, a predictable routine could offer health benefits that extend beyond improved sleep.
The discovery could be especially important for older adults, who frequently experience sleep difficulties. According to the National Council on Aging, roughly half of adults age 60 and older report symptoms of insomnia, a condition that can make it difficult to fall asleep, stay asleep, or get restful sleep.
Daily Routines Linked to Less Pain and Depression
To investigate the relationship between sleep, daily habits, and overall health, Eunjin Tracy, an assistant professor in the College of Education and Human Development at the University of Missouri, examined survey responses from 67 older adults. Among the participants, 37 reported experiencing insomnia.
As researchers expected, those with insomnia generally reported more physical pain and higher levels of depression than participants without the condition. However, another pattern emerged when Tracy examined their daily routines.
Participants who maintained more consistent schedules tended to report less pain and fewer depressive symptoms, regardless of their sleep quality. This suggests that keeping regular daily habits may be associated with better health even when sleep problems persist.
"Regardless of sleep quality, those who reported having a regular daily routine had lower levels of physical pain and less depression compared to those without a daily routine," Tracy said. "If we are consistent with when we wake up, eat, work or study, interact with others and go to bed, those time cues help synchronize our internal body clocks. Over the long term, that seems to be linked with improved health outcomes."
Why Your Body's Internal Clock Matters
One possible explanation involves the circadian rhythm, the body's natural 24-hour timing system. This internal clock helps coordinate when we feel awake or sleepy and influences numerous biological processes, including hormone activity, metabolism, and mood.
Rather than operating independently of our surroundings, the circadian system responds to signals that help it keep time. Light and darkness are especially important, but regular activities such as eating, working, interacting with others, and sleeping can also provide timing cues.
When these signals follow a predictable pattern, they help keep the body's biological rhythms aligned. Irregular schedules, on the other hand, can interfere with that coordination.
"When we regulate our circadian rhythm well, our bodies function well, but if it gets too distracted, our bodies don't function as well," Tracy said.
Although the study did not establish that regular routines directly reduce pain or depression, the findings point to circadian regulation as one possible explanation for the connection.
The Hidden Effects of Social Jet Lag
Even relatively small changes in daily schedules may disrupt the body's internal clock. One common example is social jet lag, which occurs when a person's sleep schedule shifts between workdays and days off.
Someone who wakes up early throughout the week but stays up late and sleeps in on weekends may experience this mismatch. The resulting disruption resembles some of the effects of traveling across time zones, even though the person has never left home.
Tracy suggests that maintaining reasonably consistent schedules throughout the entire week, including weekends, may help limit these disruptions and support healthier circadian rhythms.
"As someone who wakes up and goes to bed at the same time every day, I think a daily routine can be helpful for people of all ages across their lifespan," Tracy said. "There is growing awareness about the concept of social jet lag -- waking up and going to bed at different times on weekends compared to weekdays -- and the disruptions it causes to our circadian rhythm, so hopefully this research helps more people consider the health benefits of a daily routine. Since one-third of our lives will be spent sleeping, I think health and well-being research should be looked at holistically from a 24-hour perspective and not just focus on when we are awake."
A Simple Habit With Potential Health Benefits
The research highlights an aspect of healthy living that can be easy to overlook. While getting enough quality sleep remains important, the consistency of activities throughout the day may also be connected to how people feel physically and emotionally.
Because the study relied on survey data from a relatively small group of older adults, it cannot prove that adopting a regular routine will relieve pain or depression. Larger studies would be needed to establish whether changing daily schedules directly improves these outcomes.
Still, the findings suggest that a predictable daily routine may be a useful component of a broader approach to health, particularly for people experiencing insomnia.
For older adults and potentially people of other ages, simple habits such as maintaining regular waking times, eating meals on a consistent schedule, and limiting major changes in weekend sleep patterns may help support the body's natural rhythms.
The study, "Behavioral-social rhythms and insomnia symptoms: associations with pain, body mass index, and depressive symptoms among older adults," was published in the Journal of Behavioral Medicine.

title: This Week In Space podcast: Episode 236 — Alienspotting
text:

title: SpaceX’s Starship returns to launch pad from orbit in victory for company
text:
SpaceX’s megarocket Starship returned to its Texas launch tower on Saturday, a milestone in the company’s efforts to make the craft suitable for human spaceflight.
The 171ft (52-meter) bullet-shaped upper stage descended into the clutch of the tower’s mechanical arms, ending a 22-hour mission where the craft orbited Earth 14 times.
Starship’s 15th test flight was envisioned as a historic double-catch mission, where all parts of the rocket would be returned intact to the launch site, rather than recovered from the ocean as with some previous test flights.
The hulking spacecraft is comprised of two parts: a lower booster stage called Super Heavy, whose Raptor engines powered the orbital ascent, and an upper stage also called Starship.
Those double-catch ambitions were dashed on Friday, when the booster diverted a few minutes after takeoff and exploded in the Gulf of Mexico.
The guidance, navigation and control (GNC) system triggered the no-go.
“It was doing what it was supposed to do. Basically, it detected that the booster was not in the place it was supposed to be to proceed with a catch,” SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot said early on Saturday. The booster was also “slightly low on fuel”, according to SpaceX’s chief executive, Elon Musk.
This week’s test flight was still a victory for SpaceX, marking the first time that the company caught its upper stage.
It was also only the second time Starship has entered Earth’s orbit.
The feat comes as the 2028 date nears for Nasa’s plan to return humans to the lunar surface. The agency has contracted SpaceX and Jeff Bezos’s Blue Origin for the mission.
“Making more believers by the day,” Nasa’s administrator, Jared Isaacman, wrote on X, praising the 15th flight. “One step closer to [the moon].” Isaacman is an ally of Musk, who advised Donald Trump to appoint him to lead Nasa.
SpaceX has plans to ramp up its Starship test flights to a weekly, then twice-weekly cadence, Musk said on a recent earnings call. He has sought to make Starship rapidly reusable so that it can land and take off much like standard airplanes. Musk has touted the rocket’s reusability as a way to reel in the enormous costs of space travel.
Beyond another moon landing, Musk has also pushed a plan of carrying humans to Mars.
Starship’s advances have also aided the expansion of Musk’s satellite internet empire. The spacecraft deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites during this recent flight.

title: California sues OpenAI over hacking risks
text:
California sued OpenAI Monday, alleging that the frontier AI company failed to protect the public from its systems' advanced cyber capabilities. The lawsuit stems from OpenAI's agents' attack on open-source software platform Hugging Face over the summer but also touches on a wide range of other related incidents tied to the company's agents acting without authorization.
"Just because the technology is new or rapidly evolving doesn't mean the people behind it are above the law," said California Attorney General Rob Bonta during a press conference. "Whether it's a car or a toy, the law is simple: don't build or test things that can hurt people without proper safeguards." The lawsuit cited potential concerns about cyberattacks "on power grids, emergency infrastructure, hospital systems, and financial institutions."
In the complaint, California alleged that OpenAI misled the public about how unsafe its products are. The state said the company admitted to the attorney general's office that "it lost control of its autonomous AI agents over 80 times during testing."
That number is higher than what OpenAI has so far disclosed publicly and more than what outside researchers have independently discovered, but OpenAI has otherwise provided little information, California said. The state also accused OpenAI of poor security practices, stonewalling the state's investigation into the company and discouraging employees from speaking up about safety.
In a statement to NPR, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the lawsuit "appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that's been identified by every major AI lab" and that the company has "engaged—and will continue to engage—constructively with the Attorney General's office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry."
After the most notorious of cyber incidents involving OpenAI's agents – the attack on Hugging Face over the summer – the company admitted that it did not monitor its agents in ways its own researchers deemed important. Since then, outside researchers as well as OpenAI itself have found more incidents in which AI agents have interacted with websites and communicated with each other on the internet in ways that OpenAI did not intend. The lawsuit mentions these events as well as other incidents that OpenAI started disclosing voluntarily to the public.
Other AI companies have also had to wrestle with their systems behaving in unexpected and undesirable ways. Anthropic and Meta have both said they found that their AI systems have hacked into places they shouldn't have. Major AI companies have since signed onto an agreement organized by the White House to develop AI responsibly, but the agreement is nonbinding.
Drawing from reports including from OpenAI's own disclosures, California alleges that the top AI company has engaged in unfair competition and created a public nuisance. It asked the court to stop the company from further engaging in such activities and order it to pay monetary damages.

title: Meteorite found in the Sahara Desert turns out to be piece of Mars
text:
A rose-colored meteorite found in the Sahara Desert in 2022 has been identified as a 4.1-billion-year-old chunk of the Red Planet, a NASA study determined.
The nearly two-pound meteorite was found in Mali. It was named Teghaza 001, after the salt plain where it was discovered, NASA said in a news release.
Study of the meteorite allowed NASA scientists to determine it was one of . Meteorites can be verified as having been part of Mars by comparing their chemical and mineral makeup to samples and data collected by NASA's Martian missions.
Age-dating of the meteorite led researchers to conclude it was about 4.1 billion years old, making it one of the three most ancient Martian meteorites found on Earth, NASA said. That provides "a rare snapshot" of the planet's crust and formation, the agency said.
"It was only after we started looking closely that we realized this meteorite is really unique," said Yang Liu, the lead author of a paper detailing the age-dating process and related discoveries. Liu is part of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. "One of the paper's reviewers called it a Rosetta Stone for Mars."
Previous ancient Martian meteorites provided narrower glimpses into the planet's history. But Teghaza 001 shows how Mars' crust formed from cooling magma and was then changed by water on the planet's surface.
The meteorite is made of a unique mix of volcanic minerals, including zircon crystals, NASA said, matching samples observed by the agency's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter in the planet's southern highlands. Francis Tissot, a geochemistry professor at Caltech, helped the researchers use a pioneering age-dating method that studied a piece of meteorite smaller than a fingernail. The precise method allowed scientists to analyze single grains of minerals.
That analysis showed the rock had been altered by Martian water about 4.1 billion years ago. The rock itself may have been formed even earlier, NASA said. The data also showed that early Mars may have had a more dynamic water cycle than scientists previously believed.
Paper author Lee Saper said that the meteorite "records interactions of water and rock and maybe even an imprint of the Martian atmosphere as it was losing water." Another study of the meteorite, published in June, focused on the rock's water content and considered how water might have shaped the early topography of Mars.
"This is really our first piece of Martian crust from a part of Mars we've never had a sample of before," Lee, a scientist at NASA's Ames Research Center, added.
Liu said that further research on the meteorite is likely.
"We've only scratched the surface," Liu said.

title: Supreme Court declines to hear challenge to Maryland 'sensitive places' gun law
text:
The Supreme Court has declined to consider a challenge to a Maryland law restricting where people can carry guns
WASHINGTON -- The Supreme Court declined Monday to consider a challenge to a Maryland law restricting where people can carry guns.
The law prohibits carrying concealed weapons into schools, mass transit, bars and other areas deemed sensitive places.
The high court declined the case without comment. But Justice Clarence Thomas wrote to say he’s skeptical about the law and others like it. He expressed support for weighing the issue again in a “more narrowly focused case.”
The refusal comes as the court prepares to hear arguments over state laws banning AR-15s and similar semiautomatic firearms, measures that are often called assault weapons bans.
The conservative-majority court has handed down several decisions backing Second Amendment rights, including a recent ruling striking down wide-ranging gun-carry restrictions in Hawaii.
The high court has upheld some gun restrictions, though, including a law aimed at protecting victims of domestic violence.

title: German economy returns to growth, so why is the country still worried?
text:
Is Germany's economy back on the up? The answer to that question depends on your perspective.
At the 2026 Mechanical Engineering Summit in Berlin this week, the mood was sullen. "A year ago, I said here: We are angry. Today I must say: We are stunned," Bertram Kawlath, president of the Mechanical Engineering Industry Association (VDMA), said in his opening remarks on Tuesday.
The mechanical and plant engineering sector was the backbone of German industry for decades. It once employed more than a million people; now 15,000 positions are being cut every month. Production has shrunk about 20% since 2018.
Kawlath criticized the federal government's infighting and lack of reform, as well as what the companies consider a continued high bureaucracy and tax burden.
"[We are] stunned by the whitewashing in so many government statements. Stunned by the increasingly visible decline of our country as a business location."
Germany's economy is growing again — a little
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz promised quick reforms and a rapidly noticeable economic upswing when he took office in May 2025. A year and a half later, reality has caught up with him.
Merz's coalition of his conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), its Bavarian sister party the Christian Social Union, (CSU), along with the center-left Social Democrats(SPD), keeps running into trouble. In addition, there are crises and wars. The German economy is facing more headwinds than seldom before, Merz said in October at the German Employers' Day conference in Berlin.
Given the circumstances, small successes are even more meaningful. "A heartfelt thanks for the good news you bring," Merz said when he received the autumn report of the Council of Economic Experts in Berlin, which predicted economic growth of 1.3% for 2026 and 1% for 2027.
The economic experts have a German government mandate to independently analyze business activity and make recommendations for economic policy. Earlier this year, they were much more pessimistic.
"The German economy has recovered quicker than expected from the energy price shock sparked by the war in Iran," said Monika Schnitzer, chair of the expert advisory board, explaining the prognosis. "We see a significant economic recovery, driven by surprisingly strong exports and high government spending."
The chancellor, who celebrated his 71st birthday on November 11, spoke of "encouraging signals" in his address. "The economy in Germany is slowly on the rise again. Considering the many crises in Germany, it was not totally expected that we would manage that."
Why 1% growth is not enough
But these improved prospects do not change the long-term problems. An ageing society means the bills for pensions, health and caregiving are constantly rising.
At the same time, the number of working-age people who finance these services is sinking. That puts increasing pressure on the public purse. According to Berlin's financial planning, social welfare costs, defense and interest on debt will account for 80% of the spending in the federal government's budget.
"We must realize that in the long term the expected revenues in the federal budget will not be enough to cover the planned expenses," Schnitzer warned. The growth rates are far below what is needed to secure the same level of prosperity as previous decades in the long term.
"To grow out of this budgetary predicament, we would need levels of economic growth which we haven't experienced in Germany for the past 50 years," she said.
The government is currently in final deliberations over its 2027 budget; spending upwards of €555 billion ($615 billion) is planned. Because revenue won't be enough to cover it, the government is planning to take on more than €118 billion in new debt. Adding the debt-financed special funds for infrastructure and the military, the new borrowing adds up to almost €204 billion.
Could Germany lose its top rating?
The economic experts have warned that if Germany continues with this path, the debt-to-GDP ratio could rise to 100% by 2040. This ratio indicates how high the national debt is in relation to annual economic output. At the end of 2025, it was 63.5%.
Germany is the only country of the world's leading democratic industrialized nations (G7) to still hold a AAA rating, the best possible credit rating in finance markets. It signals to investors the smallest possible default risk for German government bonds. "I want it to stay that way," Merz emphasized.
However, taking on less debt will not be simple. "A reduction in debt-based financing presents policymakers with a consolidation task of historic proportions and will require tough decisions," said Schnitzer. The belt-tightening must, however, be designed to enable growth. Some recommendations include reducing environmentally harmful tax benefits — like the energy tax breaks for diesel fuel.
The so-called "mothers' pension", a pension subsidy for older parents, should be revoked, said the experts. Tax increases could become necessary in the medium term, for example with value-added tax.
"The burden should be shared fairly between generations and societal groups," Schnitzer said.
Merz wants austerity throughout Europe
According to the chancellor, the experts' message has been received. Solid state finances are an issue in Germany but also throughout the European Union. Merz said there needs to be a consolidation course, adding that politicians have a duty to the younger generation. Reforms are needed, especially when it comes to social security systems.
Economic researchers are setting their hopes on increasing companies' productivity. Put simply, productivity describes how much a company can generate with its employees, machinery and resources in a set time.
According to the Council of Economic Experts, there is enormous variation even within the same industries. In Germany, the top companies are up to five times as productive as the weakest enterprises.
If the less productive companies caught up, economic growth could increase significantly, it said in the report. "New technologies and business models could drive peak productivity and allow new highly productive companies to develop."
Germany needs startups, venture capital
But innovations need capital. It's here that the Ifo Economic Research Institute sees considerable deficiencies.
New evaluations show that German universities produce significantly fewer successful business startups than their counterparts in the United Kingdom or United States. For example, for every 1,000 students, about 14 venture capital-backed founders emerge from the vicinity of Stanford University each year. In Cambridge, the European leader, it's 3.5. In Munich, by contrast, it's only 0.5.
There continues to be an abundance of inventors and tinkerers in Germany, especially in mechanical engineering. However, the message from the industry summit in Berlin was that for renewed success, labor costs must come down. Suggestions included longer working hours and more flexibility for employers around job protection.
The intention was not to cut employees' wages and salaries. However, a new study by the German Economic Institute commissioned for the German Mechanical Engineering Industry Association showed that extending the working week by an hour alone would increase real gross domestic product by 1.5% in the coming five years.

title: Rassie Erasmus banned for six matches for questioning integrity of match officials
text:
The South Africa head coach Rassie Erasmus has been handed a six-match ban after his comments about match officials following the Springboks defeat to France.
The coach, 54, made reference to “match-fixing” in wide-ranging comments on Monday related to what he perceived as inconsistencies in the officiating of his side, and possible offences missed during the game in Paris.
Erasmus previously served a 10-month ban for comments made about referee Nic Berry during the British and Irish Lions series in 2021. He was also banned in 2022 for criticising referee Wayne Barnes.
“South Africa men’s 15s head coach Rassie Erasmus has been suspended for six international matches with immediate effect,” a World Rugby statement said. “The sanction follows a review of wide-ranging comments made by Erasmus at a media conference this week concerning officiating during the Springboks’ Nations Championship match against France last Friday.
“Having considered the comments which related to the match TMO, the standing Match Official Abuse committee, chaired by senior officer Adam Casselden SC (Australia), determined that the threshold for serious misconduct had been met. The panel determined that the comments suggest that match officials acted with bias/prejudice or deliberately influenced the outcome of a match, and when the conduct is considered as a whole a reasonable person would conclude that the conduct constituted an unacceptable attack on the credibility and competence of the match officials.
“In respect to the sanction, the panel determined that the conduct clearly amounts to disrespecting the authority of the match officials by impugning their integrity. Therefore, the panel reviewed a number of elements of the commentary including the timing and reach of the statements, combined with the allegations of bias or bad faith, and found that the comments attracted a six-match automatic suspension.”
Erasmus was sanctioned under World Rugby’s new expedited match official abuse sanction process. He will be entitled to a full misconduct hearing, with SA Rugby confirming in a statement they would be exercising that right.
The sanction applies with immediate effect, and “includes any match-day involvement including coaching, direct or indirect contact with team management or players on match days; entering the stadium, coaches’ box, playing enclosure, technical area, approaching and/or communicating with match officials on match day”.
Erasmus will also be unable to engage in any media duties during the suspension, or in a feedback process with match officials.
It leaves the Springboks, as things stand, without their head coach for the Nations Championship clash with Ireland rugby in Dublin on Saturday, and their fixture on the inaugural competition finals weekend at Twickenham’s Allianz Stadium next weekend.
Though South Africa’s fixture list for 2027 is yet to be confirmed, it is likely that Erasmus’ ban will expire well in advance of the World Cup as his side seek a third consecutive crown.
Erasmus’ claims had included that the matchday officiating team, led by referee Andrea Piardi, had missed up to 17 “knee-drop” tackles by French players, and that the scrum half Maxime Lucu had been permitted to return before serving a full 10-minute period in the sin bin.
The double World Cup winner also inferred that Ireland fly half Sam Prendergast, who is believed to have been cited for a dangerous tackle against Fiji, would be cleared to play against the Springboks.
“We are in the northern hemisphere,” Erasmus said. “I think there is going to be a technicality and he is going to play.”
An SA Rugby spokesperson said that “the organisation respected the process but had requested an opportunity for its coach to contextualise his comments and assure the panel that it was not his intention to allege that any match official had acted with ulterior motives”.
The union also made clear that it hoped for that misconduct hearing to be expedited.

title: Egypt pitches reforms and energy plans at World Economic Forum meeting
text:
At a World Economic Forum meeting in Cairo, Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi pledged to simplify business procedures and outlined plans for industry, energy and AI. The government is preparing a 2027–2030 economic programme to boost productivity and give private businesses a larger role.
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi called for more foreign investment on Tuesday, outlining business reforms at a World Economic Forum meeting in Cairo.
He said Egypt would announce an economic programme in December covering 2027–2030, aimed at increasing productivity and giving private businesses a larger role.
Reforms had cut the average time for goods to clear customs to two days, he said.
He also said Egypt’s shift to a flexible exchange rate had helped foreign investors transfer their profits abroad. Knowing they can bring their earnings home could encourage companies to invest in Egypt, where their projects can create jobs, generate business for local suppliers and bring in tax revenue.
Representatives of around 80 organisations, including major companies and international financial institutions, attended Tuesday’s discussions, part of the two-day Country Strategy Meeting on Egypt, according to the presidency.
El-Sisi cited economic growth of 5.1% in the 2025–26 financial year and net foreign direct investment of $18 billion (€16.4bn).
The investment drive comes as Egypt faces pressure to reduce debt and open more of its economy to private businesses. In an August report, the International Monetary Fund warned that high debt and borrowing needs left the country exposed to economic shocks. The fund has also said sales of state assets have progressed more slowly than expected.
Industry and investment targets
As part of Egypt’s industrial strategy, el-Sisi highlighted the country's target for industry to account for 20% of economic output by 2030.
The government also wants private investment to reach 67% of total investment by 2030, according to a cabinet statement issued on Monday.
Investment and Foreign Trade Minister Mohamed Farid Saleh set out a foreign direct investment strategy developed with the World Bank in an article published by the World Economic Forum on Monday.
The initial priorities include IT services, solar and wind power, food processing, clothing and transport. Further reforms are planned for sectors including data centres and green hydrogen.
Farid wrote that simpler licensing and online government services would help businesses get projects running. Under Egypt’s existing Golden Licence scheme, eligible projects can receive a single cabinet approval to build and operate.
El-Sisi also discussed whether the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development could help establish new investment zones during talks with its president, Odile Renaud-Basso, on Tuesday. No funding agreement was announced in the presidency’s account.
Energy exports and AI ambitions
El-Sisi reiterated plans to bring Cypriot gas to Egypt’s Idku and Damietta liquefaction plants for export to Europe by 2028.
Egypt also aims to generate 45% of its electricity from renewable sources by 2028, he said, alongside plans to expand electricity connections with neighbouring countries and Europe.
Shipping through the Suez Canal was improving, the president said. He repeated his estimate that Egypt had lost about $20bn (€18.2bn) in canal revenue in recent years.
He also highlighted opportunities for investment in data centres, cloud computing and AI research as part of Egypt’s national AI strategy.

title: Roth 401(k) matches are 'surging,' report finds. What workers should know
text:
Many more workers can now or will soon be able to accept a 401(k) match as a Roth contribution — giving them a new avenue to build a bucket of tax-free savings for retirement.
Historically, workers could only accept 401(k) match money from an employer as pretax, meaning they had to defer income taxes on those funds until they withdrew them in retirement.
Until a recent rule change, workers generally couldn't elect to receive a match as a Roth contribution. With Roth savings, investors don't get an up-front tax break — they pay income tax on the funds now but can take out the contributions and growth tax-free in retirement.
A law known as Secure 2.0, which former President Joe Biden signed into law in 2022, gave employers the option to add a Roth match as a feature of their 401(k) plans. If a plan offers a Roth match, it's not automatic; workers must opt in.
The number of employers that now let workers accept a 401(k) match or other employer contribution as Roth savings has "surged," according to a new report from the Plan Sponsor Council of America, a trade group representing employers.
About 42% of surveyed businesses that sponsored a 401(k) plan in 2025 have added or will add an option to accept employer contributions as Roth savings, according to an annual PSCA report published Nov. 10. That's more than double the share — about 20% — that did so in 2024, the report found.
Another 11% are still considering the option, according to the report.
The PSCA report is based on data from 753 employers that sponsor 401(k) plans of various sizes.
"My guess is we will continue to see [the share] increase," said Hattie Greenan, the group's research director. "Roth is becoming mainstream," she said.
But just because employees have the Roth match option available to them doesn't mean it will be their best option.
There are pros and cons to pretax and Roth savings, and the right choice can vary from person to person, financial advisors said.
"[Roth] is not a bad idea if you're not so worried about your taxes today," said Philip Chao, a certified financial planner and chief investment officer at Experiential Wealth, based in Cabin John, Maryland. "It's personal preference."
1. Pre-tax advantage
While there are ample benefits to saving at least some money as Roth funds in a 401(k), most investors opt against it.
In fact, while almost all 401(k) plans already allow workers to save part of their paychecks as a Roth contribution, only a quarter of workers actually do so, according to the PSCA report.
"The list of cons may be short for Roth 401(k)s, but missing tax deferral is a big one," according to a May article written by Fidelity, a retirement plan administrator. "When faced with a choice of paying more tax now or later, most people choose to pay later, hence the low participation rates for Roth 401(k)s."
Tax deferral has long been a "key driver" of retirement savings, Fidelity said.
Saving on a pretax basis effectively increases a worker's take-home pay. It also reduces their adjusted gross income today, and may therefore positively impact the calculation of eligibility for child tax credits, financial aid for college or federal aid, according to Fidelity.
A Fidelity example shows the financial benefit of an up-front tax break: Let's say a saver with a $75,000 annual income in the 22% federal income tax bracket makes a $400 monthly 401(k) contribution. Making the full contribution as Roth would reduce their paycheck by $400. Making the contribution into a traditional — i.e., pretax — 401(k) would reduce their paycheck by just $312.
2. Roth advantage
For those who can stomach the up-front tax hit, Roth provides for powerful tax-planning opportunities in future years, according to financial advisors.
"Roth gives you a lot more flexibility at retirement," Chao said. "But you have to be OK with paying years of tax on it first. It's never something for nothing. There's always a trade-off."
For example, the government doesn't require investors to withdraw a minimum amount from Roth accounts in retirement, as it does with pretax savings. These annual "required minimum distributions," or RMDs, generally start at age 73 for traditional 401(k)s and IRAs, among other accounts.
Additionally, withdrawing money from Roth accounts in retirement can help limit taxes on Social Security benefits and reduce Medicare premiums, which are based on taxable income. Roth withdrawals don't count as taxable income.
Retirees can also make strategic withdrawals from Roth accounts in certain years to avoid jumping into a higher federal or state income tax bracket, advisors said.
"Once you pay the taxes [on a Roth contribution], the government is out of your hair," Chao said. "There's no amount you must draw out. It's your money; it's all tax-free when you take it out."
There are a few caveats.
For example, many investors must wait until at least age 59 1/2 to withdraw funds tax-free from a Roth 401(k) account. Additionally, due to a so-called five-year rule, investors must have had Roth 401(k) funds for at least five years to make a tax-free withdrawal.
Because Roth employer matching contributions are included in the saver's income, investors should ensure they have enough tax withheld from their paycheck to cover the income tax, according to Fidelity.
The ultimate goal for savers choosing whether to make Roth or pretax contributions is to pay income taxes when their tax rate is lowest, advisors said.
For example, Roth savings can work well for younger savers over the long term if they anticipate their incomes — and tax rates — will grow over time, said Andrew Bachman, director of tax and retirement income on Fidelity's financial solutions team.
Similar logic applies to people who plan to move from a low-tax to a high-tax state in retirement, such as from Texas to California, he said.
While it's impossible to know future tax rates, investors can hedge by splitting contributions between both types of accounts, advisors said.
Similar to contributions, workers may be able to split a 401(k) match between pretax and Roth savings. However, workers will be constrained by what their employer does and doesn't allow, Chao said.

title: A 19-year study reveals a troubling link between napping and death
text:
A surprising new study suggests that when and how often older adults nap could reveal hidden warning signs about their health. Researchers followed 1,338 people for up to 19 years and discovered that longer, more frequent naps were linked to higher mortality, while morning nappers faced a 30% greater risk of death than afternoon nappers. Each additional hour of daytime sleep was associated with a 13% increase in mortality risk.
A daily nap may seem like a harmless way to recharge, but new research suggests that certain napping habits could provide important clues about a person's health as they age. Scientists have found that taking longer or more frequent naps, particularly in the morning, is associated with an increased risk of death among older adults.
Researchers from Mass General Brigham and Rush University Medical Center examined the napping patterns of 1,338 older adults over a period of up to 19 years. Their findings, published in JAMA Network Open, suggest that monitoring daytime sleep could help identify underlying medical conditions or early signs of declining health.
"Excessive napping later in life has been linked to neurodegeneration, cardiovascular diseases and even greater morbidity, but many of those findings rely on self-reported napping habits and leave out metrics like when and how regular those naps are," said lead author Chenlu Gao, PhD, an investigator in the Department of Anesthesiology at Mass General Brigham and an affiliated research fellow in the Division of Sleep and Circadian Disorders in the Department of Medicine. "Our study is one of the first to show an association between objectively measured nap patterns and mortality and suggests there is immense clinical value in tracking napping patterns to catch health conditions early."
Why Scientists Are Studying Daytime Napping
Daytime naps are common among older adults, with estimates suggesting that 20% to 60% regularly nap. An occasional nap can help restore energy and improve alertness, but excessive daytime sleeping in later life has been associated with several health concerns.
