Despite these connections, researchers still have an incomplete understanding of how specific napping behaviors relate to long-term health. Many earlier studies depended on participants remembering and reporting their own sleep habits, which may not provide an accurate picture. They also often overlooked important details, such as how long naps lasted, when they occurred, and how much napping patterns changed from one day to the next.
To obtain more reliable measurements, the research team analyzed information from the Rush Memory and Aging Project. Launched in 1997, this long-running study was designed primarily to investigate memory, thinking abilities, and neurological decline among older adults in northern Illinois, most of whom were white.
Starting in 2005, participants wore wrist activity monitors for 10 days to record their daily periods of rest and movement. Researchers used these measurements to identify daytime sleep and assess nap duration, frequency, timing, and daily variation.
Longer and More Frequent Naps Linked to Higher Mortality Risk
By 2025, researchers had assembled up to 19 years of follow-up information from 1,338 participants. They then examined whether napping habits measured during the initial assessment were associated with the likelihood of dying from any cause during the subsequent years.
The results revealed several notable patterns. Older adults who slept longer during the day or took naps more frequently had higher mortality rates. The timing of naps also appeared to matter.
Each additional hour spent napping per day was associated with approximately a 13% higher mortality risk. Taking one additional nap per day was linked to about a 7% increase in risk.
One of the most striking findings involved morning naps. Participants who napped in the morning had a 30% higher mortality risk compared with those who napped in the afternoon.
However, not every aspect of napping was associated with poorer outcomes. Researchers found no increased mortality risk linked to irregular napping schedules, suggesting that changes in nap timing or duration from day to day were not necessarily indicators of greater risk.
Could Napping Habits Reveal Hidden Health Problems?
The researchers emphasize that their findings do not mean daytime naps directly cause health problems or shorten lives. Instead, excessive napping may reflect medical conditions or changes in the body that have not yet been recognized.
"It is important to note that this is correlation, not causation. Excessive napping is likely indicating underlying disease, chronic conditions, sleep disturbances, or circadian dysregulation," said Gao. "Now that we know there is a strong correlation between napping patterns and mortality rates, we can make the case to implement wearable daytime nap assessments to predict health conditions and prevent further decline."
These findings raise the possibility that wearable activity trackers could eventually become useful tools for monitoring health in older adults. By identifying changes in daytime sleep habits, healthcare professionals might be able to recognize warning signs of underlying illness, disrupted sleep cycles, or neurological decline earlier.
Although further research is needed to determine how effectively napping patterns can predict specific medical conditions, the study suggests that something as ordinary as a daily nap could provide valuable information about a person's overall health.
Study Authorship, Disclosures, and Funding
Authorship: In addition to Gao and Li, the Mass General Brigham researchers involved in the study include Ruixue Cai, Xi Zheng, Arlen Gaba, Lei Gao, and Kun Hu. Other contributors include Lei Yu, Aron S. Buchman, and David A. Bennett.
Disclosures: Li received a financial gift from iFutureLab to support research and has received consulting payments for serving on the iFutureLab-HEKA Scientific Advisory Board as Chair of Cardiac Dynamics and Honorary Life-Time Co-Founder. Li also received an honorarium for delivering a lecture at Shandong University.
Hu has received consulting fees for serving on the iFutureLab-HEKA Scientific Advisory Board as Chair of Medical Biodynamics and Honorary Life-Time Co-Founder. Mass General Brigham reviewed and managed the interests of both Li and Hu under its conflict of interest policies. These interests are unrelated to the present research.
Funding: The research received support from the American Academy of Sleep Medicine Foundation (290-FP-22), the Alzheimer's Association Research Fellowship to Promote Diversity (AARFD-22-928372), and the National Institute on Aging (RF1AG064312; R01AG083799).
Gao C. received additional funding from the National Heart Lung and Blood Institute (5T32HL007901). Li received support from the BrightFocus Foundation (A2020886S) and startup funding from the Department of Anesthesia, Critical Care and Pain Medicine at Massachusetts General Hospital. Hu also received startup funding from the same department.
Gao L. received additional support from the Alzheimer's Association (AACSF-23-1148490), National Institute on Aging (R03AG087439), American Academy of Sleep Medicine (352-DS-24), and National Institute of General Medical Sciences (R35GM160254).
The Rush Memory and Aging Project was funded by the National Institutes of Health (R01AG056352 and R01AG017917).

title: 'Alien: Fireteam Elite 2' is a good old-fashioned bug hunt, ironically plagued by bugs
text:
The first Aliens: Fireteam Elite was among my favorite Alien video games, and there were a lot of reasons to be excited for a sequel.
At Summer Game Fest 2026, we learned of many smart changes and improvements to the formula, and I was eager to go bug-hunting again. A new campaign, fully reworked classes, and four-player co-op. What could go wrong?
Months later, Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2's debut has been difficult, mostly due to glaring tech issues. Despite this, it's still a welcome jolt of action for a franchise that's been focusing on making the Xenomorphs scary again in recent years.
Alien: Romulus (2024) and Alien: Earth (2025) have reestablished the acid-blooded Xenomorphs as bona fide horror icons, while games like Aliens: Dark Descent bet on tense real-time tactics and squad management; Rogue Incursion spooked VR and non-VR players alike; and we even have Isolation 2's pure survival horror to look forward to.
Rough edges aside, Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 is a necessary return to mindless shooting and treating the Xenos as a relentless horde, dropping the stalking and slasher-inspired murders in favor of sci-fi shootouts and macho one-liners. It's far from a novel idea — even the original game is only five years old — but a classic for a reason.
Another glorious day in the Corps
Believe it or not, another colony has fallen prey to the Xenomorphs in Fireteam Elite 2. The familiar setup takes a new team of Colonial Marines to a mining facility on LV-558, where contact has been lost with the first wave of Marines that went in to deal with the threat.
This isn't first contact; the Marines are more than used to bug hunts by now, which means there's less exposition to cut through before getting to the Xeno-blasting chaos. The writing certainly won't stun the Academy (and there's definitely too much of it in between missions), but the agility here is appreciated. We've fought these aliens many, many times before. Fireteam Elite 2 is smart enough to sidestep fake tension and just hit the ground running.
All the design changes and upgrades reinforce the intent to make the ultimate Aliens action game. Classes have more defined roles and access to better, more destructive sci-fi weapons, and the upgrade to four-player fireteams is welcome when aliens and hostile synths won't stop pouring in. Tired of replaying campaign missions on higher difficulties and with modifiers? Prepare for the worst in this shooter's version of the classic horde mode.
At its best, Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 understands why James Cameron's masterpiece still holds up. During the biggest Xenomorph onslaughts — when the bullets are flying and acid is spraying — the game's shortcomings and jankier elements fade away.
Game over, man
There are still some scares hiding in here, though, ready to make complacent players jump out of their seats. Special Xenomorphs have tricks to pounce on distracted players, throwing chaos into the middle of their carefully coordinated rain of fire. Others have the ability to spit from afar, breaking tight defenses that count on the Xenos' predictable tactics from other games and the movies.
It's been 40 years since Aliens first graced the big screen, but Fireteam Elite 2 manages to refresh that mix of horror and action well enough, despite sharing much of its bones with the original game. But the disturbing lack of polish threatens to undo Cold Iron Studios' best ideas.
Those ideas include more varied enemies, which can disrupt almost any tried-and-tested team composition, and even a late-game class that rewards an extensive knowledge of the game by letting veterans pick weapons from all over the roster to create a custom loadout.
These playful creative swings somewhat offset the frustration caused by glitched objectives, enemy AI that often goes off the rails, and performance issues that have often given me flashbacks to its predecessor's worst moments on PS4. Sometimes, you can just tell when six extra months would've done a game a lot of good, and it's obvious that Fireteam Elite 2 will be in a much better place by spring.
That said, its loose and confident approach to design is rare to see when dealing with games that adapt well-established IPs like Alien.
Recent Star Wars games have achieved just that, and even if Fireteam Elite 2 misses some of its shots and has faced more initial trouble than the USCM's first incursion on LV-426, it's safe to say its heart and mind are in the right place. No one can take that away from the devs. Show me another modern Alien video game that allows you to zap Xenomorphs to death with a big cannon or to hold them off with combat drones.
We've seen developers win uphill battles before, and we know for a fact the huge Alien fandom is as enduring as the deadly extraterrestrials, so Daybreak and Cold Iron have a chance to turn things around and solidify Fireteam Elite 2 as the iterative but satisfying sequel it actually is.
Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 is available now for PS5, Xbox Series X|S, and PC. A Nintendo Switch 2 version is coming in 2027.
Fran Ruiz is our resident Star Wars guy. His hunger for movies and TV series is only matched by his love for video games. He got a BA of English Studies, focusing on English Literature, from the University of Malaga, in Spain, as well as a Master's Degree in English Studies, Multilingual and Intercultural Communication. On top of writing features and other longform articles for Space.com since 2021, he is a frequent collaborator of VG247 and other gaming sites. He also serves as associate editor over at Star Wars News Net and its sister site, Movie News Net.

title: Palestinian woman, 72, shot dead by Israeli settlers in West Bank, health ministry says
text:
A Palestinian woman in her 70s has been shot dead, and several other people wounded, in a village in the occupied West Bank where Israeli settlers recently moved in, the Palestinian health ministry says.
There are conflicting accounts of what happened. Local Palestinians said there was an attack by settlers in part of al-Duyuk al-Tahta, near Jericho, which is meant to be under the full control of the Palestinian Authority.
According to the Israeli army, there was a Palestinian car-ramming attack on an Israeli vehicle. It said rocks were then thrown at the Israelis, who opened fire in response. It did not mention the fatal shooting of a woman.
There have been high tensions in the area since a group of settlers recently set up a new outpost.
They moved into eight houses in the village on 4 November after buying them, they have said, in a secretive operation. The properties are in an area where Israel retains full security control.
All settlements are illegal under international law.
Local Palestinians said that the events in al-Duyuk al-Tahta on Monday night began with harassment by Israeli settlers. Palestinian children threw stones, they said, and the settlers opened fire, killing Fadda al-Fahidat, who was 72, outside her home.
Fadda's daughter-in-law, Nema al-Fahidat, told the BBC that she died from a single bullet wound to the head. "It destroyed her brain," she said.
According to the Palestinian accounts, Fadda's son, Arafat, rushed to the scene in his car after hearing the news and collided with an empty Israeli settler car parked outside his family home, injuring settlers who were standing nearby. The settlers then fired more shots, they said, injuring several Palestinians, including Arafat.
"My husband, when he saw his mother, was not paying attention. He crashed into the vehicle. The vehicle was empty," Nema said.
"My husband got out of his car and tried to reach his mother and the injured young men. Then he was shot."
She added: "We tried to gather the injured people and move them away from the settler. We brought them here. But he kept firing, firing, firing. Even after we had brought the wounded young men here and moved them away from him, he continued shooting."
Nema said young Palestinians threw stones at the settlers after seeing what happened, but asked: "What can stones do against bullets?"
The statement from the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said that "terrorists accelerated their vehicle toward an Israeli vehicle and rammed it", and then "exited their vehicle with weapons and attacked and harmed the occupants of the Israeli vehicle".
Afterwards, it said, "rocks were hurled at the Israelis, who responded by firing in order to remove the threat."
Later, an Israeli military source said Fadda was shot by an Israeli civilian and that there was no evidence that she had been involved in the confrontation near her home.
Meanwhile, a spokesperson for Israel's police force said it had opened an investigation, and that officers and forensic technicians had been collecting evidence and interviewing witnesses.
The Israeli human rights group B'Tselem says there has been a prolonged campaign of settler attacks, intimidation and land seizures in al-Duyuk al-Tahta, with Israeli troops now stationed nearby to secure the new settlement.
Residents and activists say armed settlers walk and drive quad bikes around the neighbourhood as they threaten Palestinian residents.
A BBC team saw settlers at the end of the street where Fadda was shot on Tuesday, as well as Israeli flags flying from four of the houses that they had moved into earlier this month.
In a separate incident on Monday evening, eight Palestinians were injured when they were hit by a vehicle driven by an Israeli settler on a main road in Tuqu, south of Bethlehem, according to Palestinian officials and the Palestinian Red Crescent.
The IDF said the incident was a traffic accident. But the Palestinian foreign ministry called it a "terrorist attack", saying the driver hit a group of Palestinians who had gathered near the scene of an earlier traffic accident.
Also on Monday, the Civil Administration - the body that implements Israeli government policy in the West Bank - announced the allocation of more than 28 sq km (6,945 acres) of land in the northern Jordan Valley to nine settlers for grazing, according to the Israeli anti-settlement watchdog Peace Now.
It said handing over vast tracts of land to settlers for grazing outposts constituted "direct support for the systematic expulsion of Palestinians from their lands and the rampant criminal violence in the West Bank".
The UK government announced on Tuesday that it was imposing sanctions on eight companies building Israeli settlements in the West Bank.
It is the first sanctions package since Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband's pledge in September to respond to the accelerating rate of settlement expansion in the West Bank, which he said risked rendering a two-state solution unviable.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar called the sanctions a "hostile act targeting private, law-abiding companies".

title: Pope Leo calls for "less controversy, less war, less division"
text:
Rome — Speaking to reporters on his return trip to Rome after an , Pope Leo XIV called for less political polarization in the United States following the recent midterm elections.
"I would like to see a greater capacity for dialogue, building bridges, reconciliation, less controversy, less war, less division," the told reporters. "I know this is also a dream, but I know it is possible, so we shall see."
Leo, who that he had voted in the 2026 midterms and was proud to "exercise my right" to do so, said it was the duty of all American citizens to participate in elections. He spoke on the flight back to Italy about his American identity, calling himself "a gringo in many ways."
"My deep faith in democracy, of democratic participation, is also part of being a North American," he said.
The pontiff said being American was also likely why he had been forthcoming about his .
"Not at 100%, but I'm doing quite well"
"When I speak in general, I am very direct. I say things as they are," he told reporters. "The issue of my health and the fact of openly speaking about it … it's not so typical in many countries and cultures. In U.S. society, it is a bit more of a common attitude."
"I'm not at 100%, but I'm doing quite well," he said, crediting his doctors, prayers and personal determination for his recovery, calling stamina "one of the gifts the Lord gave me."
Leo underwent surgery in October after doctors discovered a lung tumor and diagnosed him with cancer. His medical team said the cancer was confined to a lobe of one lung that was removed, and that no further treatment was necessary. The tumor was discovered during a routine annual medical examination.
"The initial news was a surprise," the pope said. "I had no symptoms and felt fine."
Leo, who set off on the trip to Latin America just 24 days after his operation, said he had decided to proceed quickly with the surgery because he was determined to stick to the plans for his Latin American tour. He said the diagnosis did not change his agenda, or his priorities.
Asked whether he had signed a conditional resignation letter in the event of permanent incapacity, as previous popes have done, Leo said he had not.
"For now, I don't see the need," he said.
Pope doesn't rule out married priests
Leo also addressed one of the most divisive issues in the Catholic Church on the return flight — the ordination of married men to the priesthood.
He acknowledged that allowing married priests could help address severe shortages in remote regions such as the Amazon, but cautioned that the issue was "complicated" and could create division within the church.
"It's a solution which, in certain areas of the church, can cause division because there is not universal, if you will, acceptance, of that concept," he said.
Leo did not completely rule out the possibility, but made it sound unlikely any time soon.
"It may be in the future that some things will change. However, for right now, what I believe, an important part of my ministry of the church is to heal, bring people together," he said.
The pope also joked with reporters about being hit in the face with a flying rosary during his final mass in Lima.
"The affection of Peruvians — including that person who, with great faith, simply wanted to offer me a rosary — these are things one carries in one's heart, perhaps in one's eye," he quipped.

title: AI cheating fears spook South Korea ahead of high-stakes college entrance exam
text:
South Korean officials are scrambling to prevent cheating on a national college entrance exam using technology
SEOUL, South Korea -- Days before South Korea comes to a standstill for its all-important college entrance exam, the nation is reeling after the top scorer on its tax accountant test was found to have cheated with a hidden camera and artificial intelligence.
The scandal has left authorities scrambling to prevent cheating on the exam, which will be taken Thursday by more than 500,000 students, as concerns grow that AI and smart devices are making fraud harder to detect.
Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin on Monday rejected calls by some lawmakers to postpone the exam until stronger anti-cheating measures are in place, telling a legislative hearing that a delay would cause “even a larger disruption” to students.
Choi said that he was confident that proctors could spot AI-powered smart glasses, which typically have thick, horn-rimmed frames. Education authorities are also offering guidance on detecting devices such as microcameras, Education Ministry officials said.
Worries about cheating deepened over the weekend after a 34-year-old man who scored the highest on a national tax accountant exam confessed to using a hidden microcamera and smartphone to get answers from AI.
Han Won-seok’s unusually high scores had drawn suspicion after he discussed them during recent media interviews. The case follows other incidents involving AI-assisted cheating in the past several months, including test-takers caught using AI-powered smart glasses on an English standardized test in June and on some university essay exams in October.
In a video posted Sunday on his lawyer’s YouTube channel, Han said that he used a concealed camera to capture the questions, fed the images to a generative AI tool and received answers on a smartphone. He said that he would cooperate with police, who are investigating the case.
Han had previously said that he scored 397.5 out of a possible 400 points on the first-stage, multiple-choice test in April, and 663 out of 800 on the second-stage essay exam in July, unusually high marks that one Korean newspaper likened to “running a 100-meter sprint in under five seconds.”
The national college entrance exam, known as “Suneung,” or the College Scholastic Ability Test, is a high-stakes annual event in a country notorious for intense academic competition, where prospects for jobs, social standing and even marriage can depend on which university a person attends.
South Korea goes to great lengths each year to create an ideal testing environment, effectively bringing the country to a standstill by delaying the start of the workday and stock market trading to ease traffic for test-takers and pausing flights during the English listening section of the exam. Police officers often use cars and motorcycles to escort test-takers who are running late, while the military sometimes suspends training in areas near testing sites.
But it’s difficult for authorities to come up with equally sweeping measures to prevent cheating with AI devices, which the Seoul-based Hankyoreh newspaper warned in an editorial Monday could threaten “the very foundations of the examination system.”
Education authorities had focused for months on preventing the use of AI-powered glasses, but Han’s case has raised doubts about whether they are prepared for cheating involving other, less conspicuous devices.
Education authorities will deploy at least one specially trained supervisor at each of the 1,300 test sites nationwide to identify such glasses. Officials also are considering requiring test takers to hand over their smart devices and shutting down public Wi-Fi connections at test sites, according to Prime Minister Han Seongsook's office.
Song Geun-hyeon, another senior Education Ministry official, said that the ministry has provided proctors with new guidance on detecting test-takers using hidden cameras and other devices, including watching for suspicious movements involving “their sleeves, collars or buttons, and certain gestures.”
The ministry was working with the Ministry of Science and Information and Communication Technology on anti-cheating measures for the college entrance exam, which are due to be announced on Tuesday.
Vice Education Minister Choi Eun-ok said that the discussions with the science ministry also include temporarily restricting telecommunications at test sites. It wasn't immediately clear whether that's feasible, considering laws prohibiting electronic signal jamming, or concerns that it could interfere with communication in surrounding areas.
Song said that metal detectors and radio detectors would be limited, while deploying thermal cameras would be highly unlikely because of privacy concerns. Supervisors can't search belongings without the consent of the test-takers.
“At the government-wide level, we would also need to give further consideration to measures that will make it easier to identify (AI) smart devices,” said Song, adding that officials are debating whether to require manufacturers to design the devices to emit “flashing lights or sounds” while in use.

title: Despite restrictive abortion laws, Poland's 'Abortomat' — a locker that dispenses abortion pills — helps women who want to end a pregnancy
text:
Women's rights activists in Poland have opened what they say is the world's first delivery locker supplying abortion pills in a country with one of Europe's most restrictive abortion laws.
Known as the "Abortomat," the locker is in a building opposite the Polish parliament, in what activists say is a clear message to politicians like Donald Tusk. The Polish prime minister pledged to introduce abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy before the 2023 parliamentary election, but his coalition has been unable to agree on a common position.
Only two European Union member states, Poland and Malta, do not allow abortion on request.
In Poland, abortion is only allowed when the pregnancy is the result of a crime — rape or incest — or when it endangers the health or life of the woman.
Pink lockers and PIN codes
Justyna Wydrzynska, an activist from a nonprofit organization called Abortion Dream Team, showed DW the "Abortomat" in a small room behind a tasseled portiere at Abotak, Poland's first abortion center.
Inside, the pink lighting is subdued. Glitter tassels, baubles and spotlights make it feel a bit like a disco, she said.
The "Abortomat," which opened in late September, has 22 pink lockers. To open one, a woman receives a PIN code from the organization Women Help Women after completing a medical questionnaire, which is then checked by a doctor.
Parcel lockers have sprung up like mushrooms after rain in Poland in recent years. Even the smallest villages have them.
"When you walk around Poland, vending machines are everywhere. This is our culture. People in the US have Amazon, we have vending machines for everything," said Wydrzynska.
Convicted of helping a woman to have an abortion
Women in Poland who have an abortion are not criminalized. But anyone who helps them terminate a pregnancy risks up to three years in prison.
In 2023, Wydrzynska was the first activist to be convicted in Poland of helping a woman to have an abortion by sending her pills. The conviction was later overturned, and the court ordered a retrial.
Inside each compartment at the "Abortomat" is a package that normally contains two drugs, mifepristone and misoprostol, usually taken up to the 14th week of pregnancy.
Because mifepristone is not registered in Poland, the drug must be ordered from abroad where it is legal. Information on how to do this is not easy to come by, which is where Abortion Dream Team and Abotak come in. They help women find information about accessing medication, which is sent from abroad by Women Help Women, or help them to travel abroad for a termination.
A 'complicated' legal situation
Wydrzynska said she believes the "Abortomat" does not break the law because it is a machine, not a person, that is delivering the pills, although she admits she is not sure.
Dr. Sabrina Mana-Walasek, a reproductive rights lawyer representing Wydrzynska, said the legal environment for abortion pills is "complicated."
She said that although mifepristone is not registered in Poland, it is registered in the European Union and, as EU citizens, Polish women can order it and take it.
"If a woman orders pills for herself and pays for them herself, it's not a crime," she said.
Opposition from Catholic groups
The ultra-Catholic legal group Ordo Iuris disagrees and has notified the prosecutor's office that the activists are committing a crime.
"In the case of an 'Abortomat,' the actions enabling a woman to have an abortion are theoretically performed by the woman herself using the device, but the reality is that this machine is operated by people — they send the code required to open the compartment containing abortion pills, they order and procure the pills, and they restock the compartments," said Katarzyna Gesiak, director of the Ordo Iuris Center for Medical Law and Bioethics.
Wydrzynska said anti-abortion activists regularly demonstrate outside Abotak, using horns and loudspeakers to generate loud noise to annoy the center's residential neighbors and pressure the landlord to revoke their rental agreement.
At one demonstration, a woman holding an image of the Virgin Mary told DW she believes abortion "is the work of Satan."
"Abortion is evil, it's demonic, it's against the fifth Commandment, 'Thou shalt not kill,'" she said.
Support for women seeking an abortion
Earlier this year, Diana, a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman living in Warsaw, used abortion pills during her sixth week of pregnancy before the "Abortomat" started up. She got the pills using information provided by Abortion Dream Team.
Diana told DW that she has never wanted to have children.
"I was expecting something like a headache, stomachache, maybe vomiting, but I had nothing like that. It was just like a normal period. I didn't feel any pain. It was really easy for me," she said.
"I felt relief because I knew that it was the right choice for me. I knew that I can live my life," she added.
Another Abortion Dream Team activist, Natalia Broniarczyk, said they help about 130 women daily in Poland. About 125 of these women use pills that cost about €75 ($83), while the remainder travel to a clinic abroad.
In contrast, just 851 abortions were performed in Polish hospitals last year.
Rising support for right-wing parties
Broniarczyk is concerned about the rising support for right-wing parties ahead of next year's parliamentary election, but she's also furious at the inactivity of liberals in Tusk's coalition.
"I'm mad at the liberals because for three years, they did nothing to protect us. They lost three years and now, when we're close to an election, they are fighting for our voices and respect. People are more progressive than politicians," she said.
After taking office in 2023, Tusk's coalition, which includes left-wing and conservative partners, were unable to agree a common position and their separate bills failed to obtain parliamentary approval in 2024.
Afterwards, Tusk said abortion on request would not be possible during the current parliamentary term.
Two bills approved by parliament
In October, however, two bills were resubmitted to the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, and were narrowly approved.
One reinstates severe irreversible fetal defects as a justification for a legal termination. This justification had been ruled illegal by the Constitutional Court in 2020 when the previous right-wing Law and Justice (PiS)-led government was in power.
The 2020 ruling led to tens of thousands of people, mostly women, taking part in street protests in towns and cities across the country, some of the largest since communism fell in 1989.
Lawmakers also approved a bill partially decriminalizing anyone who helps a woman terminate her pregnancy.
According to the results of a recent poll conducted by SW Research for Onet.pl, almost 61% of respondents said they want the country's right-wing president, Karol Nawrocki, who is backed by PiS, to sign into law the bill on the fetal defect justification.
Nawrocki opposes abortion, and both Wydrzynska and Broniarczyk think he will use his power of veto to block the bills, preventing them from becoming law.

title: Migrant arrivals from Africa to the Canary Islands spike as Spain's general election nears
text:
More than 11,000 migrants have reached Spain’s Canary Islands in the first half of November, Spanish government figures show, an increase over the same period last year that has become political fodder ahead of the country's Nov. 29 general election.
The archipelago off northwest Africa is a major entry point for migrants, mainly from West and North Africa, who attempt the dangerous Atlantic Ocean crossing in makeshift boats fleeing poverty and conflict and seeking a better life in Europe. Most of those arriving are from Senegal, Mali, Gambia and Guinea, said José Antonio Rodríguez, spokesperson for the regional Red Cross immediate response team.
For much of the year, fewer migrants had reached the Canary Islands compared to last year, but a sharp increase since late October through mid-November has placed pressure on reception and emergency services on smaller islands, like El Hierro, where many boats have arrived and which has a population of about 12,000 people.
Their timing coincides with Spain's general election campaign. Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right, anti-immigrant Vox party, called the migrant arrivals “an invasion,” kicking off his campaign on Monday night in the Spanish archipelago.
Several opinion polls show the ruling Socialist Party led by Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez behind the combined support of the conservative Popular Party and Vox. Sánchez has been roundly criticized by conservative politicians for his party's immigration-friendly policies, including a push earlier this year to legalize more than 1 million undocumented immigrants already in the country.
Then, in July, tens of thousands of people crossed from Morocco into Spain’s North African territory of Ceuta in just two days, causing chaos and reigniting debate over immigration in Europe and beyond. More than 140 people died attempting the journey.
“Whoever enters Spain illegally will leave Spain and will never be made legal,” Abascal told a few thousand supporters Monday on the island of Tenerife. “Some disguise themselves as defenders of the Canary Islands, and all they want is to spread the problem throughout Spain."
Spain declared an emergency on the archipelago last week due to the increasing migrant arrivals, earmarking additional funds to create more space in state-run reception centers.
The Atlantic crossing between West Africa and the Canary Islands is one of the world’s deadliest migration routes. Although the islands lie about 65 miles (105 kilometers) from the nearest African coast, many migrants take longer routes to evade security forces. The journeys can last days or weeks.
Many migrants arrive unaware of what island they have reached, Rodríguez said. They often reach with health issues requiring medical attention such as hypothermia, dehydration and “trench foot," a type of bacterial infection caused by prolonged exposure to salt water contaminated with fuel and human waste.
“It's very complicated, like a gangrene,” Rodríguez explained, adding that at least a few people on every boat have the infection.
Migrant arrivals to the Canary Islands tend to rise in the fall, when sea conditions along the Atlantic route are calmer and more favorable for crossings.
In 2025, 17,788 migrants reached the Canary Islands irregularly by boat from West and Northern Africa, according to data from the International Organization for Migration, a 62% decrease compared with the previous year.
Spanish authorities usually transfer migrants from El Hierro to larger islands in the archipelago with more infrastructure to shelter and process them.
Regional leader Fernando Clavijo has called the boat arrivals in El Hierro unsustainable, and has asked for more help from Spain's national government.
“We are deeply concerned — very concerned — about the situation and the reactions we are seeing,” he said.
Associated Press writers Monica Pronczuk and Babacar Dione in Dakar, Senegal, contributed.

title: Computer love or hate: Charlotte de Witte's AI singer collaboration divides techno fans
text:
The international DJ released the EP Azadi with NAVA, a virtual AI singer, to represent Iranian women banned from performing publicly, but techno star's choice has not gone down well with some of her fans.
What if the undisputed queen of global techno crossed over to the "dark side"? That is what many people thought when on Thursday 5 November (and even earlier, to be fair) Charlotte de Witte, the 34-year-old Belgian DJ and record producer who boasts 6.5 million Instagram followers, released her new EP.
Azadi (in Persian, "freedom", a word we came to know during the protests in Iran in 2022), released on her own label KNTXT, contains three tracks (Azadi itself, Omid, which means "hope", and Tales of the Desert) with the acid techno sound that has always set her apart, as do the 140 BPM, but this time with a rather unusual vocalist.
De Witte, voted the world’s No. 1 techno DJ for the seventh year in a row in the DJ Mag Top 100 DJs 2026 ranking, has in fact used an AI singer for the first time. This is NAVA, developed by British-Iranian artist Farbod Mehr.
In an official statement, the artist said that "NAVA represents Iranian women who are forbidden to perform in public" and that the EP is conceived as "a small act of resistance", with all proceeds donated to the NGO FEMENA, an organisation that supports women’s rights activists and feminist movements in the SWANA region and in Asia.
The EP is therefore not a record produced entirely by artificial intelligence, but a musical collaboration in which only the lead voice is that of a virtual singer.
Who is NAVA?
NAVA is a project created in 2025 by Farbod Mehr, a British digital artist of Iranian origin. The virtual singer was developed using artificial intelligence and her visual identity is inspired by Persian art and cultural tradition.
Mehr has said that his aim is to symbolically represent Iranian women, who cannot freely perform as solo singers in front of mixed audiences. One only has to think of the case of Parastoo Ahmadi, who in June was sentenced by a court in Qom to 74 lashes, a two-year travel ban and a two-year suspension from artistic activity. Her offence? Having posted a concert streamed on YouTube in December 2024, in which she performed without a headscarf and wearing a sleeveless dress.
Reactions from fans and experts
The intention is certainly good, but it has not been welcomed unanimously, as de Witte may have hoped. Her fan base has been extremely voiciferous with its criticisms. The decision to use an artificial voice to represent women who have been deprived of the possibility of expressing themselves through music has in fact raised numerous objections among electronic music fans.
Many are asking why the voice of a real person was not used. For instance, on Reddit one fan states: "I have completely stopped enjoying her music. There are other ways to give voice to Iranian women, without resorting to 'an artist' created by artificial intelligence". For another fan the initiative is to be praised, but they believe she could have chosen a different path: "Apparently, artificial intelligence is supposed to represent Iranian women living under oppression, but is it really possible that there were no Iranian artists in the flesh to sing on the track?"
Some users also fear that normalising AI-generated voices could reduce professional opportunities for singers, backing vocalists and musicians, replacing human artistic performances with artificial tools.
Criticism has also come from within the Iranian techno scene. AliPink, a DJ and producer, a pioneer of the country’s underground scene and founder of the label Techno Tehran Records, has challenged the decision to rely on an artificial singer to represent Iranian women.
In a comment posted on Instagram and later picked up by the platform Tehran Herald, AliPink described as "deeply questionable" the idea that an artificial voice is needed to represent these women, stressing that there are already Iranian artists in the flesh, with talent and stories to tell.
AliPink has also questioned the very value of the project, adding: "There is a fundamental difference between raising awareness of the difficulties faced by Iranian women and using their struggles as a concept to promote music generated by artificial intelligence".
There are, however, also those who defend the project, pointing out that if de Witte had used a real Iranian artist she would have put her at risk by having her sing those songs. One Instagram user commented under the post in which de Witte shared a preview of the EP before its official release: "Wow, as a Persian woman and artist, this really hits me deeply. People do not realise how much Iranian women have to fight, much harder, just to do what artists in other countries are free to do every day". Another Instagram user wrote: "I have been waiting for this release, thank you Charlotte, for highlighting the voices of Iranian women, who are repressed by their government and denied the chance to express themselves creatively".
The debate is therefore more complex than a simple clash between supporters and opponents of AI. For some, NAVA represents a missed opportunity to involve artists of flesh and blood directly, while for others it is a tool of expression and solidarity when there are no alternatives.
The thin line between creativity and copying
The story is part of a broader debate about the role of artificial intelligence in the music industry. In recent years, generative tools have become capable of creating voices, melodies and entire compositions, calling into question the relationship between human creativity, technology and intellectual property.
So far the music industry has mostly proceeded through self-imposed limits. For example, Spotify requires that every use of unauthorised voice cloning be explicitly flagged and is prohibited, while Bandcamp (a direct-sales platform for record producers) categorically bans music generated "entirely or largely" by AI. Since 2026, moreover, Beatport has refused to accept tracks for upload if they are deemed to be fully AI.
Charlotte de Witte’s decision to use an AI voice reignites a question that is now increasingly central in the music industry: whether, and what, space artificial intelligence should have in artistic creation? Above all, where does technological experimentation end and the replacement of human labour begin?
With Azadi, the Belgian DJ has taken this debate into a particularly sensitive area, that of freedom of expression and women’s rights. Whatever the intentions and the solidarity message behind the project, one crucial question remains: when we use artificial intelligence to give a voice to those who cannot speak freely, are we really giving their voice back to them or are we simply speaking in their place?

title: French troops secretly deployed inside Ukraine as ex-NATO chief praises Macron's 'guts'
text:
French troops have reportedly been operating secretly inside Ukraine for months, training Ukrainian forces and maintaining military equipment and, as NATO experts claim, President Emmanuel Macron is taking a more assertive role in supporting Kyiv against Russia.
The covert mission, codenamed "Volia," has operated since at least summer 2026, with small teams of French military personnel deployed on short-term assignments under the supervision of a French general, Radio France Internationale (RFI) reported Monday.
Agence France-Presse (AFP) also separately reported the French military presence, citing sources who said the troops were not involved in combat.
The reports come as the United States and European allies pursue renewed, high-stakes negotiations to end Russia's war in Ukraine, raising questions about the extent of Western military involvement in the conflict.
Former NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe Gen. Philip Breedlove meanwhile, told Fox News Digital that the covert French mission sends a powerful message to Russian President Vladimir Putin at a critical juncture for Europe.
"The timing of what the French are doing and their announcement of what they're doing is important," Breedlove said.
"A very powerful NATO ally — both politically and militarily — is making a strong statement of support for Ukraine.
"And this is what Mr. Putin needs to see. He needs to look across the line and see that the Western alliances, NATO in this case, are standing up for Ukraine."
"It's very important to remember that if Mr. Putin stops fighting, this war ends. If Ukraine stops fighting, Ukraine ends," he said before adding that this is "an existential war that we in the West need to support to the appropriate conclusion."
The French mission reportedly focuses on training Ukrainian troops and maintaining French-supplied equipment, including CAESAR self-propelled howitzers, Mirage 2000 fighter jets and precision-guided missiles.
French personnel have rotated between France, Poland and Ukraine under what RFI described as a "light and flexible" operational structure.
French newspaper Le Monde separately reported Monday that personnel had also worked alongside Ukrainian intelligence units on observation missions closer to the front lines.
The deployment would mark a significant step in Macron's military support for Kyiv despite repeated Russian warnings against Western troop involvement.
"I cannot imagine the French military would deploy into Ukraine without their commander-in-chief approving it," Breedlove said of Macron while noting that Western military training missions inside Ukraine predate Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.
"It's not new to have training facilities inside of Ukraine. But almost all of them, and almost everyone, left Ukraine when the war started, which I disagree with, but that was the decision," he said.
Breedlove also pointed to the Yavoriv military training facility in western Ukraine, where NATO countries helped train Ukrainian forces following Russia's initial intervention in 2014.
"In 2014, we had a training area called Yavoriv," he said.
"We had a large facility of NATO training ability there, and we trained Ukrainians all the time. When the war started back in 2014 — remembering this is a 12-year-long war — most of those nations left, to include the United States."
"I would congratulate and thank France for having the guts to go in there and do what we all should be doing to help Ukraine fight this illegal, immoral, inhumane war that Russia is persecuting the Ukrainian people with," Breedlove said.
RFI reported that French lawmakers had not been formally informed of the deployment, with authorities maintaining that parliamentary approval was unnecessary because the mission did not involve combat operations.
France has trained approximately 25,000 Ukrainian soldiers in France and Poland since 2023, according to Le Monde.
Macron raised the possibility of sending Western military instructors into Ukraine in 2024, prompting concerns among allies, including the United States and Germany, about a potential escalation with Moscow.
France has also helped lead efforts to establish a multinational force to support a potential postwar security arrangement for Ukraine.
Russia has repeatedly opposed the presence of Western troops in Ukraine, while Putin has characterized Western military assistance to Kyiv as evidence of a proxy conflict between Russia and NATO.
The reports surfaced as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced fresh talks Monday with American and European representatives aimed at ending the war.
Zelenskyy said Ukrainian officials held online discussions with U.S. presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, along with European representatives, about prospects for a negotiated settlement with Russia.
The Ukrainian leader also warned that intelligence indicated Russia was preparing major strikes against Ukrainian targets Monday evening, overnight and Tuesday.
Breedlove suggested that France's reported mission could now encourage other NATO members to further expand their support for Ukraine.
"I think that there are more than a few NATO nations that would love to be in there helping," he said.
"They're the ones that call themselves the Eastern Front, those nations that border Russia in various parts of the eastern flank of NATO."
"And so I'm sure there are other nations that want to do this, but they're looking for leadership to go do it," he said.
"It seems now that France may be stepping up to the task."

title: Euclid discovers ancient cosmic beacons from the dawn of time, shining like a trillion suns
text:
ESA’s Euclid space telescope has discovered 31 ancient quasars, including two record-breaking objects that shone with the brightness of a trillion Suns when the Universe was just 670 million years old. Powered by supermassive black holes, these extraordinary cosmic beacons reveal a time when the first galaxies were still taking shape.
The European Space Agency's Euclid space telescope has discovered 31 exceptionally ancient quasars, including two that have set new records as the earliest ever observed. These brilliant galactic centers, powered by enormous black holes, were already radiating as much light as a trillion Suns when the Universe was only 670 million years old, about 5% of its present age.
Quasars are among the brightest objects in the cosmos. They appear during a relatively short period in a galaxy's history when huge quantities of gas and other material spiral toward its central supermassive black hole. This process releases extraordinary amounts of energy, causing the galaxy's core to shine hundreds or even thousands of times more brightly than the rest of the galaxy combined.
Astronomers have spent decades searching for quasars from the Universe's earliest years because they offer valuable clues about the formation of the first galaxies and supermassive black holes. Finding them, however, is extremely challenging. Few galaxies had grown large enough to host such objects at that early stage, and the light reaching us today is incredibly faint. These distant sources can also be difficult to distinguish from stars much closer to Earth.
Launched in 2023, Euclid is transforming that search. Its ability to survey enormous regions of the sky and detect faint objects has already produced an unprecedented collection of 31 quasars from the early Universe, including some dating back to when the cosmos was just 5% of its current age.
"These early quasars date back to the Universe's infancy," says Daming Yang of Leiden University in the Netherlands, lead author of the Euclid discovery paper. "By finding and studying them, we can better understand how these enormous systems formed and grew so quickly - one of the greatest mysteries in astrophysics."
Euclid Reveals a Hidden Population of Ancient Quasars
Until now, astronomers had identified only a small fraction of the quasars that existed during the Universe's earliest period. Most known examples were exceptionally luminous objects that stood out because they were easier to detect. This limited sample made it difficult to understand the broader population and how these powerful systems developed.
Euclid is changing that picture by identifying not only the brightest quasars but also much fainter examples that previous searches struggled to find. Its discoveries are providing scientists with a far more representative view of the ancient quasar population, opening the door to more detailed studies of these early cosmic objects.
"Euclid is a true game-changer," adds Daming. "Before, we could only find a handful of the very brightest ancient quasars, but Euclid lets us search far more efficiently across huge areas of sky to capture much fainter light. It's a unique tool for quasar hunting."
Among the 31 newly identified quasars, 12 have a redshift of 7 or greater. Redshift describes how light is stretched as the Universe expands and helps astronomers determine how far away an object is and how far back in cosmic history its light originated. A redshift of at least 7 places these quasars within the Universe's first 770 million years.
Two Record-Breaking Quasars From Cosmic Dawn
Two objects stand out as particularly extraordinary. The most ancient, EUCL J172902.75+641018.1, has a redshift of 7.77, while EUCL J125308.55+705432.3 has a redshift of 7.69. Both are located just over 13 billion light-years from Earth and were already shining within the first 670 million years of cosmic history.
These discoveries establish new records for the earliest known quasars. The previous record belonged to an object discovered in 2021, which has a redshift of 7.64.
"This finding more than doubles the number of quasars we know of that are so ancient," says Antonio La Marca, an ESA Research Fellow in the Euclid team.
The pace of discovery is especially remarkable. Astronomers needed more than a decade to identify roughly the first 10 quasars with redshifts of 7 or higher. Euclid has already surpassed that number in just one year, demonstrating how dramatically the telescope is accelerating research into the early Universe.
"The Euclid team has taken a true 'census' of quasars at the dawn of the Universe for the first time," adds Antonio. "It's a big step towards understanding these fascinating objects on a more fundamental level."
Ancient Black Holes Reveal Clues About the First Galaxies
One of the newly discovered objects is already offering additional insight into conditions during the Universe's infancy. Silvia Belladitta and colleagues recently conducted a more detailed investigation of the second most ancient quasar identified by Daming and his team.
Their observations revealed that the quasar sits inside a galaxy filled with gas and dust where new stars are forming at a tremendous rate. This provides an important glimpse of the environment surrounding an early supermassive black hole and could help researchers understand how the first massive galaxies evolved alongside the black holes at their centers.
These quasars also belong to a transformative chapter in cosmic history known as the epoch of reionization. During this period, the Universe emerged from a cold, dark state (the 'dark ages') as increasingly energetic radiation heated the surrounding gas and ionized it (split apart by energetic light). This fundamental transition helped establish the conditions that shaped the Universe we observe today.
"Ancient quasars are rare discoveries. They're interesting in themselves, but also time machines that enable us to explore the early Universe and understand how the first generation of galaxies came to be," says ESA Euclid Project Scientist Valeria Pettorino.
How Euclid Is Transforming the Search for Cosmic Giants
Euclid's success comes from a powerful combination of capabilities. The telescope can examine enormous portions of the sky while collecting detailed images and detecting faint infrared light from extremely distant objects. Together, these features make it exceptionally effective at finding rare sources that earlier surveys could easily miss.
"Euclid's capabilities are unrivaled. The telescope combines a large area, depth, sharp imaging, and unique space-based infrared vision in a way that lets us pick out rare, extremely distant objects far more efficiently than before.
"And it's not just the telescope: the data processing is only possible thanks to thousands of Euclid Consortium scientists and engineers working together to deliver scientific discoveries, sifting through enormous datasets to identify rare, distant quasars that we can study further using telescopes on the ground."
All 31 quasars were identified using observations from the Euclid Wide Survey, an ambitious project that will eventually examine more than one-third of the entire sky.
Although Euclid's primary mission is to investigate the dark Universe, its observations are revealing much more. By studying billions of galaxies, the telescope is helping astronomers investigate the Universe's composition, history, evolution, and vast cosmic structure. At the same time, its sweeping survey is uncovering rare ancient quasars that offer a remarkable opportunity to explore how the first galaxies and giant black holes emerged.
As Euclid continues mapping the cosmos, astronomers expect its growing collection of distant quasars to provide new clues about one of astrophysics' most enduring questions: how supermassive black holes became so enormous in such a remarkably short time after the Big Bang.

title: Why did Starship Flight 15 booster abort 'chopsticks' landing catch? SpaceX still investigating (video)
text:
Update for 3:40 p.m. ET on Nov. 14: SpaceX's Kate Tice provided more information about the booster abort at about 3:30 p.m. EST (1830 GMT) on Nov. 14, during the company's Flight 15 webcast. "Early indications are that the booster ended its boostback [burn] early due to a low fuel mass alarm," she said. "The team is still investigating the root cause on that."
SpaceX is looking into why its latest Starship megarocket test flight missed the first of two planned landings on Friday (Nov. 13), triggering an automatic abort that destroyed the booster.
The giant Starship rocket, a massive two-stage vehicle that's the largest launcher on Earth, soared into orbit from SpaceX's Starbase in South Texas on Friday on the company's ambitious Flight 15 test flight. The goal: To land both the Super Heavy first stage and the Ship upper stage, for the first full Starship recovery — and the first complete recovery of an orbital launch system in history.
The Super Heavy stage, called Booster 22, came back to Earth mere minutes after liftoff as planned. Instead of returning to its launch tower to be caught mid-air by the tower's metal "chopstick" arms, however, the rocket veered offshore and detonated its flight termination system. SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot initially said that a guidance issue appeared to be the cause.
Starship Die Cast Rocket Model Was $47.99 Now $39.99 on Amazon.
Even if you can't see SpaceX's Starship in person, you can score a model of your own. Standing at 13.77 inches (35 cm), this is a 1:375 ratio of SpaceX's Starship as a desktop model. The materials here are alloy steel and it weighs just 225g.
"We were initially 'go' for a catch," Huot said during live commentary on Friday, about seven hours into the mission. "But in the later stages of the coast, the booster aborted itself for a GNC issue that it detected, and that put it into its contingency landing offshore." Super Heavy exploded a few feet above the waves of the Gulf of Mexico about 6.5 minutes after liftoff.
GNC is short for Guidance and Navigation Control, a criticial system used by rockets to control their flight and ensure they remain on their planned course. Such a system is vital for any landing attempt by a Starship Super Heavy or Ship upper stage to ensure the vehicle returns to its landing site safely and doesn't veer off course to damage SpaceX's Starbase or surrounding populated areas.
In an update during SpaceX's Flight 15 coverage on Saturday, however, Huot said that Super Heavy's GNC system actually performed well.
"I did a disservice to our booster GNC guys last night," Huot said. "It was not a GNC issue that caused us not to come back. GNC triggered that abort; it was doing what it was supposed to do. Basically, [it] detected that the booster was not in the place that it was supposed to be to proceed with a catch, did an automated abort and then headed out to that offshore splashdown location."
SpaceX is "still digging into the root cause on how we got there, and so, more to come on that," he added on Saturday.
You can follow our Starship Flight 15 live updates for the latest on the mission.
Super Heavy is powered by a cluster of 33 Raptor rocket engines that fire simultaneously during liftoff to send the 41-story Starship megarocket into orbit. During Friday's launch, all 33 engines fired as planned for the ascent, Huot said.
One engine did drop out after stage separation, when Super Heavy dropped away from Ship and flipped over for a "boostback" burn to begin its trip back to Earth, Huot said on Friday.
"We had 32 out of the 33 booster engines lit for boostback, which started sending it back here to the launch site," he added.
That firing was followed by the booster's landing burn. In SpaceX's launch video, Super Heavy can be seen activating 13 of its Raptor engines as planned, followed by the abort and the booster steering itself to a contingency landing zone in Gulf waters.
"It did that hover, cut the engines off, the FTS — the flight termination system — triggered, and it splashed down in the water," Huot said on Friday. (The FTS is designed to destroy a booster in the event of an emergency.)
As its name suggests, Starship Flight 15 is SpaceX's 15th test flight of the giant rocket, but it will be the first to attempt to catch a Ship upper stage with the chopsticks. SpaceX has successfully caught Super Heavy boosters on three test flights to date.
Flight 15's Ship vehicle is in good health and will orbit Earth a total of 14 times before landing back at its launch pad in Starbase at around 4:20 p.m. EST (1920 GMT) today, if all goes well.
"Our heat shield team reviewed all the data we got from our ground-tracking cameras, and from those satellite cameras and confirmed the heat shield is in a good posture for a reentry and return to the launch site," Huot said in Friday's mission update. (Flight 15 hauled 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink V3 satellites to orbit, and a few of those spacecraft carried cameras for heat-shield inspection.)
SpaceX designed Starship to be fully reusable, with the company banking on that reusability to make it an affordable heavy-lift booster capable of a wide range of missions to low Earth orbit, the moon and eventually Mars.
NASA has picked Starship as one of two commercial landers to carry Artemis astronauts to the moon in 2028, and SpaceX sees the rocket as vital to building out a 100,000 constellation of Starlink V3 internet satellites, as well as a new AI data center network in orbit called Starmind.
But first, SpaceX has to successfully land a Starship upper stage from orbit. That's the next step for Flight 15.
Huot said that flight controllers will make one last check at the 20-hour mark in the mission to decide whether to proceed with the landing at Starbase or make an "early return" splashdown off the coast of Hawaii.
That final check is expected by about 2 p.m. EST (1900 GMT). Space.com's Starship Flight 15 landing livestream will begin at that time, and will be carried on our live updates page, Space.com homepage and our VideoFromSpace YouTube page.
Editor's note: This story was updated at 11:50 a.m. ET on Nov. 14 with the latest information from SpaceX's Dan Huot, who clarified that the booster tower-catch abort was not caused by a GNC issue.

title: These economists say in-person work boosts creativity, but office mandates fall short
text:
A pair economists argue in a new book that people are more creative and productive when they work together in person. But it's not enough for employers to simply order workers back to the office.
SCOTT SIMON, HOST:
Years ago, Natalia Emanuel was a graduate student at Harvard, sharing a small basement office with another budding economist, and the two wound up forming a lasting professional partnership.
NATALIA EMANUEL: We had many, many years where we were only a few feet away from each other. You could say, oh, is this a brilliant idea? Or someone could very easily say, no, that's a waste of time. Please stop.
SIMON: Emanuel and her one-time office mate, Emma Harrington, have now written a book on the advantages of working side by side with colleagues. It is called "In Person," and the book comes as many businesses now contend with just how in person they want their workers to be. NPR's Scott Horsley reports.
SCOTT HORSLEY, BYLINE: The book opens with a story about Steve Jobs, who insisted that Pixar's headquarters have a central atrium where animators and engineers would naturally bump into each other. Emanuel says the man who's responsible for putting screens in all of our pockets nevertheless understood the value of connecting coworkers face to face.
EMANUEL: You do need to have some friction, the unexpected serendipitous encounter, and those things are much, much more likely to happen in person.
HORSLEY: But in-person contact on the job is less common since the pandemic. Emanuel says nearly 1 out of 4 employees still works remotely, almost seven years after the outbreak began. As economists, she and Harrington have documented some of the drawbacks of that - a 20% drop in on-the-job feedback, less mentoring, which makes it harder for young people to find jobs, and more isolation, which wears on mental health. Some companies have begun to backtrack on work-from-home policies they adopted during the pandemic. In leaked audio, published by Barron's last year, JP Morgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon told employees remote work wasn't working.
JAMIE DIMON: It slows down decision-making. The young generation is being damaged by this. They're being left behind socially, ideas, meeting people. I can't stand it anymore.
HORSLEY: But Emanuel says just ordering workers back to the office is not enough. In a survey this fall, she and Harrington found even when they're in the office, nearly half of all workers had no in-person meetings. Fifteen percent didn't have a single face-to-face conversation with a coworker.
EMANUEL: And that's sort of one of the most demoralizing things. So you commute into the office only to achieve a different background for your Zoom screen. And so then you feel like you have a lonely, isolated workday bookended by a pointless commute.
HORSLEY: That sounds familiar to Tom Robinson (ph), a 36-year-old data scientist who used to drive at least 45 minutes each way to a job in Austin, Texas.
TOM ROBINSON: There are days where I would just have Zoom calls. My productivity was measured by how long I was sitting in my chair versus what my actual, like, output was.
HORSLEY: Robinson ultimately took a pay cut for a new job that allows him to work from home.
ROBINSON: My perspective is completely biased because I'm also a single father. My kids - they needed me to be present. I just was never around.
HORSLEY: Emanuel, who has four kids herself, acknowledges that remote work has been a boon for parents, especially women. Though she knows parents who try to combine work and childcare often feel like they're shortchanging both. The challenge for employers, she says, is to figure out how to balance the flexibility of remote work with real connection when people are in the office. That might mean realigning schedules or locating the coffee machines in a way that encourages chance conversations.
EMANUEL: Encountering other people, fueling friendships is a profoundly important experience, and we tend to undervalue how much even small encounters are going to make us joyful.
HORSLEY: Emanuel and her co-author no longer share that small basement office, but they still make time to get together regularly to brainstorm and collaborate in person.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.

title: Groups raise concerns over DOJ's new Civil Rights Division chief
text:
Washington — Eighteen civil rights organizations asked President Trump on Tuesday to withdraw his appointment of Craig Trainor as the new acting assistant attorney general for the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, saying he has a track record of undermining the laws he is tasked with enforcing.
Trainor was appointed last week to replace Harmeet Dhillon, who from her post shortly after the midterm elections.
Trainor most recently served as assistant secretary for fair housing and equal opportunity at the Department of Housing and Urban Development. Prior to that, he held several senior roles at the Department of Education.
He also previously served as a senior special counsel to GOP Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio on the House Judiciary Committee as well as the Select Subcommittee on the Weaponization of the Federal Government.
Tuesday's statement opposing his appointment was signed by a variety of organizations, including the National Center for Youth Law, the Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights, National Council of Jewish Women, Human Rights Campaign, the Sikh Coalition and Stop Sexual Assault in Schools, among others.
"In the midterm elections, the American people rejected an agenda to divide, discriminate against, and diminish our communities," the groups said.
"Instead of rebuilding a Civil Rights Division decimated under Harmeet Dhillon, the Administration has chosen to elevate the official behind a court-blocked classroom censorship agenda who seeks to undermine the rights of survivors and equal opportunity in our schools and communities," they added.
CBS News has reached out to the Justice Department for comment.
The civil rights groups said that Trainor took action in his prior roles at the Department of Education and HUD that scaled back civil liberties.
After a court struck down a Department of Education rule that broadened the definition of what constitutes sexual harassment under Title IX of the Civil Rights Act, Trainor issued a directive to schools in February 2025 that ordered them to revert to less-stringent standards that were adopted in 2020.
Many civil rights groups have long criticized the 2020 standards and referred to them as "anti-survivor" rules because the definition of what constitutes sexual harassment is narrower.
The 2020 rules also only require schools to investigate allegations of sexual assault or harassment under Title IX that occur on school grounds, excluding conduct that may occur abroad or off campus.
The groups also pointed to threats that Trainor directed toward schools in a Feb. 14, 2025, letter, in which he threatened to withhold federal funding if they had diversity, equity and inclusion programs.
Several federal courts later enjoined the Department of Education from following through on its threats to withhold the funds.
After he left and went to HUD, Trainor also shuttered many discrimination investigations under the Fair Housing Act, the groups said.
In announcing his appointment, Attorney General Todd Blanche praised his actions at HUD, saying he helped to "cut the Biden-era Fair Housing case backlog in half."
Trainor is taking over the helm of a Civil Rights Division that was largely gutted under Dhillon's leadership, as more than 75% of its staff left since January 2025.
Although Dhillon later hired more attorneys, the staffing level is still not what it once was.
Dhillon away from its historical mission of protecting some of society's most vulnerable and marginalized groups. She shifted its focus to other priorities that included protecting gun owners' rights, curbing the use of equity, diversity and inclusion policies at universities, and adopting legal positions that oppose civil rights protections for transgender people.

title: Germany news: Germany holds national day of remembrance
text:
The German and Austrian presidents spoke at events marking Volkstrauertag
- The day commemorates soldiers and civilians who died in war but also victims of the Nazi regime persecuted for their sexual identity
- Solar energy output in Germany is drawing close a record total of more than 100 terawatt-hours in a single calendar year
- Economics experts are warning that the country is living beyond its means
- Health care cuts mean people might have to pay privately to avoid long waiting times, says the national association for statutory physicians
- Experts in Germany have warned against too much reliance on a sole provider after a major outage at Microsoft affected German businesses
This live blog is now closed. Read on for a roundup of the top stories from and about Germany on the weekend of November 14-15, 2026:
Thank you for reading
Thank you for reading this weekend's Germany news blog.
We'll bring you more from the heart of Europe on Monday. We wish you a very Schönen Abend!
Austrian president urges compassion at German memorial
Austrian President Alexander Van der Bellen has urged Europeans to defend compassion and humanity during Germany's national day of mourning for victims of war and oppression.
Speaking at a ceremony in the Bundestag in Berlin, Van der Bellen warned against becoming desensitized to suffering despite the constant images of war and violence.
"Compassion is not a weakness; it is a human strength; it is the foundation of humanity," he said.
He also addressed the responsibility of later generations for the crimes of the past.
Although people today bore no personal guilt for their ancestors' actions, he said, they were responsible for what they learned from history and how they treated others.
"Let us ensure that our home, Europe, remains a place where people can live in peace, freedom and dignity," he said.
Bundestag President Julia Klöckner also called for the defense of democracy, pointing to Ukrainians risking their lives to protect freedom.
Germany's Volkstrauertag commemorates soldiers and civilians killed in war, as well as victims of Nazi persecution and other forms of oppression.
Three arrested after car rams German jewelry store
German police have arrested three suspects after thieves rammed a car into a jewelry store in the Bavarian city of Bayreuth and stole valuables worth around €10,000 ($11,600).
Bavarian Interior Minister Joachim Herrmann said the stolen items included jewelry and silver coins.
The burglars drove a car into the store early in the morning before fleeing in a second vehicle, police said.
Officers spotted the getaway car on the A9 highway and gave chase. The suspects left the highway near Weidensees, abandoned their vehicle beside a wooded area and fled on foot.
Police launched a search involving patrol cars, dogs, drones and a helicopter.
All three suspects were subsequently arrested, with some of the stolen goods recovered.
Prosecutors are expected to decide whether to seek pretrial detention for the suspects.
German-American NFL star St. Brown makes Munich debut
Detroit Lions receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown played his first NFL American football game in Germany in Munich.
St. Brown made his professional debut in Germany as the Detroit Lions faced the New England Patriots at Munich's Allianz Arena. The 27-year-old grew up in Southern California, and his mother, Miriam, is from Leverkusen. Both his parents were due to watch from the stands.
The NFL player spent childhood summers with his grandparents in the Rhineland.
"This is awesome. A dream come true," St. Brown said before the game. Asked by German broadcaster RTL what he had been looking forward to most, he reeled off a list that included schnitzel, potato dumplings, sauerkraut, currywurst and fries with mayonnaise.
"I'm really excited. I can't wait," he said. "Being in Germany with my teammates and my family — I want to enjoy it and take it all in."
Two injured in firework attack on Frankfurt gay bar
Two people were slightly injured after an unidentified man threw a firework into the entrance of a gay bar in Frankfurt, police said.
The attack took place at the Zum Schwejk bar, a venue popular with the city's gay community, on Saturday evening.
Police said the bar was clearly identifiable as an LGBTQ+ venue because of a rainbow flag displayed outside.
The motive remains unclear, and police have not said whether they suspect a homophobic attack.
Officers are investigating suspected aggravated assault and have appealed for witnesses.
The bar said it was "shocked and stunned" by the incident and apologized to guests who witnessed it. It said it wanted to be a place where everyone felt welcome, respected and safe, and pledged to do everything it could to prevent a repeat.
Andreas Ewald, LGBTQ+ policy spokesperson for the Greens in the Hesse state parliament, condemned the attack and called for those responsible to face the full force of the law.
He also urged the state government to establish a roundtable on LGBTQ+ safety involving community representatives, police and victim support organizations.
The bar's name refers to a Czech soldier in the satirical anti-war novel "The Good Soldier Svejk."
Berlin police file 28 criminal charges against Gen Z protesters
Police in Berlin have filed 28 criminal charges against demonstrators who marched throught the capital on Saturday as part of the Gen Z regelt (Gen Z Takes Charge) movement.
Some 1,200 demonstrators took part in the march, although only 100 had registered for the event under German laws regulating public protests.
The protesters complained about dilapidated schools, the threat of compulsory military service, cuts to university and social funding and other issues.
Police said there had been some clashes with participants.
A police spokeswoman said the criminal charges were filed for riot, assault, resisting officers and violations of explosives regulations.
Three police officers of the 700 deployed to ensure securty were injured during the demonstration.
November 20 is likely to see more large protests in both Germany and Europe, with some 15,000 demonstrators registered for a march in Berlin.
Steinmeier condemns rising antisemitism in Germany
German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier has expressed solidarity with the Jewish community in Germany amid what he described as ever "louder and more aggressive" antisemitic voices.
Speaking at the presentation of the Prize for Understanding and Tolerance awarded by the Jewish Museum in Berlin, Steinmeier said: "For all those to whom our country, its constitution and the values it enshrines mean something, there can be only one answer to such antisemitism: to stand side by side with Jewish people in our country."
Steinmeier said he deplored the frequent vandalism of memorials to Nazi crimes.
"I am profoundly ashamed of that all," he said, saying that anyone who mocked the work of museums and memorial sites or collectively blamed, threatened and attacked Jews "attacks the heart of our republic."
The president also congratulated the prize winners — German journalist and author Düzen Tekkal and British philanthropist Michael Moritz — on their awards.
In a citation, the museum described Tekkal as a champion of human rights who consistently opposed antisemitism and racism while promoting interfaith dialogue, equality in education and opportunities, peace and democracy.
The museum commended Moritz for supporting artistic projects that show Jewish perspectives and strengthen social dialogue.
The Jewish Museum, which is marking its 25th anniversary this year, has been presenting the prize since 2002.
Nuremberg overrun by sheep in annual spectacle
Some 600 sheep have made their way through the southern city of Nuremberg on their way to western winter pasturage, watched by crowds of spectators.
The sheep follow an around 10-km-long (6-mile-long) route that crosses a number of streets and the market square.
The annual event is meant, among other things, to draw attention to the tradition of transhumant, or itinerant, sheep-keeping in the region and the benefits the animals have for landscape conservation.
"With their grazing in summer, sheep create great biodiversity in many important biotopes in the urban region," the city of Nuremberg said ahead of the migration.
Thieves drive car into jewelry shop in dramatic break-in
