Thieves have stolen several valuable items from a jewelry shop in the southern city of Bayreuth after ramming it with a car, police said on Sunday.
They said a black Mercedes carrying three people crashed into the shop in the early hours of Sunday morning.
The burglars then fled the scene in a second Mercedes, this time a gray one, after taking a number of articles.
The getaway car was then spotted by a police patrol on a motorway heading south, with officers setting off in pursuit.
The suspects were then said to have driven off the motorway to a patch of woodland where they abandoned their vehicle and went on by foot.
Police searched for the fugitives with patrol cars, police dogs, drones and a helicopter, a statement said.
Two men were reportedly arrested with a third still on the run. Investigators are looking into whether the detainees were connected with the theft.
Germany marks day of mourning for victims of war and oppression
Events are taking place around Germany for the Volkstrauertag (people's day of mourning), a day on which armed forces personnel and civilians who died in armed conflicts and victims of violent state oppression are commemorated.
Austrian President Alexander Van der Bellen is to speak in the parliament at the main commemoration ceremony of the German War Graves Commission at midday.
His presence reflects the large number of Austrians who were killed in action in the Second World War while fighting for the German Wehrmacht following the annexation of their country by Nazi Germany in 1938.
German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, the patron of the commission, will also hold a speech and lay a wreath.
Last year, Steinmeier decreed that the Volkstrauertag should also commemorate people who were persecuted and killed by the Nazis because of their sexual identity, as well as police officers who have lost their lives in the course of duty.
There will also be a remembrance ceremony at the Jewish Cemetery in Berlin for those of the Jewish faith killed in World War I.
In remarks to the DPA news agency ahead of the remembrance day, the speaker of the lower house of German parliament, or Bundestag, Julia Klöckner, called on society to actively defend democracy.
Klöckner said that the Volkstrauertag was a reminder of how destructive tyranny and contempt for human dignity can be.
"Democracy is the antidote here," she said. "But it is not an heirloom. It wastes away when we do not constantly renew its promise of basic rights and freedom."
We are resuming our Germany coverage
Guten Morgen from the DW newsroom on the banks of the Rhine in Bonn!
You join us as Germany holds a day of remembrance for the victims of war and oppression and also commemorates members of the police force killed while carrying out their duties.
Read on here for the top stories from and about Germany on Sunday, November 15,
Pausing coverage from Germany
It's 1 a.m. here and time for us to pause our coverage of news from Germany.
We'll be back Sunday morning with more of what's making headlines in Berlin, Bavaria and the rest of the country.
WATCH: From watching to acting: Germany's spy shift
Germany wants to turn its spies into "real secret agents." A sweeping reform could allow them to sabotage threats abroad and use AI to analyze intelligence data.
But why does Germany need these powers now? And how far can its secret services go in a country with a history of strict limits on intelligence operations?
Bavaria holds funeral for former deputy premier Hubert Aiwanger
Hundreds of mourners gathered at Munich's Frauenkirche on Saturday to pay their final respects to Hubert Aiwanger, Bavaria's former deputy premier and economy minister, who died unexpectedly at the age of 55.
The ceremony combined a Catholic funeral Mass with a state memorial service, attended by leading political figures, church representatives and members of Bavaria's former royal family.
Bavarian Premier Markus Söder recalled his disbelief when he first heard of Aiwanger's death in a Berlin hotel on November 4. He described his former deputy as someone who had always been full of energy.
Bavarian parliament president Ilse Aigner praised Aiwanger as one of the greatest political talents of his generation, highlighting his role in transforming his party "Freie Wähler" (Free Voters) from a local political movement into a governing party.
Aiwanger's partner, Tanja Schweiger, and their two sons were among those attending the service, which took place eleven days after his death.
Lufthansa largely unaffected by US flight ground stop
German airline group Lufthansa says it was only slightly affected by Friday's temporary suspension of flights to the United States.
Most flights operated as scheduled, although some were canceled or delayed. Lufthansa expects its US flight schedule to return to normal on Saturday but warned that isolated delays could still occur.
Affected passengers are being notified by email, with alternative travel options provided automatically in the event of cancellations.
The disruption was caused by problems with the US air traffic control system. Domestic flights in the US were grounded for around four hours, marking the longest nationwide ground stop since the September 11 attacks in 2001.

title: Detroit Lions star Aidan Hutchinson out for season after tearing ACL while celebrating sack
text:
Detroit Lions defensive end Aidan Hutchinson is out for the rest of the NFL season after suffering a torn ACL while celebrating a sack.
Hutchinson injured his right knee after landing awkwardly from a celebratory leap into the air, which followed him sacking New England’s Drake Maye in the first quarter of Detroit’s 35-10 win at the Allianz Stadium in Munich.
The 26-year-old immediately crumpled to the ground and clutched his knee, and while he was able to walk to the sideline after medical treatment, he did not return to the action and has now learned the severity of his injury.
“Man, what a gut punch,” Detroit head coach Dan Campbell said on local radio. “He’s such a phenomenal player. This guy's an impact player, but more importantly, he's an unbelievable teammate and he's one of our captains.
“So it stinks, man. It hits you, and I hate it for him. I hate it for him because he was on a heater, man. What a hell of a year he was having.”
Hutchinson, a two-time Pro Bowler and the 2022 second overall draft pick, had six sacks to his name in nine games this season.
This is his second season-ending injury, with a double leg break curtailing his campaign after just five weeks in 2024, though this setback comes in far more unique circumstances.
“I think we all understand what it is, and let's be smart, but no, I'm not gonna say 'nobody celebrates any more'," Campbell added.
"The number of moves that I've seen 'Hutch' make and the number of plyometrics, explosive movements, the spins, the one-leg lateral movements, lateral balances... it was one of those things, man."
The Lions host Tampa Bay on Sunday, riding an NFC-best five-game winning streak that has put them in a first-place tie with Minnesota and Chicago in the NFC North.

title: EU’s Rwanda migrant return plan faces backlash over human rights concerns rights record
text:
Kigali’s human rights record is under scrutiny as it prepares to host the first EU return hubs outside the bloc. Rwanda’s Interior Minister rejected the criticism, pointing out to the country's experience in dealing with migrants.
The announcement of a partnership between five EU countries and Rwanda to set up the first return hub outside the bloc has sparked controversy across Europe.
Although the final deal is still under negotiation, growing criticism has emerged over Rwanda’s human rights record. Furthermore, the planned deportations from the five participating countries — Austria, Germany, Denmark, the Netherlands and Greece — to Rwanda, which are expected to begin in 2027, could face legal challenges before European courts.
“I see neither future nor humanity in it,” Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said in an interview when asked about the initiative, in an indirect swipe at the five member states involved in the project.
The proposed partnership concluded in Vienna on Monday would establish the EU’s first return hub outside the bloc, with the facility expected to accommodate around 100 people at a time. Those transferred to Rwanda would be free to move around the country and would be expected to integrate into Rwandan society and the local labour market.
Many members of the European Parliament strongly condemned the political agreement, citing both the risk of abuses in Rwanda and the prospect of migrants being stranded in a country with which they have no ties.
“It is particularly disturbing that the fate of human beings is entrusted to a country burdened by documented allegations of serious violations of fundamental rights,” said Italian MEP Marco Tarquinio of the Socialists and Democrats (S&D) group.
Similar concerns were voiced by other MEPs, including Iraqi-born Swedish MEP Abir Al-Sahlani of Renew Europe, who questioned the rationale behind the agreement in an interview with Euronews’ flagship programme, Europe Tonight: “If we in Europe were not able to send them back to their countries, what makes us believe Rwanda will be able to?” Al-Sahlani asked.
The European Parliament has previously taken a hard line on Kigali. It called for the suspension of an EU-Rwanda memorandum of understanding on critical raw materials, over alleged war crimes and the occupation of territory in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo by Rwanda’s defence forces.
Humanitarian organisations also voiced their opposition. In a joint statement, a total of 45 NGOs described the partnership as a “cruel measure” that pushes migrants into further insecurity.
Rwanda's human rights record in question
Rwanda has sought to establish itself as a partner for Western countries looking to relocate migrants beyond their borders, although previous agreements of this kind have faced significant challenges.
In 2018, Kigali backed out of an agreement with Israel to accept refugees deported against their will, while a deal to transfer asylum seekers from the United Kingdom was ruled unlawful by the UK Supreme Court because of Rwanda’s poor human rights record.
In 2025, Kigali agreed to accept 250 migrants from the US under a deal with President Donald Trump’s administration but has so far relocated only a few of them.
According to an Amnesty International report, in all these cases Rwanda failed to show it could guarantee fair procedures and adequate protection for people transferred from another jurisdiction.
Rwanda’s Interior Minister Vincent Biruta dismissed the criticism in response to a question from Euronews at the conference on Tuesday.
“Human rights in Rwanda are respected for everyone, and specifically for the migrants who choose to come to our country,” he said, describing his country’s integration policy as “one of the most progressive” because it allows refugees to work.
Biruta defended Rwanda’s long experience with migrants. He pointed out that Kigali currently hosts more than 140,000 refugees and asylum seekers and has run a transit centre for people evacuated from Libya since 2017.
“Which other country has come forward to propose a solution for those refugees? We were the only ones,” he said.

title: Bush-appointed judge torpedoes Trump immigration rule, rips DHS for overstepping its authority
text:
An immigration rule drafted by the Trump administration to plug an alleged gap in the visa system has met its end at the hands of a federal judge appointed by former President George W. Bush.
District Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV of Massachusetts ruled Monday that the Department of Homeland Security overstepped its authority by promulgating a rule that placed greater restrictions on visas for international students, exchange visitors and foreign journalists. His ruling represents a victory for the labor unions and university presidents that challenged the rule, and another loss in the Trump administration’s legal crusade to crack down on immigration.
The DHS rule would have replaced a longstanding policy by only allowing international students to study in America for a fixed timeframe, generally capped at four years, requiring them to apply for an extension if they wish to continue their studies. Previously, there was no fixed time limit for international students so long as they remained enrolled in a university and otherwise maintained legal status. The rule also would have imposed new restrictions on transferring schools, changing academic programs and pursuing additional degrees, while subjecting students to additional immigration reviews intended to combat fraud and national security threats.
"DHS acknowledges that there are legitimate reasons why a student may pursue another academic degree at the same or lower level as the one he or she has completed — for example, pursuing an M.B.A. after a J.D.," the judge wrote. "But the Final Rule would effectively prohibit such a student from entering the United States to pursue those studies. And the purported reasons given by DHS for doing so — protecting national security and preventing fraud — are not reasonably related to the nature and purpose of the F-1 visa program."
"Put bluntly, DHS is seeking to prevent or discourage the very activity — providing educational opportunities for foreign students in the United States — that Congress sought to permit and encourage," Saylor continued. "The statute simply does not grant DHS such broad and open-ended authority to undermine the F-1 visa program."
Saylor had already blocked the rule from taking effect in September, but Monday's ruling went further by striking it down entirely after finding that DHS violated federal administrative law.
Lawyers representing the department disagreed with the judge’s characterization, arguing that indefinite admission periods prevent immigration officials from periodically reassessing whether foreign nationals are complying with the conditions of their visas. Mandatory extensions, in the telling of the agency, would create additional opportunities to identify fraud, security risks and immigration violations — risks it says are substantiated by past cases of fraud and abuse in the student visa system.
"The performative outrage is incredible. Where was the outrage when foreign nationals were abusing the system, violating the terms of their student visas, and making a mockery of our immigration laws? If the media really cared about legitimate international students, they would be thanking President Trump for cracking down on the rampant fraud to ensure only those truly intending to study in the United States are given the privilege," a DHS spokesperson told Fox News Digital.
Saylor, however, further argued that DHS failed to establish how its new rule would constitute an improvement over existing systems meant to catch visa fraud.
"But DHS has not adequately explained how implementing an unreviewable, completely discretionary renewal system — after a foreign student has already been in the country for four years — meaningfully enhances the ability of DHS to root out cases of fraud, or how the benefits of such a system outweigh the immense costs of abandoning the existing system," he wrote.
Currently, DHS relies on the Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS) to monitor student visa fraud. SEVIS is a federal database that monitors international students and exchange visitors, tracking their enrollment, immigration status and compliance with visa requirements through information reported by schools and program sponsors. The agency argued that the system is a "data-reporting system for schools" that is "not designed for performing all relevant fraud and security screening."
Saylor was identified as a Republican in a 2014 profile piece. The same piece noted Saylor had close ties to former Massachusetts Gov. Mitt Romney and that he was reportedly considered for a position in the Bush administration. He was confirmed by a bipartisan vote in the Senate, even winning the support of Democratic Sen. Ted Kennedy, a noted liberal, who praised him for his fair-mindedness and independence.
DHS did not tell Fox News Digital whether it intended to appeal Saylor's ruling.

title: Dinosaurs may have been eating seaweed 100 million years ago
text:
Dinosaurs may have been snacking on seaweed and other ocean foods more than 100 million years ago, according to surprising new evidence hidden in their fossilized teeth. Researchers discovered chemical signatures suggesting that coastal dinosaurs and other prehistoric animals relied partly on nutrients originating in the sea. The findings reveal that marine resources traveled through ancient food chains, supplementing the diets of everything from plant-eating dinosaurs to predators.
Dinosaurs living along ancient coastlines may have enjoyed an unexpected addition to their diets: seaweed and other food from the ocean. New research suggests that marine resources washed onto prehistoric beaches helped feed dinosaurs and their prey millions of years ago.
Today, powerful storms frequently deposit seaweed and other ocean material along shorelines, creating opportunities for animals that live on land to find additional food. Scientists call this process marine subsidization (MS). It is especially common in coastal environments and can become more important when food on land is limited, such as during droughts.
A new study published in Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution suggests that this relationship between land and sea existed during the age of dinosaurs. By examining chemical signatures preserved in fossils, researchers found evidence that ocean resources contributed to prehistoric food chains.
"We show that coastal terrestrial organisms in the greenhouse climates of the Cretaceous relied on marine resources to supplement their diets in a similar way that modern organisms do," said first author Dr. Clayton Forster, a geologist at the University of Arkansas. "We can identify that marine resources are passed along the food chain and incorporated in the minerals of bones and teeth of dinosaurs, crocodiles, turtles, and fish."
Mysterious Chemical Clues in Dinosaur Teeth
The discovery helps explain a longstanding mystery involving the chemical composition of dinosaur teeth.
Plants contain two forms of carbon known as isotopes: 'light' (C-12) and 'heavy' (C-13). Scientists can measure the relative amounts of these isotopes, expressed as δ13C, to identify a chemical fingerprint that passes from food into the animals that consume it.
As animals eat, this carbon signature becomes incorporated into their tooth enamel. The δ13C value in enamel is typically higher than that of the food consumed, with living animals generally showing an increase of between 11 and 13 parts per thousand.
However, previous measurements of dinosaur teeth have consistently revealed unusually high values. These readings also exceed what scientists would expect from animals that ate only plants growing on land, which generally have lower δ13C values than most marine plants.
One possible explanation is that dinosaurs, or the animals they consumed, were obtaining some of their nutrients from the ocean.
"By determining the carbon isotope composition of dinosaur, fish, and crocodile tooth enamel, we can determine what their primary dietary source was and if they were different between regions," explained Forster.
Fossils Reveal a Prehistoric Ocean Food Source
To investigate, researchers examined fossils from (once) coastal locations bordering the Western Interior Seaway and the ancient coastline of the Gulf of Mexico. Around 100 million years ago, the Western Interior Seaway was an enormous inland sea that divided North America into two separate landmasses.
The team also analyzed fossils from locations farther inland, allowing them to compare animals that lived near the ocean with those that occupied landlocked environments.
The fossil deposits formed during two intervals of the Cretaceous Period: the early Albian (around 113-107 million years ago) and the early Cenomanian (approximately 100-96 million years ago).
Researchers used powdered fossil material to measure carbon isotope signatures from both periods. They also determined the latitudes where the animals had lived to investigate whether geography influenced the results.
A clear pattern emerged. Fossils from coastal environments consistently contained higher δ13C values than those from the inland formation. Remarkably, the coastal signatures remained similar across different locations, regardless of latitude or geological age.
These findings provide the first evidence of marine subsidization in prehistoric ecosystems, indicating that nutrients originating in the ocean were entering food chains on land millions of years ago.
Seaweed May Have Been on the Dinosaur Menu
The researchers next considered what ocean food source could explain the widespread chemical signatures.
"Coastal-dwelling organisms must have eaten some kind of organic matter from the ocean, or prey that had done so. This pattern is shared from fish to megaherbivores and indicates that the extra carbon source must have been low in the food-chain to affect both aquatic and terrestrial animals," Forster explained.
For the same chemical pattern to appear in such a wide variety of animals, the marine food source would likely have entered the food chain near its base. It also needed to be something that existed along coastlines but was absent farther inland, while remaining available for millions of years.
Seaweed emerged as the most likely explanation.
"Few organisms meet these criteria besides marine macroalgae or macrophytes - seaweeds," said Forster. "Given the almost ubiquitous behavior of large coastal herbivores today to supplement their diet with seaweeds, it's likely that most of the sampled herbivorous dinosaurs were no different."
Modern plant-eating animals living near coastlines often consume seaweed to supplement their diets. The fossil evidence suggests that many herbivorous dinosaurs may have behaved similarly, with marine nutrients also passing to other animals through the food chain.
Not Every Dinosaur Had a Taste for the Sea
Despite the widespread evidence of marine nutrients in coastal food webs, the researchers found that not every dinosaur took advantage of these resources.
One notable exception was Tenontosaurus tilletti, a large plant-eating dinosaur whose fossils have been discovered at numerous locations dating to the Cretaceous Period.
Its tooth enamel contained δ13C values comparable to those of modern animals that feed on plants growing on land. This suggests that Tenontosaurus tilletti did not rely on marine food sources, even though other dinosaurs apparently did.
The difference also strengthens the researchers' interpretation of the fossil evidence. If geological processes occurring after death had altered the carbon signatures in dinosaur teeth, the same unusual values would be expected more broadly. Instead, the variation between species suggests that the elevated readings reflect genuine differences in diet.
An Ancient Connection Between Land and Ocean
Although the findings provide strong evidence that marine resources supported the coastal ecosystems examined, important questions remain.
The available fossils do not include specimens from polar or equatorial regions during the early Albian and early Cenomanian. As a result, scientists cannot yet determine how widespread this feeding behavior was across different latitudes.
Additional studies will also be needed to establish whether similar relationships existed during other geological periods, including the earlier Jurassic Period and the later early Cenozoic Era.
Beyond revealing a surprising possibility about what dinosaurs ate, the discovery highlights how closely life on land has been connected to the ocean throughout Earth's history.
"Our study emphasizes the connections between terrestrial and marine ecosystems," concluded Forster. "They are deeply intertwined and have been for hundreds of millions of years. It highlights the importance of environmental linkages across time and space and protecting them where they exist today."

title: On this day in space! Nov. 14, 1969: NASA's Apollo 12 astronauts launch to the moon on a 'pinpoint landing' lunar mission
text:
On Nov. 14, 1969, the Apollo 12 mission launched to the moon. This was the second moon landing of the Apollo program.
The two astronauts on board were Pete Conrad, commander, and Alan Bean, the lunar module pilot. Astronaut Richard Gordon, the command module pilot, stayed in the command module and orbited the moon while his crewmates went to the surface. The astronauts made a pinpoint landing in a lunar mare called the Ocean of Storms.
The previous moon mission, Apollo 11, drifted far from the planned landing zone. But Apollo 12 landed close to a scientific target. That target was a robotic lander called Surveyor 3. Scientists wanted to look at Surveyor 3 to see how well the spacecraft lasted on the moon since it landed there more than two years earlier.
The Apollo 12 moonwalkers also performed a lot of moon science. The astronauts picked up 75 pounds of moon rocks. Most of the rocks were basalts that formed from molten lava. These basalts showed the Apollo 12 landing site is more than 3 billion years old.
Why it mattered
Apollo 12 proved that the Apollo 11 moon landing was not just a one-off stunt while setting the stage for even more ambitious missions.
To truly explore the moon and advance our understanding of how our solar system formed, the follow-on Apollo flights needed to be able to land where the geologists had identified as areas of interest. Apollo 12, with its touchdown in proximity to the Surveyor probe, proved this was possible.
The launch of Apollo 12 also underscored the importance of having a well-prepared Mission Control team, an asset that would be critical to outcome of the next mission, Apollo 13.
The ability to recover from a complete electrical short out with the simple call of a through of a switch "SCE to AUX" proved that knowing every detail about how the spacecraft worked was key to a successful program.
Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube.

title: Nvidia dismisses 'Bring Jensen Back' campaign as Trump backs effort to reinstate ex boss
text:
Nvidia has dismissed a campaign calling for the company's co-founder Jensen Huang to be handed back his job as allies, including US President Donald Trump, supported the effort.
Trump said on Monday that he "would certainly not mind" if Huang was reinstated, joining a list of supporters including SpaceX's Elon Musk who are backing a "Bring Jensen Back" campaign.
But the BBC has been told the board of the AI chip giant is not interested in reinstating him after he resigned last week following revelations he had two affairs, including one that involved a suspected Chinese spy.
The same day, the White House also said it will further restrict China's access to AI chips from firms like Nvidia.
The reported affairs created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms - a central company in AI and the US battle against China for dominance.
Since Huang's departure, more than 175,000 people have signed an open letter calling for the board to reinstate the tech billionaire while an ongoing internal probe is conducted.
Major tech bosses, including Musk and Tim Sweeney, chief executive of Fortnite-maker Epic Games, have also supported Huang's return.
The "Stand with Jensen" campaign claims to have been launched by current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters, all demanding the return of the former chief executive.
They expressed concerns the firm's co-founder "was removed without meaningful due process".
Trump gave his views on Huang's future on Monday, saying he "would certainly not mind" seeing the former boss given his job back.
Huang had been expected to weather the storm following the revelation of the affair but resigned last Thursday after a second extra-marital relationship emerged, allegedly with an executive at Nvidia who reported to him.
The scandal-hit tech boss was discussing a possible return to Nvidia with confidants, according to the Financial Times, external, though Nvidia's board is not considering reappointing him.
A representative for Huang declined to comment on the report.
The so-called war room also wants to get support for Huang from the White House.
Trump has spoken in glowing terms about Huang since the scandal erupted, and also said he believed Huang when the former Nvidia boss told him he had "no idea she was a spy".
Trump's view is at odds with his Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has called for Nvidia to hire its next chief executive from outside the company.
The scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end Nvidia chips to Alice Huang's former firm, Megaspeed. China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy.
It has raised questions about the possibility that the chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.
New rules
The Trump administration on Monday also issued new restrictions on chip exports to overseas data centres, which have been allegedly used as a way for Chinese firms to gain access to advanced chips to train AI models.
The move comes ahead of a meeting this week between Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping, whose countries are locked in a race to lead AI development.
The interim rules will require companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for export licences for the most advanced chips in an effort to prevent them from being illegally diverted to China.
The measure is designed to ensure existing restrictions on sensitive US technology "cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the Department of Commerce said.
Huang has been a vocal advocate for easing chip export restrictions on China, arguing that broad access to global markets is crucial for the competitiveness of the US.
He said in 2025 that the market for AI chips in China would eventually reach $50bn - a sum Huang said "is like Boeing - not a plane - the entire company".
In 2025, Nvidia won an approval to sell some advanced AI chips in China after Huang's repeated lobbying efforts in Washington.
The ex-Nvidia boss' affair with Alice Huang, the former director of a Singaporean data centre firm called Megaspeed, has raised the level of scrutiny over deals abroad.
The small South East Asian business hub has been a draw for companies all around the world, many of which have set up headquarters in Singapore.
Major US firms like Anthropic, OpenAI and Google have set up offices in the business-friendly country, alongside Chinese companies like TikTok-owner ByteDance and Tencent.
But Singapore's openness to business has also made it the ideal address to place orders for restricted advanced semiconductors.
Singapore was the second-largest billing centre globally last year for Nvidia, accounting for nearly a fifth of what the chip giant earns.
But notably, only 2% of its earnings were for chips that actually entered Singapore, which acts as a hub for many Asian companies to place orders and send them elsewhere.
While Singapore does not necessarily prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.
Advanced semiconductors, crucial for the development of AI models, are at the centre of the US and China's technological rivalry.
US officials have long viewed the country's technological supremacy as a matter of national security and have expressed concerns that sharing the best chips could give China's economy and military a boost.
Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China to discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair.
Trump said he did not think Huang had put national security at risk. "You know, China plays games with us. So we play games with China," he said.
The FBI is also investigating the affair between the former Nvidia boss and Alice Huang, according to Trump.
'A handshake with Jensen'
Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation.
"Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract," he posted on X., external
"Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost."
Fellow tech boss Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, sidestepped the question of Huang returning to Nvidia at a conference, saying: "I don't think I know enough to answer that question."
But Altman, who himself was reinstated to his job after being fired back in 2023, said Huang was a "hero of mine".
Shareholders in Nvidia also want Huang back at the company's helm.
Hundreds of billions of pounds have been wiped off the firm's stock market value in recent days, but it is still worth some $3.87 trillion. Its share price was down in early Monday trading.
In an open letter to the board, Brad Gerstner, founder of Altimeter Capital and Atreides Management boss Gavin Baker called for management to leave "all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang".
Lord Sarfraz, a member of the UK's House of Lords, has also written to Nvidia's new chair, Harvey Jones, urging the firm's directors to give "serious consideration" to Huang's return following the investigation.
For the moment, Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress is leading the firm and will present the company's results on Tuesday.

title: Lewis Hamilton visits Egypt’s Rafah crossing and Gaza aid facilities
text:
Lewis Hamilton has visited Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with the Gaza Strip to meet organisations sending humanitarian aid to the territory.
The seven-time Formula One world champion has spoken out about conflict and humanitarian crises in the region, and has called for peace. He has frequently posted on social media about children killed in Israeli airstrikes in Gaza and called for a ceasefire.
“I think we need to make sure we’re pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine. I think there’s a lot of peace that I’m hoping we get to at some stage,” Hamilton said in October.
A ceasefire agreement reached last year has halted major combat operations in Gaza, but the amount of aid reaching the territory continues to fall far short of the agreed-upon minimum of 600 trucks a day.
Israeli forces have continued to advance, expanding their control from 53% of the territory to at least 60%, an independent commission of UN experts said last month.
Airstrikes also continue, and Israeli fire along the advancing front has killed at least 196 Palestinians, including 18 women, 32 boys and 11 girls, the commission said.
Hamilton toured Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with Gaza before visiting logistics warehouses operated by the Egyptian Red Crescent, which facilitates the entry of aid to Gaza.
At the crossing, Hamilton greeted aid workers with “Assalamu alaikum” a widely used Arabic greeting meaning “peace be upon you.” He shook hands and briefly spoke to workers and officials.
Khaled Megawer, the governor of North Sinai, where Rafah is located, said the visit was intended to help Hamilton learn about Egypt’s efforts to send aid to Gaza.
The visit comes after Hamilton made his 400th race start on Sunday at the São Paulo Grand Prix at Interlagos.
The first black F1 driver, he made his debut with McLaren in 2007. He is only the second F1 driver to start 400 races after his former teammate Fernando Alonso, who achieved the milestone in 2024.

title: SpaceX's giant rocket may leave NASA in the dust
text:
Later today, SpaceX is planning the most ambitious test yet of its massive new rocket Starship. If all goes well, it will lift off from a pad in South Texas, circle the Earth and then land vertically at the same pad 22 and a half hours later.
The test would be a major milestone for a rocket that company founder Elon Musk says he hopes will one day carry astronauts to Mars. But experts say the rapid development of Starship could also end up stranding one of the company's biggest boosters over the years: NASA.
That's because as SpaceX ramps up its new rocket, it has said it will stop flying a much smaller one called Falcon 9. Falcon 9 launches the company's Dragon capsule, which is currently the only American spacecraft capable of ferrying NASA astronauts to and from the International Space Station.
"Because Dragon has become such a successful and reliable vehicle, it became the de facto way for astronauts to get to orbit," said Caleb Henry, director of research at Quilty Space, a firm that tracks the space industry.
According to a NASA announcement in September, the space agency has contracted with SpaceX for three additional flights to the International Space Station. That would only allow Dragon to fly through 2028, assuming the missions were flown consecutively in six month increments and no further flights are contracted with SpaceX.
"NASA and SpaceX continue to work closely together across numerous missions and contractual agreements, including crew and cargo transportation to the International Space Station," the space agency said in an e-mail statement to NPR. "As the commercial space industry evolves, so will the technologies and services available to NASA."
The space station is currently set to retire in 2030.
"I love you guys"
The current problem facing the space agency marks a stark reversal from earlier times, when it was SpaceX that was depending heavily on NASA. In 2008, following multiple failures of the Falcon 9, the space launch company was on the ropes.
"We were running on fumes at that point, we had virtually no money," Elon Musk told CBS' 60 Minutes in a 2014 interview.
Then, just days before Christmas, NASA came through with a big contract.
"I couldn't even hold the phone, I just blurted out, 'I love you guys!'," Musk said.
For the next decade, a steady diet of NASA and eventually Pentagon contracts were responsible for a big share of the company's revenue. But all that changed in 2020, when SpaceX launched a subscription satellite internet service called Starlink. Starlink subscriptions quickly eclipsed the money made from launching rockets.
Today, according to SpaceX's latest financial report, the company made around $2.1 billion in revenue from space launches through September of this year. By contrast, Starlink pulled in around $12.8 billion, while its rapidly growing AI business made around $10.9 billion.
Winding down Falcon
Starship is central to SpaceX's newer, larger businesses. The space launch company is already using it to send its new, powerful V3 satellites for Starlink into orbit. Further down the road, Musk has said he wants the rocket to deliver data centers to space.
"Once Starship is flying reliably several times per week, it makes sense to shift super scarce SpaceX engineering and production resources to Starship to get launch rate to several times per day, which means winding down Falcon," Musk said on X earlier this year.
"We definitely want to move from the older technology to the newer technology," SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell said at the All In summit in Los Angeles in September. "A Falcon 9 with a Dragon capsule on top is like a minivan. … The road trip to Mars is six months — so you don't want to be in the minivan."
The problem is that the minivan is perfect for taking astronauts on a short jaunt to the space station. In fact, it's currently the only American option for making the trip.
Henry said building space capsules is time-consuming and expensive. And as it turns out NASA is about the only one willing to pay, making it a very small market for a company like the one SpaceX has become.
"Today there is not a strong commercial market for human spaceflight," he said.
Launch gap
The retirement of the Falcon rocket will have huge impacts beyond human spaceflight. A recent analysis by Quilty Space finds that the commercial market may end up short by some 150 launches between now and 2030, and the Pentagon has reportedly been left scrambling to find rides for national security satellites. In a statement to NPR, the U.S. Space Force said it had secured Falcon 9 launches through 2028 and that it was "confident" other suppliers would be able to pick up the slack.
None of that is likely to change SpaceX's mind, according to Tim Farrar, the president of TMF associates, a telecom analysis firm that tracks SpaceX.
The company has grown far beyond its launch business, he said. "SpaceX has now got an enormous amount on its plate."
In particular, "it's not making a lot of money out of NASA," he said. "Although it seems likely that the individual missions are profitable, they're small potatoes."
It's still not clear when SpaceX will retire the Falcon 9 rocket. The company did not respond to NPR's request for comment, but in her public comments at the summit, Shotwell implied that a rival company, Boeing, could fly to the station instead.
"Boeing has been paid, I think, probably more than we have been paid to develop their human capsule. So we're just going to let them have some business," she said. "They should fly their capsule."
The Boeing capsule, known as the Starliner, has been beset by problems throughout its development. In 2024, failures with the vehicle's first attempt to take astronauts to space resulted in a planned eight-day mission aboard the ISS becoming a nine-month stay. The astronauts returned home on a SpaceX vehicle in March of the following year. The next Starliner test flight is set to take place over the winter, with a crewed flight sometime in 2028.
For Farrar, SpaceX's choices make sense for its business, but he wonders whether NASA deserves better. "They were responsible essentially for SpaceX not going bankrupt," he said. "One would hope that there's a bit of loyalty."

title: EU-backed court convicts Kosovo ex-President of attempting to obstruct justice
text:
A European Union-backed court has convicted Kosovo's former president, Hashim Thaci, of trying to obstruct justice and contempt of court
THE HAGUE, Netherlands -- A European Union-backed court on Tuesday convicted Kosovo's former president, Hashim Thaci, of charges that include trying to obstruct justice and contempt of court.
Thaci was sentenced to 17 months in prison to be added to a 25-year war crimes sentence that he's already serving.
It was the latest legal setback for Thaci, who was convicted in September along with three other former leaders of the Kosovo Liberation Army of committing war crimes during Kosovo's war for independence from Serbia in 1998-99. In that trial, Thaci was sentenced to 25 years in prison. His lawyer, Luka Misetic, said on X that he would appeal.
After Judge Christopher Gosnell of Canada read out the verdicts and sentence Tuesday, Thaci took off a headset that provides simultaneous interpretation and said: “This is politics, not justice.”
Kimberly West, the prosecutor who brings cases to the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, a special branch of the Kosovo legal system based in The Hague, welcomed the verdicts. She said they “send a clear message: those who attempt to subvert the rule of law, reveal confidential court materials or interfere with witnesses will be held accountable, no matter their status or position.”
Thaci resigned from office nearly six years ago to defend himself against the war crimes charges. He's still considered a war hero among his supporters in Kosovo, who angrily denounced his sentence in September. At the time, Kosovo Foreign Minister Glauk Konjufca condemned the verdicts as “a terrible judgment for Kosovo, for our people and for our liberation war.”
At a hearing on Tuesday, the court ruled that Thaci “disclosed confidential information about several witnesses in his war crimes trial to persons visiting him in detention in 2023, and that he had conveyed instructions through visitors to witnesses about how they should testify in his war crimes trial.”
Thaci was acquitted of two counts of obstruction and contempt.
Gosnell called the crimes “an attack on the integrity of the judicial system, which is an essential foundation of the rule of law.”
Thaci was on trial with four other defendants, Bashkim Smakaj, Isni Kilaj, Fadil Fazliu and Hajredin Kuci, accused of trying to influence the testimony of witnesses. They had all pleaded not guilty to the charges.
Smakaj and Fazliu were found guilty of attempted obstruction of justice and sentenced to 12 months of imprisonment, but were ordered released immediately because of time they have already served in detention. Kuci was found guilty of one count of contempt of court and given a suspended one-month sentence. Kilaj was acquitted.
Most of the 13,000 people who died in the war in Kosovo were ethnic Albanians. A 78-day campaign of NATO airstrikes against Serbian forces ended the fighting. About 1 million ethnic Albanian Kosovars were driven from their homes.
In 2008, Kosovo declared its independence from Serbia, a move that Belgrade refuses to recognize. Ties between Kosovo and Serbia remain tense, despite years of EU-mediated negotiations supported by the United States.

title: How AI is likely to change Germany's job market
text:
At the German government's 2026 Digital Summit in early November, Chancellor Friedrich Merz was asked by a journalist to square a difficult economic circle: If artificial intelligence could make hundreds of thousands of people redundant in the next few years, might it become necessary for the government to give people a basic income to ease the ensuing economic disaster?
Surprisingly, Merz didn't respond with a flat dismissal — as might be expected from a conservative politician known for his neoliberal, market-friendly views.
"I've always been a bit cautious about this issue in recent years," he said, as reported by the news outlet RND. "However, I'm also well aware that the issue of AI will change our working world so fundamentally that we'll have to give serious thought to many of these issues in the coming years — including the question: Is our productivity not good enough?"
What makes this ambiguity notable is that much of Merz's policies since becoming chancellor last year have involved making Germans work more: His government's planned pension reforms would see Germany's retirement age being raised. In July, he announced a crackdown on sick leave. And in spring 2025, having barely taken office, he caused much consternation by criticizing the concept of a "work-life balance" and declaring, "We in this country must work more and more efficiently."
Germany must prepare for impending job rupture
But those policies seem to contradict the impending realities of the labor market in an AI world.
This week, the head of Germany's Federal Employment Agency, Andrea Nahles, warned that the introduction AI would cost Germany as many 800,000 jobs in the next 15 years. Though she also said AI could eventually create a similar number of jobs, clearly the socioeconomic upheaval would be considerable.
Nahles is not the only leading figure concerned about job losses caused by AI. Karsten Wildberger, Germany's minister for digital transformation and government modernization, takes any opportunity he can to warn that Germany must prepare for the economic disruptions of AI.
And even for Wildberger, a former CEO of a massive retail company, part of the future economy might come down to giving people free money. He was convinced, he told the Neue Osnabrücker Zeitung in March, "that an unconditional basic income can be part of the solution to cushion the upheavals in the labor market."
Why tech bosses love UBI
Campaigners have cautiously welcomed this new openness from unexpected quarters. "It shows that in the face of technological transformation we also need to look differently at the question of how we need to secure people's economic stability," said Kirsten Herrmann, board member at the nonprofit Mein Grundeinkommen (My Basic Income), which runs various projects examining the social and economic impact of universal basic income (UBI).
"But I also think that individual statements by politicians don't amount to a political change, of course," she told DW. "It just means that we need to enter a serious and constructive debate about what kind of a role a basic income can play."
The idea of a universal basic income is very old: English Renaissance philosopher Thomas More mentions it in his 1516 book Utopia, for instance. But since the 20th century, it has largely been seen as an idealistic notion adopted by leftists — that is, until some of the world's most high-profile tech bosses latched onto the idea as a way to offset the utopian advances they said AI would bring.
In 2017, Elon Musk, who had co-founded the corporation OpenAI two years earlier, predicted that a universal basic income would at some stage become inevitable. Since then, leading figures in the AI sector, including Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, and Sam Altman, the other founder of OpenAI, have all gone on record in support of UBI (though Altman's interest has cooled somewhat since he launched a massive UBI experiment in the US in 2019).
But Herrmann said it's a "double-edged sword" when such figures mention the idea. She isn't convinced that organizations like hers and people Elon Musk want the same thing.
"On the one hand, it's always nice when the debate about a basic income gets attention from prominent voices," she said. "On the other hand, the basic income that people from the tech business talk about is a kind of neoliberal basic income: They talk about what to do when there are no more profitable jobs for people, because they still actually do need people to do certain things, whereas we talk about a basic income that is meant to give people a secure economic base — before the crisis in the job market happens."
AI and basic income
What makes the comments of Merz and Wildberger all the more eyebrow-raising is that mainstream German economists have long since rejected the basic income idea.
Dominik Enste, director of the democracy, society, and economic ethics department at the German Economic Institute in Cologne, dismissed the idea out of hand — AI or no AI. UBI was, he said, just too expensive, especially in a country that already has plenty of social welfare costs.
"Many economists have calculated that implementing this in many countries is financially unfeasible — in Germany, for one, simply because of the need to fund commitments that have already been made (including pension payments)," he told DW in an email.
However, he also added: "We will have to change our social security systems if work is replaced by AI and, if necessary, tax AI-generated income. But it will be a conditional basic income that still provides incentives to earn a living."
Other economists are more positive about the idea. "How this plays out depends on many choices we make, and on who makes these choices, in whose interest," said Maximilian Kasy, professor of economics at the University of Oxford and author of a book on the impact of AI on society. "But a lot of the current thrust is to replace workers to increase profits and increase corporate control, though this is not the only path possible."
Kasy thinks a basic income could be a good solution, "especially if it's financed in a progressive way (so that only those at the lower end of the income distribution are net recipients)," he wrote. "The 'small print' matters very much, though!"
If the warnings of Wildberger, Musk, Altman et al. are to be believed, AI is already causing a bigger upheaval than any other technological advance in history, partly because of the speed of the innovations, but also because of the scale of the potential impact.
AI innovation is affecting the jobs of the traditional urban middle classes across the entire world. In 2024, the International Monetary Fund predicted that some 40% of employment in the world would be shaped by AI innovations, and as much as 60% in rich, industrialized nations.
For her part, Herrmann thinks we are not yet asking the truly fundamental questions about the socioeconomic implications of AI: Not just how do we replace the lost jobs and keep the capitalist system going, but what do we actually want to use AI for? As she put it: "Who actually profits when we become more productive through AI? And how do we redistribute that profit to everyone?"
This, she argued, is why there needs to be more debate about how exactly AI is used in the world of work. "Which jobs are going to be replaced by AI is not some law of nature," said Herrmann . "It's something that we can shape politically and socially — and then the bigger question is: Who gets a say?"

title: Former Nvidia boss Jensen Huang speaks out about return for first time in wake of scandal that rocked AI industry
text:
Former Nvidia boss Jensen Huang has said he would be “honoured” to return to the company after he was ousted in the wake of a scandal.
Mr Huang resigned from the chipmaker last week, amid a wave of scandal after he admitted to an affair with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy as well as a subordinate at Nvidia. Since then, petitions and supporters have called for him to return – but the company has said that it is not interested in inviting him back.
Nonetheless, Mr Huang signalled he would be willing to return and that he would work with an investigation into the incident. But he suggested that the decision was up to the board and whether it thought his return would be “in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America”.
“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said in his first public statement since he resigned on 12 November over revelations of extramarital affairs that intensified scrutiny of the chip firm's China business. Mr Huang had not been quoted in Nvidia’s original statement about his departure, though it thanked him for his “profound” contributions to the company, and he has been silent since.
“I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation,” he said in the new statement.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Mr Huang's statement, but multiple reports have suggested that its board is not planning to reappoint him. Nvidia shares pared some declines and were last down 1 per cent.
More than 180,000 people have signed a petition demanding Huang’s return, Elon Musk has thrown his support behind the effort, and US President Donald Trump said he would not mind seeing Huang reinstated as CEO. Thousands of people identifying themselves as Nvidia employees have joined the call, even as governance experts and some investors warn that bringing him back before investigations are complete could expose the company to fresh risks.
The groundswell of support for Huang has turned a corporate succession story into a test of whether Nvidia can separate itself from a founder whose influence stretches across its employees — some fiercely loyal to the former CEO — and shareholders, Silicon Valley, the Taiwanese supply chain and Washington.
Taiwan's tallest skyscraper, Taipei 101, was illuminated on Monday with messages including "Taiwan Loves Jensen." Some prominent shareholders such as Atreides Management's Gavin Baker and Altimeter Capital Management CEO Brad Gerstner have urged Nvidia not to rush to replace him before all the facts are known.
Earlier on Tuesday, before Mr Huang’s statement, Nvidia created a board-level committee to oversee national security and export controls, its first major governance move since he left.
Mr Huang's relationships have raised questions about whether Nvidia's oversight kept pace with its rapid growth and increasing importance to US national security. The crisis had erased more than $400 billion from the company's market value by Monday's close.
The National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee will be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson, a former Goldman Sachs vice chair, Nvidia said. Directors Stephen Neal, former CEO of law firm Cooley, and John Dabiri, a Caltech professor, will also serve on the committee.
Donald Trump welcomed the move, calling the launch of a national security initiative a good idea.
In the full statement, posted on X, Mr Huang thanked the public for its support and admitted to having made “serious mistakes”. He also included a message to his family, in which he suggested they were offering him “support”.
“Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I've never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me,” he wrote.
“I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. Nvidia has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like Nvidia be possible. I love our country, and I love Nvidia.
“I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation.
“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honoured to answer these calls and return as CEO.
“Thank you again to everyone who has shared their good wishes. I am profoundly humbled by your support. To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours.”
Additional reporting by agencies

title: Sean McVay Gives Injury Updates On Rams Stars Myles Garrett, Trent McDuffie
text:
Los Angeles Rams defensive end Myles Garrett expects to play Sunday despite missing practice, while cornerback Trent McDuffie is questionable for their game at the Arizona Cardinals.
Garrett was held out of practice on Friday after being limited earlier in the week because of a knee injury that caused him to miss seven games before returning to make three sacks with a forced fumble in the Rams’ 20-13 win at the Washington Commanders on Sunday.
"He’s had a really good week," coach Sean McVay said. "Played a bunch of snaps, and expect him to be able to build on that. But we’re being smart with him."
Garrett was largely pleased with his performance, in which he played 61.5% of the defensive snaps, apart from needing to build up his endurance and address what he felt was a slow get-off time.
"I'm sure Next Gen or PFF or somebody would tell me it wasn't too bad," Garrett said. "It felt terrible to me."
McDuffie is dealing with a back injury that forced him to miss the Rams’ third straight win last week, getting them over .500 for the first time this season at 5-4. McVay expressed optimism he would be able to play, provided McDuffie felt good coming out of Friday's workout.
"He was rolling, you know, doing a lot of good stuff yesterday," McVay said.
The ongoing issues with the Rams’ two marquee offseason acquisitions are indicative of their larger injury crisis that has threatened a campaign that began with them as Super Bowl betting favorites. Los Angeles is so beat up that star wide receiver Puka Nacua was placed on injured reserve Thursday to free up a roster spot, a reversal from what McVay had indicated earlier in the week when he cited the limited number of IR slots remaining to be able to bring players back later in the season.
"Some things changed where we needed that spot because of all the moving pieces," said McVay, while adding that nothing has changed with the timeline for Nacua’s return from knee and toe injuries.
Safety Kam Curl is questionable with a toe injury, but McVay indicated he is likely to play. The same is expected for the Rams’ banged-up crop of tight ends, Colby Parkinson (ribs), Tyler Higbee (illness) and Davis Allen (oblique). All three are needed to supplement the passing game with top receivers Nacua, Davante Adams (hamstring) and Jordan Whittington (back) on IR.
Tight end Terrance Ferguson (ankle/hamstring) and left guard Steve Avila (hamstring) were ruled officially out, as was previously announced.
The Rams were upset by the Cardinals 18-16 on Oct. 18, giving up a last-minute drive which ended with Chad Ryland kicking his sixth field goal as time expired at SoFi Stadium.
Reporting by The Associated Press.

title: Physicists use laser light to unlock a crystal's hidden electrical powers
text:
Scientists have discovered how to use flashes of laser light to organize tiny electrical regions inside a crystal, solving a decades-old mystery about how the material behaves. The laser-induced alignment lasts just a trillionth of a second, but the breakthrough could open the door to new ways of processing and storing information.
Physicists at Auburn University have discovered how to use brief bursts of laser light to organize tiny electrical regions hidden inside a crystal. Their findings shed new light on a mystery that has puzzled researchers for decades and demonstrate how lasers can influence the material's electrical behavior. The breakthrough could eventually help scientists explore faster ways to process and store information.
The research was led by Wencan Jin, the Thomas and Jean Walter Endowed Associate Professor in Auburn's Department of Physics, and graduate student Mohamed Kandil. Their paper, "Optical Poling of a Quantum Ferroelectric Metal across the Order-Disorder Phase Transition," received an Editors' Suggestion designation from Physical Review Letters. Scientists at Japan's National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology produced the crystals used in the study.
A Decades-Old Mystery Hidden Inside a Crystal
The researchers investigated a modified version of strontium titanate, a material with an unusual combination of electrical characteristics. Although electrons can travel through the crystal, it also contains extremely small regions with positive and negative electrical sides. Known as polar nanoregions, these microscopic "islands" can point in different directions or become aligned with one another. Understanding how and why this alignment occurs is essential to explaining the material's properties and learning how to manipulate them.
Scientists have spent decades trying to determine what happens when these regions become organized. One possibility is that atoms move together to produce the polarized state. Another is that the tiny electrical islands are already there and simply begin pointing in the same direction as temperatures fall. The distinction is similar to the difference between assembling a group of people and asking people who are already gathered to turn and face the same way. Because the regions are extraordinarily small and produce very weak signals, determining which explanation is correct has been a persistent challenge.
Laser Experiments Reveal How Electrical Order Emerges
To investigate, the Auburn researchers developed an exceptionally sensitive system that uses lasers to measure subtle changes in the crystal. By studying how the material altered incoming light, they were able to monitor the orientation of its electrical regions while repeatedly heating and cooling the sample.
The measurements revealed a clear pattern. At warmer temperatures, the tiny regions pointed in seemingly random directions. When the crystal cooled, however, they began adopting preferred orientations. This behavior provided compelling evidence that the electrical islands existed before becoming aligned, supporting the explanation that cooling organizes regions already present in the material.
A Flash of Light Creates Order in a Trillionth of a Second
The team went beyond observing this natural process. Researchers also demonstrated that short laser pulses could temporarily align the electrical islands, even at higher temperatures when the regions would ordinarily remain disorganized. Using an optical measurement, they were able to detect the pattern produced by the laser light.
The effect was extraordinarily brief, lasting approximately one picosecond, or one trillionth of a second. Nevertheless, the ability to create and detect this electrical alignment using light provides a promising approach for studying how information might be controlled at extremely high speeds.
Three Years of Experiments Lead to a Breakthrough
Achieving these results required considerable patience and technical refinement. The collaboration began at the 2023 American Physical Society March Meeting, where Jin met Japanese researchers capable of producing the specialized crystals needed for the experiments.
Back at Auburn, the team spent almost a year refining its equipment before it could reliably detect the weak optical signals from the tiny electrical regions. The next obstacle was even more demanding: measuring the extremely short interval during which laser illumination caused the regions to align.
"The breakthrough came in 2025, when Mohamed finally observed the disordered polar regions becoming aligned under laser illumination," Jin said. "Seeing that signal emerge was a thrilling moment for the team."
The achievement also represents an important personal milestone for Kandil, whose first published research paper reflects three years of dedicated experimental work.
"This experiment has truly been Mohamed's odyssey," Jin said. "It took him three years of dedication to complete the work and achieve his first publication."
New Possibilities for Ultrafast Information Technology
The discovery provides important evidence about how electrical order develops in this unusual crystal while also establishing a method for manipulating that order with light. Rather than simply observing the material's internal behavior, researchers can now briefly influence its microscopic electrical patterns and detect the resulting changes.
Although practical applications remain a future possibility, the experiments offer a new way to investigate the rapid electrical processes occurring inside quantum materials. By revealing how light can control these previously elusive patterns, the Auburn researchers have opened another avenue for exploring technologies that could one day transform how information is processed and stored.

title: 'Now everything changes': SpaceX catches Starship upper stage for 1st time ever (video)
text:
SpaceX caught the upper stage of its Starship megarocket for the first time ever today (Nov. 14), a landmark achievement that could unlock the giant vehicle's immense potential.
Starship launched on its 15th test flight on Friday evening (Nov. 13), rising into the sky from SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas. The mission plan called for bringing both of the vehicle's stages back to Starbase and catching them with the launch tower's "chopstick" arms — an unprecedented total recovery of an orbital rocket.
That didn't happen; Starship's Super Heavy booster diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown on Friday after experiencing a low-fuel alarm. But Ship succeeded in its attempt, notching a huge milestone for SpaceX and its dream of full rocket reuse.
"That was the missing link," SpaceX's Dan Huot said during the company's landing webcast today, his voice thick with emotion. "That was the holy grail of spaceflight, plummeting through fire to be snatched out of the air by steel. We caught a Starship, and now everything changes."
The Ship catch occurred today at 4:20 p.m. EST (2120 GMT; 3:20 p.m. local Texas time), roughly 22.5 hours after Flight 15 lifted off.
Many SpaceX employees went outside to watch the vehicle, known as Ship 42, descend through the clouds toward its Starbase launch tower, which the company calls "Mechazilla."
And they got quite a show: Ship 42 nestled gently into Mechazilla's waiting arms, while "Baby Come Back" played over SpaceX's landing webcast.
"This is so incredible to see," SpaceX's Jessie Anderson said during the livestream. "One of the most incredible and historic engineering feats of all time has just happened right in front of our eyes."
Why was this such a big deal? SpaceX had already caught Super Heavy — on three previous Starship test flights, in fact. But it had never tried before with Ship. The upper stage is a tougher target, for it flies higher, farther and faster than the booster. Indeed, on Flight 15, Ship 42 came all the way back down from orbit.
While the double-catch attempt, and the chopsticks success with Ship, were Flight 15's main headlines, the mission had other objectives as well. One was getting Ship to orbit, which had happened on just one previous Starship launch — Flight 14, which lifted off on Sept. 28.
Ship deployed 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink V3 broadband satellites in low Earth orbit (LEO) on Flight 14, and it did so again on Flight 15. These 52 spacecraft are the first members of a constellation that will eventually consist of 100,000 satellites, if all goes according to SpaceX's plan.
Some of those Starlink satellites took video and images of Ship 42's heat shield to check its health for today's landing attempt. Those images, combined with ground-based cameras, found Ship 42 to be in good shape and ready for its big moment.
SpaceX plans to use Starship to build an even bigger network in LEO than the Starlink V3 system — Starmind, an AI data-center constellation that will harbor a million spacecraft, according to Elon Musk. (For context: SpaceX's current-gen Starlink network employs about 11,000 satellites at the moment.)
Assembling these megaconstellations will require an incredible launch cadence. The double chopstick catch is key to that vision, SpaceX says, for it will enable quicker inspection, refurbishment and reflight of Starship.
So the company will doubtless try the maneuver again soon — probably on the next Starship flight, which won't be too far down the road.
Editor's note: This story was updated at 8 a.m. EST to include new details on SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 mission from SpaceX. Space.com Editor-in-Chief Tariq Malik contributed to this report. It was updated again at 4:45 p.m. ET on Nov. 14 with news of successful Ship catch.

title: Yellow weather warnings issued for snow as temperatures plummet
text:
A spell of cold and wintry weather is set to grip northern areas of the UK early this week, bringing the threat of ice and hill snow.
A yellow weather warning for snow comes into effect in the very early hours of Tuesday following a blast of Arctic air pushing across the UK causing temperatures to plummet.
Cold health alerts for parts of northern England also remain in force from the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) until 09:00 GMT on Thursday.
Some snow is forecast over the hills and mountains in the north over the coming days but the wintry chill will be fairly short-lived in the south, where temperatures will rebound to above average by midweek.
Coldest night of season so far recorded
Monday morning started on a chilly note for all parts. The coldest conditions were seen across the northern half of the UK with northern England, Scotland and Northern Ireland waking up to a sharp frost with some wintry flurries over the hills.
Tulloch Bridge in Scotland recorded an overnight low of -7.7C making it the coldest night of the season so far.
Temperatures in the south generally remained a few degrees above freezing.
Cold health alerts, issued by the UKHSA, are currently in force across north-west England, north-east England, Yorkshire and the Humber until 09:00 GMT on Thursday.
These alerts are only issued in England and are aimed at health and social care professionals.
A Met Office weather warning for ice from Sunday evening into Monday morning across northern and eastern Scotland as well as parts of Cumbria, Northumberland and Durham has now expired.
Though Monday will be dry and bright for many places, wintry showers will affect some eastern parts of England and Scotland, with these falling as sleet or snow over high ground.
Afternoon maximum temperatures will be a chilly 4-8C in most places - a few degrees below the seasonal average.
Later in the day, the next front will approach from the south-west bringing milder air and some heavy and persistent rain.
As this band of rain then moves northwards overnight into Tuesday, a further spell of hill snow may develop.
Met Office warnings for snow on Tuesday
A yellow weather warning for snow is set to come into effect on Tuesday from midnight until 11:00 GMT, covering parts of the Midlands, north-east and north-west England, North Yorkshire and south-west Scotland.
Where snow does accumulate, depths of 1-5cm are likely, although some locations above 300-400m could see 5-15cm.
Some roads and railways are likely to be affected, resulting in longer travel times by road, bus and train services. Power cuts are also possible.
Further south, Tuesday will be a very different day with blustery conditions and some heavy showers.
This battleground of colder, drier conditions in the north and milder, wetter weather in the south will continue into the middle of the week.
You can keep up to date with your local forecast by checking BBC Weather online and on the app.

title: Judge extends deadline for Trump’s deposition in $10bn BBC lawsuit
text:
Donald Trump has been granted a temporary delay before he must give a witness statement in his $10bn defamation lawsuit against the BBC.
In late October, Enjoliqué Lett, a federal magistrate judge,gave Trump a firm 11 December deadline to sit for a deposition by lawyers representing the BBC in his lawsuit against the British broadcaster. If he failed to do so by that date, he could be subject to penalties up to dismissal of the case, the judge warned.
But on Tuesday, the president got something of a reprieve when Jeffrey Kuntz, a federal district court judge, approved a joint motion by the parties and extended the deadline for Trump’s deposition until 22 January. The judge also pushed back the deadline for discovery in the case from 18 December to 29 January.
Trump had originally agreed to sit for a deposition on 16 October, but his team backed out, citing “matters of national importance”. That led the BBC to file a motion to compel Trump to sit for a deposition in a timely fashion.
According to the joint motion filed on Monday, the BBC has agreed to the Trump team’s proposal for the president to sit for a deposition between 11 January and 22 January after his representatives said he was unavailable to do so this year “due to his schedule and the nature of his profession”. As that timeline nears, the parties will meet to select a date and identify a secure location for the deposition.
“It is Trump’s case, so he should expect to be deposed,” Kuntz wrote in his order. “It appears he acknowledges that reality.”
The judge ordered the parties to schedule Trump’s deposition by Friday at noon. Kuntz scheduled a trial date for the case for 3 May 2027 in Fort Lauderdale, Florida.
So far, Trump’s lawyers have deposed seven defendant witnesses. As part of the agreement between Trump and the BBC, the president’s lawyers will not depose Samir Shah, the BBC chair, or a former BBC director-general – nor any current or former BBC employee – until the president sits for questioning.
While Trump’s seven-hour-long deposition will be videotaped, it will only be available to attorneys for the parties.
In addition to Trump, the BBC might also be able to depose his daughter, Ivanka Trump, his son, Donald Trump Jr, and his son-in-law Jared Kushner. “Defendant is currently conferring with President Trump and these non-parties regarding the subpoenas directed to them, given that these non-parties may be objecting to, or moving to quash, those subpoenas,” the parties wrote in their joint motion.
Last week, Kuntz, a Trump appointee, refused the BBC’s request to dismiss the case, though he threw out the president’s contention that the broadcaster violated Florida’s Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act.
The lawsuit stems from a Panorama documentary aired by the BBC that spliced together two comments made nearly an hour apart by Trump during a rally on 6 January 2021, before the US Capitol riot. The BBC has acknowledged that this specific edit was misleading, but Trump has gone on to claim, falsely, that the BBC did not just edit his speech but used AI to insert words into his speech.
“BBC tries to frame this editing as ordinary editing done to condense a 70-minute-long speech into 12 seconds,” the judge wrote in his ruling. “But the court is not persuaded.”

title: California donates 1,300 hospital beds and medical supplies to Ukraine
text:
California is donating 1,300 hospital beds and millions of bandages to Ukraine.
California is donating 1,300 hospital beds, millions of bandages and other medical supplies to Ukraine to help treat those wounded in Russia's war with the country, Gov. Gavin Newsom announced Monday after traveling to Ukraine.
The Democratic governor from the most populous U.S. state said he visited the Ukrainian city of Lviv on Sunday to show his support for the country in the long-running war. He said the donated equipment comes from surplus supplies in California and builds upon previous donations made earlier in the war.
Newsom is preparing to leave office after eight years and is considering a run for U.S. president in 2028.
Republican President Donald Trump has recently played up chances for a settlement to Russia’s war in Ukraine. But European Union countries on Monday accused Russia of trying to drag out talks on ending the war while it bombs power plants and other infrastructure as winter nears.
In October, the White House said first lady Melania Trump had brokered a ceasefire to help with the delivery of humanitarian aid and to allow civilians to evacuate from a war-torn area.
The supplies from California include a 50-bed field hospital, which includes oxygen concentrators, wheelchairs and wound-care materials. The state also is providing more than 1,300 additional hospital beds, more than 11 million bandages, thousands of wound-care kits and 20 portable generators.
“The people of Ukraine did not choose this war,” Newsom said in a statement, adding: “No people fighting for their freedom should have to wonder whether they stand alone. California stands with Ukraine.”
Newsom said he also visited the graves of Ukrainian soldiers, toured a rehabilitation center for people injured in the war and visited defense technology companies.
Earlier in the war, California provided five field medical stations, more than 4,300 ballistic vests and nearly 1,600 helmets, the governor's office said.

title: Germany's 2027 budget: A record €561 billion and a mountain of debt
text:
