It was 5:55 a.m. on Friday when the Bundestag's Budget Committee concluded its final session.
Following nearly 16 hours of negotiations, lawmakers from the conservative Christian Democratic Union(CDU) and Christian Social Union (CSU) parties, along with their coalition partners from the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), voted in favor of the 2027 draft budget. The opposition parties — the environmentalist Greens, the socialist Left Party and the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) — voted against it. With that, the way is now clear for the final vote in the Bundestag on November 27.
Reading through the nearly 1,000-page document requires a great deal of number-crunching. Next year, the federal government plans to spend around €561 billion ($620 billion).
But here's the problem: it won't collect nearly enough revenue to cover these expenses. With a shortfall of €123 billion, borrowing will be needed to bridge the gap.
But that's not the only problem. On top of all this debt, Germany also has loans for defense spending and for the renovation of the dilapidated infrastructure. Approved by the Bundestag in 2025, these special funds are set to be in place for multiple years.
If the new debt for 2027 is factored in, the total borrowing amounts to over €210 billion. This is the second-highest level of borrowing in the history of the Federal Republic of Germany. The only time Germany borrowed more was during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2021, when borrowing reached €215.4 billion.
This development has drawn sharp criticism from opposition parties. Green Party lawmaker Sebastian Schäfer and his colleague Dietmar Bartsch of the Left Party called it a "gigantic mountain of debt," an "untrustworthy" budget, "irresponsible" policies at the expense of future generations and a lack of future prospects.
Why is debt growing? Crises drive up costs
To understand the reasons behind the growing debt, one has to look beyond the numbers. Every federal budget is a snapshot of the priorities set by a government and a country — in terms of the economy, social issues, security and geopolitics.
For 2027, that story continues to be one of crises and wars. While Russia's war against Ukraine is driving up defense spending, the faltering economy is also demanding new investments. At the same time, Germany's population is aging rapidly, which is driving up social spending.
What's more, the crumbling infrastructure must be repaired and modernized, and the energy transition is costing billions. And more than half of all this debt is going toward security and defense.
Defense spending continues to rise
Russia's war against Ukraine will enter its sixth year in 2027. As of the end of June, the federal government estimated its overall support for Ukraine to have reached approximately €100 billion. In response to a request from the AfD in the Bundestag, the government stated: "The federal government will continue to provide Ukraine with political, financial, humanitarian, civil and military support for as long as necessary."
The rearmament of the Bundeswehr and spending on NATO are also putting massive pressure on the budget. The defense budget is set to grow to just under €110 billion in 2027, an increase of around €27 billion compared to last year. Added to this are expenditures from the Bundeswehr's special fund.
Largest budget item: Social spending and pensions
Nevertheless, by far the largest single budget item comes from the Ministry of Labor and Social Affairs, which is set to grow to over €200 billion. There are plans for cost-cutting measures, for example, in basic income support for job seekers. But the costs of old-age pension benefits continue to rise.
People born in the 1960s have begun to retire. Back then, more than 1 million children were born each year. But birth rates nearly halved in the early 1970s and have continued to decline since then. As a result, there will be an increasing number of retirees and a decreasing number of working-age individuals in the coming years.
The pension funds cannot be financed by the pension contributions of this dwindling workforce and have to be subsidized by the government. Already, contributions to the pension insurance system — which are split equally between employees and employers — will have to be increased. They are expected to rise to just under 20% of gross salary.
The Federal Employment Agency, too, has long been unable to make ends meet on contributions alone. In 2027, subsidies of more than €8 billion from the federal budget are planned.
Germany no longer a model of fiscal discipline
Anyone comparing Germany's current budget situation with that of past years will be rubbing their eyes in disbelief. It wasn't that long ago that Germany was considered a model of fiscal discipline. Between 2014 and 2019, the federal budget managed to avoid taking on new debt for six consecutive years. In some years, there was even money left over.
But the era of "balanced budgets" came to an abrupt end with the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. However, today Germany is still enjoying the benefits of those years of fiscal stability. Compared to other countries, Germany is still in relatively good shape.
Economic experts warn of rising debt
The key indicator is not the amount of debt along but the debt-to-GDP ratio. It indicates how high the national debt is in relation to annual economic output.
At the end of 2025, it stood at 63.5% for Germany. France, on the other hand, stands at over 110% and Italy at about 135% to 140%, while the US is well above 100%. However, in its latest fall report, the German Council of Economic Experts warned that Germany could be heading down a dangerous path. If debt continues to rise at this rate, the debt-to-GDP ratio could climb to 100% by 2040.
This would also put Germany's creditworthiness on the financial markets at risk. Germany is the only country among the seven leading democratic industrialized nations (G7) that still holds a triple-A (AAA) rating. This is the highest possible credit rating on the financial markets. It signals to investors that the risk of default on German government bonds is extremely low.
This also means that interest rates on new loans are not set as high. This is an important point, as interest payments place an increasing burden on the federal budget each year. By 2027, approximately €42 billion in interest payments are expected to be due.
What's the road ahead?
At the end of November, the Bundestag will hold its final debate on the draft budget. Should changes be expected by then? There is disagreement within the government over whether a reduction in the electricity tax might still be possible.
The prospect of such a reduction had been raised by Chancellor Friedrich Merz. On Friday, during a European leaders summit in Dublin, he reiterated: "I expect that we will discuss this again next Tuesday in the coalition committee, and I remain committed to my goal of lowering the electricity tax to the European minimum — in full — starting next year."

title: Who is standing for Fifa president – and can anyone finally topple Gianni Infantino?
text:
Gianni Infantino remains in a strong position to secure a further four-year mandate as Fifa president, even after enduring significant pushback over his governance.
However, a number of challengers have stepped forward ahead of next March’s election. So, who is in the running to potentially oust Infantino, and do they realistically have a chance of beating him?
Who is standing for the Fifa presidency?
- Gianni Infantino: Having held the post since 2016, the Swiss-Italian incumbent is seeking a fourth period in charge as Fifa chief.
- Ramon Vega: The ex-Switzerland skipper made previous bids to contest the Fifa presidency in 2015, 2019 and 2023.
- Kozo Tashima: Serving on the Fifa Council since 2015, the Honorary president of the Japan Football Association is a former international player and youth coach. He represents the first Japanese contender to campaign for Fifa president.
- Philippe Diallo: The French Football Federation (FFF) president was put forward as Uefa's candidate following the decision of Arsene Wenger - the former Arsenal boss and current Fifa chief of global football development - not to enter the contest.
How does the Fifa presidential election work?
To be eligible, candidates require backing from at least five member associations and must demonstrate active involvement as a player or official within Fifa, a confederation or a national association for two of the preceding five years.
Every one of Fifa's 211 member associations holds a single vote, meaning national size or historical success carries no extra weight. Consequently, world champions Spain possess identical voting power to San Marino, who sit bottom of the world rankings.
When two or fewer contenders stand, victory requires a simple majority - exceeding 50 per cent - of the valid votes submitted.
In races with three or more candidates, a two-thirds majority of present and eligible member associations is needed in the initial round. Should subsequent ballots be required, the candidate receiving the fewest votes is knocked out in each round until two remain.
What are the key dates and deadlines?
Formal nominations close on Wednesday, four months prior to the assembly. Voting will subsequently occur during the 77th Fifa Congress in Rabat on 18 March.
The Fifa general secretariat is required to inform member associations of the official candidates for president no later than one month before the Congress convenes.
Why has Infantino drawn criticism?
Discontent mounted following proposals for the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE), an initiative designed to introduce private funding into a fresh entity overseeing commercial rights for premier Fifa tournaments, such as the World Cup.
Opponents targeted both the structural details of the initiative and the absence of consultation and openness with which it was introduced to Fifa's membership.
The backlash grew so severe that prominent administrators urged Infantino to step down, while multiple regional confederations formed a united front, prompting the president to eventually scrap the plan.
How does Infantino still have support?
Having withdrawn the FFE plan following threats from European body Uefa to boycott Fifa fixtures, Infantino offered an apology to the Fifa Council regarding the management of the proposal.
While Uefa - among three confederations that had demanded his resignation - remained unmoved, the apology served to mend bridges with the Asian Football Confederation (AFC).
AFC head Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, who had denounced the project as a "fundamental breach of trust", subsequently changed position to offer his endorsement to the president.
Elsewhere, South American governing body Conmebol declined to demand Infantino's departure, while the Confederation of African Football (CAF) maintained solid backing.
A pledge by Infantino to distribute $25m to every member association also seems to have been instrumental in smoothing over tensions.
Concacaf, representing North America, Central America and the Caribbean, originally aligned with Uefa and the AFC in voicing opposition. However, its delegation has since split, with Mexico alongside various Caribbean nations rallying behind Infantino.
Can any of the challengers beat Infantino?
As one of the most seasoned figures in the race, Tashima has outlined ambitions to reform Fifa's governance, rebuild institutional accountability and tackle what he views as an unhealthy centralisation of authority.
Possessing deep internal knowledge of the governing body's inner workings, the Japanese administrator offers a direct proposition: "I'll keep what's good and change what's bad."
Diallo entered the contest relatively late, gathering support from Uefa member associations sitting on both its executive committee and the Fifa Council.
In charge of the FFF since 2023, the Frenchman has consistently challenged Infantino's leadership. Nonetheless, Uefa has stopped short of confirming unanimous backing from its 55 member nations, leaving his exact level of support uncertain.
Vega grounds his platform in athletic credentials, commercial background and ten years of global campaigning, with the former defender stating he has travelled to over 140 nations to build support.
His bid is far from impulsive given his prior campaigns for office, yet three prior failures create doubts over whether his ambitions can translate into meaningful voting power.

title: Serbian MiG-29 fighter jet crashes near Belgrade, killing pilot
text:
Developed by the Soviet Union's Mikoyan-Gurevich Design Bureau in the early 1970s, the MiG-29 entered service with the Soviet military in 1983.
A Serbian armed forces MiG-29 fighter jet crashed near Belgrade on Tuesday morning, killing the pilot, according to the country's defence ministry.
The incident occurred at around 8:45 am local time in the vicinity of Stara Pazova, northwest of the capital.
The pilot has been identified as Major Goran Bulajić, 53. Bulajić had served in the Serbian military since 1996 and is survived by two children, the defence ministry said.
Military police are at the scene.
"A commission has been established to investigate the accident, with a mandate to establish the circumstances surrounding the incident and determine whether there was any responsibility on the part of the military organisation," it added in a statement. "An expert commission from the air force has also been appointed to establish the cause of the aircraft crash."
Video footage circulating on social media appears to show the aircraft on fire in a field.
The fighter posed a "formidable threat" to Western air forces, according to the National Museum of the United States Air Force. It is equipped with one 30 mm cannon and can carry six air-to-air missiles as well as bombs and rockets.

title: Pope Leo XIV hit in the face by flying rosary during farewell Mass in Peru, video shows
text:
Pope Leo XIV appeared to be struck near the eye by a rosary Monday as he reached out to catch prayer beads tossed toward his popemobile ahead of a massive farewell Mass in Lima, Peru.
Video shows the 71-year-old pontiff wincing, clutching his face and rubbing his eye after the beads appeared to hit him as his vehicle slowed near the altar at Las Palmas Air Base.
Leo showed no obvious signs of injury and continued with the Mass, marking the end of his six-day visit to Peru and a grueling 12-day tour of South America, Reuters reported.
An estimated 1.5 million people attended the farewell Mass, where the pope thanked Peruvians for their hospitality and reaffirmed his deep connection to the country, which he considers his second homeland.
"I wish to confirm you in faith and charity and assure you that I will always carry you with me. Yes, the Peruvian people are my people, too," he told the crowd.
The incident came as the pontiff traveled through crowds of faithful Catholics in his popemobile, a specially designed vehicle equipped with security features to protect the leader of the Roman Catholic Church.
Leo has previously been seen catching dolls, flags and other gifts tossed by worshipers as he travels in his popemobile.
During an appearance in St. Peter's Square, he even accepted pizza offered by fellow Chicagoans, according to Reuters.
At another event in Rome, the pope accidentally struck a Vatican cameraman riding behind him while reaching for a flying gift, prompting him to apologize to the operator.
Born Robert Prevost in Chicago in 1955, Leo became the first American pope in May 2025, when 133 cardinals gathered in the Sistine Chapel and elected him to lead the world's 1.4 billion Catholics.
Stepping onto the balcony of St. Peter's Basilica before thousands of cheering faithful, he had greeted the crowd with the words, "Peace be with you."
He also paid tribute to Peru at the time, since he spent decades serving as a missionary and bishop there before becoming pontiff.
Switching to speaking in Spanish at the event on Monday, Leo told the crowd, "I would particularly like to say hello to my compatriots from Peru. It was a great pleasure for me to work in Peru."
Pope Leo's South American tour began in Uruguay and carried on through Argentina before ending in Peru.
The trip included 12 flights, two helicopter rides and nine Masses, as well as 36 speeches.
The trip came weeks after Leo underwent surgery to remove a lobe of his right lung.

title: Scientists discover a bizarre paradox among endangered penguins
text:
A groundbreaking drone survey has revealed a startling split in the fate of New Zealand's endangered Erect-crested penguins. While one population has remained stable for decades, another has declined by more than 40%, apparently due to a combination of predators, worsening storms, and changing ocean conditions. Even more surprisingly, the tiny Bounty Islands support nearly as many breeding pairs as the Antipodes Islands, despite being 40 times smaller.
A new study from the University of Otago, Ōtākou Whakaihu Waka, has revealed a surprising divide in the fortunes of one of New Zealand's least understood penguin species. Although Erect-crested penguins breed in just two remote island groups, their populations are experiencing dramatically different outcomes.
Published in PLOS ONE, the research found that one population has remained stable for at least 25 years, while the other has declined by more than 40 percent over the past three decades.
The study was led by Dr. Thomas Mattern of the Tawaki Project, which brings together scientists from the university's Departments of Zoology and Marine Science. Researchers also collaborated with the Antarctic Research Trust and the Global Penguin Society.
Drone Surveys Reveal a Surprising Penguin Population Divide
Erect-crested penguins breed exclusively on the Bounty and Antipodes islands, two isolated island groups located approximately 800 kilometers southeast of New Zealand's South Island.
To determine how many penguins remain, researchers conducted extensive drone surveys between 2022 and 2024. They photographed and counted every breeding colony across both island groups, producing the first comprehensive population survey of the entire species.
"The results overturn a long-standing assumption," Dr. Mattern says.
"The tiny Bounty Islands, at just 50 hectares, were found to hold almost as many breeding pairs (about 27,800) as the Antipodes Islands (about 29,800), even though the latter is 40 times larger and historically considered the species' stronghold."
The difference in population trends was even more unexpected. Despite their small size, the Bounty Islands have maintained a relatively consistent number of breeding penguins for decades. Meanwhile, the much larger Antipodes Islands have experienced a substantial decline.
"Comparing the new counts with historical records going back to the mid-1990s, the Bounty Islands population has remained essentially unchanged for at least 25 years.
"The Antipodes Islands population, by contrast, has declined by more than 40 percent since 1995."
Why Are Penguins Disappearing From the Antipodes Islands?
Researchers believe several overlapping pressures may explain why the two populations are heading in opposite directions. Natural predators, increasingly destructive storms, and differences in where the birds travel and feed could all be contributing.
One particularly troubling factor involves skuas, native subantarctic birds that prey on penguin eggs and chicks. As penguin colonies become smaller, the birds lose some of the protection that comes from nesting together in large numbers.
"As Antipodes colonies have shrunk over recent decades, the collective defense they once provided against native subantarctic bird, the skua, a natural predator of eggs and chicks, has weakened, allowing predation losses to increase and colonies to fragment further."
Co-author Dr. Klemens Pütz of the Antarctic Research Trust suggests that changes involving another penguin species may have intensified this pressure.
Eastern Rockhopper penguins suffered a "catastrophically" severe population collapse during the second half of the 20th century. Similar declines occurred across their Southern Ocean breeding range, likely driven by warming ocean waters. Today, fewer than 1,000 breeding pairs remain on the Antipodes Islands.
"As Rockhoppers disappeared, skuas may have turned to Erect-crested penguin eggs and chicks instead," Dr. Pütz says.
Stronger Storms and Different Migration Routes Add to the Threat
Predators are not the only challenge facing the Antipodes penguins. Increasingly powerful storms, consistent with wider climate trends across the Southern Ocean, have caused landslides that break up breeding colonies and leave the birds more vulnerable.
Differences in ocean habitats and seasonal movements may also help explain why the two populations have experienced such contrasting outcomes.
According to Dr. Mattern, penguins breeding on the Antipodes Islands migrate considerable distances into the Antarctic Polar Frontal Zone when the breeding season ends. In contrast, birds from the Bounty Islands remain closer to their nesting grounds, where the surrounding waters are more sheltered and may offer more abundant food.
These differences could leave the two populations exposed to very different environmental pressures, despite belonging to the same species.
The Strange Paradox of Schrödinger's Penguin
The researchers have named this unusual situation "Schrödinger's Penguin," drawing inspiration from the famous physics thought experiment involving a cat inside a sealed box.
In that experiment, the cat is imagined to be both alive and dead until the box is opened and its condition is observed. But Dr. Mattern explains that the penguin discovery turns the familiar concept around.
"With Schrödinger's cat, opening the box settles the question one way or the other.
"With Erect-crested penguins, it's the opposite. From a distance, without proper surveys, everyone assumed there was a single answer for the whole species.
"Once we actually opened the metaphorical box and looked, we found there wasn't one state at all, but two: stable on the Bounty Islands, declining on the Antipodes Islands."
In other words, looking at the species as a whole can conceal what is happening within individual populations. Only by examining both island groups separately did researchers uncover how dramatically their circumstances differ.
A Hidden Conservation Crisis for Endangered Penguins
The Erect-crested penguin is currently one of only four penguin species worldwide classified as "Endangered" on the International Union for Conservation of Nature Red List. Another New Zealand penguin, the hoiho/yellow-eyed penguin, shares that designation.
However, the two species have received very different levels of attention. While the plight of the hoiho has attracted ongoing public interest and conservation efforts, the Erect-crested penguin has remained relatively overlooked.
Dr. Mattern explains that the species' current conservation classification relies on population estimates from the 1970s that were considerably inflated. When the new survey results are considered, the "Endangered" designation remains broadly appropriate for the declining Antipodes population, but not for the stable Bounty Islands population.
This creates a difficult conservation dilemma. If the two populations are combined into a single assessment, the species' overall threat classification could actually improve, even though one population continues to decline sharply.
"Averaged across both populations, the global ranking would actually improve to "Vulnerable," masking the severity of the Antipodes decline, and downplaying how exposed the Bounty Islands, likely the species' last secure stronghold, are to industrial fishing."
The researchers warn that a more favorable overall classification could create a misleading impression of security. Although the Bounty Islands population remains stable, it may still face significant threats, particularly from industrial fishing activity.
"A single, ostensibly improved threat ranking is like putting the lid back on Schrödinger's box, trading a convenient illusion for the stronger protection the Bounty Islands population actually needs," Dr. Mattern says.
The findings highlight why conservation efforts must account for the circumstances of individual populations rather than relying exclusively on a species' global status. For Erect-crested penguins, recognizing the differences between the two island groups could be essential to protecting their future.
The study received funding from the Vontobel Foundation (Switzerland) through the Antarctic Research Trust and from the Global Penguin Society. The research was carried out under permits issued by the New Zealand Department of Conservation.

title: See Jupiter and Mars make a spectacular close approach overnight Nov. 15-16
text:
Heads up stargazers! Mars meets Jupiter for a spectacular rendezvous in the heart of the constellation Leo on the night of Nov. 15-16, and they won't be this close again until July 2029.
Jupiter and Mars will appear a little over 1 degree from each other as they rise over the eastern horizon around midnight for viewers in the U.S., as the blue-white light of the main-sequence star Regulus glows below, according to In-The-Sky.
It's all a trick of perspective, but spectacular nonetheless. In reality Mars and Jupiter are separated by a gulf of over 368 million miles (592 million kilometers), while the light from Regulus has travelled for some 79 light-years before reaching Earth.
The spectacular display occurs just once every 2-2.5 years, when Mars catches up to Jupiter as it plies its more distant orbit, making the pair appear side by side from our Earthly vantage point — an event known to astronomers as an appulse.
Both Mars and Jupiter are "superior planets" whose orbits exist beyond that of Earth. As a result their disks always appear full to us through the eyepiece of a telescope, unlike the inner planets Mercury and Venus, which exhibit moon-like phases as they circle the sun.
A 6-inch telescope can reveal the wildly differing natures of the solar system worlds. Slew your scope to Jupiter to spot the gargantuan cloud bands (and zones) that ring the gas giant, formed from masses of ammonia and water that travel in different directions through Jupiter's hydrogen and helium atmosphere, driven by powerful jet streams.
Mars, meanwhile, appears as a reddish, ochre disk complete with dark surface features, where basaltic rock has been scoured clean of the iron-rich dust that covers much of its surface, according to NASA.
Interested in seeing and capturing the planets for yourself? Then be sure to read our guide on everything you need to observe and photograph the planets of the solar system, along with our picks of the top telescopes, cameras and lenses for exploring the night sky in 2026.
Editor's Note: If you would like to share your photos of Mars and Jupiter with Space.com's readers, then please send your photo(s), comments, and your name and location to spacephotos@space.com.

title: England's Atkinson set for All Blacks dream date
text:
England centre Seb Atkinson says he is living a childhood dream as he prepares to face New Zealand in Twickenham on Saturday.
The Gloucester pivot has recovered from a hip knock and is set to return to the starting XV at number 12 for the visit of the wounded All Blacks.
For Atkinson, this weekend's game comes a fortnight after he made his first Allianz Stadium appearance with England in the 45-22 thumping of Australia.
"It's sort of ticking off wishes and dreams that you have as a young aspiring rugby player," Atkinson told BBC Sport.
"Watching [England against New Zealand in 2012] when Manu [Tuilagi] scored that try and set up that try, the big performance in the semi-final of the World Cup a few years ago [in 2019].
"And obviously I was frustrated to not be available last year when the team put in a good performance.
"So a lot of things spring to mind and to be able to be out there and show what I can do on that stage will be really exciting for me personally."
England v New Zealand
Nations Championship
Saturday, 21 November at 14:10 GMT
Allianz Stadium, Twickenham
Listen to match commentary on BBC Radio 5 Extra, BBC Sounds, BBC Sport website and through your smart speaker
New Zealand - beaten 33-19 by England on the same stage last November - will recall several big-name players this weekend.
They are looking to make amends for a shock defeat by Wales in Cardiff, with Atkinson set to line up against the heralded Jordie Barrett in midfield.
Atkinson has observed and admired Barrett at his best, but he is determined to be his own man.
"I love rugby and I love watching rugby and I love watching the likes of Jordie and [South Africa World Cup winner] Damian de Allende and try and take bits from their game," Atkinson said.
"But I know that fundamentally for me to get better as a player I need to be myself. I can't just replicate other people.
"You're trying to take away what they're good at - but also show what you're good at too."
New Zealand head coach Dave Rennie said his group would "poke each other in the chest" at the start of this week as they pick the bones out of a chastening first loss to Wales in 73 years.
Rennie said the All Blacks "let the country down" against the Welsh, but with an expected 500 caps of experience to come into the New Zealand matchday squad, England senior coach Richard Wigglesworth says the home side are preparing for the highest standard of opposition regardless of what happened in Cardiff.
"It changes nothing," Wigglesworth said.
"We get a different team. It is a massive challenge for us. England against New Zealand is an historic game. We just want to bring the best of us and give it a good rip."

title: ‘Chloe’s policy’ aims to prevent repeat of case of Treasury worker who took her own life
text:
The parents of a Treasury worker who took her own life last year have launched a policy that directs employers to treat staff in a kinder and more commonsense way, and are asking HR departments across the country to adopt it.
Chloe Moffat’s parents also said the government department plans to plant a memorial garden in her honour at its Horse Guards Road offices.
Moffat, a 26-year-old personal assistant, took her own life the day after she was called into a surprise disciplinary meeting about anonymous complaints alleging she had disclosed sensitive information at work, which she denied. A coroner found in August that the Treasury had “materially contributed” to her death.
She had been convinced she would lose her job, the coroner heard, despite that not being a likely outcome. Moffat’s managers declined to allow her to bring a colleague to the “informal” meeting, did not give her any advance notice of it and refused to tell her whether she was likely to lose her job. They also removed access to her director’s email and changed her work responsibilities.
She had worked at the Treasury for almost three years, loved her job and had an exemplary employment record, the coroner heard.
Her parents, Anne and David Moffat, have been working with the Global Kindness Institute, an NGO, to come up with “Chloe’s policy” for HR departments to adopt to prevent such tragic incidents from happening in future. They are calling on organisations across the country to help develop and take on the policy.
“All we want is for nobody else to go through this,” Anne Moffat said. “If it goes through HR departments, even people considering making allegations, everybody can hopefully follow the Chloe policy and ask if this is really necessary.
“So many people are so policy driven and so into disciplinaries and making people accountable when it may not be necessary. People aren’t being treated in a commonsense, human way.”
The policy calls on HR departments to consider the harms of disciplinary processes to those subjected to them, particularly when complaints are anonymous or unverified. It emphasises prioritising psychological safety and supporting those going through any disciplinary process, as well as minimising these processes in the first place by considering alternatives.
It also calls on HR departments to provide clarity to those going through disciplinary processes, including letting people know if their role is safe.
David Moffat said: “It’s a powerful leadership standard. If it raises the profile of the process that Chloe went through and avoids it happening to anyone else, that is good enough for me.”
The Treasury’s response to the coroner’s prevention of future deaths report acknowledged the department’s role in her death and committed to safeguards. A review of the civil service by the Cabinet Office found that the conditions to which Moffat was subjected had been replicated in other disciplinary meetings.
Anne Moffat said: “If you think about what happened to Chloe, if HR had thought ‘we know that she was very well thought of, nothing else had ever happened, these were the first ever allegations, they were anonymous,’ was this process necessary?”
The prevention of future deaths report issued by the coroner last month found there was still a risk at the civil service due to its disciplinary procedures. The civil service has put in place multiple safeguards to address these issues.
This guidance includes allowing staff to have a supporter in disciplinary meetings, giving proper notice of any such meeting, and informing staff if a dismissal is not likely. The Treasury is also hiring an on-site occupational therapist to support staff wellbeing.
The Moffats met James Bowler, the permanent secretary at the Treasury, at the end of last month. David said: “We felt listened to, and as part of their response to the coroner as well we felt reassured that change was being implemented.
“If the changes they have put forward to the coroner had already been in place, we certainly feel that Chloe would be with us today. It was a very emotional meeting.”
Anne added: “It is the first time we felt that the Treasury had been compassionate to us and it wasn’t defensive or legal speak. They are looking at how to remember Chloe, and looking at the possibility of a memorial garden within the building and marking the garden with a plaque.”
David said: “We feel that Chloe is finally being acknowledged and remembered.”
A Treasury spokesperson said: “The Treasury’s deepest sympathies continue to be with Chloe’s friends and family, and the department continues to mourn our colleague.
“Our response to the coroner’s prevention of future deaths report sets out the action we have taken following this tragic case. An independent review found staff acted in good faith and with a duty of care throughout.”

title: U.S. tightens controls on remote access to AI technology amid Nvidia fallout
text:
The U.S. government has announced a rule to prevent remote access to advanced artificial intelligence chips and servers, closing a loophole that could let adversarial governments access American AI technology through overseas data centers.
The move comes amid the fallout at Nvidia, the world's dominant producer of AI chips, following revelations that CEO Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with a woman who U.S. intelligence officials suspected of being a Chinese intelligence operative. NPR has not independently verified the claims. Huang stepped down as CEO last week.
Alice Huang, who is not related to Jensen Huang, is a former executive at Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based data center company. Jensen Huang has personally lobbied President Trump to loosen restrictions on Nvidia chip sales to China. It is not known if Alice Huang influenced this activity.
The rapid advancement in cloud computing and AI infrastructure has made it possible to access advanced U.S. computing capabilities remotely, including through data centers located outside countries subject to U.S. export restrictions, the U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) said in a statement on Monday.
The rule is designed to reinforce existing restrictions on access to sensitive American AI technology through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in other countries, which could threaten national security
However, a loophole existed where Chinese companies could still access those chips remotely, despite U.S. restrictions on their physical sale to China.
"The United States is the global leader in advanced computing and super intelligence technology and is committed to promoting the global adoption of American technology for legitimate commercial purposes while ensuring that sensitive technologies are not exploited in ways that threaten U.S. national security," the BIS statement said.
The government refers to artificial intelligence as "super intelligence" following an executive order signed by President Trump in September.
Since October 2022, U.S. companies have typically needed a BIS export license to sell advanced computing chips meeting specified technical thresholds to China, including Hong Kong and Macau. These restrictions covered advanced Nvidia chips, some high-performance semiconductor components, and certain AI computing systems.
Megaspeed is based in Singapore and operates facilities in Malaysia.
"Megaspeed conducts legitimate and lawful business. The company has retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation," the company said in a statement emailed to NPR and other news organizations on Sunday.
In a joint statement late Monday, the Department of Commerce and the Department of Justice said that U.S. authorities had launched a criminal investigation into Megaspeed in 2025 after conducting an "on-site, in-person, end-use check" at the Singaporean-based company and interviewing its then CEO Alice Huang.
"Following this enforcement action, the Department of Justice took the lead role in the criminal investigation against Megaspeed," the statement said.
In the statement posted on X, the two departments said they "will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred."
The statement also provided a timeline of the ongoing probe against Megaspeed, detailing how the investigation was initiated in 2024 by the Department of Commerce "for potential export control violations" after "identifying suspicious activity through proactive monitoring of potential sensitive semiconductor diversion." It said that the probe involved a request to Nvidia to provide records of "direct or indirect sales" to the company. According to the statement, by June 2025 Nvidia had placed Megaspeed on their "no sell" list.
Prior to the Nvidia scandal, the Trump administration had resisted imposing additional regulations to prevent foreign access to American AI technology.
The Biden administration had written a framework designed to control worldwide distribution of advanced AI chips on January 15, 2025 – five days before Trump's inauguration. In May 2025, Trump's Commerce Department announced it would not enforce the rule and intended to rescind it, calling it "ill-conceived and counterproductive."
Biden's framework would have also limited access to AI chips by countries considered security risks, required licenses for certain chip exports, and created restrictions on the power of advanced models and computing infrastructure.
The New York Times reported that Trump was first briefed by intelligence officials about Jensen Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy in October 2025. Both Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick are expected to testify before Congress this month and next month and there will likely be further investigations into what Trump knew about the affair when the Democrats take control of Congress in January 2027, Rep. Yvette Clarke, D-NY, told NPR.
"We need to get the facts investigated, bring in individuals to give us as much information as possible under oath, so that we can get to the bottom of why this happened, how it occurred, and how we could prevent this type of compromise from happening again," said Clarke.

title: Greenhouse gas levels set records again in 2025, U.N. says
text:
Geneva — Greenhouse gas concentrations in the atmosphere rose to record highs in 2025, locking in impacts that will persist for centuries, the United Nations said on Tuesday.
Levels of the three main greenhouse gases -- the climate-warming carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide -- all rose to unprecedented figures in 2025, the U.N.'s weather and climate agency said.
The World Meteorological Organization said the rise would lead to more long-term temperature increases for the planet.
The WMO's 22nd annual Greenhouse Gas Bulletin comes ahead of the COP31 U.N. climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, from Nov. 9 to Nov. 20.
"Another year, another new record," said WMO Deputy Secretary-General Ko Barrett.
"Greenhouse gases are trapping an unprecedented amount of heat in the atmosphere, providing energy for more extreme weather and associated risks to our economies and societies.
"The past 11 years have been the warmest on record and this trend is set to continue. Carbon dioxide (CO2) has a very long life-time and so will affect the global climate not just for years but for decades and even centuries."
El Nino's impact
The bulletin looks at greenhouse gas concentrations -- the amount of those gases in the atmosphere -- rather than new annual emissions amounts as the world burns more coal, oil and gas.
In 2025, carbon dioxide concentrations were at 426.8 parts per million (ppm); methane at 1,948 parts per billion, and nitrous oxide at 339.1 parts per billion.
That takes them, respectively, to 153%, 267% and 126% of the pre-industrial levels witnessed before 1750.
Of the three major greenhouse gases, CO2 accounts for about 66% of the warming effect on the climate.
Around half of the total CO2 emitted each year remains in the atmosphere; the rest is absorbed by the land and oceans.
From 2024 to 2025, the global average concentration of CO2 rose by 2.8 ppm -- smaller than the record surge from 2023 to 2024 of 3.6 ppm.
WMO senior scientific officer Oksana Tarasova said this reflected the "recovery of the land carbon sinks and reduced fire carbon emissions in 2025 after the strong 2023/2024 El Nino," the naturally occurring, climate-warming weather phenomenon.
"However, a 2.8 ppm annual increase is still a substantial addition of carbon to the atmosphere from fossil fuel burning."
It is also above the average growth rate for the past decade of 2.6 ppm -- a figure that stood at 0.8 ppm in the 1960s.
"We can expect to see a further increase in concentrations in 2026 because of fossil fuel burning and the development of a powerful El Nino which will impact land carbon sinks, as it did in 2023/2024," Tarasova warned.
Methane accounts for about 16% of the warming effect on our climate by long-lived greenhouse gases, though it has a much shorter lifetime than CO2.
Around a third of methane emitted into the atmosphere comes from natural sources like wetlands, with the rest from anthropogenic sources such as cattle, rice farming, landfills and biomass burning.
The bulletin said that as countries shift their energy systems toward decarbonization, more attention should be paid to two potent but less abundant trace gases closely related to electricity production and distribution: molecular hydrogen (H2) and sulfur hexafluoride (SF6).
SF6 has been rising steadily over the past three decades. It is used primarily as a spark suppressant in electricity distribution.
Why hydrogen levels have increased over the past decade is unknown but it has begun to be used as an energy storage medium.

title: Fans cheer as popular online platform for spinoff stories nears full return after security incident
text:
The Archive of Our Own, a popular global fandom site, is making a limited return after a security incident led to a shutdown on Oct. 29
In a comeback tale like one from Harry Potter battling back his nemesis or a “Heated Rivalry” hockey hero rebounding from injury, a top global fandom site that was sidelined by a security incident is now on the mend.
The activist group behind the popular Archive of Our Own, or AO3, platform, a collaborative online space which serves up fans’ spinoff narratives derived from well-known published stories, says it’s undergoing a limited return after a shutdown on Oct. 29.
“AO3 is now up!” said a status page for the Organization for Transformative Works, an activist group behind the platform, on Sunday.
The outage sent fans of the platform — readers and authors alike — into a desperate void for the past two weeks with a “Bad Gateway” message stirring frustration. The return drew many expressions of joy Sunday.
The organization, in a summary it posted on Instagram of its 2025 results, said nearly 2.6 million AO3 works were created, with nearly 40 billion page views. Nearly 2 million accounts have been created, it said.
AO3 hasn't been without its critics, who have warned about sexual content that could be available to minors and fandom racism through the platform.
The group said some features like user icons have been disabled and importing of external work isn’t available, while downloads are currently only possible in the web-language HTML format. It promised those features will ultimately return.
The team predicted that the security incident would take up to four weeks for AO3 to get back up, while floating the prospect of a partial revival “in a degraded state” — which appears to be what was taking place on Sunday.
The organization said contributors’ “works, bookmarks, kudos, etc., are still safe” and that no drafts were deleted during the outage — but it couldn’t rule out that the user database might have been compromised.
“We understand that the wait and uncertainty surrounding AO3’s return have been difficult, and we apologize for the inconvenience,” the status update said.
AO3 is a hub of content from fans who have produced content that riffs off fiction, art and other culture and entertainment: Imagine a repository of sequels, prequels and derivatives dreamt up by adoring aficionados of some of the world’s best-known titles.
The result is catchy products like “fanfic” — fiction from fans — and similar fanart, as well as “podfics,” readings of narratives shared in audio form.
A recent listing of “ship stats” — or the number of references to relationships of stars from literature — shows that pairings of characters featured in the Harry Potter, Heated Rivalry and anime fandoms were the most prominent this summer.
The reaction from fans of the fandom platform was swift and exuberant.
“So, we've all agreed we don't need to sleep tonight, now that AO3 is finally back, right? Right!?” quipped yet.another.loon on the Threads social media site.
User Verkielos gushed: “Just got email from AO3 about a fic update. The world is healing!”
Associated Press writer Stefanie Dazio in Berlin contributed to this report.

title: Werner Holzer Prize awarded to Katja Gloger and DW's Jaafar Abdul Karim
text:
At a time when press freedom is under pressure and international newsrooms are shrinking, the Werner Holzer Prize celebrates a profession that many consider indispensable to democracy: foreign correspondence.
Presented in honor of Werner Holzer, the veteran reporter and former editor-in-chief of the German daily newspaper Frankfurter Rundschau, this year's award coincided with what would have been his 100th birthday. Holzer spent decades reporting from some of the world's most important hot spots and championing international journalism.
At the award ceremony in Frankfurt's Römer, the city's historic town hall, Mayor Mike Josef recalled that fundamental rights such as freedom of speech and freedom of the press were first enshrined for all Germans by the Frankfurt Parliament in the nearby Paulskirche in 1848.
The 2026 winners reflect the breadth and ambition of the award. First prize went to Katja Gloger, a veteran Russia correspondent who moved to Moscow in 1989 and accompanied Vladimir Putin during the early years of his presidency.
In her recent nonfiction book, "The Failure: An Investigative Report of Germany's Russia Policy," Gloger and co-author Georg Mascolo offer a searing critique of the misjudgments and illusions that shaped German policy toward Russia for decades.
Second prize was awarded to DW journalist and presenter Jaafar Abdul Karim. His talk show JaafarTalk reaches millions of viewers across the Arab world and in Germany. Whether in Tunis, Beirut or Cairo, Abdul Karim tackles subjects that are often considered taboo.
A research grant went to freelance journalist Luise Land, whose current project explores why her German-Namibian family still owns extensive landholdings in Namibia today. By tracing that history, she examines the enduring legacy of the genocide against the Herero and Nama peoples by German colonial forces in the early 20th century.
Call for more international coverage
"Katja Gloger is one of the leading foreign policy reporters. For decades, she has been among the foremost experts on Russia and speaks out on uncomfortable truths," the jury stated on Friday, explaining its decision to honor Gloger. "Like almost no one else, she has gained access to the very heart of the Kremlin's power elite — from Mikhail Gorbachev to Vladimir Putin."
At the prize-giving ceremony, Gloger delivered a passionate plea for more journalism — and more international coverage — in the German press. "We must defend trustworthy, reliable and fact-based journalism with everything in our power," she said.
Gloger worked for Reporters Without Borders for 12 years. "The latest rankings show that only one in 100 people can get their information from free, independent journalism and a free, independent press. That shows what's at stake," she said.
The prize winner also said she would dedicate the award to journalists in exile and to her colleagues at Novaya Gazeta, the independent Russian newspaper long known for its critical reporting on the Kremlin. Earlier this week, the paper was forced to shut down its operations in Russia and leave its Moscow newsroom.
Belief in the power of dialogue
In his acceptance speech, Jaafar Abdul Karim said journalism has become more challenging and exhausting than ever. The DW host spoke of hatred and incitement, attacks and threats, both online and offline, in the regions he reports on as well as in Germany.
Such pressure, he said, takes a personal toll — yet giving up is not an option. "When I listen to my heart, I know I have to keep going," he said. The answer, he argued, is a form of journalism that fosters dialogue, embraces multiple perspectives and helps bridge divides rather than deepen them.
"I firmly believe in the power of dialogue, today more than ever. That's why we must talk to one another. Even when it gets difficult. Even when we disagree. Or perhaps precisely because of that," he said.
Listening doesn't mean agreeing, and understanding doesn't mean being in agreement. "Especially now, in times of polarization, when those who believe they're always right are often the loudest, we as journalists have a special responsibility. When everyone is just shouting into their own bubbles or communities, we need journalists who connect these bubbles with one another," he said.
The jury praised Abdul Karim for creating programs at DW that reach millions of young people across the Arab world and in Germany. "His journalism fosters dialogue between countries, between generations, and between religions. He has set new standards," the jury stated.
So far in 2026, JaafarTalk has already garnered more than 1.1 billion views across all platforms, and its community has grown to more than 9 million followers. Its motto: "Diversity fosters dialogue."
"We need fact-based journalism that promotes dialogue and reflects the diversity of our society," Abdul Karim stressed. "By that, I mean an honest and open dialogue in which we do not look away or remain silent. On the contrary, we must take a clear stand against racism, antisemitism, Islamophobia, discrimination, sexism, and hate speech — no matter which side they come from."

title: Classified network used by US intelligence to share information goes down in latest tech failure: report
text:
A “highly classified network” used by the National Security Agency went down Tuesday, multiple sources familiar with the matter told CNN.
NSA employees use the network, known as NSA Net, to share classified materials internally. CNN reported that there was no indication of a cyberattack. As a precaution, the Maryland-based intelligence agency has “enacted staggered arrivals for personnel.”
The NSA collects and analyzes foreign electronic communications and protects sensitive government communications. Its exact workforce is classified, but it is estimated to employ tens of thousands of workers.
A source familiar with the matter told The Wall Street Journal that a software update had taken NSA Net offline, adding that the disruption would be temporary.
“The National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance,” the agency said in a statement provided to The Independent. “While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues. NSA's infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.”
The outage is the latest in a string of high-profile technology failures, several of which have disrupted daily life across the U.S.
On Thursday, Microsoft Outlook, Teams and AI Copilot were hit by a massive outage that threw workplaces around the world into disarray and stretched into Friday. Microsoft attributed the disruption to a software bug compounded by heavier traffic and reduced server capacity.
On Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration ordered a rare nationwide ground stop — the longest since 9/11 — that led to thousands of flight cancellations and left passengers stranded across the country. Trump administration officials blamed the disruption on a routine router upgrade in Arkansas, and have called on Congress to authorize “emergency” FAA funding.
Then on Monday, a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase rippled through the U.S. financial system, preventing thousands of customers from accessing their online accounts. A spokesperson said the bank had sustained “a temporary issue related to a software bug in an on-premise hardware system.”
None of these disruptions have been linked to one another, nor have they been attributed to cyberattacks or malicious behavior.
The spate of outages prompted tech experts to warn of weaknesses in the infrastructure underpinning the modern economy.
“The real lesson is how many separate services quietly depend on the same few providers,” Danielle Lemons, vice president of operations at Nashville-based IT firm DirecTech Connect, told The Independent on Monday. “When one of them goes down, email, file sharing, sign-ins and even phone systems can fail together, because they were all built on the same foundation.”
”The real cause for concern isn't a single master threat—it is the underlying reality that our digital economy has become so hyper-connected that isolated software bugs, database corruptions, or routing errors now trigger immediate, high-visibility disruption across millions of lives,” added Fran Villalba Segarra, founder and CEO of INTERNXT, a cybersecurity company based in Spain.

title: ASRA NOMANI: Far-left US groups battle Trump plan to rival China's tech dominance
text:
As President Donald Trump attends the 49th ASEAN Summit in the Philippines, American communist and far-left organizations are mobilizing internationally against an American initiative designed to reduce reliance on China.
According to a Fox News Digital investigation, a network of 120 mostly communist, socialist and far-left U.S. groups – many of them pro-China – are joining protests in Asia opposing the Trump administration's effort to build an artificial intelligence and semiconductor hub in the Philippines that would reduce U.S. dependence on China in the AI war.
The target is the Pax Silica tech industrial hub in the Philippines, which Undersecretary of State for Economic Affairs Jacob Helberg, a former senior adviser at Palantir Technologies, said last year would strengthen American control over AI infrastructure, semiconductor production and critical mineral supply chains. Two days ago, Helberg described Pax Silica as key to the world's "superintelligence revolution."
The dispute centers partly on the proposed Clark Advanced Manufacturing Park, a roughly 4,000-acre development in New Clark City, Tarlac, in the Philippines, that would be a hub for the Pax Silica project.
A Fox News Digital investigation traced support for the protests to a transnational pro-China activist network stretching from Manila to New York, Washington, D.C., Los Angeles and Canada, including the Democratic Socialists of America East Bay, Calif., chapter and organizations with ties to American-born, Shanghai-based Marxist tech millionaire Neville Roy Singham. The protests also include indigenous groups in the Philippines that allege Pax Silica is being built on ancestral land.
About eight of 10 of the organizations in the network of 120 are openly communist, socialist or "anti-imperialist."
In addition, most of them are openly "anti-Zionist," opposed to the existence of a Jewish state of Israel, according to a Fox News Digital analysis of the groups in the network.
CodePink, a pro-communist, pro-China nonprofit co-founded by Singham's wife, Jodie Evans, has used its media programming to criticize Pax Silica as a "military-industrial-surveillance complex."
For Washington, experts say, the Pax Silica plan is about securing the technology and resources needed to compete with Beijing. For opponents, the protests are a way to curb American economic and military domination.
The campaign also reveals how opposition to Trump's China strategy is being organized not only overseas, but through pro-China activist networks inside the United States.
The U.S. network, organizing behind a campaign called "Shut Down Pax," includes familiar faces in the Singham network's protest circuit: BAYAN USA, a pro-communist Filipino American alliance helping lead the campaign; Anakbayan USA, a pro-communist youth organization; and the International League of Peoples' Struggle, or ILPS, founded with the help of Jose Maria Sison, the late founder of the Communist Party of the Philippines.
The campaign has also reached the U.S. Congress. A letter, headlined "Shut Down Pax Silica in the Philippines" calls on lawmakers to halt the initiative pending review of environmental protections, labor rights and the treatment of Philippine communities.
The activism intersects with other nonprofits in the network funded by Singham, including the People's Forum and BreakThrough News, that have promoted opposition to American foreign policy and challenged Washington's confrontation with Beijing.
On Sept. 20, the U.S. chapter of the International League of Peoples' Struggle, the International Coalition for Human Rights in the Philippines-US and Bagong Alyansang Makabayan USA, or BAYAN USA, launched the "Shut Down Pax Silica Campaign Network" in Queens, New York, with organizers claiming about 500 participants in person and online.
An article, published by Bulatlat, invoked a term popular in communist, "anti-imperialist" circles, claiming that a movement had begun in "the belly of the beast," with "resistance" to Pax Silica "rising."
"We unite to confront and oppose the Trump/U.S.-led Pax Silica Initiative in its competition with China to dominate the AI/tech supply chain," the coalition declared in its organizing platform.
"We Filipinos in the U.S. must also take action," BAYAN USA declares on its campaign website, urging opposition to U.S. investments associated with Pax Silica.
A month later, on Oct. 24, CodePink Radio published Episode 374, with host Marcy Winograd interviewing sociologist William Robinson about his new book, "Pax Silica: The New Ruling Class," examining the "rise of a new transnational capital complex" that combines big tech with global finance and the "military-industrial-surveillance complex" to "colonize the world unless we continue to protest, disrupt, divest and withhold our labor."
The Black Alliance for Peace, which participated in CodePink's November "Taxpayer Uprising" campaign in Washington, D.C., last week, also promoted the anti-Pax Silica campaign's launch.
Anakbayan USA, its local chapters and GABRIELA USA, a Filipino women's organization, appear among the American coalition's participants. Their Philippine counterparts are involved in the demonstrations surrounding Trump's visit.
The coalition's published platform also identifies "Migrante USA," student organizations and other activist groups.
The overlapping campaigns bring together Filipino American organizations, socialist activists and groups that have previously organized against U.S. military operations, Israel and American foreign policy.
Singham, an American-born technology entrepreneur who sold his consultancy ThoughtWorks for an estimated $785 million in 2017, has financed an extensive network of U.S. nonprofits.
A Fox News Digital investigation traced $278 million into six core American nonprofits, including CodePink, People's Forum, Tricontinental and BreakThrough BT Media Inc., which operates BreakThrough News.
In July, the House Ways and Means Committee subpoenaed three organizations as lawmakers investigated the financial network and potential foreign influence. The organizations have challenged the investigation.
One connection to the anti-Pax Silica campaign from the Singham network is "Nodutdol for Korean Community Development," an American group listed among the coalition's endorsers.
Nodutdol member Winter Oh participated in the September launch in Queens.
BreakThrough News has amplified the Philippine protests and criticism of Pax Silica, this summer promoting a BAYAN and Kilusang Mayo Uno demonstration with the slogan "The Philippines is not for sale!" As Trump was still in flight to Manila, BreakThrough news highlighted growing opposition to Pax Silica with a story headline, "ASEAN summit in Manila met with protests over Trump’s participation."
Philippine officials have previously accused organizations such as Gabriela, Anakbayan, Karapatan and Kilusang Mayo Uno of acting as communist fronts. The groups have denied those allegations.
The ideological roots of the campaign extend to the Communist Party of the Philippines, founded by Sison in 1968.
The United States designated the Communist Party of the Philippines and its armed wing, the New People's Army, as a foreign terrorist organization.
In a Nov. 7 editorial, the party's official newspaper, Ang Bayan, urged Filipinos to organize "widespread protests" against Trump and to "reject and drive him out."
The editorial accused Trump of advancing Pax Silica to strengthen American control over Philippine resources.
The publication also reported that clandestine organizations associated with the National Democratic Front of the Philippines staged demonstrations. One teachers' group, KAGUMA, reportedly chanted, "Join the New People's Army!"
The American campaign includes explicitly communist organizations, including the Workers World Party, a Marxist-Leninist organization, and the International Action Center.
Separately, "Fight Back! News," published by the Freedom Road Socialist Organization, a Marxist-Leninist group that has organized many anti-ICE protests this year, republished an editorial from Ang Bayan criticizing Trump's Pax Silica initiative.
The International League of Peoples' Struggle called for global protests under the slogans "Trump Out!" and "Reject Pax Silica!" The organization said groups planned demonstrations in 23 cities worldwide, including locations in the United States, Canada, Europe and Asia.
American organizers identified planned actions in Los Angeles, Oregon, Washington, D.C., New York and Honolulu.
In Ottawa, International League of Peoples' Struggle Canada, Anakbayan Ottawa, Migrante Ottawa and "Ottawa for Palestine" announced a demonstration for Wednesday outside the U.S. Embassy under the slogan "Shut the Pax Down!"
In an April proposal to the U.S. State Department, Philippine officials outlined plans involving critical minerals, industrial infrastructure, investment and technology development.
Protesters allege the project could displace Ayta Indigenous communities, expand mining, and strain electricity and water supplies.
Philippine officials dispute allegations that the project would create a U.S.-controlled enclave or include the massive AI data centers described by activists. They say the development remains subject to Philippine law.
As Trump arrived, demonstrations escalated.
Reuters footage showed students marching with anti-Trump banners. SunStar reported more than 200 arrests during demonstrations in Metro Manila, while GMA News reported that activists condemned police dispersals and disputed the government's response.

title: AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death
text:
Scientists have uncovered a hidden warning sign in routine heart scans that could predict sudden cardiac death before it strikes. The AI-powered discovery outperformed conventional screening methods, potentially revealing thousands of people at risk of a fatal heart malfunction that doctors might otherwise miss.
More than 300,000 people in the United States die from sudden cardiac arrest each year. This deadly emergency occurs when the heart's electrical system suddenly fails, causing the heart to stop pumping blood. It can strike older adults with known heart conditions as well as seemingly healthy young athletes. Although implanted defibrillators can prevent some of these deaths, doctors have long struggled to determine which patients need them most.
Now, researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a previously overlooked warning signal in routine heart scans that could make it easier to recognize people at risk before a fatal event occurs.
The discovery was made using artificial intelligence trained on more than 440,000 electrocardiograms, or EKGs, collected in Sweden. By comparing the electrical patterns recorded in these scans with information from death certificates, the researchers taught an AI system to recognize subtle differences between healthy individuals, patients with known heart risks, and people who eventually died from sudden cardiac causes.
The team then evaluated the technology using thousands of additional patient records from the United States and Taiwan, testing whether the patterns could reliably identify people at heightened risk in different populations.
AI Detects Hidden Heart Risks That Standard Tests Miss
The results suggest that AI can identify vulnerable patients more effectively than the conventional tests doctors typically rely on. Current screening methods largely focus on how much blood the heart pumps with each contraction, a measurement used to assess whether someone might benefit from an implanted defibrillator.
Using these traditional measurements, doctors can identify a group of patients with an annual sudden cardiac death rate of 4.6%. The AI system, however, identified a group with an annual death rate of 7%, demonstrating a greater ability to distinguish patients facing serious danger.
Importantly, the algorithm also recognized a broader population of people at elevated risk, including thousands who would not normally raise concerns under existing medical guidelines. Most of these individuals would have been classified as relatively low risk using conventional methods.
Another major advantage is that the AI system works with ordinary EKG images, which are already routinely collected in hospitals and medical centers around the world. This means the technology could potentially improve screening without requiring an entirely new type of medical test.
The findings, published in Nature, could eventually help physicians make more informed decisions about who should receive an implanted defibrillator. They also raise an intriguing scientific question about what changes inside the heart produce the electrical patterns that AI has learned to recognize.
"Medical decisions are really hard, and I think that's why AI is so exciting for me," said Ziad Obermeyer, an associate professor at UC Berkeley's School of Public Health and the study's lead author. "We can not only make better decisions, but also start to understand what's actually going on with these patients before their heart stops."
Why Sudden Cardiac Death Is So Difficult to Predict
Sudden cardiac arrest is different from a heart attack. A heart attack happens when blood flow to part of the heart becomes blocked or severely restricted. Cardiac arrest, by contrast, results from a failure of the electrical signals that coordinate the heartbeat.
Immediate CPR and an electrical shock from an automated external defibrillator can sometimes restore the heart's rhythm. However, roughly 90% of people who experience sudden cardiac arrest outside a hospital die within minutes, making early recognition of those at risk especially important.
For Obermeyer, an emergency physician whose research combines artificial intelligence, medicine, and health policy, sudden cardiac death remains one of medicine's most frustrating unsolved problems.
Because victims often die without warning, researchers have limited opportunities to observe what happens inside the heart immediately before it stops. An autopsy may uncover blocked blood vessels, hardened tissue, or other structural abnormalities, but it cannot fully reveal how the heart was functioning in the moments leading up to death.
"One thing that makes the problem very tragic, but also very well suited for AI, is that we have the cure for this problem," Obermeyer said. "If you knew you were one of the people who was going to drop dead, you would go to a cardiologist and you'd get a defibrillator implanted. The problem is that doctors can't figure out who needs one before it's too late."
The Problem With Current Heart Risk Screening
Doctors currently rely heavily on a measurement of how effectively the heart pushes blood out with each beat. Patients whose hearts pump below a specified threshold may be considered candidates for an implantable cardioverter defibrillator, a device that can deliver an electrical shock when a dangerous heart rhythm develops.
But obtaining this measurement generally requires a more extensive medical evaluation. Many people who eventually experience sudden cardiac arrest never receive such testing because they have no obvious reason to suspect they are in danger.
The approach also has limitations for patients who are identified as high risk. About two-thirds of implanted defibrillators in these patients never need to deliver a shock. As a result, many individuals undergo expensive, invasive procedures for potentially fatal emergencies that may never occur.
At the same time, thousands of people who are not recognized as being at risk die unexpectedly each year.
"In some fraction of those people, we could have prevented those deaths if we had just known it in time," Obermeyer said. "There are a lot of lives being lost from people who are dropping dead of sudden cardiac death that are preventable if we just had better AI tools to find these things."
The researchers hope that identifying more accurate warning signs could help doctors direct preventive treatments toward the patients most likely to benefit.
How Researchers Trained AI to Recognize Deadly Heart Patterns
Developing the algorithm required three independent collections of medical data gathered from different parts of the world.
The researchers began with six years of EKG recordings from Sweden's unified healthcare system. By linking these scans to death certificates, they could examine the electrical patterns of patients who later experienced sudden cardiac death and compare them with those of other patients.
The AI learned to identify combinations of spikes, waves, and other characteristics in the recordings that appeared to be associated with increased risk. Once the system had been trained, the team tested it against two additional datasets: two years of anonymized EKG records from a San Diego hospital system and a separate collection of patient data from Taipei.
This international testing helped researchers evaluate whether the algorithm's predictive abilities extended beyond the Swedish population used to develop it.
"Good AI starts with good data," said Obermeyer, who is also part of the joint UCSF-UC Berkeley Computational Precision Health program. "Unfortunately, data like the ones we used for this study are incredibly hard to access. It's a big part of why there's so little clinical AI in use today."
Obtaining and organizing the information was itself a massive undertaking. According to Obermeyer, assembling the datasets took approximately 10 years and involved contributions from two organizations he helped establish, Dandelion Health and Nightingale Open Science. Both organizations work to advance medical research through better access to data and artificial intelligence.
"It's one of the tremendous luxuries of being at Berkeley," Obermeyer said. "You can pursue these projects that just are a slow burn and then have -- hopefully -- a big return when they get over the finish line."
From Hidden Heart Signals to Lifesaving Treatments
The researchers have already begun exploring how the system might be used in actual healthcare settings.
Obermeyer is collaborating with medical systems in Sweden, Taiwan, and the United States to introduce the algorithm into hospital EKG databases. The goal is to examine existing heart scans for signs of elevated risk and identify patients who may benefit from additional monitoring.
Under the proposed approach, physicians would contact patients whose EKGs receive a high-risk assessment and offer them the opportunity to wear a patch that continuously records their heart's electrical activity.
These longer recordings could provide valuable clues about the biological processes responsible for the warning signals detected by the AI. Understanding those processes could help researchers explain why certain hearts are more vulnerable to suddenly developing fatal electrical disturbances.
For some patients, the additional information might ultimately support a recommendation to receive an implanted defibrillator, potentially preventing a sudden and otherwise unexpected death.
Obermeyer has also created a website where people interested in learning about their own risk can provide basic personal information and an email address. The research team can then contact them about EKG analysis when the technology becomes more widely available.
Could AI Reveal New Secrets About the Human Heart?
Beyond its potential to improve the prevention of sudden cardiac death, the discovery highlights how artificial intelligence could help scientists investigate medical mysteries that have resisted conventional approaches.
Rather than simply identifying patients who might need treatment, the algorithm has uncovered patterns in heart activity that researchers do not yet fully understand. Studying those signals could lead to new insights into the electrical disturbances responsible for sudden cardiac death and potentially reveal additional opportunities for prevention.
Obermeyer believes this ability to uncover previously unrecognized biological patterns could become one of AI's most important contributions to medicine, opening new directions for research while helping physicians make better decisions.
"There is also going to be a new way of doing science that comes out of these tools," Obermeyer said, "and it's fun to think about how that starts happening."

title: SpaceX launches Starship on ambitious 22-hour Flight 15 test, but aborts booster 'chopsticks' catch (video)
text:
STARBASE, Texas — SpaceX launched the 15th test flight of its massive Starship rocket today (Nov. 13) and is preparing the vehicle's upper stage for its first-ever return to the launch site in less than 24 hours.
Flight 15 lifted off from SpaceX's Starbase facility here in South Texas at 5:47 p.m. ET (2247 GMT; 4:47 p.m. local Texas time). The towering Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage cleared the tower without incident and climbed into the skies under more than 18 million pounds of thrust from the booster's 33 Raptor 3 engines.
The flight continued nominally through its initial ascent, with the successful execution of Super Heavy's main engine cutoff and Ship's subsequent hot-staging — firing its own Raptors during separation from the booster — about 2.5 minutes after launch. Following stage separation, Super Heavy reoriented for a planned return to Starbase as Ship powered its way toward low Earth orbit (LEO).
SpaceX originally planned to catch Super Heavy with the Starbase launch tower's giant mechanical "chopstick" arms. But it wasn't to be: The company called off the catch attempt and brought the booster down for a controlled splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico about 6.5 minutes after launch, for reasons that were not immediately clear.
A successful catch would have been a significant milestone for SpaceX and its efforts to design Starship as a fully and rapidly reusable launch vehicle. It would have been the first successful recovery of a Version 3 (V3) Super Heavy, which SpaceX began flying earlier this year. The company previously recovered three of its V1 Super Heavy vehicles and reused two of those in later flights.
Ship goes to orbit
Ship's Raptors continued to fire following stage separation, completing their first burn just after eight minutes into flight. All went according to plan after that for Ship as well: A second engine burn lasting about 20 seconds parked Ship in LEO at an altitude of around 170 miles (275 kilometers) at T+26 minutes and 10 seconds.
"We’ve got a nominal orbit insertion, so Starship now in orbit around Earth for the second time ever," SpaceX's Dan Huot said during today's Flight 15 launch webcast. "That’s a really great moment."
Ship first reached orbit on Flight 14, which launched on Sept. 28.
Ship carried 26 of SpaceX's Starlink V3 spacecraft, which were deployed into LEO on schedule today over a 42-minute span starting 35 minutes after launch.
The upgraded wireless internet satellites are the second V3 batch to reach orbit, after a set of 26 that were delivered on Flight 14 . V3s are significantly more powerful than SpaceX's V2 Starlinks, which currently number more than 11,000 in LEO. The addition of this new set of V3s will add a terabit of data capacity to the constellation, according to SpaceX's Flight 15 mission outline. That's equivalent to the amount contributed by 10 Starlink V2 launches, which are carried out by SpaceX's Falcon 9 rocket.
Three of the V3 Starlinks flying today were equipped with cameras to point back at Ship after deployment in order to analyze its heatshield tiles and other hardware following its ascent to orbit. Their data will help SpaceX determine if Ship can indeed come home to Starbase on Saturday.
