"Starship will only execute a return to launch site if the flight control team has ensured that the vehicle systems critical for reentry maneuvers and final landing burn and tower approach are healthy," SpaceX wrote in its Flight 15 mission description.
SpaceX engineers will have ample time to go over Ship's systems before making a final landing decision. Ship is scheduled to circle Earth 14 times, spending more than 21 hours in space before coming home.
You can follow all of the action on here at Space.com via our Flight 15 live updates page.
To catch or not to catch?
SpaceX has reserved three contingency checkpoints during Flight 15's mission timeline to allow for an early Pacific Ocean return, should engineers determine a catch attempt to be unfeasible or unwise. The first comes just 10 minutes after the completion of Starlink satellite deployment, the second at T+7 hours and 15 minutes, and a final one at T+20 hours and 41 minutes.
Should Ship continue to look good through each of these milestones, SpaceX will proceed with a 10-second deorbit burn at approximately T+21 hours and 36 minutes, setting the spacecraft on a trajectory back toward South Texas. Its plunge through Earth's atmosphere will begin about 35 minutes later. SpaceX has also designated a contingency splashdown zone in the Gulf of Mexico, should conditions prevent a safe catch during Ship's final approach.
If all goes according to plan, Ship will return to Starbase on Saturday at approximately 4:17 p.m. EST (2117 GMT; 3:17 p.m. Texas time), about 22.5 hours after liftoff. A successful catch would be a major milestone for SpaceX — the first-ever recovery of a Starship upper stage.
Full reusability is central to the company's ambitions for launching its V3 Starlink satellites, as well as a proposed constellation of orbital data centers envisioned by company founder and CEO Elon Musk. The next-gen Starlink constellation will consist of about 100,000 satellites, while the AI network will be 10 times that size, Musk has said. Building and maintaining those constellations will require a mind-boggling number of launches. Indeed, SpaceX is targeting 10,000 Starship liftoffs per year by 2030, according to Musk.
Some of Starship's other planned missions won't necessarily require full reusability, but the spacecraft's reliability will be critical to NASA's Artemis program and its efforts to return astronauts to the moon. The space agency selected Starship as one of the program's crewed lunar landers, and it's slated to fly a demonstration mission with NASA's Orion spacecraft and Artemis III astronauts to Earth orbit in the summer of 2027.
Editor's note: This story was updated at 7:10 p.m. ET on Nov. 13 with news of successful payload deployment.

title: American soldier arrested by UK police on suspicion of spying taken into US military custody
text:
A US Army officer arrested in the UK on suspicion of spying for Russia earlier this month has been taken into US military custody, British counter-terror police have said.
The serviceman has been identified as Lt Col Brandon Carroll Tyner, BBC News understands. The 41-year-old - who served in the US Army since 2008 - was arrested near Gloucester last week by British counter-terror police.
Tyner was based at Imjin Barracks in Innsworth, Gloucestershire, the headquarters of Nato's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps.
Counter Terrorism Policing said he is now in US custody over suspected national security and espionage allegations. At the time of his arrest, Russia said it had "nothing to do with it".
British police previously said he was being held in London after he was arrested under section one and section three of the National Security Act 2023, which relate to obtaining or disclosing protected information, and assisting a foreign intelligence service.
The day after Tyner's arrest on 10 November, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he was "unaware" of what it was connected to.
"We have nothing to do with it, and it has nothing to do with us," he told reporters in Moscow.
On Tuesday, Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing, said: "Subsequently, a decision was made to pass the investigation to them [their American partners] to progress."
"These are extremely serious allegations, and our collective response should send a strong message that we will act swiftly and robustly where we suspect this kind of espionage activity taking place," he added.
Tyner's arrest was the result of a long-running operation by MI5 - the UK's domestic intelligence and security agency - in collaboration with the FBI, the BBC understands.
He had previously served in Afghanistan and Iraq, but at the time of his arrest was working with NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps near Gloucester - where he was said to be entrusted with sensitive information which would have been extremely damaging if leaked to Russia.
Detectives sent the Crown Prosecution Service a file on the senior US soldier's alleged spying for consideration - allegations described by the head of Counter Terrorism Policing as "extremely serious."
But at that stage the Attorney General's Office in London got involved. As did the US authorities.
And now the decision has been taken that Lieutenant Colonel Tyner should be taken into custody by the US Military.
It means he will not stand trial in the UK, but under US Uniform Code of Military Justice.
FBI director Kash Patel said an army officer was in custody "as the result of an espionage investigation and the close cooperation" between the bureau, US Army and various UK partners.
"Together we worked to identify a potential threat to national security and take swift action," he said.
"This FBI has zero tolerance for anyone who betrays their oath to the United States or puts our national security at risk."
US Brig Gen Sean Stinchon said the case should serve as a "stark warning to any service member suspected of violating the oath" they all take.
"Whenever we suspect somebody of betraying the trust of their fellow soldiers and jeopardising our collective defence, we will identify you, and we will ensure justice is served," he added.

title: UK unemployment unexpectedly eases to 4.6% as government releases Milburn report
text:
The UK unemployment rate has unexpectedly fallen as the government released an important report on the youth jobs crisis.
The unemployment rate was 4.6% in September, dipping from 4.7% in August and down from 5% earlier in the year, according to the Office for National Statistics.
However, the number of vacancies fell as employers delayed hiring in response to global economic uncertainty and the use of artificial intelligence, which many analysts expect will lead to widespread job losses.
Business groups said the slump in vacancies posed a problem for the government as responded to Alan Milburn’s report on young people not in employment, education or training (Neets).
Milburn, a former health secretary, unveiled his long-awaited report into youth unemployment on Tuesday morning in London, urging ministers to cut disability and sickness payments for under-25s and invest the money in back-to-work schemes.
The British Chambers of Commerce said it was “alarming” that the number of vacancies had tumbled to its lowest level since 2014 and unemployment for 18- to 24-year-olds was nearly triple the average for UK adults, at 13%.
“This will put further pressure on today’s Milburn review to deliver a sea change in the government’s approach to tackling youth joblessness,” it said.
The number of vacancies dropped to 690,000 in October after soaring to more than 1.3m after the pandemic.
Wage growth also fell to 3.5%, excluding bonuses, in the latest official figures for the three months to the end of September, down from 3.7% in the three months to August.
City economists had expected unemployment to remain steady and wages, excluding bonuses, to fall slightly to 3.6%.
With inflation also at 3.5% and expected to rise for a fourth consecutive month to 3.7% when figures are released on Wednesday, the average worker faces a fall in real wage growth to zero or even negative figures.
Martin Beck, the chief economist at the consultants WPI Strategy, said: “The UK labour market remained relatively resilient in late autumn, but beneath the surface, there were more signs that the economy is struggling to generate jobs. The jobs market isn’t falling off a cliff, but is going nowhere fast.”
The jobs market has proved difficult for analysts and politicians to assess in recent years. It has been called weak after a dramatic slide in the number of vacancies, which illustrates the reticence of companies to hire new staff.
Ministers are known to be concerned that some large employers, including several banks, have said they intend to use AI to reduce their staffing levels.
Economists are divided over whether AI will enhance productivity across all the big sectors of the economy – after signs it has boosted GDP – or lead to improvements in certain industries such as healthcare.
Employer groups have complained that Labour’s increase in employer national insurance contributions, a higher minimum wage and changes to employee rights have increased costs, leading to a fall in the number of advertised vacancies.
The Bank of England increased interest rates earlier this month after a rise in the consumer prices index to 3.5% in September.
It has said that its own surveys showed employers did not expect to increase pay beyond 3.5% to 4% next year, despite the higher level of inflation, and also reported little change looking ahead in their own prices.
However, a growing number of the Bank’s policymakers believe the prospect of high oil and energy prices next year as the Iran war drags on will push inflation towards 5% and force employers to offer higher pay, which will be passed on in higher retail prices.
A spokesperson for the Department for Work and Pensions said the Milburn review would “shape our next steps for young people”. “Despite the difficult global backdrop, the unemployment rate is falling, and the number of people in work is rising,” the spokesperson added.
“We are determined to go further. Our £2.5bn youth employment support will give almost 1 million young people opportunities to earn and learn, while wider reforms including improving jobcentres, will create a more personalised work and skills advice service for all.”

title: Scientist fired after 6-year-old girl dies in gene-editing trial
text:
A Chinese scientist who concealed the death of a 6-year-old girl in a gene-editing trial has been fired following a government probe, according to state media.
The girl died last year after receiving experimental gene therapy to correct a non-life-threatening condition — which was not disclosed in published research, an investigation found in July.
Neuroscientist Zilong Qiu, the trial's lead researcher, had made no mention of the girl in a paper published in the prestigious journal Nature, according to the joint investigation by Science and Retraction Watch.
"According to official documents and accounts provided by the girl's parents, the hospital had allowed Qiu's experimental treatment to proceed under a regulatory provision that does not require approval from national regulators," Science reported in July. "After the child's death, the hospital paid a modest fine to a local health authority but Qiu was not publicly sanctioned."
Qiu was dismissed as deputy director of the Songjiang Research Institute affiliated with Shanghai Jiao Tong University, state broadcaster CCTV said Friday, citing a statement from Shanghai authorities.
The reported statement included only Qiu's surname, but referenced the Nature study published on Feb. 18.
Qiu was given a five-year suspension from participating in scientific projects and recorded in a database for "serious breaches of research integrity," the report said.
Another researcher on Qiu's team was fired and handed a five-year suspension, while several others with ties to the hospital where the trial took place were also punished.
The child who died had a rare neurodevelopmental condition called Snijders Blok-Campeau syndrome, according to the report.
The hospital's ethics committee had approved a gene-editing trial to treat the disorder in January 2025, the report said.
The committee terminated the study after the girl died in March due to complications from gene therapy.
"Unusual and dangerous"
Shanghai authorities found that Qiu's team failed to properly inform the hospital of possible safety issues from earlier tests on primates, according to the report.
AFP has reached out to Qiu for comment.
The July investigation by Science and Retraction Watch found that the girl's parents, who paid more than $800,000 to fund the experiment, were not adequately informed about the risks.
"Learning the reality of these missing safeguards has fundamentally changed how we now view the entire project," the girl's father, told Science. "We did not realize how unusual and dangerous many of the arrangements were."
The scandal is a blow to China's ambitions to rival the United States as a biotech power following the 2018 scandal around , a biophysicist who secretly produced gene-edited babies. He was later to three years in prison.

title: Ukraine: Zelenskyy says security deal could go to referendum
text:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said US peace envoys asked whether Kyiv would withdraw from its eastern region of Donbas in exchange for joining NATO, according to remarks to the media published on Saturday.
The suggestion was made following the latest round of peace talks in Abu Dhabi to bring Russia's nearly 5-year war in Ukraine to a close.
What did Zelenskyy say?
The Ukrainian leader told reporters: "The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?'"
Zelenskyy repeated Kyiv's position that it was not willing to cede territory to Russia. But he added that if the country reached a comprehensive deal, including security guarantees, a strong and well-funded Ukrainian army and funds to rebuild, he would put the question to the public in a referendum.
"That is why I believe NATO is back on the agenda. But you have also heard [Russian President Vladimir] Putin's signals, and this is an extremely difficult conversation."
Zelenskyy said the prospect of NATO membership in exchange for withdrawing from Donbas has not been raised before.
He also warned about Moscow's plan to change the continent's security architecture, saying it could lead to more conflict.
Putin has demanded that NATO pull back its troops from the Russian border, which European Union leaders have strongly criticized.
"This is dangerous because, in my view, it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations," Zelenskyy added.
"Real security in Europe means the EU and NATO. That's it. There is no other security in Europe."
Europe to play bigger role in peace talks
On Friday, the EU said several European diplomats would take part in future Ukraine peace talks, including Germany, France, the United Kingdom and Poland.
Moscow has long insisted that European states be excluded from the negotiations because they support Ukraine.
Russian forces strike Zaporizhzhia
The comments come as Russia’s Defence Ministry said its forces had captured the settlement of Tersianka in Ukraine’s southeastern Zaporizhzhia region, news agency Interfax reported.
Interfax cited the ministry as saying that Russian forces had struck Ukrainian energy and transport infrastructure used by the military, along with ammunition depots and drone production and storage sites.
Russia has targeted power stations across Ukraine in waves of ballistic and cruise missile attacks, cutting power and heating to millions of people as temperatures plunge.
Zelenskyy warned that Putin was "betting everything" on this winter's war campaign, which Kyiv insists is aimed at hurting public morale.

title: The WTA Finals’ future is bright – but can it ever be ‘the Super Bowl of women’s sports’?
text:
As 19-year-old Mirra Andreeva beamed and lifted aloft the WTA Finals trophy after a stunning unbeaten run in which she did not drop a set, WTA chair Valerie Camillo could similarly reflect on a job well done.
The flagship tournament of the women’s tour, bringing together the eight best players in the world – this year all grand slam winners or finalists, or WTA 1000 champions – has often felt like an afterthought in recent years. But this reset edition in Indian Wells felt like a moment of course-correction – and the signs for the future are largely bright.
The last few years have been turbulent for the WTA: the Telegraph reported in September that it could run out of money entirely by next autumn. To condense a long story: the Covid-19 pandemic hit the tour hard, given it held nine significant events in China, including – after signing a 10-year, nearly $1bn deal – the Finals in Shenzhen. The WTA, under Steve Simon, then suspended all events in China over the Peng Shuai scandal, before it was forced into a humiliating climbdown nearly a year and a half later – by which point China pulled the plug on the Shenzhen deal.
So the WTA’s biggest tournament, pitting the best athletes against each other, has endured a nomadic, ramshackle existence since then. A last-minute event in Guadalajara in 2021 was followed by a similarly short-notice edition in Fort Worth, Texas the following year, which was poorly promoted and suffered from low ticket sales. Then followed a truly farcical edition in Cancun, where gale force winds and torrential downpour, coupled with hastily-assembled courts and infrastructure players worried was unsafe, made a mockery of the entire thing.
The WTA’s three-year partnership with Saudi Arabia brought the prize money to an astonishing high of $15m and gave it a slightly more permanent home. But it always left a sour taste, bringing the pinnacle of women’s sport, and a sport with as long and proud history of trailblazing for gender equality as tennis, to a country with one of the poorest human rights records in the world. (Amnesty International’s April 2026 report into ‘The State of the World’s Human Rights’ detailed how in 2025 the Saudi government “executed the highest number of people on record in any given year” and “severely restricted the rights to freedom of expression and association”, while women “continued to face discrimination in law and practice” and a law passed in 2022 “codified gender-based discrimination in most areas of family life, including in marriage, divorce, child custody and inheritance”.)
From a purely commercial viewpoint, the Finals in Riyadh was under-promoted and ill-attended and ultimately ended after just two years, with the Saudis scaling back their sporting investments and war in the Middle East bringing yet more uncertainty to the event - a painful end to a high-risk and ultimately reputation-sullying experiment. The Telegraph’s report said the WTA expected operating losses of $23m in 2026, with the loss of revenue from the Saudi Finals deal a major contributor.
It was against this rocky backdrop that the WTA Finals came to Indian Wells for a placeholder year in 2026, before a three-year stint in Charlotte, North Carolina from 2027.
There have been positive signs under the new leadership of Camillo, who took over in November 2025 and had previously worked at the top of the Philadelphia Flyers and Washington Nationals, with the WTA adopting a savvier commercial approach.
The most obvious is the decision to take greater control of its media rights and assume operational control of the WTA Finals – for the first time in more than 20 years – rather than licence it to third-party operators for lucrative fees. Previous editions including in Qatar, Shenzhen and Riyadh upped the prize money dramatically and put the tournament on a par with the ATP Finals, but at significant cost in terms of control over the event and its image, with local organisers running everything.
And the decision to head to California has proved inspired: the hub for an existing tournament, the well-promoted and popular joint-ATP and WTA 1000 tournament in March, with all the infrastructure in place to host another event at late notice, and a place with a well-established tennis fanbase. Another savvy move was using the 7,500-capacity Stadium 2 – which sold out on the opening day – at the Indian Wells Tennis Garden rather than risk the look of a sparsely attended bigger arena, like the 16,100-seater Stadium 1.
Day two’s group stage matches were similarly well attended, even without the attraction of the two American players in the eight-woman tournament, Jessica Pegula and Coco Gauff. Gauff acknowledged the strong turnout after her opening win over her compatriot: “Really happy that you guys are here supporting women’s tennis and women’s sports in general,” she said.
Brand partnerships with the likes of Hello Kitty and Mercedes-Benz, with winner Andreeva inspired to get her driving licence after leaving Indian Wells with a swanky new Mercedes-AMG SL 55 4MATIC+ along with her trophy, have also provided a boost on the commercial side.
And the tour’s decision to bring the Finals back to the US, home to a colossal sports market in general and a particularly booming one in women’s sport, expands its reach and commercial heft, with a huge number of potential sponsors based there. “The United States is the core commercial market in the world, it just is,” Camillo told The Athletic earlier this year. “The money is here.”
The WTA has also relocated its base from St Petersburg, Florida to Charlotte, throwing all its weight behind the new home of its Finals and its new operational strategy – moving away from years of partnership with repressive sportswashing governments, from China to Saudi Arabia, and shifting tack to prioritise its own financial independence and long-term stability.
There remain plenty of issues for the WTA’s leadership to iron out over the coming months and years. Camillo insists the Tour will return to “normal operations, normal financials” in 2027 and said all seven joint ATP and WTA 1000 events – the level below grand slams – will offer equal prize money, rather than the four which currently provide it.
But where will that funding come from? The joint ATP and WTA 1000 event in Indian Wells offered a total prize pot of $9.4m per Tour and $1.15m for the male and female champions; by comparison, the Canada Open provided a total purse of $9.4m on the men’s side and $7.4m on the women’s. That is a major gap to bridge, and it is unclear how much the WTA will have to contribute to close it.
Adding to the financial pressure is the fact that some of the WTA’s funding will dry up next year – the final payment in a $150m injection of cash over five years from private equity firm CVC Capital Partners, which bought a 20 per cent stake in the WTA’s commercial arm in 2023, comes in 2027. How it makes up that shortfall, and more, will be critical.
While there is optimism over the move to Charlotte its venue, the Spectrum Centre, is home to the NBA’s Charlotte Hornets, and the Finals could be cut from their usual eight-day schedule to five to accommodate the team needing the stadium.
Camillo has said no decision has yet been made on the format, but it would feel regressive for the tour’s biggest sole event to be squeezed just when it began to be making strides towards greater self-sufficiency and a bigger profile. Issues over the promotion of the event by the WTA itself, particularly compared to how visibly the ATP promotes and advertises its counterpart in Turin, also continue to shadow it.
Camillo has memorably described wanting to make the WTA Finals the “Super Bowl of women’s sports”. That is a hugely ambitious target, but it has many of the elements it needs to make this tournament a huge success – the athletes, hugely marketable stars in their own right; the drama and tension of the world’s best colliding; and now the chance to finally put down some roots and take control of its future.

title: Dutch Romp Greece, Germany Cruises In UEFA Nations League Action
text:
The Netherlands routed Greece 7-0 in a statement Nations League victory to stay unbeaten under new coach Xavi, while Jürgen Klopp's Germany cruised to a 3-1 win over Serbia on Friday.
That now sets up a decider between the two big-name coaches for first place in their group.
Tijjani Reijnders scored a hat trick and Jurrien Timber had two goals in a rampant win for the Netherlands.
Beaming and holding up three fingers, Reijnders celebrated a hat trick which came off a series of slick team moves to tear apart the Greek defense in Amsterdam.
Crysencio Summerville got the Netherlands started with a sixth-minute opener before Reijnders scored three in the space of 21 minutes, Timber added two more and Donyell Malen a seventh.
Germany is three points behind Group A2 leader the Netherlands before they play on Monday in Berlin.
The top two in the group advance to the quarterfinals, with head-to-head record as the tiebreaker. The Netherlands, Germany and Greece are all able to qualify. Serbia is last after losing all of its five games.
Germany Wins In Front Of Serbia's Sparse Crowd
Goals from Florian Wirtz and debutant Brajan Gruda lifted Germany to its second win in five games with Klopp as coach after a slow start to his tenure.
In driving rain, Germany was ahead after just three minutes when Serbia defender Srdjan Babic turned Germany forward Kai Havertz’s header into his own goal.
It was 2-0 soon after when Wirtz flicked a rebound over goalkeeper Vanja Milinkovic-Savic, who had parried a shot from Havertz.
Klopp’s experimental squad, with Freiburg winger Derry Scherhant but no place for Barcelona’s Karim Adeyemi, added a third when Leipzig's Gruda dribbled through the center of the Serbian defense to score Germany’s third.
Babic canceled out his earlier own goal by scoring for Serbia on a rebound, but chances of a comeback were ended when Vanja Dragojevic was sent off for a reckless tackle on Joshua Kimmich's ankle.
The 50,000-capacity Rajko Mitic stadium was almost empty because Serbia was supported by only 5,000 accompanied children and teenagers. That's because UEFA was punished the Serbian soccer federation for fans’ offensive behavior in the previous rounds.
Swiss Promotion Bid On Track
Switzerland is playing in the second tier of the Nations League for the first time, but its bid to rejoin Europe's elite stayed on course in a 0-0 draw with Slovenia, its closest rival in Group B1. Scotland won against North Macedonia 2-1.
Reporting by The Associated Press.

title: Yale scientists reveal what really slows aging and what doesn't
text:
Yale researchers have discovered that certain prescription drugs, healthy diets, and exercise can measurably slow biological aging, while popular anti-aging supplements appear largely ineffective. Their analysis of 51 studies could transform how scientists evaluate anti-aging treatments, although whether these biological changes actually extend life remains uncertain.
A growing body of research suggests that aging may be more flexible than once believed. Now, scientists at Yale have taken an important step toward identifying which treatments can actually influence biological aging and which ones show little measurable benefit.
Their findings suggest that certain prescription medications and lifestyle changes can reduce biological age as measured by DNA-based blood tests. Popular over-the-counter supplements examined in the research, however, showed little evidence of producing the same effects.
The findings, published in Nature Medicine, could help scientists evaluate anti-aging treatments more effectively, although researchers emphasize that changes in biological age markers do not necessarily mean people will live longer or avoid age-related diseases.
From Fighting Cancer to Understanding Aging
When Raghav Sehgal began graduate school at Yale several years ago, he planned to use advanced computer science techniques to investigate cancer. His background in engineering and experience launching a computational biology startup had given him a strong foundation for that work.
However, a question from his Ph.D. adviser at the Yale School of Medicine changed his research direction. Rather than focusing on individual diseases such as cancer or cardiovascular disease, why not investigate the aging process that contributes to their development?
"That put me on a different path," said Sehgal, now an associate research scientist in psychiatry who specializes in computational biology and bioinformatics. "As researchers, we have a long way to go in understanding the aging process and whether the steps we take to manage it really work."
Sehgal now studies the biological mechanisms behind human aging, how scientists can measure those changes, and why getting older increases the likelihood of conditions such as cancer, diabetes, and dementia. His work also explores whether interventions might reverse certain aspects of biological aging, even if eliminating aging itself remains beyond reach.
New DNA Tests Reveal Which Anti-Aging Treatments Work
Sehgal is the lead author of the new study, which was conducted in the laboratory of Albert Higgins-Chen, an assistant professor of psychiatry at the Yale School of Medicine. The research team set out to determine which existing approaches to slowing aging produce changes that can be reliably measured.
Their analysis found encouraging results for certain medications and lifestyle interventions. In contrast, the over-the-counter supplements included in the study generally failed to produce meaningful reductions in biological age.
The project involved the entire Higgins-Chen laboratory, including Daniel Borrus, Jenel F. Armstrong, John Gonzalez, Jessica Kasamoto, and Yaroslav Markov.
"For the first time we've shown that certain therapies have measurable impacts," said Sehgal. "This wasn't previously possible, because we didn't have enough data to say these biomarkers are consistently responsive to these interventions."
Biomarkers provide measurable information about what is happening inside the body. In aging research, they can help estimate a person's biological or functional age, which may differ from their chronological age.
How Scientists Measure Biological Age
To investigate whether treatments could influence aging, the Yale team relied primarily on blood-based measurements called epigenetic clocks.
These tools analyze chemical patterns attached to DNA, particularly methyl groups (basic chemical structures that act like tags). Previous research has shown that these chemical markers change as people grow older. Some interventions may reverse certain age-associated patterns, and computer algorithms use those changes to estimate a person's biological age.
The researchers brought together findings from 51 clinical studies investigating different anti-aging strategies. These ranged from dietary supplements and medications to lifestyle changes and medical procedures.
Across those studies, the team examined more than 110 DNA methylation biomarkers (including 16 major epigenetic clocks). By comparing measurements taken before and after interventions, they could evaluate which approaches were associated with reductions in biological age.
"What we did was pretty unique," Sehgal said. "We already know that certain things might prolong health span and lifespan. There is data from retrospective analysis as well as from animal models. We took all that knowledge along with the real-world clinical studies to identify which interventions in humans were slowing down aging across the board in these known biomarkers."
Which Anti-Aging Treatments Showed the Best Results?
The researchers divided the interventions into four main groups: prescription drugs, lifestyle modifications, over-the-counter supplements, and medical procedures.
One of the clearest findings involved diet and exercise. Combining regular physical activity with a healthy eating plan consistently reduced epigenetic age. The dietary approaches examined included Mediterranean, low-fat, and low-carb diets.
The strongest reductions in biological age markers were associated with certain pharmaceutical treatments. These included metformin and semaglutide, prescription medications used to manage metabolic conditions and body weight, as well as anti-TNF therapies that target a protein involved in the body's inflammatory response.
(TNF, or tumor necrosis factor, is an immune-system protein that helps fight inflammation-related injury.)
The findings were less encouraging for over-the-counter supplements and some medical procedures. In the studies examined, these approaches did not produce measurable reductions in epigenetic age.
The researchers also discovered that newer biological age clocks performed better than older versions. Another important finding was that people living with diseases generally experienced larger changes in their aging biomarkers than healthy participants.
Could DNA Blood Tests Transform Anti-Aging Research?
According to Sehgal, the next priority is to test these findings in larger, more diverse populations. This would help researchers determine how consistently different treatments influence biological aging across people with different health conditions and backgrounds.
The improved blood tests could also dramatically shorten the time needed to evaluate potential anti-aging therapies.
"If these new biomarkers are eventually validated to predict long-term health, scientists will be able to evaluate anti-aging therapies much faster," he added. "Instead of waiting decades for evidence from clinical trials, we'll be able to see which interventions are effective and in which people in a few years or even months."
That possibility could represent a major advance for aging research. Instead of relying entirely on clinical studies that follow participants for decades, scientists might eventually use validated biological age measurements to identify promising treatments much earlier.
However, senior author Higgins-Chen stressed that scientists must be careful about interpreting what changes in aging biomarkers actually mean.
"We have developed a rigorous, systematic approach to evaluating and comparing how biomarkers change across a wide variety of interventions, and that is a critical step in the right direction," he said. "However, the true meaning of that change must be fully understood."
Important Questions About Slowing Aging Remain
Although the results are promising, several major questions remain unanswered.
For example, researchers still need to establish whether changes in biological age are directly caused by a treatment or influenced by other factors that were not accounted for. They also need to understand how quickly those changes occur, whether they persist after treatment ends, and which biological processes produce them.
Most importantly, scientists have not yet established whether lowering epigenetic age leads to meaningful improvements in long-term health.
"And most importantly - what does the change mean for our long-term risk of age-related disease and functional decline?" Higgins-Chen said.
Further investigations into these questions are underway, with additional studies led by Borrus, Armstrong, and Grace Zou.
The Higgins-Chen laboratory is also affiliated with Yale's Department of Pathology, the Computational Biology and Bioinformatics Program, and the Y-Age Yale Center for Research on Aging.
What Appears to Work Against Biological Aging?
Based on the improved DNA-based blood tests, the Yale researchers identified two particularly promising approaches for reducing biological age markers:
- Prescription medications: Drugs used for metabolic regulation and weight management, including metformin and semaglutide, were among the treatments associated with the strongest reductions in biological age.
- Healthy eating combined with exercise: Regular physical activity paired with nutritious diets, including Mediterranean, low-fat, and low-carb eating plans, consistently produced favorable changes in aging biomarkers.
The analysis also identified benefits from certain anti-TNF medications, while the tested over-the-counter supplements and some medical procedures showed little measurable effect.
These results provide a clearer picture of which interventions may influence biological aging. However, more research is needed to confirm the findings and determine whether reductions in biological age markers ultimately translate into fewer age-related diseases, better health, or longer lives.

title: On this day in space! Nov. 13, 1971: NASA's Mariner 9 becomes 1st spacecraft to orbit Mars, revealing close looks at the Martian surface
text:
On Nov. 13, 1971, Mariner 9 became the first spacecraft to orbit Mars. At the time, scientists didn't know much about the Red Planet.
NASA had several Mars flybys before Mariner 9. Those flybys showed that Mars had a cratered surface, so some scientists thought that Mars looked just like the moon. Then Mariner 9 blew blew their minds.
When Mariner 9 got to Mars, it arrived in the middle of a dust storm. It saw some tall structures sticking through the clouds. When the dust settled, images from Mariner 9 revealed that these structures were the tops of huge volcanoes.
One volcano, Olympus Mons, is the tallest in the solar system. Mariner 9 also spotted an enormous canyon called Valles Marineris. This canyon is five times longer than the Grand Canyon in Arizona.
Mariner 9 worked for one year in orbit. When it ran out of gas, NASA shut it off. But the spacecraft remains one of the most famous Mars voyagers of all time.
Here's why it mattered
Mariner 9 cemented its place in space history when it entered into orbit around Mars, the first human-built spacecraft ever to do so.
The NASA spacecraft actually beat the Soviet Union's own Mars 2 spacecraft to the Red Planet, even though Mars 2 "had an 11-day head start," NASA said in a mission description. (Mars 2 would go on to be the first human-built craft to impact the surface of Mars when it crashed into the Red Planet.)
But it was the science from Mariner 9 that transformed Mars from a mysterious Red Planet into a full world for humans to explore.
Mariner 9 carried four primary instruments to study Mars, including a camera system for imaging, an ultraviolet spectrometer, an infrared spectrometer and an infrared radiometer. The probe mapped 85% of Mars with those tools during its nearly one-year mission.
The Mariner 9 spacecraft discovered 20 giant volcanoes on Mars (including Olympus Mars) and made key observations to map Valles Marineris, which runs 2,500 miles (4,000 kilometers) long acros the Tharsis region and is 120 miles (200 km) wide.
"The canyon was named in honor of Mariner 9," NASA said in an overview.
In all, Mariner 9 took 7,329 photos of the surface of Mars, mapping the planet down to a resolution of between 1/2-1 mile (1-2 km). It also snapped at least 80 photos of Phobos and Deimos, the two small moons of Mars.
By February 1972, Mariner 9's supply of gaseous nitrogen, which it used to feed its attitide control thrusters, had run dry. NASA finally shut down the mission in October 1972.
Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube.

title: Ministers to end Palantir’s contract with NHS in England in 2029
text:
Ministers will end the NHS’s contract with the controversial tech firm Palantir – but not until 2029, to allow time to line up British companies to replace it.
The Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) has decided to extend Palantir’s contract to provide the federated data platform (FDP) – the software that links different healthcare providers – for two more years rather than exercise a break clause that would have let them axe it next spring.
Ministers have come under growing pressure to end the NHS in England’s relationship with Palantir, which is run by the Donald Trump-supporting US tech billionaire Peter Thiel.
James Frith, a health minister, said Palantir’s role would end in 2029 to boost public trust in NHS tech, end its “over-dependence” on one supplier and let UK companies start providing crucial digital infrastructure. The DHSC will in the meantime select UK tech firms to replace it.
However, Labour and Liberal Democrat MPs criticised Palantir being given a further two years.
“My committee has repeatedly called on the government to exercise the 2027 break clause in Palantir’s federated data platform contract with the NHS,” said Chi Onwurah, the chair of the Commons science and technology select committee.
“It’s deeply disappointing to hear that it won’t do so and is instead choosing to extend the contract for two years, during which time it says it will procure a UK-based supplier.
Martin Wrigley, a Liberal Democrat MP, said: “After months of campaigning by the Liberal Democrats, the government has finally admitted that the Palantir contract has to end.
“However, ministers have kicked the can down the road to March 2029. That leaves a company co-founded by Trump ally Peter Thiel, and criticised by human rights groups over its work with ICE [the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency], holding the keys to our health data for years to come.”
Campaign groups such as Amnesty International and Just Treatment have been urging ministers to activate the break clause in February in the contract that NHS England agreed with Palantir in 2023.
Many NHS care trusts have declined to use the FDP, amid widespread doubts in the service that it is as good as Palantir insists. NHS England last week deleted a claim from its website that 137 trusts were benefiting from the FDP after the Guardian disclosed that 29 were using it never or rarely.
“The current contract will remain for two years, before coming to an end,” Frith told MPs. The DHSC will soon invite British tech outfits to bid to be part of whoever replaces Palantir. “A process this important must command public trust as well as clinical confidence,” Frith added in a tacit admission that many hospital bosses and doctors are sceptical about Palantir’s claimed benefits.
Ben Coleman, a Labour member of the Commons health select committee, who last week urged ministers to replace Palantir with a group of British firms, said: “I’m glad the government is ending reliance on a single supplier and shaking off the Palantir albatross. This must be done without disrupting patient care or creating new dependence [on a new single supplier]”.
Amnesty International said the decision was “a victory for healthcare workers, patients and campaigners who refused to give up”.
“Doctors and nurses … should never have to work in a health service that partners with a company supporting a military committing genocide.
“Palantir has openly acknowledged supporting Israel’s military in ‘war-related missions’, while Israel is committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza. ‘First, do no harm’ should apply not just to NHS staff, but to the companies the NHS contracts with,” said Tom Guha, its crisis campaigner.

title: Is there an opening for Nvidia's competitors, now that Jensen Huang is out?
text:
NPR's Scott Detrow talks with Dylan Patel of the AI and semiconductor research firm SemiAnalysis about Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia, and whether it opens up the field for Nvidia's competitors.
SCOTT DETROW, HOST:
Nvidia has long been the kingpin of the semiconductor industry, a company whose huge technological bets paid off, making its chips the most in-demand chips in the world and crowning the company, for a time, the most valuable in the world. But with Nvidia's leader, Jensen Huang, out, does that leave an opening for Nvidia's competitors to catch up? We're going to put that question to Dylan Patel. He is founder and CEO of SemiAnalysis, an AI and semiconductor research firm. Welcome to ALL THINGS CONSIDERED.
DYLAN PATEL: Thank you for having me.
DETROW: So you and others have estimated Nvidia is probably a year, two years ahead of its competitors. With Huang out, can other companies catch up?
PATEL: I think that's the biggest risk at least. Over the last, you know, handful of years, Nvidia's lead has actually lessened, and so therefore, they've lost market share, albeit, the market has grown so fast, Nvidia's revenue and profits have skyrocketed so fast. But now, with, you know, many barbarians at the gate, when sort of Jensen is needed most, he sort of is disappearing or (inaudible) the game.
DETROW: Needed most by the company, the industry?
PATEL: I think most - the most to the company. The industry has for a long time tried to roll their own solution, you know, at least as far as the biggest customers. Google, Microsoft, Meta, Amazon all have been working on their own AI chips for, you know, a number of years. And yet, they all still relied on Nvidia. But their reliance is reducing to some extent, and that's their goal and has been their goal. And now, you know, the only way Nvidia can keep their market share and stay on top of the world is if they out execute everyone - right? - they keep innovating and bringing new technology to the market. But without Jensen, you know, the founder and the visionary of the company, it's going to be a lot harder for them to keep on top.
DETROW: One of the things you've written about that I think is really important to understand is the way that - like, sometimes I feel like a CEO's role in a company is overblown. But how much came to (ph) his personal decisions, his personal decision-making? Let's talk about this first on the supply side. How was his personal relationships with supply chain managers in Korea and Taiwan so key to Nvidia getting what it needed?
PATEL: There's no other company in the supply chain, including in the semiconductor supply chain, where the CEO is, every quarter, meeting with all his suppliers. And, you know, chips are such a complex supply chain. He has hundreds of suppliers. He's talking to every single one of them, going to Korea, going to Taiwan, going to China, meeting, having drinks with them, going to local fried chicken spots, or, you know, night food markets, everything to woo them. And given this is such a complex industry where, you know, products are improving by 2x a year - right? - it's at an incredible pace - you need your suppliers to have full focus and put their best engineers on your product. And this just keeps Nvidia ahead of everyone.
DETROW: I mean, a big part of the reason the company dominated this field the way it did was the really risky big bets that Jensen Huang took. Do you see another CEO taking those bets, or do you see another company trying to establish itself taking the types of bets that he took?
PATEL: You know, there's many visionaries within the company. The challenge is, are there visionaries who are willing to bet the entire company, right? Jensen with CUDA, the software that makes Nvidia what it is, he developed it in 2010, you know, and the company developed it in 2010. And everyone who was a technologist at the time, everyone who was on Wall Street at the time thought it was a waste of money, thought it was a waste of effort. And then it turned out to be the bedrock of all AI software. You know, is someone going to do something that is such a waste of money that, for a decade looks like a terrible bet? It really takes a visionary, and I don't know if too many people will make those kinds of bets. You know, if someone were to ask me, hey, Nvidia without Jensen, a decade from now, are they the one that's bringing the most important new technology to market? I'd probably wager no.
DETROW: Do you have any sense what some of Nvidia's next big bets could be?
PATEL: Yeah, so Nvidia sort of had this history where they started making chips, and then they started making servers, and then they started making systems. Nvidia now is really focused on the end applications. They're making - they're helping companies make medical devices. They're helping companies make satellites. They're helping companies make entire systems that include AI as a part of it. If they don't do this, then most small and medium-sized healthcare companies, and even many of the not - large-but-not-so-largest-ones can't afford to build their own systems out of AI.
And so I think that's where Jensen was heading - right? - was, hey, in automotive, in healthcare, in manufacturing, how do we make it so medium-sized companies, small companies can all start deploying AI throughout their businesses to make them more efficient, increase production, make their products better, make people healthier? Without that, only the biggest companies can do this. And then the profit motive sort of makes it so, you know, all of the profit is captured by a few, not diffused to the whole ecosystem.
DETROW: That is Dylan Patel, founder and CEO of SemiAnalysis. Thanks so much for talking to us about this.
PATEL: Thank you.

title: Wolf Biermann at 90: The singer who defied East Germany
text:
He mocks Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin as "political lovers," denounces the "endless fratricidal war" over the Palestinian territories, and repeatedly invokes "Lady Liberty." It is a celebration of the freedom he once so painfully lacked in the former East Germany, and of the freedom people around the world still yearn for.
These themes run throughout Wolf Biermann's new album "Unterm Haar nur Himmel" ("Beneath Hair, Only Sky") released to mark his 90th birthday. The album's title is a characteristically poetic phrase coined by Biermann himself. It evokes the idea that however restrictive the world may become, the human mind and spirit remain free. Beneath the hair lies open sky: a metaphor for inner freedom, independence and imagination.
Biermann remains one of Germany's most influential singer-songwriters, and at 90, he shows little sign of putting down his guitar. Often described as Germany's answer to Bob Dylan, the outspoken troubadour continues to weigh in on the issues shaping the world today.
In his recent song "Moritat von den Liebespaaren" ("Ballad of the Lovers"), he delivers a simple but urgent message: no single person can save the world, yet everyone can help make it a better place. Above all, the song is a call to take responsibility for one's own life rather than remain a bystander.
A child caught in the Allied firestorm
This outspokenness was instilled in Biermann early on. When he was born in Hamburg in 1936, Adolf Hitler was already in power. His father was a dockworker, a committed communist, a resistance fighter against the Nazis — and Jewish.
Wolf was just three months old when the Gestapo, Hitler's secret police, arrested his father. He initially served time in prison before he was murdered by the Nazis at Auschwitz in early 1943.
Just a few months later, British and American bombers attacked Hamburg, unleashing a devastating firestorm. "Nothing in my life has shaped me more," Biermann has repeatedly said in interviews. When the sirens sounded, his mother took him into an air raid shelter. The house above them was burning.
Yet Biermann has said his memories of that time are rooted in a profound sense of trust in life. In an interview with the German magazine Chrismon, he recalled: "I pressed my face into my mother's soft coat so I could breathe. A sense of security in the midst of the end of the world. We stumbled out over the neighboring house and into the open. The firestorm lifted a burning roof into the air. Roaring corrugated metal, smoke everywhere. We searched for a way out. [...] Death was everywhere. 40,000 people died. They had no chance. But I did. My strong mama."
Avenging his father
Biermann's mother instilled communist and anti-fascist ideas in him with almost religious fervor. "My mother had only one goal after those dark years," Biermann once recalled. "I was supposed to survive so that I could, as she put it rather grandly, one day take revenge for my father's death. I was supposed to build communism."
In 1953, while countless people were fleeing East Germany, Biermann moved there of his own free will — after all, communism was the official state ideology. He was just 16 at the time. In East Berlin, he studied political economy, mathematics and philosophy. His role models were writers Bertolt Brecht and Heinrich Heine. He began working as an assistant director at the Berliner Ensemble, and also began writing and performing his political songs.
Biermann soon realized that life in East Germany was far from the communist paradise he had imagined and he wrote about this openly in his songs. "The party bosses were torn," Biermann said. "They were delighted by this young poet who could play the guitar so beautifully and sing such cheeky songs. They thought they just needed to bring me into line. Even today, I'm amazed that I wound up cast in the role of the heroic dragon slayer."
Exiled from East Germany
In 1965, East Germany's ruling Socialist Unity Party, the SED, imposed a blanket ban on Biermann performing or publishing his work. His East Berlin apartment, which was under constant surveillance, soon became a gathering place for dissidents and critical thinkers.
Yet, to his great surprise, the East German authorities allowed him to travel to Cologne, West Germany in 1976. There, around 7,000 people flocked to see him. For four and a half hours, he strummed and sang, mocking the East German regime. His songs were so popular that bootleg copies found their way back to East Germany.
On November 16, while still on tour in West Germany, Biermann heard the news on his car radio that he had been stripped of his right to continue residing in the German Democratic Republic. The regime accused him of betraying and slandering East Germany. "
I felt like the ground had opened up beneath me. I was overcome with fear, everything went dark," Biermann wrote in his memoirs.
Protest over expulsion
In a petition, leading East German intellectuals spoke out against the decision. In response, the regime stepped up surveillance of dissidents, imposed professional bans and jailed its critics. Several prominent public figures left the country.
"The SED leadership expected an angry media response from the West. What they hadn't reckoned with was that, for the very first time, a group of respected East German writers and artists would make their protest public, disguising it as a humble petition," Biermann wrote.
'Always the same struggle for freedom'
Afterward, Biermann sank into a deep depression. "Not just because I had been torn away from the friends I knew and loved in East Berlin, but also because I had lost my familiar mortal enemies," he said.
He became involved in the peace and anti-nuclear movements and continued singing about the injustices of the world. "The world's conflicts take different forms in each generation," he said. "But it's always the same struggle for freedom."
The singer-songwriter plans to spend his 90th birthday at home in Hamburg with his wife and manager, Pamela. For the first time in his life, he said, he's skipping the birthday party, even with his 10 children.
"I'm so old and I can feel my strength fading. And I know that the next day I have a major concert at the Berliner Ensemble," he told the German Press Agency.
And should he ever die, he said, he wants to be buried at Berlin's cemetery where some renowned German writers and intellectuals have been laid to rest, among them Bertolt Brecht, Anna Seghers and Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel. He still has a thing or two to discuss with them.

title: Fox News is already starting the culture wars over the new Grand Theft Auto VI
text:
As gamers anxiously await this week’s release of Grand Theft Auto VI, Fox News hosts are already starting the culture wars over the crime-fueled video game series.
Fox & Friends Weekend hosts Rachel Campos-Duffy, Charles Hurt and Griff Jenkins recently looked at a preview of the new game, featuring characters Jason Duval, an Army veteran working for local drug runners, and Lucia Caminos, who was previously jailed after fighting for her family.
“I’m gonna push back a little,” Campos-Duffy, wife of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, said. “I’m not thinking that this is a good thing for our culture.”
Jenkins then suggested Campos-Duffy could play as Luicia, prompting her to ask, “Is she the hooker?”
“No, she’s a partner-in-crime,” Jenkins said. Campos-Duffy then laughed it off. “You can maybe play and get her to go straight,” Jenkins added.
Conservatives and liberals have long fought over cultural beliefs, typically when it comes to civil rights, including diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives and LGBTQ+ issues.
Fox News is known to promote the conservative view, railing against DEI and trans rights. And now, the network is coming after your favorite video game.
In Grand Theft Auto VI, set to be released at midnight on Thursday, Jason and Lucia will find themselves in the middle of a criminal conspiracy in the fictional state of Leonida, where they will need to rely on each other to make it out alive.
Grand Theft Auto, or GTA for short, is one of the most popular gaming franchises of the century. GTA fans have been waiting more than a decade for a new game in the series, making Thursday’s release even more exciting for them.
Roughly 15 million copies of Ground Theft Auto VI have been preordered, CNN Business reported, citing Sensor Tower data.
Strauss Zelnick, the CEO of GTA’s publisher, Take-Two Interactive, told Variety that presales of the new game are “running far in excess of our expectations.”
Violent games like GTA, Call of Duty and Mortal Kombat have faced scrutiny over the years for potentially leading to bad behavior in players, such as aggression.
But a study published in Molecular Psychiatry in 2018 found no changes in behavior between participants who played Grand Theft Auto V, the non-violent video game The Sims 3 and those who played no game at all.

title: Uzbekistan’s mountain lakes and trails draw visitors in every season
text:
Emerald lakes, mountain trails and boat trips offer different ways to experience the Tashkent region, where seasonal landscapes and growing tourism are bringing more visitors into the mountains.
In the mountains of the Tashkent region, the landscape changes with every turn. At Urungach, the lower lake takes on an emerald hue as water gathers in spring and recedes by summer. Further along, Chimgan draws hikers and skiers, while Charvak Reservoir offers boat trips beneath the surrounding ridgelines.
Together, these places offer different ways to explore the region’s mountains, from walking remote trails to spending time by the water.
Urungach’s changing emerald lake
Known for its jade-coloured water, Urungach attracts visitors looking for a distinctive mountain landscape. The smaller lake, also called Jade Lake, sits among rugged rock formations and steep terrain, with a larger lake above it.
According to Efrat Turaboyev, a representative of the tourism department, the smaller lake is around 180 metres long and reaches a depth of 16.5 metres at its deepest point. Water flows into it from the upper lake through underground channels, as well as from nearby mountain streams.
The water level changes throughout the year. It generally rises in April, reaching its highest point during spring, before receding around the middle of June. The cycle repeats the following year, giving the lake a different appearance depending on when visitors arrive.
The main visitor season runs from mid-April to June. Daily numbers can range from around 50 to 500 people, with weekends generally busier than weekdays.
For visitors from Germany, the scenery remains appealing even when the weather is cloudy or rainy.
Frank Karis says the changing weather gives the landscape a dramatic quality, while Simone Rode describes the mountains and natural surroundings as peaceful and relaxing.
Tourism and village life
Urungach’s growing popularity is creating opportunities for nearby communities, where livestock farming, agriculture and beekeeping remain important sources of income.
Residents also sell honey and other local products to visitors. Guesthouses are beginning to open in nearby villages, offering travellers a place to stay and meals prepared with local produce.
Most visitors currently travel by private car, often using four-wheel-drive UAZ or Niva vehicles suited to the mountain roads. Access is improving as roads are developed around the villages, although the journey to the lake still requires planning.
Tourism representatives are also considering camping areas and tent accommodation in lower parts of the mountains. Plans for 2027 include creating places where visitors can stay overnight before making the trip up to the lake.
For local communities, the lake has become a source of pride as well as a growing attraction. Its distinctive colour is the main reason many people make the journey.
Chimgan throughout the year
A journey from Urungach to Chimgan brings a different mountain experience. The area is known for its trails, broad views and access to outdoor activities in both summer and winter.
Shahzod Abduvaliyev of the Tashkent region tourism department says Chimgan has a long history as a recreational destination, dating back to the late 19th century. Its accommodation options now include hotels, hostels and family-run guesthouses.
During winter, visitors come for skiing and other snow-related activities. In warmer months, horseback riding, trekking and time by natural lakes and swimming pools are among the options.
The area also attracts travellers interested in village life. Some communities have retained traditional ways of living, and visitors can find local bread, honey and other regional products.
Tourism has become an important source of income for residents who provide accommodation, food and other services. According to Abduvaliyev, transport and visitor facilities have also improved, with connections from Tashkent and accommodation options ranging up to four-star hotels in the Bostanlyk district.
Safety measures are part of the area's tourism infrastructure. Warning signs identify places where swimming is prohibited and alert visitors to potential wildlife risks in forested areas.
A boat trip on Charvak Reservoir
Near Chimgan, Charvak Reservoir offers another way to experience the mountain scenery. Visitors can take boat trips across the blue water, with steep rocky slopes rising along the shoreline.
For tourist Ekaterina Sidorchuk, the colour of the reservoir and the surrounding rocks made a strong impression. She describes the boat ride, the movement of the waves and the traditional music on board as part of the experience.
She says she would like to return with her children to share the landscape with them.
Andrey Sidorchuk, who first visited the area 18 years ago, has returned with his wife to explore places she had not seen before. He says the trip has left them with many impressions and that they plan to continue travelling through Uzbekistan.
Different ways to experience the mountains
Urungach, Chimgan and Charvak each offer a different way to experience the Tashkent region. At Urungach, the lake’s emerald colour and changing water levels give the landscape a seasonal character. Chimgan draws visitors throughout the year for hiking and winter sports, while Charvak’s blue waters are best explored by boat, with mountain slopes rising along the shore.
Tourism is also creating new opportunities for people living in the surrounding villages, from guesthouses and local food to guiding and other visitor services.
As access improves and more travellers discover the area, the region’s mountain landscapes are becoming an increasingly important part of Uzbekistan’s outdoor tourism offer. The lakes, trails and villages each provide a different perspective on the same mountainous region.

title: Ukraine hits Putin's prized bridge in record drone blitz as Kremlin tells lawmakers to prepare for 'victory'
text:
Ukraine launched what Russia described as the largest overnight drone attack of the war Monday, striking President Vladimir Putin's prized Crimea bridge and setting industrial facilities ablaze, as separate reports revealed a covert French military mission in Ukraine and preparations in Moscow for a possible return of Russian troops.
The developments came days before President Donald Trump is expected to meet Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in China, amid renewed U.S.-brokered efforts to end the nearly five-year conflict.
"The sheer scale and effectiveness of these drone attacks are remarkable," retired Air Force Lt. Gen. Richard Newton told Fox News Digital. "Ukraine has developed the capability to produce large numbers of drones and strike targets once considered a safe haven deep inside Russia."
Russia's Defense Ministry claimed its forces intercepted 1,336 Ukrainian drones across 16 regions, exceeding the previous overnight record of 1,254 on Oct. 29, Reuters reported Nov. 16. The numbers could not be independently verified.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said about 600 drones had been launched toward the capital region since Sunday evening, with 191 intercepted.
Russian-installed Crimean governor Sergei Aksyonov confirmed that the Kerch Strait bridge, linking occupied Crimea to mainland Russia, had been struck. The Kremlin characterized the damage as minor. Road traffic was temporarily suspended for repairs, while trains continued running, according to Russian transportation officials.
The bridge is both a strategically important supply route and a symbol of Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014.
The strikes also hit Russia's energy sector. Rostov regional governor Yuri Slyusar reported fires at four industrial sites in Azov, where three people were injured. Officials in neighboring Krasnodar said a separate fire broke out at an industrial facility in Ilsky. Falling drone debris reportedly injured six people in the Krasnodar region.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy claimed Sunday that strikes had disabled more than half of Russia's refining capacity, a figure Fox News Digital could not verify. Two industry sources separately estimated that recent attacks reduced refining capacity by approximately 30%, Reuters reported.
"Putin has a serious problem on his hands," Newton said. "Russia is enormous in terms of size; there’s simply no way to 100% defend every refinery, airfield, and military installation."
Newton said Ukraine's campaign was designed to strengthen its negotiating position while disrupting Russia's military and logistics networks.
"I don’t believe Ukraine has reached a culminating point yet, by any stretch, to change Putin’s mind, but sustained military and economic pressure just may eventually at some point force him to reconsider his position," he said.
Secret French military mission
In a separate development, Radio France Internationale reported Nov. 16 that French troops had been operating inside Ukraine since at least summer 2026 as part of a confidential mission codenamed "Volia."
The mission reportedly consists of small teams making short visits to train Ukrainian personnel and maintain equipment. RFI said French lawmakers had not been informed and alleged that an established French training operation in Poland, known as "Gerfaut," provided a gateway for deployments into Ukraine.
An anonymous source familiar with the mission confirmed French personnel's presence to AFP, while stressing that they were not combat troops.
"The rotation of French trainers supporting Ukraine in France, Poland, or occasionally in Ukraine is a reality," the source told AFP. "But this is not a military operation. There is absolutely no intention of engaging in coercive actions."
France's military general staff did not immediately comment to AFP. The number of troops involved remains unknown.
Kremlin reportedly prepares for 'victory'
Meanwhile, Russian newspaper Vedomosti reported Nov. 16 that Kremlin officials had instructed lawmakers from Putin's United Russia party to prepare for "victory" and the return of personnel from the battlefield.
The message was reportedly delivered during a closed-door seminar attended by senior presidential administration official Sergei Kiriyenko. A source described lawmakers being told to anticipate the possibility of soldiers returning home simultaneously.
The report provided no timetable and did not establish that Putin had ordered a withdrawal or decided to end the war.
The reports emerged after U.S.-brokered talks in Abu Dhabi last week resulted in a major prisoner-exchange agreement but no breakthrough over territory.
Trump, Putin and Xi were due to meet Thursday, Nov. 19, in Shenzhen, China, with Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov describing the trilateral summit as a potentially significant event.
Newton expressed skepticism about an immediate diplomatic breakthrough. "I don't anticipate a major breakthrough on any issue, including Russia's war against Ukraine," he said.
"If President Trump has any discussions with Xi and Putin regarding Ukraine I would advise him to look those two leaders in the eye and underscore the U.S. is not backing down in our support to the Ukrainian people as they valiantly defend their homeland," he concluded.
Reuters contributed to this story.

title: A new fiber supplement could help millions suffering from irritable bowel syndrome
text:
Scientists have developed a promising new fiber supplement that improves gut health in people with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) without worsening bloating, pain, or other digestive symptoms. The specially designed blend also improved gut-related anxiety and produced surprisingly rapid changes in gut bacteria, potentially offering a new way to manage IBS.
A specially designed fiber supplement may offer a promising new way to improve gut health for millions of people with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). Researchers at Edith Cowan University (ECU) have developed and tested a fiber combination that supports beneficial gut bacteria without making common digestive symptoms worse.
The research team at ECU's Nutrition and Health Innovation Research Institute (NHIRI) found that the supplement, called ur gut®, improved gut health in people with IBS without increasing abdominal pain, bloating, diarrhea, or constipation.
IBS affects people around the world, including nearly 11 percent of Australians. Although its exact cause remains unclear, stress, infections, and certain medications may contribute to the condition. Symptoms can also become worse because of particular foods, inadequate sleep, psychological stress, hormonal changes, and lifestyle factors.
Why Common IBS Diets Can Affect Gut Health
People with IBS are frequently advised to follow a low-FODMAP diet, which limits certain carbohydrates that are easily fermented by gut bacteria. Although this approach can help control uncomfortable symptoms, restricting these foods may also have unintended consequences for the gut microbiome.
"For years we've known that a diet low in Fermentable Oligosaccharides, Disaccharides, Monesaccharides and Polyols (FODMAPs) can relieve symptoms, but they can also reduce beneficial gut bacteria and negatively impact fiber intake over time," lead author Dr. Tina Yan said.
"We wanted to find a way to build better gut health while following a low-FODMAP diet."
The new findings suggest that a carefully formulated fiber supplement could help address this problem, allowing people with IBS to support a healthier gut microbiome while continuing to manage their symptoms through dietary changes.
How the New Fiber Blend Works
The researchers attribute the supplement's promising effects to its combination of two ingredients: resistant starch and psyllium husk.
Psyllium appears to slow the breakdown of resistant starch by gut bacteria, allowing more of it to reach deeper sections of the colon before fermentation occurs. This process may increase the production of beneficial compounds that support intestinal health.
Ordinarily, fermentable fiber can be challenging for people with IBS because bacterial fermentation can produce excess gas and increase digestive discomfort. The new formulation appears to offer a way to obtain the benefits of fermentation without aggravating these symptoms.
"Traditionally, fermentable fibers can be difficult for people with IBS because they can increase gas production and discomfort," Dr. Yan said.
"What's exciting about this study is that participants maintained stable symptoms while showing meaningful improvements in their gut microbiota as well as in their gut-related anxiety."
Significant Changes in Gut Bacteria and Anxiety
The researchers observed substantial shifts in the composition of participants' gut bacteria during the intervention. These changes were particularly notable because they occurred over a relatively short period.
"Changes of this magnitude are rarely seen with such a short intervention," ur gut® co-creator Professor Amanda Devine said.
"The study demonstrated that our targeted dietary fiber blend positively reshaped the gut microbiome in people with IBS following a low-FODMAP diet, supporting beneficial bacteria linked to gut and mental health. This was great to see."
Alongside improvements in gut bacteria, participants also experienced reductions in gut-related anxiety. These findings suggest that the supplement's potential benefits may extend beyond changes in the digestive system, although further research will be needed to establish its broader effects.
A New Approach to Managing Irritable Bowel Syndrome
The researchers believe their findings could help shift IBS care toward improving the underlying health of the gut rather than focusing exclusively on avoiding foods that cause discomfort.
"For many people with IBS, success has traditionally meant simply avoiding certain foods," ur gut® co-creator Associate Professor Claus Christophersen said.
"Our findings suggest we may also be able to actively rebuild gut health and the microbiome while not making IBS symptoms worse. That's an important step forward."
By demonstrating that beneficial gut bacteria can be supported without increasing IBS symptoms, the study points toward new dietary strategies that could complement existing treatments.
The ur gut® supplement is already available for purchase. The research team has also created a cookbook featuring recipes designed to help people incorporate the supplement into a healthy diet.
The study, "Dietary fibre blend improves gut health in patients with irritable bowel syndrome following a low FODMAP diet: a randomised, double-blind control trial," was published online in the European Journal of Nutrition.

title: 60 years ago the Leonid meteor shower produced 144,000 meteors per hour. Could it happen again?
text:
This year marks a rather auspicious anniversary for meteor watchers. Sixty years ago, one of the most stupendous Leonid meteor displays lit up the predawn skies over the central and western U.S. So, what will the 2026 Leonids bring us? And what might they bring in the years to come?
The Leonid meteor shower is one of the most celebrated of the year's annual displays of "shooting stars." The mere mention of the Leonids usually elicits mental images of a sky filled with shooting stars pouring down through the sky like rain. Such meteor storms have indeed occurred with the Leonids, such as in 1833 and 1966 when meteor rates of tens of thousands per hour were observed. In more recent years, most notably 1999, 2001 and 2002, lesser Leonid displays of up to "only" a few thousand meteors per hour took place.
Unfortunately, that's not likely to be the case this year. In fact, comparatively speaking, this is going to be a lean year for the Leonids chiefly because of the expected lack of any significant activity. Although the Leonids are one of the most famous of all the annual meteor displays, this year they're not likely to be very productive. It's probable they are going to be rather weak and there probably will be long stretches when not a single Leonid will be seen. I'll explain why in a moment. First, let's find out about this shower's lineage.
What causes the Leonids?
The Leonids are so named because the shower's radiant point, from where the meteors seem to fan out, is located within the constellation of Leo the Lion, from the backward question mark pattern of stars known as "The Sickle." The meteors are caused by the Tempel-Tuttle comet, which sweeps through the inner solar system every 33⅓ years. Each time the comet passes closest to the sun it leaves a "river of rubble" in its wake: a dense trail of dusty debris. A meteor storm becomes possible if the Earth were to score a direct hit on a fresh dust trail ejected by the comet over the past several centuries.
The "lion's share" (no pun intended) of comet dust can be found just ahead and trailing behind Tempel-Tuttle. That comet last swept through the inner solar system in 1998. That's why spectacular meteor showers were seen in 1999, 2001 and 2002, with declining numbers thereafter.
When is the best time to look for Leonids?
According to the International Meteor Organization's 2026 meteor shower calendar, the Leonids are expected to reach their regular maximum at 23:45 UTC (6:45 p.m. EST) on Nov. 17, with around 15 meteors per hour possible under ideal viewing conditions.
Other forecasts place the peak at slightly different times. Margaret Campbell-Brown and Peter Brown, meteor experts for the Royal Astronomical Society of Canada, predict that the peak of this year's Leonids will occur at 00:00 hours UTC on Nov. 18. Russian meteor expert Mikhail Maslov feels that the peak will come about a third of a day earlier, at 16:00 UTC on Nov. 17.
Several weaker encounters with older debris trails are also predicted between Nov. 17 and 19, although no major meteor storm is expected.
Hardly any crumbs this year
Back in September 2014, comet Tempel-Tuttle was as far from the sun as it can get: 1.84 billion miles (2.96 billion km). The comet has since spent the last dozen years slowly approaching the inner solar system, but it's still 1.11 billion miles (1.79 billion km) from the sun, which is still well beyond the orbit of Saturn.
In contrast, at the point in the comet's orbit where we will be passing by on Tuesday morning, there is nothing save for a scattered few particles; bits and pieces likely loosened from the comet's nucleus a millennium or two ago.
So, this year's Leonids are expected to show only low activity; "maybe" at best 10 to 15 Leonids per hour might be seen, but more likely hourly counts will be less than that. The moon will not pose a problem; it's at first quarter phase, but it will set before 11 p.m. local time Monday evening, leaving the rest of the night dark.
What to look for
Watching a meteor shower consists of lying back, looking up at the sky... and waiting. Keep in mind that any local light pollution or obstructions like tall trees or buildings will further reduce your chances of making a meteor sighting. Leo does not start coming fully into view until the after-midnight hours, so that would be the best time to concentrate on looking for Leonids. As dawn is about to break at around 5 a.m., the Sickle will have climbed more than two-thirds of the way up from the southeast horizon to the point directly overhead (called the zenith).
Because the Leonids are moving along in their orbit around the sun in a direction opposite to that of Earth, they slam into our atmosphere nearly head-on, resulting in the fastest meteor velocities possible: 45 miles (72 km) per second.
