Such speeds tend to produce bright meteors, which leave long-lasting streaks or persistent trains in their wake. A mighty Leonid fireball can be quite spectacular, but such outstandingly bright meteors are likely to be very few and very far between this year (if any are seen at all).
1966: Stormy times
It was a different story 60 years ago, in 1966, when anticipation ran high for a potentially heavy display of Leonid meteors. The previous year, comet Tempel-Tuttle swept around the sun and was accompanied later that year by an unexpected surge of Leonid activity, with brilliant meteors darting across the sky at one or two per minute as seen from Hawaii and Australia. The most sanguine prediction for 1966 came from Dr. Kenneth L. Franklin (1923-2007), chief scientist at New York's Hayden Planetarium. Dr. Franklin had carefully examined the orbit of comet Tempel-Tuttle and concluded that " . . . the position of the comet is roughly what it was in 1833. So, a dramatic shower like the one that occurred in that year may yet be in the offing for 1966."
Based on Dr. Franklin's prediction, a "meteor party" was planned for the peak night of the Leonids in Central Park. New Yorkers of all ages were invited to gather on the Great Lawn at midnight to watch for the shooting stars. Ten thousand people turned out, but unfortunately skies were hopelessly cloudy.
But across the central and western US, where skies were mostly clear, Leonids were falling at a rate described by many as "too numerous to count." One observer stationed north of Mission, Texas said that meteors falling in all directions gave the impression of a "gigantic umbrella," appearing to "waterfall" out of the head of Leo. Perhaps the best views were from California and Arizona. At the Table Mountain Observatory, near Wrightwood, California, one resident astronomer commented that he and a colleague " . . . watched a rain of meteors, turn into a hail of meteors and finally a storm of meteors, too numerous to count by 3:50 a.m. Pacific Time. Instinctively we sought to shield our upturned faces from imagined celestial debris." From 6,850-foot Kitt Peak in southern Arizona, thirteen amateur astronomers saw Leonids falling at the staggering rate of 40 per second (144,000 per hour)!
Looking ahead. . .
In 2005, French meteor expert Jeremie Vaubaillon published a technical paper with two colleagues in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics that forecast Leonid activity for years up to 2100. Sadly, in the year 2029, Jupiter is expected to throw Comet Tempel-Tuttle off its current path through space, making it all but impossible — at least through the beginning of the 22nd century — to see a repeat of the Great Leonid Storm of 1966.
But Vaubaillon expects the next big Leonid outburst in the year 2034, when rates could reach up to 2,000 per hour.
That's just 8 years from now. Mark your calendars.
Joe Rao serves as an instructor and guest lecturer at New York's Hayden Planetarium. He writes about astronomy for Natural History magazine, Sky and Telescope, The Old Farmer's Almanac and other publications.

title: The AI start-ups fixing India's broken roads and messy land records
text:
In 2020, Sanjay Mandava flew down from Chicago to Chennai in southern India to resolve a personal land dispute.
Over the next few months, he was running around between government offices to access a dozen records that would conclusively prove that the property belonged to his family.
Just a sale deed dating back to when his parents bought the land was not enough. Authorities asked him to produce a string of other documents.
Frustrated by the experience, he built Landeed - an AI-led digital platform that enables users to aggregate fragmented, multi-source land-records, verify titles and conduct legal checks at the click of a few buttons, across 24 states in India.
He's solving a problem that is uniquely Indian.
"In the US or UK, when you purchase a property, the government verifies ownership. In India by contrast, we follow presumptive titling - the buyer is responsible for establishing ownership. A sale deed merely records the transaction - multiple other documents may be needed to prove title," Mandava told the BBC.
These include building certificates, property tax receipts and land survey maps among others.
The system is rife for misuse - property disputes account for a bulk of civil litigation cases in the country where some 80% of household wealth is held in real estate.
Landeed has mapped large swathes of India using geo-spatial technology and data from state land revenue departments, registration offices, survey records and municipal databases.
Using this, it has linked registered properties to their official land identification and survey numbers and ownership records.
An additional AI-layer can read these titles, extract information and spot inconsistencies within minutes - a process that takes lawyers and brokers several days.
With the largest repository of title data in the country, consisting of 1.8 billion documents, the app is now used by millions of individual and enterprise customers while doing real estate transactions.
The app is among a burgeoning list of Indian start-ups trying to address some of India's most complex challenges in sectors ranging from legal-tech to healthcare, infrastructure, education and agriculture using AI.
Unlike the US and China which have a global dominance in building frontier language models like ChatGPT, India's AI revolution is happening downstream in data centre infrastructure and consumer applications rather than in research.
Start-ups are solving issues for everything from pothole detection to tribal language translation to assisting overworked public-health professionals with medical tasks - often working with highly fragmented, multilingual datasets in extremely cost sensitive industries.
Bengaluru-based YouTube teacher Gaurav Sen's AI app detects potholes using a dash-cam, satellite-based navigation and an AI vision model to analyse images.
It then identifies civic officials responsible for fixing them and sends them this data. He got viral attention recently given how widespread the menace of potholes is across India's urban sprawls.
On last count, there are at least half a dozen other similar offerings that map and report road damage to authorities across the country.
"A municipal corporation can take the app and use it on public buses and taxis, to access real-time, updated data on road conditions," Sen told the BBC.
In Mumbai on India's western coast, Fractal Analytics - among the few Indian listed AI companies - has deployed its AI tool "Vaidya" in hospitals run by the local civic authority.
The app allows citizens to receive AI-generated, simplified summaries of their lab reports in multiple languages, identify nearby healthcare facilities based on their needs and gives doctors AI-guided pre-consultation support such as medical history and medication details of patients.
It also provides hospital administrators with a public health dashboard based on aggregated, anonymous insights from lab reports accessed through its tie-up with municipal hospitals, giving them crucial visibility into emerging infections or other disease trends.
This boom has led to a surge in funding for AI start-ups - up 265% year-on-year according to Inc42, external, a start-up information platform. They raised over $1bn in the first nine months of this year amid a relatively muted fundraising environment for the broader ecosystem.
Yet, these companies face an uphill task in commercialising their ideas and taking them beyond pilot.
"The cost of building in India is sometimes much higher than what Indian customers are willing to pay," Fractal's co-founder Srikanth Velamakanni told the BBC at his sprawling office overlooking Mumbai's film city.
"The computing power needed to run an AI model is the same whether it is built in India or the US - but American customers have a far bigger paying capacity than those here."
Indian AI founders are also being forced to build around scarcity, with availability of high quality chips at the right scale and price, a major impediment for many.
"I believe I am building one of the most impactful things for this country," says Mandava.
"But I am starved for GPUs [chips that perform millions of calculations and help train AI models]. I have a hellish time trying to acquire them," he says.
The country has promised its start-ups 38,000 GPUs through its government-led AI mission, external, but demand for this compute power is far greater than supply.
Cumbersome regulation and bureaucracy are other major challenges.
Without these fundamental issues being addressed, there's a risk that Indian AI companies will build shallow solutions that a next generation of founders will immediately make redundant, say experts.
"Someone like a Google will probably laugh if I tell them of my pilot. To make it sustainable and hard to replicate, it will have to be much more sophisticated," says Sen, displaying a self-awareness of where his product currently stands.
From a lack of experienced talent to the struggle to turn successful pilots into recurring government contracts to heavy dependence on expensive foreign technology, Indian founders are powering through many odds.
"We can still do it. We don't want protection, but propel us, give us the weapons to compete against the best," Mandava says, when asked what he wants from policymakers.
"To quote Jay-Z - I can't help the poor if I'm one of them," he adds.

title: ‘Ahead of his time’: AI helps unlock discoveries hidden in notebooks of man who transformed maths
text:
The Austrian logician Kurt Gödel was one of the most original thinkers of the 20th century. His two incompleteness theorems, published in 1931, transformed mathematics and paved the way for the digital age.
After his seminal results of the 1930s, Gödel published only a few papers. His unpublished work, however, runs to tens of thousands of pages, and is of great interest to historians of science.
Since 2017, the Finnish logician Jan von Plato has led a project at Helsinki University to understand the contents of 16 notebooks that Gödel wrote in the early 1940s. This material – the “workbooks” – is 1,009 pages of densely written text about maths and logic. Much of it is written in a German shorthand, Gabelsberger, that was obsolete even when Gödel was using it.
Progress in the mathematical understanding of the text was painfully slow – about a page a week – until September, when von Plato enlisted the help of the AI model Claude. Within a couple of days, Claude had provided a comprehensive digest of the entire material, revealing Gödel had proved hundreds of theorems that no one knew about.
The most famous logician of modern times had, in fact, discovered significantly more than anyone had thought.
“I was flabbergasted,” said von Plato. “The workbooks not only contain dozens of anticipations of results not known until the 70s and 80s, but they also contain 14 themes in logic that have not been pursued. Gödel was far ahead of his time.”
Gödel changed the course of logic because he revealed the limits of mathematical knowledge. His incompleteness theorems show that in all mathematical systems there are true statements that can neither be proved or disproved. Yet while this result was a blow to previous generations of logicians, who had hoped that all truths were verifiable, Gödel’s work pushed the field in new directions, inspiring Alan Turing to write his 1936 paper that began the theory of modern computation.
In 1940, Gödel fled Austria under the Nazis. He settled in Princeton, New Jersey, and became a close friend of Albert Einstein at the Institute of Advanced Study. Increasingly paranoid in his later years, he refused to eat food that was not cooked by his wife, and died of starvation in 1978.
Von Plato said he had started his Gödel project in 2017 because he was facing mandatory retirement from Helsinki University. “What should I do to make myself indispensable? Oh yes, I’ll start reading Gödel’s enigmatic shorthand pages!” He received a €2.5m (£2.1m) grant from the European Research Council, taught himself Gabelsberger shorthand – “I am one of only six people who can read it in the world” – and assembled a small team.
In August, at a conference in France about AI and theorem proving, von Plato met computer scientists who suggested that he co-opt the help of Claude in trying to make sense of the workbooks. On his return to Helsinki he began the process, showing Claude his transcriptions of the workbooks, as well as six books he had previously written on Gödel and other secondary scientific literature.
“In a couple of days, I got to see a 650-page explanation of the workbooks. It had to be controlled page for page, but it’s basically a work that is impossible to do for human beings,” he said. “Humans read one page at a time and we tend to forget things. It takes us a year to read about 50 pages. We just are not able to keep in mind all the different parts.
“The AI can connect all the pieces in a thousand pages. It can see all of Gödel’s writings as one piece.”
Gödel’s incompleteness theorems revealed the existence of statements whose truths were independent of the system they were written in: that is, they could not be proved or disproved within the system. In 1966, the American mathematician Paul Cohen won the Fields medal, the highest honour in maths, for showing the independence of two well-known mathematical statements: the continuum hypothesis and the axiom of choice.
Gödel reacted to Cohen’s Fields medal by saying that he had already proved the result in the 1940s. Yet when pushed for a proof by his peers, Gödel was unable to reconstruct one from his notes.
The first task von Plato set Claude was to discover if Gödel’s workbooks had a proof of the independence of the axiom of choice, which would reveal that Gödel had been telling the truth in 1966. The answer came back: yes, almost. “He was just one step away,” said von Plato. “There’s one definition that Gödel got wrong, but he had the right definition two years earlier, and so the thought is that he would have arrived at the right definition anyway if he had just continued for a few months. For me, the architecture of his proof is just wonderful. It makes all of these results of set theory follow a uniform pattern.
“What strikes me especially is that he starts from ideas. He’s not like someone who plays with formulas and hopes to arrive somewhere. He has very, very clear ideas, and then he’s methodical. Step after step he goes ahead and he manages to fulfil the aims that he has in this formal work.”
Von Plato said that when Claude presented him with the reconstructed proof of the independence of the axiom of choice, he ran it through the proof assistant Coq, a program that verifies the validity of mathematical proofs, and it passed. Von Plato believes that had Gödel published his work on the axiom of choice, he would have won the 1940 Fields medal. “Maybe he felt that when Cohen got the medal, that that was something he sort of missed.”
In further discussions with Claude, von Plato asked the AI model to extract all theorems in the workbooks for which Gödel either had a proof, had sketched a proof or had an idea for a proof. Claude found 663. When these results were put into Coq: “About 400 were verified as stated, about 200 were repaired, meaning that perhaps the statement of the theorem had to be made more precise, or some assumption had to be added. About 50 were false, and this is no wonder. Gödel himself, when rereading his notes, would occasionally add a marginal remark: falsch! [incorrect] or schlecht! [bad].”
Von Plato added: “I am sure that the continued study of Gödel’s manuscripts will reveal further treasures. The workbooks contain, Claude says, more than a dozen themes in logic and foundations of mathematics that have not been found in the 80-plus years since they were written down. So this is one thing to explore. But there are many others. His physics and cosmology notebooks are an unknown territory I plan to start exploring once I am finished with my present logic projects.”
Joel David Hamkins, a professor of logic at the University of Notre Dame, Indiana, has not seen Claude’s reconstruction of Gödel’s proof of the independence of the axiom of choice, but said that if it stood up “it is remarkable and historically interesting. Although how much is Claude and how much is Gödel is a job for the historians.”
Hamkins said: “The fact that there are things in there that resemble [Cohen’s proof] does not mean he had it. It shows he was on the path. You don’t get credit for work you don’t tell anyone about. But Gödel had so many ground-breaking ideas that it is maybe not surprising that his notebooks are full of exciting things.”

title: This week in science: PTSD prediction, phishing while tired, an exoplanet
text:
The regular news roundup with NPR's science podcast Short Wave covers a possible use for AI in emergency rooms, a distant planet and the link between cybersecurity and Daylight Saving Time.
SCOTT DETROW, HOST:
It's time now for our science news roundup from Short Wave, NPR's science podcast. I am joined by the show's hosts, Emily Kwong and Regina Barber. Hello to both of you.
REGINA BARBER, BYLINE: Hey.
EMILY KWONG, BYLINE: Hey.
DETROW: You were in stereo just now.
BARBER: Yeah.
DETROW: It was great.
BARBER: We planned that.
DETROW: So you've brought us three science stories that caught your attention. What are they?
KWONG: How AI can help emergency room workers identify patients who may develop PTSD.
BARBER: A new technique that helps us find really faint planets beyond our solar system.
DETROW: You know how I feel about space.
BARBER: That's right.
KWONG: We put it in there for you.
BARBER: That's why I picked it.
KWONG: (Inaudible) put this story in there for you (laughter).
KWONG: And why daylight saving time could be bad for cybersecurity.
DETROW: All right. Let's start with - this is interesting. There's been so many stories about AI identifying healthcare trends that might be hard for doctors to spot. Let's talk about this. Identifying...
KWONG: Yeah.
DETROW: ...PTSD in emergency departments.
KWONG: This is very interesting. So researchers took trauma patients answers' to a routine screening question - what brought you to the emergency department today? They fed the answers to that question into an AI model that was designed to predict the patient's risk of developing PTSD a month later.
DETROW: Huh. I mean, how good was the model making that prediction?
BARBER: So it got it right around 95% of the cases. A psychologist and lead researcher, Katharina Schultebraucks, says that these results are exciting because they're using a patient's story in their own words.
KATHARINA SCHULTEBRAUCKS: Some people talk, like, very elaborative of what happens. Some are in such high distress they may only say a few words and a few sentences. And we are looking not on PTSD symptoms right now, but we're looking in what happens in the future.
BARBER: They published their findings in the journal Nature Communications.
DETROW: I'm curious, is this something that clinicians have been missing?
KWONG: Yeah, so when trained clinicians are screening for PTSD risk, they do tend to find it. The problem is that giving a PTSD risk assessment is an extra step that a lot of emergency departments just simply do not have time for. You know, they're, like, tending to the emergency. There's also the stigma around mental health that might clam up some patients. So using this model could streamline the process, and medical professionals can act sooner to prevent PTSD from developing.
BARBER: And Scott, what's unique about this work is that the model gave its reasoning at each step of the analysis.
MUNMUN DE CHOUDHURY: What this work does, it says that the AI doesn't have to be a black box.
BARBER: So this is Munmun De Choudhury, a computer scientist not involved in the work. She said this work has real potential to guide clinicians to the right kind of interventions.
DETROW: Perpetual question with this stuff - are there worries about privacy of sending a patient's words to an AI model?
KWONG: Good question. Katharina says that the model did not share the data on a cloud service and was HIPAA-compliant. But she adds that it is important any patient consents to having their information recorded and used by an AI model.
DETROW: So new topic.
DETROW: Gina.
DETROW: Exoplanet.
BARBER: (Laughter) Yeah.
DETROW: New exoplanet. Let's - this is a - meaning a planet beyond our solar system.
DETROW: What is this technique that scientists used to find it?
BARBER: So this exoplanet was actually already known. A team of researchers studied existing images of the star it orbits to see if light from 51 Eridani b could be found, just to kind of verify this technique. And this is important because often it's hard to see exoplanets in images.
KWONG: And that's because the light that exoplanets reflect from the closest star is often much fainter than the light the star gives off.
DETROW: Right.
KWONG: So the star, like, kind of hides the planet.
DETROW: I mean, so how did they uncover it, then? Because again, stars, very bright.
DETROW: Planets, when they're far away, not very bright.
BARBER: So they subtracted light from the image until they could clearly see the planet and not the stars. The paper was published in Nature last week. And this new technique corrects that issue and corrects for millions of more issues that can make it harder to find an exoplanet, like the telescope being unstable or instrumental errors or temperature fluctuations.
DETROW: Is this kind of like in a - in, like, a cops TV show where they're looking at the security camera and they say, oh, enhance on that one image, and they zoom in?
BARBER: I mean, kind of (laughter). But Scott, what I'm actually surprised about is that they did all of this with just physics knowledge and algorithms and no AI.
DETROW: No AI.
DETROW: All right.
KWONG: (Laughter).
DETROW: So what can these images tell us about this planet?
KWONG: So yeah, because these images were taken in infrared by the powerful James Webb Space Telescope, they can tell us more about what these exoplanets are made out of.
RODRIGO FERRER-CHAVEZ: With this, it is the first time that we can actually get this specific information-rich image of this planet that might tell us a lot about how it formed.
KWONG: That's lead author Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez, a Ph.D. candidate at Northwestern University. He also says that this tool can be used to find even more exoplanets hiding out in James Webb Space Telescope images.
BARBER: This technique can also be used to make future telescopes, that are already supposed to be more powerful, even better at finding exoplanets. But I do want to say that other astronomers I talked to said that this is just one cool technique of many that scientists are developing for future research in finding these faint, distant worlds.
DETROW: OK. All right, back here on Earth. Third story. It's about sleep.
KWONG: Mm-hmm.
BARBER: Mm-hmm.
KWONG: And daylight saving.
BARBER: Yeah. So, Scott, did you know that nearly one-third of U.S. adults don't get enough sleep?
DETROW: Honestly, I would assume the number is higher.
DETROW: One-third actually sounds promising (laughter).
KWONG: Oh, gosh.
BARBER: And we know that it's bad for our health, right? It's bad for decision-making.
KWONG: But just how bad is it for decision-making if you lose a modest amount of sleep? That's what Eitan Schechtman, an assistant professor at the University of California, Irvine wanted to know. And he found a fun way to test this with phishing attacks.
BARBER: (Laughter).
KWONG: His university regularly sends fake phishing emails to staff to train them on cybersecurity. These emails contain suspicious links you are not supposed to click. But would they click if they were a little sleepy?
DETROW: Interesting. Did this become a full experiment?
BARBER: Yeah, so Eitan worked with the university's security team to divide 11,000 participants into two groups. Some people got the fishing email the Monday before daylight saving, and some got it the Monday immediately after, you know, when we can assume some may have lost an hour of sleep. So people emailed after daylight saving were 13% more likely to fall for the phishing attack the following morning and click that bad link. The study was published in the Proceedings of National Academy of Sciences this week.
KWONG: I spoke to Muhammad Adeel Rishi, a sleep specialist at Indiana University School of Medicine who wasn't involved in this study. He found the finding compelling and said it adds to growing evidence about the consequences of daylight saving. Spring forward has been linked to an increase in heart attacks and fatal traffic accidents.
DETROW: And apparently cybersecurity problems. What's the solution here?
BARBER: So Eitan wants cybersecurity companies to be aware of this finding so they can beef up their security for any moments where there's widespread sleep loss. So think about holidays or major sporting events.
EITAN SCHECHTMAN: There might be more of these - more susceptibility to click these links or generally to make impulsive decisions, whether it's on the road, in the stock market or cybersecurity-related decision.
DETROW: Some places have just, like, gotten rid of time changes, right?
DETROW: Like most of Arizona and Hawaii.
KWONG: Yes. This is a whole other debate. But just to put science's finger on the scale, multiple studies have shown that standard time is healthier for our bodies. Standard time has more natural light in the morning, which better aligns to our bodies' circadian rhythms.
DETROW: All right. Good thing we're in standard time right now.
DETROW: That is Emily Kwong and Regina Barber with NPR's science podcast Short Wave, where you can listen for new discoveries and the science behind the headlines. Thanks to both of you.
KWONG: Thank you.
BARBER: Thank you, Scott.

title: Trump's handpicked party chair faces a rebellion as midterm losses challenge president's grip on GOP
text:
A rebellion is forming against President Donald Trump’s handpicked chairman at the Republican National Committee
NEW YORK -- A nascent rebellion is underway against President Donald Trump's handpicked chairman at the Republican National Committee, and it’s already getting ugly.
Some members are calling for a forensic audit of spending decisions, including hair and makeup services for Trump and other officials, as well as the hiring of the daughter of Trump's former chief of staff. Feuding Republicans are leaking emails and opposition research on rival factions. The White House is threatening to cut off fundraising assistance if the rebels don’t fall in line.
The emerging fight, which will shape the 2028 presidential nominating contest, represents a rare challenge to Trump's dominance, even after the party's worst midterm performance in a generation. Despite the heavy losses, Republican leaders across Washington have shown little desire to move past Trump and have largely stood behind his most unpopular policies.
But inside the RNC, an organization of 168 members elected from every state who oversee the party’s national political operation, a small yet growing group is backing an attempt to depose Joe Gruters. Trump wants to keep him in charge.
The dissidents are rallying behind Kentucky’s KC Crosbie, the RNC's second-in-command, who launched her bid just two days after the Nov. 3 election in a letter that drew the fury of both the White House and Gruters' allies.
Crosbie remains a vocal Trump supporter who backs his “Make America Great Again” agenda, but her opponents view her gambit as a direct challenge to the president and his power.
“We have an obligation to serve the Republican Party the most effective way we can. And if all we do is say yes to what the White House wants, I’m not sure that’s doing what’s best for the Republican Party,” said RNC member Oscar Brock of Tennessee, who is supporting Crosbie’s candidacy. “Our job is to elect Republicans broadly, not to support one man all the time.”
He said that requires a change in leadership.
“There’s so much frustration that Chairman Gruters didn’t pull his weight in this election, that the RNC was far less effective than it should have been,” he said.
In her letter, Crosbie described the midterms as “a serious setback" and called for the RNC to provide “an honest account” of what went wrong.
“We should preserve what we built and be equally willing to confront where we fell short,” she wrote.
Crosbie declined to be interviewed. The leadership election will be held in January at the RNC’s winter meeting in Arizona.
It’s unclear how many RNC members will back Crosbie, although the number so far is believed to be small. Some would-be supporters privately acknowledge that they're worried about a backlash from the White House, especially with Stephen Miller taking over as Trump's new White House chief of staff. Others believe in the committee's tradition of having presidents pick their own party chiefs.
Gruters also has vocal backers.
Lauren LePage, an RNC member from Maine, praised the chairman's leadership and his efforts to help her father, Paul LePage, flip a congressional seat — a rare bright spot for Republicans this election cycle.
She described Gruters as “highly responsive” during the campaign and praised his “record-setting fundraising."
“From my perspective, as chairman, he did his job," she said, adding that Trump's endorsement is “something that the committee should take very seriously.”
Nevada Republican Party Chairman Michael McDonald called Crosbie a “dear friend," but said Trump is “the leader of our party” and “you always have to fall in line with the leader.”
“I don’t have a bad word to say about KC at all. It's just that the president wants to go with Joe Gruters," he said. “The president made his choice.”
The Republicans who have lined up behind Crosbie insist a leadership change is needed to send a clear message that the party will do things differently after losses even in conservative strongholds such as Texas, South Carolina and Mississippi.
Patti Lyman, an RNC member from Virginia, said it would be “catastrophic” and “insulting” to the party’s base “to keep the same leadership and pretend that we don’t need to do anything different, that we don’t need new players and a new plan.”
Lyman described Crosbie as “by far the best candidate currently running to lead the RNC forward to victory in 2028.”
Sue Cienki, an RNC committee member from Rhode Island, predicted that Crosbie would have the backing of at least two members from 10 states — for a total of 20 — at the committee's January meeting. That number is the minimum required for a successful nomination.
She insisted that she wouldn't be scared off by backlash from Trump or the White House, which has been actively lobbying RNC members.
“We should not be influenced by any one person or other. It’s our organization," Cienki said. “We have to hold an election, not a selection.”
Trump and senior White House officials were livid about Crosbie’s Nov. 5 letter and the fact that they were given no heads-up.
During a White House meeting Nov. 6, Trump threatened to punish the RNC if members crossed him and said he would refuse to help the organization, including appearing at fundraisers or allowing his name and image to be used in mail and digital solicitations. That’s according to a senior White House official with direct knowledge of the meeting who was not authorized to publicly discuss the private gathering and spoke on condition of anonymity.
Such a threat would be catastrophic to the party because Trump remains its most effective money raiser.
An Axios story that first reported the threats was distributed via text message to all 168 RNC members.
The same senior White House official said staff convinced Trump that he should not go after Crosbie personally that day. Instead, he released a lengthy statement on his Truth Social social media platform hailing Gruters as a “MAGA Warrior” and giving him his “Complete and Total Endorsement.”
The leadership fight comes as Trump has shown no interest in relinquishing power
The Constitution bars Trump from seeking a third term, but he is expected to play a central role in picking the party's next presidential nominee. Trump's team contends that he remains the most popular Republican in the country, and House Republicans this week elected a slate of new leaders closely aligned with him.
The White House referred questions about the leadership fight to Trump’s Truth Social post.
The RNC will oversee the party's presidential primary process, including setting the nominating calendar, the debate schedule, the national convention and the rules governing the selection of the White House candidate.
People close to Gruters, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss private conversations, said Crosbie’s campaign was “100% a challenge" to the president’s power and described the RNC as “the president’s political operation.”
Allies argued that a leadership change now would put the RNC at a severe disadvantage heading into the next presidential cycle because a new team would need time to get up to speed and they warned that friction between the president and the committee's leadership would curtail their ability to organize and raise money.
They also rejected Crosbie's call for a postelection review, which they said would do little more than rehash the past and put all their grievances on paper. Similar demands for a retrospective were a headache for Ken Martin, the embattled leader of the Democratic National Committee, after Trump won in 2024.
But they said Gruters has taken the criticism seriously and has been soliciting feedback to make adjustments heading into 2028.
Gruters spent much of this week holding private phone conversations with committee members. Those who participated in the calls said Gruters listened to their grievances but said little about what he would do differently.
The opposition to Trump's choice to lead the RNC has little to do with Trump's leadership or policy decisions, according to nearly a half-dozen Crosbie supporters.
Instead, they focused on the RNC's spending decisions under Gruters. Republicans had a massive fundraising advantage and still lost the House and Senate.
“There’s clearly a groundswell of support for a forensic audit,” said Brock, the RNC member from Tennessee.
In a letter to RNC members sent Thursday night and obtained by The Associated Press, Gruters acknowledged concerns.
Gruters defended a $22,500 expenditure for hospitality space at the Presidents Cup, a golf event, saying it was offered to major donors and "resulted in $2.5 million in renewed contributions to the RNC.”
He also addressed concerns about “a brief contract” between the RNC and Caroline Wiles, a longtime Republican consultant who is the daughter of Susie Wiles, Trump's former chief of staff. Gruters said she was hired by his predecessor at the committee, Michael Whatley.
“While I have no reason to doubt Caroline Wiles’s value to the RNC or Chairman Whatley’s reasons for bringing her on, this was a brief six-month engagement that ended when I was elected Chairman,” he wrote.
Gruters also defended the RNC's decision to pay for “hair and make-up services” for senior White House officials, including Trump, Vice President JD Vance and former press secretary Karoline Leavitt.
“This was a request made of us so that the expense did not fall to taxpayers,” Gruters wrote. He said the beneficiaries “generously gave so much of their limited time and energies to help the RNC this cycle” and “did not ask for much of us in return, so we felt this was a request we could accommodate.”
Gruters promised to provide members “honest and direct answers to concerns raised” as conversations continue.
“I pledge to listen and learn from you about what happened in the field,” he wrote, “so together we can move forward stronger than ever.”

title: Turkey uses espionage accusations to pressure government critics
text:
When police officers appeared at her home in Istanbul last Wednesday evening, Yonca Verdioglu Sik was surprised — even more so when they took her in for questioning. Her lawyer says she was accused of political and military espionage.
But, according to transcripts of the interrogation that were published later, Verdioglu Sik was never asked any questions about espionage. Instead the public prosecutor's office appeared to be more interested in the activities of her German employer, the Heinrich Böll Foundation.
For 18 years, Verdioglu Sik, who was born and raised in Germany, has been the foundation's project coordinator. In her role, she organizes projects that focus on democracy and the rights of women, minorities and LGBTQ+ people.
During the interrogation, transfers of money from the foundation into her bank account were discussed. Verdioglu Sik found out that she was now also subject to a travel ban.
Pressure on politicians
Verdioglu Sik was eventually released, but her arrest caused outrage among critics of the Turkish government. She is married to investigative journalist and member of parliament, Ahmet Sik. He belongs to the left-wing Workers' Party of Turkey, or TIP, and is known as one of the harshest critics of the current government.
Sik has recently been looking into a stock market scandal, which allegedly benefited members of the ruling Justice and Development Party, or AKP, headed by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, and associates.
Opposition critics drew a clear conclusion: As a member of parliament, Sik has parliamentary immunity. So instead, the justice system is putting pressure on him through his wife.
"If you take away a state's law, what is left is no longer called a state, but a gang," Sik responded to the arrest in writing.
Verdioglu Sik's arrest is not the first such case in Turkey. Ever since the attempted coup against the Erdogan government in 2016, accusations of espionage have been leveled at a wide variety of groups in Turkey: journalists, opposition figures and human rights activists as well as employees of foreign embassies and staff of foreign institutions like nongovernmental organizations and foundations.
Diplomatic disputes
Such accusations have often been followed by acquittals or convictions for other offenses, albeit sometimes years later. But what the many instances have in common is what's known as a "chilling effect." Any investigation can mean lengthy pre-trial detention, reputational and professional damage and even social isolation.
In the past, such cases have even triggered diplomatic spats.
In 2015, for example, Can Dundar and Erdem Gul, both senior journalists at the opposition daily Cumhuriyet, were accused of espionage after reporting that Turkey had tried to ship arms to rebels fighting the Syrian government. Dundar now lives in exile in Berlin.
In 2017, Erdogan said that reporter Deniz Yücel, then working for German newspaper Die Welt, was a "German agent." That led to a serious diplomatic crisis between Berlin and Ankara.
Espionage charges have also been laid against local employees of the US diplomatic corps and against a lawyer working for the German embassy. US pastor Andrew Brunson and his wife were also arrested because of alleged links to Kurdish anti-government groups. Turkish philanthropist and human rights activist Osman Kavala, who was charged with espionage and attempting to overthrow the constitutional order, remains in prison.
Most recently, espionage charges have been brought against the former Istanbul mayor and Erdogan's political competitor, Ekrem Imamoglu, and a number of journalists.
'Hostage diplomacy'
Hakki Tas, a research fellow and expert on Turkey at the German Institute for Global and Area Studies, said the number of such cases have been increasing over the past few years.
On the one hand, Turkey has the right to protect itself from foreign intelligence services — especially given geopolitical competition and conflict in the region, he argued. On the other hand, there's a long tradition of bringing the Turkish opposition to court to face security charges.
"What foreigners or employees of foreign institutions have experienced in recent years is a continuation of this pattern," Tas told DW.
Media outlets and NGOs critical of the government have faced investigations, trials and other sorts of state sanctions for years. The ruling AKP party has also brought in its own version of a so-called "foreign agent law."
These sorts of espionage cases serve both a domestic and foreign policy function, Tas said.
For locals, "contact with a foreign institution, foreign funding or even a perfectly normal salary could become part of an investigation someday," he explained. "For opposition figures and civil society organizations, in particular, this can become a security issue."
In terms of foreign policy, the cases also show other countries that there are limits to their activities inside Turkey. These kinds of accusations seem to become more frequent when there's some sort of foreign policy tension — for example, after Western criticism of how opposition groups were dealt with after the alleged coup in 2016, the aforementioned disputes about arms deliveries in connection with Syria, or criticism from abroad about the removal of elected mayors in Turkey.
It can also serve as a kind of "hostage diplomacy," Tas said.
Punishing process
The case of US pastor Brunson is a good example. After his arrest, the Turkish government proposed a trade with the Americans. They wanted to exchange Turkish preacher Fethullah Gulen, who lived in the US and who the Turkish government blamed for the 2016 coup attempt.
This suspicion of foreign institutions isn't something that the Erdogan government invented, Tas points out. In the early 2000s, several representatives of German organizations were already made to stand trial in Turkey. At the time, it was alleged that, among other things, the German spy service was using German foundations as a front for conspiracy.
In some of the best-known cases, defendants often don't end up convicted of espionage. In the case of activist Osman Kavala, he was initially acquitted of espionage several times and spent two years in prison, just because of those charges.
But Tas said that's no surprise, referring to a 1979 work about the sociology of law written by US law professor Malcolm Feeley. It's title: "The Process Is the Punishment."

title: Tiger Woods confirms playing return on PGA Tour
text:
Tiger Woods is set to make his return to the PGA Tour at the Hero World Challenge in December.
Woods has not played competitively in a regular event since missing the cut at the 2024 Open at Royal Troon, but is in-line to make his comeback at the limited field event in the Bahamas.
The 15-time major champion took a break from the sport after his involvement in a car crash in March, for which he received a five-year ban from driving after a reckless driving plea.
The 50-year-old’s Tiger Woods Foundation is attached to the Hero World Challenge, which features 20 of the world’s best players.
Rickie Fowler and Gary Woodland have also earned invites into the event, which begins on 3 December. Scottie Scheffler and Matt Fitzpatrick are among those also slated to play.
Woods has struggled increasingly with injuries over the last few years. He ruptured an Achilles tendon and had a seventh back surgery before his arrest on suspicion of driving under the influence in March.
"I am stepping away for a period of time to seek treatment and focus on my health. This is necessary in order for me to prioritise my well-being and work toward lasting recovery,” Woods said then after revealing he would be taking his break.
“I'm committed to taking the time needed to return in a healthier, stronger, and more focused place, both personally and professionally.
"I appreciate your understanding and support, and ask for privacy for my family, loved ones and myself at this time.”
Woods won his last major at The Masters in 2019, and sits three titles behind the record tally of Jack Nicklaus.
He is also set to play in TGL, the indoor golf league he co-founded with Rory McIlroy.

title: Deutsche Bank shares fall as leak reveals Trump tax document error
text:
Deutsche Bank shares fell more than 6% on Tuesday after reports based on 15 million leaked records shed light on its dealings with clients including Donald Trump.
Deutsche Bank shares fell more than 6% in Frankfurt on Tuesday before paring losses to 3.8% by early afternoon, after an international media investigation shed new light on the lender’s dealings with Russian oligarchs, convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and US President Donald Trump.
Germany’s largest bank said some of the cases dated back as much as two decades and that it had reviewed them at the time and worked with regulators where relevant.
It said it had spent €7 billion strengthening its internal controls between 2019 and 2025 and told Reuters news agency it expected no significant financial impact from the reports.
The investigation, dubbed Inside Deutsche Bank, drew on more than 15 million files supplied by two whistleblowers whose identities the consortium has kept confidential.
More than 200 journalists worked on the project, including reporters from the Financial Times, Der Spiegel, Le Monde, The New York Times and German public broadcaster ZDF.
What the records revealed
The Financial Times reported that Deutsche Bank accidentally sent a Trump tax document to another client’s accountant in 2017, during his first term as president, and did not tell the White House.
Speaking to reporters in Manila on Tuesday, Trump called the disclosure “illegal”. The bank declined to comment on his reaction, Reuters reported.
The FT also reported that Deutsche Bank processed $582 million (€528 million) in payments linked to the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein that it later flagged as suspicious.
Other reports described tax arrangements the bank set up for wealthy clients and suspected money laundering through services it provided to other banks.
The records show that Deutsche Bank sought to expand its Russian business shortly before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, despite internal warnings about regulatory and money-laundering risks.
Chief executive Christian Sewing took part in the working group that prepared the strategy, according to reports based on the documents.
Deutsche Bank said in March 2022 that it would wind down its remaining business in Russia and take on no new business there. Its annual report shows that it still had 162 full-time equivalent staff in Russia at the end of 2025 and recorded a pre-tax profit of €61 million in the country that year.
German finance minister calls for answers
German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil called for “full transparency” about how Deutsche Bank had addressed past failures and gaps in its internal controls, and how it would prevent them from recurring, according to AFP.
He also called for regulators and law enforcement authorities to scrutinise the bank.
Deutsche Bank chair Alexander Wynaendts backed Sewing in a statement emailed to Reuters, saying he had been comfortable with every decision Sewing had made during his tenure as chair.
Deutsche Bank said it had already taken steps to protect confidential information about clients, employees and others and would continue to do so. It gave no details of those steps in its public statement.

title: Conservatives launch $10M anti-socialism blitz after Democrats dominate youth vote
text:
FIRST ON FOX: A conservative organization has launched a nationwide campaign of more than $10 million targeting at least 30 Democratic strongholds to combat the growing popularity of socialism among young Americans ahead of the 2028 presidential election.
The Young America's Foundation (YAF), led by former Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker, announced its "Freedom Not Socialism" initiative, which will bring prominent conservative leaders, including possible 2028 contenders, scholars and activists, to schools and communities across the country to challenge the influence of democratic socialism among younger voters.
"Our mission is to explain to people that their high cost of living is due to big government," Walker told Fox News Digital, explaining that the initiative will mobilize speakers to engage directly with young Americans at colleges, high schools and other institutions.
The announcement comes after Democrats captured the majority of the youth vote in Tuesday's midterm elections. The group launched its first event in Santa Barbara, Calif., over the weekend.
"YAF's initiative is vital for the future of our country because young Americans continue to get behind these false narratives of free this and free that, and they don't realize that the reason they are in the place where they cannot afford to live is because of big government," Rep.-elect Michael Alfonso, R-Wis., said.
During his interview with Fox News Digital, Alfonso, the 26-year-old grandson of immigrants who escaped communist Cuba, argued that the American education system had failed the next generation by not teaching the history of socialist regimes.
"The American education system has failed us," Alfonso said. "Young Americans do not know the truth about communist Cuba, communist Russia and communist Venezuela. All it takes is a simple look at these countries to realize how prosperous they were before communism came, and then what happened to them after."
"If we started teaching kids real history in the schools, maybe we wouldn't have so many people that come out hating this nation," said the congressman-elect, who will become the youngest member of Congress.
The group also announced plans to host a Freedom Conference in Dallas in early 2027 to prepare young conservatives to promote free-market principles and challenge socialist policies on college campuses.
"Young Americans are going to be the majority of voters in 2028, and they are increasingly being sold the promises of socialism without understanding the devastating consequences that follow," Walker, YAF's president, told Fox News Digital.
"As socialism gains ground in cities and states across the nation, we must teach the next generation what it truly is and act today," he continued. "The next generation cannot afford to sit on the sidelines while socialism infiltrates our communities and our schools."
The organization expects prominent Republican figures and potential 2028 presidential contenders to help carry its message, including former Virginia Gov. Glenn Youngkin, Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis.
"I can't think there's a more challenging place than college campuses to make this decision to embrace our foundational principles that not only laid the groundwork for the greatest nation ever, but were the foundational principles that guided us when we were lost," Youngkin said at the initiative's inaugural event on Sunday.
YAF argues that young Americans are increasingly exposed to socialist ideas in schools, universities and communities without learning about what the organization describes as socialism's historical failures.
Walker attributed the growing appeal of socialism among younger voters to a lack of understanding of its consequences, arguing that many are embracing the ideology without fully considering its implications.
"Freedom, not socialism, is about informing people of those ideas," Walker said.
Among the speakers expected to participate are Daniel Di Martino, a Columbia University graduate who fled socialist Venezuela, and Yeonmi Park, a North Korean defector who has spoken publicly about her experiences under the country's communist regime.
Walker said their firsthand accounts will help demonstrate why he believes socialist policies, including those championed by progressive leaders in Seattle and New York, "do not work."
The initiative is expected to expand throughout 2027 as conservatives seek to regain support among younger voters ahead of the 2028 presidential election.

title: A giant icy world hiding beyond Pluto could be our sixth dwarf planet
text:
Astronomers have uncovered a potentially enormous new dwarf planet beyond Pluto, hidden for years in one of the most crowded regions of the night sky. The discovery of 2026 ED138 could expand the solar system's official dwarf planet family and hints that more mysterious worlds may be lurking far beyond Neptune.
An enormous icy world discovered beyond Pluto could soon become the sixth officially recognized dwarf planet in our solar system.
The object, temporarily named 2026 ED138, was identified by an astronomer analyzing observations from the Simonyi Survey Telescope at the NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory. Early estimates suggest it ranks among the largest dwarf planet candidates ever found beyond Neptune. If its status is confirmed, it would join the five dwarf planets currently recognized by the International Astronomical Union: Pluto, Ceres, Eris, Haumea and Makemake.
The discovery was announced at a press conference featuring Matthew Holman, a senior astrophysicist at the Harvard & Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, and Mario Jurić, a University of Washington astronomy professor who leads Rubin's solar system team. Holman made the initial discovery, while Jurić helped gather the additional evidence needed to verify it.
"If confirmed as a dwarf planet, ED138 would join a very small family of worlds," Holman said. "Rubin will image the whole southern sky again and again for 10 years, so any others hiding in the places earlier surveys skipped are now within reach."
"Finding an object this big, roughly 1,000 kilometers across, is something that happens maybe once in a generation," Jurić said. "It's the largest trans-Neptunian object found in about 20 years, and Rubin turned it up while we were still commissioning the telescope."
How Astronomers Discovered the Hidden World
The breakthrough occurred on the evening of October 13, when Holman examined observations gathered by Rubin earlier in 2026. He was using specialized software developed with his colleague Kevin Napier to search for previously unidentified objects moving through the solar system.
The program compares billions of telescope detections, looking for individual points of light that appear in multiple observations and move in ways that suggest they belong to the same object. When the software identified ED138, Holman quickly realized that its apparent brightness and enormous distance pointed to something unusually large.
"My first reaction was one of excited disbelief," Holman said. "Objects like this are very rare, so I immediately started checking whether I or the code had done something wrong."
To check the finding, Jurić examined Rubin's stored observations and located 20 additional detections of ED138, including some captured as early as March 2026. The researchers then searched historical records from other astronomical surveys and identified images of the object dating back to 2016.
Together, these observations allowed the team to reconstruct more than a decade of the distant world's orbital motion, strengthening the evidence that the discovery was genuine.
Could This Be Our Solar System's Sixth Dwarf Planet?
ED138 currently lies approximately 46 astronomical units (au) from the Sun. One astronomical unit represents the average distance separating Earth and the Sun. By comparison, Pluto's average orbital distance is about 40 au.
Because ED138 travels beyond Neptune, astronomers classify it as a trans-Neptunian object (TNO). These distant bodies are valuable to scientists because their physical properties and orbital paths preserve clues about the solar system's distant past.
By examining their sizes, compositions, and movements, researchers can better understand how the solar system developed, how its giant planets shifted positions, and how smaller bodies were redistributed during that process.
However, being a trans-Neptunian object does not automatically make ED138 a dwarf planet. An essential requirement is that the object's gravity must be strong enough to shape it into a nearly round body.
Using measurements of ED138's brightness and distance, along with estimates of how much sunlight its surface reflects, astronomers calculate that it could measure anywhere from 600 to 1,500 kilometers across.
An icy object within that size range would generally be expected to have enough gravity to become round. Nevertheless, scientists will need more observations to establish ED138's actual dimensions and determine whether it qualifies as a dwarf planet.
Why Such a Massive World Remained Undiscovered
One of the most surprising aspects of the discovery is how an object this large managed to escape detection for so long.
ED138 occupies a region of the sky near the plane of the Milky Way, where millions of stars create an exceptionally crowded background. Against that dense field of light, the distant object's faint movement was difficult for earlier telescopes and surveys to distinguish.
Rubin Observatory has an important advantage. Its ability to repeatedly observe the Southern Hemisphere sky, combined with advanced computer algorithms, makes it possible to search enormous quantities of astronomical data for subtle changes in the positions of objects.
By examining millions or even billions of individual light detections, these systems can recognize the movement of small solar system bodies that might otherwise disappear into the surrounding stars. This capability was essential to finding ED138 in such a challenging part of the sky.
Rubin Observatory Could Reveal More Hidden Worlds
The newly identified object adds to a growing collection of solar system discoveries made by Rubin Observatory as it began gathering observations ahead of its ambitious Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), which officially started in June 2026.
Even before the survey began, the observatory was producing remarkable results. In April, Rubin's solar system researchers reported observations of more than 11,000 previously unknown asteroids, including approximately 380 new trans-Neptunian objects.
The team described that enormous collection of discoveries as "the tip of the iceberg," anticipating that the full survey would uncover many more objects. The identification of ED138 offers an early indication of just how significant those future findings could be.
Rubin's combination of extensive sky coverage, sensitivity, and rapid observations is also changing how astronomers investigate new discoveries. Once an object has been identified, researchers can search older telescope images to find instances when it was photographed but went unrecognized.
"Rubin is giving us an unprecedented capacity to explore the sky through a combination of speed, depth, and precision," Jurić said. "And the discovery is just the beginning: Once we identify a new object, we can search back months, and sometimes even decades, finding it in images where nobody knew to look. This ability to both discover and 'precover' objects is transforming how quickly and accurately we can determine their orbits and understand the distant solar system."
As Rubin continues surveying the southern sky over the next decade, astronomers expect its observations to uncover additional objects that previous searches missed, potentially revealing more large, icy worlds in the outer solar system.
Anyone interested in exploring ED138 can view its location and orbit using Orbitviewer, an interactive web-based application that displays the solar system in three dimensions and allows users to explore its structure in real time.
Operations of the Vera C. Rubin Observatory are funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation and the U.S. Department of Energy's Office of Science.

title: 'Arrival' at 10: Denis Villeneuve's alien visitation classic that reminded us it's good to talk
text:
In many of the biggest science fiction franchises, conversing with alien races is an absolute doddle. In "Star Trek", universal translators come as standard, while C-3PO has spent the last 49 years reminding everyone in "Star Wars" that he's fluent in over six million forms of communication.
But in "Arrival" — which was released 10 years ago in November 2016 — making first contact proves to be rather more challenging than maintaining your Duolingo streak. In fact, working out how to establish a dialogue with extraterrestrial visitors becomes the whole point of this powerful and heartbreaking story, as the fate of planet Earth hinges on the interpretation of a single noun.
The film's journey to the big screen began when a screenwriter best known for his work on horror franchises such as "Final Destination", "A Nightmare on Elm Street" and "The Thing" read a short story in an online magazine. Eric Heisserer was so impressed by Ted Chiang's "Understand" that he bought himself a collection of the author's short stories. One in particular, the Nebula Award-winning "Story of Your Life", piqued his interest.
"It had a very profound emotional effect on me," he reminisced to Deadline. "I was in tears, and I was both heartbroken and uplifted. My head was just full of big ideas. I had to walk around the block a couple of times afterward and just hug my friends. The next day, I was like, 'Oh god, I want to give this to other people.'"
So when 21 Laps (the production company that later went on to make "Stranger Things") invited Heisserer to discuss possible future projects, the writer mentioned "Story of Your Life". The producers were also smitten.
"I was so excited, but I had that dread that a lot of producers get, which is, 'Are the rights available?'" 21 Laps' Dan Levine told the Hollywood Gold podcast. "You read something that blows you away, and then you find there aren't the rights, and there's no chance, you have to move on. So we were trying to track down this Ted Chiang, and he had no agent. He had a day job. He was impossible to find, so we started the hunt for Ted Chiang."
An up-and-coming Canadian director named Denis Villeneuve had also found his way on to 21 Laps' radar after his 2010 French-language drama "Incendies" earned rave reviews and an Academy Award nomination. He told the producers that he'd always wanted to direct a science fiction film — a hint of things to come? — and they showed him "Story of Your Life".
He was also drawn to the story, while the now-located Chiang was suitably impressed by the director's work on "Incendies" to make a deal for the rights. And with Amy Adams also interested in playing the lead role of linguist Dr Louise Banks, the film that would eventually become "Arrival" was ready to proceed — or, at least, it would be once Villeneuve had completed his first three Hollywood movies, "Prisoners" (2013), "Enemy" (2013) and "Sicario" (2015).
With 12 alien spaceships arriving simultaneously around the globe, "Arrival"'s poster-friendly elevator pitch could almost have been borrowed from "Independence Day". Indeed, the question of whether these whisper-quiet, chocolate button-shaped craft belong to the "Day the Earth Stood Still" / "Close Encounters" friendly extraterrestrial camp, or have the invasion of planet Earth on their minds is a mystery the world's governments are desperate to solve.
"Denis didn't really see this as an alien invasion movie — more an alien arrival movie," producer Aaron Ryder told SFX magazine. "What would be the protocols that were in place? How would they be implemented? How would people react? What would the government be doing? What would the news organisations be saying? That was the tone and the texture, which is established right up front."
These Hollywood blockbuster components were not part of "Story of Your Life". But even though Heisserer's script was not a direct translation of Chiang's tale, he retained the most important bits — namely Dr Banks' efforts to establish a means of communication with seven-legged extraterrestrial heptapods, and the profound effect their language has on her perception of time.
Designed by Carlos Huante, the heptapods themselves are like giant elongated hands, alien visitors light years away from the "Star Trek" tradition of actors with a few ridges glued to their foreheads. Like the evil 456 in "Torchwood: Children of Earth", they're enclosed in gaseous chambers and make sounds imperceptible to the human ear.
This, however, is where "Arrival" gets really interesting. Working alongside physicist colleague Dr Ian Donnelly (Jeremy Renner), Banks gradually exchanges foundational vocabulary with two heptapods they name Abbott and Costello. They discover that the alien visitors use a sophisticated written language of circular "logograms", squirted into their atmosphere as if it were sentient squid ink.
"The idea in the short story is of circular language that has no beginning and no end," Villeneuve explained in an interview with IndieWire. "We were looking for no relation to any human language. I had to figure out how to produce logograms from my aliens while avoiding being long and boring. The sounds were an expression of their emotions, with more intellect coming from the signs. This beautiful species uses written language as their first means of expression instead of movement or gesture. They produce words out of their bodies."
But Banks and Donnelly's research project has a purpose. With the world's military on high alert — and, ironically, struggling to communicate — they need to work out how to ask the aliens a fundamental question: Why are you here?
The heptapods' answer — "offer weapon" — is tantalizingly ambiguous. Are they planning to attack? Or is, as Banks suggests, 'weapon' simply being used as a synonym for 'tool'?
SPOILERS AHEAD
Aside from a bomb planted on the heptapod ship by a rogue US soldier, "Arrival" is mostly free from the big-budget explosions that are part-and-parcel of most alien visitation movies. Instead, the film's denouement delivers a twist — the crux of Chiang's story — that rivals "The Sixth Sense", "Fight Club" and "The Prestige" in its audacious sleight of hand.
It turns out the "weapon" in question is actually the heptapod language, which, thanks to their non-linear perception of time, gives speakers a unique perspective on the past, present, and future. Therefore, those scenes we assumed to be flashbacks to the life and tragic death of Louise's daughter, Hannah, are actually flashforwards, as her increased understanding of heptapod-speak gives her memories of a life she hasn't yet lived.
Villeneuve put on multiple test screenings to ensure the big reveals hit properly.
"I wanted to screen it with people who knew nothing about the project," he said. "What we discovered is when someone in the audience felt too lost — if intellectually they were not engaged — the ending was less powerful from an emotional point of view. So we tried to give as few clues as possible, but enough clues to be able to stay engaged and follow the story."
Those subtle hints become obvious on second and third viewings, whether it's a lingering shot of a wedding ring absent in the movie's "present" or a conversation about the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis (the notion that the structure of a language can influence the way its speakers think). The absence of young Hannah's father also takes on tragic new meaning when we realize it's Ian, who'll leave after Louise tells him about their daughter's sad fate.
"We were walking on this tightrope of trying to play things so it could play both ways, because of the reveal at the end," Adams recalled in a Vanity Fair conversation with Villeneuve. "I had to do so much work to understand how I play a character so that the first time you watch it you think that it's one thing, and the second time you watch it you can see it from a totally different perspective."
While Adams didn't get the Oscar nomination her performance deserved, everything else paid off, with the film making over $200 million worldwide from its reported $47 million budget. (The film did win an Academy Award for sound editing, while receiving further nods for best picture, director, and adapted screenplay.)
Villeneuve has famously gone on to become Hollywood's go-to guy for intelligent sci-fi, thanks to "Blade Runner 2049" and the smash-hit "Dune" saga, and will next be given the opportunity to resurrect James Bond.
Normally we'd take this opportunity to say no one could have foreseen Villeneuve's subsequent ascendancy but — in a story involving heptapods and some clever people at 21 Laps — who can be so sure?
"Arrival" is available to stream on Paramount+ in the US, and Netflix in the UK.. It's also available on Blu-ray via Amazon.
When mysterious spacecraft touch down across the globe, an elite team — led by expert codebreaker Louise Banks (Amy Adams) — is brought together to investigate.
Richard's love affair with outer space started when he saw the original "Star Wars" on TV aged four, and he spent much of the ’90s watching "Star Trek”, "Babylon 5” and “The X-Files" with his mum. After studying physics at university, he became a journalist, swapped science fact for science fiction, and hit the jackpot when he joined the team at SFX, the UK's biggest sci-fi and fantasy magazine. He liked it so much he stayed there for 12 years, four of them as editor.
He's since gone freelance and passes his time writing about "Star Wars", "Star Trek" and superheroes for the likes of SFX, Total Film, TechRadar and GamesRadar+. He has met five Doctors, two Starfleet captains and one Luke Skywalker, and once sat in the cockpit of "Red Dwarf"'s Starbug.

title: Gas starts flowing from Jackdaw after government green light
text:
Gas has begun flowing from the Jackdaw gas field, with the UK energy secretary saying it will help to heat millions of homes and businesses this winter.
Ministers last month announced the Jackdaw field, which lies 150 miles east of Aberdeen, had been approved after years of uncertainty and a court case.
It has now been announced that it has begun producing gas which will start flowing into Britain, according to its operator Adura.
The UK government approved production from the gas field in the North Sea last month, amid intense debate about the project's environmental and economic impact.
Jackdaw is operated by Adura under a joint venture between Shell and Norwegian state energy firm Equinor.
A decision is yet to be taken on whether production can begin at Rosebank, the UK's largest known untapped oil field, which is located off the coast of Shetland in the North Atlantic.
Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said: "Last month, I gave Jackdaw the green light and today its gas will start flowing into Britain, thanks to the hard work of the skilled North Sea workers.
"It means homegrown gas from this project will help to heat millions of British homes and businesses this winter and beyond, in a boost for our energy security.
"It also will help minimise the UK's use of imported higher emission gas as we continue our transition to renewables and nuclear."
Claire Mueller, Jackdaw project director at Adura, said the gas field was "now helping to power Britain".
She added: "At a time of considerable uncertainty around the world, Jackdaw will provide secure energy from our own waters to heat British homes and power our economy, while reducing our reliance on imports with higher emissions.
"Jackdaw also demonstrates what can be achieved when Britain makes pragmatic, evidence-led decisions about the energy it needs, while properly accounting for our climate responsibilities."
Mueller said the decision was a "positive step towards restoring confidence in the North Sea".
She added that Adura was "proud to be producing the oil and gas our country will continue to need for decades".
Adura has said Jackdaw will provide about 6% of UK gas production, enough to power 1.4 million homes. After imports are included, that amounts to about 2% of total UK demand.
The gas will be pumped to the existing Shearwater platform for processing – known as a tie-back in industry terms – before being piped to the St Fergus gas terminal in Aberdeenshire.
The UK government said that over its expected 11-year lifespan, Jackdaw would support the UK's gas supply, protect hundreds of jobs and add £2.9bn to the economy.
The timeline of Jackdaw and Rosebank
The decision to green-light Jackdaw drew criticism from some Labour backbenchers and environmentalists, while Conservatives called on the government to also approve the Rosebank oil field.
Both projects were approved for development by the previous Tory government in 2022 and 2023 respectively but these decisions were struck down by the Scottish courts after a challenge from environmental campaigners.
This followed a Supreme Court ruling that developers had to account for the climate impact caused by burning fossil fuels in their planning applications.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has pledged to stick to the UK's net zero target despite giving the green light to Jackdaw.
He previously said the decision would "significantly strengthen our energy security by increasing domestic gas production by about 6% and support the UK's energy supply for more than a decade".
A decision on the larger Rosebank oil project is yet to be made.
The co-leader of the Scottish Greens, Ross Greer, described the Jackdaw approval as "climate vandalism".
He said: "It is a devastating betrayal of our children's future and it won't even lower energy bills in the here and now."
Environmental campaigners argue that this summer's heatwaves demonstrate the need to tackle climate change by rejecting both Jackdaw and Rosebank.
Areeba Hamid, the co-executive director of Greenpeace, said approving Jackdaw was "the wrong decision" in terms of lowering energy bills, providing energy security, and addressing climate change.
Oxfam said the government had "drilled straight through the UK's climate commitments" and accused the prime minister of sending "the wrong signal as the impacts of climate change intensify".
The charity says the government must commit to not approving any new oil and gas licences, including the proposals for Rosebank.
Jackdaw sits close to the boundary between the British and Norwegian sectors of the North Sea, in an area where Westminster originally granted licences to explore for oil and gas in 1970 and 1989.
The field was discovered in 2005 but it was expensive and technically difficult to exploit.
Shell did not commit to its development until 2022, shortly after the Conservative government had granted consent for production.
But in January 2025, after a challenge by environmentalists, the Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled that consent for Jackdaw and Rosebank had been granted unlawfully.
The judge, Lord Ericht, said the developers should have provided a more detailed account of the fields' impact on climate change as part of the permitting process.
The judge allowed the companies to continue with preparatory work short of producing oil and gas while they crafted new environmental impact assessments taking into account the eventual effect of actually burning the fossil fuels, not just the emissions which would be created in extracting them.
When BBC News visited the platform this summer, Adura CEO Neil McCulloch said its approval was vital to avoid domestic supply shortages this winter.
However, the UK government has previously suggested that Jackdaw will have little impact on energy security and none on reducing domestic gas and electricity bills.
In August, in an interim response to a consultation on the future of the country's gas supplies, Energy Minister Michael Shanks said the UK would inevitably become more reliant on imports as domestic production declined, external.
"With diminishing output from the North Sea over the past decades, any gas produced from the UK Continental Shelf represents a tiny fraction of global demand and so will not lower prices nor materially boost supply," wrote Shanks.
Labour has previously said it is opposed to the issuing of new exploration licences but it will consider new production projects if they are tied back to existing facilities.
McCulloch described the Jackdaw decision as "an important and positive step forward" - but said attention now turned to Rosebank.
He has urged the UK government to approve production from the field, in which Adura owns an 80% stake. The other 20% is held by London-based Ithaca Energy.
Rosebank contains an estimated 300 million to 500 million barrels of oil.
But while most of Jackdaw's gas is likely to be consumed in the UK, Rosebank's oil will be taken off by tanker and sold on international markets.

title: Surge of US datacenters adds equivalent of Denmark’s annual emissions, study finds
text:
The frantic buildout of “hyperscaler” datacenters in the US has collectively caused planet-heating emissions of about the same scale as Denmark emits in a year, new research has found.
In that period, 403 “hyperscalers” – the largest datacenters used primarily to handle the growth of artificial intelligence – emitted about 25.7m metric tons of carbon dioxide, according to the study.
This is equivalent to the entire annual carbon pollution of Denmark, a country of 6 million people, and is about two to three times more than a previous estimate of hyperscale emissions in 2018. The latest research, published in Nature Sustainability, found that these datacenters were responsible for about 1.8% of total US electricity consumption.
Researchers said this vast datacenter energy demand, centered on states such as Virginia, Oregon, Ohio and Iowa, is almost certainly a conservative estimate. The study used federal government data to determine emissions from the facilities over a year until April 2025. Since then, the rapid expansion of datacenters has only accelerated further.
“There has been an explosion in these datacenters and the CO2 emissions are pretty substantial,” said Francesca Dominici, a professor of biostatistics at Harvard University and co-author of the study, which was led by Gianluca Guidi. “Since 2025 there have been many, many more datacenters so we need to think of this level of emissions as a lower bound. This is something that needs study and for policymakers to think about how to do this in a responsible way.”
Datacenters use an enormous amount of energy – the new study estimates the hyperscale group consumed 68 to 99 terawatt-hours of electricity over the year – and largely draws upon dirtier sources of power to meet this demand.
More than half of the generation used by hyperscalers came from the fossil fuels that are dangerously overheating our planet, the research found. The growth of AI is being underpinned by a rise in new gas-fired power, sometimes built at the site of the facilities themselves, which is being favored over installed renewables such as solar and wind.
“Sadly, it doesn’t surprise me that the majority of hyperscale datacenters rely on fossil fuels for their power generation despite the profound and lasting climate and health impacts that could be, and should be, avoided,” said Gina McCarthy, a former climate adviser to Joe Biden’s administration who said that the study is an “important step” to assessing the impact of datacenters.
