The rise of datacenters has caused alarm among climate groups amid worsening global heating that may surpass previously agreed “safe” levels and cause an acceleration of the sort of deadly events seen this year, such as roasting heatwaves in Europe, wildfire smoke in North America and the disastrous landslide on the Nepal-Tibet border.
In the US, the epicenter of this AI boom, developers have defended the use of energy and water used by the facilities as marginal when compared with other industries, such as agriculture, and have touted associated jobs and raised local taxes as beneficial for communities. Donald Trump, a vocal supporter of the AI industry, has said people who oppose the growth of datacenters will end up “backwards and poor”.
But a bipartisan public backlash against datacenters shows little sign of abating in the US. Local opposition has focused on several big developments, such as a cluster of datacenters in the greater Memphis, Tennessee, region that are central to Elon Musk’s AI ambitions but have faced protests and lawsuits over their noise and air pollution. Musk’s AI company has responded to this by buying the homes of those who live nearby.
The vast water use of one of the world’s largest planned datacenters in drought-hit Utah, meanwhile, has mobilized grassroots opprobrium. The site, called Stratos, will also emit a large amount of air pollution, a separate study recently found.
Stratos could cause health-related economic costs of up to $690m each year if it uses the dirtiest of the fossil fuel options to power itself, this research concluded. Burning this fuel will release up to 3,140 tons of soot-like particulate matter, linked to an array of cardiovascular and respiratory problems in people, in plumes that will waft across Utah and into Idaho, Wyoming, Colorado and Illinois.
“Stratos is a modern-day Trojan horse that would unleash deadly air pollution linked to serious, life-threatening health damages upon Utah communities and millions of people living downwind of this massive datacenter,” said John Walke, director of federal clean air at the Natural Resources Defense Council, which commissioned the report.
“Pollution from Stratos will contaminate the air and compromise the ability to live a healthy life both around the facility and in states hundreds of miles from the datacenter.”
The developers for the Stratos project have been planning to use combined-cycle natural gas but are also reportedly considering using renewables and other options; they have been under political pressure to reduce its scale. Last month the project filed a new water application that reportedly claimed its water demands would be lower than historical agricultural uses at the property, which some environmental critics have questioned.

title: Nvidia's board of directors opposes restoring Jensen Huang as CEO
text:
Nvidia board members are not interested in reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO or in any other role at the chipmaker, according to a source directly familiar with their thinking.
Huang from Nvidia on Thursday amid an investigation into his extramarital affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies for China. His departure from the chipmaker he co-founded more than three decades ago came within days of the relationship becoming public.
At the same time, thousands of Nvidia employees and technology executives, including Elon Musk, have signed a petition asking the chipmaker to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, with the organizers arguing that he "may have been forced out without due process and without even a few days to make his case."
The push to reinstate Huang comes as the company named Colette Kress, Nvidia's chief financial officer, as its interim CEO and said it would seek a permanent replacement. Nvidia's stock has amid the controversy, chopping more than $500 billion from its market valuation.
"For thirty-three years, Jensen poured his heart and soul into building Nvidia," according to the petition, which described itself as an "independent, volunteer campaign" that is "not affiliated with, authorized by or endorsed by Nvidia Corporation or Jensen Huang."
The petition added, "He bet it on ideas that most of the industry dismissed, carried it through years when the bets looked foolish, and stayed long enough to see them change how the world computes ... That deserves more than gratitude after the fact. It deserves fairness now."
The petition has gained more than 180,000 signatures, including from what it says are more than 9,000 Nvidia employees representing about one in five company workers. Executives, including Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and Shopify CEO Tobias Lutke, have also signed the petition, according to its website.
"A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen and I'm signing it too," Musk wrote on X on Friday.
At the same time, Huang is said to be discussing his return to Nvidia with allies, the Financial Times reported on Sunday.
President Trump suggested to reporters on Monday that he would support Huang returning to Nvidia.
"I would not mind seeing that," Mr. Trump said. Later, the president said he recommended former as Nvidia's next leader.
Long-shot bid
Huang's return to Nvidia is a long shot, according to Wall Street analysts. On Sunday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for the chipmaker to hire its next CEO from outside the company, arguing that the company needs a major leadership shakeup amid questions about whether sales of its chips to companies in Singapore and other Asian countries circumvented U.S. export controls and ended up in China.
"We will see if Nvidia intentionally ignored the warning signs of these shell companies, many of them in Singapore," Bessent said on Fox News on Sunday.
Given Bessent's push for Nvidia to look outside the company for its next leader, Huang's return appears unlikely, according to Vital Knowledge analyst Adam Crisafulli, who told investors in a research note that the "odds of him being reinstated seem quite low."
Dan Ives, a well-known tech stock analyst at Yorkville Ives, downplayed the likelihood that Huang would resume his duties at Nvidia.
"Any talk of a damaged Jensen coming back to Nvidia is ridiculous in our view given the legal/board/DC scrutiny/moral compass/China tentacles," he said in a note to investors. "For the company, the best path forward is with a new external CEO or Colette [Kress]."
Prediction market users aren't giving much credence to the idea of Huang's return, with Kalshi traders assigning only a 10% chance of the former CEO returning to that role.
Nvidia shares are poised to continue their decline on Monday, with the stock down $2.39, or 1.5%, to $160.46 in early trading.
Investors will be tuning into Nvidia's earnings call on Tuesday afternoon to hear more about the company's guidance in the wake of Huang's departure.
"The critical question in the immediate term is what management has to say about the 70% sales growth guidance for next fiscal year — does Nvidia reiterate confidence in that or withdraw it given uncertainty about export rules in Washington," Crisafulli said.

title: Megaspeed says Alice Huang left in 2025, company conducts probe over Nvidia fallout
text:
Singapore-based company has been at the center of the claims involving Nvidia.
Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed International said Sunday that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, whose relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang sparked U.S. national security concerns, left the company last year.
Megaspeed, which is under scrutiny over alleged transfers of advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese companies, also announced an internal investigation led by outside lawyers.
The company told The Associated Press that it runs a “legitimate and lawful business” and was aware of media reports containing claims about its business, supply chain and global operations “that are not supported by verifiable evidence.” It did not address specific allegations.
“The company has retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation,” it said in an emailed statement.
Alice Huang “left Megaspeed effective Aug. 30, 2025, and currently has no role with the company,” the statement said. “Megaspeed does not comment on Ms. Huang’s personal and private matters.”
A customer and cloud partner of Nvidia, Megaspeed has faced scrutiny in recent months, including from U.S. authorities, over allegations that it circumvented U.S. export restrictions to route large quantities of advanced chips to Chinese companies. Last December, it said there was “no evidence” of illicit chip transfers.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday that “it doesn't matter to me” whether Alice Huang is a spy. He said his concern is “whether Nvidia had a culture of compliance around the U.S. export restrictions” or not.
“Jensen’s foibles are his foibles. Obviously, it’s a problem if in fact he was having relationships with subordinates,” Bessent said in an appearance on Fox News Channel's “Sunday Morning Futures.” “I want to keep coming back to: ‘What was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?’”
Bessent said the Nvidia board of directors should look outside the company for a new CEO because “they need a dramatic shake-up.”
Singapore’s government said Thursday that it initiated an investigation into Megaspeed in February 2025, including possible “false declarations in relation to the purchase of servers.”
Authorities also investigated Alice Huang, whom the government identified as Megaspeed’s then-CEO, chairperson and one of its key controllers.
Singapore authorities questioned her and withheld her passport last year. They later concluded there was insufficient evidence that she had committed a crime, despite suspecting she had provided “inaccurate” information to downplay her role at the company.
An earlier New York Times report suggested U.S. officials believed Alice Huang was a Chinese spy recruited to potentially influence Nvidia to make its advanced chips more available to China.
As scrutiny intensified and reports of her romantic relationship with Jensen Huang gained attention, Nvidia announced Thursday that he was stepping down as CEO.
U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said Thursday, however, that the Justice Department had not concluded whether Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. Asked whether she was a spy, President Donald Trump said: “I don’t know if that’s been determined yet.”
Beijing rejected the allegations as unsubstantiated.
The Associated Press has been unable to reach Alice Huang for comment.
Megaspeed began as the overseas arm of a Chinese video game developer and was incorporated in Singapore in 2015 as 7Road International. It adopted its current name in March 2023, when all its shares were transferred to Huang Le Limited, a British Virgin Islands company. Alice Huang is also known by her Chinese name, Huang Le.
By November 2023, she was no longer listed as a Megaspeed director, and all her shares had been transferred to an entity owned by Singaporean businessman Tan Yong Pong, also known as James Tan.
Despite those public records, short seller Culper Research cited a Megaspeed employee in a report released this May as saying Alice Huang was “actually still our boss” and remained involved in daily operations.
The company’s finances have also attracted attention. Singapore corporate records show its total assets rose roughly 90-fold from end-2023 to 2024, reaching almost $3 billion.
In a separate statement Thursday issued under James Tan’s name, Megaspeed said it takes its obligations under U.S. export control laws “extremely seriously.”
The company said it had cooperated with inspections by the U.S. Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security and was ready to cooperate fully with other relevant U.S. authorities.

title: Gen Z protests: Do Baby Boomers really have it better than young people?
text:
Young people across Germany and Europe are taking to the streets, voicing fears of a bleak future.
But is that really the case? Does Gen Z face greater challenges than Baby Boomers did in the 1990s? What do the two generations have in common, and where do their experiences differ?
"Of course, it's fair to ask, 'Were things just as tough for you back then?'" youth researcher Simon Schnetzer tells DW. "But young people see that things are difficult for them now, and say that's why they need support today."
Schnetzer, who wrote the annual Youth in Germany study, highlights one key question raised by the recent demonstrations across Europe as: "Have we given young people the conditions they need to live and work here with confidence, and to keep this system funded?"
His straightforward answer is no. A survey of the statistics shows that both Gen Z and the Baby Boomers are affected by major societal changes, but in different ways. DW surveyed data on pensions, education, housing and climate change to find out more.
Pensions and poverty among the elderly
The facts point to a clear trend: Fewer and fewer young people are having to support an ever-growing number of retirees. According to the Germany's public pension insurance system, there were 3.73 contributors for every retiree in 1957. By 2025, that figure had fallen to just 2.1.
By 2045, this number is projected to drop to just 1.73 contributors per retiree. In absolute terms, this means 35.35 million contributors will be financing pensions for 16.82 million retirees.
To cushion this trend and keep contribution rates stable, the pension system already receives around €118 billion [$131 billion] in annual government subsidies. This amounts to roughly 25% of the federal budget. That means an increasing share of the population will be called upon to help fund pensions.
There are also signs that many people's pensions are already falling short of covering their living expenses. The number of retirees relying on federal basic income support has risen from 257,000 in 2003 to 738,000 in 2024.
Rent and housing costs
Rising rents hit low-income households particularly hard. According to a report by the German Institute for Economic Research (DIW), the share of income spent on rent by low-income households rose from around 24% in 1990 to nearly 36% in 2021.
This means that in 2021, the lowest-income households spent an average of 14 percentage points more of their income on rent than high-income households.
According to Germany's Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), in 2025, an average of 11% of the population spent more than 40% of their disposable income on housing costs. Among people at risk of poverty, the figure was as high as 35%.
However, according to calculations by real estate platform Jacasa, Boomers could actually help ease pressure on the housing market in the coming years. They currently own around 4.8 million owner-occupied houses and apartments.
Over the coming decades, these properties are expected to change hands as former occupants sell them, move into assisted living, or hand them down through inheritance. In some regions, this could lead to an oversupply of properties and, consequently, lower prices, according to Jacasa's projections.
Investment in education
According to the federal government's Education Finance Report, public spending on education for people under 30 has doubled since 2011, rising from around €4,000 to approximately €8,000 per person annually.
Despite this increase, Germany ranks only in the middle of the pack internationally. According to the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), public education spending accounted for 4.6% of Germany's gross domestic product (GDP) in 2022, compared with an OECD average of 4.7%.
However, the additional funding cannot solve the problem of teacher shortages. According to estimates by the Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education and Cultural Affairs, Germany will be short of around 27,000 teachers by 2035. The main reasons are the wave of Baby Boomer retirements and declining birth rates, which have contributed to a shortage of young teachers.
Climate change
Back in 1972, the Club of Rome warned of the consequences of global warming in its landmark publication The Limits to Growth. According to the United Nations, the planet is on track for 2.6°C of warming by the end of the century compared with pre-industrial levels.
If the world maintains its current climate policies, children who are six years old today could experience heat waves two to seven times as often as Boomers did over their lifetimes. That was the finding of a 2025 study by Vrije University in Brussels.
The deadly impact of extreme weather is already evident in rising death tolls during recent heatwaves. According to Germany's Robert Koch Institute (RKI), an estimated 16,000 people died from heat-related causes across Germany by mid-September 2026. The vast majority — more than 14,000 — were over the age of 65.
"Gen Z and Baby Boomers are in the same boat. We need to bring them together, because otherwise younger people have no prospects for prosperity, and neither do older generations," youth researcher Schnetzer concludes.
He suggests that both generations take to the streets and protest together, adding that would just be the beginning. "What needs to follow is a constructive process to define goals and measures that everyone can support," he said. "Even if it means making sacrifices."

title: Prince William’s presents Earthshot Prize winners with $1.3M each in Mumbai
text:
Prince William presented five Earthshot Prize winners with 1 million pounds ($1.3 million) each on Tuesday, recognizing their efforts to tackle the world’s climate challenges.
The annual ceremony, held this year in Mumbai, marked the centerpiece of William and Princess Catherine’s three-day visit to India.
The Earthshot Prize winners were selected from 15 finalists for their work in areas ranging from clean transport and renewable energy to forest conservation and marine protection.
Four were Mahindra Last Mile Mobility, for its electric transport initiatives; PFAS-Free France, for its campaign to ban toxic “forever chemicals”; Niue Ocean Wide Trust, for protecting marine ecosystems; and Ørsted, for advancing offshore wind energy.
The fifth recipient was the country of Bhutan for its work in conserving Himalayan forests.
William, the Prince of Wales, established the prize through his Royal Foundation in 2020 to encourage inventors and entrepreneurs to develop technologies to combat global warming and mitigate its effects.
The ceremony at Mumbai’s Jio World Convention Centre brought together Bollywood celebrities, innovators, entrepreneurs and environmental advocates.
William and the Princess of Wales, commonly known as Kate, began their visit Monday. The couple have played street cricket in Mumbai, ridden in an electric rickshaw and met leading figures from India’s cricket, fashion and film industries.
They are scheduled to meet Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Wednesday.
The trip marks a significant step in Kate’s return to overseas royal engagements. She announced in March 2024 that she was undergoing cancer treatment following major abdominal surgery. In January 2025, she said she was in remission and has since gradually resumed public duties.
She traveled to Italy without William in May for her first overseas engagement since her diagnosis.

title: High tobacco use among European women and girls is ‘worrying,’ WHO warns
text:
Women’s tobacco use is falling at a much slower rate than men’s, according to WHO Europe.
Every part of the world is meeting global targets for cutting women’s tobacco use — except Europe and Central Asia, according to a new report from the World Health Organization (WHO).
More than 22% of adults use tobacco in the WHO’s European Region, which includes 53 countries in Europe and Central Asia. Tobacco kills 1.6 million people annually in the region.
Tobacco use is falling faster among men, who have higher smoking rates overall, according to the WHO Europe analysis. Among women, tobacco use is declining at a stubbornly slow pace — and in 15 countries, women’s tobacco use is on the rise. Around 63 million women in the European region use tobacco.
Men’s tobacco use fell from 39.3% to 30.3% between 2010 and 2025 — a 23% decline — while women’s use fell from 19.6% to 17.3%, a 12% drop. Both men and women fell short of the WHO’s goal of a 30% reduction in tobacco use by 2025.
Globally, tobacco use among women fell by 42% in that 15-year period. Europe is the only region that missed the WHO’s 30% target. In every other region, women’s tobacco use fell below 10% by 2025, the report found.
“The European Region is not making sufficient progress in reducing tobacco use among both men and women. But women and girls, in particular, are being left far behind,” said Kristina Mauer-Stender, WHO Europe's regional advisor for tobacco control.
These trends hold up among teenagers. About 14% of 13- to 15-year-olds in the region use e-cigarettes, roughly twice the global average. Girls are at least as likely as boys to use tobacco in 29 countries, while they’re at least as likely to use vapes in 35 countries.
“Teenage girls are now smoking and vaping as much as boys, or more,” Mauer-Stender said. “None of this is inevitable. We know which policies work.”
WHO Europe called on countries to raise tobacco taxes to at least 75% of the retail price, enforce smoke-free policies, ban tobacco advertising, regulate e-cigarettes and “protect tobacco control policy from industry interference.”
The European Commission, the European Union’s executive arm, is preparing a major overhaul of its tobacco rules. The legislation is expected to address nicotine products, including vapes and pouches, and packaging requirements. A separate plan to raise tobacco taxes has stalled.
Last year, a watchdog group accused Commission officials of holding undisclosed meetings with tobacco industry representatives, in apparent violation of transparency rules. The industry is estimated to spend €8 million to €10 million lobbying EU institutions each year.

title: That Was Fast! Vikings HC Kevin O'Connell Reveals Kirk Cousins Timeline
text:
That didn't take long!
Minnesota Vikings head coach Kevin O'Connell revealed in a press conference on Friday afternoon that recently acquired quarterback Kirk Cousins will start in the team's Week 10 road matchup against the Green Bay Packers (1 p.m. ET on FOX); the Vikings defeated the Packers at home in Week 1, scoring 29 consecutive points to get a 39-22 victory.
"I cannot give him enough credit for coming in here with how he's gone about the week, both him and the coaching staff getting him ready to go, working extremely hard, using all the time we possibly can," O'Connell said of Cousins. "It's been really impressive what he's been able to do with the command and just getting right back in the huddle with a lot of guys he's played with, but certainly some guys he hasn't.
"And it's been something that everybody's been very, very impressed with, so exciting to start Kirk."
Of course, Cousins' arrival in Minneapolis marks his second stint with the Vikings, as the four-time Pro Bowler played for the franchise from 2018-23 and for O'Connell from 2022-23. Minnesota acquired the 38-year-old Cousins from the Las Vegas Raiders on Tuesday afternoon for a 2027 third-round pick.
Across the nine starts he made for the Raiders this season, Cousins totaled 2,340 passing yards, 20 passing touchdowns, eight interceptions and a 97.1 passer rating, while completing 64.1% of his passes.
After starting the season 0-6, the Vikings have lost back-to-back games. In the second of those two losses, a 23-6 defeat at home on Monday night against the Buffalo Bills, Vikings quarterback Carson Wentz tossed two interceptions, threw for only 81 yards and completed just eight passes.
Wentz was starting in place of Kyler Murray, who's dealing with a hamstring strain and will be inactive Sunday, per O'Connell. The Vikings also have quarterback Max Brosmer, who took over for Wentz late in the fourth quarter on Monday night.

title: Stanford scientists discover hidden brain signals that predict Alzheimer’s years before symptoms
text:
Stanford researchers have discovered that hidden patterns of brain activity can predict Alzheimer’s risk years before memory problems appear, potentially offering an earlier warning than traditional biomarkers. The same patterns also reveal which brains are unusually resistant to aging, raising hopes for future treatments that could help protect memory.
Subtle patterns of brain activity may reveal the risk of Alzheimer's disease years before memory problems develop or harmful proteins begin accumulating in the brain, according to new research led by Stanford Medicine. The same approach can also identify people whose brains show exceptional resistance to cognitive decline, suggesting they may eventually become "super agers."
The study, published November 4 in Science Advances, points to a potentially powerful new way to detect early warning signs of cognitive decline. Unlike conventional biomarkers, these patterns of brain activity might eventually be possible to change through targeted interventions.
To investigate, the research team examined brain activity in adults aged 75 and older who represented opposite ends of the cognitive aging spectrum. One group had Alzheimer's disease, while the other consisted of super agers, older individuals whose memories remained comparable to those of people decades younger. Using the differences between these groups, the scientists created a scoring system to evaluate brain activity in cognitively healthy adults between 55 and 70.
The results revealed a striking connection between brain activity and future cognitive health. People whose brain patterns more closely resembled those of Alzheimer's patients were more likely to experience cognitive decline, accumulate amyloid-beta plaques, and receive an Alzheimer's diagnosis during follow-up periods extending up to 12 years. Those with activity patterns resembling super agers were more likely to maintain their cognitive abilities and avoid these outcomes.
A New Way to Detect Alzheimer's Before Memory Loss
The new scoring system predicted future cognitive decline more effectively than several established indicators, including demographic characteristics, genetic risk factors, and amyloid-beta and tau biomarkers. This suggests that examining how different regions of the brain communicate could reveal Alzheimer's risk earlier than existing approaches.
"We want to address a major challenge in the Alzheimer's field nowadays -- most studies are looking at well-known Alzheimer's disease biomarkers, such as amyloid-beta or tau. But those are observable at relatively late stages of the disease," said Yu Zhang, PhD, assistant professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences and senior author of the study. "What we really care about is defining early markers that can detect earlier signs of cognitive decline and potentially help us deliver timely interventions to people."
Zhang envisions a future in which treatments could potentially move someone's brain activity toward the patterns associated with greater cognitive resilience. Possible approaches include cognitive training and transcranial magnetic stimulation, which uses magnetic pulses to influence brain activity.
Transcranial magnetic stimulation has already demonstrated potential for changing brain activity in people being treated for depression. However, neither of these proposed approaches has been tested in this context for preventing cognitive decline, and researchers do not yet know whether changing brain activity would alter the course of Alzheimer's disease. The new findings provide a starting point for identifying which brain regions might be useful treatment targets.
"There are two main components: One is to know which part of the brain to target, the other is how we should change it," Zhang said. "That's why identifying the super-ager brain resilience pattern is a critical component -- so we know what a good pattern should be."
What Makes Super Agers' Brains Different?
Depending on how they are defined, approximately 10% of older adults may qualify as super agers. For this research, the term referred to people at least 75 years old who performed on memory tests at a level typical of a 45-year-old while maintaining normal executive function for their age.
Scientists have become increasingly interested in these unusually resilient individuals. Most earlier studies, however, compared super-agers with other older adults who performed normally on cognitive assessments.
Zhang recognized that this approach could overlook important biological differences. Two people might receive similar scores on memory tests despite having very different underlying brain health. One might already be developing amyloid-beta plaques or showing other biological changes associated with aging, while the other might not.
"Normal, cognitively unimpaired individuals are pretty heterogeneous in terms of their biological abnormalities," he said. "Simply comparing super agers with such a heterogeneous population makes it challenging to define what is critical in terms of resilient or vulnerable brain patterns."
In other words, comparing super agers with a broad mixture of seemingly healthy older adults makes it difficult to determine which brain characteristics actually protect against decline.
The Stanford team took a different approach. Rather than using typical older adults as the comparison group, they examined people with Alzheimer's disease who were approximately the same age as the super agers. This created two more clearly defined groups at opposite ends of the cognitive spectrum.
Brain Scans Reveal a Hidden Pattern
The researchers drew on imaging information collected through several major research initiatives, including the Open Access Series of Imaging Studies, the Harvard Aging Brain Study, and the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative.
They examined resting-state functional MRI scans from 180 super agers and 110 people diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease. This imaging technique records patterns of brain activity while a person lies quietly inside a scanner.
The comparison uncovered distinctive differences in activity across multiple brain regions. Some areas showed greater activity while others showed reduced activity, producing recognizable patterns that distinguished the two groups. Scientists refer to the relationships among these regions as functional connectivity, or the functional connectome.
Using these patterns, the team developed a measurement called the Alzheimer's resilience-vulnerability connectome, or ARC score. This scoring method distinguished super agers from Alzheimer's patients with approximately 85% accuracy.
The researchers then investigated whether the same brain signature could help predict what would happen to people who had not yet developed any noticeable cognitive problems.
Predicting Alzheimer's Risk Years in Advance
The team applied the ARC scoring system to more than 1,300 cognitively healthy adults between the ages of 55 and 70. Their scores fell across a broad range, with lower values reflecting brain activity more similar to super agers and higher values indicating patterns closer to those observed in Alzheimer's patients.
At the beginning of the study, people with high and low ARC scores showed no obvious differences in cognitive performance. As researchers examined follow-up data collected over subsequent years, however, important differences became apparent.
"We used the ARC score to make a prediction of how likely this patient will convert into mild cognitive impairment or Alzheimer's disease," said Kanhao (Alex) Zhao, PhD, a postdoctoral scholar in psychiatry and lead author of the study.
The available follow-up periods differed across the datasets. Some participants had records extending as long as 12 years, although most were tracked for approximately five to six years. Even within these shorter periods, the initial ARC scores helped predict subsequent changes in cognitive abilities.
People whose scores indicated more Alzheimer's-like brain activity experienced more rapid declines on standard tests of memory, attention, and executive function. In contrast, those with patterns most similar to super agers generally experienced the slowest cognitive decline.
"We compared the ARC score with existing biomarkers in predicting people converting to Alzheimer's disease," Zhao said. "Our model shows comparable or better prediction ability, and it can do so at an earlier time point. And if we combine our score with the existing biomarkers, the prediction performance improves."
A More Precise Measure of Brain Aging
The team also investigated how ARC scores related to another measure of neurological health called brain age. This measure estimates brain aging using functional MRI information collected from healthy individuals.
Although the two measurements showed some correlation, Zhang emphasized that ARC provides more targeted information about a person's vulnerability or resistance to cognitive decline during aging.
"I'm excited we established a signature that can help us better understand the difference between people who can maintain excellent cognitive performance and people who show cognitive decline," he said.
The findings suggest that patterns of communication between brain regions may offer valuable information about future cognitive health that cannot be captured through standard memory testing alone.
They also raise the possibility that combining brain activity measurements with established Alzheimer's biomarkers could improve the identification of people who would benefit most from earlier monitoring or future preventive treatments.
Could Brain Training Help Prevent Alzheimer's?
Despite the encouraging results, researchers caution that ARC scores are not intended to diagnose Alzheimer's disease. For now, the system should be viewed as a potential tool for tracking cognitive health and estimating future risk.
Zhang also stresses that a person's score is not a permanent prediction of their future. Brain activity can change over time, and an individual who initially shows a resilient pattern may not maintain it indefinitely.
For example, the proportion of people with super-ager-like ARC scores generally declines with advancing age. Brain injuries and neuropsychiatric conditions can also influence the patterns associated with cognitive resilience.
Importantly, this potential for change may work in both directions. If brain activity can shift toward patterns associated with vulnerability, Zhang hopes future treatments might also encourage it to move toward greater resilience.
His research team is preparing a trial that will measure ARC scores before and after cognitive training. The goal is to explore whether targeted training can influence the brain activity patterns associated with healthier cognitive aging.
"But the critical part is that we have to intervene at an early stage," he said. "That's why we focus on the cognitively unimpaired population to identify super-ager-like versus Alzheimer's-like individuals. If we can precisely identify such as early indicator, I'm optimistic that we can reverse or prevent this process through advanced intervention technologies."
Although it remains unknown whether modifying these brain patterns can prevent or delay Alzheimer's, the discovery offers a potentially important new direction for research. By identifying differences in brain activity before symptoms emerge, scientists may eventually gain a valuable opportunity to intervene while cognitive function is still intact.
Researchers from Children's National Hospital; the University of Texas at Austin; Lehigh University; Penn State College of Medicine; New York University Grossman School of Medicine; and the University of California, Los Angeles also participated in the research.
Funding was provided by the National Institutes of Health (grants R21AG080425, R01MH129694 and R01AG081768), a joint Rosenkranz Foundation-Knight Initiative program, an Alzheimer's Association grant, and a Lehigh University CORE grant.

title: 100 launches! Rocket Lab sends Earth-observing satellite to orbit on milestone mission (video, photos)
text:
Rocket Lab just hit the century mark.
An Electron rocket topped with a private Japanese Earth-observing satellite lifted off from Rocket Lab's New Zealand site on Saturday (Nov. 14) at 12:30 a.m. EST (0530 GMT; 6:30 p.m. local New Zealand time).
The mission, which Rocket Lab called "The Mountain God Rises," was a big one: It marked the 100th launch to date for the California-based company.
Rocket Lab launched for the first time in May 2017, sending the brand-new Electron up on a test flight from New Zealand. That effort failed, but Electron bounced back on its second-ever liftoff, delivering several cubesats to low Earth orbit (LEO) in January 2018.
In the years since, the 59-foot-tall (18 meters) Electron has become one of the most prolific and reliable rockets in the world, carrying small payloads to the final frontier for a variety of customers.
And it hit the century mark on Saturday in record-breaking fashion: No commercially developed rocket has gotten there faster, not even SpaceX's workhorse Falcon 9, according to Rocket Lab founder and CEO Peter Beck.
"It's an unprecedented milestone for a commercial small-lift orbital rocket, and a threshold rarely crossed in modern spaceflight," Beck said on Monday (Nov. 9), during Rocket Lab's third-quarter earnings call with investors. "But what matters most to us and our customers is that we have achieved a 96% reliability rate across 99 launches."
Electron met the moment in style on Saturday morning, thanks to some fancy livery.
"Black rocket 🤝 Golden milestone. Electron is all dressed up for launch 100," Rocket Lab said via X on Tuesday (Nov. 10), in a post that shared a photo of the specially painted first stage.
Not all of Rocket Lab's missions have gone orbital, it should be noted: A suborbital variant of Electron known as HASTE, which customers use to test technologies in a hypersonic flight environment, has nine missions under its belt to date.
"The Mountain God Rises" was Rocket Lab's 11th launch to date for the Tokyo-based company iQPS, which is building a constellation of three dozen synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellites in LEO. And all went to plan on the mission: Electron's upper "kick stage" deployed a single iQPS spacecraft 357 miles (575 kilometers) above Earth.
SAR satellites can see through cloud cover and image our planet at night as well as during the day, offering key advantages over spacecraft that are optimized to view in optical wavelengths.
Editor's note: This story was updated at 12:40 a.m. ET on Nov. 14 with news of successful liftoff, then again at 1:30 a.m. ET with news of satellite deployment.

title: Liverpool lead Chelsea in Camara race - Wednesday's gossip
text:
