title: Peter Storey, Arsenal Double winner and England international, dies aged 81
text:
Arsenal have paid tribute to Peter Storey, a key member of their 1971 Double-winning team, after the death of the former England midfielder at the age of 81.
Storey was part of the Bertie Mee team that secured the First Division title and FA Cup in a season that remains one of the most celebrated in Arsenal’s history and played 501 times for the club. That places him eighth on their appearances list.
Storey, who represented England on 19 occasions from 1971-73, earned respect for his uncompromising approach and versatility, also featuring at right-back.
Storey died in hospital after a short illness, surrounded by his family. Arsenal said: “Everyone at Arsenal is deeply saddened by the passing of 1970-71 Double winner Peter Storey. All our thoughts are with his family and loved ones at this incredibly sad time.”
Born in Surrey, Storey began his career at Arsenal and made his debut shortly after his 20th birthday in 1965. He is fondly remembered by the club’s fans for scoring a stoppage-time penalty in the 1971 FA Cup semi-final against Stoke that forced a replay and kept the Double dream alive.
Storey left for Fulham in 1977 and retired eight months later when his contract was cancelled, going on to own a pub in north London. He was later convicted of several criminal offences, including financing a plot to counterfeit gold coins and smuggling pornography. He released an autobiography, True Storey: My Life and Crimes as a Football Hatchet Man, in September 2010.
Storey’s family said: “We are deeply grateful for the many kind messages, tributes and good wishes we have received. It has been a great comfort to see the affection and respect in which he was held by so many, both within the football community and beyond.”

title: U.N. talks seek to rein in 'killer robots' as fears over AI weapons grow
text:
GENEVA — Negotiations on possible rules for the use of lethal autonomous weapons, also known as 'killer robots' are underway at the United Nations in Geneva.
Supporters of controls on autonomous weapons say this week's U.N. conference on Certain Conventional Weapons (or CCW), which meets just once every five years, is the last best chance to agree rules before it is too late.
Warfare technology has advanced rapidly in the last few years, with some experts warning that the world is just months away from having weapons that can choose targets and make the decision to kill autonomously.
In Ukraine and Gaza, AI-assisted weapons have already been used to take out targets, with Ukrainian civilians reporting being 'hunted' by drones as they shop or go to school. But these are still controlled remotely by humans.
Humanitarian organizations say the decision to kill – and responsibility for that choice – must stay in human hands. Ahead of this week's meeting, the United Nations, the International Committee of the Red Cross and the Pope have all called for legally binding rules. U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned that allowing fully autonomous weapons to kill would be 'crossing a moral red line'.
What are the risks?
The Red Cross is especially worried that existing rules of war – the Geneva Conventions – cannot be fully respected by autonomous weapons. War is often chaotic and confusing, and the situation can change rapidly. Under the Conventions, soldiers who are wounded or in the process of surrendering can no longer be targeted.
Georgia Hinds, a legal adviser with the Red Cross, worries that autonomous weapons will not be able to distinguish between a soldier who is still fighting, one who is wounded and one who wants to surrender.
'The risk is that, based on the technology we are seeing, they are not able to understand in the same way that a human is the contextual signals. And so the risks are incredibly high that there will be a misidentification of a target," Hinds says.
Meanwhile, human rights groups warn that the technology behind AI-assisted weapons is becoming increasingly cheap and easy to use. The more it is adopted by the military, the greater the danger of proliferation and its use by terrorist groups or law enforcement agencies in repressive regimes. In theory, a swarm of autonomous drones could be programmed to kill everyone wearing a red sweater, everyone carrying a poster or even everyone speaking a certain language.
Many of the countries now meeting in Geneva take such concerns very seriously. At least 50, including Ireland, Italy, Brazil, Mexico, France and Germany, are calling for a strict timetable to agree on binding rules governing autonomous weapons.
But among states that are already developing and using semi-autonomous weapons, there is pushback. The United States, Russia and Israel have indicated they are set to oppose legally binding rules, with Washington proposing a five-year timetable to draft non-binding guidelines instead.
The U.S. is traditionally a late adopter of international treaties. It did not ratify the Ottawa Convention on landmines, for example, although it did, over time, stop deploying them and reduce its stockpiles.
Under President Trump, doubts about international law have grown. Washington has imposed sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court, and just this weekend, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, in a keynote speech to the Federalist Society, warned against "quoting laws to men with swords."
The problem for states meeting in Geneva is that U.N. negotiations on limiting specific weapons are supposed to be conducted by consensus. This was achieved in 1995, when countries agreed to a ban on blinding lasers, but other agreements have proved elusive. With landmines, countries frustrated by the delay finally took negotiations outside the U.N. process to create the Ottawa Convention.
This week, there may be a compromise: a longer or even open-ended negotiating period to come up with rules that individual states can adopt as binding or non-binding. For diplomats supporting such a solution, it is a way to ensure at least some progress. For campaigners, it is less than ideal, with one likening it to kicking a very dangerous can down the road.

title: Mars rover sets new driving record on surface of another world
text:
NASA's set an otherworldly driving record this week, traveling the farthest of any vehicle ever on the surface of another planet.
The space agency said its rover, which has been exploring Mars since 2021, had driven 28.1 miles as of Sunday, exceeding the previous record set by NASA's Opportunity rover, which drove 28.06 miles during its 15-year exploration of the red planet, from 2004 to 2018.
Perseverance reached the milestone distance while traveling along the western rim of of Mars' Jezero Crater, where the rover has been tasked with investigating what scientists believe may be some of the oldest terrain in the solar system. They hope Perseverance will find traces of ancient hydrothermal systems — underground networks that heat water — in that area.
The rover has made important discoveries at since first landing on Mars in February 2021. Several years into its mission, Perseverance had collected enough data for scientists to develop a timeline of the crater's formation, dividing its history into "three major periods" after water originally entered it. In 2023, NASA said it was possible that microbial life once existed there.
Perseverance has been able to cover as much ground as it has in a relatively short time, compared with its predecessors, because of its self-driving capabilities. The rover is equipped with an autonomous navigation system, called AutoNav, that allows it to collect images of surrounding terrain, map out hazards and plan its own route as it's rolling along.
Scientists overseeing the rover have dubbed that skill "thinking while driving." They said Perseverance is also able to navigate itself while traveling at top speeds, up to 1,351 feet over the course of one sol, which is how scientists count a single solar day on Mars.
"It is an honor to be working on Perseverance at a moment when the technology has evolved to the point that drives like these are routine," said Steven Lee, the project manager of the Curiosity and Perseverance rovers at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, in a statement.
Lee said the rover has "blown well past" the 12.4 miles of driving initially expected during the mission, and now, it's likely that Perseverance will "keep adding to this record for many years to come."
NASA said it recently extended the Perseverance mission to allow to explore the rim of the Jezero Crater until the end of 2028.

title: The dangers of revising Europe's security architecture
text:
European leaders have so far found compromises in response to many of US President Donald Trump's demands.
But they were surprised to hear Trump say that he raised Europe's security framework with Russian officials.
"It's going to be a big agreement and it's going to involve more than Ukraine," Trump said after meeting Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev at the White House last week.
He said that deal might include all of Europe. But what he meant by "all of Europe" was not clear.
US envoy Jared Kushner also wrote that Europe and Russia had struggled to establish a sustainable security framework for more than 30 years and that he was looking at "broader" European security architecture before he was to fly to Abu Dhabi.
That sent off alarm bells in European capitals, with diplomats having pushed back on Washington's approach to secure a peace deal in Ukraine.
They feared that a peace settlement could restore Russia's sphere of influence and undermine NATO.
"We already have European security architecture in place. NATO and the European Union both have their respective roles. We must make sure Ukraine is integrated into this architecture," said Kaja Kallas, the European Union's foreign policy chief.
The issue with revising Europe's postwar security framework
Russia made clear during talks in Abu Dhabi earlier this week that they were keen to discuss a broader European security framework before tackling the specifics of the war.
"Phrases about the European security architecture are certainly Russian talking points and not only talking points but, to a degree, part of a media propaganda effort that Russia makes to frame the war as it wishes to frame the war," said Michael Kimmage, a historian of the Cold War.
Russian leaders, including Vladimir Putin, have long alleged that the US and NATO repeatedly violated pledges they made in the early 1990s not to expand the alliance into the former Soviet bloc.
They have seen NATO's enlargement during this period as having put them in a humiliating position in which they could do very little.
At the same time, in the 1990s, the European project saw the birth of the European Union, the single market that ensured the free movement of goods and people across member states, the Schengen agreement for border-free travel, and the euro.
The core idea was to extend peace across the continent.
"Europe can mean so many things, but the European project was not designed for war. It was designed for peace," said Kimmage.
During this period, there were even suggestions of Russia becoming a NATO member.
But that relative period of stability changed after Russia invaded Georgia in 2008, annexed Crimea in 2014 and launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
"Russia wants to redraw all of this by force. And I think that that's fundamentally unacceptable to Europe with all the diversity and variations that you get within the European landscape on what's acceptable and not acceptable. I think the large-scale redrawing of borders by force is just not the European project," said Kimmage.
"So to the extent that the redrawing of borders by force is the lifeblood of Russian foreign policy, and I think that's a pretty easy case to make, Russia and Europe are at an impasse," he said.
What was to happen to Ukraine's security?
The Trump administration very quickly turned to making sure that "existing European security institutions" would be intact, with Jared Kushner having said late Thursday that the next round of negotiations would include "our European partners."
Kushner, along with Steve Witkoff, flew to Moscow to talk to Putin after talks in Abu Dhabi. Then they flew to Dublin, Ireland, to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Kushner had earlier Thursday signaled some "really incredible" postwar plans for Ukraine, saying that it could not be concluded without Europeans at the table.
"We should not allow a diktat from Russia that would result in some kind of neutralization or significant reduction in the military forces of Ukraine going forward, because that would make Ukraine very, very vulnerable to future aggression and pressure coming from Russia," said Hiski Haukkala, the director of the Finnish Institute of International Affairs.
That would mean that Ukraine would also be completely dependent on the security guarantees that the US or Europeans are able and willing to provide.
"We are supporting Ukraine because we are supporting international law and the basic norms of decency and international security when it comes to European security architecture. And this is the vantage point from which we are operating," he said.
The European Union has repeatedly pointed to some of the basic treaties that Russia broke, including:
- The UN Charter
- The Helsinki Act of 1975, which established the ten core principles of European security, including the non-use of force or threat against territorial integrity.
- The Charter of Paris for a New Europe that built on Helsinki commitments
- The Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE), which was one of the few multilateral security forums where the West and Russia engaged.
- The Budapest Memorandum of 1994 in which Russia, the US and the UK provided security assurances to Ukraine and others in exchange for them giving up their nuclear weapons.
"Russia walked away from these principles and smashed them to pieces in the process. And they are not interested in reinstating the previous security architecture order. They want something different in its stead. And as long as this is not on the table, the Russian form of negotiation is to wage war. War is a form of bargaining," Haukkala said.
"And they are signaling strategic intent to change the makeup of European security, to subdue Ukraine and to change the very essence of European security," he added.
What is the way forward?
Daniel Fried, a former assistant secretary of state for European Affairs in the George W. Bush administration, said Russia is very good at sticking to its demands.
He said Russians know how to negotiate and "right now, they are not negotiating," referring to talks in Abu Dhabi.
Some experts said there was no possibility of having a new security architecture with the Russians at this point because there was no trust or common vision to align with Russia at the moment.
"There is no obvious compromise — dismantling NATO and the EU is not an option for Europe," said Maria Snegovaya, an expert on Russia at the Center for Strategic and International Studies think tank.
"Repeatedly offering Putin peace deals he is unwilling to accept will not produce that outcome," Snegovaya said.
Others like Balazs Jarabik, an expert on post-Soviet politics, said that Russia was part of the European security architecture whether Europeans liked it or not.
"And the question is whether it's included as our enemy. Obviously, Russia is not going to be a partner, right? We have to find a modus operandi to reduce the risk of a horizontal escalation and potentially a bigger European war, even a bigger one than what we have now."
A host of European leaders on Friday rejected the Russian demands to discuss Europe's security framework as well, with a spokesperson for the German government saying that Berlin was looking to host a meeting of the "Coalition of the Willing" to secure funding for Ukraine's defense and reach a unified position regarding future peace talks.

title: Bryson DeChambeau joins DP World Tour after collapse of LIV Golf
text:
Bryson DeChambeau has joined the DP World Tour for the 2027 season after leaving the now-defunct LIV Golf.
The European tour said on Tuesday that DeChambeau is “joining as a member for the first time in Category 1” status. He is joined by Jon Rahm in making the jump.
The American’s inclusion could eventually offer him a route to regaining his PGA Tour card for 2028.
Former major champions Dustin Johnson, Cameron Smith, the 2022 Open winner, and Bubba Watson will also feature on the DP World Tour next year, having signed agreements to receive invites to a “specific number of tournaments”.
At the start of November, LIV Golf announced it intends to “transition to an orderly wind-down of its operations”, bringing an end to the controversial breakaway tour.
It had been reported BC Partners Credit, who had been lined up as potential backers following the withdrawal of Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, had pulled out of a deal worth more than £200m due to an exodus of star players.
LIV, which launched in 2022, was forced to apply for chapter 11 bankruptcy, effectively cancelling playing contracts – with the likes of Rahm, Sergio Garcia, Ian Poulter, Tyrrell Hatton, Louis Oosthuizen and Lee Westwood all departing.
Former Masters champions Garcia and Patrick Reed – who left LIV Golf ahead of the 2026 season and has since earned back his PGA Tour card – have also been confirmed among the 22 former major champions in exempt membership on the DP World Tour for 2027.
Johnson, Smith and Bubba Watson are among nine players who have signed agreements with the DP World Tour for specific tournaments next season.
The DP World Tour said these would will be in effect from the Bahrain Championship, which starts at the end of January, onwards, but would exclude those in the Rolex Series.
The designated events for each player which were prescribed by the DP World Tour “to add value to those tournaments,” it said, with the invites across the season carefully managed by the Tour’s Player Relations Department, following “extensive modelling to ensure and preserve playing opportunities for existing members”.
DP World Tour’s chief executive Guy Kinnings expects the 2027 season to be “one of the most keenly contested campaigns in our 55-year history.”
Kinnings said in a statement: “There has been significant change in the landscape of men’s professional golf over the past 12 months. As golf’s global tour, we have taken a pragmatic approach to this unique and unprecedented situation as we go into next year, always with the best interests of our entire membership at the forefront of our minds.
“We realise there are different viewpoints, but this approach, discussed and agreed with our Tournament Committee and allied to this responsibly managed programme of invites, will add value which, in turn, will benefit the Tour as a whole.
“We therefore look forward to beginning our 2027 season at the BMW Australian PGA Championship next week, a season where our fans will enjoy enhanced and competitive fields at our historic tournaments around the world.”

title: Spain's Canary Islands flooded by thousands of migrants as country declares emergency
text:
Thousands of migrants flooded Spain's Canary Islands this weekend as the nation's government remains under a migration emergency.
The Canary Islands have received the brunt of migration from West Africa and Sub-Saharan Africa in recent months. Authorities there processed over 2,200 migrants in just two days, all arriving in dinghies and makeshift boats.
One flotilla of 14 boats landed on the island of El Hierro carrying 1,324 people. The island's Spanish population is just 12,000.
The Spanish government declared an emergency over the archipelago last week. The latest surge comes just months after tens of thousands of migrants crossed into Spain's North African territory of Cueta in July.
The country also faced internal unrest this month after a general strike turned violent last week and rioters began clashing with police, setting fires and bashing storefronts in hotspots across the country.
Violent scenes unfolded in Barcelona, where some demonstrators vandalized stores along the city's popular Paseo de Gracia shopping boulevard, set small bonfires and launched fireworks at officers arriving in riot gear and armored vehicles.
The violence erupted as Spain experienced its first general strike in 14 years, with workers demanding relief from skyrocketing rents and the rising cost of living.
Housing activists claimed 400,000 people marched through Barcelona, while city officials estimated attendance at 55,000. Government officials reported another 120,000 demonstrators gathered in Madrid despite heavy rain, The Associated Press reported.
The nationwide walkout disrupted public transportation, forced some businesses to close and blocked major roads. Police made arrests across the country, while officers used pepper spray against demonstrators in Madrid.
Both the migration and housing crises are expected to play a major role in Spain's Nov. 29 parliamentary elections.
Fox News' Jasmine Baehr and The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Scientists discover a surprisingly simple way to turn coffee waste into fuel
text:
Scientists have developed an efficient method to transform used coffee grounds into a potential source of biodiesel while preserving the leftover material for other renewable fuels and valuable chemicals. The discovery could turn millions of tons of discarded coffee waste into a surprisingly useful resource for sustainable energy.
Used coffee grounds may be far more valuable than they appear. Instead of ending up in the trash, this everyday waste could provide ingredients for renewable fuels and a variety of useful chemicals. Researchers at Universitat Rovira i Virgili (URV) have identified an efficient way to recover oil from discarded coffee grounds while keeping the remaining material suitable for other industrial applications.
The findings, published in Biomass and Bioenergy, highlight the untapped potential of spent coffee grounds, a waste product generated in enormous quantities worldwide. Global coffee bean production reaches approximately 10 million metric tons annually, but only a small fraction of the beans' material makes its way into the brewed beverage. Much of the rest is discarded as solid waste. These leftover grounds contain roughly 15% lipids, or fats, which can serve as ingredients for producing biodiesel.
Finding a More Efficient Way to Extract Oil From Coffee Grounds
To determine how best to recover these valuable oils, researchers Jorge F. Romero, Alberto Tampieri, Daniel Montané, Magdalena Constantí, and Francesc Medina from URV's Department of Chemical Engineering examined three variables: extraction temperature, processing duration, and the amount of solvent used relative to the coffee grounds.
The team used n-hexane, a solvent widely employed to separate fats from other materials. Through a series of carefully designed experiments, they evaluated how changes in temperature, extraction time, and solvent quantity affected the results, both individually and in combination.
"We have found that the optimal conditions are at 45°C for 60 minutes with a ratio of 35 milliliters of hexane per gram of dry residue," explained Magdalena Constantí, one of the study's authors.
Under these conditions, the researchers recovered approximately 90% as much oil as could be extracted using Soxhlet, a standard laboratory method known for its high extraction yields. Although Soxhlet is effective, it generally takes longer, consumes more energy, and is less practical for large industrial operations.
The newer approach also produced considerably cleaner oil. The optimized extraction yielded just 0.3% impurities, compared with 3.9% using Soxhlet. Chemical analysis revealed that the oil's fatty acid composition remained consistent across the different experimental conditions, with linoleic and palmitic acids making up the largest shares. This composition supports the oil's potential use as an ingredient in biodiesel production.
Coffee Waste Could Produce More Than Just Biodiesel
Recovering oil is only one part of the opportunity. The scientists also wanted to ensure that extracting the fats would not destroy the remaining coffee material, which contains compounds that could be used to manufacture additional fuels and chemicals.
"In our study, we also demonstrate that extracting the oil does not mean that the rest of the material cannot be used for something else," pointed out Francesc Medina, a researcher at the Department of Chemical Engineering who participated in the research.
A central goal was to protect the structural components of the leftover coffee grounds, collectively known as the lignocellulosic matrix. This material contains cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin, substances that can be processed into products such as bioethanol, lactic acid, polyhydroxyalkanoates, phenolic compounds, and ingredients used to produce sustainable aviation fuels.
Removing the oil may actually make the remaining material easier to process. Fats can form a barrier that prevents solvents and catalysts from reaching other useful components within the plant matter. By extracting the oils without substantially changing the underlying structure, the researchers created a residue better suited for further processing.
In this way, the method serves two purposes. It recovers a potentially valuable source of biodiesel ingredients while preparing the leftover biomass for conversion into other products.
A Simpler Approach to Sustainable Biofuel Production
The team also investigated whether more advanced extraction methods could deliver better results. These included techniques that use ultrasound or microwaves to accelerate oil recovery.
Although both alternatives can speed up the early stages of extraction, neither offered a sufficiently compelling overall improvement. When the researchers considered oil purity, extraction efficiency, energy requirements, and the potential to expand production to an industrial scale, the conventional batch process using n-hexane under moderate conditions emerged as the more balanced option.
That combination of efficiency and practicality could make the method useful in biorefineries, facilities designed to convert biological materials into fuels, chemicals, and other products.
The research also supports the broader goal of creating a circular economy, in which materials that would otherwise be thrown away are reused to generate additional value. This approach is particularly relevant as industries search for renewable fuel alternatives in sectors that are difficult to electrify, including heavy transportation.
By finding ways to make use of both the extracted oils and the remaining coffee grounds, the scientists hope to reduce waste while expanding the range of materials available for sustainable fuel production.
As Daniel Montané, another researcher involved in the study, explained, the goal is "to transform a typically underused waste product into various energy vectors and bio-based chemical products, and to reduce the environmental impact associated with its accumulation."
The findings suggest that discarded coffee grounds could eventually become an important feedstock for producing renewable fuels and other valuable materials, turning a familiar source of everyday waste into a resource with multiple industrial uses.

title: California's brand-new Air & Space Center, home of the space shuttle Endeavour, opens today
text:
LOS ANGELES — The California Science Center officially opened its brand-new Samuel Oschin Air & Space Center to the public today (Nov. 13).
After more than three decades in development, folks can finally visit the Los Angeles science museum's massive new wing. For most of us, the biggest draw is its centerpiece: the retired space shuttle Endeavour, sitting upright in launch position, towering at nearly 200 feet (61 meters) tall.
"It just takes your breath away when you see that reveal and the doors open and you get to look at it for the first time. It's just — it's overwhelming," former NASA astronaut Garrett Reisman told Space.com during a visit to the museum. Reisman flew on two space shuttle missions during his astronaut career, the first of which was on Endeavour.
"There are people that come from all over the world, and when they come to Los Angeles, they're going to have the opportunity to see it, too," Reisman added. "The exposure it's going to have is just a force multiplier. There are so many people that can have that opportunity to bring their kids here and show them [the shuttle] and have that experience."
Entering into this exhibit is an experience in and of itself, as I can personally attest; I was among of group of reporters who got a sneak peek at the new wing on Oct. 28. A video presentation ends in a dramatic reveal: Visitors walk into a space where the enormous shuttle, which flew 25 missions to Earth orbit from 1992 to 2011, feels truly larger than life.
There are a number of interactive exhibits around the base of Endeavour, which you can slide down to (though, of course, you can also take the elevator or stairs). From a shuttle landing simulator to a replica of a shuttle cockpit that you can sit in, to shuttle tires and space tech from across decades of spaceflight history, there's an incredible variety of space artifacts to both observe and interact with.
As for Endeavour itself: It is open, so you can peer inside to see the robotic arm tucked away among a myriad of handles, straps and electronic gear inside. And you can see the shuttle from underneath all the way to the top.
You can lie on the floor underneath the shuttle's engines, for example, and then take an elevator up the launch tower to come face-to-face with Endeavour's nose. There's even a transparent floor at the top that allows you to stand above the shuttle (though if you have a fear of heights, this might not be for you).
This is the abbreviated description, but know that if you are visiting the California Science Center, you will want to budget a serious amount of time to explore all that this new center has to offer.
The new air and space center is designed for all ages, and for civilians and astronauts alike. For instance, looking at Endeavour spurred some memories for Reisman: He reflected on his time aboard the shuttle and his time as an astronaut and pinpointed specific places on the shuttle that played important roles in his mission.
"I'm looking at handrails that I held onto during a spacewalk," he said. "They're the same handrails. My hand was in the glove, but it was wrapped around those handrails. And I practiced for a long time exactly how I was going to do that, how I was going to root my tether, and all that kind of stuff. And I get to stand [here] now. When you go up the elevator there, you can actually have a direct view of those handrails, and every time I see that, I'm thinking about that spacewalk."
But you don't need to have completed a spacewalk to get that view. And, as of today, the general public is welcome to visit the museum, which is free to the public — as is the new aerospace center with its Endeavour exhibit.
However, due to the excitement over this new center opening, you will need to make a reservation online to attend. And, while the museum is free to the public, there is a cost associated with reserving slots during these busy first few days.

title: Caribbean nations fear economic impact of shuttering citizenship program after EU threats
text:
The decision by St Kitts and Nevis to end a lucrative programme offering citizenship to wealthy foreigners in exchange for investment threatens its economy and ability to support people in need, the premier of the island of Nevis has warned.
On Friday, Terrance Drew, the prime minister of the twin-island Caribbean nation, announced he would wind down the citizenship-by-investment (CBI) programme, after the European Union threatened to end visa-free access for St Kitts and Nevis.
Mark Brantley, the premier of Nevis, which has autonomous self-governance in some aspects, said he understood that the “country was given very little choice”, but did not “support the winding down of the program”.
The 42-year-old CBI programme, which St Kitts and Nevis pioneered, allows wealthy foreigners to obtain citizenship and ultimately a passport by investing in infrastructure and other development projects. It has brought billions of dollars into the country and in some years accounted for the largest share of government revenue.
In June, the European Commission wrote to the five Caribbean nations that currently operate CBI programmes: St Kitts and Nevis, Dominica, Antigua and Barbuda, Grenada and St Lucia. It warned that countries may lose visa-free access to its 29-country Schengen area if they did not phase out CBI.
In Friday’s statement, Drew blamed concerns over the programme on mismanagement by previous administrations, including years of underselling to undercut other countries, a controversial prison project, weak escrow protections and investment sums not being properly paid into the citizenship unit.
He said his government had led major reforms to the Caribbean’s programmes with international partners, including the US treasury, but argued that continuing the programme risked visa-free travel to parts of Europe and access to international banking. That could disrupt services allowing visitors to use overseas cards and families abroad to send money home.
Brantley, however, argued it was unfair for the EU to force St Kitts and Nevis to make a move without offering assistance to navigate the transition to other industries.
“I have not yet seen from the EU any corresponding suggestions of assistance. And we have to realise that these citizenship-by-investment programs, not only in St Kitts and Nevis, but … smaller countries of the Caribbean, have contributed significantly to our gross domestic product and also to ensuring that our people … can get adequate access to water and to education, to healthcare and the like,” he said.
Brantley described the 1 June 2028 deadline the EU gave the country to phase out the lucrative programme as “frankly ludicrous”.
In his statement, Drew said the CBI programme “did a lot of good, but it also created a danger”.
“When one source pays for half or more of everything, you are at its mercy. If it stops, everything stops. That is putting all of your eggs in one basket,” he added.
The prime minister said the government aimed to diversify its economy by strengthening tourism, yachting, and digital and creative industries, among others. He added that the sale of clean, geothermal energy was “at the heart of it” with drilling and exploration already planned.
“I will not pretend that the road is easy. Less CBI money means we must spend wisely and plan carefully. We will. Our plan is to make this change by growing our economy. Raising taxes is not part of that plan,” Drew said.
Antigua and Barbuda has also expressed willingness to end the programme, though it is trying to negotiate a longer transition period. The five Caribbean governments have taken differing positions on the EU demand. According to local media, Grenada has indicated it wants its programme to continue until 2032, while Dominica and St Lucia have responded to Brussels without publicly committing to ending their programmes.
Jermine Abel in Basseterre contributed reporting

title: More than 200 people jailed over crackdown on illegal gold mining
text:
A court in Guinea has sentenced 22 former officials and 202 miners to prison over illegal gold mining in the northeast
A court in Guinea sentenced 22 former local officials and 202 miners to prison over illegal gold mining in the country’s northeast, the latest in a crackdown that has sparked deadly clashes and sent tens of thousands of people fleeing into neighboring Mali.
The government announced a crackdown on unauthorized gold mining earlier this month, saying it aims to curb environmental damage, including the destruction of farmland by heavy machinery and the pollution of rivers by chemicals.
The crackdown turned violent last week, when clashes between protesters and security forces enforcing restrictions on gold mining in northeastern Guinea killed 10 people and injured 13 others.
On Monday, the Court for the Repression of Economic and Financial Offenses in Conakry, Guinea’s capital, sentenced the 22 former officials from Siguiri, a major gold-producing area near Guinea’s border with Mali, to two years in prison each for complicity in environmental degradation, destruction and water pollution. Each official was also fined 10 million Guinean francs (about $1,120).
The 202 illegal miners — who included several foreign nationals — received three-year prison sentences on the same charges, in addition to illegal mining. They were ordered to pay a combined fine of 10 billion Guinean francs ($1.1 million).
The court also banned the foreign nationals involved in the case from Guinean territory for 10 years.
The 224 defendants sentenced on Monday were among more than 1,200 people arrested in Siguiri earlier this month on suspicion of illegal gold mining.
Unauthorized gold mining has been the livelihood of more than 300,000 people in Guinea, according to the U.N. Environment Program. Guinea’s gold mines have long attracted workers from across West Africa.
The crackdown has sent tens of thousands of miners and their families, many originally from Burkina Faso, fleeing into neighboring Mali, according to Malian authorities.

title: What's going on with the polar vortex?
text:
High up in the atmosphere, there's a ring of cold air swirling over the Arctic that can intensify, weaken, and shapeshift through the seasons. This is the polar vortex.
If it gets disrupted, this twisting pool of chilly air can influence the weather we experience, increasing the risk of a cold snap in the Northern Hemisphere.
Current observations show the vortex has weakened unprecedentedly early this year, with its winds reversing directions.
Earliest vortex disruption on record
It's not yet clear how the current disruption to the polar vortex will affect the Northern Hemisphere winter, but scientists agree it is a record-breaking event.
"As far as we know, this is the earliest stratospheric vortex disruption that has been observed," European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecast (ECMWF) principal scientists Tim Stockdale and Frederic Vitart told the AFP news agency.
The French meteorological agency Meteo-France, meanwhile, called it "an unprecedented event."
The early breakdown of the vortex "really increases the chance of cold air outbreaks across the latitudes where most of the densely populated population centers are across the Northern Hemisphere, US, Europe and East Asia," Judah Cohen, a climatologist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology told AFP.
What exactly is the polar vortex and how does it work?
The polar vortex is an enormous band of cold, low-pressure air that spins counterclockwise around the North Pole, about 10 to 50 kilometers (around 6 to 30 miles) above the surface.
It's closely connected to the jet stream, another band of powerful winds just below the vortex. The jet stream forms a boundary where the cold Arctic air meets warmer air from the tropics and subtropics.
The vortex can sometimes be a tight circle, keeping the coldest air locked around the North Pole over winter. It can also form uneven waves that dip southwards. And as it changes in strength and shape, that can influence the atmosphere below and alter the position of the jet stream, which drives the weather on the ground.
So, if the jet stream is more "wavy," and plunges south, it may also allow freezing Arctic air to spill southward.
One of the biggest influences that can provoke this kind of disruption is known as "sudden stratospheric warming." This is when temperatures in the polar stratosphere rise dramatically within a few days, causing the vortex's strong westerly winds to weaken.
This can push the vortex off its spot at the North Pole, make it split apart into multiple rings, or — as is happening now — cause the westerly winds to change direction.
It can take several weeks for the vortex to recover.
What does this mean for winter weather?
A previous polar vortex disruption contributed to the deadly Great Texas Freeze in February 2021, which caused more than a week of freezing temperatures that sparked power outages and killed hundreds of people.
But bone-chilling cold isn't a foregone conclusion. The Met Office, which is the UK's national weather and climate service, stresses that what's happening with the polar vortex can nudge odds in that direction, but it's not a switch that turns cold weather on and off.
Other weather patterns can also influence the outcome.
For example, there's a possibility El Nino, which is associated with milder winters, could "moderate or modify" the impacts, Cohen told AFP. But he added this was not certain.
The El Nino weather phenomenon, caused by the warming of surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, is currently intensifying and is expected to peak at the end of the year. The ongoing event has been classified as exceptionally strong and is disrupting weather around the globe.
Some research has also linked the rapid warming of the Arctic driven by climate change to increasing disruptions to the polar vortex. That means that, even as the planet warms, some areas may still experience more severe cold spells. But this connection is not conclusive and is still debated by scientists.

title: Teen accused of beating homeless man to death and leaving shoe prints on his face
text:
A 19-year-old teen was arrested after beating a disabled homeless man to death — leaving shoe prints on his face in the horrifying attack, cops say.
New Orleans police arrested Antonio Myles in connection to the November 8 murder of 68-year-old David Hyde, a New Orleans Police Department spokesperson confirmed to The Independent. Myles allegedly approached the victim just before 1 a.m. and began to argue with him before taking his belongings from a backpack and destroying them, police said.
He then began to brutally beat up the victim, who was unable to defend himself due to health issues, police said.
Authorities found Hyde outside a Walgreens just before 7 a.m., “with severe contusions to his face” as well as shoe prints left on his face, police wrote in court documents obtained by The Guardian.
There were also numerous prescription medication bottles left near Hyde. He was pronounced dead at the scene.
Surveillance video from a nearby store showed Hyde sitting near the pharmacy’s front entrance when his attacker grabbed his backpack, dumped its contents on the ground and beat him up, according to the court documents.
According to the report, most of the fatal beating occurred out of the camera’s view. However, investigators said that the attacker could be seen using Hyde’s shirt to wipe his shoes before fleeing the scene.
Police said they received a call the following day reporting that Myles had been “bragging to unknown subjects that he was responsible for beating a homeless man to death.”
While Myles was interviewed by police, he was released pending further investigation. Days later, police released footage of a man in a parking lot, noting that he was a “suspect wanted in connection with a brutal beating that left a disabled man dead.”
An informant told police the person in the video was Myles. During an interview with investigators, they said that Myles had called hours after Hyde was found dead and told the person “he loved them, and that he killed a homeless man, and continued to kick him after he was already dead.”
“The known subject also advised … that Mr. Myles advised a known subject that he killed the homeless man and took his prescription medication that was inside his backpack,” the police statement said.
In the police statement, investigators noted that they believed the information the subject was giving them was true since “no specific details of the investigation were released” to the public and news media.
“Only a person who was there when the homicide occurred would know that the victim was kicked to his head repeatedly, and that the victim was in possession of prescription medicine inside of a backpack,” the statement added.
Myles was arrested Friday on a count of second-degree murder. He would receive a life sentence in jail if convicted on the charge.

title: Fresh public sector strike in France under way over pay as government struggles to pass budget
text:
Tuesday's demonstrations follow talks with Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, which left unions dissatisfied, as they continue to push for across the board pay rises.
Another major day of protests took place in France on Tuesday, as part of a nationwide strike led by public sector workers calling for pay increases, despite government efforts to ease tensions as demonstrations roil the country.
This come as France races to adopt a 2027 budget against a backdrop of strained finances, eight weeks after social unrest erupted in mid-September, amid student anger at school conditions.
The movement has since broadened in scope, taking aim at the cost of living crisis and rising fuel prices. Tuesday's demonstrations follow talks with Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, which left unions dissatisfied, as they continue to push for across the board pay rises.
In an attempt to meet union demands, the government has announced eight additional index points for the lowest-paid public sector workers. It has also brought forward an increase in the national minimum wage from 1 December, in reaction to inflation.
Despite this, in its draft budget, the government has ruled out any general pay rise for the fourth consecutive year, citing the country's finances, amid a mounting public deficit and national debt.
This is unacceptable for the unions, which put the loss of purchasing power for public servants at 16 percent since 2017, leading to increasing numbers of public employees ending up on or close to the minimum wage against a backdrop of inflation.
Demonstrations have seen a decline in turn out in recent weeks, according to figures from France's Interior Ministry.
Sophie Binet, Secretary General of the General Confederation of Labour (CGT) trade union told Euronews that "records" couldn't be "broken everyday."
"This is the first time in social history that eleven days of national protests have occurred in under two months. So, yes, there have been ups and downs. We don't break records every day, but this is significant", she said.
"Everyday we are also learning about other protests across Europe. They have been inspired by France", she added.
Protests have been largely peaceful, however there have been instances of fringe violence, including attacks on journalists and police, public buildings, the use of firecrackers, as well as looting and attacks on 17 October.
Meanwhile, police forces have been accused of using disproportionate measures to clamp down on demonstrations, prompting a number of investigations into law alleged police misconduct.
France's protests erupted as the country nears elections in spring.
Manuel Bompard, deputy for the hard left France Unbowed party told Euronews that primary goal is to address the demands of young people and unions."
He added that "during the election campaign, all candidates present their own proposals. Our proposals align with the demands being voiced in the streets today. The primary goal is not the election campaign itself."

title: American veterans targeted by schemes to steal benefits and exploit the sick, disabled: DOJ
text:
FIRST ON FOX — Fraud schemes drained veterans’ disability benefits and left a promised cancer treatment center unfinished before it was demolished, according to the Justice Department.
In launching a nationwide crackdown on abuse of veterans’ programs, the DOJ is levying charges against 15 defendants in schemes involving more than $3.4 million in intended losses, announcement materials obtained first by Fox News Digital detail.
Prosecutors also secured guilty pleas, trial verdicts and sentencings in cases involving more than $19 million in intended losses during the operation, which began Sept. 1, 2026.
The operation marks the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division’s first coordinated nationwide surge focused on VA benefits, bringing together federal prosecutors, the Department of Veterans Affairs and its inspector general.
"For veterans, benefits are not simply government payments," Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald said in a statement. "They are earned benefits -- earned through service, sacrifice, deployments, injuries, time away from loved ones, and a willingness to serve something larger than themselves."
Asked during Tuesday’s press conference whether uncovering $19 million in fraud represented a meaningful success given the scale of fraud nationwide, McDonald pointed to the veterans whose benefits and care were affected.
"I would ask the question of the veterans who didn't get the care whether the $19 million that was stolen from them, whether it matters to them," McDonald said. "Whether the cancer center that was not built, did it matter to them that they did not have the cancer center that the taxpayer funded to be able to serve our warfighters and to seek to help them in their moment of need?"
In Florida, the government paid approximately $4.8 million toward a veterans’ cancer treatment center that was never completed — and ultimately was demolished without being rebuilt, according to DOJ.
The VA awarded the $8.9 million construction contract for the Cancer Infusion Therapy Center at Bay Pines VA Medical Center through a program reserved for businesses owned by service-disabled veterans.
Evidence at trial showed that Matthew West, Kevin Kutina and their co-conspirators secured the contract while concealing arrangements under which ineligible companies would perform most of the work and receive most of the payments.
West and Kutina were convicted of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, wire fraud and major fraud against the United States. Two co-defendants pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit wire fraud.
Construction failures plagued the project, leaving the partially completed facility to be torn down, according to the DOJ.
Other cases involved alleged theft directly from veterans’ benefit payments.
In Texas, prosecutors allege that VA National Call Center employee Heidi Brady used her access to veterans’ personal information and knowledge of payment procedures to change their direct deposit details shortly before monthly disability payments were issued.
The money allegedly went to an account she controlled.
Her neighbor, Raymond Audie Davis, is accused of helping by impersonating veterans during calls to the VA and using their identifying information to redirect payments, according to the indictment.
In Ohio, Darlene Toman allegedly stole from disabled veterans whose finances she was entrusted to manage — including a Marine severely wounded in Iraq who received the Purple Heart and Combat Action Ribbon.
Prosecutors say the victims included people with traumatic brain injuries, schizophrenia, amputations and other serious conditions. Some required around-the-clock care.
Rather than safeguard their benefits, Toman allegedly used fraudulent checks and diverted payments intended to cover veterans’ living expenses and care for her own use.
The allegations against Brady, Davis and Toman have not been proven in court. Defendants are presumed innocent unless and until convicted.
Alongside the VA enforcement announcement, DOJ is establishing a Texas Federal Fraud Task Force comprising all four U.S. attorney’s offices in the state, with support from federal, state and local law enforcement.
Fox News Digital's Stephen Sorace contributed to this report.

title: A surprising brain difference may explain why some kids struggle with math
text:
Stanford researchers have discovered that children who struggle persistently with math may have underlying differences in how their brains manage problem-solving strategies. Children with developmental dyscalculia were slower to switch strategies, less responsive to changes in difficulty, and less able to improve their approach over time. Distinct patterns of brain activity were linked to these difficulties and could even predict certain math-related abilities.
For some children, learning math is much more difficult than it is for their classmates. Even when they practice and receive instruction, they may continue to struggle with problems that other children their age can solve more easily. Researchers are now uncovering clues about why these difficulties persist, and the answers may involve more than an understanding of numbers.
One possible explanation lies in differences in how the brain selects and manages strategies for solving problems. A new study from Stanford University suggests that children with persistent math difficulties may have trouble adjusting their approach when faced with different mathematical challenges. The researchers also identified distinctive patterns of brain activity associated with these struggles.
The findings, published in JNeurosci, come from research led by Oliver Lasnick and colleagues at Stanford University. Their work focused on children with a condition that causes ongoing difficulty with mathematical problem solving (developmental dyscalculia). Although the condition has been recognized for years, scientists are still working to understand the specific thinking processes and brain mechanisms that contribute to it.
Why Some Children Struggle With Math Strategies
To investigate these challenges, the Stanford team studied 68 children between the ages of 8 and 10. They examined how the children approached math problems, how effectively they used different strategies, and how their brain activity related to their performance.
Solving a math problem often requires more than knowing numbers or remembering arithmetic facts. Children must also decide which approach will work best. For example, a child might count individual numbers to find an answer or use a more efficient method based on a familiar mathematical relationship. As problems become more difficult, the ability to recognize when a different strategy is needed can become increasingly important.
The researchers found that children with developmental dyscalculia were generally less effective at using different mathematical strategies than children without the condition. They took longer to shift from one method to another and were less responsive when the difficulty of a problem changed.
Another important difference involved learning to choose better strategies over time. While other children became more effective at selecting appropriate approaches, those with developmental dyscalculia did not show the same improvement. This suggests that their difficulties may involve not only performing calculations but also deciding how to approach a problem in the first place.
Brain Activity Reveals New Clues to Math Difficulties
The researchers also examined patterns of brain activity to better understand what might be happening behind these behavioral differences.
They discovered that activity within a particular brain system differed between children with developmental dyscalculia and those who were more skilled at selecting and using math strategies. These neural patterns were not simply unrelated differences. They could also predict how effectively children counted and how well they switched between approaches when solving problems.
The findings highlight the possible importance of several mental abilities that extend beyond mathematics itself. These include attention, memory, and cognitive flexibility, which is the ability to adjust thinking or behavior when circumstances change.
Such abilities are part of what researchers often call executive functions. These mental processes help people organize information, stay focused on a task, hold relevant details in mind, and change plans when an approach is not working. In mathematics, they can help a child keep track of numbers, compare possible solutions, and recognize when to try a different method.
The Stanford findings suggest that difficulties involving these processes may contribute to the development of dyscalculia. Differences in brain activity may also help explain why some children have persistent trouble choosing and changing problem-solving strategies.
However, the observed connections do not establish that the brain activity differences directly cause the condition. They provide new evidence about the cognitive and neural processes associated with these mathematical difficulties.
Understanding Why Math Struggles Differ Between Children
An important conclusion is that developmental dyscalculia does not appear to involve one simple problem shared by every affected child. Instead, different children may experience difficulties involving several interacting mental processes.
As Lasnick explains, "Importantly, this study also emphasizes the individual variability observed in dyscalculia, further demonstrating that the disorder reflects cognitive and neural dysfunction across multiple processes."
By connecting children's mathematical behavior with measurable differences in brain activity, the research offers a more detailed picture of why math can be persistently challenging for some students.
The findings also point toward the importance of looking beyond whether a child gets the correct answer. Understanding how children choose strategies, adapt to more difficult problems, and manage the mental demands of mathematics could ultimately help researchers develop better ways to identify and support those with developmental dyscalculia.

title: Think you have good eyesight? Try counting the stars in the Pleiades tonight
text:
Every autumn, I conduct an eyesight test that no reputable optometrist would understand.
I go outside, find the Pleiades and count how many stars I can see. Usually I start confidently. One, two, three, four, five. Then things become contentious. Is that another star? Did I actually see it, or did I decide I ought to see it because I know it's there? I look away, look back and begin again.
This is not, I should emphasize, a meaningful test of eye health. What it tests, rather, is how badly I've prepared for looking at the night sky.
The Pleiades sit roughly 444 light-years away in Taurus and are right now becoming extremely convenient in the evening sky. You don't need a telescope to find them. You don't even need binoculars. In fact, you're likely to catch their collective brightness in your peripheral vision every time you go outside and look up.
But every November the Pleiades remind me that naked-eye observing isn't as simple as opening the back door and looking up. How many Pleiades I can see can change depending on what I do during the next 10 minutes.
What's happening and when to look
The Pleiades, also known as Messier 45 (M45) or the "Seven Sisters," are an open star cluster in Taurus. They're one of the closest clusters to the solar system and some of the youngest stars you can see with the naked eye — just 100 million years old. They're basically newborns.
In mid-November, they rise in the east in the early evening and climb higher as the night progresses, making this an excellent time to get acquainted with them. Look east after dark for a tiny, compact group of stars. If you know Orion, which rises later, the Pleiades are above and to the right of it from mid-northern latitudes. Nearby you'll also find orange Aldebaran and the much broader V-shaped Hyades cluster. The Hyades are closer to the sun, but their stars are about 625 million years old.
The name "Seven Sisters" creates an immediate observational trap: people assume they're supposed to see seven stars. That's not necessarily true. In fact, six is a common naked-eye result under decently dark conditions (note that the shape of the six brightest is like a mini Big Dipper/Plough), while people with sharp eyesight under darker skies may see more. The cluster itself contains about 1,000 stars. The number you personally distinguish depends on eyesight, sky brightness, atmospheric conditions and how well your eyes have adapted to darkness.
That makes M45 much more interesting to me than a simple tick-box target. So tonight, don't just find the Pleiades — count them.
How and when I'm watching it
I'm going to run my Pleiades eye test in stages. First, I'll step outside and look almost immediately. I'll count the individual stars I can distinguish without spending ages convincing myself about marginal ones. Then I'll wait. After about 10 minutes (without looking at my phone or bright outdoor lights, of course), I'll count again. Full dark adaptation takes considerably longer, but even 10 minutes can make an obvious difference when you've just come from a brightly lit house.
I'll then try my trusty 10x50 binoculars. This is where the experiment stops being subtle. The little naked-eye knot of brightness suddenly becomes a field filled with stars. The Pleiades don't just become brighter through binoculars. Their whole character changes because stars that were below my naked-eye threshold appear. I'll also use the averted vision technique, looking slightly to one side rather than directly at M45. It's one of the best demonstrations of the technique, with its fainter stars seemingly popping into view as your more light-sensitive peripheral vision takes over.
Stargazer's corner: November 13-19, 2026
The moon is returning to the evening sky this week, waxing from a thin crescent toward first quarter. It reaches first quarter around Nov. 17, so moonlight becomes progressively more noticeable during the first half of the night. Look southwest during twilight, and you'll see the beautiful sight of a crescent moon sporting Earthshine, sunlight reflected from Earth onto the moon's night side.
Overnight, Nov. 15-16, don't miss Mars and Jupiter in conjunction. The two planets will appear just over a degree apart, rising in the east during the evening before climbing high into the southern sky in the hours before sunrise.
The following night, Nov. 17-18, the Leonid meteor shower peaks. This is one shower where staying up later actually matters. Leo, the constellation containing the shower's radiant, doesn't rise until late, so the better opportunity comes after midnight and toward the predawn hours.
Asterism of the week: The Kids
Auriga, "the Charioteer," is easy to see in the northeastern and eastern sky during November evenings, but have you spied the asterism close to its brightest star, Capella? It's known as the "Goat Star," though its Latin name is the diminutive of capra, meaning "little she-goat." The reason is esoteric — Capella represents Amalthea, the mythological goat that suckled the infant Zeus — but there is a neat asterism (shape of stars) nearby that suddenly makes sense. Close to Capella is a triangle of faint stars that are known as The Kids — Epsilon, Zeta and Eta Aurigae — traditionally imagined as the offspring of Capella. It's one of those little patterns that makes a constellation much easier to recognize.
